The *Śrī Tantrāloka*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Abhinavagupta, the illustrious Great Māheśvara,
together with the commentary titled *Viveka* composed by the venerable Rājānaka Jayaratha.
The First Daily Lesson:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
From which indeed arise these desires, cognitions, and actions, as well as the planes of bliss and consciousness.
May that abode— the non-dual reality of the Trika, whose sovereign power is this entire universe of such a nature, and which is the full manifestation of absolute freedom—
reside in my heart, destroying the veil that obscures the secret of the scriptures of the Śiva-revelation. (1)
I am indeed liberated from the body by the mere droplets of the compassion of that glorious ocean of auspiciousness; I take refuge in that true guru within my heart. (2)
His instruction was quickly taken to heart— even though their hearts were hardened by the accumulation of worldly existence— by all the kings, as if it were placed upon their heads.
I have not set out here to attain the status of an author, nor to display unprecedented skill in speech;
rather, this conceptual elaboration arises from the thorough investigation of this very subject matter.
And may he be endowed with refined conduct; this is our wish. || 4 ||
Some have come and gone; some remain; some are ignorant, others are envious; some are full of doubt—what can I say of those listeners who have not yet arrived? (5)

Not having heard that speech— which was sweet, possessed of hidden meaning, and displayed skill in his own intention— he wavers in mind because of what was said by others with intentional implication.
That which may here flow forth without restraint, even though my speech is powerless, is the unfolding of the glorious Great Bliss belonging to the Supreme Lord. (7)

In this work, at the very beginning, the author of the treatise invokes the appropriate chosen deity by means of a non-worldly benediction, thereby internalizing the meaning of the *Trika* (Six-and-a-Half) scripture that is about to be expounded.
The Mother is the great new creation, whose foundation is the stainless arts, and her body is full; the Father is the one with five faces, whose splendor is hidden;
and [the reality] consists of the emission of the state vibrating from the union of those two.
May my heart, the family of the unsurpassed nectar, radiate forth! 1-1.

"May my own heart"— the true reality denoted by such terms as *jagadānanda* (the bliss of the universe) and so forth— "shine forth," that is, may it blossom as being unconditioned by space, time, and the like, through the unfolding of the state of total immersion (*samāveśa*), preceded by the complete suppression of the habitual tendencies of subjectivity associated with the body, vital breath, and so on. This means it should expand as being devoid of limitation by the three periods of time.

— such is the meaning. And what is that like? It is said: "that pair. "That" refers to both [the subject] which will be explained in the first half [of the verse], and "that pair" (ubhayam) is their "union" (yāmalam)—as it is stated:
"Whatever is the united form of those two, that is known as *saṅghaṭṭa*."
Thus, according to the principle to be explained, *saṅghaṭṭa* (the union) consists of the state of equilibrium between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*);
from that arises "the manifestation of being"—that which has its existence spontaneously surging forth by its own nature, independent of anything else—as it is said:
"Therefore, this emission (*visarga*) consists of the unmanifested element *ha*."

By this statement, [the term] refers to that whose nature is the desire to manifest externally—the *visarga*, which consists of half of half of the letter *ha* and comprises the essence of both the *kula* and *akula* aspects; for this very reason, he says:
"the family of the supreme nectar (*anuttarāmṛtakula*). "Supreme" (*anuttara*)...
And that [state] is superior because it differs from death resulting from the firmness of a few moments or from other causes:
"Where there is no fear whatsoever, nor old age, nor even diseases; where there are no obstacles, nor indeed death, nor does Time reckon him."
Because it is not limited by time (*akāla-kalita*), that in which death does not exist is the "Kula," which is the body; its essential nature is the *kalā* called *Amā*. This is the meaning.
As it has been said:

"The seventeenth digit (kalā), which has the form of nectar. Furthermore, what are those two? He says: "The mother and the father. Of what nature is the mother? "She who is the support of the pure digit."

The meaning is as follows: that whose "limb" (*kalā*)—characterized by agency whose sole nature is supreme reflective awareness—is "free from stains" (*vigatāmalā*), meaning devoid of limitations, and which has such a "limb" as its "basis" (*āśrayaḥ*), i.e., its support or essential nature, is the power of pure sovereignty. For this very reason...
In the "new," that is, the primordial creation, on the path of the Pure Way (śuddhādhvan)— according to the principle that "on the Pure Path, Śiva is the agent"—
it is called "Greatness" (mahaḥ) because Śiva alone is the direct manifestor there.

It has been stated that she is one whose splendor (*tejas*) is expansive, characterized by complete fullness. For here, in the non-dual system (*advayanaya*), the Lord alone, through the majesty of His own sovereignty, manifests the universe as if distinct—even though it is not distinct from Himself—by virtue of having mere manifestation as His sole essence; thus, He is independent of anything else.

It has been stated that absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) alone is the cause of the world's manifoldness; for since [factors] such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are afflicted by the conceptual dilemmas of difference and non-difference, it is logically untenable to designate them as the cause of the world's manifoldness.
For this very reason, although the Lord possesses infinite powers such as consciousness (*cit*) and the rest, [the world arises] merely from the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of those [powers].
Among those [powers], she alone is mentioned here because of her preeminence, as he will say:
"Therefore, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is joined with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone.
And what is the nature of the progenitor? It has been stated: "one whose body is full" (*bharitatanuḥ*). "Full" (*bharitā*)...

He whose "body" (tanuḥ)— that is, his essential nature— is completely filled by the total exhaustion of all desires, and who is therefore independent because he does not look toward anything else; for this very reason, [he is endowed] with "five faces," which consist of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.

By the statement, "...the Śaiva [nature] is here called the mouth," [it refers to one] whose "desire"— meaning aspiration— is "guarded" by the powers (*śakti*) and "fulfilled" as it continues through the [spiritual] composition; since no specific object is mentioned, this desire pertains to the fivefold set of duties (*kṛtyapañcaka*), and such a person is always...
The meaning is: "the performer of the fivefold activity. As it has been said:
"I bow to the Lord who is the agent of creation and withdrawal, the cause of dissolution and maintenance, the bestower of grace, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who seek refuge."

Thus, here, for the sake of destroying the multitude of obstacles, that which is the unnameable (anākhyātmaka), denoted by the term *paratrika*— consisting of the union of Śiva and Śakti, which is the seed of the world's manifoldness due to its nature as the expansion of emission (*visarga*)— has been contemplated. As it has been said:
Even there, when Maheśvara, accompanied by his own power which consists of his very self,
attains union and enters the supreme state of absorption (samāpatti);
Then his supreme mouth, the locus for the unfolding of emission,
becomes beautiful with the bliss of the world arising from the expansion of the Absolute (Anuttara).
The seed of everything exists undivided from the future speaker;
that [seed] is considered to consist of the heart-throb, the emergent supreme flow, the nameless, the wave, and so forth.
"This supreme triad is subtle and characterized by the non-differentiation of all powers.
And furthermore: "The Heart"—

By the statement beginning with, "The heart is indeed the thread of power (śaktisūtra)... may the abode of Śrī Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī, whose form flashes forth through the threading together of the entire wheel of powers such as Śrī Sṛṣṭikālī and the rest, shine brilliantly.
The meaning is: "I would become one with that through identity.
And what is that like? It has been said: "the family of the nectar of the Absolute" (*anuttarāmṛtakula*).
Because all things, such as emanation and the rest, dissolve right here, there is no other "higher" (*uttara*) state than this; therefore [it is so called].

"Amṛta" is the ultimate reality consisting solely of the wonder of one's own Self; for this very reason, it is "Kula"—meaning it has the form of the Inexplicable (Anākhyarūpa), as in the verse: "Kula is that which is called the Nameless... Furthermore, what is it like? To this he says: "That which is both."
Thus, that which is about to be explained—the "duality" consisting of emission and withdrawal—is its "union," which is the state of being merged (*lolībhāva*). From that:
"The supreme state, having become merged, shines within the two wheels."
Thus:
"By reason of the state of agitation between emergence and dissolution, there is a sequence called 'descent'";
according to this principle, the manifold creation—which consists of persistence—is composed of that [sequence] as its manifesting reality.

The intended meaning is this: the supreme, ineffable, and divine consciousness, by virtue of its own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), manifests and dissolves within itself the processes of emanation and so forth. As it has been said:
"Whose single, eternally arisen light brings about the destruction of time..."
It shines within the hollow of the sky that is the blooming lotus of the heart.
"She whose nature consists of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal is intent upon sustaining them.
He explains both things referred to by the word "that" as "the Mother and the Father.
She gives birth to the universe—thus she is the "Mother," the Supreme Goddess, the source of the wheel of emission and the other cosmic functions.

And because its intrinsic nature is pure consciousness alone, she is "immaculate" (*vimalā*). This "digit of the moon" (*cāndramasī kalā*), which is the primordial source, is the "support"—meaning that of which she is the objective basis and the course.
The meaning is that she consists of the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) which effects the nourishment of the entire world. As it has been said:
"But established above is the creation, whose nature is supreme bliss;
raining down a shower of nectar, it is the supreme *kalā* of Bindu.
Thus, and likewise—
"The lunar digit (candrakalā) situated above is tranquil, the Goddess [filled] with the essence of the bliss of full nectar.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Abhinavā*:

She is she whose "mahaḥ"—the splendor characterized by absolute freedom—resides within the manifestation that is eternally shining forth according to the principle beginning with "always for the sake of the sport of creation," and which consists of externalized form; thus it is said. She brings [all things] into being.
Regarding the phrase "the withdrawal of existence": the "progenitor" is the supreme subject (*pramātā*), who is the beautiful one;
and he [acts] "through the mouths" of the five, namely the channels of power (*vāha-śakti*) beginning with Vāmeśī, which consist of the functions of the senses such as sight and so forth.
"By whichever sensory channel whatever object appears,
the yogi, through the power of his own firm resolve, should become absorbed in that and identified with it."

According to this principle, by means of the withdrawal of each respective object, that whose "lustre"—its radiance—is "guarded," meaning protected by the power of its own self-support, has the state of the supreme subject fully ignited through its devouring of all objective existents; this is the meaning. For this very reason, it is "one whose body is full."

The meaning is that [the subject] is "full" because, through the relishing of each respective state, a lack of further desire (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) arises, resulting in repose within one's own self alone. Thus, although the author here manifests the nature of the three sequences beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*), she shines forth by transcending them.

It would be said that the supreme, ineffable, and transcendental consciousness of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī saṃvit*), whose nature consists of both succession and non-succession, is being grasped. As has been stated by our supreme preceptor:
"By means of the continuous interplay based upon the three sequences..."

"I place within my heart that divine Supreme Consciousness (Parā Saṃvid), which shines forth loftily while transcending the three stages; she who, though her very body is the sequence, radiates as the nature of the non-sequential."

Thus [it is said]. And furthermore, "the heart" (hṛdayam) means that reality characterized by the emergence of one's own power should "throb" or "blossom"—that is, it should expand—by means of the complete manifestation and narration of everything, since no specific [object] is being taken up. And what is that like? It is "that which is both. That...

The definition of the mother and father, which is to be explained in the first half [of the verse], is "both"; that which is their "pair" (*yāmala*), the couple mounted upon the primordial sacrifice, whose "state" (*bhāva*) is "vibrant"— meaning full of joy— due to its connection with the gradations of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arising from their mutual orientation toward one another.

It is that which has as its nature the emission— that is, the projection or outflow of a specific substance known as *kuṇḍagola*— arising from a particular intention (*āśaya-viśeṣa*). And for this very reason,
it is "supreme" (*anuttara*) through the contemplative realization of its being composed of the deities whose natures are white and ruddy, and so forth.

Because it is distinct from the semen and blood of animals, it is superior; in that essence called "Amṛta" (Nectar)—according to the statement, "Kula is the sphere of origin"—that which has "Kula" as its form (*ākāra*) is [the object]. What are those two? He says: "The Mother..."
"And Janaka. What is the Mother like? "The support of the stainless arts (vimalakalā). "Stainless" refers to the phoneme-art;
she whose "support" is that—that is, she who has the name Vimalakalā—this is the meaning.
Likewise: "The greatness of fresh creation. Of the "fresh"—
"The birth of the illustrious Abhinavagupta is that very [revelation]:
'His ancestors rejoice, and his grandfathers rejoice;
today a devotee of Maheśvara has been born, who will deliver us.'"

Because of such statements, she is one for whom there is a "mahaḥ"—a festival—due to the birth of a virtuous son, which brings fulfillment and produces an extraordinary sense of wonder. Furthermore, what is her father like?
He is "one whose splendor is protected by five faces. "Pañcamukhaḥ" means a lion; thus, [the father] is known by the name Siṃhagupta.
He whose "ruciḥ"— meaning radiance or renown— pervades everywhere:
"His son was Narasiṃhagupta, known among the people as Cukhulaka, and possessed of an intellect as pure as the moon."
The meaning is that he is known by the name Narasiṃhagupta, according to the perspective that will be explained below.
For the parents of this author were Śrīnarasiṃhagupta and Vimalā; thus, the teachers (guravaḥ), being peaceful (śāntaḥ), employ parts of names in place of the full names.

According to this principle, just as in the expression "Bhīma is Bhīmasena," so too here there is the use of both the terms Narasiṃhagupta and Siṃhagupta. Regarding the phrase "bharitatanuḥ" (one whose body is filled):
"One should contemplate the form consisting of Śiva and Śakti as mutually [pervasive]."
One should not form a human-like conception associated with passion, delusion, and the like.
"Everything should be accomplished by the best of practitioners through the cultivation of gnosis (*jñāna-bhāvanā*).

According to this stated principle, since it is desired that both [Śiva and Śakti] are described as consisting of the immersion (*samāveśa*) of Śiva and Śakti, this should be applied according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣi-nyāya*). Thus, in this way...
Because he has arisen from a gathering of ancestors consisting mostly of such accomplished Yoginīs—[as it is said]:
"He who, while in the womb, possesses a body formed by such a *melaka*-germ, is declared to be a 'born of Yoginīs' (*yoginībhūḥ*); such a devotee is himself a vessel of knowledge."
According to the principle thus stated, the author— who declares himself to be a vessel for the unsurpassed, non-dual knowledge of the *niruttara* stage within his own self—
possesses the qualification even for composing this work, which is a compendium of the essence of all the Trika (Six-and-a-Half) scriptures.

[This has been] glanced over. And here, although other interpretations are possible, they have not been provided for fear of increasing the bulk of the work and because they are of no use to the present subject. Even though the inconsistency of certain other interpretations is exceedingly evident, it has not been disclosed. For thus:
"...one should not act as a cause for that [reproach].

According to this view which will be stated later, the seed of censure toward the great-souled ones—the great gurus—which brings about a violation of the *samaya* within one's own self, has been sown—it might be so; who indeed [could prevent it]?

One who is about to begin rites for pacification (*śāntikarma*) should perform the rite of raising a *vetāla*; however, since we have already pledged here to compile only the essence of its commentary, that alone is being done. Let the wise discern for themselves elsewhere that everything other than this is devoid of essence—thus [it is said].
Even with these words, we shall here state the subject at hand. || 1 ||
Thus, having contemplated the supreme Triad, and now beginning to contemplate the intermediate [Triad] as well, he first contemplates the Supreme Goddess:
"I bow to the Goddess, the supreme Cit-pratibhā (the creative intuition of consciousness), the Yoginī of Bhairava."

She has made her abode upon a lotus that has sprouted from the trident [of Śiva], which consists of the portions of the knower (mātṛ), the means of knowledge (māna), and the object of knowledge (prameya).

"Supreme" (parām) means full; therefore, she protects even the differentiated world within her own self in a form of non-difference, and is "excellent" (prakṛṣṭām) because she is not oriented toward anything other than herself—[as it is said]: "That power which is declared to be the inherent (samavāyinī) power of the Creator of the world..."
By such statements as these, [the Goddess] is "Bhairavayoginī," because she is eternally inseparable from the supreme subject and is thus identical with his very self; for this very reason:
"O Goddess, she becomes the Will of Him when He desires to emit."

By such statements as these, she is *pratibhā*, which is wisdom (*prajñā*) whose nature is consciousness; she is characterized by the desire to manifest outwardly through her primordial state of surging forth, and for this very reason she is the "Goddess" (*devī*), shining as the form of valid cognition (*pramiti*) because she is the locus of rest even for the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). And for this very reason...

Even externally, the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) are the "spokes"—the wheel-like parts—of the "trident. Within that trident are the lotuses of the *unmanas* state; there, I "bow" to her who has "taken up residence," appearing as transcendent beyond them, by way of subordinating the subjectivity of the body, vital breath, and so forth.
The meaning is: "I enter into its very nature. || 2 ||

Even though the nature of Parā has been thus described, without first explaining the nature of Aparā—since it is impossible to speak of the nature of Parā as consisting of both [Parā and Aparā]—the Goddess who is Parāparā, who follows in sequence, is set aside for now, and first the Goddess Aparā is brought into focus: [The verse continues: "Obeisance to You, O Mother, who are the Supreme Reality (paratattva), the very essence of the supreme consciousness (parasaṃvit) that is free from all conceptual constructions (vikalpa), and who, through Your own power, have assumed this form of the world (jagadrūpa). [Commentary: The phrase "Obeisance to You" is used because she is the one who bestows grace upon those who bow down. She is the "Supreme Reality" because she is the ultimate truth. She is the "essence of supreme consciousness" because she is the very nature of the highest awareness. She is "free from all conceptual constructions" because she transcends all dualistic thought-forms. She is said to have "assumed this form of the world" because, by her own sovereign power (svātantrya), she has manifested herself as the universe. The word "this" (idam) refers to the world that is currently being perceived. The word "form" (rūpa) indicates that she has taken on a specific appearance. The word "assumed" (kṛta) signifies that she has voluntarily accepted this state. The particle "ca" (and) implies that she is not merely the source of the world, but is also its sustaining ground. The word "Mother" (mātaḥ) is used because she is the one who gives birth to and nourishes all beings. The word "obeisance" (namaḥ) expresses the act of prostration and surrender. Thus, the meaning is: "I offer my salutation to You, the Supreme Reality, the essence of the highest consciousness, who, being beyond all mental constructs, have freely manifested Yourself as this visible world. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the term "Supreme Reality" (paratattva) is used here to distinguish her from the lower levels of reality; it signifies that she is the ultimate ground of all existence. The expression "essence of supreme consciousness" (parasaṃvitsvarūpā) emphasizes that she is not an unconscious material principle, but is the very light of pure awareness. By saying she is "free from all conceptual constructions" (sarvavikalpavarjitā), the author shows that she is not limited by the categories of subject and object, nor by the fluctuations of the mind. Finally, the statement that she has "assumed this form of the world" (jagadrūpakṛtā) reveals her creative sovereignty: she is the one who, through her own freedom, projects the universe while remaining essentially unchanged. The use of the vocative "O Mother" (mātaḥ) conveys a sense of intimate devotion and the recognition of her role as the source of life and liberation. Thus, this verse serves as an introduction to the Goddess Aparā, establishing her identity as the dynamic power of the Absolute that bridges the transcendent and the immanent.
I bow to the Goddess who resides within the body of the dancing Bhairava, who shines with the playful grace of a streak of lightning in a sky thick with monsoon clouds. 1.3.

Regarding the phrase "of the dancing one": according to the perspective of the *Śiva Sūtras* (*Śiva-sūtra-vimarśinī*, Uddyota 9, Sūtra), it refers to the one of "Bhairava-form," who, by means of the support of his own concealed essential nature, manifests the expansion of the various stages of manifold diversity.
Regarding the Supreme Self whose nature is complete:
"When [the will arises], 'Let this object exist in such a way,' at that very moment it brings that object into being; this is what is called 'action' (kriyā) here."

By such statements as these, she is one who has entered into her own essential nature (*svarūpa*) by producing the manifold variety of infinite appearances consisting of various subjects (*pramātṛ*), objects (*prameya*), and so forth; therefore, the connection is: "I bow to the Goddess," the Supreme Lady (*aparā bhagavatī*), who performs the play of manifesting the universe. For this very reason, even externally, she exists as the self of the entire universe.
Even while shining—
“And because it swallows the portion of light belonging to Māyā, which produces duality,
it is black by virtue of being the destroyer of all, assuming the form of darkness.”
Because she rests precisely within the Supreme Subject, whose nature has been described in such terms as these, she is of a dark-tawny form—
thus it is said:
"She who sports like a streak of lightning in a sky thick with monsoon clouds."
Thus [ends section] 3.
Now, he contemplates the Goddess Parāparā, whose nature consists of both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā):

"May the throbbing trident of knowledge—which has burnt away the three bonds of duality with its mass of blazing light, and which is capable of cutting through both the proponent's and the opponent's positions—be present. (1.4)
"Knowledge"—
that which makes known with absolute certainty that "this object is thus and not otherwise" is called the power of knowledge in this world.

Thus, although its essential nature is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) as previously described, it also contains within itself the powers of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*), which are implicitly woven into its structure;
for this very reason, it is designated by the term "the Supreme-Non-Supreme" (*parāparā*).
And for this same reason, it is said: "Therefore, that triad of powers, having become fused together, is the Trident."

Thus, according to the method to be explained, it is a "trident" (triśūla) precisely because of that; and for this very reason, it is "with blazing masses of light"— that is, with unimpeded flashes of light consisting of the various functions of the sense organs.
"Wherever rays of light converge, there the All-pervasive Lord alone unfolds"— according to this principle,
because the nature of that which will be described hereafter, characterized by duality, serves as the cause of bondage,
[this state] is the burner of the three impurities (mala), such as the *āṇava* and others, which constitute bondage; for this very reason, it is "throbbing" (*sphurat*).

Its essence is the manifestation [of reality] through its nature as pure consciousness alone; therefore, this "wing" (pakṣa) is the bliss of the universe. Its "opposing sides" (vipakṣāḥ) are those joys—such as innate bliss (nijānanda) and others—which, being of the nature of non-manifestation, are non-blissful. Their "excision" (utkartana) is their destruction by means of their transformation into the nature of full manifestation.
In this context, the meaning of the sentence is: “*Kṣamam*—it should be capable. As it has been said:
“Victorious are the rays of the moon of knowledge, which have emerged from the mouth of the Supreme Lord and are capable of destroying the adversaries of the world’s bliss.”
Thus [ends section] 4.

Now, in order to examine another triad as well, he says: "The power of absolute freedom, the desire to emit in succession, and the nature of succession— these are the manifestations of the All-pervasive Lord."
May that very triad of goddesses abide within me as my unsurpassed, expanding true nature. 1-5 ||

The Lord Śiva possesses infinite power (*anantaśakti*), being one whose nature is autonomous power (*svatantryarūpā śakti*). Regarding this, it is said: "By means of the variety of forms, the Lord manifests spatial succession;
by means of the manifestation of the variety of actions, He manifests temporal succession as well" (Rauravāgama 2.1.5).
According to the principle stated above, regarding the creation (*sarga*)— the manifold variety of space, time, and the self—
the Supreme Lord’s power in the form of will (*icchārūpā śaktiḥ*), which consists of the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*) through differentiation for the purpose of creating the universe,
is "the nature of succession" (*kramātmatā*).
According to the principle expressed in the verse, "The sequence is based on difference, and difference [arises] from the presence or absence of manifestation" (Rauravāgama 2.1.4),

that which is characterized by human-nature (*naratva*)— consisting of a contracted self-form intermingled with those various infinite manifestations and dominated by difference— is thus this very state consisting of Man (*nara*), Power (*śakti*), and Śiva.

"Of the All-pervasive One" (*vibhoḥ*)— of the Blessed One, the Supreme, the unsurpassed Light— "the manifestation" (*vibhūtiḥ*) is His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting of those various pulsations; "that very thing," being the essence of that expansion in succession, is the "Triad of Goddesses" (*devītraya*) whose nature was just described, and because it consists of supreme light, it is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).

"Manifesting" the "form"— the unique nature— of [Śiva] as the universal agent and so forth, "let it abide within me," meaning let it flash forth in a state of oneness with my own self, without being obscured even when those various states of differentiation arise. || 5 ||
Thus, immediately after the contemplation of the deity appropriate to one's own tradition, by entering into the very nature of that deity,
one simultaneously brings Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka before oneself—
[the latter] being the great radiance arising from the manifestation of that deity.

May Gaṇapati, the son of the Goddess, who alone abides as the sovereign of the wheel and possesses the luster of the shimmering moon, cause the ocean of my consciousness to surge forth perfectly. 1-6.

"Ekas eva"—alone, without support due to independence from anything else—"of the gaṇa"—that is, of the circle of instruments—"he who bears the lordship over the host beginning with Mahat and the Sun; homage to him.
According to such a perspective, he is the "Lord"—the sovereign whose nature is ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra); for this very reason, "of them..."
"Whatever does not rest within that expansion of the 'deities' just mentioned— whose nature is supreme light— is like a flower in the sky."

Thus, according to the principle to be explained, those "great rays" (mahāmarīcayaḥ)— the deities of the respective sense organs— who are habituated to becoming manifest through identification with that [reality], constitute a "circle" (cakra); acting as the Lord within that circle, my own self, whose state is consciousness itself, [is the subject].

Because it is unfathomable, it is called the "ocean" (*abdhi*). By completely—that is, from every side—dissolving the turbidity of the objects of the senses, [the teacher] should "cause it to overflow"—that is, cause it to expand, producing a state of identity with that [Reality] through the gateway of consciousness as it issues forth via each respective sense organ; this is the meaning.
And because he is appropriately characterized by the surging upward of the *abdhi* (the ocean of nectar), it is said that "he possesses the luster of the throbbing moon.

In reality, however, this refers to his possession of the pervasion of the *apāna* [wind]. Furthermore, Vaṭuka, the son of the Goddess, is also of such a nature; yet, due to the whiteness of his body, he "possesses the luster of the throbbing moon."

For the teachers point out that he indeed possesses the pervasion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The designation "Son of the Goddess" is appropriate for both according to the Kula scriptures. As it has been said:
"In this context, Vaṭuka is the Son of the Goddess, surrounded by his own powers."
Thus it is said: "Gaṇeśa, the remover of obstacles, the son of the Goddess... and so forth. (6)
Indeed, at the beginning of this treatise:
"One should proclaim the division of the streams as well as their enumeration;
by failing to mention one's own Guru, one becomes a thief."

According to the view expressed in such passages, the authors of the scriptures must necessarily mention their own gurus and others; therefore, although the scripture to be described here is twofold in nature— consisting of both the Kula and Tantra systems— ...
Just as stars situated in the sky do not shine when the sun is present,
so too the Siddhānta and Tantra systems do not shine in the presence of the Kula Āgama.
"Therefore, apart from the Kula, there is nothing else for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra"—by such statements, the Kula method is superior to other methods.
Thus: "O Dear One, having pervaded the Yoga obtained by Bhairavī from Bhairava, [she taught it] from that [source]..."
But from his presence, O fair-faced one, it was obtained by the Siddha named Mīna.

In accordance with the state established by such passages as "In the great seat of Kāmarūpa, by the high-souled Macchanda," he first extols Turyanātha, who is the one who brought that [tradition] down:
He who spread the net, reddened by passion, strewn with knots and openings, functioning as a warp and woof,
across the external path.
May He, the Lord who is my own will, being pleased, be mine. || 1-7 ||
Śaḥ— renowned as the one who brought down all the Kula scriptures— "The 'mats' are said to be the fetters, which are the flickering fluctuations of the mind;
because they were cut by him, he is celebrated as Macchanda."

By such statements as these, Macchanda himself, whose nature is the severing of bonds, being possessed of immersion into the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), is "all-pervading" (*vibhu*); the meaning is that he should become gracious to me—may he manifest his state as a vessel for the sharing of the vision of one's own Self (*svātmadarśana*). He who is the "net" (*jāla*)...
He performed the "catching of fish" and illusions consisting mostly of sorcery on the outer path—
according to the statement beginning with, "The eight great-souled Siddhas, radiant and with nets upon their backs," by means of being absorbed in the nature of the Fourth State (turyatā).
The meaning is that [the mind] was rendered inattentive by the casting aside of contraction.

And that [mind], being "reddened"—meaning made red—by "color," such as substances like ochre (*gairika*), and by the *rāga-tattva* (the principle of passion), according to the derivation of the word as "that which moves" (*iyarti*) or "goes" (*gacchati*), takes on the form of the expansion of various states of duality; and likewise...

"With knots"—meaning with bonds—and with "caves," which are the outlets for the flow of water; [this refers to] being "strewn over"—pervaded—by "knots," that is, by the second division of Māyā, and by "caves," meaning those places of enjoyment known as *bhagas* which have the form of caves. Thus...

"Functioning as warp and woof" (ātānavitānavṛtti) means possessing length and lateral measurement, and having a form that extends in all directions due to its universal nature; likewise, it is "woven" (umbhitam)—that is, commenced—by "Kalā," meaning by a specific differentiation and by the principle of Kalā, which, by implication, extends down to the earth. As it has been said:
The one who contemplates the Kula should tear asunder the net of illusory forms;
the great net of universal manifestation is strung upon the threads of the channels.
"Endowed with the worlds and the senses, made firm by the knots of the principles (tattva), and joined with the digits (kalā) and passion (rāga)...
and so forth. (7)

By the power of the command of the illustrious Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the Siddhas descended: those known as Tryambaka and Āmardaka, and the venerable Nāthas, who were experts respectively in the non-dual, the dual,
and the dual-cum-non-dual teachings within the Śiva-scripture.
And from the daughter of the first, the second was born through the line of daughters.
"And that lineage known as Ardhatryambaka is well-established;
therefore, there are three and a half monasteries here according to the sequence of the lineages," as will be stated according to the established rule.

In general, first of all, there is a traditional lineage of transmission for the system of the Tantra to be described, which relies upon the Traiyambaka Maṭhikā among the three and a half monastic lineages known as Śrī-santati, Āmardaka, Traiyambaka,
and Ardhatraiyambaka.
He brings the gurus before him—
those who possess the particular splendor of a multitude of fine pearls from the Tāmraparṇī river of the lineage proclaimed by Tryambaka.
Victorious are the former teachers, who served as stainless helmsmen in the playful sport of the waves of the ocean of the great scriptures.
The lineage designated as "Traiyambaka" is the *maṭhikā*—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
Thus:
"The secret teachings beginning with Śaiva formerly resided within the cavities of the mouths of the great-souled sages; it was within those very [teachings] that the act of grace was performed."
When the Kali age had set in and they had departed for difficult regions,
the teachings of Śiva were destroyed, beginning with the village of Kalāpi.
Wandering on Mount Kailāsa in the form of the deity Śrīkaṇṭha,
he descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of bestowing grace and issued his command.
"O Blessed One, act in such a way that the sage named Durvāsas, who is a perpetual celibate,
does not cut off our lineage, in accordance with the secret injunctions of the scriptures."
Then that Blessed One, having received a command from the God of gods,
diligently created a mind-born son named Tryambakāditya.

According to such statements [found in the Śivadharmottara, chapter 7], [this lineage] of the essence of all scriptures and Upaniṣads, which had been interrupted due to the impurity of the Kali age, [was restored].
Because he is the one who introduces the consciousness of the *Ṣaḍardhakrama* through the lineage of Tryambaka,
[the author] incidentally extols the primordial Guru residing on Kailāsa, known as the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, as well as the Gurus belonging to other lineages (*maṭhikā*).
Victorious is the one and only Guru, proclaimed on earth as the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha;
he is the Lord Maheśvara and Bhūtirāja, who is his other form.

By the phrase "the Guru is indeed one," his status as an *avatāraka* (an avatarer or revealer) is indicated. By the term "Maheśvara," he is referred to elsewhere by this author as "Parameśa" and "Īśa," in his capacity as the Guru of the two monastic lineages (*maṭhikā*) known as the Śrīsaṃtati and the Ardhatraiyambaka.
As it is said:
"The venerable sequence of the arising of the Siddhas begins with Bhaṭṭārikā and ends with Ādibhūti;
the venerable sequence of the arising of the Lineage (Santāna) begins with Bhaṭṭa and ends with Parameśa."
"May the glorious lineage of gurus, beginning with Bhaṭṭa and ending with Īśāna—
the supreme sequence consisting of three forms for the sake of the Trika— greatly increase my intellect.
Thus [it is said].
By the phrase "an image of that [same] other," the fact that these two consist of the descent (āveśa) of the Blessed One is demonstrated.
Even though it is said:
"Whoever is authorized in a particular scripture is the teacher therein..."

Thus, according to the method to be explained, there is no occasion for a salutation here because the gurus of other monastic lineages (*maṭhikā*) lack the status of being gurus in the sense of the *trika*. Nevertheless, since the instruction of a guru exists everywhere— according to the view expressed in such passages as, "For me, who am a disciple of all [gurus], there is no poverty regarding instruction"— [the salutation is appropriate].
By demonstrating his own possession of extensive knowledge, the author has revealed that this work also intends to be a compendium of the essential essence of all other scriptures. As he will state:
"The extraction of the vital sap which constitutes the essence of the streams of the three and a half lineages..."
"Having been established, this Tantrāloka flows forth with all aesthetic flavors.
Thus [ends the verse]. 9.
Although the salutation has been performed in a general sense according to the principle that "the elders are victorious," and although it is equally an ancillary limb of yoga—
as it is said: "Logic (*tarka*) is the supreme ancillary limb of yoga"—

By such statements, the authors and commentators of the *Tarka*— which is intent upon bringing about the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the Lord as one's own self, which is self-luminous and supremely worthy of being accepted— are most worthy of salutation; thus, with this specific motivation, [the author] again [offers salutations] to the Guru, the Paramaguru, and the Parameṣṭhin.
To introduce [the subject], he says:
Victorious are the compositions of the fragrance of consciousness, which have issued forth from the venerable Somānanda and the illustrious Utpala, and which spread in all directions. (1.10)
We pay homage to the bee-like intellect of the teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, which is nourished by its immersion in the fullness of that aesthetic savor and is enchanted by the inner sound (nāda). 1.11.
Now,

according to such statements as, "An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya, and a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya," there is a traditional remembrance of his superior dignity even over that of an Ācārya; therefore, [he offered] even his own...

He touches upon his father by way of a benediction: "May that most excellent teacher, the illustrious Cukhulaka, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures resting in perfect bliss, grant my desired wish. (1.12)

"Cukhulaka" is another name for him, well-known in the world. Regarding the phrase "the supreme guru," the very reason for his status as supreme is the recollection of the extraordinary weight accorded to the teacher; for this very reason, it is said elsewhere:
"To my father, named Cukhulaka, who was even more venerable than my gurus."
Thus it has been stated, and so forth. || 12 ||

And thus, immediately after bringing face-to-face the Guru who has approached through the Tantric method (*tantraprakriyā*), he further extols even the Guru of the Kula method (*kulaprakriyā*) as the place of ultimate rest:
"May that one, capable of uplifting the world, be victorious!"
Śambhunātha alone is one with the Blessed Lady;
by the rays of the teaching uttered by him, this profound path of the scriptures has been made manifest to me. (1.13)

The Bhagavatī is his messenger (dūtī); for in the Kulaprakriyā, there is no entitlement to perform any rite whatsoever without a messenger; therefore, her association with him is established. "Success is declared here for men who are fearful-souled after a year."
That perfection is attained by women established in reality within twelve days.
Therefore, having taken a woman who is beautiful, fortunate, well-formed, and of purified intent, one should perform worship, sacrifice, and oblation.
Thus [it is said].
By the statement "the path of the scriptures has become stainless," his status as a commentator on the *Trika* and other Āgamas is also revealed.
As he himself has said:
Having correctly received this scripture from the mouth of the illustrious Śambhunātha— the great treasury of all sciences—
within this treatise, which is beautiful with the continuous flow of the essence of the secret [teachings],...
"This commentary on the profound speech has been composed by me.
Now, explaining the purpose of his own undertaking and so forth, the author pledges to compose the work:
"There exist many diverse manuals (*paddhati*) within the various streams [of the teachings]."
But in the sequence of the meaning of the unsurpassed Six-and-a-Half [Verses], not even a single one is seen.
And since nothing else is possible in this regard— thus proclaiming his own reliability— he demonstrates his capacity for making such a formal proposition:
"Thus have I [been instructed] many times by the virtuous, my disciples and fellow-students."
Being requested, I shall compose this clear and complete exposition of the subject matter.
The lineage of gurus which has arisen from the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Bhaṭṭanātha and likewise from the pair of feet of the venerable Bhaṭṭārikā,
removes the poison of the fetters that are other than awakening through the practice thereof.
Abhinavagupta, radiant with awakening, composes this. || 1-16 ||

The "cultivation" (*upāsana*) of that knowledge which has been transmitted through the lineage of gurus is its repeated mental application; from that arises the "awakening" (*bodha*)—the direct realization—concerning the subject matter to be taught. Being "radiant" (*ujjvala*) by means of that, one who has correctly understood the nature of reality (*dharma*), [perceives] "this."

Having realized the nature of the system of the unsurpassed threefold purpose (*anuttara-trikārtha-prakriyā-lakṣaṇa*) through the teacher’s instruction, free from doubt, error, and the like, [the author] "composes"— meaning he teaches— it with the desire to explain it to others.
By uttering his name, "Abhinavagupta," which is well-known to all the world...
The very nature of being an authoritative person (āpta) has been further reinforced. For it has been said:
"An authoritative person is one who has directly perceived dharma and, being motivated by the desire to communicate an object exactly as it was seen, acts as a teacher."

Thus [it is said]. He explains that which is referred to by the word "that" (tat) with the words, "the lineage of the Guru," meaning the lineage of Gurus—knowledge taught by them that remains unbroken. And what is it like? It is said: "the antidote to the poison of the fetters other than awakening."

According to the principle that will be stated later— "Whatever is other than the Supreme Śiva, who is beautiful through the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness (*paramādvaitasaṃvitsvātantrya*), is called a bond (*pāśa*)"— that which consists of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) [is the bond] arising from the Supreme Śiva, who is "from awakening" (*bodhāt*).

That which consists of the manifestation of differentiation (*bhedaprathātmaka*) is "the other"; that itself is the "fetter" (*pāśa*), and because it causes delusion, it is "poison. She who dispels that [poison] is [the Goddess]. Likewise, "Śrībhaṭṭanātha" refers to Śrīśambhunātha.
"Śrībhaṭṭārikā" is the name of his consort, the Bhagavatī, who is his messenger (*dūtī*). As has been stated by him himself:
The venerable Lord Bhaṭṭārakanātha Śrīkaṇṭha, who has beheld Bhairava; Nṛsiṃha, endowed with the glory of the power of prosperity; and the fierce hero Vīra.
"I bow to Śambhu, the great Guru, who has various names and is both beginning and end.
Thus [it is said].
"The wise man should deposit it into the mouth of a woman, and again cause it to be received from the mouth of a woman."

Because of such statements as these, and because of the tradition in the Kulaprakriyā that knowledge is imparted to the disciple solely through the mouth of the messenger (dūtī), the Guru and his messenger are here mentioned as being of equal status.

Now, one might object: "Having first made a general declaration regarding the method of presenting the Trika system, why is this being carried out specifically by taking the *Śrī Mālinīvijayottara* as the authority, when there exist other scriptural collections that also express that same meaning?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
There is nothing here that has not been taught by the God of gods in the *Śrī Mālinīvijayottara*, either by its own explicit term or through its indicative mark. (1.17)

"In the Śrīmālinīvijayottara": [it is called this] because it is the *mālinī* consisting of the letters from *na* to *pha*; by its "victory" (*vijayena*), that is, by its preeminence over all, it "surpasses" (*uttarati*) all other currents (*srotas*), for it is the essence of all scriptures. || 17 ||
He says this very thing:
"The teaching of the All-pervasive Lord is divided into ten, eighteen, and sixty-four [tantras];
the essence of that is indeed the Trika scripture, and the essence of that is the Mālinīmata. (1.18)

Indeed, here in this supreme speech— which consists essentially of the awakening that discerns the other— because it is replete with all things, the entire scripture unfolds as having the nature of awakening the other, while in the state of *paśyantī*.

By virtue of its nature as the inseparable unity of the signified and the signifier, the self characterized by the reflective awareness of "I" arises within as something unique; for this very reason, when the object to be signified is being reflected upon there by the cognizing subject, it shines forth precisely as enveloped in "I-ness," and subsequently, that very [object].

Within the intermediate stage (*madhyamābhūmikā*), because the proliferation of the perceived and the perceiver arises therein, it manifests with the nature of a distinct signified and signifier. For there, the Supreme Lord himself unfolds by means of the projection of the five faces consisting of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.
Reposing in the state of Sadāśiveśvara, through the union with His five faces, He brings down the entire scripture— which consists of the five currents—

by delineating the states of non-duality, duality-cum-non-duality, and duality; this scripture, which exists as a manifold variety of various divisions and sub-divisions, shall attain clarity in the external state of Vaikharī speech.

To explain: first, by those who were about to manifest (*udbubhūṣubhiḥ*) as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Sadyojāta, three divisions were brought forth; and by those who had already manifested (*udbhūtaiḥ*), [another three were brought forth], thus making six divisions for each one.

A single division is manifested by all three of these acting together: namely, Īśa-Tatpuruṣa, Īśa-Sadyojāta, and Sadyojāta-Tatpuruṣa. Thus, even though they combine in pairs, these three divisions are fully manifested by these three [faces]—these are the ten Śiva-divisions (śivabheda) in which the divisions are predominant.
As it has been said:
"By those born from the *ṛṣi*, *tattva*, and *puruṣa* [categories], by those already arisen and those desiring to arise— by six single units, one triad, and three dual-natured units."
Thus, in this manner, the state of the ten divisions of Śiva was established.
And by combining these very [ten] with Vāmadeva and Aghora, there arise eighteen divisions of Rudra.
Accordingly, in that regard, even though there is a fivefold nature, there are only two divisions for each individual division consisting of Vāmadeva and Aghora.

Because the three faces of Īśa and the others have already been mentioned among the divisions of Śiva, it is improper to state what has already been stated; likewise, because the three divisions [of the other faces] are of a dual nature, and thus the three divisions of the five [faces] are of a triple nature, they have already been mentioned among the divisions of Śiva.

However, because Tatpuruṣa and Sadyojāta lack such a nature and do not associate with those two, the fourfold division [of the former] does not exist; thus, only three dual divisions remain: Īśa and Vāma, Īśa and Aghora, and Aghora and Vāma—these are the three dyadic divisions. Likewise...

Regarding the five [faces]—Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aja, Vāma, and Aghora—when they are merged through their triadic nature, there are six [forms] by the sequential union of Īśāna with the other faces; three for Tatpuruṣa; and likewise, even when Sadyojāta is united with the remaining faces, there is only one. Thus.
Although there are ten aspects, because the first triad— consisting of Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Sadyojāta—
is already mentioned among the divisions of Śiva, and because the remaining triad— consisting of Īśa, Vāma, and Aghora—
is to be employed through other functions.

Only the eightfold division consisting of the triads remains—thus, there are exactly eight triadic divisions. For this very reason, one should not say that the mention of the single [unit] is to be questioned; for there is a prohibition against the conjunction of Tatpuruṣa, Ajāta, Vāma, and Aghora when they produce cognition as dual-natured or four-natured.

If that were intended—even if there were such a state of being composed of three—then the negation of many differentiations would follow as a consequence, and thus even the statement of seven types of differentiation would not be logical;
so, enough of this prolixity. Likewise, because these five are also fourfold in nature...

Although there are five types of *saṃmīlanā* (fusion), because of the absence of a logical connection for *narajāti*, *vāmā*, and *aghora* according to the aforementioned reasoning, there are four [types] with four divisions each; yet, when all of these are fused,
there is only one division consisting of the pentad— thus, there are "eighteen" divisions, primarily characterized by both difference and non-difference.
The divisions of Rudra.
As it has been said:
"When there is a union of the left and right of the three faces..."
Then there are seven varieties consisting of dyads and eight consisting of triads.
There are four groups of four and one group of five;
thus, from among these twenty, there is no connection with the human birth.
Having entered into the pair of Vāmā and Aghorā through [His] sovereignty, the Eastern and Western [faces] do not partake in knowledge at all; thus the sixteenfold division is established.
Therein, one belongs to Vāmadeva situated above that, and another is the essential nature belonging to Bhairava; thus, the state [of the system] is eighteenfold.
"The divisions of Rudra have been thus described by Śiva himself in the scriptures.
This has been stated at length, preceded by its formal designation, in the venerable *Śrīkaṇṭhī*, as follows:
In the upper ear-canal, knowledge arises in two forms known as Śiva and Rudra;
furthermore, there are Kāmaja, Yogaja, Cintya, Maukuṭa, and Aṃśumat.
After the [section on] Dīpta...
once again, the divisions of Śiva have been fully declared; now hear these divisions of Rudra.
Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Madgīta, Pārameśvara,
Mukhyabimba, Siddha, Santāna, and Nārasiṃhaka.
Candrāṃśa, Vīrabhadra, Āgneya, Svayambhuva, Visara,
the five Rauravas, Vimala, and likewise Kiraṇa.
"O Maheśvarī, they say the Lalita and Saurabheya tantras are twenty-eight; thus they have emerged from the Ūrdhvasrotas.
And here, by this very [statement]—

"...the division called Śiva was spoken of by the Śivas, and the division named Rudra by the Rudras; thus the division has been described. "By the Vasus" means multiplied by eight; "eighty-eight" refers to the sixty-four divisions of Bhairava.
And thus, within the non-dual nature of one's own essence— which consists of Śiva, Śakti, and their union, the very self of the Yoginī’s face— there exists the southern face. This [face],
being fourfold in its nature as that which is about to manifest, that which has manifested, that which is about to disappear, and that which has disappeared, [is present] in each moment.

When the other four crooked [mandalas], which consist of sixteen divisions each, simultaneously attain internal absorption, then, through their mutual union, there arise the Bhairava divisions characterized by two groups of sixty-four.
As it has been said:
And that which is at the end, the southern, the heart-centered *liṅga*, is considered the supreme heart;
it too is entirely filled with all created states that have been brought forth within.
And because it effects the withdrawal of all things, it is black, assuming the form of darkness;
its nature consists in swallowing the portions of light belonging to the *māyīya* (illusory) energy, which produces the sense of duality.

Therein, it reaches a state of internal absorption as long as its four faces remain unmanifest; likewise, when they are about to emerge or have emerged, and when they are about to vanish or have vanished, it remains in that same state.
In this way, this very [consciousness], consisting of sixteen divisions,
enters simultaneously into Śiva— who is autonomous, who resides in the heart as the power of emission (vaisargika), and who is on the right.
"That scripture, consisting of eight times eight [sections], is simultaneously named Bhairava.
This has been stated at length, preceded by its formal designation, in the venerable *Śrīkaṇṭhī*. As follows:
I shall now briefly describe another song sung by the Supreme Lord;
I will explain it in its sixty-four divisions according to their respective classifications.
Bhairava, Yāmala, that which is called Mata, as well as Maṅgala;
the Cakrāṣṭaka, the Śikhāṣṭaka, and Bahurūpa as the seventh.
And Vāgīśa is declared as the eighth; thus, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, these are the eight.
I shall now describe this Sādāśiva-cakra in brief.
Svacchanda, Bhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava,
Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, and likewise Kapālīśa.
These, whose forms are according to their own will, have been described in many forms;
they are called the Brahmayāmala and likewise the Viṣṇuyāmala.
Svacchanda and Ruru, and the sixth is remembered as Atharvaṇa;
the seventh is called Rudra, and Vetāla is remembered as the eighth.
Henceforth, O Great Goddess, hear from me the different systems of doctrine:
the one called Raktāmata, the one called Lampaṭāmata, and likewise the Lakṣmīmata.
The fifth is Ālikā, and Piṅgalādya is the sixth;
Utphullaka is considered another, and Viśvādya is recorded as the eighth.
These fierce divisions are indeed remembered in the Bhairava [Tantra] worshipped by heroes;
Bhairavī is declared to be the first, originating from the Picu-tantra.
She is known to be twofold by way of division; thereafter the third is spoken of as the *brahmī* digit (*kalā*), while the fourth is indeed named *vijayā*, and the fifth is [the *jitā*].
Candrā is the sixth, as well as Maṅgalā and Sarvamaṅgalā;
this is the classification of the Maṅgalās as spoken by Krodheśa.
The first is the wheel of mantras, the second is the wheel of phonemes;
the third is the wheel of powers, and the fourth is the wheel of digits.
The fifth is the bindu-cakra, while the sixth is indeed known as the nāda-cakra;
the seventh is the guhya-cakra, and the eighth is remembered as the kha-cakra.
This indeed is the division of the Cakra as proclaimed by Asitāṅga:
the Andhaka, the Ruru, the Bheda, the one called Aja, and that known as Mūla.
O Supreme Goddess, Varṇabhaṇṭha, Viḍaṅga, Jvālina, and Mātṛrodana have been proclaimed by the Supreme Lord Ruru.
Bhairavī, Citrikā, the one called Haṃsā, Kadambikā, Hṛllekhā, Candralekhā, Vidyullekhā, and Vidyumān.
These varieties of Vāgīśa have been spoken by Kapālīśa;
Bhairavī is declared to be the Śikhā, and Vīṇā is the second.
The third is Vīṇāmaṇi, while the fourth is Saṃmoha;
the fifth is named Ḍāmara, and the sixth is Atharvaka.
The seventh is known as Kabandha, and the eighth is remembered as Śiraścheda;
these, O Goddess, are the varieties of the Śikhā-mantra proclaimed by Unmatta.
"This is the Sādāśiva-cakra, divided into eight groups of eight.
The meaning is that it is manifold, differentiated by them through the variety of divisions and subdivisions. As for that which...
In the *Śrīśrīkaṇṭhī*, with reference to the face of Tatpuruṣa, it says: "In the past, the Gāruḍa-hṛdaya [consisted] of twenty-eight divisions," and so forth. Likewise—
"In the west are the Bhūta-tantras...
and likewise:
"In the south is the southern path, consisting of twenty-four divisions."
And so forth. Likewise:
"Now hear that other [form] which was born from Vāmadeva," and so on;
thus the manifold variety of other divisions and subdivisions has been described for each individual face.

Because it consists of five faces, it is essentially composed of the various divisions and subdivisions arising from them; therefore, they are included therein, and no separate effort has been made here for them. As it has been said:
"Since each individual face is proclaimed to possess five faces..."
"Therefore, there is an incalculable number of divisions within the tenfold and eighteenfold divisions.
And thus, [the scripture] known as Śiva, Rudra, and Bhairava, which establishes both difference and non-difference among these divisions, [is established].
The established conclusion is that this scripture has arisen in three ways; as it has been said:
"This Tantra, known by the names Rudra, Śiva, and Bhairava, was born in three ways;
for in reality, this very essence of knowledge unfolds in these three forms."
"By way of division, by way of both division and non-division, and likewise by way of that which partakes in non-division.
And thus, although this scripture consists of division and so forth, it is composed of the Supreme Lord, Īśa, Vāma, and Aghora.
Having embraced the sixth triad by way of being the locus of rest for the triad of goddesses beginning with Parā—
just as "there is fragrance in the flower, oil in sesame, the soul in the body, and taste in water," so too is the Kula established within all scriptures."

By such statements as these, one should cause [the mind] to be completely saturated with the nectar of supreme non-duality; for otherwise, it would not serve as the cause for attaining the supreme state. As it has been said:
"Therefore, [the yogi becomes] perfectly full, having withdrawn all limiting adjuncts of phenomenal existence."
Bhairava is he whose power is nourished by the surging flow of ultimate reality.
In those [powers] located on the left and right of the penis, the three powers—
beginning with the *apara* and ending with the *parā*— are situated, having embraced the triad in due order.
"The Tantras and Kulas— namely Urdhva, Vāma, and the others—
having been brought to the plane of non-duality, they are established within the limit of that stream.
Thus [it is said].

But what is the proof that no such scriptural passage is found? Is it not the case that the proof for this has already been stated by him as being the characteristic of the lineage of gurus? As he said:
"In this manner, that very triad, though distinct in the middle, [manifests] in such and such ways."
"The scripture remains in our teacher’s house according to the sequence of the tradition.
Now, it may be objected that the very same point which was raised here as a challenge— namely, that [the scripture] originates from human intellect— is here made the very answer.

Thus, this is a novel kind of scholarship; therefore, some scripture must be brought into agreement with it so that this [position] may be established. This is not so, for it is said that undisputed renown alone constitutes scripture, as it has been stated:

Whether it possesses logical justification or otherwise, what is well-known as tradition in the world is an authoritative means of knowledge, free from contradiction, regarding both true knowledge and ignorance.
For well-established, uncontradicted usage is considered the truthful speech of the Lord;
likewise, wherever something is established as such, it should be accepted by those free from doubt.
Thus it is said.

And since this [tradition] exists here without contradiction among the great-souled ones, the supreme teachers, what is the use of seeking further means of valid cognition? If such [a tradition] were even for those of limited vision like yourself—
It cannot be said that this [teaching] is untenable merely because it has not reached the range of one's hearing;

for the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not entail the absence of the object of cognition (prameya). Nor are these [teachers] deceivers who would thus instruct otherwise, since the root of all this is precisely this very instruction.

Because the practical application of the meaning of the Śaiva scriptures and Āgamas is observed, it should be understood here as well that, just as in the case of the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, a foundational *śruti* is inferred for the *aṣṭakā* and other sacrifices due to the loss of their original Vedic branches (*utsanna-śākhā-mūlatva*),
so too is it to be known in this instance. Indeed, [this would not be possible] without having seen such a *śruti*.

Those who have directly realized the true essence of the entire Śaiva Āgama would teach in this manner; therefore, enough with this ill-advised practice of scrutinizing the instructions of the great gurus. Indeed, the scriptures state: "Since all [teachings] originate from Śiva, they bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva."

Because of such statements as these, there is an identity between the cause that determines oneness and its fruit; so, what is the basis here for saying that these very [principles] possess such diversity? True—but their diversity is conceptually constructed due to the difference in the dispositions (*āśaya*) of those to be graced. As it has been said:
All of this is for the sake of engaging the listeners;
however, due to their differences, this distinction is conceived through metaphorical usage based on a difference in meaning.
"No distinction of fruit should be imagined here; if one were to imagine it, it would be incorrect.
Now, if this is so, then [it is said]:
"The Śaiva system is superior to the Vedas and so forth; from the Śaiva, the Vāma and the Dakṣiṇa [are superior]."

If it were as stated in such passages as, "The Kaula is superior to the Dakṣiṇa; there is nothing higher than the Kaula," then their respective degrees of excellence would not be logical. This is not so, because their relationship as means and goal (upāya-upeya) has been explained through the relation of door and doorkeeper (dvāra-dvāribhāva). Therefore...

It should be understood that this very treatise, which establishes the instruction on supreme non-duality, has as its sole fruit the attainment of the true being of Śiva. Precisely because it serves as the direct means for attaining that supreme state, it is preeminent.
This has been explained at length by him himself in the *Śrīmālinīślokavārtika* and other works; therefore, one should consult those very sources.
This should be understood by oneself; however, for fear of excessive length, I have not provided a word-for-word comparison.
For this very reason, he says: "The essence of that is the Trika scripture. As it has been said:
"From the Veda comes the Śaiva [scripture], from that the Vāma, from that the Dakṣa, and from that the Kula."
"Then the Mata, and even beyond that, the Trika is the supreme among all.
With this very intention, it is said:
"Even a teacher consecrated in the Vāmamārga who knows the supreme reality..."
"He is also to be refined in Bhairava, as well as in Kula, Kaula, and Trika"—
thus it is stated in the *Śrīniśācāra* and other such texts.

And that [scripture] is threefold because it consists of three sections (*khaṇḍa*) named Siddha, Nāmaka, and Mālinī. Among these, the *Siddhātantra* has ritual action (*kriyā*) as its primary focus, the *Nāmaka-tantra* has knowledge (*jñāna*) as its primary focus, and the *Mālinīmata* consists of both; thus, the latter alone is the principal one, as it is said: "Its essence..."
[This is] the *Mālinīmata*. And thus, it is rightly said: "There is nothing here that does not [exist]," and so forth.
Furthermore, because it is all-enduring (*sarvasaha*), it is logical that the fulfillment of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) occurs precisely through its authority;
thus he says:
Therefore, by the command of our venerable Guru, we shall reveal everything contained herein that has remained unseen by scholars who are devoid of the oral tradition. 1.19

The word “therefore” (*ataḥ*) refers to the preeminence of this very scripture according to the reasoning already stated. “We shall reveal” (*prakaṭīkurmaḥ*) means by means of composing this *Prakriyā* (treatise). And thus, the underlying thought is: “For effort expended upon that which is primary becomes fruitful. “By the command of the Lord Guru” (*gurunāthājñayā*)—for indeed, without his command, there would be no qualification (*adhikāra*) for this work at all.
The meaning is "it would come into being. ||19||
And to show that the sole cause for the revelation of that which has not been seen by others within one's own self is indeed the grace of the Lord, he says:
"This is the work of Abhinavagupta, whose name was proclaimed by his gurus."
He attained renown through the contemplation of the lotus-like feet of the Three-Eyed One. || 1-20 ||
The sense is this: what indeed could be unattainable for one who has acquired supreme siddhi through the grace of the Three-Eyed Lord?
And so, in order to demonstrate that this work should be accepted by everyone, he says:
"That which has had its contraction removed by the light falling from the feet of the sun-like Śrī Śambhunātha..."
For the sake of worshipping the Great Lord, pluck this lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta. || 1-21 ||
The opening statement:

The heart is the true essence of the self of the scripture; it is the worship of Maheśvara. As for worship, it is said: "Worship is not that which is performed with flowers and the like; rather, it is the firm resolve of the mind."
In the non-conceptual great void, that worship is indeed absorption through reverence.
By such statements as these, there is the recognition [of all things] as one's own self (*svātmatayā*) through the sequence of cognitions that will be explained hereafter.

And for this reason, in order to demonstrate that by means of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), the entire work consists of a single sentence whose nature is that of the opening statement, he says: "The opening statement. Although, in this regard—

Apart from the descent of the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*), no other motive for engaging in such activities as listening to that scripture is admitted; nevertheless, it is the custom of the authors of scriptures to set forth the subject matter, the purpose, and so forth, as a cause for such engagement.
This is the composition of the opening statement. Therein,

the sequence of the meaning of the six-and-a-half [verses] of the Anuttara, which was indicated by the first five verses and explicitly stated by this [verse], consists of the nature of the supreme, the non-supreme, and the other [the inferior], and so forth.
The subject matter to be expressed consists, first of all, of the three-fold meaning in its many varieties;

and in order to demonstrate the excellence of this very [subject] by means of skill in presenting its author, as well as by declaring the preeminence of the Kaula Āgama over all other scriptures, [the following is stated].

The five verses beginning with "Śrībhaṭṭanātha" are presented here. And that [lineage], having descended through the succession of gurus, becomes effective for one's own purpose according to the principle stated in such passages as: "Therefore, by imparting what has come down through the lineage of gurus, one attains supreme Śiva. It is precisely as an ancillary to this [purpose] that...

A group of seven verses has been set forth, dedicated to the glorification of the lineage of gurus for the purpose of demonstrating the traditional succession. Consequently, its purpose is the bestowal of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), through the recognition of this very [tradition] as one's own self by means of the sequence of methods to be described hereafter.
Although [this] was already indicated in another verse, it is stated explicitly by the verse beginning with "Śrī Śambhunātha.

With this as its objective, what conscious being—purified by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (parameśvara-śaktipāta)—would not proceed? Thus, it serves as the motive for engagement; and even for one who has engaged, it serves as the means of attainment.
Because of such statements as, "The Vināyakas join one to impermanent enjoyments," obstacles arise;

therefore, the praise of Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka is performed for the sake of their removal. Furthermore, this [work] is being composed by me here in the *Tantrāloka*, according to the method promised in the words, "Requested [by you], I shall compose."
The title *Tantrāloka* is established by relying on what will be stated later, beginning with the words "in the teaching" (*śāsane*). Thus,

the relationship characterized as that between the signifier and the signified, and between the means and the goal— pertaining respectively to the title and its subject matter, and the subject matter and its purpose— is also implied by the sense of the text.
Thus, a single initial statement, consisting of the synthesis of many sentences, has been stated as the cause for engagement—this is the summary meaning. || 21 ||
In this regard, although for all proponents liberation alone is to be accepted and its opposite,

cyclic existence, is to be abandoned, and while false knowledge is the cause of that [existence] and knowledge of reality is its antidote— thus, through the direct realization of that [reality] alone, liberation is attained by the removal of ignorance.
There is no dispute on this point; nevertheless, because they do not know the nature of knowledge and ignorance as restricted solely to that [Self], it is said:
"Indeed, Māyā deludes them by means of the desire for liberation in what is not liberation."

By such statements, it is shown that the liberation accepted by that [system] is not liberation at all; for, in order to demonstrate this, an examination of that system— distinguished from other scriptures— is set forth hereafter, and thus its primary importance is indicated right at the outset.

The author sets forth the examination of bondage and liberation: "In this regard, it is proclaimed throughout all the scriptures that ignorance is the cause of transmigratory existence, while knowledge is the sole cause of liberation. (1.22)

Nor has this been stated by us merely as our own invention; thus he says: "They maintain that impurity is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence. This has likewise been declared in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*: na caitadasmābhiḥ svopajñamevoktam -- ityāha -- malamajñānamicchanti saṃsārāṅkurakāraṇam | iti proktaṃ tathā ca śrīmālinīvijayottare || 1-23 ||
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is a darkness whose true nature is the concealment of one's own form, manifested solely by the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord;
its essence consists in the false identification of the self with the non-self, and it is an incomplete knowledge. This very state is the *āṇava* [impurity].
"Mala," however, does not refer to the form of a substance (dravya) which will be refuted at the beginning of the ninth chapter. And it has been said:
"The loss of freedom of consciousness and the lack of consciousness regarding freedom—this is the twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala), arising from the forfeiture of one's own true nature."
Thus [it is said].
And what is that like? To this he says: "transmigration" (saṃsāra). Regarding transmigration: "The manifestation of a divided object of knowledge right here is that which is called Māyā..."
"Thus, for the impurity (*mala*) of the nature of *māyā* described above, karma— which is the cause of transmigratory existence— is called the 'sprout' (*aṅkura*) of *saṃsāra*.
According to the principle to be stated later, the 'sprout' is the causal impurity of action (*kārmamala*), and [karma] is its cause."
As it has been said:
"Impurity (mala) is caused by karma, while that which follows is occasional (naimittika).
This was taught in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*; indeed, this entire treatise is composed under the authority of this very subject matter.
The word "engaged" (pravṛtta) provides further reinforcement. ||23||
Although ignorance is twofold—consisting of both the personal (*pauruṣa*) and the intellectual (*buddha*)—it is intended here that only the personal type is meant, not the other; thus he says:
"By means of the qualification [‘future’], [ignorance] residing in the intellect [is excluded], as it pertains to the period after transmigratory existence."
Having cast aside all expectations, he declared that liberation occurs in their absence.
Regarding the qualification “the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra”:

since the Buddhist ignorance, which consists of wrong resolve, is not the cause of karma, but rather [ignorance] is the cause of that [wrong resolve], how can this qualification be consistent? For that [wrong resolve] exists only when the body has karma as its cause.

This is possible because it consists of both cause and effect, and because the intellect (buddhi) is included within the category of causes; for this very reason it was stated [in the *Sāṃsārottarakālika*]:
"The form of the body and the world is proclaimed to be māyīya."
Because of such statements as these, the meaning is: [it occurs] immediately after the body within saṃsāra.
"What is the point of refuting that possibility?"—to this it was said: "In the absence of this [other], he spoke of liberation.
For liberation would not occur through the mere cessation of mental (bauddha) ignorance, because when that has ceased, only mental knowledge arises;
and even though that [mental knowledge] consists of pure conceptualization (vikalpa),...

"Every conceptual construction (vikalpa) is saṃsāra... According to this principle, since [conceptualization] is the cause of the manifestation of saṃsāra, how could this be so even in its absence? It is with this intention that even outsiders [have said]:
It has been stated: "The wise person should not become attached even to conceptualization regarding the ultimate reality;
for what difference is there between a conceptualization that is auspicious or one that is inauspicious?
This being so, when human ignorance has been removed through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, if [the practitioner] possesses intellectual [knowledge]...

Then that knowledge would become a cause even for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) according to the method to be described; however, by that [knowledge] alone, nothing at all will be accomplished—this has already been stated.
But human effort (*pauruṣa*), once arisen as knowledge, is the cause of liberation independently of anything else.
As it has been said:
"The bonds belonging to the individual soul (puruṣa) are to be purified during initiation, but not those residing in the intellect;
therefore, even when that [intellect] is defective, initiation is not fruitless."

Thus, that [liberation] has the nature of pure consciousness alone; for the absence of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is indeed full apprehension (*khyāti*), and that alone is the true essential nature of the Self, which is a mass of light and bliss. The manifestation of that very nature is liberation;
thus it is rightly said: "In the absence of this, he declared [it to be] liberation. (24)
Now, one might ask: what is the basis for the claim that the meaning of the word *ajñāna* is "incomplete knowledge," rather than simply the absence of knowledge?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
Ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge, because that would lead to an over-extension;
for such absence exists even in a clod of earth and the like, yet it does not undergo transmigration. (1.25)
"What is this over-extension?"—to this he says: "For he... and so forth. Thus, it has been rightly stated:
