that the meaning of the word *ajñāna* is "incomplete knowledge. ||25||

Thus it is said: "Therefore, that very knowledge which consists in the non-manifestation of the reality of the object of knowledge in its totality is ignorance; this is proclaimed in the Śiva Sūtras. (1.26)
Therefore, for the reason already stated, [there is] the "knowable," such as blue, pleasure, and so forth;

and the "supreme reality of the knowable," which is Śiva whose nature consists of light, as will be described in the passage beginning with "the supreme reality of the knowable..."; [there is] the "totality" (*kṛtsnatayā*) of that "reality."

Because there is no distinction anywhere [in that state], it is "not consisting of manifestation" by virtue of having a single, compact form; whereas this "knowledge" which consists of the manifestation of duality—such as "this is blue" or "this is pleasure"—is incomplete, and that very thing is "ignorance," not merely the absence of knowledge. This has been "illuminated"—that is, stated—in the *Śivasūtras*: *na tadasti vinā yatsyāttanmātraṃ na ca bhāsate | tasyaivārthamayaṃ bhāgaḥ śuddhabhāgastu kevalaḥ ||* [That which exists apart from Him does not exist, nor does that which is merely His own essence shine forth. Its portion consisting of objects is [the world], while its pure portion alone is the Absolute. Furthermore: *ajñānenāvṛtaṃ jñānaṃ tena muhyanti jantavaḥ |* [Knowledge is covered by ignorance; therefore, living beings are deluded. And: *jñānena tu tadajñānaṃ yeṣāṃ nāśitamātmanaḥ |* [But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self... Thus, it is taught that ignorance is the state of duality, not a simple lack of cognition.
This is the meaning. || 26 ||
Anticipating the question, "Where is this demonstrated therein? he says:
"In the two aphorisms, 'Consciousness is the Self' and 'Knowledge is bondage,' this meaning is demonstrated through the conjunction and the alternative application [of the terms]. (1.27)

By means of *saṃhitā* through the conjunction (*praśleṣa*) and otherwise through its separation (*viśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*, the meaning is as follows: "Knowledge is bondage; ignorance is bondage. Thus, the word *ajñāna* (ignorance) has the characteristic of denoting incomplete knowledge (*apūrṇajñāna*).

He explains this very point: "Consciousness" (caitanya)—this word ending in an abstract suffix—denotes nothing but absolute freedom (svātantrya), without implying any specific attributes; so it was stated in the ancient Sūtra. (1.28)
But by the second Sūtra, which speaks of either action or an instrument, duality is asserted for that [Self] whose nature is pure consciousness alone. (1.29)
The manifestation of duality is ignorance of that [Reality]; because of its worthlessness, it is called bondage.
For this very reason, it must be completely eradicated; thus it is described as having the nature of an obscuration. (1.30)
In this [system], nothing whatsoever remains unperceived, for the act of consciousness (*citikriyā*) is the universal form of all things.

That which perceives is the conscious (*cetana*), one who possesses full knowledge and action; its state is "consciousness" (*caitanya*), which is the possession of full knowledge and action, and that alone is the very nature of supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*).
Freedom is being described. Thus it says: "merely freedom" (*svātantryamātrakam*).
Freedom alone, in its entirety, is "merely freedom. For this very reason, it says: "without implying any specific qualities" (*anākṣiptaviśeṣam*);
that is, "specific qualities" such as eternality, omnipresence, and so forth—even those which are its own concomitants—are "not implied."

That by which there is differentiation. For a word ending in an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) expresses precisely the exclusion of other concomitant properties; for this very reason, it is distinct from a word denoting a substance (dravya). As they say:
The exclusion or non-exclusion of other properties in those two cases is the basis for the distinction between conventional designations; it follows the desire of the cognizer.

"This very distinction exists everywhere between those [words] denoting substance and those denoting state. By the phrase "by the second," it is meant by the word *jñāna* occurring in the second sūtra; for through the etymologies "cognition is knowledge" (*jñaptir jñānam*) and "that by which one knows is knowledge" (*jāyate yena iti jñānam ca*), it denotes both "action" and "instrument."

By primarily denoting that [Self]—whose nature has been stated as "consciousness is the Self"—it is therefore called "cognition" (*cit*), because it cognizes; it is the agent in the act of cognition. Of that whose "form" is solely and exclusively that [act of cognition], "duality" is spoken of, namely, between agent and object, and between agent, object, and action.

By the apprehension of distinct limiting conditions (*avacchedaka*), the manifestation of duality is brought about; the meaning is that its full nature is not revealed. Therefore, from that non-manifestation of the full nature—which is of the essence of the non-duality of consciousness—there arises precisely the manifestation of duality.

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is incomplete knowledge; and because of that incompleteness, it is precisely this state of considering oneself incomplete—which, by way of being various contracted forms of knowledge consisting of the body, worlds, and the nature of auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), takes the form of the three impurities (*mala*)—that is called "bondage. And it is for this very reason, because it is of the nature of bondage, that it is ignorance.
"The impurity and karma, as well as everything pertaining to Māyā and the individual soul (āṇava)—
all this is declared to be that which is to be abandoned..."

By this statement, [ignorance] is to be abandoned—this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: how is it understood that here, because it consists of the manifestation of duality, incomplete knowledge itself is ignorance?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "It has been defined by way of repetition. By "by way of repetition," [it means] as "ignorance."
"By means of reciting the *saṃhitā* again and again"—this is the meaning. ||28-30||
Now, one might object: "In that case, let the definition of liberation be stated. Anticipating this, he says:

"But there is no such thing as liberation—whether it be something insubstantial or substantial—that exists apart from the independent Self; therefore, not even a separate name for it is even grasped. (1.31)

"There is nothing else whatsoever"—this is the completion of the sentence. If it were insubstantial (*tuccha*), then by the logic previously stated, it would indeed be bondage; if, however, it is not insubstantial, then because of its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), there is no existence of it as something independent or distinct from the Self.
As he will say:
"For liberation is indeed nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature; and the true nature of the self is consciousness... and so forth.
What is meant by this? Here, first of all, there is no dispute that the knowledge of the self is liberation.

Therefore, since the very characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Self is the same as that of liberation, its characteristic is established by the very fact of being inseparable from it; thus, a separate characteristic has not been formulated. For this very reason, by the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "not even the name," it is indicated: what further need is there to speak of [its] characteristic and so forth? || 31 ||
Even so, in order to cast a glance upon its distinctiveness from that [other view] and to state the nature of liberation as taught in other systems, he proceeds:
"But that which consists of the full and complete manifestation of the true reality of the object of knowledge..."
Each subsequent knowledge therein grants the pacification of each corresponding cycle of worldly existence.
Furthermore, regarding the "reality" (*tattva*) of the "knowable" (*jñeya*)— the path (*adhvan*) consisting of the *kalās*, *tattvas*, worlds (*bhuvanas*), and so forth—
which exists in a state of differentiation both progressively higher and mutually [among its parts],

there occurs a "successive ascent" (*uttarottaram*) by way of moving upward and upward through the sequence of transcending each respective world and so on, due to the disappearance of those respective limitations.
Although there is contraction due to the manifestation of duality arising from various degrees of excellence,
"knowledge whose nature is the manifestation of the full and the complete" arises, because it transcends and subordinates the entire web of objective categories.

Based on the statement beginning with, "And that which is called the fourteen-fold mandala of saṃsāra," the meaning is: [knowledge is] "the bestower of peace and the liberator from that very saṃsāra," which consists of those fourteen types of births. For the very nature of knowledge is liberation.
But rather, it is the non-contracted state of that which was contracted. 32.
He demonstrates this very point:
"I am untainted by passion and the like; I am inwardly empty; I am abandoned by agency.
In this way, through both summary and detail, knowledge releases one from that much [bondage]. (1.33)

The connection is as follows: "knowledge," whose nature has been described in the first half [of the verse], "in this manner," liberates one from "that much"—meaning limited—bondage, namely that which pertains to the Buddhists and others.
In that regard, the knowledge of the Yogācāras is: "I am unstained by passion and the like."
As they have said: "The mind defiled by passion and so forth is saṃsāra; its liberation is [nirvāṇa].
In brief, this is what liberation has been described as by the Victors who have abandoned all obscurations."
Likewise:
"This mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious.
When they are removed, that indestructible light [of the mind] realizes all objects."

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning here: although the mind—which possesses the inherent power of its own nature—is manifested as *saṃsāra* due to being veiled by adventitious impurities such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth through the force of beginningless ignorance, [liberation occurs] by means of abandoning those various adventitious impurities through the power of practicing the path consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like.

The claim that liberation is the manifestation of one's own nature as an imperishable light-form through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is untenable; for you maintain that meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause here, yet it is incapable of producing a distinction in mental moments that perish in an instant. This is because of its...
Because it is capable of receiving specific qualities by virtue of residing in a single stable substratum;
for instance, stable substances such as sesame seeds are perfumed only by stable flowers, and this [mental continuum] might be likewise;
therefore, regarding that which arises as something entirely new at every moment—

What is the meaning of this [argument]: that for a momentary state of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*) which has not attained any excellence—just like the practice of jumping without a continuous connection (*niranvaya*)—cultivation (*bhāvanā*) would not be capable of producing a luminous momentary state of consciousness? Furthermore, impure moments of consciousness possess an inherent power to produce their own similar [successors].

They are capable of producing only mental moments similar to themselves, not dissimilar, luminous ones. And thus, because of the momentary flux of mental states, cultivation would not even be able to effect the removal of impurities; so what need is there to speak of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)? Enough said.

For those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness, liberation [is impossible]. Furthermore, bondage and liberation are tenable only under the view of a stable, unitary entity; for it is one who is bound that strives for liberation, and having attained it, becomes liberated. Yet a single continuum does not exist, because such a concept is undermined by the dilemma of its being either identical to or different from its constituent moments. [The word] "antaḥ" [means]...
Even regarding the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatā*), the Mādhyamikas possess the cognition: "I am empty.

Indeed, they are proponents of the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) in all entities; because they assert that even consciousness lacks intrinsic nature and is therefore false, they [abide] precisely in emptiness.

They would declare liberation. As they say: "The teaching of the Sage that 'this entire universe is mind-only' was for the sake of removing the fear of the ignorant; it is not [the truth] in its ultimate sense."
"That state of being established in mind-only is also destroyed by those of great fortune.

This too has been said: for even if the independent nature of consciousness is set aside by treating it as false, its very existence would not cease; because, unlike blue and other objects, it lacks a dependent nature.

For although blue and other objects, being false, may have their independent forms set aside, they still persist as having consciousness as their essence; however, in the case of consciousness itself— which has nothing but its own luminous manifestation as its core—
there would be non-existence due to its falsity, and thus nothing at all would manifest, resulting in a state of mere unconsciousness.
And since it is impossible to deny consciousness, whose very essence consists in the mere radiance of manifestation, this [objection] is trivial. Now:
"By all objects of perception and by all sentient beings without exception..."

If it is argued that, according to such statements as "It is empty of all latent tendencies of the afflictions, but not empty from the perspective of ultimate reality," [the self] is empty of imagined forms such as the state of subject and object, but not empty of consciousness itself— then by asserting this, one would simply be accepting the position of the Vijñānavāda.

For that [world] too is empty of the nature of the imagined, the dependent, and so forth; thus: "This world is the manifestation of the internal organ itself, which appears as diverse and whose true reality has not been realized."

Because of such statements as these, [the opponent] has accepted that representation (*vijñapti*) alone is ultimately real; thus, nothing new has been conceived by the Venerable One. And the fault regarding that has already been stated: for the Sāṃkhyas, there is the cognition, "I am a non-agent. For they have accepted the self (*ātman*) as being entirely devoid of activity; otherwise, indeed...

And it would follow that he possesses no consciousness, since activity is observed only in insentient things such as milk and the like. This is untenable—for if the Puruṣa were not an agent, there would be no liberation; for if the Puruṣa were incapable of action, then even when discriminative insight has arisen, liberation could not occur.

There could be no abiding in its own nature, because it is impossible for *prakṛti*, whose very essence is activity, to remain indifferent; furthermore, the possibility of such a state would arise again even with respect to that [Puruṣa].
Nor does *prakṛti* think, "I have been seen by him," and thus, "I shall not act for his sake again."
Thus, because this [prakṛti] lacks consciousness, there is no such thing as purposeful deliberation; and so,
just as she would act toward sound and other objects even after they have been perceived,
she will likewise act toward that end again even after discriminative discernment has been achieved.
Because it does not deviate from its own nature, even in this way, that which has been done does not become undone;
thus, even the contracted knowledge of the Buddhists and others would perform its own appropriate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For instance, the Buddhists—

"By the reasoning stated in such passages as 'We perceive this single nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa) as the manifestation of various forms such as joy, sorrow, and so forth,' they have accepted that knowledge consisting of the fluctuations of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) alone is the ultimate reality;
thus, for them, liberation is simply the attainment of the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva). As it has been said:
"Brahmā is established there as the presiding lord within the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva);
and they call him alone the Omniscient One, the supreme state of the Buddhists."

Thus, for this very reason, there is the cessation of this transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) which resides below the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva). And so, it is rightly said: "Knowledge liberates from that much. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that liberation consists in the person (puruṣa) abiding in its own essential nature through its separation from primordial matter (prakṛti), which is composed of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Since they have realized the *tattva*, this attainment of the *tattva* itself is their liberation. As it has been said:

"And for the Sāṃkhyas, [liberation] consists in the Puruṣa alone, which is devoid of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Furthermore, for the Sāṃkhyas, the view of the Self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is superior to the view of selflessness (*nairātmyadṛṣṭi*).
For the Buddhists, knowledge consists of full manifestation (*pūrṇaprathā*);

thus, for these [schools], there is the attainment of the *puruṣatattva* situated above the *buddhitattva*. And so, knowledge becomes increasingly higher, consisting of full manifestation, and so forth.
The meaning promised in the previous sūtra has been fulfilled.

Thus, although there is equality between the Sāṃkhya and Pātañjala systems regarding knowledge through the separation from *prakṛti*, the Pātañjalas are distinguished from the Sāṃkhyas by their devotion (*praṇidhāna*) to the Lord (*īśvara*). This is [the point] for them.
The attainment of the *niyati-tattva* situated above the *puṃs-tattva* has been described:
"O Mistress of the Gods, the twenty-sixth [principle], however, is the supreme state in the Yoga-śāstra.
And thus, for the Mausulas, Pāśupatas, and others as well, [the attainment occurs] according to their respective [levels].
"Through the excellence of knowledge, there is the attainment of higher and higher principles; this is the supreme state. As it has been said:
"In the Mausula and Kārūka [traditions], the principle of Māyā is proclaimed.
Likewise:
"In the Pāśupata vow, the supreme state of Īśvara is proclaimed.

Thus, in that regard, for the Buddhists and others, [this occurs] through a portion-by-portion [removal] of the impurity belonging to Māyā; for the Mausulas, even from the impurity of Karma (kārmamala); and for the Pāśupatas, due to the conceit of self in what is not the self (anātmany ātmābhimāna).
It has been stated [in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*] that "knowledge is the liberator even from the individual impurity (*āṇavamala*), both by way of summary and detail.
Now, one might object: "Even if the bondage has dissolved in this manner according to the principles of one's own system, why is such a person not considered liberated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, even one who is liberated remains as if unliberated because of the persistence of one limitation after another;
however, the truly liberated one is devoid of all limitations.

Because of the statement, "......... the path (adhvan) is the cause of bondage," the path is indeed that which binds. In this regard, the Buddhists and others, through the dissolution of bondage up to the level of the *buddhi-tattva*, are also liberated.

Because they remain delimited by the intervening path situated above that [level], they are indeed not liberated; for this very reason, since they are created once again at the commencement of a new creation, there is the manifestation of saṃsāra, as the cause of bondage has not been entirely exhausted. As he will say:
"At the dawn of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha indeed creates again those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, the Vedas, and so forth; therefore, such liberation is not complete.
Thus it is stated also in the venerable Svacchanda-śāstra:

Having stated this in general terms, beginning with: "Furthermore, for worldly beings there is repeated creation and repeated dissolution; they are mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel," and so forth—
"And if the Lord were to bind again that one who has been liberated from bondage,

then bondage would occur once more through saṃsāra as long as one does not find the Divine"— this was stated specifically with the intent of characterizing the liberation [claimed] by the various sub-schools such as the Buddhists. He who...
Furthermore, he states that one whose bonds throughout all the paths have been completely exhausted is truly liberated:
"But the liberated one is devoid of all limitations. As it has been said:
"The supreme state of the Śaivas is that which has emerged beyond the entire path."
Thus:
"The perfected Śaiva shines at the head of the others; once liberated, he does not return to a lower state in creation."
Thus [ends the section]. 34.
And in this regard, such complete knowledge alone is the cause; thus he says:
"But that knowledge of the true reality of the object of knowledge which is free from limitations within one's own self—nowhere is there ignorance therein; it bestows true liberation. (1.35)

The meaning is: that which is "abandoned"—that is, whose essence is the reflective awareness of supreme I-ness—in every respect (sarvātmanā), even by way of mere latent impressions (vāsanāmātreṇa), by means of "limitations" (avacchedaiḥ), i.e., those reflective awarenesses of "this-ness" (idantā) that produce contraction. And for this very reason:

Because its nature consists of full manifestation (*pūrṇaprathā*), there is no ignorance whatsoever; and thus, it bestows "liberation"—which is distinct from the semblance of liberation—and shines forth as the essential identity with the subject whose core is the reflective awareness of "I. This is the meaning. || 35 ||
Now he analyzes the very nature of knowledge and ignorance as they were just mentioned:

"This nature of knowledge and ignorance, each of which has been described, is said in the teaching of Śiva to be twofold, distinguished as being either personal (pauruṣa) or intellectual (bauddha). (1.36)
"In the teaching of Śiva" means in the supreme Lord's philosophy consisting of the five currents (pañcasrotas)—this is the meaning.
For this has been stated everywhere without distinction. ||36||
He defines that very [nature] as follows:

"In that regard, the ignorance of the person, which is called 'impurity' (mala), and that which arises from it, consists in the veiling of the sharpness of one's own perfect consciousness and action. (1.37)
That [state] of the bound soul (paśu), whose nature consists of contracted vision and action, is non-conceptual (avikalpita).

Now—the word "atha" signifies immediate succession; for after the mere mention (uddeśa), there arises the occasion for definition (lakṣaṇa) and examination (parīkṣā)—this is the intended meaning. "Therein" means from between the two kinds, namely knowledge and ignorance.
Regarding the statement, "... [it] manifests as supreme for the person," that which is the very nature of the Self just described—
known as *mala* (impurity)— is conjoined with knowledge and action that are unconditioned and not shared by others.

The meaning is that [the world] has been born—that is, manifested—from Śiva alone, who is the nature of the supreme subject. For it is the Supreme Lord himself who, through his own sovereignty, conceals his own self by casting aside his full knowledge and agency and by manifesting the causal impurity (*mala*) consisting of non-recognition (*akhyāti*). As it has been said:

"That which is the supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, the accomplishment of the impossible, is the Goddess Māyā-śakti; this is the self-concealment of Śiva. (Pañcārthabhāṣya 15kha) Due to the influence of the appropriation of Māyā, consciousness becomes defiled and the person becomes a bound soul (paśu)."
Thus [it is said]. And he will state:

"Therefore, it is merely the autonomy of one's own nature that is manifested as impurity. That very [nature] belongs even to that bound soul (*paśu*), who is joined with the three impurities, beginning with the *āṇava*.
Because the Mother [of limited subjects] is delimited by space, time, and so forth, her knowledge consists of the perception of the manifestation of restricted vision and action.

Indeed, it was the Supreme Lord himself who, having brought his own Self— which had attained the state of a limited atom (*aṇu*) through the casting aside of omniscience and other attributes— again established its connection with *kalā* and the other categories, whereby its [vision and action] became restricted.
It is characterized by cognition, agency, and so forth. As it has been said:
"She gave birth to the principle of *kalā*, through union with which the person (*pums*) came into being; having acquired the capacity for agency, he then produced *vidyā* and *rāga*."
Knowledge discriminates for him between action and its causes and effects;
passion, moreover, colors him even toward his own impure enjoyments.
"Fate yokes this person to their own action;
Time also measures them, abiding in moments (*tuṭi*) and so forth.
Thus it is stated even in the first mention of the nature of knowledge.

In order to demonstrate that [ignorance] must necessarily be eradicated, the nature of ignorance is first defined. Now, one might object: "Since knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is said by the followers of Pañcaśikha to be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), how could this [ignorance] not be included within a portion of the intellect?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That is not ignorance."
The aspect of intellect [is absent] due to the absence of determination and so forth. || 38 ||

For even so, since it has been stated that "intellect (buddhi) is determination (adhyavasāya)," determination alone is its primary form; how could this [intellect] possess that as its attribute in the absence of such [determination]? || 38 ||
Therefore, it is said:
"When [the cognition] determining 'I know this in this way' arises from the reflection produced by the individual soul (aṇu) within the cavity of the six coverings... (1.39).
Then, from that [intellect], there arises a corresponding cognition designated as "ignorance" (ajñāna);
it is both mental and innate, being both that which is nourished and that which nourishes. (1.40)

And the reason for her being thus possessed of the capacity for determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the phrase "the six coverings" (*ṣaṭkañcuka*). Bound by the six coverings—by the force of time, limited agency (*kalā*), necessity (*niyati*), and the power of attachment (*rāga*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—she thinks:
"Only now do I know this very little, and only with my whole self."
This is said to be the internal factor for the six coverings (*kañcukas*) and for action, along with *māyā* (as stated in *Paśupārameśvara*, chapter 16, verse 17).

By means of those whose essential natures have been defined by such passages, the "individual soul" (*aṇu*)— who is "turbid," meaning one who is almost withered due to the arising of limited knowledge, agency, and so forth— is [described].

The self is limited; therefore, from that which arises—namely, from "reflection," meaning the transference of the shadow of consciousness (cicchāyā)—it follows that because this [intellect] is the ground for the manifestation of the individual's cognitive awareness, its nature must be such as described. This is the intended meaning.

The term "tādṛk" (such) refers to that which consists of this kind of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). To demonstrate the mutual relationship of cause and effect between these two, he says "of that," and so forth. "Of that" means of the mental (*buddhi*) [cognition]; "pauruṣam" means pertaining to the person (*pums*), i.e., the spiritual (*pauruṣa*)—this is the meaning. "To be nourished" (*poṣaṇīya*) means the effect—this is the meaning.

For indeed, in one who is possessed by desire, grief, and so forth, a non-conceptual cognition consisting of the direct perception of those respective objects may arise through the contemplation of being absorbed in them (*tanmayatānusaṃdhāna*) and other means. As they say:
"Those who are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, dreams of thieves, and so forth..."
"They see even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.

Here, "the nourisher" (*poṣṭṛ*) refers to the cause. For even in dreams and the like, prior experience alone is the causal factor; indeed, even the desire for a conceptualization of fire would not arise in an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*Nārikeladvīpa*). (Verses 39–40)

Having thus defined ignorance, he speaks in order to define knowledge as well, which is also twofold: "But when the latent impressions of the bound soul have perished, for the person who has attained the supreme state, that superconscious knowledge of the Self blossoms forth, free from conceptual construction. (1.41)

To the extent that the knowledge whose nature is non-conceptual and ever-expanding conforms to its fitness, that [knowledge] is "born of the Buddha" (bauddha); for whomsoever it belongs, that is "human" (pauṃsna), and as before, it is both that which is nourished and that which nourishes. (1.42)

Since even for the bound soul (*paśu*) there is said to be the destruction of mere latent impressions (*vāsanāmātra*), by the maxim "in the absence of the cause, the effect also ceases to exist," the *kārmamāyīya* [fetters] are also destroyed; thus, for the "Person" (*pumsaḥ*) from whom all bonds have ceased, for this very reason—

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: for one who has attained supreme identity with consciousness (*cidaikātmya*), there arises a human cognition (*pauruṣaṃ jñānam*) that is "expansive"—consisting of the reflective awareness of supreme subjectivity (*parāhantā-vimarśa*), "free of conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpaka*), and distinct from artificial conceptualizations such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). The phrase "by way of fitness" (*aucityena*) means by means of that same full Self.
This is the meaning. And for this reason, its nature is such that "all this is my own manifestation.

"Of which" refers to the Buddhist cognition. "As before" means that just as there is a relationship of nourished and nourisher between the two types of ignorance, so it is here—this is the sense. Likewise, by way of being full or incomplete.
Furthermore, a distinction must be grasped; otherwise, the very nature of knowledge and ignorance would not have been stated. || 41-42 ||
Indeed, there is no dispute that such ignorance remains indeed beginningless;
however, when will this knowledge, which consists of the absence of that [ignorance], arise? And what is the cause for its arising?
Anticipating this objection, he says:

"In that case, although the ignorance pertaining to the individual soul (pauṃsna) is destroyed by initiation and other means, nevertheless, that knowledge becomes clearly manifest at the end of that body. (1.43)
Although the nature of "ignorance pertaining to the person" has been stated thus:
"The true state of knowledge is bestowed and the latent impressions of the bound soul (paśu) are destroyed;
because it is joined with both bestowing and destroying, initiation (dīkṣā) is so celebrated here."

By means of initiation (*dīkṣā*) whose nature has been described in such passages as these, [ignorance] indeed perishes; nevertheless, that knowledge of the Self—which consists merely in the absence of ignorance—even when oriented toward manifestation—[remains], for it is said:
"One should not purify that which is [already] under the influence of *prārabdha* karma."
Because of such statements as these, since the *kārmamala* (the impurity of karma) that initiates this body exists, [it is said]: "At the end of 'that'—of the present body—it is clearly manifested":
"...upon the fall of the body, one goes to Śiva."
The meaning is that [the reality] flashes forth as direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) by virtue of such statements; and by the word "etc.

(*ādi*), the remaining modes of activity are included, but not the most intense descent of power (*tīvratara-śaktipāta*) and so on, for since that is the cause for initiation (*dīkṣā*), its inclusion is already established by that very mention. It is not [included here].
And in this regard, there is nothing other than initiation (*dīkṣā*) that serves as the cause for liberation. As it has been said:
"Therefore, from that extensive bondage which obstructs the supreme state, initiation alone liberates one upward and leads one even to the abode of Śiva."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, when there is the most intense descent of power (*tīvratama-śaktipāta*) and so forth, initiation may occur through the sequence beginning with the "no-means" (*anupāya*), by which his liberation (*apavarga*) occurs at that very moment.
As it has been stated:
"Through that connection, someone may be liberated from that very moment.
This [liberation] cannot possibly be a cause for liberation independent of initiation (*dīkṣā*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
In passages such as, "For him, even without initiation, through the transformation resulting from self-purification,
perfect knowledge arises— this is established in all the scriptures," the intended meaning is a prohibition of that [initiation] with reference to external ritual initiation (bāhyakriyādīkṣā).
Otherwise, how could the very meaning of the term "self-purification" (ātmasaṃskāra) be consistent here? Enough of this prolixity. || 43 ||
Now, one might object: "If liberation occurs only at the end of the body through initiation in this way, then how is it stated that 'he is liberated even while living' and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

But when that which is manifested by the ignorance of the Buddha's [nature] dissolves through the knowledge of the Buddha, then liberation while living (jīvanmukti) rests in the palm of one's hand. (44)
"By means of Buddhist knowledge" refers to that which has arisen from hearing the non-dual scriptures of the Supreme Lord and so forth.
As it has been said:
"When, at the proper time, the tradition has been fully explained by the Guru alone..."
"From that time forward, he is liberated; only the machine remains.

This should be understood as applying specifically to one who has received initiation (*dīkṣita*), for one who has not undergone initiation has no authority even to hear the scriptures, so how could there be [liberation] resulting from the comprehension of them?
The manifestation of that knowledge would occur. As it has been said:
"One should not recite the manual of Śiva in the presence of those who have not been initiated.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that nothing happens for one whose human ignorance (*pauruṣājñāna*) has not been destroyed by this [initiation].
Otherwise, there would be no engagement at all in initiation for those who possess discernment,

because the goal to be accomplished would be absent precisely due to the absence of a creator; therefore, one must not say that there is a lack of firm resolve regarding initiation, since it is that very initiation which is the fundamental cause for liberation.

Thus, although spiritual knowledge (*pauṃsna-jñāna*) may be oriented toward manifestation through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, it does not grant liberation at that very moment, because its manifestation is said to occur at the end of the body; this [knowledge], however, grants it immediately. Therefore, its preeminence is also indicated by this. || 44 ||
This is not the only reason for its primacy; there is another as well—thus he says:
"Initiation too, when preceded by Buddhist gnosis, truly brings about liberation.
Therefore, even in that case, Buddhist gnosis possesses primacy. (1.45)
In this regard—

because of such statements as, "Even one devoid of all auspicious marks is an excellent guru if he possesses knowledge," it is only a guru who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures who has the authority to bestow initiation; therefore...

Thus, his defining characteristic has been stated primarily as: "One who knows the prescriptions of the Śiva-scriptures and is proficient in both knowledge and the object of knowledge"; otherwise, however—

"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, without the scripture (śāstra), initiation (dīkṣā) would not be effective for liberation," according to such statements, initiation itself would not be liberating; therefore, because intellectual knowledge (bauddha-jñāna) is the cause of initiation, for without that [knowledge], its very accomplishment would not occur. || 45 ||
And this is not our own invention alone—thus he says:
"This duality pertaining to knowledge and ignorance has been established in the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Ruru*, the *Mataṅga*, and other scriptures by the venerable teachers such as Kheṭapāla. (1.46)
As it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as the impurity of the self and māyā,
and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva proceeds."
Thus [it is said]:
"Now, the beginningless impurity (*mala*) of bound souls is proclaimed as their state of bondage (*paśutva*).
Under the power of its existence, the multitude of fetters (*pāśaugha*)—beginning with ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth—is known as pertaining to the person (*pauruṣa*)."
"Therefore, that [reality] should be known in its true essence by one who desires imperishable liberation.
And in the venerable *Ruru[-tantra]* it is said:
"Those proficient in the reality of mantras worship with various sacrifices."

"Those whose doubts have been severed by the sword of initiation authorized by the Guru, the Tantras, and so forth—[such people] should not examine or deliberate upon mantras with a limited intellect.
Thus [it is said].
"Mantras are not to be scrutinized or deliberated upon by men of small intelligence."
Taking scripture as the authority, it should be trusted by the wise.
"All deities have the nature of mantra; all mantras have the nature of Śiva.
Having realized that this [universe] has the nature of Śiva, one should contemplate only Śiva.
Thus it is said. Also, in the venerable Mataṅga:
Then that Blessed Lord Īśa, whose crest-jewel was shimmering with rubies,
[was] the King of Mantras, by means of the power of the flames arising from the fire of his speech.
"It burned away all the sage's ignorance like a heap of straw.
Thus [it is said]:
"It is stainless, born from the lotus-face of Śiva, and facing in every direction."
"The unfolding of Śiva-nature is the truth, the knowledge that destroys ignorance;
by means of this, the perfected ones (siddhas) behold that state which is free from affliction.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the *Cillācakreśvarīmata* and other such texts is intended. As it is said therein:

That impurity is traditionally held to be twofold: intellectual (*bauddha*) and personal (*pauruṣeya*). Among these, the personal impurity goes to destruction through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means; however, the intellectual impurity remains inexhaustible as long as it continues to be sealed.
As long as there is no Buddhist [teaching] that dissolves this very [notion], which is of the same class [as it].
"Knowledge has arisen correctly, effecting the distinction between the essential and the non-essential.

Thus, initiation cannot manifest the masculine (pauṃsna) knowledge as long as his previously existing intellectual (bauddha) knowledge does not exist, by virtue of which its primacy over even that [intellectual knowledge] is stated. || 46 ||
Thus, how could even Buddhist knowledge arise without the scripture of the Supreme Lord?
Therefore, that [scripture] alone is the primary cause here; as such, he says:
"For the attainment of such Buddhist wisdom, which consists of definitive discernment..."
The scripture alone is primary, for it reveals the reality that is to be known.
The phrase "for the sake of attainment" means for the purpose of generating that [realization].

This is because the "reality" (*tattva*) of the "object of knowledge"—such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—is its nature as Śiva, whose essence is light, since its manifestation would otherwise be impossible; and this [text] demonstrates that reality.

The meaning is that because it brings about the instruction on supreme non-duality, it is the designator of that [reality]. For this very reason, its distinction from other scriptures is also implied by its not being a mere indicator of that [reality]. || 47 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so, what is the cause here that liberation occurs at the end of the body upon the cessation of the ignorance pertaining to the person (pauruṣa), whereas upon the cessation of the ignorance pertaining to the intellect (bauddha), it occurs right then? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when the internal ignorance consisting of the personal self has dissolved through initiation..."
For because the state of having attained wisdom has not ceased, conceptual construction would indeed still be possible. (1.48)

The term "of that which has gone to [the state of] intellect" (*dhīgatasya*) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*). For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consists in the manifestation of duality, is indeed ignorance because it takes the form of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*); this has been stated at length. || 48 ||
An objection might be raised: "If the ignorance residing in the intellect has not ceased, what does that matter to the Self?
Anticipating this, he says: "Because the sense of self persists in the intellect as long as the body exists."
And even at the end of the body, liberation occurs through human effort and the destruction of ignorance. || 1.49 ||

For even in one who has been initiated, there may persist for a fixed period the grasping at the self within the intellect (*buddhi*); thus, because of the non-difference between those two, it is possible that even the ignorance residing in the intellect could be attributed to the self—this is the sense. Therefore, at the end of the body, due to the cessation of the grasping at the self in the intellect, [the removal] of the personal ignorance occurs through initiation and so forth.
Since it has already been destroyed beforehand, it is rightly said that "liberation occurs"; thus, it is stated: "At the end of that body, that knowledge is clearly manifested. (49)
Thus, since conceptual construction (vikalpa), when present here, acts as an obstacle to liberation, liberation does not occur at that very moment;
rather, liberation occurs even while the body persists once that [construction] no longer exists. Thus he says:
"But upon the cessation of intellectual ignorance (bauddhājñāna), because of the uprooting of conceptual construction, liberation is certain."
"At that very moment liberation occurs," so it was said by the Creator in the venerable Niśāṭana.
And this is not without authority; thus he says: "It has been stated," and so forth. || 50 ||

One whose mind is joined with conceptual construction may attain auspiciousness through alms-gathering, whereas another does so immediately; such is the primary teaching of the scripture in this regard. (1.51)
"The other" refers to the non-conceptual [state]. "At that very time" means while the body still exists—this is the sense.
As it has been said in that very same place:
"But one whose mind is joined with conceptual thought shall go to Śiva upon the falling of the body."
But one whose mind is free from conceptual construction perceives oneself as auspicious and immutable.
"He who perceives through the purity of his being is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.

Now, he concludes the previously asserted primacy of the scripture itself with the words beginning with "iti": the word "iti" is to be applied according to the maxim of the crow's eye (kākākṣinyāya), by which [it functions both as a concluding marker and as a connector]. Thus:

It should also be explained as the cause for the completion of the *Śrīniśāṭana* treatise; and that [cause] was already stated previously with the words, "that which demonstrates the reality of the knowable," and so forth. || 51 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the reality of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-tattva*) that, when demonstrated, would also lead to an understanding of the preeminence of this scripture?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For the supreme reality of that which is to be known is Śiva, whose nature is light;
for that which is not of the nature of light can possess neither luminosity nor even substantiality. (1.52)
The very blueness of the object of knowledge, such as blue—that is, its state of being manifest—is not identical with the self [of the subject].
For if it were so, it would be manifest at all times and to everyone; it would not be the case that it is manifest only at certain times and only to certain people.
Consequently, everyone would be omniscient. Therefore, there arises the distinction: "it is manifest to him," or "it is manifest to me."

It is logical that this [object] is indeed conjoined with the subject whose nature is light; thus, blue and the like do not have a self-nature established in independence. Śiva alone is the subject whose nature is light, because anything else distinct from Him is afflicted by the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference. And therefore:

It has been stated that because objects of knowledge such as blue appear, they alone are the ultimate reality (paramārtha), as expressed in the words: "Śiva, whose nature is light, is the supreme principle. Now, one might object: "Even if this [object] is not of such a nature in itself, it will become so through its connection with light. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For... and so forth.
For even when blue and other objects appear through a connection with light, they appear only while being themselves of the nature of light;
it cannot be that something which is not of the nature of light appears as light—
for a palace that is not white does not become white— and in this way, its status as a real entity would also not be possible, for indeed...
The sense is that no other entity could possibly exist apart from the nature of luminosity. || 52 ||
And thus, Śiva, whose nature is light, is not only the reality because the objects of knowledge such as blue appear as light, but also because of their non-existence;
so he says:
Even the non-substantiality of entities is the sole domain of aesthetic wonder; for this cognition, "this is a non-entity," is not like that [cognition] directed toward a wall. (1.53)
Since even a cognition of the form "there is no jar here," because its nature is consciousness, is distinct from insentient objects such as walls, for this very reason,
the absence of the jar and so forth [is also established].
The meaning is that, because it is being awakened, it is precisely the very nature of Śiva, which consists of a single mass of supreme bliss and consciousness.
As they say: "Even non-consciousness, when being awakened, is indeed the Lord, whose essence is consciousness."
Thus [ends the verse]. 53.
Now, one might object: "Granted that once light (*prakāśa*) is established, the knowable—consisting of both existence and non-existence—is proven to have that [light] as its sole ultimate reality;
but by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that very light itself established? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This which is called light shines everywhere indeed."
Since it cannot be denied, what is the use of postulating means of valid cognition regarding it? (1.54)
Indeed, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object that which has not been previously known. As they say:

"A means of valid cognition has for its object that which has not been apprehended, or it is the illumination of an unknown object. Since [the self] is always already manifest, there is no manifestation of it as something previously unknown.

Since it cannot be denied by virtue of its being manifest, the postulation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard is redundant. For instance, its manifestation would have to be as something previously unknown only if it had not been manifest prior to that; and such a state [of non-manifestation] does not exist.

If there were a recollection of a prior time devoid of that [light], it would be possible; however, even recollection does not arise without such an experience, because its nature consists in the non-forgetting of an experienced object.
And there is no experience of the prior time, since that very experience itself is devoid of illumination.

Because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśātmakatva*), that very thing is indeed light; how then could there have been an absence of it even previously? And thus, because it is established as primordial due to being manifest at all times, its establishment does not depend upon the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And by the principle that "the light itself is the illuminator, the subject (*pramātṛ*)," [it is so].
It is rightly said that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, is the nature of the supreme subject: "And the supreme reality of the object of knowledge is Śiva, whose essence is light. (54)

Not only are the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) of no use for the establishment of this [Reality], but on the contrary, their own establishment is dependent upon it— thus he says: "Even those means of valid cognition which extend the life-force of objects..."
Even for those, the supreme life-principle is that very same Supreme Lord.

In this regard, among entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth, there is no distinction whatsoever—either between themselves or from one another—in their own essential nature independent of manifestation. For within its own self, blue is not "blue" [in relation to something else], nor is yellow "yellow. Indeed, if it were the case that blue or yellow [existed] within its own self...

It might be yellow or blue; why then would that not result in a contradiction? If you argue that "just as something appears, so it must be established within itself," and thus blue is not yellow, nor is yellow blue—then, in that case, there would be no distinction among these things within themselves.

Someone might say: "But it is manifest"—thus, manifestation (*prakāśa*) alone would be their form, which, because it is the basis for the establishment of each respective determined nature, would extend their very life-force, by means of which [distinctions] such as "this is blue" and "this is yellow" are established. And that [manifestation], through the coloring (*uparāga*) of blue and so forth...

Only by assuming a fixed form could it be designated by the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it has no requirement for anything else regarding its own self-establishment, because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), and because luminosity illuminates both itself and others. Nevertheless, even such luminosity [requires] the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Otherwise, there would be no basis for establishing the luminous nature of either an object or the self;

for luminosity alone could not establish itself and others, as in that case even blue would be so established simply by being "blue. Therefore, the establishment of the luminosity of both self and other [is required].
For him as well, one must admit a light whose essence is the reflective awareness of "I," which constitutes his very life, by means of which everything is established. As it has been said:
"The repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed to be the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva)."
Thus it has been said: "And that very Supreme Lord Śiva is of the nature of supreme illumination;
he alone is the supreme life-principle (jīva) even for those [others]. (55)

Since this is established in such a manner, not only is the proving means of knowledge (sādhaka-pramāṇa) ineffective, but even the subverting means of knowledge (bādhaka) is so; thus he says: "For even one whose nature is the habit of denying everything proceeds in this way."
The notion that "knowledge is for the sake of the self"—this does not appear so to me.

The "denial" (*apahnava*)—that is, the refutation—of all knowers, means of knowledge, and objects of knowledge; that which has this very "love for such denial" (*hevāka*) as its "nature" (*dharma*) or intrinsic character is the Buddhist. Among them, the Mādhyamikas are proponents of the non-existence of the triad [of knower, means, and object], while the Yogācāras are proponents of the non-existence of the knower and the object of knowledge.

The Vaibhāṣikas are proponents of the non-existence of a knower. Even for them, this [statement]—"for thus knowledge is for its own sake"—appears as "no" to me, the investigator, because [knowledge] has the nature of self-awareness; that is to say, it exists in the form of the cognition "it does not exist. By that [means]: [The text continues: ...therefore, since the very nature of cognition consists in the manifestation of objects through the power of the light of consciousness, even those who maintain that there is no external object are, by the very fact of their own assertion, established as having admitted the existence of an object within the sphere of cognition. For if they were to deny the existence of an object altogether, they could not even formulate the negation "there is no object," because a negation requires a substrate (pratiyogin) to be negated. Thus, even the proponents of non-existence are compelled to accept the existence of an object as a mental content. Consequently, the distinction between the existence and non-existence of external objects is merely a matter of convention; in reality, all things are established as existing within the domain of consciousness. Therefore, the entire universe is nothing other than the manifestation of the Light of Consciousness. This is the meaning.
In the refutation or even in the proof of the self and so forth,

the prover is necessarily implied at the prior limit and is established; for without a prover, there could be no such thing as the proving of objects, and he is self-established, of the nature of light, and the ultimate reality.
The Supreme Lord is indeed Śiva. 56.

And for this reason, even the postulation of a Buddhist means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there is entirely useless; thus he says: "In the denial or in the proof of things, such is the primary [nature of reality]. What, then, is the utility or the application of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein? (1.57)

Of "entities"—that is, those consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable—the "first" is such because it is established as the primordial [reality], namely, the nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*). "Therein" refers to the subject who is established from the beginning. Indeed, that which cognizes the object of cognition (*prameya*) is called the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the object of cognition...

It is established in dependence upon a distinct manifestation and is characterized by the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*). However, the subject (*pramātṛ*) does not possess such a nature whereby he would be determinable by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for he, being engaged in the determination of objects and so forth, is not distinct from the Light itself because his very nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

Nor is this [Self] something to be deliberated upon, because it consists of the reflective awareness of "I. If that [awareness] were itself an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then in that act of cognition there would have to be another cognizer (*pramātṛ*);
and if there were yet another [cognizer] for that one as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the means of knowledge does not apply here.

There is a certain justification for its manifestation [in the world]. As for the conventional usage in the teachings on meditation and so forth, such as "this Self, the cognizer, has shone forth once and for all," expressed through the objective case (*idantā*), that is not real, because it is not perceived there directly; rather, it is perceived therein only through the mediation of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*).
Let this suffice; for this will indeed be elaborated at every step.

However, the lack of utility regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has already been demonstrated immediately following [the previous point] due to its being established from the very beginning, and thus it is not elaborated upon again. || 57 ||
Not only is there reasoning here, but there is also scripture; thus he says:
"In the Kāmika, for that very reason, it is stated—free from discursive argumentation—that for that God of gods, no dependence upon another exists. (1.58)

Because it depends upon another, this [consciousness] is established as independent. "From that"—because there is an absence of both the validity and the utility of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein; for this reason, [the text] says "by discourse" (*vādena*), which refers to inference (*anumāna*). For this very reason, he says "of that," and so forth; "of another"—that is, of an external object.
"Of the means of valid cognition, etc.; therefore"—that is, for the reason characterized by independence from anything else. || 58 ||
Thus, because he is independent of anything else, just as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not his delimiters, so too are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); thus he says:
"For the independent and sovereign Lord, there is no sequence of place, time, or form. (1.59)
"He is not subject to necessity; he is the all-pervasive, eternal Śiva, the creator of the universe.

The reason is provided by way of the qualification "of the master"—that is, of the independent one. "In this case as well" refers to Śiva, whose nature is light and who is independent of anything else.

It has been stated that because [the Self] is afflicted by the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference regarding place, time, and form, it is impossible to impose limitations upon It; thus, It is said to be "not limited. For this very reason, he says that such a one is "all-pervasive, eternal, and the form of the universe. "All-pervasive" means being devoid of limitation by space. "Eternal" means—

Because it flows without being delimited by time such as the past and so forth; "having the form of the universe" means that it causes the manifestation of the manifold variety of forms, such as the conscious and the unconscious. ||59||
He elaborates on this very point:
"Because of its omnipresence, it is all-pervading; because it is an eternal state, it is devoid of beginning and end. (1.60)
Because he is the maker of all forms, he is the illuminator of the manifold variety of the conscious and the unconscious;
for this very reason, his possession of various forms is declared in the scriptures—thus he says: "Therefore, his multiformity is taught in the *Dīkṣottara* and other [texts]. (1.61)
He states that very point: "The world, the body, light, space, sound, and the mantra—divided into bindu, nāda, and so forth, Śiva is said to be sixfold. (1.62)

The term *bhuvana* refers to each respective world that is presided over [by a deity], which serves as the substratum for experience (*bhoga*). By the word *vigraha*, those possessing a body (*vigrahin*) are indicated through figurative usage (*upacāra*).
And although they possess various forms such as Rudras, Kṣetrajñas, and so forth, they are [referred to here] because of their capacity to bestow the respective supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

Rudra and the others are indeed the causes. Light (*jyotis*) is the *bindu*, for its nature as light is described in such passages as: "It has the form of a *kadamba* bud, resembling a shimmering star. Space (*kha*) is the void (*śūnya*), namely Śakti and Vyāpinī.

The characteristic of the *samanā* is that sound (*śabda*) is the essence of resonance (*nāda*), and the mantra consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. Its qualification is that it is "interpenetrated by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth.
As it has been said:
"The Bindu, the Nāda, as well as Vyoman, Mantra, Bhuvana, and Vigraha—the sixfold essence of Śiva is to be meditated upon by practitioners according to the distinction of their desired fruits.
Thus it is said. Furthermore—
The state beyond the mind (unmanā) is the supreme nature; its other [manifestation] is considered gross.
Again, there is the void (śūnya), the ethereal self (vyomātman), and after that, tactile contact (saṃsparśa).
"Sound, light, as well as mantras, the causes, and the worlds. And likewise:
"Through the divisions of the paths of space, form, the bindu, phonemes, and the worlds..."
"The piercing of the target (lakṣyabheda) is said to be sixfold... and so forth. || 62 ||
And in this regard:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is directed to that very place; he becomes a possessor of accomplishment..."

According to this principle, whoever has firm devotion toward that which he seeks attains it; thus it is said: "Whoever is firmly established in the nature of a particular state attains that very state.
Through the thorough knowledge of the [levels] beginning with space (vyoman), supreme liberation is attained; of this there is no doubt. (1.63)

The meaning is this: whichever practitioner is established in the state of identity with—that is, in the nature of—a particular world or other such object, he attains the corresponding accomplishment, which is determined by the specific form of that very world or object.
As it has been said:
"Whoever meditates upon the Bhuvana, which has the single form that will be described hereafter,
attains the state of a Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa)..."— beginning thus:
Whoever constantly meditates upon the form of the causes, beginning with Brahmā,
shall attain identity with that which possesses the characteristics previously described.
Through mantras, the accomplishment of mantra arises from recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;
it is accomplished here through meditation on the previously described forms—of this there is no doubt.
Through meditation on the light, the lord of yogis shall attain perfection in yoga;
he becomes one with that [light] and becomes the sovereign of yogis.
"And from the meditation on emptiness, one becomes empty-souled, pervasive, and all-pervading;
through the yoga of meditative absorption (*samanā-dhyāna*), the yogi attains omniscience.
Thus, because these six [powers] are also of the nature of Śiva—
"...having meditated upon Śiva, one becomes absorbed in Him.
Because of such statements, even when entering into each [element] individually by means of being solely composed of Śiva, there occurs the attainment of a nature whose essence is Śiva—thus he says:
"From the thorough knowledge of the words 'space' and so forth," etc. Of these, space and the others...

Of the six types of sound, the supreme sound is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); from that consciousness— which is experience (*anubhava*)— because it consists of that [reflective awareness], liberation, characterized by the attainment of identity with Śiva whose sole essence is reflective awareness, will undoubtedly occur.
This is the meaning of the sentence. However, if the reading is *vyomādiṣaṭka*, it should be explained as:

"from the specific, unconditioned knowledge of the group of six beginning with space (*vyoma*). Furthermore, the sequence of the worlds and so forth is not intended here; thus, the term "beginning with space" (*vyomādi*) is employed in this context. || 63 ||
Now, one might object: "If this [Lord] possesses the form of the entire universe (*viśvākṛti*), how is it that only his sixfold nature has been mentioned?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The fact that the Lord possesses the form of the entire universe is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of this very [sixfold nature]."
And when there is the ascent into the state of non-limitation and the dissolution of limitation for this [consciousness], || 1.64 ||

This is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), since by this alone the inclusion of the entire universe is established. This is not an illustration only for its having the form of this [universe], but also for other cases—as he says with the words "in the ascent of the undivided state," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the dissolution of limitations" (*avacchedalaye*)—[it refers to] the limitations (*avacchedānām*).
The meaning is: "in the dissolution of the worlds and so forth, which cause contraction, [and thus] in the state of transcending the universe.
The intention is that even while consisting of the universe, there is no falling away from its own essential nature.
Now, one might object: "In either case, since this is understood to have a determined nature, would it not simply be said to be limited?"

Anticipating this objection, it is said: "in the ascent of the undivided state. For even though this [consciousness] consists of the universe, because it transcends the universe, its growth occurs precisely within the state of being undivided; for the one independent consciousness alone manifests itself in such and such ways. || 64 ||
Now, one might ask: "How is it possible for a single entity to be both identical with the universe and transcendent of the universe at one and the same time?
To pacify this doubt, he corroborates this with scripture:
"And it is said in the Kāmika: 'The Lord has all forms and yet is formless.'"
By him, all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded, like a reflection in water or a mirror.
Just as a jar or similar object reflected within a mirror, although appearing as distinct from the mirror, is nonetheless not separate from it— otherwise,
the mirror and the jar would appear to each other with mutual distinctness— in the very same way, [objects appear] through the nature of Light (prakāśa).
Even by Śiva, this universe— consisting of the mobile and the immobile— is manifested by his own will as if it were something distinct from his own nature; yet, being pervaded,
it is embraced as not exceeding his own nature, since its very manifestation would otherwise be impossible.
For this very reason, although he consists of the universe (*viśvamayatva*), he transcends the universe; and although he transcends it, he consists of it.

Thus, in either case, there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore it has been said: "He is of all forms and yet formless. "Of all forms" means consisting of the universe; "formless" means transcending the universe—by way of repetition [of the two qualities].

And even within reality, He transcends it—thus it is said. Therefore, in this way, this one alone, the Supreme Lord whose nature is light, unfolds everywhere; thus, from the ultimate standpoint, there is only the non-duality of the Lord (Īśvarādvaya). ||65||

Now, since it is impossible for entities to have a manifestation separate from that [Light], let it be granted for now that the Lord is essentially light in relation to those entities, rather than existing as something distinct from them. As for the collection of attributes such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth that have been predicated of Him—

Anticipating the objection that— since the mutual distinction between the substrate (dharmin) and its attributes (dharmas), as well as among the attributes themselves, cannot be denied in relation to that [consciousness], how can this manifested difference be prevented so that the non-dualist position (*advayavāda*) that "the Lord is one alone" might be maintained— he says:
Furthermore, this property of his, such as omnipresence (*vibhutā*) and so forth, does not differ from one another;

nor is this omnipresence and so forth some property distinct from his essential nature (*svarūpa*) that serves to enhance it, but rather it is his very nature itself. For omnipresence is said to be pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and that [pervasiveness] exists in relation to what is other than itself.

Pervasion could only occur if there were something to be pervaded; however, since nothing such as space and so forth can exist in dependence upon supreme light, what indeed would it pervade? Furthermore, eternality is not its attribute, because that [eternality] consists in a nature persisting through the three times, whereas this [supreme light] is not delimited by time. It is with this very intention that [it is said]:

It has been stated that "this Self shines forth once and for all," and so on. Likewise, it possesses the form of the entire universe (*viśvākṛtitva*). For there exists nothing called the "universe" apart from this [Self] such that it could possess the form of that [universe]. And thus, since these [entities] cannot in any way be distinct from the Supreme Light, their mutual distinction as well—

It has been stated that "it does not exist" and "it is not differentiated from one another. Now, if this is so, how is it that these distinctions of attributes have been stated, such as "it is all-pervasive, eternal, and universal in form"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This single attribute of his exists by encompassing everything. (1.66)
Therefore, the direct injunction is that [the Lord] is endowed with the power of absolute freedom (*svatantrya-śakti*) alone.

Indeed, He possesses this one single inherent attribute called the "self-reflective awareness" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*), which encompasses the entire collection of attributes such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth. The meaning here is as follows: for He...

The name "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) refers to the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*), which, in its illumination of itself or another, does not depend on anything else. For this very reason, it possesses the nature of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), which is the capacity to bring forth thousands of appearances of various places, times, and so forth; by means of which...
Although the class of subjects, though manifested by its own [light], is contracted, it may, from its own perspective,
employ such designations as "pervasiveness" and "eternality"; yet, in reality, it possesses none other than the power of absolute freedom known as the reflective awareness of "I," by means of which—
"This sovereignty is the primary [attribute]; that is the supreme lordship of the Supreme Self. (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 1.5.13).
Thus it has been stated. For this very reason, he says: "By that," and so forth. || 66 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated everywhere that he possesses an infinite number of powers, such as will and so forth, how can it be said here that he is joined with only a single power called sovereignty? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even his possession of many powers is simply his inseparability from that very [sovereign] power. (1.67)

For it is the very power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) that is designated as manifold due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as the objects of desire; thus, its possession of infinite powers consists precisely in its union with that [power of freedom]. As it has been said:
"That power which is declared to be the inherent (*samavāyinī*) power of the Creator of the universe..."
O Goddess, that desire of his, when he wishes to create, becomes the power of will (icchā-tattva).
"Listen to how even that which is one attains multiplicity," beginning thus,
[the text continues]: "In this way, although she is of two forms, she again reaches infinity through her divisions."
"By the power of the limiting condition of the object, the Sovereign Lady becomes [manifold], like a wish-fulfilling gem. || 67 ||

One might object: "Even so, the doctrine of the non-duality of God has not been fully established, since there is still the mention of an autonomous power (svātantrya-śakti) that is distinct from Him. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And what is called 'power' is the very nature of an entity as conceived by the cognizer (mātṛ)."
Therefore, even when the possessor of power is postulated, that very [power] is non-dual. (1.68)

Since the very nature of any existing entity whatsoever is conceptually designated by cognizers as "power" (*śakti*)— due to the attribution of difference based on the diversity of results— and this [power] is not in reality some distinct entity, therefore, even when there is the conceptualization of power and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), [it remains so].
While [the world] is being created, that very omnipresent Lord consists of non-duality; there is no fragmentation of non-duality whatsoever.
As it has been said:
"Power is the essence of the categories of existence, whose distinctions are superimposed due to the difference in results."
Thus [ends the verse]. 68.

One might object: "Let it be so that there is no difference between power and the possessor of power; however, since powers themselves are mutually distinct, does not that same defect remain in its original state? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For, in each respective body of the Lord as conceived by the subject..."
What difference is there in reality, other than that between the fire's capacities to burn and to cook? (1.69)

Just as, due to the difference in results such as burning and cooking, the burning power and the cooking power of fire are conceptually distinguished as different, yet in reality they are unable to differentiate from one another because they possess the single nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*); for it is only a separately established entity that can differentiate another entity, not a power.

If there were no distinction other than the possession of power (*śaktimat*), then what could be distinguished from what? For it is simply the nature of fire itself that is conceived as being capable of burning and so forth. Likewise, even though the powers of the Supreme Lord are conceived as infinite, there is no actual difference [between them]; thus, it is not the case.
In some cases, there would be a contradiction of the doctrine of the non-duality of God. (69)
Now, one might object: "Even if conceived in this way, the distinction between powers certainly appears; so how can that be denied? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this [distinction] does not exist in the ultimate sense, for there is nothing other than manifestation."
For there is nothing whatsoever; even the distinction between the power and its possessor is not real.

There is nothing else whatsoever apart from manifestation; thus, even this difference, because it is manifest, is not in reality nothing at all, but rather is indeed ultimately real. Therefore, the meaning of the statement is that the difference between the powers and their possessor is also ultimately real. Such is the case with difference.

Since [the powers] have manifestation alone as their essential nature, there is no excess over that; thus, there is no injury to the doctrine of non-duality (advayavāda), nor is there any denial of worldly transaction (vyavahāra) which exists through the distinction between the powers and their possessor—therefore, everything is well-established. || 70 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "It has been stated that the Supreme Lord possesses only one power called sovereignty (*svātantrya*); are then will (*icchā*) and the others merely its manifestations, or are they independent, distinct powers?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

For that which, through identity with the reality, generates an intensification of its own power—that too is indeed the Goddess; thus, even while appearing as something else, she is of a different nature. (1.71)

For that which is called the "variety of internal powers" belonging to an entity such as fire— the intensification (*udreka*) of that power characterized by capacity, which consists solely of undifferentiated action and serves as the ground for the application of the designation "its own power"— is what is meant.

The surging forth [of the object] as the essence of another power, consisting of specific forms such as burning, cooking, and so on, is its generator—that is, its illuminator. And that too, because of identity—due to being of one nature with its own such power—is none other than its own power in the form described above; such is the connection.
For the meaning is this: fire, being capable, would indeed perform the entire range of effects such as burning;

in the same way, although the Power of the Supreme Lord appears in the form of subordinate powers such as Will and the rest, that Goddess, even when manifesting those various distinctions, possesses a nature non-different from the Supreme Light.

It is rightly said that this [reality] is indeed called "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*), characterized by a radiant manifestation: "This single attribute of His exists by encompassing everything. Thus it is established that His single power, called sovereignty, shines forth through the various forms of differentiation created in such and such ways. || 71 ||
It is not only His power that appears as such through an imagined differentiation, but He Himself as well—
thus he says:
"And Śiva, whose glory is undiminished, likewise appears as if created."
In the mirror of the subject who is one's own self-awareness, [this occurs] through freedom in acts such as creative contemplation (bhāvanā). || 1.72 ||

And Śiva is that subject who is established in the intellect and so forth, having grasped a self-identity within them, characterized by his own contracted consciousness; he alone, due to his transparency, is like a mirror capable of receiving reflections, [and this occurs] therein through the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*), instruction, and so on.

Through its own sovereignty, by means of an imagined differentiation such as being "manifested as such," it appears as if created and reduced to the status of an object of knowledge (*prameya*); yet even so, it does not actually become that way because its nature is exclusively that of the subject (*pramātṛ*), as it has been said: "its power is undiminished," meaning it has not abandoned its state as the knowing subject.
This is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"By virtue of its sovereignty, [the Self] is non-dual in nature; by virtue of its sovereignty, [it appears] in creative contemplations and the like."
"The Lord, having created [the world] through the volitions of Īśvara and others, would engage in worldly activity.
He concludes this very point:
"Therefore, by whichever aspect this [Reality] appears—even though it is partless—it is so [designated].
