And the body and so forth assume agency and subjectivity within themselves, while everything other than that assumes objectivity and knowability. For this very reason, they are designated as "insentient" (jaḍa) and "sentient" (ajaḍa); thus it is said:
"The self is both veiled and unveiled. Even so, its infinity arises from the diversity of its modes.
Thus he says: "insentient," and so forth. Regarding "manifoldness": first, that of the insentient is manifold through the distinctions of sound and so on;

even that [sound] is of many kinds through distinctions such as high and low pitch. Furthermore, although the non-insentient is infinite due to the distinctions between individual successions (*santāna*), there is a diversity among the three bonds (*bandha*) due to distinctions such as their relative intensity. [This state is] contracted.
For cognizing subjects, wandering about in accordance with their respective latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*),

recognize even their single self as having manifold forms and variety across various states— due to its being devoid of the mental states of merit, demerit, and so forth, and due to its being refined by those respective desires— whereas they perceive the insentient [world] otherwise.
And they experience the object as manifold, by virtue of its producing pleasure, pain, and so forth.
(Verses 134–135) Having raised the doubt as to what the cause of such diversity is, he says: "For what indeed could His state of absolute freedom not conceive?"
As it is said in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*: "He who knows [this] is called the Fully Awakened One. (1.136)
He corroborates this very point by way of its meaning with the words beginning with "tad uktam" (so it has been said).

"He who knows this manifold variety is *saṃbuddhaḥ*—the meaning is that he is one who has awakened perfectly (*samyagbuddhaḥ*). In the *Triśiraḥśāstra*, that is, in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*. For there [it is said]: 'Otherwise, however, one whose awakening is slight [is bound] by threads...'"
"Like a silkworm, mounted upon its own thread of impurity, it plays within the cage of the body.
Having begun thus—
And by the passage beginning with "The Perfectly Awakened One is to be known...
and so forth:
"Just as a dancer is made to whirl about through various forms and manifestations,"...
"Devoid of the existence of one's own intellect and excluded from desire and security"—thus much has been said at length. || 135 ||
Now, one might object: "Even though the body and so forth are considered the subject (the grāhaka), they are nonetheless merely objects of knowledge (jñeya) due to their insentience;
how then can such [an insentient thing] possess this kind of knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the state of being an object of knowledge is a property of consciousness; its shadow cannot obscure that [consciousness]. (1.136)

For knowability (*jñeyatva*) is indeed a property of cognition; for when one thinks "I know the object," there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to the object itself, but rather it is the cognition alone that possesses the nature of knowing that [object]. As it has been said here as well: "The knowability of the knowable is nothing other than cognition itself."

Thus, for this very reason, the reflection (*chāyā*) of those objects of knowledge—the body and so forth—which exist as such, cannot conceal or cover the consciousness (*cit*), because it is impossible for something to obscure itself by its own nature; whereby such knowledge would not arise. Therefore, even when there is the grasping of the self in the body and so forth, [the true nature] of the self is not [obscured].
There is no loss whatsoever of its nature as consciousness. As it is said in that very same work:
"The nature of the object of knowledge is consciousness; its reflection cannot conceal it. (136)
Therefore, he says:
"Thus, within the non-inert portion designated as the *pudgala*, atoms, and so forth, a manifold variety resides in the aspect of the unobstructed portion. (1.137)

"By that" means by the cause of the non-veiling of consciousness (*cidanācchādana*). "Unobscured" means in the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness—this is the meaning. For although the body and so forth possess the nature of consciousness, their impurity may still occur because they initially manifest as objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). || 137 ||
Now, one might object: "Since differentiation is impossible within consciousness, how can its manifold variety be logically consistent?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:
"Although no real differentiation exists within the eternal nature of consciousness,"
Nevertheless, it is perceived through the gradations of the diminution of its veils. (1.138)
Regarding "obscuration"—that is, the *āṇava* impurity—the "diminution" is its complete exhaustion;

its "gradation" is the intensity consisting of the mild, medium, and intense degrees. It is "perceived through that," meaning it is not possible [to perceive it] directly—this is the sense. For this very reason, it was previously described as "real."
The qualification has been employed. || 138 ||
Furthermore, what is that gradation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"We shall explain that in detail in the *Śaktipātavinirṇaya*; having concluded the discussion on the supreme state, it will be examined in the context of the gross. (1.139)
"We shall explain"— as he will state: "In the manifestation of gradation, those [levels] which are intense, moderate, and weak,
each of these are established as threefold according to the descent of power (śaktipāta)."
"Thus, in many ways, it will be discussed"—the meaning is that it will be characterized (*lakṣyate*) and examined (*parīkṣyate*).
For here, indeed, there would be a mere enumeration (*uddeśa*) of the entire collection of objects of knowledge (*prameyajāta*) that is about to be spoken; this is the intention.
As he will say:
"In the section on the shattering of consciousness, there is a sequential enumeration of everything.
This has not been shown by us word-for-word for fear of excessive length; therefore, it should be understood by oneself. ||139||
Thus, in accordance with the degree of the diminution of impurity, the nature of the Lord also manifests to individual selves; so he says:
"Therefore, the All-pervasive One manifests Himself toward a certain perceiver."
One's own nature is indeed complete, [yet it appears] through a certain sequence of parts and sub-parts.

"Something"—namely, the gradation of the intensity of the obscuration (*āvṛti*) through its sharpness; "by way of parts and sub-parts"—because of the predominance of the gradations of the intensity of the obscuration, such as being dull and so forth. || 140 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is meant by the fullness and the non-fullness of the form of the Supreme Lord?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For that which is the manifestation of one's own essential nature as the single being of all existents..."
That [knowledge] regarding atoms is the supreme knowledge; other than that, there is much inferior knowledge.

That which is the single being of all entities— such as blue, pleasure, and so forth— which, because its manifestation would otherwise be impossible, is characterized as supreme luminosity and constitutes primary existence; the unfolding of that very form of one's own self through non-conceptual activity.
Direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is precisely that supreme, perfect, and supreme-lordly (*pārameśvara*) knowledge of the atoms (*aṇu*s).
From such perfect knowledge, other forms of knowledge—consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as that of power (*śakti*) and so forth—are inferior;
they are imperfect because they lack the manifestation of the true nature of consciousness, according to the many modes that will be explained hereafter.
The meaning is "in many ways. || 141 ||
He demonstrates that very multiplicity of modes:
"And that [consciousness], manifesting both directly through the means and also through the means to those means, is differentiated here by various artistic modulations. (142)

"Regarding the word *tat*—it refers to either supreme or non-supreme knowledge. "By means of the direct method" (*sākṣādupāyena*) refers to the Śāmbhava [means]. For that alone is the immediate cause for the attainment of supreme knowledge; and when that very [means] has reached its ultimate limit, it is called the *anupāya* (the "no-method"). Therefore, *anupāya* does not merely signify the negation of a method."

Thus it will be stated. The means (*upāya*) for that Śāmbhava [state] is the Śākta; from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it follows that its means is also the Āṇava. "It is differentiated"—the meaning is that it undergoes a figurative differentiation. (142) Not only is it thus, but there is yet another cause for this variety; he says:

Even there, a great variety of distinctions arises due to being mediated or unmediated by the doors of self and other, and due to being total or partial, as well as through intervention or lack thereof. (1.143)

By its own [nature], as follows: from the Śāmbhava [state] to the Śāmbhava; therefore, by means of the door characterized by both self and other, that which is at the door is accompanied by a means (*sopāya*). "In every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*) means by its full nature; "partially" (*aṃśaśaḥ*) means by an incomplete nature.
"Obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*) is due to the absence of being a direct means (*sākṣād-upāyatva*). Thus, first—

Thus, the means (upāya) is threefold, according to the division into Śāmbhava and the others; and since each of these is twofold by way of the relationship between the door and that which is entered through the door, there are six. Furthermore, since each of those is twofold by way of being complete or incomplete, there are twelve. And since each of those is twofold by way of being mediated or unmediated—
There are twenty-four [types]. Furthermore, there is intervention by many heterogeneous factors; thus, the varieties are numerous. || 143 ||
Now, since knowledge has been proposed as the goal (*upeya*), there must be some means (*upāya*) to attain it;

yet that means cannot be knowledge itself, because it is the goal, nor can it be ignorance, because ignorance is not a means to that end. What, then, is the nature of this means? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which is the means for attaining knowledge is not called ignorance;
rather, it is considered to be a subtle form of knowledge itself, yet of a higher order consisting of will. (1.144)
However, the connection is as follows: that [knowledge] is considered subtle, being distinct from conceptual, gross, Śākta, and other forms of knowledge.
For this very reason, it is "supreme"—meaning it is Śāmbhava. For this same reason, it is said to be "consisting of will."
The intended meaning is that the Śākta and Āṇava [powers] indeed consist of knowledge and action. || 144 ||
Now, one might object: "Even so, how can the relationship of means and end (upāyopeyabhāva) be consistent for that which is one and the same? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the relationship of means and end is merely the repose of knowledge in its grossness.
And this very thing is the power of action (kriyāśakti), the sole cause of both bondage and liberation. (1.145)

Coarseness (*sthaulya*) is the manifestation as a duality consisting of infinite objects of perception and perceivers, resulting from the submergence of one's own supreme subtle nature— which is a single mass of consciousness and bliss;
it is this that produces the delusion that "this is the goal" and "this is the means."

In reality, Śiva alone, whose nature is self-luminous, is the goal; and He shines forth from every side, for there is no occasion whatsoever where He is absent. Therefore, there is no purpose here for means (upāyas), since their function consists in making known what was previously unknown. As it has been said:
"When the reality of Being is immediate and stands manifest everywhere, those by whom means (*upāya*) are elaborated certainly do not know You.
With this very intention, the description of the non-means (*anupāya*) will be undertaken. Now, if it is thus...

Anticipating the question, "How then does this worldly transaction (vyavahāra) attain growth? he says: "This very [power]," and so forth. Regarding "the power of action" (kriyāśakti): it is because she brings about the establishment of the various diversities of those [objects].
Therefore, the intention is that this is indeed the expansion of the Supreme Lord himself. For this very reason, it is such [an expansion].
When unknown, it is a binder; when known, however, it is a liberator. Thus it is said: "The sole cause of bondage and liberation.
As it has been stated:
"This power, whose nature is action, belongs to Śiva and resides within the bound soul (paśu)."
"Bonding [the breath], abiding on its own path, and being known, it brings about accomplishment. || 145 ||
One might object: "Even so, what exactly is considered the means (*upāya*) in this context? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, within the first [means], which is self-reflection—the singular abode of the non-conceptual—that which flashes forth manifest and directly is proclaimed as 'Will' (*icchā*). (1.146)

This being so, in that [first moment]— which consists of the initial cognition of bare perception (*ālocana-jñāna*), and for that very reason arises as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), and for that very reason, because there is no emergence of a distinct object to be reflected upon— the manifest reality flashes forth within self-reflection in the form of pure radiance (*sphurattā-mātra*), which, by virtue of its nature as direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), is what truly shines.

That vibration is directly proclaimed as that which is called "Will" (icchā), because it is independent of any other means; thus, the means known as Śāmbhava is said to be the expansion of the power of Will in its unmediated form—this is the meaning. || 146 ||
To clarify this very point by means of an illustrative teaching, he says:
"Just as for those with wide-open eyes, an object appears clearly even without [conscious] synthesis, so too does the nature of Śiva manifest to some. (1.147)
That reflective awareness which one attains through the repeated contemplation of the sequence of determining the various portions of conceptual construction,
the wise know that to be the means of knowledge (jñānopāya).

In the same way, although the conceptualization of the Self as "all this is indeed the Self" implies two parts— the Self and the non-Self— there is a repeated determination consisting of these parts preceded by the negation of the counter-correlate; the sequential contemplation (*carcana*) of that [determination] is, as appropriate, [the practice].

Refinement occurs through the cultivation of clarity and other such qualities; therefore, they know that means of knowledge to be that which, when being conceptualized, attains an undivided realization of its own essential nature— such as the cognition "this is exactly thus"— thereby reaching the state of direct perception.
The meaning is: "They should know the Śākta means, which consists of the expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

The word *tu* (but/however) serves to distinguish this from what preceded. For it has been stated here that conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) itself gradually attains the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*). In that case, however, the direct realization occurs precisely through non-conceptuality.
Form; and for this very reason, there exists the relationship of door and doorkeeper between these two. || 147-148 ||
However, that which establishes external objects constructed by conceptualization is taught as having action as its means; there is no difference here regarding the attainment of liberation.
Thus, that very nature of the Self is taught as having action as its means;
it is declared in all the scriptures to be attainable through the individual means (*āṇavopāya*), which consists of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
For by those conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) consisting of the manifestation of duality, [the Self] is fashioned by its own artifice.
The means for that [realization] is that object—such as the utterance (*uccāra*) and so forth—which is imagined, external, and delimited;
the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. For in the Śākta [tradition], the object is indeed only the mental construct (*vikalpa*), whereas here it is also external;
therefore, the utterance and so forth do not exist there. [Objection: But surely, from a difference in the means (*upāya*), there would also be a difference in the goal (*upeya*)?

Anticipating this objection, it was stated: "There is no division here pertaining to liberation. For liberation is the manifestation of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and that occurs through all [means] by way of the relationship between the door and the doorkeeper; such is the intended meaning. [Objection:
But it was generally asserted that knowledge alone is the means (*upāya*); how then is it so in the *āṇava* [means]?
Anticipating the question, "How is it that action is said to be the means? he says:
"Since there is no such thing as action other than knowledge itself, for that [knowledge] is indeed such;
having reached the culmination of yoga through its established usage, so it is stated in the venerable Gamaśāsana. (1.150)

"Other" means other than knowledge; for that very knowledge, through its firm rooting and growth, is the end and supreme pinnacle of yoga. Having attained that reality, it is everywhere designated as "action"—this is the meaning. But what is the proof for this?
Anticipating this objection, it was stated:
"In the Śrīgamaśāsana. The meaning is that [this] is what was said; "thus" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 150 ||

He recites the very text from that [work]: "Yoga is not one thing and action another; for that intellect which is ascended upon reality, when it brings to rest the latent impressions of one's own mind, is designated as 'action'. (1.151)
Thus [ends the section]. || 151 ||
And he explains this himself:
"The latent impressions (vāsanās) in one's own mind are born from karma, impurity (mala), and māyā;
that cognition which is the very nature of consciousness (saṃvit-svabhāvikā) exists for the purpose of their pacification. (1.152)

That very activity, which presides over the principles (tattvas) that constitute the body and those situated externally, becomes yoga when it effects the dissolution of those principles into consciousness. (1.153)
By the word "ṅimittam," the locative case is explained. By the phrase "saṃvitsvabhāvikā," it is stated that the word *mati* has the meaning of "knowledge.
That *mati*—
By means of the *praṇava*, one should sequentially place all those causes for the arising of the body, numbering thirty-one, O Goddess of Gods; thus,
by such statements as these, one rests upon the common *tattvas* through the initiation into the *tattvas* (*tattvadīkṣā*) and other rites.

Action (*kriyā*) would exist because it brings about the pacification of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of one's own mind; likewise, according to the statement, "They desire yoga to be the oneness of one thing with another thing," yoga would be the conjunction of the principles (*tattva*) within consciousness. Thus, there is no excess of knowledge (*jñāna*) over these two.
Thus it has been rightly said: "Yoga is not one thing and action another. (152–153)
Now, one might ask: "How can knowledge itself be an action? He establishes this by means of an illustration:
"Even in the world, that which is indeed the internal vibration [of the thought] 'I am going'..."
That activity of motion enters into the body, the place, and the senses as well. (1.154)

The consciousness that manifests within the inner self as the vibration "I am going"—a vibration consisting of the nature of being an agent—is itself the act of going when it enters the body and so forth; by manifesting a state of involuntary immersion, it brings about its own identity [with the body]. Thus, it is rightly said: "For knowledge itself is indeed that [act] in such a manner."
For when the flash of awareness "I am going" arises in the goer,
the accomplishment of the act of going occurs through the immersion of the body, feet, and so forth, which constitute the agent, the instrument, and the object. || 154 ||
He concludes that very point:
"Therefore, even that which is called action is indeed nothing but knowledge; consequently, it is knowledge alone that leads to liberation, and this has been rightly declared. (1.155)
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thence): because action (*kriyā*) consists of knowledge (*jñāna*).

By that [statement], namely, "Initiation alone liberates and leads one even to the supreme abode of Śiva," and so forth, it has been stated that action is also a cause of liberation (*apavarga*). And thus, what was said is correct:
"Knowledge is the sole cause of liberation. Thus he says:
"And this which has been stated is indeed logical. (155)

One might object: "Since it was previously stated in the passage beginning with 'nanu śvatantrātmātiriktastu' that there is no such thing as liberation (mokṣa) distinct from the knowledge of the Self, how can the relationship of cause and effect between these two—expressed by the statement 'jñānameva vimokṣāya'—be consistent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

For liberation is indeed nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature; and the true nature of the self is consciousness, and nothing else. As for those [states] which, however, [occur] therein— ||| 1.156 ||

Those powers, such as action and the rest, are not additional to the nature of consciousness; for it is impossible for them to be non-conscious in nature, and because no substratum [apart from consciousness] can be established. (1.157)

One might ask: "Is not liberation simply the manifestation of one's own essential nature (svarūpa)? To this he says: "The essential nature. By that, the essential nature of the self is consciousness (saṃvit-caitanya);
its manifestation is knowledge according to reality, and that alone is liberation—thus, what has been stated is indeed logical. He who...
Furthermore, this relationship of cause and effect that has been described is merely conceptual (*kālpinika*), not real (*tāttvika*);
as he will state:
"Since the relationship of cause and effect between knowledge and liberation has been declared..."
That is not the primary [meaning]... ||

"Thus. "Anything else" means that which is distinct from consciousness—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "If the Self has no form apart from consciousness, how can it possess other powers (śakti)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says "therein," etc.; the word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). (156–157)
Now, [one might object]:

"By such statements as 'The powers (śaktis) must be the attributes (dharmas) of the Lord (pati)...', [it follows that] the Lord is directly the substratum (dharmin) and the powers are his attributes (dharmas)."
Anticipating the objection that "this reason is unestablished because the subject has not been defined, as no definition has been provided," he says:
"For in the scripture of the Supreme Lord, [the process] is not like the view of the Kaṇādas."
Some [entity] is said to be the substratum of the powers (śaktis) which consist of the nature of attributes (dharmas). || 1-158 ||
Just as the followers of Kaṇāda,
having defined the self as the substratum (dharmin) through such statements as, "The self [is so called] because of its connection with selfhood," and so forth...
By stating, "Its qualities are intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction," and so forth,
they accepted a collection of distinct attributes inherent in that [self] which arise and pass away.

In this context, no relationship of attribute and substratum (*dharma-dharmin*) is asserted between power and its possessor. For consciousness alone, being independent, is designated as having the form of various powers by virtue of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, in reality, there is no difference whatsoever between power and its possessor, as was stated previously:
"For when the body of an entity is fully fashioned by the *mātṛkā* in this or that [particular form], what difference is there in reality? It is like the burning and cooking capacities of fire.

Now, one might object: "If here too, as in the systems of Kaṇāda and others, the relationship between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is being defined, then what would be the fault? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And therefore, if the powers such as vision, action, and will were likewise distinct..."
The statement "Śiva is one" arises as something entirely devoid of any real entity.

For if there were indeed a real difference between the power and its possessor according to the principle of the relationship between attribute and substrate, then [the following would not be possible]: "In this way, through various forms, both stationary and moving..."

"In play, the Lord Śiva alone is eternally diffused"— in such passages, the statement "Śiva alone" is a proposition asserting the non-duality of the Lord; yet, because there exist numerous entities consisting of powers (*śakti*) and their possessors (*śaktimān*), this [statement] is devoid of reality— that is, it lacks a literal referent.
It would mean that there is a refutation of the teaching of non-duality; such is the sense. || 159 ||

Now, one might raise this doubt: "If, in reality, Śiva alone exists as the single nature of consciousness, then how is this worldly transaction, consisting of the manifold powers such as consciousness and so forth, otherwise performed?
To pacify this doubt by way of a concluding summary, he says:
Therefore, this very nature of consciousness is its sovereignty;
even when analyzed in detail, it is fully established within its many powers. (1.160)
And since this has already been determined previously, no further effort is made here. As it has been said: "Even its possession of manifold powers is its inseparability from that very power.
In this context, since there is in reality no causal relationship between knowledge and liberation—
according to the principle that "causes do not necessarily possess their effects"—
it may be that for the knowers, even though the cause called "knowledge" exists, the effect consisting of liberation does not occur.
Should one not suspect that this *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) results in an undesirable conclusion? To this he says:
"Since liberation is the manifestation of the Self, such a [consequence] need not be suspected here;
for an effect does not necessarily follow from its cause, and thus even a knower of that [cause] is not liberated. (1.161)
The meaning is that for the knower (*jñānin*), liberation is indeed inevitable. And for this very reason:
"Among them, the knower, who is ever-disciplined and single-mindedly devoted, is distinguished;
for I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me."
Thus, likewise:
"The man of knowledge, however, is in my view none other than Myself," and so forth, is sung in the Gītā. || 161 ||

But surely, by such statements as, "Knowledge alone leads to liberation... and so forth, the causal relationship between knowledge and liberation has already been stated; so how is it that this [is not the case]?
What is the consequence? He says:
Since that which has been declared as the relationship of cause and effect between knowledge and liberation is not primary, it is certain that this consequence does not apply. (1.162)
And since this has already been determined, no further effort is made here. || 162 ||
Concluding this and introducing another point, he says:
"In this way, action, whose very nature is knowledge, carries a state of grossness within itself; therefore, let its manifold variety indeed be observed therein. (1.163)
"Having the nature of knowledge" means that action is inseparable from knowledge, as it has been said:
"Action is never devoid of knowledge.
"Coarseness" refers to its manifestation through the internal differentiation of the grasped and the grasper; by that [coarseness],...
"Thus"—by means of the reason that it brings about grossness. "Variegatedness"—due to the manifold diversity of the various distinctions between the grasped objects and so forth. || 163 ||
Therefore, he says:

"Because of the diversity of divisions and subdivisions among the various means within the means of action—which distinguish between what is internal and external—there is an infinity of intermediate [methods]. (1.164)

The objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) consist of [the internal processes of] utterance (*uccāra*) and so forth; the external [objects] consist of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala (*maṇḍala*), and so forth. For although utterance and the rest have entered the domain of the apprehended and are determined as being external, they are nonetheless not [external] because they do not fall within the range of the external senses such as the eyes, and because they are not common to other subjects (*pramātṛ*).

The external [objects]—namely, the sacrificial pits, mandalas, and so forth—are called "external" because they fall within the range of the external senses and because they are common [to all]; thus it has been said:
"of those who distinguish between the graspable and the external. Even though these possess such fixed distinctions, [it is of these very things that...]
The meaning is that due to internal divisions, and the multiplicity of distinctions and sub-distinctions, there is an incalculability—that is, a manifoldness of types.
To illustrate: in the first [category] of utterance (*uccāra*), there are five divisions based on the distinctions of *prāṇa* and so forth;
even therein, there are many sub-divisions such as *bindu*, *nāda*, and others. It is thus for those being uttered.
The infinity of mantras means their state of having innumerable divisions. || 164 ||

And thus, the fact that action is essentially knowledge— which was introduced with the words, "Since there is no such thing as action other than... and so forth— is established through both reasoning and scripture.
"Extinguished"—thus, there is only one means for the attainment of liberation, which is the nature of knowledge itself; therefore, there is no plurality of means.
For this very reason, there is also no difference whatsoever in liberation, which is the fruit thereof. Thus he says:
"And by this, that which some have suspected has been destroyed."
The wise maintain that due to the difference in means, there must also be a difference in liberation. (1-165)

The connection is: "which some wise ones have suspected. "Some wise ones" refers to the proponents of dualism (*bhedavādinaḥ*), for in their view, there is indeed a real distinction between cause and effect;
thus, from a difference in the cause, there would also be a difference in the effect. But here, however—

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "A portion of Brahman does not transcend its omniformity and is beyond conceptualization," consciousness alone is everything; so what indeed is the distinction between cause and effect?
Even if a distinction between cause and effect is merely conceptual, the means is accepted as being one and the same—the very nature of knowledge.
Since there is indeed no plurality of means, what kind of difference could there possibly be even in liberation, which is the fruit?
Now, one might object:

since it was stated in the passage beginning with "And that [attainment] is directly through the means... that there is a direct multiplicity of means, why is there not also a difference in the goal (upeya) due to that difference in the means?

Anticipating the objection, "What is the difference [between these]? he says: "Even though there is a difference in their causes, they are not distinct, because they consist in the destruction, the concealment, and the emergence of impurity and its power; this is like the occurrence of the destruction of a jar and so forth. (1.166)

Even where there exists a truly real relationship of cause and effect, although there may be a difference in the cause—such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth—there is no difference whatsoever in its result, namely the destruction of impurity (mala) and its power (śakti);
for even though initiation differs according to the categories of *kalā*, *tattva*, *bhuvana*, and so on, that [result] remains undifferentiated. And thus:

Even when there is a difference in the means—such as a hammer, a hand, a wall, or a pot—the destruction, concealment, and so forth of the jar remain entirely indistinct. Therefore, the rule that "a difference in cause necessarily entails a difference in effect" is not an absolute one. However, in cases where the relationship between the means and the end is merely conceptual, what [then]?

The meaning is that this is merely a matter of terminology. Thus, although the means (upāya) is threefold because it consists of will, knowledge, and action, it is established that there is no difference whatsoever in liberation (apavarga), which is the goal to be attained through them. || 166 ||
This is established not only through reasoning, but also through scripture; thus he says:
"Indeed, this threefold nature was taught by the Supreme Lord in the scripture named Śrīpūrva, in the determination of the states of immersion (samāveśa). (1.167)
He recites the very text found therein: "The immersion that arises for one who thinks of nothing at all, through being awakened by the Guru, is declared to be the Śāmbhava [immersion]. (1.168)
One who, contemplating an object with the mind alone, free from vocal utterance, attains a state of immersion—that is here designated as the Śākta. || 1.169 ||

That immersion which occurs through the performance of the utterances (uccāra), meditation (dhyāna), the visualization of colors (varṇa), and the arrangement of locations (sthāna) is called the perfect individual means (āṇava). || 1-170 ||

And in the alternative reading, this is the intended meaning: that through the relationship of means and end, or door and that which is entered, the primary resting place is in the Śāmbhava means alone. (167–170)
He explains that very point in sequence:
"For one who thinks of nothing" indicates the uselessness of conceptual construction;
and by means of that, the immediate absorption into the object of knowledge is described. (1.171)
"By that" means by the uselessness of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For when conceptual construction is employed, at that very moment—

according to the perspective expressed in such passages as, "He whose being consists of the object of knowledge is stable, full, and all-pervading"— there is the [realization] of the object of knowledge, that which must necessarily be known, namely the ultimate Self consisting of consciousness (*cidātman*).

There would be no attainment (*samāpatti*) of form; for conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), through the power of practice, by way of manifesting another conceptual thought similar to itself, and by means of a gradual process of generating increasingly superior conceptual thoughts characterized by the fading away of indistinctness and so forth, arrives at identity with non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpātmaka-saṃvit*).
As he will say, beginning with:
"One desiring to enter [the state beyond] should immediately perform the purification of conceptual thought," and so forth.
"Consciousness attains a stainless state whose very nature is free from conceptual construction.
For this very reason, there is a distinction between this [means] and the śāktopāya. || 171 ||
One might ask: "How could this be so simply by the uselessness of conceptual thought?
To show this doubt, he says: "How does that come about? He says: By the most venerable Guru."
By means of an awakening directed toward the object of knowledge, which is characterized by its sudden and fully developed growth. || 1-172 ||

The prefix *prati* denotes facing toward (*ābhimukhya*), and this facing toward is dependent upon another entity; and here, by virtue of what is appropriate, that [other entity] is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—thus it was said, "facing toward the object of knowledge" (*jñeyābhimukha*). To explain its very supreme gravity, it was stated, "having immediately become fully developed," and so forth; by the word "immediately" (*drāk*), [this is indicated].
The absence of ascending through the sequence of conceptual constructions as previously described has been indicated. || 172 ||

One might object: "How can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two words which have different case endings? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The suffix *tasi* is explained as having the sense of the third case, or [it may be understood] through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇyataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the third case": the form *tasi* is used here with the elision of its *anubandha* (indicatory letter). "In the sense of the third case" means...
The suffix *tasi* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in any case-ending. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative view.

The meaning is: "from that [realization] which has been produced by the Guru through the method of non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, there is an immersion (*āveśa*) for one who is not independent, resulting from the submergence of one's own limited nature into that [universal] nature. (1-173)

The state of being that [divine] nature belongs to Śambhu, who is primordial and inseparable from His Power; whereas for the insentient intellect and so forth— which are dependent— and for the limited subject, their own specific,
contracted form undergoes immersion, that is, subordination, by relying upon that [divine nature].
The connection is as follows: that state of being of the same nature—identity—with another independent awakening is "immersion" (*āveśa*). As it has been said:
"The primacy belongs to agency and to awakening, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*)."
"In emptiness and so forth, when that quality [of consciousness] is present, knowledge arises characterized by absorption into that.

From where, then, has this come? He says: "From Śambhu. It does not, however, come from Śakti or the individual soul (aṇu). Regarding the word "from the First" (ādyāt): for from Him alone indeed is the origin of both Śakti and the individual soul.

This is the state of being. For this very reason, power (*śakti*) here is will (*icchā*), and not knowledge (*jñāna*) or action (*kriyā*), because those two will be described as falling within the interior of immersion (*samāveśa*). ||173||

In this context, since the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of its constituent words, he says the following in order to connect the meaning of the sentence after having connected the meanings of the words: "Therefore, the meaning of the sentence here should be understood as follows: that which is to be known unfolds by itself... (1.174).
Even without a conscious determination, it immediately eclipses the mother who is reflected in the mirror, displaying its own sovereign splendor. (1-175)
It abides according to the degree of the excellence of the heart's purity.

That which is to be known as "pure consciousness" (cinmātra) is the ultimate form; the "knower" (mātṛ)—because she is the cause of the production of the entire collection of instruments—is the intellect (buddhi), and that very [intellect] is...
Because it is capable of receiving the reflection of consciousness, the mirror—

therein subjugating the limited subject who has grasped a sense of self through that reflection— renders the identification with the self in the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties secondary. Thus, by way of degrees of intensity...
Fashioning a manifestation that is not shared by others and in which the nature of awakening is predominant,
it is— by virtue of the reasoning just stated and because it is independent of anything else— suddenly [realized] without the ascent of conceptual construction;
for this reason, it is declared to be the essence, the Heart of the Supreme Lord.

Because of such statements as these, "the heart" is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Its "purity" is its unfading state due to not being directed toward anything else. Its "excess" is its supreme limit (*parākāṣṭhā*).
In that state, it "remains unfolding by itself," meaning it shines forth through its own self-luminosity—this is the meaning. (174–175)

Now, an objection may be raised: surely the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is twofold by nature, consisting of both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*). Since there is an immersion (*āveśa*) even of the insentient, such as blue and so forth, into consciousness (*saṃvit*), how can it be said that "immersion is of the very nature of awareness (*bodha*) alone"?
To this, he says:
The object of knowledge is twofold: pure consciousness and the insentient; and the former is further considered to be imagined.
The other [aspect], however, is likewise real; such is its division:
that which is an immersion into the insentient has the form of a reflection. (1.177)
"Penetration by consciousness is indeed identity, and nothing else.

Anticipating the objection—"But how can that which is self-luminous consciousness be made manifest by another, namely, be an object of knowledge?"—it is said: "And the first is imagined. Here, the particle *ca* (*and*) indicates the objection.

For the Supreme Lord alone, by virtue of His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), even while not abandoning His nature as the Knower, presents Himself as an object of knowledge through such reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) as "Śiva alone is to be known as the agent of all actions" in the context of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and instruction; He does so by internalizing the cognition of "I" (*ahaṃpratīti*) and then manifesting [Himself] as an object of knowledge. This very [point is as follows]:

Indeed, supreme sovereignty is that which, while being its own self-nature as the knower alone, manifests itself as the object of knowledge. For this very reason, it is said to be "imagined" and devoid of objective reality. "The other" refers to insentient things such as blue and so forth. "In that manner" means by way of being an object of knowledge. In that context, regarding [expressions] such as "the cognition of blue," [it is the] consciousness...
The meaning of *samāveśa* (immersion) is merely a reflection—according to the analogy of a mirror and a face—by means of blue and so forth, and not identity;

for if that were the case, since blue and the rest would have become one with the cognition, only the cognition itself would remain, and thus the very distinction of the reflected image would not exist. This applies to the contracted consciousness (*saṃkucitāyāś citaḥ*).

Furthermore, because that [consciousness] alone exists in reality, its identity with the uncontracted consciousness is precisely what constitutes immersion (*samāveśa*). Thus, it is rightly said that immersion is the state of the dependent being the very nature of the other. (176–177)
He concludes that very point:
"Therefore, non-conceptual consciousness is independent of cultivation and the like. (1.178)
The state of having attained identity with Śiva is here the Śāmbhava immersion; it is consciousness that has [previously] assumed a contracted form. (178)

Now, one might object: "Let there be no dependence on conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) regarding this initial arising; for if that were the case, there would be no distinction between this [means] and the *śāktopāya*. But what of subsequent conceptual thoughts? Are they required here or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Furthermore, by his grace, the definitive conclusions regarding future events will subsequently arise here.
Let them be attained as having reached identity [with it], but they do not possess the status of being means (*upāyatā*).

By the word "that" (*tat*), there is a reference to non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpaka-parāmarśa*). Since the realization of the nature of Śiva has been accomplished by such non-conceptual consciousness, it is impossible to perform what has already been done.
He states that the conceptual constructions (vikalpa) arising subsequent to that have no efficacy therein: "but they do not possess the status of being means (upāya). || 179 ||

For this very reason, those who claim that the validity of non-conceptual [cognition] depends upon conceptual [cognition] are refuted; thus he says: "One who asserts that non-conceptual [cognition] is a means of valid knowledge in dependence upon conceptual [cognition]... (1.180).
This has already been answered: for that which is established is indeed apprehended by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have as its object an entity not yet cognized. As they say:
"A means of valid cognition has as its object an entity not yet cognized, or it is the illumination of an unknown object."

Thus, since the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows immediately after it determines only that object already grasped by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), it lacks validity in itself because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhakatva*).
How, then, could it serve as the cause for the validity of another [cognition]? Therefore, he says: "For [the object] is established..."

"It is followed by conceptual construction" (vikalpenānugamyate). "Established" (siddham) means understood (adhigatam). "Followed" (anugamyate) means followed after (anu paścāt), that is, understood—this is the meaning. ||180||
Now, one might object: "Granted that conceptual construction (vikalpa) may indeed proceed with respect to an object already grasped;
however, since this [conceptual construction] consists essentially in a subsequent determination (adhyavasāya), its status as a grasper is not tenable.
Therefore, how could there be for it the cognition 'I grasp what has been grasped'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For the manifestation of the certainty "it has been grasped" is perfectly clear. (1.181)
However, one realizes "I am grasping" through the power of non-conceptual unity.

For the manifestation that "it has been grasped" arises logically from the existence of conceptualization, since this [conceptualization] operates only upon an object already grasped; yet, that which one realizes as "I am grasping"—that [is non-conceptual].

It is rightly said—namely, that "that which has been grasped by conceptual thought is grasped"—by virtue of relying on the identity with non-conceptual [awareness] through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object, and so forth. || 181 ||

Now, one might object: "Knowledge is indeed informative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*); therefore, there may be the cognition (*jñapti*) of an object, but not its actual establishment (*siddhi*). How then can it be said that 'the established is followed by conceptual construction'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the non-conceptual self-awareness, that which is the very radiance of the object itself.
That accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is devoid of dependence upon a real entity (*vastu*).

For in the doctrine of manifestation (*ābhāsavāda*), it has been stated that accomplishment is simply the state of appearing; indeed, the accomplishment of a real entity is its very state of vibrating manifestation (*sphurattā*).
Now, one might object: even for conceptual constructions, there exists a state of manifest form because they are non-conceptual with respect to themselves.

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why should the establishment of the object not follow from that [conceptualization] as well? he says: "Not from conceptualization. According to the principle that "every conceptualization is memory," the very nature of conceptualizations is indeed memory; and that [memory] operates only with respect to what was previously experienced and is no longer present.

Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are independent of real objects; for even though there is a joining together of things fashioned by the knower (*kṣetrajña*) in the case of independent conceptual constructions and the like, nevertheless those objects are produced solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous experience, as stated in the phrase "devoid of dependence on an object. And for whatever [construction], there is dependence on something else.
The sense is: since that [object] does not exist, how could it serve as the cause for its establishment? || 182 ||

If conceptualization (vikalpa) operates only upon an object already established by non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka) and does not produce anything additional, then why is it required in some cases? To this he says:
"This [conceptualization] is merely the resting place for consciousness, whether in its state of purity or otherwise. (1.183)
Regarding the independence from conceptualization and dependence upon it within its own nature:
having thus set aside the dependence on conceptualization in the case of consciousness during worldly transaction and so forth— which is established by all disputants—
he provides an example to clarify its very independence from conceptualization:
Even at midnight, one who possesses knowledge of jewels [can recognize] those displayed during a flash of lightning.
A jeweler indeed discerns the various specific qualities of even a great many gems;
for even when the light is brief and limited, he perceives the exceedingly subtle mutual distinctions among many gems solely through the excellence of his experience, even without formal analysis.
He knows that by which there may be discernment such as: "this is small," "this is large," and "this is a jewel even greater than that. || 184 ||

Furthermore, what is the cause for this excellence of experience, by which the establishment of the object occurs even without dependence on conceptual construction? To this he says: "This purity of consciousness arises either from [innate] nature or through the force of prior practice. (185)
That [the descent occurs] by the will of the Lord who is not bound by constraints will be discussed [later].
That "prior practice" refers to that of a previous birth; for this very reason, it will be discussed in the thirteenth chapter and elsewhere.
Not only does this immersion (*āveśa*) possess a threefold nature, but it also possesses various intermediate modes.
Thus he says:
"And this fifty-fold nature of this immersion has been described. (1.186)
"Because of the intention to clearly explain the distinctions residing within these thirty-six principles, they have been described"—thus it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*. As it is said there:
"Indeed, the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the power of Rudra is discussed as being fivefold."
O fair-faced one, [this occurs] due to the distinction between the Bhūta, Tattva, Ātman, Mantra, Īśa, and Śakti [levels].
In this context, that which is designated as the "elements" (bhūta) is fivefold; likewise, the other is thirtyfold.
That which is called the "self" (ātman) is said to be threefold, while that designated as "mantra" is tenfold.
"Even that which is designated as *śakti* should be understood as twofold from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
This immersion (*samāveśa*) is proclaimed to be divided into fifty varieties.
And the reason for this is stated as "the principles" (*tattva*); for these thirty-six principles are situated therein.

The "contemplation" (*anusaṃdhāna*) refers to the clear differentiation, in the manner that will be described, of the thirty-six principles— including the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and the rest— which fall within [that system] and whose individual natures will be explained separately. || 186 ||
He defines that very division:
"That triad consisting of the individual soul (puruṣa), knowledge (vidyā), and power (śakti) which exists within these principles (tattvas)... (1.187).

Since there are divisions numbering four oceans, eight, and three fires (483) respectively, the word "distinct from that" (*tadbhinnam*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Therefore, in that regard, the Person (*pumān*)—as it is said:
"This Self is indeed fourfold."
By such statements, [the universe] is divided by the four oceans— characterized as the Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānākala, and Śuddha—
and likewise by the Vidyās and Kāṣṭhās, namely the phonemes (varṇa), points (bindu), half-moons (ardhacandra), and so forth.

The Śakti is divided into ten distinctions consisting of Nirodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā; likewise, it is divided by the three fires—the three distinctions consisting of Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā). || 187 ||
Now, one might ask: "Why have these three principles been specified separately? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because that which is designated as the Person (puṃs), Knowledge (vidyā), and Power (śakti) is all-pervasive. (1.188)
Therefore, this [category] is indeed enumerated as distinct from the non-pervasive;

"from the non-pervasive" means from the other pervasive principles (*tattva*). For [the range] ending with Māyā belongs to the *ātmatattva*, that ending with Sadāśiva belongs to the *vidyātattva*, and that ending with Śiva [belongs to the *śivatattva*].
This is the pervasion of the state of Śakti. As it has been said:
"Indeed, she is the successive pervader of Māyā, Sadāśiva, and ending with Śiva. (188)
This [reality] is not only distinct from other principles, but even from one another; thus he says:
"But that [reality] is also mutually [distinct] by virtue of being impure, being purified, and being pure. (189)

The individual soul (puruṣa) is impure because it consists of duality; limited knowledge (vidyā) is being purified because it consists of both duality and non-duality; and power (śakti) is pure because it consists of non-duality. || 189 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so, what is the reason for the separate mention of the elements?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The elements are established by direct perception, whereas [the rest] are inferable from the evidence of their effects."
For this very reason, it is designated as distinct from the category of reality (tattva). || 1.190 ||

The elements (*bhūta*) are established by direct perception; this is precisely the reason for their inclusion as distinct from the other principles (*tattva*). For those [other principles] are indeed only inferable through inference. Thus he says: "from the group of principles which are inferable through the effect as a logical mark" (*kāryahetvanumeyataḥ tattvavargāt*). And so, in this context, the elements—

The inference is as follows: [the elements] are preceded by causes because, while being insentient, they possess multiplicity, like jars and other such objects. And that which is their cause consists of these:
"And from the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise the gross elements..."
Because of such statements as "the tanmātras," their inferability follows from their effects, which are the gross elements (*bhūtas*).

In this same manner, by means of this very inference, the entire range of categories (*tattva*) ending with *māyā* is to be inferred. And since this will occur in the section on the path of the categories (*tattvādhvan*), no effort has been made here. For this very reason—namely, because it is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Now, one might object: "Let the fact that the elements (*bhūta*) are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be the reason for their distinction from the category of principles (*tattva*) that are inferable (*anumeya*); but how can that same reason apply even to their status as 'elements'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the element alone is the object of the existence of all cognition."
And the wise know that their abiding is here within this fourfold [system], which provides the necessary scope.

Indeed, that which exists as an object of cognition for all people, whether learned or unlearned, by virtue of its ultimate reality, is called "bhūta" (the real). For "bhūta" means "truth," and that is truth wherein there is never any disagreement whatsoever on the part of anyone. However, regarding the object of inference, this is not the case for the unlearned.

The meaning is this: there is no consensus at all; and even among the learned, despite their consensus, there are various mutual disagreements, so that even the possibility of its being unreal might arise.
The word "ca" (and) indicates a reason; and for this reason, everything here has its scope [in it], and because it provides space, it is called *ākāśa* (space), together with those [qualities].
Since that state of being an element (*bhūtatva*)— which pertains to the four ending with air and the pentad of elements beginning with earth—

is the domain of universal empirical perception, it is rightly said that "the designation 'element' [applies] for this very reason," meaning they know its established presence or abiding. Thus, possession (*āveśa*) is elemental (*bhautika*).

The immersion into the self (*ātmāveśa*) is fivefold, and [the immersion into the *tattvas*] is threefold. Although the single division of the self (*ātmabheda*), which consists of the *puruṣatattva*, must be established within the *tattvas*, otherwise the immersion into the *tattvas* would not be thirtyfold.
And [the immersion] into *vidyā* is by means of the previously mentioned general form belonging to *mantra*.

The immersion (*āveśa*) is tenfold. However, by virtue of its specific nature as consisting of the Mantra, Mantreśa, and Mantramaheśa, it is included within the category of *tattva*. Thus, having established one division of Śakti within the *tattvas*, her immersion is twofold; whereas Śiva is solely that which causes immersion (*samāveśya*).

Thus, there is no immersion (*āveśa*) therein, because its nature is that of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaya*); for in relation to that, the distinction characterized by the immersed and the immerser is untenable. Therefore, it is rightly said: "This immersion is of fifty kinds. (191)

But has not the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, having promised an investigation into the fivefold nature of the immersion into Rudra’s power (*rudraśaktisamāveśa*), proceeded to define the essential nature of the elements and so forth? To this he says:
"Indeed, the immersion into Rudra’s power is investigated as being fivefold."
What opportunity would there be for describing such things as possession by spirits and the like?

If it is argued that this [objection] arises as a mere incidental consequence (*prasaṅga*), then although such a resolution is possible, it does not win over our minds; for the world has diverse tastes. (1.193)

"What opportunity [is there]?"—since [topics] such as possession by elemental spirits (*bhūta-āveśa*) are not relevant to the present context, this indeed constitutes an irrelevant statement, namely when one thing is introduced and something else is discussed;

thus it was not asked, "What opportunity is there for describing possession by elemental spirits and so forth? Now, regarding the description of immersion into the power of Rudra (*rudra-śakti-samāveśa*):

Although this was stated as a consequence (*prasaṅga*) even though it had already been established, that too is incorrect; thus he says, "this [was said] as a consequence. When a matter under discussion has been almost fully resolved, whatever is stated as being incidentally connected, though not relevant to the subject at hand, the resolution for that case is as follows:

Regarding the statement, “This was said by way of an incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*): — since the subject matter at hand has already been introduced here, yet the description of possession by spirits (*bhūtāveśa*) and so forth has been provided quite abruptly without first stating their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) or critical examination (*parīkṣā*), what indeed could this “incidental discussion” possibly be?
For, in this way, there would be an infinity of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that are not relevant to the context.
"Would there not then be the consequence of having to explain infinite internal objects of cognition? To this it was said: "It does not win over our minds. (192–193)
If this is so, then what is to be understood? To this he says:

"It is said that in the dualistic scriptures, the differentiation of the elements and so forth from the Supreme Lord exists; as it does there, it does not exist here in that which is devoid of duality. (1.194)
Regarding the word "here" (atra)—it refers to the non-dual scripture, the venerable *Śrīpūrva*. Regarding the word "that" (sā)—it refers to differentiation.
However, the reason for its negation is the state of being devoid of duality. || 194 ||
Then, raising the doubt as to what would follow from that, he says:
"Whatever constitutes this group of thirty-six [principles], and whatever else there may be—this much is the Great Goddess, the unimpeded power of Rudra. (1.195)
"Other" means that the worlds and so forth are indeed its specific manifestations (*tadbhedāḥ*). "Unobstructed" means unimpeded due to its all-pervasiveness—this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"This universe, consisting of the object of perception, the perceiver, and the act of perception, is indeed composed of the wheel of Your powers;
it shines eternally in its beginning, end, and middle. There is nothing whatsoever that is absolutely distinct from You. (195)
And he confirms this very point with the meaning found in that [text] itself:
"For that very reason, it was described in this second chapter that the universal form (viśvarūpatva) of the earth and the other elements consists of fifteenfold divisions and so forth. (1-196)
"From that very [source]" means, first of all, because it is the expansive form of Rudra's power itself. "In this" refers to the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*. As it has been stated in that very same work:
"The principle of earth (dharātattva) is divided according to the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself;
together with its own essential nature, it should be known as fifteenfold," and so forth.
"...Śiva is not different [from him] in person.
This ends [the citation]. And this will be treated in the *Tattvabhedana*; therefore, for fear of excessive length, no effort has been made here. || 196 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "If this is so, then let such immersion be described as occurring in the power of Rudra alone; what is the use of immersion into the elements and so forth? Does not that same fault apply? Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes this very point by demonstrating an analogy through the manner of a conclusion:

Therefore, just as in the case of an object situated before one, there arises an awareness of its partless nature through the predominance of certain parts such as qualities, so too should it be understood in this case as well. (1.197)

Just as when an object such as a jar is present, there occurs a correct cognition of its specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*)— that is, of the partless and undivided object consisting of the synthesis of various appearing universals— by means of the appearance of partial aspects such as redness, so too here [in this case] it occurs by way of the partial aspects beginning with the elements (*bhūta*).
It should be understood that this is the manifestation of the power of all Rudras. ||197||
Anticipating the question, "Even so, what would follow?", he says: "Therefore, by means of [qualities] such as non-conceptuality, permanence, sovereignty, and majesty—
or by other qualities inherent within itself that consist of its own powers— " (1.198)

Furthermore, those who, due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from what they have heard, worship that supreme Lord as either entirely [identical] or as possessing partiality, [worship Him through the flood of conceptual constructions]. (1.199)

Through the intensity of those respective attributes flashing within their own corresponding conceptual constructions, they superimpose the substratum—possessing the full flood of attributes—upon it non-differently. (1.200)

"For this very reason" means because the substratum (*dharmin*) is understood by way of understanding its mere attributes (*dharmamātra*). "Stability" (*dhrauvya*) is the state of being stable, which is permanence (*nityatva*). "By others" refers to [attributes] such as fullness (*pūrṇatva*) and so forth; "inherent in itself" means non-different from it because they exist in the form of its powers (*śakti*). Whosoever they may be...

Relying upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the flood of conceptual constructions (*vikalpaugha*) whose objects are the various specific dharmas arising from hearing, reflection, and so forth,
they enter into the Supreme Lord— either by means of all the powers (*śakti*) just mentioned together, or by means of a single power alone. Having thus entered, those very ones who...

Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are those [mental states] which manifest internally by way of their own forms; they are the powers (*śakti*), whether fixed or unfixed, which are the phenomena (*dharma*). Based upon their proficiency—that is, their awakening—one perceives the substratum (*dharmī*), which possesses a full nature because it is inlaid with infinite powers and contains the entire flood of phenomena.
The meaning is that they rest non-differently upon the omnipotent Supreme Lord and manifest as His very nature. || 198–200 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even for a single object endowed with various attributes, its manifestation as an object of cognition occurs only through its indivisibility (*ākhaṇḍya*) and not otherwise? Why, then, has this been said?
To pacify such a doubt, he confirms this very point by saying: "For this very reason, he [the author] has stated..."
The Lord of Śrīvidyā respectfully recites this very [verse]:
"If the sense-born [cognition] does not take your own nature— which is free from conceptual construction— as its object within the realm of mental construction..."
If the cognitions of the various forms inscribed within were not present, our experiences would not be manifest. || 1-201 ||

Even if sensory perception were non-conceptual and your own nature were indeed free from conceptualization and division, it would not apprehend it by resorting to differentiation through the mediation of specific, determined attributes within the process of conceptualization; rather, it would do so clearly by way of the manifestation of one or another determined attribute.

The meaning is this: those experiences—experiences consisting of the manifestation of the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*), which are internally delineated in their various aspects through intermediate manifold attributes (*avāntara-nānā-dharma*) by virtue of having indistinct forms—would not come to be; they would not arise—if indeed... [the rest of the sentence follows].

If all properties were to pervade the substratum, then all experiences would occur [simultaneously]; thus, in cases such as "the wandering ascetic" (parivrāj), there would be three possible conceptual constructions for each individual [term]— whether by the force of one's own will,
in accordance with a specific purpose, or due to proficiency.

It is logical that the manifestation of the substrate (dharmin) occurs only by way of the manifestation of attributes (dharmas) restricted to each individual cognizer, and not otherwise; for even though the Supreme Lord possesses infinite powers, His manifestation occurs by way of the manifestation of only one particular power. || 201 ||
And this is established not only by reasoning but also by scripture; thus he says:
"It is stated in the venerable Mataṅga and other [texts] that 'Now, the presiding ground of the Lord consists of the rays of His own powers,' and so forth, described with such qualifiers. (1.202)
In that [state], he is intensely radiant in soul, unwavering, and possesses an immovable form;
that very state is the supreme limit (kāṣṭhā), subtle, and of the nature of the nectar of all directions. (1.203)
With her veils destroyed, she is peaceful, intensely longing for the pure reality alone; free from beginning and end, this virtuous one is figuratively designated as having a form. (1.204)

The connection is as follows: that reality which consists of the rays of its own power is described by the qualifiers beginning with "the locus of the Lord" (*patyuradhiṣṭhānam*) as being "distinguished" (by those attributes) through implication.
Thus: "Now, the locus of the Lord consists of the rays of its own power."

This is the original reading; however, the author has provided an alternative reading in order to demonstrate the relationship between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*). To show those very qualifiers, the scriptural passage beginning with "in that" (*tasyām*) and ending with "is metaphorically designated" (*upacaryate*) is cited.
It has been recited: "His own" means those powers (*śakti*) that are not shared with others;

these very powers, by virtue of being non-different, luminous, infinite, and so forth, are the "rays" (*kiraṇa*) or beams. That which consists of them is the "abode" (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—meaning the locus of manifestation—of the Lord (*pati*), who possesses power. Power alone [is this].
The means for making that known is as it has been said:
"Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun, in the same way, O Dear One, Śiva is known through His power."

Thus, because that power shines in the heavens (*divi*), he too is one whose self is perfectly radiant, having the nature of great light; for this very reason, he is unwavering, established in his own very form. For if there were a falling away from the essential nature of that which consists of light, all this would become blind. And for this very reason:

He is endowed with an immovable, highly luminous, and praiseworthy form; and because he is of such a nature within such a state, that very state is the supreme limit, the transcendent ground of rest. For this reason, it is subtle and impossible to delimit.

Because it is of the single nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), for this very reason, its intense longing for the ultimate form which is mere reality (*vastumātra*) consists in its own manifestation; that is to say, it is of the nature of that [reality’s] flashing forth. And thus, she by whom external veils have been thoroughly destroyed through the absence of residual impressions (*niḥsaṃskāra*) is "one whose differentiation has been stilled" (*praśāntabheda*).

This is the meaning; for this very reason, she is "quiescent" (śāntā), meaning her nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra). Even so, she is "present in all directions" (sarvadikkā), existing in every direction because she takes the form of the entire world consisting of the mobile and immobile; that is to say, her essential nature is manifold (citrasvabhāvā).

Furthermore, she is "of the nature of nectar" (amṛtātmikā) and eternal; for this very reason, she is "devoid of beginning and end," since that which is impermanent—indeed, [is characterized by such limits].
The beginning and the end exist; for this very reason, she is "excellent" (*sādhvī*), meaning she is free from the impurities of defects such as impermanence.

And such as she is, she is metaphorically designated as the "form" (*mūrti*) of the Supreme Lord, the Possessor of Power; that is to say, she is expressed as being of His very nature through figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). || 202–204 ||
Now, one might object: "In a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), there must necessarily be a triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning;
does that exist here, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, the cause for the metaphorical usage here is as follows, and it possesses its purpose."

The term *nimitta* means "cause," for it is by virtue of that alone that metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) occurs—this is the intended meaning. In that context, when the power (*śakti*) is designated as having the nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), the primary meaning is indeed sublated;
and the relationship between the two is that of the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*).
Regarding this, he says:
"From that [state], clarity toward the subject arises quickly, and there is a state of identification with it. (1.205)
Those very dharmas, known as powers, are worshipped through various appropriate forms and aspects for the sake of attaining identity with them. (1.206)

That power (*śakti*) is whose "mouth" (*mukha*), that is, its means (*upāya*). What is called "clarity" (*sphuṭatā*)? It has been stated: "the state of immediate identification with that. The intention is that when this power is attained, Śiva himself is indeed attained. And this alone is the primary purpose. || 206 ||
Therefore he says:
"In that case, some power—whether infinite or limited—may project [its effects] according to the principle of existence and non-existence, based on distance and proximity. (1.207)

"Endless and limited" refers to the powers (śaktis) by implication. Regarding the phrase "according to the logic of being a *dhava* tree": for "being a *dhava*" excludes non-*dhava* trees and thus implies only its own individual instances; therefore, it has the quality of implying a limited number of entities. "Being," however, exists everywhere, in both *dhava* and non-*dhava* things.

Thus, this [latter type] possesses the capacity to imply infinite entities. For this very reason, those which imply limited entities are distant, because they are not present everywhere due to their non-pervasive nature; whereas those which imply infinite entities are proximate, because they are present everywhere due to their pervasive nature. || 207 ||
He applies this very point to the subject at hand:
"Therefore, fullness of being, luminosity, the nature of consciousness, and the state of Bhairava—these project all powers because of their pervasiveness. (1.208)
However, because Sadāśiva and the others lack upward pervasion, they occupy the lower [levels] and would project their powers [only] near or far from their respective objects of worship. (1.209)
Regarding the phrase "those who abide below"—this refers to the powers beginning with Īśvara.
The word "that" [refers] to the state of being Sadāśiva, which consists of a full nature;
this is because of the reason that such a nature is both pervasive and non-pervasive. For it is in the form of the full nature [that this occurs].
Those who have approached [the teacher] attain the full fruit characterized by enjoyment and liberation;
however, for one whose nature is incomplete, there is only incompleteness—this is what is meant by the statement, "from proximity or distance regarding worship.
For this very reason, there is a difference in philosophical perspectives (darśana). || 208-209 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely, by the power of that mental construction (*kalpanā*), it is conceptualization itself that appears as a determined property (*dharma*) whose nature is universal (*sāmānya*);

thus, through that [property], there would be an appearance of the substratum (*dharmin*)—this sequence would apply to the Śākta means (*upāya*), but not to the Śāmbhava [means], which consists in the appearance of the undivided reality and is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) by nature."
Anticipating the question, "How is this stated here?", he says:
"In this context, the sequence of the path of conceptualization called 'Śākta' exists in the sense of 'being thus' (itthambhāva).
Since that is what is taught here, therefore [the state] corresponding to it is non-conceptual. (1.210)
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the occasion of the Śāmbhava state; "therefore" (*tasmāt*) means from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For when the opposing position has been thoroughly examined, the establishment of one's own position is effectively accomplished—thus, the sense is that nothing irrelevant has been stated here. Indeed, within conceptual construction, there occurs the manifestation of the undivided reality through a gradual process.

Furthermore, in the state of non-conceptuality, it occurs without sequence—wherever one who has attained the state of non-conceptual stability fixes their attention, at that very moment, the attainment of Śiva-hood occurs for them. || 210 ||
Thus it is said: "Established on the path free from conceptual construction, by whichever path one may enter—down to the level of Dharā or Sadāśiva—one becomes Śiva through that very path. (1.211)

He illustrates this very point: "In the stainless heart, which shines with the manifestation of the foremost portion of the levels, within that light, by means of that very [heart], there is the nature of Paraśiva-consciousness. (1.212)

Indeed, here in this stainless heart, which consists of the full self-reflection of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃvimarśa*), and for that very reason preeminent— having made it supreme by way of its indivisibility— there is the thirty-sixth part, characterized as the ground of manifestation, which, in relation to other principles, is a constituent portion; [this occurs] within that which consists of the self-manifestation of that [part].
The meaning is that, through the means consisting of the very nature of a portion of that ground within the Light, there occurs the absorption into the state of Paraśiva-consciousness. || 212 ||
He concludes this very point:
"Thus, those dwelling with Sumati and others know this immersion called Śāmbhava, which possesses a truly effective means consisting of a portion of the Supreme Will-power. (1.213)

And this Power of Will (icchā-śakti) is the supreme form of the Blessed Lady (bhaṭṭārikā), and this portion consists of that very essence, according to such statements as: "But the Supreme is considered to consist of Will. Because it is a direct means in comparison to the Śākta and other [means], it is both real and a means (saṃś-cāsau upāyaḥ).

"Those who dwell at the end of Sumati," namely Śrī Somadeva and others. For those who know the lineage of transmission maintain that Śrī Somadeva was the disciple of the venerable Lord Sumati, and his [disciple] was the venerable Śambhunātha.
As he will state:
"From Śrī Soma, indeed, [came] Śambhunātha, the knower of all...
Thus it is said. As for that which states:
"A certain glorious and all-pervasive Bhairava, dwelling in the sacred seat of the southern land..."
In the world, there was the author of the treatise *Pañcasrotasi-sātimārgavibhava*; from him arose his foremost disciple, the illustrious Sumati,
