who became renowned as Śambhu from the sacred seat of Jālandhara.
Thus, what is stated elsewhere should be understood solely with reference to the intention of the Supreme Guru. Or else:

"Thus, the illustrious Śambhunātha, whose darkness has been dispelled by the moonlight of the wisdom of the venerable Sumati, has described the true nature [of reality] in the waking state and the others."
This should also be understood in cases such as these. || 213 ||
Having now established the Śāmbhava means, he also describes the Śākta: "Next, the Śākta is said to be clearly the mind (cetas), intellect (dhī), thought (manas), and egoity (ahaṃkṛti);
because it is characterized by conceptualization (savikalpatayā), it consists of Māyā; in reality, however, it is the Will (icchā) and the other [powers]. (1.214)

And this is not merely a matter of mental construction here—thus he says: "intellect, mind, and ego-sense. For this very reason, it is "clearly"—meaning its essential nature is directly manifest. And consequently:
"every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is *saṃsāra*..."
By such reasoning, it is said that [the universe] consists of the manifestation of duality—"as consisting of *māyā* due to its conceptual nature.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this [universe] consists of will, knowledge, and action as appropriate; thus it is said:
"in substance, it is will and so forth. For indeed, the Lord [creates] the universe through these powers of will and the rest.
In the same way, the bound soul (*paśu*) creates even conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and so forth by means of the triad of internal organs beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*).

This is the intended meaning; for in the case of conceptual construction and the like, the sovereignty belongs primarily to the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and its manifestation is entirely dependent upon this triad—thus it has been stated. (214)
Therefore, he says:

"That which, through the sequence of conceit, conceptualization, and determination, is empowered (śākta), is also a means characterized by Māyā; yet at its conclusion, it is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka). (1.215)

For here, having conceived agency within one's own self through the grasping of the ego (ahaṅkāra), and having conceptualized external objects of desire as being either of that nature or not, and having determined that very object by the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), there arises this conceptual state belonging to the power of Śakti: "I alone am situated everywhere," or "everything is situated in me alone. This is the nature of the self.
Although that cognition arises as a means consisting of *māyā* because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are grounded in differentiation,

nevertheless, through the power of the repeated practice of those very conceptual constructions, they generate increasingly superior conceptualizations until, at the end, it culminates in the direct perception of the object in its most vivid clarity.
The meaning is that the Śāmbhava immersion (*samāveśa*) would be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
As he will say:
"In this nature of the Supreme Lord, which was described in the immediately preceding chapter..."
"One who wishes to enter into the state beyond conceptualization should immediately perform the refinement [of consciousness]," beginning thus, and continuing:
"Then [the cognition] is augmented by a most vivid and noble identity with that [object]."
"Consciousness attains a stainless state whose very nature is free from conceptual construction.
For this very reason, it is said that the Śākta means (upāya) is a "means-to-a-means" (upāyopāya). || 215 ||

Now, one might object: "Since for everyone, including ourselves, there exists a spontaneous, effortless, and non-conceptual cognition, why is it said that this possesses the nature of the Śāmbhavāveśa state, which is taught as the very goal to be attained? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The state of the bound soul (paśu) consists of various degrees of limitation; that which is the lowest is the supreme Śāmbhavī state.
It is incomplete due to the wretchedness of the subject (mātṛ), yet it becomes fully blossomed when that [limitation] is removed. (1.216)
"She" refers to the state free from conceptual construction (*avikalpā bhūḥ*). As it has been said:
"In that state, even for a bound soul (*paśu*), there exists the divine nature (*aiśvaro bhāvaḥ*).
If this is so, then what is the use here of effort such as instruction and the like? To this he replies: "supremely full" (*paramapūrṇā*).
For when the subject is contracted, his knowledge and action become contracted as well;
thus, how could this evil-minded one possess the state of Śambhu directly therein? This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, upon the removal of that wickedness of the subject and the emergence of fullness, that is the state of Śambhu.
The meaning is that [consciousness] becomes blossoming, characterized by full knowledge, agency, and so forth; therefore,

this effort consisting of instruction and the like must necessarily be undertaken for the purpose of making one recognize one's own self, preceded by the casting aside of contracted knowledge, agency, and so on.
Success! 216.

He applies that very principle to the subject at hand: "In this way, the stage of conceptualization belongs to the Śakti, wherein agency and cognition are manifest; however, according to the previously stated principle, there is contraction within this [stage]. (1.217)
Likewise, for one who is intent on dissolving the accumulation of contractions, that radiant power which brings about internal manifestations at will [is attained]. (1.218)

In this case, although within the means of power (*śāktopāya*), which consists of conceptual knowledge, cognition and action are more manifest than in the non-conceptual state, nevertheless, due to the wretchedness of the subject (*mātṛdaurātmya*), they remain contracted; thus, even here,
one must necessarily employ effort such as instruction and so forth, by which [the state] becomes so for everyone.

Because she is intent upon dissolving contraction, that Śākta ground is radiant and blossoming; the meaning is that she brings about the manifestation of that internal light—which is the desired goal and whose nature is identity with the subject—and shines as the single form of the supreme subject. || 217-218 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that a distinction between the Śākta and the Śāmbhava [means] is established by their respective forms as conceptual and non-conceptual;

however, how can there be a distinction between them and the Āṇava, which is of the singular form of conceptualization? Having presented this doubt, he explains the distinction between those two [the Śākta and the Āṇava]:
Now, is it not the case that discursive thought exists in the Āṇava [means]? It does exist there;
however, he has described the absence of vocalization (uccāra) here as being due to other means. (1.219)
In this context, by the words "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth, *samādhi* is indicated; "other" (*anya*) refers to [practices] such as the upward movement of breath (*uccāra*).

For in the *āṇava* [path], the conceptualizing intellect exists by relying solely on external [objects] such as the upward movement of breath; here, however, in the *śākta* [path], it is distinguished by being devoid of that [external reliance]. Therefore, the phrase "by the mind alone" (*cetasā eva*) is used with restrictive emphasis.
In this context, it is stated that there is merely reflection. || 219 ||

Now, is [the state of being] "devoid" here meant only by the absence of utterance (*uccāra*), or also by the absence of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth? To this he says: "By the word 'utterance' (*uccāra*) mentioned here, that which begins with it is intended; these do not exist in the means of power (*śaktyupāya*). For in the state of power (*śaktitā*), there is neither difference nor non-difference. (1.220)

The sense is that by the plural ending in *bahvantena*, the meaning of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is obtained; therefore, the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) should be shown as "devoid of utterances" (*uccāraiḥ rahitam*). "These" refers to utterance, the instruments [of speech], and so forth. "They do not exist" because these are solely dependent upon duality. For here, due to being devoid of external utterance and the like—
Furthermore, because non-duality is of the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), duality also arises; thus, there is a state consisting of both. He says this:
"For duality and non-duality are indeed power (*śaktitā*). In the *āṇava* [means], however, duality alone is predominant. || 220 ||
Thus it is said: "The 'atomic' (aṇu) is a manifest duality; the means thereto here is the atomic (āṇava).
Consisting essentially of conceptual determination, it becomes non-conceptual in the end. (1.221)
By the statement "at the limit, it is non-conceptual," it is shown that even this [state] finds its rest solely in the Śāmbhava [state].
Now, [it may be asked]: "But Sadāśiva and the others, due to the absence of upward pervasion, are situated below."
They would completely subvert the powers... || 221 ||

By the reasoning stated above, since there is no activity of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties within Śiva, how can it be said that they are even means for attaining Him? To this, he says:
"But surely the intellect, mind, ego, and the person would pervade Śiva."
Since he was situated below [her], how could he have spoken in such a manner? || 222 ||
He provides the resolution for this very point: "It is said that, in reality, for us Śiva alone is of such a nature;
having performed the concealment of his own form, he again becomes self-luminous in that manner. (223)
In reality, for us non-dualists, Śiva alone is [the self]—
according to the reasoning stated in such passages as "Śiva himself has assumed the state of a bound soul"— having concealed his own nature through the majesty of his own sovereignty.
Such a limited cognizer, consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, would indeed exist;

yet, through the process of "unwinding" (*udveṣṭana*), by means of the gradual removal of the intellect and other faculties, he becomes Śiva himself, self-luminous. Thus, it is not the case that the intellect and other faculties must necessarily function even within Śiva, nor that they do not.
There is no fault whatsoever. || 223 ||
"This is not only stated in the non-dual (advaita) scriptures, but even in the dual (dvaita) scriptures"—thus he says:
"In the dual scriptures such as the Mataṅga and others, this is also well-established:
that light belongs exclusively to Śiva, who pervades the lower [realms]. (1.224)
By which the supreme state shines even upon the mental plane of the Buddha.
As it is said there:
"In this way, from that virtuous principle (tattva), another irreproachable principle emerges below— great, pervasive, and enriched by thousands of shimmering rays."
Thus [it is said]. He concludes this very point with the words “of the one who pervades below,” and so forth. “He” refers to that which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest;
“by which” means by the reason that the intellect and the rest have as their sole nature the light of Śiva. (224–225)
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"Both of these two modes of immersion (*samāveśa*) proceed toward the ocean of the non-conceptual; for indeed, without being rooted in that [ocean], there is nothing at all. (1.226)

The prefix *prati* signifies "facing toward" (*ābhimukhye*); therefore, the meaning is that both of these rest solely within the *śāmbhavāveśa*, which is the nature of the Supreme Light. For whatever does not rest therein would be nothing at all, because it would not be manifest.

Thus it has been said: "Indeed, without that rootedness, nothing at all [is possible]. And so, it would be stated that the supreme Light, whose nature is free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), is the means for all these [levels].
And this is not our own invention alone; thus he says:
"Therefore, he stated that no distinction in the fruit of consciousness should be postulated here;
indeed, the primacy of conceptualization (kalpanā) is indicated right here. (1.227)
"Therefore"—that is, because of entering into that very single consciousness which is of the nature of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).
As it has been said:
"Wise men should not conceive of any difference here in the fruit of consciousness."

Thus [it is said]. And here, because of the diversity of the means (*upāya*), the assumption of a difference in the fruit (*phala*) would necessarily follow; otherwise, since a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence, that very prohibition would not exist here. By the statement "it is not to be imagined," this [consequence] is implied—thus he says: "of the imagination. [This refers to its] primacy (*mukhyatva*).
Thus, the state of being denotable is indicated—not explicitly stated—this is the sense.
The reality of resting in the non-conceptual is not only found here [in our own system], but even in the view of outsiders;
thus he says:
"Even in the opinion of one who asserts that validity depends upon conceptualization..."
The state of non-conceptual valid cognition is attained through the sequence of conceptualizing that [object]. (1-228)
Even in the view of the Vaibhāṣikas and others who maintain that non-conceptual cognition is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by depending upon conceptual construction,

those very conceptual constructions have a sequence or succession; by that [sequence], the validity of the non-conceptual itself is acquired or produced— that is, through the ascent of conceptual construction, there is a final resting point (*viśrānti*) in the non-conceptual alone.
—this is the meaning. || 228 ||
He illustrates this very point:

"One who previously did not know the true nature of the jewel, but through the investigation of the means for certain knowledge, attains it by means that are effortless and free from conceptual construction, is called a 'knower of the jewel. (1.229)
Any jeweler or similar artisan, though initially unaware of the true nature of the gem through non-conceptual functioning,
relies upon inquiry by way of conceptualization— such as "Is its essence thus, or not?"— until,
upon the spontaneous arising of a non-conceptual state that is free of [deliberate] means, he becomes a knower of the gem and realizes its essential reality.

The meaning of the sentence is that one who knows [reality] as non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) is so described; the same should be stated regarding one who possesses higher knowledge (abhijña) of the individual soul (āṇava) and the other [powers]. || 229 ||
In this context, indeed, that which was stated regarding knowledge as being threefold by way of its nature as difference, difference-and-non-difference, and non-difference—namely:
"In reality, this existence of knowledge unfolds in only three ways:
through difference, through difference-and-non-difference, and likewise through that which partakes of non-difference."
Thus, among these, the *āṇava* [means] has been described as primarily characterized by duality (*bheda*), and the *śākta* as primarily characterized by both duality and non-duality (*bhedābheda*).
Raising the question, "What, then, is the primary characteristic of the *śāmbhava*? he says:
"In this context, the *śāmbhava* is said to have non-duality as its means (*abhedopāya*); the *śākta* is now being described."
The means consisting of both difference and non-difference, the means of difference, and that which is the individual (āṇava) [means].

But surely, since it has been stated in such passages as, "And liberation [is attained] through Śiva-initiation," it follows that ritual action such as initiation is also a means to liberation; therefore, that—
Anticipating the doubt— whether there is some other additional means or whether it is included within this very [means] in some way— he says:
"In the end, within this knowledge accompanied by its means, the entire expansion of ritual action [is contained]."
In its very manifest form, that which is yet to be will become internalized.

"With the means" (*sopāye*) means accompanied by the means such as utterance (*uccāra*) and so forth—this is the meaning. For this very reason, it was previously stated: "there, with the means. "The entire expansion of ritual action" (*samastaḥ karmavistaraḥ*) refers to the various collections of rites, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so on, which are yet to come and will be described. By the phrase "it will be included"—
It has been explained that there is no other means beyond this. || 231 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the inclusion of a homogeneous thing within another homogeneous thing is logical, and not otherwise? Therefore, how can ritual action (*kriyā*) such as initiation be included within *āṇava* knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For that which is called 'action' is not a reality other than consciousness; it is merely consciousness itself assuming a sequential nature."
It was previously stated that what is attained through the power of skillful means is "action" (kriyā). (1.232)
The word *tat* refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); the word *purā* (formerly) refers to [the passage] beginning with "since there is no such thing as action other than this," and so forth. ||232||

Now, it has been asserted by such statements as "Knowledge is the sole cause of liberation" that liberation arises from knowledge; however, does that [knowledge] effect liberation while residing in its own substratum, or while residing in another's substratum?
And if it resides in its own substratum, does it effect liberation when initiation (*dīkṣā*) is present or when it is absent?
If [the teacher] is unreal—

given the statement, "And there is no eligibility for the yoga of Śiva without initiation," and so forth— it follows that there is no eligibility even for the attainment of knowledge; so what could liberate whom?

If [it is argued that] this might be so, [we reply: since initiation cannot logically occur within one's own self by means of the self alone through dependence on another, and if [the self] were the locus of another, there would be the great fault that the cause is in one place and the effect in another? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And right knowledge, which is the sole cause of liberation, abides in both oneself and others;
for the manifestations of self, other, and so forth are merely conceptual constructions. (1-233)

"It is mere conceptual construction" (kalpanāmātra) means that, in reality, consciousness is indeed one alone, yet it manifests as various appearances of self, other, and so forth—this is the intended meaning. || 233 ||
Therefore he says:
"And since their conceptual nature is equal, when the Guru consists of the manifestation of unity, he is established as the one Self and is called liberated. (1.234)
Even when the conceptualization of self and other is equal in relation to the teacher and the non-teacher and so forth, that teacher—

who is essentially the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) consisting of a single, undivided mass of consciousness through the manifestation of that unity (*aikya*) or unification by whichever disciple or teacher [is involved], characterized by the absence of any distinction between the appearances of self and other— is indeed "that much" (i.e., he is the full extent of that reality).

The limit of the manifestation of oneness (*ekyasphuraṇāvadhi*) means that one who has become such—possessing a single self—is established and liberated, and is said to consist of nothing but supreme sovereignty; this is the meaning. What is being stated here is this: as long as there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of this [reality] as having a single self-nature through one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*), for that long he remains truly one.
It shines forth as having attained identity with the supreme light. As it has been said:
"He who thus knows the pervasion according to the division of the supreme and the non-supreme, he shall become a direct liberator, Śiva, the supreme cause."
Thus [ends the section]. || 234 ||
Therefore he said:
"For as long as his lineage is great, so far is it proclaimed to consist of perfect knowledge; and by means of that, one is liberated through one's own self. (1.235)
Therefore, it is established through both reasoning and scripture that the knower liberates his own continuum; for the Sage is one and the same [for all]. (1.236)
The lineage consists of the form of disciples, grand-disciples, and so forth; this is because, for the time being, it manifests as a single self. "From that" means from such a lineage.

For, by relying on such a lineage, because of the identity with consciousness (*saṃvid-ekātmya*), this teacher is one and the same; thus, when those belonging to the lineage are liberated, it is he alone who is liberated.
There is no fault whatsoever, because the distinction between self and other is merely conceptual; one is liberated by means of one's own self.
For this very reason, he says "from that very [source]" and so forth, [meaning] "it delivers.
As it has been said:
"The Teacher, through the thorough knowledge of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, will cause all his own kinsmen and thousands of millions of lineages to cross over.
Herein the reason is given: "For he alone is a sage (muni)," where "sage" refers to the Guru. (235–236)
And this being the case, the refutation of the objections raised by others is established without effort—thus he says:
"Therefore, those who here raise the objection: 'Surely liberation comes from knowledge;
how then can this ritual action, such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth, lead to liberation? (1.237)

If it is argued that she is of the nature of knowledge (*jñānātmā*), then [the soul] should be liberated from wherever that knowledge resides. Or, even if it were to liberate another, would that not be inconsistent?
Thus, what has been supported by others here has been refuted by you from its very root. (1.238)
The term "ye" refers to the various types of proponents of dualism; "te" refers to those who raise such objections; they have been "kṣiptāḥ," that is, refuted.

Since it has been accepted from the very outset that knowledge and action are one and the same, and that the distinction between self and other is merely conceptual, this very point constitutes the rebuttal here.

He says, "It is not other," with the words beginning "But that which... The connection is as follows: we shall refute later on that which has been propounded by others who maintain the doctrine of a distinct God (Bhedeśvara). || 237-238 ||
Now, one might object: "If the nature of impurity as a substantial entity (dravyarūpatva), as asserted by the proponent of duality, is not accepted, then what is its nature?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
It is said that "impurity" (mala) is indeed a substance, like a cataract or film on the eye;
initiation (dīkṣā) is the action that destroys it, like the application of collyrium and similar treatments. (1.239)
We shall refute that [view], which is censured by both reason and scripture, in what follows; and we shall demonstrate the nature of impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and karma. (1.240)
He concludes this very point by adding further elaboration:
"Thus, regarding that knowledge which has the three powers as its means, the last is the root; the one following it is the middle; and the first is the highest of the high. (1.241)

"Western" refers to the individual means (āṇava); "root" refers to its resting within the Śāmbhava [means] by way of the Śākta sequence. Thus it is said: "subsequent to that," meaning subsequent to that individual means.
Because it is the place of ultimate rest, the Śākta is superior; and superior even to the Śākta is the Śāmbhava. As it has been said:
"Due to the connection with the pervasive Power (Śakti) and the individual soul (Aṇu), immersion (Samāveśa) is considered to be threefold."
"Through the union of will, knowledge, and action, it is accumulated in ever-increasing measure. (241)
Not only is the Śāmbhava knowledge superior as the resting place for the Āṇava and other means, but there is yet another known as the Anupāya that is even more excellent than this; thus he says:
"Even higher than that is the supreme knowledge, which is devoid of means and the like."
That which rests in the power of bliss is here called the Unsurpassed (Anuttara). || 1-242 ||
"Supreme" (*paramam*)—because its nature is solely that of the goal (*upeya*); for this very reason it is said: "devoid of means and the like.

And for this same reason, it is said: "resting in the power of bliss" (*ānandaśaktiviśrāntam*). For in the case of will and the other powers, because they are directed outward due to the limitation imposed by objects such as that which is to be desired, there is even the possibility of duality.
Furthermore, as for the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti)— since,
according to such statements as "Bliss is the nature of Brahman," it is indeed the very essence of consciousness, there is not even a trace of a means (upāya) here.
The intended meaning. || 242 ||
And this is not my own invention, but is stated everywhere in the scriptures; thus he says:
"That self-luminous consciousness, whose true nature is difficult to attain even for the Vidyās and the Lords of Vidyā (Vidyeśvaras) and others, is described in the Śrīsiddhātantra. (1.243)
And this has been clearly indicated in the eighteenth chapter of the Mālinī [vijayottara-tantra] by the statement: "And this [is not attained] unless Śaṅkara is pleased. (1.244)
By this very reading in the *Mālinīvijayottara*, for therein it says:
"Effortless, without undertaking, without means, yet of great fruit."
"I wish to hear about Yoga, O Lord of Yoga, best among the knowers of Yoga.
When the Goddess had thus asked, [He replied]:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed nectar of Yoga."
Attaining which, mortals obtain the state of Śiva, free from all exertion.
"And this is not taught by Śaṅkara unless he is pleased;
even if [the truth] is somehow attained, the latent impression (vāsanā) does not arise.
Beginning with these words—
Therefore, one should practice that constantly with a mind free from detachment;
for that, O Great Goddess, is the emission (visarga) wherein one finds rest.
"That alone is called the mouth of the Guru; that is said to be the wheel of power (śakticakra).
That indeed is the supreme place of origin for all mantras. Thus it has been stated [in verses 243–244].
And this indeed is the meaning of the treatise; thus he says:
"This fourfold knowledge, which is the great arising of both accomplishment and liberation, is set forth by me here in this teaching named the *Tantrāloka*. (1.245)
Regarding the word *iti*: in the *Tantrāloka*, it is called "light" (*āloka*) because it is like the light of the Tantras belonging to the Supreme Lord;

or rather, it is so called because it illuminates—that is, makes manifest—those [Tantras]. Regarding the word *iti*: it refers to that tetrad of knowledge whose nature has been described. Of what nature is it? It is considered such because it is the great arising (*mahodaya*) of both spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*).
"Of great excellence"—that [reality] is "expounded" (*tantryate*) here in this teaching, the *Tantrāloka*; that is to say, it is revealed in detail. || 245 ||

Now: "In that regard, reasoning (nyāya) does not operate upon an object that is not perceived, nor upon one that is already certain; rather, it operates upon what is doubted. Therefore, doubt is a constituent part of it."

By such statements, it is said that the composition of a treatise— which consists of a definitive determination— is undertaken precisely regarding a matter that is subject to doubt; therefore, since doubt is an essential limb of that [treatise], he begins by first defining its very nature:
In this regard, whatever is perceived here, whether internally or externally, that which has not yet had its form disclosed shines forth even beforehand. (1.246)

"Internally," that is, within mental cognition (*mānasavijñāna*) and so forth; "in an unmanifested form" means having its specific qualities not yet delineated, consisting of a universal property (*sāmānyadharma*)—this is the meaning. || 246 ||
And this is generally what is called "doubt. Thus he says:
"In that way, an appearance whose form is not disclosed, by means of an inexpressible nature, is doubt; [this occurs] when some aspect has been ascertained, and not otherwise. (1.247)

Likewise— by that indefinable form consisting of general properties such as verticality and so forth, which, being primary, remains unmanifested because its specific attributes such as hands and feet have not been perceived, and thus has not yet been disclosed.

Doubt is that cognition (*pratīti*) characterized by its own nature (*svarūpa*), which— due to the absence of a determination regarding the specific nature of either one of the two possible subjects (*dharmī*)— is impossible to describe in a determinate form because it rests upon both parts; for it [perceives] a property (*dharma*) such as verticality, which is common to both [possibilities].

It would arise when there is the non-apprehension of specific properties such as having a mouth or a hole, despite the apprehension [of the general]. Thus he says "in some place" (*kutracit*), etc.—the meaning is: in some locus (*dharmin*) delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*).
"Not otherwise" means: whether the subject (dharmin) has been determined in its entirety or remains undetermined.

He shows this very point by analyzing it: "In this primary [subject], 'What is this?', the aspect of 'this' is well-ascertained; doubt consists in the non-revelation of attributes such as existence, non-existence, and so forth. (1.248)

"What is this?"— this doubt, whose essence is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), is primary because, in comparison with other forms of reflective awareness such as "Is it a post or a person?", none of the specific attributes have yet been disclosed. And therein, that aspect which corresponds to the element "what" [is the primary one].

Because it apprehends the mere substratum (dharmin), it is well-ascertained. Now, one might object: "Doubt is a reflective awareness that rests upon two fixed alternatives"—this is the definition of doubt; if, in that case, some single aspect is ascertained, then what is the point?
"Therefore, he says: 'Doubt,' and so forth. "Existence and non-existence"—that is *astitva-nāstitva*;

by those specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*) of which existence and non-existence are the first, [the object] is "unopened," meaning its nature (*ātman*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) has not been disclosed. For in that case...
Since even the two categories of phenomena known as "sentient" and "insentient" are indeterminate, no definitive resolution has occurred there;
what then can be said of other phenomena? Because all phenomena lack any delineated form and one does not rely upon fixed attributes, this is the primary doubt.
The sense is that the interrogative particle *kim* indeed expresses a form of an object that has not yet been delineated. || 248 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Why does no further meaning shine forth from this word?"—
the word "further" (adhika) meaning [a meaning] beyond the referent of this word.
If one asks, "Then for what purpose is it employed?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But rather, this [word] denotes the very object whose form has not yet been unfolded. (1.249)
"This" refers to the interrogative pronoun "kiṃ. || 249 ||

Since the primacy of doubt is only tenable when there is some secondary status [to other factors], he says the following to demonstrate its secondary nature as well: "The doubt 'Is it a post or a person? is not primary;
for it is indeed the production of certainty regarding the multitude of properties residing more abundantly [in one alternative]. (250)
"It is not primary"— because, as before, there is no absence of the unveiled nature of all dharmas,
since [the reality] cannot otherwise be accounted for by the specific conceptualization of a post and so forth.
This cognition, consisting of ascertainment, pertains for the most part to those properties that abide in non-pillars and so forth.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since there is here the possibility of a confusion of meanings and because that which is fixed cannot be determined, there would necessarily be an option (*vikalpa*), according to the logic of the 'offering at sunrise or after sunrise'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, by virtue of not disclosing the two-fold nature of that which is to be contemplated..."
That [cognition] is doubt when it concerns the aspect "what might it be?"; otherwise, it is clearly a conceptual construction (vikalpa).

The "object of deliberation" (*āmarśanīyam*) is that duality characterized as either a post or a person; its "non-disclosure" (*anudghāṭanam*) is the failure to manifest it in its specific forms, such as having a face or being a hollow. Therefore, this cognition is indeed a doubt because it is permeated by the element of "what [is it]?"—as in the case of "Is it a post or a person? For in this instance:

The true meaning of doubt is precisely "Is it a post? Is it a person? At most, the primacy belongs to the mere element "what" (*kim*) because all specific attributes remain unmanifested therein; and in this case, there is no cognition of any fixed specific attribute.

The distinction is that [in the case of doubt] there is a lack of primacy (*amukhyatva*). In the case of an alternative (*vikalpa*), however, since both *vrīhi* and *yava* are equally certain, there is no state of having an unrevealed form; thus he says: "But an alternative is clearly otherwise.
"Otherwise" means by way of the specific attributes of both the *vrīhi* and *yava* which are to be reflected upon.

Because of this certainty, it has already been stated that such a doubt serves as the occasion for the commencement of the treatise (*śāstra*). For a treatise consists of definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), and definitive determination generally proceeds only with respect to an object that is indeed doubted; for that which is already perceived [as certain] cannot be the subject of doubt.

One does not comprehend what has not been apprehended; and since doubt is a property of the cognizer, even if an object is doubted by someone who is doubting and that object is then comprehended, there would be an apprehension of it.
Furthermore, the very presentation of that [object] constitutes the question; thus, it too, like its own cause, [is preceded by apprehension].

It should serve as the occasion for the commencement of the treatise; and the operation of a treatise undertaken for its definitive determination is threefold: enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṇa*), and examination (*parīkṣā*).
Enumeration is merely the naming of categories by their designations, and of that...
First, the enumeration must necessarily be performed, because the definition and investigation of that which has not been enumerated are impossible; therefore, without enumeration,
the composition of a treatise consisting of definitions and investigations would not even be feasible— this too [is established] therein.
The status of being a subordinate member. || 251 ||

If it is asked, "Since the composition of a treatise is accomplished by just one [of these], for what purpose are there three?", we say: this is not so, because here they are designated as causes precisely through their mutual interconnection. For it is only an object that is already subject to doubt, when being expressed by someone through a treatise by means of enunciation (*uddeśa*) and the rest, [that becomes established].

It is thus determined; and for this very reason, even though there is a difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa*), he says the following in order to demonstrate that they possess causality through a common form consisting of an unmanifested self-manifestation (*anudghāṭitātmaprathātmaka*) when the scripture functions in this manner:
Therefore, that which is the manifestation of the state of the self not being disclosed is, first of all, the enunciation here, as well as the question and the doubt. (1.252)

By the aforementioned reasoning, the very first manifestation of a thing— that is, of any entity— whose nature remains unopened, is here the *uddeśa* (enunciation), which consists of both question and doubt. Regarding that, the nature of doubt has just been described, as has its place within the enunciation.

The very nature of a thing is its manifestation as something unopened—that is, because objects are denoted by their mere names alone. This must also be stated regarding a question; otherwise, if it were of the nature of a definitive conclusion, there would be no distinction between it and a reply. || 252 ||

In that regard, since a question arises concerning a matter that is subject to doubt, the question must be resolved immediately after its determination; thus, as the occasion has arrived, he speaks in order to explain its true nature: "In that way, by means of the path of the unfolding of existence whose form remains unmanifest..."
Self-awareness, expanding forth, becomes the questioner who has attained the state of being a disciple.

In this non-dual system, since "consciousness alone is everything in the ultimate sense," the distinction consisting of the questioner and the respondent, the teacher and the disciple, and so forth, is first of all untenable. Likewise, in the manner previously described, its form remains unmanifested because it is replete with all things.
That reality which is of the singular nature of consciousness is the ultimately real, full-svabhāva entity;
its "expansion" (prasara) is its descent through the sequence of stages beginning with Paśyantī, and that alone is the path.
Expanding by means of that path and assuming the forms of Vaikharī and so forth, it is one’s own consciousness itself that has become contracted.
The meaning is that she who manifests the state of being the disciple, whose nature is the knower, is called the "questioner. || 253 ||
Wherein and how does she possess the nature of being questioned? To this he says:

"Thus, because her nature as internal reflective awareness and certainty is concealed, she also participates in the emergence of withdrawal that arises immediately after the outward expansion. (1.254)
To whatever extent there may be an external expansion within that which is of a manifest nature, to that same extent she is said to be the questioner, whose form has not yet unfolded. (1.255)

Likewise— by virtue of consisting of supreme non-duality— the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which is of the nature of identity with the subject, possesses certainty— that is, firmness— due to the concealment of its own essence,
because each subsequent form does not abide within each preceding one, through the process of unfolding.

She partakes of both dissolution— which is the resting within one’s own self of that form consisting of Parā and the others— and emergence— which is the external manifestation in the form of Paśyantī and the rest— because she arises immediately after the outward orientation [of consciousness]; for to whatever extent that consciousness exists, it possesses those very forms.

In the external expansion—which has as its nature the manifestation of the primordial pair consisting of the grasped and the grasper—she remains with her form unmanifested, meaning she does not appear as the nature of consciousness; because she manifests precisely to that extent with her essence unrevealed, she is called the "questioner"—this is the meaning. (254)
Not only does consciousness possess the quality of being the questioner, but it also possesses the nature of the question and so forth—
as he says:
"In this way, consciousness itself consists of both the question and the answer."
Even in the relationship of teacher and disciple, this distinction of bodies is indeed non-ultimate.
As it has been said:
"The Lord Sadāśiva himself, assuming the roles of teacher and disciple,
brought down the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and succeeding words."
Thus it is said:
"The Goddess herself is established as both the questioner and the respondent.
Now, one might object: since a mutual distinction between the teacher and the disciple is directly perceived, what [is the point]?
"What is the nature of consciousness in these two? To this he says: "This," and so forth. "Atāttvikaḥ" means unreal (*avāstava*).
The sense is that consciousness itself, through the majesty of its own sovereignty, manifests within itself the state of various bodies and so on. || 256 ||
Thus it is said:
"For consciousness, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, indeed causes the various forms existing within to appear externally in an instant, both in their general and particular aspects. (1.257)
For the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, because He is characterized as the agent of the act of cognizing and because His essence is consciousness,

projects the various forms— the multitude of all those objective entities— internally; then, "instantly"— that is, without delay due to independence from anything else— He projects them externally through differentiation, in the form of both universals and particulars.
The meaning of the sentence is that it indeed illuminates. || 257 ||
Regarding that, what is meant by the external manifestation of the universal (*sāmānya*)? To this he says:

"The creation of a certain attribute (*dharma*) which is capable of and expectant of the particular aspects yet to be created—that is the creation of the universal; it is essentially characterized by doubt. (1.258)
Regarding those particular aspects which are about to be emitted— that is, which are about to be manifested through their own specific characteristics—
it has been said: "For a universal devoid of particulars would be like the horn of a hare."
By the reasoning stated in such passages, because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with that [consciousness], *ākāṅkṣā* is "orientation" (*aunmukhya*).

In that regard, even in the absence of such orientation, there occurs the manifestation externally— which is the nature of emission— of some specific, determinate property such as "cowness," which is "suitable" (*anuguṇa*) because it is omnipresent and its own essential nature is never lost.

"The creation is universal, and that very [creation] is doubt because its manifestation as a specific self-nature has not yet been disclosed"— the meaning is that the cognition of doubt is precisely the perception of a universal in accordance with a desire for particulars. || 258 ||

Thus, even the creation of specific particulars consists of the cognition of certainty; so he says: "But when the portion of the particular that is about to be created ceases [its activity], then there is a determination according to the will of the subject, and not otherwise, even in ten million aeons. (1.259)

Furthermore, when— because all particularities have been emitted by that which serves as the means for ascertainment— the portion of particularities yet to be emitted ceases— that is, when the emission directed toward particulars is completed— then that very [consciousness],
being of the nature of the manifestation of its own unveiled self, is the ascertainment consisting of the cognition: "This is indeed a post."

It may be so. And in the arising of this [cognition], the very will of the subject (*pramātṛ*) is the cause—thus it was said, "according to the subject's pleasure. For as long as the subject is satisfied by the thought "this has been known by me," to that extent it becomes certain; such is the sense. Otherwise, however, it would never [be certain] at all.
This would be so because [the object] does not rest within the very desire of the knower. Thus he says:
"Not otherwise, even in ten million aeons. (259)
Not only does this [cognition] possess the nature of mere ascertainment, but it also possesses the nature of definition and so forth—
as he says:
"Then, because of its proficiency in ascending the power of its own self with respect to that object..."
The unsealing [of the channels] by means of that form, and the determination of the characteristics and their transcendence. || 1-260 ||

Of that entity which consists of particularity—that which is its own inherent vitality (vīrya)—there is its "exclusion from others," its "assault" (ākramaṇa), which is the making it an object by means of one's own self; therein lies "proficiency," which is intensity due to freedom from further desire; and from that, [arises] that very form.

Unsealing (*unmudraṇam*) is the manifestation of one's own specific essential nature (*svasvarūpa*). Because that [manifestation] consists of the unfolding of the self (*ātmaprathā*) without distinction, it is called a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), a "conclusion" (*uttara*), or a "determination" (*nirṇaya*). In this context, it is a unique property that brings about the awakening to reality (*tattva*).
The definition [of debate], the means for the realization of truth, the refutation [of objections] as the reply, and the realization of truth as the final determination. || 260 ||

An objection might be raised: "Since the essence of both [the definition and] the investigation is the realization of reality without distinction, why is investigation not also included by means of the definition itself, just as the determination is?
Anticipating this, he says: "Furthermore, because it follows upon the aspects of the properties already determined..."
The repeated examination of the nature of the [subject] through its indications and characteristics. || 1-261 ||

"Decided" means made the object of a determination; "to that extent" means characterized by a fixed definition; "that which is a portion of the property"—the repeated mention (*samuddeśa*) of it as the object, and the "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), which consists of the description of common and uncommon properties—that is its nature.
Furthermore, "paritaḥ" means "from all sides"—that is, an examination (*īkṣaṇa*) by way of the complete rejection of every opposing view; this is the meaning of the sentence. || 261 ||
And this triad of enunciation and so forth exists everywhere; thus he says:
"In all cases—whether in perception, inference, analogy, authoritative testimony, and so on—the triad of enunciation, definition, and examination flashes forth for living beings. (1.262)
He demonstrates this very point in sequence:
"The non-conceptual is the enunciation (uddeśa), while conceptualization is the definition (lakṣaṇa);
likewise, in perception, there is a succession of examinations (parīkṣaṇa) of conceptual constructions. (1.263)

"This is a mountain" is the designation (uddeśa), and "it possesses fire because it possesses smoke" is the definition (lakṣya); however, the complex of cognitions concerning pervasion and so forth constitutes the examination (parīkṣaṇa) in this context. (1.264)

"This is the enumeration (uddeśa)," says the former; "that which is similar to a cow is called a gavaya"—this is the definition (lakṣaṇa); the remainder constitutes the examination (parīkṣā) regarding analogy (upamiti). (1-265)
"One who desires heaven should sacrifice"—such is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of this [injunction];
"by means of the Agniṣṭoma and so forth"—this is the investigation (*parīkṣā*) that follows as a subordinate element (*śeṣavartinī*). (1-266)
"Enumeration" (uddeśa) is so called because mere sensory perception (ālocana) consists of the manifestation of the self in an unopened state.

"Definition" (lakṣaṇa) is so called because, through the thought-construct "this is blue," the very non-conceptual [perception] itself takes the form of the manifestation of the self in an opened state.

"Of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpānām*) means: those that occur prior to and subsequent to the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*); and precisely because of that, there arises the determination of the reality of the object—this constitutes their nature as "examination" (*parīkṣā*). "Indication" (*uddeśaḥ*) means:
because [in the statement] "This is a mountain," there is the manifestation of the mere locus (*dharmimātra*) alone, without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) having been disclosed.
"The subject" (*lakṣya*)—because its manifestation is disclosed as being qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

"Pervasion" (*vyāpti*)—namely, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), for it is precisely through these that the certainty of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the probandum and the probans arises; thus, this [pervasion] has the nature of an investigation.
"This" refers to the mere physical form present before one, which manifests as something whose nature has not yet been disclosed.

"The former" means the initial [cognition], which is not delimited by specific attributes. "This is similar to a cow" refers to the stage of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); "this is denotable by the word *gavaya*" refers to the stage of the result (*phala*).
Because the delimitation by specific qualities (*viśeṣāvaccheda*) is yet to come. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction;

thus, because both the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇadaśā*) and the state of the result (*phaladaśā*) consist in the manifestation of the unveiled self, they possess the nature of a definition (*lakṣaṇatva*). "The rest" refers to [definitions] such as "that which possesses a dewlap and performs the functions of carrying and milking," and so forth.
"Apprehension" (*parāmarśaḥ*). "Of this kind"—namely, "one who desires heaven" (*svaḥkāmaḥ*). "Of him"—of the one desiring heaven.
"The definition"—because the connection of qualification (*adhikārānubandha*) cannot be determined without the connection of the object (*viṣayānubandha*).
"Residing in the remainder"—because of the statement: "The remainder [is the means], because it is the ultimate reality. That [is what is meant].

The meaning is that the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) consists in the function of the *arthavāda* (explanatory passages). This has been stated. But is it not improper for a specific detail to be required [as an object of expectation], since at that time, because it is yet to come, there is not even a mere report of its existence?—this is the doubt [to be addressed].
He refutes [the opponent's position] by restating the previously mentioned definition along with its supplementary details:

"The manifestation of a real entity as being such-and-such, while tolerating other aspects that are not desired and are to be projected by conceptual construction—that is designated as 'uddeśa' (brief indication). (267)

At that very moment, consciousness discerns as many [entities] as there are to be created by means of conceptualization— since the universal has already been created by the subject, whose primary activity is that conceptualization— and in relation to those,
the "to-be-created" are those which are about to be manifested through their defining characteristics; for this very reason, they are "other" than those [already created].
Because they provide satisfaction to the cognizer,

those portions— the particularities— which are "rucitāḥ," meaning desired, are what it tolerates as being pervaded; that which has such a nature belongs to this kind of entity whose essence is the universal, and [the cognition arises] by virtue of its being so.

Because it possesses the capacity for particularity characterized by such qualifiers as "about to be created," that which is the creation has an objective referent— namely, its designation— and at that very moment, during the occasion of that designation, consciousness gathers all the particularities required to the extent that they are about to be created.
—he connects—this is the meaning. || 267 ||
The reason for this is: "For that which is not limited by time encompasses all times. (1.268)
The word "hi" serves as an ornament for the sentence. || 268 ||

Now, one might object: "If the definition consists in the manifestation of its own unveiled nature, then since both the universal and the particular are manifested, there would be no fixed rule due to a lack of distinction as to which is the definiendum (lakṣya) and which is the definition (lakṣaṇa). Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The creation of that which is about to be created and the withdrawal of the portion already created—when a property is being restated, that is called the defining characteristic of consciousness. (1.269)
In this context, consciousness— which consists of the creation and withdrawal of both the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*)— is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that is,

the seed of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therein, the particular aspect being emitted must be stated as the defining characteristic by virtue of its being the object to be produced (*vidheya*), and likewise for the universal aspect being withdrawn.
There is indeed a distinction: that which is being restated possesses the status of being the indicated (lakṣya). || 269 ||
But is it not the case that it has been said:
"The examination consists of repeated and intense investigation"?
And since there would be no cause for cessation therein, would the examination not simply never come to rest?
He refutes this doubt, which contains an implicit restatement [of the opponent's position]:

"The examination, which rests upon the repeated cycles of emanation, withdrawal, and repose of the various aspects following that [initial state], is described as having limits constructed according to the inclination of the subject. (1.270)

But has it not been stated that in each respective instance— such as perception and so forth— it is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), consisting of the wonder of one's own self, that unfolds sequentially in the form of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*? So how is it that here another sequence,
unknown to our own established doctrine, is introduced through the nature of enunciation (*uddeśa*) and the rest?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"First Paśyantī, then Madhyamā, and another, Vaikharī—these are they; [the first] is Parā, the second is Parāparā, and the final one is of the nature of Aparā. (1.271)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the triad beginning with *uddeśa* (enumeration) possesses the nature of *paśyantī* and the other levels of speech merely by virtue of their numerical correspondence?
What, then, is the point of this [following statement]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This very triad of powers, beginning with Will (*icchā*), is what is being described."
The connection is with what precedes:
it is only when animated by this [consciousness] that this worldly transaction is extended. || 1.272 ||
The intended meaning is that this entire conventional reality, consisting of both the pure and the impure, indeed manifests upon the very wall of consciousness.
As it has been said:
"Thus, within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the appearance of objects that are extremely diverse,
worldly transaction— whether accompanied by impurity or free from it— is experienced.
Not only do these [connections] possess such a nature, but furthermore: "The connection in the Tantra is sixfold: supreme, great, proximate, divine, mixed, and non-divine..."
He says this regarding the relationship that was also mentioned by the words "and so forth":

"In the teaching of the Supreme Lord, within the fivefold set of relationships, these [latter ones] consist of the nature of question and answer, and they possess the character of the supreme relationship. (1.273)

The meaning is: "when that reality exists"—that is, when the reality (*tattva*) whose nature (*ātman*) consists of the question and answer just mentioned exists. The sense is that the relationship belongs only between the questioner and the speaker. "In the fivefold relationship" refers to [the relationship] beginning with *mahat* and so forth; for the sixth is indeed...
The supreme relation (para-sambandha) underlies all of these as their vitalizing principle;
therefore, it is not mentioned here separately. || 273 ||
And this has not been stated by us as our own invention; thus he says:

"As it is stated in the *Ratnamālā*: 'Everything consists of the supreme *kalā*; [the types are] the Great (*mahā*), the Intermediate (*avāntara*), the Divine (*divya*), the Mixed (*miśra*), and another which is the fifth. (1.274)
"In the *Ratnamālā*," that is, in the *Śrīkularatnamālā*, it is "stated"—that is, by way of meaning and not by the literal words. Therein [it says]:
"That which is unseen, devoid of qualities, and free from what is to be rejected or accepted..."
That reality is taught as the foremost among all realities.
"He whose form is unseen is indeed sung of as 'the Peaceful' (Śānta).
From Him, His Will has emerged as Śakti, endowed with His attributes and qualities.
By such passages, it is shown that the supreme power of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī Parā Śakti) itself has emanated through the nature of various relationships.

It has been stated that every relationship, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), consists of the nature of another's power (parakalā). For this very reason, it is precisely this [power] which, following the path of emanation, has arrived upon the surface of the earth.
"O Goddess, the sixth [type] has been described according to the nature of its possession (*āveśa*).
With this, [the section] is concluded. "Mixed" (*miśra*) means divine-and-non-divine (*divyādivya*).
Regarding "mutually" (*anyonya*): in relation to the divine, the other is the mixed; and in relation to that, the other is the non-divine (*adivya*).

Indeed, conceptual construction arises in exactly three ways: as divine, non-divine, and both divine and non-divine. For this very reason, it is described here by the term *itaretara* (mutually). As it has been said:
"The great, the intermediate, the divine, and the fourth, which is both divine and non-divine."
"By way of the successive transmission, its characteristics are divided fivefold.
And this fivefold relationship [extends] from Śiva to Sadāśiva, from him to Anantanātha, from him to Śrīkaṇṭha, Nandikumāra, and the others, and from them as well.
This should be understood as occurring in sequence from the sages such as Sanatkumāra and others, and from them to humans and so forth.
As it is stated in that very same place:
Of Śiva, who is perfectly complete, supreme, and of immeasurable splendor,
there is his power known as Sādākhyā, whose sphere of activity is the agency of his own will.
The wise know that through that [Sattva], the first relationship is attained;
and furthermore, by means of Yoga, there is an intermediate [relationship] with Sādākhya, occurring in due order.
The second was proclaimed by the god Ananteśa;
furthermore, O Goddess, the third was Śrīkaṇṭha together with Nandin.

Having thus considered it as originating from the gods (deva) by means of two [factors], it is proclaimed as "divine" (divya) through the application of the sequence of exposition during the worship of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
"The fifth [type of relationship] is mutual, consisting of the nature of disciple and teacher;
thus this fivefold relationship has been proclaimed. || 274 ||
He explains the very nature of being the self of another's power:
"That which is the identity between the two distinct parties—the questioner and the speaker—is what is called [the state of being the self of another's power].
The questioner is, for example, Sadāśiva; the speaker is, for example, Śiva; by the word "that" (tat), [he refers to this identity].

The reflective awareness of the act of questioning: although these two [the questioner and the question] are distinct, there exists a relationship between them because of their identity within the firmness of consciousness regarding that very object;
for that [relationship] consists of both difference and non-difference, since in the state of absolute identity, even a trace of difference dissolves, characterized by being the self of all.
When fullness is attained, then there is the supreme connection.
Thus it is said: "Its relation and its transcendence consist in the manifestation of perfect oneness. (1.275)
For "otherness" (paratā) is characterized by the manifestation of perfect identity. Indeed, everything exists within the Perfect, and the Perfect exists everywhere;
this is present even in all five types of relations. Thus, it is rightly said: "Śarva consists of the supreme power. As it has been stated:
"O Supreme Sovereign, every relationship consists of the supreme power (parakalā);
it is great, intermediate, divine, mixed, non-divine, and beyond that. || 275 ||
He extends this very principle to other types of relationships as well:

"By this same method, other relationships expressed in the scriptures are also sufficient, through their connection with the state of being complete, such as the results [of practice] and so forth. (1.276)

He summarizes this very point: "In this way, this Goddess of Consciousness, by her very nature, is always animated by the triad beginning with the enunciation (uddeśa), and she is the embodiment of all scriptures. (277)

In this way—that is, in the manner described—this blessed Consciousness alone, by virtue of its own sovereignty, is at all times the very essence of the scripture through its threefold life-force consisting of the enunciation (uddeśa) and so forth;
the meaning is that Consciousness itself manifests in the form of the scripture. || 277 ||
In that regard, he first states the nature of the summary (uddeśa):

"Therein, the preliminary summary (puroddeśa) is said to consist of the divisions of the 'previously born' (pūrvaja) and the 'subsequently born' (anuja); the means consisting of the penetration of consciousness (vijñānābhighātōpāya) is the second, and the supreme means (parōpāya) is the third. (1.278)

The means of power (śāktopāya), the means of the person (naropāya), and then the seventh, the means of time (kālopāya); then the arising of the wheels (cakrodaya), the path of space (deśādhvā), the path of principles (tattvādhvā), and the differentiation of the principles (tattvabhedana). || 1-279 ||
The path of the levels (kalā) and so forth, the application of the paths, the descent of power (śaktipāta),
concealment, the commencement of initiation, and initiation itself— these [are discussed] in the ritual concerning the Samayin and the Pautrika.

The procedure for the objects of knowledge, the subtle initiation, the immediate departure [of the soul], the initiation by scales, the indirect initiation, the extraction of the mark, and the consecration. || 1-281 ||
The funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), the arrangement of the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), the description of the remaining modes of livelihood,
the worship of the Liṅga, the various festivals, the Pavitra rite and others, and that which arises from specific occasions.

The secret practice, the flood of mantras, the mandala, the ritual of the mudrās, unification within one's own essential nature, entry [into that state], and the integration of the scriptures. (1.283)
The statement of the purpose (*āyātikathana*) and the demonstration of the treatise’s worthiness of adoption (*upādeyatva-nirūpaṇa*).

It has been stated elsewhere that "enunciation" (*uddeśa*) is the mention by a general name, while "subsequent enunciation" (*anuja-uddeśa*) is the mention by a specific name; this latter is also called "division" (*vibhāga*). In that regard:
He states the preliminary summary with the words beginning "the breaker of consciousness" (*vijñānabhid*) and ending with "determination" (*nirūpaṇa*);

that is, [the state] wherein the consciousnesses, such as the *śāmbhava* and others, are differentiated. "One for whom the means has passed away" (*gatopāya*) means one who is without means (*anupāya*). "In the *pautrika* rite" means by resorting to the *pautrika* procedure. "Initiation" (*dīkṣā*)...
The connection is with what precedes. By implication, the phrase "the treatment of the objects of knowledge" (prameyaprakriyā) should be construed with the words "in the Pautrika rite.
As he will state:
"That was explained in the subsequent enumeration of the daily ritual, regarding the Pautrika rite."
Thus [ends the section] 278–283.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of composing such an extensive work?", he says:
"The wise person who always [recites] these thirty-seven... (1.284).
One who practices these daily recitations thoroughly shall become Bhairava in person;
for when one possesses complete awakening regarding the thirty-seven [topics], one becomes Bhairava. (1.285)
"What wonder is there that even ordinary men attain the state of Bhairava by his glance?
Thus has the description of the elder brother been told; now the younger brother is described. (1.286)
In the section on the shattering of consciousness, there is a sequential enumeration of everything;
in the second section, the distinctions regarding the means that have been traversed are explained. (1-287)

The state of being a reflection of universal consciousness, the sequence of the arising of reflective awareness, and the non-differentiation from the nature of mantras and so forth are discerned in the supreme means (paropāya). (1.288)

The refinement of conceptual thought, the reality of reasoning, and the true nature of the Guru; the lack of utility for the limbs of yoga, and the disregard for imagined icons and the like. || 1-289 ||

The arising of the wheel of consciousness, the potency of mantra, and the true nature of recitation and so forth—the equality of prohibition and injunction regarding these is discussed here in the context of the Śākta means (śāktopāya). (1.290)

Meditation on the intellect, the utterance of the principle of vital breath (prāṇatattva), and the nature of the conscious self—utterance is the characteristic of the path for entering into the interior of the supreme reality. 1.291

In the Āṇava [upāya], however, the instrument and the reality of the phonemes (varṇatattva) are described, as well as the conceptualization of the movement [of breath], the measurement of time, day and night, the transits [of the sun], and so forth. (1.292)
The diversity of withdrawal and the emergence of phonemes occur in the conceptualization of the path of time;
this emergence of the wheels occurs within the wheel [of consciousness] through the distinction between mantras and vidyās. (1.293)

The measurement of the worlds, their compendium, and the application of the principles—these two [topics] are contained within the description of the path of space and the determination of the path of the principles. (1.294)

The relationship of cause and effect, the determination of the sequence of the principles (tattvas), the properties of entities, the rule of the principles, and the description of the waking state and so forth. || 1.295 ||
This distinction of cognizers is examined within the division of the principles (tattva).
The nature of the kalās consists in the conceptualization of principles by means of numbers such as one, three, five, and so forth. (1.296)

The sequence of the division of the castes, the description of the foundational power (sarvādhāraśakti), and the investigation into the paths beginning with Kalā—up to this point, these matters are being analyzed. (1.297)

The shaking and laughter resulting from the contemplation of non-duality, the application of the [three] paths, the excess of number regarding impurities and so forth, the true nature [of reality], and the manifold variety of powers. (1-298)
The establishment of independence and the variety of concealment—this is the summary of what is to be said in the examination of the descent of power (śaktipāta). (1.299)
The disappearance of concealment, the attainment of fullness through knowledge, and the lack of utility for the upward departure (utkrānti) are established at the commencement of initiation. (1.300)

The examination of the disciple’s suitability and so forth, the conceptualization of the locations and the divisions of the sites, the varieties of the general placement (sāmānyanyāsa), and the vessel for the offering (arghapātra)—this is the purpose [of this section]. (1.301)
The suitability of the substances, the worship, the external worship at the door, entry, the nature of the directions, and the purification of the body, vital breaths, and so forth; || 1.302 ||

The variety of specific placements, the vessel for the special *argha* offering, the worship of the body, and the worship consisting of the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*cit*), and the internal sound (*adhvan*). (1.303)

The excellence of the collection of other scriptures, the worship of the cakra in every respect, the acquisition of the sacred field, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the worship of the Earth and Gaṇeśa. (1–304)

The worship of the weapon-mantra, the fire-ritual, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) pertaining to the fire, the libation (tarpaṇa), the preparation of the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the purificatory rites ending with the tooth-stick; || 1-305 ||
The ritual of Śiva’s hand, the consideration of the preparation of the bed, the ritual concerning dreams, and the observances—this is the summary. (1.306)
In this fifteenth chapter concerning the procedure for initiation,
there shall be the contemplation of the nature of the mandala and the detailed ritual for the offering of the sacrificial victim.

The satisfaction of the fire, the illumination of one's own essential nature within the body of the disciple, the procedure for the deposition on the paths (adhvan), and the manifold variety of the purified and the purifier. (1.308)
The varieties of initiation, the supreme deposition (nyāsa), the purpose of the existence of mantra,
and the varieties of the rite of union (yojanikā) and so forth— these shall be treated here in the sixteenth chapter.
The arrangement of the thread, the purification of the principles (tattvas), the burning of the bonds, and then the union;
likewise, the divisions of the paths—thus has it been described in the ritual concerning the *pautrika* [offering].
The state of being devoid of birth and so forth, as well as the clear distinction between mantras—this shall be found in the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Concise Initiation. (1.311)
The examination of the digits (kalā), the placement (nyāsa) of the sword and other implements, the movement within the body,
and the procedure for the knowledge of Brahman— thus has the immediate transference (sadyaḥsamutkrama) been described.
The examination of authority, the internal purification, and the procedure for the scales—
this constitutes the entirety of what is to be said in the twentieth chapter.
The procedure for the dead and the living, the instruction on the net, the group of consecrations, and the consideration of strength and weakness—this is the rule in the twenty-first chapter. (1.314)

In the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*, it must be clearly stated: "hearing [the teaching]," "authorization," "purification," "falling away from sin," and "the cutting off of doubt. (1.315)

The examination, the acting as a teacher, the vow, the seizing of the intellect, its division, and the state of being a means of accomplishment—this much constitutes the procedure for the consecration (abhiṣeka). (1.316)
Now, the qualified candidate, the consecration, and its purpose—these matters are to be discussed and examined in the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Final Sacrifice. (1.317)
The purpose here is the bestowing of enjoyment and liberation; the procedure is clear.
This is the summary of contents for the twenty-fifth daily lesson, the *Śrāddhaprakāśa*. (1.318)

The purpose [of this work] is the remaining conduct, the daily worship, the supreme [worship] on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the various forms of the Liṅga, and the description of the rosary (akṣasūtra). || 1.319 ||
The classification of worship shall be stated in the exposition of the adoration of the *liṅga*;
thereafter follows the division of occasional rites and the rule for their purpose. (1.320)

The divisions of the chapters, their specific details, the discussion on the wheels (*cakras*), their worship, and the determination of the purpose of the worship on the days of the Guru and others, as well as at the beginning and end of the day and so forth. || 1-321 ||

The examination of death, the ritual for the assembly of the Yoginīs and so forth, the method of exposition, the method of hearing [the teachings], and the method of worshiping the Guru—this much [is the scope]. (1.322)

In the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Occasional," it is established that there is a distinction between the qualified subject and the Self, as well as the Kula lineage of the Siddhas and their consorts. (1.323)
The ritual of worship, the ritual of the messenger, the sequence of the secret Upaniṣad, initiation, consecration, and awakening—these are treated in the twenty-ninth chapter. (1.324)
The true nature of mantras and their potency are described in the thirtieth [chapter];
as well as the varieties of tridents and lotuses, and the description of the Vyomeśa, Svastika, and other [mudrās]. (1.325)
It should be explained in detail in the thirty-first chapter:
the distinctions between the subordinate and the primary, the essential nature, and the investigation of *vīrya*. (1.326)

"The division of the *kalās* has been declared in the exposition of the *mudrās*"—and so forth. It is not only thus; there is yet another greatness of this [work]. Thus he says, ending with: "Thus, [he taught] the seven-plus-... in the phrase "in the exposition. Here, by the author of the text, in accordance with reality...
Thus, thirty-seven chapters have been composed in both collective and individual form.

Just as everything exists in a gross form within the earth-element due to the predominance of duality (*bheda*), so too will that which is to be explained here [be understood]—as it has been said: "The enumeration of everything in due order."

Regarding the phrase "in the supreme means" (*paropāye*): this refers to the Śāmbhava means, and its nature is essentially free of conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*), as has already been largely explained.

That [non-conceptual state] can only exist when there is an absence of duality; and that [absence of duality] occurs when the entire universe, consisting of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), is of the single nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-ekarūpatva*). In that state, because the universe, which is of the nature of the signified, exists as a reflection within consciousness (*cit-pratibimbatvena*).

Because the universe—which is twofold, consisting of both the general and the particular, as well as the expressive aspect—is non-different from mantra and so forth through the sequence of the arising of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is said to be of one and the same nature with consciousness (*saṃvit*) due to its non-excess over it; herein, these three objects of knowledge are introduced. And [the same applies] to that which pertains to Śakti.

Since form is indeed conceptual, the cultivation of conceptualization itself was taught first; and since that [cultivation] is expressed by means of reasoning (*tarka*) through the discernment of what is to be abandoned and so forth, the reality (*tattva*) of that [reasoning] follows immediately after. Furthermore, it is the very manifestation of reasoning, whose essence is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), by the power of which alone—

Thus, it has been stated that the attainment of the true guru constitutes its essential nature (*satattva*). Furthermore, since reasoning (*tarka*) alone is the direct limb of yoga, other limbs of yoga are of no utility;

for reasoning, being of the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), strikes down the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) born of Māyā which produce the sense of duality, as these are merely imagined.

From that very [state] comes disregard for ritual worship and the like, because the impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-conceptuality has become firm; from that arising alone comes the emergence of the wheel of consciousness (*saṃvic-cakra*), and in that emergence alone lies the supreme vitality (*vīrya*) of mantras. Furthermore, such reflective awareness (*amarśa*) itself is the true essence of recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
For this very reason, since there is no duality within consciousness, prohibitions and injunctions are equal.
Thus, these nine objects of knowledge (*prameya*) have been introduced. Similarly, in the case of the individual soul (*āṇava* [impurity]) and so forth,

the fact that meditation (*dhyāna*) and other such practices are directly conducive to them has not been stated word-for-word by us, because it is self-evident, for fear of excessive prolixity, and because it will be determined later on.
"It has been explained" is to be understood by oneself. || 284–326 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Why was the subsequent enumeration not made at the beginning of the *Ekīkārāhnika* and other chapters?", he says:
"Because [the manifestation] from the thirty-two principles starting from the one called Īśa is clearly evident. (1.327)
Since there is no difference [between them], that other heading was not mentioned here;
therefore, that chapter on Mudrā, whose essential nature is the thirty-second principle (*tattva*),
follows immediately after the one numbered thirty-two, which is called Īśa.

The thirty-third chapter is titled "The Unification" (*ekīkārāhnika*); from that point onward, because differentiation no longer predominates, no further enumeration was made—this is the meaning. || 327 ||
Now, one might object: "If there is no difference from this point onward, why was the enumeration of separate chapters (āhnika) performed at all? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And because it is to be known as the primary [subject], there is the sequence of further chapters. (1.328)
Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says:
"Thus the method of enumeration has been declared for the sake of easy comprehension;
now its definition and examination are set forth in due order. (1.329)
"Of this"—that is, of the collection of objects of knowledge (prameyajāta) that has been indicated. || 329 ||
Now he summarizes the very subject matter of this daily lesson:

The Self is the abiding state of the light of consciousness; it is partless consciousness that has assumed a multitude of powers, and its essential nature, due to the veiling of its own majesty, takes on a bound form.
