Through the method of manifesting the nature of the light of the Self, there is liberation for him; and this liberation, which is manifold for that which possesses manifold forms, has been revealed here—this is the summary of the meaning. || 330 ||
In this context, first of all, the essential nature of the Self is a manifestation that is consciousness itself, distinct from the external manifestations belonging to the three domains;
and since consciousness is partless, it follows that it is one alone, consisting of an undivided manifestation. And for this very reason—

By the reasoning stated in such passages as, "And what is called power (*śakti*) is the very nature of the entity as conceived by the subject," the true nature of that Self consists of infinite powers embraced within itself;
thus, even while its essence is non-dual, it is precisely through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), characterized by the capacity to accomplish the most difficult tasks, that—
By concealing his own light— characterized by knowledge and agency that is unique and not shared with others— he manifests the duality consisting of the grasped and the grasper.
"Śiva himself has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu)."

By the reasoning stated in such passages, he is called "bound"; nevertheless, for that Self, liberation is indeed nothing other than its own return [to its true state], for "liberation is truly the manifestation of one's own nature, and the nature of the Self is consciousness... [and so forth].

By the reasoning stated in such passages, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the manifestation of one’s own splendor alone, characterized by the qualities of knowledge and agency; and it is for this very purpose that there exists this extensive apparatus consisting of those various infinite scriptures. Thus he says:
"And this [liberation]," and so forth; and this liberation—

For this [individual], whose level of experience is determined by the perception of various objects grasped [by the senses]—whose nature is manifold according to the reasoning stated in such passages as, "I am internally untainted by passion and the like; I am empty; I am devoid of agency"—or rather:

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "Thus, within the non-obscured portion of that non-inert part which is designated as the *pudgala*, the atom (*aṇu*), and so forth, manifold variety resides in many ways," [the reality] possesses variegated forms.
"Therefore, the Lord reveals His own full nature to a certain cognizer, while to another He does so through a gradual succession of parts and sub-parts.
By such statements, the manifold [nature]—consisting of the *śāmbhava* and other types of immersion—is made manifest; this is what is meant by "here."
In this chapter: the connection is with the phrase "this matter has been revealed by way of a summary"—that is, a concise treatment—of those two, namely bondage and liberation. || 330 ||

Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that liberation (*mokṣa*) is simply the manifestation of the true nature of the Self? And since the Self is one and indivisible, from where could there be any diversity even in liberation, which consists of that manifestation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
False knowledge is a cataract that gives rise to unequal defects of vision;
because of its presence, even that which is pure appears as a locus of impurity.
But that which is to be perceived, when encountered by the eye, [removes] the seal of the defect of cataracts.
Since it obstructs [the path] from afar, how could any suspicion of impurity arise therein?
*Timira*— which is indeed the *āṇavamala*, false knowledge consisting of the manifestation of duality and incomplete cognition—
produces defects such as the conceit of "self" (*ātman*) in what is not-self within the perfect vision of consciousness; thus, it exists because of the presence of false knowledge.
Although that knowledge is pure and full, it appears as the locus of impurity;

the meaning is simply this: by its own sovereignty, it manifests itself through an incomplete self—this is what is conventionally designated as that which must again be perceived as the goal, that which must necessarily be known.
I am the full knowledge whose sole essence is the supreme subject;
I am neither the vital breath, nor the body, nor the mind;
I am not the intellect, nor am I the notions of ego and mentation.

According to the principle that "I am indeed that which is the portion of knowledge here," when [the self] has ascended to the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through the process of unwinding,
it casts far away the seal of defect consisting of the false identification with the non-self, which arises from erroneous cognition.

"Should obstruct"—meaning he should conceal [the Self] within himself alone through the conceit of self-identification (ātmābhimāna). In that case, what suspicion of impurity could possibly arise? Not even the mere possibility exists; thus, according to the actual nature of reality, there is no such thing as bondage or liberation at all.
So what room is there for the possibility of any diversity therein?
And with this intention [it was said]:
"In reality, saṃsāra does not exist for embodied beings; what talk can there be of bondage?
For one who has never been bound, the act of liberation is futile."
"This delusion, which produces false ignorance, is like the error of [seeing] a snake in a rope or a ghost in a shadow;
do not abandon anything, do not grasp at anything, but desist and remain established in your own natural state.
Thus it has been said elsewhere. Furthermore, regarding "by darkness"—that is, by a specific eye disease affecting the vision—

Having observed that the collection of defects arising from ignorance—which is otherwise produced—is obstructed by the discerning eye acting as a salve and so forth, even the suspicion of impurity does not arise therein; thus, the simile is suggested (*dhvanita*).
Now, considering this treatise to possess supreme profundity, the author—

To those others who, not knowing the true nature of this matter, speak superficially and erroneously due to a mistaken understanding, he speaks as follows to mock them by means of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise): "O multitude of emotions, having forcibly invaded the hearts of people and making them dance..."
You sport about, concealing your own heart with various artful turns of expression.

As for that dullard who calls you "dull"—I consider him poorly trained by his self-conceited notion of being a man of taste; his very dullness is, I think, a matter for praise, since it allows for the possibility of his being equal to you.
That multitude of existents— the objects such as blue and so forth— having concealed the heart of the Self, which is the true nature of the Self,
forcibly overcomes the hearts— that is, the inner dispositions— of all people, that is, of every proponent.
"Today he will make us, who are non-existent, existent; or perhaps he will make us twofold—whether stationary or perishable, or distinct from one another or non-distinct.
Thus, through the states existing in the world that are intent on beholding the face of the Existent, I believe [he will transform us]."

"With hearts constrained by silence, they remain in a state of suffering"—by such and various other modes of expression, You cause them to dance; You sport—like an actor, You manifest in a non-ultimate form. Therefore, every disputant, even one who lacks aesthetic sensitivity (*asahṛdaya*), [is moved].

Considering himself to be possessed of a sensitive heart, and for that very reason ill-instructed, he— knowing nothing due to false pride— speaks of you, the multitude of states of being, as "insentient" (jaḍa), meaning unconscious;
therefore we conjecture that this speaker, in reality, [denies] the nature of consciousness.

If it is argued that because of the possibility of its similarity to you, it must possess existence and is therefore of an insentient nature (*jaḍātmā*), then this is a praise of it in a place where censure is due. For if those entities had no form whatsoever, then those who do not even know this are more insentient than the insentient themselves.

And how could there be a similarity with those things consisting of volition that results in censure?—this is the sense. Likewise, in the present case as well, let him who does not know the true nature of this treatise remain ignorant; on the contrary, he who speaks something else entirely is the one who is dull-witted, and not this [treatise].
The meaning is: there is some defect in the book. || 332 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then a request should be made to certain other learned persons for the sake of understanding this treatise, so that having understood the reality as it truly is, they do not harbor aversion toward it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

In this matter, those gurus who have shed their impurities, who know the higher and the lower, and who consist of the true being of Śiva, are authorized for this investigation; therefore, the request for the removal of the stain of fruitless hatred is rendered useless.
In this world, there are two kinds of persons: those upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has not occurred, and those upon whom it has occurred.

Among these, for the former—who though they may entreat hundreds of times—their minds do not even incline toward attaining this [knowledge]. One must pay heed to this point; one should not harbor aversion, as is the intent of the entreaty.

There is a lack of capacity [on the part of the teacher]. Furthermore, since others may proceed toward this realization of their own accord even without being requested, in that case too such a request would be useless. Thus he says: "The request for the removal of the stain of aversion. And what are those who have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) like?
Thus he says: "those whose impurities have fallen away. Those for whom impurity—that is, ignorance—has fallen away are such [as described].

And for this very reason, those who know the supreme (para), the primordial (ādimam), the unsurpassed (anuttara), the inferior (avaram), and the final (antya) emission (visarga)—the meaning is that they are knowers of the potency of mantra, which consists of the reflective awareness of the supreme "I" (parāhaṃparāmarśa). For this very reason...

"Consisting of the true being of Śiva" means, in other words, that they possess the knowledge whose sole essence is the supreme subject; for this very reason they are "gurus"— that is, teachers of the ultimate reality— and thus it is said that they alone are the supreme qualified candidates for the attainment of this [knowledge], since they are authorized for its investigation.
As he will say:
"The characteristic of the Guru is this much: he should make known both the first and the last [letters].
He is to be worshipped like me; he is a knower, Bhairava, whose very self is the deity."
Thus [ends the section]. || 333 ||

In this work, the author’s style is such that he employs a single verse to provide both the conclusion of one daily lesson (*āhnika*) and the commencement of the next, thereby demonstrating their mutual interconnection through the logic of cumulative accumulation; this is shown by the first half of the verse.
He concludes the meaning of this daily lesson (āhnika):

"In this *Tantrāloka* composed by Abhinava, completion has been reached in this first chapter (*āhnika*), which is skillful in manifesting the emergence of the distinctions within the reality of consciousness."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Divisions of Consciousness," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 1.
In the word *paṭau*, there is optional masculine inflection (*puṃvadbhāva*). May there be auspiciousness!
Having obtained a faultless birth from the illustrious Śṛṅgāraratha,
having acquired supreme proficiency in all branches of knowledge from the venerable Śaṅkhadhara,
and having attained mastery even in all the scriptures from the auspicious Śiva;
The first chapter has been explained by Jayaratha; it should be attended to here by the wise.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Varieties of Consciousness," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 1 ||
May this be an offering unto Śrī Śiva.
The Second Daily Lesson:
Viveka.
May Rudra—who is ever-victorious, who brings victory to those who bow before him, and who is himself without need of external means—be triumphant.
By virtue of being the Lord of Desire, whom does he not satisfy with every wish?
Now,

according to the principle that "he who is superior in qualities compared to another is said to be above him," the respective superiority of the *āṇava* and other means [of knowledge] is established here.
Since each preceding means is held to be [superior], the *anupāya* (the "no-means") is superior even to the *śāmbhava* [means] by virtue of its singular nature as the goal;
thus, with the second half [of the verse], he announces the commencement of another chapter in order to first describe the very nature of that [anupāya]:
Since the first word therein consists of uninterrupted and unsurpassed cognition, I shall commence this second treatise in order to determine its meaning. (2-1)
He states that very determination:
"Indeed, if the nature [of reality] were without means, what would be the purpose of teaching here?
The teaching would occur only once; thereafter, it would be called 'without means'. (2-2)

The word *vai* is used for emphasis; thus, the meaning is that there is no objective referent whatsoever. He provides the resolution right here with the words beginning "it would be [produced] all at once," and so forth. The term "teaching" (*deśanā*) is illustrative;
by this, the visions of the Siddhas and other such phenomena are also to be included, as it has been said:
The vision of the Siddhas and Yoginīs, the consumption of the sacrificial pap (caru),
the exposition [of the teachings], the transmission [of authority] in the scripture, the spiritual practice (sādhana), and service to the Guru.
"O fair-faced one, this is the summary of the methodless [approach], beginning with these words."

The word *sakṛt* means that the experience of the means (*upāya*) does not occur repeatedly; this is the sense. For this very reason, he says: "Thereafter, the state of being 'without means' (*anupāyatva*) is taught. For in the case of the individual means (*āṇava*) and so forth, instruction and the like, when cultivated repeatedly, bring about the attainment of the goal; thus, that status [of being a means] was stated there. But here, it is not so.

The word "thus" (*tathā*) signifies the lack of means (*anupāyatva*). Even though the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) has the sense of "smallness"—as in the expression "the girl is thin-waisted" (*anudarā kanyā*)—it implies here that [this method] is a "small means" (*alpopāyatva*). The underlying thought is: once that which is to be attained has already been attained, what is the use of meditations (*bhāvanā*) and the like, which are useless and cause only exhaustion? As it has been said:
Śiva does not appear through means; rather, they appear by His grace. He alone am I, self-luminous, shining as the very nature of the universe.
Having heard these words of the Guru once, some become resolved;
without further investigation, they shine, established as consisting of pure consciousness.
Thus [ends the verse]. 2.

One might object: "Why has the primary meaning—that this reality is indeed devoid of means by resorting to the position of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—not been explained here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This reality is without means; how [could it be realized] without a means?"
But as for those [beings] themselves, who possess such a nature, what indeed can we say to them? || 2-3 ||
"There must necessarily be some means, such as instruction, by which [one realizes] 'this is the reality that is without means';
otherwise, how could the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) be established without a means? Thus it was said:
'How [could it be] without a means? Therefore, there must necessarily be some means, such as a single instruction.
It must be cultivated; otherwise, there would be no realization of the supreme reality through the proper means. One might object:

"Since some are seen to attain what is to be attained by themselves alone through the power of their own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), what is the use of a small amount of unrefined instruction consisting of a single teaching and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

By the words "by itself" (*svayam*) and so forth, [the author means]: "that" refers to the nature consisting of supreme light, which is beyond all means; what can we say of it?—for the scripture does not proceed by virtue of that [nature] as its primary subject; such is the intention.
As it has been said:
"For one who knows reality, the scripture is as a blade of grass... and so forth.
It is with this very intention that it was said:
"Whoever is an excellent person desiring to cross the ocean of saṃsāra— neither one who knows it perfectly nor a fool— is fit to be a student of this treatise."
In such passages, it is stated that one who knows [the truth] absolutely has no further need for the scripture;

therefore, we—who are ourselves limited perceivers—speak something only for those who, though possessing the scripture as their sole divine eye regarding the unseen reality, desire to ascend [to it] and have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). For them:
It has been stated that without such a means (upāya), the attainment of the goal (upeya) can never occur; as he will say: "For a person whose mind is not pure, there is no grace without a means."
Thus [ends section] 3.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then let some small portion of a means be taught, by which the attainment of the goal may occur with ease for those to be instructed; what is the use of other means that entail great exertion? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That fourfold form which has been described as belonging to the all-pervading consciousness should be understood as its very nature; for that [nature] is eternally manifest and all-pervading. (2.4)

That form of consciousness which has been described as fourfold— by way of the divisions beginning with *anupāya*— should be understood as the very sovereignty of the all-pervasive Supreme Lord; for it is He alone who, through His own sovereignty and by means of the application of various degrees of extreme diminution and so forth, [manifests] in the diverse nature of those to be instructed.

Vibrating, it would manifest the various diversities of those respective means (upāya) in accordance with that very [vibration]. Now, one might ask: "How is it that the One alone manifests in manifold forms? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For He... and so forth. "Ever-arisen" (nityodita) means His primordial nature is never lost; for this very reason, He is "all-pervasive" (vibhu), that is, omnipresent.
The meaning is that it persists even at the time of perceiving those various diversities. || 4 ||
Therefore he says:
"That which shines forth through these countless inherent natures—some enter it by way of parts and sub-parts, while others enter it without parts. (2.5)
"By so many"—that is, by four; "innumerable"—due to their various internal subdivisions; "by that"—because of being manifested through manifold natures. || 5 ||

Not only is there this variety here, but there is yet another as well—thus he says: "Moreover, because of the connection with difference due to dependence on means and so forth, the variety of even the means itself cannot be denied, owing to its difference from that [result]. (2.6)

Regarding the phrase "of the means (upāya) also"—the word "also" (api) is displaced in its order; therefore, it should be explained as: "or rather, it is not to be warded off, because it is other than that.
And this has been determined at length in the very first chapter, so no further effort is made here.
Having thus spoken by way of digression, he states the subject at hand:
In that regard, the procedure for those pure-souled ones who worship their own consciousness as Bhairava, which is without means (nirupāya), is now being proclaimed.

For those who have been pierced by the most intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*), who are liberated from the stain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and who are possessed of the Bhairavic self-awareness— which is full and therefore without means (*anupāya*) or dependence— their *vidhi* (rule/method) is the manner consisting of the sequence of immersion into that full consciousness.
"It is proclaimed pre-eminently"—that is to say, it is spoken as being endowed with logical reasoning. || 7 ||
He says that very thing:

"In that regard, first of all, the yoga of action does not deserve to be the means (*upāya*). For a means indeed exists when an instrument (*karaṇa*) has been set forth; and therefore, it must necessarily be complete."

There is no dispute among all [schools] regarding this, yet it is not so in this case: since action and the rest are established solely within consciousness because they are objects of awareness, how could they attain the status of means toward that [consciousness] without the power of consciousness itself? On the contrary, therefore—
It is logical that consciousness is the means for the external manifestation of action and the other [categories].
Therefore he says:
"On the contrary, that [effect], having arisen from that [cause], is clearly perceived as distinct from it. (2.8)
"Therefore" means from that reality of consciousness which is devoid of means. || 8 ||
Now, if it is argued that its action and so forth are not a producer (*kāraka*) but rather a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), that too is not tenable; thus he says:
"If it is said that [the means] is merely a means for cognition, then let it be called cognition."
Luminosity belongs to that which is self-luminous; how then could that [luminosity] come from another in that case? (2.9)

In this regard, the insentient (*jaḍa*), being by nature non-luminous, does not manifest itself to its own self, but rather to another; thus, its manifestation is solely that of another. The sentient (*ajaḍa*), however, being by nature luminous, manifests only to its own self and not to another; thus, its manifestation is not that of another, but its very own.
Light; for if that too were illuminated by another, it would be insentient (*jāḍya*) because its nature would be non-luminous.

Therefore he says: "In self-luminous [consciousness], how could that [luminosity] come from another? Thus, luminosity is established. In this way, even another [entity] must either be self-luminous or otherwise; if it were self-luminous, it would be identical to the first one.

Let it be said that [the Self] exists as such; what is the purpose of this [argument]? For if it were otherwise, even that [Self] would fall into insentience. Thus, since it is luminosity, if there were a dependence on another cognizer to illuminate it, an infinite regress would result; therefore, for all [beings],...
Because its nature would be non-luminous, nothing at all would be manifest; thus, this entire world would be blind.
Regarding this, he says:
"What need is there for arguments to establish that the reality of consciousness is self-luminous?
In its absence, the entire universe would be non-luminous due to its insentience. (10)
"What is the use of many arguments?"—he says this because there is no purpose in numerous arguments;
for there is indeed this one argument that transcends all others: if consciousness were not self-luminous, nothing at all would be manifest. || 10 ||
Now, one might object: "If external means such as ritual action (*kriyā*) and the like are indeed ineffective here, then should one resort to means such as the knowledge of the Guru?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Whatever means there may be, whether external or internal, all of that depends upon Him; how then could it possess the status of being a means toward that [end]? (2.11)
"Whatever" means that which is taught in various scriptures; "all" means whether external or internal;
"subsisting on its very face" means that its accomplishment is dependent upon consciousness (saṃvit). The underlying sense is:
how could that, depending upon whose accomplishment something else is established, itself become a means (upāya) for that [latter]? || 11 ||
Therefore he says:
"Abandon your attentions; indeed, where exactly do you apply your attention? Discern that for yourself."
Indeed, it is not fitting for that which is incomplete to be focused upon, nor does that which is incomplete attain the state of reality. (2-12)
In this context, one who is being instructed must first reflect for themselves on what is to be attended to:
Is it the complete form or the incomplete form? Now, attending to the complete form is not appropriate;
for "attending" (avadhāna) is indeed a state of one-pointedness directed toward a specific object of attention, and therefore—
That which is dominated by differentiation is incapable of attaining any fruit whatsoever. || 12 ||

Therefore, since even attention (*avadhāna*) is afflicted by incapacity and futility, what can be said of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like, which are animated by that [attention], when they lack the status of being a means? Thus he says:
"Therefore, for cultivation and the like, whose life-breath is attention, on the supreme path..."
In the tradition of Bhairava, how can there be direct means? (2-13)
"In Bhairavī" means in the Full [state]. || 13 ||
What, then, can be said regarding those who, even by this means, pursue the supreme reality which is beyond all means?
To this he says:
"Even those who discern that very nature directly through the means..."
Surely those dull-witted ones desire to hold up glowworms for the purpose of perceiving the sun.
As it has been said:
"While Your true nature is immediate and remains manifest everywhere,
those by whom means are elaborated surely do not know You."
Thus [ends the section]. 14.
Right here he states another reason as well:
"Furthermore, whatever is considered an external or internal means, that is merely the nature of Light, the very innate body of Śiva himself. (2.15)

In this context, whatever is intended as a means (upāya), is it non-manifest or manifest? If it were non-manifest, it would possess no form whatsoever; thus, how could it assume the status of a means? If, however, it is manifest, then it is Śiva, whose very nature is light.
It remains thus established, for nothing else whatsoever can be logically established apart from that;

so, of what could there be the state of being a means? For a means must be distinct from the goal to be attained (*upeya*), and since that is not tenable here, what indeed is the meaning of the relationship between means and goal? || 15 ||
It is not only meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like that are intended as means; rather, even other things are so. Thus he says:
"Blue, yellow, pleasure, and so forth—pure consciousness alone is Śiva. In this supreme non-duality, whose nature is light, what else could there be? (2.16)
The relationship between means and end would be nothing other than mere manifestation. || 2-17 ||

Even though the status of meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the like as means is well-established, [the author] has stated "what else? so that there may not be even the slightest possibility of anything else being considered a means—something where the very possibility of being a means might otherwise arise. (17)

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can this universally established dualistic convention be denied? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This is duality, this is difference, and this is non-duality."
This Supreme Lord shines forth as having the very nature of light.
The intention is that even dualistic discourse, because it is manifest, is of the very nature of manifestation;
and this is to indicate that this is the view of many disputants, which is why the phrase "this difference" is taken up again.
And just as in the manifestation of non-duality, the Supreme Lord alone, whose nature is manifestation, appears.
Likewise, in order to hint at the analogy even when there is the appearance of duality, the phrase "even this 'non-duality'" has been employed. || 18 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the external object, because it is manifest, is of the nature of light itself; but what follows from its mutual difference [from the subject]? Does this not result in duality? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"On this level, pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, consciousness, and the insentient..."
Like the words "ghaṭa" and "kumbha," those words have a single meaning, and that [meaning] is indeed one and the same. (2-19)

"On this ground" means in the state of supreme non-duality; "having a single object" means those for whom the sole object or denotable referent is Light itself. For if pleasure, pain, and so forth were to possess some fixed, individual form distinct from Light, then [the following] would indeed be the case.
The intention is that there may even be such a possibility; for this very reason, others have stated:
"The jar knows through my self, and I know through the jar's self," and so forth. Now, if this is so, then...
Might there still be duality even with the intention that words denote those [objects]? To this he says:
"And those words too are one alone. "One" means that, because they are being experienced, they are nothing other than experience itself. || 19 ||
Now, one might object: "If blue, pleasure, and so forth are indeed manifestation because they are manifesting, then in what form do they manifest?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For how indeed could an unmanifest portion manifest within that which is manifest?
Or, if that [portion] were manifest, its dualities would be sublated. (2.20)
Alternatively, if that [object] is not manifest, how can it be said to have the nature of a real entity?
For this very reason, its being a particularity of manifestation is not tenable. (2.21)

Regarding the phrase "the non-luminous aspect": it refers to an insentient object such as pleasure and so forth. The question "how indeed" means "in what form. In that regard, if it were to manifest solely through the nature of luminosity, then there would be a defect in the very essence of that blue, pleasure, or other object—namely, its fixed external nature as blueness and so on.
One should not fear that [the object] would be reduced to mere light; rather, if it were to manifest through a fixed form whose nature is non-luminous,
there could be no certainty regarding its existence at all,
for the essential nature of blue and other such objects has never been perceived without luminosity.
Furthermore, the verbal expression "it shines by means of a non-luminous nature" would be empty;

thus he says "non-luminous," and so forth. Moreover, luminosity shines even in what is not blue and so on, setting aside blue and the like, for blue and such are merely adventitious conditions (*upādhi*). That...

And because [these distinctions] consist merely in the unfolding of its own sovereignty, they are not real; thus, the one undivided Light alone unfolds, by whose very majesty this universe—consisting of various appearances such as blue and so forth—manifests. For this very reason, he says: "The state of being a particularity of the Light is not tenable. The word "therefore" (ataḥ) refers to this.
Because the one and undivided Light alone manifests itself through various appearances (ābhāsa). [Objection:

But surely there is indeed a difference between these, such that "the manifestation of blue is one thing, and the manifestation of yellow is another. Why, then, was it said that "it is not tenable for them to be specific instances of the Light"? [Response: This is not so; [the difference] is merely adventitious (aupādhika).

This is the distinction, and it has been demonstrated many times that it is not real: for blue and other such objects, being manifestations, are essentially of the nature of manifestation; thus, what could be differentiated by what? Indeed, a thing is not differentiated by its own self—this has been stated: "And [there is no differentiation] within consciousness, whose sole form is manifestation."

"There is indeed another consciousness. For if one were to employ the conventional usage of difference based on a distinction in essential nature (*svarūpa*), it would amount to stating nothing other than that [consciousness] has the form of the manifestation of a single difference; thus, it would be like an elephant's bath (uselessly washing away only what was already clean).
Consequently, it would again result in the conclusion that "there is only one undivided consciousness," and so forth. And thus...

Space and time as well, resting solely upon the state of manifestation and being manifest themselves, penetrate into the very identity of manifestation; how then could they be the instigators of difference within manifestation? Or, if one were to admit that these two are distinct from manifestation, [then they would not exist] here at all.

Since [the concepts of] permanence and omnipresence lack the capacity to produce differentiation, there is only one undivided manifestation; thus, those others who desire to establish alternative doctrines have been thoroughly refuted.
Thus he says:
"Therefore, when this doctrine that 'this is a single light' is well-established here, those who maintain the theory of distinct cognitions are truly shut out from afar. (2.22)
Now, one might object: "If distinct cognitions are not possible, then for what purpose is the word 'one' (eka) employed here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Pure luminosity alone has been declared, because of the negation of non-luminosity."
The meaning of the word "one" (eka), however, is not a number that pertains to a distinction between individual consciousnesses. (2-23)
It is non-manifest—first of all, external objects such as blue and so forth, which are to be manifested, have been negated;
therefore, in the phrase "only manifestation exists," the word *eka* (one/alone) functions here in the sense of being without a companion (*asahāya*). As it has been said:
"The meaning of the word *eka* is declared to be pure manifestation alone," and not that it possesses a differentiation within manifestation.
Thus, the meaning of number, characterized by one, two, three, and so forth, is that by which even other philosophical systems may be conceived as objects to be excluded. || 23 ||
For this very reason, even a mere conventional usage that suggests duality is not perceived here; thus he says:
"This is not the Great Goddess Śakti, because she does not depend on another;
nor is this the God Śaktimat, because he does not serve as the support for anything. (2.24)
This is not the object of meditation because of the absence of a meditator; it is not the meditator because of the exclusion of the object of meditation.
It is not the object of worship because of the absence of a worshiper; it is not the worshiper because of the absence of an object of worship. (2.25)

There is no mantra, nor is there one who is to be addressed with a mantra; there is no master who utters the mantra. There is no initiation, nor an initiator, nor even Maheśvara as the recipient of initiation.

"This" refers to the supreme light whose nature has been explained. For words such as "power" (śakti) and "possessor of power" (śaktimat), being relational terms, are eternally dependent; thus, they find rest only in their own referents without implying another. Therefore, the linguistic usage performed by them—

It would necessarily be established upon difference; however, in this light (*prakāśa*), which is the single self of the supreme subject, there is no difference whatsoever. Thus, it could never descend to the level of mere conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-mātratā*).
For this reason, this is not *śakti* (power), for that [power] exists only by depending upon a supreme possessor of power (*śaktimant*).

Thus, because there would be no dependence [on anything else] when difference manifests, the thesis that "light alone is one" would be undermined; likewise, this linguistic usage of the term "possessor of power" (*śaktimat*) would also not be possible, for that too functions only by presupposing an object characterized as "power," and thus difference itself would result. In this way...

It should be understood that this applies even to the object of meditation and so forth; [the term] "mantra" refers to the one who is addressed by the mantra, such as the *praṇava*, or the one who instructs, the reciter of the mantras.
It does not refer to initiation (*dīkṣā*), because that depends upon an agent and an object;
and in this context of Maheśvarī, sovereignty (*prabhutva*) is the cause. (24–26)

For this very reason, he states that nothing whatsoever which could produce differentiation exists here: "In this state, which is devoid of agent, object, and action, there is no [rite] beginning with the selection of a place, the posture, the suspension [of breath], the offering of water, and the invocation, and ending with the dismissal. (2.27)

*Sthāna* (the place) is the Lord’s abiding by means of the *sthāpana-mudrā*; *āsana* (the seat) is the orientation toward worship by means of the *saṃnidhāna-mudrā*; *nirodha* (restraint) is remaining motionless in that very state; the *ardha-aṣṭāṅga* (eightfold half-offering); and *saṃdhāna* (unification).

The subject matter concerns mantras and so forth: *āvāhana* (invocation) is the act of making present that which was not present; *visarjana* (dismissal) is the act of making absent that which has been made present.
Regarding these [ritual acts] beginning with invocation and ending with dismissal, the qualifying term "the agent" contains the reason for their existence as named entities.

And so forth. Since agents and the like have as their sole ultimate reality conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and since Light—being of the singular nature of the supreme subject—is beyond conceptualization, it cannot be designated by any designation whatsoever; thus it was said: "This is not a power," and so on. (27)
And this is not established by reasoning alone; rather, it is also established by scripture. Thus, he corroborates it with the *Śrībhargaśikhā*:
"It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor is it devoid of both."
For that state is difficult to discern; this unsurpassed [state] is something beyond description. (2-28)
For that entity which appears as "this" and consists of limitation is, in the world, like a jar; however, Bhairava is not such. (2-29)

In the world, whatever object appears as being present before one as "this," a positive entity (bhāva) distinguished from its own class, that alone is designated as "existent" (sat), just as in the case of "a jar"; this is the manifestation whose nature was explained immediately above.

Furthermore, that which is overflowing with infinite manifestation is not "thus"—that is to say, it does not possess such a form—because it is undivided by virtue of being the essence of the Great Being (mahāsattā); consequently, it cannot be designated by the term "existent" (sat). This is the meaning. (28–29)
If that is so, would it not then be subject to the linguistic convention of being "non-existent"? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Non-existence is non-manifestation; it has no utility whatsoever.
Manifestation alone is the supreme existence of all things; thus, what is called 'non-existence' is simply non-manifestation."

It is said to have the nature of being nothing at all, like, for example, the horn of a hare; and for this very reason, it is not useful for any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) whatsoever—it does not perform any purposeful action at all. Light (*prakāśa*), however, is not like that—thus he says:
He is the life of the universe, truth, and his sole nature is light. (2.30)

Of the universe—of everything consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious—it is the ultimate life-force; it is the animator by virtue of its nature as *sphurattā* (vibrant manifestation), for without it, nothing at all would manifest, as it has been said: "and [it] is whose sole essence is light."
Thus, because it possesses manifold forms, the implication is that it would not even be subject to the linguistic convention of being called "non-existent. || 30 ||
For this very reason, He is not even of the nature of both existent and non-existent; thus he says:
"But for these very two reasons, He is neither dual-natured nor devoid of both.
For since He shines as the self of all, in what form could He be described? (2.31)
By these two—namely, by the two characteristics just mentioned, which consist of being uninterrupted and being manifest—[the author] raises the objection:
"But if this is so, would he not then transcend the two forms consisting of existence and non-existence? Anticipating this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "I am the two," etc.: even at the time when existence and non-existence appear, it is indeed that very [Self] which shines supremely; so how could it be abandoned by both the existent and the non-existent? Therefore, he says: "For this shines as the soul of all. In this way, this [reality] truly becomes one with the nature of the supreme subject; otherwise, it would not.
The intended meaning is that, because its nature is unconditioned, it can never fall into the state of conceptualization; as it has been said:
"O All-pervasive Lord, [the Absolute] is necessarily beyond both the supreme non-existence and existence."
"And since you are other than both the non-existent and the existent, you consist of both existence and non-existence.
Likewise:
"Neither is your form quiescent, nor arisen, nor even intermediate."
"O Hari, Your form is form, which cannot be described by anything.
Therefore, we do not know by what imagined form this is being said;
for this state is difficult to discern for those limited subjects (māyā-pramātṛ) whose intellects are afflicted by conceptual construction (vikalpa).
The meaning is that [this state] is indeed impossible to know by means of the aforementioned reasoning; however,

for those who have directly realized the reality of the Supreme Self and whose mental activity is free from conceptual construction, this shines forth as surpassing all else, being a dense mass of the wonder of supreme bliss consisting solely of their own direct experience.
Thus it has been said: "This is some unsurpassed [state]. || 31 ||
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:

"In the venerable *Triśirobhairava*, the supreme state is described as having the nature of supreme gnosis (*parajñāna*), being the womb of power (*śaktigarbha*) by virtue of the power residing within its interior. (2.32)

The intention here is that this form of supreme knowledge (*parajñāna*) has been taught by the Lord in order to resolve the Goddess’s question, "O God, what is supreme knowledge? He recites that very [teaching] beginning with "by power" (*śaktyā*), etc.;
for that which is this supreme state is pregnant with power; it is power itself.

That whose essence (*garbha*) and core (*sāra*) is denoted by terms such as "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*) and "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*), and which is not distinct from that [consciousness]—thus he says: "by the power (*śakti*) abiding within the womb. For by that very power called sovereignty, the "womb" is the interior, which is identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-aikātmya*).

The meaning is that it proceeds by means of that supreme limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*), characterized by its own nature which consists of that [limit]; for otherwise, this [consciousness] would not possess supremacy at all, as it has been said:
"They know the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of manifestation to be its very nature; otherwise, [it would be nothing]."
"Even though light is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient thing such as a crystal.

For this very reason, [the Lord] abides in His own nature within power, which is His freedom—meaning He exists at all times in that very form; for this same reason, He is "pregnant with power" (śaktigarbha).

The meaning is that apart from the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), no other powers exist for Him; for it is that very [power] which is designated by various names due to the influence of the limiting conditions (upādhi) of this or that object to be desired and so forth—this is the intended sense.
As it has been said:

"Therefore, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is endowed with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone; even His possession of manifold powers is inseparable from that very power. Thus, autonomous consciousness is the ultimate reality.

The essential meaning is this: according to the principle stated above, the supreme reality is precisely the Light (prakāśa) itself—unconditioned in its essential nature, endowed with absolute freedom (svātantrya), and free from conceptual construction (avikalpaka). || 32 ||
For this very reason, because it cannot tolerate any fixed exclusion, it does not fall within the scope of conceptualization; thus he says:
"It is neither existence nor non-existence, nor both, because it is beyond the range of words. It has ascended to the state of the ineffable, abiding in power while yet devoid of power. (2.33)

The term "from the non-domain" (*agocarāt*) is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is emphasized; thus, the meaning is that because it is beyond the domain of words, it has ascended to the level of the ineffable (*akathyapadavīrūḍha*). And all of this has already been explained more than once, so no further effort is made here. || 33 ||
And those who are attentive to this are indeed the ones who have accomplished their purpose; thus he says:
"Those who are purified by the supreme reality of established consciousness, having ascended the path of the Absolute (Anuttara), are no longer constrained by means. (2.34)

Thus— by means of what has been stated, such as the teacher’s instruction and so forth— that consciousness which has taken root, having attained its growth through the realization of identity with that [Reality],
is purified by its ultimate reality— the manifestation of all things as being the self of all.

Having been rendered fit vessels for supreme non-duality through the removal of the impurities of differentiation and transformation, they are therefore unrestrained by any external or internal means distinct from themselves— being independent of such means— they abide on the path of the Absolute (anuttara-patha) due to its density as the wonder of full bliss.

The meaning is: those who have come to rest on the path of the expansion of consciousness—which transcends all—having attained identity with that [reality] through abiding in their own innate nature (*svarasa*). As it has been said:
"Abide exactly as you are; do not go outside or within."
"Abandon the multitude of transformations through the expansion of pure consciousness alone.
Likewise:
"The yogi, resting in the power of bliss, becomes one with the equal flavor [of all things]."
Thus it is said:
"There is no other means whatsoever than the realization of one's own true being;
the yogi who follows that very [realization] and remains established in himself shall become happy."
Thus [ends the section]. 34.
And what follows from that? He says:
"To them, this entire circle of existence appears as if standing right before them, dissolved by the fire of the Bhairava of consciousness. (2.35)

For them—those characterized by immersion through the *anupāya* (the methodless)—this entire circle of objective phenomena (*bhāvamaṇḍala*), although appearing as something external in relation to the body and so forth, [is understood thus]:
"This has arisen from me alone; it is reflected in me alone."

The meaning is that, according to the principle beginning with "And this [universe] is non-different from me," it manifests as consisting solely of full consciousness (*pūrṇasaṃvinmayatayā*). As it has been said:
"Just as wood, leaves, stones, and the like, having fallen into a salt-lake (*rumā*),"
"So too do all phenomena [contribute] to the state of saltness within the conscious self.
Thus [ends verse 35].
Therefore, he says:

"The conceptualizations of these [beings] regarding the portions of pleasure and pain, as well as fear and anxiety, have come to rest solely in the state of the supreme, thought-free immersion. (2.36)

For these, there is no mantra, no meditation, no worship, nor even conceptualization; there is no delusion whatsoever, from the level of the initiate (samayin) up to that of the master (ācārya). (2.37)

Not only do their mundane conceptualizations amount to nothing because they have fallen into a state consisting of non-conceptual immersion, but even their supramundane conceptualizations do so as well—thus he says, “of these,” and so forth; “conceptualization” refers to [the visualization of] the abode and so on. (36–37)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how could there be a 'subsistence on remnants' (śeṣavṛtti) for him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one whose nature is to shatter the entire system of constraints, there is no purpose whatsoever in subsisting on remnants other than [the act of] bestowing grace. (2.38)

"All"— meaning every restriction prescribed in the scriptures, such as the rules "this must be done" and "this must not be done"— is itself the *tantra* because it is that which is stretched out (like a warp), namely the web of threads that initiates a cloth or similar object; [the term refers to] the severing or breaking of that [web], by one who possesses the nature of a chisel, like a sharp weapon.

—this is the meaning. For just as a saw cuts wood, so too does this [yogin], having entered into the state beyond means (anupāya), cut through the constraints of the scriptures; the sense is that for one who has already ascended, there is no longer any contraction resulting from those [scriptural rules]. Indeed, scripture is intended only for those who desire to ascend and are still to be instructed.

It was stated immediately prior that [the Lord] is the "director"; for this very reason, because He has already accomplished all that was to be done within His own self, His activity exists solely for the sake of favoring others—thus he says: "Not out of favor," meaning "nothing whatsoever," such as the maintenance of the rules of conduct (*samaya*). || 38 ||
To this he says:
Perceiving some task of its own to be performed, this world exerts efforts; it does not direct any of its activities toward the sake of another.
But for one whose impurities of all worldly existence have been destroyed and who is filled with the state of Bhairavī, his manifest duty is simply this much: the welfare of the world. (39)
This world— the limited group of subjects— is such that:
"In this context, desire is indeed the impurity."

According to this principle, due to the connection with the worldly impurity of finitude (*āṇavamala*), the self possesses a sense of incompleteness; because of the general indication "something," everything belonging to the self must be accomplished through effort—
that is, by being desired— as one conceives it, [realizing] that "that which is unestablished is established by what is unestablished."

According to this principle, how could one for whom even their own purpose (*svārtha*) is not established effect even the slightest activity toward the purpose of others (*parārtha*), or how could such activity, even if established, accomplish anything at all? This is the intended meaning; moreover, for one who is [otherwise] possessed of the *anupāya* (the "no-means") state...
Having rendered all bonds obsolete, and for that very reason, through the state of Bhairavī—

by attaining non-dual knowledge of the Lord— and by having fulfilled all duties within one's own self, there is an absence of anything whatsoever to be desired; thus, being "full," one remains solely within oneself due to the lack of orientation toward anything else.

He is at rest; for him, by this much, the task of composing the entire work must necessarily be performed as a means of making himself recognized. This alone is clearly his unflagging duty—the meaning is that his only task is the grace toward the world—not indeed [anything else] within his own self.
The sense is that because everything to be attained has already been attained, there is nothing further to be done; as was sung by the Blessed One:
"But the person who should find delight only in the Self, and be satisfied with the Self..."
"And for one who is content in the Self alone, there is no duty to be performed.
Thus [it is said]:
"O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me."
"And there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to abide in action.
Thus [it is said]. || 39 ||

And there are two kinds of favor toward others: that directed toward those with pure consciousness and that directed toward those with impure consciousness. Regarding the former, His capacity to bestow favor is entirely independent of external instruments; thus he says:
"Those of pure consciousness who perceive Him through the process of becoming identical with His nature..."
They too possess that same nature, and their quality of being gracious toward him extends to that very extent.
Those whose consciousness is stainless due to prior practice and the like, or who are recipients of the most intense descent of power (*tīvratīvra-śaktipāta*),

perceive— that is, they directly realize through prior knowledge— that [reality] whose nature was just described, according to the sequence of identification with it, thinking, "This one partakes in the effortless immersion (*nirupāya-samāveśa*). Therefore, they...
By the mere sight of another, through the transference of that consciousness—

according to the principle to be stated later, "like [light] arising from lamp to lamp"— they become identical to that very [consciousness] by virtue of participating in the effortless immersion (*nirupāya-samāveśa*).
The word "occur" is to be supplied; and such a vision of the Siddhas and others is the cause for immersion (*samāveśa*) without [external] means, as was already explained previously:
"the vision of the Siddhas and the Yoginīs..."

And so forth; for this very reason, his nature as grace consists solely in the act of mere vision, and does not depend upon the means (upāya) and other factors that will be described hereafter—this is the meaning. || 40 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: since it has been stated everywhere that initiation is a means to liberation— based on such statements as "And liberation [is attained] through Śiva-initiation"— how can it be that here [liberation occurs] even without initiation?
Anticipating the objection, "Is it not said that [the goal] is attained through mere vision alone?", he says:
"In the venerable Siddhayogīśvarīmata, the Lord has declared that the thorough knowledge of this reality is the primary sacrifice and so forth, ending with initiation. (41)

The connection is as follows: the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of this very reality (*tattva*) just described—which is essentially devoid of means—is what is primarily designated by the term "sacrifice, oblation, and so forth" (*yāga-homādi*) everywhere in the scriptures, such as the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata* and others, by the "All-pervasive Lord" (*vibhu*). For this very reason, external sacrifice and the like are considered secondary (*gauṇa*).

This is established by the sense of the passage; otherwise, this [practice] would not even possess primary importance. It is with this very intention that it is prohibited even in the sequence of conduct (*caryākrama*), as it has been said:
"For him, nothing at all—such as mandalas or sacrificial pits—is of any use."
"And one should not perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, nor the bathing and so forth, beforehand as one pleases.
Thus [ends verse] 41.
He recites that very point:
"After the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) comes the drum (tūra); after the drum, the cloth (paṭa);
after the cloth, meditation (dhyāna); after that, the object of meditation (dhyeya); and after that, concentration (dhāraṇā) follows. (2.42)
Higher than even that is the form born of yoga, and higher than that is knowledge;
for by means of knowledge, one becomes a great adept, a lord of yogis. (2.43)
*Sthaṇḍila* is a portion of ground taken for the purpose of sacrifice; *tūra* is a specific carved design on a vessel or similar object. He states the reason for the supreme excellence of knowledge:
"by means of knowledge"—the meaning is that by means of knowledge, one becomes even the Lord (*īśvara*) of yogis; therefore...
Thus, for the purpose of strengthening that very point, there is also the employment of the words *mahat* and *īśvara*. || 42–43 ||
Furthermore, for those whose consciousness is impure, His capacity to bestow grace is necessarily accompanied by external means; thus he says:
"Even if He, through the power of His sovereignty, desires to bestow grace upon those of impure consciousness, He must resort to the procedure appropriate for their state. (2.44)

[This occurs] through the power of absolute freedom (svātantryadhāman), and not through the constraints of the scriptures, because the breaking of those [constraints] was mentioned immediately prior. || 44 ||
And what is the nature of the future ritual procedure? To this he says:

"It is said to be manifold according to those to be graced, through the distinctions of the various mixtures of the streams of means beginning with the supreme (parā) and the intermediate (parāpara). (2.45)

The term *parāpara* is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member of a pair); by this, *para* refers to the Śāmbhava [means], *apara* to the Āṇava, and *parāpara* to the Śākta. Its "mixed nature" (*saṅkīrṇatva*) arises from its association with other means (*upāya*). || 45 ||
Not only is his recourse to future injunctions appropriate for the sake of favoring others, but even the scripture and so forth that express those [injunctions] are so; thus he says:
"And for that very purpose, even for him who is of the nature of the Supreme Lord..."
Then there is respect for hearing and studying the scriptures and other means [thereto]. (2.46)
The meaning of the word *api* (also/even) is that the scripture is to be adopted not only by those who desire to ascend [the stages], but by this person as well; as it has been said:
"Even one who is free from doubt and knows reality [should follow] the procedure for those seeking liberation."
"One must not abandon the boundaries of the scriptures"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus [ends verse 46].
One might object: "In that case, because this [consciousness] depends upon the means (upāya), would its autonomy not be lost?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For there is no impairment whatsoever, anywhere, of that which is autonomous."
For a person whose mind is not pure, there can be no grace without the proper means.
For this [Lord], unlike one who desires to ascend [the path], there is no dependence upon means whereby his sovereignty might be compromised;

rather, because he has already accomplished all that was to be done within himself, his acceptance of such means is solely for the sake of others. This is because, since other beings possess impure minds, their grace cannot be accomplished without a means. Thus it is said:
It has also been stated by resorting to the future tense, as it is sung: "O Bhārata, just as the ignorant act with attachment toward their duties,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world."
Thus [ends the verse]. 47.

Nor is this merely our own invention; rather, it has been stated everywhere by the Blessed One and by the ancient masters. Thus, in order to demonstrate that the entire subject matter of this chapter is free from contradiction, he says:
"In the venerable *Ūrmi-mahāśāstra*, which embodies the lineage of the Siddhas..."
This has been stated likewise by the venerable teachers beginning with Somānanda. (2.48)

Regarding the phrase *ūrmimahāśāstre*—in this work which embodies the lineage of the Siddhas of the venerable *Ūrmikaula*—by this [reference], the unfading nature of the tradition (*pāramparya*) within the *Pādovallī* is demonstrated. For therein it is said:
"The Void is nothing at all; that Void is not a non-void, nor is it [merely] emptiness."
"How can that which is nothing at all be capable of cutting anything?
Thus questioned by the Blessed Lady, the Blessed One replied: "The self is to be known here as empty, devoid of the qualities of Śiva."
"Śiva is to be realized as empty, stainless, and formless.
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"Indeed, the conceptual extremes of 'it exists,' 'it does not exist,' 'it neither exists nor does not exist,' and 'it neither exists nor does not not exist' do not touch [Him]."
Because that reality is beyond the range of words, it is described here as "thatness" (tattva).
What is not destined to be will not come to be, and what is destined to be cannot be otherwise;
having reflected thus, the wise person should not rely on conceptual construction.

And he has spoken extensively, up to the point of saying: "That [consciousness] is all-pervading, subtle, and free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This was stated by the venerable teachers beginning with Somānanda in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* and other works, as it has been said:
In that regard:
"What is the use of cultivation (bhāvanā) and means (karaṇa) for Śiva, who is eternally manifest?
Thus [it is said].
Once gold has been known, what need is there for cultivation to serve as the means?
[It is known] once through a valid means of knowledge, whether from scripture or from the words of the guru.

"And: 'Once Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, has been known through firm realization, there is no further need for any instrument or even for meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) anywhere. Thus [it is said]. (48)
That very point must be kept in mind in all cases— thus he says:

"Whether from the words of the Guru, through the power of purification by the composition of a multitude of arguments, or from the confidence arising toward the scripture due to what has been stated in its entirety."
Now that the cloud of doubt has dissolved, touch the feet of the Lord—who, like the sun, conquers the darkness and shines with splendor from the sky of the heart. (2.49)

By means of that systematic arrangement of the scriptures— the sequence of the treatise which establishes the refutation of opposing views and the proof of one's own position, consisting of the composition of a multitude of logical arguments such as "the Self alone is the Lord, omniscient and the creator of all," based on the single instruction [received] from the Guru and other such statements— [one attains realization].

"Unmārjana" means the eradication of the ignorance born of the Buddhist [view]. "By its power"—that is, by the firmness of one's own self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*) arising from the dawn of Buddhist knowledge—this is the meaning. Regarding the scripture (*śāstra*):
it is said that one attains conviction through trust in the non-dual tradition (*advaitāgama*), which is equal to a sovereign master; this is understood from the individual [words] (*vyasta*).

For those possessing the most intense-intense (*tīvratīvra*) power, [liberation arises] from the Guru, from the scripture, or from themselves; or else, for those possessing the intense-middling (*tīvramadhya*) and other degrees of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), it arises from all three combined as described.
When the cloud of doubt and conceptual construction—which acts as an obscuration—has dissolved, the heart, which is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [is revealed].
Thus, because it is undivided, the sky shines intensely therein— that is,
that whose light (*mahaḥ*) or splendor (*tejaḥ*) is characterized by the nature of knowing and acting; for this very reason,
[it is the opposite] of darkness (*dhvānta*), which consists of the manifestation of duality and is ignorance (*ajñāna*) resorted to through the concealment of one's own self.

"Of the victorious Lord"— of the Supreme Self, whose nature is to manifest as the soul of the universe— "the feet"— since the root *car* means "to move," [this refers to] the knowledges beginning with the *āṇava*— you,
who have just been mentioned and who possess the most intense descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), "touch."

The meaning is: "Cultivate [the reality] by making it consist of your own self, each subsequent stage more so than the last. For this very reason, its comparison with the sun has been stated; for even the sun, when the clouds have cleared away, is fit to be touched by the feet as it dispels the darkness by shining forth in the sky. || 49 ||
Now he concludes the meaning of the daily lesson with the first half of the verse:
"This daily lesson, which discerns the abode of the Absolute (anuttara) and in which all means have dissolved, has been completed. (2.50)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Anupāya," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The means itself is that which is conducive to the goal; may there be auspiciousness.
Jayaratha, being occupied with the pursuit of hundreds of means for mastering various texts, has quickly explained this "Day on Non-means."

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Methodless" (*anupāyaprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 2 ||
The Third Daily Lesson:
"Discrimination. Although it is one's own self, this entire universe, consisting of the signified and the signifier, is manifold.
Shining within the self like a city in a mirror, Vijaya reigns supreme. || 1 ||

Now, following the sequence, he promises to explain the Śāmbhava means (upāya) by means of the second half [of the verse], immediately after the means that is not a means (anupāya): "Next, the supreme means is proclaimed— the very unsurpassed state of the Great Lord."

Now, one might object: "If even the supreme means (paropāya) is indeed of the nature of the unsurpassed, then since its meaning has already been conveyed by what preceded, for what purpose is this subsequent chapter commenced? To this he says:
"That which was proclaimed as pure luminosity, the supreme splendor of Bhairava..."
In this regard, only its independence is further analyzed. (3-1)

"It is mere light" is said because of its predominance; for there exists no light devoid of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), nor is such a thing logically possible. This was stated in the chapter on "The Absence of Means" (*Anupāyāhnika*). The term "furthermore" (*adhikam*) refers to a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*);
for in reality, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing does not differ from itself—otherwise, it would not be that very nature at all.
It may be argued that "independence" consists in being the agent of the act of manifestation; and its measure is this: that it manifests everything by its own will upon its very own screen. || 1 ||
He says that very thing:
"That which is light bestows the state of being manifest upon everything;
it is indeed the agent in the act of manifestation."

The Light, which is the Supreme Subject and is denoted by the term "Anuttara," bestows the state of being manifest—the state of appearing—upon the entire universe consisting of subjects and objects; it causes [the universe] to shine forth through its identity with its own self. This is the meaning. For there is no such thing as a "universe" apart from this.
Because it is manifest, nothing can possibly exist apart from it; for if one were to admit its separation, its manifestation would be impossible, and thus it would not even appear at all.
Regarding this, it is said:
"And there is nothing apart from that [consciousness], for the universe appears as real. (3.2)
The word "or" (vā) is used in the sense of admission. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then only light shines, and thus there would be no manifestation of the universe at all; yet the universe does manifest—what is this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, that Supreme Lord, unimpeded within the ether of His own Self..."
He is the exhibitor of this vast display of creation and dissolution.
"Thus"— because it is impossible for the universe to appear as something distinct from Light. For the Supreme Lord,

by virtue of the majesty of His own sovereignty characterized by unimpeded freedom, displays this manifold variety of the universe upon the wall of His own Self, making it appear as if distinct even though it is not distinct from Him.

Thus, even while the manifold variety of the universe unfolds, nothing additional whatsoever has arisen within one's own self, whose nature is pure luminosity (*prakāśa*); this is what is intended to be indicated here by the description [of the universe] as "space" (*vyoman*). For this very reason, the entire universe possesses the status of being a reflection within consciousness (*cit-pratibimbatva*). — Thus ends the subsequent section.

An opportunity has been provided for the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*) to be examined. For just as specific forms reflected in a mirror or similar surfaces—though their natures are mutually distinct and not actually different from that [mirror]—appear as if they were distinct, so it is here as well. || 3 ||
Thus it is said:
"Just as earth, water, and so forth appear unmixed in a spotless mirror, so too do the functions of the universe appear within the one Lord of Consciousness. (3-4)
In the Subodhamañjarī:
"This entire universe consists of nothing more than this group of five, namely form and the rest;
and it is perceived by the five sense organs, beginning with the eye."
By such statements as these, it follows that all things are indeed only five: form and the rest. || 4 ||
He shows the objective aspect through their reflection and its systematic arrangement:
"It appears as a likeness in the eyes, mirrors, the sky, and water.
"A likeness" means belonging to the same class; "in the sky" refers to that which is situated in the sky, being neither too intense nor too faint.
Whether it be solar or lunar light, for therein a reflection of the body's configuration is seen by those who know the instruction on the Shadow-Person (chāyāpuruṣa). As they say:
"In light situated in the sky, there occurs the conjunction with the reflection of form."

Alternatively, it should be explained as having the reflection of sound as its object by way of indicating other objects; thus, there is an echo in the sky, and likewise, the bitter, pungent, and other tastes being experienced by others, as well as the touch of women and so forth, and odors, [are perceived] in the saliva and the *kanda* [root-center], respectively.
Reflection occurs respectively in the field of touch, namely the skin, and in the field of smell, namely the nose.
He demonstrates this very point: for in a pure form, only form itself appears. (3-5)

In this world, among the three elements of earth, water, and fire alone, there exists a translucent quality called "form" (rūpa) within the earthen— such as a mirror and the like— the aqueous— such as still pools of water and the like— and the luminous— such as the eye and so forth;
this quality consists of the configuration and structural arrangement [of atoms], and it is precisely the reflection of that which appears therein.

It does not [arise] from touch and so forth; rather, that [consciousness] indeed reflects upon the supports such as the *kanda* (the bulbous root), which consist of states of bliss and the like, because touch and the other qualities are possible therein. Therefore, whatever pure quality exists in a particular place, that very quality reflects there—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||
And this is not unrelated; to establish this point, he provides an illustration:
"A woman whose passion is concealed does not reach satiety as she touches with her jar-like breasts a mirror made beautiful by the reflection of her beloved. (3.6)
In this case, since the presence of elders and other such obstacles prevent a woman who secretly harbors passion from seeing her beloved directly, even though she does not obtain direct perception,
she nonetheless experiences— through the medium of a reflection in a mirror— a state that can be cognized by no one else: "I have seen my beloved."

Due to the pride of contentment, her gaze became fixed upon her beloved; by the word "beautiful" (*sundara*), it is also indicated that it produced an excess of joy arising from the power of that very sight. Thus, even though she made an effort toward the mirror, thinking, "May this touch of his also be mine—something otherwise imperceptible," [she was thwarted].
Because there is no transition of contact, not obtaining that [contact], she is neither satisfied nor delighted—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "If form is reflected here, why is touch—which is inseparable from it by its very nature—not also reflected? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For its touch is not pure, whereas its form alone is so."
And purity is the extremely dense conjunction of homogeneous [atoms] alone. (3-7)

The word "asya" refers to the mirror; "tathā" means "pure. For it is only that which is pure and transparent, like a mirror, that receives the reflection of that which is not pure, such as a face—this is the intended meaning. And what is this so-called "purity"? To this he says: "And purity... [referring to] those that are exceedingly dense.
Those homogeneous entities which are unpolluted by heterogeneous entities— such as the atoms of form within a mirror— their conjunction, being solitary due to the absence of heterogeneous factors,
consists in their state of proximity without intervals, characterized by smoothness through the exclusion of unevenness and the like.

This very state of being integrated is purity (*nairmalya*). For when the form of a mirror or similar object is perceived as unclouded by heterogeneous factors and by the absence of homogeneous ones, then there is the connection with the reflection of form. But when [it is clouded] by heterogeneous factors such as vapor, dust, or [other] forms...
It is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that turbidity is not brought about at that time;

for it is established that only that which possesses a specific quality called clarity (*svacchatā*), relative to the object that provides the reflection, grasps that reflection. And for this very reason, it is said: "Only form appears as form."

In such cases, it has also been explained that even a mirror, which was proposed as an example, does not possess the relationship of original object and reflection in an unrestricted sense—such that a face would reflect [in it]. || 7 ||

He explains this very point by means of another formulation: "That very capacity to perceive what is distinct [from it] within itself, due to non-difference [from it], while not abandoning its own self-luminosity—that is called 'purity' (nairmalya) by the Guru. (3.8)

Even when another object is reflected as an image that has not abandoned its own nature, because there is the manifestation of that very non-conceptual [mirror], the self-luminosity of the mirror or similar object remains unobscured;
this occurs by relying on non-difference within itself with respect to that which is distinct and located in a different place— the object that provides the reflection.

The perception of mountains and the like is a manifestation because it involves the internalization of the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*); for a reflection does not occur even a particle’s breadth outside the location of the mirror—this is the intended meaning.
In that regard, "capacity" refers to the ability to receive a reflection, distinguished from walls and other such surfaces.
That very [state] is purity. And this has not been stated by us merely on our own authority; thus he says, "spoken by the Guru," meaning by the Guru, the supreme teacher, the illustrious Utpaladeva:
"Now, according to the form of the object... [and so forth].
And so forth.
Likewise, "Nor is this appropriate for that which is insentient...
and so on—all of this is found in the *Ṭīkā* on the two verses of the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-Kārikā*.
The true nature of the reflection has been declared as joy—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
To show that this purity is of two kinds—primary and secondary—he says:
"The primary purity belongs in every respect to the one Lord of Consciousness;
other things are pure in some measure or degree here and there, according to His will. (9)

Regarding the word "primary" (*mukhyam*): because the entire universe, consisting of form and so forth, is capable of receiving a reflection, it is said [in the text], "from everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*). For the universe is perceived only as being closely joined with consciousness; therefore, this [consciousness] possesses transparency in every respect, and likewise in no other place.

In mirrors and the like, there is a secondary, non-primary purity that depends upon various parts characterized by form and so forth; for if it were otherwise, everything would appear everywhere. Thus, even in a mirror, touch would grasp a reflection, and in this way—

Otherwise, there would be no distinction between this [limited subject] and the primary [Lord]. And the cause of its purity is precisely His sovereignty—thus he says: "It is pure by His will. "That" refers to form and so forth; for that very reason, it includes touch and so forth.
In that context, it is established by implication that it is impure; therefore, it is His power alone that has thus emanated.
The state of being. || 9 ||
Therefore, he says:
"That form of entities which is obstructive is indeed of the nature of *māyā*;
however, that which belongs to those very same entities and consists of true knowledge (*sadvidyā*) is non-obstructive. (3-10)

"Obstructive" (*pratighāti*) means that, because it strikes back, it does not allow others to enter—this is the sense. For that [power] consists of the creative energy (*kriyāśakti*) of the Supreme Lord, since its nature is to conceal the essence of *māyā*;
therefore, due to the predominance of duality, there is a grossness of objectivity (*vedyatā*).

In this context, "lack of clarity" means the incapacity to receive a reflection. On the other hand, that form of entities which is non-obstructive consists of *sadvidyā* (pure knowledge) and has the nature of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*);
