therefore, in relation to that [form], it is "clear," meaning it possesses the capacity to receive a reflection. Consequently, as before—

However, this [world] consists of reflections and exists outside of that [original object]; such is the distinction. Thus, the essential meaning is that the Supreme Lord alone, through the majesty of His own sovereignty, manifests by means of the various diversities of appearances such as those original objects and their reflections. || 10 ||
Thus it is said: "In this way, manifesting an appearance of both forms, the Giver of Boons shines forth in all things through the analogy of the original image and its reflection. (3.11)

It has been stated that this [duality], consisting of both the resistant and the non-resistant, is essentially nothing more than a mere appearance (*ābhāsa-mātra-sāra*) and is not ultimately real (*na tu tāttvika*), as expressed in the phrase "manifesting the appearance. And it has also been said:
"Therefore, Mahādeva is one, whose state is endowed with absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)."
It appears as a duality through the nature of the emergence of the original image and its reflection.
Thus [ends the section]. 11.

Thus, having established the true nature of the reflection according to common perception, [the author] addresses certain Naiyāyikas who claim that even when one's own face is apprehended by the rays of the eyes turned back,
this notion of "the mirror-face" is merely an error; it is not, however, something distinct from either reality or error.

In order to refute the view that there exists something called a "reflection" because of the absence of a third category [of entity], he says: "But as for him who says that the visual rays, being reflected back from a clear surface, [produce the perception]..."
Turning their own faces away, they seize [him]; thus he is questioned. (3-12)

The use of the singular number (*yaḥ*) in the aphorism indicates that this is not the view of all Naiyāyikas, as it was not formulated by the author of the Sūtras; rather, the implication is that this was stated only by certain individuals driven by dogmatic insistence. For this very reason, even the name of this doctrine has not been touched upon by the authors of the Vṛtti, the Bhūṣaṇa, and others.

"From a clear [surface]" means from an external object such as a mirror; "having turned back" (viparyasya) means having returned—this is the meaning. And here, the phrase "reflecting" serves as the reason by way of a qualification; for otherwise, these [images] would not even face one's own body, so how could one see one's own face?
They would accept it. It is asked: "What is your intention in accepting this? || 12 ||
He states that very point:
"The light which exists apart from the body belongs to the Self, who is its substratum.
If cognition occurs by means of that very light, what would be the purpose of a mirror? (3.13)

If the knower, with eyes opened, were to experience the cognition of his own face through that very same ocular light which has issued forth from the body—only now inverted—then what further purpose would a mirror serve? [It would be none. Before [the mirror].

For other causes of reflection, such as walls and the like, are also possible there. If it is argued that mirrors and the like alone are the causes of reflection, while walls and the like are not, this is merely a statement made according to one's own whim; for although they are equal in being causes of obstruction, mirrors and the like [are distinguished].
In this way, we do not perceive any cause for [the claim] that walls and the like are not so [transparent].
If it is argued that there is an additional property called "transparency" (svacchatva) which serves as the cause here, this is not so;
for transparency is not the cause for resistance (pratighāta), since [otherwise] light would [also possess it], owing to its transparency.

If that were the case, there would be no room for anything else in the sky; on the contrary, it would be the very cause for the perception of reflections. Thus, the reason leads to a contradiction: since resistance is caused by corporeality and the like, and that [corporeality] is common to both cases—or rather, to the reflection by means of a mirror—[the reason is inconclusive].
Since it is round, one should now be able to perceive one's own face even without a mirror;
what, then, is the purpose of it? || 13 ||

And thus, if the visual rays, having returned by the power of reflection, grasp their own face, it is logical that this occurs in its own location and not elsewhere, such as inside a mirror; thus he says:
But by those [faculties] whose luminosity is inverted and has attained the nature of a grasper, form would be seen in one's own face and not within a mirror. (3.14)
"Form" (*rūpa*) means "connected with one's own face"—that is, "in one's own face," meaning precisely in the location of one's own face;
for the sense is that the perceiver grasps only that which is situated in its own location.
Indeed, the cognition of blue does not determine the blue object by bypassing the location of the blue.

In some cases it is observed that the nature of being a grasper (grāhakātmatva) is indeed connected with a grasper (grahītṛ); for it is only of those things presided over by a self (ātman) that there is the conventional usage of "being a grasper. Furthermore, regarding the ocular rays (nayanatejas) that have issued forth externally, is their presiding by a self done by one who is bodiless?

Or [is it] with a body? In the first case, that which is bodiless could not be the locus of experience—because experience, characterized by external cognition, would arise even without it—and thus its own established tenet, namely that "the body is the locus of experience," would be contradicted. || 14 ||
His perception [of the reflection] would occur only through the body and its substratum, like a statue, and not otherwise; thus he says:
"If this form were to appear as 'mine' with the same tactile sensation as one's own face..."
But this [consciousness], which is distinct from the tangible and whose essential nature is exclusively that of the object of cognition, [is not so]. || 3-15 ||

If this form were to appear as the very nature of the self by virtue of having one’s own face as its locus, then there would be a cognition of reversal in the form of "this is my form," wherein it would be the substrate of the *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness); but it is not so, for this [face] is the substrate of the *idantā* (this-ness) as "this is the form of that which is solely of the nature of the object of knowledge. For in this case:

For those who are unlearned, such as children and others, there is a single-flavored cognition that it is simply "this"; however, let the learned person indeed maintain the conceit that "my face is reflected here"—what is the harm?
Nevertheless, regarding its status as a reflection, there is certainly a cognition of it as distinct from the original object (the *bimba*). In that regard:

Because such a nature cannot be denied. Furthermore, if the manifestation of the self's own form were to occur within its own mouth, then its touch would also have to manifest; for while it is possible that the form and its configuration might be devoid of qualities such as weight or odor, they cannot be so [devoid of touch], because [touch] is an inseparable characteristic of their very nature.
In some cases, two things are seen to be devoid of touch; however, in the case of a reflected image of form, a form is perceived that is indeed distinct from its touch.
For instance, no heat is ever perceived in a mirror that reflects an image of fire.
Just as when there is the appearance of that form, its property—namely its configuration—must necessarily appear, so too [is it with other properties].

"The same would apply to the touch that is inseparable from it, if one's own face were actually being perceived; therefore, it is not correct to say that 'only one's own face' is being grasped. [The opponent replies: "But for this very reason it was said that 'this is an illusion,' because one mistakenly imagines that one's own face is being grasped when it is not."

If it is argued that [the face] is apprehended in the mirror, then let it be so; what is the use of postulating the apprehension of the actual face which is not being experienced? For in an illusion, only the superimposed object appears, not the reality of the thing itself. Indeed, if in the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, the mother-of-pearl were also [to appear], then...

If it were merely produced by the appearance of silver, it would not be an error at all; likewise, if the face itself were truly perceived, what indeed would constitute an error? Furthermore, even in the case of an error, does the mirror appear as the face, or does one's own face appear as another's face? The first alternative is certainly not the case.

Because it is the undivided mirror itself that appears; for at the time of the appearance of silver, there would not be an appearance of the mother-of-pearl shell either. Nor is the second [alternative] valid—for if that were so, then everyone, maintaining an attitude of indifference, would [perceive] their own face...
One would be indifferent toward the arrangement of ornaments, decoration, and so forth;
therefore, because there is no error [involved], this must be accepted as a distinct entity called a reflection, which is different from the original object. || 15 ||
Therefore, he says:
"That object, consisting merely of form and configuration, joined with touch, smell, taste, and so forth, which are indeed subordinated, is what is reflected therein. (3.16)
Therefore— for the reasons stated, such as the absence of error and so forth— because it is devoid of touch and other qualities,

that mere configuration of form reflected there in the mirror and such is indeed a real entity (*vastu*) and not a non-entity; however, it is endowed with those [qualities] only insofar as touch and the rest are suppressed (*nyagbhūta*), for otherwise, its...
It would be no different from the original object (bimba) itself; therefore, the intention is that there certainly exists a third category characterized as a reflection (pratibimba). || 16 ||

"What indeed is this state of being subordinated (*nyagbhūtatva*) of touch and the other [sensory objects]? To this he says: "Subordination [is] due to the absence of being an object of perception; that absence is due to the lack of means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); and that [lack of cognition] is due to the absence of contact with the object; and that too is because [the mirror] does not abide [in the object], as in the case of a reflection. (3.17)

"That" refers to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). "Because of non-abiding" means, by implication, that [the sense organs] do not abide in touch and so forth; or rather, if there were indeed an abiding of touch and so forth here, then the sense organs would come into contact with them, and the cognition arising precisely from that contact would be directed toward them.

The sense is that [the cognition] would attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)—in which case there would be an absence of the object of apprehension (grāhya) for the touch and so forth being cognized by it. || 17 ||
Furthermore, for this very reason, properties such as weight are not perceived in this [reflection];
for it does not reside in the mirror, though it serves as the means for its perception. (3.18)

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): because touch and the other qualities are not present [in the reflection]. For if this reflected object, which consists merely of form and configuration, were to possess touch and so forth, then its various attributes such as weight would also appear; and in the absence of those, what proof is there for its existence? To this he says: "For in a mirror..."

"He is situated there"—this refers to properties such as weight belonging to the reflected mountain and so forth. By the word "this"—meaning that if properties such as weight were present [in the reflection], then due to their connection with it, even the mirror would become immovable;
but this is not the case, and thus it is said that those [properties] do not exist in the reflection either: "Properties such as weight do not belong to this."

"It is perceived. Now, one might object: since form is everywhere seen to be invariably concomitant with touch, and this is likewise the case with the original object (*bimba*), why is it that only the form is reflected in the mirror?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the perception of that, it is the means. Regarding the phrase "in the perception of that": of that...

The meaning is: "in the vision of mere form and configuration," that is, in its manifestation; for, according to the reasoning stated previously, only pure form exists in the mirror, and thus it serves as the means (*sādhana*) only for the manifestation of that [form], not for touch and so forth—this is the intended sense. The word *upāyaka* is formed by adding the suffix *kan* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
Now, one might object: "Just as the mirror is a means for perceiving that [reflection], so too are other factors such as light;

since there is no difference in their status as means, why is this [mirror] alone called its substrate? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, because this does not appear as something distinct [from the object], it is so called."
In that regard, the supports are the means [consisting of] the lamp, the eye, and consciousness, respectively. (3-19)
Furthermore, because this reflection does not appear as distinct or separate from the mirror and so forth,
for that reason its support is said to be all-pervasive, like oil in sesame seeds; moreover,
light and other factors are the means for the cognition of the reflection once it has arisen therein.
Its distinction from those [other reflections] is stated as follows: "In that case, however... [and] "gradually," because of the manifestation of its arising as non-different from the mirror.

Even though the mirror remains present and the reflection has arisen at a later time, what practical usage could there be for it without the lamp? For who would know of a face in a mirror in total darkness?

Regarding the term "transferred" (*saṃkrāntam*): even when [the reflection] has been transferred thus to the mouth of a blind person, despite the presence of light, there is no such conventional usage [of "seeing"]. However, for one who is not blind, even though such a causal complex exists, if that cognition does not arise due to some deficiency resulting from the absence of contact between the sense organ and the object, then who indeed [could deny it]?
"One should discern"—this indicates that their collective nature as a means lies in the act of cognition;
for the true essence of a reflection consists solely in its being a mere manifestation. This is what has been stated here as the primary point. || 19 ||

Now, one might object: "By the reasoning already stated, the capacity to receive a reflection belongs equally to lamps and other such objects as it does to a mirror; so why do they not also manifest that [reflection] as non-different from themselves? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because it lacks solidity, because it is superior to lamps, eyes, and consciousnesses, and because it is entirely translucent, it does not appear separately like a mirror. (3.20)
It is true that lamps and the like possess the capacity to receive reflections within themselves;

however, while a reflection appears in a mirror as if it were distinct from it even though it is not actually separate, such is not the case here. Therefore, he says: "It does not appear separately like a mirror," because...

There is an absence of solidity in lamps and the like; whereas in solid objects such as mirrors, a face or other features reflected therein appear as distinct from their support due to the stability of that support, the light of a lamp and so forth, however, appears as one because of the absence of solidity; in that case, it is thus because of instability.

The sense is this: just as in a clear body of water and the like, although a face or similar object is reflected due to its stillness, it is not perceived [as distinct], so it is here as well. Now, one might object: even in water, because of its fluidity and lack of solidity, even when there is stillness, why does the reflection not appear as something separate?

Could it be so? No; for water indeed possesses solidity, since there is no lack of resistance here as there is when one swings an arm in the sky. For this very reason, when a man crosses [a river] with his arms, the exertion required to break through that [solidity] is great; however, that [solidity] is merely relative. For it is not...
Just as there is solidity in earth, so it is in water; and just as it is there [in water], so it is not in fire.

It is not said that there is no solidity in fire, but rather that, in comparison to that [solidity of water], it is very slight and unfit for the distinct manifestation of a reflection. Otherwise, indeed...

Because they are formless, even lamps and the like would be just like space; however, this is simply not the case with consciousness—thus, due to its formlessness, there is no separate manifestation of a reflection within it.
Furthermore, a mirror and such are clear only on the front side, not on the back; therefore, it is sullied [on the latter].

In other cases, a reflection appears by relying on the rear portion as if it were a wall, while the reflection shines forth in the clear front portion; here, however, because of the transparency on all sides, even a face or similar object reflected through one part is not perceived, since it is [simultaneously] reflected through another part, ultimately by means of light and so forth.

Because that [lamp] is transparent; or rather, just as pieces of glass, crystal, and the like— due to their being transparent on all sides— are not obstructors of the visual rays, since the perception of objects screened by them would otherwise be impossible,
so too are lamps and such, provided there is an absence of solidity.

Because it is transparent on all sides, the reflection emerges through another part [of the mirror]; thus, the reflection does not take root there, because there is no other part that is opaque enough to obstruct it.
Consciousness, however, is self-luminous due to its purity in every respect; therefore, [the reflection] does not [take root] in it.

Since even the scent of being an object of cognition exists there, how could there be a separate manifestation of a reflection? Furthermore, as for the reflection that is perceived in a lamp at the time of its expansion, or in the light situated in the sky during the cognition of a shadow-person, or the reflection that occurs even in the eye due to the power of mantras and so forth— [these are explained as follows].
That [light] is not seen in the fiery visual faculty, because that is eternally beyond perception; rather, it is seen in the watery eyeball (golaka), so there is no fault whatsoever. || 20 ||
Nor has this true nature of the reflection been stated by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"And this has been shown by the God of gods for the increase of awakening.
For the deluded, it becomes a real object, and elsewhere it is not even sufficient. (3.21)
"It is not resistant, nor independent, nor is it stable or unstable;
this is merely the majesty of some translucent [reality]," so [it was said] by the Compassionate One. (3-22)

The connection is as follows: this true nature of the reflection was shown by the compassionate God of gods for the sake of increasing the awakening of [beings], in the manner that will be stated with the words "of the deluded.
By the general statement "it was shown," the intended sense is that it was shown everywhere; as it has been said:
"One should worship the goddesses as rays [of light], as instruments, like reflections.
Likewise:
"By him, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded, like water or a mirror."
Thus: "Likewise, it manifests as both real and unreal objects, like a reflection in a mirror.
And likewise:
"Just as contradictory objects appear unmixed in a mirror that is perfectly clean at its core, so too do the functions of the universe appear in this Lord of Consciousness.
Thus it is said. And likewise:
"Objects reflect within him like [images] in a clear gem. Likewise:
"I have neither bondage nor liberation; these are merely terrors for the individual soul (jīva)."
"This reflection is the intellect, like that of the sun in waters.
Regarding this, first of all, this reflection is a real entity because it is being manifested;
for there is no dispute among anyone here that what has been manifested cannot be non-manifested, nor is there any [dispute] in this regard.
There is no subverting cognition [to the contrary], because such a cognition does not arise at a later time.

Now, if this is so, then it is logical that this [object] should belong to the same class as those well-known entities; otherwise, the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*) would be indeterminate.
Therefore, [the claim that] "the horn of a hare consists of form, touch, and so forth" [is untenable].
It might be argued that [the object] exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*);

however, since it does not possess the same genus (*jātīyatva*) as other well-known real entities, how could it be a real entity? For indeed, an external entity that has arisen would travel from one location to another, yet this [consciousness] does not do so. To this, he says:
"Not elsewhere than from that either"—"from that" means from the location of the mirror; "elsewhere" means in another location.

The word "occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be connected everywhere [in the following clauses]. Furthermore, external form and so forth are invariably concomitant with touch and so forth; it is not thus [with the reflection], as he says: "nor even sufficient."

This is not sufficient—this is the meaning; because here there is the manifestation of the mere configuration of form (*rūpasaṃsthāna*) alone, to the exclusion of touch and other qualities. The word "not" (*na*) is to be applied here like the "crow's eye" (applying to both preceding and following terms).

An external object such as a mountain is an obstructor for everyone, and everything [is an obstructor] for this [consciousness], because of its corporeality (*mūrtatvāt*); it is not [the case that consciousness obstructs anything].
And this is indeed so; therefore he says: "It is obstructive. Here too, the word *na* (not) must be connected [to the preceding].
Otherwise, when the mirror is broken, how could there be entry into its interior? Nor is this [entry] possible behind the mirror; for if that were the case, the mirror would not be visible.

Furthermore, there is a dependence on causes for the production of everything external; indeed, no entity whatsoever can exist as self-born (*svayambhū*). Once produced, however, it remains independent of anything else, just as a jar exists even when the wheel and other [causes] have ceased. This [consciousness], moreover, disregards such things as mirrors which serve as the cause for its production.

Nothing whatsoever attains existence independently; for indeed, no reflection is ever seen apart from a mirror or some such surface. As it has been said: "It is not independent. For this very reason, it is neither inherently stable nor unstable; thus he says: "Neither stable nor unstable."
"No," [he replies]. For an external object, having arisen, is called "enduring" because it persists over a long duration;
otherwise, it is non-enduring. But this [reflection], apart from the mirror and so forth, does not even possess existence;
therefore, for what could there be a connection with time, by virtue of which it might be either enduring or non-enduring?

Therefore, because it lacks the nature of belonging to the class of those well-known entities, this is indeed non-existent, like a hare's horn; thus, its manifestation is not logical. Yet, since there is a manifestation, what is this being called? To this he says: "This is the power of some utterly pure [reality]."

This is the power of a clear mirror or similar surface: that this so-called "reflection"—which is distinct from both a real entity and a non-entity, and whose essence consists solely of appearance—manifests.
By that Blessed One, it was shown that in a mirror or the like, entities consist solely of appearance.
Just as they appear [externally], so too do they appear within consciousness; therefore, their existence does not consist in having an external form.

This was taught for those who are attached to external objects, in order to increase their understanding that all this has nothing but appearance as its essence. Thus, one should not be attached to external objects.
The delusion of duality shall be stilled. || 21-22 ||
Therefore he says:
"There is no location, nor form, nor connection with time, nor dimension; there is neither mutual contact nor its cessation, nor density."
"There would be neither unreality nor any inherent essence;
thus delusion would surely cease"—this was the method of the mirror that he taught. (23)

It has already been established that a reflection does not possess an independent existence apart from the mirror; consequently, it has no location separate from the mirror—as it was stated: "no location. And likewise, it possesses no density, characterized by solidity.

The meaning is that even its form does not exist; for otherwise, it would have to occupy a location distinct from the mirror, because it is impossible for another corporeal object to occupy a portion of space already occupied by one corporeal object, since there is a contradiction in two corporeal objects occupying the same location. Therefore—

And thus, for him there is no form—meaning there is no connection with the quality called *rūpa*. For that [quality] exists only in what is corporeal (*mūrta*)—this is the sense. And for this very reason, he has no connection with time;
for that [connection] would belong to something that has acquired its own existence separately by depending on something else that occurs earlier or later, but not for him.

Furthermore, it has been stated many times that there is no existence separate from the mirror; for this very reason, it has "no dimension" (*na parimāṇam*), because dimensionality is only possible for that which exists. Otherwise, how could a large-sized object such as a mountain be reflected within the limited space of the mirror? Nor...
Even when many objects appear simultaneously within a mirror, there is no mutual cohesion through density; thus he says: "and there is no mutual contact. Now, [one might object]:
in the case of the appearance of a city and so forth, if many objects situated in different locations [appear] in one and the same...

The reflection appears within a limited area of the mirror; therefore, since its appearance in a single location would otherwise be inexplicable, it is logical that these [reflected objects] must merge with one another into a single mass. If this were not the case, then there would be no appearance of the city at all—thus he says: "And there is no loss of that [city]."

Since all objects indeed appear with mutual distinctness, and it has been stated many times that what has appeared cannot be non-existent, for this very reason there is no unreality for this [appearance]—
thus he says: "And there would be no unreality," because all objects indeed appear.

Even so, there is not even the slightest inherent, real form of this [reflection] that establishes its status as a substantial entity; thus he says: "And there is no inherent essence whatsoever. In this way, for the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), the true nature of the reflection—which has mere appearance as its essence—is certainly of the nature of the manifestation of duality.

"The contracted knowledge must be stilled"—for this purpose, the procedure concerning the mirror was taught; [the author] pointed out the specific type of object capable of reflecting an image by way of its distinction from walls and the like. And this being so, the following meaning is demonstrated: that this entire universe...

That which exists in consciousness by the analogy of a reflection in a mirror does not exist as a real entity with an external form apart from that [consciousness]; therefore, one should not be attached to it. || 23 ||
Thus, when the path of reflection has been established in this way, that which is the reflection of a word is also denoted by another synonymous term through its inherent connection; thus he says:
"In this manner, once this path of reflection has been demonstrated here..."
That which is the reflection of sound is called an echo. || 3-24 ||
Nor is that sound produced by sound, because it is heard as something arriving;
for even by those standing at a distance from that very speaker, the sound would not be heard [if it were merely produced]. (3-25)
Because this word is variegated, its reflection—like that of a face and so forth—is perceived in conjunction with the apertures distinguished by the parts of the covers of pots and the like. (3.26)

It is called a "reverberation" (*pratiśrutkā*) because hearing occurs by returning to it; or else, *prati* means similar, and *śrut* means hearing, thus it is that very thing which is a similar hearing. Indeed, in this context, according to the Naiyāyikas, due to the reflection of visual rays upon a mirror or similar surface, there is the perception of one's own face.

The intention is this: since it is impossible for the ear and other sense organs to reflect in a reflection of form, even by imagining that echoes and the like possess the nature of primary sound and so forth, one would still be denying that [reflection]; thus, a reflection does not exist anywhere at all. In that regard, as for the reflection of form...

Thus, the existence [of the echo] has been established simultaneously. In this way, having raised the opponent's view in order to establish the existence of reflections for sound and the other sense objects as well, he refutes it with the words beginning "And this... Here, "this" refers to the echo; it is born from sound (*śabdaja*), and not, however, produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*).
Or else it is produced by division—this being the primary sound, because it arises from its own cause by itself; such is the sense.

And that [sound] is perceived only as it proceeds from the region of the speaker. For this very reason, the perceivers situated in close proximity hear the very first sound as being exceedingly intense.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the final [sound] is the weakest, nor that for those situated at a great distance only the final sound is heard and not the first; rather, the echo is heard by that very speaker or by perceivers standing near him as something approaching and proceeding directly toward them. Therefore...
And thus, it is not heard by perceivers situated at a distance, such as those in mountain caves or forest thickets, because the sound does not proceed toward them; for the primary sound,
while occupying the space of the auditory ether of many listeners, does not [reach] them.

It attains a distinct and diverse nature; for if that were not the case, all listeners would not act with a single object in mind. Furthermore, the echoes take the form of coverings over vessels containing boiling, noisy water situated below.
Regarding those specific types of material objects such as cooking pots and the like,

their particular gross and subtle forms contain cavities and porous parts; when sound encounters these, through its union with the space therein, it undergoes a variety of manifestations consisting of a single sound.
Because it is not perceived as belonging to the same class as a sound produced from a substantial object, this sound is not born of sound;

therefore, just as there is a reflection of a face in a mirror or similar surface, so too is there a reflection of this primary sound in space—thus he says: "The reflection of this sound is like that of a face and so forth."
It is not only because of the absence of the nature of a primary word denoting a real entity that there is the state of being a reflection here;
rather, it is also because of the possession of the nature of a reflection of form—thus he says:
"This appears as the form of another object of cognition."
"Just as in a mirror, so too do I listen to whatever has been spoken by anyone. (3-27)

Just as in a mirror or similar surface, even the form belonging to one's own face— which is associated with the notion of "I"— is perceived as something not belonging to another, being known as an object of cognition; likewise, even a word uttered by oneself, which is to be reflected upon as "this was said by me," appears as if it were "said by someone else."

"I hear [it]," and for this reason, because it belongs to a different class from other reflections, it possesses the nature of a reflection here—this is the intended meaning. The word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and), and it refers back to what precedes;
the word *iti* marks the conclusion of the sentence. || 27 ||

Now, one might object: "If a sound uttered by a certain speaker undergoes a transfer into the space of a cave or similar location at a distance, would its hearing not belong only to those residing in that place, and not to others? To this, he says:
Because a reflection necessarily faces its original object, those perceivers situated between them hear the echo. (3.28)

Since, as in the case of a mirror and the like, the reflection necessarily possesses a direct orientation toward the original object (*bimba*), therefore only those perceivers situated between that original object and its reflection hear the echo— which proceeds with a direct orientation toward the original object— and not others.
Furthermore, those [senses] that go far away are situated in places such as deep chasms and caves beyond that [object], because they do not function toward it. || 28 ||

Now, if this is so, then even though they are situated between those two, how could cognizers— whose mental forms (*śabdākāra*) are not intended as the heard reflection due to some cause— grasp the echo that proceeds toward the source of the reflection?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even without the perception of the primary object, the perception of the reflection occurs;
one may see the beloved standing behind oneself, reflected in a mirror. (3.29)

The phrase "it might be" [is used] because she is situated in a place suitable for perceiving a reflection; the expression "standing behind the dog" serves as a reason, conveyed through a qualification, for the sight of her beloved who has appeared as a reflection unexpectedly. || 29 ||

Now, one might object: "According to the reasoning already stated, since a reflection does not possess a separate existence apart from the mirror and so forth, how can it face its original (bimba)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And such 'facing' is said to exist because of its abiding in non-difference from the mirror. (3.30)
That mirror which faces such a reflection—non-difference from it means identity with the mirror; by that identity, there is the existence or abiding of the reflection.
This alone constitutes its "facing" (sāṃmukhya), namely, that the mirror exists facing the object, because the reflection does not exist apart from that [mirror].

Furthermore, for a mirror and the like, there must necessarily be the presence of the original object (bimba) facing them; otherwise, the very production of the reflection would not occur. Likewise, it should be understood that even space and so forth possess the capacity to receive reflections of sound and other phenomena only through the presence of an original object facing them. || 30 ||
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, the space of the mouth, reflected in the space within a vessel such as a well, appears together with its sound, just like the mouth of another speaker. (3.31)

Therefore, due to the aforementioned cause—the identity with the specific substratum facing the original object (*bimba*)—the space associated with the speaker, which constitutes that original object, becomes reflected in the space of the well and so forth; existing as a function characterized by non-difference from that [reflected space], it appears—that is to say, it manifests—as sound. This is the meaning regarding sound.

Since a quality is inherently dependent on its possessor because it inheres within it as a quality, it is logical that its reflection occurs only together with that possessor; thus it is said: "the ether in the ether.
This is stated in order to make the face-to-face encounter between the space of the well and the space of the mouth intelligible to the heart.

He provides an illustration: "like another speaker facing that [first speaker]. This means: like the space associated with the listener who faces the speaker other than the one under discussion—the space associated with the speaker of the sound.

Just as [the eye] perceives a reflection, so too does the space within a well and the like. Indeed, in this world, the cognition produced by each respective sense organ must determine its object precisely as that which has already grasped a corresponding reflection; otherwise, for a cognition that is devoid of form (nirākāra), [no object could be determined].

Because it would be common to multiple objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, there would be no restriction such that "this is the cognition of blue" and "this is the cognition of yellow. Therefore, cognition possesses a form (sākāra), for without possessing a form, its determination according to each respective object would be impossible. Nor is it the case that... [the same object] of this [cognition].

It would not be correct to say that the restriction of objects to specific cognitions (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) is thereby established on the grounds that "that alone is the cause," because if there is no distinction in their status as causes, it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs would also be the objects of that cognition.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "existence is produced by the object, blue, but not in this way by the eyes and so forth": [this is untenable].

If it is asked, "Is that [the object] a single objective domain?"—this is not so; for being an object (*karmatva*) is indeed being a factor (*kārakatva*), and that arises by virtue of being permeated by an action (*kriyā*). Otherwise, it would be merely a thing (*vastumātra*) and not a factor.
And since it is precisely the permeation of the action called "cognition" (*jñāna*) in the case of "blue" that is proposed here for investigation, how [could there be a single objective domain]?
In that case, its status as an object would have to exist even prior [to the cognition]; nor could its having that single object be established merely by way of being a generator.

As for the claim that, despite the lack of distinction in their generative capacity, this difference is produced solely by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing—that is merely sketching a mode of escape; so enough of this prolixity. By this—

The sense organs, too, are capable of effecting the discernment of their respective objects only when they have grasped the reflection of those [objects]; thus, the analogy has been well illustrated by the phrase, "like another speaker. Although this applies to any hearer whatsoever, [it is particularly relevant here].

Nevertheless, this has been illustrated by the fact that, due to attachment and so forth, a mutual confrontation between the speaker and the respondent is inevitable; however, for the listeners, even a lack of such confrontation is possible.
For instance, worldly listeners are seen speaking in this manner: "No..."

"I have heard what was said by him. Alternatively, the meaning is that the space of the mouth reflected in the space of a well or similar object appears as another speaker, and the sound uttered—as if by another mouth—is heard. Thus it is with the reflection as well.

Because it exists as non-different from that [original object], it is rightly said that the reflection is indeed facing the original object; thus, by necessity, the reflection possesses the quality of being oriented toward the original object. — 31 ||
For this very reason, he states that only the cognizer situated in the space between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) perceives them, and no other:
"And just as one standing behind a mirror does not perceive the face."
In that same way, one situated behind such a space does not perceive the sound.

"Face" refers to the reflection of a face belonging to another; "of such a kind" means facing the original object (bimba) while situated behind it in a place resembling a hollow or a cave—this is the meaning. "Sound" refers to the characteristic of an echo; by the negation of "he does not know," the mere act of perceiving the reflection is denied.

In reality, it is indicated that there is no such thing as "standing apart" (atathāsthitam); for the point is that the absence of the object of knowledge does not follow from the absence of knowledge.

Therefore, even though a reflection has arisen, one does not perceive it due to the absence of its abiding in a suitable location—this is the meaning; although this [point] is indeed already established by the passage beginning with "the fixed orientation toward the original object" (niyatād bimbasāṃmukhyam).
The meaning has already been explained; nevertheless, it is mentioned again in order to reinforce the similarity with a reflected image of form. || 32 ||
Now, in this case, does the state of belonging to the same class as a reflection of form apply by way of some partial similarity or by way of total identity?

Regarding the first alternative, since even the state of belonging to the same class as an actual sound produced from another sound exists through some aspect such as being manifest and so forth, it would follow that the latter also possesses that same nature.

He shows the following doubt: "This is not the case for every single instance—that upon the arising of a reflected image of form, there is a cognition of the original object (bimba) such as a hand; however, here it is not so.
Therefore, he states: "And sound certainly does not reflect when it is unmanifested."
The audition of its manifestation occurs simultaneously with the second [moment]. (3-33)
In that very moment, however, there is the state of being a reflection, and the scripture is simultaneous with it.
In this context, sound— so long as it remains unmanifested— that is, unuttered— does not attain the nature of a reflection; therefore,

having been manifested in the first moment through the impact of the articulatory places and organs, it necessarily enters the domain of audibility for the sense of hearing, while in the second moment, again...

It is heard that [the reflection] attains the state of being a reflection; however, there is no perception at the moment of its becoming a reflection of that which is considered the original (bimba), which perishes as soon as it is uttered. Therefore, this does not belong to the same category as a reflection of form (*rūpa*), because in that case, the original object is perceived even at the time of the reflection. // 33 //
This is not so; for he says: "For us, the determination of the form of a hand and its shadow occurs at the same time. (3.34)

"Certainty" (*niścaya*) is an appearance whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); even in that case, there is no cognition of the original object (*bimba*) at the time of the reflection (*pratibimba*).

For it is not logical that when the reflection is cognized, there is also a cognition of the original object, such as a hand and so forth, because of the contradiction in the simultaneous arising of two cognitions. Nor is this [cognition] a single one, like the cognition of a variegated painting (*citrajñāna*).

It has both as its object, because the original form (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*) exist at a great distance from one another, and thus there is no appearance [of them] without separation. If it is argued: "But surely, even though there is no appearance of the hand and so forth, the thing itself still exists"—[we reply: that is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*).

It is that which establishes all things, for without it, it would be impossible to determine the existence or non-existence of objects; yet that very [means of knowledge] is not present here. Thus, what proof is there for the actual existence of an object such as a hand, and likewise for sound, even in its second moment?
In the case of that which is in a state of perishing, although it lacks actual existence, its cognition does not fail to occur at the moment it is reflected;
thus, even here, since there is no simultaneous cognition of the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*), its belonging to that same class remains established. || 34 ||
Thus, having established the ultimate reality of the reflection by refuting the view of the Naiyāyikas, he resumes the subject at hand:
"In this way, once the true nature of the reflection has been demonstrated here,"
We shall now speak of the subject at hand; therein, it is worthy of being reflected. (3-35)
In the blissful ether, sound is beautiful, as is the touch within the domain of touch;
yet there is also another kind of touch arising from firm blows, pain, cold, and so forth.
Standing outside, because he is a reflection, he effects the smearing of one's own body.

He says this: "In that case," and so forth. "In that case" means: such being the situation. "In the ether" (nabhasi)—the connection is as follows: because sound possesses purity (*nairmalya*) precisely there, and being situated in that which is beyond (*para*), it is capable of reflection; and this [principle] is to be applied everywhere. "Accompanied by bliss" (*sānanda*)—meaning, having the nature of the locus of bliss (*ānanda-sthāna*).

"In specific locations such as the bulb (kanda), the heart, and the surface of the palate; for it is precisely there that, due to the purity of touch, a touch appropriate for the enjoyment of a couple is transmitted, by which even the bliss resulting from the flow of the bodily constituents (dhātu-niṣyanda) occurs. Therefore, because it produces an excellence of bliss, it is called *śundara*."

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, another touch—though unpleasant because it causes suffering and so forth—is transferred by implication (*arthāt*) into a specific substratum (*ādhāra*) consisting of suffering and the like, such as the stomach, the tortoise-channel (*kūrmanāḍī*), or the throat of an elephant in rut (*mattagandhaja*), whereby even fainting and other states may occur; this is what is meant by "located elsewhere" (*parastha*).

The sense is that he is the primary [subject] when being experienced by another; this is an illustration, and by extension, he would likewise exist in the form of what is being remembered, imagined, and so forth. To the question, "From what is his status as a reflection (pratibimba) perceived? he says:
"Because it is a reflection, it causes the smearing of one's own body. And this is common to the experience of both pleasure and pain; thus, it is stated without distinction. (35–36)
One might object: "In that case, since it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), why is this not considered primary *sparśa*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this is not primary, because the succession of its effects is not manifested. (3-37)

"Primary" (mukhya) means having the form of the *bimba* (the original image). Because there is no manifestation of the succession—that is, the continuous flow—of the effects of that touch, such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth;
for when a cause is directly present, its effect arises without interruption, but it is not so here.
Thus, this [interpretation] does not possess primacy. || 37 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"In the same way, fragrance is clearly present within the nose, and taste within the saliva of the teeth. (3.38)

Regarding the phrase "dantodake" (in the water of the teeth): the meaning is [in that which serves as] the locus of the sense organ of taste, which is endowed with the quality of a stainless essence. || 38 ||
Thus, indicating that reflections of taste and so forth are of the same nature as reflections of form—just like an echo—he demonstrates their systematic arrangement according to what is possible:
"And just as a form reflected in the eyes... [is not seen].
For indeed, it is perceived by means of one sense organ;
likewise, taste, touch, fragrance, and so forth are not perceived even when they are present, without their respective sense organs. (3-39)
It has been stated many times that the true nature of a reflection consists solely in its being a mere manifestation (*avabhāsanamātra*).
And this manifestation depends upon the presiding of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) over the sense faculties that grasp their respective objects; for:

Even when a mirror or similar object is present, if the collection of sense organs such as the eyes is not presided over by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), how indeed could there be the manifestation of a reflection of the face and so forth? Consequently, this applies to the two eyes, which are to be presided over by the visual faculty.
The meaning is that the form reflected in the two pupils is not perceived by one eye-faculty belonging to another [person], nor does it appear without the operation of a different eye-faculty.

It has been stated— "of the two eyes"— in order to demonstrate that the employment of the eye-faculty belonging to another is required not only for the manifestation of a form reflected in a mirror or similar object which lacks the skill of discerning it, but even for one's own eyes when they are similarly [unskilled]. Indeed, it is not the case that...

The sense is that, like eye-salve and such, it is capable of being discerned due to its extreme proximity. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this does not manifest without the operation of the senses. In this same way, even though [the object] exists, it remains as something reflected in the taste and so forth.
The meaning is that, without the operation of its own sense organ, it is not perceived nor does it appear.

In this context, since the manifestation of the sense organs such as the eyes would otherwise be impossible, the presiding of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is implied; thus, this has not been stated explicitly by the author himself.

Otherwise, even though the eye and other senses are active, they would not discern anything at all. Now, one might object: "In this case, there is a connection with a reflection of both form and sound—internally within the eye, ear, and so forth, and externally within a mirror, space, and so forth; thus, the external reflection belongs to two different related entities."

It is logical that [an object] is delimited by the eyes and ears; however, touch and so forth migrate only within the body, such as into the *kanda* (the vital center), and thus remain there. Furthermore, because the continuum of another person is always to be inferred, it cannot be the object of an external sensory cognition belonging to someone else.
This would be so; how then was it said that "this is not perceived without the eye, like a reflection of form"?
Regarding this, it is said: "Nor is that which resides within the locus of touch the object of other sensory cognitions that perceive external things. (3.40)

Regarding the term *āntare* (internal): it is because [the senses] function within the internal body (*antardeha*). The phrase "the locus of touch" (*sparśanadhāmani*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the domains of smell and taste are also included. Furthermore, the reason for the other sensory cognitions not perceiving internal touch and so forth is provided through the qualification "touching the external" (*bahiḥspṛśaḥ*). The word *śa* is dependent on the word *gocara* (domain).

The explanation: Thus, because they exist within the body—such as the *kanda* and so forth, as well as the fields of touch and so on—it is not the case that they fall within the range of the senses for another perceiver, just like the eyeballs and such. || 40 ||
In that state, touch and the other [objects] manifest solely through the activity of their own respective sense organs presided over by the internal organ; thus he says:
"Therefore, from the nearby, similar sense organs of one's own..."
When [the object] is grasped by the senses along with the purpose and the internal organ,
then that reflection, having been taken up, indeed produces its own corresponding activity within the sense-faculty. (3.41)
Therefore, for the reasons stated— such as their internal nature and so forth— the internal organs, beginning with the mind (*manas*),

can sequentially come into contact with all the sense organs. Consequently, that which is proximate, conjoined, specific to its own object by virtue of its suitability, and unperceived due to the absence of such things as injury to the respective organ, [is apprehended].

That sense-organ is the skin and so forth; when there occurs an impulsion toward an object such as touch, having the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its agent, then— due to the contact with the external touch and so forth which serve as the prototype (bimba)— there arises in the sense-organ a sensory cognition (indriyajñāna), which is a cognition that possesses only the apprehended form.

Since it has already been stated that the determination of each respective fixed object is possible, the reflection—which consists of touch and so forth—having been taken up or grasped, produces (sūyate) or performs its own corresponding causal function (arthakriyā), characterized by bliss and so on, which is considered to be its source (bimba); this is the meaning. And for this very reason, here...
Reality [is established], because everywhere the relationship between the grasped and the grasper exists in this very way.

Furthermore, in the absence of an external object, even touch and other sensations that are being remembered—even when they have been transferred into their own respective domains—do not perform real causal functions; thus he says:
"But [the power of action] does not arise from what is remembered, which is an object of the mind."
That action indeed exists by virtue of its present state;
therefore, the most excellent touch, being present and having come into contact with that sense organ, is known as such through its activity. (3-42)

By the phrase "from memory" (smṛtāt), its impossibility outside [the mind] has been stated; for since that [memory] has past objects as its domain, even things like fragrant bandhūka flowers—which are impossible outside [of the mind]—may become the objects of mental cognition. This is the sense. The intention is: "It may exist [as such], but it would certainly not be non-existent."

For pleasure and the like could indeed arise even from a touch that is being remembered; however, that [pleasure] is not real, because there is an absence of its continuous occurrence. The reason for this is: "that [activity], it is said, arises from the present" (*sā kila vartamānataḥ*); the particle *kila* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). This is because that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs externally in the present.
This is what follows from the sense of the passage—this is the meaning. Thus he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Therefore, the excellent touch that arises from the aforementioned external object, having arrived—that is, having imparted its reflection—at the sense-organ, namely in the cognition of the tactile organ (*sparśanendriya*), and being thus known, [is perceived].
The meaning is: he becomes one who performs his own true purposeful action according to how it is to be done. || 42 ||

Now, one might object: "Since only an existing object is capable of casting a reflection, and since touch and so forth cannot exist externally [in the mirror], they do not undergo transference at all; therefore, what indeed could perform a causal function (arthakriyā) within memory and the like, such that its unreality would even have to be postulated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the absence of such an external object, that very [organ], being of a similar nature, reflects itself within it; thus,
the excellent touch produces that state which consists of bliss.
And that too [occurs] within some particular series of channels.

In the absence of an external object, it is not an external thing such as touch that has become a form through its own nature— inscribed by mental constructs such as memory and the like, resembling that [external object]— but rather that which is reflected within the field of touch and so forth; thus, according to its own fitness, it possesses that [feeling] characterized as pleasure, even though it is unreal.

"It performs purposeful action"—this is the meaning of the sentence. Now, since there exist many fields of touch such as the *kanda* and so forth, one might wonder: does the touch transfer everywhere, or only in certain places? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that [touch] occurs within any particular series of channels (*nāḍi*)."

The meaning is: "in some particular locus of support," such as the *kanda* (the bulbous root) or others, which consist of a continuous series of channels (*nāḍī*). For, due to the predominance of the *kanda* and other such sites, certain specific loci of support arise for some [practitioners]; it is precisely there that their excellence of purity occurs, just as the palate is for the neuter vowels.
The meaning is that it is precisely there that their transition of tactile sensation occurs. || 43 ||

Having thus established the true nature of the reflection, he applies it to the subject at hand: "Therefore, by offering the universe as its own self within the mirror of consciousness, this Lord proclaims His own stainless universal form. (3.44)

By that reason just mentioned, the universe is consciousness itself; because of its extreme transparency, it is like a mirror, and by offering itself— that is, by giving its own reflection— within that mirror,
it [confers] the stainless [glory] upon this Lord whose nature is consciousness, for that glory has been established through both reasoning and experience, and is therefore beyond reproach.

It expresses—that is, it manifests—the state of being the universal form (*viśvarūpatā*) as non-different from its own self; the meaning is that nothing flashes forth apart from consciousness. Indeed, the reflection of a face or the like does not appear independently or separately from its own support, the mirror and so forth—this is the intended sense. Therefore, this entire universe...
The essential meaning is this: it is the very form of the one Supreme Lord, whose nature is pure consciousness.
As it has been stated in the *Prajñālaṅkāra*:
"If that is so, then the world belongs to a certain single, partless [entity] alone."
"Let the form be according to the stated rule; what is lost for us?
Regarding the word *vadate*, [the rule] is *bhāsanopasaṃbhāṣājñānayatnakṣepavācanavyavasāyasvatantraprayogeṣu* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.47).
By such statements as these, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the sense of "shining forth. || 44 ||

Now, if the universe is indeed not distinct from consciousness, then because it consists of the nature of consciousness, would it not also possess the status of being both a property and its substratum? True—this is certainly the case;
thus he says, preceded by an external example:
And just as odors, forms, tangibles, tastes, and so forth, when reflected, appear with the coloring of their substratum—as a face and such do in a sword-blade—so it is here. (3.45)
In the same way, this entire universe, reflected within consciousness, partakes in the full range of attributes such as luminosity and sovereignty. (3.46)
In this world, indeed, forms and other objects, when reflected, appear only as qualified by the specific limitations (*upādhi*) of their respective substrates;
just as a face appears in a sword as colored by its attributes such as verticality,
so too does it appear in a large or small mirror according to that [substrate's] nature— likewise, this entire universe appears within the Light of Consciousness.

The meaning is that once reflected, it must necessarily take on—that is, appropriate—the entire collection of its attributes, such as being manifest; for it is only when the universe is not distinct from the Light (prakāśa) that its state of being manifest can exist.
Otherwise, because manifestation would be impossible, nothing at all could shine forth. And for this very reason:

Its sovereignty consists in its self-luminosity; for if the universe—consisting of insentient objects such as blue or pleasure—were distinct from light, it would, by virtue of its insentient nature, not be manifest through itself, but rather through another. Thus, in dependence upon another, there would be a state of heteronomy.

Existence; and for this very reason, this entire collection of objects of knowledge has become the body of the Supreme Lord whose nature is Light. Thus, because his nature is Light, he is the Self of the universe itself. As it has been said:
"Even a single point of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization."
Thus it is said; likewise: "Each individual principle (tattva) also possesses the nature of the thirty-six principles. ||45-46||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not previously established that among form and the other [sensory objects], only a certain thing reflects in a particular instance? So how could the entire universe, consisting of form and the rest, undergo reflection within a single cognition? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And just as a reflection appears on all sides in a crystal that is transparent in every respect, so too does it appear in awakening, which possesses transparency in every respect. (3.47)

Regarding the term "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*): in the case of the crystal, it refers to every direction such as east, west, and so forth; in the case of consciousness (*bodha*), it refers to every [object] such as form and the like. Although, in a crystal that is transparent on all sides, there would only be a reflection of mere form from every direction—and thus this [specific] example might not apply—[the point remains].
Although there is equality in consciousness regarding its capacity to receive reflections of form and so forth,

this [distinction] has been introduced with the desire to demonstrate the excellence of objects in receiving reflections, due to the occurrence of varying degrees of clarity according to their respective natures; for instance:

Just as there exists a gradation in the capacity for receiving reflections according to each respective object— namely, the front surface alone of a mirror, both the front and back surfaces of a sword, and the extreme transparency of crystal on all sides—
so too does such a gradation exist for consciousness in every respect.

Because of its transparency, consciousness possesses the capacity to receive the reflections of form and other objects; thus, consciousness is even more utterly transparent than crystal—this is the intended meaning. || 47 ||
Now, what indeed is this extreme transparency of his even beyond that? To this he says:
"That extreme transparency consists in the non-manifestation of one's own form;
therefore, consciousness is the most transparent, whereas a gem is not, because its form is perceived. (3.48)

In this context, indeed, Light, because it is self-luminous, shines by its own self alone and not for another; thus, due to its independence from anything else, it does not touch even a trace of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*). Consequently, it does not possess the property of being graspable by another cognition—like a crystal or similar objects—by which even the appearance of a form (*ākāra*) might occur. Here, however...

For only that which is transparent can receive the reflection of that which is non-transparent, just as a crystal gem receives that of a white silk cloth; and there exists nothing else more transparent than the Light— which is of the singular nature of the supreme subject and dependent upon that Light— capable of grasping even its form.
This has been rightly stated: "That absolute transparency consists in the non-manifestation of one's own form.

On the other hand, objects such as crystal are not transparent in comparison to this [consciousness], because they are themselves objects of perception (*grāhya*). For the more distinct the state of being an object of cognition, the more there is an absence of transparency—this is the intended meaning.
And with this very intention, it was previously stated:
"The primary purity of this Lord of Consciousness is absolute;
anything else [found] anywhere is merely a fragment of a fragment."

By these and other such statements, the twofold nature of clarity—both primary and secondary—is described for consciousness and for certain other entities. The intention is as follows: a mirror and the like are clear, crystal is clearer, but consciousness is the clearest of all. || 48 ||

Thus, although the universe arises in every respect through its reflection in consciousness, there exists a certain distinction between this and an external reflection— a distinction established by the force of reasoning— as he says:
"And a reflection is presented by means of an external prototype (bimba)."
If that very [object] is the reflection, what remains of the original object? (3.49)

In this world, indeed, there is no disagreement that a reflection is projected onto a mirror or similar surface by means of an external object such as a face; however, when that very external object which is generally accepted as the "original" (bimba) is itself understood to be the "reflection" (pratibimba), then what indeed remains as the original?

The meaning is this: let there remain only that object capable of casting a reflection; nothing else whatsoever is possible. For no one accepts that there exists another object separate from that [reflection], in the same way that an object such as blue or pleasure is separate from cognition. || 49 ||
Now, one might object: "Even if this is so, how could a reflection arise without a cause?
In that case, some cause existing as the original object (bimba) must be stated. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Or rather, whatever cause is designated as the original object..."
That too becomes a reflection within consciousness; otherwise, it is non-existent.

In this context, whatever cause is intended as the "original object" (*bimba*)—insofar as it is capable of imparting a reflection—is that [cause] non-different from consciousness, or different? If it were non-different, then by the reasoning already stated, it would be merely the reflection and not the original object; and if it were different, it could not be so because it lacks the quality of being cognized. Therefore, it is neither.
Thus it has been rightly said: "If that very thing is the reflection, what remains of the original object?
He concludes this very point:
"In this way, this sovereignty of the reflection unfolds everywhere, protected by the weapon of the firm logic of self-awareness. (3.51)
The particle *eva* is displaced [in its position]; its meaning is that [the reflection belongs] to the reflection alone, and not to the original object (*bimba*) as well.
The phrase "everywhere" means not in the external face and so forth, for in that case, the capacity belongs to both the original object and the reflection—this is the intended sense. || 51 ||

Now, since those two are mutually dependent, how can there be the existence of the reflection alone in the absence of the original object? To this he says: "But in the absence of the original object, how could the reflection exist?"
"What can we do? For that is indeed seen; surely it should be called a reflection. (3.52)

He provides the resolution for this very point with the words "What can we do? and so forth. The phrase "it is seen" implies the principle that "indeed, there is nothing inconceivable regarding what is perceived. Now, one might object: "Certainly, we do not deny what is perceived when this is said; rather, [we deny] this universe which is currently being perceived."
He says: "We maintain that [the object] is not to be called a reflection (*pratibimba*), but rather the original image (*bimba*). To this, he asks:
"Well then, let that *bimba* be described. (52)
He refutes this very point:
"It is not so, because that characteristic is absent; for what indeed is called a 'reflection'?
It is like a face appearing as something unmixed with anything else and independent. (3.53)

"Because of the absence of the characteristics of an image" means because of the lack of connection with the characteristics of a reflected form (*bimba*). What, then, are the characteristics of an image?
To this he says: "The image," and so forth. "Unmixed with others" means excluded from both similar and dissimilar things—this is the meaning.
For this very reason, it is "autonomous" (*svatantra*), being established solely in its own nature, and not dependent on another.
Because its ultimate perfection would otherwise be impossible; for if that were the case, it would not be distinct from that [perfection]—this is the intended meaning.
And regarding its being of such a nature, the fact that it is uncontradicted is itself the proof, as stated:
"while appearing. || 53 ||

Thus, immediately after the characteristics of the original object (*bimba*), in order to establish the foundation for the reflected image (*pratibimba*)— which is to be characterized as being of equal status with it— and first to illuminate that its substratum is established by all disputants:

"He defines the characteristic by incorporating the meaning of the *Prajñālaṅkāra-kārikā*: 'The imitation of another's form without abandoning one's own nature is called the nature of a reflection, as in the case of a sword-blade or the surface of a mirror.'"
They say that the nature of a reflection consists in its similarity to another form while not abandoning its own essential nature, as in the case of a sword-blade or the surface of a mirror. (3.54)

In this regard, all theorists maintain that the nature of a reflection consists precisely in the similarity with the form of another— such as a face— even while the mirror or other reflecting surface does not abandon its own unique form, such as its thinness or circularity; it is not, however, the actual acquisition of that [other's] form.

They say: "The meaning is that there is no disagreement here by anyone. For if [the mirror] were identical [to its reflection], then even for a mirror with a single smooth body, there would be an absence of smoothness when it assumes the reflection of a face with depressions and elevations—since even upon the conjunction with the reflection of a city and so forth, it assumes multiple forms.

There would be a lack of unity in the mirror; therefore, just as in the case of a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), although there is the perception of many [colors], because the unity of the variegated cloth and so forth is not lost, it is indeed unity and not plurality due to its having forms resembling many [colors]. Likewise, even in the case of a mirror and the like, when there is the conjunction with multiple reflections, there is no multiplicity of form.
There is no consequence of identity, but rather merely similarity to that;
and from mere similarity alone, there is no identity of nature, for a cow does not become a *gavaya* simply by virtue of its similarity to a *gavaya*.
Therefore, the essential meaning is this: the state of bearing a reflection consists precisely in having a form similar to the original object (*bimba*). || 54 ||
He corroborates this very point by way of its meaning:

"And it has been stated by the Buddhists that even when an external object exists, the intellect—because it perceives both the one and the many—has a form similar to the many, but is not itself multiple. (3.55)
"It has been said"—in the *Prajñālaṅkāra* and other works. As it is stated there:
"Therefore, even though an external object exists, because the intellect perceives both the one and the many, it manifests as having a form that resembles the many, yet it is not itself manifold."
Thus [ends the section]. 3-55.
One might raise the objection: "Even so, would not the definition of a reflection remain unstated?
Having presented this doubt, he states that very definition:
"But if this is so, what is said to be the definition of a reflection?"
Because it is impossible for anything else to be mixed with it, its differentiation cannot be manifested.
They say it is a reflection, just as a face [is seen] in a mirror. (3.56)
In this regard, indeed, all disputants maintain that it is a reflection;

for it is due to its conjunction with a mixture—namely, identity—with another object such as a mirror which serves as its own substratum, and because of the reason that it is not distinct from that [other object]. Therefore, it is other than that.

The meaning is that it is "dependent" (paratantra) because its manifestation cannot occur separately or independently—that is, apart from the mirror or other such objects—which are capable of assuming its form. By this, its contrast with the original object (bimba) is shown; for that [the original object] is said to be unmixed with anything else and independent.
And this has already been stated at length previously; therefore, no further effort is made here. || 56 ||

He applies this very principle to the subject at hand: "Since this [world], mixed with consciousness, cannot appear as distinct from consciousness, why is the supreme reality (paratattva) and so forth not called a reflection within consciousness? (3.57)
Indeed, why is this universe— which consists of reality, the worlds, and so forth— not called a reflection within consciousness?—
the meaning is that it must necessarily be so designated—
because this [universe] too has attained identity with consciousness through consciousness, just as a face does through a mirror; for this very reason, [it is like] from a mirror.
That which cannot manifest separately from its face—that is, from consciousness—because apart from light nothing at all in this collection of entities could ever shine forth; such is the meaning.
As it has been said:
Knowledge manifests both externally and internally in the form of this or that object;
there is no existence of an object apart from knowledge, and therefore the world is of the nature of knowledge.
"For entities have never been made objects by anyone apart from cognition;
therefore, it is determined that cognition has attained the nature of those [entities].
Thus [it is said].
Likewise: "Because they are perceived simultaneously, the knowledge and the object of knowledge possess a single form. (57)

Thus, even though the universe possesses the characteristics of a reflection, if it is asserted that its status as the original object (*bimba*) is entirely without cause, let it be so; what fault is there? Indeed, there is no dispute here, nor is the burden of proof upon the learned in this matter, for they are intent only upon the reality itself, and that cannot be made otherwise.

This is possible, because it has been established here that [the object] possesses the characteristics of a reflection, and because it is impossible to apply the characteristics of an original object (bimba). Thus he says:
This is the established rule for defining characteristics; if it were otherwise, let the original object itself be called [the word].
Wise people apply themselves to real entities, not to conventional sounds. (3.58)
"Accidentally" means without cause—this is the meaning. || 58 ||
Now, one might object: "Let it be that the universe is called a reflection because it possesses those characteristics;
we have no insistence on this point. But how could its very existence possibly occur without a cause known as the original object (*bimba*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Is it not the case that a reflection cannot exist without an original object (bimba)? He answers this very point: "What of it? For in a reflection, the original object does not exist through identity (tādātmya). (3.59)
"What follows from that?"—if the original object (*bimba*) does not exist, what then? The meaning is: nothing at all.

For the original object does not exist within the reflection as a single identity, in the way that "treeness" exists within the "śiṃśipā-ness" [of a specific tree], such that in the absence of the original object, the reflection would also cease to exist. || 59 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Therefore, even if that [object] which was described as the definition is impossible, there is no loss; for this question merely results in an inquiry into the cause. (3.60)

"From this"—because there is an absence of the state of identity between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). "Of what has been stated"—meaning, with respect to the entire universe. "The impossibility of that"—namely, [the reflection] in the presence of the original object. Now, it may be argued: "We do not dispute the definition of a reflection; rather, we ask how it could exist without an original object."
We reply: Is it not the case that the arising of entities without any cause whatsoever is logically untenable?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the mere cause," and so forth. Furthermore, the cause is of two kinds: the material cause (*upādāna*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). The material cause is, for example, clay and so on in the case of a jar; the instrumental cause is, likewise, in that very same case [the potter's wheel and so forth].

[The example is] a staff and so forth. Furthermore, the original object (*bimba*) is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the reflection; for that [material cause], like a clay pot, exists as a modification of its own substance (the clay) by following along with the effect. This is not the case here with the original object, because even when the reflection arises, it is perceived separately and remains entirely unmodified. Therefore, in this case, it is like a staff.
In the case of a jar, the original object is the efficient cause. || 60 ||
And therefore, this question concerns only the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and nothing else; thus he says:
"In that case as well, [the question] does not apply in any way to the material cause (*upādāna*), nor is there ever any possibility of efficient causes existing anywhere. (3.61)
