Nor is it the case that all instrumental causes must necessarily exist everywhere; thus he says, "In the case of an instrumental cause," and so forth. Indeed, here in this world, even by setting aside a staff, a potter might fashion a jar by merely whirling the wheel with his own hand. However, even one who is extremely skillful [could not do so] by setting aside the clay.

A potter might not be able to make a jar. Therefore, unlike the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the employment of an instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is not strictly necessary; thus, even without the original object (*bimba*), a reflection (*pratibimba*) may arise, because there exists another cause that serves as its substitute and is capable of producing it. 61
Thus he says:
"Therefore, let the form of the beloved be transferred [into consciousness] by means of the dense causal factor of recollection and so forth, directed toward the light present before one. (3.62)
"From this"—because even in the absence of the original object (*bimba*), the production of a reflection is possible through another cause.
"Light"—because it is capable of receiving the reflection of form. "By the dense"—the meaning is:
by that which has attained the nature of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*); for otherwise, [this would apply] to every rememberer whatsoever.

That which is constantly remembered in the past should appear [as a reflection]. In this case, however, there is no original object (*bimba*), because the beloved is absent due to being separated by distance of place and so forth. Nevertheless, since her effect—the reflection (*pratibimba*)—is perceived, there must necessarily be some other cause, such as memory, present here.
For there could not be an occasional manifestation resulting from the separation of a beloved who has been transferred [to another] without any cause whatsoever. || 62 ||
Thus it is said:
"Otherwise, why would a beloved woman who has ascended into consciousness appear as one joined with separation? Indeed, consciousness does not proceed toward separation before itself. (3.63)

"Otherwise"—that is to say, if the beloved were not reflected [in consciousness] through some other cause such as memory; "ascended into consciousness"—the sense is that there can be no manifestation of an object once it has ascended into consciousness if it were to appear as something fragmented. For, indeed, if there were fragmentation of consciousness...
Due to the occurrence of insentience (*jāḍya*), nothing at all would manifest; thus, this entire world would be blind.

Furthermore, an object mounted upon consciousness is such precisely because it is being experienced, and not as something additional to that; therefore, even that [object] would not appear as something separate. Hence he says: "Consciousness has not gone before [it] as something divided."

[Objection: But if this is so, then the very relationship of grasped and grasper would not exist, and thus there would be a total collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). [Reply: True—but with respect to supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*), not even a trace of duality exists; everything is consciousness alone. So what, indeed, could be called the "grasped"?

Or it may be the subject; yet that very [consciousness], by its own sovereignty, when it conceals its own nature and manifests as the essence of contracted cognition, then this entire worldly transaction of duality consisting of the grasped and the grasper occurs. Thus he says:

Therefore, let there clearly be some intermediate state designated as "intellection" (dhī), wherein its manifestation occurs through interruption, as in the case of volitional imagination and dreaming. (3.64)
For this very reason— that is, because of the impossibility of any separation from the perspective of supreme consciousness—
let there be an internal state known as "knowledge," which consists of a slightly contracted subject, is perfectly clear and non-conceptual in form,
and exists between supreme consciousness and the object of knowledge; wherein [the following occurs]:
The manifestation of a reflection would occur through its separation or distinction from the original object, as in the case of mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*) or dreams;

for even in the mental constructs of one separated from a beloved, since the original object is absent, [the reflection] appears only as something presented by other causes such as intense recollection.
The reflection of the beloved would appear—this is the intended meaning. || 64 ||

Just as in external recollection and so forth, a reflection may arise through another cause even in the absence of the original object, so too is it here; thus he says: "Therefore, let the powers of the Lord be the cause in such a case."

Therefore— from the aforementioned reason characterized by dependence upon nothing more than efficient causes— let the powers of knowledge, action, and so forth serve as the efficient causes for such a reflection of the universe within the Divine, whose nature is the luminous principle of consciousness (cittattva); in this way, no defect whatsoever can be imagined.

This is the meaning. And as for being "capable"— according to the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Even its possession of manifold powers is its inseparability from that very power," they have as their ultimate reality nothing other than the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone.
The summary meaning is this: by virtue of his own sovereignty alone, he assumes the form of the universe within his own self. As it has been stated by the author of the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"In that regard, however, the assumption of that form [by the Self] arises from the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)."
"But [this occurs] through the innate sovereignty of the reality of consciousness.
Thus [it is said].
Even that which is produced by subsequent recognition was shown by you, O Lord, for this very purpose:
the reflection of the circle of existents (*bhāvamaṇḍala*) within your own pure self, through your power, just as [an image] is seen by Prasenā (or Prabhā) in a mirror.
Thus it has been said.
In this way, he concludes that the universe is indeed a reflection within consciousness:
"In this manner, this entire universe [is reflected] in the Lord, within the ether of Bhairava’s consciousness."
Indeed, a reflection appears clearly in that which is pure; it certainly does not arise from the clarity of another.
"Anyeti"—the sense is that if he were dependent on another's perspective, his sovereignty (*svātantrya*) would be undermined.
For sovereignty is said to be *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and that is his primary nature. Indeed, a light devoid of *vimarśa* is neither possible nor logical; for this very [awareness] is its—
The distinction of the [Self] from insentient things, in its capacity to assume all forms, is that it perceives everything.
As has been stated by this very author elsewhere:
"The entire universe shines within the Self here."

"Just as a diverse arrangement [of objects] appears within the interior of a mirror, consciousness, moreover, perceives the universe through its own essential function of self-reflection; a mirror, however, does not do so."

And this reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) is not merely conventional; rather, it is proclaimed by all to be the nature of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*), which arises spontaneously and is inseparable from the very essence of consciousness. Thus he says:
"That independence of the Lord with respect to his being the self of the universe..."
Let them indeed recite that supreme goddess Pratibhā, who is unsurpassed.
"Anuttarā" means consisting of the wonder of unsurpassed, supreme sovereignty and freedom (*svātantryaiśvarya*).

For this very reason, it means *pratibhā* (intuitive insight) which is characterized by the manifestation of the infinite multitude of powers beginning with the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). By this, space has also been granted for the sequence of the arising of supreme reflective awareness (*paramarśa*). || 66 ||

For here, the manifestation of the universe occurs in two ways, as the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). In this regard, it has been stated by way of emphasizing that the universe is a reflection within consciousness: "It is *prakāśa* (light) itself that primarily flashes forth as the universal form of the signified. [And] "Vimarśa (reflective awareness) also..."
He also describes the sequence of the arising of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), stating: "She arises as the essence of the reflective awareness of those respective unsurpassed joys and so forth.
"She is that supreme Kaulikī Śakti, who possesses the expansion of the Kula of this God who is Akula; by her, the Lord is never separated. (3.67)

In this regard, O Pūrṇa, the supreme reality is indeed the unsurpassed Light (*prakāśa*) itself, which is ineffable (*anākhyā*), whose essence is the supreme self-reflection (*parāmarśa*), and which cannot tolerate any fixed designations such as Śiva, Śakti, and so forth. And that very [Light],
desiring to manifest the universe through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), first assumes the form of Śiva and Śakti.
It manifests within its own self, as they have said:
"I am always the wheel of rays belonging to the Lord Anuttara,
renowned as Śiva and Śakti, which bestows both the supreme and the lower fruits."
Thus, with this very intention, it has been stated elsewhere: "Rudra and Rudra-śakti have both dissolved into the Amanaska," and so forth. And therefore:

From that *Kula*, characterized by the nature of the full supreme consciousness (*pūrṇa-parasaṃvitti-tattva*), which is defined as follows: "O Omniscient One, know that *Kula* to be devoid of Śiva and Śakti, wherein this variegated universe arises and wherein it sets. From such a *Kula*.

That which is otherwise manifested as the unconditioned (*akula*) characterized by Śiva, shining forth as having the singular nature of light—of that [Śiva], she is the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), whose essential nature is the filling of the universe; for this very reason, it is said: "His powers are the entire universe... and so forth.

By such statements as these, [it is shown that] because she shines forth— that is, possesses the nature of expanding— that universe which is the *kula* consisting of the flow of Śakti, she is therefore called "Kaulikī Śakti," since the *kaula* (that which arises in *kula*)— which is essentially *akula*— exists within her through identity; and by her, the Lord, whose form was just described, is never separated.
The meaning is that its nature is inseparable from that [consciousness].
Thus, the first letter is also designated as "the body" (śarīra) of this family (kula), which is characterized by the letter A;
for he too is indeed the Lord.
"There is no one to utter it, nor is there anyone to obstruct it;
it utters itself, O Goddess, abiding in the chest of living beings.
From such a nature as described, [there arises] the *anāhata* (unstruck) sound, and from the *hata* (struck) sound produced by the impact of the articulatory places and organs.
Shining eternally as the nature of the most brilliant light, characterized by the supreme self-reflection of having transcended [all states],
it is said:
"Transcending both the unstruck (*anāhata*) and the struck (*hata*), he is the movement of consciousness in the great and formidable."
"The cry of the Goddess expands, intent on crushing the hearts of heroes.

And her supreme power is that which causes the expansion of the *kula*, the body; she is praised by means of that [expansion], meaning she is the originator of that body. For this very reason, she is called "Kaulikī."

Thus it has been said; for instance— the supreme, subtle Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, having attained a friction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) with Śiva consisting of the state of being the churner and the churned in a form of mutual aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*),
and having arisen, assumes the nature of Will, Knowledge, and Action, while manifesting the state of Raudrī.
Assuming the form of a triangle as Ambikā,
abiding in the crescent-moon form of the syllable *ukāra* as Jyeṣṭhā,
and taking on the form of a distinct line resting upon the point consisting of the letter *ra*, which is the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) arisen from the lunar dot (*bindu*).
"It illuminates"—that is, it causes the body of the initial phoneme to shine forth. As it is said in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"That power which is supreme, subtle, and proclaimed to be beyond conventional conduct (*nirācārā*)."
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"When that subtle *kalā*, Kuṇḍalinī, has arisen by means of that [breath],
she is the Bindu consisting of four *kalās*, the Lord residing within the womb of Śakti."
O beloved, through the process of churning and rubbing, straightness is produced;
that is known as the Jyeṣṭhā Śakti, situated in the center between the two points (bindus).
When she has reached the point of union with the *bindu*, she is like a line of the *amṛtakuṇḍalī*;
she should be known by the name *rekhinī* when both *bindus* are situated at her ends.
She is proclaimed as the three-pathed one and is sung of by the name Raudrī;
she is observed to be the Obstructress because she blocks the path to liberation.
"Ambikā, shaped like a crescent of the moon and possessing half-moon radiance, is indeed one;
thus that supreme power (parā-śakti) arises in three ways.
Thus it is stated in the venerable Vāmakeśvarīmata as well.
"O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial Śakti; she has arisen here," beginning thus, [the text continues]:
"She abides as the state in which all seeds and sprouts have been completely swallowed up."
Then the left [channel] is Śikhā, and the superior [channel] assumes the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭaka).
O Supreme Goddess, Raudrī is she whose form is the devouring of the universe;
the goddess Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
O Dear One, she consists of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti).
"She creates the three worlds; therefore she is celebrated as Tripurā.
With this very intention, it is stated elsewhere as well that she consists of the three abodes (dhāmatraya), which are characterized by creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
As it has been said:
"Established above is the emanation that bestows supreme bliss;
the supreme digit of Bindu rains down a shower of nectar."
Below, one should know the Great Fire (Mahāgni), the bringer of dissolution,
the end-maker, terrible, endowed with rows of flames, invincible, and a treasury of light.
Between those two is the supreme splendor, beautiful with the bliss of both;
that is to be known as the descent, Śiva, who pervades both.
When the moon and fire are mutually interpenetrated within the constellation Āśleṣā,
one should know that the moon represents creation, while fire is said to be dissolution.
"The sun is declared to be the descent (avatāra), while the Supreme Lord remains in the center.
Likewise:
"And the radiance has issued forth from Kālāgnirudra..."
It should be meditated upon as vast, manifest, and most radiant;
and above it, O Goddess, stands the tranquil digit of the moon, filled with the essence of the bliss of full nectar.
Since both [the Sun and Moon] are subject to fire and poison respectively, and therefore the fire and the moon are melted,
[the result arises] from the clear conjunction of the fire and the moon.
Then that very form would be the sun in its descent.
"And the wise one, having understood the nature of the object, should meditate through reasoning on the form of the sun of self-consciousness.
Thus it is said; and likewise:

"Then, the single Light arises, devoid of sound, possessing the expansion of the seeds of the digits of the sun, moon, and fire, bestowing the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower. And here, it follows that only three primary powers of the Supreme Lord are possible.

Primarily, its nature as that [form] alone has been stated; however, elsewhere it is said: "Raudrī is proclaimed as the head of the letter 'A', Vāmā as the face, Ambikā is said to be the arms, and Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as the weapon."
By such statements, its fourfold nature has also been described through another intended meaning.
Thus, this very supreme Kuṇḍalinī Śakti is not distinct from His own essential nature—as it has been said: "That by which the Lord is never separated. This has also been stated:
"The letter *a* and the letter *ha*—these two exist simultaneously;
there is no distinction between them, just as there is none between wind and space.
Thus, even though these two are inseparable, [they function] through the predominance of each one respectively.
Resting solely in its own essential nature constitutes its state as the solitary hero (ekavīra) and its nature as the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 67 ||
Furthermore:
"Śiva is not devoid of Śakti, nor is Śakti devoid of Śiva;
the entire expansion of the universe is their union."

According to the principle taught by the Great Guru in such passages, when these two possess a *yāmala* (conjugal) form consisting of mutual orientation toward one another, then the emanation of the universe occurs; thus he says:
"If the form of those two is *yāmala*, that is known as *saṅghaṭṭa* (the creative union)."
That very [power] is called the power of bliss (ānandaśakti), from which the universe is emitted.

"Of those two" means of Śiva and Śakti, who are designated by the terms *akula* and *kaulikī*. "Union" (*saṅghaṭṭa*) means a perfect friction, a movement, a state of vibration, and the surging forth of one's own nature—this is the meaning.
And therefore, [it occurs] precisely within the two *anuttaras*, whose essence is light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

From the friction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of the second phoneme, whose nature is the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), there arises the emission (*sarga*) of the universe, which consists of will (*icchā*) and the rest. Even in the sequence of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), emission occurs through the arising of bliss from the very friction of the woman and the man. Here, however, because Śiva and Śakti transcend the universe, [the emission is of a different order].

Furthermore, while one form is fragmented by virtue of being composed of the universe (*viśvamayatva*), this [other] form, despite being composed of the universe, transcends the universe; thus, due to the absence of any fixed limitation, it is the full (*pūrṇa*) form. || 68 ||
For this very reason, she is proclaimed in all the scriptures as the supreme goal to be attained; thus he says:
"The reality that is higher than both the supreme and the non-supreme is declared to be this very Goddess.
She is the essence, she is the Heart, and she is the Supreme Lord, the emission (visarga). (3.69)
In the Devīyāmalaśāstra she is called Kālakarṣiṇī;
likewise, in the Mahāḍāmara sacrifice, she is Śrīparā at the summit.

In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, she is described as the "Essence of the Mothers" (*mātṛsadbhāva*). From the supreme form of Śiva, which transcends the universe, and from the lower form of Śakti, which consists of the universe—she is the supreme, the full, the essence; thus it is stated in the *Śrīsārabhaṭṭāraka* and other texts. She is the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*).

The Secret of the Heart-Essence of Śrī. Regarding the term "supreme" (para): this is because both the supreme-inferior (parāpara) and the inferior (apara) emissions (visarga) are about to be described. The phrase "in the Mahāḍāmara sacrifice" is to be construed in grammatical apposition with the *Devīyāmala* scripture; therefore, it refers to that which expounds it.
This means: in the first part of the book. As it is stated there:

"In the middle of that is the Supreme Goddess (Parā); on the right is the Supreme-Non-Supreme (Parāparā); and on the left horn is the Non-Supreme (Aparā). Now listen to [what is] above the middle horn."

"That goddess Saṅkarṣiṇī, who is situated beyond the Supreme," [is so called] "by way of being the true essence (sadbhāva) of the Mothers"— as it is said there: "For this is taught as the supreme essence of the Mothers."
Thus [ends the section]. 69–70.
Having thus described the powers of consciousness and bliss, he speaks of the power of will: "In this union, that reflective awareness which arises from the nature of consciousness... (3.71).
The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the supreme mistress of the non-terrible powers (*aghorāṇāṃ śaktīnām*);
in this very conjunction (*saṅghaṭṭe*) whose nature has just been described, [it is said]:
"Bliss is the form of Brahman..."

By such statements as these, because of the primacy of consciousness (*cit*), this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which arises in the supreme subject as the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*) is the power known as Will (*icchā*). Indeed, it is that which—
“like before, bestows upon the multitude of living beings the fruit of the abode of Śiva.”
"The supreme powers known as Aghorā have been proclaimed by those who know that [reality] to be the Śiva-energies.
Regarding these aforementioned Aghorās,
because they consist solely of pure sovereignty (*svātantrya*), they do not possess the nature of the "terrible" (*ghora*) form characterized by the existence of duality and the like.
The Lord of the powers (*śaktīnām prabhuḥ*) is the cause of their manifestation—meaning that He contains within Himself the entire multitude of infinite powers.
For this very reason, She is "Supreme" (*parā*), being endowed with the highest excellence, and is designated by that name; such is the meaning.
In the present context as well, by this [term], the emergence of the third phoneme (*varṇa*) is stated. And that is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
But when, through the unfolding of the joy of the manifestation of His conscious nature, He proceeds with the creation of various effects in diverse arrangements;

"The first *tuṭi* of will is the thought of being oriented toward [the object]. Thus, as described in such passages, it consists of the initial vibration (*ādyaspanda*), whose nature is merely an outward orientation;
or rather, it may consist of the mere will that has not yet been colored by the objects to be created.

This [power] is twofold: either it assumes the nature of effort characterized by agitation through the coloring (*ārūṣaṇā*) by various objects to be sought, or it partakes in sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) by way of its external form.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"One [intention] consists of mere desire and is remote from that which is to be created;
another, however, having attained the state of effort, is proximate.
In that regard, the nature of the first [power] has been described; now, in order to describe the second, he says:
"If that very [power], in its agitated form, becomes the Sovereign (īśitrī), [she is the second]. (3.72)
Then the terrible, supreme goddesses were born as guides upon the path of Śiva.

Then, when the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) possesses sovereignty through its agitated form, the supreme (*parā*) non-terrible (*aghorā*) goddesses are born; that is to say, they manifest externally. For this alone is her sovereignty: that she shines forth externally in the form of those various infinite powers (*ananta-śakti*). And they are thus...

Because differentiation lacks clarity, they possess only the activity of manifesting their own essential nature. Thus he says: "the teachers of the Śaiva path. Therefore, the implication is that they do not obstruct the path to liberation like the Ghorā and other [obstructive] powers. This also applies to the present context.
The arising of the fourth caste has been described. || 72 ||

Having thus described the power of will (icchā-śakti) as being of two kinds, he also speaks of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti): "That self-reflection which previously existed as the solitary hero (ekavīraka)... (3.73).
The Self, whose nature is the unfolding of the entire universe to be known, exists as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

Indeed, in this context, because it was previously in a state of agitation and because there was at first no object of reflection distinct from itself, it was established solely in its own self; therefore, that very reflective awareness which existed as the "solitary hero" (*ekavīraka*)—that is precisely [what is meant].

The determination of the fifth seed-syllable (*pañcamabīja*) is as follows: it exists in the form of that primordial vibration (*unmeṣa*), which is the first pulsation of the universe that is intended to be inwardly known as the power of consciousness (*jñānaśakti*).
He connects this very point through the method of his own philosophical system: [The text continues: "He who, being of the nature of that [vibration], remains established... and so forth.
This is the goddess Parāparā, who [presides over] the formidable circle of Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍalī).
She incessantly creates that which is the sole lamp for the pure and impure paths;
[she is] called Ghorā. As it has been said:
"Those [powers] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma..."

"The terrible [powers], both higher and lower, would be fixed upon the cessation of the path to liberation. Thus [it is said]. Regarding "pure and impure"—the sense is that they do not fall further and further down like the *ghoratara* and other [lower powers]. || 74 ||

In this context, just as the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is twofold according to whether the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) exceeds [the subject] or not, so too is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) twofold.
Among these, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) when there is no excess of the object of knowledge has already been determined. Now, he describes its essential nature when there is an excess:
When the objective aspect, opening up due to its intensity, undergoes agitation, [it becomes the state of the subject]. (3.75)
At that time, when consciousness exists as pure awareness (*saṃvinmātra*), the appearance of deficiency arises;
for, in relation to knowledge, the objective aspect becomes manifest due to its predominance.
When it undergoes agitation by assuming various forms—such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—it then attains a state of manifoldness.

Because the object of knowledge is greater than the knowledge itself, when knowledge exists in the form of mere cognition, there arises the manifestation of deficiency or incompleteness; that is, the attainment of contraction occurs—this is the emergence of the sixth phoneme.
He elaborates upon this very point:
That which has become firmly established is said to be the commencement of the stability of the category of objects to be known. (3.76)
This is the conventional usage of the ocean of awakening, which encompasses the three aspects;
yogis discern this as the seed within the arrangement of that seed. (3.77)

That manifestation, which consists of nothing more than pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) and has become established—that is, having taken root—is said to be the beginning of the persistence of the various objects of knowledge, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; it is not, however, their direct persistence itself, because that [direct persistence] exists within the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). What indeed is this?

"What is this growth?"—to this he says: "This is its rootedness," and so forth. By this it is indicated that there is no object of knowledge whatsoever that exists apart from consciousness; rather, that very [consciousness] itself flashes forth in the form of various manifestations. Therefore, for this reason—that consciousness alone assumes diverse forms—this very [is the case].

It has been explained that pure consciousness alone is the cause of the sixth arrangement of differentiation; this applies to the yogin, and not to the non-yogin, because the latter perceive gross differentiation through the power of action (kriyā-śakti). "Cinvanti" means they know—this is the sense.
In this context, indeed, there are these very six primary reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) whose essence is the supreme contemplation (*paravimarśa*),
from which the arising of all reflective awarenesses occurs when there is a mutual conjunction with the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
As he will state:
"In this world, for the lineage of castes, the group of six vowels alone shall be the root.

In that regard, because Anuttara (A) and Andha (Ā) consist solely of pure consciousness, there is no differentiation in relation to them; thus, even the mention of an object of knowledge does not exist. || 77 ||
He begins to demonstrate that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) itself possesses four forms through its coloring by the object of desire:
"The power of will is said to be twofold—disturbed and undisturbed—for it takes upon itself the object of desire in its two forms. (78)

Because that which is being desired consists essentially of mere manifestation and of repose; for this very reason, there is the phonetic substitution of *ra* for *la* here, since those two possess the nature of manifestation and stability respectively. || 78 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Then, through the power that flashes like lightning and has the nature of fire, there is the attainment of the desired object;
or else, through stability, by means of the earth-nature. (3.79)

Based on the statement, "All this universe is His power...," this twofold power— which consists of the nature of fire and the nature of earth— is that which is desired; by that [power], therefore, [is meant] that which belongs to the twofold power of will (icchā-śakti).
"Attainment" (samāpatti) means appearing as non-distinct; therefore, its nature is formless—this is the meaning.

Although the attainment of the object of desire was previously described as the very form of the desire itself, by which its state of agitation was established, nevertheless, that was not so in a clearly manifest form.

"Just as now"—thus it was said with regard to "stability. And here, even though it is intended to be stable like an external object, it is not perceived as such; for if that were the case, it would be its effect, not something intended.
Therefore, because of the lack of clarity here, there is merely the auditory perception of the sounds *ra* and *la*, but not—

It exists as a direct manifestation, like a syllable. Thus it is said: "shining like a flash of lightning. For just as lightning, due to its momentariness, shines for only a brief duration, so too here that which is desired appears merely as a shadow. Therefore, in this case, there is only the hearing of the phoneme, not the phoneme itself directly.
The mere hearing of the phonemes is not itself the phoneme; for this very reason, the venerable author of the Mahābhāṣya states that this is a distinct genus (*jātyantara*), like Narasiṃha.
And for this same reason, these four phonemes are considered to possess a dual nature, because they serve as the substratum for both [the individual and the universal].

By the statement beginning with "The group of four— ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ— is likewise the neuter class," [these vowels] are everywhere designated as neuter; therefore, *akṣubdhā* (the Unagitated) is the Will (*icchā*) permeated by the power of Fire (*jvalana-śakti*).
The letter *ṛ* is indeed agitated; likewise, when permeated by the power of the earth (*dharā-śakti*), it becomes *ḷ* and *ḹ*.

Since the nature of that which is sought here—consisting of fire and the other elements—is obtained simply by taking up its essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*), no further qualification is required for that purpose. || 79 ||

Now, one might object: "If it is held that from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) there arises another reflective awareness through its absorption into the object of will (*iṣyamāṇa*), why is this not also the case for the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) through its absorption into the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Although this [absorption] exists to a great extent within the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*)."
Nevertheless, that was her place of residence, but not the land of her previous birth.
Although this object of knowledge, consisting of fire and so forth, exists predominantly within the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), nevertheless,

that power of cognition is merely the locus of the manifestation (*vibhava*) of the object, and not its place of birth characterized by the primordial power of will (*icchāśakti*). Like the power of will, this [power of cognition] is not the site of its origination.

—this is the meaning. Indeed, for the multitude of existing entities that have arisen within the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) as objects of desire, there is a manifestation within the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); their externalization occurs through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Therefore, within the power of knowledge, there is no production of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as something previously non-existent. Thus, it is not the case [that the object is newly created].
In that state, through immersion in it (*samāpatti*), there arises another act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*);

by means of that, because the object of desire is produced as something unprecedented within the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), it is designated in this way. Although all entities are possible even in the supreme consciousness (*saṃvit*) because it is filled with all things, [it is so called] for this reason.
Nevertheless, they remain therein as pure consciousness alone. || 80 ||
In this context, however, it has been stated that because of the attainment of a slight swelling [of consciousness], there appears as if something distinct;
therefore he says:
"Therefore, they say that the supreme nectar consists of the fourfold form of the power of will."
Because no other agitation exists, this is not the seed of anything whatsoever. (3-81)
"Supreme nectar" (parāmṛta) means that which consists of supreme wonder through resting solely within one's own self.
As he will say:
"And by resting in the Self alone, that is said to be of the nature of nectar."
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object:
by such statements as "The vowels are considered to be the seeds," their status as *bījas* (seeds) has been declared because they are included among the vowels; and that—
It is said that [the seed-syllable] possesses the quality of agitation (*prakṣobhakatva*), yet this does not apply here because its nature consists solely in resting within its own self;
for such agitation would only occur if another agitation were present. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"This is not a seed," because when there is rest within one's own self alone, no other agitation can arise.

This is because they are as if burnt, being unable to perform their own function, and not because the nature of the seed is entirely absent in every respect. For there is nothing distinct from the seed and womb consisting of Śiva and Śakti;
[as it is said: "Due to the division into seed and womb, the seed is considered to be twofold; the vowels are regarded as the seed."
Because of such statements as, "And the Yoni is remembered by the letters beginning with Ka," there exists another zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) by which this could be so. As for that which was said:
"But she who is described as participating in the impurity of the object of knowledge, through the conjunction of the mobile and the stable..."

"The pair of groups beginning with *ṭa* and *ta* is born from that which has two forms"—this and so forth will be explained further on, and it will be resolved in that very place; thus it is rightly said that this is not the seed-syllable (*bīja*). || 81 ||
Now, one might object: "If these [elements] do not possess the nature of seeds in this way, then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), they must have the nature of wombs (*yoni*"?
Anticipating this doubt, he says the following in order to refute it and to establish the distinctness of these [elements] from both seeds and wombs:
He first states its essential nature:
"The state of being a seed is the quality of being an agitator, and the state of being a womb is the substratum of agitation.
Now, one might object: a seed, which is considered to be a cause, is insentient; how can it [function] independently?
Anticipating the objection, "What is the capacity for manifesting another form?", he says:
"The nature of consciousness is that which causes agitation; it is both agitated and it agitates. (3.82)
"Agitation" (kṣobha) is the state of being an object of knowledge, while "agitating" (kṣobhaṇā) is its externalization.
Since consciousness itself is primarily the agitator, that very consciousness "is agitated" (kṣubhyati), because the causative sense is internalized within the non-causative root *kṣubh*.

The meaning is that, according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock's egg, it sustains the entire range of objects of knowledge—which, though primarily woven within, seem as if oriented toward external manifestation—and being thus agitated itself, it causes agitation and manifests them in the form of externality. Thus he says: "agitation," and so forth.
The meaning is that "impulsion" (preraṇā) consists of forms such as agitation (kṣobhaṇā) and dispatching (preṣaṇā), and so forth. || 82 ||
He also aphoristically indicates this very point by incorporating the process of the secret [teaching]:
"The desire to emit, which consists of a single seed-syllable portion that is non-different from the universe situated within. (3.83)
They know that agitation (*kṣobha*) is the non-desire for that [object], while the manifestation of the desire for reality (*tattva*) is what they call "agitating" (*kṣobhaṇā*).

The entire universe— the collection of objects such as those to be desired— which exists within [the subject] in identity with the perceiver, is non-different from that [subject] in its nature as consciousness, [even when appearing as] the object of desire and so forth.
That very nature of consciousness— which is undifferentiated by specific qualities and for that reason alone is one and non-dual—

is the seed-portion (*bījāṃśa*), the specific cause, because it manifests the universe by being filled with all existents. Its particular will to create, characterized by its independence from anything else, is [the power of will].
The desire to manifest the universe— which consists of the grasped and the grasper— as if it were divided,

and the relationship that arises through that [desire], is precisely what constitutes *kṣobha* (vibration/disturbance). Likewise, as in the expression "he causes the arrow to go," even when there is no such desire [on the part of the object], in the case of the collection of entities such as the body, the color blue, and so forth— which, due to indifference, are not oriented toward external existence— [the same principle applies].

The manifestation of the desire for that [object], which is an appearance characterized by a turning toward externality through the departure from indifference—that is "agitation" (*kṣobhaṇā*); this is what the teachers and others know—this is the meaning.
For in the process of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), a person desiring to emit a seed becomes agitated himself.

"But he agitates the young woman"—this has not been elaborated upon here because it is an extreme secret and because it is irrelevant to the present context; it should simply be inferred according to its application. || 83 ||
Having thus described the nature of the seed (bīja), he states the nature of the womb (yoni): "When, having attained unity with that [seed], her will becomes effective," (3.84).

The spiritual sons of the venerable Somānanda have declared this to be the support of agitation (*kṣobha*): by means of that collection of entities— such as the body, blue objects, and so forth, which are perceived as "this-ness" (*idantā*)—
and [the phonemes] *ka*, etc., having attained identity with them, the Will belonging to that supreme perceiver becomes effective (*kṛtinī*).

"By the principle expressed in such passages as 'These [powers], which shatter the universe, have emerged from me, Bhairava alone,' she becomes fulfilled and complete through resting solely in her own self. This very object, the substratum of the agitation of the sovereignty of consciousness— [this] Śrī Somānanda’s objects of compassion..."
The sons, beginning with the illustrious Utpaladeva, and the disciples, say—meaning they declare:

"Even in the course of spiritual practice (*caryākrama*), that state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) which, having been attained, brings the male desire to its fulfillment, is the 'womb' (*yoni*), characterized as the substratum of arousal. (84)
And this very nature of the seed and the womb has been aphoristically indicated by the words "situated within" (*antaḥstha*) and so forth.
Because it contains the secret methodology and is supremely worthy of being adopted, [the author] himself explains it so that it may reach the hearts of those to be graced:
It is that which does not manifest the distinctions of consciousness, such as the desire for acquisition (īṣaṇā) and so forth.

That which is the mere object of knowledge (*jñeyamātra*) is the seed; through connection with that, the state of being a seed exists within the vowel. It is the undivided [reality] of the cognitions of desire and so forth. That which is the object of knowledge—meaning that which must necessarily be known as the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).

The very nature of consciousness, because it does not assume the specific forms of particular cognitions such as will (*icchā*) and so forth, is the purely unconditioned form of the Supreme Lord. That alone— indeed, the Lord whose essence is consciousness, by the power of His will, [manifests] what was situated within externally...
"The yogi, like [the Supreme], may manifest the multitude of objects without any material substrate.

By such statements, because He is filled with all things, the seed is the primary cause, since the universe residing within Him manifests externally solely by His own will—this is the meaning. Now, if this is so...
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how can vowels also possess the nature of seeds (bīja)? it is said: "By virtue of whose conjunction there is seed-nature in the vowel.

The meaning of "by virtue of whose [conjunction]" (udyogāt) is "because of being animated by which [power]. Therefore, the intention is that the status of being a seed is appropriate for the vowels because they cause the manifestation of their respective phonemes; for indeed, [otherwise...]
The meaning is that, apart from the sovereignty of consciousness, nothing else possesses the capacity to manifest another form. || 85 ||

Having thus explained the meaning of the word "seed" (bīja), he also explains the agitation (kṣobha) consisting of the desire to emit (visisṛkṣā), which is of two kinds— both with and without the causative suffix— as follows:
"The very emergence of that seed is said to be that same desire to emit."
For this object of perception appears as if it were distinct from the conscious self. (3-86)

This is agitation; however, "agitating" refers to forcibly displacing the state of indifference from consciousness by its own power, even when it has become silent and has entered into another subject. (3.87)

"Arising" (udbhava) means the state of emerging—this is the sense. For this reason, this collection of objects to be grasped, such as the body, blue, and so forth, as well as [phonemes] like *ka* and so on, although not distinct from the conscious self (*cidātman*) and not exceeding it, appears as if distinct;
it is that which has appeared, or will appear, at a later time. This is that very [process].

Agitation (*kṣobha*) consists solely in the nature of being an impeller. For even in the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*), bliss and the rest occur immediately after agitation; however, the act of agitating (*kṣobhaṇā*) itself becomes silent due to indifference, no longer oriented toward external objects. As for those others who remain by means of the exclusion (*apoha*) of blue and so forth—

The body and so forth are the subjects (*mātṛ*), and by implication, objects such as blue and so forth are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); having forcibly relied upon their own inherent vitality (*vīrya*) characterized by autonomy— which is the agency of consciousness— there occurs,
through a violent imposition characterized by the manifestation of a will toward that [object] even when there is no such will, a state of indifference.

Because there is no engagement in the orientation toward external existence, "falling away" (cyāvana) is indeed the manifestation [of consciousness] precisely through that orientation toward external existence. || 86–87 ||
Having thus explained the *Bījasūtra*, he also elucidates the *Yonisūtra*:

"Even though this desire to emit has already arisen, it becomes fulfilled through its unification with another reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); that which serves as the basis for this agitation is proclaimed here [as the *yoni*]. (3.88)

That which is the desire to create, characterized by agitation, though it has arisen in another subject— namely, that reflective awareness consisting of "this-ness" (idantā), which is distinct from the original reflective awareness of "I-ness" (ahantā) grounded in pure consciousness— and which,

through the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the object of reflection and the act of reflecting, constitutes the collection of entities such as the body, blue, and so forth, that are to be reflected upon.
And because of that [the letter K], having resorted to oneness, she becomes fulfilled and complete by resting solely within her own self, having achieved her purpose;

this very point is what has been correctly proclaimed as the "substratum of agitation" (*kṣobhādhāra*) in the *Yonisūtra* in the passage beginning with "having attained the state of oneness" (*yadaikyāpattimāsādya*), and so forth—this is the meaning. || 88 ||
Having thus explained this by way of the meaning of the words, he now states it also by way of its intended purport:
"Therefore, at that time, one should know that [the internal] desires a state of being as if separate from the seed of the universe; hence, the entire external reflection will evolve. (3.89)

Then, from that immediately mentioned agitation characterized by the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), that object of knowledge— which exists internally in identity with the subject— attains a state of being almost manifested, a state of differentiation, and a state of appearing as something separate; therefore:

Beginning from the seed of the universe— the primordial letter— and from Mahāmāyā, the entire collection of entities, such as bliss and the rest, as well as the principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), which appear externally through differentiation,
shall evolve as having the nature of a reflection characterized by the form belonging to the knowledge of the original image (*bimba*).

The meaning is that [the seed-syllable] will manifest clearly, as appropriate, in the form of various bodies, such as blue and so forth, and as words, sentences, and so on. For even in the sequence of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), the seed-syllable itself, having emanated through differentiation, will assume the forms of female, male, neuter, and so forth. || 89 ||
And this was not stated merely as my own invention; thus he says:
"The true nature of the relationship between the agitated and the agitator has been shown by me, through the grace of my teacher, the venerable Maheśvara. (3.90)

The connection is as follows: I have demonstrated that true nature (*satattva*) which was previously taught by the Guru—who was saluted with the words "the Blessed Maheśvara, whose form is none other than That"—and so forth. || 90 ||
Having thus spoken in connection with this incidental discussion, he introduces the actual subject at hand:
"We speak of the subject at hand: these four phonemes are not the seed (bīja), nor are they the womb (yoni), because they do not attain the state of being a substratum for agitation. (3.91)

For, unlike in the case of *kādi*, there is no attainment of unity here such that the desire of anyone would reach fulfillment; thus, this [system] does not become a locus for arousal (*kṣobha*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "this is not the seed," there is no mention of a reason—such as "because another arousal is impossible"—as was previously provided. Therefore...
And thus, because these four classes [of phonemes] lack the quality of agitation, they consist of supreme wonder through resting solely within their own self. || 91 ||
Thus it is said:
"And because of resting in the Self alone, that [consciousness] is called immortal.
Not only does another reflective awareness arise for these [subjects] through their union with the object of knowledge as far as possible," [but also...]
Even mutually—thus he says:
"In this way, that pentad which was previously mentioned [is] mutual. (3.92)

"Arising in various forms through mutual intermingling"—this refers to the pentad (*pañcaka*) consisting of the forms of Anuttara, Icchā, Īśana, Unmeṣa, and Unmanā; for the power of Bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) is indeed "Bliss is the form of Brahman... [and so forth].
By such statements as these, [the world] is indeed non-different from consciousness; thus, there is no separate designation for it.
This very [world], though mutually—meaning not each individually—becomes a surging variety of forms, manifesting in the nature of manifold colors. And this is so even in its succession.
"But when there is a fusion while abiding in one's own nature alone," he says:

"because of mutual intermingling. For example, when the letter *a* or the letter *ā* is intermingled with the letter *i* or the letter *ī*, the form "e" arises; likewise, when those same two [letters] are [intermingled] with the letter *u* or the letter *ū*.

In the process of mutual blending (*vyatimiśraṇa*), the form "o" arises. Furthermore, the blending of the vowel *i* with the vowel *a* results in "ya," and the blending of the vowel *u* with the vowel *a* results in "va. And this blending does not occur through any other reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) beyond the five [phonemes]. Thus it was said: "mutually" (*anyonya*). As for that which—
Śiva [is said to be] "stained by the impurity of the objects of knowledge acquired swiftly or steadily;
through the orientation toward that which is of a different nature, he undergoes the states of *ratva* and *latva*"—
as he will state in such passages, that refers to the domain of the arising of another supreme reflective awareness (*paramārśa*) and should not be conflated with this [present context].
Because it is precisely the arising of the diphthongs that is under discussion here. || 92 ||
He demonstrates this very point: "That which is the unsurpassed, supreme vibration (spanda), and that which is the surging bliss (ānanda)."

These two, designated by the terms *anuttarānanda* (the unsurpassed bliss) and the syllables *a* and *ā*, undergo extreme variety through their conjunction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) with *icchā* (desire) and *unmeṣa* (expansion)— that is, with the syllables *i* and *u*— in a manner of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) according to the rule *ād guṇaḥ*.

Therefore, by virtue of being distinct from the two phonemes that are being joined with excellence, they attain— that is, reach— a "variety," namely the variety characterized by the sounds *e* and *o*.
(93) Having thus stated merely the emergence of the sound *e*, he now also declares its essential nature through its internalization:
When the consciousness of unsurpassed bliss is joined to the power of will, || 3-94 ||
They call that the "triangle" (trikoṇa), beautiful with the fragrance of the emission (visarga).

Since the Absolute (anuttara) and Bliss (ānanda) are, by implication, joined through conceptualization within the Will (icchā)— that syllable characterized by the letter *e*, whose parts are being conjoined, is the triangle.

As stated in such passages as: "The triangle is the eleventh [letter], the abode of fire, the womb, the rhombus (śṛṅgāṭa), and it is celebrated by the names beginning with the letter E," and because it consists of the three corners known as Will, Knowledge, and Action, even in the sequence of the script—
Because it is arranged in such a manner, they call it "the triangle," designating it by the term *trikoṇa*—
this is the meaning of the sentence; and that [triangle] is said to be "the emission (*visarga*) of that Lord, which is called the Kaulikī Śakti."

According to the principle to be explained hereafter, *visarga* is the supreme power (*parā śakti*). Its "fragrance" (*āmoda*) is its radiance extending up to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) through the sequence of the arising of bliss. Therefore, it is "beautiful" (*sundara*), meaning it consists of supreme bliss because the power is eternally manifest therein. By the term "triangle" (*trikoṇa*),...

It is also indicated that this [reality] has the nature of the *janmādhāra*, which is another synonym for the *yoginīvaktra*. For it is from that very place that the supreme power (*parā śakti*) arises—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"When she who is of crooked form flashes forth from the seat of the *śṛṅgāṭa*..."
Thus [it is said]. Likewise: "The triangle is called the *bhaga*; situated in the void, it is the secret maṇḍala.
Its corners are Will, Knowledge, and Action; in its center is the lineage of Ciñcinī.
And with this very intention, even by those outside [this tradition]...
"It is divine, having the form of the letter *E*, adorned in the center with the six syllables;

it is the abode of all blisses, a jewel-casket for awakening"—thus it has been said. For even in the stage of practice (*caryākrama*), it is connected with the emission (*visarga*) which has bliss as its fruit.
Through its expansion, it is the locus of emanation consisting of supreme bliss. Thus, [verse] 94.

Not only in the case of the union of the Absolute (anuttara) and Bliss (ānanda) does there arise an emergence of another reflective awareness characterized by a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*), but here too as well— thus he says: "When the Absolute and the power of Bliss have attained firm establishment therein" (3.95).

By the conjunction of two triangles, they proceed to abide in a hexagon. When, even within that triangle, Anuttara and Ānanda attain firm establishment— reaching their full growth through the process of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) according to the rule *vṛddhireci*— then, by the previously mentioned method, [the state] of Anuttara [is realized].

Because bliss (*ānanda*) also consists of the three powers beginning with *raudrī*—its essence being nothing other than their expansion—it possesses the form of a triangle; thus, through the union of two triangles characterized by the vowels *a* and *e*, they attain the state of a six-spoked [figure], a hexagon, manifesting the nature of the vowel *ai*. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, this nature of the *lipi* (phoneme) is not revealed here because it is a profound secret; rather, the placement of the line above is for the purpose of manifesting the doubling of the single vowel *e*. For even in the sequence of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), by the union of two triangles of the *siddhayoginīs*, a state consisting of the six-spoked mudrā arises.
Thus [ends verse] 95.

Just as there arises another level of reflective awareness when the unsurpassed (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda) come together through the letter *E*, so too does it occur through the letter *O*; thus he says:
"These very [energies], even in the union of Unfolding (*unmeṣa*), again attain identity with that. (3.96)

When those very [powers] of Anuttara and Ānanda, which clearly manifest the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), mutually unite with the unfolding (unmeṣa) represented by the letter *u*— that junction characterized by the attainment of the letter *o*— even while that [junction] exists, when there is furthermore absorption into that state (*tanmayatā*)...

As they proceed through the sequence of conjunction toward a state of oneness with the nature of the syllable *o*, then the two supreme joys (*anuttarānanda*), having merged together into the nature of the syllable *au*,
manifest clearly in every respect the distinct form characterized by the syllable *au*, which is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

The meaning is: "making manifest. By the phrase "clearly revealing the form on all sides," it is shown that within the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) exists respectively in its unmanifested particularity; therefore, that very form of consciousness which is one and without a second—[is what is meant].

Because it is replete with all things, the seed-aspect (*bījāṃśa*) is a specific cause characterized by the manifestation of the universe; its particular will to create— which, being independent of anything else, is the desire to manifest the universe consisting of subject and object as if it were something separate— is that which...

That very [connection] is agitation (*kṣobha*). Thus, as in the expression "he causes the arrow to go," even when there is no desire for that [external object], in the collection of entities such as the body and the color blue— which, due to indifference, are not oriented toward external existence—
there occurs the manifestation of the will of reality (*tattvecchābhāsanam*) by way of causing a fall from indifference and an orientation toward external existence.

The meaning is that the masters and others should know—that is, understand—that "illumination" is that very agitation. For in the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*), a man desiring to emit the seed becomes agitated himself and then agitates the woman; however, this [is not explained here] because it is an extreme secret and because it is irrelevant to the present context.
It has been explained; one should simply infer it according to its application. || 83 ||
Having thus described the nature of the seed (bīja), he states the nature of the womb (yoni): "When, having attained identity [with it], that will (icchā) becomes effective. (3.84)
The disciples of the venerable Somānanda have declared this to be the support of agitation (*kṣobha*):

by means of that collection of objects—such as the body, blue things, and so forth—which are perceived as "this-ness" (*idantā*), and [phonemes] such as *ka* and so on, one attains identity with it; and then the will belonging to that supreme perceiver becomes effective (*kṛtinī*).

"By the principle stated in such passages as, 'These [powers] that shatter the universe have emerged from me, Bhairava himself,' she becomes fulfilled and complete through resting in her own self alone. This very foundation and object of agitation— the sovereignty of consciousness— is [the subject of this work] for those who are the objects of Śrī Somānanda’s compassion."
The sons, beginning with the illustrious Utpaladeva, and the disciples, say—meaning they declare:

"For even in the course of spiritual practice (*caryākrama*), that which, having attained a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), brings the male desire to its fulfillment, is the source characterized as the womb (*yonilakṣaṇa*) and the substratum of arousal (*kṣobha*). (84)
And this nature of the seed and the womb, which was aphoristically indicated by the words "situated within" (*antaḥstha*) and so forth,
he himself explains in order to make it reach the hearts of those to be graced, because it is supremely worthy of being adopted due to its containing the secret method (*rahasyaprakriyā*).
It is that which does not manifest the specific distinctions of consciousness, such as desire and so forth. (3.85)

That which is the mere object of knowledge (*jñeyamātra*) is the seed; by connection with that, the state of being a seed resides in the vowel. This refers to the cognitions of desire and so forth, in which no differentiation has yet arisen. That which is the object of knowledge—meaning that which must necessarily be known as the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).

The supreme form of the Lord is indeed the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), because it is not grasped as having the specific forms of consciousness such as will (*icchā*) and so forth; it is simply the unconditioned state.
That very [form] is described thus: "The Lord, whose essence is consciousness, projects outward from within by the power of his will."

The meaning is that, because it is filled with all things— as expressed in such passages as "Like a yogi, it may manifest the multitude of objects without any material substrate"— the seed is the primary cause, since the universe residing within it is manifested externally solely by its own will. Now, if this is so...

"How then can vowels also possess the nature of seeds?"—anticipating this doubt, it is said: "By virtue of which [vowel] there is seed-nature in the consonant. The meaning of "by virtue of which" (udyogāt) is "because of being animated by which. Therefore, the intention is that the status of being a seed is appropriate for the vowels because they cause the manifestation of their respective letters; for indeed... [the text continues].
The meaning is that, apart from the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*), nothing else possesses the capacity to manifest another form. || 85 ||

Having thus explained the meaning of the word *bīja* (seed), he also explains *kṣobha* (agitation), which consists of the desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*) and is of two kinds— both with and without the causative suffix— as follows:
"The very emergence of that seed is what is called the desire to emit."
For this object of perception appears as if it were distinct from the conscious self. (3.86)

This is "agitation" (kṣobha), whereas "agitating" (kṣobhaṇā) is the forceful displacement from the state of indifference of consciousness by its own power, directed toward another subject who has become silent [inwardly]. (3.87)

"Arising" (*udbhava*) means the state of emerging—this is the meaning. For this reason, this collection of objects to be grasped—the body, blue and so forth, as well as the letters *ka* and so on—which, though not distinct from the conscious self (*cidātman*), appears as if distinct and not exceeding it, is that which is being manifested and will be manifested at a later time; such is this [arising].

Agitation (*kṣobha*) consists solely in the nature of being an initiator. For even in the sequence of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), bliss and the rest occur immediately after agitation; however, the act of agitating itself becomes silent through indifference, no longer oriented toward external objects. As for those others who remain by means of the exclusion (*apoha*) of blue and so forth—

The body and so forth are the subjects (*mātṛ*), and by implication, objects such as blue and so forth are the objects of cognition (*prameya*); having relied upon their own inherent vitality (*vīrya*) characterized by autonomy which resides within them, consciousness acts as the agent through force— that is,
by means of a compulsion characterized by the manifestation of the will toward that [object] even when there is no such will, arising from a state of indifference.

Because there is no engagement with the orientation toward external existence, "falling away" (cyāvana) is indeed nothing but manifestation through that very orientation toward external existence. || 86–87 ||
Having thus explained the *Bījasūtra*, he now also expounds the *Yonisūtra*:

"Even though this desire to emit has arisen, when it becomes fulfilled through its unification with another reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), that which serves as the substratum for agitation (*kṣobha*) is proclaimed here [in this sūtra]. (3.88)
That which is the desire to create— characterized by *kṣobha* (disturbance)— which has arisen in another subject,
[and] that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is distinct from the aforementioned reflective awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) grounded in pure consciousness;

[and] because of the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the object of reflection and the act of reflecting, that collection of entities such as the body, blue, and so forth, which is the object of that [reflective awareness].
And because of that [the letter *ka*], having resorted to oneness (*ekātmya*), she becomes fulfilled and complete by resting solely within her own self, having attained her purpose;

this very point is correctly proclaimed as the "support of arousal" (*kṣobhādhāra*) in the *Yonisūtra* in the passage beginning with "having attained oneness" (*yadaikyāpattimāsādya*)—this is the meaning. || 88 ||
Having thus explained this by way of the meaning of the words, he now states it by way of its underlying purport:
"Therefore, at that time, one should understand that [the internal] desires a state of being as if distinct;
from this seed of the universe, the entire external reflection will evolve. (3.89)

Then, from that agitation characterized by the desire to emit (sisṛkṣā), which was just mentioned, that object of knowledge— which exists internally as one with the subject— attains a state of being almost projected, a state of appearing as if distinct or separate; therefore:

Beginning from the seed of the universe— the primordial phoneme— and from Mahāmāyā, the entire collection of entities, such as bliss and the rest, as well as the principles (tattvas) and worlds (bhuvanas), which appear externally with a sense of separation,
shall evolve as reflections characterized by the forms of the knowledge of the original image (bimba).

The meaning is that [the seed-syllable] will manifest clearly, as appropriate, in the form of various bodies such as blue and so forth, and as words, sentences, and so on. For even in the sequence of ritual practice (*caryākrama*), the seed-syllable itself, having emanated through differentiation, will assume the forms of female, male, neuter, and so forth. || 89 ||
And this was not stated merely as my own invention; thus he says:

"The true nature of the relationship between the agitated and the agitator has been shown by me, [that which] was taught by the venerable Maheśvara, my Guru, through whose grace [this was possible]. (3.90)

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "I have demonstrated that true nature (satattva) which was previously taught by the Guru—who was saluted with the words 'the Blessed Maheśvara, whose form is other than that'—and so forth. || 90 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he introduces the actual subject at hand:
"We shall speak of the subject at hand: these four phonemes are not the seed (bīja), nor are they the womb (yoni), because they do not attain the state of being a substratum for agitation. (3.91)

For, unlike in the case of Kādi and so forth, there is no attainment of unity such that the desire of anyone would reach fulfillment; thus, this [Kādi] does not become the substratum of *kṣobha*. Furthermore, regarding the statement "this is not the seed," there is no mention of a reason, as was previously stated in the passage beginning with "because another *kṣobha* is impossible. Therefore...
And thus, because these four phonemes lack any capacity to cause agitation, they consist of supreme wonder through resting solely within their own self-nature. || 91 ||
Thus it is said:
"And because of its resting in the Self alone, that [consciousness] is declared to be of the nature of nectar (*amṛta*).
Not only does there arise, according to the possibility, another reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) through the contact with an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for these [perceptions],..."
"Even mutually"—thus he says:
"In this way, that pentad which was previously mentioned is [related] to one another. (3.92)

"Arising in various forms through mutual intermingling"—this refers to the pentad consisting of the forms of Anuttara (the Absolute), Icchā (Will), Īśana (Mastery), Unmeṣa (Expansion), and Unnata (Elevation). For the power of Bliss is indeed described as:
"Bliss is the form of Brahman... and so forth.
By such statements as these, [the world] is indeed non-different from consciousness; thus, there is no separate designation for it.
This very thing—neither one nor the other—becomes variously manifest in rising forms, appearing in the nature of diverse colors. And this is not so even in its succession.
"But when there is a fusion while abiding in one's own nature alone," he says:

"because of mutual intermingling. For example, when the letter *a* or *ā* is intermingled with the letter *i* or *ī*, the form "e" arises; likewise, when those same two [letters] are intermingled with the letter *u* or *ū*.

In the process of mutual blending (*vyatimiśraṇa*), the form "o" arises; likewise, from the blending of the vowel *i* with *a*, "ya" arises, and from the blending of *u* with *a*, "va" arises. Furthermore, this blending does not occur through any other reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) apart from the five [phonemes]. Thus it has been said: "mutually" (*anyonya*). As for that which...

As he will state in such passages as, "The Śiva-consciousness, stained by the impurity of the objects of knowledge acquired quickly or stably, attains the state of *ra* and *la* through its orientation toward heterogeneous [objects]," that refers to the emergence of a different kind of reflective awareness (*paramārśa*) and should not be conflated with the present context.
Because it is precisely the arising of the diphthongs that is under discussion here. || 92 ||
He demonstrates this very point: "That which is the unsurpassed, supreme vibration (spanda), and that which is the surging bliss (ānanda)."
These two,

designated by the terms *anuttara* (the unsurpassed) and *ānanda* (bliss)— namely, the letters *a* and *ā*— attain extreme variety through their union (*saṅghaṭṭa*) with *icchā* (will) and *unmeṣa* (expansion), that is, with the letters *i* and *u*, via the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) of the form "ād guṇaḥ."
Therefore, by virtue of being distinct from the two phonemes being joined with excessive intensity, they attain— that is, reach— a "variety" (*vaicitryam*), characterized by the letters *e* and *o*.
(93) Having thus stated merely the emergence of the letter *e*, he now also declares its essential nature through its internalization:
When the consciousness of unsurpassed bliss is joined with the power of will, || 3-94 ||
They call that the "Triangle," beautiful with the fragrance of the emission (visarga).
Since the Absolute (anuttara) and Bliss (ānanda) are, by implication, joined through conceptualization within the Will (icchā),
that syllable characterized by the letter *e*— whose constituent parts are being conjoined— is the Triangle.

Because of such statements as, "The triangle is the eleventh [letter], the abode of fire, the womb, the rhombus, and the letter *e*; thus it is celebrated by these names," and because it consists of the three corners known as Will (*icchā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), and Action (*kriyā*), even in the sequence of the script—
Because it is arranged in such a manner, they call it "the triangle," designating it by the term *trikoṇa*—
this is the meaning of the sentence; and that [triangle] is said to be "the emission (*visarga*) of that Lord, which is called the Kaulikī Śakti."

According to the principle to be explained below, *visarga* is the supreme power (*parā śakti*). Its "fragrance" (*āmoda*) is its unfolding up to the level of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) through the process of the arising of bliss. By that, it is "beautiful";
the meaning is that, because the power is eternally manifest there, it consists of supreme bliss (*parānandamaya*). This is indicated by the term "triangle" (*trikoṇa*).

It is also indicated that this [receptacle] has the nature of the *janmādhāra*, which is another synonym for the *yoginīvaktra*. For it is from that very place that the supreme power (*parā śakti*) arises—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"When she who possesses a curved form flashes forth from the seat of the *śṛṅgāṭa*..."
Thus [it is said]. Likewise: "The triangle is called the *bhaga*; it is the secret mandala situated in space (*viyat*).
Its corners are Will, Knowledge, and Action; in its center is the lineage of Ciñcinī.
And with this very intention, even by those outside [this tradition]...
"It is divine, having the form of the letter *E*, adorned in the center with the six syllables;
it is the abode of all blisses, a jewel-casket for awakening.
Thus it has been said. For even in the Stage of Conduct (*caryākrama*), [it is taught] by means of that which pertains to the emission (*visarga*) whose fruit is bliss.
Through its expansion, it is the locus of emanation consisting of supreme bliss. Thus [ends verse 94].

Not only in the case of the union of the Absolute (anuttara) and Bliss (ānanda) through desire does there arise an emergence of another reflective awareness characterized by a diphthong, but here too as well— thus he says: "When the Absolute and the power of Bliss have attained their rootedness therein" (3.95).
By means of the conjunction of two triangles, they proceed to abide in the hexagon.

When, even within that triangle, Anuttara and Ānanda attain firm establishment— reaching their full growth through the process of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) according to the rule *vṛddhireci*— then, by the previously mentioned method, of that Anuttara...

Because bliss also has the nature of a triangle— since it consists of the three powers beginning with Raudrī and its essence is solely their expansion— it attains the state of a six-spoked [figure], that is, a hexagon, through the union of two triangles characterized by the letters *a* and *e*, thereby manifesting the form of the letter *ai*. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, because of its extreme secrecy, this nature of the *lipi* (syllable) is not revealed; thus, the placement of a line above [the letter] is for the purpose of manifesting the doubling of the single vowel *e*. For even in the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*), by the union of two triangles of the *siddhayoginīs*, the state consisting of the six-spoked mudrā arises.
Thus [ends the section]. 95.

Just as there arises another level of reflective awareness when the unsurpassed (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda) are joined by means of the vowel *e*, so too does it occur through the vowel *o*; thus he says:
"These very [energies], even in the union of Unfolding (*unmeṣa*), again attain identity with that. (3.96)

When those very [energies] of Anuttara and Ānanda, which clearly manifest the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) through their mutual union, join with the vowel *u* by means of unfolding (*unmeṣa*)— that conjunction characterized by the attainment of the form of *o*— then, even while that [conjunction] exists, when there is once again absorption into that [state]...

As they proceed through the sequence of conjunction toward oneness with the nature of the syllable *o*, then the two supreme joys (*anuttarānanda*), having merged into the nature of the syllable *au*, clearly manifest the form characterized by the syllable *au*— the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— on all sides, completely.

The meaning is "of one who illuminates. By the phrase "manifesting the form clearly on all sides," it is communicated that within the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), there exists a form of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) that is, respectively, indistinct, distinct, more distinct, and most distinct. || 96 ||

Now, one might raise this objection: "Just as it was stated that through the friction (saṅghaṭṭa) of the desire (icchā) and the unfolding (unmeṣa) of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda), another reflective awareness arises, why does the same not occur through Īśana and Unmanā, which likewise consist of that agitation (kṣobha)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even for one who has attained that state, there is a disturbance described as occurring through the opening of desire.
Those two powers themselves partake of that very nature and do not remain otherwise.

Even when they have entered into that previously mentioned agitation— which consists of the emergence of will characterized by the desire for movement— and have reached a phonetic combination (*saṃdhi*) with it according to rules such as *ād guṇaḥ*, those two [powers]...
In the two powers called Anuttara and Ānanda, which indeed partake of that very nature,
they necessarily assume that form characterized by the letters *e* and *o*; for this very reason,
"not otherwise situated," they do not remain as having the nature of other reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), and thus [they arise] through their conjunction.
The arising of another reflective awareness between the unsurpassed [bliss] and bliss has been described. || 97 ||

Now, one might object: since "only the one, unsurpassed Light shines," nothing else whatsoever can possibly exist, because any such thing would be undermined by the dilemma of whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from that Light; so how can it be said that "He alone manifests through this manifold variety extending up to the power of action"? To this, he says:
Indeed, the state of unsurpassedness and bliss are, by their very nature, devoid of differentiation. (3.98)
"How is it that this [Lord] has taken such a vast variety within Himself?
To this, He provides the following answer:
"Listen first: this Lord of Consciousness is of an unlimited nature. (3.99)

The Lord of Time (Kaleśvara), who is the locus of the emergence and dissolution of the manifold variety of infinite powers—this indeed is the Lord of Consciousness (Saṃvinnātha), whose nature is unsurpassed bliss.
[As it is said: "His powers are the entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."

The meaning is as follows: because of such statements, regarding the diversity of the powers of the Infinite (Ananta), there is a "reckoning" (*kalana*)—that is, a projection through differentiation—of its dissolution and emergence, or its closing and opening; in that regard, due to its sovereignty, it is of an immeasurable nature, and because it does not assume a restricted form, its essential nature is unconditioned.
Now, one might ask: why indeed does this Lord of Consciousness not manifest with a fixed form?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If Maheśvara were to abide with a body of a single, uniform nature... (3.100).
He would forfeit His state of being Maheśvara and His nature as consciousness, just like a jar or other such objects.

For if Maheśvara were to abide in some specific, limited form, then, according to the logic of a jar and so forth, His sovereignty and His nature as consciousness would not exist. Indeed, this alone is [His essence].

The state of being Maheśvara and the nature of consciousness manifest as various pairs of signified and signifier in an unrestricted manner.
