For instance: "We perceive this single nature of consciousness as the transformation (*vivarta*) of many forms such as joy, sorrow, and so forth; therein, one may apply names according to one's will."
According to the reasoning stated in such passages as "let [these] be performed," consciousness indeed manifests in manifold forms;

of this there is no dispute. Nor is its manifestation in those various forms caused by ignorance (*avidyā*) or other factors—on the grounds that such causes would be undermined by the dilemma of whether they are distinct from or non-distinct from consciousness—but rather, it is caused by consciousness itself.

It is proclaimed everywhere that "intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is autonomy," and "it is the state of being the Great Lord (*māheśvarya*). If this [nature] were to manifest in a restricted form, then its state of being the Great Lord and its nature as consciousness would not exist, and thus it would fall into mere insentience (*jāḍya*). For only an insentient thing, such as a jar, [can be thought of as] "this is here now."
It would appear as a manifestation restricted to itself in this way—"it shines"—and not as another light. || 100 ||

Indeed, this alone constitutes its distinction from the insentient (jaḍa): that because it is self-luminous (svaprakāśa), it is not delimited by anything else. For being delimited in its manifestation is precisely what is defined everywhere as the characteristic of the insentient—namely, being cognized by something other than itself.
Regarding this, it is said: "The defining characteristic of the insentient (jaḍa), it is claimed, is indeed the state of having a limited manifestation. (3.101)
Since consciousness, which is distinct from the insentient, is not limited, and because it is thus, the expansion of this entire universe proceeds from that very source; so he says:
"Therefore, its own powers emerge as waves from the great ocean of consciousness. (3.102)
They assume a variety of forms through their own mutual friction, like waves; for that reason— namely,

by virtue of this vibration consisting of many manifested forms— the powers such as Will (icchā) and the rest, which are one's own (svāḥ), meaning identical with one's self, surge forth from consciousness like waves from the ocean, being by nature prone to such surging.

By means of their own internal union—that is, by becoming mutually fused—they assume a state of manifoldness; they manifest as various objects of perception and subjects of perception, and as the nature of various reflective awarenesses—this is the meaning. || 102 ||
And this indeed is the supreme form of the power of action; thus he says:
"That which is the mutual variety of the collision of powers within one's own self. (3.103)
This alone they call the supreme, manifest form of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
"Supreme" and "manifest" mean most clearly manifest; for this very reason, because of the predominance of duality (*bheda*), it belongs to her.

"Those others, however, who are even more terrible (ghorataryaḥ), embrace the Rudra-entities (rudrāṇūn) and cause the individual souls (aṇūn) who are utterly absorbed in sense objects to fall further and further down. Thus are characterized those most terrible powers (ghorataryaḥ) who preside over the impure path (aśuddhādhvan).

It should be understood that the powers (*śakti*) possess the nature of being instrumental causes (*nimitta*). For it has been stated that the birth of the powers beginning with Aghora arises from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). || 103 ||

And because this Blessed One consists precisely of the union of the three powers (śakti), he is said to possess the nature of a trident; thus it is said: "In this fourteenth abode, wherein the three powers have become manifest... (3.104).
Therefore, the Teacher declared the state of being a trident (*triśūlatva*) in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana*.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers to the fact that [the power of action] is more manifest than the other two; this is also the reason given in the passage, "in that which has become manifest as the three powers. Furthermore, the state of having the three powers become manifest is the reason for the statement regarding its being a trident.
The sense is that the triad of powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action exists here; as it is said therein:
"The fourth [power] is by means of the trident. (104)

Not only has the Lord described this as being a trident due to the convergence of the three powers (*śakti*), but even as being "stainless" (*nirañjana*)—according to the teachers who have mastered the meaning of the various scriptures. Thus he says:
"And this has been called 'stainless' by the teachers who perceive reality. (105)

Since that which possesses power (the possessor) is manifested, but power itself is never manifested by anything— where the word *ca* is to be understood as displaced in the sequence— the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Therefore, this fourteenth abode, characterized by the vowel *au*, is called *nirañjana*."

For, as it is said: "Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known by means of the light of a lamp and the rays of the sun, so too, O Dear One, is Śiva [known] through His Power (śakti).
According to such statements, the Supreme Light is the Possessor of Power (śaktimān), and by means of His Power, the limited [subjects] are illumined.

The meaning is that [the power] is manifested and conditioned (*upādhīyate*) with respect to the subjects (*pramātṛ*). For the manifestation of the supreme light, which is self-luminous, is itself the condition brought about by another agent. Furthermore, the power, once manifested, is the means for its own manifestation; thus, there is no further manifestation of that [power] by anyone else.
It could so arise; for an instrument that is not itself cognized cannot truly function as an instrument—this is the sense.

Now, one might object: "Since powers such as will (icchā) are indeed conditioned by their own objects, such as the desired object, how can it be said that 'power is not manifested by anything'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Will, knowledge, and action—these are each manifested separately. (3.106)

That very [reality] is clearly endowed with powers (*śaktimat*) through its own respective [powers], such as that which is desired and so forth; for indeed, the powers characterized by will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) are each distinct from one another through their own respective objects, consisting of the desired, the knowable, and the effect.
It is colored by differentiation; that very [reality] is clearly manifest—the possessor of power whose essential nature is full.

This is the supreme Light (para-prakāśa) which has internalized infinite powers—this is the meaning. For what is called "power" (śakti) is indeed the very own-nature of the possessor of power, yet it possesses an imposed differentiation due to the diversity of its effects. By means of this...
The linguistic usage such as "desire" (icchā) and so forth arises from the coloring [of consciousness] by the object of desire and other factors. || 106 ||

Now, one might object: "If each of these—desire and the rest—possesses a nature endowed with power when colored by its respective object of desire and so forth, then what is the nature of them when they are combined? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But when this triad flashes forth in unity... (3.107).
Nothing can be conditioned [by another], because of the mutual exclusion between each thing and its own nature.

Furthermore, when this triad— characterized by will, knowledge, and action— manifests in a state of equilibrium as the essence of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), then it cannot be limited by any object such as that which is desired and so forth.

Because of their mutual exclusion—namely, that desire and the rest [of the faculties] are not colored by the object of desire and the rest by virtue of their own respective oppositions; that cognition and action are not colored by the object of cognition; nor are desire and action [colored] by the object of cognition; nor are desire and cognition [colored] by the effect—due to such mutual contradiction, they cannot be the substrata of superimposition (*upādheya*).
The meaning is: "it is not to be anointed. As he will say: "The Goddess of action is the stainless (nirañjana). || 107 ||
And for this very reason, this is expressed by the term "trident" (triśūla); thus he says:
"Therefore, that trident is the triad of powers (śaktitritaya) which has become liquefied (lolībhūta), through immediate immersion into which the yogin becomes stainless (nirañjana). (108)

Therefore, because it is unconditioned (*anupahita*), this triad of powers— which has become a unified mass (*lolībhūta*) and attained non-differentiation even while in a state of mutual rivalry— is designated by the term "trident" (*triśūla*). In that unconditioned form, not only is there its own stainlessness (*nirañjanatva*), but through the immersion into its very existence, one attains identity with it.
Even one who is fit shall become stainless. || 108 ||
Now, he concludes this very point by introducing another object of knowledge:

"In this way, starting from the state of supreme nectar (parāmṛta), such a group of eight clearly attains the state of eight groups of eight through the differentiation of forms beginning with that of Brahmā. (3.109)

This group of eight, which begins from the four neuter vowels following the state of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) and extends up to the seed-syllable *ŚA*, possesses the aforementioned form; as such, it constitutes the all-encompassing nature of the group of eight starting with Brahmī, and thus each individual letter therein serves as the signifier (*vācya*) for the group of eight goddesses.

Through their mutual blending, they clearly attain the state of eight times eight—that is, they manifest in the form of sixty-four; this is the meaning. Thus, Brahmī is the phoneme *ṛ*, and in this sequence up to the phoneme *au* she is Yogīśvarī; then Māheśvarī is the phoneme *ṛ*, while here Brahmī is the phoneme *au*.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the same applies elsewhere, such as in the case of the letter *ṛ*. || 109 ||

Thus, in order to illuminate that even as supreme consciousness vibrates with such diversity extending up to the power of action (kriyā-śakti), there has been no loss of its essential nature, he shows the nature of the Bindu:

In this regard, although that unsurpassed power manifests its own form as clearly present, it takes on the form of the *bindu* due to the impurity caused by the subtle divisions of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). (3.110)
Even though things are established in this way, that aforementioned supreme power (*anuttara-śakti*),

by virtue of its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), effects a limitation (*kalana*)— that is, a determination of measure (*iyattā-pariccheda*)— of the multitude of objects (*bhāva-jāta*) consisting of the grasped and the grasper; through that, there arises a turbidity which is a contraction (*saṅkoca*) characterized by the concealment of its own true nature.

Relying upon that very self-luminous body which remains manifest, even while making it abide as the object of all perception, she is "of the nature of the *bindu*. The *bindu* is the knower who is independent in the act of knowing (*vidikriyā*); its form is the supreme, undivided state.

"Light" means that which has that very [light] as its existence—that is, whose essential nature is that—such is the meaning. Even so, she does not deviate from her own nature; this is the intended sense. || 110 ||
Therefore, he says:
"When the power of action (kriyāśakti) has arisen in the abode of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, that undivided light is indeed for us the supreme Bindu. (3.111)

In this world, even when the power of action— which serves as the substratum for the sun and other luminaries that possess fixed natures delimited by qualities such as coolness and sharpness— has arisen and is manifesting in the form of various diversities as the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, there remains no division.
That full light which is devoid of the limitations of adjuncts such as pleasure and sharpness is the supreme;

even so, because its essential nature is never lost, it is most excellent in our system— the "Bindu," the Supreme Lord Śiva, who is autonomous in the act of knowing and whose sole form is the supreme subject.
This is the meaning. As he will state:
"In this context, that which is mere luminosity while the three abodes (dhāman) exist is described in the scripture as the 'Bindu'; this is considered the Bindu of Śiva."
Thus [ends the section]. || 111 ||
And this was not stated merely as his own invention; thus he says: "And in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*, it was said by the Supreme Lord:
'Abiding within the circle of the heart-lotus, [the Self] consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva. (3.112)
The Bindu, which is the stainless Savior, is to be understood through the divisions of its states of absorption (laya).
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "the heart-lotus" and so forth. The Bindu is the supreme Light that makes known, desiring to manifest the universe through its own sovereignty.

By the statement beginning with, "One should contemplate the *bindu* located in three places as being in one place alone," [the reality] should be understood as consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, due to the distinction between the dissolution and the rest in the locations characterized by the *dvādaśānta*, the space between the eyebrows, and the heart.

The meaning is that he manifests as the nature of the three principles (*tattva*) characterized by Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, beginning with *icchā* (will). Even so, because the state of contracted selfhood (*saṃkucitātmatā*) predominates within the circle of the heart-lotus, he has taken root specifically on the level of duality—this is the meaning. Nevertheless, even so, he is not...
He says that [the Guru] has not fallen from his own essential nature: "the pure deliverer" (*vimalatāraka*).

He is "pure" (*vimala*) because he is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), even while the various diversities [of phenomena] manifest; for this very reason, he is the "deliverer" (*tāraka*) from the ocean of transmigratory existence. || 112 ||

Not only does this [Universal Consciousness], which manifests as the manifold variety of all objects of cognition, not deviate from its own essential nature, but it remains so even in its aspect as those various individual cognitions—thus he says:
"That sound whose essence is *nāda* (resonance) resides within all living beings. (3.113)
Then, through the division of lower and upper, it abides in a state of non-action.

Here, that which is the *bindu*, desiring to manifest its nature as various forms of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), flashes forth in the form of "sound whose essence is *nāda*"; this is the meaning. It makes the universe resound by means of its own non-duality.

The word "parāmṛśati" (it reflects) refers to reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of supreme speech (*parāvāk*), and that is of the nature of resonance (*nāda*). It is called *nāda* because it "resounds" (*nadati*), manifesting itself as the very life-force (*jīvakalā*) within all beings. This is precisely the "measureless digit" (*amā kalā*), whose form is half of half of the letter *ha*, which is primarily designated everywhere as being without vowels (*asvara*).

This means that his own self manifests in that very form. And by such statements as, "The letter A stands as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all phonemes," he [the Self] exists within all phonemes indeed, through the division of above and below, from the Unsurpassed (anuttara).

The meaning is that [the Absolute] exists as the very nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), extending from the end of the *śūla* (the letter *Ṣ*) and the *bīja* (the letter *Ś*), or up to the letter *Ha*;

indeed, the entire mass of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-rāśi*) has nothing other than its expansion (*sphāra*) as its essence. Furthermore, that same [Absolute] exists for all living beings according to the division of below and above.

He also exists in the form of the flow of the sun and moon, which are the nature of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; for that indeed is the "supreme portion of the individual soul" (*parā jīvakalā*)—this is the sense. Even so, he remains in an inactive form, even while manifesting through various diversities up to the limit of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). His [nature] does not [change].
The meaning is: a falling away from one's own essential nature. || 113 ||
Now, once the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) has arisen, the limited light of the moon, sun, and so forth—determined by qualities such as coolness or sharpness—manifests;
this [limited light] illuminates both itself and everything else. But what, then, is that supreme light which has been described as being without division?
Is that [object] identical with that [consciousness], or is it something else manifested by it?—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whatever variety there is, such as pleasure and sharpness, or white, red, and so forth... (3.114).
And the Guru has said that this supreme Light is itself independent of those [objects]:

"Indeed, that variety consisting of joy, sharpness, and so forth, as well as whiteness, redness, and so forth, which resides in the moon, the sun, and other such things— that the supreme Light does not depend upon by means of its own self."

Because it lacks a fixed form, it cannot consist of that [form] alone; nor, because it is self-luminous, can it be illumined by that. Therefore, it is neither of the nature of the sun and so forth, nor is it illumined by them;
rather, it is the vitalizing principle of the three abodes of the sun and so forth, whose sole nature is the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*).
And from the two words beginning with "ādi," one should also understand combustibility arising from the diversity of combustible objects, as well as the possession of various colors.
Furthermore, this has not been stated by us alone, but even by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—thus it was said:
"And the Guru says. As it is sung:
"The sun does not illuminate that, nor the moon, nor fire;
that is My supreme abode, reaching which they do not return. (114)
He shows this very point by way of its meaning: "That which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even fire illumines," (3.115).
And there is no inherent radiance belonging to the sun, moon, or fire apart from that [universal] light; rather, it is consciousness that shines forth in this manner. (3.116)

That supreme abode does not manifest as a fixed, singular form such as the sun and so forth; for, being self-luminous (*svābhāsa*), it cannot be illumined by the sun or other such sources. On the contrary, since the sun and others are what are to be illumined, they would lack the very quality of being manifest without its light—thus, it is "supreme" (*para*).
In this very way, the Light flashes forth as the various forms of the sun and so on. For this reason it has been said:
"But consciousness shines forth in this manner. (115-116)

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since all three are indistinguishable in their nature as fire (*tejas*), from where does their diversity—consisting of sharpness and other qualities—arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Joined with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) arising through the power of its own sovereignty..."
Light undergoes various internal diversities such as sharpness and so forth. || 117 ||

By the majesty of its own sovereignty, that light— which, having attained a state of differentiation through an adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of emergent substances such as earth and water, has thereby also assumed the form of fire—
undergoes another variety of internal diversity characterized by sharpness and so forth, and manifests in that very form.

This is the meaning: for the Supreme Light alone, when blended with the manifestation of earthy and other substances, flashes forth as fire; when conditioned by the manifestation of watery substances, as the moon;
and when colored by the manifestation of pure light alone, as the sun.
It would manifest a manifold variety consisting of such forms as burning, refreshing, sharpness, and so forth. || 117 ||
One might object: "How can such a diversity, which even surpasses the essential nature [of the object], arise from the mere association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) alone?
He pacifies this doubt by showing an illustrative example:
"Even the sun, though difficult to behold, when fallen upon the path of the waters..."
Behold how it attains the state of being a delight to the eyes through the influence of its limiting adjunct! (3.118)
Even the sun, though it destroys vision, when reflected in a pond or similar body of water that possesses stillness,
becomes easily and beautifully visible by abandoning its state of being difficult to behold; thus,
this power of an adjunct (*upādhi*) is observed everywhere— that it enhances the very nature of that which is conditioned (*upādeya*).
Precisely because it thus assumes all forms, the light of the sun and other luminaries requires the light of consciousness for its own manifestation; thus he says:
"In the sun and other [luminaries], this light is rendered turbid by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)."
Therefore, it indeed depends upon the light of consciousness belonging to Maheśa.
By the word *saṃvit* (consciousness), the distinction of this supreme light from the inert light of the sun and other sources is shown here. || 119 ||
Thus, he shows their essential nature as it occurs:
"That which is clearly manifest as pure light is explicitly called the Sun;
that which showers down the essential portion of the objects to be illumined is called the Moon. (3.120)
"Clearly manifest" (suvyakta) means not obstructed by water, substances, and so forth—this is the meaning;

the sense is that the sun's form is pure light alone. For this very reason, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for its intended form is indeed nothing but knowledge itself. This is evident and witnessed by all people.
Since those objects which are to be manifested and are the objects of knowledge consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion,
that essence which— relative to two portions— is the superior portion consisting of the form of joy and so forth, which is the effect of pleasure.

By such statements as, "Soma rains down nectar," and so forth, that which rains— that by which this entire collection of entities is sprinkled and made to consist of nothing but bliss— is called Soma, being essentially that very manifestation of consciousness.

The meaning is that it is designated by the word *soma*. For this very reason, because the aspect of the object of knowledge (*meyāṃśa*), which consists of bliss, is predominant, it possesses the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*); with this intention [it is said]:
"This power of knowledge of the Supreme blazes forth in the form of the sun."
Thus it is said:
"The power of action (kriyā-śakti) of Śiva shines forth in the form of the moon.
And so they say that the sun is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), while they declare the moon to be the object of knowledge (meya).
Having thus described the essential nature of the Sun and the Moon, he now describes that of Fire as well:
"Though both are independent, they remain inseparable from one another. (3-121)
This [universe], consisting of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, has attained a state of mutual orientation;
therefore, it is proclaimed as Citrabhānu, whose nature is the blazing consciousness. (3.122)
That which is the supreme reality of fire is precisely this [reality] of the knower.

Both of these— the sun and the moon— though independent and capable of being treated separately as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), are nonetheless inseparable from one another.

The meaning is that because they are necessarily perceived together, they have attained non-difference; for indeed, knowledge is never perceived anywhere without being colored by the object of knowledge, nor is an object of knowledge perceived without knowledge.
As they say:
"For the nature of cognition, when devoid of an object of support, is indefinable, like that of a crystal.
Likewise:
"Therefore, that which is not cognized cannot be an object of cognition..."

Thus, for this very reason, these two— the sun and the moon— having attained mutual orientation due to their nature as the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), the limited subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); and because it is composed of that [duality], the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also the enjoyer.

The object of enjoyment consists of blue, pleasure, and so forth; that which has attained a state of fusion (*lolībhāva*) is that whose essence is both of these—meaning its nature is the union of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. And because it is thus, for that reason, from the cause characterized by the union of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, [arise] variegated forms of manifold aspects.
He in whom the manifestations take the form of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so forth, is called Agni; as it has been said:
"The fire named Śuci has arisen from the friction of the Moon and the Sun.
And he is so called because he burns away duality, which consists of the distinction between the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge.
He whose nature is consciousness, in which fire is predominant, is one whose form is that of a limited subject—this is the meaning.

For his very nature is the union of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—this is the meaning; since this is also the case for fire, it possesses the status of a subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, he says "this one who... and so forth; "supreme" (*param*) means unique or extraordinary (*asādhāraṇa*).
Now, one might object: "Since fire requires another for its manifestation, its insentience was stated immediately [before];
how then can it be the true nature of the cognizer, whose sole essence is consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But consciousness itself, because of its identity with the object of knowledge, is independent. (3.123)
Because of its autonomy, it is called the "knower" (*pramātṛ*); it is diverse due to the differentiation of the objects of knowledge.

For consciousness itself, through its own sovereignty, by attaining identity with the object of cognition—which consists of the enjoyer and the enjoyed—like fire [with its fuel], is called the "knower. Therefore it has been said: "independent" (*anapekṣiṇī*).
The meaning is that even upon assuming the form of fire, there is no falling away from the essential nature of consciousness. Now, one might object:

"If the state of being a subject belongs to consciousness alone, then because of its indivisibility, how can the diversity of the subject—who is of that very nature—be logically accounted for? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The phrase "variegated due to the differentiation of the objects of knowledge" means that there is variety because of the differentiation— that is, the manifoldness— of the collection of principles (tattva) consisting of *kalā* and the rest.

For although *kalā* and the others are not distinct in terms of their general capacity for limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and so forth, they are nonetheless perceptible to all as possessing specific presiding powers over their respective functions.
This gradation is that by which this differentiation of subjects is brought about through the greatness of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 123 ||
For this very reason, fire also is likewise; thus he says:
"It is augmented by the appearance of variety arising from the objects to be burned, which are portions of the moon. (3.124)
For that very reason, Agni was called Citrabhānu by Maheśin.

Precisely because of the manifoldness of the subject (*pramātṛ*), the Lord has declared Agni to be one whose "lights" (*bhānavaḥ*)—namely, the various objects of enjoyment such as the enjoyer and the enjoyed—are manifold; for it is from him that the expansion of the various [categories] such as the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the objects of knowledge (*meyātman*) proceeds.
The meaning is as follows: the portions of Soma, consisting of parts such as the *kalā*s, are the very objects to be consumed and assimilated;
by the appearance of diversity arising from them through gradations and so forth, [the subject] is "augmented," that is to say, brought to a state of particularity (*vaiśiṣṭya*). || 124 ||

Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that the diversity [of consciousness] arises from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the cognizer (pramātṛ), and since the object of cognition (prameya) does not manifest as something separate from the cognizer, let alone any discussion of diversity, how can the very status of being a cognizer even be possible for this consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The consciousness [of the yogin] is indeed independent of the collection of means such as the objects of knowledge and so forth. (3-125)

The state [of consciousness] consisting of the reflective awareness "I am," which is independent of the objects of knowledge— such as various blue forms, pleasures, and so forth— which serve as the means for the knower, just like one who knows the scriptures, is the "Mātṛ" (the Knower). This state of consciousness,
whose essence is the awareness "I am," is the Mātṛ.

The meaning is that the knower has the nature of the supreme reflective awareness of "I. Furthermore, by its independence from an object of knowledge, the distinction of this reflective awareness of "I" from conceptual construction (vikalpa) is demonstrated. For in cases such as "I am thin," the reflective awareness of "I" is indeed a conceptual construction, because there exists a counter-correlative, namely the negatable state of "not being thin," and so forth.
Because of its possibility; for its very nature consists in its dependence upon a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) that is a subject possessing both that form and a non-that form.

However, in the light whose essence is the supreme subject, the reflective awareness "I" (ahaṃpratyavamarśa), as it proceeds, cannot have any counter-correlative whatsoever, because it is afflicted by the dilemma of being either distinct from or non-distinct [from that light].
Because it is impossible [for such a thing to exist], there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As they say:

"That reflective awareness of 'I' which, though its nature is light, has speech as its body—is not that a conceptual construction? For a conceptual construction is defined as a determinate cognition that depends upon a duality."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Let the very nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*) be the reflective awareness of 'I' (*ahaṃvimarśa*), or let that too be distinct from conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); what need have we for this? For without an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), his status as a knower (*jñātṛtva*) would not be possible. Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Because [he is] like one who knows the scriptures."

Just as one who knows the scriptures is said to possess the status of a knower with respect to them— even in the absence of a desire to explain— because the scriptures exist non-differently from his own self, so too for the supreme subject, because he is filled with all things, the entire range of objects of knowledge resides within his own self. || 125 ||

Now, one might object: "The knower is so called because of his connection with valid cognition (*pramā*), and valid cognition arises from a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose object is a distinct cognizable thing (*jñeya*); therefore, how can this [Self] possess the status of a knower while setting aside the distinct cognizable object and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For the knower is essentially the experience of what is known, not [known] by way of its own form. (3-126)
But that state of being a knower does not depend upon a pure object of knowledge and so forth.

For he who is called a "knower" by depending on specific cognitions, such as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the rest, is actually ignorant and is not truly a cognizer (*pramātṛ*)—this is the meaning. Indeed, for the cognizer...

Because it is not directed toward anything else, its nature is indeed independent of anything else, as previously stated; it cannot, however, have a dependent nature, for it is impossible for one thing to reside in another. Thus he says: "But not... and so forth. (126)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can the fact that he is called the 'knower' (jñātṛ) in all circumstances be denied?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that state, his status as a knower is spoken of by virtue of his inherent capacity. (3.127)

But that [state] is indeed the very nature of the ego-sense (mānata) as imagined by the primordial subject; "in that"—meaning, in that which consists of the limited subject—is the sense. "By virtue of fitness" means by virtue of the characteristic of performing the delimitation of the object of knowledge. Furthermore, this state [is brought about] by the primordial [subject].
The meaning is as follows: she has been conceptually constructed as the nature of the means of knowledge by the supreme subject who is established from the beginning;
because her essence consists of contracted cognition, she appears as such. For it is the supreme subject alone who, through his own sovereignty, conceals his own true nature.
Having manifested the nature of consciousness as contracted, it should also manifest the object of knowledge as distinct [from itself]. || 127 ||
Now, one might object: "If supreme consciousness itself manifests even in the form of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth, would that not be its very disappearance?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even as consciousness surges forth, because it is devoid of temporal succession... (3.128)
Being already arisen and full, consciousness— though appearing externally in the form of the knower, the known, and so forth— is [in truth] the knower, the known, and so on;
for according to the maxim, "This Self is once and for all manifest."
Because there is no interruption in the activity of manifestation, consciousness is "ever-risen" due to the absence of temporal limitation;
because it does not fall away from its nature as pure consciousness, it is "necessarily of a non-setting form"—this is the meaning.
For this very reason, it is "full," meaning that because its nature consists in resting solely within itself, it is independent of anything else—this is the meaning.

One might object: "Is consciousness not indeed an action? And since, like any other action, it must necessarily be subject to temporal limitation, how can it be said to be devoid of temporal succession? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] refers to worldly actions such as cooking and so forth.
To show that there is a delimitation by time for action (kriyā), but not for this [consciousness], he says:
"But action such as cooking, because it is delimited by time, is characterized by succession" (3.129).
Even that which is considered barren of its final moment does not attain the state of being "cooked.

For here, cooking and the like are worldly actions intended to be pervaded by a sequence due to their limitation by time; since that final moment is immediately followed by the production of the result in the second moment, even by that [moment], when—

Then it would be empty; even if it possessed an accumulation of multiple moments, because its own nature would remain incomplete, it would not engage in such conventional activity. For if that manifestation-activity itself were not delimited by time, then [it would do so] in the very first moment.

"...one would arrive at the conventional usage [of terms] such as 'the act of cooking' and so forth. And for this reason, it is only worldly action, such as cooking, that possesses succession, and not the eternal action characterized by pure consciousness.
As they have said:

"And the state of being Śakra [the lord of gods] arises from the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) regarding worldly activity; however, it does not apply to that which is eternal and sovereign, as is the case with the Lord. Therefore, because it is not delimited by time, it exists in the form of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
Even while persisting [in its state], the reality of consciousness would not be divested of its primary nature, which is characterized as pure consciousness alone. || 129 ||
Thus he says:
"In this way, the state of being the moon, the sun, and the fire resides within the principle of Light. (3.130)
Moreover, its primary nature as pure luminosity is not negated.

Now, let it be so during the state of the manifestation of the universe as the signified (*vācya*); but in the manifestation of the universe as the signifier (*vācaka*), what indeed has been said regarding the very form of the moon, sun, and fire, by whose manifestation this [universe] is revealed?
Might there not even be the thought that "there is no exclusion of the essential nature of the principle of Light"?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is the first form of these, the short [vowel], is called the Sun. (3.131)
Due to the power of the bliss of agitation and through long-lasting repose, it is called Soma; that which is known as the supreme *pluta* stands beyond the bliss of Soma. (3.132)
Those learned in the scriptures call that [state] of the nature of light *āgneya* (fiery).

Among these seeds (*bīja*) just mentioned, that first form which is attained and remains unagitated is "short" (*hrasva*), consisting of a single measure due to its subtlety; and because of the predominance of pure illumination (*prakāśa*), it is the Sun.

Likewise, due to the power of agitation (kṣobha) and bliss (ānanda), because it rests in an externalized form, it is "long" (dīrgha) as it possesses two measures (mātrās) owing to its state of being agitated and gross; and because it bestows delight, it is called "Soma.
Since this is stated generally, it is designated in this way by all those who are experts in the scriptures—this is the meaning.
Likewise, beyond those two— one mora and two moras, namely the short and the long—

there is another which consists of three moras and is called *pluta*; those learned in the scriptures call that form *āgneya* (fiery) and *prāmātra* (the measure of three moras), because it is rooted in and has taken root in the Sun, whose nature is light and measurement.

The meaning is that [the vowel *i*] rests most intensely upon the supreme *somānanda*, which consists of the object of knowledge (*meyātmaka*), and manifests as the nature of the subject (*mātṛrūpatayā*). For it was stated previously that the nature of the subject indeed consists of the union of the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. Thus, for these [vowels], shortness is their solar nature (*sūryatva*) and length is their lunar nature (*somatva*).
The state of being flooded and the state of being fire constitute the nature of the three abodes. || 131-132 ||
Even so, there is no deviation from its own essential nature for the supreme Light here;
thus, its state as the *vindu* (the point) has been described—as he says:
"In this context, that which is pure Light exists while the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*) remain. (3.133)
It is stated in the scripture that, by virtue of being the *bindu*, this is considered the *śivabindu*.

And this is not a mere *bindu* [in the sense of a phoneme], because, being of the singular nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), it does not reside within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) such as mantras; thus he says:
"this is considered the *śivabindu*. This is because, by its nature as the undivided supreme light, it is [the agent] in the act of knowing (*vidikriyā*).

The meaning is that the supreme subject is autonomous. As was stated previously: "When the power of action has arisen in the abode of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, that undivided light is indeed for us the supreme *bindu*."
Thus [ends the section]. || 133 ||

Now, it may be objected that a distinct reflective awareness (parāmarśa) called the "bindu" is not tenable, since it is already subsumed under the specific reflective awareness known as the letter *m*, which will be discussed later. Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever in the cognition (*pratīti*) of these two;
for a difference in cognition arises only from a difference in the object of cognition (*pratyeya*). Therefore, how can this [bindu] be [distinct] from that?
Fearing that [the letter *ya*] might be distinct [from the letter *ma*], he says:
"This [letter *ya*] is indeed other than the letter *ma*, just as it bears only its shadow. (3.134)

The letters *ra*, *la*, and *ha* are established as having the form of the sixth letter, the visarga (*ḥ*). Just as the letters *ra*, *la*, and *ha* have resorted to the state of being the sixth letter, the visarga— even though they maintain only the resonance (*śruti*) of that [visarga]— they are distinct from those [letters] which are about to be described.
The meaning of the sentence is that this bindu, like [the vowels] beginning with *repha*, is distinct from the letter *m*.
It was established previously that "a letter is not merely the auditory perception of a phoneme. || 134 ||
Now, it might be argued that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is colored by the letters *ra* and *la*, which possess the nature of being desired;
therefore, it is appropriate for it to assume a distinct form of reflective awareness (*parāmarśāntaratva*) because it merely bears their reflection.
But as for the letters *ma* and *ha*, whose coloring of what could possibly be admitted? For whom [is this coloring] even asserted?
Fearing that there might be a difference between [this] and other forms of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), he says:
"Just as the letter *i* itself becomes another vowel through the shadow of a portion of the letter *r*. (135)

In the same way, that other [letter] "aḥ," although itself devoid of vowels (asvara), becomes twofold through a slight portion of greatness; just as the vowel *i* itself, by means of the shadow of a portion of the letter *r*, takes on the form of another vowel whose nature is that of a neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*), so too this [letter] "aḥ," while remaining devoid of vowels and consisting of the light of the Absolute (*anuttara*), [becomes twofold].

The meaning is as follows: the first phoneme, whose essence is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), assumes the trace of the letters *ma* and *ha* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and, by merely bearing their resonance, becomes twofold—namely, in the form of the *bindu* and the *visarga*. Thus, the other [phonemes] come to possess the nature of further reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). For indeed, it is the Absolute (*anuttara*) alone that is the Light (*prakāśa*).

By concealing its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) through its own sovereignty (*svasvātantrya*), [the Absolute] manifests the state of power (*śakti-daśā*) and causes the appearance of the form of the contracted subject (*saṃkucita-pramātṛ*). Therefore, according to the statement beginning with, "The letter *A* and the letter *Ha*,
these two stand as one," the letter *Ma* [is produced] by the power in the form of the letter *Ha*.
By the statement beginning with "situated in the heart," there is a coloring by the letter *ma* in the form of the contracted subject; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 135 ||
Now, one might ask: why should the Absolute (anuttara) itself undergo such a manifestation as the nature of emission (visarga) and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which has been called the supreme Kaulikī is this internal desire to emit. (3.136)
By virtue of that very agitation, she certainly attains the nature of emission (*visarga*).
Of this first letter, whose essence is the light of the Absolute (*anuttara*), it was previously stated: "She is that supreme Kaulikī power, inseparable from whom the Lord [exists]."

In such passages as these, that which is called "kaulikī" or "parā"— the desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*) which exists internally in identity with the subject and whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— itself, by virtue of the agitation characterized by an outward orientation, certainly attains the state of emission (*visarga*), and through the sequence of the arising of bliss, reaches the limit of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
It illuminates a state that is surging forth—this is the meaning. || 136 ||
And this is not our own invention alone; thus he says:
"And it has been stated in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*, in the discussion concerning the extent of the pervasion of the *kalās*. (3-137)
Therefore, the seventeenth digit has the form of the nature of nectar;
it has spread forth by means of the movement of the bindu, which is the essential nature of both the transcendent and the immanent.
She is the illuminator of all things, yet she is devoid of emission;
she is indeed Śaktikuṇḍalikā as well as Prāṇakuṇḍalikā. (3.139)
At the terminal point of the emission (visarga), however, is what is called the Supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
it is called the Sky of Śiva, the supreme Brahman, and the station of the Self.

"The emanations of the Lord consist of mere emission (visarga) alone, [which are] the fluctuations of creation and withdrawal; this is during the discussion on the extent of the pervasion of the *kalās*," meaning: at the occasion of investigating the established doctrine regarding the expansion of the essential nature of the *kalā* called Amā. For therein—

When the Blessed Lady asked, "O Mahādeva, [what is] the pervasion of the *kalās*, O Maheśvara, and what is the designation of the *padas*? Tell me very briefly..."— [the following is] for the purpose of determining that:
"That which is the seventeenth digit...

and so forth was spoken by the Blessed One. Whatever has been corroborated here, whether by way of words or by way of meaning, therein [it is said]: "In the Puruṣa of sixteen digits, they call that digit immortal."

By such statements as these, because she nourishes all sixteen digits (kalās), beginning with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and because her form is never-setting due to being eternally risen, this [reality] whose nature is pure consciousness and whose form is the nature of nectar is called "Kaulikī" and "Parā."
The seventeenth *kalā*, known as *Amā*, which consists of half of half of the letter *ha* and is designated by such terms as these,

abides in the essential nature of that *visarga* which is both supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*). This is because the *visarga* whose nature is bliss (*ānanda*) has been described as supreme, while the *visarga* whose nature is the letter *ha* will be described as non-supreme.
The two *bindus* denoted by the term *visarjanīya* constitute the "self-nature" (*ātmabhūta*); their "movement" (*gati*) is their expansion through the manifestation of those respective forms.
By that movement, she is "flowing forth," meaning she surges up with the desire to manifest each of those specific forms. And for this very reason:

The meaning is that, although all things— consisting of subjects, means of knowledge, and objects of knowledge— are not distinct [from consciousness], they are manifested as if they were distinct, having as their essence a specific, determined manifestation; furthermore,
when that very [consciousness] is devoid of *visarga*, which is the orientation toward externalization, [it remains as such].

Because it has the form of a slumbering serpent, the power Kuṇḍalinī rests solely within her own self—meaning that she is the supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*) consisting of pure being alone. For this very reason, at the terminal point which is the initial stage characterized by the orientation toward the external manifestation of emission (*visarga*), there is the Prāṇakuṇḍalikā. "Previously..."

According to the principle that "consciousness (saṃvit) is transformed into vital breath (prāṇa)," the meaning is that [consciousness] first manifests itself in the form of the vital breath. Likewise, by way of the process of reversal, it reaches its ultimate limit within its own essential nature, which consists of the orientation toward internal absorption; this is "the Supreme Kuṇḍalinī."
The meaning is that its nature consists solely of supreme consciousness resting within itself. Thus,

this very seventeenth digit, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, is called the "Sky of Śiva" (*śivavyoma*), the "Supreme Brahman," and the "Abode of the Pure Self" by various conventional terms used by those belonging to the [esoteric] traditions.
This is the meaning. For instance, in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* itself: "That which is known as the 'void of Śiva' (śivavyoma) is the state that is the Supreme Brahman.
Likewise: "What is declared to be the abode of the Self..."

When the Blessed Lady had been asked thus, [the Lord] began: "She should be known as named Kuṇḍalī, abiding above all paths," and continued: "It is devoid of arising from means of knowledge, free from distinctions of analogy, transcending the state of the elemental ether, the supreme state at the end of the ether of consciousness."
The cessation of the agitation of conceptualization regarding existence is the supreme goal;
that should be known as the void of Śiva, characterized by being the support of all.
"It is vastness and the quality of expanding; it is subtle and yet abides within.
It is called the Supreme Brahman—the unmanifest that is the object of realization.
Thus, and likewise:

"The division of the words has been proclaimed previously as that which is to be abandoned; nevertheless, the state of abiding in the Self, which transcends the stages (*bhūmikā*), is now being described.
By such passages, the Lord has declared their true nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, it is indeed the supreme, transcendental state of the Supreme Lord.

It would have been stated that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the basis for manifesting the delusive appearances of the emission and reabsorption of the entire universe, which consists of various subjects and objects of knowledge. For this very reason, he says:
"merely emission," and so forth. (137–140)
An objection is raised: "If there is only one undivided consciousness (*akhaṇḍasaṃvit*), then nothing whatsoever can exist apart from it;
so for whom could there be creation or dissolution, by virtue of which she could possess the agency of performing them?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The state of emission is the projection of one's own self into one's own self by one's own self. (3-141)

This very state, characterized by the power of emission and reabsorption, consists precisely in [the activity] of one's own self—and not from a material cause such as *māyā* or *prakṛti*; it occurs within one's own self—and not in some place or time separate from it; and it belongs to one's own self—and not to anything else whatsoever.

The "projection" (*kṣepa*) of the knower, the knowable, and so forth, is their manifestation as internal and external forms through the variety of their respective appearances. Therefore, the supreme consciousness itself—being full because it is independent of anything else—manifests in the form of the letters from *ka* to *ha*; this is the intended meaning. || 141 ||
Therefore, he says:
"The emission (visarga), thus emitted and having reached a state of solidification, is designated as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the consonant, and the contact (*sparśa*). (3.142)

In this context, the meaning is that the visarga itself, having attained a state of grossness in the form of the letter *ha* through the process of ascending various diversities, is designated by such words as "haṃsaḥ"; this is stated thus in all the scriptures. As it has been said in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka*:
"Hamsa, Śūnya, Prāṇa, and Hakāra—these are its names. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the Nighaṇṭu: "The thirty-third [letter], the consonant, the double-curved, and the contact [consonant] as well.
In this way, it may be said that "Hakāra" is the gross form of the Visarga itself. || 142 ||

Now, it is beyond dispute that, according to such statements as, "His powers are this entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power," the universe is the expansion of the mere power of the supreme, unsurpassed Light; yet, here again—
"The Lord's emission alone is the play of creation and withdrawal"—this and other such statements have been spoken otherwise; what does this mean? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Absolute is the supreme abode; that very same thing is called Akula."
The emission (visarga) of that Lord is called the Kaulikī Śakti.

Thus, the point is that what was already introduced here with the words, "Of this god who is without a clan (akula)... and so forth, has been brought to its conclusion; nothing new has been stated. || 143 ||
Now, one might ask: "By what cause is the word *visarga* applied to Śakti? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And that very [Śakti] possesses the state of *visarga* when her condition is one of surging forth, extending up to the point where the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) becomes manifest through the process of the arising of bliss. (144)
This very state of the Kaulikī Śakti is its "state of emission" (visargatā), which is the agency in the act of emission;
when this has become manifest— that is, attained clarity— through the sequence of the arising of bliss, will, and so forth, due to its nature as a differentiated manifestation,
it is that surging condition culminating in the power of action (kriyāśakti).
It is the manifestation [of consciousness] in the form of the variety of various subsequent reflective awarenesses (parāmarśa). || 144 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Let emission (*visarga*) be the cause of this much diversity; but how is it logical that emission itself is, in turn, that [diversity]? He pacifies this doubt by means of presenting an illustration:
"Emission itself is of such an extent that it implies within itself this entire nature."
Such is the nature of the ocean that it consists of an infinite succession of waves.

The emission (*visarga*) itself is of that measure—that is, its extent is precisely that—but it is not the cause of that [measure]. For the relationship of cause and effect is based on differentiation (*bheda*). Since there is no differentiation here at all, how could this be?—this is the intended meaning. Because [the emission] implies and contains within itself everything up to the limit of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The meaning is: he by whom such a self is [constituted]—that is, one who consists of infinite manifestations in the form of various signifieds, signifiers, and so forth. || 145 ||
Thus, because he is the agent of the act of emission (*visarjana*), there is another designation for him elsewhere; so [the author] says:
"For this very reason, this emission, whose nature consists of the unmanifested *hakalā*, is called the 'Principle of Desire' (*kāmatattva*) in the venerable *Kulaguhvara*. (3.146)

Therefore, for the reason stated above, this *visarga* consists of that *hakalā*—the half-part of half of the letter *ha*—which is unmanifest (*avyakta*) because its division into phonemes has not yet emerged, being merely the nature of sound (*nādamātra*).

In the venerable scripture known as the *Kulaguhvara*, it is called the "principle of desire" (*kāmatattva*); "desire" (*kāma*) means will (*icchā*), and its "principle" (*tattva*) is its essential nature.
The meaning of the sentence is this: that which is everywhere of an unimpeded nature is called the "Full Form" (pūrṇarūpa).
(146) He recites the very passage from that [text]:
"That which is the imperishable, unmanifest syllable situated in the throat of the beloved..."
But that which does not desire the form of sound is devoid of meditation and concentration.
Having concentrated the mind there, one should bring the world under control simultaneously.
And therein: "Now, O lady of beautiful hips, the reality of desire and likewise the supreme reality of poison are being told to you, especially out of devotion and affection."
Having begun thus and having stated, "That which is the imperishable...
and so forth, [it continues]: "In that, the high-souled practitioner should fix the mind."
The women of the gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas.
"O Subhagā, even yakṣa maidens, nāgas, piśācas, and celestial women come under one's control; what need is there to mention men and women?
Thus it is said. And here [in this context]: "Having concentrated the mind there, one may bring the world under control simultaneously."
Thus it is recited by way of its meaning: that which is "akṣara" (the imperishable), because it is always of a radiant nature, is established solely through one's own experience;
and because it is eternally arisen, its primordial nature is never lost.

Precisely for this reason, because its nature is to manifest spontaneously—as stated in such passages as: "Therefore, there is no one who utters it, nor is there any who obstructs it; the God, residing in the chest of living beings, manifests Himself by Himself"—there is no desire to utter [the mantra] belonging to another.

It does not depend [on anything else]—this is the meaning. For if it were dependent on that, then because of its occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*), its state of being eternally arisen (*nityoditatva*) would not exist; this is the intended sense. For this very reason, it is described elsewhere as "spontaneous" (*sahaja*) and "self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*). For this same reason, it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), for manifestness (*vyaktatva*) indeed...

It would arise through the impact of the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the organs of pronunciation (*karaṇa*), and since that is dependent on volition, how could this [Sound] be so? For this very reason, it is of the nature of resonance (*dhvani*):
"That supreme seed called 'Sound' (*nāda*) which resides within all beings."

The meaning is that its nature consists solely of the eternally manifest sound (*nāda*), according to such statements as: "It is extremely subtle, all-pervasive, pure, and the designator of the principle of *prāṇa*. Precisely because of this extreme subtlety and pervasiveness, and because of that [nature] which resides there, as opposed to that which resides in gross objects of meditation and so forth—

The meaning is that [the state] is devoid of meditation and so forth, and is unshakeable by virtue of being fixed in the nature of the object of meditation and the like. Even while possessing such a form, at the time of enjoyment, because the internal organ has its perception of other objects dissolved through the helplessness of immersion in the bliss of passion, it is like a beloved woman whose deficiencies have been cast away.

Arising spontaneously within the throat and being manifested, it therefore has a particular presence at that moment despite its state of being perpetually arisen. And thus, because the *visarga* is of the nature of the *anāhata*,
even in its subtlety, through the occurrence of a slight swelling within the throat of the beloved, it is [expressed as] "hā-hā."

The meaning is this: its manifestation is clear, by which it is made into a demonstrable example for him; therefore, this is not accessible to yogis alone, but is perceived by everyone as well. And thus, by this very [explanation], the nature of the letter *ha* has also been indicated by way of incidental discussion, but that of [the letter *a*]—

The difference is merely this: [the former] exists in a manifest state due to its grossness, whereas this [latter], because of its subtlety, does not; for this very reason, it was stated immediately thereafter:
"Emission itself has clearly attained a state of solidification."

Thus it has been stated. It is with this very intention that the higher-lower (parāpara) and lower (apara) nature of these two have been described. For this reason alone, the essential form of the letter *ha* is not mentioned here later on. And it has been said elsewhere:
"That supreme, unshakeable syllable which has arisen from the throat of the Beloved..."
"The innate is called *nāda*; this reality is the ever-arisen recitation (*japa*).
Likewise:
"From the savoring of the essence of eternal bliss, 'Hā-Hā' arises within the hollow of the throat."
"The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) is the utterance that bestows bliss; He is the knower of the reality of desire.
Thus, within such an emission (visarga) whose nature is the Unstruck (anāhata), the practitioner [should fix] his mind correctly—[as it is said]:
"For one whose consciousness is rendered helpless by the immersion into supreme bliss..."
They recite this continuously during the festival of union with women.
Those lords of yogis whose minds are unattached here attain the supreme yoga;
he is Kāma, devoid of a head, whose abode is the hearts of women.
"Then, by means of that which has ascended to the eye, one should bring about the gaze of power (śaktidṛṣṭi);
there is no doubt that one will agitate even a proud and excellent woman.
According to this stated principle, [one should contemplate] the emission (visarga), which consists of the vowel-less phoneme (anackakalā) and is denoted by the word "Kāma."

One should meditate on [the light] emerging from one's own eyes and entering the eyes of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and [then] meditate on it emerging from the eyes of the person to be accomplished and entering one's own eyes; in this manner,
by means of the sequence of a swing-mechanism (dolāyantra), one should repeatedly maintain the movement of going and coming until it is complete on all sides.
Having become attentive without depending on anything else, one should "subjugate" the world—the cycle of living beings as it arises—simultaneously and not sequentially;
that is, one should cause everything to appear as identical with one's own self, or bring it under the control of one's own self—this is the meaning. || 147 ||
Now, taking the very nature of emission (*visarga*) as described above as an illustration, he begins to speak of the emergence of the consonants beginning with *ka*:
"Therefore, just as the state of emission is clearly manifest in the *haṃsa*... (3.148).
In the same way, there is the abiding of the vowels beginning with Anuttara (A) as the consonants from Ka to Sa.

Therefore, for the reason just mentioned, just as the visarga itself exists in a gross form as the nature of the letter Ha, so too do the vowels beginning with Anuttara exist as the consonants from Ka to Sa. Thus, the vowels beginning with Anuttara [are established].
They appear in that very way—this is the meaning. || 148 ||
He says that very thing:
"From the unsurpassed [letter] comes the clear birth of the fivefold *ka*-group. (3.149)

The penetration into the nature of the five powers (*pañcaśaktyātmatāveśa*) is clearly evident in each individual [power]; this is the reason for their fivefold nature—namely, "the penetration into the nature of the five powers. Regarding the phrase "in each individual," this refers to the Anuttara, Icchā, and so forth; for even though the Anuttara is characterized primarily by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), everything exists everywhere.
By this logic, since [the letter *ka*] consists of five powers, its progeny—the *ka*-group (*kavarga*)—likewise possesses a fivefold nature;
the same should be understood for other cases as well. || 149 ||
From the single nature of the power of will, which abides in its own essential form. (3.150)

The *cavarga* consists of the five powers and is characterized by the gradual manifestation [of consciousness]; however, that which was described as being subject to the turbidity of the knowable arises through the application of rapid movement. (3.151)
From that [dual form] arises the pair of groups beginning with *ṭa* and *ta*;
however, from *unmeṣa* (the opening) comes the group beginning with *pa*, since within it the universe is fully encompassed.

"Abiding in its own nature" means being uncolored by any desired object. "In a single form" means that this is so of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) precisely when it is undisturbed, and not even when it is disturbed—this is the meaning.
Even for the powers beginning with consciousness (*cit*), there is a clarity corresponding to their respective outward orientation.

Thus, by virtue of this propriety, it is stated that the *ka*-group and the others, which are its expanded forms, possess the same nature—as expressed in the phrase: "consisting of the progressive manifestation [of phonemes]. The word "she" (*yā*) refers to the power of will (*icchā-śakti*); "the object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) is that which is desired, such as an external object; and "of the two-fold form" means of the form of the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*.

Thus, it has been stated that the five groups (vargas), beginning with the *ka*-group, arise precisely from the five [phonemes] beginning with *a* and *u*; for this very reason, their shared place of articulation (*sasthānatva*) has been declared by such statements as "the throat is the place of articulation for *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya*," and it has also been stated elsewhere:
From Akula, the second group, consisting of the five powers, has arisen;
and beyond that is the Will, whose form is uncolored [by objective determination].
"Then, for that [consonant] which resides in fire (v) and earth (ṣ), there are eight; then the first two, followed by 'p' and so on, born from Unmeṣa—thus the Sparśas are proclaimed.

But is it not said: "The principles beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa are [located] in the five groups of consonants beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', in due order, O lady of good vows"?

By such statements as these, the twenty-five phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are established as corresponding to the principles (*tattva*) starting from the earth-principle up to the principle of the Person (*puruṣa*). Since other principles also exist, how can it be said that the entire universe (*viśva*) is exhausted by this much alone?
—“From what point does the universe come to an end? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

“Since this world, consisting of the knowable, clearly extends up to the twenty-fifth principle, it is stated that, because it is clearly the object of knowledge, its nature consists of touch to this extent. (3.153)

Since this entire universe— beginning from the earth-principle (*pṛthvī-tattva*) and ending with the twenty-fifth, which is the principle of the Person (*puruṣa-tattva*) according to such statements as "the Person is the twenty-fifth"— is of the nature of the knowable due to its manifestness, it has been so stated.
Regarding the phrase "from which the universe is completed": since the group beginning with Niyati— namely,

the six coverings (kañcukas) together with Māyā— is said to be "the innermost [sheath] of the individual soul," and by such statements is understood to be entirely non-different from the knower due to its extreme proximity, as if clinging to his very throat, it is not [separate].

The meaning is that it has been described as having the form of the universe, which consists of the self and the gross objects of knowledge that are distinct [from consciousness]. For this very reason, this entire universe, up to the end of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), is "of the nature of touch" (*sparśarūpa*) because it is clearly an object of knowledge; for things are called "touches" (*sparśas*) because they are touched by the senses. Furthermore, [the letters] beginning with *ka* are preeminently...
The consonants ending in *m* are the *sparśa*s; with this in mind regarding their denotation, [the Lord said]:
"But the contacts of the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold, heat, pleasure, and pain, are transient, coming and going; endure them, O Bhārata."

And this was stated with the intention of referring to what is expressed [in words]. Furthermore, although the person (pums) is the knower (pramātṛ), and although the instruments (karaṇa) are indeed means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by virtue of being instruments, the fact that they are said to be objects of knowledge (jñeyatva) is intended with respect to other knowers such as those who are void (śūnya) and so forth; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 153 ||
Having thus described the arising of the *sparśas*, he now describes those that are internal (*antaḥstha*):

"And that power of will (*icchāśakti*), which is twofold according to its being either agitated or unagitated, becomes the nature of *yā* when it is oriented toward a portion of a heterogeneous power. (3.154)

That very [consciousness], when defiled by the turbidity of the objects of knowledge acquired more rapidly, undergoes the states of *ratva* and *latva* due to its orientation toward heterogeneous [objects]. (3-155)

In the same way, the power of unfolding (unmeṣa-śakti), which possesses two forms and resides in the power of differentiation (vaijātya-śakti), attains the state of the letter *va*, which rains down the essence of emanation (sṛṣṭi). || 3.156 ||

This power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which is twofold by virtue of being both agitated and unagitated, becomes oriented toward that supreme, dissimilar aspect of consciousness which is of the nature of *cit*— the Absolute (*anuttara*)— and,

undergoing a phonetic combination (*saṃdhi*) according to the rule "a vowel *i* [or *u*, etc. becomes a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) before a vowel," it attains the state of the letter *ya*, becoming identical with the essence of *ya*.
"It throbs"— this is the meaning. That very will-power (icchā-śakti), though possessing two forms,
acts swiftly and steadily according to the manner described in the passage beginning with "shining like a flash of lightning," and thus,
being colored by the turbidity of the object of knowledge (jñeya)— namely, the thing desired such as wealth and so forth— [it becomes manifest].

The state of being directed toward that which is dissimilar to the unsurpassed Self (*anuttarātman*) constitutes a *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) according to the rule "iko yaṇ aci"; by means of this, it undergoes the transformation into *ra* and *la*, and thus shines as that very essence—this is the meaning.
In this way, the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*) is also twofold, "reaching the power of dissimilarity"—that is, together with the unsurpassed.
Just as before, having formed a union, it manifests as the letter *va*. As it has been said:
"Through conjunction with distinct powers, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) assumes the forms of *ya*, *ra*, and *la*;
the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*) likewise attains the state of *va*, O fair-faced one."

Thus, by the phrase "pouring down the essence of creation," its nature as a nourisher is shown because it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Varuṇa; in this same way, it should be understood that the letters *ya*, *ra*, and *la* possess, respectively, the qualities of drying, burning, and paralyzing. || 156 ||

Now, even when there is the coloring by the object of desire, according to the principle to be explained later, it is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) alone that is capable of generating another act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

Thus, let it be granted that for that [will] which possesses the union with the Absolute (*anuttara*), an effect characterized by another reflective awareness may indeed arise; however, regarding that—

Furthermore, how could there be a distinction based on the forms of the letters beginning with *ya*? For it is said that "the difference in effects arises from the difference in causes," yet here the cause consists solely of the single, unified friction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of will and the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
What, then, is this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Will itself, having attained unsurpassed bliss through its association with swiftness, is called wind; it is fire because of its luminosity, and earth because of its stability. (3.157)

In this context, it is desire itself— and not even the object of desire— that, having joined with the two unsurpassed joys (anuttarānanda) by means of conceptual thought (vikalpa), assumes the characteristic of momentum (vega) defined as a latent impression (saṃskāra) due to its rapidity, and thereby takes on the limiting adjunct (upādhi) and is called "wind" (vāyu), taking the form of the seed-syllable *ya* of wind.

The meaning is "has been attained. Thus, from its shining, fire assumes the attribute characterized by luminosity; likewise, from its stability, earth assumes the attribute called steadiness, which is the cause of support. Having taken hold of these attributes as coloring factors (*uparañjaka*), fire gradually attains the nature of the seed-syllable *ra* (repha), and earth attains the form of the seed-syllable *la* (lakāra).
And it causes [the object] to appear—this is the meaning. The word "Ānanda" (Bliss) is stated with the intent of manifesting other heterogeneous powers, such as Unmeṣa (Expansion) and so forth.
Therefore, for the Will-power (*icchā*), which possesses the union of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and the rest, through its connection with such limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [it manifests].
Since there is a distinction [in the cause], there must also be a distinction in the effect; thus, what was stated previously alone is logical. || 157 ||
And here he shows the reason for the application of the term "inner" (*antaḥstha*):
"This group of four is called 'inner' precisely because it is contained within [the powers] such as Will (*icchā*), and because it abides in its own completion. (3.158)

For this very reason, from the cause previously stated—namely, because by the word "etc. in the phrase "will, etc.," the *unmeṣa* (the upward-expansion) is included, and thus will and *unmeṣa* abide within [the Self] non-differently—there is likewise the "perfect attainment" (*sam-yag-āpti*), which is the manifestation as one with the Self whose sole nature is that of the subject; therein...

Because it exists as one with the subject through its very constitution (*saṃsthiti*), this tetrad beginning with "this" (*idam*) and ending with "vomited" (*vānta*) is said to be "internal" (*antaḥstha*) in all the scriptures; such is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"Because they enter into the interior of desire and the rest, they are proclaimed as the 'Antasthas' (the semi-vowels). || 158 ||

Now, one might object: "Just as the powers such as will (icchā) and the rest, when conjoined with heterogeneous powers, bring forth other types of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), does the same occur—or not—when they are connected with homogeneous powers? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

They say that this [state] consists of agitation (*kṣobha*), which is the conjunction of homogeneous powers such as will (*icchā*) and the rest, even for those whose nature is both agitated and non-agitated. (3.159)

When there is a conjunction (*yojana*)— that is, a union characterized by *saṃdhi* according to the rule "a long vowel occurs before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*)— of powers such as Will (*icchā*) and the rest, which are of the nature of agitation (*kṣobha*) when they are long and of the nature of non-agitation (*akṣobha*) when they are short, even though these powers are of the same class (*sajātīya*), then [the result] is "of the nature of agitation."

Thus they say—the meaning is that those learned in the scriptures declare that [the vowel *i*] has the nature of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of its own long form belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*), and not the nature of another reflective awareness belonging to a different class (*vijātīya*). Therefore: *i* + *i* = *ī*; *ī* + *i* = *ī*; *i* + *ī* = *ī*.
In a conjunction such as *ī* + *ī* = *ī*, the intended meaning is that, due to the nature of agitation (*kṣobha*), the long form itself becomes the phoneme *ī*. || 159 ||
Furthermore, even though the unsurpassed (anuttara) is of such a nature, there is a distinction; thus he says:
"In the case of the similarity of the unsurpassed, there may be a twofold course: if that which is one among them is for the sake of generating bliss... (3.160)
In conjunction with that, the yoga consisting of agitation will clearly manifest;
here too, the second unsurpassed abode serves for procreation. (3.161)
At that time, without agitation (*kṣobha*), the state of being the Unsurpassed (*anuttarātmatā*) is not sufficient.
Furthermore, when the Unsurpassed joins with its own kind, there are two possible courses;
for in that case, if that one [element] is the Unsurpassed, it will then become capable of producing bliss (*ānanda*).

Therefore, in that connection with the supreme *anuttara* itself, the yoga consisting of arousal (*kṣobha*), which is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), is clearly the yoga; it is an unimpeded junction (*sandhi*) just as before. For example, in the phrase "the tip of the staff" (*daṇḍāgram*) and so forth, there is one mode, yet nevertheless, from the perspective of the meaning, it belongs to the single *anuttara*.
Even a second instance of the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) friction would not suffice to produce bliss;

for, without the manifestation of the bliss consisting of arousal (*kṣobha*), when the *pararūpa* substitution is applied according to the rule "ato guṇe," there would result only the state of the unsurpassed itself—as in the case of the word "śīmantam" and so forth. This is the second [point].
Having thus explained this as a digression, he now describes the actual subject at hand—the arising of the *ūṣman*s:
"That desire which is devoid of action, and that which is colored by the object of desire. (3-162)
Divided into three by its qualities of swiftness and stability, it exists in three states:
the unblown, the blossoming, and the fully blown. (3.163)
That which is desired is threefold within this [will], because it does not fall away from its own nature;
for that very [will] is impelled by its own heat, which consists in the impulse of the sovereignty of its own self. (3.164)
The triad of *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* has been clearly cast out externally and remains [there].
Thus, he shows the state of even that which is to be desired (*eṣṭavya*) by dividing it, starting with the words "unmanifested" (*anunmiṣita*). In this [state]...
When the Will has attained a threefold state, that which is desired also exists in a threefold state;
for it is said:
"That [Will], being of the nature of mere Will alone, is remote from that which is to be created."
