According to this principle, [the state] is "unblown" (anunmiṣita), meaning not yet emerged, in the pure form of the vowel *i*;

it is "blooming" (unmīlat), meaning emerging, in the form of the vowel *ṛ*, which is colored by the object of desire (*eṣṭavya*) in its rapid aspect; and in the form of the vowel *ḷ*, it is colored by the object of desire in its stable aspect.

"Unfolded" (*pronmīlitam*) means "shining forth. Now, one might object: since the desired object possesses distinctions such as speed and so on, does this not result in a deviation from its essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by its uniqueness? Thus, one should say that there are three objects here, rather than one single object appearing in three ways? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Regarding the phrase "because of the non-deviation from that nature":
the sense is that even though there are differences such as speed and so forth, there is no falling away from this [nature] characterized by the state of being desired.
Thus, in this way, even the threefold object of desire, by its own heat characterized by absolute freedom (svātantrya),...
Having manifested as an external form, it flashes forth as the triad consisting of *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, which are designated as "heat" (*ūṣman*). Therefore, he says: "That very [desire], etc.
Thus, since it is impossible for that which is desired to exist apart from desire itself, even this threefold [object] is indeed just desire, by virtue of its own internal heat (*svoṣma*).
The intended meaning is that [the power] flashes forth as the essence of the three types of conceptual grasping (*parāmarśa*). As it has been said:
"Will itself, overcome by its own heat, rests upon the three *kalās*.

For this very reason, regarding these [consonants] and will, [it is taught]: "The palatal [sounds] *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* [arise from the palate]," and "the retroflex [sounds] *ṭu*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa*..."

By the statement beginning with "The head is the [abode] of the Ṛtu-lasas; the teeth... and so forth, the state of having a common place of articulation (*sasthānatva*) has been declared. By this, it is also revealed that the expansion (*visphāra*) extends only up to this point. (162–164)
Therefore he says:
"From that very [source], the universe shines forth clearly in this letter SA. (3.165)
And yogis declare that to be the nectar and the supreme abode;
for it is from *tataḥ* (that) that even what has emerged and is being desired unfolds as an external form.
And it is with this very intention [that it is said].
It has been stated [in the scriptures], "The three eggs are pervaded by the Śārṇa [syllable]," and so forth. For this very reason, because it causes the nourishment of this entire universe,
it is the Moon, the Lord of Nectar, the essence of ambrosia, and the treasury of nectar.

The meaning is: because it is described as the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*) through such perspectives as, "The letter *sa* is proclaimed by its names as the support of the six flavors," the Gurus declare that supreme abode of nectar;
they speak of it in all the scriptures. || 165 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is this nature of his perceived anywhere, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that very supreme nectar [is found] at the cessation of the beginning and end of agitation. (3.166)

The connection is as follows: within the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of immersion into the reality of the bliss of the *sītkāra* sound, there are the beginnings, ends, and cessations of the agitation that constitutes the primordial sacrifice (*ādiyāga*). Within those [moments] characterized by the *sītkāra* and so forth, that very nectar—the supreme abode—is manifested; this is the meaning.
Thus, through the intensification of his nature as consisting of supreme bliss,
the wheel of the rays of his instruments (the senses) impetuously brings about its arising;
it attains stability therein by means of the culmination in the essence of the flavor of supreme happiness.
"And here, through the destruction of the weight of supreme awakening, it goes to dissolution;
and herein, the supreme *kalā* shines forth in its stainless isolation.
By such reasoning as this, first, due to the inclination toward agitation (*kṣobha*) of the wheel of instruments (*karaṇacakra*),...

When the *sītkāra* (the sound "sit") and so forth have arisen, immediately thereafter, through resting in that very state, there occurs an immersion into the bliss whose nature is supreme *sāmarasya* (harmonious integration); and following that, through firm establishment in that very same state, one realizes:
"Śat is the Supreme Brahman."

By this reasoning, the existence (*sattā*) of the supreme Brahman is its being; therein, that which is immersion—namely, the emergence of the consciousness-subject (*cit-pramātṛtā*) through the submergence of the subjectivity of the body and so forth—is itself *samādhi*, which is the radiant manifestation as the form of the digit of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit-kalā*). Thus it is said.
The meaning is that there is manifestation in such states of bliss and so forth. || 166 ||

Thus, it would be said that this [consciousness] is indeed of the nature of the supreme Brahman; therefore, he says: "That very [consciousness] they declare to be the supreme, undivided Brahman. (167)
"Brahman"—
the meaning is that this refers to the all-pervasive form, according to such statements as "All this, indeed, is Brahman. For this very reason, it is said to be "undivided."

The sense is that there would indeed be a division of that which has a fixed form. They "declare"—that is, in the *Śrīparātriṃśikā* and other texts. For instance, in the extraction of the *Parā*-seed-mantra therein, it says: "The third Brahman, O lady of beautiful hips."
Thus it has been said: the third Brahman is the syllable *sakāra*, as it is sung [in scripture]: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally known to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*. || 167 ||
And because its nature is both all-pervasive and immortal, for that very reason there is another designation elsewhere as "the principle of poison" (viṣatattva); thus he says:
"The Blessed Lord himself declared this in the venerable Kulaguhvara."
In that which has acquired its literal designation from the identity of power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat). || 3-168 ||
Having the shape of a crow’s beak, devoid of meditation and dhāraṇā, and called "without phonemes" (anacka), the reality of poison has been revealed out of affection for you. (3-169)

Regarding the phrase "anvarthābhidhānake" (having a name according to its meaning), it is stated in that very same work: "Kula is declared to be Śakti, and Gahvara is the possessor of Śakti (Śaktimat);
the oneness of the realization of both is called Kulaguhvara."

Thus [it is said]. He recites the very passage from that [work], beginning with "the crow’s beak," and so forth. Because the referent of the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*) consists essentially in an address—[namely], "O Goddess, out of affection for you"—and because [you] are to be instructed and are thus worthy of compassion, there is that reality of the pervasive form of poison.

The meaning is that there is non-obstruction everywhere, which has been brought into the range of experience at the occasion of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) resulting from the mutual friction (*anyonyasaṅghaṭṭa*) manifested by that [power]. And because its nature is unstruck (*anāhata*), it is denoted by the word "without phonemes" (*anacka*). For this very reason:

Because it is perpetually manifest, it is independent of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the like; for that [consciousness] is fixed upon a specific object of meditation and so forth—this is the intended meaning.
Even so, its form is like the beak of a crow, because the vowel-less [consonant *ha*] is arranged in such a way due to its double curvature (*dvikubjatā*). (168–169)
But surely, the seed-syllable of immortality (*amṛtabīja*) was introduced here at the outset, and its form cannot be such [as you suggest],
since it has been stated to belong to the domain of the syllables of desire (*kāma*); for what purpose, then, has this been corroborated here, even by the Blessed One?
"What is this principle of desire (*kāmatattva*), that is indeed the principle of poison (*viṣatattva*).
Listen now to this in brief, O deer-eyed one."—
What is the intention behind this restatement of the very principle of desire as the principle of poison?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The reality of desire is its fullness, which is clearly perceived in the state of union;
and the reality of poison is nectar, once the concealment of the individual soul has fallen away. (3.170)

Surely, in the venerable *Kulaguhvara*, the Blessed One has described the essential nature of the reality of desire (*kāmatattva*) and the reality of poison (*viṣatattva*) with reference to the sixth *prāṇakalā*— which consists of nothing but the name "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) and is the common substrate of the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*— and not merely the *prāṇa* alone.

Because such a state is impossible for that [prāṇa]. For in its states of exhalation (*recaka*) and so forth, since its activity is dependent on another's will, there could indeed be the occurrence of being uttered or being obstructed. Furthermore, the "distinction" consists in the *kāma*-tattva having the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and likewise the *viṣa*-tattva.
The nature of the *apāna* [wind]. For this very reason, these two consist of the letters *ha* and *sa*. As it has been said:
"The letters *śa* and *ha*, which are the names for night and day, move respectively below and above;
they are intent on mutual enmity and are considered to have the form of a snake (*naga*) and a lizard (*huḍu*)."
"Who is capable of obstructing those two, except by exerting his own great heroism?
Likewise:
"The *bindu* above is the sun, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the day, and indeed half a portion."
The portion presided over by the Siddhas consists of the propitiation of Khecarī.
"Below is the *nāda*, as well as the *apāna*, the *mattagandha*, the night, and the moon;
this portion is presided over by Khecarī, is served by the *siddhas*, and consists of dissolution.
Thus, even though these two possess such specific characteristics, because the universal resides within the particular, [the general principle applies].
Since the nature of being mere vital breath (*prāṇana*) is possible in both cases, they are designated with a single form;

it is with this intention that the Lord has described the reality of desire (*kāmatattva*) itself as the reality of poison (*viṣatattva*), and here this is corroborated. For this very reason, there is the fullness of desire, even of the reality of desire (*kāmatattva*).

The state called "desirelessness," which consists in resting solely within one's own self, is the ultimate reality, the supreme form; it is "discerned" during the *saṅghaṭṭa*—that is to say, it is directly realized by everyone at the moment of the internal agitation consisting of mutual aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*). This applies even to the limited individual (*aṇu*) who is [otherwise] a "poison-principle."
When the state of being limited— the nature of the subject who perceives the body and so forth, which veils innate, full vision and action— is cast off as the object of concealment,

and when the full form arises through the dissolution of the division between the known and the knower, the immortal reality consisting of the state of expansion is manifested within the union; thus, as before.
The connection. || 170 ||
Now, one might ask: "Even though its innate, perfect vision and action are obscured, what is the cause [of this]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since the pervasive power is like poison, it would obscure the light of the non-pervasive."

"Power" (*śakti*) refers to the supreme Lord's power called *māyā*, which consists in the concealment of His own nature. "Greatness" (*maha*) refers to the innate, perfect form of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*). For even poison, due to its external pervasiveness, would indeed cause the obscuration of the vision and action of the limited self who does not pervade; such is the point here.
The superimposition of that.
Thus, not only does this [reality] possess the nature of *kāmatattva* or the nature of *viṣatattva*, but it also possesses the state of being *nirañjana* (the stainless)—as he says:
"The supreme abode is *nirañjana*; its *tattva*, however, is *sāñjana*. (3.171)
Since the supreme filling [consciousness] flashes forth from that [source] as consisting of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) and comprising the universe—
because even that which is intended [as an object], though already manifested, is made to emerge as an external form—
it consists of the power of action; for this very reason, it comprises the universe.
*Dhāma*—the lunar light whose essence is the letter *sa*; that is *nirañjana*.
As it is said: "When these three flash forth as a unity, then nothing can serve as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because each negates its own [limitations]."

The meaning is that, according to the reasoning previously stated beginning with "ityādi," nothing at all can be superposed upon it. Furthermore, that which is the *tattva*— the state of ultimate luminosity characterized as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and the place of rest— of that lunar abode whose nature is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), is "with ointment" (*sāñjana*).

The meaning is that it is logical for manifestation to be brought about by the power (*śakti*) as its agent, according to the reasoning previously established in such passages as: "Since that which possesses power is manifested, while power itself is never [manifested] by anything.
Therefore, he says: "Therefore, since it shines forth..."—that is, for that reason, because...
From the power (*śakti*), it "shines forth"—the meaning is that it is manifested by its own power alone, according to such statements as: "The Śiva-power is here called the mouth. || 171 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the three principles beginning with *kāma* consist of the three powers beginning with *icchā*, how can it be said that the single seed-syllable *amṛta* possesses this nature? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] first explains their differentiation and then confirms their non-differentiation:
Desire is the poison; knowledge is the Goddess, the stainless action.

The convergence of these three is called Śiva-Bhairava—Bhairava because of his fullness by virtue of consisting of the entire universe. For this very reason, it has been stated: "That alone is the supreme Brahman," and so forth. || 172 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"In this regard, one should always cultivate firm mastery; so our teachers have declared. (3.173)

Having fully entered into the reality of poison, one should manifest through the contemplation: "I am neither the element, nor the poison, nor even the seizing spirit; I am solely the Absolute. (3.174)

Here, in this pervasive form which consists of the reality of poison (*viṣatattva*), "establishment" (*rūḍhi*) means penetration. Anticipating the question, "What would be the result of establishment here?", he says: "In the reality of poison," and so forth. "Element" (*bhūta*) refers to a *yakṣa* or similar being. "Seizure" (*graha*) is the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding that which is not the self; for that [seizure] belongs to one who is limited.

The intended meaning is that this would belong to the knower. Furthermore, for one who has attained immersion (*samāveśa*) in the pervasive form that is the nature of the supreme subject, through the practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-abhyāsa*), the supreme non-duality consisting of "I" alone should manifest; by means of this, there remains for him nothing whatsoever that could cause affliction beyond that [non-duality].
"One should fear"—this is the intended meaning. As it is said in the *Śrīkulaguhvara*:
"When [the state] is empty, without support, devoid of meditation and concentration, bearing all phonemes yet peaceful, and free from all phonemes..."
Pure consciousness alone is absolute, pure, and the means for neutralizing poison;
there is no poison, no planetary influence, no sin, no yakṣa, and no rākṣasa.
"One should not conceptualize any [entity] such as a *piśāca*, nor this, nor 'I';
[one should do so] merely by way of its appearance (*bhāva-mātra*).
Now, since no other agitation is possible prior to the desire colored by the object of desire,
its neuter nature was asserted through such statements as, "...and this is the seed of nothing whatsoever"; and immediately thereafter, here—
"That which was stated as 'the turbidity of the object of knowledge'... and so forth;
likewise, "O Śiva, that which is most swiftly acquired...
and so forth; likewise...
By such statements as, "...and this [nature] is colored by that which is to be desired," the existence of another agitation (*kṣobha*) even from the neuter vowels (*ṣaṇṭhavarṇa*) is asserted;
how, then, could their previously promised status as neuters be maintained?
Anticipating this objection, he provides the following response:
"But surely, since birth from the neuter vowels has been taught here, how could they possess the state of being neuter?
If this is asked, we reply: in this case, there is no generative power belonging to the neuter. (3-175)
For it is thus: that very power of will (icchā-śakti) which has been described as residing therein produces its own effect, which exists within itself in the form of its own desired object. (3.176)
Whatever cause for defilement is sought here remains [unproduced] from that portion; there is no production from it, and the turbidity born thereof is its very nature. (3.177)

Regarding the phrase "janmoktam" (spoken as birth)—this refers to the *ṭa*-group and so forth. Regarding "we say"—the answer is that "here the neuter has no generative power. He establishes this very point with the words beginning with "for instance" (*tathāhi*). Since this very power of will (*icchā-śakti*) residing in the neuter, although existing non-differently from itself within the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), [acts] according to its own nature...

One's own fixed form, the effect beginning with the *ṭa*-group [of consonants], should be made to manifest externally; however, one should not seek the nature of being slow or quick, which serves as the cause for coloring that [form]. For that would only produce turbidity. And by this much alone, this [process] has fulfilled its purpose; thus, [it is unnecessary].
The sense is that she is also capable of manifesting other effects. Furthermore, that turbidity, its cause, or the very body of this will (*icchā*) is identical with her—this is the meaning.
For there is nothing whatsoever distinct from the will, whose sole nature is light (*prakāśa*).

The sense is that something might possibly arise. Therefore, since in reality it is *icchā* (will) alone that is predominant, it is rightly said that it brings forth its respective effects; thus [it is said in the] Śivasūtra: "Śiva begets. || 177 ||
One might object: "Even so, would not the status of the neuter vowels as seeds be refuted by the principle that every [vowel] possesses every [quality]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"They know the [seed-mantra] to consist of a composite whole, joined with the coloring (ārūṣaṇā) of the object of knowledge."
The neuter [state] arises from the conjunction of the absence of both the state of being an agitator and the state of being the locus of agitation. (3.178)

For they know the neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) to be the form of the union between the object of desire and the desire itself; because herein there is neither the state of being an agitator (*kṣobhakatva*) nor the state of being a substratum of agitation (*kṣobhādhāratva*). Therefore, even though desire alone brings about the manifestation of another agitation, its status as a seed-syllable (*bījatva*) would not be excluded for these [neuter vowels].
Since the state of being neuter consists of a composite nature, it is rightly said: "In this case, there is no procreative power for the neuter. || 178 ||
Having thus explained this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"Because of the manifestation of its own *ūṣman* (aspirate) by this group of four letters, it was given the name 'ūṣman' by Bhairava, whose nature is stainless. (3.179)

"Of the group of four"—that is, together with the letter *ha*. For its birth is from the Absolute (*anuttara*), as has already been stated by way of this methodological turn. Indeed, the power of the Absolute is emission (*visarga*), and its congealed form is this very [letter *ha*]. Therefore, it shares the same place of articulation (*saṃsthānatva*) with the Absolute. "By its own heat" (*svoṣmaṇā*).

The meaning is: "by the light of one's own self, characterized by autonomy. For this manifestation does not appear through dependence on anything else, as is the case with other reflective awarenesses such as will (*icchā*) or the Absolute (*anuttara*);
rather, it arises solely from its own majesty—this is the intended sense. Even though...

Although it is stated that the birth of the *kavarga* and the other classes arises from each of the vowels beginning with *a* (anuttara) alone, this is nevertheless due to the employment of other powers [within those vowels]; thus it is rightly said: "by virtue of the manifestation through the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
Not only is there a separate designation for each individual phoneme from *ka* to *ha* by way of being "contacts" (*sparśa*) and so forth, but this is done even without such separation; thus he says:
"The wise declare that this [series] from *ka* to *ha* is the substratum of agitation."
The phrase "by being the substratum of agitation" means "by being the womb (yoni)"—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"And the womb is remembered as [denoted] by the letters beginning with *ka*... and so forth.

Not only does the manifestation of another agitation occur through the union of one seed with another seed according to the aforementioned principle, but this also applies to the womb through its union with another womb; thus he says:
"Through union with that [seed] in the form of the womb, it too shall undergo another agitation. (3.180)
By way of illustration of that, there is the state of being the fiftieth letter.

"Of that" refers to the source-form (yoni-rūpa) such as *ka* and so forth. And thus, by the method of illustrating that other agitation (*kṣobha*), that very same other agitation is exemplified in the *Mātṛkā* by means of the fifty [letters].
The connection is with the "filling color," namely the "peak seed-syllable" (kūṭabīja) called *kṣa*.

For that [syllable] is taken as a comprehensive contraction (*pratyāhāra*) of the letters *ka* and *sa*, which constitute the beginning and the end [of the alphabet] and are vitalized by the Absolute (*anuttara*) and the Emission (*visarga*), by means of which the entire true nature of the Mother-phonemes (*mātṛkā*) is simultaneously [manifested].
This has been demonstrated. As it was stated by the venerable Kṣemarāja:
"That which is the reality of Mātṛkā up to this extent is precisely the union of the Absolute (anuttara) and the Emission (visarga) through the pratyāhāra of the letters *ka* and *sa*."
"It has been demonstrated at the end by means of the essential seed-syllable (kūṭabīja). || 180 ||

Now, by such statements as, "Since this [universe] ending with the twenty-fifth is clearly of the nature of the knowable," the twenty-five phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are [established] as being of the nature of the knowable.
Having specified those whose essential nature is solely differentiation, he raises the doubt—"What, then, is the form of the two subsequent sets of four?"—and says:
"It is well-established on the levels (bhūmi) as previously described, known by the name 'the twenty-five'. (3.181)
The fourfold group and the fourfold group, pertaining respectively to difference and non-difference, follow in sequence. He elaborates upon this very point:
"The first fourfold group is skilled in the unification of the differences of consciousness. (3.182)
"Differentiation has as its sole cause the firm establishment of non-difference; the other fourfold [cause] is as follows.

Regarding "differentiation"—the meaning is that which is severed from consciousness. For this very reason, it is said to have the nature of gross elements such as air and so forth. Regarding "non-difference"—because it arises from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
Because its nature consists solely of the light of power (śakti). || 182 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate that the entire collection of phonemes from *ka* to *ha*, thus established, is indeed animated by the vowels, he says:
"In this way, that entire collection of phonemes was previously composed of vowels. (3.183)
Because the consonant (vyañjana) is indeed animated by the vowel (svara) through its union with individual manifestation,
according to the principle just stated, the entire collection of phonemes previously mentioned exists prior to its emergence as consisting of vowels alone—
abiding within the vowels themselves in the form of the nature of power (śakti).
This is the meaning. Otherwise, through the mere joining and disjoining of those respective phonemes, there would be no manifestation of them in such a form—this is the intention.
For this very reason, that collection of phonemes, having been manifested externally, is itself manifested [by others]; thus it is called a "consonant" (*vyañjana*).
Furthermore, [one might object that] it must be produced as something previously non-existent, since it did not exist before in its own nature;

and moreover, for that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*), its true essence would only exist upon the proximity of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), and not otherwise?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because the Lord's breath is [the cause]," meaning that it is indeed already manifested.
This collection of phonemes must be animated by vowels; otherwise, due to being vowel-less (anacka), its very utterance would not be possible. || 183 ||
And thus it would be said that the vowels alone are the root cause of all phonemes;
to this he says:
"In this world, the group of six vowels alone shall be the root in the succession of phonemes. (3.184)
The six deities are indeed those which are the primary rays of the sun.
The "group of six" refers to [the vowels] beginning with *a* and ending with *ū*. By the use of the particle *eva* ("indeed"), there is an exclusion of the other vowels;
for their form is also merely an expansion (*sphāra*) of these—this is the intended meaning. Thus, of these...
It would thus be said that their nature as illumination (*prakāśarūpatva*) consists precisely in the manifestation of the other six phonemes.

And because their nature is indeed that of illumination, it is stated elsewhere that they possess the nature of the rays of the Sun, which consist of the six deities; thus he says, "the six deities," and so forth. As it has been said:
"Burning, cooking, smoky, attracting, raining, and the essence.
Regarding the term "primary": this is because the powers such as burning and the rest are grounded solely in Light (prakāśa), as it has been said:
"Only six vowels here are declared to be the primary root causes; and because they are of the nature of light, they should be understood as the rays of the sun. (184)
Not only does their form consist of solar light, but even lunar light is present within it—as he says:
"Because the lunar digit resides within the very solar rays. (3-185)
Therefore, the triad of long vowels here is clearly the lunar body;
this has already been established previously, so no further effort is made here. || 185 ||
An objection may be raised: "Since all entities are mutually exclusive, how can lunar digits exist within the solar rays? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is called the moon is not something other [than the sun], nor is the object of enjoyment anything other than the enjoyer. (186)
The enjoyer alone exists established in a twofold state by way of the nature of the object of enjoyment;
for the pot does not possess the status of being an object of enjoyment in its own form, since that [status] resides in the subject. (3.187)
Therefore, that which is established as "Mother" (mātṛ) is said to be His state of being the object of enjoyment (bhogyatva).

For what is called "Moon" (candra) is not other than the Sun; hence, it is His object of enjoyment. Indeed, the "object of enjoyment" is termed the "object of knowledge" (prameya). And the object of knowledge does not exceed the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), because it exists as subordinate to it.

— this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, such an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) cannot be distinct from the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because in reality all things rest solely within the subject (*pramātṛ*); therefore, the enjoyer alone manifests in the form of both [subject and object]. This is the point. Hence he says: “The enjoyer alone...”

"By way of being the object of enjoyment," and so forth. Now, one might object: "How can there be identity between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, given the contradiction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the jar. For that which is called "knowability" is not a property belonging to the jar itself; for if it were, then since it would be indistinguishable for all [perceivers], everyone [would perceive it].

[If it were so,] all would be omniscient. Therefore, that property [of being known] belongs to the knower alone, because an excellence is observed in him alone through the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Consequently, the very fact that this jar or other object finds its rest in the knower is what is called "knowability" (*jñeyatva*). As it has been said: "The object of enjoyment for the enjoyer..."
"there is no further"—thus [ends the verse]. 186–187.
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand:
"The Absolute (Anuttara) [is established] by virtue of the relationship between the object to be reflected upon and the reflecting subject. (188)
Likewise, the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), such as will (*icchā*) and the rest, having attained a state of friction (*saṅghaṭṭa*),
[merges] with the Absolute (*anuttara*)— the supreme form characterized by the first letter— which,
having manifested within itself the relationship of subject and object, attains a state of friction through their mutual orientation toward one another.

Once attained, it is called "the object of enjoyment" (*bhogya*); otherwise, there could be neither the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) nor the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*), because these two are mutually dependent. Therefore, the intended meaning is that through the conjunction of these two aspects, the object of enjoyment, characterized by form, comes into being. And here, the object of enjoyment...

Since that [desire] was what was undertaken to be explained, it has been presented here as the primary subject. In this way, Will (*icchā*) and Expansion (*unmeṣa*) also, having reached a union within the Self through the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed, attain the nature of the object of enjoyment consisting of the essence of seeking and exertion; thus, what was stated is logical.
"Therefore, in this context, the triad of long vowels is clearly the lunar body. || 188 ||
Now, one might object: "Let it be that the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) remains as such; there is no fault in this.
However, if the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) possesses multiple forms, would there not be a loss of non-duality (*advaya*), resulting in the collapse of your own established doctrine?
Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates that desire and the rest possess only the status of being objects of enjoyment, and not the status of being the enjoyer:
When [the elements] beginning with will have attained the state of being objects of enjoyment within the plane of unsurpassed bliss. || 3-189 ||
The emergence of the diphthongs (saṃdhyakṣara) is said to be the nature of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ).

Although desire and the other [mental states] possess the status of enjoyer with respect to themselves, nevertheless, in relation to the Absolute (anuttara), their state of being the enjoyed (bhogya) comes to rest; at that time, there is the emergence of the diphthongs.

Creation would come into being. The use of the plural number in the expression “of the planes of Anuttara and Ānanda” should be understood as referring to individual instances. And it has been stated that this emergence occurs when the subject (bhoktṛ) is predominant, in the words “and it is described as having the form of the enjoyer”; for this very reason, the [powers] beginning with Will (icchā) are subordinate here. Therefore...
Although there is no difference in their being composed of the union of Anuttara, Icchā, and the others,

this is the specific distinction of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) from the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*): whereas the diphthongs have Icchā as a subordinate element and Anuttara as the primary element, the semi-vowels, however—

Since the supreme [consciousness] is subordinate while desire and the rest are primary, it is thus established that the one supreme alone is the ultimate enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); for, because he is self-luminous, he does not tolerate even the mention of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*) within his own self— how, then, could he possess the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*)?
Furthermore, since desire and the like are exclusively objects of experience, they possess the nature of being experienced.
Therefore, he says:
"The deity, consisting of the unsurpassed bliss, is said to be the enjoyer alone. (3.190)
Desire (*icchā*) and the rest are indeed objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*); for that very reason, they possess the nature of power (*śaktitā*).

Although bliss (*ānanda*) is an object of enjoyment, its inclusion here is intended to illuminate that it also possesses the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), because it is non-different from the Absolute (*anuttara*). By the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "only an object of enjoyment," [the distinction is made].

This is the exclusion of [the Self's] being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). Furthermore, that which was stated regarding its being an enjoyer in relation to desire (*eṣaṇā*) and so forth is not ultimate; for it is merely the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) that is conceptualized as such. "From that" means from being an object of enjoyment. Indeed, being an object of enjoyment is itself the state of being power (*śaktitva*), with reference to which—
"Its powers are the entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power"—thus it has been said. ||190||
One might object: "In that case, does not the duality of the enjoyer and the enjoyed once again follow? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If the object of enjoyment is dissolved into the enjoyer, then the enjoyer alone remains manifest in reality. (3.191)
Therefore, among the six, the triad consisting of consciousness, will, and expansion is the essence.
In this context, the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) cannot even attain existence within itself without a subject who enjoys (*bhoktṛ*);
thus, how could it possess the status of being an object of enjoyment? [It can do so] only if it rests in the enjoyer.

Only that enjoyer remains; there is nothing whatsoever called "the object of enjoyment" apart from him. Thus, it is the enjoyer alone who directly unfolds. There is no loss whatsoever to the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*).
In this way, each of the three long vowels of the nature of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) rests within each of the three short vowels of the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).—Thus.
The intended meaning is that the triad of short vowels alone constitutes the primary element. Thus he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
*Cit* is the Absolute (*anuttara*). *Iṣiḥ* is will (*icchā*). || 191 ||
One might object: "Even so, since the enjoyer is not one, the doctrine of non-duality (advayavāda) is abandoned; thus, that very same defect remains as before?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That very triad they call the supreme majesty of Bhairava. (3.192)
In that regard, the triad is proclaimed as the full power (*pūrṇā śakti*) of the Supreme Lord.

That very triad— just mentioned, consisting of *anuttara*, *icchā*, and *unmeṣa*— is the supreme Śākta radiance (*tejaḥ*) of Bhairava, which fills the universe, because it is the full reality that is independent of anything else.

They say that, according to the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Even His possession of manifold powers is inseparable from that very power," that same Triad, when fully integrated, constitutes the Supreme Lord.

Power characterized by absolute freedom (svātantrya) is accepted everywhere, because from it proceeds the expansion of this universe consisting of the signified and the signifier; for it is this very Triad that exists by encompassing everything—this is the intended meaning. || 192 ||
Thus it is said:
"Since the entire universe is projected by that [consciousness], therefore, when this [consciousness] is worshipped... (3.193).
Since worship has arisen within the Universal Power, which is devoid of all limitation,

and since by means of that Trika all this [universe] is encompassed, therefore, for those who possess immersion (*samāveśa*) in this very Trika— the ultimate reality of which is solely the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*)— [all things are realized].

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: by means of that very [door], because its nature is unconditioned, immersion (*samāveśa*) occurs effortlessly even within the full form of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), according to the statement beginning with: "...the Śaiva [power] is here called the mouth. (193)
And all this is to be projected as having an expansive essence that is beyond limitation; thus he says: "In this way, it is not possible to say that its majesty is merely this much. (3.194)
Who could determine the limit of the power of that which is unlimited?
"It cannot"—that is, it cannot be determined by its meaning. 194.
And for this very reason, that same Blessed One has attained the state of universal form through his own absolute sovereignty;
thus he says:
"Therefore, the God is unsurpassed because of the unsurpassability of his own freedom. (3.195)

Because it is endowed with the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), it is perfected as the universal form (*viśvarūpaka*). In the union with the power of emission, autonomy (*svācchandyam*) and the state of being unsurpassed (*anuttaratvam*) are the cause. For it is only that which is independent (*svatantra*) which possesses the capacity for emission, owing to its performance of the fivefold act; and this capacity belongs only to the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
Regarding the expression "designated by the word *visarga*": as was stated previously— "The supreme abode is the Absolute (*anuttara*); that very same [abode] is called *akula*.
The *visarga* of that Lord is called the *kaulikī* power."
Thus [ends the section]. || 195 ||
One might object: "In this way, if he possesses the nature of the manifold universe, would there not be a lack of unity for him, resulting in the loss of his non-duality?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, the Great Lord is the one whose power is full of the fifty-fold awareness. (3.196)
The other powers are established in this very one, whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
There are fifty such awarenesses, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. It is "one" because of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power.
Now, it was just stated that the powers are unlimited; how then [can they be fifty]?
One might ask: how is the fixed limitation of "fifty" consistent? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:

"The other powers are established right here. "The others" refers to those arising from the conjunction and disjunction of those [primary powers], such as "jar," "cloth," and so forth. "Established right here" means—
Because a reflective awareness exceeding fifty is logically untenable. || 196 ||

For this very reason, by means of the sequence of counting half-measures (*ardhamātrā*), even the Goddess consisting of eighty-one words will be included within the fifty phonemes (*varṇa*) alone; thus he says:
"The Goddess of eighty-one words shall indeed be included here. (3.197)
It will be included herein; it will be brought to its final conclusion precisely by being centered upon this, as he will state:
"The time of the thirty-three letters beginning with 'ka' is said to be half-mātrās."
The short vowels have five morae; the long vowels have eight; but the protracted vowel *ḷ* has two or three.
Our Guru has stated that this consists of eighty-one half-measures (ardhamātrās),
by virtue of which the Blessed One proclaimed the mantra of eighty-one [syllables].
"The Goddess, whose nature is Śiva, is declared to be the Power (Śakti) consisting of eighty-one parts. ||197||

One might object: "In that case, since all other reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) are ultimately resolved within this very one, there would be only fifty primary reflective awarenesses; thus, the restriction [of the number] would once again fall back upon its necessity?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] proceeds to demonstrate their unreality in order to show their incapacity for imposing further limitations.
He demonstrates that the specific reflective awarenesses arise from their association with various limiting adjuncts (upādhi):
"When its nature is a single reflective awareness, it is the Mass of Sounds (śabdarāśi), that Bhairava;
through union with the shadow of the object of reflection, it is that very same [awareness] as Śakti and Mātṛkā. (3.198)

That Mālinī, however, arises from the friction of the mass of sounds and possesses diverse origins; like the previous [Mātṛkā], she takes the form of distinct groups through the reflective awareness of her ninefold nature. (3.199)
But when each one is established as an act of reflective awareness (*āmṛśa*), that very [consciousness] consists of fifty [phonemes].

"One" means being without a companion due to the emptiness of anything to be reflected upon. "Reflective awareness" (*āmṛśa*) is the act of reflecting; it is the subject who performs the reflection. When the fifty phonemes possess that nature through their synthesis, [they become one].
The designation "the mass of sounds" (śabdarāśi) and "Bhairava" [is applied to Him]. Because of union even with that which is to be perceived, He is called "Power" (śakti) and "Mātṛkā.
That very Mātṛkā, through the convergence of the mass of sounds—which is characterized by the identity of Power and the Possessor of Power—[attains this state].

Due to the mutual blending of salt and sour gruel, its constituent *yonis*—the consonants—are differentiated by the seeds (*bījas*). Being of such a nature, she is the "Ma"—the reflector (*alinī*) of the absence that is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the signified object. She sustains (*malate*) the universe, holding it within her own essential nature.
It is designated as *mālinī* because it "strings together" (*mālayati*) and "makes whole" (*antaḥkaroti*) everything.

Precisely because its constituent elements (*yonis*) are distinct, and because the seed-syllables (*bījas*) and matrices (*yonis*) are not arranged in a fixed order, it consists of the letters from *na* to *pha*.
The phrase "as before" means according to the previous sequence, by way of the forms consisting of sixteen, five groups of five, two groups of four, and one.
This is what was stated—this is the meaning; as it has been said:
"It is ninefold according to the division of the groups (vargas);
by the distinct differentiation of the groups, it shines with fifty rays."
Thus [ends the section]. || 199 ||

Thus, having here described the essential nature of each of the fifty phonemes both individually and collectively, he now also indicates— in connection with that— their identity with the mantras and so forth, as previously mentioned in the general enumeration of the human race.
Thus, through the penetration of the *nāda*, [the self] has the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). (3-200)
Śiva, as the agent existing everywhere in the form of mother and father,

is indeed the Supreme Lord Śiva himself— the Absolute— by virtue of that "pervasion" (anuvedha), which is the attainment of identity with the Sound (nāda) in the form of the letter *ha*, according to the manner already stated and to be stated hereafter.

By such statements as, "The letter *a* and the letter *ha*, these two stand as one; there is no distinction between them, just as between wind and space," [the mantra] consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is the supreme potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*), namely the letters *a* and *ha*.

This would be so, because that very agent—who is of a single nature with the supreme subject—is established as both mother and father within the totality of the fifty phonemes; he flashes forth in the form of the Absolute (anuttara) and the Emission (visarga)—this is the meaning. || 200 ||
One might object: "Even so, would not the nature of the fifty phonemes have been described only in terms of difference, and not in terms of non-difference?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This very emission (visarga) is Śākta; furthermore, by way of the Śiva-bindu... (3.201)
Containing the infinite universe within itself, it abides in the state of the Absolute (anuttarātmatā).

Indeed, in this context, this emission of the Supreme Lord, the Anuttara, is purely Śākta— it is the manifestation in a gross form extending up to the phoneme *ha*, and then, having returned [to its source].

Having embraced the entire collection of denotable objects and their denoters as the *śivabindu*— that is, as being of a single nature consisting solely of the subject who is the undivided self and supreme light— it takes recourse in the state of the Absolute (*anuttarātmatā*), that is,
it assumes the form of the *bindu* whose essence is undivided supreme light, by which [it is expressed as] "I."

The meaning is this: there occurs a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in that the Absolute (*anuttara*) itself, having manifested as the nature of the power (*śakti*) whose essence is the letter *ha*, comes to rest within its own self, which is the form of undivided light. As he will say:
"The universe shines within consciousness; indeed, it also [shines] within that [consciousness] by means of consciousness."
Thus, this triad, through the conjunction of pairs, has attained the state of a composite whole.
"The supreme form of Bhairava is indeed one alone, consisting of my own self. (3.207) || 201 ||
But is it not the case that even when resting in the supreme light which is undivided, the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa) still consists of duality? To this he says:
"In the Lord’s own self, whose inner essence is the unlimited universe... (3.202).
That very reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is said to be characterized by the perfection of the dyad;

it is that reflective awareness as "I" within the self of the Lord, the Supreme Śiva, which is unsurpassed and excels even amidst the infinite world. That [awareness] alone [is the negation] of the counter-correlate, the object to be excluded (*apohya*).
Since even the non-apprehension of "this-ness" (idantā) is possible, [the state] is described as being characterized by the attainment of the dyad;
that is to say, it appears as having differentiation as its basis. || 202 ||

Now, one might object: let it be granted that the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*) with respect to the body and so forth is based on difference because it possesses a counter-correlative (*sapratyogitva*); however, why is it not the same in the case of the Light which is the Self of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛātman*), since that [Light] lacks a counter-correlative (*apratiyogī*) due to being undermined by the dilemma of whether the counter-correlative is distinct from it or not?
Thus he says:
"In that which consists of the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti, whose nature is the Absolute (anuttara) and Emission (visarga). (3.203)
The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the All-pervasive Lord is called "I" because of its fullness.

It is the non-dual state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, whose essence consists of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and Emission (*visarga*). In that state, there is no separate reflective awareness of "Śiva" or even "Śakti," for if such were the case, there would be a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
The sense is that there might even be a mere possibility [of such a thing]. For in this way,

because the Supreme Lord— the Absolute (anuttara)— is full, being replete within His own nature as the all-pervasive Light of the Other due to the absence of anything else external to Him that could be required;—
"The resting of the Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva)" (A.Pra. 22).
According to this and other such views, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is the manifestation of one's own Self alone is called "I" (*aham*);
the meaning is that this is stated without contradiction in all the scriptures. || 203 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the reflective awareness of 'I' (ahaṃparāmarśa) may indeed consist of the manifestation of one's own self alone; what business is this of ours? Does this not fail to state the essential nature of the fifty phonemes in their non-differentiation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The emanation beginning with Anuttara and ending with Ha is the very nature of Śakti.
Having withdrawn the entire universe back into herself, she merges into the Absolute (Anuttara).
Because she brings about the manifestation of internal reflective awarenesses such as Bliss (Ānanda) from the Absolute, which is the primordial phoneme, she is of the nature of Śakti.

That which is the expansion (*prasṛti*) ending in *ha*— the vibration in its gross form up to the letter *ha*— is itself, moreover, by the rule "the first [letter] with the last one including [all in between]" (Pāṇini 1.1.72), in the form of the letters *a* and *ha*; thus, everything from *Ānanda* down to the seed-syllable of *Amṛta* is withdrawn and internalized.

Being thus constituted by that through which the universe [is manifested], she dissolves into and rests within the supreme form, which is unsurpassed and whose nature is undivided luminosity; thereby the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) arises, by which,
through non-duality alone according to the method of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), there occurs the reflective awareness of all phonemes as well.

Now, if it is intended that all the phonemes be grasped simultaneously according to the sequence of *pratyāhāra* in the Pāṇinian system, then that specific grasp should occur through the very nature of the phonemes *a* and *ha*; yet, [the text] further states, "resting precisely in the Absolute (*anuttara*)."
Having raised the doubt, "For what purpose was that said?", he says:
"This entire universe resides within Śakti, and she resides within the supreme Anuttara. (205)
The truth is that within her, there is an encapsulation by the Pervasive Lord (Vibhu).

Although the apprehension of all phonemes could be accomplished through the method of *pratyāhāra* by means of the very form consisting of the letters *a* and *ha*, nevertheless, [this occurs] through the universal form (*viśvarūpā*) whose nature is *hakalā*.
This has been stated here in order to demonstrate the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*) by the unsurpassed agent (*anuttarakartṛka*).

For instance, according to the principle beginning with, "His powers are this entire universe...," the universe is first of all of the singular nature of power (*śakti*); and power, too, [is of the nature of] the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).

According to the principle that "power is non-different [from the possessor of power]," [all things] rest in the Absolute (anuttara) alone; and for this very reason, because the power and the possessor of power are inseparable from one another, that form of the possessor of power is also the Absolute, which resides within that very power.
Thus, the emergence of power occurs from the Absolute alone, and its repose is likewise in that very place.
Thus, by the Supreme Lord alone, through the union of the beginning and the end of power (śakti), there is indeed a formation of a "seal" (saṃpuṭīkṛti).
For this very reason, the scripture also speaks thus; so he says:
"Therefore, in the venerable Trīśikāśāstra, the form of power is sealed. (3.206)
The *Trīśikā*—the venerable *Parātriṃśikā*—is so called because it is the mistress (*īśā*) of the three scriptures that establish the supreme power (*parā-śakti*). As it is stated therein:
"In that regard, the hero should worship emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and then likewise the seat (*āsana*)."
"Having encapsulated the creation, one should thereafter begin the sacrifice. (Parātrīśikā, verse 29). || 206 ||
He summarizes that very point:
"The universe shines within consciousness; and indeed, within that [universe] as well, it is by means of consciousness.
Thus, this triad, through the union of pairs, has attained the state of a composite whole. (3.207)

The supreme form of Bhairava is indeed one alone, consisting of the self of "I" (aham). This meaning is as follows: this universe, whose nature is the letter *ha* and which is the form of power (*śakti*), shines within consciousness—the supreme, unsurpassed self—and has arisen from that very source. Even there, [it continues...]
Even in such a form, it indeed shines as consciousness alone; the meaning is that it rests within that very nature of the unsurpassed Self (anuttarātman). As it has been said:
"In which this manifold universe arises, and in which it sets."
Thus, this triad— consciousness, the universe, and consciousness—
having attained a state of integration through the union of pairs and their mutual friction, reaches a state of fusion;
and because there is no other counter-correlative reflection such as "I," it becomes truly one.
Because it is the locus of rest for the manifestation of the knower, the known, and so forth, it is supreme (*param*)—that is, most excellent.

It is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Bhairava’s own self, which consists of the supreme reflective awareness (*paravimarśa*); for Bhairava, who is filled with all things, is independent of anything else, possesses full activity, and has light alone as his body. This is his innate nature.
This is the meaning. || 207 ||
Now, an objection may be raised: "It was previously stated that 'the Kaulikī power is the emission (visarga) of the supreme, undisturbed abode.
And since that [power] is not distinct from the possessor of power, its manifestation as something separate from him is logically impossible;
so what is the point of resting within it once again? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That power of emission belonging to Śambhu exists thus everywhere. (3.208)
From that very source arises this entire play of the essence of bliss.

Indeed, that which has been described as the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) of the Unborn (*akula*), the abode of the supreme good which is the cause of ultimate liberation, exists everywhere in the manner that will be explained below.

The meaning is that [the Absolute] manifests itself through the nature of difference, non-difference, and the identity of both; by virtue of which alone this external expansion, consisting of the signified and the signifier and composed of bliss, unfolds. || 208 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "Since external objects consist of pleasure, pain, and so forth, how can it be said that they are composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes that very point:
"For instance, in the case of sweet song, or the touch of sandalwood and the like... (3.209)

That vibration within the heart which occurs when neutrality has ceased is called the power of bliss (ānandaśakti), for by means of it one becomes a person of aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya). || 3-210 ||

Indeed, here, when for any cognizer whatsoever there is the departure from neutrality— that is, the abandonment of indifference— toward an object such as a song, and there arises a state of one-pointed absorption through identification with it,
then that which is a state of vibration within the consciousness that is the locus of the foundation of the universe occurs through being composed of that [object].
The state of being a throbbing form—this very thing is called the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) in all the scriptures;
this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"For one whose self is unified with the incomparable happiness of tasting objects such as song..."
"For the yogin, through identification with that [object], because it has ascended into the mind, there is identity with it. (Vijñānabhairava, verse 73).
Thus, this radiance—the Great Being which is not limited by space or time—does not fail to attain the commonality of the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which constitutes experience.
"This very [consciousness] is declared to be the essence, the heart of the Supreme Lord" (Ri.Pra. 1.5.18).

Thus, its nature as defined by such passages is that its very state of radiant manifestation (*parisphuradrūpatā*) is called sovereignty (*svātantrya*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and bliss (*ānanda*). This is proclaimed everywhere; and it is precisely due to its majesty that even the insentient [attains its being].

"All these people are said to possess consciousness; for this very reason, there is a well-known saying in the world that 'one who experiences the effect of supreme bliss is a *sahr̥daya* (a sensitive heart). Although this entire cosmic manifestation (*viśvaprapañca*) is an expansion of the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), nevertheless, because it is clearly perceived here [in such persons], it is described in this way. || 210 ||

Thus, it is the majesty of the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) alone that constitutes this vast expansion of the universe, whose nature consists of difference, non-difference, and both; and it is precisely by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that even the power of emission itself possesses a threefold character. As it has been said: "Having first emitted everything that was to be done into the fire of emptiness..."
This is the stage known as the repose of the mind (cittaviśrānti), following that [stage of āṇava]. || 3-211 ||

The state of being directed toward those objects such as what is seen or heard within one's own consciousness is called the awakening of the mind (cittasaṃbodha); it consists essentially of the fullness of the unfolding of power (śāktollāsa). (3.212)

In that state, due to being oriented toward it, from the impact with that reality, and because of its establishment in the heart, there occurs an immersion into Śiva through fullness and the dissolution of the limited mind. (3.213)

This supreme Śāmbhava emission, known as the dissolution of the mind, arises from the abode of the immeasurable, which is conceivable through its orientation toward the future, just as before. (3.214)

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the partless form whose nature consists in the dissolution of all entities; because it dissolves them, it is opposed to every entire form composed of entities. It has functioned from time immemorial (*anidaṃprathamatayā*), and that which is to be emitted is neither something to be established nor something to be withdrawn.
The entire universe, consisting of the subject and the object, is that in which there occurs such an activity as the manifestation in various forms; that indeed is called *citta*.

As it is said: "Consciousness itself, having descended from the state of pure awareness (*cetana*) and being constricted by the objects of consciousness (*cetya*), is *citta*" (Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya, Sūtra 5).
According to this principle, contracted knowledge consists of the friction between consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*cetya*).

Its repose in the state of being oriented toward duality is the supreme limit; designated by that [repose], this gross emission (*visarga*), consisting of the letter *ha*, pertains to the individual soul (*āṇava*) and is connected with the human level due to the predominance of duality.

Immediately following this, wherever there is the seeing or hearing of the "beginning" (the word *ādi* being used to include touching, smelling, and so forth)— that is, whatever object characterized as the world, well-known in its form as the moving and the unmoving— therein lies that which is an intense orientation toward the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvit*) of that [object].

It is the manifestation [of consciousness] through the casting aside of all forms characterized by the duality of grasped and grasper, and through the intensification of its undivided (niṣkala) nature, by becoming one with the self-awareness of its own essence. That very thing is the awakening—the perfect awakening—of the mind, that is, of knowledge whose nature was contracted, due to its resting in the self-awareness of its own essence; this is what is meant by that name.
The emission (*visarga*) belonging to Śakti is said to be subtle, consisting of the *visarjanīya* sound, and characterized primarily by both difference and non-difference.

Likewise, within that self-consciousness, because of its being oriented toward [the object], there occurs a mutual orientation through the very conjunction of that reality which is characterized as the world; and of that very reality...

In that very heart, within the ultimate nature characterized by pure consciousness (*saṃvit*), because of its sprouting within Śiva— the awakened Self whose essence is consciousness— there occurs an immersion (*āveśa*) resulting from the subordination of the limited subject (such as the void and so forth),
who is contracted and finite, through the full activation of agency and other powers. From that [immersion],...

As previously [stated] regarding the *āṇava* [means], when there is an orientation toward the future—that is, a manifestation as an external form—the "limitedness" (*mitatā*) that is thereby conceived, which consists in the nature of contracted cognition, undergoes dissolution;
this is the absence of even the conceived contraction. Consequently, there is the thorough dissolution (*prakarṣeṇa layaḥ*) of the mind.

By means of the withdrawal of contraction and by resorting to fullness, there occurs a manifestation as pure self-consciousness; this is the supreme Śiva-issuance (*visarga*), which is of the nature of bliss and characterized primarily by non-duality.
Thus, it is the very power of emission (*visargaśakti*) of the Supreme Lord that manifests itself in such various ways.
Its threefold nature has been described in terms of the self consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva. Therefore, it is rightly said that the power of emission (visarga-śakti) exists everywhere. || 214 ||
For this very reason, the Blessed One has also spoken thus—as he says: "Therefore, in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*, the threefold nature of emission (*visarga*) is taught.
"Therefore" means according to the reasoning already stated.
He recites that very same point by way of both sound and meaning:
"The friction between those two is held to reside in the center of the lotus-bud of the heart. (3.215)
The first emission (visarga) is said to be the end, characterized by the resting of the mind;
the second emission, however, is characterized by the awakening of the mind. (3.216)
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings shines here as a single unity;
indeed, when any distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject is perceived here, it is merely something slight.
Then that [consciousness] is called "with parts" (sakala) and "without parts" (niṣkala) through union with Śiva;
it consists of the complete act of grasping, characterized by the cessation of the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject. (3.218)
That third emission, however, is characterized by the dissolution of the mind;
it consists of oneness, is subtle, has consciousness as its essence, and is the bliss of the Self. (3.219)

The heart is the ground of awakening; that very thing, because it blossoms outwardly, is the lotus (*padma*). Its interior calyx is the supreme limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*). Residing therein is this very conjunction (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of consciousness (*citi*) and the object of consciousness (*cetya*), which consists of contracted cognition. That alone is what is called the "resting of the mind" (*cittaviśrānti*), situated between the two emissions (*visarga*), namely the Śiva and Śakti emissions.

The third, or alternatively the first, is the *āṇava* emission (*visarga*), which is described as being characterized primarily by differentiation. The second, however, is the *śākta* [emission]; furthermore, that emission is named the "awakening of consciousness" (*cittasaṃbodhana*), because herein this world of manifold appearances—the moving and the non-moving, consisting of the grasped and the grasper—is unified.

It shines forth, manifesting as the very nature of self-awareness alone; for this emission of power (*śākto visarga*) is said to be "with parts" (*sakala*) and consisting of the universe when there is the appearance of the distinction between subject and object,
but it is "without parts" (*niṣkala*) when there is the unification with self-awareness that effects one’s own spiritual welfare through supreme liberation.

That which transcends the universe is this third Śaiva emission (*visarga*), characterized primarily by both difference and non-difference; it is called the dissolution of the mind (*cittapralaya*). For, through that severance (*vicchitti*) or breaking (*troṭa*)—which occurs because the subject and object are firmly established as pure consciousness alone—it is perfectly [unified].

The meaning is that it consists of that perfect apprehension which, due to the absence of any fixed limitation such as "void" and so forth, is of the nature of supreme luminosity. For this very reason, it consists of unification and takes the form of immersion in the pure consciousness of one's own self. For this very reason, it is subtle, because it is of the singular nature of the subject alone.

He is not cognizable by another; therefore, because even contracted knowledge—which might otherwise be suspected—is absent, the *vijñānātman* has the nature of full knowledge (*pūrṇajñāna*). Consequently, because there is nothing else whatsoever to be desired, he is self-contented (*ātmanirvṛta*).
It rests solely within its own self; for this very reason, it is characterized primarily by non-duality.

Thus, the essential meaning is that the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord—designated by terms such as *kaulikī* and so forth—manifests itself through the nature of various reflective awarenesses (*āmarśa*). || 219 ||
Nor has this been stated by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"This matter has been determined in the Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata.
He recites that very [text] by way of its meaning:
In this context, Kuṇḍalinī is the seed-syllable, consisting of consciousness and functioning as the individual soul.
From that arises the triad known as the Stable (dhruva), Will (icchā), and Expansion (unmeṣa), and from those, in turn, the phonemes (varṇas).

That very power of emission (visarga-śakti), which is the supreme consciousness of the Lord (pārameśvarī) consisting of pure awareness alone, is designated by the term *kuṇḍalinī* because it contains the entire universe within itself; she is the form of the vowel-less digit (anacka-kalā).

The sense is this: since ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like are far removed from being the cause of this entire universe—which consists of the signified and the signifier—[consciousness] is its seed; and even though it is that [reality], it is the life-force (*jīvabhūta*) because all established orders reside within consciousness, for nothing whatsoever could manifest without consciousness.
As it is said there:
"That which is Kuṇḍalinī is proclaimed here as the womb of the universe;
she should be known as being in the form of a *tuṭi*, existing as the life-force (*jīva*) within the world."

"She is declared to be of the nature of the seed (bīja) and is also proclaimed to be of the nature of consciousness (cit). Here, the reading "mātrā" is a corruption; for there is no scriptural meaning whatsoever to be grasped by this [term] for which such a usage would be intended.
On the contrary, a lack of connection with the intended meaning and the use of ungrammatical words would result; so, enough of this prolixity.

Thus, from that [state] as it has come to be, there arises a triad of reflective awarenesses known as *anuttara* (the unsurpassed), *icchā* (will), and *jñāna* (knowledge). And from that triad of reflective awarenesses, according to the method already stated and to be stated hereafter—
It is the arising of all other forms of reflective awareness. As it is said there:
"From that arises the manifestation of the three powers, and from that, the manifestation of the phonemes. (220)
He analyzes this very point:
"The letter 'ā' [arises] from the vowel 'a', and so forth, up to the phonemic unit (kalā) consisting of the visarga. (3.221)
The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*, along with the *visarga*, are fivefold;
they exist externally, internally, in the heart, in the resonance (*nāda*), and in the supreme state.
The *bindu* extends from the heart to the crown of the head; for it is all-pervasive within the self.
The first word "iti" refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), while the other [word] indicates the manner [of its arising].
Thus, just as bliss arises from the Absolute (*anuttara*), so too does the state of diminution arise from the Will (*icchā*) through the unfolding of consciousness (*unmeṣa*).

The meaning is that the entire collection of phonemes has arisen, such that the letter *ha*—which begins with *ka* and ends with *sa*—has become the *vaisargikī* (emissional) power (*kalā*). As it is said there:
"From the letter *a* is born the letter *ā*, and from the letter *i* and so forth [the others] are remembered."
The letter ū arises from the letter u, and the neuter [gender] arises from the letter ṛ.
"The letter *e* and *ī*, as well as *o* and *au*, the letter *aṃ*, the *anusvāra*, and *aḥ* is traditionally known as the *visarga*.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"The thirty-two *kalās* are remembered as beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *sa*.

Although it should have been stated as "ending with the letter *ma*," the expression "beginning with the letter *ka*" and so forth is used to indicate that the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) possesses the nature of a consonant and that its birth originates from the vowel *a*—as in the rule: "Of the letters *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya*... [and so on].

According to the principle beginning with "the throat," the *ka*-group, the letter *ha*, and the *visarjanīya* arise from the letter *a*. Since it is stated generally that "the power (*kalā*) belongs to the *visarga*," the *visarga* whose nature is both transcendent (*parā*) and immanent (*aparā*) is indicated by the term *visarjanīya*. Furthermore, all this has arisen from the *visarga*, and is indeed the *visarga* itself.
The meaning is that He flashes forth as the very essence of the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of each respective [object].

For He alone, whose single nature is the supreme subject, while flashing forth as the nature of the unsurpassed *Ha* (the letter *ha*) through the embrace of the entire universe, manifests Himself as the nature of *nara*, *śakti*, and *śiva* by way of being both internal and external. Thus it has been said:
In this regard:
"Thus, the Bindu is described as pervading and abiding within this entire universe;
through the differentiation of thirty-eight kalās, it is established as the Bindumāla."
"All [the phonemes] are said to be traversed by the Bindu, joined with the first and the last.

For this very reason, he says: "And that is fivefold. The word "and" (ca) indicates the cause; because that very Visarga is the Bindu, the independent subject in the act of knowing, who exists as the human state within the Heart by way of external form.
—because even while possessing an external form, it finds its ultimate rest solely in its internal nature; thus, as the *nāda* (sound), it exists as *śakti*;

as the internal nature, it exists as *śiva* in the supreme state at the *dvādaśānta*. For this very reason, within the body as well, from the heart to the crown of the head, it manifests in five ways.
It resides, by implication, in the heart, throat, forehead, the end of the *śakti*, and the *dvādaśānta*.

Thus, although it is fivefold in terms of its substrates (*dhātu*), in reality it culminates in a threefold nature; therefore, one should not suspect any contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Now, [one might ask]: how can this one [reality] be...?
He says that [the Self] exists in the heart and so forth: "For He is all-pervasive. As it is stated there:
"The outer self is indeed one, the inner self is the second;
the heart-self is the third, and the sound-self (nādātman) is the fourth."
Thus, O Goddess, these five kinds of Bindus reside in the Great Hero, the Supreme Self, located in the heart, the throat, and the forehead.
"And likewise at the end of the *nāsā* (the *nāda*) and at the end [of the *ha*], there is the *bindu*; by that very [bindu], it is all-pervasive.

Thus, this supreme power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, having manifested a gross form extending up to the letter *ha*, again, without falling away from its own essential nature, [rests] in the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) Self alone.

It comes to rest; for it has been said: "The I-consciousness is indeed proclaimed as the repose of Light within itself," that supreme reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which consists of the potency of the Supreme Mantra, whose single form is the subject, and from which the entire universe has been withdrawn for the sake of its illumination.
This is proclaimed in all the scriptures, beginning with [the verse] "(ajaḍa pra. si. 22 ślo.). And that alone is the supreme reality of Mātṛkā, with reference to which indeed—
"...the supreme *mātṛkā* is not [attained] by those who do not possess knowledge.

(Svacchanda Tantra 11.197) Thus it is traditionally taught. And it is only for those yogins who possess such thorough knowledge that this [science] shall bestow the accomplishment characterized by both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Otherwise, however—

By means of being permeated by their respective designators, these [energies] assume the form of joy, sorrow, and so forth, thereby acting as bond-makers for bound souls (*paśus*). Thus, because they would be incapable of yielding fruits characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) or liberation (*mukti*), they would be entirely fruitless—this is the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*). As it has been said:
"This power of Śiva, whose nature is action, resides within bound souls (paśus).
When it remains on its own path, it is the binder; when known, it brings about accomplishment. (Spandakārikā 4.18) || 222 ||

This possibility does not apply to this [mantra] alone, but extends even to mantras whose nature is to reflect and protect; thus he says: "But mantras devoid of the first and the last [letters] would be like autumn clouds. (3.223)

The word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). The first [letter] is *A*, the unsurpassed; the last is *Ha*. Therefore, even mantras, when devoid of the first and last letters—which consist of the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*)—and when not recognized as being of that nature, would be like autumn clouds: they would be utterly ineffective.

This is the meaning. As it has been said there: "Those mantras that are devoid of the first and the last [syllables], and whose root-source is unknown, do not grant success; they are as fruitless as autumn clouds."
O Goddess, just as a flower in the sky is fruitless, as is the horn of a hare,
the offspring of a barren woman, and the semen of a eunuch;
When Brahmins have uttered the fire [mantra], these then become fruitless;
likewise, so too are those mantras that lack both the beginning and the end.
"In this way, they become entirely fruitless for one who drinks [only] the mirage.

Otherwise, however, when they are fully recognized as being of the nature of the supreme mantra-virya, which consists of the self-reflective awareness (*aham-parāmarśa*), they will indeed perform their respective specific functions.
This is the intended meaning. As he will state: "They say that this unartificial and stainless self-reflection of this very form—'I am'—is the luminosity of the Light."
For this vigor is indeed the heart-essence of all mantras;
without it, they would be inert, like living beings without a heart.
"Whatever one may perform, whether breathing or reflecting, once this [state] has ascended into the heart as something uncontrived— all that is considered his *japa*. (4.294) || 223 ||
For this very reason, the thorough knowledge of this [reality] alone is the primary characteristic of a Guru; thus he says:
"The characteristic of a Guru is this much: he should make known both the beginning and the end.
Such a one is to be worshipped like me, for he is a man of knowledge, Bhairava himself, whose nature is the deity. (3.224)

For this very reason, by virtue of his union with knowledge and other such qualities, he—whose nature is luminosity and who is replete with the universe—is worthy of worship by all, just like me; such is the statement of the Lord. As it is said therein:
"The teacher who discovers both the beginning and likewise the end..."
He shall become worthy of worship by the assembly of yogis, and he shall become even more worthy of worship.
They ensure his practice remains flawless,
they bestow their favor upon him, grant him boons, and protect him like a son.
O Goddess, he shall be honored everywhere, just as I am honored by you;
O lady of excellent limbs, he is indeed a man of knowledge and the best of practitioners.
"The astrologer is declared to be the best of all, the bestower of all accomplishments;
he is proclaimed as a renunciant, a scholar, and indeed Bhairaveśa.
Thus [ends verse 224].

And for this very reason, such a guru does not only know the mantras— which consist of the vibrating power and vitality of supreme Śakti— by their very nature, but even whatever is mundane, such as verses and so forth; thus he says:
