Whatever there may be, such as verses or songs, provided it is joined with the beginning and the end—from that, the knower likewise perceives everything as being nothing other than mantra. (3.225)

That teacher, indeed, because of his union with unsurpassed knowledge, perceives everything whatsoever— whether external verses or the like— as being of the nature of the reflective awareness of "I," and thus as mantra alone:
"Mantra is the state of knowing all and the protection consisting in grace toward those in transmigratory existence."
Thus, one realizes [it] through its efficacy as an effect;

for even that is of the nature of the supreme reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) which is devoid of beginning and end—this is the meaning. The point is that nothing whatsoever could manifest apart from the state of the supreme subject, whose essence is Light (*prakāśa*).
It is stated there: "When the śloka, gāthā, vṛtta, gītaka, vacana,
as well as stuti and daṇḍaka, are joined with the beginning and the end..."
Even those [other] mantras certainly exist; how much more so, then, the seizing of that [object]?
Thus [it is said]. || 225 ||

And this entire expansion of the universe is nothing but the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*). Thus, it has been stated by the Lord not only in those scriptures that are sister-systems to our own, but even in those external to them; as he says:
"The power of emission is determined to be the cause of the universe."
In the Vedānta known as the Aitareya, it has been explained at length by the Supreme Lord. (3-226)
"By the Supreme Lord"—meaning, by one who has assumed the role of the Itara-śākhin sages. "In detail"—the sense is that this alone is the primary subject matter of this entire work. || 226 ||
He confirms that very point by way of its meaning:
"That which is red is fire; that which is virility has the form of the sun and moon.
'A' is the supreme Brahman, consisting of the nature of their union. (3.227)
That which is the supreme abode, red and blazing because its nature is pure luminosity,
is itself Fire (Agni) because it is of one form with the subject; and that which is its vitality— the expansion of Power (Śakti) consisting of knowledge and action—
is itself the form of Sun and Moon by way of appearing as the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth.

The union (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of these two, which are of such a nature and possess the vitality of *lohitavīrya*— that is, their emergence as a single identity (*ekātmya*), their state of being perpetually manifest by virtue of never setting— that supreme Brahman, whose essence is this and which consists of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti in the form of the letters *A* and *Ha*, is so called; for from this [arises]...
The supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the singular form of the supreme subject— expressed as "I"— should arise,
by whose majesty this entire manifestation of creation, consisting of the signified and the signifier, comes to be. As it has been sung:
"The imperishable Brahman is the supreme; its inherent nature is called the *adhyātma*.
The emission (*visarga*) that brings about the arising of the state of beings is designated as *karman*. (Gītā 8.3).
This very essential nature has already been explained at length previously, so no further effort is made here. And in the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*)...

That which is the blood, in the form of the essence of digested food, is the *ārtava* (menstrual flow); that is fire, and its ripening is food. Or rather, whatever is the potency (*vīrya*) of all the *ārtava*, which has bliss as its fruit and corresponds to the sixth *graha*:
"Now, this semen is indeed the luster (*tejas*) drawn from all the limbs."
"Having come together, it sustains itself within itself" (Eka-ūrmikā Upaniṣad 4.2).
According to such statements from that source, because it consists of light and because it is nourishing, it takes the form of the sun and the moon.
For this very reason, as its nature comprises the three abodes (*dhāman*), both of these are designated by terms such as *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.

It is supremely purifying, by which its status as the most excellent object of attainment has been stated according to the principle that will be explained later in the passage beginning: "...therein, the *argha* [offering] arises from the union with Śakti" (29.25). And precisely from that union...

Even the Supreme Brahman, which is eternally risen, becomes fixed within the body and so forth when it assumes the sense of "I," by which this creation consisting of female, male, neuter forms, and so on, comes into being. As it is said therein: "That which is red in the woman is the form of fire; therefore, one should not feel loathing toward it."
"Now, that which is this seed in man is the form of the sun; therefore, one should not feel loathing toward it. (EaU) Thus, likewise:
"Aḥ is Brahman; therein I have arrived," so it is said in the *Ekaśloki Upaniṣad*. || 227 ||
And for this reason, the entire universe is His very manifestation; thus he says:
"And His supreme vitality consists of the five elements, taking the form of food as an object of enjoyment, and consisting of sound, touch, and taste. (3.228)

This pentad of objects, such as sound and the rest, which consists of parts and sub-parts of the five elements beginning with earth, is the supreme potency (*paraṃ vīryam*) of the Supreme Brahman whose nature has been described above, according to the teaching: "His powers are this entire universe... and so forth.

By such statements, the meaning is that the expansion of Śakti has reached its supreme limit in the form of the universal majesty (viśvavaibhava). Now, one might object: "If sound and the other objects are indeed this very expansion, then since they are of the same nature as their enjoyer, why should they not also be exactly like that? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:

The phrase "as the object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatvena*) means not as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvena*). The expression "that which has the form of food" (*yadannarūpam*) does not mean that it has the form of the eater of food. And in the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*), it is said: "From the union of the red [blood] and the semen, there is the assumption of this very body composed of the five elements, and so forth. And this is stated in that very same place:
"Verily, he who knows the fivefold Self that has been described—from which all this arises—is one who possesses true knowledge: earth, wind, space, water, and light. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)
Beginning with these words, [the text continues]:
"Therefore, he who knows both food and the eater of food—'I am born in this eater of food; water and earth are his food'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
Much has been said in this manner, and so forth. || 228 ||
Now, one might ask:
"What is the proof for the statement that 'sound and the other [objects] are the expansion of this very [consciousness]'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because even a sweet sound brings about an increase in vitality."
For that energy is considered supreme, pure, and characterized by the desire to emit. (3.229)

The word "sound" refers to the five [objects] beginning with sound; since these, when they are pleasing to the heart, are causes for the accumulation of the vitality (*vīrya*) of the Supreme Brahman-self, there arises for those whose minds are focused upon them an instantaneous flash of supreme consciousness—this is the meaning. As it has been said:

"For the yogin whose self is unified with the incomparable bliss of tasting objects such as song and the like, there arises identification with that [object] because the mind has ascended into it" (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā 73).
With this very intention, the venerable Praśastibhūtipāda also stated:

"Whatever objects are seen here that are delightful, possessing auspicious and beautiful forms—the nourishment of their own abiding state at the time of their experience is the worship of the virtuous.
Thus it has been said. For if these [objects] did not possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, [this would not be so].
The sense is: how indeed could its expansion occur for those whose minds are not attentive to each of these?
Having raised the doubt—“Is such a supreme Brahman quiescent or is it variegated?”—he says, “For that...,” and so forth. The word *hi* (for/indeed) serves to dispel the doubt.

"Consisting of the desire to emit" means that, by its very nature as the will to create, it is always characterized by the manifestation of the manifold variety of the universe—this is the meaning. "Is held [to be]" refers to everyone;
the intention is that no one at all would be able to hold a contrary opinion on this point. || 229 ||
Even so, one might wonder: is His form transcendent of the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*) or is it composed of the universe (*viśvamaya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"That is His power (*bala*), that is His vigor (*ojas*), those are His vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and that is His loveliness (*kāntatā*). The meaning is that He Himself manifests as those various forms. As it has been stated there:
"This very Śa is the vital breath (asu), he is the life-force (prāṇa), and he is prosperity (bhūti).
(E.U. Likewise:
"This very Śa is both death and immortality. (E.U.)
Thus it is said; likewise:
"This is Brahmā, this is Indra, this is Prajāpati" (Eka-Upaniṣad). And it has been sung:
"That is the vigor of all vigors; that indeed is the strength of the strong. That is the entire vitality of all vitalities—eternal, immovable, and constant.
Thus [it is said].
And he shows the structural process (*prakriyābandha*) in its manifestation as the universal form (*viśvarūpa*):
"From that vitality (*vīrya*), those creatures arise; and that vitality is said to reside in actions. (3.230)
In sacrifices and the like, that [power] resides in them; then in medicinal herbs, and again in those [herbs];
that [power] resides in their potency, and that in living beings—thus, in the process of emission, there is the manifestation of universal form.

"Progeny" refers to those in the form of women, men, and so forth. And the connection is that these progeny are said to be the "vīrya"—the causal agent—in rites such as sacrifices; this should be applied similarly in the subsequent cases as well. "That" refers to the ritual action beginning with sacrifice, [which resides] in the plants—consisting of food and so forth—and "vīrya" refers to that which consists of semen and blood.
Thus, it is the Supreme Brahman alone that, through the state of coming and going (*ajavañjavībhāva*), acts as the cause of the universe by assuming various forms;
therefore, it is said that this entire universe is its very form. As it is stated there: "In this way, even in emission (*visarga*), there is the nature of being the universal form.
Regarding this, it has been said:

"Now, therefore, follows the creation of semen: the gods are indeed the semen of Prajāpati; rain is the semen of the gods; herbs are the semen of rain; food is the semen of herbs; semen is the semen of food; and offspring are the semen of semen. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)
Thus it is said. Likewise elsewhere:
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings" (Manusmṛti 3.76).
And thus it is sung:
"From food beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice rain comes into being; and sacrifice originates from action."
Thus [it is said] in the *Bhagavadgītā* (Chapter 3, Verse 14).

Thus, it is the power of emission itself that, by assuming various forms of reflective awareness (*āmarśa*), manifests within its own self the state of being the universal form; it is designated by various terms in the *Āgamas*—
so he says:
That very [totality] is called the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), and she is celebrated as Mātṛkā;
through the penetration of the state of the agitated and the agitator, they call her Mālinī.

O illustrious one, the undivided nature of gross sounds— which are differentiated as words, sentences, and so forth— is the causal aggregate known as *mātṛkā*, which belongs to all mantras and *vidyās*.

The meaning is that the Mother (Mātṛkā) is "unrecognized" in her own form as described in such passages as: "This is declared to be the source (yoni) in all mantras at all times. Thus, because she remains undisturbed by abiding solely in her own self, there is a twofold designation for the power of emission (visarga-śakti) according to the Āgamas.
This has been shown. Furthermore, there is another designation for that which is agitated; thus he says "the object of agitation," and so forth.

The "objects of agitation" are the *yoni*s (wombs/sources), and the "agents of agitation" are the *bīja*s (seeds); their state—the relationship consisting of agent and object within the act of agitation—is the "immersion" (*āveśa*) therein.
The state of *lolībhāva* consists of mutual friction; from that, the "yoni-s" (vowels) are differentiated and "seeds" (consonants) are distinguished by them.

Being of such a nature, she is Mālinī—the meaning is that she who "maintains" (*malate*) the universe, that is, she who "bears" its own essential form, and is thus the embodiment of the universe. || 232 ||
Now, one might ask: "How is it that by this much alone she possesses the nature of the universe? To this he says:

"For Mālinī is indeed determined to be the supreme Śakti, whose form is the universe, beautiful through the emergence of emission [visarga] resulting from the union of the seed [bīja] and the womb [yonī]. (233)
For Mālinī is indeed the supreme power whose nature is unsurpassed light;

through that union—which is the state of equilibrium consisting of mutual friction—of the seed (bīja) and the womb (yoni), which are the forms of Śiva and Śakti who have become her rays, there occurs this emergence of emission (visarga). By means of that [emergence], [it is attained].

She is radiant in form; by that [form], she is beautiful and unsurpassed, whereby her nature as the universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) has been determined in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* and other texts. || 233 ||

Now, one might object: "Is there not only one supreme, unsurpassed consciousness (anuttarā parā saṃvit), since it is impossible for anything else to exist apart from that which is being cognized? Therefore, it is illogical for there to be even the nature of Śiva and Śakti as distinct from that;
what then can be said of its having the form of the entire universe? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In reality, this is the one supreme power that draws forth time;
through its union with the possessor of power, it attains the state of being a couple (yāmala). || 3.234 ||

"This" refers to supreme consciousness (*anuttarā saṃvit*). She is "Kālī," meaning she is Bhairava as Time (*kāla*), because she "measures" (*kalayati*)—that is, she emits—the universe from Śiva down to the earth. She is his "attractor" (*karṣiṇī*), in the sense that she manifests [the universe] by bringing it under her own control. The implication is that nothing whatsoever could manifest without her will.
As it has been said:
"Time, in the form of Bhairava, creates the universe from its primary cause down to the smallest insect by the power of her will; O Mother of the Worlds, you who are she, are victorious!"

Thus, however, by manifesting a conditioned difference characterized by light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it attains a state of duality (*yāmalatā*), whereby it is designated as "power" (*śakti*) and "the possessor of power" (*śaktimān*). For in reality, reflective awareness does not differ from light, nor does light exceed it—this has been stated many times. || 234 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then let it be just that; what further room is there for the state of having manifold forms (viśvarūpatā)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"His reflective awareness, which consists of the perfect 'I'..."
Because of its sovereignty over itself, it manifests division within itself. (3.235)

"Of that" means of the *yāmala*; "consisting of the 'I'" means having the nature of the non-conventional supreme reflective awareness—this is the meaning. "Perfectly full" means that if it were limited (*pārimitya*), it would possess the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—this is the intended sense. "Division" means the state of being the universal form (*viśvarūpatā*)—this is the meaning. || 235 ||
If this were the case, it would possess a threefold nature denoted by such terms as *paśyantī* and so forth; thus he says:
"And when its differentiation manifests, its body is declared to be threefold, designated as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and the gross *vaikharī*. (3.236)

"Of this"—that is, of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the *aham* (I) which is the nature of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*). Regarding "gross," the supremacy and subtlety of the other two [levels of speech] are implied by the sense. Furthermore, the supremacy of the supreme speech is independent of anything else; thus, its form is even more supreme (*paratara*), for she alone is the Supreme Goddess (*Parameśvarī*).

Desiring to manifest external form through its own sovereignty, yet because the sequence of signifier and signified has not yet arisen and the division is therefore indistinct, it is designated by the term *paśyantī* as the nature of the Seer, due to the predominance of the light of consciousness itself. Following that, [it manifests] the sequence of signifier and signified...
Although its divisions have not yet been fully articulated, because it exists solely within the intellect in both manifest and unmanifest forms,
and because of the predominance of perception, it is designated by the term *madhyamā* (the intermediate) as it resides in the interval between the seer and the seen. Beyond that—

Because of the power of the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of articulation (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*), and because of the clear manifestation of the division (*vibhāga*) through the sequential apprehension of each respective phoneme, and because of the predominance of that which is visible, and because it arises within the manifest body (*viśvara-śarīra*), it is designated by the term *vaikharī*.
Thus, there is a threefold nature in the manifestation of its universal form (*viśvarūpatā*). || 236 ||
Thus, not only do these [energies] possess a threefold nature each through their grossness and so forth, but even individually— so he says:
"Their form is also threefold, by way of being gross, subtle, and supreme."

He analyzes this very same [process] for the triad of speech as well, beginning with the gross level: "In that regard, that which consists of sound (nāda), beautiful due to its arrangement of vowels... (3.237).
That [perception] is indeed gross (*sthūlā*), because it does not differentiate between phonemes and so forth.

In that state, there is a composition consisting of the mutual blending of the vowels, such as *ṣaḍja* and the others; for this very reason, while fixed within the unity of any one of them, such as *ṣaḍja*, the differentiation of phonemes and so forth remains unmanifest.

Speech (*ālāpa*) is "fortunate" (*subhagā*) because it consists of an excellence of sweetness and takes the form of delight; for this very reason, that speech which is by nature merely the initial sound is indeed the gross *paśyantī*—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, [one might ask]: if such is the case regarding the speech of the Self...
One might raise the objection: "Since it is possible for [this sound] to arise from the friction of the places of articulation, the breath, and so forth, why should it not simply be *vaikharī*?
Anticipating this, he says: "Because of the non-differentiation of phonemes and so forth.
Its sweetness is caused precisely by this non-differentiation of phonemes and so forth, and it is because of this that... here.

There is no dispute that all people are attached—indeed, the world is attached only to what is sweet; whereas elsewhere, due to the division of phonemes and so forth, there is harshness, and for nothing that is harsh is there attachment in anyone. Thus, the point is that this difference between the two is established by one's own direct experience.
Thus it is said: "Sweetness is said to be the power (śakti) consisting of a single, undivided nature. (3.238)
Furthermore, there is a bursting forth arising from the friction of the winds of the locations and so on, which constitutes coarseness (*pāruṣī*).
Thus, he says that for yogins who possess attachment to this [practice], the state of becoming one with consciousness (*saṃvinmayībhāva*) occurs instantaneously:
Therefore, within this [state] which is of the nature of resonance (nāda), by virtue of its function being in close proximity to consciousness, || 239 ||

The internal absorption (*antarmayībhūti*) consisting of that very same nature is perceived instantaneously, because it functions in the immediate vicinity of consciousness; thus, unlike the intermediate [state] and so forth, there is no emergence at all of an external form, even to a great distance.
For this very reason:
"The tasting of objects such as song... (Vi.bhai. 73, verse).
Thus it has been stated elsewhere. || 239 ||
An objection might be raised: "But surely, for some whose minds are attentive even to the *Gītā* and other such works, there may still be no state of identification (*tanmayībhāva*);
so how can this have been said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For those in whom there is no identification with That, there is no submergence of the body and so forth. (3.240)
"Those who do not know [this] are called 'heartless' because their consciousness is submerged in mere measurement.

For in the world, those who possess aesthetic wonder (*sacamatkāra*) through becoming absorbed (*tanmayībhāva*) in objects such as songs that are full of excellence are known as "connoisseurs" (*sahṛdaya*); otherwise, they would be known as "those whose hearts go elsewhere" (*parahṛdayaga*), that is, "heartless" (*ahṛdaya*).

Having thus examined the gross form for one who perceives in this way, he now speaks also of the intermediate [form]: "But as for that sound which exists there in whatever is covered by skin and so forth... (3.241).
Because it possesses both manifest and unmanifest forms, this middle [level] has a gross form.
In that regard, the sound produced by the striking of a hand upon a drum or similar instrument covered with leather—
which is manifested as one specific form such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth— is more manifest than the preceding [unmanifest] state.
And because it does not manifest the distinctions of phonemes and so forth, it is indistinct; for this very reason, it is designated by the term "Madhyamā" (the Intermediate Speech).
Thus, since there is the presence of an undivided portion here, sweetness (*mādhurya*) may also occur; for this reason, even the world has an attachment to this—so he says:
"And because of the presence of an undivided portion in the *madhyā* [rhythm], there is passion (*raktatā*). (3-242)

"That which consists of indivisible phonemes (*avibhāgasvaramayī*) is what is truly captivating. Anticipating the objection—"But will even this produce attachment in the same way as the *paśyantī* [level of speech]?"—he says:
"consisting of indivisible phonemes," and so forth. Here, in certain cases, that which consists of indivisible phonemes is, by implication, speech; that is excellent.

"Rañjaka" means capable of generating attachment; the sense is that through such attachment, even here, there arises a state of identification with that [object]. By this, its distinction from *vaikharī* is also indicated. || 242 ||
"Surely, what is the proof for the claim that non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) alone is the cause of non-attachment?"—anticipating this objection, he says:
"For non-differentiation leads to liberation; let this be seen from the reading of the *Tāla* [scripture]. (3.243)

The meaning is: "Indeed, when that indistinct sound is being played, one is satisfied; let this very non-differentiation be seen—that is, let it be directly realized. The sense is that what has been seen cannot become unseen. The particle *kila* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

The meaning is that because this entire world finds satisfaction and attains bliss by relying on the rhythmic performance (*pāṭha*) and singing (*gāna*) of tāla, the beak, and other instruments— in that instrumental music which consists of indistinct sound and is of an undifferentiated nature— it is for this reason that one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*) alone is the authority here.
The intended meaning is that [this] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 243 ||
Having thus described the gross form of the *madhyamā* [speech], he now speaks also of the *vaikharī*: "That which, however, becomes the cause for the production of distinct phonemes... (3-244).
That [speech] is the gross *vaikharī*, whose primary effects are sentences and the like.
"Of the distinct" means those being heard by the ear while abiding in a state of mutual differentiation.
For this very reason, due to its harshness, people have no attachment to it. (244)
Having thus described the three gross divisions, he also speaks of the subtle one:
"In this triad of gross [levels], that which is the contemplation (anusandhāna) [of them] is like the first. (3.245)
This triad, taken individually, is designated as "subtle. Within this aforementioned triad of gross divisions, that first one—
which consists of the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) in the form of the desire of the self, such as the wish to go and so forth— is itself [the subtle division] for each case respectively.
The subtle triad of divisions is said to consist of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. || 245 ||
He illustrates this very point in sequence:
"I produce the *ṣaḍja* note, I play it sweetly, and I utter speech. (3-246)

Therefore, the essential meaning is that this subtle triad of divisions consists of the three forms of mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), namely: the desire to know (*jigāsā*), the desire to dispute (*vivādayiṣā*), and the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). || 246 ||
"What is the proof for this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, a triad of distinct unifications is experienced.
The phrase "is experienced" means that this is established by one's own direct experience.
Having thus described the threefold subtle division, he speaks of the supreme as well:
"Of this triad also, that which is the first form is free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhimat). (3.247)
Beyond that triad, Śiva exists there as the supreme conscious self; that which is the unconditioned,

primordial form of this triad of contemplations— consisting of the desire to go forth and so on— which is devoid of adjuncts and free from the coloring of the desire to go forth and the rest, and which constitutes the prior limit even of will.

"This very reality of consciousness (saṃvittattva) is that supreme triad of divisions. Now, one might object: "In this reality of consciousness, which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (anupādhimat), not even the slightest possibility for division can exist; so how can it be said here to possess a threefold nature?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Śiva is of the nature of supreme consciousness."
The meaning is that here the triad beginning with Paśyantī appears as being in a state of identity with Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness alone. As it has been said:
"The manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self of the Lord..."
"Indeed, it exists; without that, the reflective awareness of desire does not proceed. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 9.5.20) || 247 ||
Now, one might object: "If the supreme light is partless, its manifestation through division is simply not possible;
even so, what is the cause for its threefold nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And in the manifestation of division, there are here three primary powers. (248)
What are they? He says:

The Absolute (Anuttara), the Supreme Will (Parā-icchā), and that which exists as the Intermediate (Parāpara) [Power]; the Power of Expansion (Unmeṣa-śakti), called Knowledge (Jñāna), is declared to be the Lower (Aparā). (3.249)
Furthermore, the triad of short vowels has been previously determined to be the nature of power (*śakti*) belonging to Bhairava, the supreme reality; as it has been said:
"Therefore, the essence of the six [vowels] is the triad consisting of consciousness, will, and expansion."
"That very triad they call the supreme splendor of Bhairava. (3.92) || 249 ||
Now he elaborates upon the manifestation of division:
"Furthermore, from that form of agitation, six pure consciousnesses of those [powers] are said to arise.
Regarding the phrase "of those," it means by relying on the agitated form of the three powers; furthermore, there are six.

Consciousnesses ending in deficiency were previously described; and even when they are agitated, they are stainless because they do not fall away from their own essential nature. For this very reason, they are capable of manifesting other consciousnesses through mutual conjunction. As it has been said:
"In this lineage of castes, the group of six vowels alone shall be the root;
those very six deities are the principal rays of the Sun. (3.184)
Therefore, he says:
"Because of the immersion into these very [powers], arising as the power of action (kriyāśakti). (3.250)
Twelve consciousnesses have been proclaimed, in which everything is fully contained.
Through the mutual friction of those very six consciousnesses, arising as the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), twelve consciousnesses are proclaimed, excluding the neuter ones.
The meaning is that they are manifested as the essence of the twelve vowels by assuming the forms of the diphthongs and so forth.

And within these very cognitions, because everything— from the object of knowledge (*prameya*) up to the supreme subject (*paramātmā*)— is established according to the sequence to be described, and because there is nothing beyond this, there is the complete fulfillment of all things.

"In which everything is completed. And this alone is the primary wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), because all other powers are included within it according to the method already stated and yet to be stated. || 250 ||
Thus it is said: "This much is the primary wheel of powers (śakticakra) belonging to the God of gods. (3.251)
To the extent that this is so, that Bhairava, the God of gods, possesses full power;

and it is these very twelve consciousnesses that have been shown in the Kramadarśana and other texts by means of names that correspond to their actual meaning— as he says in order to demonstrate this:
By virtue of its nature as reflective discernment (parāmarśa), through its connection with emission (visarga) and projection (ākṣepa). || 3-252 ||
Because they possess the knowledge that measures [the extent of] this much, they are in some places called *kālikā*.

Following the meanings of the verbal roots— *kala* in the sense of "to throw," *kala* in the sense of "to cast aside," *kala* in the sense of "to count," and *kala* in the sense of "to go"— they respectively measure (i.e., perceive), cast aside, and emit.
They are called *kālya* because they withdraw, count, and know [the time]; those very [verses] are the *kālikās*. || 252 ||
These [energies] have been described not only in the Kramadarśana and other such works, but even in the scriptures that are siblings to our own system; thus he says:
"And it is also stated in the Śrīsāraśāstra that the supreme single-syllabled [energy] resides in the center. (3.253)
One should worship the one called Bhairavātmā, surrounded by twelve Yoginīs, as stated in the *Sāraśāstra*, namely the *Śrītrikasāra*. As it is said there:
"But the Supreme [Parā], consisting of a single syllable, is in the center, beautiful like a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon."
"Having four arms and four faces, surrounded by twelve Yoginīs.

Regarding the phrase "named Bhairavātmā"—it refers to that which, through its nature as both the internal and external form of the universe, consists of protection and fulfillment; thus, by following the etymological meaning of "Parā," she exists with a full Self.

"It shines forth and manifests everywhere"—this is the meaning. Furthermore, by the phrase "the Yoginīs of Kālikā," it is indicated that this distinction exists merely at the level of names and not in reality.
Moreover, the fact that these consciousnesses consist of the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of those respective [principles] such as Anuttara and so forth is also stated in the *Śrītrikasāra*.
This was stated by way of a stylistic device; for there,
having commenced with the primacy of speech itself in the words, "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed method of speech," it continues:

"That seed-syllable is indeed differentiated by the twelve vowels in sequence, and those [vowels] are likewise the goddesses... and so forth has been stated. This will be examined in detail specifically in the chapter on the Śāktopāya. Thus [it ends].
No effort has been exerted here. || 253 ||
And he elaborates upon that very primacy which was stated regarding these [energies]:
"From these alone arises the wheel of energies (śakticakra) up to the number sixty-four. (3-254)
Beginning with the single-spoked [wheel] and proceeding up to the thousand-spoked, their names appear in many ways in the scriptures according to the distinction of their functions. (3.255)
And the attendants (upāsā) arise from the conjunction of the forms of duality, non-duality, and their mixture; this has been explained at great length in the venerable *Traiśirasa*. (3.256)
It has not been written here out of fear of prolixity and because of its lack of utility.
Since "scripture" (āgama) was mentioned in general terms, the specific [text] is indicated by the phrase "the venerable Traiśirasa.
The intended meaning is that this [work] is to be followed from that very first chapter. || 256 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then as for those powers such as Aghorā and the rest that abide even within the sequences of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and so forth, are they not simply the expansion of these [very same powers], or are they not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Those very [powers] are proclaimed as the stainless, pure Aghorās. (257)
Because they are the creators of even the most terrible and most terrible [beings], they are identical with them;
[this applies] during creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as upon the cessation of those three limiting adjuncts.
"Their very established form is divided manifoldly;

even when their impurities have been exhausted, they are said to be 'stainless and pure' because their vision and action are predominant. The transcendence (*atyaya*) of that triad of adjuncts (*upādhi*), which consists of emanation and the rest, is the "Inexplicable" (*anākhyam*), just as it is for them.

The phrase "upon the cessation of those three limiting adjuncts" is employed to express the synthesis [of all states], showing that just as the nature of the twelve consciousnesses is differentiated within the sequence of the Unnameable (anākhyakrama), it is likewise so within the sequences of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and the rest. || 258 ||

Now, one might ask: "In the Anākhyakrama, this transcendence of the three limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of emanation and so forth that has been described—is it of the nature of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) or of the nature of posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The nature of that which transcends the adjuncts, the teachers have declared to be twofold. (3.259)
"Either due to the non-manifestation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), or through the application of pacification.

Regarding "due to non-manifestation": this refers to their prior absence. For at the initial stage, the supreme reality is like a waveless ocean, from which, by its own sovereignty, the manifestation of limiting adjuncts occurs when there is an outward orientation.
It may be so; [it is said] "by means of the application of pacification" because it consists of the nature of non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva). || 259 ||
For tranquility is indeed twofold; thus he says:
"And tranquility is twofold: by means of peace (śānti) and by the process of forceful digestion (haṭhapāka). (3.260)

"By means of tranquility"— that is, by means of a peaceful process of sweet maturation, preceded by the propitiation of the Guru and others, through the accomplishment of initiations such as that of the *samayin*, and by being intent upon the performance of various daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. This is because [the fire] is characterized by a constant burning known as the "taste for voracious consumption."

The meaning is that at the end of the body, there occurs the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as creation and so forth. Furthermore, "peace" (śānti) is not to be described as the natural subsiding of the limiting adjuncts of creation and so forth; for if that were the case, the instruction of the scriptures and the like would be rendered purposeless, since the occasional [cessation] of the adjuncts would occur quite naturally.

Because of the absence of tranquility; likewise, *alam* means excessively, in its entirety—that which has the name *Alamgrāsa-bhairava* and so forth, whose essence is *rasa*, meaning greediness (*gṛdhnutā*) regarding the "swallowing" (*grāsa*), that is, the assimilation into one's own self (*svātmasātkāra*) of creation and the other cosmic acts; for this very reason, it is constant and uninterrupted.

By that sequence of the process of ripening— which consists of the reduction to the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*)— by means of a forceful method (*haṭha*) characterized by a sudden instruction, which bypasses the gradual stages and possesses a nature whose essence blazes forth as it burns its respective objects of combustion.

The meaning is that there must be the cessation of the three limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as emanation (sṛṣṭi) and the rest. Indeed, in this world, the cessation of all three limiting adjuncts—emanation and so forth—is what is truly desired by everyone; therefore, some specific means capable of accomplishing that result must necessarily be investigated, and it has been stated that this [means] is threefold. Among those, that which...

The claim that the mere non-manifestation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is what has been taught is far-fetched, for it is precisely the cessation of those [adjuncts] that have already manifested which is intended. And although the specific means called "quiescence" (*śānti*) is capable of bringing about their cessation gradually at the end of the body, nevertheless...

Since this [work] proceeds under the authority of the mild descent of power (*manda-śaktipāta*), it is appropriate that the third [chapter] teaches a specific means for the pacification of the "forced ripening" (*haṭhapāka*) through the authority of the intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*), by which the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) may occur instantaneously. || 260 ||
Regarding that, it is said:
"That which is the third [state], the pacification of violent ripening (haṭhapāka), is precisely what is suitable for instruction, as it burns away the fuel of duality. (3-261)

The reason why it is appropriate [to say this] is given here as "that which burns the fuel of duality. For its very power is supreme in dissolving duality all at once—this is the intended meaning. || 261 ||
Therefore, he says:

"All objective entities, when forcibly offered into the fire within the belly of one's own consciousness, abandon their division into duality, fueling that [consciousness] by means of their own power. (3.262)

For indeed, all entities such as creation and the rest, when forcibly offered into the fire of consciousness, abandon their division into duality and manifest as the singular form of consciousness—this is the meaning. Now, one might ask:
if all entities were indeed distinct from consciousness by virtue of their respective forms, then why is this so?
Anticipating the objection, "Do they not manifest as being of that same single nature? he says: "kindling Him by their own power.
The meaning is that they too, being of the nature of consciousness, appear as kindling that very consciousness through their own power; for if they were not of the nature of consciousness...
The sense is that for them, there would be nothing but a state of non-comprehension. || 262 ||
Anticipating the question, "What would happen if this were so?", he says:

"When the differentiated forms of all things have been dissolved through forceful digestion (haṭhapāka), the deities of consciousness consume the universe, which has been transformed into nectar. (3.263)

Through the process of "forceful digestion" (*haṭhapāka*), preceded by the awakening of the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*), the diversity of entities such as creation and the rest is dissolved; thus, the universe becomes transformed into nectar and attains the singular nature of pure awareness.
Then, the Goddesses of Consciousness—the sovereigns of the senses—consume it, meaning they perceive it as being of the single nature of supreme awareness.

—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the worldly transaction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is also implied here, because the subject at hand is understood precisely as being characterized by that [transaction]. || 263 ||
What follows from that? He says: "Satiated, they rest non-differently upon the god Cidvyomabhairava, who is their own full self and dwells in the absolute solitude of the heart. (3.264)
And those deities of consciousness, being satisfied by attaining the singular nature of supreme awakening, become independent of anything else;

they rest solely within the heart, finding repose only in the essential reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and for that very reason are full and free from any further longing; and for that same reason, they are divine, having as their sole essence the act of luminous manifestation.

The supreme reality, which is the Bhairava of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyomabhairava*) and whose essence is supreme light, they rest upon as non-different from their own self and their own nature; that is to say, they manifest as being of one form with it. Furthermore, as before, the worldly conduct of a hero is here implied. || 264 ||
Now, one might object: "Since these [powers] rest within the supreme nature which is consciousness itself, and since there is nothing else apart from that, how can there be a twelvefold form?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Thus, due to the engagement in various ritual functions and the multiplicity of names and modes of worship, their form appears in many ways even though there is no difference [in essence]. (3.265)
The *kṛtya* (function) consists of the perception of forms and so forth; the *nāman* (name) consists of the deities of the eyes and so forth;
and the *upāsā* (mode of worship) consists of the dissolution of the functions of the self, such as the perception of forms and so forth.
By the statement, "Even though there is non-duality, it appears in many ways," its conceptual nature (*kālpānika*) is expressed. || 265 ||
Now, if these [energies] are manifold due to the distinction of their functions (*kṛtya*) and so forth,
then even their function consisting of the perception of form and the rest would be twelvefold,
since there is no other function beyond that; thus, they [would arise] from only twelve kinds.

One might object: "If there were no form less than or greater than the [sixty-four] forms, then how could it have been stated that 'from those very [forms] up to sixty-four is the wheel of powers' (3.54), and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And by means of the combination of the addition and subtraction of these very goddesses—
by one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or more [than nine]— 3-266.
The detailed expansion of divisions begins with the armies of eleven Rudras, twelve Suns, and so forth;

*āvāpa* is contraction, while *udvāpa* is expansion. The sense is that from their own inherent freedom (*svātantrya*), these very [energies] undergo the constant occurrence of contraction and expansion like a lotus. There are ten in the subsequent [group].
The others are thirteen; the *kalās* are sixteen; and the armies consist of eighteen *akṣauhiṇīs*. || 266 ||
Thus, concluding this matter which has arisen through a series of related digressions, he introduces the subject at hand:
"Enough with this further elaboration; let us now apply ourselves to the topic under discussion. (3.267)

"By another" means by the intermediate exposition of the Śāmbhava means (*upāya*). For its nature has been primarily described in three ways—such as being the reflection of the universal consciousness (*viśvacit*)—so that for those who have approached it, there may be the immediate attainment of the state of non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*); [this is so] because that [means] is crowded with many objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

Lest those to be instructed forget that very [reality]—namely, the fact that the universe is a reflection in consciousness—that same point is stated to them in brief: thus he says, "Now, one is joined to the primary subject.
Here, "now" (atha) signifies immediate succession; therefore, immediately after this, the primary subject is precisely that the universe is a reflection in consciousness and so forth.
It is being introduced—this is the meaning. || 267 ||
Therefore, he says:
"He in whose conscious self this entire manifold category of entities shines as a reflection—he indeed is the Lord of the Universe. (3.268)
Thus, he who possesses such a non-conceptual awareness (*parāmarśa*) within himself that it is ever-arisen—he alone is sealed with the Śāmbhava means. (3.269)
This reflective awareness of full subjectivity which has been discerned here—apart from this, there are no other mantras, mudrās, rituals, or forms of worship whatsoever. (3.270)
For that practitioner or others who possess the intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*), this entire range of objective phenomena— consisting of subjects and objects,

though manifold through its various divisions and subdivisions— shines within the self of consciousness as a reflection, according to the analogy of a city in a mirror, even while appearing as if it were separate from it.

It manifests as nothing other than its own self-nature, without any addition; indeed, that Lord of the Universe shines forth in identity with the Blessed One, whose essence is supreme light—this is the meaning. Even for that multitude of entities which thus appears as if it were a reflection, [the Lord remains] "I myself" in this way within His own self.

The meaning is as follows: there would be a continuous, ever-arisen reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is the direct realization of the Self, manifesting as the essence of the category of existence;
that very [awareness] is "sealed" by the Śāmbhava means, being regulated by the attainment of its own appropriate goal. Therefore, of this...
This reflective awareness of "I" (*ahantā-parāmarśa*), which has been analyzed as being full by virtue of having all things as its object—

in other words, it is precisely this that constitutes the various forms of mantra, mudrā, ritual action, and worship within this Śāmbhava means; they are not distinct from that full reflective awareness of "I," because they are non-different from one's own Self, whose sole nature is the Supreme Subject.
"They quiver"—this is the meaning. The implication is that for one who has ascended to this plane, there is no further need for these [lower states]. As it has been said:
"For him who has attained even a slight portion of this rasa, and who is intent upon acting according to his own will..."
"The practice of meditative absorption (samādhi), yoga, vows (vrata), mantras, mudrās, recitation (japa), and so forth, appears like poison.
And he will say:
"Bathing, vows, purification of the body, concentration (dhāraṇā), and the application of mantras..."
The arrangement of the path, the ritual procedure of sacrifice, as well as oblations, recitations, and meditative absorptions.
"No conceptual construction whatsoever of this kind is appropriate here as a distinction," [as stated in Tantrāloka 3.290]. || 270 ||
Thus, the great-souled one who practices this threefold Śāmbhava means attains liberation even while living; so it is said:
"Having repeatedly resorted to this thought-free immersion..."
It attains the state of Bhairavī, which is also designated as "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti).
Surely, previously [it was stated]: "In that regard, first of all, the application of ritual action does not deserve to be a means," and so forth;
thus, because the Bhairavīya consciousness is eternally manifest and primordially established, it is [not something to be produced] but rather something to be made known.

It has been stated that there is no means whatsoever that acts as an agent; how then is it now said that "this non-conceptual immersion (nirvikalpa-samāveśa) is the means here"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From this point onward, this liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is being investigated."
In this regard, even according to the method of the Sūtras, this conceptualization of means and the goal to be attained [is as follows].
In the previous daily lesson, however, there was not even the slightest conception of difference;
therefore, in that "no-means" (anupāya), who is liberated, how, or from what? (3.273)
"Also by way of the Sūtras"—the sense is that this will become even clearer in other chapters (āhnika).
"Of duality"—that is, of the agent, instrument, point of departure, and so forth. For this very reason it was said:
"Who, how, from what? (273)
And here he demonstrates the very relationship between the means and the goal:
"The wise man should apply the fiftyfold division previously indicated to the non-conceptual reflective awareness known as the Śāmbhava means. (3.274)
Perceiving the earth itself as reflected within one's own self through non-conceptualization, one attains the state of Bhairava; this same method applies even to water and other elements. (3.275)
Finally, that which is conceived as Śiva is the supreme reality, transcending all veils, all-pervasive, independent, and omniscient. (3.276)
"In the first chapter" refers to what was stated:
"And the fifty-fold nature of this immersion has been described,
based on the intention toward the manifest divisions residing within these thirty-six principles" (Tantrāloka 1.187).
And so forth. "One should join" means that one should conceive of [the elements] individually as being the means (*upāya*)—this is the meaning.

He says this with the words "the earth," and so on. Seeing the single reality of the earth-element (*dharātattva*), reflected within one's own self by means of non-conceptual knowledge (*avikalpajñāna*) and not by mere conceptualization (*vikalpa*) alone, as being of the nature of nothing but one's own self-consciousness (*svātmasaṃvinmātra*);...

By directly realizing the state of Bhairava through the fact that everything is the self of all, one shines forth as the nature of supreme light—this is the meaning. And he extends this very principle to other categories as well with the words, “even in water and so forth,” and so on. This is the method.

Beholding the web of principles (*tattvajāla*), from water up to the principle of Śiva, reflected within one's own self through non-conceptual activity (*avikalpavṛtti*), one attains the state of Bhairava. Now, if the supreme principle is indeed all-pervasive, how is it that [the text] omits the thirty-five principles?

Anticipating the question, "Is it stated as having exactly thirty-six forms? he says: "It is conceived as rising above all coverings. For in reality, it has been stated that its nature is solely that of the supreme subject—the knower and the agent—being autonomous (*svatantra*).
"The Omniscient One. || 276 ||

Now, one might object: "If the supreme reality is indeed of the nature of Bhairava, consisting solely of the supreme subject, then how can it serve as a means (upāya) both for the act of seeing and for the state of being Bhairava?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Seeing even that [world] reflected in the mirror of noble, non-conceptualized consciousness, one who is free from conceptual construction spontaneously becomes Bhairava himself. (3.277)
Not only the other categories of reality, but even the supreme reality— which is of the nature of Bhairava, consisting solely of that subject—
is liberated through its own sovereignty; [he liberates] himself through the sovereignty of the non-dual self.
"The Lord, having created [the world] through the volitions of Īśvara and others, would engage in worldly transaction.

According to the reasoning stated in such passages as this (Rju-vimarśinī 1.5.16), the practitioner and others—who, though free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), are immersed in the Śāmbhava means—possess within their own self the relationship of means and end imagined by their own sovereignty; and because they are indeed non-conceptual (*akalpita*), they are real.
Because it is free from the contraction caused by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this consciousness is expansive;

and because of its supreme transparency, it is like a mirror. Beholding that which is reflected therein, and realizing it as being of the same nature as itself, it becomes *Bhairava*—that is, it attains the state of Bhairava spontaneously, without depending on anything else.
The meaning is that [it] shines forth through the nature of non-conceptual, sublime consciousness. || 277 ||

Now, one might object: "If it is said that immersion into the full nature occurs through the gateway of the supreme reality (paratattva), then let that be; but how could this [immersion] occur again by way of the partial aspects (aṃśikā) beginning with Earth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as one seeing a red object before oneself through non-conceptual consciousness..."
Firmly established in the single, partless perception of the jar through each respective sense-door.
In the same way, by reflecting upon one's own self through the successive collection and integration of each element beginning with earth, one shines forth as truly full. (3.279)

In this world, indeed, every perceiver, through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), directly perceives first of all— right here before him— the red or crimson quality, as well as the configuration such as the broad base and bulbous belly that characterizes it, appearing according to their respective inclinations and so forth.

That which has "redness" and so forth as its parts is the door or means; such is this perfect cognition (*samyag-vitti*)— neither deficient nor excessive— of the primary, unitary reality, which is partless, indivisible, and consists of a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) characterized by the confluence of multiple non-universal appearances.

Through that [cognition], awakening occurs perfectly; by producing satisfaction such as "this jar has been well known by me," one comes to abide in a state free from further desire, resting solely within one's own Self. In the same way, each individual principle—beginning with earth, such as earth, water, and so forth—as well as the elemental self beginning with earth, [is likewise realized].

The meaning is as follows: by relying on that aggregate consisting of fifty elements—such as the earth and so forth—and perceiving his own self through a non-conceptualizing mental state (*nirvikalpaka-vṛtti*), he appears as truly full; he flashes forth in the form of pure self-awareness alone. || 279 ||
Now, one might object: "This universe, consisting of the collection of principles beginning with Earth (dharā), appears as something distinct;
how then can it be of the nature of pure self-consciousness through such a reflective awareness alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This has arisen from me alone," "this is reflected within me alone," and "this is non-different from me"—this threefold means is that of Śambhu. (3.280)

Regarding the word "matta" (from me): according to such statements as, "In all cases here, the word 'I' denotes exclusively pure consciousness" (Tantrāloka 1.132), [the world] arises from the supreme consciousness and not from ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth; this [world] consists of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*).

The entire universe is thus rejoicing; even though it is of such a nature, it is reflected within my consciousness. Although it is not distinct from me, it appears as if distinct, yet it does not exist as something separate.
Even so, when this [universe] is withdrawn, it remains non-different from me, in its ultimate form which is the very nature of consciousness.

It is not, however, by means of a process of disintegration of parts that leads to the state of dyads and so forth, resulting in the form of atoms; thus, it is entirely logical that the universe is of the nature of pure consciousness solely through reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). And this very reflective awareness is the essence of this Śāmbhava means (*upāya*).
Its essential nature has been described as follows: "Thus, that Śāmbhava means is threefold. (280)
And since the emanation (sṛṣṭi) and the other [phases] are the basis for this self-reflective awareness (ahaṃparāmarśa), he has also performed its preliminary sketching (āsūtraṇa); thus he says:
"This very sketching of emanation, persistence, and withdrawal has been made."
Regarding where it is situated and from whence it arises, he has said this in the Spandaśāsana: || 3-281 ||
And this has not been stated by us alone, but even by our teachers—as he says in the passage beginning with "where," etc. It is said there:
"That wherein this entire universe resides as an effect, and from which it has emerged..."
"Because its nature is unobstructed, there is no cessation anywhere.

(Svacchanda Tantra 1.2.2) Since it has "emerged from" [the source], it is called emanation (*sṛṣṭi*); since it "abides in" [the source]—both as non-different and yet appearing as if different—it is [thus characterized by] persistence (*sthiti*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). || 281 ||

Now, one might object: what is this that has been called the agency of consciousness in creation and so forth? Should not some other definition be stated, as by the proponents of Brahman—such as "That experience which is unborn, immeasurable, infinite, and whose very form is the bliss of the Self"—by means of which [the nature of consciousness] would be established? For its...
Lest it be suspected that a unique nature established by another school of thought has been asserted, he says:
"For by this much alone, the supreme sovereignty of consciousness is made manifest;
and since its being the self of the universe [is also established], what other definition could possibly be stated? (3.282)

The meaning is that by this much— namely, by her very agency in creation and so forth— the sovereignty and universal nature of consciousness have been most excellently proclaimed as distinct from other philosophical systems;
for this alone is her primary and unique defining characteristic.

"Because it manifests as the self-nature of the universe through its sovereignty. For this very reason, what other definition could possibly be stated for it? By stating such a thing, nothing at all would have been said—this is the intended meaning.
For if that were the case, on the contrary—

Because [ignorance] is undermined by the dilemma of whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from [the ultimate reality], it cannot even be established as the cause of the manifold variety of the universe. Therefore, its primary characteristic is precisely its agency in creation and so forth;
thus, what has been stated is indeed logical. || 282 ||
Therefore, by reflecting upon his very own capacity to perform acts such as creation within himself, he attains identity with supreme consciousness; thus he says:
"I am manifesting the universe within my own self, the space of consciousness."
Through the expansion [of the realization] that the Creator is the soul of the universe, there is the state of being Bhairava.
The entire collection of the six paths is reflected within me alone;
"I am the sustainer"—thus this universal form becomes manifest. (3.284)
Seeing that "this entire universe dissolves into me, whose nature is filled with the mass of flames of ever-arisen great awakening," one attains peace. (3.285)

One might object: "Even so, since the universe persists as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of that which is being created and so forth, how can its state of utter tranquility arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Of the dream-palace of transmigratory existence, which contains within it an infinite and variegated reality..."
The consumer is the blazing fire itself, which exults in the thought, "I am indeed Śiva."
According to the principle that will be explained regarding space and time,

[the worlds] are variegated because they are innumerable and consist of infinite diverse configurations; for this very reason, the *saṃsāra* (cycle of existence) is one whose "wombs" (*garbha*)— that is, its worlds (*bhuvana*)— are "good" (*santaḥ*), meaning auspicious.

The meaning is this: that very Self of all principles (*tattva*), which is the expansion of the universe, is itself the "dream-abode" because it is devoid of substantiality; for indeed, even the possibility of a residue might remain after the burning away of the "waking abode. Its burner is [the consciousness] brought forth by the power of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as "I am the creator," and for this very reason...

The meaning is this: the fire of supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*)—which, through constant practice, has the nature of flashing forth and consists of uninterrupted consciousness, and which realizes even the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the universe as one's own self-consciousness—is Śiva himself, who is "I. For just as when a fire arises in a house, even though it is filled with many coverings, [the darkness does not remain].
In the same way, even when the state of being Śiva has dawned for the universe, something remains yet to be accomplished.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the realization of consciousness within one's own self, by virtue of performing acts such as creation, is itself delimited by those very acts? Therefore, how could there be identity with undelimited consciousness through that means?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The entire world originates from me and appears manifold through differentiation; yet it is rooted in me, and when this [differentiation] dissolves, nothing else remains.
Thus, he who—by virtue of unifying them—perceives creation, maintenance, and dissolution as partless, [is liberated].
For from this, the fourth state vibrates forth. || 287 ||

This entire world, in all its manifold variety, arises from supreme consciousness alone; though thus arisen, it rests within that very consciousness. Even when this world is withdrawn, nothing else remains, but rather consciousness itself. In the manner thus described:

Because consciousness alone is the underlying thread throughout all states, he who— by means of unification characterized by the identity of creation and so forth with consciousness alone— should perceive that which is partless,
and through the dissolution of the divisions of creation and so forth, should directly realize it as being of the single nature of undivided consciousness; he [is one].

The meaning is that one who is indeed fully immersed in the *śāmbhavopāya*, having attained the fourth state (*turīya-pada*), vibrates and manifests as the nature of the supreme, inexpressible consciousness (*anākhyaparasaṃvid*). By the use of the singular pronoun "he" (*saḥ*), it is indicated that many do not possess the qualification for this. || 287 ||
Therefore he says:
"Only a few, graced by the Supreme Lord, attain faith in this supreme means which abounds in the non-duality of Śambhu. (3.288)

The term "cultivated" (*bhāvitāḥ*) means that they have been consecrated by the Lord as being eligible for this [teaching] due to the intensity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). For this very reason, it is said that "only some" [are so]. Indeed, such eligibility for the descent of power does not belong to everyone.
— This is the intended meaning. As they say:
"There are hundreds of worshippers; there are thousands of devotees;
but those who are vessels of grace and full of confidence toward the Lord are two or three, not five or six."

Thus [it is said]. And its state of being supreme is caused by its possessing the non-duality of Śambhu. For others, such as those belonging to the *āṇava* and other [means], are indeed not supreme because they consist of duality—this is the intended meaning. Therefore, in this context, no separate collection of means, such as ritual bathing and so forth, is of any use. || 288 ||

Thus it is said: "Bathing, vows, purification of the body, concentration (dhāraṇā), application of mantras, the arrangement of the paths (adhvan), the ritual of sacrifice, fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa), and meditative absorption (samādhi). (3.289)

No such conceptualization whatsoever is appropriate here as a distinction. Now, one might object: "If no diverse collection of means is applicable here, then how indeed can a teacher, being himself devoid of means, perform the favor of grace for others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For one established in this state, the capacity to bestow grace upon others is clearly manifest. (3.290)
If such a person worthy of grace approaches the teacher—
"such a person" meaning one who is a fit vessel for the Śāmbhava means—
then for him, [liberation occurs] merely through the sight of him, conversation with him, and so forth.

With the intention that "it is like a lamp rising from one lamp," the sense of having accomplished all that was to be done arises within one's own self; thus, what indeed is the purpose of a variety of different means? This is the underlying meaning. || 290 ||
Now, one might object: "If there should be someone who is not of such a kind yet has set out to worship Him, what should be done by this [teacher] in that case? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But if he were not such a person, yet were permeated by devotion to Bhava... (3.291).
And when he has propitiated him, impelled by such grace as has been cultivated, then the wise one should learn the various rites of initiation and so forth. (3.292)

"One such as that" means a fit vessel for the Śāmbhava means; "he would not [be so]" because of the absence of the most intense descent of power (*tīvratīvra-śaktipāta*). And furthermore: "In this regard, this is the first sign: unwavering devotion to Rudra" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.14).

According to this principle, [the disciple] is presided over by the first sign, known as devotion to Bhava (bhavabhakti), which indicates the descent of power (śaktipāta); and because only this single sign called devotion to Bhava is specified here as an indicator of the descent of power, while other signs are not mentioned, [it follows that the descent of power is of the] very mild (mandamanda) type and so forth.

This has been indicated. Thus, even though he possesses only a very weak descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and so forth, he does not set out to propitiate a Guru who is merely proficient in the appropriate means such as the *āṇava* and others;
rather, he is one who is permeated by the *śāmbhava* means—this is what was stated in the words, "and he propitiates him. For he...

The meaning is this: impelled by such grace that has been cultivated, one does not receive even future grace appropriate for the Śāmbhava-upāya from a Guru who is only knowledgeable in the Āṇava-upāya. Therefore...

"And there shall be no contempt at the time of the ritual regarding the rescue from saṃsāra"—because of such statements, and because the disciple has no other recourse according to the aforementioned reasoning, the various means (upāyajāta) must necessarily be employed out of a desire to uplift him. Thus he says: "Then..."
"Variegated," and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated previously:

"If He, by means of the abode of His sovereignty, desires to bestow grace even upon those whose consciousness is impure, He should resort to the procedure appropriate for that [state]. (Tantrāloka 2.44)
Thus it has been stated. Regarding the term "variegated" (*vicitram*)—it is so called because of the differences among those to be graced (*anugrāhya*). As was said previously:
"And that [grace] is variegated according to the recipients; this will be explained" (Tantrāloka 2.45).

Now, if grace has been bestowed through the process of the *āṇavopāya* upon such a recipient— one who is worthy of favor and partakes in the immersion (*samāveśa*) of the *śāmbhavopāya*— from the presence of a Guru, then, according to the maxim:
"By the practice of weaving with a coarse thread, one attains the variety of weaving with fine threads," and so forth;
Anticipating the objection— "Since the relationship between cause and fruit is fixed, how indeed can there be for this person a future grace (anugraha) appropriate to the Śāmbhava means?"— he says:
"For even those future forms of worship reach their final consummation right here."
Having attained this supreme state of being composed of that, the auspicious [reality] is described.
The [means] beginning with the individual (āṇava) will be explained later.
For, since there is nothing further to be sought beyond these in their relationship as door and doorkeeper, the sprouting occurs only within the Śāmbhava means;
thus it has been said: "In this very [means] they reach their final consummation. Therefore...
Thus, this very state of being composed of that (evaitanmayatva), which is the supreme goal in the form of ultimate welfare, is proclaimed everywhere.

For nothing at all could exist without resting in this—such is the intended meaning. Therefore, even though there is a plurality of means (upāya), there is no plurality of the goal (upeya). It is with this very intention that it is said:
Both of these modes of immersion proceed toward the ocean of the non-conceptual; indeed, without being firmly rooted therein, nothing at all exists.
"Therefore, one should not postulate a difference in the fruit of consciousness here," as was stated previously in [Tantrāloka] 1.227 and so forth. || 293 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half of the verse:
"Thus has been described in great detail this supreme realization of the Self belonging to Śambhu."

One named Jayaratha, consisting of the state of identity with the taste of the peerless flavor (asamarasa) shining forth through the power of Śiva’s possession (āveśa), has explained this third daily lesson (āhnika).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Śāmbhava [Means]," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 3.
The means itself is that which is conducive to the goal—may there be auspiciousness.
Jayaratha, being occupied with the pursuit of hundreds of means for mastering various texts, has quickly explained this "Day on Non-Means."

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Śāmbhava Means," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, the illustrious Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. || 3 ||
The Fourth Daily Lesson:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
To him who, in the destruction of the obstacles of false conceptualization, possesses the status of Gaṇapati among the host of true conceptualizations.
May Jayanta, whose very self is the supreme power of the highest mantra, carry [you] and be victorious.
Now, following the Śāmbhava means, he promises to explain the Śākta means as it follows in due order by means of the latter half [of the verse]:
"Now we shall describe the sphere of the Śākta means for the sake of the consciousness of the Supreme Self. (4.1)
"The mandala of means" [is so called] because of the non-identity of the purification of conceptual constructions and the other [stages]. || 1 ||
Therein, he begins first to explain the purification of conceptual constructs, which was indicated in the summary of the first chapter:
"In this nature of the Supreme Lord, which was described in the immediately preceding chapter..."
One who wishes to enter into solitude should immediately perform the purification of conceptual construction.

"In this very nature" means in that which has a single, non-conceptual form; by this, it is made known that his repose lies solely in the *śāmbhavopāya*. Regarding "the latent impression" (*saṃskāra*): through the power of repeated hearing, reflection, and so forth, it refers to the process beginning from indistinctness and culminating in the attainment of the state of extreme clarity.

The infusion of another quality, by means of which there would be an entry into one's own nature that is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). "Directly" (*añjasā*) means swiftly; for otherwise, due to the arising of other contradictory conceptual constructions, the growth of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would not occur. || 2 ||

Now, it may be argued that there is no dispute among anyone regarding the momentariness of cognition; since its conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is also of the nature of cognition, it too is momentary. How, then, could a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) take root in something whose very essence has vanished immediately upon arising? For such a thing must be stable, as for example:
Anticipating the objection—"In the case of sesame seeds and the like, [the effect is produced] by *sumanas* flowers; how then can this be said?"—he says:

A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), when refined, produces another conceptual construction that has been refined by its own nature and is similar to itself. That one also produces another, and that one yet another, each being of a similar nature. (4.3)
Just as here, from a conceptualization of blue, only another conceptualization of blue arises and not a conceptualization of yellow,

so too— even though it is not yet clear— a conceptualization that is being cultivated for the sake of becoming clear possesses an infused latent impression (*saṃskāra*), because otherwise there would be the consequence of its clarity failing and its lack of clarity persisting, just like its own nature.

The conditioned [conceptualization] alone would produce another conceptualization; for generally, the production of an effect occurs in accordance with its cause—this is the sense. This should be understood to apply to other conceptualizations as well.
"That too" refers to the second [conceptualization] born from the conditioned conceptualization; "that too [produces] another" refers to the third.

Furthermore, that [third] is also compared to another, which constitutes the fourth [type]. Here, although the quality of being identical to oneself (*svatulyatva*) can tolerate a relation [with a further term], by the statement "consisting of similarity," it is made known that even when the chain of conceptual constructions (*vikalpamālā*) extends far and far, there is no loss whatsoever of its similarity. || 3 ||
Now, one might object: "If a second [moment] of exactly the same kind arises from a single conditioned conceptualization, let that be so;

but if a third and subsequent moments arise in this very same way, would there not be pointlessness, or else, if there were any distinction, would there not be a loss of similarity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Among these very four conceptualizations, that formative activity (saṃskāra) is, in sequence: unclear, about to become clear, becoming clear, and having the nature of being clear. (4-4)
"Capable of becoming manifest" (*sphuṭatābhāvī*) means fit for manifestation; "becoming manifest" (*prasphuṭan*) means having a state of manifestation arising;
"consisting of manifestation" (*sphuṭatātmaka*) means having a perfected state of manifestation. "Gradually" (*kramāt*) refers to the degree of excellence in practice.
Therefore, because an excellence is observed here according to the respective stages, there is neither futility nor [mere] similarity.

"Diminution"—because no dissimilar subsequent cognition arises; for it has been stated that the very first impression (saṃskāra) has reached full development through the excellence of repeated practice as appropriate. || 4 ||
Nor could such a degree of refinement (saṃskāra) be possible for him alone; thus he says:
"From that point, [it becomes] clearer and clearer until at the end it becomes most clear.
The word "from that" (tataḥ) refers to immediately after the four [stages].

Now, one might ask: "Even due to the intensity of practice, how can a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is initially unclear in nature suddenly attain a state characterized by clarity and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:
"And even in a conceptual construction that is unclear and so on, there exists an intermediate differentiation. (4-5)

"Differentiation" (*bheda*) means a particularity; "intermediate" (*āntarālika*) means situated in the middle. For instance, in the interval between that which possesses indistinctness and that which possesses distinctness, there occurs [the state] where indistinctness is falling away, and likewise: slight distinctness, sprouted distinctness, and outlined more distinctness.
And [the state of] being most clearly manifest as it arises. || 5 ||
Anticipating the question, "If this were done, what would happen?", he says:
"Then, nourished by that most vivid and noble identity [with the object], consciousness attains its stainless nature free from conceptual construction. (4.6)

Then— from that aforementioned cause, which is the latent impression (saṃskāra)— it becomes most vivid, and for that very reason "magnificent" (udāra), that is, great because it shares the same level as non-conceptual [cognition]; being augmented by that "conformity"— namely, by its state of being conceptual— and thus rendered independent of other latent impressions, it takes on the form of a conceptual construction.

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), by casting off the stain of contraction, attains a state of purity that is essentially free of conceptual construction (*avikalpa*); the meaning is that it shines forth as consisting of full, non-conceptual knowledge. And for this reason, it is also said: "One must not rest in mere conceptual construction alone."
By this it is said: as they have declared—“A wise person should not become attached even to conceptualization regarding the ultimate reality;
for what difference is there between a conceptualization that is auspicious or one that is inauspicious?”
Thus [ends the sixth].
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand:
