"And therefore, for those who reflect again and again upon that Bhairavian light whose nature is consciousness, its state of manifestness arises. (4.7)

Therefore— because conceptual consciousness itself manifests through the power of its respective latent impressions (saṃskāra) in the form of non-conceptual consciousness— the light whose nature is consciousness, called knowledge and action belonging to Bhairava, [manifests] repeatedly as "I," precisely in that form, through the sequence beginning with indistinctness.

For those great souls who possess the most intense descent of power (*tīvratīvra-śaktipāta*) and who contemplate [reality] through the process culminating in its most vivid manifestation as it arises,
there arises the state of clarity of that very splendor of Bhairava, which consists of consciousness and is the object of such contemplation.
The meaning is that through the power of the Śāmbhava immersion (āveśa), there occurs the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of that [reality]. || 7 ||

Now, one might raise the following objection: "Since consciousness is of a single nature with the subject, it is logical that it possesses only the quality of being the reflector (*parāmarśakatva*), not the quality of being the object of reflection (*parāmṛśyatva*); for if it were so, the consequence would follow that it is insentient (*jāḍya*), just like blue and other such objects.
He shows this doubt as follows:
Surely consciousness is by its very nature the subject that cognizes and consists of reflective awareness; how could it be an object of cognition?
For if it were created as having such a form [of an object], it would be insentient.
"In that form" means "of being graspable. || 8 ||
He provides the resolution for this very point:
It is said that self-awareness is, by its very nature, full;
it has been stated previously that in this [awareness] there is nothing to be removed and nothing to be added. (4.9)

In this context, consciousness, being of the nature of one's own self, is inherently full because there is no external object to be required; thus, it has no longing for anything else. Since it is eternally manifest, within this self-consciousness nothing such as lack of clarity is to be removed, nor is anything such as supreme clarity to be added. Previously—

In the *Anupāyahnikam*, it was stated: "In this regard, the yoga of action (*kriyāyoga*) does not deserve to be considered a means," and so forth. It is with this very intention that even by outsiders [it has been said]:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
The reality should be seen as it has arisen; one who sees reality is liberated. Thus it has been said. (9)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then from where does this expansion of consciousness—characterized by such qualities as lack of clarity and so forth—arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But rather, because of its power to accomplish the difficult-to-accomplish, this [expansion] arises from its own stainless freedom."
The Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing his own nature. || 4-10 ||

Furthermore, this Supreme Lord, the supreme Light— by virtue of His pure sovereignty (*svācchandyam*), which is characterized by the power to accomplish the impossible through the concealment of His own nature— conceals His own Self, even though that Self is essentially one with the supreme subject.

The manifestation as suchness through the emergence of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth, is itself "play" (*krīḍā*)—an activity that proceeds without regard for specific results. In this regard, one who is "learned" (*paṇḍita*) means one who is proficient. For this very [activity] is his power called *māyā*, which consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

That which, although its own nature is unobscured, manifests itself as if it were obscured; for this reason, there is this manifestation of duality consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth. || 10 ||
Regarding this, he says:

"Even though its own nature is unobscured, that which is the self-concealment of the All-pervasive One is indeed Māyā, from which arises this entire extent of differentiation consisting of the activities of the universe. (4.11)

Thus, it is precisely this manifestation of his in the form of the manifold universe that is called duality, by virtue of which this endless bondage of saṃsāra occurs; and for the very purpose of dispelling that [duality], there is this reflective awareness—that consciousness itself, when reflected upon again and again, shall attain clarity. || 11 ||
Thus it is said: "The manifestation of this Great Lord as duality has been described;
by means of the removal of that duality, this [true] reflective awareness is designated. (4.12)
"The removal of that duality"—this is said because of the metaphorical treatment of the effect as non-different from the cause. || 12 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Is it not the case that there is no dispute among anyone that what has appeared here cannot become unappeared? Furthermore, this body, blue color, and so forth, manifest as distinct [from consciousness].
Therefore, how can it be said that 'by the removal of those [objects], there remains the manifestation of consciousness alone'?
In order to dispel this doubt, [the author proceeds] with the sequence of the purification of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

He introduces the true nature of reasoning (tarka-tattva) as it was taught in the subsequent instruction: "The wise cut the root of this tree that is so difficult to split with the axe of sound reasoning (sattarka) raised on its edge; such is the certainty. (4.13)

Because it is the sole cause of bondage, that duality consisting of the grasped and the grasper and so forth is itself a "tree" (*pādapa*) due to its being difficult to uproot; of this very tree which is currently being experienced, the "wise ones" (*kovidāḥ*)—
those who have recognized their own Self— are "real" (*san*), meaning they are directly established in reality, and for that very reason...
That reasoning which is distinct from other forms of reasoning, having reached its supreme limit—

arising from an intellect purified by contact with the portion of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) and whose essential nature is the recognition of one’s own Self— that alone is the well-sharpened axe; by means of it...

The root text: [The wise] cut away the very cause characterized by non-recognition (akhyāti), so that for this manifestation of pure, perfect supreme consciousness, there may never again be a recurrence; such is the conclusion, for that alone [is achieved] by the great-souled ones through the contemplation of the body and so forth.

By means of the excellence of practice according to its respective degree, bringing about the purification of conceptual thought, and having reached the highest limit, one should attain the state of being composed of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), by which even the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), though not yet manifest, shall attain clarity. || 13 ||
Therefore he says:
"The wise call this very cultivation the 'cow of plenty' that milks all desires; it makes manifest the reality that is even beyond the reach of the mind's longing. (4.14)

"That which is reasoning (tarka), they call cultivation (bhāvanā)"; thus, there is an infusion of the grammatical marker (liṅga) being prescribed, for it is reasoning itself, when it has reached its highest limit, that is called cultivation. As it has been said:
"That very supreme knowledge is held to consist of cultivation."
Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, she is described by means of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) with the word "her" (*enām*);
and it has been stated that when she is fully perfected, the attainment of the desired fruit occurs—namely, that she is "the milch-cow of all desires. As it has been said:

"Remaining there, one attains samādhi in just a moment; and having become fully perfected therein, one obtains the desired fruit. For that very cultivation indeed transcends even the objects of desire—even for those who possess independent conceptual constructions.

Because it is beyond conceptualization, it is not an object of the senses; one should make manifest—that is, directly realize through non-conceptual activity—the reality which is ultimate, characterized solely by the supreme subject, and whose nature is consciousness. By the power of what [is realized], what indeed would not be accomplished for the yogin? || 14 ||
And for this reason, it is stated in our system that "this alone is the supreme limb of yoga"; thus he says:

"In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, reasoning (tarka) is declared to be the supreme limb of yoga. Because it involves the discernment of what is to be abandoned and so forth, effort in that regard is praised. (4.15)

Even if the mind has become steady on the path, one should urge it away from the desire for objects that are to be abandoned, and by means of that [mind], lead it until the state free from affliction is reached. (4.16)
Although it is said: "Prāṇāyāma, as well as dhyāna, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, tarka, and samādhi— this is called the six-limbed yoga."

According to this principle, although reasoning (*tarka*) is equal in status to breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the other limbs of yoga, it is nevertheless the most excellent internal limb of yoga because it involves the discernment of what is to be abandoned and so forth. For by means of reasoning,
the yogi— who reflects, "this is to be abandoned, this is to be accepted"— quickly becomes a knower of reality (*tattvajña*).
As it has been said:
"Discrimination (ūha) is internal to yoga; by means of it, one abides on the path. Although this [discrimination] is common [to all], it indeed greatly assists in liberation."
Thus:
"He who investigates by means of reasoning that is not contradicted by the established tenets [of his own school] for the sake of dharma,
knowledge, and liberation— he, and no other, knows reality."

Thus, for this reason, it has been stated that one should strive here [in this very path] by means of the primary mode of practice: "Therefore, effort therein is praised. For the yogi who has exerted effort therein [in this path] will not seek elsewhere for the means to liberation characterized as that which is to be abandoned, even though such means are taught in other scriptures such as Sāṃkhya; rather, he thinks: "This alone is mine."
Even if the mind has become stabilized through the arising of the conceit that "the reality is to be longed for" and so forth,
one should, by means of that reasoning, impel it— having turned it away from the path of what is to be abandoned—
and lead it until it rests upon the path of what is to be adopted, until the state free from affliction is reached.
The meaning is that it should manifest as having the nature of a supreme light that transcends everything. || 15-16 ||
And here, because of the unevenness [of the meter], he himself explains the four terms:
"The path here is the means to liberation; that which is taught in other scriptures is to be abandoned.
That will which, conjoined with Niyati, pervades—that is, binds—[is what is meant]. (17)
That which was called *rāgatattva* by him is that by which one becomes attached to that [object].
Since the fact that the path taught in other scriptures is to be abandoned has already been established, no further effort is made here.
The word *viṣaya* is derived from the root *ṣiñ* meaning "to bind," preceded by the prefix *vi-*, with the suffix *ac*. By that [word],...

That desire which consists of objective forms and acts as a binder—namely, that particular kind of conceit such as "let this alone be mine"—is what is generally called the *rāgatattva* (the principle of attachment) in conjunction with *niyati* (destiny). For the very nature of the *rāgatattva* is simply the mere longing for all objects; that indeed is it.

Because it arises from the principle of necessity (*niyati*) by virtue of having a restricted object, it is appropriate that "the principle of attachment" (*rāgatattva*) be designated as its [specific] name; for this reason, by means of that attachment, the mind becomes colored toward that restricted path which is to be abandoned—it becomes stabilized, is the meaning. Now, [one might ask], is this not the case everywhere else?
Those lowest of men who are not devoted to the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, and the Scripture; who are experts in the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic.
"Indeed, Māyā causes them to wander, desiring liberation when there is no liberation.
Likewise: "And that which is the science of logic (hetu-śāstra) in the world, which mocks the eternal and the non-eternal..."
For those who are uncertain indeed engage in disputes by means of formal debate, informal chatter, and destructive criticism.
O lady of excellent vows, those statements which are based solely on causal reasoning are devoid of reality;
they are bereft of the yoga of knowledge and lack a presiding deity.
Certainty regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa does not arise at all;
for [the mind] is bound by ignorance and, by means of signs, by unrighteousness.
By censuring this reasoning with the words, "Those people who take delight therein lead [others] to hell," and so forth, the Blessed One illuminated its inferiority;
and it is with this very intention that even a teacher who knows such [reasoning] is said to be avoidable, as it has been stated:
"One should not make a logician one's guru...
and likewise,
"...in the case of a logician, there shall be execution or imprisonment."

Thus it is said. Following this very line of reasoning, even those who are proficient [in logic] have declared: "We feel ashamed of those dialectical intellects which, devoid of any determination of reality, merely communicate with one another, having as their sole essence mere conceit."
Such has been stated; how then is its superiority here asserted? For in that case, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti.
Moreover, since the single cause of authority exists in both cases, it is impossible to suggest a lack of authority in even one of them. What, then, is to be understood in this matter?

A distinction between the objects [of these two types of reasoning] must be understood here, so that everything may remain in its proper place; for reasoning is indeed twofold: one is devoid of the determination of reality, primarily consisting of quibbles and the like, culminating merely in the defeat of an opponent, and being essentially a form of wrangling (*jalpa*); while the other...

That which results in the determination of a real object (*vastu-nirṇaya*) through the discernment of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, which is free from quibbles (*chala*) and the like, and which is primarily debate (*vāda*), is [the first type].
Among these, the former is censurable because it lacks the determination of a real object; for this very reason, it is said:
"Those [arguments] which are devoid of a real object..."
Thus, it has been stated:
"...no certainty whatsoever arises," and so forth; for this very reason, even those who perceive that [consciousness] lack knowledge of the actual object.

It has been stated that [the former] is to be avoided; however, for one who, through the investigation of what is to be abandoned and so forth, effects the purification of the reality and, having abandoned that which is to be abandoned, comes to rest in the means and the goal—that is the supreme limb of yoga. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, this is our own sound reasoning (*sattarka*), whereas that belonging to other systems is unsound reasoning (*asattarka*).
The division. || 17 ||

But surely, people intent on their own welfare proceed by themselves to abandon what is to be discarded and to adopt what is to be adopted, even without depending on scripture; for scripture is of no use to one who is hungry regarding food,
nor to one who is dirty regarding bathing— so what is the need for reasoning here?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Just as [one might feel] upon seeing the enjoyment of imperial sovereignty, or even upon not seeing it in an inferior [state]," (4.18).
A person of poor intellect might become attached to enjoyments; likewise, one might be attached even to liberation through passion.

Just as some ignorant person—failing to discern what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—might regard imperial sovereignty as fit for full enjoyment, whether he understands it correctly or not, [yet remains] base—

One might become attached—that is, one might become infatuated through passion—toward wealth that is to be enjoyed by those in a miserable state, due to the ripening of previously formed latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that have long since taken root; likewise, one might do so even toward a false liberation, while directly abandoning true liberation. This is the meaning of the sentence; therefore, [this is taught] for the purpose of abandoning what is to be abandoned.
And since reasoning (*tarka*) is necessarily required for the adoption of what is to be adopted, it is rightly said: "Reasoning is the supreme limb of yoga. || 18 ||
Is it not the case that all these people are attached to this or that philosophical view by their very nature, with the intention that:
"For a person born empty [of wisdom], who does not perceive what ought and ought not to be done..."?

"Alas, by whom have these malignant planets of dogmatic tenets been unleashed?"—since such things have been said elsewhere, [one might ask: "In that case, even his liberation would be appropriate; so what is this thing called 'attachment'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That very [state] is called a "portion" (aṃśaka), and it is clearly designated as "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva). || 4-19 ||
The learned declare that what is an auxiliary to accomplishment is an obstacle to liberation;
for it is stated in the scriptures that "it is indeed attachment itself, the aspect known as the state of being a beast.
Thus, it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda-śāstra*:
"O Goddess, I shall describe the sixfold *aṃśaka* in due order," beginning thus, [it continues]:
"The *bhāvāṃśaka*, that which is called *svabhāva*, and the *puṣpapātāṃśa*."
Having thus indicated their natures, I shall describe their activities in due order.
One who is a portion of Brahmā is devoted to the Vedas; now learn from me the nature of one who is a portion of Rudra.

"He is a devotee of Rudra, of virtuous character, and always intent upon the scriptures of Śiva"—by such [descriptions] he is characterized. Now, if this were so, then all these people would attain their own appropriate liberation simply by the force of their own nature; what then is the purpose of this [scripture]?
Anticipating the question, "What is the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted?", he says: "But that," and so forth.
That is to say, such a nature is clearly [described] as:
"And the human [agency], according to the Sāṃkhyas... and so on.

Because this is established by the authority of such scriptural passages (*āgama*) and is thus unfading, even the attainment (*siddhi*) consisting of the enjoyment appropriate to those respective levels is an obstacle; furthermore, when invited by others, one must avoid attachment and pride, lest undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭa*) arise again.

As stated in such passages as *Yoṣū* (3-51), those who know the scriptures consider [the attainment of supernatural powers] to be an obstacle to liberation; for one who possesses such a nature regards the very accomplishment (*siddhi*) characterized by the attainment of those respective principles as liberation itself.
He rests in that very [state] which is of the nature of a semblance of liberation and is to be abandoned. || 19 ||
Precisely because of this very nature, one might abandon the direct means to liberation and become attached to something else;
thus he says: "For this very reason, even while knowing the greatness of the teaching of Śiva... (4.20).
A fool, colored by passion, might become attached to Vaiṣṇava and other [traditions].
Now, if he truly knew the excellence of the power of Śiva’s teaching as being the direct means to liberation, why would he be attached elsewhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For to that extent, his divine power called Vāmā exists.

The [power] called Vāmā manifests for the Pāñcarātrikas, the followers of Brahmā (Vairiñcas), the Buddhists (Saugatas), and others, bestowing only their respective limited accomplishments (*niyatasiddhi*). Thus it is said:
"Vāmā is so called because she emits (*vamana*) the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*)."... [etc.]

By such statements, the meaning is that [this] is the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) which manifests transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); "Vairiñcas" refers to the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*). || 21 ||
One might object: "If he is ignorant of the greatness of the Śiva-scripture and thus becomes attached elsewhere, let that be;
what is the harm? But how can this be so for one who knows? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Some fools have been seen disparaging the enjoyment of imperial sovereignty. (4.22)
It is not, however, out of contentment, nor from the cessation of desire for one's own enjoyments.

Indeed, in this world, some who are mostly childish are seen to despise even the enjoyment of sovereignty—despite recognizing it as supremely excellent and desirable—precisely because of their foolishness; it is not [out of contentment].

Furthermore, because of their contentment— the implication being that since the desire for enjoyments has been cast far away from them, it is appropriate to censure such desires— whereas for the foolish, there is no contentment at all;
for even regarding their own inferior enjoyments, they think, "May this happen again and again."
Thus they offer such blessings— because there is no cessation of the desire for worldly enjoyment—
and although they know the greatness of the teaching of Śiva, these deluded ones are seen beginning to disparage it,
being attached elsewhere; by virtue of which, because they are presided over by the Vāmā [power], once again...
Furthermore, there would be a sinking back into saṃsāra itself. || 22 ||
Thus it is said:
"In this way, those whose minds are intent upon censuring the immersion into the Bhairava of Consciousness... (4.23)
Because they are struck down by extremely terrible powers (*śakti*). Regarding the phrase "by extremely terrible [powers]," it is said:
"[They] cause the individual souls (*aṇu*) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower."
The meaning is: by others [mantras] designated as such, namely those called "most terrible" (ghoratara). || 23 ||
And for this very reason, there is no emergence from saṃsāra at all for this deluded person; thus he says:
"Therefore, one who knows the majesty of Śambhu [but remains] within another teaching... (4.24).
Once reassured, one must not emerge from that great ocean of division; for, with a heart thus reassured, one remains fixed in that [state], and not otherwise—as it is said:
"Inwardly a Kaula, outwardly a Śaiva, but in worldly conduct a Vaidika."

According to this principle, by being intent on the preservation of worldly consensus (*lokasaṃgraha*) and remaining superficial, there would be no crossing over from this ocean of *saṃsāra*— because within that very state, the experience of rising and sinking would continue without interruption. || 24 ||
And he says that this was not merely stated by us as our own invention:
"And it has been clearly declared in the venerable Kāmikā, in the section on bonds (pāśaprakaraṇa). (4.25)
He recites that very [verse]:
"Those wise sages who are knowers of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, and Purāṇas; those devoted to the Pāñcarātra; and whoever are devoted to other scriptures... (4.26).
All those [followers] of the Buddhists, the Ārhatas, and others, are colored by the passion for knowledge;
because they are bound by the snare of Māyā, they do not obtain initiation into Śiva. (4.27)
The "steadfast" (dhīrāḥ) are those whose wisdom is firmly established in the subject matter of the Vedas and so forth. "Other scriptures" refers to the Vedānta and similar texts;

"knowledge and passion" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the sense of a collective whole. Here, because of its proximity to the word "passion," "knowledge" refers to impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*). For this very reason, they are devoted to the scriptures such as the Vedas.
It has been stated that because they fall within the domain of *māyā*, they do not obtain the Śaiva knowledge that transcends it:
"Because they are bound by the fetter of *māyā*, they do not find initiation into Śiva.
Furthermore, that which was previously explained by us in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*’s compendium of dialogues—

where, under the term "desire for objects" (*viṣayecchā*), the *rāgatattva* (principle of passion) was defined as that which bestows attachment toward the means to liberation taught in other scriptures such as the Vedas, and which is endowed with the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*)— is not without foundation.
To illuminate this point, he also explains the word *rāga* occurring here:

"And by the word *rāga*, the principle of *rāga* (passion) is declared to be the regulator; and that [principle] should regulate him within that [state] belonging to Māyā," according to the scripture. (4.28)

And here, by the word "passion" (rāga)—meaning by the reason that will be stated later—it is connected [to the context] that the *tattva* of passion is said to be the regulator (*niyāmaka*). "Regulator" means that which bestows attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) toward a specific, determined object; for that is the *tattva* of passion.
In that illusory scripture such as the Veda and so forth, he should restrain that deluded person, establishing them in a state of limitation by making them think,
"This alone is what I desire," even though the principle of attachment (*rāga-tattva*) consists generally of nothing more than the mere longing for all objects.
Although its own nature [is thus], nevertheless, without the ascent toward a specific object, that [nature] would not attain manifestation;
therefore, it necessarily implies the principle of necessity (niyati-tattva). Thus, it is rightly said: "The principle of attachment (rāga-tattva) is the regulator. || 28 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if liberation as taught in other scriptures such as those of the Vaiṣṇavas were attained, why indeed would this person not emerge from saṃsāra? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even regarding the liberation of the Vaiṣṇavas and others, that which is conceived through their own mental resolve..."
Either union with the nature of the Supreme, or else the state of being of the nature of bliss.

Or, it is pure consciousness alone, with its continuity extinguished like a lamp; that [state] consists of the condition of the *pralayākala*, which is characterized by the dissolution of the self along with both the experienced (*savedya*) and the unexperienced (*apavedya*). (4-30)

The connection is as follows: that which is indeed liberation according to the systems of the Vaiṣṇavas and others, even that consists of the state of the *pralayākala* in our own philosophy. In that regard, for the Vaiṣṇavas, "liberation is union with the Supreme Nature (*paraprakṛti*)," because in their system [it is attained] through the Lord known as Vāsudeva.

Because the Supreme Brahman— who is of the nature of the supreme primordial matter (*paraprakṛti*) and the ordainer of both the conscious and the unconscious— manifests through his own essential nature in various ways according to a sequential diversity,
he possesses a manifold self in the form of the universe.

Based on such scriptural passages as "Brahman is one only, without a second," because of the non-deviation from the single reality whose nature is pure consciousness through the practice of the knowledge of truth, non-unity is ultimately unreal.

Liberation is the realization of the singular Self, wherein the knots of transformation have been stilled; as the Śruti says: "All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven."
And it is said: "From that, creation manifests as a bubble.

Furthermore, for the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins), liberation is the state of being of the nature of bliss; for according to their view, the Self—which is experienced during the state of transmigratory existence under the influence of the veil of ignorance—is [liberated when that veil is removed].

From such scriptural passages as, "The Self is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," there arises, through the practice of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) and the removal of the veil of ignorance (avidyā),
a direct realization [of the Self] as being beautiful with its innate bliss and self-luminosity that is unlimited and unsurpassed.
Liberation [is defined as follows]: according to the scripture, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss";
and in that system, liberation is indeed pure mind-only by its very nature.

Although the continuum of consciousness, whose intrinsic nature is luminosity, is obscured by adventitious stains such as passion due to the power of beginningless ignorance, [it becomes purified] through the abandonment of those respective adventitious stains by means of the cultivation of the meditation on selflessness and so forth.
Liberation is the direct realization of one's own true nature, which is of the form of imperishable light, through the power of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); as they say:
"This mind is luminous by nature; the defilements are adventitious."
"When they have passed away, that imperishable light [shines] for the sake of all.

For the Vaibhāṣikas, liberation is the cessation of the continuum, like a lamp. According to their view, the five aggregates—form and so forth—which constitute the fruit, arise from causes such as afflictions and karma.
This saṃsāra consists of both of these, as they say:
"Saṃsāra is cause and fruit.
Liberation, however, is like a lamp: when the causes such as oil are exhausted, it is impossible for it to arise again.

Cessation is likewise [attained] through the abandonment of the afflictions, karma, and so forth, by means of the practice of meditating on selflessness and other [doctrines], resulting in the cessation of all five aggregates, beginning with form; as they say:
"Just as a lamp that has reached extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere,"
He goes neither to any country nor to any intermediate direction; through the mere exhaustion of craving, he attains peace.
"The yogin who has thus attained liberation goes neither to the earth nor to the intermediate space;
he goes to no region, nor to any intermediate direction, but through the destruction of the afflictions (kleśa), he attains absolute peace.
Thus, regarding the *pralayākalas*, there is the inclusion of the qualification "consisting of both the knowable and the unknowable."

This is the intended meaning: here, in the first two positions, because Brahman consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it possesses the nature of a *savedya-pralayākala* (a pralayākala with objects of knowledge) due to its self-reflective awareness; whereas in the other [position], since no single eternal cognizer is admitted, it possesses the nature of an *apavedya-pralayākala* (a pralayākala without objects of knowledge).
Since this fourfold set of positions serves as an illustration for other alternative views,
even in the liberation (*apavarga*) of the followers of Akṣapāda and others— which consists in the total cessation of all qualities of the self—
one should understand that it is essentially equivalent to the state of the *pralayākalas* who have dissolved their objects of cognition; and as for those *pralayākalas*:
Because two impurities remain, the cause of saṃsāra is not exhausted, and thus there is only the state of being a transmigrator;

therefore, it has been stated that even liberation, which consists primarily of this [state], is to be abandoned. And so, the effort made by them toward the state of a *pralayākala*—even though it occurs spontaneously through the dissolution of various respective principles—is indeed futile.

This is the intended meaning; for this very reason, by the statement "imagined through the resolve of tomorrow," the unreality of these four positions is revealed, since they are merely conceptual constructs. || 29-30 ||

Now, one might object: here, liberation is indeed defined as the destruction of bondage; and according to the maxim, "A person with cataracts is better than one bound by [the three impurities]," this refers to the *pralayākala*, who is bound by two impurities (*dvimālaba*), in comparison to the *sakala*, who is bound by all three impurities (*trimālaba*).

Having raised the objection— "Why is this [state] called 'perfected' (vṛtta), and why is liberation, which consists mostly of that [state], to be abandoned absolutely?"— he says: "Even having attained that, after a long time, because of having enjoyed the full expansion of its experiences..."
But at the end of the dissolution of those respective principles, he has come to the creation above them.

This person— namely, the Vaiṣṇava and others— having attained the state of a *mantra* through the awakening bestowed by Ananteśa, and although for a long time they have reached that liberation which is essentially the state of a *pralayākala*, they remain an enjoyer of the full expansion of experiences consisting of delusion and the like associated with the *pralayākala*.

Immediately following the dissolution of that level of experience belonging to the *pralayākala*, at the end of the dissolution of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *māyā*, and again at the commencement of creation,
[they] awaken for the sake of becoming *mantras*.

According to this principle, when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, through the awakening characterized by the stimulation of knowledge and action performed by Ananteśa, one attains the state of a Mantra upon reaching the pure creation that exists above Māyā; otherwise, however, [it is not so].

Thus it is established that there is the state of being in saṃsāra; for this very reason, even when liberation as described in other systems such as Vaiṣṇava philosophy is attained, the destruction of saṃsāra does not occur, and therefore its status as something to be abandoned has been stated therein. || 31 ||

Now, one might ask: "Even though the state of being a *pralayākala* is common to all, what is the cause for some among them to possess the status of a *mantra* while others remain subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"We shall explain this further on; let it rest for now. (4.32)

Regarding the word *agra*— at the beginning of the ninth chapter, as he will state: "This is declared to be the impurity of karma (*kārmamala*), along with which the *layākala*s remain within the depths of the cave like sleeping serpents."
Then, with their latent impressions awakened, they partake of their respective destinies and transmigrate again and again in this world, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings.
Furthermore, those who have begun the practice of meditation for the sake of destroying the formative forces of karma,
yet have passed away before reaching the perfection of that meditation—
"By virtue of the excellence of the ripening of their internal contemplation, those great ones attain the state of mantra; this is wondrous, and [it arises] from wondrous action.
As for the phrase "let this suffice," it is because this [discussion] is of no use regarding the present subject of the principles of logic (tarka-tattva). || 32 ||

Now, one might object: "If indeed the destruction of saṃsāra does not occur through the liberation taught by other philosophical systems, then why do these people, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others, take delight in them? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, he who is mocked by the doctrines fabricated by ignorant folk..."
With his consciousness firmly rooted in a false teacher, he is colored by the noose of Māyā.

Indeed, that person— whether a Vaiṣṇava or otherwise— who has been deluded by the ignorant masses through the various doctrines such as the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* imagined by groups of teachers like Kapila, [is led] by that Blessed Supreme Lord who is renowned throughout all the worlds.

By the noose of *māyā*—that is, by the power (*śakti*) called *vāmā*—he is made intensely attached to that very [world]; for this reason, his mind is fixed upon a false teacher (*asadguru*), a particular preceptor who instructs in the principles; he is one who has placed his trust [in him], and not merely one desiring knowledge. However, for one who places trust in a true teacher (*sadguru*), liberation occurs directly.

The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established by implication; for this very reason, immediately following the principle of reasoning (*tarka*), he has begun to explain the true nature of the Guru, which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration and is logically connected to it. || 33 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then because this Vaiṣṇava and the others are presided over by the Left-hand path (vāmā), no confidence can arise even in a true guru; what then can be said regarding the direct attainment of liberation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He too is led toward a true guru by means of right reasoning;
that right reasoning is indeed Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), which is the will of the Supreme Lord.
"He too" refers to the Vaiṣṇava and others whose minds are rooted in a false teacher. Now,

it has been stated everywhere that the growth [of understanding] regarding a reality consistent with logic is brought about by reasoning, and the attainment of a true teacher occurs through the power of Śiva.

"Where firm conviction arises through certainty regarding that which is joined with reason—this is the grace of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. Here, "that" refers to Pure Knowledge; "desire" refers to that form of grace which culminates in the attainment of a true guru.
And this was not stated merely as his own invention; thus he says:

"In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, it has been stated by him [the Lord]: 'He who, by the will of Śiva, desires to depart, is led toward a true guru for the sake of the attainment of enjoyment and liberation. (4.35)
He—penetrated by the power of Rudra and desiring to attain his own true nature—is led toward a true guru by the will of Śiva, which takes the form of the power called Jyeṣṭhā;
that is, he is set in motion toward the presence of a true guru, by which his worldly enjoyment and liberation are accomplished. Therefore...

Since there is no difference between right reasoning (sattarka) and the power of Śiva (śivaśakti), it is established that whatever engagement occurs through right reasoning directed toward a true guru is in fact by the power of Śiva alone. || 35 ||
Now, it has been stated that "the turning toward [the teacher], whether he be a false guru or a true guru, occurs solely by the will of Śiva";

one might then object: "Let that [turning] occur toward a true guru alone; what is the need for a gradual process? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that case, this descent of power (śaktipāta) proceeds in a sequential manner."
Having stayed with a false teacher or having resorted to another [false] scripture, he who has taken to the true path— || 4.36 ||

"In another scripture" means, by implication, on an evil path such as that of the Vaiṣṇavas and others; "the true path" refers to the characteristics of the Śaiva teacher and scripture. "Therein" means: after having relied upon an evil teacher and so forth, one subsequently relies upon a true teacher and so forth. (36)

Now, one might object: "If this world, by the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), were to take refuge in a Guru or a scripture—whether they be of the nature of existence or non-existence—let that be so; what indeed is the harm? But what is the cause for those two [the Guru and the scripture] themselves being either non-existent or existent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The distinction between the presence and absence of the [divine] essence within the teacher and the scripture, as well as the variety of the descent of power (śaktipāta), will be analyzed in detail further on. (4.37)

Regarding the phrase "herein"—referring to what was just stated—and "prior to this"—referring to the occasion of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and so forth—the "differentiator" is the cause of distinction. Thus, the teachers and others belonging to other philosophical systems are presided over by the power of *māyā* called Vāmā, whereas our own [teachers] are presided over by the power Jyeṣṭhā; therefore...
This world is presided over by that very power; one should place one's trust in it. ||37||
Nor is this without authority; thus he says:
"It is stated in the *Svacchanda Śāstra* that Māyā causes all those who propound doctrines such as Vaiṣṇavism and the like to wander, while they desire liberation in what is not liberation. (4.38)
"It causes one to wander" means because of grasping at what is not that [as being that]; thus it says, "through the desire for liberation in what is not liberation.
And here, regarding the reading by way of the meaning, this is the intention—that which has been stated there in many ways. As it has been said:
"Beyond this is Māyā, which deludes all living beings."
By that [ignorance], which is the enemy without enmity, those whose intellects are deluded...
In this world, disputants argue, "This is the truth; this is not," and by abandoning the true path, they quickly lead one onto a wrong path.
Those lowest of men who lack devotion to the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, and the Scripture; who are experts in the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic.
"For Māyā indeed causes them to wander, desiring liberation where there is no liberation.
Likewise,
those who know the Sāṃkhya, Vedas, and Purāṇas [are deluded] regarding the determination of other systems.
When other proponents of liberation are not able to transgress them, [how much less so can others]?
"Deluded by illusion, they suffer, desiring liberation in what is not liberation. (38)

Now, one might object: "If these people, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others, have been deluded by Māyā, then because their latent impressions (saṃskāra) would take root in that very [delusion], they would not descend from the false path; thus, they could never ascend to the true path. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

But he who, even while established therein, is skilled in the exertion of reflective awareness, is purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta) through the majesty of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). || 4.39 ||
He indeed ascends the true path, freed from all obstacles;

moreover, he who has taken root there through the firmness of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) in the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions, and who is proficient by means of that reflective awareness (parāmarśa) which consists of right reasoning (sattarka) and is ever-arising— by him [the path is ascended].

Being skilled in the discrimination between what is essential and what is non-essential, he— by virtue of the majesty of pure knowledge (*vidyā*) consisting of right reasoning (*sattarka*) and being sanctified by the presiding power of the *Jyeṣṭhā* energy— ascends the true path without obstacle; that is, he should become established in our philosophical system, whereby his liberation (*mokṣa*) becomes manifest.
It may be so. || 39 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for the arising of this reflective awareness (parāmarśa)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"First of all, that [reflective awareness] arises spontaneously as the reasoning (tarka) of someone. (4.40)
And that [awakening] is declared in the scripture to be innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), consisting of one's own direct realization;
it arises from itself— meaning independently of causes such as the instruction of a teacher well-known in the world— but not, in reality, without cause in an absolute sense.

Since other causes, such as the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvara-śaktipāta*), are also possible, for this very reason his name is also explained etymologically (*yaugika*) in our system; thus he says, "And he... and so forth.
"He" refers to one who has independently engaged in reasoning (*svayaṃ-pravṛtta-tarka*); "innate" (*sāṃsiddhika*) means [one who possesses] perfection together with reasoning.
The meaning is that he has arrived [at this state] by birth alone. And it has been said:
"He in whom this [knowledge] arises spontaneously, independent of a teacher or scripture, is called a *saṃsiddhika*—a great sage established in reality."

Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, it is "one's own" (*sva*), meaning it does not depend on others such as a guru; he whose self (*ātman*)—that is, whose nature (*svabhāva*)—is the well-ascertained knowledge that "this alone is it," is so described. || 40 ||
Now, one might object: "In other contexts, the realization of the supreme reality is said to have other causes as well, such as the guru;
why then is it said here that it occurs 'by itself alone'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even that which was stated in the *Kiraṇa*—from the guru, from scripture, or by oneself... (4.41).
In this regard, each subsequent stage is primary, while each preceding one is a means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, as it is stated in the *Kiraṇa-saṃhitā*, in order to know the supreme reality which is empty of the qualities of *māyā*—
"Such emptiness is to be known from the guru, from the scripture, and from oneself";
by these words, three causes have been stated. Among them, each subsequent one is intended to be more primary, as follows:
from the guru comes the scripture, and even more so than that, self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*), because each preceding one [depends upon] the former.
Just as the teacher and the scripture are means (*upāya*) [to realization], so too is that [realization] itself within one's own self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*). Thus,

according to the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Those things which are to be abandoned even by means of them are called means," the teacher and the scripture are secondary because they are merely means.
Self-reflection alone possesses primacy, which is why it is the only one mentioned here. || 41 ||
Therefore, he who possesses reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) arising from himself alone is the one authorized in all matters; thus he says:
"He for whom this sound reasoning (*sattarka*) arises spontaneously is entitled to authority in every respect. (4.42)
He who possesses this aforementioned right reasoning (*sattarka*) arising spontaneously— independently of a teacher or others— is consecrated and initiated by the goddesses of his own self-awareness;
he becomes qualified in every respect, such as in yoga and knowledge.
But surely,

according to such statements as, "Indeed, there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation," how can this [practitioner] have eligibility everywhere while setting aside initiation and the like?

Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "He is initiated and consecrated by the goddesses of his own consciousness. Those which are one's own consciousnesses—the functions of the senses—are precisely what are proclaimed as "the functions of the mantra directed toward the external."

The meaning is that these goddesses, by such statements as "these very [powers] are proclaimed to be the powers of this inward-turned [subject]," illuminate the identity with the subject; through them, by the stimulation of knowledge and action, one attains sovereignty everywhere.
And for this reason, he says that he alone is supremely excellent:
"He alone is proclaimed as the foremost among all teachers. (4.43)
By virtue of its proximity, there is eligibility for others who are conceptually constructed.
And because he is the preeminent among all the teachers to be mentioned hereafter— beginning with Akalpitakalpaka and the others—
in his presence others have no authority for bestowing grace upon others and so forth;
thus it was said, "In his presence, not [others]," and so on, as he will state later:
Just as the liberated Śivas are indeed inferior to Śiva who is established from the beginning through differentiation,
so too those who have acquired knowledge are inferior to those whose knowledge is innate.
"In his presence, they have no authority like those whose nature is that of liberated Śivas;
rather, their state is one of silence, or else it is the following of his activities. (43)

Now, there is no dispute among anyone that the mastery of the scriptures comes from a guru; so what can be said of one who has no guru at all regarding the mastery of the scriptures? Thus, even one who has engaged in independent reasoning, when beginning initiation and the like—
Fearing that one might ask, "By what means could one attain any spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) whatsoever—such as initiation and the like—if one is devoid of the scriptures? he says:
"He understands the entire meaning of the scriptures through right reasoning alone. (4.44)
They think; thus they perceive. || 44 ||
One might object: "How can there be an understanding of all the scriptures by this alone, without dependence on a guru and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) indeed—that truth does not exist which it would not illuminate."
And this is not established by reasoning alone, but also by scripture; thus he says:
"And the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises in him spontaneously. (4.45)

Thus, in the aforementioned venerable passage, by means of the word "akasmāt" (suddenly/without cause), there is the connection: that reality—which consists of the understanding of the entire scripture and is caused by right reasoning—is stated "by the word 'akasmāt'. Now, one might ask: "What does 'akasmāt' mean?"
Anticipating the objection, "How could this be stated based on the mere word alone? he says:
"That reason which is not established in the world is called 'accidental' (akasmāt). (46)
And this very [state] is the unfolding of the Supreme Lord’s Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
For "spontaneously" (*akasmāt*) is said to mean "without cause," yet this is not tenable; for if that were the case, it would have to be either eternally real or unreal. (46)

Therefore, there must necessarily be some cause for this, and it is not one established by worldly consensus, because [causes] such as the instruction of a guru are not directly perceived. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is something not established by the world;
and this very [cause] is the manifestation of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) belonging to the Supreme Lord, which is to be inferred from its fruit, and by whose power alone—
For him, there may arise a great intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) that is independent of teachers and scriptures and encompasses all objects,
as he will state:
"Furthermore, from the 'medium-intense' [level of practice], all ignorance is completely removed."
For it is this very [consciousness] that undergoes the states of bondage, liberation, and suchness.
"That great intuitive knowledge (prātibha) which is independent of scriptures and teachers.
Thus [it is said].
And because of the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a multiplicity of this [consciousness]; thus he says:
"Its divisions are many: those without a foundation and those with a foundation. (4.47)
That [consciousness], though all-pervading, is also situated in its parts; it abides in both primary and secondary aspects.
It is the foundation, its subsistence upon another, that supreme wisdom, and its creative activity. (4.48)

"Emerging from the wall, he is 'without a wall' (nirbhitti); he exists together with a wall, thus he is 'with a wall' (sahabhittika). This refers to the primary twofold division of the innate (sāṃsiddhika) [liberation]: "he who has gone to all walls" and "he who has gone to a portion [of a wall]," as it is said. That too [is explained as follows].

There are three divisions of that which possesses a wall (sabhittika)—namely, whether it is "situated in a portion" (aṃśagata), "established in the primary portion" (mukhyāṃśaniṣṭhita), or "otherwise"—and with the addition of that which lacks a wall (nirbhitti), there are four. Furthermore, there is multiplicity due to the diversity of the walls and their respective portions; herein, [the distinctions arise] through the presence or absence of these.
The *Bhedollāsa* explains that term “wall” (*bhitti*) with the passage beginning with “the wall,” etc.

Regarding the phrase “dependence on another” (*paropajīvitva*): the meaning is that the other upon whom one depends is the “wall. Anticipating the question “Who is the other? it is said: “the other is wisdom (*prajñā*) and its activity. Wisdom is one’s own self-reflexive awareness (*svavimarśa*).

"His work" refers to a treatise composed by another that expresses various specific rituals. Now, one might object: since knowledge arises for this [treatise] spontaneously, there is no "other" upon which it depends;
therefore, let it indeed be "without a foundation"—what is the harm? However, if it is further asserted that it possesses a "foundation," then...

It would not have the status of being spontaneously accomplished (*saṃsiddhika*), because it would result in being merely imagined by depending on another; nor can there be a particular (*viśeṣa*) that lacks its corresponding universal (*sāmānya*). Thus, how can its nature as "co-arising" (*sahabhittikatva*) be asserted? It is said: here, indeed, it arises from the emergence of sound reasoning (*sattarka*) by itself.
For the perfected Guru, whose every bond has been severed, who is filled with the state of Bhairava,
and who has achieved his own purpose within his own self, the sole supreme aim in his remaining life is the grace of others;
as it has been said:
"Previously,
for one whose nature is the tearing asunder of the machinery of all constraints,
there is no purpose whatsoever in remaining in a residual state of existence other than [bestowing] grace."
Thus,
perceiving that there is something to be done for oneself, this world exerts effort; it does not direct even the slightest activity of its own nature toward what belongs to another.
"But for him whose impurities of all worldly existence have been destroyed and who is filled with the state of Bhairavī, his manifest duty is merely this much: the task of the world.
Thus it is said. In that regard, for this one of stainless consciousness, toward those to be graced, [his action] is indeed without external instruments.

Regarding "the state of acting for the benefit [of others]": by the mere act of perceiving without further conceptual synthesis, he bestows grace upon them by transferring his own consciousness and bringing them to equality with himself, as was stated previously:
"Those whose stainless consciousness [perceives] Him through the process of assuming His very form—they too become of that same nature; such is the extent of His grace.
It is with this very intention that [the state of grace] is called "wall-less" (*nirbhittika*), because even in the act of gracing others, it is independent of anything else.

Thus this is said. Furthermore, for those whose consciousness is not yet pure, its capacity to bestow grace is necessarily accompanied by external instruments—since it functions here through such considerations as, "This person is to be graced by me in this manner," and so forth; therefore, everything [is required].
It requires an external collection of implements by which his favoring of others may be accomplished, as was stated previously:
"If he, even for those whose consciousness is not pure, [acts] through the power of his sovereignty..."
"Desiring to bestow grace, one should resort to that procedure which is to come about for him.
And for that very purpose, even for this [teacher] who possesses the form of the Supreme Lord:

"And thus, there is respect for hearing and studying the scriptures and other means for that [attainment]. Furthermore, even though the mind is not yet purified, because of the diversity of those to be graced, the means of assistance are also infinite according to their respective dispositions; it is with this in mind that [the scripture] declares:
The scripture, moreover, must be consulted by everyone; otherwise, the benefit of others would not be accomplished, as it has been said:
"O fair-faced one, because of the diversity of the minds of men, there is a diversity of scriptures."
Just as there is a distinction among medicines of great potency according to the different types of diseases.

"Just as a physician, having known a single medicine, does not treat every case [with it], so too a teacher, relying upon a single cause, would not be a teacher in all cases. It is with this very intention that his omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) was stated. For he is indeed one and the same for everyone.
With reference to a specific scripture, it favors only those who are suitable for it—

this is what has been stated regarding its partial nature, as he will say: "One who knows the ritual manual (*kalpa*), one who knows the collection thereof, one who knows the scripture (*śāstra*), and one who knows the meaning of the compendium (*saṃhitā*)."
"And one who knows the meaning of all the scriptures... and so forth; "Whoever has thoroughly mastered the knowledge of a particular scripture, let him perform the exposition therein."
"And not otherwise...
and so forth. Regarding even the partial systems that constitute those various scriptures:
"From the Veda comes Śaiva, from that Vāma, from that Dakṣa, and from that Kula."

Thus, by such statements as "Then the Mata, and then also the Trika, which is the supreme among all," the fact that each subsequent [system] possesses primacy while the others possess non-primacy is stated;
this constitutes their nature as primary and secondary. Nor does this [Trika], even so, depend upon the perspective of another.
The state of being spontaneously accomplished (*sāṃsiddhikatva*) is refuted— because he has already achieved all that was to be done within his own self by himself,
and because this [state] is required for the sake of others— as was stated previously:
"For there is no obstruction whatsoever, anywhere, of that independent one."
"For there can be no grace for a person whose mind is not pure without [the appropriate] means.
Thus, because this [grace] does not depend on anything else within its own self, it is indeed *sāṃsiddhika* (spontaneously accomplished); therefore, what was stated above is alone correct. (47–48)
And this was not stated merely as his own invention; thus he says:
"Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, whoever knows [this] in its true essence, shall eternally partake of accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is initiated. (4.49)
Thus, for one who knows this according to reality, initiation that leads to Nirvāṇa occurs; so it is declared in the venerable Triṃśakaśāsana. (4-50)

Because he is graced by the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*), he has no need for a guru or other such requirements; thus, he is one who— though [ordinarily] characterized by external initiatory implements (*adṛṣṭa*) and the mandala consisting of sacrificial rites and the like—
is nevertheless, for that very reason, devoid of oblations of sesame and clarified butter, and possesses [an initiation] that is free from doubt.

One who, while practicing the initiation leading to Nirvāṇa, knows his own self in this very way— namely, by himself alone, in its true essential form, because no specific attributes are assumed— is truly initiated;
for by the goddesses of his own consciousness itself, preceded by the destruction of the bonds (pāśas), he is liberated.

He has been rendered a fit vessel for the knowledge of his own self; for this very reason, he is a perpetual yogi—one who possesses identity with the Supreme Lord even during the state of worldly emergence—and for this very reason, he is a possessor of *siddhi*, meaning that while still alive, he partakes in the perfection characterized by liberation. This is what is meant.

It is stated in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*: "This is not without authority"—this is the meaning. And therein, immediately after the verse beginning with "Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala... and so forth.
Although other passages such as "By the mere knowledge of this... exist, they have not been cited because they are not relevant to the present context;
furthermore, since the maṇḍala has not been seen, it is understood that [the rite] is "devoid of oblations of sesame and clarified butter," and so forth.
That too has not been recited. || 49-50 ||
And there is another designation for him as well; thus he says:

"The unconstructed Guru is to be known as the *sāṃsiddhika* (one perfected by nature)," as recorded in our scripture. That Guru who is *sāṃsiddhika* [is not to be confused with one] by means of another teacher.
Because it has not been produced, it should be known as "unconstructed"— the meaning is that it may even be designated by the term "unconstructed.
Having thus described the unconstructed Guru, he speaks of another Guru as well, by virtue of his connection to him:
But he who, through the cultivation of a self that partakes of that very nature, [acts] without another— || 4-51 ||
The teacher who knows the scriptures is declared in the scriptures to be the "unconceived-conceiver" (akalpitakalpaka);
however, even one who possesses the nature of spontaneous realization lacks full perfection so long as that self-arisen knowledge has not reached its ultimate completion.

By virtue of the power of self-contemplation (*ātmabhāvanā*) arising from such statements as "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*," the knower of the scriptures— disregarding any external teacher or other authority— is himself the teacher, because his knowledge is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) and thus not artificially constructed through contemplation of another.
And because he conceptualizes according to the sequence of perceiving the scriptures, he is described in our treatise as "the conceptualizer of the non-conceptual.
Like the *sāṃsiddhika* [spontaneously enlightened], there are many varieties of this type as well; thus he says:
"Its varieties also arise from superior, middling, inferior, and other such means. (4.52)
The means is the descent of power (śaktipāta). || 52 ||

Now, one might ask: "Is the cultivation of the Self (*ātmabhāvanā*) alone the cause for the fulfillment of this spontaneously arisen knowledge, or is there something else as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Or rather, [it arises] from cultivation (*bhāvanā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), dreams (*svapna*), vows (*vrata*), or sacrifice (*huti*)."
The one of great intelligence attains the uncontrived and sublime consecration. || 4-53 ||

Indeed, this one of great wisdom, by virtue of the majesty of the infinite means beginning with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, and because he has not been [initiated] by another such as a guru and the like, obtains the "unconstructed" (*akalpita*), and for that very reason the "lofty"—that is, the great—consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
the meaning is that he becomes qualified for the knowledge of the scriptures and other such matters. || 53 ||
Now, one might ask: "If this is so, what is the proof for the infinity of causes such as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the attainment of knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the venerable Vājasaneyi, the venerable Vīra, and the venerable Brahmayāmala..."
This was clearly stated by the Creator in the Śrīsiddhā and elsewhere as well.
"This" refers to the infinity of the causes for [the arising of] meditative cultivation and so forth. || 54 ||
Thus, although it is stated in many scriptures, he first cites the *Śrīsarvavīra* text for the sake of illustration:
"Because its activity proceeds from its own will, an infinity of causes is maintained."
Sometimes by means of the yoga of devotion, or by ritual action, or even by knowledge. || 4.55 ||
Through the instruction of the knowledge of reality, by means of mantras, or even by initiation, and through many other such modes, the Supreme Lord [acts]. (4.56)
The Lord of the entire universe bestows grace upon those wandering in saṃsāra;
for in this regard, it is said:
"In the beginningless saṃsāra, the Supreme Lord is the cause."
"By his very nature, he is always intent upon the grace of living beings.
Having thus begun by explaining that the Supreme Lord acts out of grace solely through his own sovereignty, [the text continues]:
"Therefore, Śiva releases by his own will those beings who are bound by that [power]."
Having established that very point with these words, this passage explains that although the Blessed One possesses absolute autonomy (*svātantrya*),
his act of favoring others is characterized by other instrumental causes; for instance, [it is said] of that very Supreme Lord, the Blessed One:

By such statements as, “His very will (*icchā*) alone is the cause...,” although His own will is indeed the cause for the engagement in acts such as grace (*anugraha*), the infinity of causes is asserted because that will itself varies according to the diversity of those to be graced (*anugrāhya*).

In reality, however, there is nothing else apart from that which must be depended upon by this [Lord], as has been stated many times previously; therefore, because He is engaged in the protection and other functions of the entire circle of living beings subject to birth, this Supreme Lord is the "Master" (pati), who— according to their respective dispositions— sometimes acts through devotion and sometimes through yoga.

By means of these and many other such types of causes, [the Lord] bestows grace upon the transmigrating beings—the class of contracted subjects—meaning that He makes them manifest as the nature of full knowledge by casting off their contraction. By the phrase "by these and others," practices such as austerity (*tapas*) and recitation (*japa*) are included; thus...
The essential meaning is that many means for the attainment of perfect knowledge are possible.
Even though this has been shown in this way, in order to provide further proof for the infinity of causes,
he recites the venerable *Brahmayāmala* text:
O beloved, through the awakening of the circle of mothers, and through the refinement of ascetic practice.
Through meditation, yoga, recitation, knowledge, the propitiation of mantras, and observance of vows,
one attains the common knowledge of the Kula, which bestows the siddhis of the Kaula.

Of the Mothers— the sovereigns of the instruments such as sight— either through the thorough realization of the mandala in its aspect of power (śakti), setting aside its nature as a mere circular form,
by means of the agency of the circle of mothers; or else, through the awakening [of the disciple] via the sequence beginning with the "dear union" (priyamelāpa) performed by that circle of mothers.
By means of such infinite signs as these,

and according to the statement beginning with "The *kula* is the sphere of origin," [it refers to] the *kula*— that which is about to arise by way of appearing as something distinct from one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*).
The meaning is that in the entire universe, which consists of the knower and the known, there exists a universal (*sāmānya*)—that which persists through all things;

for otherwise, this [universal] could not even appear. Therefore, it bestows that perfection (*siddhi*) which arises within the *kula*—that is, within the Self—in the form of one's own essential nature alone.

The meaning is that knowledge whose essence is the supreme subject (parapramātṛ), which is throbbing with vitality, is necessarily attained; this is due to "refinement" (saṃskāra)—that is, from initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth. || 57–58 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then is not the primary characteristic of the Guru—who is the non-conceptualizer of the conceptualized—his abiding in the entire web of causes such as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like?
To dispel this doubt, the author himself says:
Wherever the goal, which consists of the knowledge of reality, is perceived, he alone is indeed the guru; there, let a web of reasons be fashioned.

Indeed, that very full knowledge which consists of the supreme reality (*paratattva*)—the characteristic of one's own self that one desires to realize—is precisely what is to be recognized as the unconstructed-constructing Guru whenever and wherever it is perceived;
he is not merely one who is established in a web of causes such as mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like. For it is thus:

According to the maxim, "Causes do not necessarily possess their effects," even if someone exerts effort toward the causal complex beginning with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they might at some time fail to attain perfect knowledge; how then could such a person possess the capacity to conceive what has not been conceived?
Since knowledge of such a nature occurs only occasionally, there must be some cause for it;

thus it was said, "In that regard, let a web of causes be imagined. Therefore, the essential meaning is this: here, his primary characteristic is precisely the possession of perfect knowledge, which is the result [of those causes]. || 59 ||

And this is not our own invention alone; thus he provides corroboration by way of its meaning: "In the *Brahmayāmala*, there is no other defining characteristic [of a practitioner] apart from the knowledge of reality:
'One whose self is cultivated and perfectly serene, who is always devoted to recitation and fire-offerings.'"

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: setting aside other characteristics mentioned in other scriptures, the *Śrībrahmayāmala* states that the primary characteristic of a Guru is precisely the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). It is with this very intention [that the following was said].
"Even if devoid of all auspicious marks, a teacher who possesses knowledge is supreme," and so forth,
as stated elsewhere.
Does this not contradict the scriptures, given that even for one who has exerted effort in meditation and other practices, no fruit whatsoever arises?
Anticipating this doubt, he again provides a corroboration by way of its meaning:
And it is said in that very same place: "When service has been performed without conceptual construction... (4.60)
When it is asked, "If the practitioner does not attain success, what should be done?", [the answer is]:
his own initiation into the self by means of the sequence of recognition.
Then, for the sake of establishing its state of being manifest (*sasphuratva*), the object to be proven (*sādhya*) becomes established.
Regarding this, in the *Śrībrahmayāmala* itself it is said: "Without freedom from conceptual construction (*avikalpataḥ*), one who remains in doubt does not attain success."
By such statements, "vikalpa" means doubt; because of its absence— due to the firmness of one's own position—
even when the service consisting of a hundred thousand recitations and so forth prescribed in one's own ritual manual has been performed,
for the practitioner, due to some deficiency, that which results from its fruit...

When the Blessed One was thus prompted— when the question was asked: "If accomplishment, characterized by the attainment of desired objects, were not to exist, then what would be the use of that [scripture]?"— [he spoke of] his own, i.e., pertaining to himself, the *saṃ* (perfect), meaning thoroughly free from doubt and error, consisting of the realization "all this is indeed the Self."
The sequence of that knowledge is as follows: through the progressive intensity of practice, there is an ascent to the supreme support for the sake of establishing its state of radiance;
consequently, it serves as an auxiliary cause for the intensification of the essential nature of the mantra and so forth to be recited, which is one's own self.
Initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*) is defined as the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*) of the nature of supreme consciousness;

this is what was stated by the Lord in response. The meaning is that by means of this, the object the seeker wishes to accomplish becomes established for him, reaching its final consummation in the form of the fruit. || 60-61 ||
Right here he explains the intended meaning:
"By this, one's own self-knowledge is established as being accompanied by creative vibration. (4.62)
It has been stated that, primarily, if the teacher (*ācārya*) is not "radiant" (*sasphura*),

then by this *Śrībrahmayāmala* text, it is explained that the very consciousness of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) regarding the mantra to be recited and so forth is the cause for its radiance— provided, that is, that the teacher is [absent] as the primary factor.

Due to the lack of union with the identity of the Supreme Lord, [the mantra] would not be radiant; therefore, while the Ācārya is indeed radiant, one should have him perform initiation for oneself, so that even one's own mantra may become radiant.
[Objection: But let the Ācārya be radiant or non-radiant—what concern is this of ours?
Furthermore, without that [initiation], initiation could not occur by itself; for in that case, a contradiction with the scriptures would arise.
Anticipating the objection, "Is this then a false interpretation?", he says:
"And in that very same [context], moreover, in the ritual of the worship of the venerable Raktā... (4.63).

By always performing the prescribed rite, one is called an *ācārya* after a month; an *sādhaka* after a fortnight; a *putraka* after half of that [half-month]; and likewise a *samayin* after half of that [half-month]. (4.64)
In that very [text], namely the *Śrībrahmayāmala*, again— immediately following the question and answer just mentioned—
in the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) of the venerable Raktā, i.e., Śrī Caṇḍikā, it is stated with pre-eminence— that is,
independently of a guru and so forth— the prescribed method (*vidhi*).

By performing daily—that is, every day—the taking up, recitation, meditation, and so forth of that mantra, the practitioner (sādhaka) is called an "Ācārya" within a month, even without [undergoing] consecration and the like; the meaning is that one who undertakes the authority appropriate to that status does not fall back. Thus, by a fortnight...
The *śādhaka* [attains success] in seven and a half days; the *putraka* in four days less a quarter; and the *samayin* [attains it] in [three and three-quarter days]. || 63-64 ||
One might ask: "How can one possess the status of a *samayin* and so forth without initiation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since Raktādevī initiates [the disciple] through the application of recitation (*japa*) in due order, one should perform this prescribed rite in the absence of a Guru. (4.65)
By the word "should initiate" (*dīkṣayet*), every action performed by the Guru is indicated; as it has been said:
"He offers oblations, he mutters prayers, and in all these cases, Caṇḍikā is present. "In due order" means according to the stages beginning with that of the *samayin*. Now, if this is so, then...
Fearing that the entire scripture which speaks in praise of the Guru would otherwise become meaningless, he says:

"In the absence of a Guru," and so forth. This means that when a Guru—as previously described, such as the one who is both unconstructed and the constructor, and who possesses expansive awareness—is found, then this—namely, what was just mentioned—one [attains] by oneself.

One should perform—that is, carry out—the ritual procedure consisting of the reception of the mantra and so forth; otherwise, however, one should have the teacher perform everything, such is the intended meaning. || 65 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, why has the fault of the self—namely, that those of small intellect who have merely received mantras [from a teacher] suffer, as stated in passages such as '...and those of small intellect who have studied the sciences from books suffer'—been mentioned elsewhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And since such a fault has been stated regarding the study of knowledge from a book when one is dead, it is not prohibited in the absence of that fault. (4.66)
"In the *Siddhāmata* (mate iti)" means in the *Śrīsiddhāmata*, as he will say:
"For it is stated in the *Siddhāmata*: 'Those whose knowledge has been learned from books...
By "by him" (tena) is meant by the Blessed One; "of such a kind" (īdṛśaḥ) refers to that which was just mentioned.
It is characterized by the absence of radiance; for mantras residing in books are indeed devoid of potency (*nirvīrya*).
Consequently, when they are taken from such sources, their own inherent splendor (*tejas*) does not flash forth to accomplish their respective supernatural powers (*svasiddhi*).
Thus, it is stated that those who have studied the *vidyās* from books experience only suffering, due to the absence of success.
As he will say:
"A mantra that remains in written form is considered here to be devoid of potency;
its splendor does not manifest from the book due to the power of convention."

Thus [it is said]. If that very fault were not to exist, then this would not be a prohibition at all, such as "Mantras should not be studied from books. For, according to the reasoning just stated, the innate power (*tejas*) of certain mantras studied from books might manifest; as he will say:

"But those who recognize the potency even in a mantra obtained from a book, they are said to be purified by Bhairava and are called *sāṃsiddhika*s (those perfected by their own nature). Thus [ends verse 66].
And he recites the very passage from that [text] which makes this intention known:
"When it is asked, 'What is the fruit of keeping the mantras, substances, and so forth secret? [the answer is:
Those who have studied the sciences from books, yet are devoid of initiation and the observances (samaya)... (4.67)

Those characterized by tamas engage extensively in harming others, seeking to subjugate them, and so forth; yet they do not know the true reality. Therefore, it is clear that they are the ones who incur the fault. (4.68)
"In this matter, it has indeed been said: 'Because it was told and kept secret from them, it should not be written in a book;
it can only be obtained from the mouth of the Guru, and never otherwise.'"
Thus,

having carefully considered many such statements spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with: "Likewise, the wise person should always take great care to protect the mantra," and so forth, [one should refrain] from writing the mantras and other [sacred texts] in books and the like.
