When the Goddess asked, "What is the purpose of concealment? the Blessed One gave the reply beginning with, "Knowledge learned from a book," and so forth; for when mantras are written in books and such, some who are "devoid of initiation and the observance of rules" (dīkṣā-samaya-varjitāḥ), and for that very reason "tamasic"—that is, *tamas*—[will encounter them].
Ignorance is of two kinds: that pertaining to the Buddhists and that pertaining to men. Those who exist therein are devoid of knowledge;

having studied those [scriptures], they "practice for the sake of harming others and so forth," yet it would not succeed for them because they do not know the true nature of the mantras and other elements due to the absence of a guru's oral instruction. Therefore, this is quite clear.

They would incur the fault of falling into hell and other such states, because their mantras lack potency due to being merely studied from books; because they fail to achieve success when undertaking various rites of subjugation and the like; and because, while being themselves lax in their faith toward the scripture, they likewise [lead] others to it.
They produce disrespect—thus they would become the cause for the destruction of the system of the scriptures.
Right here, due to the apparent inconsistency, he explains the pair of words: "The preceding pair of words is mutually cause and effect.
Regarding "mutually": because their learning was acquired from books, they are devoid of initiation and the observances (*samaya*).
And because they are devoid of initiation and the observance of its rules, their knowledge is merely that which has been studied from books.
Having thus described the teacher who is "unimagined" (akalpita-kalpaka), he now begins to describe the "imagined" (kalpita) one as well:
"But he who, without the scripture, does not attain the consciousness known as Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)... (4.69).
Seeking the scripture from his guru, he should practice the sequence taught therein.
However, there may be someone who, without the investigation of scripture,
does not attain that consciousness known as Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), which consists of sound reasoning— namely, one for whom sound reasoning does not arise spontaneously.

Desiring to seek out the scriptures through service and other means from some teacher who is not [limited by] conceptual constructs and the like, he should follow the sequence— consisting of such instructions as "having done this, one should do that"— which is found in the scriptures and understood through the traditional usage of the elders, so that for him...
Through the process of propitiating the Guru, the arising of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) shall occur. || 69 ||
Therefore it is said: "Having propitiated the guru with devotion by whatever means possible," (4.70).
Through the application of the sequence of that initiation, he then understands the meaning of the scripture;
however, he who attains consecration [merely] is considered "constructed" (kalpita).
Even though one is already skilled in turning back the entire flood of bonds,
it is indeed said here: "Having propitiated Him, and having then obtained the initiation of Śaṅkara from Him when He is pleased..."
According to the sequence taught in such scriptures, one must first perform the propitiation of the Guru alone;

and since that cannot occur without a means, one should strive all the more to accept him. Furthermore, he is not unique, because those worthy of propitiation are not one—some indeed [are won] through service (*śuśrūṣā*).

Some are propitiated with wealth, and some by means of counter-knowledge (*pratividyā*) and so forth; thus it is stated generally as "by whatever means possible. The sense is that one should act in whatever way the propitiation of a particular [deity] succeeds for that person. Furthermore, this should not be performed merely for the sake of a visible result.

Thus it was said, "through devotion"; from him who has been propitiated, there should arise a connection with the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*), by which his mastery of the scripture may be accomplished. For otherwise, he would lack the qualification even for merely hearing the scripture;
what possibility, then, could there be for its mastery? This is the intended meaning.
As it has been said:
"One should not recite the Śivasaṃhitā in the presence of those who have not been initiated.
And immediately after that:

"In this world, the consecration (sekha) must be performed for one who has mastered the *Śaṃhitā*, and not otherwise. According to such statements, having properly obtained "consecration" from that very guru—
meaning in the form of complete knowledge and so forth— one becomes qualified in all respects for the grace of others and other such activities.

He may indeed be so; yet, because he has been perfected by another teacher, even though he is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*), he is skilled in the complete cessation of the entire flood of fetters (*pāśaugha*)—that is to say, he is capable of bringing about their removal without leaving any residual impressions (*niḥsaṃskāram*). By this, although he is conceptually constructed, [he is effective] in terms of the result.

It has been explained that there is no distinction [between them] that is not conceptually constructed. For the Supreme Lord himself, assuming the form of a teacher, effects the removal of the entire flood of bonds; as it has been said:
"Because Maheśvara, having directly assumed a human body..."
"Out of compassion, in the form of the Guru, he uplifts the submerged subjects.
This is the sense: what, then, in reality, is the distinction between the imagined and the unimagined? || 70-71 ||

Thus, even though [the scripture] is non-constructed (*akalpita*), because it is possible for someone— through the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth— to construct it for the sake of perfecting their own self-knowledge, he is called the "constructor of the non-constructed" (*akalpitakalpaka*). Likewise, even regarding that which is constructed, there may be an understanding of some scripture through the power of one's own intuition (*svapratibhā*), without depending on a teacher or others.
Since [the teaching] arises—thus there would be the state of being unconstructed—he speaks also to designate the Guru known as "the constructed-unconstructed" (kalpitākalpita):
"He who, by means of sequential application, [teaches] some matter within a scripture... (4.72).
For he who is both the imagined and the unimagined would attain awakening spontaneously;

that is, whatever teacher is imagined in relation to some object— whether it be supramundane, scriptural, or ultimate reality— he [attains it] spontaneously, that is, entirely independent of the teacher and other such factors.

By means of the application of sequential order—that is, according to the state of things—one should attain awakening; for even though it is conceptualized, it is itself non-conceptual because the activity of awakening proceeds from within itself. || 72 ||
Anticipating the objection, "If there were even a single part of the imagined guru that were unimagined, what would follow from that? he says:
"That part of him which is unimagined is considered the most excellent. (4.73)
Excellence is produced by the gradations of the portion of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā);
for, in the state of being most excellent, excellence produced by the gradations of Pure Knowledge is the cause—
the sense being that the very internal differentiation of Pure Knowledge is the instrumental cause for [states such as] non-conceptuality (akalpita).

Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not just stated that 'there is no difference whatsoever in the fruit between an imagined and a non-imagined guru'? What, then, is the reason for the non-imagined guru being superior to the imagined one? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Just as, through differentiation, the liberated Śivas are indeed below the eternally established Śiva.
Likewise, those who have acquired knowledge through the innate knowledge (sāṃsiddhika-jñāna) are inferior;
they have no authority in his presence, just like liberated souls whose nature is Śiva. (4.75)
Rather, [the appropriate course] is either remaining silent or following whatever task is to be done;
for even in the doctrine of a distinct Lord (bhedaiśvaravāda), it is said: "In this world, there is equality with Śiva for one who is devoted to Him."

Because of such statements, since there is no distinction in the manifestation of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth among individual souls (*aṇu*), liberation is held to be "attaining equality with Śiva. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between this [Lord] and the liberated souls:
namely, that He is established from beginningless time, whereas for them, their omniscience and other qualities are adventitious (*aupādhika*), just as in the following example.

Therefore, even though there is no difference in their omniscience and other qualities, the liberated Śivas (mukta-śivas) are inferior to him; likewise, those who are "constructed" (kalpita) are inferior even to the "unconstructed" (akalpita) Guru. For his knowledge is unconditioned (*anupādhika*), arising spontaneously from himself, whereas theirs is conditioned by another (*paropādhika*). For this very reason, just as in the presence of Paraśiva...

Those who have been liberated as Śivas (muktaśivas) have no authority over the functions of creation and so forth; likewise, in the presence of a spontaneously perfected (sāṃsiddhika) Guru, those who are merely "constructed" (kalpita) and so on have no authority regarding initiation and the like.
Thus, it is rightly said that "the unconstructed (akalpita) is the most excellent. Now, if this is so, then what?

Raising the doubt as to whether even those [entities] such as the imagined (kalpita), which are like liberated atoms (muktāṇu) in his presence, perform any action or not, he says: "But rather, there is a state of silence," and so forth. (74–75)

Now, one might raise this doubt: "Even for one whose reasoning proceeds spontaneously (*svataḥ pravṛtta-tarka*), was it not previously stated that there is a dependence on scripture and so forth? Is this, then, a defect or an ornament?
Anticipating this, he says:
But that which, though not of an imagined nature, serves to establish the firmness of correspondence— || 4.76 ||
That guru who has received the consecration from another is Bhairava manifest;

moreover, that guru whose form is non-conceptual is so because he possesses the quality of making known— within others as well— the self-arisen gnosis that is the exclusive domain of his own direct experience.
By means of corroboration— consisting of the firm conviction that "it is thus and not otherwise"—

he has attained excellence from all sources, whether collectively from the teacher and the scriptures or individually from either the teacher or the scriptures; such a person, through freedom from further desire regarding his own self, is directly Bhairava himself.
The meaning is that he is permeated by the fullness of supreme consciousness. || 76 ||
One might object: "How can this be established by mere correspondence alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because [it is so] through the sequence of the scriptures and by cultivating the wisdom of a teacher who knows that. (4.77)
Knowledge that is self-validated becomes Bhairava through its fullness;
for, by means of the process of mastering the scriptures and by following the wisdom of a teacher who knows the scriptures,
it becomes consistent with reality through such deliberation as "this is thus, not otherwise."

Knowledge, having attained firmness through the arising of a certainty within the self that "it is exactly thus, and not otherwise," becomes full precisely because of this lack of further expectation; thus, it manifests as Bhairava by way of being the nature of the unsurpassed, supreme knowledge free from all longing.
It throbs; such is the meaning. || 77 ||
For this very reason, the scripture also says thus:
"Therefore, [knowledge] taught in the venerable *Kiraṇa*—whether from the guru, from the scripture, or by oneself... (4.78).
And as it is stated in the *Niśāṭana*: "This knowledge has three conditions;
it manifests accordingly through combinations, inversions, and separations. (4.79)
Regarding the phrase "having three conditions," as it was stated therein:
"This knowledge has three conditions: the self, the scripture, and the mouth of the guru.
Therefore, by virtue of the fact that even one who is unconditioned (akalpita) requires a guru and so forth, that which [is taught] in the *Śrīkiraṇa* and other texts...

Regarding the knowledge of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the three causes beginning with the Guru have been mentioned; they manifest—that is, they flash forth as something established by the experience of everyone—in the form of a "conglomeration" (*saṅghāta*) and so forth, according to the manner described. "Conglomeration" means the totality of all principles (*samastattva*); "inversion" (*viparyāsa*)—

The meaning is that there may be a deviation from the stated sequence; even if knowledge arises in someone spontaneously (*svataḥ*), its fullness may still be achieved through the teacher and the scriptures. "Analysis" (*vigraha*) means a state of being distributed;
for in some cases, knowledge arises through only one of these factors, such as the teacher alone—this is the intention. (78–79)
Now, one might object: "If indeed all [factors] such as the Guru and others are the causes for the knowledge of the supreme reality, then why has it been stated that they may also be separate?
Or, even if they are separate, since the effect can be accomplished from just one, what is the use of the others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because the instruments are diverse, one takes up an adze, a chisel, and even a saw in order to produce that very same diverse cut. (4.80)

And for that long, there is indeed only a single act of cutting, precisely because of the initial intention. For carpenters and others, due to the diversity of their tools— such as the axe, which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the act of cutting— they produce that very same kind of cut, namely, the state of being split into two (*dvaidhībhāva*).

The meaning of the sentence is that they employ [the tools] either collectively or individually to perform [the task]. For in the world, it is understood that when a large piece of straight wood is to be worked upon, the cutting is done with individual tools such as an axe and so forth, whereas for curved surfaces, hollows, and the like, they are used collectively. Now, one might object: "If there is a diversity of effects due to a diversity of instruments, [then how can there be a single agent?]"
There is a dispute: since the instruments such as the axe and so forth are distinct, the act of cutting must also be distinct for each;
thus, one might object: "How can a single effect be produced by these [instruments], whether individually or collectively? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And to that extent," and so on—meaning, to that extent, [the effect] is that which is accomplished by those respective instruments such as the axe.

That which is the act of cutting is indeed one; it is not diverse and distinct, because there exists only a single primary intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*) belonging to the agent who cuts. The point is that the diversity of the objects of cognition (*parāmṛśya*) arises solely from the diversity of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Thus, even in a single act of cutting, [the roles of] the axe and so forth...
There is no fault whatsoever in their being instruments either collectively or individually. || 80 ||
He applies this very point to the subject at hand: "In this very way, the own nature of the instrument must be stated regarding cognition. (4.81)
One should not independently establish valid cognition through forceful apprehension; for apprehension is said to extend as far as the cognizer's attainment of confidence. (4.82)
And this diverse consolation arises likewise by virtue of the descent of power (śaktipāta);
therefore, there is clearly still room for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) even regarding what has been already known. (4.83)
The "instrument"— that is, the teacher and so forth— possesses its own unique "body," which is its essential nature;

this must be expressed in the same manner as described above, through a mode that is either individual or collective, within the valid cognition consisting of inferential knowledge, even though each individual factor, such as the teacher, is present for the realization of reality.

Although there is a state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), nevertheless, the application of these [factors], whether individually or collectively, extends only as far as the cognizer’s desire ceases; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, it is not the case that what is called "means of knowledge" (*māna*) is independent by virtue of its being a means of knowledge; thus, one cannot forcibly deny its dependence upon the cognizer.

One should effect the attainment [of the goal] even without [external] means; for what is called "attainment" is the conviction of the knower culminating in the thought, "This object has been known by me. If that very conviction has not arisen, what indeed is the purpose of attainment? And that conviction [varies] according to the distinctions such as the most intense degree of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

The variety [of means] arises through a sequence beginning with the most intense degree [of intensity], by which [knowledge] is produced either from a single source such as the guru or from all of them combined;

this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, even when an object is cognized externally, because the cognizer has not yet attained full confidence, there is an unimpeded utility for other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, if the causal complex consisting of the illumination of the object and so forth has not come together, then cognition itself does not arise; what, then, could be the meaning of "comprehension" in that case? On the other hand, if it has come together, then at the very first contact with the sense organ, [cognition arises] without depending on any other conditions.

The apprehension [of an object] must be one whose object is not already apprehended by the knower; even so, if subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhīni) should arise regarding that same object, let them arise—what is the harm? However, they would no longer possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) with respect to that very object, since it has already been apprehended by the first [cognition].

Because a moment of cognition reveals an object not previously known, its very nature as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists precisely in this revelation of an unknown object; as they say:
"A means of valid cognition has an object not yet apprehended, or it is the revelation of an unknown object."

Thus, for the knower as well, the attainment of the fruit occurs by this much alone, through the pride of satisfaction in the form: "This object has been known by me. And this [satisfaction] is not possible for subsequent, continuous cognitions; so how can it be said that "[the fruit exists] even when the object has already been cognized"?
Anticipating the objection, "What scope is there for the means of valid cognition [in this case]? he says:
"What can we possibly say regarding those who, having looked again and again, embraced her, and having relished her long in their minds, find complete satisfaction in their beloved? (4.84)

"Having seen, having seen"— by this repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), the sense of both "embracing" and "relishing" is also obtained by implication; or rather, it is obtained from the word *cira* (long), meaning that [the act] occurs hundreds of times through cognitions consisting of forms, cognitions consisting of touches, and the conceptual cognitions (*vikalpajñāna*) that follow them.

Regarding those for whom satisfaction characterized by consolation arises when their beloved has been cognized through the functioning means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what can we say to them? [The goal] is achieved by the very first moment of cognition, culminating in the consolation of the knower (*pramātṛ*).
In the case of arising, there is nothing [to be gained], because it contradicts experience; therefore:
"When a single nature of an object is itself directly perceived, what other part could remain unseen that would need to be examined by means of valid cognitions?"
The point is that what was stated in such passages is indeed untenable; therefore:
"Even where there may be a further determination by subsequent means of valid cognition, surely even there, that object was not previously apprehended in that same way."
By the reasoning stated above, some entirely new aspect (*apūrva-aṃśa*), not already apprehended by previous means of valid cognition,
must necessarily be apprehended by other means of valid cognition, whereby the cognizer ultimately attains full confidence. As for that which [is apprehended] by others...
"By such statements as, 'There is certainly no further determination by subsequent means of valid cognition; what additional object is revealed in continuous cognitions (dhārāvāhin)?',
it follows that even those continuous cognitions which apprehend what has already been apprehended [are not invalid]."
Validity has been asserted [by some], but that is not tenable— because it is beset by hundreds of defects such as redundancy;
therefore, even in the case of "convergence" (*saṃplava*), which consists in the operation of multiple means of knowledge upon a single object,
there is no apprehension of an object already apprehended— and thus, there is no [need for] further means of knowledge.
Nor is there a lack of purpose, because even those [subsequent cognitions] reveal an object not previously known; if this were so,
then in the natural progression of subsequent continuous cognitions, the revelation of an unknown object would never cease, and thus there would be no infinite regress either.
It may be so—because there exists an unavoidable limit characterized by the subject's sense of security.

Nevertheless, even regarding a single object, a manifestation arises as something previously unknown through the convergence of multiple means of knowledge (pramāṇas) employed by the subject; such is the case for these [means].

There would also be no mutual dependence such that the validity of the subsequent depends on the preceding, and the validity of the preceding depends on the subsequent; for in this case, there is no validity that relies on mutual dependence,
since the validity of cognitions depends upon their illumination of an object not previously known.
Validity is that illumination which has an unprecedented object as its domain, and this exists separately for each and every [cognition]; so what room is there for mutual dependence?
For "convergence" (*saṃplava*) is spoken of with reference to the substratum (*dharmin*).
"The operation of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon a single object" means that, in reality,

when a substratum (*dharmin*) is qualified by multiple attributes (*dharma*), a certain specific attribute is revealed as something previously unknown by some [means of cognition]; by virtue of which— preceded by the comprehension of each respective attribute— the [object] is fully [apprehended].
"Having apprehended the substratum (dharmin) by means of its form (rūpa), the cognizer finally attains rest.
Thus he says this:
"And in this way, even when there is a convergence of means of knowledge, there is no further movement once [the object] has been apprehended."
There is neither futility, nor infinite regress, nor even mutual dependence. (4.85)
Now, having concluded the true nature of the Guru as connected with the reality of reasoning (*tarka*),
he begins to state that the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*) are likewise useless, which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration immediately following that:
"Thus, the limb of yoga is only reasoning and nothing else."
He [is for] the sake of the excellence of skill in internal, internal reflective awareness. || 4.86 ||

Thus, having established this much— the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of the true essence of the Guru— it is concluded that reasoning (*tarka*) alone is the supreme limb of yoga, and not anything else such as the restraints (*yama*) and so forth; for it is that very [reasoning] which, through its respective proximity to consciousness, [leads to] the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

One should generate an extraordinary proficiency in discernment (*parāmarśa*), by which the yogi may ultimately achieve the direct realization of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvitsākṣātkāra*). As it has been said:
"For one who has attained the stage and is dispassionate, [the teacher] is skillful in the means for conquering that [resistance]."
Reasoning (ūha) is defined as discursive speech, characterized by investigation and examination.
Whatever state is preeminent and presided over by enjoyment—
being perishable, rooted in doubt, and utterly defiled.
"What is the use of this [world], which consists of conceptualization, speech, and worldly transaction?
It is already fully satisfied by a superior enjoyment that is distinct from us.
And so forth.
That single state, free from discursive thought, is the abode of the Lord, undisturbed and supreme among all states that possess feet, its eyes concealed by its own splendor.
The remaining [mental states], accompanied by discursive thought (savitarka), must be abandoned by those seeking liberation;
for those practitioners of yoga cannot abandon them without first abandoning discursive thought.
"O tiger among sages, they can indeed be understood; therefore, even reasoning (tarka) is appropriate, for when it has become an auxiliary to yoga, it strives for its own benefit.
Thus ends [the verse]. 86.

Now, one might object: "Even though reasoning (tarka) is equally a limb of yoga, what is the reason that it alone possesses the status of the most excellent limb of yoga, and not the restraints (yamas) and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness..."
Thus, these five restraints (yamās) are not directly useful for direct realization (saṃvitti).
Whatever restraints there are, such as austerity and the rest, as well as the postures and the breath-controls— all this is merely an external manifestation.
By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), purity and the other observances are indicated, as it has been said:
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances" (Pātañjala Yogasūtra 2.32).
The connection is as follows: "all such [factors] as these are not directly useful for consciousness.
By the use of the word "directly," it is indicated that while some may indeed be useful through an indirect succession, they are not so here;
the reason for their lack of direct utility is as follows:
"All this is the manifestation of the external.
And this is established not only by reasoning, but also by scripture; thus he says:

"And it is stated in the venerable Vīrāvalī: 'When the moon and the sun have dissolved through the bond of the dissolution of the mind within that which consists solely of consciousness and is of the nature of Śiva... (4.89)
When the twelfth part has been reached, and the sun of one's own consciousness has arisen, that itself is declared to be liberation; [any other] breath-control is useless.
Prāṇāyāma should not be practiced such that the body is oppressed;
he who knows the secret therein is liberated and is the liberator. (4.91)

The dissolution—which is rest—of the mind within the thinker through the process of making the object of thought its own prey, that alone is bondage, whose nature is not wandering elsewhere. By that, when the sun conjoined with the moon—the flow of prāṇa and apāna—is dissolved, and because of its merger into the central channel, its own current is severed; for this very reason...
The individual soul (*jīva*)—which is indeed the *udāna* breath—is the Sun; it is Fire because it takes up as its fuel the various objects of cognition and other things to be consumed.

When that [fire], by the process of moving upward through the center, reaches the *dvādaśānta*, the supreme limit is ascended within the cognizer alone, through the cessation of the conventional activity of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge.

When pure consciousness alone— which is self-revealing, self-luminous, and consists of one's own supreme good as well as the supreme good of others— has arisen by its very nature, whatever specific experience occurs therein is declared to be liberation:
"Through the union of the moon and the sun, the individual soul (jīva) attains that state of pure essence."

"In this [state], Brahmā and the others, desiring liberation, are dissolved for the sake of release"—thus it was previously taught in that very [text]. It is not, however, attainable through some other external cause as in other philosophical systems; therefore, it takes the form of *recaka* (exhalation) and so forth.

"Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is useless"— the meaning is that by means of it, no goal characterized as liberation is accomplished. Thus, when the Lord had questioned [this], the [author] established the final conclusion (siddhānta) precisely for the sake of answering the Blessed Lady's question.
"O one of great wisdom, this is true: breath control (prāṇāyāma) is not the cause [of liberation].
Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"Breath control should not be practiced if by it the body is afflicted."

Having thus presented the subverting evidence against the opposing position with these words, he demonstrates the proving evidence for his own position with the verse beginning, “He who knows the secret in each [case],” and so on. The “secret” is that which,
because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and other such instruments do not apply to it, is beyond the reach of all ordinary people— the supreme reality of the subject (*pramātṛ*) alone.

He who fully realizes—that is, directly perceives—the reality (tattva), being himself liberated, becomes the liberator of others as well. Since the futility of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) has been stated, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpīya), the same applies to the restraints (yama) and other practices; thus, they have not been mentioned separately. [This occurs] in mere awakening...
By the phrase "in the nature of Śiva," the collection of topics previously explained in the two preceding chapters is again briefly introduced. || 89-91 ||
Now, one might object: "If the restraints (yamas) and so forth are not useful for consciousness because they are external manifestations, let that be; what is the harm?

But as for withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the rest, since they involve turning away from the external and finding their growth within, why are they not also useful there? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For this which is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is indeed the turning back of the senses from their objects; it is truly the pinning down of that unbound bondage within. (4.92)

The binding of the mind to any object whatsoever, characterized by concentration (dhāraṇā), is meditation (dhyāna); when that [meditation] has reached its culmination, it is supreme absorption (samādhi). (4.93)
But when the very identity with the object of knowledge arises within consciousness, this state of being devoid of the duality of the grasped and the grasping is *samāhiti*. (4.94)

This indeed is what is called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*): the internal pinning down of the sensory cognitions of the eyes and so forth, which have been withdrawn from their objects such as form and the rest;
it is the attainment of self-dependence by way of conforming to the very nature of the mind, as it has been said:
"When there is no contact with the objects of the dog, the withdrawal of the senses is as if they were imitating the very nature of the mind" (Yogasūtra 2.54);
and that indeed is [the means] for one who is not bound.
"Transmigration does not exist in reality; for embodied beings, what talk can there be of bondage?"—
by such reasoning, the *kīlana* (nailing down), that is, the production of firmness, even of a bondage that has not yet taken root,
occurs because the supreme consciousness, through its own sovereignty, has assumed contraction.
Bondage is indeed the state of being delimited by space and so forth; and this very bondage is reinforced here by the withdrawal of the senses from some objects and their stabilization upon others.
Thus, how can practices such as withdrawal (pratyāhāra) be of use for the direct realization of consciousness? For [consciousness] is all-pervasive.
The sense is: how indeed could consciousness be perceived only in some particular place? As it has been said:
"Wherever the mind goes, one should fix [the awareness] right there;
having moved, where would you go? For everything is composed of Śiva."

Thus it is said. In this same way, it should be understood regarding concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and the other stages as well; for in that context, the "form" (*rūpa*) of concentration is defined as "the binding of the mind to a specific location," such as the *kanda*, as it has been stated:
"Concentration is the binding of the mind to a place" (*Yogasūtra* 3.1).

Thus, even in meditation (*dhyāna*), the nature of a continuous flow belongs only to cognitions of the same kind (*sajātīya*) and not to those of different kinds (*vijātīya*); this is what is meant by being delimited by a fixed form (*niyatākārāvacchinnatva*). As it has been said:
"In that regard, meditation is the one-pointed continuity of cognition" (*tatra pratyayaikatānatā dhyānam*, *Yogasūtra* 3.2).

Thus, for this very reason, it is said: "It has set beyond. Even in *samādhi*, by setting aside the two forms known as the knower and the known, its nature consists solely in the manifestation of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) alone;
in this regard, a fixed form (*ākāra*) is indeed the delimiting factor, as it has been said:
"That very [state] in which there is the appearance of the object alone, as if devoid of its own form, is samādhi" (Yoga Sūtra 3.3).
Now, if it is argued that since all five, beginning with *yama*, are external limbs (*bahir-aṅga*), they are of no use for direct realization (*saṃvitti*), then let that be;
[the scripture states]: "The triad is internal compared to the former ones" (Yogasūtra 3.7).
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why would those [practices] not be of use there? he says:
"Therefore, this triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi does not attain any utility whatsoever with respect to supreme consciousness. (4.95)
This is because of the reason of being a binder and so forth, according to such statements as: "The pinning down within that [space] is indeed the binding of that which was previously unbound. (95)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then for what purpose are all eight limbs of yoga, beginning with *yama*, enumerated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The status of being limbs of yoga is described for everything from *yama* to *samādhi*."
Because each preceding one serves as the means for the next, and because it is employed by the final reasoning (tarka). || 96 ||
It "goes to the end" (*antyeti*)—meaning it is "good at the end" (*ante sādhu*), in the sense that it is fit as the means for attaining the eight limbs beginning with *yama*.

Thus, *yama* is the means for *niyama*, and *niyama* is the means for *āsana*; in this sequence, the status of all eight limbs beginning with *yama* as being limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*) has been described by virtue of each preceding one being the means for the subsequent one.

Just as these [eight limbs] serve as a means to the goal because they constitute the nature of that which is to be attained, they function through the relationship of door and doorkeeper in ultimate reasoning;
for it is only when the intellect of the yogin is refined by all eight of these limbs that such self-reflection arises,
by which he may immediately attain the direct realization of his own consciousness— namely, that which is here [described].

Having set aside the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) taught in one's own system, the eight ancillaries beginning with restraint (yama) according to Patañjali are stated; the intention therein is that nowhere else is there any other ancillary apart from this group of eight, thus it is everywhere.
The other limbs of reasoning are the means, and that [reasoning] is the means for the direct realization of self-awareness. || 96 ||
He demonstrates this very point:

"For that [object] which is rooted within consciousness is projected, by means of that [consciousness], onto the vital breath and the body, or onto the intellect through repeated practice; however, this principle does not apply to consciousness itself. (4.97)
For indeed, within consciousness—in a state of non-differentiation—that which is being perceived, such as the breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, has taken root;

by means of that, that is, solely through the gateway of consciousness, for not even a single object that is not cognized could be fit for worldly transaction—this is the intended meaning. Through practice—that is, by repeated cultivation.

"Entrusting to the body and so forth"—the meaning is that just as the body and so on gradually attain growth through proficiency in practice (*saṃskāra*), so too [should one proceed]. For example: postures (*āsana*) and so forth in the body; breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth in the vital breath (*prāṇa*);

withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth in the intellect (*buddhi*). But as for consciousness (*saṃvit*), this [is the case] for one who has already attained firm growth within the body and so forth.
That logic would not apply here because, through the power of practice, the sprouting [of restraint and so forth] occurs by means of that [consciousness];

for it is said that the "sprouting" of restraint and so forth within consciousness is its intensification (*paṭīyastva*), and that indeed is what is called an impression (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, consciousness itself is not something to be impressed; for an impression is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*), and that—

It could not exist within this [consciousness], because that would entail its becoming non-conscious; therefore, the intended meaning is that for one who abides in this eternally arisen state of supreme non-duality, there is no purpose whatsoever for practices such as *yama* (restraint). As it has been said:
"That which is firmly established internally within consciousness is present everywhere, even in the body, intellect, and vital breath."
"How might it be made to circulate? Thus, a sequence of means is applicable therein.
But as for those who strive to refine this consciousness through the path of practice—we are in doubt as to what they should do, where, or indeed how."
Thus [ends the verse]. 97.
Or rather, there may be an excellence characterized by the manifestation of consciousness through the medium of the body and so forth; thus he says:

"Alternatively, even for the vital breath, intellect, body, and so on, which are under our control, because they consist of everything, practice residing therein effects the exclusion of the other. (4.98)
Alternatively, according to the perspective of the supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*),

based on the principle that "even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization," the body and so forth are also of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*) and thus possess the nature of being the self of all; therein...

Even while established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, there is the practice of the restraints (*yama*) and others; for there is the removal of those things such as violence (*hiṃsā*) which consist of non-restraint and belong to others who are fixed in duality.
For just as violence should not be committed against oneself, so too it should not be committed against another. Thus [it is said].

The sense is that, through the manifestation of self and other as one's own essential nature, the distinction between them dissolves, and thus there occurs the manifestation of consciousness alone. || 98 ||
Now, one might object: "If that which is practiced here were to attain a superior proficiency due to the firmness of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), let that be so;
what is the harm? But how can it possibly exert itself to produce the exclusion of something else—by means of which another effect would also arise? To dispel this doubt, he provides an illustration:
Due to the desire to rise up through the nature of leaping and falling of the body, one causes it to leap upward by dispelling the apprehension of falling toward its opposite. (4.99)

Leaping (*utpluti*) means jumping upwards; because this occurs repeatedly, there is a convergence (*saṃpāta*), and the "flavor" (*rasa*) of this desire to rise upward is an intensity of zeal resulting from repeated practice. For that reason, [it is like] the body.
With reference to the removal of the apprehension regarding that downward or oblique fall which is the opposite of the impulse to rise upward, one "leaps up"—
meaning one is made fit for the upward flight by means of physical exertion and so forth; thus, upward.

The meaning is that by the practice of swimming, falling downward and other such [accidents] are averted from the body; thus, even for one practicing one thing, there may occur the cessation of another. || 99 ||
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand:

"When one's own self-reflection, which resembles the contemplation of the Guru’s words, becomes awakened, there occurs the elimination of its opposites through the contemplation of the [scriptural] text. (4.100)

Thus, through the disciple's repeated and intense practice regarding matters such as recitation and reflection, and through his own reflective awareness that accords with the consideration of the guru’s words, there occurs the elimination— even of those adverse factors such as delusion and the like— of that reflective awareness which has arisen. || 100 ||
One might object: "Surely the removal of his ignorance and other defects would be accomplished by the power of the Guru's words alone;
what is the purpose of one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), which is as superfluous as an internal goitre? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For it is not possible for the Guru [to impart] either his own knowledge or even the word itself to him."
Therefore, he certainly established the sequence of his own awakening within the intellect.

Indeed, it is not possible for the teacher to cause his own knowledge— consisting of thought and so forth— or his own word being recited, to take root in the intellect of this disciple by means of his own power alone,
as long as the disciple lacks his own self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*); for without his own self-awareness (*svavimarśa*), he [cannot grasp it].
He is not even capable of comprehending the words of the Guru; what possibility, then, could there be for the cessation of his delusion and other defects?
Therefore, it is certain that because of his own nature as pure *vidyā*, he possesses an elevated awareness (*bodha*) characterized by supreme reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*).
The word "there is a sequence" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 101 ||
Because of his majesty, even an object experienced in a dream attains for those possessed of focused attention the nature of direct perception, culminating in effective action; thus he says:
"Therefore, even regarding that object heard at the time of dreaming..."
The practice of meditating on identity is not said to be without fruit. || 4-102 ||

Therefore— precisely because of the existence of self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*)— even during the time of a dream, which consists in the perception of unreal objects, the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanāyoga*), characterized by repeated cultivation toward some object heard (such as a woman or the like), is said not to be without fruit when performed in its true form.
The meaning is that it is directly realized by virtue of its capacity to perform the purposeful action appropriate for the waking state. || 102 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the essential nature of those two—recitation (pāṭha) and reflection (cintana)—which are intended as the objects of this self-reflection? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Recitation is the reflective awareness residing in the word when there is no regard for conventional signs."
Therefore, let it be considered that when there is respect for that [object], its meaning is indeed "reflection" (cintā). (4.103)

Disregard for the convention— that is, indifference toward the conventional meaning— for this very reason it is said to be "resting in the word" (śabdaniṣṭha) and not resting in the object (arthaniṣṭha) as well; because if that [object] were attended to,
then upon the requirement of the word, the cognition of the object would necessarily be preceded by the cognition of the word.
The state of being. || 103 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he returns to the subject at hand:
"In that non-dual consciousness, practice is of no use;
it serves solely to uproot the suspicion of the defilement of duality. (4.104)

The word "tat" refers to the reason already stated; "practice" (abhyāsa) refers to the [observances] beginning with *yama*. Now, one might ask: "If this is indeed useless, for what purpose was it mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says "kevalam" and so forth.
But if this is so, then how [is it related] to reasoning (*tarka*), which consists of the reflective awareness of self and other?
Having raised the doubt, "Was it not already stated that the suspicion of duality is rootless? he says:
"And it has been described that suspicions of duality are investigated by means of reasoning;
furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing that reasoning, practices such as the restraints (yamas) also serve as means. (4.105)

This has been described during the discussion on the principles of logic (*tarka-tattva*), and it was said: "By means of this, the yogi should discern that object which sets in motion the perfections of yoga (*yoga-siddhi*) and that which causes their cessation, and which exists in manifold ways."

Thus, because it has been stated that the [observances] beginning with *yama* serve to uproot the suspicion of duality, this occurs indirectly through the medium of reasoning (*tarka*); therefore, it is precisely that [reasoning] which should be declared as their primary function.
Thus he says: "That reasoning... and so forth; by this, it is shown that reasoning alone is the direct means (*sākṣādupāya*) for the realization of consciousness.
It would thus be said that this does not apply to others. || 105 ||
And this is not without authoritative proof; thus he says:
"And it has been stated by Śambhu in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, beginning with the words 'There is neither duality nor non-duality, [yet] all such things as the worship of the *liṅga*... (4.106).

Whatever is prescribed here, or even whatever is prohibited, [is of no consequence], because yogas consisting of the ancillaries such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth are merely artificial. (4.107)

Therefore, these do not merit even a sixteenth part of this uncreated [reality]. This is the connection with what was stated by Śambhu in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, beginning with the words “neither duality nor non-duality,” which has not been cited here due to the requirements of the meter; [the text continues] with “the worship of the liṅga and so forth.”
In the phrase "all," there is also a connection with the negative particle *nañ*, as it was stated therein:
"And there is no worship of the *liṅga* and so forth.
By the word "all," there is the acceptance of the non-abandonment of the worship of the *liṅga* and other such practices, as it was stated therein.
Furthermore, neither the renunciation of those things, nor the state of being without possessions,
nor even the state of possessing them— such as the gathering of matted hair, ashes, and so forth— is [the cause].
The renunciation of those [worldly things], as well as the performance and non-performance of vows and other observances,
the entry into sacred sites (kṣetra) and so forth, and the preservation of the rules of conduct (samaya) and the like.
"Neither the nature and so forth of another's gender, nor names, lineages, and the like—
nothing whatsoever is prescribed for this [state], nor is anything prohibited.
Anticipating the objection that such being the case, one would fall into a state of total silence (tūṣṇīṃbhāva), he says, "It is prescribed," and so forth.

If "everything" were being enjoined or prohibited, then something would be prohibited and something else enjoined, which would necessarily manifest duality. Consequently, it would follow that for the yogin who abides in the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*), there is no distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done; therefore, [the text] says: "Therefore..."

It has been stated that because they are artificial— being produced through the performance of ancillary practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma)— the yogas of other systems are not even capable of attaining mere equality with yoga, which consists of non-dual consciousness established in its own natural state, even in its smallest part.
"By means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth," and so on. || 107 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then because it does not depend on any cause due to its being uncreated, would it not always be either existent or non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But here, O Goddess of Gods, this is established as a rule. (4.108)
"The mind must be made steady upon reality, and that [steadiness] should be such as belongs to each [individual].

But what exactly is to be enjoined here by way of rule—that "the mind should be steady upon reality"—is not something where the steadiness of the mind occurs merely by chance; rather, in this regard, by someone...
Anticipating the objection, "Must there necessarily be a cause? it is said: "And that [state] belongs to whomever it may be, in whatever manner.
This means that "that"—the steady mind—belongs to any given yogi, in whatever way it may exist, namely, by not depending on fixed external causes. As it has been stated therein:
"And whatever [practice] may be for whomsoever, in whatever manner it may be, he should perform it in that very way.
For this very reason, due to the absence of restrictive rules (niyama), it has been stated that everything is both prescribed and prohibited.
In order to demonstrate the syntactic unity of the eighteenth chapter, this [verse]—remaining unfragmented and complete—is [presented].
The text has been verified. || 108 ||
He concludes that very point:
"In this way, for the sake of destroying the perception of duality, the Supreme Lord... (4.109).
In some cases, he remains constantly contemplating his own stainless nature.

Indeed, the supreme nature of the Lord consists of pure consciousness alone, whose reflective awareness takes the form: "I am everything," and this awareness never undergoes any modification whatsoever, at any time or place.
"How can it be said that he 'might exist'—that is, that he remains perceiving his own stainless nature?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is the awareness of one's own nature [occurs] by means of the senses, objects, and so forth. (4.110)
"Either without that [means] or by another means, the conceptualization of that occurs through independence. Here, indeed, one who is independent of means such as the senses and their objects,
and who rests solely upon the form internally manifested, is "one whose face is toward that"— meaning one who possesses the means such as the senses and their objects.

The meaning is that "conceptualization" (vikalpa) refers to conceptualization in both forms— that which arises subsequent to non-conceptual [perception] and that which is otherwise— as well as the reflective awareness of intrinsic nature (svabhāvaparāmarśa), all of which are manifested by the sovereignty of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 110 ||
And that is of two kinds; thus he says:
"And that [is clearly] manifest in the jewel of the self, which is pure and autonomous. (4.111)
In the flood of objective existents, that which unites diversity is called the "night" of one's own self;
yet that very same [consciousness], when its sole object is the Self filled with all things, [is called the day]. (4.112)
All this is indeed of the nature of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), namely "I"—this is sufficient.

And that [I-consciousness] is a conceptualization (*vikalpana*); it is transparent because it is not manifested by another; for that very reason, it is independent because it does not depend on anything else.
That which is the Self, whose sole form is the subject, the supreme Light—that alone is [it].

Because it is capable of receiving reflections, it is like a crystal; for, although the flood of existents— consisting of both subject and object— is by nature manifest as non-different from it, [the intellect], having made this distinction clear,
acts as a unifier of difference by means of its nature as the exclusion (*apoha*) of everything other than itself, and is therefore "nocturnal" (*naiśa*).

The term *māyīya* (pertaining to Māyā) is used because, as stated generally, it is designated by all [the categories]; that very conceptualization (*vikalpana*) takes the form "all this is indeed I," and for this very reason it is grounded solely in one's own Self which is filled with all objects; for this very reason, being sufficient (*alaṃ*), it is complete.
"It is said to consist of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā)," this is the connection with what precedes. || 111–112 ||
Indeed,

according to the principle beginning with "every conceptual construction (vikalpa) is saṃsāra," all conceptual construction whatsoever is to be abandoned; thus, by this very distinction that has been stated, [it is established].
Anticipating the question "What is the meaning?", he says:
"This conceptualization, which is of the nature of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), is of a manifest character. (113)

"It strikes down the conceptual construction belonging to Māyā which consists of the perception of duality" means that it has attained the state of direct realization through the previously described sequence of purifying conceptual constructions; for, in the striking down of the conceptual construction belonging to Māyā, its nature as the perception of duality [is destroyed].
This is the reason; therefore, because it brings about non-differentiation, this [state] is to be adopted—this is what would have been said. || 113 ||
And that [reflective awareness] is of many kinds due to the diversity of the objects to be reflected upon; thus he says: "That very reflective awareness of Śuddhavidyā is indeed manifold. (4.114)
Through the practice of bathing, purification, worship, fire-offerings, meditation, recitation, and so forth— [one attains this]. Now,

how indeed can this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), whose essence is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), counteract the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) belonging to Māyā which is grounded in duality— for the sake of employing even this [conceptual construction]?
Anticipating the objection, "Is this not the indication of another method?", he says:
"This entire universe, out of its own relish, is filled with the essence of its own self-awareness. (4.115)
Having entered, the pure one should satisfy the entire circle of the paths (*adhvamaṇḍala*).

Indeed, in this world, the yogi who possesses such reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), by means of the sequence to be described, having entered this universe through the fullness of the wonder of his own Self and with great intensity of devotion, for that very reason—
Because it is of the singular nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), the pure [consciousness] should satisfy the entire circle of paths (*nikhilamadhvamaṇḍala*);

the meaning is that it should directly realize [them] through being filled with the essence of the relish of self-awareness (*svātmasaṃvitti*). And by this [statement], while casting a glance toward the absence of any fixed, imagined external objects of worship and so forth, [the author indicates the true nature of ritual].

By the immediate sequence following the lack of utility of the limbs of yoga, an opportunity has been provided for the disregard of imagined images and the like, which was previously mentioned. || 115 ||
One might object: "Since even acts such as ritual bathing serve to maintain the sense of duality, it is more appropriate for them to be of the nature of the reflection of Māyā;
how then can it be said that this [bathing] is a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of Śuddhavidyā? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When the fuel of the universe has been consumed by the blazing fire of awakened consciousness... (Kārikā 116).

Immersion of the body in white ashes is called bathing. That cognition which, by its nature as a means of knowledge, is prone to manifesting due to its outward orientation, is itself fire because of its luminosity; by that [fire], it is "burnt"—that is, assimilated into one's own self.

The universe, which consists of forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, is itself the fuel because it is combustible; from that [fuel], having attained its established state through the friction of these two arising together, [it is consumed] in the white ash— which is the supreme reality (para-tattva), consisting solely of the infinite subject and free from all limiting conditions— [the ash] of the body and so forth, that is, of the limited.
The "immersion" (*majjana*) of the knower— which consists of his primary absorption therein by means of subordinating his own [limited] qualities—

is what is called "bathing" (*snāna*), and not that which consists of external water and so forth; this distinction is obtained through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), and it is precisely with this intention [that the following is said].
"If liberation comes from bathing in water, why would it not also happen for fish?
and so forth, as stated elsewhere. || 116 ||
One might object: "Surely, through external bathing, one gains the qualification for rites such as the daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) and the purification of the body and so forth;
what, then, is the fruit of this [internal] kind? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, having performed the prescribed bath and having satiated the infinite deities... (117)
From that point, one should also purify the principles (tattvas) that constitute the body.

Now, according to the principle expressed in such passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," all of this—the body and so forth—is of the very nature of Śiva, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman; so what indeed could there be therein that is either pure or impure?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Even though these [elements] have Śiva as their essence, that cognition which perceives them as distinct... (4.118).
That very impurity is called *parā* (the supreme); purity is the crushing of that [notion of] it.
"Distinct" means having the nature of duality; "that notion" refers to the notion of distinctness.
As it has been said: "There is nothing whatsoever that is impure; everything is established within That."
Whatever is devoid of that [discipline] becomes somewhat impure because of it. || 118 ||
And what follows from that? He says:
"In this way, one's own body becomes a unique vessel of consciousness, with all duality dissolved. (4.119)
Perceiving [all things] as being nothing but consciousness, the Lord remains established in His own sovereignty.
In this manner— that is, by way of suppressing the conceit of self in what is not-self,
and by making the attributes such as sovereignty inherent in the Self— He abides in the state of pure consciousness alone.
The meaning is that one should directly realize it. || 119 ||
Having thus stated that bathing and the other [limbs] are not to be conceptually constructed, he demonstrates this for the other ancillaries of worship as well:
"Whatever gladdens the mind, wherever the senses may be situated... (4.120).
For that very instrument of worship is joined within the abode of Brahman—
whatever indeterminate object, pleasing to the mind, arises in any activity of the senses;
it is joined within the beautiful form of Brahman, a splendor distinct from the sun, moon, and other such lights.

By abandoning external form, it is directly realized as the essence of pure consciousness; that indeed is the implement of worship—the meaning is that by that alone the fulfillment of worship is attained. || 120 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Is this not a definition of worship that has never been heard before?", he says:
"Worship is indeed the unification of even the manifold flow of objective phenomena. (4-121)

The union of the manifold flow of existence— such as form, taste, and so forth— which, though distinct, is [united] with the self of consciousness belonging to Bhairava, who is independent, stainless, and infinite; that is, with the self of supreme consciousness which is unconditional, full, and unconditioned by space, time, and the like.

This unification is considered to be worship— the meaning is that this is not something conceived by us alone— as it has been said: "Worship is not merely that firm resolve which is formed through flowers and other such offerings."
"In the non-conceptual great void, that worship is indeed absorption through reverence.

Thus, since fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth are likewise merely instruments of worship, such a nature is established by implication; therefore, it was not stated explicitly. This has been explained at length previously and will be explained further—therefore...
This is how it should be understood. || 121 ||
Now, one might object: "How can there be a unification of one thing with another such that even acts like worship could be said to be its defining characteristic?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For indeed, this very consciousness exists internally and externally as both. (4.122)

Existing solely through its own freedom, this [consciousness], whose nature is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), is of the character described above; for consciousness itself, by virtue of its own sovereignty, manifests as both internal and external. Thus, in reality, there exists nothing whatsoever other than that.
It has been rightly said: "The unification of the manifold stream of phenomena with the conscious self. Now, one might object:

even when this [consciousness] manifests in an external form, how can its own nature remain essentially the reflective awareness of "I"? Anticipating this doubt, it was stated that it is "indeed of the very nature of reflective awareness"; for even in this state, its...
The meaning is that there is no falling away from its own essential nature. || 122 ||
For this indeed is its nature as reflective awareness—that it flashes forth as the form of the universe; therefore he says:
"And that [awareness] is twelvefold, because everything is contained within it. (4-123)
For the sun itself has the nature of the moon, and it exists as consisting of the universe;
in ultimate reality, that consciousness consists precisely of twelve digits (kalās). || 4.124 ||

The meaning is that he—the supreme subject—and reflective awareness (parāmarśa) shine forth in twelve ways as the universal form; by this, following the disregard for the constructed image and so forth, the emergence of the wheel of consciousness (saṃviccakra), which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration, has also been introduced. Now, [regarding] the universe...

Since there is also a manifoldness consisting of the forms of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the knowable (*prameya*), and so forth, how could their inclusion be established by means of the measure (*pramāṇa*) alone—conceived as the sun consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: “In that regard,” etc.; “everything” refers to the knower, the knowable, and so forth.
In this context, indeed,

by such statements as, "This fire which is the supreme reality— that is precisely this [reality] of the cognizer," the cognizer, whose nature is supreme consciousness, is first of all "fire" because he burns the fuel of duality.

And that very [Self], whose nature consists solely in the cognition of "I," by virtue of its own sovereignty, manifests twelvefold as the intellect, the senses, and so forth; resting in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is called the "Subject" (*śūrya*). And the means of knowledge is nothing other than the outward-turned form of the subject itself.

In this regard, the knower (pramātā) must first be included; and that which is called the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is cognition (jñāna), and that [cognition] cannot possibly exist anywhere without a substratum.
Thus, it necessarily exists by implying the object of knowledge (meyākṣepa); therefore, that too is indeed included here. As he says in the Śūrya [Tantra]:
And so forth; "Soma" is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). As was stated previously:
"They say that Sūrya is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while they declare Soma to be the object of knowledge (*meya*).
Though both are independent, they remain inseparable from one another."

Thus: "consisting of the universe" (*viśvamaya*) means that the universe has the nature of being an object of knowledge (*meyātmaka*); and because everything is included herein, it is logically stated by Śrī [Somānanda] that the supreme consciousness, which manifests as the form of the universe, can in reality only possess a twelvefold nature.

Regarding the phrase "twelvefold," for this very reason he says: "the twelve *kalās*, etc. *Kalās* are the constituent parts (*aṃśas*) consisting of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth. || 123-124 ||
Now, one might object: "Has this [power] not been described by others as being thirteenfold?
Why, then, is it stated here to be twelvefold alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And she [resides] in the subject (mātṛ), in consciousness (vijñāna), and in the means of knowledge (māna) which is within the sphere of the instruments."
O lady, it always appears in fourfold form, depending upon [the elements]. || 4-125 ||

"In cognition" (*vijñāne*) is a qualification of "man" (*māna*); for others, the definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is intended to include both the nature of awareness and non-awareness. "Within the sphere of the instrument" (*karaṇa-gocare*) means having attained the status of being an object of a means of valid knowledge; for otherwise, that which is called the "object of knowledge" (*meyam*) would be nothing at all in itself—this is the sense.
For what reason? Because that ultimate consciousness,

having assumed a fourfold form consisting of emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhāra), and the nameless (anākhyā), shines at all times within the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object— remaining uninterrupted within each of these fourfold states.

The meaning is that it manifests in twelve ways, as it has been said: "He who is all-pervading and immeasurable brings to clear manifestation the form of the splendors of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, through the application of the sequence beginning with emission (sṛṣṭi)."
Thus:
"In whichever stage of awakening the knower of reality enters,
having attained identity with that very stage, he reaches the state of the fourfold self."
Thus [it is said]. Now, it may be objected that this supreme consciousness has been described by others, in this very same manner, as being thirteenfold, as it was stated:
"The single nature of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower..."
It exists by pervading [the universe] consisting of creation, descent, and withdrawal.
By virtue of their individual conceptualization in accordance with their own essential nature,
they too exist in a fourfold manner through the divisions of emission, maintenance, and so forth.

Since dissolution is fourfold, arising from the emergence [of the powers] up to the end of the "devouring of time" (kālagrāsa), its repose is indeed one alone; therefore, there are thirteen goddesses.
"They abide in the *anākhyacakra* as the primary objects of worship.
Now, we do not understand this: what is meant by the statement here that [the deity] is twelvefold? To this it is replied:
indeed, in this context, the Supreme Consciousness itself, through its own sovereignty, becomes twelvefold according to the reasoning already stated.
That these [forms] are manifest is, for now, beyond dispute; in that regard, if this supreme consciousness were to appear as distinct from those twelve forms, then it would constitute a thirteenth.
Otherwise, to what else could that state of being thirteen belong? For apart from consciousness, there are only twelve.

Since forms (*rūpa*) lack the nature of consciousness, they would not manifest at all; thus, only consciousness alone, devoid of appearances (*nirābhāsā*), would remain. In that case, what room is there for a thirteenfold form? Alternatively, even if [consciousness] were distinct [from its forms], according to the logic of universality (*sāmānyanyāya*), consciousness would pervade all twelve forms by its very own nature.
If it is argued that its status as thirteen is already established because it appears [as such], this is incorrect;

for a universal, being distinct from its particulars, pervades them, whereby there arises a non-differentiated, inclusive cognition such as "cow, cow"; however, in consciousness, those various forms [themselves]...
"They manifest, yet they do not exceed [consciousness]; for if they were other than that, their manifestation would not even occur.
Therefore, when those various forms manifest, it is said that 'consciousness itself manifests.
How can this be accepted? Because the example is dissimilar; this is quite trivial.
It is precisely with this intention that it is said:
"In the consciousness [that] 'entities appear,' it appears as 'the Self appears'; in the consciousness [that] 'the Self appears,' it appears as 'entities appear.'"

This and more has been stated elsewhere. Now, one might ask: does this supreme consciousness manifest in a form colored by the nature of the twelvefold [senses], or rather in its thirteenth aspect as pure consciousness alone, uncolored?
This is not so; for here, it is indeed the supreme [consciousness] itself that is without limiting adjuncts, uncolored, and free from objective manifestation.
It is our established tenet that pure consciousness exists; and by virtue of the majesty of its own sovereignty,
it conceals its own true nature and manifests as the form of the universe,
appearing only in a form colored by the twelve-fold [subjective] self, for at that time [otherwise], it would not.

Even that form which is beyond [the universe] and uncolored by it would appear; for it has been stated many times that if it were otherwise, only the colored form would manifest. Now, even though she consists of the universe (*viśvamayatva*), her transcendent and uncolored form must be possible; otherwise, indeed, of her—
Stupidity might arise; indeed, what is the intention of this question?

Is it that even while consisting of the universe, her nature could exist as something devoid of it and uncolored by it, according to the maxim of the cow's horn? Or rather, [is it] that even as she manifests the form of the universe through her own sovereignty...

Is it that no deviation from one's own essential nature, which is non-dual consciousness, occurs? Among these, the first position is already effectively refuted— for it has been stated more than once that its very manifestation could not exist apart from the manifold universe— and he will state it again:
Indeed, this Śiva, known as "the Peaceful," is someone distinct from all others;
excluded from every other path, he exists somewhere like a jar.
For that consciousness which unfolds as the nature of great light is indeed Śiva; and his very state of being Śiva is the manifestation of his universal form.
"Therefore, the yoga of appearing as such unfolds by its own inherent nature.
With this very intention, the venerable Tapasvī also said:
"Whatever form I perceive as being higher than the highest, each of those is actually lower than You."
It has been stated: "There is not even the slightest notion in which You are not present on all sides.
Regarding the second position, however, although [the Self] is in reality uncolored, its manifestation occurs through various colored forms projected by its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*). Thus...

Furthermore, it does not possess a thirteen-fold nature; for that [thirteen-fold nature] would belong to these two [the subject and object] as they flash forth in a state of rivalry, being like iron rods [separated by a gap], just as, for example, an actor, at the time of assuming various roles, is in reality still an actor even while [portraying other characters].
It manifests precisely in those respective forms, and not even as a "dancer" (naṭa); in the same way, consciousness (saṃvit),

although in reality it is pure consciousness alone, manifests in its state of being composed of the universe solely through the form of the twelvefold [perceptual powers], and not even through the thirteenth form, which is the nature of pure consciousness alone.
It appears as form; thus, what has been stated is indeed logical.

Therefore, consciousness, manifesting itself as the totality of all forms (*viśvarūpatā*), must shine forth in exactly twelve ways; otherwise, it would ultimately be reduced to being only one. As the scripture says:
"As long as the deities remain established in their respective individual functions, so long does the designation based on that sequence exist; it is not otherwise."
"When everything, by virtue of its state of oneness, abides in the inexpressible, then it should be known as 'simultaneous' (akrama), since it has transcended all [limitations].
And thus, even unity is the counteragent to duality; therefore, it too cannot serve as a qualification.
"It endures," thus it would be "consciousness alone" (*saṃvid eva*). And the particle *eva* serves to exclude connection with anything else;

yet since there is nothing else whatsoever here, what could it exclude? Thus, not even tolerating such a connection, it would be "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) alone. And consciousness is grounded in the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*), and that which is called the "object of consciousness" is...

Since there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from its own self, and thus failing to obtain even a designation, it is everywhere described as "the undesignated," "the nameless," and "the ineffable"; enough of this prolixity.
But if this is so, how is it appropriate that elsewhere its state of having thirteen forms has been stated? For indeed—

It cannot be said that this is untenable, because there exists the authority of scripture (*āgama*), which is itself an uncontradicted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, let it be explained how this [objection] is resolved. It is said:
In this context, those subjects (*pramātṛ*) who are permeated by duality and belong to the realm of *māyā* are indeed the ones to be instructed.

Just as in the case of acting for a common purpose (*samānārthacaryā*), instruction that proceeds here in accordance with that [common aim] may easily take root; thus, relying on a distinction brought about by the force of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the thirteenfold nature of consciousness was described. However, in this [present context], one relies solely on the actual non-duality (*abheda*).
Such is the instruction; thus, everything has been fully resolved. Now, regarding this supreme consciousness: "Its powers—Parā and the others—these three shine forth."
"Because [they arise] in creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the fourth state, these twelve have thus arisen.

By such statements, the twelvefold arising was previously described in one way, whereas here it is described differently; thus, a contradiction between what precedes and what follows would ensue. What is this? To this it is replied: for here, insofar as...

The twelvefold arising of supreme consciousness is intended [here]; let it be thus, or otherwise—since there is no difference in that [consciousness] despite the differences in its formal procedure—and precisely by internalizing this intention, it is stated elsewhere by him: "These four powers, through their sovereignty, each..."

They exist in exactly three ways—in creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—and thus they become twelve. By such statements, her twelvefold emergence is described through another method of exposition; thus, everything is beyond reproach. || 125 ||
Now, one might object: "Since this [consciousness] appears in such a form, its specific distinction (vaiśiṣṭya) must necessarily be admitted;

otherwise, there would be no non-duality at all. But where does that [distinction] reside, and of what nature is it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the prior cognition, it consists of pure consciousness; in the [subsequent] cognition, it takes the form of verbalization."
For this reason, in the *Śrīyogasañcara*, it is said that the instruments have the form of grasping. (4-126)

This indeed is the supreme consciousness (saṃvit) in the primordial subject— pure because it remains the very nature of the subject even when there is some emergence of contraction, and not impure like the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and so forth;
this consciousness has as its essential nature that contracted, non-conceptual cognition (jñāna).

And in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is characterized by the instruments consisting of the intellect, the senses, and so forth, there is "verbalization"—meaning that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists of the reflective awareness of differentiation (*bhedāmarśamayī*) and takes on that form. For this very reason, it is said to be "of the nature of apprehension" (*grahaṇākārā*); for apprehension indeed depends upon both the object to be grasped (*grāhya*) and the subject who grasps (*grāhaka*). But [one might object]: [The text continues: ...But [one might object]: [Is not conceptual construction merely a mental construct? No, for... [the passage continues with the argument that conceptualization is grounded in the reality of the object]. (Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly; the translation above reflects the full logical flow of the argument as presented in the source.)
