Raising the doubt, "Even at the stage of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the proof that consciousness exists solely as the form of the apprehended (*grahaṇākārā*)?", he says "since," etc.; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "because it has been stated [in the scripture] that is about to be mentioned, namely, 'In the Śrīyogasañcara'. || 126 ||
He says that very thing: "O Supreme Goddess, those two white circles of the eyes which are directly perceived—therein resides the supreme wheel consisting of sixteen spokes and twelve spokes. (4.127)

The word "ye" (which) is in the dual number with reference to the two eyeballs; the same should be understood for what follows. Those two white circles of the eyes which are seen—being visible and not hidden like the red circles [of the pupils]—are there the "Supreme," because they encompass the universe, consisting of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*).

Because it is the self-nature of all things, the sixteen-spoked wheel abides—meaning it manifests as that very form; it is with this very intention that it is said in the venerable *Kramasadbhāvabhaṭṭāraka*: "In the Wheel of the Ineffable (*anākhya-cakra*), there are exactly sixteen goddesses."
"They are described as objects of worship," as it is said therein:
"O Hara, listen with a one-pointed mind to these sixteen in brief," and so forth.
"That existence (sattā) in which [all] dissolves is known as Kālī, who possesses sixteen digits.

Thus ends [the passage]. Here, although she is the Inexplicable (anākhyatva), because the object of knowledge (prameya), whose nature is emanation (sṛṣṭi), predominates, she is of the nature of Soma (the Moon) and is therefore white (śvetatva). || 127 ||
Now, one might object: "If a sixteen-spoked wheel is established here, how can there also be a twelve-spoked one?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is outside of that, red like a lotus, is what is called [the twelve-spoked wheel]."
The second [pair] is those two mandalas, black and white, situated in the middle.
Within that, O beloved, two pure [lotuses] are situated, possessing a luster like split collyrium; they should be known as having four petals and being of the nature of Agni and Soma. (4-129)
O Supreme Goddess, when the two wheels are situated in a state of union,
they perform for one another the acts of closing and opening.

Outside of that— that is, outside the white circle— according to the principle of successive circles (*pratimaṇḍalanyāya*), there are two red circles situated there; that is called the second twelve-spoked wheel, which takes the form of Śrī Sṛṣṭikālī and the others, even though it belongs to the state of the Inexplicable (*anākhyatva*), because here resides the means of knowledge whose nature is persistence (*sthiti*).

Its redness is due to its predominance, for it is indeed colored by the object of cognition (*prameya*); and since the object of cognition exists in non-difference from that [consciousness], the fourfold form residing therein lacks any separate existence, resulting in twelve spokes. For this very reason, because it incorporates the object of cognition within itself, it also exists externally while remaining in the center.

— [located] within the white and black circles; therefore, because they are sprinkled with the black circle on the inside and the white one on the outside, those two circles which are predominantly greyish-white are also [included],
since the measure of that [object] comes to rest in the subject (pramātṛ) who possesses it.

Because the fourfold group of forms does not exist separately [from the subject], the wheel of eight spokes is said to consist of the three Bhairavas, the three Goddesses, Kuleśvara, and Kuleśvarī— predominated by the subject who is the nature of withdrawal; this is how the meaning is to be understood, as he will state:
"From the sixteen and twelve-spoked [wheels], into the eight-spoked ones in every respect"—
thus, within that very white mandala, which is exceedingly black and designated by the term *kumārikā*, those two mandalas situated there belong to the subject as well.

The meaning is that because they rest within valid cognition (*pramā*), they flash forth in the four-petaled lotel of the objects of knowledge as the triad of goddesses and the venerable *Mātṛsadbhāva*, appearing in the form of the "Inexplicable Wheel" (*anākhyacakra*) whose true essence is pure cognition. For this very reason, because it effects the withdrawal of all things, it exists here in an undifferentiated state.

Because it is of the nature of *tamas*, it possesses blackness (*kārṣṇya*). Thus, it has been stated that the fourfold sequence of emanation and so forth resides in the eye as the form of its specific constituent parts; therein, he describes its essential nature as it occurs accordingly, beginning with the words "Agni-Soma," regarding this fourfold wheel.
In the sixteen-spoked and eight-spoked wheels, which consist of Agni and Soma,

and are composed of the subject and the object, there exist two wheels that take the form of a couple by virtue of being both the enjoyer and the enjoyed; these two perform the mutual closing and opening [of their petals]— that is, they effect contraction and expansion.

This is the meaning: for the knower (pramātā), by effecting a closing within his own self, brings forth the object of knowledge (prameya); and by closing the object of knowledge, he brings forth his own self. The same applies to the object of knowledge as well; such is the meaning of the word "mutually" (anyonya). And this very [process] is said to be the nature of emission (sṛṣṭi) and withdrawal (saṃhāra).

Furthermore, that which is to be known (prameya) cannot attain rest within the subject (pramātṛ) without ascending into the means of knowledge (pramāṇa); thus, even the [subject’s] abiding [in itself] is implied by the object. Moreover, the subject, through its orientation toward the object, becomes free from further desire upon the arising of satisfaction—thinking, "This object has been known by me"—and thus rests within its own self.
One should attain rest—thus, from the friction between the subject and the object, there shall arise the manifestation of the full and supreme consciousness. (128–130)
Therefore he says:
"Just as the womb and the linga flow with nectar through their union, so too, through the union with the fire of nectar, they will flow; of this there is no doubt. (4.131)
According to the principle stated in such passages as, "In order to accomplish the means of enjoyment for this one who desires enjoyment, the King of Mantras,
having entered Māyā through His powers, brought forth the universe," the *yoni*— which is Māyā— attains a union characterized by mutual penetration.
And the *Liṅga* [Purāṇa] states:

"By the word *liṅga*, the wise call that imperishable state of all beings the cause of creation and dissolution, because of the merging (*laya*) [of things] into it and their emergence (*āgamana*) from it."

By such statements as these, the Supreme Lord is the performer of the fivefold acts beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*). Just as those two flow—that is, they perform emission—so too do they [flow] in the sixteen-spoked and eight-spoked wheels;
namely, of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) which is the moon-natured nectar, and of the subject (*pramātṛ*) who is fire. This is beyond doubt.

From the conjunction characterized by mutual orientation, the nectar—the supreme reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which is without beginning or end because it is not limited by time—flows; that is to say, it expands in that very form. For it is consciousness itself that, having become solidified, rests upon the forms of blue and so forth.

The intention is that, by means of ascending through the levels of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), having dissolved its own form [into consciousness], it attains rest in the subject (*pramātṛ*) and shines forth by way of its own nature as being one with the subject. || 131 ||
Now, one might object: "This worldly transaction consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, which are all illusory;
therefore, how could such a state occur even while that [transaction] exists? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From the pressure of that wheel, a light shines at night reaching both the sun and the moon."
Having seen that supreme moonlight, the knowledge of time proceeds.

From the pressing— characterized by the extraction of the essential meaning— from those two wheels consisting of sixteen and eight spokes, which are of the nature of the subject and the object; at night— even while Māyā still exists— that which goes beyond the sun and the moon, transcending both the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge.
The light characterized as the subject shines forth indeed; that which, in relation to the means of knowledge and so forth,
is designated by the word "moonlight" because it supremely nourishes the universe and so on— having seen it, that is,
having perceived it as being one's own essential nature.

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "Time, in the form of Bhairava, creates the universe from its primary cause down to the smallest insect," Time is the manifestation (*kalana*) of the entire universe consisting of creation and so forth;
it is the full Light whose sole nature is the Supreme Subject. Knowledge of that [Light] proceeds—that...
The meaning is that it appears in that very form. || 132 ||
Now, one might object: "If this were so, would there not be no manifestation of the universe at all? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The thousand-spoked wheel exists situated above those two.
From "those two" means from the presence of those very two wheels consisting of sixteen and eight spokes.
The thousand-spoked wheel— the universe, which possesses infinite divisions in the form of the elements, states of being, worlds, and so forth—
should be situated above; the meaning is that even while appearing as something separate, it should manifest as being entirely contiguous with itself.
From that wheel characterized as the universe (viśva), further intermediate wheels have emerged; thus he says:
"The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is said to have arisen from that wheel. (4.133)
"The cosmic egg" (brahmāṇḍa) is an elliptical expression that also includes the egg of primordial nature (prakṛtyaṇḍa) and the others. || 133 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But how could the universe manifest in so many diverse ways with such uninterrupted continuity?", he says:
"For the Moon, ignited by Fire, releases the stream situated therein."

For when Soma, whose nature is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), is ignited by Agni— which is of the singular form of the supreme subject— through its own sovereignty, being thus inflamed in its outward orientation, it releases the stream situated therein— that is, existing everywhere— in an uninterrupted flow in the form of the subject, the object, and so forth.
It vibrates as a continuous flow, by which this expansion of the universe has come to be.
He states that this [Lord] creates not only the common universe, but even the uncommon one as well:
"In this manner, he creates the entire infinite world within each and every self" (4.134).
The repetition "in each self" (ātmanyātmani) signifies "in every individual soul" (pratyātmam). || 134 ||
And how is that? He says:
"Then, from the sixteen- and twelve-spoked [cakras] into the eight-spoked ones, and everywhere in this manner, the supreme nectar [flows] through all the cakras. (4.135)
Soma flows as long as the sequence of the five wheels;

by the use of the plural "in the eight-spoked [wheels]," the sense of "and so forth" is obtained, which implies the four-spoked wheel as well— thus, together with the sixteen- and twelve-spoked wheels, it refers everywhere to all of these four.

In the wheels (*cakreṣu*), thus— in the sequence of descent according to the stated reasoning— *sarvaśaḥ*, in every way, the supreme nectar— the innate essence consisting of externalized form, which is Soma, whose nature is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— flows out for as long as it is fivefold.
The "method" (paddhati)— that is, the sequence— of the four wheels beginning with the faculties of cognition (buddhīndriya) and so forth,
means that [the reality] should manifest in a gross form as the nature of the objects of knowledge (prameya-prakṛti), extending up to the earth-element (pṛthvī-tattva). For the Supreme Lord indeed...
Desiring to manifest the nature of the universe through its own sovereignty,
it assumes the form of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth, by way of the manifestation of limited subjectivity and the like.
The meaning is that it manifests in the form of the body composed of the five elements, consisting of cause and effect;
moreover, this [consciousness] not only creates the world but also withdraws it, as he says:
"Furthermore, vibrating as 'haṃsa, haṃsa,' the Swan drinks it with delight. (4.136)
But by hearing this even once, one is no longer stained by merit or sin;

for through an unartificial, innate, and creative-reflexive awareness (*vimarśa*) that effects both emission and reabsorption, one realizes: "I am the nature of the supreme subject, yet I am the expansion of the universe," or "Even as the expansion of the universe, I alone am."
Because it proceeds continuously and vibrates without interruption,

the Supreme Self, Śiva, is the *haṃsa*; according to such statements as "The *haṃsa* is the Supreme Self, Śiva," the term *haṃsa*— possessing the qualities of abandoning (*hāna*) and taking up (*samādāna*)— is designated by the word "fire" (*agni*).

The supreme subject—that is, the universe consisting of the knower, the known, and so forth—furthermore, after the time of emanation and the rest, is "drunk" by means of "joy"—that is, bliss and sovereignty;
he makes it his own essence and withdraws it, which is the meaning. This belongs to that supreme Self, the *haṃsa*, who has performed [this act] once.

Even by hearing it but once—that is, through direct realization—every person is no longer tainted by merits and sins; the meaning is that they are not touched by their own performed good and evil deeds such that those would grant further experience, but rather they are indeed liberated. Therefore...
It would thus be said that only for a person who possesses this direct realization is there the fulfillment of all purposes, and not for anyone else;
as it has been stated:
"A man remains one whose purpose is unfulfilled so long as he does not find the *haṃsa*."
Thus [ends the verse]. 136.
Having thus explained how he brings about withdrawal as an incidental consequence, he returns to the subject at hand:
"Then, having become possessed of transformation within the five-spoked [wheel], from the nectar flowing from the moon... (4.137).
This pervasive Lord runs through the secret wheels (*guhyacakras*) which possess three spokes and three essences.
Now, this "Lord"— designated by the term *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self, Śiva—
having assumed contraction through His own sovereignty, [runs] within the five-spoked [wheel], that is, within the body composed of the five elements.

Having become subject to modification by being nourished with the nectar flowing from the moon according to the reasoning just stated, and thus increasing through connection with modifications such as birth, [the central channel] possesses three spokes of the three rasas:
"The left channel, Ambuvāhā, carries [menstrual] blood; the middle one, Śukravāhinī, carries semen."

By the statement beginning with "Dakṣasthā, Raktavāhā, and... and so forth, there are three flavors (rasas) such as water and the rest; those [cakras] are of such a nature that their spokes (arās) consist of channels (nāḍīs) numbering that same amount. Alternatively, they have three spokes when in the state of being single (viyuta), and six spokes when in the state of being coupled (yāmala).
Because they are non-manifest, they are secret; for this very reason, the cakras, beginning with the place of birth, are of the nature of mysteries.
"He runs" means that he proceeds with an orientation toward them out of a desire to emit the universe.
Now, one might object: "If this [Lord] indeed desires to emit the universe, what is the purpose of his activity directed toward that end? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From whom the world is born and in whom it is dissolved by his own play. (4.138)

From which—namely, from those very secret wheels (guhyacakras)—the world has arisen through its own play (*svakalīlayā*), that is, through its own sovereignty (*svasvātantryāt*); although it has thus shone forth as something appearing to be separate (*atirekāyamāṇatayā*), it is said to be non-different from them precisely because its manifestation would otherwise be impossible: "And in that very place..."
"Līnam" (the dissolved state): thus, the intended meaning is that this very world is the supreme cause of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, who desires to emit it. || 138 ||
Not only is this [power] the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for them when directed toward external objects, but also when resting within one's own self; thus he says:
"In that state, there is bliss for everyone, and the celibate student (*brahmacārī*) is devoted to that."
Therein, both accomplishment and liberation are attained together as a pair.
"Of everyone" means even of the common folk and others; "intent upon that" means having that as one's sole refuge;
furthermore, whether he be a man of knowledge (*jñānī*), a yogi, or a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), [it is said]: "Bliss is the nature of Brahman... and so forth.

By such statements as these, it is meant that Brahman, whose nature is bliss, "moves"—that is, it shines forth in identity with the Supreme Brahman. For this very reason, there is "attainment" (siddhi), which consists of worldly bliss; and "liberation" (mukti), which consists of the state of being a true seeker of Brahman (brahmacāritva). They are "equal" because bliss itself is the very nature of Brahman. || 139 ||

Now, one might object: "If the creation of the universe were thus accomplished from this single secret wheel (guhyacakra) known as the place of birth, for what purpose is this indicated by the plural term 'secret wheels'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
From there, he ascends again as far as the state whose nature is Brahman;
there, Agni and Soma are produced equally by the Self within the Self. (140)

Therefore— from the secret wheel (guhyacakra) known as the place of birth as previously described— further upward is the supreme state consisting of Brahman, situated at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta),
which is the secret wheel designated by the term "emission" (visarga) and joined with the triad of spokes consisting of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
The meaning is that as long as [the mind] moves, it proceeds with an orientation toward that; the word "ca" (and) indicates the reason, for there, within the Self—

by the Supreme Lord designated by the term *haṃsa*— within His own creative ground (*svabhitti*), the two principles of subject and object, consisting of the natures of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), are emitted as the equalized *agni* and *soma*.

The meaning is that, according to the logic of such passages as "For there is co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the cognition of 'Being' (sadvidyā) and the cognition of 'I-this' (aham-idam-dhī)," these two appear as being of equal status. || 140 ||
Furthermore, when there is an overflow of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) whose nature is the Moon (*soma*), then there is the blossoming of the universe; thus he says:
"Situated therein and heated, the Moon is established in two ways in the shanks.
Therein—meaning while situated in the state of equilibrium—the Moon, which is the nature of the object of knowledge, is illuminated in two ways.
Being thus inspired by differentiation, he is established in the shanks; the meaning is that he shines forth in a gross form as the universal self, extending down to the earth-element.
And how is this so? He says:
"One should cause the fire below to fall; in an instant, nectar flows forth. (4.141)
Clearly manifested in the ankles, knees, and other parts, that power, ignited by the curved sun and further heated, brings forth the sequence beginning with the five spokes. (4.142)

The word *adha* (down) refers to the state of external manifestation; *tam* (him) refers to Soma; and "flowing with nectar" means that Soma, being heated by fire, [flows] because that power—which is the nature of the *prāṇakuṇḍalinī*, which is curved (*kuṭilā*), consists of Soma, and is of the nature of action—is [heated] by the *arka*, that is, by the subject alone.
Abiding in the state of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is ignited— meaning awakened— with the desire to manifest externally;
for this very reason, being heated again— that is, further stimulated— as an external form,
it would create the sequence beginning with the five spokes— the meaning is that it would illuminate the universe consisting of the five elements.
He extends this [principle] to the other sense organs as well:
"In the same way, it should be understood regarding the ear, up to the range ending with the feet.
By the phrase "up to the range ending with the feet," it is stated that the organs of action (karmendriyas) also possess this same nature.

This nature exists not only in the sense organs, which are of the nature of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but extends even to the five elements, which are of the nature of objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Thus he says:
"Beginning from the big toe up to the vision of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). (143)

The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: "In this same way, it should be understood even within the body composed of the five elements, starting from the big toe up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Thus, even in the state of being an object of knowledge, the supreme consciousness itself exists in the form of the perceived. In this regard also—
That this alone is the means of valid cognition is established by implication; for this very reason, it will be corroborated later on. || 143 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of describing the sense organs and so forth in such a manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, the yogi who does not know [this] is no yogi at all; by knowing it, he becomes the Lord of the Universe.
Blazing as it were, this Supreme Lord is beheld even by Brahmā and the other gods. (4.144)

"By Brahmā and the others"—the sense is that the entire world is indeed an expansion of this very [reality]. Furthermore, although the sequence of conduct (*caryākrama*) is situated within this very process, it has not been elaborated upon in such detail here because it is both very clear and secret; thus, it should be understood by oneself. || 144 ||
Having thus corroborated the scripture, he explains its intended meaning:
"In this regard, the fourfold sequence has been taught with respect to each sense-faculty (akṣa) according to its essential purport; therefore, the nature of being twelvefold is proclaimed. (4.145)

"In each individual sense-organ" (ekaikatrākṣe) means, in short, in all the senses collectively; therefore, because the fourfold sequence beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi) exists individually within the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, for this reason—since—the twelvefold nature is said to arise in each individual sense-organ. One.
The meaning is that the single sense-faculty has the form of twelve rays. || 145 ||

One might ask: "Why has only the explanation of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) been provided? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It has not been explained by dissecting [the text] because it is exceedingly secret.
It is not only the supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*) that takes the form of apprehension during the state of valid cognition (*pramāṇadaśā*)."
Even in the state of being an object of knowledge, she possesses the form of the apprehended; thus he says:
"The Goddess, remaining even within the object of knowledge, takes the form of the lunar mansions, the zodiac signs, and so forth. (4.146)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the vowels and so forth, delimited by the number twelve,
as it has been said:
"The vowels are declared to be exactly twelve, excluding the neuter ones."
The twelve Ādityas are proclaimed to be stationed within the twelve spokes.

"The months are said to be twelve; the digits (kalās) are designated as twelve. The sense is that even in the state of being the object of measurement, this [power] possesses precisely a twelvefold nature. || 146 ||
Thus, this one supreme consciousness alone manifests everywhere in various forms; so he says:
"Therefore, this consciousness abides as both internal and external;
having manifested itself, it shines as if manifesting something else therein. (4.147)

Therefore— on account of this reason, namely, that she abides everywhere as has been demonstrated— this supreme consciousness, whose essence is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), although she remains having manifested her own self through her own majesty in the form of both subject and object (such as the knower and the known) by way of being both internal and external, [remains] therein.

It shines forth as if manifesting something else, distinct [from itself]— the meaning being that this fact is established by the experience of everyone; for although in reality it is only supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvid*) that shines, and nothing could appear if there were anything separate from it, nevertheless, at the very outset, through its own sovereignty alone, it appears as if the subject and so forth were distinct from it.
By which it shines forth, its twelvefold nature manifesting. || 147 ||
Now, demonstrating this very point through analysis, he makes known the affinity of this vision with the method of sequential progression:
"And therefore, previously, this pure [power], eager to manifest in such a way..."
The Goddess brings forth creation; therefore, it is called Āgama by that name.

Therefore— because it is precisely the supreme consciousness that manifests as the various forms of subjects and so forth— for that reason, prior to such manifestation, this "Śrī Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī" is pure— that is, uncolored by the fixed forms of subjects and the like.
The Goddess Parā Consciousness, who is expressible through words, shines forth by devouring the stain of the measurement of time;

thus, although not distinct from her own Self, she manifests through her sovereignty as if she were distinct, and being intent upon emission, she is eager for creation and brings about the world-emanation.
*Kalayate*—she contemplates the multitude of objects that are almost externally projected;
for this very reason, she is called by the meaningful name *Śrīsṛṣṭikālī* in the scriptures, such as the *Śrīpañcaśatika*, which means she is designated by that term. As it has been said therein:
Arising from mantra, having the nature of space, abiding in space, yet devoid of space;
she is all things, yet liberated from all, the destroyer of creation within the universe.
"That digit which possesses universal power and is capable of performing the act of creation, within which it attains peace—that is remembered as Sṛṣṭikālī.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:

"I perpetually bow to that Sṛṣṭikālī, who consists of the dense waves of bliss from the ocean of Kaula, who inwardly partakes in both the unfolding (unmeṣa) and the closing (eṣa), and who dissolves within the blue abode of Kula. (148)
Having thus described the nature of emanation as it pertains to the object of knowledge (*prameya*),
he speaks in order to describe its nature as maintenance (*sthiti*) as well: "In that same way, that [power], directed outwardly, effects the coloring of the portions of the manifested objects."
Then, by means of its own wheel of activity, it fully brings forth [the effects] from that as well.
This alone is the stability of existence... Therefore— even after the emergence of the venerable Sṛṣṭikālī— that very consciousness, which is the supreme subject and of a single nature,
becomes extroverted by its own sovereignty, abiding in the state of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

That wheel of functions (*vṛtticakra*), consisting of the perception of form and so forth, which belongs to one’s own self and is connected to the sense organs such as the eye— along with that [wheel], the objects characterized as the universe appear as if they were identical with it or as if they were distinct from it; of those [objects]...

By such statements as, "This entire universe consists of nothing more than this group of five, beginning with form," [it is shown that] the aspects beginning with form, while intensely— *alam*— bringing about a coloring (*rañjanā*) produced by their own agent, even by way of having the Self as their object, and while cognizing through non-conceptual functioning (*avikalpavṛtti*), [constitute] "the means of knowledge" (*mānam*).

"It would indeed be colored by the object of knowledge"—of this there is no dispute; and since the cognizer alone would manifest through the outward-turned form that constitutes the means of knowledge (*māna*), its coloring by the object occurs precisely through that [means], and not directly—this is the intended meaning. This very [process] constitutes the established state of the entire collection of entities, such as form and the rest.

The meaning is that manifestation has the nature of illumination; for that which is called an "object of knowledge" (meyam) is nothing in itself, and its existence can only occur through its ascent into the means of knowledge (pramāṇa)—this is the intention of the particle *eva*. And such a manifestation, due to its attachment to the object of knowledge alone, is designated by the term *Raktakālī*; thus, here too, it is referred to by that name.
"Scripture is said [to be this],"—this is the connection with what precedes. As it is stated in the venerable *Pañcaśatika*:
"She is not to be grasped by the eye, nor does she abide in any of the senses;
free from qualities and free from ego, she colors the entire circle of the universe."
"That digit which has arisen should be known as Raktakālikā.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:
"She who is intent on drinking the essence of the blood of the lords of heroes (*vīrendra*) from the circle of Mothers (*mātṛcakra*) offered in great play..."
"And I bow to that Viśvākṛti-Raktakālī, who at the end of the dissolution has been made red.
Now, one might object: everywhere else, after the mention of Śrī Sṛṣṭikālī, there is the mention of Śrī Sthitikālī, as it has been said:
In the *Śrīsārdhaśatika*, it is proclaimed: "The great wheel with twelve spokes is described as being in the form of rays;
I shall now declare the names of those rays as they exist."
Creation, maintenance, and destruction, as well as Raktakālī,
Svakālī, Yamakālī, and likewise Mṛtyukālī.
Rudra, Paramārka, and beyond that Mārtaṇḍa;
then Kālāgnirudra and Kālī, and again she who is named Mahākālī.
"And the word Mahābhairava, followed by the word Ghora, and finally the word Caṇḍakālī—these thirteen have been declared.
Thus it is said; so how is it that here, immediately after that, the mention of Śrī Raktakālī and the others has been made? For in this way:

Would there not be a contradiction with scripture? True—but in the scripture, this formulation is made in a fragmented and disjointed manner for the purpose of concealing the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*). This is as it stands even in the *sthitikrama* of the venerable *Pañcaśatika*, and it is by following that very [sequence] that the great teachers have commenced the ritual procedure of worship (*pūjākrama*); however, here...

For the sake of concealing the sequence of worship, it is established by means of one's own bed— that concerning which the *Saṃvitkrama* reaches its culmination; for this very reason, even though the *Śrīkramastotra* proceeds by taking refuge solely in the scriptures, the author [Abhinavagupta], in his commentary on it, demonstrates precisely that *Saṃvitkrama*.

It was stated previously that after the commentary on the verses of praise beginning with Śrī Sṛṣṭikālī, the presence of the Blessed Lady Śrī Raktakālī is to be expected hereafter; however, in this instance, such a statement is made explicitly and directly according to the perspective of the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*). Thus, [there is no contradiction].
There is no fault whatsoever. || 149 ||

Having thus described the nature of persistence as it pertains to the object of knowledge (*prameya*), he speaks in order to describe the nature of withdrawal as well: "... because of the savor of inwardness."
Desiring to withdraw [the world], she is described as "kalayantī" (measuring) the destruction of its stability.

She alone is the supreme Goddess of Consciousness; desiring to withdraw that state— which is the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and has "attachment" as its synonym— into the internal orientation toward the oneness of the subject, out of the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) consisting of the wonder of resting in one's own self in the form of the thought "the object has been known by me," [she desires to withdraw it].
"Desiring to make [the object] one with herself, she is therefore described as 'conceiving the destruction of persistence' (*sthiternāśaṃ kalayantī*);
the meaning is that in the *Śrīkramabhaṭṭāraka* and other texts, she is designated by the term *Sthitināśakālī*.
As it is said therein:"
The pure one, by whose radiance the setting sun was sent away— that [radiance] which possessed the power of constant collision and movement within the circle of wind embraced by two horses.
"I bow to Śāntā, who is Kālī at the time of the destruction of the state [of duality].
Also, in the *Śrīpañcaśatika*:
"This Hāsinī, who belongs to the individual soul (paudgalī), is conceived as being as subtle as the tip of a hundredth of a hair."
Abiding within the entire body, it is conceived as that which brings about the persistence of creation.
"When that goddess has arisen, she dissolves once again right there;
know her, O Maheśvara, Lord of the Gods of Gods, to be Sthitikālī.
Thus [ends the verse]. 150.
Having thus described the nature of withdrawal as it pertains to the object of knowledge (*prameya*), he also speaks of the nature of the Inexplicable (*anākhyasvarūpa*):

"Then, when the flavor of withdrawal is full, [the Absolute] itself produces within that portion a doubt consisting of the principle of Yama which acts as an obstacle, and it also withdraws that. (4.151)

Then— following even after the emergence of Śrī Sthitināśakālī— in this manner, within the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of the subject-self which consists of the aforementioned form of withdrawal (saṃhāra), when it has become full— that is, when it has ascended to the supreme flow— it is that very consciousness which has assumed the level of a limited subject, [and] itself—

By the power of its own sovereignty, it restrains—that is, it establishes within the limit of necessity—within a single aspect consisting of outward orientation, [determining] "this is to be done, this is not"; thus, *yama* is conceptual thought (*vikalpa*).
Animated by that [conceptual thought] is this doubt, arising from the infinity of scriptures.

Because one observes even the reversal of the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, the state of being bewildered as to what should be performed is doubt; for this very reason, it is said:
"[... one who is possessed by doubt is a vessel for obstacles."

By such statements, she creates an obstacle to the entry into one’s own true nature; she gives birth to that [obstacle], causing it to flourish up to the level of the object of knowledge (*prameya*); and she withdraws it within—the second part consisting of the state of *unmukhya*—into the nature of supreme consciousness, wherein the rules of injunction and prohibition, which are the contraction of *niyati*, have dissolved away.
It vibrates by its own expanding form, as it is said:
"Just as the vulva of a female donkey throbs at the time of urination," and so forth; thus, it is characterized by an incessant and indeterminate process of contraction and expansion.
Incapable of being described by form, she who thus restrains (yama) is defined as "Yamakālī"; this is the objection [raised] as before. As it is said in the *Śrīpañcaśatika*:
"She who abides in the very nature of Yama’s form, yet moves within a nature that transcends form."
"That digit (kalā) in which [all] dissolves is remembered as Yamakālī.
Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:
"For the restraint of the world, for the sake of Yama, the controller, who is the restraint that withdraws all objects..."
"I bow to Kālī, who draws [all things] toward herself through her passion for the playful relish of swallowing the great mouthful of the body.
Thus, the four goddesses of emanation and the rest, who delight in swallowing the portion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), have been described. (151)
Now, however, he describes the group of four goddesses beginning with Saṃhārī, who are intent upon devouring the portion of the means of knowledge (pramāṇāṃśa):
"Having withdrawn doubt, or [having withdrawn] the object of doubt from the sphere of objective existence..."
He indeed effects withdrawal by dissolving [everything] into the fire of his own self.

Thus, having withdrawn that doubt consisting of the self, or having set aside— that is, having withdrawn— the objects of doubt, namely the matters consisting of what is to be done and what is not to be done,
that supreme Goddess of Consciousness [manifests] through a function inseparable from that.

Because of the cause, which is the dissolution characterized by the reduction of all things to the fire of one's own self, she indeed effects the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) within the entire circle of existents (*bhāvamaṇḍala*).

For this reason, she is designated by the term *Saṃhārakālī* in the venerable *Pañcaśatika* and other texts; thus, it is by that name that the scripture (*āgama*) is spoken of—so it is said at length.
The connection [is as follows]; it has been stated therein:
"Caṇḍakālī, of pure color, intent upon devouring the nectar, liberated from existence and non-existence, she whose form is the dissolution of the universe."
"Wherein she goes to dissolution, that is the time of withdrawal (saṃhārakālikā).
Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:
"The infinite Unmanī, who contains all objects within her womb, attains the closing of her eyes in the withdrawal of all states of being."
"I bow to Muditā, who is eternally arisen for the sake of the arising of truth, who is void at the time of withdrawal.
Anticipating the question, "What is the nature of the conceptualization of the entities being withdrawn here?", he says:
"And one contemplates within oneself that withdrawal of entities, which consists of dissolution, by means of which [the thought] 'this has been swallowed by me' flashes forth. (4.153)
Indeed, the very dissolution of entities— which consists in their production within consciousness— is their withdrawal [into it]; that is,

by means of the effacement of their external form, there occurs a non-dual reflective awareness within consciousness as it rests in the state of the means of knowledge, for this is precisely what consciousness is.

"It must shine forth as having the form of a radiant flash, such that one thinks: 'This entire collection of objects has been manifested by me within myself without distinction. Thus it is said: "By which [consciousness] this [world] shines forth as 'swallowed by me'.
For this alone is the "creation" within the state of consciousness as a means of valid cognition—that it is colored by each respective object.
"May it shine forth. || 153 ||
Having thus described the nature of emanation as it pertains to the means of valid cognition,
he speaks in order to describe the nature of persistence as well:
"For the very nature of this consciousness is its own self, which has the limiting adjunct of withdrawal."
In the unconditioned, perfectly pure nature of consciousness, it sets.
Even when that which is to be withdrawn has been so withdrawn, there remains the consciousness consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
which is of the nature of death because it withdraws all objects;

and from this [consciousness], there is one's own [nature] which is everywhere free from the distinctions of objects such as those to be withdrawn— whether they be things to be done or not to be done.

Such is this unique nature that it could not even maintain its existence without resting within the consciousness of its own parts; thus, like the object of knowledge, it resides within the means of knowledge when that means is free from adjuncts—that is, uncolored by various objects—and for that very reason, perfectly pure: namely, within the self of the knower, whose essence is consciousness.

"It sets" (*astamīyate*)—it should attain rest in that very [state] in the form of attachment, whereby its nature as the power of withdrawal (*saṃhartṛtva*) alone remains established; thus, because this consciousness—even though it is of the nature of death—is an act of creative ideation (*kalanā*), it is proclaimed everywhere as "the Time of Death" (*mṛtyukālī*). This is what is obtained by implication.
As it is said in the venerable *Pañcaśatika*: "OṂ—this is the Mistress of the Kula, who brings about the end at the time of death.
O Śiva, if the digit of the time of death should enter her body..."
"Then she should be known as Mṛtyukālī, O Consort of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:
"Death is the pride exulting in the expansion of the entire range of the digits of egoism, such as 'mine'."
"I bow to that Mṛtyukālī, arisen beyond time, by whom even the devouring consciousness is swallowed.
Having thus described the nature of persistence as it pertains to the means of knowledge, he also describes the nature of withdrawal:
"Even when the flood of entities has been dissolved, she at that very moment causes some entity to solidify—namely, that which remains in the form of the latent impression of doubt. (4.155)

"By virtue of being auspicious or inauspicious, he shall bring forth the abundance of fruits. For in this way, even when the flood of objective phenomena (*bhāvaugha*) in the form of effects has been withdrawn through resting in the consciousness of the pure subject (*nirupādhi-śuddha-pramātṛ-saṃvit*), that supreme consciousness, immediately following its own manifestation (*vilāpa*), [produces] something..."
One should cause the entity, which possesses a specific form, to solidify— that is, even though it has been dissolved,

one should bring it to a state of density by means of its nature as the manifestation of some degree of differentiation. That very thing which has become solidified and exists in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) "remains as doubt," because it serves as the cause for that [doubt].

The meaning is that [the mind] remains fixed; for it is due to this very [ignorance] that a cognizer, failing to attain certainty regarding the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done amidst the infinite scriptures that display various modes of conduct, thinks: "Enveloped by darkness, she perceives non-dharma as dharma."
According to this principle— that whatever takes root in the heart in a certain manner will bear fruit for that person in that very way—

it is this very latent impression (*saṃskāra*), established by the fixed nature of things characterized as "to be done" or "not to be done," which, having been awakened, will produce an abundance of results consisting of both auspicious and inauspicious forms; this is the cause of doubt.
By means of which this world, through its status as a vessel for heaven, hell, and so forth, becomes an experiencer of pleasure, pain, and the like.

(155) Now, one might object: "If the cognizer suspects this, then because no certainty regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done arises, he would not perform anything at all; thus, how could [action] bear fruit as being auspicious or inauspicious?"— [The response follows: ...[as the text continues].
Anticipating this objection, he says: "For this doubt persists either prior to or after experience. (4.156)

In this world, because of the diversity among all people regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, as well as their experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth, a doubt arises even before [action]— namely, "What should be performed by me?"— though it occurs only in some cases due to the varying degrees of the awakening of one's own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

In someone, a certain conviction arises; following that, by virtue of partaking in the results of good and evil through the performance of those actions, there would be for him the state of being an experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Subsequently, due to the affliction caused by pain and the like, this doubt arises in him: "Surely, that which was not to be done..."
"I performed this as a duty, by which I have thus become overcome by suffering"—
this very doubt, arising at that moment, loosens even that [action] such as the immolation of a Brahmin previously committed,
so that it cannot yield its fruit, whether auspicious or inauspicious, by virtue of its residual force (*anuśaya*).
He would be able. || 156 ||
He says that very thing: "This [power] would melt even that which has solidified at another time, just as the act of killing a Brahmin [is dissolved] by rites such as penance. (4.157)
Neither the limited subject nor his mental factor known as doubt is capable of effecting this; thus he says:
"By means of obstructing and dissolving, consciousness fashions form in this manner."

Thus, even for an object that exists in the form of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), this supreme consciousness—by obstructing and dissolving it while fashioning its form in the manner described—is designated as "Rudrakālī" in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva-Ṭṭāraka*. This is the meaning. As it has been said:
In that regard:
"All this is non-all, for it is eternally subject to dissolution;
it is swallowed by the end of the line of the curved glance, and it has set."
Then, permeated by the essence of awakening, throbbing and undisturbed,
she both vomits forth a thousand rays of light and drinks them in profusely.
"That power (kalā) in which [all] dissolves is remembered as Rudrakālī.

Furthermore, in the *Śrīpañcaśatika* and other texts, she is called "Bhadrakālī"; thus, although there is a difference in name, there is no difference whatsoever in the reality itself—whether it be that which obstructs or that which dissolves the differentiated object.
Thus, in both ways, there is a correspondence with the meaning; as it was said therein:
"She is easily accessible through coming and going, beholding great awakening, liberated from the impurity of *māyā*, and delighting in the nectar of pure consciousness."
The auspicious Rudrā, who bestows happiness upon the entire world—
wherein every fragment [of worldly existence] is stilled— is remembered as Rudrakālī.
"Because she dissolves all differentiation, she is Bhadrā, who brings about auspicious success.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Śrīkramastotra*:
"The universe [is consumed] by her who wanders with a terrifying frown at the end of existence, at the conclusion of the Great Kalpa, and at the end of the Kalpa..."
"I bow to that auspicious Bhadrā Śubhabhadrakālī, who consumes [all things] with her infinite, powerfully blazing radiance.
Thus it is said.
This [power] not only dissolves an object that has already been solidified, but may also solidify even that which has been dissolved; thus he says:
"It may indeed dissolve that, and then it may solidify that as well" (4.158).

And thus, although it possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in this context, the primary importance belongs solely to the cognizer who effects the withdrawal of those respective objects; for this reason, the author places his emphasis on the word "Rudra."
Having thus described the nature of reabsorption as it pertains to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he speaks in order to describe its nature as the "Inexplicable" (*anākhyā*) as well:
"In this way, when even the object of enjoyment has been enjoyed, its instruments [are also absorbed]."
Withdrawing [them], she manifests the twelve [suns] within herself as the "I. || 4-159 ||

Even when the object has been thus withdrawn, consciousness—while withdrawing all twelve instruments (*karaṇa*) that determine it—merges within the "I" in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); the meaning is that it leads them to dissolution right there. || 159 ||
Now, one might ask: what are these twelve instruments, and what constitutes their instrumentality?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The group of the organs of action and the organs of cognition, ending with the intellect, consists of twelve."
Because it is illuminating, the solar self unfolds within distinct objects. (4.160)
"They awaken"— together with the mind— because they are illuminators, that is, because their nature consists in the observation of objects;
"the solar self"—
for they say that the sun is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)........."

By such statements, the meaning is that [consciousness] has the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for it is said that "the means of valid cognition is that which delimits a distinct object of knowledge (*prameya*)," as expressed in the phrase "it unfolds within a differentiated reality. || 160 ||

Now, one might object: since the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is also included within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), how can it be said that "there are only twelve instruments"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the ego-sense is an instrument whose sole function is self-identification (abhimāna)."
Because it possesses uninterrupted reflective awareness, it dissolves therein. (4.161)

Furthermore, *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-sense) is the instrument whose nature is to reflect upon every object, because it is the sole means for the conceit "I hear," "I see," and so forth; it functions as an uninterrupted, undifferentiated unity with the subject (*pramātṛ*), since it does not assume any specific distinctions. Thus it is.
The entire group of twelve instruments also dissolves into that ego; the meaning is that it comes to rest solely within it. || 161 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even though there is no difference in their status as instruments (*karaṇa*), how is it that the group of instruments beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) dissolves specifically into the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)? He pacifies this doubt by presenting an illustrative example:
Just as the various instruments such as the sword and the noose are dissolved into one's own hand and so forth, which are non-different from them, so too is this rule. (4.162)
In this case, if the instrument (*karaṇa*) were distinct [from the agent], what would constitute its status as an instrument? For such a consequence would apply to everything.

Furthermore, if it were that which is impelled (*preryatva*), it would be the object (*karman*) in the act of impelling, not the instrument; nor can there be an action without an instrument. Thus, in that case too, another instrument would have to be postulated, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

It may be so; for just as an instrument such as a sword, though distinct from that [agent], functions as an instrument through the contemplation of its non-difference from the hand and other parts which are non-different from the agent, so too, because the intellect and the rest dissolve into the *ahaṅkāra*— which, by touching upon the "I-portion," is non-different from the knower— the same applies here.
This has been rightly stated: "The intellect dissolves into the ego. || 162 ||
This very point is applied to the present context:
"Therefore, by her own sovereignty, the Goddess of Consciousness herself should draw forth the solar orb of the multitude of senses within the constructed self of egoity. (4.163)

By that— by the aforementioned sequence— the Goddess of Consciousness, through her own sovereignty and not through the mediation of limited subjects and so forth, [projects] the solar orb of the senses beginning with the intellect, delimited by the number twelve.
Due to the deep-seated attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to the body and so forth, one should conceive of the imagined self consisting of egoity (*ahaṃkṛtātman*);
that is, one should bring about its state of being composed solely of that [consciousness], by which she is called "Mārtaṇḍakālī" in the *Śrīkramastotra* and other texts.
As it is said there:

"I perpetually bow to that Mārtaṇḍakālī, who, like a moth, makes the sun— the consumer of the orb of the sun— a fuel for the fire of Time, thereby bringing about the end of the essence of the universe.
Thus it is said in the *Śrīpañcaśatika* as well:
Transcending the state of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), she reaches the end of the thirty-six principles and the nine peaceful states;
having emerged from the fragments of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), she is the imperishable form of Mārtaṇḍī.
"That digit (kalā) in which [the sun] dissolves is called Mārtaṇḍī Kālikā. ||163||
Thus, the group of four goddesses inclined toward consuming the objective aspect of cognition (*prameya*) has been described;
now he describes the group of four goddesses adept at savoring the subjective aspect of cognition (*pramātṛ*).
That very Supreme Sun, the thirteenth, who is nearly full—
Because it is an instrument, it clearly undergoes dissolution into the agent. (4.164)
In this way, when the twelve instruments beginning with the intellect have been withdrawn into the supreme sun named *ahaṅkāra*,

that very [sun] named *ahaṅkāra*— the thirteenth— is as if full because it is oriented toward the subject; thus, the supreme sun, by virtue of being an instrument, clearly undergoes dissolution into the agent alone.
"Prayāti" means that one should attain identity with that [reality]. || 164 ||
Now, an objection may be raised: "The agent is indeed twofold—both contracted and uncontracted; so where, then, does this [agent] go to dissolution? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the agent is declared to be twofold, consisting of the imagined and the unimagined."
It is conceptualized as being defined by the exclusion of the body, intellect, and so forth.
In the scriptures, his designation as Kālāgnirudra is defined as follows:
"Kāla" (Time) is that which possesses the quality of delimitation, and "Agni" (Fire) is traditionally held to be the enjoyer. (4.166)
The Lord is so called because He obstructs and dissolves [the world] through the non-construction and construction of saṃsāra;
therein, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛt) of one whose state as a bound soul (paśu) has not yet ceased becomes dissolved. (4.167)

Regarding the phrase "of this"—that is, of the imagined subject who possesses the delimitation of the body, intellect, and so forth—what is the cause for the application of this designation? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Time," and so on;
"delimited" means delimitation (*vyavaccheda*), and by that time, there is that delimitation.

Agni is the enjoyer; and he, due to the non-awakening of certain latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the object of enjoyment, restrains it with the thought, "May this not be mine," while through awakening, he melts it away. Rudra, by means of enjoyment, assimilates it to his own self; for this very reason, because of his orientation toward the object of enjoyment, the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) has not yet ceased.
The meaning is that there is a connection with the *āṇavamala*, which consists of a burgeoning desire;
"therein" means within the limited subject known as Kālāgnirudra.
Thus, because of this reckoning, [the light] of the supreme sun named *ahaṅkāra* resides within the limited subject known as Kālāgnirudra.
In the *Śrīkramastotra* and other works, she is called "Paramārkakālī," as it is said therein:

"I bow to that infinite Paramārkakālī, in whom the crest-flame of Bharga— like a flame entering the sun— meets its destruction of radiance upon reaching her, who possesses the twelve suns that have both set and risen within her tranquil abode."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīpañcaśatika*:
"The solitary one, the sole heroine, exceedingly subtle, yet devoid of subtlety;
she is the state of the plane of the Supreme Self, whose nature is both transcendent and immanent."
"O Śiva, O one whose limbs are adorned with ashes, that digit (kalā) in which [the other] dissolves by means of its supreme form is to be known as the Supreme Sun.
Thus [ends verses 165–167].
Having thus described the nature of emanation as it pertains to the subject, he also speaks of the nature of persistence:

"That [subject] too, because its activity is imagined, dissolves into the expansive Great Time, which consists of 'I' and 'this' and is characterized solely by non-difference from the universe. (4.168)
In this way, when the ego (ahaṅkāra) has been swallowed, there must also be a swallowing of its swallower— the constructed subject designated by the term Kālāgnirudra. Thus, that constructed subject,
precisely because it is constructed, consists of "I" and "this," since for that very reason the sense of "this-ness" (idantā) comes to rest within the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā).

It dissolves into Mahākāla— the supreme, unconstructed [reality] whose nature is described in such passages as, "Time, in the form of Bhairava, emits the world from its primary cause down to the smallest insect"— which is characterized solely by the non-differentiation of all things and is therefore ever-expanding.

She is called "Kālāgnirudrakālī" in the venerable *Pañcaśatika* and other texts because she brings about the creative activity (*kalana*) of Kālāgnirudra, who is essentially the limited subject, so that he may come to rest within the subject consisting of the full self-reflection of "I. As it has been said:
The bestower of boons, possessing universal form, she is the supreme digit who transcends the qualities;
she is soundless yet resounds with the eternal note, intent upon swallowing the fire of time.
"That in which one clearly becomes tranquil— free from affliction and free from form—
is to be known as Kālāgnirudrakālī, who is worshipped by the immortals.
Thus it is said in the *Śrīkramastotra* as well:
"I bow to that Kālānalarudrakālī, in whom the fierce Kālāgnirudra— the mass of whose fire is embraced by the solar orb as it is overtaken by the succession of time— attains dissolution. (168)
Having thus described the nature of persistence as it pertains to the subject, he also states the nature of withdrawal:
"In this self-awareness, the consciousness shines forth in its expanding form as 'I am the all-pervasive Lord of all this. (4.169)
Then, consciousness—though perfectly full and colored by the enjoyment of the state of being the self of all that exists within—dissolves into the abode of Akula. (4.170)

In this way, when the limited cognizer in the form of Kālāgnirudra has been swallowed, there must likewise occur a swallowing of Mahākāla— the supreme cognizer who consists of the perfect state of "I-ness"— by means of a swallowing that is essentially the repose within one's own self-awareness.
Thus, within this consciousness— which has been described as such and which belongs to one's own self, the Great Time (Mahākāla)— [one realizes]:
"All this is my own manifestation..."

As stated in such passages, the All-pervasive One (Vibhu) is "I alone am all this. Thus, there manifests a particular experience—a consciousness characterized by the absolute non-duality of the universe, and for that very reason, possessing a fully blossoming form, which is adept at relishing the limited subject. Even that [consciousness], immediately after such a manifestation, [is absorbed] within—
The experience of all entities— which exist in identity with the subject and are therefore of the nature of the Self of all, since everything is the Self of everything—

is the act of assimilating them into one's own self through the method of "complete swallowing" (*alaṃgrāsa*) by means of the process of "forceful digestion" (*haṭhapāka*); it is by this that [consciousness] becomes colored.

She has the singular nature of withdrawal; for this very reason, she is perfectly complete; and for this very reason, because she does not become an object of enjoyment for anyone, she is consciousness (*vitti*) whose form consists of the agency of the act of knowing.
She is the imperishable, the unmanifested (*akula*), the immeasurable, in whom the waves of discrimination between existence and non-existence have subsided.
"He triumphs, the supreme abode of Kālī, vast with the glory of light. Thus,
one dissolves into the abode of Akula, which possesses the nature described in such passages—
that is, one should attain the state of resting upon the reflective awareness of "I," whose essence is the wonder of repose in one's own self.
Thus, because of the reckoning of Mahākāla, she is called "Mahākālakālī" in the *Śrīkramastotra* and other texts;
as it is said therein:
"She is described as being at night in the cremation ground, the dissolution of the great elements, together with the assembly of the Dikkhecarīs."
"I bow to Kālī, who completely devours Mahākāla, who is inconceivable, and whose splendor is like that of wind and fire.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīpañcaśatika*:
"Blazing with the seasons, greatly radiant, she possesses a luster equal to ten million suns."
Free from the stain of parts (kalā), she is intent on the reckoning of time (kāla).
"Where she attains dissolution, she is remembered as Kālakālī.
Thus [ends verses 169–170].
Having thus described the nature of withdrawal as it pertains to the subject, he now describes the nature of the Inexplicable (anākhyā) as well:
"The class of subjects, the flood of means of knowledge, and the various forms of valid cognition abide in manifold ways."
That which is called the flood of objects of knowledge is, in this context, nothing but pure consciousness alone.
That which constitutes the absolute freedom of self-awareness as it assumes such a manifold variety of forms, independent of anything else, is the Supreme Goddess, Parā. (4.172)

Thus, here—in the abode of Akula, which consists of the self-reflective awareness of "I"—all this, namely the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing, though manifesting in diverse forms, is nothing but pure consciousness alone;
the meaning is that it shines forth as having that single essence. Therefore, to this extent...
Of that supreme consciousness, which is self-luminous and assumes a manifold variety of forms delimited by the knower and so forth, there is that which is independent [of anything else]:
"Of that God beyond gods, whose nature is supreme awakening..."

"Vimarśa (reflective awareness) is the supreme power, endowed with omniscient knowledge. Thus, [the text describes] freedom (*svācchandyam*) consisting of the reflective awareness of "I," whose nature has been described in such passages. This [freedom] proceeds through the process of objects of cognition:
by the term "subject" (*pramātṛ*), the word "Mahābhairava" is intended; and by the term "object" (*meyapada*), the word "Caṇḍa" is intended.
By the implication of the word *pramā* for the term *ugra* and the word *māna* for the term *ghora*,
[the goddess] "Mahābhairavacaṇḍograghorakālī," who is declared in our system to be the fully supreme (*parā*) Parameśvarī, is indicated; as it is said in the venerable *Pañcaśatika*:
Abiding in the seventeenth emission, she who is terrifying as the Great Bhairava shall withdraw all the Bhairavas and the entire universe, O you who are worshipped by the gods.
"And that in which the tranquil one becomes stilled shall be Bharitabhairavī;
she is Mahābhairava, Caṇḍograghorakālī, and the Supreme (Parā).
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīkramastotra*:

"I salute Mahābhairava-ghora-caṇḍakālī, whose splendor is like the moon in the sky of the creative arts (kalā), and who possesses the supreme reality consisting of the skillful movement of the wheel of rays [of consciousness] through the three stages.
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is its 'supremacy'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Since these aforementioned modes of manifestation (*kalanā*) are said to be its unfolding (*vijṛmbhā*), therefore, because they consist of that very unfolding, each one of them possesses the nature of being everything-in-everything."

In consciousness, all consciousnesses exist in a state of non-separation; therefore, because each single consciousness possesses a twelvefold nature, one hundred and forty-four [deities] are said to be worthy of worship in the sequential worship of their movement, as the scripture states:
"One should worship the Goddess in twelve ways through the separation of the twelve spokes";
for this very reason, there is not even a slight opportunity to designate a thirteenth form.
Thus it is rightly said: "In the ultimate sense, consciousness consists of twelve aspects alone."
Now, in the Kramadarśana, the name of the Blessed Lady Śrīsukālī occurs everywhere in the midst of the goddesses beginning with Śrīsṛṣṭi;
by virtue of this, there are thirteen goddesses in the Anākhyacakra, and for this very reason,
the venerable Mahābhairava-caṇḍograghorakālī-bhaṭṭārikā also possesses the number thirteen.
As it is said in the venerable *Pañcaśatika*:
"The syllable Ḍa is terrifying, fierce, the unagitated Kulakālī;
she is unperceivable, yet perceivable and beyond perception—the one named Sukālī, who bestows accomplishment."
Thus it is said; and also in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka*:
"She is Sṛṣṭikālī in withdrawal, and that Supreme Goddess is [Sṛṣṭi-]Kālī in emission;
likewise Ghorā is Sthitikālī, and thereafter Saṃhārakālikā."
Raktakālī devours the flood of blood without distinction;
Sukālī, Yamakālī, and the terrifying Mṛtyukālī likewise consume it.
Bhadrakālī, as well as another, Paramādityakālikā;
Mārtaṇḍakālī, and Kālāgnirudrakālamaholbaṇā.
"In the family of Mahākāla, Kālī is Mahābhairavakālikā;
Kālī is to be known as being of thirteen kinds according to the distinction of names.
Thus [it is said]. The venerable *Sārdhaśatika* has just been corroborated [by this], so here [in this context]:

Even if one intends to assert that [the Krama system] is of equal status with the Krama method (*kramanaya*), how can it be stated that this is contradictory by saying, "there are only twelve goddesses"? To this it is replied: here, in the Krama system, according to the universal rule (*sarvasarvikayā*), it is accepted that there are indeed thirteen goddesses to be worshipped in the Wheel of the Inexplicable (*anākhyacakra*); thus, [the claim of only twelve] does not exist [as a contradiction].

This is the rule (*niyama*), because in the venerable *Śrīkramasadbhāvabhaṭṭāraka*, seventeen goddesses are declared to be worshipped within the Wheel of the Ineffable (*anākhyacakra*). As it is said there:
"O Great God, she who has arisen from Time is Nandinī, the blissful Śivā."
She is the mass of consciousness, situated between the pair, imperishable, yet within the sphere of the perishable.
"The eternal Akalā, who is beyond all agitation (nirākula), is Kālakālī;
she in whom that Kalā dissolves is remembered as Sṛṣṭikālī.
Beginning with these words...
The wheel of the three steps, which is great, most terrible, and even more terrible than the terrible,
is the form of Time (Kāla), beginning with Marīci and others, belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, and reaching the end of the dissolution at the end of the kalpa.

And in that state, one should practice with the very skillfulness of the Great Conduct; that auspicious Śivā who is the most terrible and fierce art (kalā) therein is she who has reached the Fourth State (turyagā).
Mahākālī, the destroyer of time, who is of a fierce form and utterly terrifying like Mahābhairava, devours all things as the sixteen-year-old.
"But know that this seventeenth [verse] is Kālī, the accomplisher of all aims.
For this very reason, it should not be understood that the sequence of worship for the author of the *Śrīstotra* follows this intention; as they say:
"And here, according to the intention of the scriptures such as the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*,

there are thirteen goddesses intended for worship in the Wheel of the Ineffable (*anākhyacakre*) within the lineages beginning with Śrīstotrakāra and Bhāskarakuladhara. For indeed, [there are] twelve [goddesses].

Or rather, regarding that under whose authority this investigation was commenced: if it is thus stated here that only twelve goddesses are to be worshipped, excluding Śrī Sukālī, what is the fault? As the Āgama says:
"By those who are red with creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, and by Yama and Mṛtyu..."
[He is worshipped] with the Rudra, Mārtaṇḍa, Paramāditya, and Kālāgnirudra [mantras].

"And with words joined at the end with the term *kālī*, preceded by *mahākāla*, one should lead to the words *mahābhairava*, *caṇḍa*, *ugra*, *ghora*, and *kālī*. Thus, in the *Kramakeli* as well, the author of this work has included this [sequence] within its core.
It has been explained there as well that nothing else is conceivable; for here,
his lineage of guru-instructions exists in many branches through the sequence beginning with Śrī Govindarāja and Śrī Bhānuka,
which even today remains by the hundreds in the heart-paths of great-souled and supreme gurus.
It flashes forth clearly, as has been stated by him in that very same place: "Just as the one illustrious Vīravara, whose name is auspiciously invoked, [known as] 'Govindarāja';
the second, the illustrious one named 'Bhānuka'; and the third, the illustrious one called 'Eraka'—all three received the instruction simultaneously."

Having received grace from Śrī Śivānandanātha, who obtained instruction at the Northern Seat (uttarapīṭha) from the Pīṭheśvarīs, they received it from Śrī Keyūravatī, Śrī Madanikā, and Śrī Kalyāṇikā. Among them, the first one, having thus received the instruction, [said]:

He reflected in his mind: "Now that this much has been attained, what further duty remains? Thus, with his mind fully satisfied, for as long as he lived, his activity was limited to merely passing the enjoyments that presented themselves, while remaining intent on instructing those disciples who were worthy vessels for the teaching of this knowledge until the end of his body.

He perceived it and transmitted this secret to the Guru named Śrī Somānanda. The second [lineage] was likewise; and from him alone comes this succession of various lineages of Gurus, beginning with the venerable Ujjaṭodbhaṭṭa.

This has been demonstrated by us, who have attained greatness through his grace. Śrī Māniraka strove for perfection, and having achieved it, he reflected in his mind: "What is the use of enjoyments, since I have undergone such great hardship; how could I [accept them]?"
I was not merely intent on uplifting the world as one who has entered the lifelong vow of the fellow-practitioner (sabrahmacārin);
for even in the state of the glorious Sadāśiva, there is Mahograkālī.

Thinking, "Bhīmotkaṭa, with his frowning brows, will come as a ground for my defeat," one should contemplate this and, attaining the supreme state, forcibly take recourse in the Goddess Akālasaṅkarṣiṇī.

Therefore, even now, thinking "I shall favor the world by propagating, even through the medium of a hymn, the secret instruction regarding my own inner state," [I act]; and thus, for those of the present day who do not know this lineage of gurus...

As for what was stated, beginning with: "There was another teacher named Śrī Bhūtirāja, a disciple of Cakrabhānu, who indeed held the position of a guru in the Kālī-naya of the master Abhinavagupta," that is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination and should be disregarded; for it is not [the case].
Śrī Cakrabhānu has taught this approximately as follows to someone; for even now, hundreds of instances of this teaching are seen to be rooted in that very [tradition], and therein also,
the sequence of worship according to Śrī Bhūtirāja is presented differently from what is found here.

By saying, "And by relying on the intention of the *Devīpañcaśatika* and those beginning with Bhūtirāja," you yourself have stated this; yet, if you now intend that "only twelve goddesses are established as objects of worship," then you do not even understand the meaning of the *Śrīpañcaśatika*.
—Therefore, go and ask your own guru: "What is the use of our revealing this?

Even in the *Śrīdevīpañcaśatika*, from the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Somānanda onwards, the lineage of gurus is exactly like that of the Trika system; thus, even there, the venerable Bhūtirāja is not his guru."
He remained [in that state], and it was not as if "this one were not his teacher," as he will say: "Now it is said that the knowledge of Brahman bestows immediate realization—
the very knowledge which Śiva, the illustrious Bhūtirāja, imparted to us."
Thus:
"The illustrious Bhūtirāja— who was Śrīkaṇṭha himself, the glorious one, assuming a human body— expounded this triad of vidyās."

And thus, what certainty is there here that [this is] not so? Furthermore, it has been understood from this that Śrīmadanikā and Śrīkalyāṇikā were likewise graced by the illustrious Avatārakanātha, just as Śrīkakāradevī was; such is this.
"The Lord, through the teaching on the distinction and non-distinction based on the fourfold support of Krama and Kula,
thus made seventeen disciples [possessing] both lineage and the absence of lineage"—
this restriction is not logical, because these two disciples have not been included, nor has anyone else.
Because it is possible for there to be some disciple [of the latter],
it is said: "Thus, from Śrī Keyūravatī up to the disciples of Śrī Cakrabhānu,
sixteen lineages of Atinaya are celebrated here in this manner."
This should also be understood in such passages as follows: here, regarding the venerable Kakāradevī,

one should not say that she had only three disciples— namely, "her disciples, the great leaders of the current tradition, were three, along with their lineages"— for [the lineage] also includes the venerable Govindarāja and the venerable Bhānuka.
Because he was her disciple, Naverakanātha was also her disciple; as they say:

"I bow to that celebrated goddess Keyūravatī, who dwells in no fixed abode, in whom the all-pervading [reality] shines forth through the constant obstruction of the *khecarī* gaze, as described without interruption."
"I bow to that glorious one named Navara, who has destroyed the power of all objective phenomena, and from whose falling flood of rays the unfolding of touch arises and expands.
Thus [it is said] also by the venerable Hrasvanātha.
"The venerable Vīranātha made five disciples in the system of the Goddess (Devīnaya).
This does not mean there were only five disciples, because there was also a sixth named the illustrious King Bhoja; as stated by the illustrious Somarāja while explaining his own lineage:

Victorious is the illustrious Vāmanabhānu, who is skillful in causing the lotus-feet of [his lineage] to bloom; he has established a continuous tradition in the supreme sky that is free from the six paths.
By him, the entire dense and most profound darkness of the terrible great delusion has been destroyed.

"I praise King Bhoja, who has been honored by the most excellent gurus and revered within by the Arhats; he has bestowed the perfect illumination which consists of the repose of the blossoming lotus-forest of the Krama, and by whom consciousness has attained the enjoyment of union with the taste of incomparable aesthetic essence."

Thus, although many such kinds of inconsistencies are possible here, they have not been demonstrated because they are irrelevant to the main point. Now, one might ask: how can this [inconsistency] also apply to the lineage of the Guru (*gurukrama*), given that it is stated here—"these goddesses are exactly twelve"—since even for the venerable Avatārakanātha...
In this context, only thirteen [authorities] are intended, among whom he who stands as the supreme guru even to Śrī Govindarāja and others is included; as he himself said:
"The one essential nature is threefold, according to the distinctions of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution."
Each of these is also fourfold, according to its arising, persistence, dissolution, and repose.
Having thus established one's own innate nature as numbering five *vasus*, [one says]:
"Victorious is Your form, which sets in motion the whirlpools of the universe's manifestation.
This is true—indeed, who here would disagree? However, [it is said that] "of this [nature], even the twelve..."
We state that they are "intended," by virtue of which the instruction of Śrī Govindarāja and others was set in motion, which has reached even our own time;
as he said:

"O Kālī, having divided the body of Time (Kāla) into five parts according to the number of sages, you are victorious as you manifest that very form shining within yourself. This is the meaning here: O Blessed Kālī, whose nature has been thus described!

By such statements as, "Time, whose own nature is solely self-luminous and yet possesses differentiation, being of the form of Bhairava, emits the universe from its primary cause down to the smallest insect," the nature of Time is [described] as the cause of the manifestation of the universe; and thus, by the reasoning already stated, [it is established].
Having divided [the universe] twelvefold by means of the number five of the Sages— thus manifesting it externally—

you then cause that very form, which is in excess, to shine within your own nature, which is a single mass of light; making it appear as non-different [from yourself], like a reflection in a mirror, you are victorious.
"You alone, as the ineffable form that performs the most difficult of tasks, manifest at all times.
Indeed, this is so:
"The one form of one's own essential nature... and so forth.

By such [an argument], there would be a contradiction— namely, how could one, having described the twelvefold arising of the supreme consciousness in one place, then describe it as thirteenfold? Therefore, in this context,
it must be stated that the thirteenfold nature belongs to the Blessed Lady herself, who exists as the agent.

How could there be syntactic unity between these two? This is not so—for if this were intended, then a fourteenth form would result in the subsequent statement, implying that the Blessed Lady exists here as well by virtue of being the agent; however, in reality, in both cases, it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
