For in the Vedic scriptures, impurity is said to exist in a dead body, in filth discarded from the body, and so forth; but elsewhere, it is not said to exist in a living body, nor in the filth situated within the body—hence [the conclusion follows].

The meaning is that whatever has fallen away from, or is distinct from, consciousness—due to the cause consisting in its being either co-existent or non-co-existent with consciousness—is impure; this everyone should understand, as no specific exception is mentioned. And for this very reason, whatever has attained identity with consciousness [is pure].

"Everything is pure. Thus, it is established as a proven conclusion that the distinction between purity and impurity everywhere depends on whether [the object] is identical to or different from consciousness. || 240 ||
And this is established not by reasoning alone, but also by scripture; thus he says:
"And it is stated in the venerable Vīrāvalī, in the determination of purity and impurity. (4.241)
He recites that very point by way of words:
"The individual soul (jīva) is the sustainer of all; there is nothing whatsoever that is soulless. Know that whatever is devoid of the soul is impure. (4-242)

He gives life to this entire collection of beings by enkindling their knowledge and action; he vitalizes them—thus he is the *jīva*, the Supreme Light. He carries and sustains the entire universe, which consists of subjects and objects—thus he is the *vāhaka*, the manifestor through his intimate union with one's own self.

This is the meaning. The reason for this is stated as: "There is nothing whatsoever that is lifeless. The sense is that nothing at all could appear apart from Light (prakāśa). Furthermore, whatever is devoid of the living principle (jīva) is not experienced as being of one essence with it; therefore, know that to be impure.

The meaning is that one should understand [the other] as something to be avoided because it is defiled by the refuse-heap of logical impossibility (*anupapatti*). Thus, since that which is distinct from consciousness is described as impure, it follows by implication that the other is indeed pure. || 242 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, that which is not too far removed from consciousness should bring about purity.
This has been stated in that very same place:
"There is nothing whatsoever that is impure; everything is established therein.
Whatever is devoid of that [Brahman] becomes impure thereby.
Thus it is said.

Now, one might object: "In that case, this distinction between purity and impurity has not been accepted by any great souls; how, then, can there be confidence in this matter for the wise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even the sages became thus through a state free of conceptual construction. (4.243)

The meaning is that, through the consciousness of "so be it," they partake in the distinction between purity and impurity by means of oneness and non-oneness with that [consciousness]. As it has been said there:
"Previously, beef and human flesh were eaten by the Ṛṣis."

Thus: for if they did not indeed know that "the purity of substances consists precisely in their identity with consciousness," then how could they consume beef and the like, which is excluded by the scriptures and opposed by the world? For this very reason, in the case of external conduct (*bāhyacaryā*), [it is said:]...

By such statements as, "Whatever substance is loathed by the world, whatever is excluded by the scriptures, and whatever is contemptible and censurable— that indeed must be consumed by heroes," a collection of substances contrary to worldly and scriptural norms is prescribed for the purpose of abandoning conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

If indeed the nature of all substances—such as being contrary to worldly norms and so forth—is not real, but rather is supreme consciousness itself, then what could possibly be loathsome or censurable? For in every case, there is no difference in their being the very form of consciousness; therefore, in that regard, there is merely the observation of the mind itself.
The purpose [of this inquiry] is: "Is the mind one-pointed within consciousness, or not? As it has been said:
"The practice that was described as having a terrifying form is not [defined] by enjoyment;
rather, it arises from the introspection of one's own mind: is the mind stable or wavering?"
Thus [ends the section]. || 243 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, why did the sages teach that meat, fish, and so forth are not to be eaten?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"However, for the sake of protecting the world, they concealed that reality."

For if this were taught in such a way, even though the world has not yet attained the consciousness of oneness with the Self, it might— driven by greed and restlessness— engage in various [prohibited] acts and thereby destroy the course of worldly life; therefore, that ultimate reality, whose nature is the non-duality of consciousness,
must be established by them preeminently through means such as the censure of those respective substances.
The meaning is that it was concealed and not revealed. As it is said in that very same place:
"Having realized everything to be of a single flavor (samarasa), one may again perform [acts such as] reviling and so forth.
It is with this very intention that it is said: "One should not do what they tell you to do; one should practice what they tell you to practice."

This and more has been stated elsewhere. Now, if this collection of entities does not exist as having an external form, then for whom would there be purity and impurity, on whose account this inquiry is even undertaken? Or, if it does exist, then it must exist exactly as it exists; what [is the point]?
Anticipating the objection—"How can there be [distinctions] through a thorough knowledge related to that subject?"—he says:
"Even though external entities exist, purity and impurity are not like the color blue. (4.244)
This [distinction] is indeed a property of the subject (*pramātṛdharma*), arising from the perception of identity with or difference from consciousness.

Even when entities such as blue and so forth are accepted as having an external form, purity and impurity are not properties of the object itself, because they do not produce modifications in the manifestation [of the object], following the same logic as [the case of] blue. Rather, [they belong to the subject].
[This pertains to] the knower (*pramātṛ*); for the knower, being endowed with excellence by virtue of perceiving both identity and non-identity with consciousness, determines accordingly:

"this is pure, this is impure. For this very reason, purity and impurity are not fixed, since what is impure for one person is not so for another. This would indeed be the case if these were properties of the object itself.
This is the fixed rule—that this is pure and that is impure—for indeed, for no one could even the blue be non-blue. || 244 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the mind of the knower becomes serene and free from doubt simply by seeing this or that particular object, how could purity and impurity not be attributes of the object itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Or rather, even if they are attributes of the object, they are dependent upon the perceiver. (4.245)
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, wine is pure for the Hotṛ priest, while for another it is the opposite.

Even if one were to admit that purity and impurity are objective properties of things, the determining factor here would still be dependence upon the subject (the cognizer). For instance—whomever [it concerns]...

The cognition of duality arises in dependence upon a cognizer; its apprehension would belong to that [cognizer] alone and not to another, because it is possible for a cognition of unity and so forth to arise in that other person as well. Likewise, that which is apprehended by whichever cognizer as pure belongs to that cognizer alone as pure, and not to another.
For instance— the meaning is that in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the wine (surā) itself is pure for the officiating priest (hotṛ/yājaka) and fit for smelling, consuming, and so forth.
"The smelling of the wine must be performed."
Thus [it is said]. For another person who has not performed the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, [the remains] are again impure and unfit for smelling and so forth; this is the meaning. As the Smṛti states:
"Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling what should not be smelled, and consuming intoxicants—"
"And deceitful sexual intercourse with a man is recorded as causing loss of caste.
Therefore, even if these two [liquor and sex] are inherent properties of things (*vastudharma*), if they were not dependent upon the specific person [concerned],
then for everyone alike, liquor would be either pure or impure.

Thus, while the general impurity of liquor has been established, it must be understood that this is set aside by a specific scriptural injunction regarding the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice and the *hotṛ* priest, due to the contradiction between the general rule and the specific revelation. || 245 ||
Now, one might object: "If the Vedic injunction is indeed sublated by the Śaiva injunction as you have stated, let that be;
however, it does not seem logically sound to us that everything is subsequently sublated by the Vedic injunction itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
By this, there is also the sublation of injunctions by their own statements. (4-246)

"In some places, [the teaching] is shown like the injunctions and prohibitions regarding the killing of a Brahmin, by means of 'dog-words'—that is, by way of exceptions (*apavāda*). By the phrase 'in some places,' it is meant that this occurs within the domain of general rules (*utsarga*).
By the phrase 'is shown,' it is indicated that, according to the reasoning already stated, this does not result in irrationality."

"No fault whatsoever"—thus it has been made clear. By the word "api" (also/even), it is stated that this is not only by means of statements from other scriptures; therefore, nothing new has been imagined by us—namely, what was said [in the passage]: "By the specific injunction of Śiva..."

"The Vedic injunction, being of a general nature, is sublated"—and this is not merely accidental, but rather occurs for the most part; to demonstrate this, the example "like the injunction and prohibition regarding the killing of a Brahmin" has been cited.
Thus, just as—
"A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed"—thus a general prohibition against killing a Brāhmaṇa has been enjoined; [yet there is also the injunction]:
"One should sacrifice a Brāhmaṇa for a Brāhmaṇa."
Thus, being sublated by this specific scriptural statement, the meaning is that liquor (surā) likewise possesses impurity.
Thus, having conducted an investigation regarding purity and impurity, he extends this analysis to other matters as well:
"The rules concerning what is fit to be eaten and so forth have also been discussed by relying on this same principle. (4.247)

Regarding the phrase "the consideration of what is edible and so forth," the meaning is that even those injunctions obtainable through the force of the context, such as "here there is nothing edible and nothing inedible," have their purpose already fulfilled by this very principle. || 247 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as the Vedic injunction, which is general in nature, is sublated by the specific Śaiva injunction, why should the Śaiva injunction not likewise be sublated by the Vedic one?
Anticipating this doubt, he begins by demonstrating the very meaning of the Āgama:
And Maheśvara spoke in the *Sarvajñānottara* and other scriptures;
he recites that very same [teaching] by way of its meaning:
"That which was uttered by sages, gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others... (4.248).
Because each subsequent [scripture] possesses greater excellence, it sublates each preceding one.
That which is spoken by a seer (ṛṣi) sublates that spoken by a human; likewise, that spoken by Rudra sublates that spoken by Viṣṇu. Thus he says:
"each preceding one is sublated. In this context, the reason is the increasing excellence of each successive [revelation].
The meaning is that it is logically correct for a general rule to be sublated by a specific one. || 248 ||
For this very reason, he states that there can be no sublation by way of the opposite: "The Śaiva [teaching] must never be sublated by Vaiṣṇava statements. (4-249)
One should deliberate upon [the passage] beginning with "Not by those born of Brahmā," which refers to the Vaiṣṇava [tradition].
"Born of Brahmā" means by Vedic statements; as the Śruti says:
"The four Vedas were created by Prajāpati."

Thus, where even the Vaiṣṇava [tradition] is not sublated by Vedic statements, what need is there to mention the sublation of the Śaiva?—this is established by implication. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand that even those [teachings] originating from Brahmā are not sublated by the words of the gods, and so on. As it has been said therein:
I have not [seen] the words of the Ṛṣis by men, nor the Vedic [words] by the Ṛṣis;
nor the words of Brahmā by the gods, nor the words of Viṣṇu by those born from the lotus-born [Brahmā].
"The Śaiva [teaching] is never sublated by the words of Viṣṇu. Thus [it is said]. (249)
"Surely, what fault is there if the sublation occurs even by way of reversal?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He who sublates [the scripture] through inversion is a fool and shall partake of sin. (4.250)
The sublation of the latter by the former is due to their contrariety. As it has been stated therein:
"For that sinner who sublates [the former] is a fool, devoid of consciousness;
the progressive excellence of all [the levels] has been proclaimed."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 250 ||
Thus, because it is the most excellent, one should practice steadfastness primarily in the Śaiva scripture alone and not elsewhere; so he says:
"Therefore, O Skanda, one should not practice worldly duties as the primary focus."

The intended meaning is that there is no fault whatsoever for one who, by means of a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) based on ultimate emptiness, practices worldly conventions for the sake of protecting the world. As it is said therein:
"But as for those worldly conducts of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), and the penances (*prāyaścitta*),"
One should not scrutinize established family connections or local customs.

"Having performed the rites beginning from conception up until the marriage itself, one should then practice the Vedic ritual; thereafter, O Skanda, one who is devoted solely to Śaivism should not follow worldly customs as a primary duty."
Thus it is said:
"Internally Kaula, externally Śaiva, and in worldly conduct Vaidika;
one should remain having extracted the essence, just like a coconut fruit."
This and more has been stated elsewhere.

Now, one might object: "If he does not follow worldly customs according to their primary sense, why should he not do so as a subordinate part of the Śaiva scriptures? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One should not practice what is prescribed in other scriptures, even if it is stated in one's own stream [of revelation]. (4.251)

In one's own stream—that is, in one's own scripture—one should practice (caret), that is, carry out, the very meaning already stated in such passages as, "One should drink wine up to the throat... and so forth; one should not, however, abandon it.

"Wine should not be drunk," and so forth, as prescribed in other scriptures. For the Blessed One has taught various scriptures that are mutually distinct according to the differences among the respective qualified practitioners; thus, with respect to another [scripture]:

How could that which has been taught [in one system] be practiced by another? As it is said therein: "One should not follow what is prescribed in another scripture, nor should one meditate upon another deity; rather, endowed with pure contemplation, one's mind should be focused solely on Śiva."

Thus [it is said]. And this should also be applied with respect to the *samānatantra* (the shared tantra), for even those are indeed distinct due to the differences in ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth—so say the knowers of the *Āgama*. As they have said:
"Since the distinction of tantras is traditionally held to arise from the distinctions of ritual action and the rest..."
Therefore, whatever has been stated in a particular [tantra] should be performed according to that, and not according to another tantra.

Thus it is said. When, however, a further requirement arises, one must look to another scripture; otherwise, there would be an incompleteness regarding the various sets of procedural details (*itikartavyatā*). For instance, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:

Regarding the question— how is there a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) for the gatekeepers in such passages as, "Having sacrificed there to the gatekeepers, one should cast a flower consecrated with a great mantra (*mahāstra*), while meditating on the blazing [fire], for the sake of dispelling the manifestation of obstacles"?— it is stated from a related tantra (*samānatantra*):
From the *Śrītriśirobhairava*: "Then, at the base, one should worship Nandirudra and the Gaṅgā to the north,
and Mahākāla with his fangs and the Yamunā to the south."

Such [passages] are to be consulted. And precisely here, regarding the expectation of how one should cast the "blazing flower," since its casting is not explicitly stated in the *Samānatantro*, one should look to the *Śrīsvacchandaśāstra*, which belongs to the same ritual manual (*samānakalpa*).
Having recited the Bhairava-weapon mantra and taken up a flower while remaining in meditative absorption,
one should empower it seven times so that it becomes filled with blazing crests of fire.

"One should enter through the middle of the house by means of employing the nārāca weapon"— this and similar [passages] must be consulted. Furthermore, as to what kind of employment of the nārāca weapon is intended— since such [an employment] is not found even in a scripture of similar ritual class (samānakalpa), let alone in one that is entirely dissimilar— [it remains to be determined].
From the Siddhānta scripture known as the *Anantavijaya*: "Having placed the hand palm-upward, one should extend the three fingers;
the middle finger and the thumb, joined together, should be moved repeatedly."
"For the *nārāca* is indeed proclaimed thus... and so forth;

this [text] must be consulted. For our goal is the cessation of dependence, and whatever source that [cessation] may arise from is precisely what should be consulted—what is the use of the stubborn grasping at similarity or dissimilarity? Thus, regarding such dependence...
When there is another treatise— whether it be similar or dissimilar— one should rely upon it only so long as that reliance remains necessary; in its absence, however,

there would be no basis at all for relying on what is stated in another treatise, because if that were the case, it would follow that everything [else] must be relied upon, resulting in an infinite regress.
The practice of the meaning of the scriptures would [be required]. As they say:
"Even when there is dependence, dependence itself is the authority;
only as much as is required [from another source] should be done from elsewhere, for anything more would lead to an infinite regress."
Thus [ends the section]. || 251 ||
Now, is it not the case that this entire collection of scriptures was taught by the Blessed One himself out of a desire to uplift the whole world?
Therefore, the performance of the various meanings taught therein must necessarily be carried out, so that the delusion of saṃsāra may be stilled.
Thinking, "Let it be so; what is the use of this deliberation?", he says in response:
"For although even the Vedas and other scriptures were expounded by the Lord, nevertheless, [they differ] due to the conceptualization of the presence or absence of contraction. (4.252)

There is no dispute that the Supreme Lord alone is the teacher of all scriptures, beginning with the Vedas; however, He has taught the scriptures in two ways according to the distinction between the state of limitation (*saṅkoca*) and non-limitation (*abheda*)—some being primarily characterized by duality (*bheda*), and others primarily characterized by non-duality (*abheda*). In this regard:
The Vedas and other scriptures primarily emphasize difference, whereas the Śaiva and other scriptures primarily emphasize non-difference.
Thus it is said:

"Knowledge belonging to the bound (pāśava) is described according to the degree of its contraction; however, the knowledge of the Lord (pati), which is the sublater [of that bondage], is according to the degree of its expansion. (4.253)
Contraction (*saṅkoca*) is the manifestation of duality. This [Vedic tradition] and so forth belongs to bound souls (*paśu*), hence it is called "pāśava" (pertaining to fetters).
Expansion (*vikāsa*) is the manifestation of non-duality due to the absence of contraction; therefore, because the manifestation of duality is sublated, this [expansion] is the sublater.
For duality is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and it must be eradicated by everyone—of this there is no dispute.
And thus, if the sublated and the sublator were practiced in a state of confusion, the performance [of the rites] would be corrupted;
therefore, that which has been stated above alone is correct. For this very reason, it is said elsewhere:
"Having abandoned the knowledge of the bound (pāśava), one should take refuge in the scripture of the Lord (pati)."
Thus it has been stated, etc. || 253 ||
Now he explains [the statement], "There is neither duality nor non-duality":
"This is duality, this is not"—through such mutual negation, that which is fashioned by the distinctions of Māyā might exist; how could it exist in that which is beyond conceptualization? (4.254)

"Having cast aside whatever this duality— that is, the state of manifold forms— may be called, one should take refuge in non-duality characterized by absolute unity"— this and other such statements spoken elsewhere refer to that state which consists solely in the flashing forth of one's own Self, wherein the entire collection of various conceptual constructions has been swallowed up in the non-conceptual.

"How could it be in the supreme reality? It is not tenable," is the meaning. Since that [reality] consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there is mutual negation; therefore, it is "fashioned" or animated by that "division" which arises from *māyā*—the power of will belonging to the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the concealment of one's own essence.
The meaning is that its true nature consists solely of conceptual construction. || 254 ||
"What is the proof for this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And it is stated in the *Bhargaśikhā* that the one of perfected intellect devours death, time, the kalās, and so forth, which arise from the conceptual constructions of duality and non-duality. (4.255)

In this context, the yogi is one whose intellect (*dhī*)—meaning his cognition—has achieved its purpose through the power of immersion into supreme non-conceptual self-awareness, and who has attained identity with that supreme consciousness. For him, there arises [a state] risen above the conceptualizations of duality and non-duality, which no longer flashes forth as animated by the perception of difference; herein, there is no longer anything such as birth or death, nor any form consisting of the means of knowledge (*māna*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and so forth.
And the meaning is that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) does not exist there. As it is said in that [text]:

"Then he swallows up all of this: death and time, the multitude of parts, the collection of transformations, the web of cognitive apprehensions, and the entire mass of discursive thoughts concerning unity and diversity."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 255 ||
Now he explains the statement, "And there is no worship of the *liṅga* and so forth":
"In the Siddhānta, the worship of the *liṅga* is prescribed for one who knows that the universe consists of the paths [of emanation];
in the Kula systems and others, it is forbidden for one who knows that the body is the self of the universe. (4.256)
In this context, why [is there] the prescription and prohibition regarding that which consists of all things?

In the Siddhānta, within the dualistic perspective (*bhedadarśana*), the ritual for the worship of the *liṅga* is prescribed so that one may know the nature of that "path" (*adhvan*) which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and is called "the universe. For it belongs to the Supreme Lord.

The *liṅga* contains within it the entire expansion of the paths (*adhvan*); thus, the sense is that by its worship, this entire universe becomes directly realized. As they say: "In the *liṅga*, the pervasion ending with Paramaśiva; in the pedestal (*pīṭha*), that ending with Sadāśiva."
"By these [practitioners] who meditate upon [the universe] from the Brahma-stone up to Māyā," and,
"By means of the desired Śiva-liṅga, the entire universe becomes fully satisfied."

And thus it is said: "In the Kula and other [traditions] of non-dual vision, moreover, this worship of the *liṅga* is prohibited," because the body itself consists of the entire cosmic path (*adhvan*); therefore, its direct realization is easily attained right there.
What, then, is the use of an external *liṅga* or the like, which is logically untenable? As it has been stated:
"One should worship the internal *liṅga*; one should not worship the external *liṅga*. Likewise:
"Having abandoned the omniscient and omnipresent [Lord] who has entered the cave of the heart..."
"The one of limited intellect bows to the inauspicious with the hope for the auspicious, as if praising a stone and such.

However, in this Trika system, which is of the nature of supreme non-duality, there is no purpose whatsoever in either its injunction or its prohibition; thus it has been said: "In this [system], there is neither the worship of the *liṅga* nor its abandonment."

Thus [it is said]. Since this [world] consists of all things—for as far as this universe is to be known, it exists by virtue of being the expansion of the supreme consciousness of the Supreme Lord—and since that [consciousness] is the expansion of the consciousness of everything itself, let it reside within the body or otherwise; what does it matter?

The sense is that this [realization] might be obstructed by the identification with the body, external objects, and so forth, which stands as an impediment to the attainment of the universal self-nature (sārvātmya). As they say:
"Those who, having gone nowhere and abandoned nothing, [perceive] only this..."
"The fortunate behold Your abode; salutations again and again to them.
Thus [ends the verse]. 156.
Now he explains the adoption of matted hair, ashes, and so forth, for the purpose of attaining identity through entry into the observances (niyama): || 4.257 ||
In the Kaula tradition, the renunciation of matted hair and other such practices occurs through the instruction on the easy means [of liberation].
Regarding the "observances": "He may wear matted hair, be shaven-headed, have a single lock, or carry a staff, and be adorned with the five mudrās."

"O Maheśvarī, having committed sexual intercourse through negligence, he becomes my enemy"—by such statements, detachment and other qualities [are indicated]. In that context, "entry" (anupraveśa) means practice;
by means of that, "the realization of identity" (*tādātmyapratipatti*) is the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, for the sake of which [this is taught].
In the Siddhānta, practices such as matted hair and the smearing of ashes are prescribed as being accomplished through great effort. As it has been said:

"Having divided the hair according to the number of the Kalās, Tattvas, Pavitras, Aṇus, Śaktis, Mantreśvaras, and [other categories], and having applied [the ashes] to each portion with the corresponding mantras..."
"One should bind [the thread] in front of Vrateśvara by means of Śiva’s splendor.
Likewise: "Among those who observe vows, some have matted hair and others are shaven-headed; among them, the foremost are those white with ashes."
"Kings and others are adorned with *tilakas*, *puṇḍrakas*, and [silk] bands.

Thus, in the *Kaula*—that is, in the Kula doctrine—the "abandonment" of this, namely matted hair, ashes, and so forth, is prescribed; the meaning is that its prohibition is enjoined. As it has been said:
Whoever on this earth should bear the marks of matted hair, ashes, and so forth, the banner, the vow of the Kāpālika, the trident, and the extremely fierce skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga);
"One should not form an attachment to that [world] through action, mind, or speech.

For here, by the statement, "Wherever the rays meet, there the All-pervasive Lord alone unfolds," it is shown that even amidst attachment to sense objects, one attains the essential nature of the Supreme Lord; thus, with ease—
Regarding what was stated as "the teaching of the means without effort":
"The ancients taught cessation through the yoga of dispassion and practice;
but by us, this cessation is taught without effort."

Thus, the state of being without possessions (*niṣparigrahatā*) and so forth has not been explained separately again, because its meaning is already understood through this very [text], as the sense of these matters was indeed expressed by the first and fourth quarters [of the verse]. The intention is that here, however, because of his universal nature (*sārvātmya*), neither injunction nor prohibition applies to him.
The connection is with what precedes. For here, what is to be attained is indeed oneness with consciousness;
and in that regard, whatever is proximate at a given time is what should be grasped, while the rest must be abandoned.
Thus, whether there be an injunction or a prohibition regarding matted hair and so forth—what business have we with this? As he will say:
"But when entering into the supreme reality, whichever means one perceives as being nearest at that time, that should be adopted; or else, it may sometimes be abandoned.
Now he explains the performance and non-performance of the observances (*vrata*) and so forth:
"And the practice of the observances is for the sake of realizing identity with the meaning of the mantra. (4.258)

However, its negation is stated in the Siddhānta for the sake of realizing the universal nature (*sārvātmya*) of the mantra’s meaning—the word *ca* (and) implies this. One should supply: "The meaning of the mantra is restricted to the expressed deity and so forth; its 'negation' [occurs] in the Kaula sense. "Universal nature" means non-difference from the universe.
Furthermore, in this case, there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition regarding her; all of this has already been explained previously, so no further effort is made here. || 258 ||
Now, in order to explain the entry into the fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth, he says:
"Entry into the fields, seats (*pīṭha*), and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) is for the pacification of obstacles. (4.259)
Now, for one who seeks to propitiate the mantra and so forth, [the following] is taught for the sake of attaining that:

"Field" (*kṣetra*) refers to a place of assembly (*melāpasthāna*); "Seat" (*pīṭha*) refers to Kāmarūpa and so on; "Sub-seat" (*upapīṭha*) refers to Devīkoṭṭa and so on. "For the sake of attaining that" means for the sake of attaining those mantras and so forth through the sequence of beloved assemblies and the like.
The attainment of the Siddhas and so forth, or that which is caused by them; as it has been said:
"One becomes stainless by resorting to the kṣetras, upakṣetras, saṃdohas, and so on. || 259 ||
Furthermore, a prohibition has been made in this regard; thus he says:
"But the rule regarding the absence of going to sacred fields and so forth applies likewise to one's own self. (4.260)
It has also been described that [this is] for the purpose of knowing fullness through its manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth are included. "In that manner" means by the method previously stated.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added here.
When the Self is perfectly complete, what indeed is the use of wandering through sacred fields and the like?
It has already been stated that in this case, however, neither of these two applies; thus he says: "Even so..."
Thus it has been described. As it was said:
"In this world, from that which is the soul of all, regarding its affirmation and negation...
Now he explains the preservation of the pledges and so forth:
"The true nature of the conduct of the pledges is taught as that which is to be preserved. (4.261)

Because differentiation is their very life-force, the prohibitions regarding the rules of conduct (samaya) and so forth are taught in the Mata scriptures for the sake of purifying the principles (tattva) through the renunciation of each respective [differentiation]. (4.262)
"One should understand one's own awakening to be complete and beyond all boundaries.
The conduct of the *samaya* consists of such [rules] as "one should do this" and "one should not do that.
By the phrase "because its life-force is duality," it is meant that something is abandoned and something else is adopted; such is its nature.
Diversity [is the obstacle], such as when one's growth occurs within one's own scripture while abandoning other scriptures. As he will say:
"One whose mantra is not [firmly] established should not remain [inactive], nor should he serve other scriptures; for unrooted gnosis wavers due to the influence of other [ideas]. (25.563)

Thus, in the "mata-śāstras," which possess characteristics both even and uneven, the prohibition of *śama* (tranquility) and so forth is further enjoined. And so he states the relevant passage from them: "without boundaries," and so on.
For that supreme reality is self-awareness (*svasaṃbodha*) and self-luminous; therefore, because it does not depend on anything else, [it is without boundaries].
It is entirely full; and precisely because its form is unrestricted, it is "limitless" (*nirmaryāda*) and "unfettered" (*niryantraṇa*).

The meaning is: let it be understood, let it be experienced. Thus, in such a supreme reality (*para-tattva*), how indeed could there be a conventional practice (*samayācāra*) divided by thousands of expectations regarding rejection, acquisition, and so forth?
The meaning is: "for the sake of purification. || 262 ||

Now, desiring to explain the passage beginning with "the form, signs, and so forth of another, as well as the name, lineage, and so forth," he describes in sequence the form and other attributes belonging to another and those belonging to himself:
"This form belongs to another and is to be meditated upon; however, this one is my own. (4.263)
"The linga of flames and so forth belongs to another, but the skull and so forth is my own.

Here, "this" refers to the nature of the meditator. "Flames and so forth" is that which belongs to another because it arises from external desires and the like. "One's own" means that which resides within one's own body. || 263 ||
He explains the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "the linga, etc. (*liṅgādi*):
"By the word 'etc.', ascetic practice, [proper] time, hospitality, and so forth are mentioned. (4-264)

"Austerity" (*tapas*) refers to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other such penances; "conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the behavior described in the section on conduct (*caryāpāda*); "time" (*velā*) takes the form of midday, midnight, and so forth; and "lunar day" (*tithi*) takes the form of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), and so on. || 264 ||
"The name of this [practitioner] of mine shall begin with Śakti and end with Śiva; it cannot be otherwise.

For this practitioner of the Siddhānta, when undertaking vows and so forth, the name—performed according to the sequence of the "falling of the flower" (puṣpapāta) and other rites—shall begin with Śakti and end with Śiva. Thus, [the name] is Śikhāśakti.

Īśānaśiva; by the word "etcetera," [it includes] everything from Gaṇa onwards, such as the Kavacagaṇa. As it has been said: "One should release the name of initiated persons beginning with that [specific deity] and ending with Śiva; for the best of the twice-born, it ends with Śiva, while for others, it ends with Gaṇa."
Thus it is said:
"In that place where [the seed] might fall unintentionally when discharged by a child,
one should perform the rite for women ending with the word *śakti*, and for men ending with the word *śiva*."
"In this way, for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, it should be the end of the group for the Śūdras.

Regarding the phrase "otherwise," it means [the sequence] ending with the Bodhyas; for the experts of the secret scriptures (rahasyaśāstra) maintain that what is called worship must indeed proceed according to the succession of one's own respective lineage, up to the Auḷlis. As it has been said:
"Bodhi is the Lord, likewise the Yogin; Ānanda is the series of feet.
This ending [of the names] is to be assigned to the heroes and the wives of the heroes.
By this, [the names] Satyabodhi, Viśvaprabhu, and so forth [are formed].
And *gotra* is the lineage of the teacher, designated by the terms *maṭhikā* and *kula*.
It has two designations: "maṭhikā" and "kula. || 265 ||
In this regard, what is a *maṭhikā*? He says:
"The lineage of Śrī, that called Tryambaka, and those known as Ardha and Āmarda—thus, there are three and a half *maṭhikās* here in the tradition of Śaṅkara. (4.266)
The lineage of the Siddhas begins with Kūrma and ends with Mīna according to the sequence of the Yugas.
He says, "beginning with the Yuga," etc., to show that there are not only three and a half monasteries (*maṭhikā*), but others as well.
The word "first" (*ādya*) is to be explained by means of *tantra* (polysemy); thus, it refers to Kūrma, who descended in the Tretā Yuga.

The first incarnation of Śrī Kūrmanātha in the Kṛtayuga was Śrī Khagendranātha; she belongs to him, and thus [the lineage] is so called. A separate explanation of the word *kula* has been provided because it is well-known in common usage in such terms as *gurukula*. || 266 ||

Regarding the phrase "the lineage and so forth," he explains the meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi): "By the word 'and so forth' [is meant] the house, the village, the sacred seat (pīṭha), and the subsidiary seat (upapīṭha). (4-267)
"Mudrā" refers to their kiss, and their ritual procedure is established for both themselves and others.
"House" (*ghara*) refers to the distinct residential sites for each of the six princes who hold office. "Village" (*pallī*) refers to the place for begging alms. As he will say:
For these are indeed worthy of worship, possessing their rightful authority, whose manifold lineage is unbroken, diverse, and composed of disciples and grand-disciples.
Those ending in Ānandāvalī, Bodhiprabhupāda, and Yogin—these are the *ovallis*;
these constitute the six mudrās in sequence.

From the right thumb to the little finger, and then from the left little finger upward to the end of the twenty-second [tattva], [the locations] are the Kuṇḍalinī, the Bindu, the Heart, the Navel, and the Kanda; these are the secret signs (chummās).
Śavarāḍa, Billakhaṭṭilla, Karabilla, Ambila,
Śarabilla, Aḍavī, Ḍombī, Dakṣiṇapallī, Kumbhāra, Bhillikā, and Akṣarapallī.
"Devīkoṭṭa, Kulādri, Tripurī, Kāmākhya, Maṭṭahāsa, and Dakṣiṇapīṭha—this group of six belongs respectively to the Gharapallīpīṭha. (29.39).
The phrase "situated elsewhere" means that each is distinct according to its own respective lineage sequence.
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of such instruction regarding the lineage of the Guru and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For indeed, in order to attain identity [with the Guru], one should take refuge in one's own lineage. (4.268)
One should eat and worship the *cakra*, but not with one who belongs to another lineage (*parasaṃtānin*).

[The term] "one's own lineage" (*svaṃ saṃtānam*) refers to whichever [lineage] may be possible for someone according to the sequence beginning with the venerable Amaranātha and others. "Another" (*paraḥ*) refers to Śrī Varadeva and so forth; "one who has a lineage" (*saṃtānaḥ*) means one who possesses such a lineage. || 268 ||
And he says that this is prohibited elsewhere:
"Moreover, this is prohibited in the Mata scriptures because it is subject to refutation. (4.269)
Even within the indivisible supreme reality (*paratattva*), differentiation arises by means of this [distinction].

The phrase "by this" refers to that which was just mentioned—the form of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—meaning by way of one's own and others' mental continua (*saṃtāna*) and so forth.
For indeed, in the indivisible supreme reality, there is no such fragmentation consisting of the forms of the abandonable and the acceptable.
This is logical—such is the intended meaning. || 269 ||
Having thus explained the text by way of its meaning, he now applies it through the connection of systematic coherence:
"In this way, from the entry into the field up to the rule concerning the lineage... (4.270).
"For in this [teaching], that which is not directly conducive to Śiva is not prescribed.
Thus, according to the previously stated method, "the entry into the field and so forth"— ending with the restriction regarding the lineage (*gotra*) denoted by the word *saṃtāna*—
"is not prescribed at all in this present scripture," namely, the field and the rest.

The meaning is that an injunction such as "one must enter" is not prescribed, because that [method] is not a direct means (*upāya*) to Śiva. And this has been determined many times previously; therefore, no further effort is made here.
One might object: "If indeed there is no rule here regarding the entry into the sacred field (kṣetra) and so forth, would that not then result in its prohibition?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And there is no prohibition of that, because it does not constitute a violation of the reality (tattva). (4-271)
Because that—namely, the entry into the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth—is not a limitation of the supreme *tattva*, which is the Self of the universe;

for in relation to that, external fields and the like do not exist at all. Thus, where could even an entry or the like take place? Therefore, this injunction or prohibition being enacted with respect to that [entry]...
The sense is this: because it functions as mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), it is not capable of undermining its own essential nature.
Therefore, he says:
"For within his own nature, the two [aspects] are conceptually constructed for the Lord, who is the self of the universe."
Prescription or prohibition does not serve to undermine the very nature of a capacity. (4.272)

For this very reason, everything—both prescribed and prohibited—is contained herein; since all meanings are thus internalized, one should not fixate upon any single point alone. This is the intended meaning. || 272 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then when there is a desire to enter the supreme reality (*paratattva*), how can the distinction that 'this is to be accepted' and 'this is to be rejected' be established, since such a distinction must necessarily be relied upon? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But at the time of entering the supreme reality, whichever [means] is nearest..."
He understands the means; he should then be accepted, or perhaps in some cases, abandoned. (4.273)
"It is stated in the venerable Trika scripture that no constraint should be applied here.

There is no disagreement that a yogi who desires to enter the supreme state must first stabilize the mind therein. Furthermore, when someone, at some point, [is situated] nearby through the process of 'forceful ripening' (haṭhapāka),"
When a means is recognized as being proximate by virtue of its capacity to cause the sudden attainment of the nature of the Supreme, that very means should then be adopted, or otherwise abandoned;
however, one should not here apply such restrictive constraints as "this must be accepted" or "this must be rejected. Therefore, even when there is attachment to sense objects—

"Sometimes there may be an entry into the supreme reality (*paratattva*). By the phrase "in some cases" (*kvacit*), it is revealed that the proximity or remoteness of the means (*upāya*) is not fixed.
And by this, the passage beginning with "But this... is [explained] in its essential purport.
This has been explained. Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for stating such a previously unknown matter? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
"Thus it has been declared in the venerable Trika teaching. (273)
He recites the very text found therein: "The equality of all deities [is established] through the *ovallī*, the mantra, and the phonemes. (4.274)
Since everything pertaining to the *āgamas* and the *gatīs* is composed of Śiva;
the term "*ovallyaḥ*" refers to the six lineages of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃtati*), such as the *Bodhya* and others, which are divided into categories such as the *Jyeṣṭha* and so forth.
The term "*gatīnām*" means the various types [of lineages] consisting of *bhāva*, *vṛtti*, *dravya*, *bhūmikā*, and so on.
The reason for this is stated as: "Because everything (*śarvam*) consists of Śiva. As it has been said:
"There is equanimity (*samatā*) toward all states of being and all mental fluctuations in every respect; there is equanimity toward all views and all substances in every respect."
"And likewise, there is equality among all the *bhūmikās*, as well as among all the *vallīs*, among all the goddesses, and among all the *varṇas* in every respect. (274)
Anticipating the objection, "Indeed, who is there that knows all things to be composed of Śiva, such that this instruction might take root in them? he says:
"For he perceives the reality of Śiva as an undivided existence. (4.275)
For he who attains the reality of the Self, whose true being is unbroken—

by asserting that the knowledge of the Self alone is the cause for the direct realization of the Śiva-reality— it follows that here, as in other philosophical systems, there is no need for the arduous pursuit of external means.
Thus it has been reported. || 275 ||
And not everyone here is a worthy recipient; rather, only someone purified by the most intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is so. Thus he says:
"In the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower, only the bee is truly connoisseur, not the fly."
Impelled by Maheśa, someone becomes devoted to the worship of the supreme non-duality of Bhairava. (4.276)
One might ask: "What would happen here through non-attachment? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For those who find rest in this sacrifice, the pomp of worldly existence dissolves of its own accord, like a mass of snow in the great heat of summer. (4.277)
And here, in order to specify by way of a concluding summary the qualified practitioner who was introduced in general terms, he says:
"Enough with this excessive digression; let there be no further prolixity."
Some wise man, Abhinavagupta, is worthy in this ritual procedure of sacrifice. || 278 ||

Alternatively, enough with this excessive elaboration— characterized by repeated examination— regarding the manifold branches of the relationship between the sacrificer and the officiating priest; for,
in this very ritual procedure of sacrifice whose nature has just been described, [the point is established] on all sides.
In the multitude of insentient and sentient entities, which is intermingled with endless divisions such as the grasped and the grasper, there is a "pride"—

a self-praise consisting of the reflection upon one's own qualities characterized by unconditioned knowledge and agency; by that [pride], he is "protected," meaning his own majesty, which consists of universal identity, is preserved even when he has been robbed of his true nature by the delusion of *māyā*.
And for this very reason, he is "someone extraordinary," that is, transcendent; furthermore, the meaning is that only this particular author is suitable for this work. || 278 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half of the verse:
"Thus, in the unfolding of the state of the Absolute (anuttara), the Śākta means has now been clearly distinguished."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Śākta Means," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.

By the word "today" (adya), it is revealed that the meaning of the term *āhnika* is ultimate reality (*tāttvika*). Thus, may there be auspiciousness! Jayaratha has clearly expounded this fourth daily lesson (*āhnika*) through the power of his perfected discernment, which has blossomed by virtue of immersion in the Śākta energy.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Śāktopāya," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Prakāśa* written by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
He who, by the power of uttering terrible sounds, terrifies the entire world;
Delighting in meditation upon his own abode, that unconquered Rudra is victorious. || 1 ||

Now, he begins to describe the means of the individual soul (āṇavopāya), which has reached its proper occasion, with the latter half [of the verse]: "Next, this is described for those who desire to reach the supreme abode by means of the individual method. (5.1)

"By means of the ritual" (vidhinā) refers to the form consisting of recitation and so forth; "this" (etat) refers to the definition of the individual means (āṇavopāya) which is about to be described. ||1||
Anticipating the objection, "Surely everything would be accomplished by the *śāktopāya* alone; for what purpose is this being investigated?", he says, while internalizing that doubt:
"When the purification of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) itself has occurred, such that it is free from all counter-correlates..."
The attainment of the desired object—whether enjoyment or liberation—is certain. || 5-2 ||

Because there is no arising of another contradictory conceptualization, for the conceptual thought (*vikalpa*)— according to the method established in the *Śāktopāya*— once it has indeed arisen within the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose nature is the attainment of the most vivid form of non-conceptuality,
it becomes "determined," meaning restricted, toward one of the two goals between enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), namely toward the "desired object."
The intended meaning is that this subsequent chapter, [dealing with] "attainment" (*prāpti*), would be entirely unnecessary to begin. || 2 ||
Now, even if this is so, there are nevertheless two possible courses for conceptual thought (*vikalpa*):

for it may be refined through its own autonomy alone, independent of any other means, or it may be so in another way. Of these, the former mode has been described in the context of the Empowered Means (*śāktopāya*).
The other [means], however, will be explained in the section on the individual means (*āṇavopāya*); thus, the commencement of another chapter is indeed appropriate. He says this:
"For someone, conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is firmly established by the very sovereignty of its own self."
It arises precisely through the absence of dependence on any other means. || 5-3 ||
However, for someone whose conceptualization depends on other means for the sake of purifying one's own self, the previously mentioned rule is prescribed therein. (5.4)
By the statement "the previous rule has been stated," it is established by implication that another [rule] will be stated—this is the meaning. || 3-4 ||

But surely, since even conceptual thought (vikalpa) consists of the manifestation of an object, it is of the very nature of consciousness (cidātman), just like non-conceptual [awareness]; so what kind of latent impression (saṃskāra) could there be therein? For a latent impression is a specific excellence (atiśaya), and that is not applicable to pure consciousness.
Thus, for whom indeed could there be dependence upon or independence from another means?
Anticipating this objection, he says:

"Although that which is called conceptual construction (vikalpa) exists as having the nature of pure consciousness alone, nevertheless, being of the nature of ascertainment, it bestows sovereignty upon the individual soul. (5)

Even though this is so, nevertheless, this conceptual construction (vikalpa)—because it consists of a determination that "this is a jar" by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), such as "this is not a non-jar"—bestows sovereignty upon the "atomic," i.e., the contracted, cognizer; for its sovereignty is established precisely with respect to the object being conceptually constructed. Therefore...

Thus, it has been stated that the activity of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For instance, even though the opposite of a jar does not appear when a jar appears, the subject grasps it solely through his own sovereignty (*svātantrya*) for the sake of its utility in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); otherwise, in the realm of *māyā*, [such activity would be impossible].

Without the cognition of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārapratīti*), even the conventional reality (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the nature of the grasped and the grasper would not be established. Therefore, although consciousness is of a single nature, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—being of the nature of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—is composed of duality; thus, for its removal, it requires a refinement (*saṃskāra*) within itself, for the sake of instilling that [refinement].
In some cases, this [conceptual thought] depends upon other means; thus it was rightly said: "This conceptual thought, in its own purification, is dependent on other means.
And its purification extends from the stage of indistinctness through successive stages until the attainment of the state of extreme clarity.
The attainment of the nature of non-conceptual knowledge, which consists of the realization of one's own ultimate self.
As was stated previously:
"Then, [the consciousness] is nourished by a most vivid and noble identity with that [reality]."
"Consciousness attains a stainless state whose very nature is free from conceptual construction. (Tantrāloka 4.6) || 5 ||

And since there are many means, such as meditation and so forth, for instilling that impression according to the method to be explained, its diversity follows from their diversity; thus he says: "This certainty is manifold, and the means therein are diverse."
And those are designated by the word "atom" (aṇu) according to the distinction of being distant or near. || 5-6 ||
The reason for the multiplicity of means is stated as: "In that regard, the means are diverse. The reason for their diversity is stated as:
"Due to the distinction between the distant and the near. For some means are proximate to consciousness, while others are remote. And thus:
According to the principle that "prior to this, consciousness is transformed into the vital breath," because the vital breath is more internal than the intellect and other faculties,
the upward movement (*uccāra*) and so forth residing therein are proximate; and in comparison to that, meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth residing in the intellect are [more remote].

[The means are] remote, and even more so than that, those pertaining to the body such as the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth. One might ask: "How is it known that these means are possible only here [in the Āṇava system] and not in the Śākta? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "They are called by the word *aṇu*. Therefore, they exist among the *aṇu* means, which are characterized by differentiation (*bheda*).
Thus ends the section on the individual soul (āṇava).

Now, one might object: "Since the vital breaths and so forth are insentient, they are not ultimately real; how then could the utterance and other such acts residing within them be the cause for attaining the ultimately real nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard, [this occurs] in the intellect, as well as in the vital breath, in the body, and also in the subject."
Even though this [world] is not ultimately real, the ultimate reality shines forth within it. || 5-7 ||

The phrase "in the cognizer" is to be applied everywhere, including in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. The term "non-ultimate" refers to the fact that although the intellect and other such entities are in reality of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), they are nevertheless conceptualized as such [as subjects]. || 7 ||
One might object: "Has not that which was questioned been made the very answer? What does this mean? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Since [the vital breaths] are non-different from the Light, which is pure Consciousness (cinmātra), just as they are non-different from it—thus, because they are non-different from Consciousness, the vital breaths and so forth possess ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) alone. This is the intended meaning.

It is precisely with this intention that it is said: "Even though the stability of objects is obstructed in the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), it nevertheless remains established in the Supreme Self. (Āgama-prāmāṇya, verse 20).
This and more has been stated elsewhere.

Now, one might object: "Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as blue and other objects, are non-different from consciousness (*cit*), their ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) is equal [in both cases]; we have no disagreement on this point. However, in the realm of *māyā*, how can consciousness be consistent with the insentience (*jāḍya*) of the vital breath and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But because that very [Self] is independent, its nature consists of both the insentient and the sentient, possessing a twofold form. (5.8)

The word *tu* (but) indicates a reason. Because that very light of the conscious self (*cidātman*) possesses sovereignty, [the vital breath and so forth]—by implication—are "twofold," meaning they are endowed with two qualities characterized by insentience and sentience; this is the sense. For it is the Supreme Lord alone who...
In the desire to bring about the illusory creation, by means of its own sovereignty, it causes certain [entities], even though they are insentient such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
to become subjects (*grāhaka*) through the consecration of agency characterized by the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*) inherent within itself; and this applies to some of them as well.
It renders sound and the other objects into the state of being grasped by presenting them as objects of "this-ness" (idantā), thereby transcending their nature as consciousness;
thus, although the vital breaths and so forth are insentient, they possess the quality of consciousness solely through the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord.
This is established not only by reasoning, but also by scripture; thus he says:
"And this was stated to the Goddess by the one whose crest is the half-moon of the moon in the *Traiśirasa*.
He recites that very passage:
The individual soul (jīva) is indeed the power (śakti) of Śiva; although it is present everywhere, it remains so.
Established in the cognition of its own essential nature, it is supreme due to the unfolding of consciousness.

Although this "supreme power," which consists of the expansion of the universe, belongs to Śiva alone— the supreme light whose essence is pure consciousness— it is nonetheless present everywhere, even in the insentient.

Although [the power] abides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the jar, and so forth, and manifests as their very form, nevertheless— by the "unfolding of knowledge" consisting of the agency whose nature is the I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*) in the form of the vital breath and so on,
and of one's own self and of objects such as blue— it takes the form: "I know this."

The meaning is as follows: that "cognition" (*pratyaya*), which is conceptual in nature and characterized by the activity of a contracted subject, when it has "taken root"—that is, attained growth—therein, is designated as the "living being" (*jīva*) in the form of subjects such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the intellect (*buddhi*). || 9 ||
Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how the manifestation of the ultimate reality occurs therein, he says:
"Because of the conceptualization of the unfolding of his sovereignty, his true nature is that of consciousness" (5.10).
"Beholding [it], one becomes non-dual by concealing the portion that consists of insentience.
Having concealed "one portion"— the insentient form— of that "insentient" breath and so forth which possesses a conscious body,
and having suppressed the identification with "I" (*ahaṃtā*) therein, one attains the state of pure consciousness through the manifestation of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

"Seeing" the ultimate reality (*paramārthikī*) means experiencing it as the locus of the uncreated supreme *ahantā*; "he becomes non-dual" (*advayo bhavet*) means he shines forth as the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*)—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"The insentience that resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), likewise in the body, and in space..."
"A wise person should become composed of the rays of consciousness for the sake of overcoming that [duality].

Thus, although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are insentient, their ultimate reality is precisely the nature of consciousness; this means it has been stated that they serve as the instrumental cause for attaining their ultimate essential nature. || 10 ||
He states this very point from another perspective as well:
"In that regard, it may be through the vision of absolute freedom (svātantrya), like the reflection of a face in a mirror. (5.11)
He determines his own pure consciousness to be non-identical with that [object].

Or rather, just as this world determines its own reflection in a mirror to be distinct from the mirror because of its coming and going, so too does this yogi [determine it] "there," within the vital breath and so forth.

By virtue of the majesty of its own sovereignty, it is “pure,” meaning unstained by the impurity of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) and so forth. For this very reason— according to such statements as,

“I am not the vital breath, nor indeed the body, nor the mind” (Hastāmalaka-stotra, verse 36)— it is “not of that nature,” meaning it does not consist of the vital breath and the like, but is distinct from them, one's own innate self.
Thus, its attainment of the ultimate essential nature would consist precisely in this: that its very being is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*). — 11 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not already been determined that just as a reflection has no existence apart from the mirror, so too this manifold variety of the universe—consisting of subjects, objects, and the like—has no existence apart from consciousness?
Why, then, is it stated here in a different manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Consciousness is definitively established by force as distinct from the intellect, the vital breath, and so forth. || 5-12 ||

In reality, it would be non-different from that, because of its mutual distinction from cognition and the rest. Even though consciousness (*caitanya*) is determined to be "different" or "separate" from cognition and so forth by force of an untenable sequence, in fact it must be non-distinct from them; for [it exists] only through that very cognition and the rest.
There is a mutual distinction [between them], because they are cognized in their own respective and determinate forms;

consciousness (caitanya), however, appears as permeated by the intellect (buddhi) and the other faculties, for otherwise the intellect and the rest would not even possess the status of being objects of cognition. || 12 ||
An objection may be raised: "How can consciousness, which is indeed one, become undivided from the infinite forms of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth?
Anticipating this, he says:
"The state of being undivided from the universal form arises precisely from its purity. (5.13)
Because of the contradiction between one established, vibrating form and another form;

for here, indeed, since consciousness— which is of the nature of supreme light— is "pure," it cannot be manifested as stained by any fixed, particular form, owing to its characteristic of self-luminosity.

Due to its supreme purity, it "indeed arises as non-different from all"—that is, from all forms such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; it does not fail to arise—this is the meaning. For this alone is the name's purity:
that it manifests by assuming those various manifold forms, like a mirror and so forth. And it is not thus...

There is a certain contradiction; for [the object] is "established" (*niṣṭhitā*), having attained its firm standing through the non-universality of limitations such as place and time. Precisely because of this, it is "one" (*ekā*) since it is excluded from everything else, and thus "shining forth" (*sphurantī*)—that is, appearing in that manner—it is the "form" (*mūrti*) belonging to that [object], such as a cognition and so forth.

There is a contradiction [with scripture] because of another form associated with the vital breaths and so forth, since it is impossible for one embodied being to enter into another embodied being. || 13 ||
Now, [it may be objected]: "The manifestation of entities appearing as present is possible only as external forms of those that already exist within. (Ri. Pra. 1.5.1)

According to this principle, it has been established everywhere that the external manifestation of entities occurs precisely because they abide in identity with the subject; therefore, would there not likewise be an external manifestation of objects— even those residing within the subject such as the intellect (*buddhi*)— or would there not?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Although everything exists within internal consciousness, otherwise [it would not appear] in the intellect. (5.14)
Why would it migrate from the vital breath or the body, by what means, or how?
Even so, in this state free from conceptual construction, there is no conceptualization; without that [conceptualization], it does not exist. (5.15)

Even when perceived, it is as if unseen; however, certainty arises through conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Although this entire collection of entities might exist as one with consciousness within [the subject], otherwise, why would all this appear within the cognizer—such as the intellect and so forth—if it were of a nature distinct from consciousness?

The meaning is: by what cause other than [His] sovereignty (*svātantrya*), or in what manner other than through the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I-ness" (*aham*) and "this-ness" (*idam*), could [the object] "transfer"—that is, manifest as if it were a reflection? For otherwise, even the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth [would not appear].
The sense is that there would be no manifestation of those respective objects. Nevertheless, "in this"— that is, in the subject consisting of the intellect and so forth—
"even for a bound soul (paśu), the divine state exists in that state of non-conceptualization."

By the reasoning stated above, within the non-conceptual state whose nature is the manifestation of the non-differentiation of all entities, there exists no "conceptualization" that determines [them] as such internally, by virtue of which all this would manifest as non-differentiated. For—

By the statement, "Even that which is seen is as if unseen if it is not reflected upon," the meaning is that without conceptualization (*vikalpa*), even when something is seen, it is as if it were not seen—it has not taken root exactly as it was perceived. The word *tu* (but/however) indicates a reason; for...

"By means of conceptualization alone" (vikalpenaiva) there would be a "certainty" (niścaya) of the nature "this is thus. And that conceptualization is the operation of the limited subject; it would therefore determine [the object] only through the distinction of part and part, and not through non-distinction—thus, for the intellect and so forth, [such certainty] does not exist.
The manifestation occurs through the non-differentiation of all entities; thus it was rightly stated: "due to their mutual differentiation. || 15 ||

Now, one might object: "If it is the case that even though cognition and so forth are not ultimately real, they are said to serve as the instrumental cause for the manifestation of ultimate reality by means of meditation and the like, why is this not also the case for the Void?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The supreme sovereignty of the Lord is directly [manifest] in the intellect, the vital breath, and the body. (5.16)
Conceptualization occurs within the void-form, not within the cognizer.

Indeed, here in the cognizer such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, because it is the locus of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*), the "supreme sovereignty of the Lord," characterized by the nature of knowing and acting, is to be directly conceptualized; that is, having made it manifest through the various means of limitation (*avaccheda*).

This is certain, because by means of that [determination], the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth directed toward it would become the cause for attaining the ultimate nature. Furthermore, even though a subject (*pramātṛ*) whose form is empty might exist in reality,
since it is impossible for the supreme Lordship (*pārameśvaryam*) to be limited by fixed boundaries, it cannot even be conceptualized.

Thus, how indeed could this [scripture] serve as the cause for the illumination of the ultimate reality? In this way, it would be stated that only these three—intellect (buddhi) and the others—are the causes in this matter. || 16 ||

One might ask: "What indeed is that which exists for these [faculties] such as the intellect (buddhi), by taking recourse to which they might attain their ultimate, absolute nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The intellect there consists of meditation; the vital breath (prāṇa) consists of upward movement (uccāraṇa). (5.17)
"It consists of meditation" (dhyānamayī) because of the predominance of continuous contemplation (anusaṃdhāna). || 17 ||
It defines utterance (*uccāraṇa*):
"Utterance consists of the five functions beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *vyāna*.
[The word] 'five' refers to what was stated:"
"Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "Is there not a twofold vital function (*vṛtti*) belonging to the vital breaths? Namely, one is the general vital function that serves as the foundation for all five, beginning with *prāṇa*, while the other consists of the specific vital breaths themselves.
Therefore, how can it be said that 'the five functions are utterance'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But the first [state] consists of the supreme utterance known as the vital breath (prāṇa). || 5-18 ||
The meaning is that [the power] called *prāṇanā* consists of internal exertion; it is synonymous with "living" (*jīvana*) and has the nature of mere vitalization (*prāṇana*). As he will say:
"This is that power of vitalization (*prāṇanā-śakti*), which bestows the longing for internal exertion."
Vibration, throbbing, repose, the individual soul, the heart, intuition, and the intellect.

"That function of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), by means of its fivefold forms beginning with *prāṇa*, makes the body its own through consciousness; therefore, this [body] shines forth as full of consciousness. (6.12).
Thus, it is specifically these particular functions of *prāṇa* and the others that are intended here.
It has been rightly said: "the five functions are the utterance. And the nature of this will be explained later; therefore, no effort has been made here [to elaborate]. || 18 ||
Having thus described the specific nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he now describes that of the body as well:

"The constitution of the body consists of the senses, their objects, and these [elements] such as the vital breaths. Here, "senses" (*akṣāṇi*) refers to the organs; "objects" (*viṣayāḥ*) refers to their effects; and "these" refers to the vital breaths and so forth. Their—[the body's]—constitution is by way of being a mass (*piṇḍatvena*).
The meaning is: by way of being a "piṇḍa," that is, through unification, the "saṃsthiti" (establishment) is the unique form of the one afflicted by the body.
Now, immediately after defining the qualified practitioner, he begins to describe the nature of meditation and the other practices:
"In that regard, first, the unsurpassed [practice] consisting of meditation is described here. (5.19)

Thus, although [the goal] is to be accomplished through many means, that which has "meditation" (*dhyāna*) as its primary cause is here described as having such an "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) ultimate form; the meaning is that it is now being stated as the occasion for its exposition has arrived. For this very reason, the word "first" (*tāvat*) is used.
It indicates the sequence, for in the subsequent enumeration, the opening begins with "meditation on the intellect" (buddhidhyāna) and so forth. || 19 ||

Regarding this, he says: "This light, which is independent, whose nature is consciousness, and which abides in the heart, consists of all the principles (tattvas); and this has been declared in the *Triśiromata*. (5.20)

"This very nature of consciousness, which is distinct from the light of the sun and other [physical luminaries], is for that very reason autonomous because it is self-luminous; and for that very reason, it consists of all principles (*sarvatattvamaya*). It is the Light (*prakāśa*) that, manifesting in various forms within the heart during self-reflection, [is the ultimate reality]."
"Although this entire body is pervaded by the Witness and resides therein, nevertheless, His supreme abode is the ocean of the heart-lotus.
According to this principle, He is situated in the heart; there alone is He to be directly realized by those who know the reality (tattvavid).
This is the meaning. Now, what is the authority for this? It has been said: "And this has been taught in the Triśiromata. || 20 ||

He recites the very text found therein: "The knower of reality perceives that which resides within the heart, shaped like the hollow of a plantain leaf, possessing outer, inner, and innermost layers, like a flower. (5.21)

In this context, the knower of the Self [regards] that Supreme Brahman—which is the nature of independent luminosity—as being like a flower, because it bestows an excellence of bliss and is thus the supreme object to be attained; as it is said: "It is to be meditated upon in the heart by the wise."
By such statements as these, the meaning is that one "beholds what resides within the heart," i.e., one should directly realize it.

For that [reality] is like the "sheath of a plantain tree" (*kadali-śampuṭa*), which refers to the arrangement of the petals of a plantain flower joined together in the manner of being both internal and external to one another.

That whose form is interwoven with the principles (tattvas) such as the elements, subtle elements, and sense organs, which exist in a state of being woven together like warp and woof; for this very reason, it is the totality of both the "external"—the common collection of principles—and the "internal"—the uncommon [collection]—which constitutes the "external and internal. Of that...
"Internal" means having the singular nature of the supreme subject—this is the sense. What is meant is this:

just as someone, having removed the outer sapless layer of a plantain tree, gradually takes the innermost layer after layer until finally attains the supremely worthy flower; [so too does one attain the supreme reality].

In the same way, the knower of reality (tattvavid), having abandoned each successive external and bodily category of reality, should directly realize his own Self (svātmāna) vibrating within the heart—this is the meaning.
(21) Now, one might ask: even though the Self pervades all bodies, how can there be such direct realization (sākṣātkāra) specifically in the heart?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There, with undistracted mind, one should meditate on the union of the moon, sun, and fire.
For in that "place"—the heart—the attentive yogi [meditates] upon those consisting of prāṇa, apāna, and udāna.
One should meditate on the conjunction of the moon, sun, and fire; that is to say, one should maintain the continuous flow of the unfolding of the kumbhaka state.
Now, one might ask: "What is the fruit for one who meditates in this manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From the friction of the fire-drill of that meditation, the sacrificial fire of Mahābhairava [arises]. (5.22)
Blazing intensely in the great sacrificial pit called the Heart, it attains expansion.

That very "meditation"—which was just mentioned and consists of the union of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—is the "fire-drill"; by means of that [drill], through the complete severing of the movement of the prāṇa and apāna, one reaches a state free of conceptual construction.

Because of that "agitation," which consists of entering the central channel (*madhyadhāmānupraveśa*), the fire of Mahābhairava blazes intensely within the heart-pit (*hṛtkuṇḍa*) by casting aside all limitation; the meaning is that there occurs the direct realization of one's own self in the form of the perfect subject (*pūrṇapramātṛ*).
As it has been said:

"The power, in the form of the vital breath, neither goes out nor enters when [the lotus] is opened; by means of that [power], through its state of non-conceptuality, one assumes the form of Bhairava in the center. (Vijñānabhairava, verse 26)
Thus [ends the section]. || 22 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But how can this be so on this basis alone?", he says:
"Of that possessor of power, whose power is expanded, who is the splendor of Bhairava... (5.23).
One should contemplate the triad of abodes known as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge as non-different from the Light.

For one should contemplate— that is, realize as having become one with— that triad of abodes consisting of the limited subject and so forth, as being non-different from that supreme Light which is Bhairava, endowed with absolute freedom.
By which transcendence of limitation, identity with the supreme subject may arise. || 23 ||
Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that meditation, consisting of the union of the moon, sun, and fire, is the cause for attaining the state of the supreme subject?
