How is it then that you have just now spoken of even the existence of the mere cognized object and so forth as being non-different from that [supreme subject]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That very triad constitutes the powers of Fire, Sun, and Moon. || 5.24 ||
The meaning is that this triad, beginning with the knower (*pramātṛ*), belongs exclusively to the powers such as Fire (*vahni*) and so forth; it is of their very nature. || 24 ||
This is not only in the form of powers such as fire and so forth, but even in the form of the *parā* (supreme) and others; thus he says:
"This [power] is *parā*, *parāparā*, and *aparā*, eternally arisen.
She is "arisen" during the states known as emission (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthitī*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
There is a connection with each individual [term].
Therefore, he says:
"By means of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, each of them is threefold. (25)
Now, one might object: "Since these [powers] are eternally arisen, their emergence should also be possible even in the state that is beyond description;
so how is it said that each one possesses a triad consisting of emission (sṛṣṭi) and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And their fourth form is uninterrupted and unconstructed."
"Unconditioned" (anavacchinna) means devoid of limitations such as creation and so forth; for this very reason, it is "unconstructed" (akalpita), meaning it is the ultimate reality (tāttvika).
He summarizes this very point:
"In this way, those twelve goddesses are situated like the orb of the sun. (5.26)
Each one of these possesses the radiance of fire, sun, moon, and their pacification.
The word "those" refers to the powers beginning with Parā. Here, the phrase "each one" and so forth serves as the reason for making them penetrate the heart;
this has already been determined in detail in the immediately preceding chapter, so no further effort is expended here.

To show that this is established by the experience of everyone and is not something unprecedented, he says: "This unsurpassed wheel [emerges] from the heart through the eyes and other [senses]. (5.27)
"It indeed issues forth through the cavities (*vyoma*) into the range of each respective object.
This aforementioned "supreme wheel," which consists of twelve aspects, [emerges] from the heart—
from the Self in the form of the Supreme Lord— by way of the path of the cavities of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth.
The meaning is that it indeed "emerges" in the form of various mental modifications (*vṛtti*) for the purpose of grasping objects such as those specific forms;
it does not mean that it never emerges at all. This is what is being said:
that which, whether in one who is awakened or one who is unawakened, occurs quite naturally...
The twelvefold activity of the sense organs, such as the eye, proceeds by extending toward the perception of objects such as form;

this very [activity] is this unsurpassed wheel. However, because it is not recognized as being such by one who is unawakened, it is a cause of bondage; but for one who is awakened, it is a cause of liberation.
This is the distinction. As it has been said:
"This power, whose nature is action, belongs to Śiva and resides within the bound soul (paśu).
When remaining on its own path, it is the binder; when known, it brings about accomplishment. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.18)
Thus it is said:
"By whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound,
by that very same means, when employed with skillful method, they are liberated from the bondage of existence."
Thus [ends the section]. || 27 ||
This is not only the case here, but even with respect to the object itself—as he says:
"By the rays of that wheel, in that object, through the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal... (5.28).
The form of the essence consisting of the light of the Moon, Sun, and Fire becomes established.

Of that "wheel" (cakra)— just mentioned— which consists of the twelve goddesses beginning with Dṛk, by means of the "lights" (bhās) whose nature is their respective functions, "in that object," that is, in each respective domain.

By assuming the form known as creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, it "abides perfectly"— that is, without any differentiation from its own essential nature— in the form characterized by the expansion of the object, the means of knowledge, and the subject, which consist of the moon and so forth, yet with a slight contraction through outward-facing orientation.

The meaning is that it "throbs. For the subject first creates the object by way of its being manifested; thereafter, becoming attached to that very object for some time with unblinking steadiness, he subsequently [establishes it] through the conceit of satisfaction, thinking, "This object has been known by me."

Reflecting within himself, he withdraws [the senses] and, immediately thereafter, through the process of forceful digestion (*haṭhapāka*) by means of the method of "seizing" (*alaṅgrāsa*) and bringing about fullness, he causes them to reach the state of being assimilated into the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*).
This meaning also, like the goddesses of sight and the other senses, attains a fourfold form, because everything consists of the nature of everything.
One perceives that very identity. Thus [ends the verse]. || 28 ||

And therefore, wherever this circle of rays consisting of the eyes and other senses may fall, one should contemplate that very form [of consciousness] therein, by which the meditation on one's own Self (svātmadhyāna) is accomplished. Thus he says:
"In this way, regarding objects such as sound, through the path of the ether of the ears and other senses... (29).

"One should contemplate identity with this falling wheel. Now, one might object: "Since sound and the other objects are to be known through the specific functions of the ear and the other senses, how can the entire wheel of the functions of the ear and so forth descend upon each single [object]? Why was this said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
By this sequential method, wherever this [consciousness] falls— || 5.30 ||
The *cakra* is the essence of all, like various universal sovereigns of the earth; this very thing is the *cakra*. Words that function by denoting a whole also apply to its constituent parts.

According to this principle, each individual limb of the wheel, characterized as the ear and so forth, "falls" upon its respective object— such as sound and the rest— "wherever" it may be; that is to say, in each such instance, because everything consists of the nature of all things through the aforementioned sequence of emanation and so forth, it is of the nature of the Wheel (cakra).
The meaning is that it effects the enjoyment of its respective objects by swallowing all other functions without exception.
On this very point there is an illustration: "like a universal sovereign king. Just as when a universal sovereign king enters any foreign kingdom whatsoever, the other kings therein—
They necessarily follow for the sake of assistance; likewise, wherever even a single mental modification (*cidvṛtti*) extends toward any object, other modifications also run after it.
As it has been said:
"And even when a single mental modification of consciousness spreads forth for a moment,
all those deities of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) run toward that very place.
Thus [ends verse 30].
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this teaching that everything consists of the nature of all? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, the entire array of the six paths dissolves effortlessly. (5.31)
In the great wheel of Bhairava, which is surrounded by the goddesses of consciousness— meaning,
for one who meditates in the manner thus described on that which is surrounded by the circle of goddesses consisting of the consciousness of the eyes and other senses— within the [wheel] of Bhairava.

In the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), whose nature is that of the supreme subject, the "sixfold universe"—the entire range of the paths—dissolves "without effort"; the meaning is that it becomes one with Him. For, since individual entities are infinite, their dissolution into consciousness would not be accomplished even in a thousand ages [if it were approached piecemeal].

Because everything consists of the nature of all things, when even a single entity—consciousness itself—is dissolved, the entire universe would likewise be dissolved effortlessly and simultaneously; this is the meaning of the word "without effort" (ayatna). || 31 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Even so, what [follows]? he says:
"Then, through the mere residual impression (saṃskāra), even when the entire universe has been dissolved," (5.32).

One should contemplate the great wheel whirling through the surging forth of one's own self. Then, immediately thereafter, when the "destruction" of the "universe"— which remains as a mere latent impression— occurs by way of its externalization on all sides, [this takes place] because of the swallowing up of separate objects.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the "wheel"— which consists of the perceptions of the senses such as sight and so forth— as "wandering," that is, expanding everywhere, having made it "great" by its own self (ullasattayā), through its own surging forth (ucchalattayā). || 32 ||

Now, it is undisputed that even when external objects are present, the sequence of consciousness consisting of the activity of the senses, such as the eye and so forth, arises. If that very [sequence] has perished, how could this cycle manifest within itself? Anticipating this objection, he says:
Then, from the dissolution of that which is to be burned and from the complete exhaustion of its latent impressions (saṃskāra), || 5.33 ||

"One should meditate on the wheel as subsiding, then as stilled, and then as peace. From that—that is, from the aforementioned cause, the complete exhaustion of the "combustible," which is the external collection of objects—one should contemplate that wheel in its state of subsiding; immediately thereafter—

The meaning is that because even the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that [experience] are completely exhausted, it is "peaceful" (*śānta*); and finally, through the cessation of that wheel, one should maintain awareness of pure consciousness alone, which is "quiescent" (*śama*). He summarizes this very point as follows: || 33 ||
By means of this yoga of meditation, the universe is dissolved into the Wheel.
Consequently, within that consciousness, consciousness itself appears as having its objects dissolved.

Now, if it is the case that consciousness alone appears with its objects dissolved, then the entire universe—consisting of both subject and object—would shine forth according to the analogy of a flash of lightning; thus, there would be dissolution and emergence at all times?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Because of its nature as consciousness, the Great Goddess of Consciousness brings forth further creation from that [state]. (5.35)

Now, one might ask: what indeed is this nature of consciousness such that it possesses agency once again at the beginning of creation? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "because she is the Great Sovereign of Consciousness. (35)
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose for a meditator who thus contemplates the dissolution and emergence of the universe?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, dissolving the universe at every moment into his own consciousness..."
And by emitting it even more than that, one will constantly fall into the state of a Bhairava. || 5.36 ||
It is not only this wheel that the yogi should meditate upon, but also other wheels; thus he says:
"In this way, from the trident onwards, through the sequence of four and five spokes, the yogi should contemplate the wheel up to fifty spokes" (5.37).
With undistracted mind, one should meditate upon a wheel having sixty-four spokes, or a hundred spokes, or even a thousand spokes, or indeed thousands of innumerable spokes. (5.38)
And this has already been explained previously; thus, no further effort is made here. || 37-38 ||
Now, one might ask: what is the reason for its being beyond number? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the Great God, the Lord of Consciousness, whose consciousness is ever-shining, there is no conceptualization whatsoever regarding the Maheśvara who is the power of the universe. (5.39)
Anticipating the objection, "But what is the proof for this?", he says:
"The entire universe is his power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power;
thus did the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha describe it in the Māṅgalaśāstra. (5.40)
As it is stated there:
"Power and the possessor of power are said to be the two fundamental categories;
the entire universe consists of powers, and the Great Lord is the possessor of power."
Thus [ends the verse]. 40.
Nor is this merely our own invention; thus he says:
"The venerable Lord Sumati [taught] this meditation, which is of the nature of the first means, to Śrīśambhunātha, who was pleased with him. (5.41)

He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "In this same manner, one should also rely upon other meditations which, without following a gradual sequence, arrive at the pinnacle of the Unsurpassed Means. (5.42)
The term "others" refers to the various forms of the cakras mentioned in other scriptures. || 42 ||
Having thus defined the nature of meditative absorption (dhyāna), he now begins to explain the "emission of the reality of breath" (prāṇatattvasamuccāra) which was mentioned immediately thereafter:
"Now, that function of the breath which has been described as 'vitalizing' (prāṇanā) and so forth..."
As a means to that end, we shall explain the manifestation of the Unsurpassed.
He says that very thing:
"Abiding first in the heart, which consists solely of the aspect of the subject within innate bliss, one should contemplate the 'blissless' state through resting in pure emptiness. (5.44)
When the object of knowledge arises at the emergence of the vital breath (prāṇa), one should contemplate supreme bliss;
therein, one finds fulfillment through the apāna breath which is filled with the infinite portions of the objects of knowledge.
One should remain established in supreme bliss, adorned by the moon of apāna;
then, one is uniquely tranquil through the friction of the infinite, throbbing mass of objects of knowledge.

Having reached the level of equality, one becomes composed of the bliss of Brahman; even from that state, one remains intent on devouring the conceptualization of the multitude of means and objects of knowledge.
Resting in the fire of the *udāna*, one should contemplate great bliss (*mahānanda*).
Indeed, in this context, the yogi [realizes] that "first" (*purā*), the non-empty is called empty, and the empty is said to be non-existence (*abhāva*).

Having taken refuge in the repose within the "mere void" (*śūnyatāmātra*)— whose nature is defined by such passages as, "That is designated as non-existence (*abhāva*) wherein all existents (*bhāva*) have come to an end" (Svacchandatantra 4.291)— which is the single essence of consciousness (*saṃvidekātman*),
one [attains] the "natural" (*nija*) [state] in the "heart" (*hṛdi*), the locus which is the ground for the arising and resting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest.
In one who is thus characterized by bliss that has become his very nature due to being free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhitva*), and who—

remaining solely in the aspect of the subject (*pramātraṃśamātre*) in relation to other partial aspects such as the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— abides while directly realizing his own self in its absolute isolation, immediately thereafter...

According to the principle that "prior consciousness is transformed into the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," when the "vital breath," which is the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), arises from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* by way of exhalation (*recaka*), it is "devoid of bliss" (*nirānanda*) due to some degree of outward orientation.

The meaning is that one should "discern"—that is, perceive—the particular state that has emerged from the bliss recognized as one's own subject (*pramātṛ*). Furthermore, when [the consciousness] arises again within the "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) consisting of the *apāna*, one should discern the "bliss" produced by the "supreme" object of knowledge; for "there," in that state of the emergence of the object of knowledge, [this occurs].

He should abide established in supreme bliss; for that which is the "filling"—the state of being free from desire through the grasping of various objects—performed by those "parts" characterized as objects of cognition (prameya) which are "infinite" in relation to the subject (pramātṛ) and so forth, that very filling is the "drinking," the act of drinking. By means of that...

“Nirvṛta” means resting solely within one’s own self; because the “apāna” itself acts as a nourisher, it is the “moon,” and by that [moon] he is “adorned,” meaning he abides in that state from the *dvādaśānta* down to the heart through the process of inhalation (*pūraka*). Furthermore, from there, for a moment, by means of the function of retention (*kumbhaka*) in the heart—

Having rested, [one perceives] that which is the "clash" (*saṅghaṭṭa*) consisting of the mutual fusion of those "objects of knowledge" (*meyānām*)— which were just mentioned and appear as infinite in their forms such as blue, pleasure, and so on—
and being "completely" (*ekāntena*), that is, unerringly "satisfied" (*nirvṛtaḥ*), simultaneously...
By accepting all objects of knowledge (*meyasvīkārāt*), having reached a common ground, and because it is produced in conjunction with the object of knowledge,

one becomes composed of that bliss which is expanded and of the nature of Brahman; the meaning is that one would experience a state of bliss even more distinguished than the state of supreme bliss (*parānanda*).

Immediately after that, [it says]: "Of the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge," that is, of the Prāṇa and Apāna which are of the nature of the Sun and Moon, there is a "current" (*ogha*)—the flow of which consists of "twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths], O fair lady" (Vi.bhai. 156).

The yogi— whose nature has been defined by such passages as these— is intent upon devouring those "vibrations" (kalanās), being dedicated to their dissolution; moving upward through the central channel (madhyamārga) into the "fire of udāna," he comes to rest through the process of excellence, having abandoned the intermediate disturbances of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth.

"One should contemplate 'Great Bliss'" (mahāntam ānandam) means that one should reflect upon it as resting solely within one's own self— bliss which is superior because it transcends the ten measures (*pramāṇa*) and is distinct from [ordinary] bliss such as *nirānanda*, and which is recognized as the subject (*pramātṛ*). || 47 ||
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what would happen to this [consciousness] through such reflective awareness (parāmarśa)? he says:
"Having attained rest therein, it becomes tranquil in this great flame" (5.48).

The meaning is that, having attained rest therein in Great Bliss, it becomes one with that [state] within this "Great Radiance," which is the fire of the udāna breath in the nature of the subject; thus it "subsides. || 48 ||
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what indeed is called its 'peace' (śānti)? he says:
"The unconditioned great pervasion, devoid of the limiting adjunct known as vyāna;
at that time, there is indeed the bliss of consciousness (cidānanda), which is not augmented by the insentient. (5.49)

And that peace is "without limiting adjuncts" (*nirupādhi*); it is such because its "limiting adjuncts"—consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—have departed from it and do not manifest as differentiated.
For this very reason, because it abides pervading everything from *kalā* down to the earth, it is the "great pervasion" (*mahāvyāpti*); for this very reason, it is present everywhere.
Because it pervades all, it is called "Vyāna"; the meaning is that it rests upon the state of Vyāna.

Thus, although it consists of everything, it is said to be "transcending everything" by being described as "devoid of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhivarjitā*). For this very reason, "then"—in that state—bliss is indeed of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Indeed, at that time...
It has been stated that there is room for non-conscious things, whose nature consists of objects such as "mine," in the phrase "that which is not augmented by the insentient."
The presentation of the reason for this is as follows:
"For here there is no separate existence whatsoever of that which is insentient in nature.
The word "separate" implies that, on the contrary, these [insentient things] do indeed possess existence through non-separation—this is the intended meaning.
As it has been said:
"But for the Immeasurable One, all things appear full within Himself, just as His own Self appears [full] within Himself. (Rigpāda-prakaraṇa 2.1.7).

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since the supreme reality is the undivided self of the subject due to its being free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi), as has been stated, how could there be any delimiters here even in the absence of division?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In which there is no exclusion whatsoever, which vibrates everywhere.
That which is the unstruck consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar, wherein there is no primary application whatsoever of meditative cultivation and the like. (5.51)
Śambhu has declared that very bliss of the universe to us:

"Where there is no one at all"—meaning there is no exclusion whatsoever—because this "shines forth in every way" (*viśvataḥ*), in every form; for nothing else whatsoever can possibly exist apart from this.

The sense is that, from this, even its differentiation (*vyavaccheda*) occurs. For this very reason, it is said: "That which is [the state] of *anāhatā*—that consciousness which flashes forth everywhere as the nature of the subject, the object, and so forth—and for this very reason, it is 'nourished by the supreme nectar' characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)."

"Full" means independent of anything else. Precisely for this reason, because there is an absence of any fixed or determinate form, "there is no primary applicability whatsoever of [practices such as] meditative cultivation (bhāvanā)"; the meaning is that they do not possess direct status as means (*upāya*). As it has been said:
"Therefore, how can the non-apprehension of objects, whose very life is concentration, serve as a direct means on the supreme path of Bhairava? (Tantrāloka 2.13).
This supreme reality, which is the self of the subject and consists solely of consciousness, [is related] to the world...

The meaning is that Śrī Śambhunātha has taught us that which is designated by the term "world-bliss" (jagadānanda)—that in which bliss exists and from which it arises, both as one's own innate bliss and as the universal form; it is not, however, something stated by us as our own original invention. || 51 ||
One should not stop merely with this instruction; thus he says:
"In that regard, rest should be established through the yoga of the heart's utterance. (5.52)
The "utterance from the heart" refers to the utterances of the *hṛdayas*— both those already mentioned and those yet to be described— which consist of the nature of emanation and so forth.
One might ask: "What would come of resting here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which is perfect rest therein is the state consisting of the Absolute (Anuttara).
He concludes this very point as follows:
Thus, even though [the heart and so forth] possess a single nature within their own abode, [this distinction arises]. (5.53)
Now, that form born from the upward movement of the six vital breaths (*ṣaṭprāṇoccāra*) is described by way of its pervasiveness (*vyāpti*).

Although the nature of the light of one's own Self is one and the same in the heart and elsewhere— for there is no distinction whatsoever for that which has departed from the heart to the *dvādaśānta*, or from the *dvādaśānta* back to the heart— it has been said:
"Having moved, where will you go, since everything is composed of Śiva? (Svacchanda Tantra 4.310).
It is with this very intention [that it is said]:
"Those who have lost their discernment wander in the forest of the cakras and ādhāras, which is unreal."
Thus it has been stated by others; nevertheless, because differentiation arises through the gradation of contraction,

this form— which consists of *nirānanda* and so forth— is born from that utterance (*uccāra*) of the sixfold vital breath (*prāṇa*), which exists in the nature of both the universal and the particular, and whose essence is *prāṇana*, *apānana*, and so on.
The word "iti" implies that it has been stated in the manner just described; now this very point is also expressed by way of the pervasion of the mantra—thus he says "atha" and so forth. || 53 ||
He says that very thing:
"By means of the application of the staff of breath (prāṇa), through the equalization of the preceding and the following. (5.54)
One should take refuge in the palace of the hanging *lambikā*, which hangs down from the lotus of the crossroads (*catuṣkikā*);
having then traversed the ground of the trident (*triśūla*), where the three channels (*nāḍī*) converge. || 5-55 ||

The wise one should enter into the state of equality among the powers of will, knowledge, and action. Indeed, here in this world, the yogi— by means of the sequence beginning with the contraction of the "intoxicated scent" (*mattagandha*) and so forth, through the cessation of the transverse flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by abandoning the state of being coiled (*kuṇḍalatā*)— performs what is called the "application of the staff" (*daṇḍaprayoga*).

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "Just as a snake struck by a stick arises in the form of a stick, so too does she awaken when awakened by the Guru," there is the attainment of the state of being shaped like a stick through the state of awakening; by that—

The "four-way junction" (*catuṣkikā*) is the support named Cintāmaṇi, which takes the form of a crossroads situated below the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), resulting from the pacification of the flows of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* in the anterior and posterior [channels] through the support of the form of the equinox (*viṣuvat*) and the consequent entry into the central abode (*madhyadhāman*).

The "lotus" (*ambuja*) is the support named the "knowledge-lotus" (*vidyākamala*) situated between the eyebrows; she who "takes hold of" (*ālambate*) it—that is, whose nature is to grasp it by being positioned above and below—is this "pendent one" (*lambikā*).
Above that is the "palace" (*saudha*), the support of nectar (*sudhā*); [the text refers to] that support of nectar. Furthermore, this [belongs] to the nectar...
One should cause the letter *śa* (the *śaudha*) to rest; the meaning is that one should find repose therein.

Immediately after this, the pure (*śuddhiḥ*) yogi [perceives] the channel called Ādhārā, which resides above the Brahmarandhra and is characterized by a trident because it consists of the convergence of the three channels.
Having ascended the plane—
"For by ascending that triad of powers within the Bhairavian self, which is consciousness, that [universe] is indeed emitted... (5.187).

By the reasoning stated in such passages, one should "enter" with intensity into the form of Bhairava— which is designated by terms such as *visarga* and is filled with that [divine nature]— when there is an equilibrium of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), and which contains within it the reflective awareness of the phonemes of the *śūla*.
The meaning is that one should become a partaker of that immersion. || 55 ||
One might object: "How can entry into this [reality] be accomplished by this much alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The one [consciousness], which is expansive, further uncontracted, and ever-blossoming... (56)
One should resort to the series of steps consisting of the brow-point (*bhrūbindu*), the resonance (*nāda*), the end (*anta*), and power (*śakti*).

The word *tu* is placed out of its logical order and functions as a reason; for, first, because it is difficult to pierce, the "one" is primary, and by the term "brow-point" (*bhrūbindu*), [the path] begins from the surface of the brows.
Bindu, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā— these are the "steps" because they serve as the means for ascending higher and higher.
One should "resort to their garland," which means one should ascend by way of the process of extraction (*uddhātaka*) out of a longing to attain the state of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī.
Now, one might object:

according to the principle stated in [Svacchandatantra 4.27], "O fair-limbed one, the infinite web of bonds extends up to the level of *śamana*," the contracted form alone would be possible for the *bindu* and other [principles]. How then [can they be otherwise]?

One might ask: "Could this very name serve as a means to attain a state of ever-expanding abundance of bliss, because it is eternally arisen? Anticipating this doubt, he says "expanding" (*vikāsinīm*), and so forth. For by this, [he shows] their respective...
It would thus be said that because of the existence of varying degrees of expansion, even the state that is eternally expanded is appropriately an *upāya*. || 56 ||
Now, one might ask: "What would be gained even by attaining the state of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There, on the plane of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, [resides] that which is beautiful with the interior of its vibration. (5.57)
In that state, which partakes of the condition of the "fish's belly," the emission (*visarga*) should find its rest;

for there, in the transmental (*aunmanasa*) plane, the "belly" (*udara*)— the essence consisting of the non-dual manifestation of the "surging forth" of one's own self— is the "emission" (*visarga*), which is beautiful and desirable because of its movement.

The supreme form of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*), consists of two *bindus*; the meaning is that one should "rest therein," in the emission (*visarga*), which is to say, one should manifest in identity with it.

Although its essential nature has already been stated by the phrase "beautiful within the belly of vibration" (*spandanodarasundara*), [it is further specified] as "abiding in the state of the fish's belly" (*matsyodaradaśājuṣi*).
By this it would be stated that he always, at all times, abides in the state of vibration (spanda), and not merely at some particular time. || 57 ||
To pacify the doubt—"What would come of resting even there?"—he provides an illustration:
"Just as a she-donkey [rests] in the mare's own abode, the temple of bliss. (5.58)
Having entered [the heart] which consists of expansion and contraction, one rejoices;
likewise, [one rejoices in the heart] which is completely filled with the multitude of states that are repeatedly dissolved and projected. (5.59)
One should take refuge in the union of Bhairava and Bhairavī, which is established in the nature of expansion and contraction;

just as a she-ass or a mare, at the time of urination and so forth, possesses that which consists of "expansion and contraction"— the characteristic of the generative organ— which vibrates incessantly through being oriented both outwardly and inwardly.

Having entered that abode, the temple of supreme bliss, and becoming one-pointed in mind toward it, he "rejoices in his heart," experiencing an excess of bliss within his own self; likewise, [the powers] are repeatedly "dissolved," withdrawn into his own self, and "emitted," projected outward.
All "entities" (bhāvas), whose nature consists of the knower, the known, and so forth, [are] "thoroughly filled" (nirbharām) by them—
meaning they have no further requirement— and for this very reason, [they exist] within "expansion and contraction," that is, within emission and reabsorption, as appropriate.

"Established" means manifested as suchness (*tathātvena*). By the rule of *ekaśeṣa* in the form "man and woman" (*pumān striyā*, Pāṇini 1.2.67), there is a "pair" (*yāmala*) consisting of Bhairava and Bhairavī.
One should "take refuge" in such a ground of emission (*visargabhūmi*), which is the cause for the consciousness of one's own bliss.

The meaning is that he should enter [into it]. For this very thing is the nature of this supreme Light, whose essence is non-dual—that it is always characterized by the performance of both emission and withdrawal; otherwise, its distinction from insentient things would not exist.

This has been established many times. Thus, in emission (*sṛṣṭi*), there is the growth of power (*śakti*); but in withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), it belongs to the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). As it has been said:
"The universe is the accumulation of his own powers" (*Śivasūtra* 3.30).
Thus it is said;
and also: "The Lord of Heroes is the enjoyer of the triad" (Śivasūtra 1.11). || 59 ||
He summarizes this very point: "In the heart, which is the state of emission (vaisargika) where the great root-piercing (mūlaśūla) has been unified," (60).
"Resting in the Supreme" means resting in that which is beyond all, by virtue of the yoga of filling everything.
"Unified" means established as the essence of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) and made into a single whole.
And the "Great Root" is *Māyā*, because it is the supreme cause.
"From that very [source], the universe clearly shines forth within this letter *sa*. (Tantrāloka 3.165).

According to such statements, because it is the locus for the establishment of the universe, the letter *sa* is the "trident" (*śūla*), and the letter *au*, which consists of the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*), is the "emissional" (*vaisargika*) state, the location of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī.

And where there are two *bindus*—in such a state, within the "supreme" (*parasmin*) which is the nature of the supreme subject, distinct from the heart of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-hṛdaya*) and so forth, and within that "heart" (*hṛdi*) which is consciousness and the supreme seed-syllable (*parā-bīja*)—there occurs the "filling" (*āpūraṇam*) of everything, whether internal or external; that is, its assimilation into one's own self (*svātmasātkāraḥ*) and the manifestation of duality (*bhedollāsaḥ*). Of that...

"Yoga" means *yukti* (logical consistency); therefore, "he attains rest" means he should abide established solely in his own self by way of the nature of the supreme *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness). For it is precisely the state of being the mere form of the reflective awareness of "I," which contains the entire universe within itself, that is the supreme abode of rest—this is our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, he says:
"In this regard, it exists as consisting of universal immersion by means of that very full manifestation. (5-61)
When light rests within itself, let it be perceived as simply "I. Here,

on the plane of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, through a full mode of being that encompasses the entire universe, that very supreme Heart— which consists of the reflective awareness of "I"— is realized.

It abides as the locus of rest; for it abides as the locus of rest within the self of the Light, and not within the body or other objects of manifestation. Observe that when there is rest within the Light—not within the body or other objects of manifestation—the reflective awareness is precisely "I."
The meaning is: "Let it be examined. For in this case, there could not possibly be anything else to be excluded (apohya) apart from light;
what then can be said of another reflective awareness? This is the intended sense. || 61 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since there exists only the unsurpassed, peaceful, supreme Brahman, what indeed is this 'I-reflection' (ahaṃparāmarśa), which could even serve as a locus of rest? To pacify this doubt, [the author] proceeds immediately after the exposition of the principle of breath (prāṇatattva) to that which was indicated in the subsequent section.
He introduces the utterance of the conscious self (cidātman):
"In the supreme reflective awareness (anuttaravimarśa), which is initially devoid of activity and the like... (5.62).

The supreme egoity (*parāhaṃkṛt*), which consists of the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cidvimarśa*), flashes forth as the first emergence. This occurs within the "supreme Self," the ultimate Light of manifestation, which is the reflective awareness prior to all else— unconditioned by activities such as the desire to emerge (*ullilasiṣā*) at the initial limit (*prāk*), and resembling a waveless ocean.

First, she is of the nature of radiance; therefore, because there is no object of reflection distinct from her, she is "supreme reflective awareness of consciousness" (*cidvimarśaparā*), intent solely upon the self-reflection of her own Self. She is the "I-maker" (*ahaṃkṛt*), the reflective awareness of "I," by whose flashing forth autonomy arises for her everywhere.

Indeed, by the very majesty of His own sovereignty, the Supreme Lord— whose essence is the unsurpassed Light— conceals His own true nature and, abiding in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, manifests the multitude of separate entities. 62.
Regarding this, he says:
"Then, by that [power] consisting of twelve kalās, which is intent on exertion... (63).

One should illuminate the objective entity with the sun, then fulfill it, and subsequently contemplate it. Then, for the reason that there is the vibration of the reflective awareness of "I," that supreme Light— preceded by the manifestation of the stage of the contracted subject— is "exertion."

The desire to manifest the object, by one who is capable therein, is always extroverted; through the twelve *kalās*— the phonemes from *a* to the visarga, excluding the neuter ones— which are the reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*),
and by means of the sun that is the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) having attained its full essential form, [one perceives] each individual entity.
One should "illuminate" (bhāsayet) by means of a slightly contracted form such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, which is to say, one should project it externally;

one should "fill" (pūrayet) it, meaning one should maintain it for some time precisely as that [externalized state]; one should "contemplate" (carcayet), meaning one should withdraw it by assimilating it into one's own self. For anyone who seeks purposeful action (arthakriyā)...

The cognizer should first perceive the multitude of objects as they have ascended into the means of knowledge; immediately thereafter, he should conceptualize them as "this is thus"; following that, through the pride of satisfaction in thinking "this object has been known by me," he should dissolve their external form and cause them to rest within his own self.
Thus, this matter is attested by direct experience. || 63 ||
Now, one might ask: "What would the multitude of entities do once they have attained this state of being characterized by manifestation and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Then the moon, possessing sixteen digits, becomes slow in swallowing the emission (visarga). (5.64)
Vibrating, he pours the nectar of Sañjīvanī into the fire of awakening,
[the nectar] which has reached the tip of the sacrificial ladle formed by the subtle apertures of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

Thus, this very nectar is divine and satisfies the goddesses of consciousness. Now, following the ascent of the means of valid cognition (*pramā*), it "throbs," manifesting in its own form; for this reason, it is that which possesses the "sixteen" digits (*kalā*), beginning with *a* and so forth, as well as those beginning with the faculties of perception (*buddhīndriya*).

Having attained his own full essential nature, he is therefore characterized by the "swallowing of the emission" (*visargasya grāsaḥ*), which consists internally in the obscuration of that [emission] through the attainment of an overflowing state of being; by means of that, the moon— which is the body and other objects of cognition— is "sluggish" (*mantharaḥ*) and "relaxed" (*visrabdhaḥ*),
while [the teacher] is the "life-giving herb" (*sañjīvanī*).

By such statements as, "In the person consisting of sixteen parts, they call that the immortal part," it is taught that the seventeenth part, named Amā, is the cause of the vitalization of the universe;
it consists of a specific constituent that nourishes even the group of sixteen parts— the "immortal nectar" within the fire of consciousness.

The meaning is that when the limited subject "emits," it shines forth in a gross form as the nature of the subject, the object of knowledge, and so on. Having made this nectar—which has shone forth in the manner described above and has long since taken root in the form of blue, pleasure, and so on—divine by placing the ladle consisting of will and the other [powers] at its tip; |||

The meaning is that one should cause the goddesses of sight and the other senses to rest entirely within the pure self (sarvātmamātra) by means of the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of objects such as form, which satisfies the goddesses of consciousness (saṃviddevī). The subtle apertures are the gateways of the senses in the form of the physical orbs (golaka). This is what is being said: whatever collection of entities exists...

Thus, preceded by the attainment of its state as an object of desire, it reaches the status of being knowable through its ascent upon the gateway of the senses; then, by performing various purposeful actions and generating a repose within the entire measure of the self, it brings about the fullness of consciousness. || 65 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of thus satisfying the Goddess of Consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This much is the nectar of emission [to be offered] into the consumer of the oblation called Awakening. (5–66)
If everything were thus released, the entire mandala of the sixfold path would be offered as a sacrifice— namely,
that mandala of states consisting of all states, within the sacrificial fire of power which consists of the power of the universe, as taught by the excellent Guru.

"For who else is equal to me, who am sacrificing with this Viśvamedha-sacrifice consisting of the sacrifice?"—here, the extraction of the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*) and so forth has already been explained by the previous commentary;
thus, because of its extreme secrecy, no further effort is made here. || 66 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if this much nectar of emission (*visargāmṛta*) has indeed been apprehended by means of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), what does that have to do with the sixfold circle of the paths (*adhvamaṇḍala*) such that it was described in this way?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Since the emission (*visarga*) of the Unsurpassed Lord is the Mistress of the Kula, its agitation is the series of letters from *ka* to *ha*, and its expansion is the sequence of the principles (*tattva*). (5–67)
The term *kulanāyikā* refers to the *kaulikī* power (*śakti*). As was stated previously:
"The unsurpassed supreme abode is called *akula*; the emission (*visarga*) of that Lord is called the *kaulikī* power. (3.144)
"The wise declare this [alphabet] from *ka* to *ha* to be the substratum of agitation" (3.180).
Regarding the phrase "its agitation," this means the agitation of that *visarga*, which is the substratum of agitation.
As it has been said: "Its expansion" refers to that [expansion] of the substratum of agitation, which consists of the letters from *ka* to *ha*.
"Expansion" (*prasaraḥ*) means the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
As it has been said:
"The principles beginning with earth and ending with the *puruṣa* [are contained] within the five."
O Subratā, [these are] sequentially within the classes beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma'.
There is a tetrad of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on wind, fire, water, and earth;
above that is the well-known group beginning with *śa*, and before that is the pentad beginning with *bha*.
"From that sequence, it should be known as rootless; [this] emission is declared to end with *kṣānti*. (Paṭrī. 7).
Thus [ends verse 67].

Now, one might object: "If the emission (visarga) of the Unsurpassed Lord is indeed the Kaulikī Śakti, then why has this not been demonstrated in the arising of the Mātṛkā? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the Lord of Kula is indeed accompanied by the Mistress of Kula as 'aṃ aṃ'."
As it has been said:
"That which is pure luminosity here, existing when the three abodes are present, is described in the scripture as the *bindu*; this is considered the *śivabindu*. (Tantrāloka 3.134)
Thus:

"That supreme Kaulikī power, which is said to be the desire for emission within this [consciousness], necessarily attains the nature of emission (visarga) through the force of agitation. (Tantrāloka 3.137)

And so it is said. Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated through such reasoning as 'the power is indeed non-different from the possessor of power,' there is no separation between the possessor of power and the power; how then can their emergence be shown as distinct? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The supreme separation of emission is said to be the universe consisting of that.

The term *viśleṣa* of the *visarga* means that the *visarga* is disjoined; for this very reason, because it is differentiated from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), it is said to be "supreme" (*para*). Furthermore, it is stated that the universe is indeed its expansion, as expressed in the words: "the universe is said to consist of that. Thus it has been said:
"It is said that there are two categories of reality: power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).
His powers are this entire universe, while the possessor of power is Maheśvara.
Thus, when the nectar of emission (*visargāmṛta*) is contemplated as being identical with the supreme subject, even that which is sixfold [is so realized].
The path (adhvan) must indeed consist of that alone; thus it was rightly said: "The oblation becomes the maṇḍala of the sixfold path. || 68 ||
And for this reason, should all these external acts of worship and so forth be performed solely under its authority? To this he says:
"One should worship, offer oblations, and meditate upon this life-sustaining *kalā*, which consists of consciousness, vital breath, qualities, the body, and internal and external substances. (5.69)

"In this manner"— that is, by the method described above— one should perform worship, the realization of universal identity, and so forth, by relying on this very power of the *sañjīvanī* (the life-restoring) aspect known as *amā*, which nourishes the entire universe; for supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*) is the true knowledge, while the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and the individual subjects (*pramātṛ*) are [its manifestations].

O Sacrificers, that which has as its *prakṛti* (material cause) the five jewels and their substitutes such as saffron—which, in relation to that [consciousness], take the form of internal and external substances serving as the means for sacrifice; the meaning is that it has the expansion (*sphāra*) of those [jewels] as its essence. || 69 ||

One might object: "In that case, worship and the like would only succeed if this ground of emission (*visargabhū*) were attained; for the great exertion required for its attainment alone might not reach its conclusion even in a thousand yugas—thus, the practice of the meaning of the scripture would remain endless. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Remaining attentive to the vibration of the pair of channels of bliss,
he attains this ground of the nectar-flowing mansion of emission.

That which is characterized by bliss, associated with the accomplished Yoginīs, and possessing the marks of the excellent limbs—the pair of *nāḍīs*—its "vibration" (*spandana*) is the mutual orientation toward one another through the desire to move;
"attention" (*avahiti*) therein is one-pointedness through the sequence beginning with the entry into the six-spoked mudrā; [the practitioner] is "established" (*sthita*) therein.

Having attained growth, this art of *sañjīvanī* is the very place of repose (*viśrāntisthāna*) and the pure ground (*śaudhabhūmi*) of that "outpouring" (*niṣyanda*), which is the expansion of the Supreme Lord’s form consisting of the desire to emit (*visisṛkṣātmaka*) and His final constituent (*caramadhātu*). It is that very [ground].

Because it produces an excess of bliss, one attains the "ground" (*bhūmi*) of the "pure nectar" (*śaudha*), which is a mass of ambrosia; the meaning is that one should reach identity with that. This is what is being said:
here, indeed, the practice of all worldly customs is established even without being explicitly stated.

If, by relying on even a mere fragment of reasoning in that very context, one simply applies focused attention, then the ground of emission (visarga) would be attained without effort; so what need is there for such exertion here, the failure of which would render even the practice of the scriptural meaning incomplete? || 70 ||
Granted that this means may indeed be an easy method to accomplish [the goal], but where even the entire web of means has become powerless, what can be achieved there by this single one alone?—
anticipating this doubt, he says:

When there is agitation through power (*śākta-kṣobha*), when there is the immersion into *kula*, when [consciousness] has reached the tips of all the channels, during the state of pervasion, and during the contraction of the entire self—the wise one should enter the heart. (5.71)
"In the agitation of Śakti" refers to union with an external Śakti. As it has been said:
"The bliss that concludes the immersion of power, agitated by union with Śakti—that is the bliss of the reality of Brahman; that is called one's own innate bliss. (Vijñānabhairava, verse 69).
Thus:

"Kulāveśa" (the immersion into Kula) means that even in the absence of external power (*bāhya-śakti*), through the intensity of contemplation preceded by recollection, there occurs an identification with the "Kula," which is the essential nature of Śakti. This is the meaning.
As it has been said:

"O Goddess, through the recollection of the fullness of a woman's pleasure—arising from licking, churning, and piercing—even in the absence of actual power, there occurs a flood of bliss. (Vi.bhai. 70)
Thus,
in the foremost range of all the channels, in the primary or ultimate object, namely at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta),
as it has been said:
"In whatever manner and wherever one may cast the mind at the *dvādaśānta*, a distinct transformation of the diminished mental fluctuations will occur within days.
(Vi.bhai. 51)

Thus [it is said]. Or else, "in the foremost region" (*agragocare*) means in the peripheral area where, as in the armpit and so forth, great bliss arises through gentle stimulation with the fingers. As it has been said:
"By this deceptive application, O fawn-eyed one, immediately..."

"By which great bliss arises through which reality is discerned. (Vi.bhai. 66, śloka). Regarding the term "in pervasion" (*vyāptau*), it means in the *vikāsa-samādhi* (the meditative absorption of expansion), which effects the inclusion of all things through the realization of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*). As it has been said:

"The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading; I am indeed He, a follower of the Śaiva dharma"—through such firm conviction, one becomes Śiva. (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā, verse 109).

And as it is said: "Just as waves belong to water, the flickering flames to fire, and the radiance to the sun, so these various manifestations of the universe are differentiated from me alone, Bhairava" (Vi.bhai.
110). And regarding the phrase "contraction of the self of Śarva," when there is a contraction of the external by means of the entire self, [one thinks] "this is not a real thing."
The meaning is: "in the contemplation that 'something exists'. As it has been said:
"Knowledge would be without support, without cause, and of the nature of delusion; in reality, for no one is this so—the Śiva who is dear, O Beloved. (Vijñānabhairava, verse 99).
Thus it is said:
"The universe is composed of a magical illusion (indrajāla), or it is laid down like a painted picture."
"Or for one who meditates or perceives everything through delusion, there is the arising of happiness.
(Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā, verse 102).
Regarding such a subject, "one who possesses pure intellect"—that is, anyone whose knowledge is complete and who is in their final birth—[is the one qualified].
"He should enter the heart" means he should rest upon the ground of the Visarga. || 71 ||
Now, one might object: "If there are indeed many such means possible here, why has the predominance been assigned specifically to the *kṣobha* of Śakti? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From the mutual friction of the web of digits of the Moon and the Sun..."
In the abode consisting of Agni and Soma, the bliss of emission shall manifest.

The "web of digits" (*kalājāla*) consists of the objects of measurement and the means of measurement— namely, the moon and the sun— which take the form of sound and so forth, as well as the senses such as hearing; the mutual friction between these two,
which consists of the relationship of grasped and grasper, results from the inclusion of both, and thus takes the form of the goddesses of the *cakra* and *anucakra*.
The "web of digits" (*kalājāla*) is the friction consisting of their mutual union; from that—

according to the statement beginning with, "The fire named *Śuci* arises from the friction of the Moon and the Sun"— there occurs the bliss of emission (*visargānanda*) through entry into the central abode, which consists of Fire and Moon (*agnīṣoma*).

It would "open" by its primary function; through the emission of the final element, the supreme state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) would arise, which is metaphorically designated as "bliss" (*ānanda*) elsewhere so that it too may serve as a means for entering into supreme consciousness. || 72 ||
He concludes this very point: Enough with secret talk; this is hidden by its very nature.
The wise man who finds rest therein is one who has accomplished his purpose. (5.73)
Since this is the "heart" of the Yoginīs—the supreme place of rest—it is for that very reason described as being secret by its very nature; with this very intention it is said:
"Neither one born of non-Yoginīs, nor even one who is not Rudra, attains this" (Paṭtriṃśattattvaprakāśa, verse 10).

This and more has been stated elsewhere. Regarding the word "therein," it refers to the unfolding of emission (*visargonmeṣa*) which is the very heart of the Yoginīs; by the word "wise one" (*budha*), it is indicated that here the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*) alone is primary—thus it is hinted at. (73)
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the sign of recognition for one who has found rest here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Having attained firm rootedness in the state where rejection, acceptance, and disregard have ceased, one should perceive the universe through non-dual functioning as the wonder of Consciousness. (5.74)

Regarding the rejection and acceptance of objects to be abandoned and adopted, there is a state of disregard based on such teachings as, "Do not abandon anything; do not grasp anything" (Anu. 7, verse). In that regard, this is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which consists of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

In this context, the phrase "he should see" means that, having attained growth through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of identity with consciousness—the wonder of consciousness—he should know the universe as being one with his own self by way of non-dual functioning.
Therefore, this alone is the primary characteristic for entering into the supreme reality: that [the universe] is known as identical with one's own self.

It is the abiding in one's own self alone, through the transcendence of rejection and acceptance. For this very reason, immediately following the utterance of the conscious self (*cidātman*), he has begun to determine the entry into the supreme reality (*paratattva*), which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration. For it is only when duality exists that there is a distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted; [this is the case] for whomsoever...
For one in whom [all duality] has dissolved, what indeed is there to be abandoned and what to be accepted? Thus, his supreme consciousness shines forth in its fullness. || 74 ||

Thus it is said: "Having abandoned the wretchedness of seeking purposeful action within the outer and inner self, and having attained fulfillment in one's own true nature, one should resort to the blossomed state of Nāda. (5.75)

In this context, indeed, the yogin who has entered into the ultimate reality (tattva), having abandoned the wretchedness of desiring specific causal functions for various objects— due to the absence of any distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding the external and internal nature of objects such as blue or pleasure— [perceives] all phenomena...

Because it is being withdrawn, there is the extraction of the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*). Following that, "one should resort to the state of *ṅāda*, which is expansive due to the sprouting of that very [seed]," means that one should attain the consciousness that transcends the universe, whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And thus, first—

Since the dissolution of the universe has commenced, there arises the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*); following that, from its very sprouting, there arises the seed-syllable of the *saṃhārakuṇḍalinī*.
Thus, by this [process], even the first two syllables pertaining to the venerable Piṇḍanātha have been extracted. || 75 ||
One might ask: "Even if this [state] is attained in such a way, what purpose would there be? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of that [attainment], one should properly cause the internal crookedness of consciousness to expand;
then the wheel of the senses, the vital breaths, and consciousness becomes non-different from the object of knowledge. (5.76)
By that state of *nāda*, which is the nature of consciousness transcending the universe, and which—
preceded by the complete withdrawal of the universe and through the sublation of duality— brings about the purification of the path;
[it is] the "inner mouth" of the supreme consciousness, which, though transcending the universe, consists of the universe.

The inward-turned form— such a yogi "should cause it to blossom," meaning he renders it fit for blossoming. "Thence," that is, from the reason of bestowing upon consciousness the fitness for blossoming,
[he causes] the "blossoming of the senses," namely, of the cognitions of blue and so forth.

The wheel consisting of the nature of the knower (mātṛ), the means of knowledge (māna), and the object of knowledge (meya)— which belongs to the "winds" (marut), that is, the senses that serve as the cause for the arising of those [objects], existing in the form of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth through their common function— is the universe (viśva) in relation to the empty subject (śūnyapramātṛ).
That which is to be known as having the nature of an existent would be non-different from that which has the nature of nothingness. || 76 ||
One might object: "Even so, since the latent impression of objective existence (bhāva-saṃskāra) still persists, the dissolution of duality has not occurred in an absolute sense;
therefore, how can entry into the nature of pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra) be established?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That object of knowledge is dissolved by the fire called consciousness;
once dissolved, it merges into this triangle, the fire of Śakti.

That [object], whose nature is non-existence, is to be known as dissolving—meaning it melts away completely without leaving any residual impression—by means of the fire called consciousness (*saṃvit*), which has the nature of the supreme subject; the meaning is that only the fire of consciousness remains.
By this, through the dissolution even of non-existence, the extraction of the seed-syllable *agni* (the letter *ra*) is accomplished. Thus...
Although that object of knowledge has "dissolved," having attained the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*),

it nevertheless dissolves into this "triangle of power and fire"— which consists of the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*)— that is, into the power of absolute freedom (*svātantryaśakti*) which embraces all powers, because otherwise its status as consciousness would be untenable.

The meaning is that it flashes forth as having the *tanmātras* (pure potentials) as its essence. Thus, by resting in pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) alone, the extraction of the seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*) has also been accomplished. Indeed, in this context, the very nature of consciousness is nothing other than supreme subjectivity, whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), vibration (*spanda*), and heart (*hṛdaya*) [are one].
There are thousands of such designations, such as *visarga* and so forth. As it has been said:
"The supreme power of that God of gods, whose nature is supreme consciousness, is *vimarśa*; she is omniscient and endowed with knowledge."
Thus [ends the verse]. 77.
And for this reason, one should rest in that very state through the primary mode of operation, so that the direct penetration into the supreme reality may be accomplished; thus he says:
"There, perfectly tranquil in the existence of the noble point (bindu) of consciousness..."
The yogi who rests in the seed-syllable of withdrawal becomes supreme.
This being the case, because it bestows the state of being a knower upon the supreme subject— the self of consciousness—

there exists this "exalted," that is, great, "reality of the bindu," which consists of the supreme stage of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the agency of the act of knowing; by means of that, [it is] perfectly...

Being "satisfied through the absence of further desire," he possesses the excellence of the wonder of his own self; for this very reason, because the point (*bindu*)— which is the seed of withdrawal and whose essence is the supreme subject— arises even within the venerable Lord of the Body (*piṇḍanātha*), he is "rested" therein, having attained identity with it, and thus "he becomes a yogi of the supreme nature."
The meaning is that one becomes a partaker of identity with the supreme reality. || 78 ||

Now, one might ask: "Why has it been stated that, even in relation to consciousness (*saṃvit*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is primarily the locus of repose? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whether internal, external, or both, [reflective awareness] is beautiful in its universality and its particularity."
The vibration of consciousness consists of the three powers and possesses both contraction and expansion.

For that very vibration of consciousness (*saṃvitspanda*) is, within the reality of Śiva—the supreme subject as the "inner"—of a universal nature due to its appropriation of all particularities; for this very reason, it is expansive as the "I.
On the other hand, as the "outer," from Māyā down to Earth, it is of a particular nature due to the manifestation of duality. Therefore...

Thus, through mutual exclusion, it is contracted as "this"; in the state of *vidyā*, which consists of the pair of internal and external forms, by the logic of two scales held in perfect equilibrium, it is the nature of both the universal and the particular as "I am this. For this very reason, it possesses both contraction and expansion, and for this same reason, it brings about the manifestation of the entire universe.
Consisting of the triad of powers beginning with will (icchā)—He alone is the supreme place of rest; this is what should be understood therein. || 79 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then because it possesses contraction and expansion, it would follow that it is insentient (jaḍa);
thus, its status as the locus of rest is undermined. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even though it is devoid of contraction and expansion, it appears as such through its own manifestation."

In reality, because its essential nature is consciousness alone, this vibration of consciousness—even though it lacks actual contraction or expansion—manifests through its own sovereignty in the form of contraction and so forth;
thus it is said to "possess contraction and expansion," but the point is that it does not actually exist in that way in reality. Now, [an objection]: "But..."
If indeed contraction, expansion, and so forth do not exist for it in reality, then what is the cause for their manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, one attains the supreme state. (80)
For here, regarding that which is externally perceived as "this"—such as the body, a jar, and so forth—it is said:
"Cognition shines forth both externally and internally in the form of each respective object;
apart from cognition, there is no existence of objects; therefore, the world is of the nature of cognition."
"For entities have never been made objects by anyone apart from consciousness;
therefore, it is determined that consciousness has attained their very nature.
According to such statements from the *Śrīkālikākrama*, these [entities] have as their essence the expansion of pure awareness (*saṃvit*).

Thus, by means of this view of the Self, the yogi— being attentive precisely within the reality of consciousness whose nature is the internal reflective awareness of "I," and because he is intent on the awareness of his own true nature even while in contact with external objects— enters the Bhairava-mudrā and attains the supreme state.

The meaning is that [the external form] rests upon the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By this, according to the principle that "ignorance itself is the means to knowledge," even the contracted external form may become the instrumental cause for attaining the expanded essential nature—this is what is being stated. And in that case, there must be an appropriate reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Thus, there is also the manifestation of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this" with respect to the specific nature [of the object]; therefore, it is rightly said: "in that manner, by virtue of appearing in that manner. || 80 ||
Therefore, he says:

"Then, within the manifestation of diverse purposeful actions fashioned by absolute freedom, there is a reflective awareness called 'particularization,' which is designated as 'orientation' (unmukhya), a vibration (spanda). (5.81)

"Therefore," from the reason just mentioned, that reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) directed toward the multitude of entities— which arise from one's own sovereignty and perform their respective causal functions— is the vibration (*spanda*) known as "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), because it proceeds according to the degree of desire for those respective causal functions; it is "designated as 'orientation' (*aunmukhya*)."
The meaning is that it would be designated by the term "orientation" (aunmukhya). || 81 ||
And one must not rest right here; thus he says:

"One should attain rest therein [in the maṇḍala], for whatever power exists in the circle of mantras, from that [power] arise the accomplishments such as pacification (śānti) and the rest, through identification with their respective forms. (5.82)
In this regard:

"The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of 'this,' which is [initially] fragmented, is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is 'I am this'. (Aparāpūrvaprakriyā, verse 15).

By such statements as these, one should bring about repose within the "I-reflection" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which is the abode where this reflective awareness finds its rest; for it is not only here, but even within the circle of mantras (*mantramaṇḍala*), that there is vitality (*vīrya*), since it is precisely through the identity with the circle of mantras permeated by the "I-reflection" that the fruit [of mantra] arises.
The meaning is that the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth would possess various ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
The underlying sense is that, without resting in pure consciousness (*saṃvid-viśrānti*), nothing at all could come to be. As he will state:
"Whatever does not rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky" (*Tantrāloka* 8.3).
Thus [ends the verse]. 82.
Not only is this so, but even the sense organs are likewise; thus he says:
"This divine collection of senses, known as the sovereignty of consciousness, remains ever-unblinking and would make this entire world consist of its own self. (5.83)

Indeed, here, although directed toward external objects, this aggregate of senses— which, because it has the internal as its objective focus, is divine, and precisely because it consists solely of pure consciousness, is designated by the terms "consciousness-sovereignty" (*bodhasvātantrya*) and not by the terms "intellectual organs" (*buddhīndriya*) or "organs of action" (*karmendriya*)— is [the subject].

Remaining externally "unblinking," that is, fully active, one should make this world identical with one's own self through the process of entering the Bhairava-mudrā; the meaning is that one should perceive it as having pure consciousness (*saṃvid*) alone as its essence. || 83 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But how could this be so?", he says:
"With all its mental fluctuations dissolved through union with the Great Courage (mahāsāhasa), it remains, having become fully saturated, within the massed stream of its own rays. (5.84)
One who does not think of what is to be done and possesses clear vision attains pure consciousness there, whose sparks are the sole cause for burning away the ashes of saṃsāra. (5.85)

By means of entering the *cakita-mudrā*, which is designated by the term "great courage," he is one whose "all sensory functions (*indriya-vṛtti*) have dissolved"— meaning they have melted away from the external and turned back— and for that very reason,
he is "one who thinks of nothing," being without attention due to the absence of outward orientation. Therefore...
When the flood of the Lord’s rays— that is, the circle of rays of the various sense organs—

becomes a "mass," having merged into its own self through the dissolution of duality, and thus, "having become full," attains plenitude and remains; therein, within the reality of the subject whose nature is the internal reflective awareness of "I."
One with clear vision and manifest awakening attains pure consciousness;
one enters into the interior of the supreme reality, by the mere expansion of which the destruction of saṃsāra is accomplished without effort. || 84-85 ||
And he says that we have not merely stated this based on our own imagination;
rather, it was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the *Triśirobhairavāgama*. He recites that very passage:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the entry into the ground of mantra.
"In the stage of mantra" means up to the ultimate reality (paratattva). || 86 ||
What is that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The upward movement through the central channel is characterized by the attainment of its [supreme] qualities;
it transcends the state at the end of emission and is defined as the ultimate limit. (5.87)
That which is called the "word ending in visarga"— the state of the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) having been intensely attained (*ita*)—

its upward movement from that point via the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*) by means of the process of carrying the *udāna* breath is said to be the entry into the plane of Mantra; this is implied by the sense of the passage, since [it belongs] to that [state].

The "attainment" (*prāpti*) of those "attributes" (*dharma*)— such as being unobstructed and free from conceptual construction— which belong to the level of mantra whose essence is the reality of consciousness, consists in its radiating forth through identity with that [reality]; its nature is such that it is therefore described as the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭi*), the supreme pinnacle everywhere— thus it is proclaimed.
This is the meaning. As it has been said:
"That which is the unobscured reality of consciousness, free from conceptual construction—that, O daughter, is declared to be the Supreme; that is the ultimate limit, that is the highest goal."
Thus [ends the verse]. 87.
And how might that be? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the obstruction of the downward flow and by the abandonment of upward projection, [it becomes] the Great Light, which bestows the manifestation of arising knowledge. (88)
Having experienced [the state] in the supreme abode through the function of the measure (mātrāvṛtti),
one should enter the city by casting aside the downward-flowing apāna and the upward-thrown prāṇa;
through the friction of those two, in the supreme middle abode—
Having drunk the divine nectar of Akula, one should enter Kula once again;
then one should go to Akula once more through the yoga of the measures (mātrā), O Pārvatī.
"And that [mātrā] is known as the carrier of the vital breath (prāṇa) in this Pārameśvara Tantra.
By such statements, the nature of that mātrā has been defined; its "repetition" (āvṛtti) means its recurrence, that is, counting it again and again.
"Rising up in the form of lightning from each successive wheel,
step by step, until reaching three finger-breadths above [the head], there occurs at the end the Great Arising (mahodaya).
According to the reasoning stated in such passages (Viṣṇubhairava-tantra, verse 29), by means of the sequence of transcending those respective wheels, one reaches the ground of the *dvādaśānta*.
According to the maxim, "This Self shines forth once and for all," because there is no interruption in the act of manifestation,
one experiences the Great Light— which is the supreme subject appearing as the manifestation of that self-knowledge which is eternally risen and characterized by its primary emergence.
Having experienced this Great Light, which bestows clarity upon that [knowledge] by appearing as its very essence;
"One should enter the city" means that one should attain the state of one's own self, which is the full manifestation of the ground of mantra. || 88 ||
And of what nature is that?—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That state, which has descended into the waveless [ocean], is one and consists of the nature of Śiva. (5.89)
Blazing with six wheels multiplied by four, six, and two, one situated therein should contemplate the void within the void; abiding in the void, one should enter into that which abides in the void.
Having abandoned the void within the void, having ascended to the void, one should utter the void that abides in the void.
By virtue of presiding over the center of the void, the rays of consciousness are established in their respective positions.
And that mental modification (*vṛtti*), whose nature is one's own Self, is "waveless" because of the complete cessation of the entire universe;
the meaning is that it is of a tranquil form due to resting solely in its own Self. For this very reason, it is said to be "one.
Nor does its form consist only of transcending the universe in this way; rather, even while being such, [it remains immanent].
He says she is "consisting of the universe" (*viśvamayī*) by stating "descended" (*avatīrṇā*), meaning she has manifested externally in various forms.
For this very reason, summarizing the meaning of the many texts therein, he says:
"blazing with the six wheels multiplied fourfold, sixfold, twofold, and twofold. As was stated previously:

"In the *Traiśirasa* doctrine, because of the application of the fourfold, sixfold, twofold, and twofold enumerations, the Lord—who possesses a manifold innate form—is said to possess mastery over the six cakras. (1.114).
Even so, there is no deviation from her own essential nature; thus it is said that she is "of the nature of Śiva."

Thus, even though this [consciousness] manifests as an external form, its repose is found only within its own essential nature, which is the supreme subject— this is what is meant, and it is precisely with this intention that the term *bhairavamudrā* (the Seal of Bhairava) is employed. And because this is an extreme secret, it must be kept concealed.
With this intention, the Blessed One speaks with a hidden meaning through the words beginning with "situated in the void" (*khastham*).

Here, indeed, the yogi, having "ascended the void"— that is, having taken recourse to the sovereignty characterized by the autonomy of the self which is denoted by the word *bhūti*— and having concealed his own true nature from space, time, and so forth...
Having manifested contraction, that which is designated by the word *aṇu* (the minute) abides in the void (*kha*); it vibrates as the nature of contractedness— the "void" (*kham*),
which is the very essence of the Supreme Self, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
By such statements as, "Consciousness is taught in all scriptures to be the nature of the Self" (Netra-tantra 8.28),

one should "investigate" the Self— which consists of full manifestation and must necessarily be known— meaning that one should bring it to the level of reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*) by considering whether its essential nature is merely contracted or not.
The sense is that in this way there would be the attainment of the ultimate form. As it is said in that very same place:
"That which is to be known as the Bhairava-sky is the end of all paths and the inner-most limit."
The wise one, situated within the pervasion of the instruments, should investigate this.
"For one who stands on the plane [of consciousness] and resides in the wheel attains [the goal] from the perspective of ultimate reality.
How is that so? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Abiding in the void, one should utter the void, and the void.
The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. "In the void" means while remaining in, or being attached to, sexual union (*rati*).

With an attentive mind, one should utter the "Kha"— the power in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa)— which resides at the "Khe," the root of the Kula, the foundation of birth that is the essence of the arising of power: "From the root upwards, she who has the luster of rays, who is more subtle than the subtle, and whose nature is the Supreme."
"One should contemplate her as she subsides at the end of the twelve-finger space, the arising of Bhairava.
