According to such statements, one should lead [the consciousness] upward to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the process of entering the central channel (*madhyadhāma*), so that—

Having abandoned the object of perception— which has entered the "ether" (kha) consisting of the power of action (kriyāśakti)— as well as the power of action colored by that [object] which constitutes the plane of the knowable; and likewise having abandoned the perceiver— which resides in the "ether" of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti)—
as well as the power of knowledge colored by that [perceiver] which constitutes the plane of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

The meaning is: even while engaged in the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the self (*ātman*), one should abandon attachment to them.

Although the coloring (*uparāga*) by the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) is possible in both cases here, it is stated thus because of their predominance. Likewise, "the ether" (*kham*) refers to that which is devoid of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the seer, the seen, and so forth.

Having presided over the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which consists solely of one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) by means of authority— that is, having taken possession of it through the strength of one's own support— one [attains] the "ether" (*kha*) denoted by the word *citi*—
"the abode of reflection, the fourth state (*turya*), the pervasive, and that which is both above and in the middle."

In accordance with the principle stated in the *Śrītriśirobhairava*, "The hollow core is the king of principles, proclaimed as the supreme space (*parākāśa*)," one should [realize] the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), which is characterized by the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and whose nature has been defined by that teaching, through the process of correctly entering into Bhairava-mudrā.

The meaning is that one should "enter," which is to say, become possessed by [the state]. And thus, the phrase "rays of consciousness" refers to the functions of the various sense organs because they lack outward orientation; "established in the plane" means they remain resting precisely in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 91 ||
Thus, one must remain vigilant in this regard—as he says:
"One should contemplate the internal state of being, remaining established in being and free from longing for objects of thought;
having blocked the movements toward existence and non-existence, one possesses the vision that obstructs both existence and non-existence. (5.92)

Even so, having blocked the movements of existence and non-existence and abandoned the agitation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the yogin should "cultivate" (*bhāvayet*) the "internal state"— that is, internal being— by repeatedly creating attachment to that very place through the process of entering the central channel (*madhyadhāman*), so that there is no falling away from it even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).

Therefore, he is "established in being" (*bhāvastha*); the meaning is that even amidst the agitation of the grasped and the grasper, his consciousness remains unimpaired by the entire range of external and internal organs, and he is firmly established in his own self alone. As it has been said in that very same work:
Free from upward, downward, or lateral movement, and devoid of the desire for sensory instruments, his form does not diminish; established in being, he is the illuminator of all states of being.
"Having realized its own nature, this [Self], devoid of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
should be known as abiding in Being when the confusion of the grasped and the grasper has collapsed.
For this very reason, by entering the central channel (*madhyadhāmā*) between the two states of existence and non-existence— that is, between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*— ...
The meaning is that he sees—that is, directly realizes—that "enclosure" (*avarodha*) which is the self of equanimity by virtue of being waveless. As it is said in that very same work:
"He for whom the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths have become equal, having reached the state of equilibrium..."
"...the vision that excludes both existence and non-existence by way of being waveless.
For this very reason, due to the absence of outward orientation, he is "indifferent to existence," meaning he is established solely in his own essential nature. As it is said in that same work:
"And for one who has abandoned that state, whose conduct consists of millions of conjunctions with the stability of his own true nature,
this [state] is indeed free from longing for worldly existence.
Now, one might ask: "Even though there is no difference in the essential nature of the word *kha*, from where does this tenfold divided meaning arise?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Self, the vital breath, the lineage, the root, power, manifestation, consciousness, and delight."
The triad of powers, colored by the seer and the seen, as well as that which is devoid of them. || 5.93 ||
This void (kha) is said to be tenfold, characterized by successive utterances (uccāra).

Ātman is the supreme self (paramātman); aṇu is the contracted self; kulamūla is the source of the vital energy (prāṇaśakti), the locus of birth; śakti is that which flows through the central breath; and bhūti is—

Sovereignty is characterized by autonomy; supreme consciousness is the nature of the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); passion is attachment; the triad of powers consists of the power of knowledge colored by the subject, the power of action colored by the object, and the power of will which is devoid of both—thus it is stated in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*.
As it has been said:
"One should know the void to be the self alone; the atom is the void, extending in all directions. The void should be known as the root of the Kula, and the void is proclaimed to be power (śakti)."
"One void (kha) is manifested here, and two voids are the delight in the consciousness of the elements;
they know the three powers, colored by the seer and the seen, as the void.
Through the completed transformation, the void became the defining characteristic of the principles (tattva)."

Thus, the meaning is that this characteristic of the successive utterances (uccāra), according to their respective [correspondences], brings about the attainment of supreme consciousness through the intensification of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). || 93-94 ||
Not only is this tenfold meaning expressed here by the word *kha* alone, but also by other words— as he says:
"Abiding in the abode, situated in the middle of the abode, enclosed within the belly of the abode" (5.94).
Awaken the abode by means of the abode; make the abode reach the end of all abodes.
By means of the movement through that abode, one must pierce the internal end of the abode.

In this context, the yogi should awaken the "abode"—the Self—which, though situated within the "abode" (the individual soul) as the limited self, flashes forth by means of that which is its true essence: the "womb" of the manifestation of sovereignty. This [Self] is "encased" on all sides, meaning it is completely enveloped and eternally inseparable from that essence; therefore, through the awakening of that [essence], one awakens the abode.

The meaning is that one should practice what is effective. He explains that very practice of effectiveness: "Make the abode situated in the middle of the abode reach the end of the abode by means of the abode. "Of the abode" (dhāmnaḥ) means of the root of Kula, the support of birth;
"situated in the middle" (madhyasthaṃ) of that "abode" (dhāma), which is the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti); [make it so] "by means of the abode" (dhāmnā), that is, by means of passion (rati).
Through attachment to that, make it reach the "end"—the supreme limit—of the "abode," which is consciousness in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta);

the meaning is that one should realize it through its identity with that alone. "Therefore" (tat), for that reason, from the direct realization of the supreme reality, [one realizes] the "abode" of the power of action colored by the visible world.

By proceeding to the ground of the object of knowledge (*prameyabhū*), the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*)—colored by the perceived object—is the "to-be-pierced" (*bhedya*), meaning it is to be differentiated or abandoned. For just as the ground of the object of knowledge is established as something to be abandoned by all disputants, so too is even cognition, which constitutes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), necessarily to be abandoned; this is the intended sense.

The word *tu* (but) is displaced [in the sentence] and functions as a reason; and thus, one should— by implication— resort to the "inner" (*āntaram*) final abode (*dhāmāntam*), which has attained identity with the subject (*pramātraikātmyam*), namely the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) whose nature is pure self-reflection (*svavimarśa-mātra*) and which is devoid of adjuncts such as the seer and the seen, so that in that very [state],...
"I shall sprout"—this is the connection between the word and its meaning. As for the meaning of the sentence, it should be inferred by oneself as before. || 95 ||

Now, one might object: "Since many other means for entering into the supreme reality are possible, why is this alone considered a secret, such that it is taught in this way as something to be concealed and its meaning kept hidden? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The division should indeed be made from the middle by means of further subdivisions.
Furthermore, whatever other distinction consisting of subdivisions of the means may exist, that should be made from the middle;
the meaning is that a middling [means] is of this nature, whereas the superior is not.
He summarizes this very point:
"Thus, this means of entry known as the individual (āṇava) has been fully described. (5.96)
"That which was declared to me by the venerable Maheśvaranātha residing within my heart—this has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well," he says:
"And it is stated in the Śrī Brahmayāmala that the venerable Rāva is tenfold. (5.97)
It is gross, subtle, supreme, heart-born, produced in the throat, and produced in the palate;
it is all-pervading and bestows the state of omnipresence. (5.98)

The term "glorious" (*śrīmān*) is used because, in its nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it constitutes even the very life-force of manifestation (*prakāśa*). Here, this resonance (*rāva*), which is of the nature of supreme speech (*parāvāk*) and consists of the reflective awareness of "I," first possesses a threefold form— namely, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*— due to its arising from the heart and other centers.
Each of these is threefold by way of being gross, subtle, and supreme; thus, there are nine states.
Underlying all nine of these is the tenth, which is the nature of supreme speech (*paravāgātmā*).
For it is that very [tenth] which, through its own sovereignty, manifests in this manner. Therefore it is said: "And he is all-pervasive. That indeed is [the Supreme].

And it is the place of rest—thus it has been said that [the Lord] "bestows the state of omnipotence. And this was stated previously: "That reflective awareness of His, which consists of the perfect 'I', may, by virtue of its sovereignty within itself, manifest differentiation."
And when this [power] manifests as differentiation, its form is declared to be threefold,
designated as Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and the gross Vaikharī.
"Even for these, there are three forms according to their gross, subtle, and supreme states," and so forth, up to:
"Therein, that supreme triad is Śiva, whose nature is supreme consciousness. (3.237–248)
This has been almost fully determined by the preceding [text]; therefore, its true nature should be ascertained from that very source. || 98 ||
Therefore, one must focus intensely on this very point so that the attainment of the ultimate essential nature may occur;
thus he says:
"The great yogi who has conquered sound shall transfer [his consciousness] while residing within another's body."
And one attains supreme pervasion; therefore, one should practice that every day.
This continues until that sounding one (rāvinī) merges into the soundless (arāva).

One who has "conquered"—meaning one who has overcome and brought under control each successive sound—is such a great yogi; by means of this, through the abandonment of each successive [level], he should transfer the sound upward, higher and higher, whereby he becomes "one who goes into another's body."

Established in the nature of increasingly superior sounds according to their respective levels, he "attains supreme pervasion," which means he obtains his ultimate, absolute nature. As it has been said:
"That [power] indeed resounds tenfold, bestowing divine bliss."
"Cinī" is the first word; "ciñcinī" is the second.
The third is the sound of bark, the fourth is the sound of a conch shell,
the fifth is the resonance of a lute string, and the sixth is likewise the sound of a flute.
The seventh was like the sound of a brass cymbal, and likewise the eighth was like the roar of clouds; the ninth was the crash of a forest fire, and the tenth was the resonance of a kettledrum.
"Having abandoned the nine sounds, the tenth bestows liberation;
by this method, one should utter the sound tenfold.
Therefore, in this context, practice must be performed every day until that [state] which is the nature of supreme speech is attained.

Because the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) manifests as the nature of each respective resonance (*rāva*), it is called *Rāviṇī*. By dissolving one resonance after another through the melting away of all divisions, it "dissolves"—meaning it comes to rest—within its own self, which is the state of non-resonance (*arāva*) consisting of the supreme reflective awareness of "I. || 99 ||
Having thus determined the entry into the supreme reality (paratattva), he speaks in order to characterize the signs of its path, which were indicated immediately following that:
"In this regard, by means of contemplation (bhāvanā) and the methods residing within the body, [one proceeds] upon the supreme path. (5.100)
For one desiring to enter [the state of fullness], bliss arises prior to the touch of that fullness;
even beyond that, in that which is devoid of the body and resembles a flash of lightning.
Through momentary immersion in the [divine] abode, emergence becomes clearly manifest as a leaping upward;
this occurs through the abandonment of the habitual identification of consciousness with the body, which is like the separation of water from dust. || 5-102 ||
From the onset of one's own power and the resulting loosening of the body, one experiences trembling;
this occurs when the certainty of identification with the body has dissolved due to inward-turned consciousness. (5.103)
Before one falls asleep while still unestablished in the Self of consciousness,
by means of that "cultivation" (bhāvanā)— which is repeated practice— of this very specific method just described,
and by means of the bodily methods such as the aforementioned and yet-to-be-described utterances (uccāra) and gestures (karaṇa), [one proceeds] on the supreme path.

This refers to one who desires to enter within the supreme reality, but not to one who has already entered it; for the latter, there would be only fullness—this is the intended meaning. From the "touch" of fullness, that is, from its mere orientation toward it, but not yet from its actual immersion, there first arises "bliss," a particular kind of aesthetic wonder (camatkāra), in its highest degree.

The meaning is that by making one's own self the object [of consciousness], one is "born," that is, one attains the path of direct experience. Then, immediately after that bliss, in the "abode" which is like the flash of lightning— just as when lightning strikes,
everything loses its own nature and becomes identical with it— so too in the supreme reality (para-tattva).
Through immersion (*samāveśa*), having made [the reality] manifest by dissolving the grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*) within the body and so forth, and thereby detaching from the lower state,
there occurs "emergence" (*udbhava*), which is a leaping upward— namely, the ascent to the supreme abode (*paradhāma*).
The meaning is "it should be. For this very reason, it is said, "in that which is devoid of the body. Regarding the word "for a moment":
the intention is that if the immersion (*samāveśa*) were to last for a long time, there would indeed be absolute fullness (*pāripūrṇya*).

Thus, the "loss" (*hāni*) refers to the separation, by means of differentiation, from that identity of consciousness and the body which has been practiced through many lifetimes like [the mixing of] dust and water.

The formal motion (*jñapti*): Then, by the "assault" upon that "power"—the vigor characterized by the ego-sense (*ahantā*)—which belongs to one's own consciousness-nature for a moment, the identification with the self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding what is not-self becomes loosened within the self alone; thus [it concerns] the body and so forth.
Because it is subject to decay, one "should experience trembling"; the meaning is that one should abandon firmness therein.

Thus, "previously"—that is, first—when attachment to the identity of the body and consciousness has ceased, one "sleeps," due to the mere orientation toward consciousness and the cessation of external mental activity, as well as [the cessation] of the internal [activity].
The meaning is that he remains as if asleep because no experience arises clearly for him.
To the question of how long he remains thus, he says: "as long as [the seed] has not taken root in the self of consciousness.
The intention is that once it has sprouted therein, another characteristic would arise. || 103 ||
Thus it is said:
"Then, established in the state of reality, [one perceives] consciousness as the self-nature of the universe. (5.104)
Because it is taught that "whirling" (*ghūrṇi*) is a great pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*),

one who has attained growth in the state of power within the Self of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvidātmani śaktyapade*) realizes that the true essence of this entire world— consisting of the body, pots, and so forth— is consciousness alone, and not [materiality]. Following that, [he realizes]...
Realizing that this is nothing other than that very [reality] itself,

he "whirls," meaning he revolves or moves, becoming one who dwells in the state of vibration (*spanda*). For the yogi who dwells in this state, the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord arises at all times through his capacity to effect both emanation and withdrawal.
Thus it has been said: "For whirling is known as the Great Pervasion. || 104 ||
Now, [it may be objected]:
"Strengthened by the splendor of his power, he gathers within himself ten states:
trembling, dizziness, as well as whirling, leaping, and even steadiness."
The manifestation of consciousness, bliss, divine vision, and wonder—
the tenth state is inexpressible, resulting from entry into the principle of Śiva.

By such statements as, "As soon as contact [with the Guru] is attained, one becomes liberated from the ocean of existence," other characteristics for one desiring to enter into the supreme reality (*paratattva*) are also possible;
that is to say, until those [other characteristics] have been indicated, how could there be entry into that [reality] by this much alone?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "For it is only when there is the conceit of the non-self in the Self that [the conceit of the Self arises] in the non-self. (5.105)
The conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth is bondage, while its dissolution is liberation.
Indeed, in this world, bondage is twofold: the conceit of non-self in the self, and the conceit of self in the non-self;
this very thing is called the atomic impurity (*āṇava-mala*). As they say:

"The loss of freedom for consciousness and the lack of consciousness within freedom—this is the twofold *āṇavamala* (the impurity of the individual soul), due to the forfeiture of one's own true nature. (Rijuvimarsinī-prakaraṇa 3.2.4). And that very [impurity], because it is the cause of both the *kārmamala* and the *māyīyamala*, is the root of this entire cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
As it has been said:
"Impurity is the cause, while action is the effect; beyond that [is the goal]" (Svacchandatantra 3.176).
Therefore, as in the saying, "This is an axe placed at the very root," one must strive for that [goal] alone.
The sense is that by this, there shall be the cessation of all bondage. That alone is stated here as the primary subject;
therefore, in its primary sense, that itself is bondage and its dissolution alone is liberation—this is the summary of the meaning. || 105 ||
And as for that [state of] "tallness," would it arise only through a sequence, or otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"First, when the sense of self in what is not the Self has dissolved and one's own true Self has been attained... (5.106).

When the notion of non-selfhood regarding the self is destroyed, the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti) proceeds. For first, when the conceit of selfhood (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth— which are not the self— is dissolved,
the destruction of the conceit of non-selfhood regarding the self occurs, whereby [the state] characterized by pure consciousness [arises].

When the arising of ego-sense (abhimāna) occurs within one's very own self, the "Great Pervasion" (mahāvyāpti) proceeds; the meaning is that the supreme state of the Lord (pārameśvarya) shall arise. || 106 ||

Thus, first, due to the arising of a distinguished and unprecedented contact, there is the experience of mere bliss, but there is no cessation of either of the two types of bondage. Following that, through the dissolving away of the identification with the self in the body and so forth, the identification with the self arises in the Self alone; however, this lasts for only a moment, as it occurs again during emergence from samādhi and other such states.

Immediately following that state, there is the direct dissolution of the identification with the body and so forth; thereafter, even the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [identification] dissolves, until finally, through the sprouting of the identification with the Self alone within the Self as appropriate, the Great Pervasion (*mahatī vyāptiḥ*) proceeds— thus, by means of these five characteristics alone.
"Sufficient"—thus, only those [five] are taken up and no others, because all others are included within these very ones; with this very intention, the scripture also says:
"Bliss, rising, trembling, sleep, and whirling—this is the pentad" (5.107).
For this very reason, it has been stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*.
As it is said therein:
"The one of great intelligence [should act] toward this disciple who is being purified by this [initiation]..."
One should attentively observe the collection of signs, beginning with bliss.
Bliss, arising, trembling, sleep, and whirling—this is the pentad. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 11.35). || 107 ||
Now, it was stated that when all the characteristics arise together for the yogin, there occurs the "great pervasion" (mahāvyāpti).
But what happens when only a single characteristic arises? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When this pentad, beginning with bliss, has been demonstrated... (5.108).
Then the yogi would forcibly attain the state of being the lord of each respective *cakra*.

However, when the yogi "enters" (*viśet*)— meaning he experiences each individual characteristic one by one, because simultaneous entry into those five [states] beginning with bliss (*ānanda*) mentioned immediately above is impossible— then, by force (*haṭhāt*), for him...
By its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*), mastery over each respective wheel—such as the triangle and so forth—is attained;
the meaning is that victory over those various wheels arises. || 108 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely such an experience arises precisely from the touch of fullness; since everything exists within the Full, how could it occur with such necessity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as the body, though pervaded everywhere by the consciousness of the Lord of All, [is perceived] in some specific place... (5.109).
Just as the eye has the power to produce the perception of form through some slight action, so too, by entering into something anywhere, someone may come into being. (5.110)

Just as the body, although pervaded by all-pervasive consciousness and having attained non-difference from it, is capable of performing only certain actions in only certain places— such as perceiving form with the eye, but not smell and so forth—
and that too only in a proximate location and not in a remote one, even though consciousness is present there; so it is in every case.

Because one enters into specific wheels such as the triangle and so forth, only a particular, singular experience—such as bliss and the like—can arise, and not every [experience]; thus it is rightly said: "One should forcibly ascend to the lordship of each respective wheel. || 110 ||
Now, raising the doubt, "What is whose wheel?", he says: "The wheel of bliss has seven spokes; the bulb (kanda) is called the source (udbhava).
Trembling occurs at the heart, sleep at the palate, and whirling is the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī. (5.111)

"Vahnyaśri" means the triangle, which is the mouth of the Yoginī. "Ūrdhva-kuṇḍalī" refers to the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths). These are designated in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of being metaphorically identified as non-different.
One might ask: "What is the proof for such a specific restriction regarding these? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this has been stated quite clearly in the venerable *Mantraiśirasa* system;
therein, in the sixth and seventh [chapters] alone, by means of many [arguments] preceded by infinite objects of knowledge..."
This has been indicated by a mere glance in the text; thus, for fear of excessive prolixity, it has not been corroborated here—it should be understood from that very source.
Thus, regarding that supreme reality which is to be attained through this manyfold collection of means, there is also another occasional designation; so he says:
"In this way, the supreme [reality] has as its heart the repose of the upward movement (uccāra) thus demonstrated. (5.112)
"That which has an unmanifest sign (avyaktaliṅga), characterized by the non-differentiation of man, Śiva, and Śakti.
Thus, in the manner described, there is this repose of the utterances (uccāra) and so forth;
of that, there is the "supreme heart."

The meaning is as follows: that supreme reality, which consists of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa), is designated by terms such as *Yoginīhṛdaya*, is of the nature of the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvitspanda*), and is the essential truth; because it possesses the non-differentiation of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, it is called the "unmanifest emblem" (*avyaktaliṅga*). || 112 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for such a designation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this [state], this entire universe is dissolved, and it is understood to be situated within. (5.113)

This is the characteristic of the consciousness of Pūrṇaśaktibhairava; the word *ca* (and) is displaced [in the verse] and functions as a causal particle (*hetau*). For, in this supreme Heart, which consists of the reflective awareness of "I," "this universe"—composed of the principles of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva—is "merged," meaning it exists in a state of non-differentiation.

Up to this point, it has been stated that this is not like lac and wood, but rather like milk and water—as expressed in the words, "And here, that which is situated within is perceived," meaning that it is cognized as having attained a state of identity.
For this indeed is the defining characteristic of the supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*) whose nature has been described: that from it...
Thus the universe arises therein and dissolves therein as well. As it has been said:
"The wise call the cause of creation and dissolution 'liṅga';
because of [the world's] dissolution (*laya*) and coming forth (*āgamana*), they call that imperishable state of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) the *liṅga*."
Thus [ends the verse]. 113.
Now, it has been stated here that there are three kinds of signs (*liṅga*): the manifest (*vyakta*), the manifest-unmanifest (*vyaktāvyakta*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Among these, it was said that the unmanifest is supreme consciousness itself. But as for the other two, are they not the expansion of that very [consciousness]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But that immersion which is manifest upon the unfolding of the paths within the body— || 5.114 ||
And that [Self], conjoined with the state of "this-ness" (idambhāva) through the emerging phenomena concealed by the sense of "I" (ahantā),
is this manifest-and-unmanifest *liṅga*, the power of the mantra, which is both supreme and non-supreme.

"Arisen from human power and differentiated from the form of Śiva. Regarding the phrase "in the emergence of the paths within the body": even while there is the conceit of self-identity with the body and so forth, that which remains unfading—the internal immersion into the supreme reality—is this very *liṅga*, both manifest and unmanifest.

The Connection. Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the distinction between this [state] and the unmanifest (avyakta)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "ahantā... and so forth. When objects "unfurl" (*unmeṣiṣu*), that is, when they manifest externally, that which is "this-nature" (*idantā*)—the state of being "this"—is joined with it; the meaning is that it takes the form of the cognition "this am I. Therefore...

Thus, one should know that through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), there exists the state of being both manifest and unmanifest;

for this very reason, because it lacks the nature of the pure self-referential awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), it is differentiated from the nature of Śiva and is characterized by the manifestation of *nara* (the individual) and *śakti* (power)—that is to say, it has the form of *nara* and *śakti*. Even so...

The meaning is that the "higher and lower" is characterized primarily by *śakti*. The intention is that the manifest *liṅga* will indeed be characterized primarily by *nara*. For this very reason, it possesses the potency (*vīrya*) of mantra;
the sense is that a mantra, when resting upon this state, becomes capable of bestowing its appropriate fruit. As it has been said:

One should not employ a mantra upon the individual soul (puṃs), nor upon the supreme reality (para-tattva), nor upon power (śakti). [If employed] upon the individual soul, it becomes inert; but upon the supreme reality, it is fruitless.
"But a mantra applied when one has the capacity bestows the fruit of all rites.
Thus [it is said]. || 115 ||
Not only is her *liṅga* (sign) manifest and unmanifest, but its expansion extends even to the manifest as well—thus he says:
"That which suppresses the immersion into the 'I'-ness of Śiva and possesses differentiation. (5.116)
That manifest sign (*liṅga*), which consists of consciousness, has the nature of a particular vibration; it is that very thing which,
having subordinated the reflective awareness of the supreme non-dual "I-ness," vibrates as a particular vibration in the form of an externalized state— thus, such a contemplation is the manifest.
The meaning is that it is called the *liṅga*. Even so, it is of the nature of consciousness; for otherwise, this would not exist at all—this is the intended sense. || 116 ||
Not only is there a distinction among these in terms of their essential nature, but even in terms of their results—as he says:

"From the manifest arises the birth of supernatural powers (*siddhi*); from the manifest-unmanifest arise both [powers and liberation]; and from the unmanifest arises the primordial power (*bala*) of the Supreme. However, this discussion does not apply to the Absolute (*anuttara*). (5.117)
As it has been said:
"From the worship of an image comes worldly enjoyment, and from the constant worship of a *liṅga* comes liberation;
through the worship of the *mukhaliṅga*, both enjoyment and liberation are attained by men."
Thus: "The power of the supreme is primary. This [power] belongs to the unmanifest, that to the manifest-unmanifest, and that to the manifest.

Now, if this is so, what is the status of this [power] again in the unsurpassed abode (*anuttara-dhāman*), which is the essence of all and the ground of all? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But this discussion does not apply to the unsurpassed. For in that [state],...
The sense is: since the state of being free from further desire arises through complete fulfillment, what indeed could be the distinction between "accomplishment" (siddhi) and the rest? || 117 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the basis for the claim that the first [state] alone is the place of rest for the Supreme, and not the reverse? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one who offers the entire universe into that manifest human *liṅga* known as the Self..."
Therefore, when that [consciousness] has dissolved, the manifest becomes unmanifest. (5.118)

Regarding that manifest sign (liṅga) called the Self— which, because it is the foremost among men, has the nature just described, and is the locus of this self-reflection— it is for one who dissolves the universe into that sign called the Self by means of the realization, "That which is this, I am indeed that."

Because for the yogin there is a manifestation through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), there is the "manifest-unmanifest" (*vyaktāvyakta*) subtle body (*liṅga*). The meaning is that when even from that manifest-unmanifest subtle body this entire universe has "dissolved"—having reached a state where only the reflective awareness of "I" remains—that unmanifest subtle body itself ceases to exist. || 118 ||
Anticipating the question, "What, then, has been stated by this? he says:

"Therefore, this sign of the Self (ātman) rests in the unmanifest (avyakta), which consists of the supreme nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu); however, this discussion does not pertain to that which goes to the abode of the Absolute (anuttara). (5.119)

Thus, this manifest "this" (etat), which is primarily characterized by the Person (nara) and serves as a sign of the Self (ātma-liṅga), by implication comes to rest within the manifest and unmanifest signs (liṅga) where Power (śakti) and the Person are predominant; and even when Śiva is predominant, because its intermediate forms are internalized within that which consists of the Person, Power, and Śiva, it is therefore "supreme" (parama).

The meaning is that [the power] "rests" in the unmanifest *liṅga*, which possesses excellence due to its distinction from other *liṅgas*, and flashes forth through identification with that. Now, one might ask: why is it not said that just as the two *liṅgas* beginning with the manifest rest in the unmanifest, so too does that [unmanifest] rest in the abode of the Absolute (*anuttara*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But this discourse does not reach the state of the Absolute (anuttara-dhāma).

For that Absolute itself manifests as the three signs beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta); thus, it is always resting within that [Absolute]. Otherwise, its very existence would not be possible. || 119 ||
For this very reason, he says:
"This threefold establishment of differentiation belongs to a single vibration.
Here, indeed, "of the one" refers to the primary [reality] whose nature is the Absolute (anuttara).

This is the "establishment"— that is, the manifestation— of this *spandana* (vibration), which is designated by terms such as *Yoginīhṛdaya*, in the form of the marks (*liṅga*) beginning with the manifest (*vyakta*),
through a threefold division; the meaning is that this is not something distinct from that [vibration].
And for this reason, one should come to rest right here, setting aside the signs such as the manifest (vyakta) and so forth; thus he says:
"One should always abide in this sign, intent upon worship and finding rest therein" (5.120).
As it has been said:
"One should not worship a *liṅga* made of clay, stone, minerals, gems, and the like;
one should worship the spiritual (*ādhyātmika*) *liṅga*, wherein the moving and the unmoving are dissolved."
"Since the state of being a sign (liṅgatva) of the *barhis*-sign has been presided over by this [deity]," (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.42). || 120 ||
One might ask: "What would arise from resting here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This Liṅga, the Heart of the Yoginī, beautiful with bliss, gives birth to an indescribable consciousness through the union of the Seed and the Womb. (5.121)

This Liṅga, consisting of bliss and denoted as the Heart of the Yoginīs (Yoginīhṛdaya), whose nature is vibration, "gives birth to an ineffable consciousness" through the identity of Śiva and Śakti—whose essences are the seed (bīja) and the womb (yoni); the meaning is that it should manifest immersion into supreme consciousness. Furthermore, this is also so according to the sequence of ritual practice (caryākrama).
It has also been hinted at that there should be an entry into the consciousness of another, as it is said:
"The triangular maṇḍala, which is the abode of the three powers, should be worshipped;
in its center, one should contemplate the conscious Liṅga facing westward."
Thus, as it is said:
"That song which flows with bliss and is the cause of all production— this is called the organ of generation (upastha), and it is described as the form of the Suṣumnā."
Thus [ends the verse]. ||121||
One might ask: "How can this be so simply by resting right here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this state, because it is free from effort, this entire host of deities abides in the abode filled with bliss, consisting of eternally emergent consciousness. (5.122)
As it has been said:
"In the triangle reside all the deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (122)
Not only does the entire host of deities reside here, but even the power of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī Śakti) is present—
thus he says:
"Here resides the [power] of Lord Bhairava, which possesses both contraction and expansion."
The power of that which neither contracts nor expands shines forth as difficult to accomplish.

In this abode filled with bliss, there shines the power called sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which performs the impossible; it consists eternally of emanation and withdrawal, and thus possesses neither contraction nor expansion, belonging to that full Light which is like a waveless ocean and is itself free from contraction and expansion.

The meaning is that by virtue of its own essential identity, it manifests as such a vast expansion of the universe through its majesty, and thus it always maintains its presiding state over the phases of both creation and dissolution. || 123 ||
Thus it is said:
"Sprinkled by the stream of the bliss of emission resulting from the absorption into this Linga, that very same real universe becomes eternally ever-new. (5.124)

In this very "sign" (*liṅga*) just described, which is the nature of the unsurpassed abode, there is "absorption" (*samāpatti*), meaning oneness; and of that "emission" (*visarga*)— which is the Kaulika power called sovereignty— there is the "stream of bliss."

"And that very [power], having reached the visarga, when its state is surging forth— extending as far as the clearly manifested power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— through the sequence of the arising of bliss (*ānandodaya*).
By such statements, [the reality] is sprinkled by that surging state through the sequence of the arising of bliss.
Having been brought to a state of external expansion, the entire universe at that very moment becomes "ever-new";
the meaning is that it perpetually attains the status of being the vessel for both creation and dissolution.
Furthermore, according to the sequence of practice (*caryākrama*), there is the designation of these two signs (*liṅga*) by such terms as *vajra* and *padma*.

The meaning is that the entire universe, consisting of women, men, and so forth, is produced incessantly when the seed is sown—that is, when it is moistened—by this stream of bliss (*ānandadhārā*) which takes the form of emission (*visarga*) through the attainment of tranquility (*śamāpatti*) and enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).

[Objection: But surely, since mental reflection (*buddhi*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the like, instill the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) whose life-force is duality (*bheda*), [how can they lead to non-dual realization]?

It is clearly the means of the individual (āṇavopāya); thus, its mention here is appropriate. But since this [other] means, characterized by entry into the supreme reality, is of a non-conceptual nature, it is not so;
how then can it be mentioned here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The supreme means is described here precisely because of its identity with that [ultimate reality];
for does not the sun shine even when lamps are ablaze? (5.125)

In this chapter (*āhnika*), although it is primarily concerned with illuminating the *āṇavopāya*, this "supreme means" (*abhyupāya*)—which consists of entering into the inner essence of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and is directly caused by the Absolute (*anuttara*)—is taught precisely because it possesses the nature of the means to the Absolute (*anuttarābhyupāyarūpatva*). Here is an illustration: just as...

The intended meaning is this: even when there exist lamps and other sources of limited light for the purpose of illuminating various objects, there is no fault whatsoever in the presence of the great light of the sun; so it is here as well. || 125 ||
Now, one might object: "In that case, the instruction on all three means, beginning with the individual (āṇava), should be given in a mixed manner;

so what is the point of devising separate chapters for each? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In objects, in the process of their enjoyment, and in the pleasure or pain arising from them, [the yogi remains] free from all apprehension."
Even without entering [the state], those whose minds are immersed [in it] know within themselves the bliss of the cessation of mental fluctuations.

Regarding "objects," such as blue and so forth; regarding "the process of their enjoyment," which is the cognition of blue and so forth; and regarding "that which arises from them," namely pleasure or pain produced by blue and so forth—in this way, with respect to the external collection of objects that have attained established status up to the point of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), those whose minds are submerged therein—even while performing the respective acts of abandoning or acquiring [them]—remain [attached] to that.

Entering with minds free from doubt, and thus experiencing that state of mastery without uncertainty— realizing, as in the case of dream-objects, that "this [world] is indeed unreal"— the yogis know within themselves the bliss of the cessation of mental fluctuations:
"With the internal object of focus and the gaze directed outward, one attains the supreme state."

The meaning is that, by the reasoning stated in such passages, even while being intent upon various external worldly transactions, one experiences a supreme excellence of wonder through resting solely within one's own Self. And for this reason, although it consists of duality, its nature is non-dual; thus it is at the outset.

This designation [of "difference"] is made because difference persists; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. For this indeed is the supreme manifestation of the yogi: that even while consisting of difference, he abides in the form of non-difference.
Thus he says:
While the self exists as the splendor of the nature of consciousness, while the internal organ likewise provides assistance to it,
and while the group of sense organs is rendered helpless by its activity,
and while objects such as pleasure and the like exist— there arises that which is most clearly devoid of differentiation.
The yogi remains possessed of the splendor of full rays; let that very reality be accumulated.

Indeed, here, while the Self alone exists— full, consisting of the supreme subject, and distinct from the light of the sun and other sources due to its nature as consciousness— at the moment of the direct realization of one's own self,
because it is of the singular form of consciousness, it is undivided; thus, "to him," that is, to the Self whose essential nature has been described.

When the internal organ (*svānta*)— that is, the group of internal instruments (*antaḥkaraṇavarga*)— is present and performs the "service" characterized by limited knowledge and agency through the manifestation of contraction, then,
in the state of the cognizing subject consisting of the intellect (*buddhipramātṛdaśā*), because division has been projected therein, [it acts] in that manner for that very *svānta*.

That which is called "activity" (*pracāra*)—the eminent movement consisting of such thoughts as "I know this"—is "dependent on that," meaning it is under its control. The intention is that if something has not indeed ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, what could the external senses do with respect to it? In such a form...

When the aggregate of the senses, such as sight and the rest, exists in the state of the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the body and so forth, and when objects in the form of the desirable and undesirable— namely pleasure and the like— are present as distinct entities; thus,
having made this clearly manifest even within the three stages whose nature consists of non-difference, difference, and both difference and non-difference.
If the yogi remains in that which is without distinction, arising free from duality— that very thing,

whose essence is the entry into the Bhairava-mudrā, should be gathered as the "Reality," the ultimate form; even while consisting of external agitation in the form of subject and object, one should abandon attachment to it.

The meaning is that one should remain established solely in one's own self. Precisely for this reason, because all longing for the external has been extinguished, and because all functions of the senses have forever perished, he is described as "the one whose full splendor of rays [of consciousness] has manifested. As it is sung:

"One whose self is unattached to external objects of touch finds that happiness which is within the self; he, whose self is united with the yoga of Brahman, enjoys imperishable happiness. (Bhagavad Gītā 5.21). || 127 ||
Having thus concluded this [section], he promises an analytical exposition of the *karaṇa* (instrumental means) which was indicated immediately following it:
"Thus the rule for the utterance has been declared; the *karaṇa* is now being analyzed."

For exhalation (*uccāra*) itself is first of two kinds by virtue of being the conscious self of the vital breath (*prāṇacidātman*). Therein, the conscious self also becomes twofold—existing as either the predominance of consciousness (*cit*) or the predominance of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—and thus it is threefold. This is because [exhalation] is also the means (*upāya*) consisting of entry into the supreme reality (*paratattva*).
Because it is a differentiation of that [consciousness], its nature consists precisely in utterance; thus it is rightly concluded: "The procedure for utterance has been declared."
And this method of exposition is not being composed by us as our own invention; thus he says:
"And this has been declared in this manner by the Supreme Lord in the Triśiraḥśāstra. (5.128)

They say that practice preceded by awakening is sevenfold, consisting of: [the contemplations on] the grasped, the grasper, consciousness, pervasion, relinquishment, projection, and immersion. (5.129)
In the context of the objection preceded by its pervasion, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is self-established.

"Consciousness" (*cit*) is awareness; "entering" (*niveśana*) is the act of settling. Here, they say that what is called the "instrument" is practice preceded by awakening, which is divided into seven modes beginning with the "object of apprehension" (*grāhya*).

The meaning is that they have described consciousness itself as having attained a state of exclusive focus on its own self through the subordination of everything else to awakening. For that is the instrument for one who fully realizes: "I am all this; this is my manifestation."
"Even in the proliferation of the conceptual constructions of the universal Self, there is the state of the Great Lord. (Ri.Pra. 4.3.12).

According to the principle stated in such passages, when the universe is subsumed through pervasion, "establishment in oneself" (*svapratiṣṭhatā*) means resting within one's own self alone. As it is said therein:
"The object of apprehension, the subject of apprehension, and consciousness as the third;
likewise, the configuration, pervasion, implication, and even abandonment."

"The instrument (karaṇa) is said to be sevenfold: practice preceded by awakening, its pervasion, and in the case of projection, the instrument is self-establishment. And regarding the objects of perception and so forth, it is stated in that very same [text]:

The cognition whose nature is that of the apprehended object, which is established as a substantial entity, should be understood as residing in the individual instance; however, the apprehending subject is that which has a clear object.
One should cause [the disciple] to grasp the nature of consciousness, which investigates the manifest and the unmanifest;
the perceiver is established within the sense-organ by means of direct perception and other valid cognitions.
The sphere (golaka) is said to be the door; from that point on, the mind does not abandon nor grasp external objects. That which neither grasps nor is grasped is known as the grasper (grāhaka).
This arises from the conjunction of the object of perception and the perceiver, and from the application of the subject matter of the proposition.
Just as it was experienced, so too is the non-separation of both remembered.
Whatever arrangement, consisting of the nature and power of anything, is being investigated, that is to be known as its "inherence" (saṃniveśa); its pervasion (vyāpti) is so designated.
For one who abides in their own nature yet has reached only a single stage,
there is indeed the expansion of the flame from the nostrils, proceeding step by step from station to station.
The knower of the awakening to reality is known through three modes regarding the object;
that pervasion has been described as all-knowing, all-pervading, and supreme.
Having realized its own true nature, it does not undergo cessation;
for by attaining the state of non-dual knowledge, it transcends all projection regarding itself.

Even when its own nature is being contemplated, the cognition of the object's form as a property [of that nature] abandons [the previous state] due to the difference from the preceding stage; this abandonment is what is proclaimed as "renunciation" (tyāga).

"One who stands on the [spiritual] plane, who possesses renunciation, and who has restrained both self and others—O Beloved, one should know that to be the 'Projection' (ākṣepa) which is present everywhere.
By such statements, its essential nature (svarūpa) is described. || 129 ||
Anticipating the objection—"Why has this not been stated here by analyzing it separately? Is it enough merely to recite the scripture?"—he says:
"Even though the instrument [of realization] is clearly to be understood from the mouth of the Guru... (5.130)
Nevertheless, for the sake of preserving the tradition (āgama), it will be described further ahead. Although here,

because it is the exclusive domain of direct experience, the true nature of the instrument (karaṇa) must be clearly understood from the mouth of the Guru alone, nevertheless, so that the meaning of the tradition may not be interrupted, this [will be explained] further ahead.
"It will be described" means that it will be discussed here and there, as well as previously. For instance:
"That very cognition of an object which consists of the form of the grasped and the grasper is indeed the power of mantra, extended throughout the continuum of mantras" (Tantrāloka 16.256).
By such statements in the sixteenth chapter regarding the grasped and the grasper:
"That which is the essence of all non-differentiation, autonomous, and beautiful as consciousness—
that they call the thirty-seventh reality, designated as Paraśiva" (Tantrāloka 11.21).
Thus, regarding consciousness in the eleventh chapter [of the Tantrāloka]:
"In this system, indeed, vision, action, and will are said to be Śiva; however, they reside within the fragmentary sphere of the object of knowledge" (Tantrāloka 15.338).
This is because of the pervasion [of this principle] as stated in the fifteenth chapter, beginning with the words:
"Thus, that which arises in the abode of the attainment of immersion into the threefold emission,
consisting of the reflective awareness of consciousness— that alone shall be the vitality (*vīrya*) of mantra" (Tantrāloka 29.140).
By such passages as:

"Behold that consciousness residing within the body, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of time, wherein all things go to dissolution and the accumulations of the principles are consumed" (Tantrāloka 25.172).
And by such statements as these, he will describe the nature of renunciation (*tyāga*) and projection (*ākṣepa*) in the twenty-ninth chapter,

and the nature of integration (*saṃniveśa*) in the thirty-second chapter, by way of defining the essential character of their respective mudrās; therefore, the true essence of this matter should be understood by oneself from those very sources.
And in this exposition, his intention is that it is not proper to teach the secret meaning all at once in a single block; as he himself has stated elsewhere:
"Our teachers maintain that what is not extremely secret should not be proclaimed in one place, yet it must not be kept entirely hidden."
Thus, regarding this very interpretation of ours, the venerable Abhinavaguptapāda himself is our authority; therefore, the learned should not harbor resentment toward us in this matter. 130.
Having thus defined the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*), he begins to explain the principle of the phonemes (*varṇatattva*) which was mentioned immediately thereafter:
"Regarding this aforementioned utterance (*uccāra*), that which exists there as a vibrating [reality]... (5.131).
That sound which is predominantly an imitation of the unmanifest is called a phoneme (*varṇa*).
It exists vibrating within that which was previously described as the self of breath (*prāṇātman*) at the time of initial utterance: "There is no one to utter it, nor is there anyone to obstruct it."
"The God, abiding in the chest of living beings, utters [the sound] spontaneously. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.57).
By such statements, it is uttered by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*). Likewise: "The single phoneme whose essence is *nāda* is undivided from all phonemes."
"Because its form has not set, it is here called the Unstruck (anāhata).

According to this and other arguments to be stated later, that sound which is essentially unmanifest and of the nature of the undividedness of all phonemes (*varṇa*)— being of the form of the Unstruck— is called a "phoneme" (*varṇa*) because it is the cause for the production of phonemes.
The meaning is that it would be denoted by the word "caste" (varṇa). || 131 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Where indeed is such a phoneme to be found?", he says:
"The wise know that its primary form is the seed-syllable of both emanation and withdrawal. (5.132)
And its two seeds—the seed of emanation and the seed of withdrawal—are its "primary body," meaning they are its principal locus of manifestation. || 132 ||
One might ask: "What would be gained by such thorough knowledge of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the power of its practice, the yogi gradually attains the nature of consciousness.
By the word "that" (tat), the *nāda* (vibrant sound) manifesting within the seed-syllable of emanation (*sṛṣṭibīja*) and so forth is referred to.
He establishes that very point:
"For thus, whether without vowels or with vowels, in the series beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*, [the same occurs] again and again. (5.133)
Whether remembered or even uttered, each respective consciousness is produced;
for here it is said:
"The first twice-born is lifeless. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 17.29)
According to such statements as these, [it is taught] regarding the "vowelless" (*anacka*), which is devoid of vowels— as in the passage beginning,

"The *jīva* is joined with the left shank... (*Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* 3.54)— and regarding the "with-vowels" (*sācka*), which is endowed with vowels, within the collection of phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*.

When [the seed-syllable] is uttered or even remembered again and again, there arises a distinct consciousness (*saṃvit*)— an experience characterized by various forms such as the cutting of one's vital points (*marman*) or nourishment— which differs from one instance to the next. Therefore,
while repeatedly uttering or remembering the *nāda* manifested within the seed-syllable of creation (*sṛṣṭibīja*), etc., [one attains this].
The yogi should experience identity with consciousness—thus it is rightly said: "By the power of that practice, the yogi gradually attains the nature of consciousness. || 133 ||
Not only are the supramundane mantra-syllables inseparable from their expressed meaning, but even mundane ones are so; thus he says:
"Even those sounds such as 'pot' (ghaṭa) which depend on external objects and conventions... (5.134).
They too would produce within themselves a mental construction of an object (*artha-bhāvanā*), like a kingdom of the mind,

regarding an external thing— such as that which has a broad base and a bulbous belly— which is impossible according to the nature of reality; they would pacify [their minds] by means of a "referent" (*artha*) imagined by elders and others in the form of "this is its denotation," consisting of such conceptualizations.
Furthermore, even those words such as "jar" which, though dependent [on other factors],

are ignorant of even the mere report regarding their own denotable objects, yet— whether uttered or merely remembered— produce a "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), that is, a direct realization, of the object characterized by a broad base and belly.

"Like a kingdom of the mind" (manorājyavat) means that just as words such as "beloved" and so forth, when cultivated through one's own imaginative conceptualization or through desire, grief, and the like, produce the effect of the object— the beloved— even though that object is not present there,
so too is it conceived here. Thus, [this applies] to those things which are independent of convention and the like.
The sense is: what doubt could possibly arise regarding the possibility of such a thing for the phonemes of mantras, which exist in a state of identity with consciousness? || 134 ||
The scripture also states this by way of its meaning, as it was said by the Supreme Lord: "Bhairava is all-pervasive throughout everything. (5.135)

Thus, through the continuous utterance of the word *Bhairava*, one becomes Śiva. According to the etymological perspective (*nirukti*), [the term] *Bhairava* refers to Him who sustains (*bhṛ*), nourishes, and fashions everything— whether internally or externally— and who, as the agent of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, is all-pervasive throughout the entire universe.

Because it is filled by encompassing the entire universe, it is "full"— thus, through the repeated "utterance" of the word *bhairava* while internalizing this self-pervasion, [the breath] moves from the heart, the central channel, to the *dvādaśānta*.
The meaning is that through such thorough contemplation (*parāmarśana*), one becomes Śiva; that is, one experiences identity with Bhairava.
As it was stated—in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
"He who creates everything through [his] power (*bhī*), the giver of all, the pervasive one in the entire universe..."
"Thus, through the continuous utterance of the word 'Bhairava,' one becomes Śiva. (Vi.bhai.
Now, one might object: "Granted that this may occur through such utterance, how can it happen through recollection?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It is also stated in the venerable *Traiśirasa*, prior to the extraction of the mantra (5.136)."
Regarding the phrase "prior to the extraction of the mantra," this refers to when the Blessed Lady asked,
"Now I wish to hear the characteristics of the extraction of the mantra," and [the Lord],
beginning the response to that question, said:

The meaning is that this very nature of recollection was stated by the Blessed One at the very outset. For this alone, when investigated, is the supreme potency (*vīrya*) of mantras; such is the intended sense.
As has been stated by this same author in the *Sūtravimarśinī*:

"Therefore, those who follow the Āgamas consider that recollection alone— animated by mantra and the like— is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) capable of bestowing all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). (Rijuvimarsinī on Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa 1.4.1) || 136 ||

He recites that very [verse]: "And memory (smṛti) is recollection (smaraṇa) which, existing previously in all things in reality, is the nature of mantra, that which effects the attainment of the nature of the object to be meditated upon. (5.137)

Here, "smṛti" (memory) refers to that power of the Supreme Lord which consists of the reflective awareness "I," manifesting as distinct from other cognitions such as direct experience (*anubhava*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); it is characterized by the non-forgetting of the light of an experienced object. And that [power]...
While entities consisting of the signified and the signifier are manifesting, that which necessarily exists "prior to"—
namely, at the initial stage preceding the desire to acquire [an object] and so forth— is required; for otherwise,
linguistic and practical activity proceeds from memory through the impulse of desire.
According to this principle, the entire worldly transaction rooted therein would perish:
since an object previously experienced does not exist now, memory itself could not arise due to the absence of an object;
or, if it were to exist, there would have to be a direct experience of it—so how could this worldly transaction, which is rooted in that [memory], be possible?

Anticipating the objection that [the goal] might not be accomplished, it is said: "In reality, the very nature of mantra. For that recollection, by its actual mode of being (*vastuvṛttena*), "mantrates"—that is, it perceives the universe as non-different from itself; thus, "mantra" is the supreme subject (*pramātā*), and its "nature" means that it rests solely within that [recollection]. But even so, what [is the point]?
Anticipating the objection, "Could this be so?", he says: "It is that which effects the attainment of the essential nature of the object to be realized.

For that essence of mantra, which is the self of the supreme subject, "effects the attainment of the essential nature"—that is, the assimilation into one's own self—of the "object to be realized," such as a jar or other external entity, by uniting [the subject] with it.

The meaning is that it establishes [the object] as being suchness (*tathātva*). For the underlying idea is this: if indeed this entire experienced object were not possible through non-differentiation from that [consciousness], then memory itself would not occur.
As it has been said:
"If all experienced objects were not preserved within by being assimilated into Your own self,
then that which is called memory— which consists in the non-deprivation of the form of a known object— would not be possible at all. (137)
He qualifies that very [power] as follows: "Memory is the generator of its own nature, the colorer of all entities, existing everywhere indeed in the form of manifold aspects. (5.138)

The attainment of one's own intrinsic nature is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, pure consciousness; know that this consciousness culminates in manifestation, and therefore it is proclaimed as the supreme existence (sattā). (5.139)

For that memory—being the "manifestation," which is the prior experience consisting in the disclosure of the object, and being "established in that" (tanniṣṭhā), having attained non-difference from it—is the "generator" of its own form as delimited by the present time; the meaning is that it makes manifest the object being remembered. It belongs to the very same prior [experience].

Recollection (*smaraṇa*) is the re-emergence of a past experience delimited by the present time; therefore, its ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this," which arises through the propriety of encompassing both the prior and subsequent times. Now, even so, since recollection is a specific type of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it would follow that it lacks an object (*nirviṣayatva*).
"How is it that she is said to be the illuminator of objects in all things?

[It is because] "she exists everywhere in the form of manifold aspects. For she [resides] everywhere—in all previously manifested entities such as jars and so forth—by virtue of [the subject's] desire for them and other factors.

The meaning is that, by means of its "multiple forms"— consisting of the pot, gold, substance, and so forth— which at no time deviate from their own specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*) but remain established solely within their own nature, [consciousness] is a "colorer" (*rañjikā*), clearly manifesting itself at its own time as the mere appearance of a pot and so on. As it has been said:

"And one should illuminate objects at their own time, reflecting upon what was previously illuminated, whether by means of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as the mere appearance of a jar, or in its entirety. (Ri.Pra. 1.4.2).
Thus, because the previous experience appears precisely without distinction from memory...

The identity of memory and experience is established—thus, that very memory is the attainment of one's own self, and it is said to be ultimate consciousness, as in: "In the highest sense, consciousness is the attainment of one's own nature. As it has been stated:
"And it is logical that when there is a difference in memory, that which is being remembered appears [as one];
therefore, the cognizer of cognitions occurring at different times is this very [one], and thus their unity [is established]. (Ri.Pra. 1.4.3).
And for this very reason—

"This throbbing, great Being, which is undifferentiated by space and time—this very [Being], because of its essence, is called the Heart of the Supreme Lord. (Rjuvimalā on Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.5.14).
Thus, the mantra-nature (*māntrī*) is defined as consisting of the supreme, non-artificial awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*).

"This is the stage of vigor; one must apply oneself precisely here," as it was said: "Know that to be proclaimed as the Supreme Being. In the word *viddhi* ("know"), the meaning of the entire sentence functions as the object. 139.

Thus, if even worldly words such as "jar" serve as a means for attaining identity with consciousness through their utterance or recollection, what then need be said of the seeds of emanation (*sṛṣṭibīja*) and so forth? To this he says:
Furthermore, how could those seeds and clusters which cause consciousness to vibrate—without depending on convention—fail to serve as means for consciousness? (5.140)
This should be interpreted with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), meaning: "How could these lead to being means for consciousness? || 140 ||
One might ask: "How is it that these [mantras] act in this way without depending on ritual conventions (samaya)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Due to the absence of a denotable object, from the vibration of indifferent consciousness, and from its own abode;
through the arousal and cessation of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is fullness within the seed-syllables and clusters. (5.141)

Because there is no denotable object existing apart from its manifestation as one with consciousness (*saṃvid-ekātmya*), [the Lord] is thus "indifferent" (*udāsīnaḥ*); that is, because he rests solely within his own self, he does not look outward.
From that state of his own abode (*svadhāmataḥ*), which is the nature of the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvit-spanda*), and likewise from the perspective of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇātman*).

"From the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)" means from its outward flow directed toward the object of knowledge; likewise, "from its restraint" means from its resting in the inward-facing state.

Because it effects both emission and withdrawal, there is "fullness within the seed-words (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*) consisting of the seeds of emission and so forth. The meaning is that this is a state of self-sufficiency (*nairākāṅkṣya*), because it does not look toward anything else.

Furthermore, it is established by implication that in the case of worldly words such as "jar" and so forth, there is a dependence on convention (*samaya*) and other factors because the existence of the denoted object and so on is incomplete [in the word itself]. || 141 ||
Having thus stated this in general terms, he shows it also by way of its specific details:
"The first consciousness of bliss, the sound 'sīt', the 'sat', the 'sam', and equanimity;
for that initial perception is indeed the touch of the unsurpassed consciousness. (142)
When the three abodes— the heart, the throat, and the lips— have fully blossomed within,
the fourteenth [vowel] is the entry which consists of their unified essence.
Then, during the phase of the pronunciation of the visarga, the practitioner intent on recitation leads both paths of the dvādaśānta into unity with the heart.
The "first," that is, the very initial cognition of the "first," which is the primordial consciousness associated with pleasure and so forth—
the sense being that immediately thereafter there would also be the coloring by the object of cognition and so on—
that indeed is the "touch" of the supreme consciousness, the direct realization of the ultimate awareness.
This is the meaning. "Bliss" (*sukham*) is the excellence of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*); "the sound *śīṭ*" is its cause;

"the beautiful" refers to external objects such as women and the like, which, even if not perfectly beautiful, are situated in a configuration appropriate to themselves; "tranquility" (*śāmyam*) is the avoidance of the dualities of passion and hatred and so forth. And furthermore—

Thus, by means of the awareness of that primordial consciousness— which consists of the mere letter *sa* and pertains to pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest— the true nature of even the nectar-syllable residing within the supreme seed has been demonstrated. As was stated previously:

"That very supreme nectar [is found] at the beginning, end, and pause of the arousal [of breath], and during the sibilant sounds (*sītkāra*), the true state of bliss, the states of immersion (*samāveśa*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)" (Tantrāloka 3.167).
And although this [sound] belongs to the dental class, its repose is in the *kanda*— the bulbous root-center.

This is to be understood from the force of the meaning of what will be stated later, beginning with: "The bulb, heart, throat, palate, tip... (Tantrāloka 5.145). Even beyond that, in the "interior"—that is, within the central abode where even the three channels are conjoined, which is extremely expanded and situated above the *brahmarandhra*— [The text continues: "...the supreme state of Śiva, which is the very nature of the Self, shines forth. (Tantrāloka 5.146) Thus, by the power of the meaning of these [verses], it should be understood. Furthermore, "within" (*antaḥ*) means in the middle abode, where all three channels are merged, in that which is utterly blossomed and located above the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The fourteenth [state] is that entry into the supreme support known as the *nāḍyādhāra*;

the meaning is that this is its place of rest. Now, one might ask: does it rest here in its absolute isolation, or otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "having become one with that essence."
"Unified" means established as non-different from oneself—

according to the principle stated in such passages as, "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*" (Bhagavad Gītā 17.23)— by which [the practitioner] becomes one whose self is inseparable from that supreme Brahman, characterized by the immortal syllable (*amṛtavarṇa*).
This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "If this is its place of rest, what then is its place of emergence?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having three abodes in the heart, throat, and lips. By virtue of being located therein (*tātsthyāt*), the letter *a* resides in the heart, and the diphthong *au* resides in the throat and the lips; because these two are conjoined, [it possesses these three abodes].

He who possesses these three "abodes"—the heart, throat, and lips—as his points of emergence is of such a nature; by means of that sequence of emergence starting from the heart, he comes to rest upon the ground of the trident (triśūla). This is the reality of the phoneme *Śū*. Even after that, in the portion consisting of the utterance of the emission (*visarga*):
The vigilant yogi, intent on recitation (*japa*), leads both "paths to the end of the twelve"— namely,
the nasal path and the Śiva-end of the twelve— to a state of unity with the heart by way of emanation;
the meaning is that he should utter the supreme seed-syllable (*parā-bīja*) up to the end of the twelve through the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with Śakti and the other powers.
He summarizes this very point:

"From the root-center (kanda), the heart, the throat, the palate-tip, and finally through the process of the Kuṇḍalinī, one should bring forth the seed-syllable as a vibration within the central channel of bliss. (5.145)
*Kauṇḍalī* is the *śakti-dvādaśānta*; *prakriyānta* is the *śiva-dvādaśānta*.

Thus, starting from the *kanda*, by means of successively transcending each respective support (*ādhāra*) up to the *dvādaśānta*, one should bring forth this seed of emanation—the vibration—within the central abode (*madhyadhāman*).
The meaning is that it should manifest as the nature of the reflective awareness of unsurpassed consciousness. || 145 ||
Thus, he also expresses this reality of phonemes (varṇatattva) according to the seed-syllable of withdrawal (saṃhārabīja):
"The seed-syllable of withdrawal is *khaṃ*; [the letter] *o* resides in the heart; the blooming [letter] *ph* is at one's own head;
the triangular fire is at the palate and throat; and the bindu is situated in the upper station. (5.146)

In this context, although the letter *kha* is produced in the throat (*kaṇṭhya*), it resides in the heart due to the predominance of its chest-located resonance (*urasyatā*). The letter *pha* is "full" (*phulla*), and it is labial (*auṣṭhya*) because it is articulated from the lips alone. The letter *ra* is "fire" (*tejas*), and because it is cerebral (*mūrdhanya*), its location is specifically in the head (*mūrdhan*). The letter *e* is triangular; of that too—

Because [the phoneme *au*] belongs to both the throat and the palate, its location is precisely the throat and the palate. By the phrase "in the upper station," it is meant the form of the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space) belonging to Śakti and Śiva.
The sense is that the utterance (*uccāra*) must occur only after coming to rest in the locations beginning with the heart. As for that which...
"Having attained rest in its own nature...

(Taṃ. 5.75), and so forth; by this, the previously mentioned *uccāra* according to the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) should also be kept in mind here, because the sequence of consciousness exists everywhere. || 146 ||
One might ask: "What would result from this aforementioned reality of the phonemes (varṇatattva)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of this reasoning, the wise and sagacious man who is devoted to the recitation of the phonemes shall, before long, enter the supreme abode, the Absolute (anuttara). (5.147)
In the passage "the wise one, the one of excellent intellect," it is shown that "the primacy of being a knower is stated here."
Having thus explained the reality of the phonemes (*varṇatattva*), he speaks again by way of another method:
"By the word 'phoneme' [is meant] blue and so forth, or as it is in the *Dīkṣottara*.
Now, has this been stated merely according to one's own ingenuity, or does there exist some other authoritative text (*nibandhana*) on this point?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "As it is stated in the *Dīkṣottara*. This means: as it has been explained in the treatise known as the *Dīkṣottara*.
He says that very thing:
"One should contemplate the [syllables] of withdrawal, fire, and wind, joined with Rudra and the Bindu. (5.148)
Then, becoming absorbed in that within the heart, one should perceive the object of focus after seven days,
variegated with blue, yellow, red, and other colors like sparks of fire.
Awakened by the lamp of the seed-syllable, it blazes intensely within the lotus of the heart;
like a lamp, the Bindu, once ignited, shines like the sun free from clouds. (5.150)

"Śaṃhāraḥ" is the letter *kṣa*; "ṅā" is the male letter *m*; "Agni" is the letter *r*; "Marut" is the letter *y*. One should meditate upon these, joined together as a single whole with Rudra—the vowel *o*—and with the *bindu*, the half-moon, and so forth, in the heart until, being one-pointed in that, [the result is attained] after seven days.

"One should see the target" (lakṣyaṃ paśyet) means that something to be meditated upon (dhyeya) becomes manifest. For that very seed, whose nature has been described as his target, is indeed the lamp; because of its identity with light, it is "awakened" (prabodhita)—that is, manifested—and by the analogy of fire characterized primarily by sparks, [it expands].

The meaning is that, within the heart-lotus, [the Bindu], variegated with many colors such as blue and yellow, "blazes intensely," which is to say it becomes clearly visible. Thus, for one who is single-mindedly focused here,
the "Bindu" becomes radiant— either like a lamp or like the summer sun— according to the degree of its cultivation.
