The knower shines as his own self; the meaning is that by the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Therefore, he [the Self] may make himself an object of knowledge" (Rigvidhāna-prakāśa 1.5.15), he becomes the object of definition (lakṣyatām eti). || 150 ||
One might object: "If this is so, what would happen to him by attaining identity with the Self that is self-luminous? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of this [Self] which is self-luminous in nature, one whose mind is focused on nothing else attains identity;
just as copper, when pierced by mercury, attains the state of gold through Śiva. (5.151)
"By this" means by oneself. "By Śiva" means that one's own self is indeed the Supreme Lord Śiva—this is our established doctrine; such is the intended meaning. || 151 ||

And it is not only through this mantra that one’s own self is directly realized by means of the emergence of various colors such as blue and yellow; rather, this applies to all [mantras]. Thus he says:
"One should observe that this is a general characteristic to be applied to all mantras."

Surely, it is beyond dispute that each and every mantra must possess its own specific result; for indeed, the seed-syllable of immortality (*amṛtabīja*) is not capable of performing acts such as killing, nor can a cruel seed-syllable perform acts such as nourishing. How then could an action accomplished by one mantra be performed by other mantras as well?
Anticipating the objection, "Could it be so?", he says:
"For whatever collection of phonemes arises from volition is indeed material. (5.152)
Due to the predominance of that consciousness, it remains as if non-material;
for indeed, it has been said:
"Words have their origin in conceptual construction..."

According to this principle, because they are born of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), the entire collection of phonemes— which is "material," permeated by duality, and belonging to Māyā— exists as if non-material due to the predominance of consciousness; for,
by the subordination of its materiality through the intensity of consciousness itself, it remains as such.
The meaning is that even though they have the nature of difference, they are nonetheless the ultimate reality of non-dual consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*). This is what is being said:

although this entire expansion belongs solely to consciousness, nevertheless, because these [objects] appear predominantly as differentiated, they possess the capacity for specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, when there is a realization characterized by preeminence, the fruit for all is indeed indistinguishable, consisting in the direct self-realization (*svātmasākṣātkāra*). As it has been said:
"In this way, upon touching the aspect of their own essential nature (*svarūpāṃśa*), their state consists of Śiva."
"If it is not sprinkled with that [nectar], one remains within the state of divided saṃsāra.
And for this reason, one who has come to rest in the unconditioned nature of consciousness, which is the self of all mantras, shall attain that very state of being; thus he says:
"Therefore, one who is rooted in such a form ascends into consciousness. (5.153)
In that which is of unobscured form and free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*), the intellect is indeed serene.

Now, it is certainly established beyond dispute here that there is a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of all mantras; therefore, that difference must necessarily apply to their results as well, since the latter is dependent upon the former’s difference. So, how can it be stated thus?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the blue, the yellow, in pleasure, and in pain, the form of consciousness remains undivided. (5.154)
"Therefore, the diversity [of means] has been taught by the Gurus.
By "the Gurus" is meant Vāmanadattācārya; it was "taught" in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*.
By this, the following is stated: regarding the universe, consisting of the expressed and the expresser, such as blue and so forth—

Since there is no difference in their nature as consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), no real distinction whatsoever can exist. Now, if this is so, how can this manifold variety consisting of the signified and the signifier be denied? For that which has appeared cannot be unappeared. What, then, should be understood in this regard? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Therefore, there is variety among the means. The meaning is this: this variety, which arises from the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*), results in being the domain of the means alone, and not even the domain of the goal (*upeya*). It is with this very intention that—
"In this regard, wise men should not conceive of any difference in the fruit of consciousness," as stated in [Mālinīvijayottara Tantra] 2.25, and so forth. || 154 ||
Thus, for the sake of attaining that single goal to be reached, this entire collection of supreme means has been taught; so he says:
"By these [means of] utterance, instrument, meditation, and phonemes, [the path] has been demonstrated" (5.155).
This is the sequential method of the means for attaining the unsurpassed state.

Now, one might object: "Since even in the Āgama the recitation of the utterances (uccāra) and so forth follows this very same sequence, why has their presentation here been made by bypassing that [order] and beginning with meditation (dhyāna)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Vigor consists in not thinking of anything, and that, moreover, occurs during meditative cultivation. (5.156)

One should follow this sequence: that [consciousness] is in meditation; it is also in the utterance; it is also in the instrument; it is in the sound; and it is in the mental construction of the [articulatory] places—thus it is external. (5.157)

"Thinking of nothing" is the Śāmbhava [means]; "contemplation" (bhāvanā) is the Śākta [means]. "That" refers to contemplation; "that" refers to the instrument. "The conceptualization of the locus" refers to what will be explained from the sixth chapter onwards.
Thus, each preceding element is the vitality for each succeeding one.
Setting aside the order of the text—

according to the principle stated in [Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.60], "For whoever is superior in quality over another is considered to be above him"— this description has been made in a different manner by following the sequence of meaning.
The meaning is that, because it is more powerful, this very sequence must be adopted. || 157 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, does the attainment of the goal occur only through this sequence, or in another way as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The supreme yogi proceeds by leaping over, but the one of dull intellect proceeds by means of the sequence."

The word "supreme" (para) refers to one who is permeated by the intense descent of power (tīvra-śaktipāta). "Yogi" means that he shall become a partaker of identity with the supreme reality (paratattva).
One might ask: "What would be the point of saying that each preceding [element] is the vitality (vīrya) of each succeeding one?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as a eunuch is without vitality, or else even he possesses strength."
This conceptualization of the internal and external would be like a dead body. (5.158)

Just as even a man, lacking the virility that brings about masculinity, is a "eunuch" and incapable of performing his own function— or rather, even he possesses some degree of virility because otherwise his physical exertion and so forth would be inexplicable— so too [is the case] because of being almost entirely insentient.

A corpse is of no use; likewise, the meaning is that even the conceptualization of external and internal means, such as the visualization of a location and so forth, would be devoid of potency and thus utterly ineffective.
Now, he concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half of the verse:
"Thus, the external method for the means of attaining the Unsurpassed (anuttara) within the Āṇava [system] has been declared by way of a clear path.
Thus ends the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Āṇava Means."
The external method consists of the utterance [of mantras] and so forth; thus, may there be auspiciousness.
One named Jayaratha, whose entire flood of erroneous conceptualizations was utterly destroyed by the grace of the feet of the most excellent Guru,
composed this commentary on the fifth chapter.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Means of the Individual (Āṇavopāya)," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by Śrī Jayaratha. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
"Viveka":
He who, indeed, constantly assumes a wide-gaping mouth in order to swallow Time itself.
Victorious is he, the truly victorious one, who is accompanied by Sañjaya in the complete destruction of worldly existence.

Now, he begins with the second half-verse to introduce the supreme object of knowledge called the "conception of the locus" (sthānakalpanā), which is a constituent part of the means for young students and was mentioned immediately after the four objects of knowledge beginning with "utterance" (uccāra).
"Now, the external means, which is clearly known as the 'conception of place' (sthānaprakalpa), is being analyzed.

Here, the word *atha* (now) indicates a new section (*adhikāra*). Therefore, everything that is said from this point until the twelfth chapter is under the heading of the "conception of place"; thus, [the discussion] begins from the fifteenth chapter.

Furthermore, this very point is stated with reference to the external sacrificial ground (*sthāṇḍila*), the mandala, and so forth—until the conclusion of the book—because the primary focus is indeed the conceptualization of the locus (*sthāna*); thus, this entire elaboration is concerned with that alone. || 1 ||
He says that very thing:

"The division of locations is declared to be threefold: in the vital breath (prāṇa), in the body, and likewise externally. He further states that there are also other subdivisions of these: "Of these too, there are further distinctions... and so on.
And the vital breath (prāṇa) is fivefold in the body, being twofold according to its external and internal nature. || 6-2 ||
The mandala, the sacrificial ground, the vessel, the rosary together with the book, the linga, the drum, the cloth painting, the manuscript, the image, and the physical form itself. (6.3)

Thus, the external [form] is elevenfold, yet it may further become manifold. "Pusta" refers to a form fashioned from clay or similar materials. "Mūrti" refers to an image associated with a Guru or others. The word "tat" (that) refers back to the external due to immediate proximity; "punar" (again/further) indicates that even though it is elevenfold, it may become "bahudhā" (manifold).
For even the mandalas and so forth possess diversity through the sequence of a single trident, three tridents, and so on. || 3 ||
Having thus described the distinction of locations according to their essential nature, he makes a formal promise to teach the procedure pertaining to them as well:
"In that regard, first the procedure based on the vital breath (prāṇa) is taught. (6.4)
He says that very thing:
"This entire path, though sixfold and exceedingly extensive, which will be described, is established all at once within the vital breath (prāṇa). (6.5)
"He will speak" refers to the exposition of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) and so forth. "Prāṇa" refers to that whose nature is general vibration (*sāmānyaspandana*). As it has been said:
"The sixfold division of the paths, however, resides as one within the *prāṇa*" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.232).
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, in its specific form, it consists of three types: words, mantras, and phonemes. As he will state:
"Of the sixfold path, that triad which is prior—this very same path of time is clearly established in the vital breath" (Tantrāloka 6.37).
Thus [ends the fifth].
He establishes that very point:

"The reckoning of the path, which exists as both succession and non-succession—for succession and non-succession are the manifold and unitary reckonings within the sphere of objective existence. (6.6)

Anticipating the objection, "Why indeed does this exist as having the nature of both succession and non-succession?", he says: "Succession, etc. Here, the manifestation of entities occurs in only two ways: through succession and through non-succession. Among these, [manifestation] through succession is as in the case of cause and effect, and so forth; [manifestation] through non-succession is as in the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), and so forth. And that [variegated cognition], in the variegated...

When there is an appearance, occurring both sequentially and non-sequentially, of a single entity at one and the same time, in relation to certain entities existing in a prior time and others existing at the same time— then that very "reckoning" (kalanā),
which is the delimitation of entities in this manner, is itself the nature of sequence and non-sequence. || 6 ||
Now, one might object: "Indeed, this entire world appears as being entirely attached to consciousness; otherwise, its manifestation would not occur at all.
And since consciousness is eternal, there is no connection with time; so how could time belong even to the multitude of entities that are linked to it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Time, whose nature consists of succession and non-succession, exists within supreme consciousness.

One might object: "In that case, such statements as 'The reality of consciousness is utterly pure, transcending all talk of succession and non-succession' would be contradicted, and there would be a lapse into the Buddhist doctrine"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
The supreme power named Kālī is indeed proclaimed to be that very [power] of the God.

That which is the connection of the Supreme Light with time is its "power" (*śakti*); it is the capacity for the manifestation of the universe—consisting of subjects, objects of knowledge, and so forth—as projected by His own will, in their respective forms.
However, within His own self, there is neither any succession nor any non-succession. Thus it is not [the case that time exists in Him].
For when fire is joined with its power of burning, there is the manifestation of a blister or similar effect within itself. || 7 ||

Thus it is said: "That very consciousness, manifesting externally through its own internal unfolding the succession and non-succession contained within itself, abides as the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti). (6.8)

That very power of time (kāla-śakti), which is non-different from consciousness itself, abides as the vital function (prāṇa-vṛtti); this means it manifests externally as succession and non-succession—which exist in a state of non-distinction from consciousness—and thus stands as the activity of the vital breath, pulsating as the very nature of life-force. || 8 ||
Anticipating the objection, "How indeed can this [consciousness] manifest as the nature of the vital function (prāṇavṛtti)? he says:
"For that which is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is light, shines forth as the void, distinct and having cast off from itself the object of knowledge. (6.9)
Indeed, because this universe— consisting of the subject and the object— is manifested as non-different from itself, its ultimate reality is Light; therefore,
being free from any coloring by that [universe], it is pure consciousness alone, which, through its own sovereignty, [manifests as such].

With the desire to manifest incompleteness within its own self, [the subject] separates from itself the "object of knowledge"— which exists non-differentiated from itself as the soul of the universe— and having reflected, "I am transcendent to the universe," the distinct sky manifests.
The meaning is that, because it is empty of all phenomenal existence, it shines forth in a form that is free from obscuration. || 9 ||
Therefore, he says:
"That very state of being void is proclaimed as the nature of consciousness.
By "the state of being void," the meaning is the state of being a void subject (*śūnyapramātṛtva*). And its voidness is...

This is because of the complete exhaustion of everything that is cognizable, but not of consciousness itself; for if that were the case, this entire world would become as if blind and mute. As it has been said:
"That which is non-empty is called 'empty,' and 'empty' is said to be non-existence."
"That is taught as non-existence where all phenomena have reached their end.
(Svacchanda Tantra 4.291). And by means of all objective supports and dharmas, together with all sentient beings without exception...
"It is empty of the latent tendencies of all afflictions, yet it is not empty from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus it is said.
And he says that this is the supreme goal for those outside [this tradition]: "That supreme state belongs to the yogins through the reflective awareness of 'not this, not this'. (10)
This is as follows:
"It is neither existence nor non-existence, according to the Middle Way"—
by such reasoning, through the two-fold reflection "not this, not this" regarding existence and non-existence.
For the "yogins" who possess the penetration of the middle state, the "supreme" (*parā*) condition—which consists of the void beyond the void—is the place of rest; such is the meaning. As they say:
"Subsequently established in emptiness, he is devoid of [ordinary] cognition."
"Having entered nirvāṇa, he becomes indefinable, like a fire whose flames have been extinguished.
Thus [ends verse 10].
And that very subject of emptiness, becoming extroverted, attains the state of being the subject of the vital breath (prāṇa);
thus he says:
"That very self of space, when this object of knowledge has been differentiated, becomes intent upon appropriating it."
By virtue of its falling and surging upward, it is designated as the wave of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa).

And that very "void-self" (*khātmā*) is the subject of emptiness (*śūnyapramātā*), because— as stated in [Svacchandatantra] 4.104, "But here, desire is the impurity"— it possesses the *āṇava* impurity consisting of the sense of being incomplete, and thus remains characterized by longing.

Furthermore, being intent on re-appropriating that [object], as this object—consisting of blue, pleasure, and so forth—is "differentiated" (bhedite), that is, separated from himself, it falls by way of surging upward;
thus, becoming extroverted, it comes to be designated by terms such as "prāṇa" (vital breath). This occurs because its nature is slight movement.

This is the primordial expansion of vibration itself, whose nature is self-reflection; thus, it is designated by that word [the "I"] only as a metaphorical convention, for it is not identical to that [vibration], since it exists even above the emergence of the void-subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*). The same applies to the term "wave" (*ūrmi*) and so forth hereafter.
This is to be known. || 11 ||
With this very intention, Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa and others have also spoken thus; so he says:

"Therefore, they indeed say that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath (prāṇa), and likewise, the wind has become the substratum for the principle of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-tattva). (6.12)

Although consciousness, preceded by the manifestation of emptiness, vibrates as the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), nevertheless, in its manifestation, it does not assume any other form—thus it was said: "Previously, consciousness transformed into the vital breath. This has not been stated by them [the opponents] without foundation; such is also the sacred tradition (*āgama*).

It is confirmed by the passage beginning with “the internal organs” (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The “essence” (*tattva*) of the internal organs is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is their core; thus, the meaning is that of the cognizer who is the intellect.
By this, it means the cognizer who is the intellect. Prior to that [intellect], there is the arousal of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus it is established. Otherwise, how could that [consciousness] be its support? || 12 ||
Thus, this very first vibration of the supreme consciousness—its entire empirical activity everywhere proceeds through a mode of non-difference from that [consciousness]. Thus he says:
"This is that power of vitalization (prāṇana-śakti) which bestows the longing for internal exertion."
Vibration, throbbing, repose, the individual soul, and the intuition of the heart are considered [aspects of this power]. (6.13)

The meaning is: she whose "longing"—that is, her desire—is for that "initial exertion," which is the vibration consisting of the state of being an agent, is one who is solely intent upon that. || 13 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this [consciousness] having thus manifested? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti), by means of its fivefold forms beginning with prāṇa, makes the body its own; because consciousness (saṃvit) fills it, this [body] shines forth. (6.14)

This very vital function (*prāṇavṛtti*), whose nature is a general vibration, takes as its own that five-elemental body— which is pervaded by the internal and external organs and consists of the five forms beginning with *prāṇa* and *apāna*— and remains there having occupied it; for this reason, this body [is called the self].
The meaning is that even though it is an object of cognition like a jar or other objects, consciousness shines as full of consciousness and manifests as the cognizer.
For this very reason, the deluded have this error:
that there is nothing whatsoever other than the body qualified by consciousness. As it has been said:
"They believe that there is no self other than the body inlaid with consciousness. (14)
Regarding this, he says:
"Therefore, the deluded perceive bodily activity as being inlaid with consciousness through its identity with the function of the vital breath (prāṇa); hence they think that nothing else exists. (15)

"The deluded" (*mugdhāḥ*) refers to those who do not know the distinction between the body and the self. This is their view: "For it is the elements themselves which, though insentient in their state as clay and so forth, possess the power of intoxication when transformed into the form of liquor—just as molasses, flour, and other ingredients [possess fermenting power]—and when transformed into the form of the body, they possess consciousness."
They proceed [in this manner], and because they undergo specific transformations over time,
they eventually arrive at a state devoid of that [consciousness]; yet for that duration,
due to the non-departure of consciousness and their proficiency in activities such as memory and mental synthesis, they continue to act.
What is the use of any other self distinct from that? || 15 ||
It is precisely those who rest upon this [view] that are called "Cārvākas"—thus he says:
"The Cārvākas, regarding as authoritative that very intellect which relies on knowers consisting mostly of children, fools, and women, consider themselves seers of reality. (6.16)

"That very view" refers to the notion that the body itself, as characterized by consciousness— as expressed in such statements as "the person is the body qualified by consciousness"— is the self, and not something distinct from it;
this form of view is shown to be unworthy of being followed by great people because it relies on the ignorant and the like.
Regarding the phrase "making it authoritative": if some self distinct from the body were to exist even after death,
then its taking up another body after abandoning its previous one would be like the recollection of objects experienced during the stages of childhood and so forth within this very body.

There would also be recollection of objects experienced in each preceding body; for since that [self] is eternal even upon the change of bodies, we perceive no specific cause by which one would remember only what was experienced in this life and not what was experienced in another life.
Therefore, it is logical that there is no other self whatsoever beyond this. As the Śruti also says:
"This mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

Thus, having cast aside all concern for the next world and such, one should live in pleasure alone for as long as life lasts—this is their essential truth, as indicated by the term "seers of reality. As they say:
"One should live happily for as long as one lives; death has no domain [over the living]."
"For one who has been reduced to ashes and is at peace, how can there be a return? (16)
Now, one might ask: "What would happen to those who thus cultivate reality? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If their cultivation in that manner attains continuous firmness, then upon the dissolution of the body, they will remain as if asleep until such latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are exhausted. (6.17)
"They are asleep" means they are for the most part *pralayākalas* who have not yet attained awakening. || 17 ||
Anticipating the question, "What would happen when those latent impressions (vāsanās) are exhausted?", he says:
"But when those latent impressions are exhausted, another unexhausted latent impression, awakened by some cause, produces a manifold abundance of fruits. (6.18)
But surely there is a similarity between these [views] and those of the Sāṃkhyas and others, since their liberation is also of this same nature;
for even then, there arises the experience of various fruits in accordance with their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*). As he will say:
"At the dawn of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha [awakens] those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, the Vedas, and so forth."
"By that [means], one creates once again; such liberation is not perfect. (Tantrāloka 6.153).
Why, then, is this very [view] everywhere designated as inferior? As they say:
"The wretched Cārvākas are simply to be rejected; what is the use here of their petty logic?"
"This is the occasion for calculation. Anticipating the question, "What does this mean?", he says:

"Because of the suspicion that [the practice] is not firm, because of the persistence of prior latent impressions (vāsanā), because of laxity regarding other duties, and because of the possibility of remorse. (6.19)
Because it causes the abandonment of duties by other people who have not attained that [spiritual state], they say this latent impression of nihilism is more evil than evil itself. (6.20)
Even though, from our perspective, other philosophical systems are equally sinful,

the latent impression of nihilism (*nāstikyavāsanā*) is even more sinful than those; for, since it is not prohibited by the "ancient" [tradition], this pre-existing latent impression of faith (*āstikyavāsanā*) remains in its original state.
For there is no firm growth of the latent impression of nihilism (nāstikya-vāsanā) by which its cessation might occur,
since here the lack of firmness is suspected due to its being rootless; just as when it is asserted with firmness that the phenomenal world is false because the Supreme Brahman is its root.
"It grows to this extent"—this is not so; for if the self did not exist, what else would remain that, being non-inert and fundamental, could serve as the basis upon which all this is well-ordered?
Furthermore, transformation belongs only to inert things; therefore, it is not tenable for the self to be characterized by sentience.

Thus much has been said by others; therefore, this should be understood from those very sources. For this very reason, because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of faith remains as it was, for "others"—those belonging to other systems of philosophy—the injunctions appear in the form of "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," "one should not harm any living beings," and so forth.

Through the form of injunctions and prohibitions—that which "must be done"—laxity arises in this [view]. For if some perform certain rites for the sake of the next world on the grounds that the self exists, let that be as far removed as possible;
yet others, even while maintaining that the self does not exist, engage in wholesome conduct and abstain from unwholesome conduct.
If some cause for this were possible here, otherwise why would everyone act in this way?

And we ourselves have no duty whatsoever to perform—thus, we have wandered in the wrong place, and why have we remained like those who are utterly deluded? Such is the remorse felt here regarding oneself.

When that [virtuous person] has arisen, it is indeed proper to honor him; setting aside the distress of formal argumentation, one should simply act with ease: "Even though the next world is uncertain, the wise must certainly abandon what is unwholesome."

"If it does not exist, what would happen? If it exists, the nihilist is destroyed"— by such advice, even from one esteemed as a friend, once that latent impression of faith has taken root, its destruction will inevitably be brought about by people belonging to other philosophical systems.
It should be performed—thus [it is said]. || 20 ||

Thus, lest the discussion of other philosophical systems (paradarśana) should further encroach upon this topic through a chain of incidental arguments, he returns to the subject at hand: "Enough with the irrelevant; now the relevant matter is being analyzed."
He says that very thing:
"This entire path, in its totality, is established in the vital breath. (6.21)
And that path is divided twofold by means of action and form;
"twofold" refers to the distinction between space and time. Therein, the path of time is divided by action, and the path of space is divided by form.
As it has been said:

"By means of the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests the succession of space; and by means of the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He manifests the succession of time as well. (Ri. Pra. 2.1.5)
Thus [ends the section]. || 21 ||
Now, [it may be objected]:
"This entire path is established in pure consciousness alone;
that which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky. (8.3)

Raising the objection—“Is it not logical that its establishment in consciousness, according to the principle to be explained below, is possible, and not in the insentient vital breath (prāṇa)?”—he says: “For that very [vital breath] is declared in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* to be the crest-lock (śikhā). (6.22)
"But when bound at the time of sacrifice and so forth, she is of the nature of Śiva because of her partless state.
The crest-lock is said to be the limited power (śakti) of Bhairava;
it is known as the power of action (kriyāśakti)..."
Thus [ends the section]. || 22 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is her bondage, by virtue of which she would be of the nature of Śiva through her partless state (*niṣkalatva*) in sacrifices and other rites?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because within the course of a day and night, her movement occurs in twenty-four ways. (6.23)
Bestowing manifold fruits through hundreds of apertures known as the emission of breaths—
within this external day-and-night (ahorātra) consisting of sixty ghaṭikās,
there are the movements of breath belonging to this supreme power of action (kriyāśakti) of the Lord, which is of the nature of breath.
She is characterized by nine hundred [channels] known as *randhra*, which correspond to the number of gates; for this very reason,
she bestows manifold fruits through twenty-four modes characterized by the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), distinguished according to whether they pertain to this world or the next.
The meaning is that the movement (cāra) would have the characteristic of flowing upwards and downwards. This is the intended sense here:
indeed, in this world, for all living beings—even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eye is cast elsewhere—[the breath flows].
"In this way, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) always proceeds effortlessly"—
according to such statements, the middle *prāṇa* flows by its own natural impulse— namely,
within an external day and night.
By the statement beginning with, “Twenty-one thousand six hundred, O fair-limbed one,
[occur] in an external day-and-night; but internally, O Lord of the Gods,” there are twenty-one thousand six hundred movements of the vital breath (prāṇa) within.
It would be as follows: "Three hundred and sixty days and nights—this is declared to be a year externally, and it is that which consists of *vighaṭikās*. (Svacchandatantra 7.51)

By such statements as these, there are three hundred and sixty movements of the vital breath (prāṇa); thus, in two and a half ghaṭikās, there are nine hundred [movements], and that itself is the individual arising of each of the transits (saṃkrānti). As it has been said:
"The twenty-four transits of the *haṃsa* always carry nine hundred [breaths] each, by the very nature of the equilibrium of the elements" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.168).
And two and a half *ghaṭikās*, multiplied twenty-four times, [is the duration of each].
There are sixty *ghaṭikās*—thus, within a single day and night (*ahorātra*), there is the arising of that many [breaths].
As it has been said:
"O fair-faced one, this occurs externally in a day and night, and internally as well."
The haṃsa of the vital breath (prāṇa) indeed undergoes twenty-four transitions.
"Twelve are said to occur during the day, and twelve indeed are recorded for the night" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.166).

Although this much must be stated here— that there are this many movements of the vital breath (prāṇa) within a day and night— even so, in that case, only their mere enumeration would have been demonstrated, and not [their true nature].
But it has been stated thus because it is also the cause for the arising of those various diverse fruits. || 23 ||

Now, one might object: "This being the case, what is this irrelevant matter being stated when the topic at hand is the binding of the crest-lock (*śikhābandha*), namely that such is the course of the movements of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)? This is not so;
for this very [course] is indeed the binding of the crest-lock of the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*).
"Praticāra" means repeated reflection with focused attention at the beginning, middle, and end.
It is with this very intention that it is said:
"Six hundred [breaths] by day and twenty-one thousand by night..."
"The recitation of the Goddess is thus prescribed; it is easily attained, yet difficult for the dull-witted. (Vi.bhai. 156).
Having stated this and other such things elsewhere, he says:
"The night, the moon, as well as the apāna breath and the nāda abide in one place. (6.24)
The sun of the individual soul does not rise; such is the twilight of half a tuṭi.
The sun faces upward, the moon faces downward, and fire is within.
The midday [meditation] bestows liberation when the sun is situated in the center of the sky;
for it is the essence that measures the infinite, awakening the wheel of living beings.
The *bindu*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the day, as well as the sun, abide together in one place;
this is the third great junction (*mahāsaṃdhyā*), which stands as the perfectly tranquil self.

When, moving from the *dvādaśānta* to the heart on the left side, the moon of the night remains in the heart with its course ceased, and the sun of the *prāṇa* does not rise from there, then such is the final half-*tuṭi* of the *apāna*, which belongs to the twilight (*sāndhya*).

The meaning is that, according to the method to be described, by the closing of the half-ṭuṭi of the rising sun of the vital breath (prāṇa), there occurs the morning twilight (prābhātikī saṃdhyā), which consists of the movement of the vital breath measuring two finger-breadths (aṅgula) divided into four parts. As it has been said therein:
Even though the moon exists within the heart as the apāna at its center,
when it reaches a state of exhaustion, the sun of the individual soul (jīva) does not rise.
It should be known as the "dawn," which awakens the reality of the Self;
there, night, moon, apāna, and sound abide together in one place.

"The half-tuṭi, by means of the splendor of gnosis, is indeed declared to be the twilight. Following that, when the sun, whose nature is prāṇa, moves upward, and the moon, whose nature is apāna, remains within the interior consisting of the palate and so forth with its face turned downward— thus.

From the friction of those two, consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the fire whose nature is the knower (*pramātṛ*) arises; this is the midday *sandhyā*, which bestows liberation,
because it is situated in the place of the palate, in the "middle" of the "void" (*vyoman*), that is, the cavity connected to the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*).

Even though [the sun] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being extroverted, because its nature as the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) does not depart, the sun—whose essence has not set—is the "awakener" (*bodhaka*) of the circle of living beings with excellence; the meaning is that even while consisting of both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, it manifests as the nature of the cognizer. As it is said there:
Beginning with: "The sun stands with its face upward, and the moon stands with its face downward," [it continues]:
"In the interval between them, [the breath] has arisen within the range of the space at the end of the palate."
One should meditate upon that which is devoid of means of valid cognition, perfectly tranquil through the awakening of peace.
The fire of the void (vyomavahni), like the void itself, lasts for half a *tuṭi* according to the calculation of time;
this should be known as the midday *saṃdhyā*, which bestows liberation.
"The Sun situated in the middle of the sky is called Parāditya;
for he is the one whose essence never sets, awakening the circle of living beings.
Following that, when the Sun, in the form of the *bindu* and so forth, resides in one place at the *dvādaśānta*...

"Abides" means that movement has ceased; and since, by implication, neither the sun nor the moon rises, then, due to the complete subsiding of the universe, she consists of her own profound tranquility. For this very reason, this great third twilight (*sandhyā*) is established—meaning it exists as having arisen through its own inherent nature (*svarasa*). As it is said there:
The *bindu*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the sun—the day—abide together in one place;
there the mind, free from all mental fluctuations, remains in perfect tranquility.
"And having established one's own nature at the point of transition upon the ground of perfect peace,
that which is known as the Great Junction (mahāsandhyā) is proclaimed as the third.
Thus [ends verse 27].
And he applies this to the subject at hand by way of a summary: "In this way, the topknot (śikhā) is bound where it bestows its respective fruits.
In the manner and sequence thus described, wherever—in a sacrifice or other rite—the topknot, which consists of the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti), [is bound].

The meaning is that, by blocking other paths and bringing about immobility within the central channel (*madhyadhāman*) alone, she becomes the one who directs the various fruits, such as the presence of the mantra and so forth,
therein. As it has been said there:
"O Goddess, when that [mantra] is bound to the body, the Lords of the Guṇas shall grant their presence to the foremost of practitioners; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is said.

Thus, since *prāṇa* is the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, that which was stated regarding the foundation of the path (*adhvan*) therein must ultimately resolve within consciousness itself; thus he says:
"Therefore, this entire path remains resting within consciousness. (6.28)
Raising the objection: "How can a formal and sequential path exist within consciousness, which is formless and inactive? he says in response:
"Because consciousness is formless and all-pervading, and because it is inactive..."
That which is the manifestation of form and action is itself the path of the Great Lord.

In this very way, the manifestation of such consciousness as having the nature of form and action is itself the path (*adhvan*) consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth, or the mantras and so forth; it is not some separate entity to be supported, by which such a doubt might arise. || 29 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the basis for applying the word *adhvan* (path) here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The path (*adhvan*) is the cause for reaching the state that is to be traversed by degrees;
for dualists it is so because of its being an object of enjoyment, but for the awakened ones, it is so because it is consumed (*adyate*). (6.30)

"In the state to be reached" means within the essence of Śiva-tattva. For in the state of differentiation (bheda-daśā), it is taught that the thirty-sixth principle, Śiva-tattva, is to be attained by means of a sequence of transcending each respective category (tattva).
"Because of its state as an object of enjoyment" means because it is to be consumed; for those who have realized the essence of consciousness perceive everything [as such].
The sense is that they make [the path] their own self. Therefore, it is called "adhvan" (the path) because it is itself the path, and it is called "adhvan" because it is traversed (*adyate*).

One might object: "Since the communication of meaning by all words is established through convention alone, what is the use here of remembering their etymological significance? For this [method] cannot possibly apply everywhere. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this context, one should everywhere investigate the etymological significance of words, because..."
Although there are three ways in which words denote their meanings— derivative (*yaugika*), conventional (*rūḍha*),
and derivative-conventional (*yogarūḍha*)— even among these, the derivative is primary because it functions based on a specific cause;
for this very reason, the other two should be included within this [derivative] category in some way or another.
In every case, an investigation into the literal meaning would reach its ultimate conclusion.
Regarding this, he says: "It is stated in the venerable *Niśācāra*: 'In this context, the designation is considered to be threefold. (6.31)

It is either based on specific characteristics (*naimittikī*), well-known (*prasiddhā*), or technical (*pāribhāṣikī*); whichever of these occurs first shall be primary, and one should then subsume the others within it. (6.32)

Therefore, even if this etymological explanation (nirukti) for the word *adhvan* has not been explicitly stated here, it should be inferred by one's own intelligence whenever appropriate; for how much can possibly be written in a book?
Regarding the term "well-known" (*prasiddha*): even though it possesses a cause (*sanimitta*), it is established only in certain specific instances. As it has been stated therein:
"In the scriptures of Śiva, technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) should always be understood as being of three kinds:
the conventional (*pāribhāṣika*), the causal (*naimittī*), and that which is established by common usage (*siddhā* or *prasiddhibhāk*)."

"In this context, the derivative designation (naimittikī saṃjñā) has arisen from a cause (nimitta). Thus, since it must necessarily be stated here that all designations possess the nature of having a cause, he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to indicate this. Now, if this is so, then [this applies] everywhere.

Anticipating the objection, "Why was it not stated in this way?", he says: "Not impelled," and so forth. The meaning is: "To what extent? for the derivation of words is not the subject under discussion here. || 33 ||
Now, it has been stated that the manifestation of form and action belongs to supreme consciousness; in that regard, one might ask:
which path pertains to the manifestation of action, and which to the manifestation of form?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In that context, the manifestation of action is called the path known as Time (kālādhvan);
within it, the three paths—known as phonemes (varṇa), mantras, and words (pada)—are clearly present. (6.34)
That aspect which consists of the manifestation of form is called the path of space (deśādhvan);
here, the triad known as kalā, tattva, and pura is included within it. (6.35)

Now, one might object: "Granted that the twofold nature of the paths (adhvan) is asserted due to the appearance of variety in form and action through the distinction of space and time, let that be so; however, what is the cause for each of those [two] being threefold?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In each of these three triads, there exists a gross, subtle, and supreme form;
because of this, this entire path is said to be sixfold.

"By that" means by reason of each being threefold—according to the gross, subtle, and supreme levels—as consisting of words (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and mantras, and as consisting of worlds (*bhuvana*), principles (*tattva*), and powers (*kalā*). As it has been said:
"Words are composed of mantras; mantras have phonemes as their sole body."
"The phonemes are established in themselves; such is their nature as gross, subtle, and supreme.
Likewise: "Their pervasion of the worlds exists within the principles (tattvas), from Ananta up to Śiva" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.96).
Thus:
"In that way, those [powers] beginning with Nivṛtti are indeed included within the Kalās" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.97).
In this regard, he introduces the topic of time and space currently under discussion:
"Furthermore, that triad which is prior to the sixfold path—this very same path of time is clearly established within the vital breath. (6.37)

"Eastern" refers to the previously mentioned [category] known as the *pada*, *mantra*, and *varṇa*. The term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) is illustrative; by this, the same applies to the downward breath (*apāna*) and so forth as well. (37)

Now, one might object: "In this way, time has been described as consisting of both succession and non-succession; is that very same [time] included among the principles (tattvas), or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This time is said to be different from the time situated within the principles."
The other is different from that, because it possesses distinct characteristics.
He says that very thing:
"For this Time belongs to the Lord, bringing about the manifestation of the universe. (6.38)

The power of action (kriyāśakti) is the supreme body of all the principles (tattvas). By "supreme body," it is meant the locus of their origination; for this very reason, she is described as "that which effects the manifestation of the universe. || 38 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not said that the supreme consciousness's capacity to manifest the universe is its external unfolding (*unmeṣa*), and thus its nature as the Lord (*īśvara*) would have been stated?
To this he says: "This is the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*); it is called the body of Śiva. (39)
Since this [reality] is the identity with the universe, whose nature consists of the activity of overflowing enjoyment,
for that reason— and because it causes the manifestation of the universe through the characteristic of external unfolding— it is called the *Īśvara-tattva* (the principle of Īśvara).

The meaning is that this nature of the universal manifestation belongs precisely to the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) of the temporal self (*kāla-ātman*); it is its outward-facing form. Now, one might object: "Since such a form could also be possible for Māyā and the other [principles], why is this stated specifically? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "the body of Śiva. This is so even when there is an outward orientation.

It rests within its own self; for, because this [consciousness] has ascended to the peak of extroversion, its expansion is intensified. Therefore, the "oneness" (*ekātmya*) of the universe—which consists of effects—is the realization of it as one's own self, meaning the assimilation of the world into one's own being. For this very reason...
"This is the state of both difference and non-difference," thus it is proclaimed by all. (39)
Now, one might object: "In this way, since time is already included within this [category], its separate enumeration would not be justified;
thus, a contradiction with such scriptural passages as 'In this manner time should proceed, and that principle is irreproachable' would arise. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This indeed is the nature of the Lord within the Supreme Self.
That principle of time (kālatattva) is said to reside in the subject under the influence of Māyā.
Now, one might object: "In the subject under the influence of Māyā, is it only the principle of time that exists, or are there other principles as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which is Śiva’s own body, beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā.

That very [nature] of the individual soul (pums), beginning with *māyā* and ending with *rāga*, becomes a sheath (*kañcukī*). By the phrase "beginning with Śiva," the venerable Lord Anāśrita is denoted by the word "Śiva. By the phrase "his own body," it is because [the soul] consists of the powers (*śakti*) such as *ānanda*. The term "of the individual soul" refers to Śiva himself.
The meaning is: "of one who has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu) due to his own freedom. || 41 ||
He analyzes this very point: "Since Māyā, Kalā, and Vidya are without support, [they belong to] Sadāśiva. (6.42)
Īśvara, Kāla, Niyati, Sadvidyā, and Rāga are said to be [the five coverings].
As it has been stated:
"The group of principles beginning with Śakti indeed constitutes the *kañcuka* (covering) of the bound soul (*paśu*)."
Śakti, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, Kāla, and Niyati.
"Sadāśiva and Īśvara are Vidyā, while Rāga is indeed [the next], O fair-complexioned one.
Thus [ends verse 42].
Not only do these possess such a nature, but they also possess the status of subjects—thus he says:
"The Unattached is the subject of the void; Sadāśiva is the subject of the intellect. (6.43)
The Lord is the subject as vital breath (*prāṇa*), and knowledge is the subjectivity of the body.
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for these [states] being the subjectivity of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, voidness is the absence of support; knowledge itself is indeed the state of the intellect (*buddhi*). (6.44)
The state of being the self of the universe (*viśvātmatā*) is the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇatva*), which is the state of being exclusively intent upon the object of knowledge within the body.

It is called "the void" (*śūnya*) because of the cessation of the universe. It is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because of the predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) in Sadāśiva. "The state of being the self of the universe" is so called because it consists of the outward unfolding (*unmeṣa*).
"Because of the state of being stretched out toward a single object of knowledge," for attachment occurs precisely there. 44.

Thus, the state of being the universal self exists within the vital breath (prāṇa); this very point is now stated here: "Therefore, this perception of the universe shines forth upon the path of the vital breath. (6.45)
"In whatever form we describe that [reality], let it be attended to by the wise.
Regarding the phrase "in whatever form," it means in its nature as time.
Surely, because the *prāṇa* pervades the entire body, its presence is necessarily established; otherwise, certain limbs would remain paralyzed, like pillars.
Why, then, is its movement described in the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra* and other texts as beginning specifically from the heart?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Although in this body, extending as far as the dvādaśānta, [the breath] is everywhere... (6.46).

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), though consisting of a warp and woof, is likewise not clearly manifest in this manner—that is, by way of being a warp and woof—not clearly manifest throughout the entire body; for in some parts of the body the breath appears with clarity, while in others it appears without clarity. (46)
Therefore he says:
"Effort is considered to be of two kinds: that which consists of mere vitality, and that which is directed toward [the goal]. (6.47)
Furthermore, it is divided into two types: that which is perceptible and that which is imperceptible.
One should consider each of these two to be twofold again, according to whether they are manifest or unmanifest. (6.48)

"Effort" (*yatna*) refers to the vital impulse (*spanda*). That which consists merely of the act of living is the natural [effort], by means of which there would otherwise be a state of rigidity in the limbs. That which is directed toward an object is preceded by volition (*icchā*). Thus, since each of the four [types of effort] is twofold, it is established that the vital impulse (*prāṇīya*) is eightfold.
In that regard, the natural effort pertaining to the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed perceived from the bulb (kanda) onwards, yet only in an indistinct manner— as he says:
"It is beautiful with the vibration of the effort known as the perceptible life-force."
The vital breath (prāṇa) begins from the bulb (kanda), yet even so, it is not clearly manifest here.
It is with this very intention that the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra* states that the abiding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest begins from that point; thus he says:
"Therefore, the systematic arrangement is said to begin precisely from the support of the *kanda*."
In the Svacchanda Śāstra, it is clearly stated that the channels serve as the support for the vital winds. (6.50)
"By that" means by the reason of the breath being an object of perception (*saṃvedyatva*).
As it has been stated therein:
"It is situated below the navel, in the bulb of the penis, and indeed in the center of the navel."
"Therefore, O Dear One, the channels have issued forth from that [center], extending sideways, upwards, and downwards. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.8) || 50 ||
Now, if this is so, it is stated in that very [text]:
"The cakras of the heart are declared to be beneficial for practitioners;
indeed, the vital breath (prāṇa) moves through them according to the division of day and night."
"I shall explain that to you clearly by analyzing it in detail," and so forth.
Having thus expanded [the teaching] starting from the heart, why was the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) mentioned again?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Moreover, even there, this effort does not exist as something perceptible.
For "there," in the foundation of the *kanda*, even this effort preceded by will is not clearly perceived;
thus, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) has not been described there in detail. Indeed, it is not [perceived] through its own inherent nature.

There is some fruit from the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) as previously described; for when the vital breath is moved by the yogi’s own will for the sake of various specific accomplishments (siddhis), it serves that purpose for which such instruction exists. And that [movement] occurs starting precisely from the heart—thus it has been indicated in that very place in such a manner.
And this is exactly what we also say; thus he says:
"But by the effort of the object of knowledge, the movement of the vital breath is differentiated from the Heart. (51)

Regarding the phrase "from the effort of the object of knowledge," this refers to that which is preceded by desire for an object. As for the word "is divided," the meaning is that it is spoken of as being divided into the nature of *tuṭi* and so forth. || 51 ||

Now, one might object: "Even though vitalization (*prāṇana*) is everywhere without distinction due to its pervasiveness, what is the cause that its effort is perceived clearly in some places and otherwise in others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The power of the Lord Śiva which is Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā..."
Of these hundred, any one of them is more vital than the life-force of the self, for it exerts effort.

In this context, indeed, the self and the vital breath (prāṇa), acting in conjunction with any one of those powers— Vāmā and the rest— belonging to the Supreme Lord, exert effort; the meaning is that these three— the power of the Lord, the self, and the vital breath— united together produce the vibration of the vital breath.
As it has been said:
"In that regard, the Self, the power of the Lord, and indeed the vital breath move through the channels" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.7). || 52 ||
Thus, although these [powers] alike require effort to be manifested, the predominance of one or another occurs in specific instances; as he says:
"The power of the Lord (prabhu-śakti) is predominant in some cases, such as in the contraction and vibration of the *kanda*;
the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) is predominant in others, such as in the impelling of the winds within the limbs. (6.53)
In some cases, the power of the self is manifest in the movement of the vital breath, as it is clearly so in the heart;
for attentive yogins, either all three or two of these may be primary.
Regarding "the movement of the limbs," such as the twitching of the eyes and so forth:

for in this case, it is the power of the Lord alone that acts primarily as the agent in the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the purpose of manifesting future auspicious or inauspicious omens. Regarding "of the *kanda*," which is the organ of bliss, [it refers to its state] consisting of contraction and expansion.

In the act of vibration (*spandana*), the Self alone possesses primacy, for its very will is the cause therein. Furthermore, in the heart, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone possesses agency in vibration due to its spontaneous flow as the primary factor; yet these two exist everywhere in a subordinate state, because otherwise such a condition would be impossible.
Having thus described their relationship as primary and secondary by virtue of being natural (*svārasika*),
he now explains it also by virtue of being effortful (*prāyatnika*) with the words beginning with "the triad. For yogins who desire various specific fruits,
wherever they apply the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through an intensity of concentration, there indeed they [apply] the Self (*ātman*) and the power of the Lord (*prabhu-śakti*).
Or any one of those [other] [54].
Not only does the relationship between these [powers] consist of primary and secondary status, but it may also be otherwise; thus he says:
"Due to attentiveness, the unseen portion, strength, or impulse, there may even be a reversal regarding the primary status of the powers of the vital breath and the self. (6.55)
For example, even a skilled person opens their eyes through their own focused attention—

herein lies the primacy of the self. For example, even in the case of cows, by the force of impressions from previous births, a specific limb [is raised] through the natural power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*) alone, due to the factor of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Since it is that [power] alone which manifests here, it possesses primacy. This is because of its strength; for example, through the mastery of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) acquired by means of practice such as wrestling and the like, feats such as various leaps are accomplished.
As for "impelling" (*īraṇa*), it refers to those overcome by wind (or *vāta*); even though their vital energy is strong, [the movement occurs] only through the sovereign power (*prabhu-śakti*).
The movement of those respective limbs occurs—thus, that [particular limb] alone possesses primacy.

In this way, it is established that wherever these [limbs] exist in a state of intensity, there alone is the effort belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) clearly perceived; otherwise, however, it is not so. || 55 ||
Now, one might object: "If the power of the Lord (prabhu-śakti) exerts a vital effort (prāṇīya-yatna) together with the self and the vital breath, let that be so;
but for what purpose has its threefold nature been stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Vāmā is the sovereign power of the Lord that ordains [the state] of transmigratory beings."
Jyeṣṭhā is for those who are well-awakened, while Raudrī is for those who desire to know.
The term "vidhāyinī" means that she performs the effort pertaining to the vital breath (prāṇa). || 56 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for this?", he says:
"Vāmā is so called because she emits (vamati) the cycle of transmigration; Jyeṣṭhā, because she consists of Śiva;
Raudrī, because she dissolves (drāvayitrī) afflictions and obstructs (roddhrī) all karmas. (57)

Are the powers beginning with Vāmā those belonging to Prabhava, whose nature consists of emanation, withdrawal, and maintenance? Thus, they exert their vital effort in such a way that for worldly beings there may be a downward fall from level to level,
while for the well-awakened there is the attainment of the state of Śiva, and for those desiring to know, [the same].

By being oriented toward the state of Śiva, one remains even within saṃsāra itself. As it has been said: "Raudrī may cast down the individual soul (aṇu) who perceives its own true nature; she may at times bestow the bliss of saṃsāra."
"But Jyeṣṭhā extends even a slight degree of independence regarding knowledge and action.
One might object: "Surely this would be established by its own inherent force; what is the point of teaching it in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Without knowing the reality of emanation and the other [phases], one is neither liberated nor can one liberate others.
Anticipating the further doubt, "What is the proof for this?", he says:
And it is said in the Śrīyogacāra: "Liberation results from the illumination of everything. (6.58)

"Because of the manifestation of everything" means because of the thorough knowledge of everything, such as creation and so forth, according to its true nature; the sense is that nothing else whatsoever could possibly exist apart from that.
Therefore he says:
"Those yogins who do not know [the Lord's] emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal are not liberated; they remain permeated solely by the bondage of ignorance regarding those [powers]. (6.59)
"That ignorance" is the lack of awareness regarding the reality of creation and so forth. || 59 ||
And what, then, is the relevance of this to the present subject? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"All those [processes], beginning with emission (sṛṣṭi), are undoubtedly dependent on time;
and that [time] consists of the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, its manifestation (uccāra) is clearly explained. (6.60)
"They are dependent on time" because creation, maintenance, and withdrawal consist of a sequential process.

"Uccāra" refers to the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa); the intention is that through its explanation, there will arise a thorough knowledge of creation and the other processes according to their true nature. || 60 ||

Regarding this, he says: "The movement of the vital breath from the heart to the end of the twelve finger-breadths at the nose is thirty-six finger-breadths long for every living being, according to the sequence of their own finger-measures. (6.61)
The *nāsikā* is the power (*śakti*) because it moves crookedly (*kuṭilaṃ gacchati*); that which belongs to it is the *ṅāsikya*. The *śākta* is the *dvādaśānta*. As it has been said:
"The movement of thirty-six finger-breadths extends from the heart-lotus up to the *śakti*" (Svacchandatantra 4.235).
Thus [ends the verse]. 61.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, how does this apply to a body related to something as minute as a mosquito, or to one as vast as that belonging to an elephant? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whether the body be most minute or most massive, it is indeed of that same nature."
"Such" means exactly thirty-six finger-breadths, but with respect to one's own fingers.

Furthermore, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) alone is not the same for every living being; rather, [their] vigor (*vīrya*), vitality (*ojas*), strength (*bala*), and pulsation (*spanda*) are also [different]. Thus he says:
"Vigor, vitality, strength, pulsation, and the movement of the vital breath are equal [to one another] from that [source]. (6.62)

This is the intended meaning here: for this entire expansion—in which the multitude of living beings, whether most minute or most vast, unfolds—is indeed consciousness alone; and there is no distinction whatsoever in it anywhere. As it has been said:
"That very consciousness which shines in the sun, the ornament of the expanse of the sky..."
"Even that same consciousness [resides] within the belly of an insect, as it does within the cavity of the earth" (Vāsiṣṭha).

Furthermore, regarding the potency (*vīrya*) and other qualities deposited therein—we perceive no cause whatsoever for any distinction among them. As for the gradation (*tāratamya*) that is observed among these, in that regard—
It is karma that is at fault for its diversity, insofar as it causes even men to excel one another in terms of vigor and other qualities. || 62 ||
Having thus explained the measurement of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) along with its foundational framework,
he now proceeds to analyze the day and night and so forth, which were indicated in the subsequent enumeration immediately following that:
"In the thirty-six-finger movement, there is a pair consisting of going and returning."
The groups of nāḍīs, lunar days, months, years, and their aggregates are clearly situated here.
"Gamāgamau" refers to the ascent and descent in the form of the prāṇa and apāna breaths. By that word, there is a reference to all [channels], such as the nāḍikā and so forth. || 63 ||
He analyzes this very [process] in sequence: "A *tuṭi* consists of one breath plus one and a quarter finger-breadths; sixteen of those constitute an inhalation (*ucchvasana*).
An exhalation (*niḥśvasana*) here is likewise a *caṣaka*, occurring at every finger-breadth plus a fifth part. (6.64)
The tube of inhalation and exhalation is said to be the day and night;
nine finger-breadths correspond to four *tuṭis*, those [four] are the watches (*prahara*), and four [watches] are a day.
"At the exit [of the breath] there is night within; by that [nocturnal period], the two twilights occupy two *tuṭis*.

A *tuṭi* is said to be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) plus a quarter-part. Thus, when multiplied sixteenfold, they become thirty-six finger-breadths, as it is stated: "The vital breath (*prāṇa*), exhaling, consists of those sixteen [twilights]."
It has been stated that this is also the case during the flow of the *apāna* in the passage, “and while breathing out”; thus, there are thirty-two *tuṭis* in both [the flows]. As it is said:
“In the flow dependent upon the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, thirty-two *tuṭis* are established.”

Thus, here, in the movement of the breath (prāṇacāra) which consists of thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula), there is one caṣaka for every finger-breadth plus a fifth part; thus, when the flow of the breath is divided into thirty parts,
there are thirty caṣakas, and it is the same in the flow of the downward breath (apāna).
Through the union of both the prāṇa and apāna breaths, there arises the *ghaṭikā*, which consists of sixty *caṣakas*;

thus it is said: "The channel (*nāḍī*) of inhalation and exhalation has been described. Regarding "in the exit," that is, in the outward expansion of the *prāṇa*, [this occurs] "in nine-finger-breadths and four *tuṭis*," meaning within the four positions of the nine finger-breadths.
The meaning is that a *prahara* arises within nine *tuṭis*, which correspond to nine finger-breadths (*aṅgulis*). As it has been said:
"A *prahara* shall consist of nine finger-breadths. Thus, those *praharas*, measured at nine finger-breadths each, are "four oceans," meaning four in number.
From the sense of "alternating," this refers to the arising of the apāna breath; thus, the night also consists of four watches. As it has been said:
"A day and night [is measured] by eight... (Svacchanda Tantra 7.28). And these two, prāṇa and apāna, are "the sun and moon," meaning they become the sun and the moon.
As it has been said:
"The sun moves during the day, while the moon moves within the stream;
for this is indeed the rising of the moon and the sun... (Svacchandatantra 7.40).
Thus, at the junctions of those two— night and day, which consist of the prāṇa and apāna breaths— occurring respectively at the dvādaśānta and the heart,

that is, at the half-tuṭi intervals, there is a conjunction of the final half-tuṭi of the prāṇic [breath] and the final half-tuṭi of the apānic [breath] during each of the evening and morning twilights.

The meaning is that the entire *tuṭi* is the locus of emergence (*udayasthāna*). For this very reason, there are two *tuṭis* for the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*) and thirty *tuṭis* for the day and night. As they say:
"Excluding the time of twilight, the day and night consists of thirty *tuṭis*."
Thus [it is said]. As for that which was stated:

"O Goddess of the gods, at the end of the fourth [tuṭi], the sun of the vital breath (prāṇasūrya) is always set; therefore, O Beloved, the twilight of setting here consists of one-quarter of a tuṭi" (Svacchandatantra 7.36).
Thus it is said:
"O lady of excellent hips, when the time of dawn has reached the heart-lotus, then half a *tuṭi* constitutes the morning twilight (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*). (Svacchanda Tantra 7.39)
Thus, what has been stated above should be understood as referring exclusively to the flow of the *prāṇa* and the flow of the *apāna*. Likewise:
"In the middle and upper portion of the Power (*śakti*), that which is proclaimed as half a *tuṭi*..."

"In this [moment], the junction of the two wings (*pakṣasaṃdhi*) is to be known... (Svacchandatantra 7.68). This same intention should be applied even to the passage concerning the junction of the wings; otherwise, one *tuṭi* would remain without an assigned function. || 65 ||
It is not only the rising of the sun and moon here that occurs, but also that of the other planets; thus he says:
"Ketu [rises] in the sun, Rāhu in the moon, and [the others] in the lords of the days beginning with Mars. (6.66)
The rising of the other planets occurs at intervals of two *praharas*.
Ketu is included within the Sun, and likewise Rāhu within the Moon; thus, the meaning is that the very rising of the Sun and Moon is itself the rising of these two. As it has been said:

"Rāhu moves with the Moon; Ketu moves with the Sun" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.42). Furthermore, the planets beginning with Mars, who possess their own days (*vārabhāgin*), rise for two watches (*prahara*);
this is because they enjoy [the day] through four half-watches at the beginning and end of each day-and-night (*ahorātra*). As for the others...
Between the sixth and fifth planets, each rises for one *prahara* every day and night, due to being enjoyed for two half-*praharas*. As it has been said:
"One should know that the first eighth part belongs to the lord of the day, and likewise at the end of the day."
"The remaining planets consume the hour by means of six revolutions at night, and by five during the day.
Thus [ends verse 66].
Right here, beginning from the first half-watch, he indicates the results in sequence:
"Success, liberation, sorcery, and that which pertains to the next world. (6.67)

Regarding the worldly [attainment], there are seven divisions based on the excellence of distance and proximity during the eight watches of the day, beginning with the statement that "success is most remote" and so forth. (67)
Raising the objection, "But how is it that although the dawn of the twilight (saṃdhyā) occurs in four ways, it is described as being only of two kinds? he says:
"At midday and midnight, Abhijit bestows liberation and enjoyment. (6.68)
It conquers all obstacles, thus it is the specific lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) called Abhijit. As it is said: "At midday and at midnight, the rising of Abhijit occurs;
therein, the desired fruit shall accrue to practitioners in this world. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.47)
Thus;
and that [should be understood] to be in the palate. As it has been said:
"............ midday is from the middle of the palate. (7.33)
Thus [ends the verse]. 68.
It is not only Abhijit that rises here, but even Aśvinī and the others as well; thus he says:
"The rising of the other constellations occurs in sequence from the middle. By "the others," he means the zodiacal signs, stars, and so forth. As it has been said:
"The lunar mansions, the zodiac signs, the stars, and likewise the degrees—
these indeed arise within the vital breath during a day and night, O lady of virtuous vows" (Svacchandatantra 7.31).
And here, the point of emergence for the lunar mansions is one finger-breadth plus a third.
In this way, the rising positions for others should also be conceived according to their respective numbers.
Furthermore, during the eight watches (prahara), it is not only the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) that rise, but others as well; thus he says:
"The Nāgas, the Lords of the World, the Mūrtīśas, and the Gaṇeśas [arise] from the water-element. (6.69)
The leaders ending with Pradhāna are the presiding lords of the Vidyā-tattva;
likewise, there are the Bhairavas beginning with Sakala and ending with Kaṇṭhyoṣṭhya.
The powers of the Supreme Lord, the Vāmeśīs, and the Vīranāyakas—those eight and those eight who thus partake in the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader. (6–71)
Their emergence, both gross and subtle, occurs sequentially during the eight watches (*prahara*).
"The *nāgas*" refers to Ananta and the others. As it has been said:
"The Sun is called Ananta, and the Moon is said to be Vāsuki."
Takṣaka is said to be Kuja, and Kārkoṭa shall be born from Soma.
Saroja is declared to be Jupiter; Mahābja is said to be Venus;
Śaṅkha is to be known as Saturn; these are the seven serpents corresponding to the planets in order.

"The eighth, named Kulika, shall be the cruel planet Rāhu. And while these [planets] rise according to the sequence of six revolutions and so forth, just like the [other] planets, the rising of Kulika occurs simultaneously with that of Śaṅkha alone, by means of a slow motion. As it has been said:
"O Dear One, Kulika consumes that time which belongs to Śanaiścara;
he too is declared to be malefic, granting no success in any ritual action.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the rising of Lokeśvara and the others occurs precisely according to the sequence of the first half-prahara and so forth; otherwise, [it would not be so].

Because there is no possibility of conjunction with the eight [categories] for the seven planets; and all these groups of eight will be described on the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*)—therefore they should be understood from that very source. So what is the use of this extensive textual elaboration? As for the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, it consists of grossness and subtlety.

The meaning is that the cause (*hetu*) is pervaded by what is subtle; just as the *nāgas* are the pervaders of the planets, and the Lords of the World (*lokeśvaras*) are the pervaders of those, and so on in an ascending sequence—therefore it is said "in order" (*kramāt*).
As it has been stated:
"Those who are the *grahas* are indeed the *nāgas*, and they are the eight guardians of the world (*lokapālas*).
They are the eight forms, and they are the eight lords of the *gaṇas*" (Svacchandatantra 7.43),
and so forth.

Thus, it should be understood that by this [verse], what was stated previously—namely, "Therefore, on the path of the vital breath, this perception of the universe shines forth" (Tantrāloka 6.45)—is being recalled. || 71 ||
Now, one might object: "If a distinction of results is stated for the eight watches (prahara) [of the day], why is it not so for day and night?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the daytime, the actions are cruel; at night, they are gentle; of this there is no doubt. (6.72)

Now, one might object: "Since the attainment [of results] is impelled by the specific mantras of the twilight rituals (saṃdhyā), and since the fruit also differs according to the distinctions in contemplation—as seen in such passages as 'due to the difference in latent impressions' (vāsanābheda)—how can there be such a fixed rule? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Cruelty or gentleness is determined even by the intention;
therefore, the implication is that at times there may even be a reversal [of these qualities].
Now, one might object: "The fruit of the two junctions has been specified; what then is not [the fruit] of the evening and morning junctions? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Liberation at the end of day and night results from the yoga of pervasive meditation. (6.73)
And these have been taught by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Vīrāvalīkula*:
"At the end of day and night," meaning at the two junctions of evening and morning;
"these" refers to the meditations on pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. (73)
He recites that very [verse]:
"The white and the black, the long and the short, merit and demerit, day and night. (6.74)
If those two are exhausted through initiation, pervasion, meditation, and yoga, then a day and night in the movement of the vital breath is said to be a month. (6.75)
If indeed the two auspicious and inauspicious wings— the white and black forms of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which exist in mutual exclusion and are designated by terms such as "long" and "short"—

are "exhausted" through the striking away of their nature as conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of negation (*apoha*), [they are so exhausted] by virtue of becoming the nature of supreme consciousness, which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

The meaning is that initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs through meditation and yoga by means of that very [consciousness] as it vibrates pervasively; through initiation consisting of knowledge, yoga, and action, liberation becomes entirely unconditioned.
For this indeed is the primary form of pervasion, meditation, and yoga, which exists throughout both the bright and dark fortnights.
Regarding what is called "destruction," it is said therein:
"The two fortnights, white and black, which are proclaimed as long and short,
are the two bonds consisting of merit and demerit— most terrible and fearsome."
Where there occurs the severance of the two, the illusory power (māyā) perishes;
when that has perished, the supreme void (śūnya) is to be known—this indeed is proclaimed as initiation (dīkṣā).
Initiation does not become otherwise effective by the mere shedding of menstrual blood;
nor indeed can liberation be attained through the scriptures, nor through performing sacrifices, nor through officiating at them.
"This is the initiation for those who know Brahman; I declare it is not otherwise.
Likewise, I shall explain the white and black [paths] by means of synonymous names.
