Having begun thus, [the text continues]: "The day is the bright [fortnight], as well as the out-breath... and so forth.
"And unrighteousness and night...
Having thus concluded the discussion on day and night, he introduces the month with the words "day and night," etc.
He states that very [point]:
The day is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*) and the night is the bright fortnight (*śukla*); the two fortnights [are assigned] to ritual acts as before.
"As before" means as in the case of day and night. Therefore, in the dark fortnight, one should perform cruel rites, and elsewhere, gentle ones. As it has been said:
"Performing cruel deeds right there, one may attain success;
however, O lady of excellent vows, auspicious deeds performed during the dark fortnight do not succeed.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"And from that time forward, auspicious actions leading to worldly prosperity will be accomplished for one devoted to meditation and mantras; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is said.
Regarding that very point, he states the division by lunar days (tithi):
"Of those sixteen lunar days that have been mentioned, those which are the first and the last... (6.76).

"Of those two, however, there is a rest at every half; the other lunar days are fifteen," so it is said—referring either to the flow of prāṇa or the flow of apāna. "Of those two" means of the preceding and following *tuṭis*. "Rest" refers to what will be described as the junction of the two fortnights. "At every half" means:

Regarding the *prāṇa* and the *apāna*: from their conjunction, the *tuṭi* (moment) becomes the place of rest, and not half of a *tuṭi*. The word "the other" (*itarā*) means that it is different from the sixteenth *tuṭi*, which was described as being divided into halves as the place of rest in both the heart and the *dvādaśānta*.
As it has been said:
"Half a *tuṭi* both below and above is proclaimed to be the rest; those fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) which are stated to be in the middle are fully described. (7.61)
Thus [ends the verse]. 76.
Regarding this, he states the division of day and night: "The day and night are divided by the lunar day (tithi) at two finger-breadths plus a quarter. (6.77)
Indeed, by virtue of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and repose (*viśrama*), those two alone constitute day and night.
The phrase "is divided" means that it is established through a division characterized by the nature of manifestation and repose.
For in some cases there is the predominance of manifestation, and in others, the predominance of bliss (*ānanda*), which is the nature of repose.

In this regard, it has been stated that when luminosity predominates it is day, whereas otherwise it is night, according to the verse: "For those two alone are day and night. Therefore, the first half of each *tuṭi*, measuring eight-eighths of an *aṅgula*, is day in the form of luminosity; the other [half]...
But the night is that which consists of rest. As it has been said:
"In the first emergence [of consciousness], from the heart-lotus, half a *tuṭi* shall be the day; and when it moves during the second half of the *tuṭi*, that is the night. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.62)
Thus [ends the verse]. 77.
Now, let it be granted that the division of day and night was described according to the varying degrees of light and rest; what is the harm in that?
However, as for that which was further stated regarding the internal form of prāṇa and apāna, even by transcending the sequence of external day and night—what of it?

Anticipating the objection—"Does not the abiding of these two, measured by the interval of a *tuṭi*, while transcending the division of day and night, appear to us as something unprecedented?"—he says:
"Because consciousness, at every moment, is conjoined with light and bliss. (6.78)
Day and night are fashioned by her to exactly that same extent;
"at every moment" means she is always composed of light and bliss. And for this reason, consciousness arises for subjects in such a manner.

Due to the gradation in the predominance of the apprehension of the object of knowledge and so forth, for one it may be a moment, for another a kalpa, or even for another a mere blink of an eye. || 78 ||
For this very reason, he says:
"To whatever extent consciousness has arisen, having become increasingly clear... (6.79).
Whether that [moment] be a single instant, an eon, or even a blink of an eye—let it be so.

Even if this were the case, what fault would there be? In that regard as well, does her orientation toward grasping the object of knowledge and her orientation toward resting within herself exist with equal status, or otherwise?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The very extent of the arising of consciousness is solely intent upon grasping the single object of knowledge. (6.80)
At that very moment occurs the setting [of the sun], which is the savoring of the knower’s own self.
The word “of consciousness” (*vitteḥ*) refers to *saṃvid*. “Setting” means the submergence of the manifestation of the object of knowledge.
“Savoring” means repose. And by the two uses of the particle *eva*, their absolute identity is illuminated. (80)

One might object: "Even if [the mind] is intent on resting within its own self, since internal objects such as pleasure and so forth—which are to be known—exist, its orientation toward grasping them would not be lost; how then could these two [states] be of equal rank?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And whether it be the object of knowledge—whether external, internal, both, or devoid of both— || 6.81 ||
In every respect, identification with that [object] is "day," while abiding in the knower is "night.

Whether the so-called object of knowledge exists externally or internally, or does not exist at all—what does this matter? For as long as there is identification with that, it is entirely "day," which is to say, abiding in the knower and resting in one's own self.
"Night" is what we intend here; therefore, as long as there is the grasping of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), that is "day," whereas otherwise it is "night. As they say:
"Therefore, insofar as there is [grasping] by this [consciousness] upon the ground of the resting of the grasper and the grasped..."

"In that state, day and night appear as those very forms consisting of light and bliss. Therefore, day and night possess an equal status, and thus there is no fixed rule. By the phrase "abandoned by both," the impossibility of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is merely reinforced; its actual occurrence in such a manner is not demonstrated.
For no object of cognition whatsoever can exist that is not of the nature of either internal or external. || 81 ||

Now, one might ask: "Is this distinction that was mentioned regarding consciousness—based on the predominance of either manifestation (prakāśa) or reflective awareness (vimarśa)—possible for subjects as well, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The knower [of objects] rests in the object of knowledge; the knower [of the self], however, abides in an inward-turned state. (6.82)

The term *veditā* means the knower; the term *vettā* means the one who deliberates or reflects—this is the meaning. Thus, there is a twofold nature even for the subject (*pramātṛ*), as in one case the predominance belongs to light (*prakāśa*) and in the other to reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). || 82 ||
The knower (*vettā*) is also twofold—thus he says:
"First reflecting, and afterwards having the nature of pure existence (*sattāmātra*).
The sense is that the attainment of one's own essential nature (*svarūpalābha*) occurs only as an inseparable concomitant of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*). Thus it is here.

The sense is that all three types of injunctions— those concerning knowledge (*jñāna*), reflection (*vicāra*), and existence (*sattā*)— must be resorted to, so that the threefold nature of the knower may be established.
In this very context, as a secondary point, he also defines the nature of the waking state and so forth:
"The waking state is the state of being the knower; the dream state is the ancient condition of the subject. (6.83)
The "other" [state] is the fourth, non-dual state, which is sleep at the end of night and day;

it is called "waking" because of the predominance of the resting within the object of knowledge (*vedya*). It is called "ancient" because its nature consists of the state of being the reflector (*vimraṣṭṛ*). It is called "dream" because the object of knowledge is, in some sense, subordinate. The "other" [state]...

Thus, [the state] rests solely in pure existence (*sattāmātra*). It is called "sleep" because of the dissolution of the agitation caused by the objects of knowledge (*vedya*). It is called "non-dual" (*advaya*) because even the differentiation of subjects (*pramātṛbheda*) has melted away. By this, the statement "being the self of the universe is breath-ness" (*viśvātmatā ca prāṇatvam*) and so forth is recalled. || 83 ||
Now, one might ask: what is the cause for the fact that the equality or inequality of night and day occurs sometimes externally? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Sometimes, through the equality of resting in the object, there is a relishing within the self. (6.84)
That equality of the object and the subject is the same as the equality of night and day.

When, indeed, there occurs a state of rest in which the object of knowledge and one's own self are of equal status, that alone constitutes the equality of the object and the subject; and it is by this that the equality of night and day is animated.

That which all yogins declare to be a time of great merit— the equinox (viṣuvat)— is as it has been said: "When, at any time, there occurs the savoring of the resting in the reality through the equality of the object of knowledge and the knower, that is the equality of night and day."
"This is declared by yogins to be the conjunction of time at the equinox. || 84 ||

And thus, through the predominance of the resting of both the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*), there would be an increase in the length of day and night; otherwise, however, there would be a decrease. As it is said:
"In that case, an excess of rest in the object of knowledge leads to the lengthening of the day. (6.85)
In the opposite case, repose in one's own self would be deficient;
for when the longing for one's own self is awakened, repose in the knowable becomes minimal. (6.86)
Regarding the term "deficiency": otherwise, there would be no excess at all in the resting within the object of cognition (*vedya*).

[The word] "would be" implies, by its sense, that it is caused by the decrease of the night. "Inverted" means when there is an excess in resting within one's own self (*svātman*) and the object of cognition is otherwise; for, when there is longing within one's own self...
When the desire for rest reaches its full expansion, the repose within the object of knowledge (*vedya*) becomes minimal, whereby the night is lengthened and the day diminished. As it has been said:
"The expansion of the state of the object of knowledge leads to the lengthening of the day."
"In the same way, the state of resting within one's own self constitutes the expansion of night.
Thus [ends verse 86].
And this very position is the one that is logical here; thus he says: "In this very way, one should state the sequence of the decrease and increase of day and night.
Now, even though the general rule regarding the sequence of night and day exists both internally and externally, [the following applies].

Just as within [the self], by the reasoning already stated, [the subject] is differentiated according to each individual perceiver due to the predominance of either manifestation (*prakāśa*) or reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
so too, externally, is there any differentiation from world to world, or not?— anticipating this doubt, he says:
Just as in bodies there is no uniformity regarding the deficiency or excess of days and nights, and so forth.
Likewise, it has not been stated that this applies specifically to the cities;
"specifically" refers to the body, for the intention is that by being so [conceived], it would serve as the cause for the attainment of various respective fruits. || 87 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for this division of night and day? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The sun in the expansive sky of the lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka. (6.88)
The illustrious Śambhu has thus proclaimed for me the sequence of day and night;

for this very reason, any other division made by others is simply unacceptable—so says the venerable Guru of the Lineage (Śrīsantānaguru): "He has declared the state of both the awakened and the unawakened. (6.89)
The division of day and night, which begins from the heart and is performed with effort, is non-existent within the bright fortnight, which partakes in the radiance of the inward entry.
How could this very "place of the non-awakened" (abuddhasthāna) become a day?
For that which is called the first vital station of the awakened one (buddha), beginning from the heart and extending as far as the *dvādaśānta*, has a measure of half a *tuṭi*. It is supreme.
It was stated [by you] that "for one who is not awakened"— and by that very statement, which describes the states of the awakened and the unawakened,

a division of night and day has been made according to the propriety of the terminology, such that the state of the awakened is day and the state of the unawakened is night; however, that is incorrect.

If, due to the lack of distinction in its location within the downward flow of *apāna* that enters the interior, the very state of the unawakened— which is conceived as night— were to become day, then there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Nor has this been stated by us out of malice, so that we have not committed the fault of censuring the learned.
Thus he says:
"Enough with this; nor is this out of any envy for my previous doctrine. (6.91)
The disciples have indeed been shown the exclusive vision of the true path. Now he introduces the subject at hand:
"The dark fortnight has been explained; therein is the moon situated within the vital breath. (6.92)
One should discard each single digit (kalā) day by day through the process of depletion;
that which is the fifteenth moment (tuṭi) near the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta), [is the one to be discarded last].

On this new moon day, that waning moon enters the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Because it is predominant therein, it is said to have "entered the vital breath. Thus, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) situated within the stations of the *tuṭis* the sun of the vital breath traverses, on each of those days, the moon of the downward breath (*apāna*) [enters].
By means of the cause consisting of the non-drinking of liquor and so forth, one should "discard each digit" (ekaikāṃ kalāṃ tyajet),
reaching a state of attenuation through the process of diminishing each digit one by one; until,
being diminished because only a single digit remains, it reaches the vicinity of the *dvādaśānta*.

On the new moon day, which consists of fifteen *tuṭis*, one should "enter the sun of the vital breath" (*prāṇārka*); that is, one should become absorbed within it, which is called its external setting. || 93 ||
And this has not been stated without foundation; thus he says: "It is stated in the venerable Kāmikā: 'The supreme Prakṛti is neither above nor below.
Māyā, which is of the nature of Śiva, moves through half-and-half [of the universe] and consists of two sections. (6.94)
One should fill and dissolve the body by means of the nature of the moon and the sun.

Here, indeed, "Parā" is the full [pūrṇā]; for that very reason, she is "of the nature of Śiva" (śivarūpiṇī), inseparable from the possessor of power (śaktimat). She is "Prakṛti," the ground of the universe's manifestation, "Saṃvit," and "Māyā," whose nature is to conceal its own essence.
First surging forth as the nature of the *prāṇa*, it becomes divided into two parts through the nature of *prāṇa* and *apāna*; yet, it does not move solely upward nor solely downward,
but rather moves "half by half" within the right and left channels (*nāḍī*) by way of an upward and downward flow, with an equal distribution.

The meaning is that it flows. For this very reason, the supreme consciousness (parā saṃvit), resting upon the state of prāṇa and apāna, should fill the body by means of the moon-nature through its quality of nourishing, and by means of the sun-nature, it should "dissolve" it—that is, dry it up—due to the waning of the lunar digits themselves. || 94 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for the waning of the lunar digits? he says:
"The nectar, in the form of the moon, is twofold and again sixteenfold. (6.95)
And all the gods drink fifteen digits [of the moon];
the sixteenth digit, Amā, which dwells within the secret cave as the remainder, is the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) that satisfies the universe.

The meaning is this: that nectar which exists divided sixteenfold in the form of the moon is further seen as twofold—consisting of the fifteen digits (*kalās*) whose nature is the visible white form, and consisting of the digit of the extremely pure *ūrṇā* which serves as their substratum. Among those, the fifteen...

All the digits (kalās), both the external ones such as the gods and others, and the internal ones which are the effects of the instruments of cognition, drink [the moon] out of a desire for nourishment, whereby there is a daily diminution of them. It is with this very intention that it is said:
"In whom the Soma is drunk day after day by the gods, the ancestors, and men..."
"Diminishing again and again, he enters... (Sāmbapañcāśikā 8, verse).

This and more has been stated elsewhere. Furthermore, the sixteenth digit known as Amā is the "residual form" (*śeṣarūpā*), because its nature is what remains after the fifteen digits—beginning with Surā—have been withdrawn; for this very reason, it is like being within a cave.
The meaning is that just as an object remains undiminished because it is well-protected, so too is this [the Moon].
Since she nourishes the universe by encompassing its fifteen digits (*kalā*s), for that very reason,
she is called "Amāvāsyā" because of the co-residence (*amā-vāsa*) of these fifteen digits with her, who is *amā* (the New Moon).

The meaning is that [the designation] applies to that [deity]. However, regarding the lunar day (tithi), the intention is that the designation "that" is applied figuratively because the deity presides over it. || 96 ||
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand:
"In this way, fifteen digits (kalās) of the moon wane successively;
however, the sixteenth digit does not [wane], because of its identity with the nectar-bearing, nourishing [digit]. (6.97)
The sixteenth digit, however, does not wane; the intention is that the sun is unable to diminish it because of its identity with the moon. || 97 ||
Now he shows the junction of the dark and light fortnights that occurs immediately following this:
"In that regard, that fifteenth *tuṭi* is when the moon has completely waned."
That half-tuṭi which follows it is proclaimed to be the junction of the fortnights (pakṣasaṃdhi).

The fifteenth *tuṭi* is the place where the new moon (*amāvāsya*) arises; for this very reason, it is called "the moon that has waned. As for the word "that," it refers to the sixteenth *tuṭi* belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 98 ||
Now, one might object: "A junction (*saṃdhi*) occurs between two things; so how could this belong to the single half-tithi of the vital breath alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, from that half-tithi of rest, the first part belongs to the new moon."
The conjunction is conceived as being half of the subsequent [syllable] and half of the preceding one.
Relying on that final half-tuṭi of the inhaled breath (*prāṇīya*),
which belongs to the first half of the month— the new moon (*amāvāsya*)— one reaches the "prior half," and then the "subsequent" second half,
which belongs to the exhaled breath (*apānīya*), is the first half of the first lunar day (*prātipada*) connected to that.
Thus, by the conjunction of these two halves, this junction (*sandhi*), which consists of a single *tuṭi* and exists within the interval between the new moons at every step, is postulated;
the meaning is that it is designated in such a manner. As it has been said:
"The junction of the fortnights is that which lies between the first day [of the lunar month] and the fifteenth.
(Amara-kośa 1.4.7). This very point has been stated elsewhere as the primary time for worship:
"One should not worship the God by day, nor indeed at night."

"One should worship the Lord of the God of Gods at the end of day and night. In this context, if the junction (*sandhi*) is explained as being divided by half of a half within the very half-*tuṭi* of rest, then both junctions would likewise consist of only one *tuṭi* each by way of that half-of-a-half division.
Thus, because there would be no application for even a single *tuṣṭi*, the result would be inconsistency; enough of this prolixity.

Having thus demonstrated the emergence of the two fortnights within the vital breath (prāṇa), he now shows the solar eclipse as well: "In that case, on the first lunar day (pratipad), during that half of a half-tuṭi, the [solar] portion enters from the front;
at the end of the lunar day (tithi), it effects a solar eclipse. (6.100)
Half and half is "half-of-a-half"; half-of-a-half of a *tuṭi* is "half-of-a-half of a *tuṭi*.
When that is conceived as a junction (*sandhi*), the meaning is: in those two halves of a *tuṭi*.
This being the case, from the middle of those two halves of a *tuṭi*, the first half belongs to *Āmāvasyā*.

By implication, when the lunar day (tithi) is cut off from the subsequent first lunar day (*pratipad*), which is designated by the term "debt" (*ṛṇa*) as will be explained later, that [cut-off] should perform a solar eclipse;
the meaning is that a solar eclipse occurs due to the conjunction of the first lunar day and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). || 100 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But how can a solar eclipse occur from this alone? he says:
"In that solar orb, the moon is dissolved, and it drips nectar."
Because it was heated, the son of Siṃhikā, who is born together with the moon, drank that [nectar].

"Madhu" means nectar (*amṛta*). The phrase "due to being heated" refers to its proximity to the sun according to its respective position. The expression "co-existent with the moon" is because of their constant association, as stated in such passages as "Rāhu [is present] during the lunar day" (*vidhau rāhuḥ*);
otherwise, the conjunction of these three would not occur—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"O Goddess, at that time the lunar orb appears within the solar orb;
within that [lunar orb], O fair-faced one, Rāhu resides, seeking the nectar."
"The moon flows with nectar, and Rāhu swallows it;
having drunk it, he releases that orb, and then he is said to be liberated. (Svacchandatantra 7.70) || 101 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the true nature when these three are conjoined? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The sun is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while the moon is the object of knowledge (*meya*), consisting of cognition and action;
Rāhu is the subject (*pramātṛ*) characterized by *māyā*, who is skilled in concealing them. (6.102)
For that very reason, being of the nature of *tamas*, it is incapable of dissolving them;

the "concealment" (*ācchādana*) of those two— namely, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— is their disappearance through the process of identifying them with one's own self, and not an absolute dissolution, since they may reappear in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Because of the greatness of the awakener (bodhaka), there is the occurrence of its arising; for this very reason it is said, "incapable of dissolving [it].
"Thence" means because of its nature as a concealer; for the very essence of darkness (tamas) is indeed its quality of obscuring. || 102 ||
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, who is capable of performing this dissolution?", he says:
"The primary subject who effects the dissolution is the manifestation of the non-dual union with That. (6.103)
The "clashing" (*saṅghaṭṭa*) of those [three]—the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object—is their state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*);

from that, the non-dual alone shines forth as the primary knower (*pramātṛ*). By the clashing of that triad, he is the one whose essence is solely supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvinmātra*), which is the meaning of the term *vilāpaka*. As they say:
The mother of the sky, longing for the nectar-essence melted by the moon that has been forcibly struck by the sun of the vital breath,
indeed veils the sun with Rāhu, yet she [bestows] the essence.
"In this auspicious planetary moment, one who knows the friction of the three [centers] should experience [the state].
Thus, [verse 103].
For this very reason, this time is of great merit; thus he says:
"Due to the conjunction of the sun, moon, and Rāhu, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower [become one].
Therefore, because of that non-duality, this great eclipse is meritorious. (6.104)

The meaning is that they exist as non-dual, having consciousness alone as their essence. As it has been said: "When these three planets—Rāhu, the Sun, and the Moon—are seen in conjunction, that becomes a 'Great Eclipse' (Mahāgrahaṇa)."
"That time shall be the most meritorious of all times for all the worlds. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.73) || 104 ||

Now, one might wonder: does this conjunction of the sun and other [planets] occur only on every new moon (*amāvāsya*), or could it happen otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even without the new moon, if this conjunction occurs, it is a 'great eclipse' (*mahāgraha*)."
Just as when the Sun is in Aries, Rāhu is situated in Aśvinī, and it is the day of Aśvinī.
Even if this conjunction should occur on the first lunar day (pratipad) while it is still pure, even without the new moon (amāvasyā),
this would certainly be a great eclipse;
just as externally, because the moon, sun, and Rāhu remain in Aśvinī alone, they are in a single asterism (ekarkṣa).

On the new moon day of Vaiśākha, after two watches have passed, an eclipse of the sun may occur on the first lunar day (pratipad) itself, provided it is pure [without overlap], because the parallax (lambana) is additive and the half-duration of the eclipse is less than the parallax. This is the case wherever...

When there is a conjunction of the new moon (amāvāsyā) with the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), a solar eclipse occurs; in that case, the commencement (pragrahaṇa) takes place on the new moon day, while the release (mokṣa) occurs on the first day of the fortnight. Otherwise, it is established by implication that both [the commencement and the release] occur on the first day of the fortnight itself. || 105 ||
He says that very thing: "When half of the new moon day has dissolved into the first lunar day (pratipad), and the pratipad is pure, that is liberation when the moon is far removed. (6.106)
And it has been stated that the cause for her liberation from that [bondage] is the moon's distancing, as expressed in the phrase "when the moon is far away.
For when he has become distant, the sense is that Rāhu, who is his companion, would likewise become so. || 106 ||
He shows the reason for the greatness of this [period of] eclipse:

"Between the commencement of the eclipse and its release, bathing, meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth—whether worldly or unworldly—shall yield abundant fruit pertaining to the next world. (6.107)
"Yielding abundant fruit" means it yields the ultimate fruit. As it has been said:
"O Goddess, whatever bathing, giving, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth is performed by practitioners there, that shall yield the ultimate fruit. (Svacchandatantra 7.74)
Thus [ends the verse]. 107.
He states the reason for its pertaining to the other world:

"Entering for a moment when the agitation of the state of being the swallowed and the swallower has ceased, one partakes of liberation; likewise, meditation, worship, and so forth [are effective] during an eclipse of the moon or sun. (6.108)

In this context, when there is an eclipse of the moon or sun— that is, during a solar eclipse— the yogi, entering into the Supreme Subject whose nature is the dissolution of that "disturbance" (kṣobha) which consists of the relationship between the "devourer and the devoured" (the subject and the object of knowledge), and relying upon the supreme state, should practice meditation and so forth for even a moment.
The meaning is that by performing [these acts], one is indeed liberated as a participant in liberation (*mokṣabhāk*). As it has been said:
"Having abandoned both sides and by means of the previously mentioned practice, remaining eternally at the end of *unmanī*, one relies upon the supreme state."
"Having abandoned everything below that and having resorted to meditation, one should apply [the mind];
for him there is liberation, no doubt; otherwise, he shall become a possessor of supernatural powers.
Thus [ends verse] 108.
Having stated that [the breath] is the "cutting of the lunar day" (tithiccheda), he characterizes it through the addition of further details:
"The cutting of the lunar day is debt, coughing; increase is exhalation, which is wealth.
That which arises without effort and that which arises with effort [are distinguished] by emission and then by retention. (6.109)

That which, due to the force of *kāsa* (coughing), causes the portion of the new moon (*amāvāsya*) to enter immediately and suddenly into the portion of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) because of the rapid flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is called "debt" (*ṛṇa*); and because of the metaphorical identification of the cause and effect—the cutting of the lunar day (*tithiccheda*)—it is also called *kāsa*. And that which...

Due to the prolonged flow of the downward-moving breath (apāna) by the force of exhalation, there is an increase in the lunar day (tithi), which, through its fullness, is called the rising of the full moon; this is termed "increase" (vṛddhi), "wealth" (dhana), and "exhalation" (niḥśvasana).
Both of these occur spontaneously even for all non-yogins through coughing, asthma, and so forth.

Thus it was said, "born of no effort" (*ayatnajam*); because of this, even when an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs in the interval, it is not perceived by others due to their lack of attention. However, for yogins, it would occur through effort consisting of the exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and so forth, directed toward the yoga of the moon and sun; thus it was said, "born of effort" (*yatnajam*).
As it has been said:

"The cutting off of a lunar day (tithi) should be known as a debt (ṛṇa), and in its increase, it becomes wealth (dhana). Coughing is indeed a debt, while exhalation is called wealth. (Svacchandatantra 7.64)
Thus it is said:
"Likewise, there may be the loss or increase of lunar days, or cough, asthma, and so forth;
these occur either without effort or through effort by means of the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa)."
Thus [ends the verse]. 109.
To extend this very principle to the flow of the apāna as well, he says:
"In this way, as the sun of consciousness enters the moon consisting of nectar within the prāṇa, it should fill it completely, one by one, with the digit of the rays of awakening. (6.110)
These fifteen *tuṭis*, beautiful as the nectar of the moon that fulfills its phases in succession, constitute the lunar days (*tithis*) belonging to the bright fortnight. (6.111)

"In this way," by the very process previously described, as the conscious self— the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇasūrya*)— descends within the *prāṇa* to the end of the heart, it enters; and at every *tuṭi*, through a single digit (*kalā*) consisting of an awakened web of rays, it should completely fill the nectar-filled moon, so that having become one digit on the first lunar day, it becomes two digits on the second.

These fifteen *tuṭis* belonging to the bright fortnight (sitapakṣa) become the lunar days (*tithis*), beautiful with the nectar of the moon which possesses the quality of gradual fulfillment through its nature beginning with "two moments" (*dvikala*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"Whenever the haṃsa of the vital breath reaches the first *tuṭi* below,
the first half is declared to be day, and the other half of the *tuṭi* is night. (7.77), beginning with this [verse].
That is to be known as the Pratipad (the first lunar day), and the moon shall possess a single digit;
on the second [day], however, it increases by one digit in due order.
"And in this same manner, starting from the lunar days (tithis), it continues up to the fifteenth *tuṭi*. (Svacchandatantra 7.79). || 111 ||
And in this very context, he extends [the rule] to the junctions of the lunar fortnights as well:
"At the end of the final *mastuṭī*, there is the junction of the fortnight as before;
and the lunar eclipse occurs at the junction of the first day (*pratipad*), due to the previous entry. (6.112)
In this context, there is great fruit for practitioners in the grasping of the *aihika* [worldly results];
as before, this other month is called the "year" (*abda*) in the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*). (6.113)

"In such a fifteenth *tuṭi* as this, when the moon is full for me," means "as before," that is, by the merging of the two halves of the *tuṭi*. "As before" refers to the entry into that half-*tuṭi* characterized by the junction (*sandhi*) of the previous full moon. And although this...
Although the meaning is already understood through the extension (*atideśa*) of the previous [rule],

it is nevertheless stated explicitly to demonstrate that the lunar eclipse occurs only at the junction (*saṃbheda*) of the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), and not on the *pratipad* alone when it is pure (*śuddhā*). [The term] "pertaining to this world" (*aihika*)...

Because of the predominance of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). "The rest is as before" refers to the union of the subject and the object, and so forth. As they say: "By the sequence of the flow of the nectar-essence overflowing from Power, the atom [of the soul] is said to seize the full moon;
here, during the great auspicious eclipse, the Great Sage drinks that which has been liquefied and concealed."
Thus [it is said]. Now, concluding the section on the month, he introduces the year with the words "This," and so forth. || 113 ||
He says that very thing:

"The Sun, staying in each successive six-finger [intervals] from the heart in the signs beginning with Capricorn, effects the group of six months beginning with Māgha; that is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa). (6.114)

The meaning is that [this applies] from Capricorn (makara) up to Gemini (mithuna); thus, by six fingers multiplied by six, they become thirty-six—this is the intended sense. For indeed, the rising of Capricorn occurs in the month of Māgha, and that of Gemini extends until Āṣāḍha. As it has been said:

"The transition [of the sun] through six finger-breadths occurs during the zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn; that which lasts from the month of Māgha until the end of Āṣāḍha for the sun is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
Thus, verse 114.
Right here he demonstrates the equinoxal transit (viṣuvatsaṅkrānti):
"When the triad of transits has occurred, one experiences [the fruit] within eighteen finger-breadths;
when the sun has reached Aries, there is the meritorious equinox pertaining to the next world. (6.115)
"Eighteen finger-breadths"—this is because of the experience (*bhoga*) of six finger-breadths for each transit (*saṃkrānti*).
"The transit from the heart, which is the place of arising, is said to occur in Capricorn;
having abandoned six finger-breadths below, it transits again into Aquarius."
Having left two finger-breadths above the throat, it then enters Pisces;
then, having left from above the throat down to the end of the palate, it enters Aries.
"The transition [of the breath] extends as far as the tip of the nose, precisely six finger-breadths; this indeed is the equinoctial transition established in the north. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.94).
It is called *viṣuvat* because it is worthy of (*arhati*) pervasion (*viṣu*), that is, equality. "The equinox is trans-worldly."
And although this is possible for the entire northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), it is nevertheless stated here specifically by its own name. As it has been said:
"O virtuous lady, beginning from Capricorn (*makara*) and ending with Gemini (*mithuna*)."
"In this context, the northern course [of the sun] is devoid of the attainment of worldly results" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.97).
Now, one might ask: "If this equinox is trans-worldly (*pāralaukika*), then what is the nature of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But upon entry [into the body], when the sun is situated in Libra, that indeed becomes the equinox."
In this world, this [practice] bestows accomplishment when it occurs during the southern solstice.

"At the entry" means up to the heart by means of the power (*śakti*). "That very [state]" means that which occurs immediately after the three transitions (*saṃkrānti*) consisting of the enjoyment of eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
As it has been said:
O Dear One, when the Sun enters Cancer, the *haṃsa* moves from the base of the *śakti* to the heart;
having traversed six finger-breadths, it then indeed enters Leo.
When six finger-breadths are further abandoned, it again moves into the Kanyā [sign];
when from the tip of the nose to the end of the palate is abandoned, the equinox (viṣuvat) indeed occurs.
"This is said to be the transition of the scale (*tulā-saṃkrānti*), which constitutes the southern equinox" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.113).
Here, it is "bestowing success," as it has been stated:
"Whatever practice (*sādhana*) is performed there, it bestows success in this very life. (116)

Now, one might ask: although the twelve signs beginning with Capricorn are generally characterized by their relation to the next world or this world, does each individual sign not possess some specific distinction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The state of being an embryo, the state of being about to emerge, and then the state of being desirous of emerging."
The state of being about to arise, the commencement of arising, and the stability of arising [are all included]. (6.117)
Birth, existence, transformation, growth, decline, and destruction occur in succession;
therefore, in this system, the action performed in Capricorn and the other signs produces a corresponding fruit. (6.118)
"Garbhatā" (the state of being an embryo) means the act of implanting. One who is about to emerge is a "bhāva," meaning one whose existence (*sattā*) is such;

this refers to the initial vibration of will. "Udbubhūṣu" means desiring to emerge; its "bhāva" or essence is the mere will conjoined with an object of desire characterized by the impulse to emerge. This is the meaning of "udbhaviṣyattvam" (the state of being about to emerge).

"Arising" (*udbhavana*) is abiding as a surging forth within one's own self. "The beginning of arising" (*udbhūtiprārambha*) is density in that very state. "The stability of arising" (*udbhavasthiti*) is directedness toward that very state. Thus, the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn occur in sequence; for it is by this means that the forms beginning with the embryonic stage (*garbhatā*) come into being.

The meaning here is that, by means of this cause, even ritual action (*japādikriyā*)—just like external seeds and so forth—bears fruit that is entirely concordant with the state of the embryo (*garbhatā*) and other stages; it "gives" [the result]. As it has been said:
"Impregnation (*ādhāna*), desire (*icchā*), union (*saṃyoga*), bliss (*ānanda*), density (*ghanatā*), and stability (*sthiti*)."
Birth, existence, transformation, growth, decline, and destruction occur in succession.
"Starting from the month of Māgha, the established rules have been proclaimed for the sake of the accomplishment of practitioners and also for the manifestation of states of being.
Thus [ends verse 118].
Even here, there is a further distinction; thus he says:
"In the practice for the sake of the next world, the Fish, the Jar, and so forth [are required] for the preliminary service of mantra and the rest;
indeed, this group of four, beginning with the Fish, becomes progressively closer. (6.119)

Indeed, at that very entrance, there should be auspicious rites such as those for peace (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi); these yield worldly results, and their fruits appear progressively further and further away.

*Jhaṣa* means the crocodile (*makara*). These two [refer to] one whose mantra is already perfected (*siddhamantra*); however, for one whose mantra is not yet perfected (*asiddhamantra*), there is the tetrad beginning with the fish (*mīna*) for the purpose of serving the mantra and so forth. Regarding the word "at entry," this refers to the flow of the *apāna* breath. As it has been said:
"Starting from that *makara*, [one should perform] meditation, fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and so on."
For the sake of the next world, its fruit shall be boundless.

"For the purpose of *puraścaryā* and the vow of mantra-grasping, one should begin everything for the sake of one's own attainment of mantra-perfection at the start of Pisces [the month of Mīna]," thus [it is said in] the Svacchandatantra (7.103).
Likewise:

"Therefore, for the sake of establishing the self and for the sake of nourishment, one should practice during the time born of the southern solstice, because from that [time] creation is produced. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.110)

Thus, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is intent upon grasping the object of knowledge (*vedya*); therefore, it possesses proximity in the bestowal of results according to their respective natures. The southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), however, is intent upon internal rest; therefore, it possesses distance in the bestowal of results according to their respective natures. For this very reason, during the northern course, [the nature] of the day...
In this case, however, the increase of the night is otherwise.
Regarding this, he says:
"During the outward movement, there is an increase of days; in the opposite case, the reverse occurs.
In this year, there are five lunar days for every finger-breadth; such is the sequence. (6.121)

In that case as well, the rule for day and night is entirely as before. Now, one might object: "Since a year begins with months, their emergence was stated to occur every six finger-breadths; yet those [months] begin with lunar days (tithis)—so why is this not the case here [for the tithis]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Five lunar days (*tithi*) per finger-joint": in that group of six [finger-joints], there are thirty, by which the arising of the month (*māsa*) therein is stated. "There too"—that is, in the fifth part of the finger—therefore, for every tenth part of a finger, there is a day and a night. "The whole" refers to the beginning of the fortnight (*pakṣa*), and by that...
In the first three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), while elsewhere is the other (the bright fortnight). As it has been said:
"In each finger-breadth here, five lunar days (tithis) are established;
half of that is the day, and the latter half becomes the night."
"Those six pentads of lunar days (tithis) constitute the monthly days and nights;
by thirty such days and nights, a month consisting of two fortnights is said to be completed. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.91). || 121 ||
Now, one might object: "According to the logic of the eight watches (prahara), do there exist some presiding deities even for the twelve months, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this solar year, [the presiding deities] are located from the right [side] during the months beginning with Kārttika. (6.122)
The Rudras, ending with Pitāmaha, will be twelve in number hereafter;
as it has been said:
"O Maheśvarī, that Rudra who is mentioned here by the name Dakṣa..."
O Maheśvarī, he indeed eats throughout the entire month of Kārttika.
Caṇḍa is proclaimed as Hara in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
while Śauṇḍī is in the month of Māgha, and likewise Pramatha is in Phālguna.
Bhīma is proclaimed in Caitra, and Manmatha is remembered in Vaiśākha;
Śakuni is in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and likewise Sumati in Āṣāḍha.
"Nanda [is the deity] in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Gopālaka in Bhādra;
and Pitāmaha and Vīreśa belong to the month of Āśvayuja. This is stated in the chapter on the Manifestation of Unification (Agra). 122.
Concluding this, he introduces another topic:
"The arising of the year within the vital breath has been explained; now follows the arising of the twelve-year cycle. (6.123)
In each finger-breadth, there are respectively thirty lunar days; these twelve, beginning with Caitra, are said to arise during the emergence of the twelve years.

Regarding the term *kharasāḥ*: *kha* signifies zero, and *rasāḥ* signifies six; thus, [the total is] sixty. By this, for every finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), there is a season (*ṛtu*); in three finger-breadths, a solstice (*ayana*); and in six, a year (*varṣa*). Thus, within a single movement of the breath (*prāṇacāra*), when the year arises, there are twelve [units] for every set of six finger-breadths.
The intention here is that the emergence of the years occurs in this manner, just as the emergence of the *saṃkrāntis* [occurs]. As it has been said:
"Just as twelve *saṃkrāntis* are proclaimed here in a year, so those years are proclaimed in the breath (*prāṇa*) upon the emergence of twelve years. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.126)
Thus [ends the verse]. 124.
Now, it was previously stated that for Caitra, the arising [of the mantra] occurs in the palate, and therefore from that point onward the service of the mantra and so forth should be performed;
however, here its arising is said to be in the heart. Raising the doubt, "In that case, where should the practitioner now perform the service of the mantra and so forth?", he says:
The arising of Caitra occurs in the palate; he too is now said to be in the heart. Therefore, the arising of Caitra is in the heart, and indeed, the arising of the mantra is there as well.
"It has been said" refers to the arising of the year (*abdodaya*). "Now" refers to the arising of the twelve-year cycle (*dvādaśābdodaya*). || 125 ||
Having thus described the emergence of the twelve-year cycle, he now describes the emergence of the sixty-year cycle as well:

"When three hundred lunar days (tithis) are assigned to each finger-breadth (aṅgula), and when one year occurs within a finger-breadth plus its fifth part, then the state of sixty years occurs within a single breath (prāṇa). (6.126)
There are three hundred and fifteen *tithis* per finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); thus, in one-fifth of a finger-breadth, there are sixty days and nights (*ahorātra*).

In this way, with each finger-breadth plus its fifth part, a year consisting of three hundred and sixty [days] arises. Consequently, since a year arises for every finger-breadth plus its fifth part, the emergence of the *caṣaka* occurs according to the previously stated duration of its emergence.
Within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there is the duration of sixty years; that is to say, sixty years come to pass. As it has been said:
"From the heart-lotus up to the end of Śakti, there is the emergence of thirty years" (Svacchandatantra 7.134).
Thus [ends the verse]. 126.
Right here, he shows the calculation of days and nights: "Twenty-one thousand six hundred;
this division pertaining to the breath is called the day-and-night of sixty years. (6.127)

And here, so that there may be no confusion among the listeners due to seeing something unprecedented, the similarity in the number of breath-movements occurring during external day and night has been brought to light. As it is said:
"Twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths]."
"But the days and nights are reckoned as sixty in a year, O fair-faced one" (Svacchanda Tantra 6.136). || 127 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this division of lunar days (tithis)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The divisions and junctions therein—pertaining to the watches of the day, day and night, months, seasons, years, and the sixty-year cycle of the Sun—are meritorious for meditation and worship. (6.128)
The term *abda* refers to twelve years; *chedaḥ* means completion, and *saṃdhiḥ* means the junction (*saṃdhyā*).

The intention here is as follows: that which is called the daily obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and so forth, might or might not reach completion even with hundreds of external efforts throughout a human lifespan, yet [all of it is accomplished] within a single movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*).
Through focused attention for even a mere moment, following the sequence of watches, days, nights, and so forth, happiness itself shall be accomplished for the yogin. As it has been said:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, and during the fortnights, months, and solstices..."
And that which occurs at the beginnings of the ages, at the ends of the ages, and also within the year;
And in the twelfth year, or in the sixtieth year, O fair-faced one,
[one attains the goal] through bathing, giving gifts, sacrifices, worship, fire-offerings, and recitation.
O lady of excellent limbs, whatever is performed externally during this time through meditation, yoga, and asceticism, one obtains its great fruit as described by him.
"Having understood the movement of the *prāṇa*-swan during its course, one should resort to it for that single [moment]. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.140).
With this very intention, he said:
"The oblations of the *agnihotra* that would amount to seventy-two thousand in the course of a human lifespan..."

"He who, knowing the path, offers oblations even once quickly by means of the conjunction of the channels and parts—he shall accomplish [the goal]," so it has been stated by others. Now, let it be granted that for a yogin, the duties of birth may be accomplished through mere internal attention for a moment; however, this is not [acceptable] to us.
It appears that, after sequentially describing the period from the movement of the internal breath (*nāḍikā*) up to the end of a year,

the mention of twelve years and so forth was made without cause by skipping the sequence of two, three, four, and more years. Even there, it is not the arising of exactly twelve years [that is meant].

Regarding the thirteen [channels], there are exactly sixty, and not fifty-nine; we perceive no reason whatsoever here for the non-mention of anything additional to those—thus we do not understand what this means. To this it is replied: first of all, this may occur here when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been mastered by yogins.

Otherwise, the mastery of the vital breath (*prāṇajaya*) would occur only gradually according to the methods taught in the Yoga scriptures and so forth; for this very reason, it is stated there: "One should step across the unconquered measure," and so on. Therefore, in this context, its arising is said to occur through the sequence of *tuṭi* and so forth, according to their respective degrees of intensity, up to the duration of a year.

Thus, if some yogi who has conquered his vital breath (*prāṇa*) were to bypass the sequence and fail to synchronize the arising of the twelve years therein, that would become a causal factor for him because of the absolute mastery over his *prāṇa*; yet here, as in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), there is no [fixed calculation] of years.

There is no specific sequence intended here by which there might be a transgression [of that sequence]; for as long as a yogi who has mastered his vital breaths (prāṇas) applies his contemplation to whatever object, that very thing becomes directly realized by him—this is what must be stated. And whether it be so or not so, what difference does it make? Nor is there any [difference] here for yogis.

In order to conquer the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there exists a certain intermediate requirement by which a gradual process must necessarily be accepted. Nor should one suddenly attempt a contemplation that is extremely remote; thus, the arising of the twelve-year cycle is taught as being like a series of steps in between. The same should be said regarding the arising of the sixty-year cycle.

Therefore, just as someone who, by consuming poison in a gradual sequence of parts, has digested it, will likewise digest even a large amount of poison if consumed non-sequentially—so too should it be understood here. And this very point is the reason for not mentioning the arising of anything beyond that [limit]. Thus, having reached the supreme pinnacle...

Whatever the yogi should connect with therein, that very thing he shall directly realize—since this is infinite, how much more could be said? Indeed, we perceive no other purpose in stating anything further than this. As it has been said by him elsewhere:
"Beyond the arising of sixty years, it is examined [further] due to its infinity" (Tantrāloka 6.15).

Furthermore, as for what is stated elsewhere regarding the arising of one hundred and twenty additional years, that too is intended merely as an illustration; thus, even a *kalpa* is not fully contained within a single movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*).

It would indeed be directly realized; what contradiction could there possibly be here? As for the objection raised—"How is it that spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*) is said to occur after exactly twelve or sixty years?"—that is indeed a "śiṃśapā" (pointless) objection.
Even if it were designated by another name, such an objection would still find scope;

nevertheless, out of compassion so that the listeners might not be utterly bewildered by the perception of an entirely unprecedented matter, the Blessed One has stated this very thing as being of the same nature as the previous sequence of enumeration. Thus, [there is no fault].
There is no fault whatsoever. || 128 ||
Having thus described the nature of internal time, he now describes it externally as well:
"Thus, this time which arises in the vital breath (prāṇa) and whose singular form is Śakti, abiding within the Self of the universe—its external form is now described. (6.129)

By implication, the phrase "the rising of the vital breath" (prāṇodaya) serves as the reason for its being the self of the universe even during the rising of the downward breath (apāna), as expressed by the words "whose singular form is Śakti.
He states this very point:
"Six breaths constitute a caṣaka; sixty of those make a nālī, and sixty of those likewise [make a muhūrta]."
Thirty such lunar days constitute a month, and twelve of those months make a year.
A year of the ancestors (pitrya) is a day and night [of the gods], measured by the northern and southern solstices;
that which is a year in the measurement of the ancestors is called a divine (divya) year.
Three hundred and sixty human years constitute [one year] here;
"likewise" means exactly sixty. "By its own measure" means by the calculation of its own day-and-night consisting of human units. That which is the year of the ancestors (pitr) is precisely that.

It is called *divya* (divine), meaning that by it the day-and-night (*ahorātra*) and so forth of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and the gods (*devas*) are exactly the same; this is the sense. And as for the measure of that year—whether ancestral or divine—it has been stated: "three hundred and sixty human years. || 131 ||
He analyzes this very point:
"And having multiplied that by twelve, the number of months is obtained here. (6.132)
Furthermore, having multiplied that by thirty, one should state the calculation of days and nights;
and having multiplied that by twenty-one thousand six hundred.
One should state the count of breaths there, and then again the emergence of the sixty-year cycle and so forth.

Regarding the word "that": having multiplied the divine year by twelve—that is, having divided it by twelve—therefore, here, the twelfth part consisting of thirty human years is a month. Regarding the word "that" (tām):

Having multiplied the number of months by thirty—that is, having divided them into thirty parts—the thirtieth part of a human year here constitutes one divine day and night (*ahorātra*). Regarding the phrase "that [measure]," it refers to the calculation of a day and night consisting of three hundred and sixty human days; [this is further multiplied] by twenty-one.
"Having struck by six hundred and [six] thousand" means having divided it into parts according to that principle.
For in this way, for every human *nālikā*, there would be a divine movement of breath (*prāṇacāra*); such is the intended meaning.
Thus, it is declared that the number of breath-movements remains exactly the same everywhere in every daily cycle.
The word "there" (tatra) refers to the enumeration of the vital breaths (prāṇa); the meaning is "again," as in the expression "as if. || 133 ||

Now, one might object: "Have others not stated that a year of the ancestors is a day of the gods? How then is their equality asserted here? Is there any supporting evidence for this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it has been stated by the Teachers in their own commentaries on the Śrīmad-Raurava and other scriptures. (6.134)
He recites that very [verse]:
"That which is one day and night of the gods is a year for humans;
by three hundred and sixty human years, there is one year of the gods. (6.135)
That which is a day for the ancestors is a year for humans; of this there is no dispute.

Since it is stated that it is likewise for the gods as well, the equality of these two is established by implication. In the phrase "of men" (nṛṇām), the word "of years" (hāyanānām) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This has been stated not only by the teachers, but the scripture as well speaks in this very way; thus he says:
"In the venerable Svacchanda Śāstra, that same view is observed, beginning with [the statement] 'that is a day and night of the ancestors,' and continuing thereafter. (6.136)
Thus, the divine day-and-night is indeed concluded as a unity.
"Behind" means subsequently. As it was stated therein:
"The southern solstice is night, and the northern solstice is day."
That is a day and night of the ancestors; by this measure, a year is as previously described.
"In this way, the day and night are divine; there too, the year and so forth are as before. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.208). || 136 ||
Thus, what has been stated by others—that a year of the ancestors (pitrya-varṣa) is a day of the gods—is indeed incorrect;
so he says:
"Therefore, those teachers who [rely] on the two statements from the venerable Svacchanda-tantra... (6.137).
Those who are deluded have falsely stated that a year of the ancestors (pitrya) is a divine day;

for they are "deluded," the reason for which is given as "due to the two statements, etc. The first statement is "of the ancestors" (pitṝṇām), and the second is "thus, of the gods" (daiva); by the word "etc.," the statement of the author of the *Ruru-vṛtti* is included. || 137 ||
Now, relying on this very [calculation], he also states the arrangement of the beginning of the ages (yuga):
"In the ages, starting from four, there are one thousand divine solar years. (6.138)
With a decrease of one hundred years for each [yuga], there are eight junctions (saṃdhi) among them;
fourteen such periods of four yugas constitute a Manvantara.
There, fourteen Indras pass away from Brahmā’s day in succession.

The "Arkas" are twelve. In all four Yugas, their distribution proceeds by a decrease of one starting from four; thus, there are four thousand [years] in the Kṛta, three thousand in the Tretā, and two thousand in the Dvāpara.

"One *kalā*—thus, ten thousand divine years is the measure of the four *yugas*. He explains the division of the remaining two thousand [years] with the words beginning with 'by those many' (*tāvadbhiḥ*).
By those same numbers—four, three, and so on—there are eight junctures (*saṃdhi*) for the four [ages]."

Because they exist at the beginning and end of the *yugas*, the two combined amount to four hundred years. Thus, one hundred years at the end of the Kali age and four hundred years at the beginning of the Kṛta age constitute five hundred years as the *saṃdhyā* (twilight period) between the Kali and Kṛta ages. Similarly, there are seven hundred years as the *saṃdhyā* between the Kṛta and Tretā ages, and [seven hundred] between the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
Having counted five [ages] for the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas and two thousand [years], the Caturyuga consists of twelve thousand divine years on both sides. As it has been said:
"The Caturyuga should be known as consisting of twelve thousand years."
But it was performed by four thousand [beings], O Goddess, in due order.

"O Goddess, Tretā is to be known [to last] for three [thousand years], while Dvāpara is remembered as being for two; O Beloved, Kali is to be understood as lasting for one thousand years. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.210).
Likewise:
In the Kṛta age, four hundred [years] are proclaimed, with the beginning and the end;
in the Tretā, three hundred are to be known, while in the Dvāpara, there are two hundred.
"And in the Kali age, it should be known as one hundred; this is remembered as the measure of the twilight period" (Svacchanda Tantra 11.212).

"Those" refers to the ends of the Manvantaras. "Therein" means within a day of Brahmā; "fourteen" implies that with each successive Manvantara, one Indra goes to his destruction. Thus it has been said:
"In a single day of Brahmā, fourteen Indras likewise pass away after having ruled in succession according to the arrangement of the Manvantaras" (Svacchanda Tantra 11.229).
For this very reason, room has been provided here even for the diversity of dissolution. || 139 ||
Regarding that, he says: "At the end of the day of Brahmā, there is a flame of the fire of time extending for a hundred thousand yojanas. (6.140)
"Having burned the three worlds with smoke, one should put the other three to sleep.
Regarding "the three worlds," the meaning is from the hells up to the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
As it has been said:
"O Goddess, she would burn the hells and the netherworlds on all sides;
she burns even the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar—to their very ends. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.237)
Thus; "the other" refers to that which is known as the austerity of Mahājana. || 140 ||
Now, one might object: "Is it not heard everywhere that all the Lords of the Worlds (bhuvaneśvaras) perform creation and withdrawal only in a downward direction? And this will be stated further on;
why then has this been stated differently here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because, prior to the hells, the manifestation [of time] arises from the fire of time (kālavahni).
The venerable *Raurava* school maintains that the Lord (*Īśa*) is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), even though he is situated below.

Indeed, his position below [the hells] is because his creation occurs prior to that of the hells, and not because of any deficiency; therefore, although he is situated below them, he is also above them due to his omnipresence.

The meaning is that he is the Lord at the beginning of the withdrawal [of the universe] and so forth. And he says—“Thus is the venerable Raurava doctrine”—to show that this has not been stated by us merely as our own invention. It is said there:
“First, its manifestation arises below the hells.”
"Even though he occupies every place, for that reason he appears as if situated below. || 141 ||
The universe does not exist only in this way, but even when it has become a single ocean; thus he says:
"In the ashes blown away by the breath of Brahman, [it remains] with the water of perspiration. (6.142)
The entire universe remains submerged by that [water] until the arrival of night.
Now, one might ask: "If this is so, then where do the lords of those worlds or the individual souls (jīvas) residing there abide? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
At that time, at the end of the night, all individuals reside within their subtle bodies.
Driven by the force of fire, they exist in this world as individuals who have attained dissolution-only (laya-kevalas);
however, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakas, and others sport in the abode of Mahat.
"Residing in the subtle body" means having the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. For this very reason, it is said that they "sport. || 144 ||
Anticipating the question, "What will happen again at the end of the night? he says:
"At the end of the night, He performs creation again, beginning from the *tāmasa* [state].
Regarding the phrase "beginning from the *tāmasa*," it has been stated as follows:

"First, he creates a *tāmasī* creation, dominated by *tamas*," beginning with this (Svacchandatantra 11.244), [it continues]: "Then, through the infusion of *tamas* and *rajas*, he creates human beings; infused with *rajas* and *sattva*, he creates the lords of the best of sages."
"Having cast off sleep and awakened, that Lord of the World, possessed by *sattva*, shall create the gods and their worlds according to the previous arrangement. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.246).
For one who performs this every day, by calculating days and nights consisting of twenty-eight *manvantaras*, his dissolution occurs at the end of his own hundred years; thus he says:
"At the end of his own hundred years, his destruction occurs—that is the day of Viṣṇu. (145)

And the night is of the same duration; thus, those designated as the hundred Viṣṇus and hundred Rudras perish in succession at the end of their respective hundreds due to the dissolution of the cosmic egg (aṇḍalopa).
He extends this very point to what follows in the subsequent [verses] with the words "That," and so forth. "That" refers to the hundred-year lifespan of Brahmā.
By the phrase "until the dissolution of the Egg" (*aṇḍalopataḥ*), he establishes the limit as the dissolution of the Egg;
thus, the meaning is that upon its destruction, the Brahmāṇḍa (the Cosmic Egg) also perishes. As it has been said:
That day of Viṣṇu is declared, and his night is indeed equal to it;
by this measurement, his year is established.
"And when a full hundred years have passed, he too goes to dissolution in the Supreme.
O Dear One, that which has been stated as the lifespan of Viṣṇu is but a single day for Rudra. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.263).
"When a hundred years have been completed, through the dissolution at the end of the day of the hundred Rudras,
he too goes to the supreme abode... (Svacchanda Tantra 11.271).

"And the hundred Rudras, O Goddess of gods, at the passing of a hundred of their own years, proceed to the supreme reality, and thereafter the cosmic egg perishes" (Svacchandatantra 11.273). And from the destruction of the cosmic egg, the destruction of Kālāgnirudra also follows— this is established by implication.
As it has been said:
"Then Kālāgnirudra shall go to dissolution in the *kālatattva*. (Svacchandatantra 11.277). || 146 ||
This same arrangement applies even up to the unmanifest (avyakta); thus he says:

"In this manner, from water up to the end of the unmanifest principle (tattva), there is a division of day and night in sequence, according to the measure of one hundred years of their respective lifespans. (6.147)
Anticipating the question, "In this established order, what would be the measure of a day for those residing in the Unmanifest? he says:
"By thousands of Brahmās' dissolutions and manifestations, [equal to] the taste-fires (sixty-three)."
While the Rudras remain unmanifest, their day and night are of equal duration.

"By the rasas and fires" means by thirty-six. "Of Brahmā" refers to him who resides in the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), and not to him who resides in Satyaloka; for the meaning is that it is impossible to calculate this [lifespan] by the same reckoning used for his lifespan.
Therefore, for Brahmā residing in the principle of intellect, up until the end of the hundred Rudras of the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*)...

Dissolution occurs at the beginning of that day, and creation [occurs] at its end; thus, in his year, there are three hundred and sixty manifestations of dissolution. When these are multiplied by a hundred, they become thirty-six thousand in number, as it has been said: "by means of the six fires" (rasāgnibhiḥ).

Regarding the phrase "with thousands of dissolutions and expansions": the lifespan of the Rudras residing in the *guṇatattva*, which is equal in measure to that [number], is said to be one day for those situated in the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). As it is stated: "For those situated in the Unmanifest, the night is of the same duration as the day. Furthermore, it has been said:
"But thirty-six thousand [years] of the Brahmas, from their dissolution until their emergence,
are declared to be one day of the Rudras who dwell therein" (Svacchandatantra 11.289).
And regarding this arrangement:
Even though there is no distinction up to the level of the Śakti-tattva, the purpose of this extended application (atideśa) up to the Avyakta-tattva is precisely this:
that here, in comparison with the lifespan of Rudra residing in the Guṇa-tattva, a fixed numerical measure for the duration of a day has arisen. || 148 ||
And here, having raised the doubt as to who possesses the authority regarding creation, dissolution, and so forth, he says:
"At that time, Śrīkaṇṭha alone is the Lord who directly performs the dissolution;
likewise, all the Rudras at the root [of the universe] are the authorities within the womb of Māyā. (6.149)
For indeed, from Viriñca down to the Unmanifest (avyakta), they abide together with Śrīkaṇṭha directly,
and not through the mediation of Viriñca and others; because at that time,
everyone from Viriñca downwards who holds office within the womb of Prakṛti are all Rudras in the form of the respective lords of those worlds.
They abide together with Śrīkaṇṭha in the root, the principle of Prakṛti, which is called the Unmanifest;
the meaning is that they remain having made Lord Śrīkaṇṭha himself the primary leader. As it has been said:
The progenitors, the lords of progeny, and the ancestors together with the Manus;
those who have attained perfection through the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, and the exponents of Brahman according to the Veda.
"The meters, the Sāman chants, the syllable Oṃ, the intellect, and their respective deities, O Dear One—
all these abide during the day within the wise Supreme Lord. (149)

Now, one might object: since his dissolution into the Supreme Śiva has been stated in such passages as, "At the end of the great aeon, Brahmā goes to dissolution in the Supreme" (Svacchandatantra 11.261), how can he remain [in that state]?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "For Brahmā, whose lower karma has ceased, [resides] there in that lower level of the intellect. (6.150)
The knower who is no longer an enjoyer, having fulfilled his office, indeed becomes Śiva.
This is the intermediate dissolution; upon its exhaustion, emanation is said to occur. (6.151)

If he has not experienced the descent of the supreme *śakti*, then because his karma has ceased below the level of the intellect (*buddhi*), there would be an absence of experience; thus, he would not be an enjoyer therein and would remain right here. Otherwise, however, if he were a knower who has directly realized the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), then immediately after the cessation of his office (*adhikāra*), he—
"He becomes Śiva" means that he should manifest through identity with Him alone. The same should be understood for the others as well.

Regarding the "intermediate dissolution," this is because the dissolution of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) has already been described, and the dissolution of the egg of primordial nature (prakṛtyaṇḍa) will be described later. || 151 ||
Indeed, it is said here: "The Buddhists are established in the principle of intellect (buddhi); the Ārhats are established even in the qualities (guṇas);
the knowers of the Vedas are established in the Person (puruṣa); but the Pāñcarātrikas are established in the unmanifest (avyakta)."

Based on such statements, some selves are liberated while others remain bound; how then can it be said without distinction that "upon their destruction, emanation is described"? For surely there can be no further transmigration for liberated selves? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
At the beginning of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha creates those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, the Vedas, and so forth;
therefore, such liberation is not truly final.

Now, by means of an extended application (*atideśa*), he demonstrates the arrangement of days and so forth according to the sequence of increasing growth, following the very same principle previously stated, with the passage beginning with "In the *pradhāna*" and ending with "in the state beyond the mind" (*śāmanase pade*).
One hundred years born from that day-and-night of Pradhāna is the lifespan of the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha; and this [lifespan] is but a single day for those who dwell in the Kañcukas.
In that sequence, Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā—these go into mutual dissolution; their lifespan is one day of Gāhanika.
At the end of that day, the universe dissolves into Māyā;
when the night of equal duration has ended, Gahaneśa creates it once again.
Multiply the duration of the unmanifest (avyakta) by ten parārdhas;
a night of Māyā is equal to that, and this is the dissolution (pralaya).
Having multiplied the duration of Māyā by a hundred parārdhas, that is a day of Īśvara; there, Nāda, whose essence is the vital breath (prāṇa), creates the world. (6.157)
And the night of Īśvara is of that same duration, wherein the vital breath (*prāṇa*) comes to rest.

This constitutes a day and night; with respect to the lifespan of Rudra, who dwells within the *guṇa*-tattva, it amounts to seventy-two thousand [years], which is the measure of a Brahmā-dissolution. "Born from that" means [a period] increased by sixty...

The meaning is that one should multiply by three hundred. "This" refers to the lifespan of Śrīkaṇṭha, which measures one hundred years. This applies to those dwelling in the *kañcukas*, namely Vāmadeva and the others who reside in the principle of *niyati* (restriction), but not to those situated in the principle of *kāla* (time) and so forth; for in comparison with them—
Since the regulation of increase and so forth occurs in successive stages starting from the principle of time (kālatattva), it is for this very reason that it is said:
"They mutually undergo dissolution in due order. The scripture also states this as follows:
"Then Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā likewise all undergo mutual dissolution in due order, each according to its own measure" (Svacchanda Tantra 11.292).
Regarding the phrase "of them," this refers to Mahādeva and the others who reside in the principle of Kalā, but not to everyone.

[This applies] to those who dwell in the *kañcukas*; for if that were the case, the multiplication to be described would be consistent with a *parārdha* increased tenfold, situated in the fifteenth place, in relation to a day of immersion whose duration is unmanifest.
Thus, for all those dwelling in the *kañcukas*, the lifespan increases progressively [in each subsequent stage].

In order to demonstrate the uninterrupted enumeration of the days of the *gāhanika* year through its increase, that which is about to be stated is thus consistent—enough of this prolixity. The calculation has not been written down for fear of making the book too voluminous; it should be inferred by oneself. Regarding the phrase "in that much":
In the context of the day to be described hereafter; *jahī* means "multiply. As it has been said:
"By means of ten times the supreme *parārdha* of Pradhāna, Māyā withdraws the entire universe, and then she creates the world once again."
"And when a hundred times a parārdha of the time of Māyā has passed, the Lord performs creation, and again he withdraws it and creates it anew" (Svacchandatantra 11.297).
By this, it would be said that here the duration of time is progressively intensified.

The same should be understood for what follows. "Nāda" refers to Īśvara, whose nature is to resound (*nadana*) by way of being the external unfolding (*unmeṣa*). He is called "the self of breath" (*prāṇātman*) because he is the subject (*pramātṛ*) of breath. He "subsides" (*praśāmyati*) because from this point upward, breath no longer possesses primacy; and "the universe" (*viśvam*) [subsides] within his very *I-consciousness* (*ahantā*).
Because of rest. || 157 ||
Not only will there be the pacification of the vital breath (prāṇa) consisting of sound alone, but it will also occur for consciousness itself, which consists of the bindu and so forth—thus he says:
"Here, the entire universe, though situated within the womb of the vital breath, [is dissolved] by way of the suṣumnā path. (6.158)
When the vital breath has become tranquil within the aperture of Brahman, consciousness alone remains;
from even a minute fraction of this [consciousness], there occurs a dissolution that is subtler than the subtlest. (6.159)
Having multiplied the time of Īśvara by a hundred parārdhas,
that constitutes a day and night for Sadāśiva, which is indeed the great dissolution (mahāpralaya).
At the end of his own time, Sadāśiva, having seized all that is moving and unmoving, ascends through the Bindu, the Half-moon, and the Nirodhikā, and dissolves into the Nāda. (6.161)

But the Nāda, having forcibly pierced the aperture of Brahmā through the function of the end of sound (nādānta), goes to dissolution in the principle of Śakti at the exhaustion of its own time. (6.162)
This much indeed should be known regarding the principle of Śakti during day and night;
when its own time has dissolved, Śakti dissolves again into the Vyāpinī.
That [time] of the Pervasive One dissolves day and night into the Unmanifested;
even when the time of Śakti is multiplied by ten million parārdhas, it dissolves into the Unmanifested.
Day and night at that time, even when multiplied by a parārdha,
also go to dissolution in the state known as Sāmya, which is beyond the mind (sāmanasa).
Regarding the term *mahāpralaya* (the great dissolution): it is so called because even the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is withdrawn [into it]. As it has been said:
"Then the god Sadāśiva withdraws [everything] according to his own measure, and then he creates once again at the dawn of his own day."
"The Great Dissolution itself is said to occur at the end of the day in the Sādākhya [tattva]. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.298).
"And having pierced the Bindu, the Half-moon, and the Nirodhikā..."
