"It dissolves into the reality of Nāda, having taken up all that is moving and unmoving" (Svacchanda Tantra 11.300). "By following Nāda" means by reaching the stage of the culmination of Nāda (nādānta). As it has been said:
"O Dear One, Nāda, having pierced the aperture of Brahmā via the path of Suṣumnā..."

"It dissolves into the principle of Śakti at the end of the day of the principle of Śakti" (Svacchandatantra 11.301). "This much" refers to the duration of Sadāśiva's life. "That" refers to the time of dissolution into Śakti. "By ten million parārdhas" refers to what was stated: [The text continues: "A parārdha is said to be the number of years in the world of Brahmā; ten million such parārdhas constitute the lifespan of Sadāśiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.302) Furthermore: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Sadāśiva constitute one day of Īśvara. (Svacchandatantra 11.303) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Īśvara constitute one day of Śuddhavidyā. (Svacchandatantra 11.304) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śuddhavidyā constitute one day of Māyā. (Svacchandatantra 11.305) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Māyā constitute one day of Kālatattva. (Svacchandatantra 11.306) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Kālatattva constitute one day of Niyati. (Svacchandatantra 11.307) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Niyati constitute one day of Rāga. (Svacchandatantra 11.308) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Rāga constitute one day of Vidya. (Svacchandatantra 11.309) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Vidya constitute one day of Ahaṅkāra. (Svacchandatantra 11.310) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Ahaṅkāra constitute one day of Buddhi. (Svacchandatantra 11.311) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Buddhi constitute one day of Manas. (Svacchandatantra 11.312) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Manas constitute one day of the five elements. (Svacchandatantra 11.313) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of the five elements constitute one day of the earth. (Svacchandatantra 11.315) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of the individual soul constitute one day of the subtle body (liṅga). (Svacchandatantra 11.316) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of the subtle body constitute one day of the Unmanifest (avyakta). (Svacchandatantra 11.317) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of the Unmanifest constitute one day of Prakṛti. (Svacchandatantra 11.318) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Prakṛti constitute one day of Puruṣa. (Svacchandatantra 11.319) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Puruṣa constitute one day of Niyati. (Svacchandatantra 11.320) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Niyati constitute one day of Kāla. (Svacchandatantra 11.321) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Kāla constitute one day of Māyā. (Svacchandatantra 11.322) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Māyā constitute one day of Īśvara. (Svacchandatantra 11.323) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Īśvara constitute one day of Sadāśiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.324) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Sadāśiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.325) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.326) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.327) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.328) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.329) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.330) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.331) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.332) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.333) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.334) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.335) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.336) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.337) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.338) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.339) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.340) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.341) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.342) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.343) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.344) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.345) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.346) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.347) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Anāśrita constitute one day of Śiva. (Svacchandatantra 11.348) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śiva constitute one day of Śakti. (Svacchandatantra 11.349) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śakti constitute one day of Śambhu. (Svacchandatantra 11.350) And: "Ten million parārdhas of the lifespan of Śambhu constitute one day of Anāśrita. (Svacchandatantra 11.351
"One day of the deity Anāśrita is proclaimed to be ten million times the *parārdha* of the *śakti*-kalpa. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.303).
He is the one called Anāśrita. As it has been said:
"By this measure, and multiplied by a parārdha, he too goes to the supreme station, which is the cause resting upon Samanā. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.304). || 165 ||
Now, one might ask: "Why is the dissolution of Samanā not also mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That [state] is Time, known as Equilibrium (Sāmya); it is eternal, undecaying, and yet consists of parts (kalātmaka).
That form which is associated with the mind (sāmanasa) is that Equilibrium—the all-pervading Brahman. (6.166)

Since he is Time (*kāla*), the creator of the manifold world, and consists of this very power of *kalā* called *samanā*, he is therefore eternal; for there is no destruction even at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) of this power known as *samanā*—this is the intended meaning. It is with this very intention that others [have stated]:

It has been stated [in the scriptures] that "Śambhu, Puruṣa, and Māyā are eternal," and so forth. For this very reason, because the entire universe—from Earth up to Anāśrita—exists in a state of equality through its nature as non-differentiation, it is designated by the term "sāmya" (equality). Precisely for this reason, there is an absence of the manifestation of duality.

"Incapable" (*akalya*) means unable to be measured. For when the dissolution of the universe has occurred up to the level of *Śakti*, this entire class of individual souls (*aṇu-varga*) comes together and abides precisely within *Samanā*; thus he says:
"That form which is associated with *Samanā* is the all-pervading state of equilibrium. And even so, it is not merely that.
Like those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*), this has been described as "Brahman," meaning it is distinct from the Supreme Brahman;
rather, its meaning is that it is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman itself. As it has been said:
"Śa is Time, known as Equanimity (*sāmya*), which removes the fear of birth and death."
Beyond that as well, the time would be immeasurable; such is the ultimate limit.
"O Goddess, he is eternal, eternally risen, and being beyond the unwholesome, he is not made wholesome. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.346) || 166 ||
Not only does the universe abide here at the time of dissolution, but even during its creation— as he says:
"Therefore, from this time which is coextensive with the mind, by the mere opening and closing of an eye..."
It is she alone who produces everything from a *tuṭi* up to the end of a *parārdha*, and she is established here as the ultimate reality.
"By means of a mere opening and closing of the eyes" means resting in the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
As it has been said:
"And he [the Lord] casts everything below, from Vyāpinī down to the earth."
"And by means of the divisions beginning with the *tuṭi*, [one perceives] the path of the Goddess, consisting of the mobile and immobile. (Svacchandatantra 11.307).

For this very reason, others who do not understand the methodology of our scripture claim that when the Great Dissolution has occurred, this entire group of individual souls (*aṇu*) remains until the end of the dissolution, ending at the level of *Śakti*.
"Since it is stated that [the levels] are situated one above the other, one would reach only the *śivatattva* as the remainder.

And since liberation is precisely the attainment of that, it would be accomplished for everyone effortlessly and without sequence; therefore, what is the use of the practice of the scriptures and so forth?"—this and other such objections have been raised.

It is indeed destroyed by their arising. For even at the time of dissolution, these do not abide within the Śiva-tattva up to the level of Śakti, because it is stated thus regarding the level of Samanā:
"O fair-hipped one, the endless web of bonds extends up to the end of Samanā" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.429).
By such statements, everything up to that point is indeed bondage—so what room is there for liberation therein?
Nor does this imply a contradiction of the doctrine of non-duality on the grounds that, like Śambhu, even the *samanā* level is eternal;
for the conventional discourse of creation, dissolution, and so forth arises precisely with reference to duality. In reality, however, [it is otherwise].
Furthermore, the discussion regarding the doctrine of non-duality has been presented here step by step, and will be presented further; so, enough of this prolixity. || 167 ||

Having spoken thus, he now demonstrates the forms of the numbers required for the measurements that will be described, in their proper sequence: ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand (ayuta), hundred-thousand (lakṣa), million (niyuta), ten-million (koṭi), hundred-million (arbuda), and billion (vṛnda).
Then there are the kharva and nikharva, followed by the śaṅkha, abja, jaladhi, madhya, anta, and finally the parārdha.
He abandons the lotus; "jaladhi" means the ocean. || 168 ||
Now, one might ask: "How could their persistence be possible in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having thus calculated in sequence ten by ten, starting from one, one should establish their persistence across the eighteen [categories] beginning with one and ending with the parārdha. (6.169)
As it has been said:
"The first [unit] multiplied by ten is ten; that multiplied by ten is a hundred;
and making the hundred multiplied by ten, it is proclaimed as a thousand."
A thousand multiplied tenfold is indeed proclaimed as ten thousand (ayuta);
ten times ten thousand is a hundred thousand (lakṣa), and ten of those is a million (niyuta).
Ten of those make a *koṭi*, and ten *koṭis* make an *arbuda*.
Ten *arbudas* make a *vṛnda*, and ten times that indeed make a *kharva*.
Ten of those [nikharvas] make a śaṅku;
ten śaṅkus make a padma; and ten padmas make a sāgara.
Ten *sāgara*s are known as a *madhya*; ten *madhya*s are said to be an *anta*; and having multiplied *anta* by ten, it is proclaimed as a *parārdha*.
Thus, these eighteen topics constitute the field of calculation. || 169 ||
Thus, although creations and dissolutions are infinite here, he speaks in order to show their primary and secondary status:
"These four are the principal dissolutions and creations, and their parts reside in Bhū, Mūla, Niśā, and Śakti; that indeed is the quartet of cosmic eggs. (6.170)

The term "primary" (mukhyā) is used because all the infinite intermediate dissolutions (pralaya) and creations (sarga) are included within these very [six]. The phrase "their parts" (tatkalā) means that the "parts" (kalā)—that is, the portions—of those dissolutions and creations consist of the fourfold division beginning with earth. "That very same" refers to...

Regarding the "roots of the earth" and so forth, it has been said: "By the weight of the majesty of His own power, the Lord has manifested this fourfold egg through division as Śakti, Māyā, Prakṛti, and Pṛthvī."
Thus [ends] verse 4 of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sañcaya-gāthā*, [numbered] 170.
Right here, he also demonstrates the distinction between the creator and the destroyer:
"Kālāgni is the destroyer on the earth; at the end of Māyā is the sovereign of the Kāla-tattva;
Śrīkaṇṭha alone is the cause of creation and destruction at the Root. (6.171)
Or rather, there is a single Tattvalaya situated between them; he is the Lord of creation and dissolution.
The illustrious Aghora, located at the end of Śakti, is both the destroyer and the creator. (6.172)
He is the destroyer and not the creator; for it was previously stated that this [role] belongs to Brahmā and the others alone.
Śrīkaṇṭha is the sovereign of the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), the lord of the principle of Time. As it has been said:
"Ekavīra and Śikhoda, as well as Śrīkaṇṭha, are dependent upon Time" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.27).
Thus [it is said]. "Śrīkaṇṭha" refers to him who resides in the Unmanifest (avyakta). The term "in one" (ekatra) is to be applied to all three [levels].

"Dissolution therein" (tallaya) refers to the withdrawal (saṃhāra) performed by Śrīkaṇṭha. Alternatively, Lord Śrīkaṇṭha alone is he who, resting upon the nature of both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), abides in all three locations beginning with Earth.
He is the agent of creation and destruction. As it has been said:
"Śrīkaṇṭha himself is called Kālāgni by means of his supreme form. Likewise:

"Maheśvara Rudra, who is the form of Time (Kāla), is established in those three alone. Regarding the phrase "at the end of Śakti," this refers to the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan). As it has been said: "Above that is the Pure Path, extending as far as the range of the end of Śakti."
"Aghora, the destroyer of the terrible, shall withdraw all that which is terrible.
Thus [ends verse 172].
He states that the greatness of dissolution extends not only up to the limit of Śakti, but also applies to creation:
"Because within that [Śāktī] creation, countless creations and dissolutions of worlds are included, the Great Creation is therefore declared to be Śāktī. (6.173)

Now, one might object: "In the dissolution of the principles (tattva) such as Earth and the rest, is the arrangement of the atoms (aṇu) dwelling therein the same for the lords of those principles or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In dissolution, Brahmā, Hari, hundreds of Rudras, and the five groups of eight [are present]."
Thus, they dissolve into one another in succession on the path ending with Māyā.
"But upon the dissolution of the principle of Māyā, these [souls] proceed to the supreme state.
What, then, is the supreme state for those situated on the pure path (śuddhādhvan)?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For those who reside on the white path above Māyā, there is absorption into Paraśiva. (6.175)

Regarding that, others maintain that even in the state of dissolution (*laya*), there is a distinction [between souls] due to adventitious limitations (*upādhi*). The phrase "regarding that" refers to the Supreme Śiva; by saying "others maintain," the intention is to show that this is not our own view.
Now, if this is so, when those who have attained liberation (*apavṛkta*) undergo re-creation (*sṛṣṭi*), who would possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for it?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Thus, when the group of Tattveśvaras has dissolved, [the process occurs] again in the supreme creation. (6.176)
Those who accomplish that, or those beloved by Śiva, occupy that station.
Regarding the phrase "those who accomplish that":
"Having superimposed [the disciple] who follows worldly dharma upon the Lord of the Worlds, according to the doctrine..."

Those who, through the sequence beginning with the aforementioned wonders, desire the sovereignty over various respective worlds, are "beloved of Śiva," meaning they are graced by His mere will alone. || 176 ||
One might ask: "Even so, what is the cause for the application of words such as 'Brahmā' to these [beings]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is called 'brahmic' is indeed the power of the Supreme; wherever one should cast that [power]," (6.177).
From this [power], Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others arise in succession from the powers of Vaiṣṇavī and so forth.
"From this" means from the Śakti. As it has been said:
"The power of Brahmā and the power of Viṣṇu have attained their respective offices."
And whatever he identifies himself with, he comes to assume the notion of that.
"Then, by the will of the Supreme Self, it exercises that authority. (Svacchandatantra 11.265) || 177 ||

Now, one might object: "If that which is called 'Brahmī' is indeed the power (śakti) of Śiva alone, then how could she go to another [being], such that he would be called 'Brahmā'? For it is not possible for the attribute belonging to one to inhere in another?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Does power ever leave one who possesses it to go to another? It is not like that. (6.178)

It has been stated in such passages as: "The one Śiva alone is thus [the Lord], whose entire power is concealed and manifested; for this characteristic of Śiva does not belong to anyone else—such as Brahmā and others—apart from the possessor of power (śaktimant), to whom Power (śakti) resorts. However, even though he is inlaid with infinite powers...
Having concealed some of its powers and manifested others, Śiva alone appears in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth. || 178 ||
One might object: "Was it not previously established that the supreme reality of the vital breath (prāṇa) serves as a means for each [level]?
Why is it that, without explaining those [levels], the nature of creation, withdrawal, and so forth is now being described by relying upon it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In this way, emanation and dissolution are both established within the single vital breath (prāṇa). || 6.179 ||
That [object] is also within consciousness, and consciousness is within pure consciousness devoid of any object of knowledge;
that Goddess is indeed pure consciousness alone, the supreme Parameśvarī. (6.180)
And that thirty-eighth reality is the Heart, which is both transcendent and immanent;
it is called "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) because it is consciousness alone, though appearing as limited selfhood when differentiated by various manifestations such as blue and so forth.
That this very pure consciousness is the thirty-eighth reality will be demonstrated immediately hereafter. Thus [it is said].

No effort is required here; that very state of resting in pure consciousness (cinmātra) remains as it is, by virtue of which there occurs this manifold variety of dissolution and emergence, ranging from the *nālikā* up to the arising of the sixty-year cycle. || 180 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Therefore, this very nature of consciousness, throbbing by its own inherent nature," (181)
"Regarding 'the arising of dissolution' (*layodayā*)," this refers to the proclamation of the arising of the sixty-year cycle within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

As for "the nature of consciousness" (*saṃvittvam*): that which is called the arising of dissolution is the sovereignty of that very consciousness. Thus, all this temporal variety is entirely dependent upon consciousness, and not independent of it.
It would have been said that some form exists externally. || 181 ||
Therefore he says:
"This investigation into the variety of actions is established solely upon will. (6.182)
Therefore, the power of time is external; its form is not fixed.

Regarding the phrase "its form is not fixed," the sense is this: if it were otherwise, how could there be the rising of a year at the very same place where the rising of a single cup [of wine] occurs? || 182 ||
Now, one might object: "How can even an extremely limited portion of time appear as something extended?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the dream-within-a-dream, likewise in a dream, in deep sleep, and within the sphere of mental construction," (6.183)
In meditative absorption (*samādhi*), when discerning the sequence of the creation and dissolution of the universe,
even a measured fraction of time indeed appears as something vastly extended.

When someone, having imagined the first state— which is merely dreamlike— to be the waking state, conceives of the second state as being a dream, that is called a "dream within a dream. Thus, it is rightly said that in a dream,
even an experience spanning many periods of time occurred in a single moment, as in the case of Hariścandra.
"—even in a minute time, there is an appearance of expansion. Regarding the phrase "in sleep," this refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*);

for even if [sleep] lasts only a moment, upon waking from delusion or the like, there arises the conviction: "For a long time, I was deeply deluded," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "within the scope of conceptual construction," this refers to independent mental constructs (*svatantra-vikalpa*) and the like; for in that case...

In an instant, even the conceptualization of an eon is possible within *śamādhi*—that is, within that which consists of the direct perception of the universe. This refers to the "discernment" (*vivecana*) of the sequence of the universe's dissolution and creation;
the meaning is: within the cognition that synthesizes the objects of knowledge belonging to time, as just mentioned. And this pertains to time...
This expansion may also reach a state of manifoldness by being perceived as both one's own and another's; thus he says:
"Whether there is non-difference or difference of the subject, this [expansion] attains a variegated extension.
By this, it is experienced in dreams and so forth through the unification with other subjects.
Or: "This is my manifestation, spread out; this has been experienced by me alone in its uniqueness."
Now he extends this same division of time to the apāna as well:
"In this way, just as time in the prāṇa arises from the power of the variety of actions... (6.185).
Likewise, in the case of the *apāna* [breath] as well, it flows from the heart to the *mūla-pīṭha*.

Although the diversity of time (*kālavaicitrya*) has been described for the *apāna* as extending from the *dvādaśānta* to the heart, it is stated thus because this [flow] is primary in its extension from the heart down to the *mattagandha* [the perineum].
As it has been said: "When the movement of the apāna is also set in motion, this [channel] becomes very extensively expanded;
from there, the wind indeed proceeds downward as far as the anus."
Thus [ends the verse]. 185.
Now, one might object: "In this case as well, is the variety of time perceived, or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the contraction and expansion of the great seat (pīṭha) called the Root (mūla). (6.186)
"He performs the creation and withdrawal of all things from Brahmā down to Anāśrita.
By the reasoning previously stated, such as "just like a she-donkey or a mare" (Tantrāloka 5.58),
those two— the contraction and expansion— belong to the power whose locus of birth has been described.

It has been stated that the creation, dissolution, and so forth of the entire universe, from Brahmā down to Anāśrita, are established through the experience of yogis: "He gathers [the universe] through creation and withdrawal. (186)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, why is this [state] not indicated everywhere as being primarily the arising of the *prāṇa*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Although this *apāna* always flows in this manner, nevertheless... (6.187).
That which is beyond the reach of effort is worshipped with effort by yogis.
Now, one might object: "If the creation and so forth of causes such as Brahmā and the others were to occur here, then where and in what state would they reside? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
They reside at the heart, the bulb, the bliss, the contraction, the expansion, and the end of the twelve.
From Brahmā down to Anāśrita, these [deities] are served here by those of excellent yoga.

The term "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta) refers to the place of the arising and resting of Śakti. By the phrase "by those of excellent yoga," it is meant that this is for those who are attentive within the prāṇa, and not for ordinary people, because for the latter, the apāna is effortless and beyond the range of objective perception; thus, its service is not possible for them.
Because it is to be accomplished through effort. || 188 ||
One might object: "Since these [powers] are all-pervasive, their abiding everywhere is established by their very nature;
what, then, is the purpose of stating this specific detail? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And these abide in the universe because they are the powers of the Supreme Lord. (6.189)
"In the Kāmika [Tantra], it is said that they pervade even the body and are its causes.
Regarding the phrase "its causes," the meaning is that they are the instrumental causes for the production of that body by means of their respective substrates. || 189 ||
He recites this very passage from the Kāmika:
"In childhood, youth, old age, death, and rebirth... (6.190).
And upon liberation, while the body remains, Brahmā and the others act as the six presiding authorities (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Among these, Brahmā acts as the presiding authority up until liberation, whereas Anāśrita [Śiva] acts as the presiding authority from that point until liberation.
[Objection: But in our own philosophical system, why would it be logical for Anāśrita to act as the presiding authority over one who is liberated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But at its end is the Supreme Goddess, united with whom one is not born again. (6.191)
By the mere knowledge of this, one becomes a bestower of initiation and grace.
Regarding the word "end," it has been said: "Through the abandonment of the six, there is dissolution in the seventh. (Svacchandatantra 4.267)
Thus:
"Yukta" means he has been joined by the Guru, according to the sense. || 191 ||
One might object: "Since the discussion has already begun concerning the variety of times for the downward breath (apāna), what is the purpose of this teaching?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because when the state that is the manifestation of all causes is well known... (6.192).
One should find that which is the causeless Śiva, for He is the cause of the universe;
the sense is that when that which is to be rejected is thoroughly known, there will be repose in that which is to be accepted, which is bliss. || 192 ||

Now, one might object: "According to the sequence of the vital breaths (*prāṇakrama*), as stated in such passages as 'the Supreme Śiva is at the End of the Twelve' (*dvādaśānte paraḥ śivaḥ*), there is repose in that Śiva by transcending each respective cause; but here [in this system], where would that repose be so that it might be likewise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Indeed, this [state] has its face turned downward, utterly destroying the stain of duality. (6.93)
Through its worship, that ostentation of above and below is destroyed;

wherein the downward breath finds rest, this is the remover of the stain of duality. That which is called the "downward-facing mouth," the form of the sixth stream, is known as the "mouth of the Yoginī"; for it is [the source] of those who teach the meaning of non-duality.

The emergence of the secret scriptures (rahasya-śāstra) serves as the cause for the cessation of the "display of above and below" for those who find rest therein through the removal of duality; the meaning is that the state of identity with Supreme Śiva, who is a single mass of consciousness and bliss, shall shine forth. || 193 ||

Now, one might ask: "In this case, does such repose occur through the sequence of *tuṭi*s and so forth, like that of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or in some other way? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Here, at the arising of the apāna, as before, there is the application of the arising of the sixty-year cycle. (6.194)

One should perform [the calculation] starting from a *tuṭi* and so forth, according to the appropriate division of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Relying on the appropriate division of finger-breadths corresponding to the *tuṭi*, one should apply the conjunction [of time units] beginning from a *tuṭi* up to the emergence of sixty years, as previously described here in the context of the emergence of the exhalation (*apāna*).
One should act in such a way that there may be rest through this very means. || 194 ||
"This is not only the case in the apāna, but also in the samāna," he says:
"In this way, the same rule applies to the samāna as well, for it resides within the channels of the heart. (6.195)
Moving in all directions, it is perceived as tenfold;
[it is said to be] in the hearts of those [energies], because of its manifestation in their hearts, though in reality their origin is from the navel.
As it has been said:
It is situated below the navel at the root of the penis, in the very center of the navel;
from there, O beloved, the channels (nāḍīs) emerge sideways, upwards, and downwards.
"There, ten principal channels are situated like the spokes of a wheel" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.8). For the *samāna* [vāyu] as well, the navel is the primary location. As it has been said:
"In the heart, the anus, the navel, the throat, and likewise in all the joints..."
"For these, beginning with prāṇa, are indeed situated... (Svacchandatantra 7.301). || 195 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for such a designation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Filling the ten principal great channels, this [breath] follows them. (6.196)
The channels situated within other channels, which traverse the body and maintain its equilibrium, are called "principal" (mukhyā), meaning primary. As it has been said:
"Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third."
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣan, and likewise Aryaman.
"Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
these are declared to be the ten principal channels that carry the vital breath. (Svacchandatantra 7.16).
"Contained within those" means they consist of the seventy-two thousand subdivisions thereof.
The forms of its subdivisions exist within other channels. As it has been said:
"Seventy-two thousand channels have emerged from those; others have emerged again from them, and yet others from these, repeatedly. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.9)
Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, it is stated that "this one is named Samāna because of its equalizing within the body; such is the state of tranquility.
(196) Now, one might object: "Even if this [prāṇa] exists by pervading the ten channels, what follows from that which would justify its being called 'tenfold'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Moving through these eight petals of the directions, he proceeds in sequence toward the lords of those respective quarters.
"Imitating the activities [of others], he appears both fierce (*raudra*) and gentle (*saumya*);
[this refers] to that lord of the direction," namely Indra and the others. "Activities" refers to forms such as paralysis (*stambha*) and so forth.
He is fierce in the south and other directions, and gentle in the west and other directions; for this very reason, for men, at every moment—
The manifestation of anger, joy, and so forth [is explained as follows]. As it has been said:
"In this manner, within the center of the eight-petaled lotus, the enjoyer of experience always resides;
for this reason, although he is omnipresent, he is clearly perceived."
By means of which, having quickly perceived sense objects, one reflects upon them with care—
whether it be sorrow, anger, despondency, wonder, or even distress.
"Or else, having reflected upon joy, it is experienced by the heart alone. || 197 ||
Thus, although he abides equally everywhere, his movement occurs primarily within the three channels alone; so it is said:
"He [the breath] himself moves within the triad of channels situated on the left, right, and middle. (6.198)
It moves and abides day and night within the three primary channels—namely *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*—which consist of the moon, sun, and fire. As it has been said:
"The sun is situated on the right, while the moon shines on the left."
As it has been said: "In the process of digestion and in its capacity as an illuminator, the fire remains indeed in the middle" (Svacchandatantra 7.52).
Furthermore: "O Goddess, among the ten [channels], the triad of channels is declared to be supreme."
"The two [energies] consisting of *bindu* and *nāda* are indeed [on either side], while that which is in the middle is known as consisting of *śakti*.
Now, one might ask: "How does this [power] remain moving day and night? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which consists of nine hundred breaths and two and a half *nālīs* remains [there]. (6.199)
Carrying [the breath] for as long as a day and night, one should perform [the movement] twenty-four times.

According to the statement beginning with, "Six breaths (*prāṇa*) make a *caṣaka*; sixty of those make a *nālī*, and likewise a lunar day (*tithi*)," there are internal movements of the breath within each external *ghaṭikā*.

Three hundred and sixty [breaths] would arise; thus, by means of two and a half external *ghaṭikās*, flowing as nine hundred [breaths], he himself—the *samāna*—would move through twenty-four modes, which constitute the external day-and-night (*ahorātra*) consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās*. By this, here...
Based on the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*), which consists of one million two hundred and twenty-one thousand [breaths], twenty-four transits (*saṃkrānti*) arise. As it has been said:
"The twenty-four transits arise by nature from the equilibrium of the constituent elements."
"Nine hundred *haṃsas* indeed always carry each and every one [of the breaths]. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.168).
And: "Externally, O fair-faced one, it is day and night; internally, however, [it is as follows]..."
The haṃsa of the vital breath should transition through the twenty-four transits.
"Twelve are said to be in the day, and twelve indeed are recorded for the night" (Svacchanda Tantra 7.166). || 199 ||
He analyzes this very point:
"On the day of the equinox, in the morning, he, situated in the center, [traverses] a nālī together with its fractional parts. (6.200)
By means of the left, the other [right], the upward, and the downward [channels], for as long as five transits [last];
thus, when thirteen and three-quarter *nāḍīs* have been exhausted.
At midday, one should carry ninety breaths during the southern equinox;
then there are five transits (saṃkrānti) consisting of south, north, and again north, south, and north.
Each [of these] consists of nine hundred [breaths];
thereafter, following the equinox (viṣuvat), when five groups of five have passed outside the equinox from the transition (saṃkrānti).
Just as there is an internal transition, so too are those nine hundred breaths;
on the day of the equinox (*viṣuvad-vāsara*), which consists of the equality of night and day, specifically on the day of the Aries transit (*meṣa-saṃkrānti*), at dawn,
[one experiences] a *ghaṭikā* consisting of four hundred and fifty breath-movements, together with a quarter-part.
Remaining in the central channel (*sauṣumna-mārga*),
that *samāna* breath moves fivefold through the left and right channels— the left and right vessels— each for two and a half *nāḍīs*, via its coming and going, until the end of Virgo (*kanyā*).

There would be a pentad of transits (saṃkrānti-pañcaka), by which, when thirteen ghaṭikās of the three equal divisions have passed, at the time of midday in the central channel (madhya-nāḍī), the southern equinox— the transit of Libra— should flow for nine hundred breaths.

The meaning is that it rises for two and a half *ghaṭikās*. Beyond that, through fivefold movements of the equal breath (*samāna*) in the right and left channels— alternating between right-to-left and left-to-right— there are again nine hundred breaths for each, which constitutes two and a half *nālīs* respectively.
The meaning is that the five transits beginning with Scorpio and ending with Pisces arise. Immediately thereafter,

in the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), at evening, the northern equinox in the form of the Aries transit arises as before, consisting of four hundred and fifty breath-movements, with an emergence of one ghaṭikā and a quarter.

In a day consisting of thirty daṇḍas, there may arise twelve transits (saṅkrānti). Among those, eleven transits are uninterrupted, while one occurs by means of two half-portions— one in the evening and one in the morning—
and [this applies] to that pair of halves.
Just as with the junctions of the fortnights, there is also integrity in the union of the two halves of the night;
thus, there are two northern solstices at evening and dawn, and two southern solstices at midday and midnight. As he will state:
"The end of night and the first part of day, midday, and the waning of the day—that is the rising of the night; such is the equinox when it rises in the middle. (Tantrāloka 6.205).
And this is with reference to the rising of the day at the Dakṣaviṣuva.
"When it moves from the south to the north, and from the north to the south,
that is the southern and northern solstice (saṃkrānti), and it is thus ordained."
When it moves from the southern channel toward the northern one,
it flows through the center from the north for as long as it remains there for half [the duration].
That indeed is declared the equinox; the northern transit occurs during the northern course.
O fair-faced one, when he moves from the north toward the south, that is the southern transit.
"As long as [the breath] carries half [the flow] there, half should carry from the right;
O Dear One, the southern equinox lasts for that long, born of the southern solstice.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda-śāstra* (7.163) and so forth. And this is not merely a preliminary stage.

He states the arising of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) with the words "the pentad," and so forth. A "transit" is of the nature of the equinox (*viṣuvat*). By the phrase "nine hundred breaths," the aforementioned measure is merely recalled. || 203 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "In the same way during the night," and so forth, from the equinoctial day onwards. (6.204)
"Beginning from day and night, this [breath] also undergoes increase, decrease, and the movement of the transits.

Thus, by means of the external day and night, everything beginning with the rising of the twenty-four transits has been explained starting from the equinoctial day of thirty *ghaṭikās*; otherwise, [it would not be so].

Otherwise, there would be no increase or decrease in the length of day and night, whereby a fixed rule of division— such as that there are twelve transitions (saṃkrāntis) in the day and twelve in the night due to their respective accumulation and diminution— even during the equinoxes, would not have been stated. || 204 ||
And here he clarifies the division of the equinoctial transits (viṣuvatsaṃkrānti):
"The end of night and the first part of the day, midday, and the waning of the day. (6.205)

That [equinox] occurs at midnight during the rising of the night; such is the equinox. The word "midnight" (madhya) refers by implication to the middle of the night. The term "udaktaḥ" means starting from the northern solstice (uttarād viṣuvataḥ). As it has been said:
One [offering] is at the vernal equinox in the forenoon; the second is at midday;
the third is indeed in the afternoon; and the fourth is at midnight.
"The Viṣuvat is said to be fourfold; by means of day and night, it bestows liberation. (Svacchandatantra 7.167). || 205 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the reason for designating these four transits (*saṃkrānti*) in this way?", he says:
"Since the root *viṣ* functions in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that pervasion is said to be equilibrium (*sāmya*). (6.206)
And that time which is worthy of this [state] is here called the *viṣuvat* (equinox).
This is because of the verbal root reading "viṣḷ vyāptau" (to pervade), and because of the use of the suffix *-vat* in the sense of "worthy of" (*arhati*) in the word "arhati. || 206 ||
Now, one might object: "If such a rule applies at the equinoxal transition (*viṣuvatsaṃkrānti*), what is the arrangement for the others?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"From the equinox onwards, there are the decrease and increase of day and night. (6.207)
By that same sequence, there is the transition, decrease, and increase of day and night.

"By that sequence" means according to the order of the increase and decrease of nights and days; thus, when the day has thirty-five *ghaṭikās*, there are fourteen transitions (*saṃkrāntis*), and when the night has twenty-five *ghaṭikās*, there are ten.
He summarizes that very point:
"In this way, there is the conceptualization of two years for the equal winds. (6.208)
The movement is unified; here there is no deliberation upon inhalation and exhalation.
"For two years" refers to the rising of the twenty-four transits (saṃkrāntis). "Unified" means that it is not, as previously, a dual movement consisting of prāṇa and apāna. || 208 ||
Now, one might ask: "Does [the breath] arise here for only two years, or for something else as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But even though it is equal, from the beginning of a *tuṭi* up to the scope of sixty years. (6.209)
The calculation of time, moving in a single subtle movement, is reckoned by the wise.
The reason for its subtlety is expressed by the term "moving in a single movement. For previously, the arising of the *tuṭi* and so forth was said to occur in two movements;
the sense is that, in comparison to that, coarseness might be suspected there. (209)
Anticipating the objection, "But what is the purpose of such a division even here?", he says: "Indeed, that which consists of twilight, forenoon, midday, midnight, and so forth... (6.210).
That which undergoes internal transition is the primary object of perception, because it is from that [transition] that its fruit arises.
Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says: "The time associated with the *samāna* has been described; now it is being defined in relation to the *udāna*. (6.211)
He says that very thing:

"That which was stated regarding the pervasion of *prāṇa* applies here to *udāna* as well; however, its locations are at the end of the nose and the power (*śakti*), and in the abode above the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (6.212)

Therefore, in this Udāna, one should contemplate the entire universe within time—from a *tuṭi* up to sixty years—as it proceeds from the heart to the head, reaching the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. (6.213)

If there is a distinction here between these two, prāṇa and udāna, it is this: the place of arising for prāṇa is the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) at the nose within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), whereas for this [udāna], it is the twelve-finger space of Śakti situated in the upper abode (ūrdhvadhāman). By "that," [he means] the twelve-finger space of Śakti.
Up to the pervasion by the *udāna* [breath]. || 213 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is such a division of time possible within the *vyāna* breath, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"But in the *vyāna*, which consists of the universal self (*viśvātman*), is all-pervasive, and devoid of succession, time exists only as a form that surges forth in an increasingly subtle manner. (6.214)

"Subtle-subtle" means having the nature of mere vibration (*spanda*). In this very context, there are three reasons expressed by way of qualifiers such as "consisting of the universal self" (*viśvātmamaya*); for this reason, because it possesses the specific quality of being all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), it is called *vyāna*. || 214 ||
And these [five breaths] perform the fivefold cosmic functions, beginning with emanation, in succession—thus he says:

"Emanation, dissolution, maintenance, withdrawal, and grace—from which [these proceed], one should accordingly rely upon each respective [breath] within the time of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the others in their proper order. (6.215)
"Each respective [one]" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. "Therein" refers to the state of performing the functions of emanation and the rest. (215)
Having thus explained everything beginning with the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
he now begins to describe the arising of the phonemes (*varṇodaya*), which was indicated immediately following that in the subsequent enumeration:
"In this movement of the vital breath, there exists the arising of phonemes, words, and mantras."
That which is produced with effort, that which is produced without effort, the subtle, the supreme, and the gross—these are described [as the types of breath]. || 6-216 ||
In this context, it is established that there is an emergence of phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras (*mantra*) during the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*).

This [emergence] is twofold: natural (*svārasika*) and effort-induced (*prāyatnika*). Of these, the first pertains to phonemes, because they occur everywhere without distinction due to their fixed necessity; the second, however, pertains to words and mantras.

And [it is] because they, like the phonemes (*varṇa*), are indefinite due to being uncountable; thus, their arising is dependent solely upon the will of the yogin. For whatever mantra or other [entity] is intended by someone, that one shall cause its arising.
And therefore, because these are dependent on the will of another, their arising is purely effortful (*prāyatnika*), and that—
This will be demonstrated in the immediately following chapter, as he will say:
"Thus has that which is born of no effort been explained; now that which is born of effort is being declared" (Tantrāloka 7.2). || 216 ||

Here, moreover, the arising of phonemes (*varṇodaya*) itself—being effortless and consisting of the supreme, the subtle, and the gross—is said to be of three kinds. Among these, even the supreme arising of phonemes is twofold due to its relative degrees of intensity; thus, he begins to describe that supreme arising:
The single phoneme consisting of sound (nāda) is undivided from all phonemes;
because its form never sets, it is here called the "unstruck" (anāhata). (6.217)

In this context, indeed, there is only one phoneme whose essence is common to all phonemes; because its form is constantly arising, it is designated as the "unstruck sound" (*anāhata-śabda*) and consists of resonance (*nādātmaka*).
It is "arisen," meaning it remains in a state of perpetual emergence. || 217 ||
And that alone is the supreme goal—thus he says:
"But that is the true being of Bhairava; this is the true being of the Mother (Mātṛ).
She is the Supreme Goddess of the single syllable, in whom the moving and the unmoving are dissolved. (6.218)
To state their second emergence as well, he says:
"Each triad of short vowels [extends] for one solar digit (*sūryāṅgula*); then the other [triads].
Thus, the six syllables on the paths of the Sun and Moon proceed in sequence during the entry. (6.219)
In the initial conjunction of the vowels *i* and *a*, and *u* and *a*, they know there are two diphthongs:
*e-o*. But in the case of entry (*praveśa*), they know there are two: *ai-au*.
The neuter vowels are at the entrance [of the central channel], at the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) and the forehead;
the nasal bindu and the visarga are situated all around the throat and the heart.
"Twelve finger-breadths" means twelve *aṅgulas*.
For this very reason, due to the emergence of the three short vowels beginning with *a*, there are thirty-six *aṅgulas* in the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*).
"The other" refers to the three long vowels. "Six letters" refers to those beginning with *a* and ending with *u*.
"Successively" means: three short vowels on the path of the sun, and long vowels on the path of the moon.
"In the initial conjunction" (ādisaṃdhau) means when the operation of conjunction has been performed between the vowel *a* and the vowel *ā*. Of this very [conjunction]...

In the initial conjunction (*saṃdhi*) of the two diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), there is the other pair of diphthongs. Each of these has an emergence (*udaya*) of eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), by which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the flows of *prāṇa* and *apāna* is accomplished.
This refers to the entry (*praveśa*), and not to the exit (*nirgama*). It is "up to the *dvādaśānta*," and not [beyond].
By means of calculating four equal parts, the letter *ṛ* is at the *dvādaśānta*, and so on is the sequence.

"On all sides" (*paritaḥ*) means everywhere. Thus, the emergence of the *bindu* occurs within the *prāṇa*, which consists of thirty-six finger-breadths, while that of the *visarga* occurs in the *apāna*; this applies to both as well.
Because it consists of the bindu and the nāda. || 221 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"The pentad beginning with *ka* is eternally arisen within the first letter;
in this way, that series of phonemes exists within the letters of their respective places of articulation. (6.222)

"Antar" (within) means that whatever is the place of origin for the vowel *ā* is the same for the *ka*-group (*kavarga*). Regarding "of the letters with corresponding places of articulation" (*sasthānavarṇānām*), this refers to *ī* and so forth; "that" (*sā*) refers to the *ca*-group (*cavarga*) and so on.
Thus, the sequence is as follows: at the place of origin for the vowel *ī*, there arises the *ca*-group, as well as the phonemes *ya* and *śa*, and so forth. || 222 ||
One might ask: "Is this rule not possible everywhere? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"But this letter *sa*, in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the heart, is the essence of life; the letter *ha* is the light (*prakāśa*), and the letter *ra* exists as the nature of filling (*pūraṇātmatayā*). (6.223)
Although, according to the rule of the six places of articulation (*ṣaṣṭhānata*), the dental is the place of origin for the letter *sa* and the throat for the letter *ha*,

nevertheless, because it is of the nature of life-force (*prāṇātman*) and vitality, the letter *sa* arises in the heart, while the letter *ha*, being of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), arises everywhere. || 223 ||
Concluding this, he introduces another topic: "The supreme emergence of the phonemes has been described; now their subtle [emergence] is being stated.
And the subtle is threefold. Among these, he first describes the subtle-subtle emergence:
At the entry there are sixteen, and at the emergence there are twelve suns, excluding the neuter ones.
In this context, the other letters are indeed the moon and the sun; however, this is the subtle arising (*sūkṣmodaya*).

It is said to be sixteenfold because the flow of the *apāna* breath is characterized by a predominance of bliss (*ānanda*). For this very reason, even regarding the supreme arising (*parodaya*), it is stated that the arising of the neuter letters occurs precisely within the flow of the *apāna*. The term "in the state of orientation" (*aunmukhye*) refers to the outward movement [of breath]. Therefore, in the *apāna*—
The emergence [of each letter] is two finger-breadths plus one-quarter for each; furthermore, in the case of *prāṇa*, it is three finger-breadths.

Taking that very group of sixteen or twelve phonemes as a basis, the other consonant groups beginning with *ka* arise together with their respective positions within the domain of the moon, the sun, *prāṇa*, and *apāna*—even in this subtle [process].
The meaning is that this arising is subtle within the emergence of the phonemes (varṇa). || 224 ||
Having thus described the extremely subtle arising of the phonemes, he now speaks of the subtle-gross as well:
"The duration of the thirty-three consonants beginning with 'ka' is said to be half a mora. (225)
The short vowels have five [mātrās], the long vowels eight; but *ḷ* is twice and thrice protracted (*pluta*).

Regarding "the eight long vowels," this includes the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*). Regarding "twice," it means two mātrās; regarding "thrice," it means three mātrās. Although the long vowels can also be protracted, that has not been mentioned here.

This is because it depends upon its utterance; the point is that, unlike their length (*dīrghatva*), their prolation (*plutatva*) is not inherent. Similarly, for the vowel *ḷ* as well, prolation alone is its inherent nature.
Thus, there is no fault in stating that very [prolation] here as its primary characteristic, rather than including its length among the enumerated qualities.

Thus, there are thirty-three half-morae (ardhamātrā) for the consonants beginning with *ka*; ten for the short vowels, thirty-two for the long vowels, and six for the protracted (*pluta*) vowel—making eighty-one half-morae in total.
Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for such a division? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Our teacher has stated that this consists of eighty-one half-measures.
Anticipating the question, "What is the intention behind his stating this? he says:
"On account of which the Blessed One uttered the mantra of eighty-one [syllables].
Regarding the phrase "on account of which," it is because this supreme subject of the mantra (mantramātṛ) possesses eighty-one mātrās.
"It consists of eighty-one" means that it is composed of that many words.
One might ask: "Even if the Lord is designated as 'Pervading the Sky' (Vyomavyāpin), what is the proof for this being the reason [for that designation]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Goddess Śakti, whose essence is Śiva, is said to consist of eighty-one words. (6.227)

In the *Śrīmātaṅga*, Śiva is said to be the self that consists of the aggregate of Dharma; thus, he is called "Śakti," whose form pervades the void (*vyomavyāpin*). This is stated in the *Śrīmātaṅga*, where it is said:
"The Goddess who consists of eighty-one words is that Śakti whose essence is Śiva. (*Mātaṅga-tantra* 1.7.31).
Thus it is said:

"Furthermore, O Sage, the mantras reside within the womb of Śakti; indeed, Śakti is the supreme power of the Lord, by whom the entire path extending to the end of the fire of time is pervaded from Śiva."
"Endowed with eighty-one forms, it has been proclaimed by me in the Vidyāpāda" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).

Now, one might ask: although this supreme power of the Lord, whose nature is all-pervasive space (*vyomavyāpin*), consists of various mantras such as the *hṛdaya* and others, how can she also possess the nature of Śiva?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that way," and so forth. Śiva is of the nature of that aggregate consisting of eighty-one powers (*śakti*)—the powers of the Lord (*pati*) as stated in such passages as: "The powers of the Lord are... (Mataṅga Tantra 1.20)—which exist in the manner previously described.
Thus, in its totality, she consists of that very nature.
As it is said there:
"All eighty-one words are indeed contained within a single one."
It is said that there are three hundred and sixty-eight letters.
"The worship of the God of gods, however, consists of his form both collective and individual.
And: "Even a single phoneme is proclaimed to be the designator of the deities."
"And all [these forms] are appropriate for the One, since they are the embodiments of the universe.
Thus it is said.
And this is established not only by scripture, but also by reasoning; thus he says:
"In such and such a way, the Lord is the sovereign of the wheel of the power of reflective awareness. (6.228)
He is manifested through the reflective awareness of the eighty-one gross phonemes; indeed,

although by the reasoning stated in such passages as "the power is truly non-different from the possessor of power," the Lord, the Supreme God, is in reality of a nature inseparable from all powers, [he nevertheless appears thus].

Śiva is the "Lord" (Īśvara) of that wheel of powers beginning with the Heart, which is of such a nature, because it consists of the eighty-one gross words formed from those respective phonemes; and because He is the one who, through various reflective awarenesses (parāmarśa) such as the Praṇava arising from them, reflects upon Himself as the universal Self, the Infinite, and so forth.
The meaning is that he who performs the severing of the fetters is indeed "manifested," such that his cognition is brought about.

For this very reason, in this context, the status of being a "word" (pada) belongs to as many [syllables] as are required for the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of the All-Self and so forth to be established, by means of which there would be eighty-one [words]. || 228 ||
Thus it is said: "From that very [point], reflective awareness continues until one [unit of] time is completed. (6.229)
To that extent, that word is said not to be constrained by the rules governing nominal endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).

There is no restriction of *sup* or *tiṅ*; for if there were such a restriction, then even though this word is one according to the aforementioned statement—"The six-syllabled mantra beginning with *praṇava* is *namaḥ śivāya*"—it would result in being three words.
The calculation would be inconsistent.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since this very Blessed Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) exists as consisting of eighty-one and a half *mātrās*, what is the purpose of teaching this Vyomavyāpin mantra, which possesses an equal pervasiveness?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
It is nourished by the sequence of the noble contemplations upon the eighty-one syllables.
"This dissolution effected by the *mātrā*s is the gross means (*sthūlopāya*), which is indeed the supreme means (*paropāya*).

By the term "dissolution" (*laya*), rest in one's own self alone is meant. By the phrase "the gross means," it is revealed that because there is a distinction among those to be instructed, there is also a distinction in the instruction itself. || 230 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he returns to the subject at hand:
"In each of the four [groups], there should be nine half-measures. (6.231)
Regarding the phrase "in the finger-breadths": there is the emergence of eighty-one half-mātrās within thirty-six finger-breadths.
Since four finger-breadths correspond to nine half-mātrās, thus within the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra) consisting of thirty-six finger-breadths, eighty-one half-mātrās arise. || 231 ||
And regarding these [fingers], there is another division at the time of their extension; thus he says:
"When a finger is divided into nine parts, there are nine sub-divisions. (6.232)
The Veda [four] is half a mātrā, while the other three [the Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan] are two, four, and six times that respectively.
When each finger-breadth (aṅgula) is divided ninefold, the measurement for thirty-six fingers becomes three hundred and twenty-four parts. Of these parts:

In that regard, it has been stated that for each individual consonant consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), there are nine parts as its place of origin (*udayasthāna*), according to the verse: "The four [vedas] are nine parts; a half-mora.
Furthermore, the other triad—characterized by short, long, and protracted [vowels]—is multiplied by two, four, and six [respectively].

Because the short vowel consists of one mora, its place of arising consists of eight or nine parts; because the long vowel consists of two morae, it consists of sixteen; and because the protracted vowel consists of three morae, it consists of twenty-four.
He summarizes this very point: "In this way, the short [vowel] resides within two sets of four parts of a finger's breadth. (233)

The long [vowel] is doubled and the prolated (*pluta*) tripled in sequence; after that, the consonant (*hal*) is half of that as well. "Of the nine parts" (*randhraṃśānām*) means of the nine divisions; "two sets of four" means eight ninth-parts. Regarding "the short" (*laghu*), it means a short vowel; "after that" (*tataḥ*) means even after the short one. By this, [the duration] of the five...
For the short vowels, since each arises in eight parts, there are forty-nine parts for each;

for the eight long vowels, by calculating sixteen parts for each, there are one hundred and twenty-eight; and for the protracted vowel, there are twenty-four for each of the thirty-three [consonants].
By calculating four parts for each of the *halāṃ*, there are one hundred and thirty-two [parts].

Although it would have been clearer to state explicitly that the rising place (*udayasthāna*) consists of nine parts— four finger-breadths for each of the eighty-one half-measures (*ardhamātrā*)— nevertheless, by stating it in this way, the following intention is conveyed:
When there is first the arising of the short vowels, immediately after that the long vowels, then the protracted vowel, and finally the consonants—thus the sequence is demonstrated. || 233 ||
Now, one might raise this objection: "If the letter *kṣa* is counted among these, then how many additional half-morae (*ardhamātrā*) are added?
And if that were so, how could they arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The letter *kṣa* consists of three and a half morae; it is thus a 'moric' [syllable] situated within. (6.34)
When that half-mora has been calculated as resting upon it, then again,
by the mountain-part (seven parts), there is another half-mora at half a finger-breadth.

The letter *kṣa*, however, is all-pervasive, its nature being the grasping of all conjunct consonants; it is the omnipresent Lord who partakes in the arising at the junctures of the beginning and end of the emergence of all phonemes.
Anticipating the question of how this [syllable] consists of one and a half *mātrās*, it is said: "consisting of *mātrās*," and so forth.
This is because it is composed of two half-*mātrās* consisting of the letters *ka* and *sa*. Regarding the phrase "in the interval of rest":
having rested for the duration of a half-*mātrā* after the letter *ka*, the letter *sa* is articulated. "In the measured" (*kalite*).
Thus, by means of eighty-one [parts], there are eighty-four half-mātrās. "Adri" (mountain) signifies seven.
For when half a finger is divided sevenfold, there are fourteen parts per finger;
thus, for thirty-six fingers, there are five hundred and four parts.
Thus, in each of the six half-fingers (ardhāṅguli), there is an increase of half a mātrā in seven parts;
consequently, in the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra) consisting of thirty-six fingers, there is the emergence of eighty-four half-mātrās.
Now, it has been stated that according to this position regarding the emergence of one hundred and one kalās, there is no emergence of the letter *kṣa* at all.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the city," and so forth. The phrase "consisting of the perception of all conjunctions" is used because it has as its ultimate characteristic the final conjunction. As was stated previously:
"When that [seed] also joins with the form of the womb, they know there to be another state of agitation."
"By way of illustration of that, there is the state of being the fiftieth letter" (Tantrāloka 3.189).

This is because, by taking the letters *ka* and *sa* as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) when they are vitalized by the *visarga* of the Absolute (*anuttara*), the entire collection of phonemes is subsumed within them. For this very reason, this...

At the beginning and end of all phonemes (varṇas), within the state of their mutual union—the *śamdhī*—it should arise as the recipient of the impulse (*codayabhāk*), being woven through all phonemes; for this reason, it is "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*), meaning it is omnipresent. || 236 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this description of the emergence of the phonemes? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this manner, within the movement of thirty-six [breaths], there is the emergence of the phonemes according to their fruit;
in the case of the cruel and the gentle, [the sequence is] in reverse order, from 'ha' down to the very last. (6.237)
"Of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) refers to [the vowels] beginning with *a*; "arising" (*udaya*) means, by implication, from the heart to the *dvādaśānta*.

"In the cruel" (*krūre*) refers to that characterized by liberation; "in the gentle" (*śaumye*) refers to that characterized by enjoyment, which consists of the respective supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
"In reverse order" (*vilomena*) means, by implication, during the arising of the *apāna* breath. He explains this very reversal: "starting from *ha* up to the last one."
As it has been said:

"Success occurs when [the breath] flows downward as far as it reaches the heart-lotus; and liberation indeed occurs when it moves upward into the Supreme Reality, O virtuous lady. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.56)
Thus it is said. In reality, however, the place of origin for the letter *a* is the heart, while that of the letter *ha* is the *dvādaśānta*.
Relying precisely upon this, he describes the subtle and supreme arising of the phonemes:
"The letter *a* is in the heart; the letter *ha* is at the *dvādaśānta*; the wise know this."
Non-duality whose essence is the Self is that repose within the nature of Light.
"Non-duality" (*advaita*) is so called because of the internalization of all phonemes through the process of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Regarding "light" (*prakāśa*), it has been said:
"The repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed to be the state of 'I-ness' (*ahambhāva*)" (Aparokṣānubhūtiprakaraṇa 22).
Thus [ends the section]. || 238 ||
And to show that this [process] occurs even at the rising of the apāna, he says:
"This single measure of eighty-one [units], through the non-differentiation of Śiva and Śakti, circulates by doubling over the seventy-two finger-breadths. (6.239)
"The inseparability of Śiva and Śakti" means in the union of both the prāṇa and apāna, which consist of bindu and nāda.
"Eighty-one" is an illustration; by it, eighty-four is also implied. "By way of doubling," [is the meaning].
Of thirty-six finger-breadths. || 239 ||
Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says:
"The subtle emergence has been described as threefold, while the supreme emergence has been stated as twofold;
now the gross emergence of the phonemes (arṇa), as taught by the Guru, is being declared. (6.240)
Now, "atha" (then) signifies immediate succession; "spoken by the Guru" is a term that applies to all [the following].

In that regard, he first describes the gross emergence of the letters according to the sequence of the groups (vargas): "The emergence of the eight groups occurs in the day at half a watch (prahara) for each; and [it occurs] at night as well. Regarding this decrease and increase, some say there is none, but others say there is. (6.241)
"Decrease and increase" refers to [the changes] in relation to or independently of the external day and night. || 241 ||
In that regard, according to the view that is independent of external days and nights, their arising occurs with equal duration; thus he says:

"This arising of the groups (vargodaya) occurs during the night and also by day, occupying half a watch (ardhayāmaga). The meaning of "occupying half a watch" is that the arising for each group is four and a half finger-breadths.
Having thus stated the view that is independent of external days and nights, he shows it for others as well:
"That [number] consists of thirteen hundred and fifty breaths. (6.242)
It is said that there is one and a half *saṃkrāntis* for each group of day and night;

that [total] amounts to one thousand three hundred and fifty movements of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*). By the term "one and a half," it is meant "with a half," because nine hundred breath-movements are specified for each *saṃkrānti*. Thus, during the day...

The arising of the twelve transits (saṃkrānti) constitutes ten thousand one hundred and eight breath-movements (prāṇacāra). At night it is likewise; thus, in the summing of day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths]. Furthermore, for each group (varga), the arising occurs at every third transit.
Thus he says:
"But when there is unity of those, there is the arising of twenty-seven hundred movements. (6.243)

Thus, it is established that, just as in the two previously mentioned transits, the increase and decrease of the emergence of the eight groups (varga) also occur in accordance with the external decrease and increase of the day and night; otherwise, there would be no fixed regularity for the movements of the breath (prāṇacāra) during each emergence of a group. || 243 ||

Now, one might object: "If there are nine groups [of consonants] including the letter *kṣa*, according to those who hold that view, what is the division of the movements of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) during their emergence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But for those who say there are nine groups, the hundred breaths are [divided by] twelve. (*prāṇaśatī ravīn*)
The transit is said to be with one-third of a part for each individual group. || 6-244 ||

Day and night, in that state of unity, there are twelve hundred [breaths] for the eyes of the Vedas—meaning twelve hundred. "With a third part" means because three hundred breaths are added. Thus, in each category (varga), there are twelve hundred movements of the breath; this is the case across the nine categories.
"One thousand and one hundred and eight" refers to the union of day and night;
"the two ears and the two eyes" refers to twenty-four.
Having thus described the gross emergence of the classes of letters according to the sequence of the *vargas*, he speaks of it by means of another sequence as well:
"This is that gross emergence of the *vargas*; now the emergence of the individual phonemes (*arṇodaya*) is being described. (6.245)
Regarding this, he says:
"In each individual phoneme, there are two hundred and sixteen breaths;
externally, there are thirty-six caṣakas in a day, and likewise at night. (6.246)
Regarding "thirty-six cups": since six movements of the vital breath arise for each cup, there would thus be one thousand eight hundred movements of the vital breath for the fifty phonemes. || 246 ||
In this regard, he shows the distinction by raising an objection:

"Therein, one hundred and eight [recitations] are for Rudra, and thereafter for Śakti; however, in the state of union (yoga) according to the Yāmala, there is the non-differentiation of Rudra and Śakti. (6.247)
"In the yoga of the Yamala-state" means in the union of both. || 247 ||
And this very [number] would be doubled when the day and night are combined; thus he says:

"In the undivided state of day and night, the emergence of external phonemes is taught as the movement of twenty-four [units]—eyes, fires, oceans, and arrows—plus one nāḍī with its fifth part. (6.248)

"Dṛgvahnyabdhi" refers to four hundred and thirty-two; these are the "impure movements," meaning the movements of the vital breath (prāṇa). "A channel with a fifth part" is so called because of the doubling of thirty-six caṣakas. || 248 ||
Concluding this and introducing another matter, he says:
"Thus has this fifty-fold [system] of phonemes been examined;
now we shall explain the opinion of those who say that it is one less. (6.249)
Thus it is said:
"The Vedas are the movements (cāras), each being half a movement less by one-fifth;
in a syllable (varṇa) it is increased, and doubled when there is no division between day and night. (6.250)
"The Vedas are four. [The phrase] "deficient by a fifth part" means, by implication, deficient by some small portion.
"Exceeding" means above two hundred and sixteen. Therefore, since each of the forty-nine phonemes consists of two hundred and sixteen [units].
There are ten thousand five hundred and eighty-four breath-movements;
with an additional four for each [cycle], there are one hundred and ninety-six. And by this, the fifth part—slightly less than a quarter—of twenty-four and a half movements [is obtained].
One hundred and eight thousand. || 250 ||
He summarizes this very point:
"This is that gross emergence of phonemes; previously, the subtle was described.
By the sense of the word "subtle," it is meant that the supreme [emergence] was also described previously. (6.251)
Now he concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half of a verse:
"Thus has the reality of time been declared, established by the scriptures, oral tradition, and personal experience.
Thus [ends] the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Reality of Time."
Regarding the term *mukhāgama*:

according to the principle stated in [the Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā], "The Śiva-nature is here called the mouth" (verse 20), the Guru is the "mouth" because he is the means for entering the supreme reality (*paratattva*); his "tradition" (*āgama*) is thus the *mukhāgama*.
The meaning is "the teaching. It is established as follows:

"Because, through the sequence of the scripture and by practicing the wisdom of a Guru who knows that [reality], knowledge that is self-validated becomes Bhairava due to its fullness" (Tantrāloka 4.77).
By the reasoning stated in such passages, one attains perfection through complete fullness; may there be auspiciousness!
Jayaratha, having reached the pinnacle of skill in investigating the movement that rests upon the flow of prāṇa and apāna, has composed this most excellent exposition in the sixth chapter.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Principle of Time," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, the illustrious Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the illustrious Jayaratha. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
One whose intense possession by Caṇḍabhairava has been rendered ready through the rising power of the respective mantras.
May Jayarudra, who has caused the seal of worldly existence to dissolve, establish auspiciousness.

Now, with the second half [of the verse], he begins to explain the arising of the wheels (*cakrodaya*), which is indeed connected to the reality of time (*kālatattva*): "Now, this supreme secret, the arising of the wheels, is being told. (7.1)
"Of the wheels" means those whose nature consists of the mantras and so forth. || 1 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated that the emergence of the Blessed Mother Mātṛkā, who is common to all mantras, occurs immediately [thereafter]? What then is the reason for describing the emergence of the wheels (cakras) as well, which consist of the specific forms of those very mantras? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Thus has that which is born without effort been described; now, however, that which is born of effort is being declared.

Anticipating the objection, "But what is the purpose of this declaration?", he says: "Everything consisting of seed-syllables (bīja) and clusters (piṇḍa) [attains] the nature of the vibration of consciousness. (7.2)
It is described as the means for effecting the consciousness of another;

this entire collection of mantras, consisting of seeds (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*), arising within the vital breath, effects the state of vibration of consciousness— that is, the immersion into the nature of Śakti.
The Śāmbhava form also enters [the path] through the lineage as a means for the consciousness of another;
thus, what was described within the *varṇatattva* in the context of the *āṇavopāya* is not without purpose—this is the meaning. 2.
Now, it was begun here to state that the arising of mantras occurs thus within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that...
And since [the result] is born of effort, when that effort is performed, only that specific result would be accomplished and nothing else;

how then could these [external means] also serve as a means for the consciousness of another?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as the driving of the multitude of water-lifting buckets at the front of a waterwheel... (7.3)
Through the effort of single-pointed concentration, one should experience the wondrous emergence of the yantra;
when the mantra constantly emerges by the power of that single-pointed concentration, [the goal is attained]. (7.4)
The deity of that mantra becomes propitiated through effort by means of identification (*tādātmya*).
Here, because the activity of the one who operates a waterwheel consists solely in the act of pulling the mechanism,
by means of a single continuous mental application (*anusaṃdhāna*), [the result arises] from the connection with the bucket situated at the edge of the waterwheel's rim.
Just as the continuous and uninterrupted movement of a machine results in its production through a variety of forms— such as the wheel of jars being empty or full, facing upwards or downwards—
so too, for the practitioner, it does not happen through a single, constant mental focus directed toward the arising of the mantra.

This alone would be established at the very moment of its arising, insofar as, by being inseparable from it, even this deity of the mantra becomes propitious through identity without requiring any further effort.
This is the intended meaning here: just as one who operates a water-wheel while driving the machine [is not separate from its motion].

Even another variety [of manifestation] would attain its state independently of any further effort; likewise, the practitioner, while striving for the very emergence of the mantra, attains identity with supreme consciousness. Thus, it must necessarily be stated that the emergence of the *cakra* is the instrumental cause for attaining supreme consciousness—this is what has been said. || 4 ||
Thus he says:
"In the sky, [there are] six, one, and two, arising eternally; half of that [is in] the pair of clusters. (7.5)
In the case of three [units], the arising is considered to be seven thousand two hundred;
but in the case of four, it is five thousand four hundred.
In the five-syllabled [mantra], the rising [of the breath] lasts for four thousand three hundred and twenty [breaths];
in the six-syllabled, it becomes three thousand six hundred. (7.7)
In the seventh [case], however, it is recorded as three thousand and eighty-six,
