when calculated by twenty-seven hundred and eight syllables.
The emergence [of breath] occurs at twenty-four hundred [breaths] for the nine-syllable [mantra], and at twenty-one hundred and sixty-six [breaths] for the ten-syllable [mantra]. (7–9)
One hundred and nineteen [syllables] are for a mantra of sixty-four syllables;
there would be one thousand eight hundred [pulses] for the rising of a twelve-syllable mantra.
In the Trayodaśārṇa [Tantra], there are indeed sixteen hundred and sixty-two;
in the Bhuvanārṇaka, fifteen hundred and forty-three.
In a fifteen-syllable [meter], there would be one thousand four hundred and forty;
however, for a sixteen-syllable [meter], it is said to be one thousand three hundred and fifty.
In a mantra of seventeen syllables, there are one hundred and twelve [repetitions];
in a mantra of eighteen syllables, it should be known by the wise that there are one hundred and seventy-one.
In a wheel numbering twenty-four, there would be nine hundred;
however, in one numbering twenty-seven, the rising consists of eight hundred. (7.14)
In the great wheel of thirty-two [spokes], there are six hundred and seventy-five;
in the wheels of twenty-four and forty-eight, there are four hundred and fifty. (7.15)
One who knows the yoga of the *piṇḍa* should observe the arising [of the breath] within the *piṇḍa-mantras*;
in the wheel of fifty-four [units], there are four hundred [breaths]. (7.16)
With thirty-seven and a half [units], there would be three hundred and eighty-eight;
with half and a third of a half, it would be two hundred and sixty-six. (7.17)
In the wheel of eighty-one squares, the arising follows the movement of the vital breath;
however, in the wheel called ninety-six, it becomes two hundred and one and a quarter.
"In the wheel of one hundred and eight, there would be an emergence of two hundred.

Here, *khe* means two zeros; *rasāḥ* means six; *akṣī* means two. "Always arisen" (*nityottha*) refers to the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), flowing continuously by its very nature, [completes] twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths].

The sense is that this should apply to the movements (*cāra*). Thus, for a mantra whose nature is a single aggregate (*piṇḍa*), there is an emergence (*udaya*) of exactly that same number in accordance with each movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
therefore, because of the emergence of each aggregate or each phoneme at every movement of the vital breath, [the result follows].

The emergence of mantras consisting of two or more syllables occurs in a reduced number, according to the sequence of one-half and one-third of the activity of the eternally arisen vital breath (prāṇa);
thus he says: "In the case of a pair of syllables, half of that. Of that [total] which consists of six hundred [breaths].
Half of twenty-one thousand—that is, ten thousand eight hundred—is the number here.
For it is intended that two natural breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) arise as a single breath-movement;
indeed, it is proclaimed everywhere without distinction that "the recitation (*japa*) should be made equal to the breath. Therefore, in this case:

It has been stated that [the number] arises from effort. "Seven thousand and two hundred" is said because it is intended to represent the emergence of three natural breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) as a single breath-movement. This should be understood similarly in what follows as well. "Abdhi" means four.

"Exceeding by eighty-six" is said by way of abundance; for in this way, there would be two additional *cāras*. Therefore, in this case, a slight reduction of some parts must be made for each *cāra* so that there may be equality in the calculation. Nor has this been stated by us based on our own imagination; rather, it is read directly from the scripture itself.

We too have not presented a detailed calculation here, for fear of excessive prolixity and because it would be of no use. By that [calculation], there is an emergence of twenty-one hundred and sixty-six, which constitutes ten vargas. "Śivas" refers to the eleven Rudras; thus, [the total] is sixty-four.

"By way of abundance" (*bhūmnā*): thus, there would be an excess of four movements; "by sixty-two" (*dvāṣaṣṭyā*) means by way of abundance due to the addition of six breath-movements; "by forty-three" (*tricatvāriṃśatyā*) means by way of abundance due to the addition of two movements; "fifteen hundred" (*pañcadaśa-śatāni*); and "worlds" (*bhuvana*) refers to fourteen.
"Khābdhi" (sky-ocean) means forty; "saikasaptati" (one-seventy) refers to the fact that there are more than seven movements by way of abundance.
Furthermore, no specific sequence of numbers is intended here; thus, there is no fault in not teaching the intermediate wheels such as the nineteenth and so forth, for in this context—

An effort must be made for the rising of each individual wheel at every movement of breath; this is what is intended to be stated, and that would be accomplished even in this way. The phrase "in the [cycle] of twenty-two and four" means consisting of forty-eight.
The phrase "in the eight-eights" means consisting of sixty-four. "Together with a half" [refers to the preceding].
By this, thirty-two remaining breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) are established. "Half" means "half of a third part," by which there would be forty and a half breath-movements, and thirteen and a half;
thus, in both ways, the numerical equality of fifty-four is maintained. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīyoginīkaula*:
"When [the breath] has risen eternally, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths];
in the pair, there are ten thousand and eight hundred."
In the triad, the emergence is recorded as seven thousand two hundred;
but in the tetrad, it is five thousand four hundred.
In the five-syllabled [mantra], four thousand three hundred and twenty rises are declared; this should be known by those who track the flow of the rises.
"In the group of six, however, that which is called the 'three-thousand' is traditionally taught to have an emergence of six hundred at its end.
In the group of seven, the three-thousand is traditionally taught to be increased by eighty-six," and so forth.

"In the wheel of one hundred and eight [spokes], consisting of the mass of mantra-syllables, the arising (*udaya*) is said to consist of two hundred [units] again; it bestows all accomplishments. Thus ends [the section from verse 5 to 18].
And one should not stop with this much alone; thus he says:
"When, in this manner, this wheel has been doubled six times in succession... (7.19).
From that [measurement], one may take double, or half of an eighth part, or one and a half, or one;
even beyond that, those skilled in subtlety may calculate by halving and so forth.
The subtle movement is perceived through its persistence for sixteen parts.
"In this way"—by the method to be described—this wheel, consisting of one hundred and eight, is doubled six times in succession; first, it consists of two hundred and sixteen.
When, at the end, it becomes six thousand nine hundred and twelve,
then, having doubled even that— which consists of thirteen thousand eight hundred and twenty-four—
and considering that this wheel contains one and a half [units] per [count], there is one and a half for each breath.
The meaning is that the rising [of the breath] would be half of one-eighth, that is, the sixteenth part.
Even after that, when the calculation of half, half again, and so forth is made while remaining within the sixteenth part,
it becomes extremely subtle and minute for yogis who are skilled in subtlety and have ascended to the supreme state.

"The movement of the vital breath (prāṇīya-cāra) is perceived," meaning it is known. The essential point here is this: in such a calculation, the sixteenth part of the movement of the vital breath constitutes the emergence of the wheel (cakra), which consists of three hundred and fifty-four thousand [breaths] plus six hundred.

It may be so; yet, if one were to conceive of even that as half, it would be the thirty-second part of a wheel consisting of six hundred thousand, two hundred and ninety-one thousand [units]; and if one were to conceive of that [part] in the same way...

The portion of the breath-movement that is perceptible to yogins is limited precisely to this extent: the sixty-fourth part of a cycle consisting of thirteen hundred and eighty-two thousand [breaths]. ||19-20||
Now, one might ask: "What would happen for yogins through such a characteristic? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, for the yogin whose movement of breath has been restrained by effort... (7.21).
Gradually, through the movement of the vital breath, the "swallowing" (grāsa) itself arises;
it is called "swallowing" because, by its very nature, there is no further arising [of the breath].
What would happen to him because of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He abides in the state of the withdrawal of time, attained through the process of devouring the vital breath. (7.22)
Consciousness alone would be one and full through the removal of the differentiation of cognitions.
He demonstrates precisely this removal of the differentiation of cognitions:
"For instance, when there is no arising of the new movement of the vital breath" (7.23).
A distinction in cognition produced by a distinction in time cannot be postulated;

for since time has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its direct substratum, when the vital breath does not arise, time also would not arise. Thus, due to its absence, even a distinction in cognition produced by that [time] would not occur.
What has been stated is correct: "Consciousness alone should be one and full. || 23 ||
But surely, through the process of swallowing the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there has also occurred the swallowing of time;

if, therefore, no differentiation caused by that [time] exists within consciousness, then there will be one caused by its object (*jñeya*), by which this distinction arises—namely, "this is the cognition of blue" and "this is the cognition of yellow. It is by this much alone [that the distinction is established].
How can its unity be established? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Knowledge is not divided by the division of its objects, just as [the perception of] a mountain peak [remains one despite its various parts]. (7.24)

For a difference in the objects of consciousness does not necessarily entail a difference in the consciousness itself. For if it were so, then even though there is a difference in the objects of consciousness—such as the names and other attributes of various houses—how could there be a single cognition of a city or the like?
This is what was stated by the phrase "like the perception of a mountain peak. For one situated on a high elevation...
The intended meaning is that for a person, there would be only a single manifestation consisting of those various appearances. As they say:

"Therefore, even though an external object exists, because the intellect is one, it does not follow that it is manifold—even though it possesses many similar forms—due to its cognition of the manifold."
Thus, time alone is its differentiator; and that [time] is intended to consist of extremely subtle moments, by which the cessation of cognition occurs immediately after its arising. || 24 ||
Thus he says:
"But time is its differentiator; that [time] is considered to be the subtle moment (kṣaṇa).
The word "but" (tu) indicates a reason. "That" refers to time.
Now, one might ask: "What is the limit of its subtlety? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The limit of subtlety is knowledge; that moment lasts as long as [that knowledge] persists. (7.25)
Therefore, its existence is a mere existence consisting of cognition alone, delimited by two fixed ends; this is the meaning. || 25 ||

Now, one might ask: "Why is this [reality], which is conditioned by other factors, described in such a way? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Otherwise, it cannot be defined even by the most skillful.
The word "otherwise" refers to [describing it] as "indivisible, partless, characterized as a moment of time," and so forth.

The meaning is "by means of its direct characteristic. For if it were stated that "destruction follows immediately after arising," then its beginning and end would be asserted; and given the existence of those two, a middle must necessarily be admitted as well.

Thus, by [asserting] that this [moment] possesses three parts—beginning, middle, and end—it would follow that it has parts; therefore, when its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) is intended to be expressed, its having parts (*sāṃśatva*) would instead be asserted. As they say:
"Just as there is an end to a moment, so too should its beginning and middle be considered."
"Because a moment consists of [these three], there is no stability of the world within a single moment.
Thus:
"Furthermore, the beginning, middle, and end must be considered in the same way as a moment."

By the reasoning stated above, if one were to apply such an investigation even to those parts that consist of beginning, middle, and end, the same objection would recur; thus, due to infinite regress, nothing at all could be established.
Consequently, even by the most skillful, it is impossible to provide a definition for it, or if one were provided, it would not hold.
It would sprout.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the limit of that knowledge by which this [state] could be defined?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Knowledge may extend as far as it does, yet the absence of that [object] does not manifest. (7.26)

"How much? means: even if [the cognition] is momentary, what is its duration? "The absence thereof" refers to the absence of cognition; the sense is that as long as that absence has not occurred, that cognition must remain as one and the same. Furthermore, this absence is both perceptible and an effect.
It has been established elsewhere; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. || 26 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, when does the absence of those [objects] arise, such that there could be a limit even for cognition?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that absence does not occur for us as long as [the object] remains on the path of the senses."
Neither in the object nor in the location of the self is there the state of being conjoined or disjoined. (7.27)

Furthermore, the non-existence of cognition does not arise as long as there is no conjunction or disjunction between the sense organs, the object, and the knower; for when cognition regarding an object such as blue arises for a knower whose sensory activity is uninterrupted, [it ceases] when there is disjunction from that blue and so forth.

Or, if there is a conjunction with yellow and so forth, then that [previous cognition] is absent. Now, since the instrument is employed at every moment—as in the case of a lamp and the like—there is no dispute among anyone regarding the momentariness of cognition; otherwise, even for a cognizer whose sensory organs are fully engaged, there would be no cognition of blue and so forth.

It would not be so; therefore, why was it said that as long as the arising of conjunctions and disjunctions of the sense organs does not occur, there is only a single cognition? For in that case, the non-existence of continuous streams of cognitions (*dhārāvāhin-vijñāna*) would have been asserted. True, but this is what you prefer.
We maintain that consciousness could not possess momentariness characterized by destruction without a trace (*niranvayavināśātman*);

for it has just been established through the determination of the moment that consciousness must persist for three, four, or more moments immediately following [the object]. Therefore, even with respect to an object such as blue, which is of a single uniform nature...

Within consciousness, the absence of [external objects] due to the differentiation of the sense organs such as the eyes and so forth is indeed established; however, it is simply not perceived in that way. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even for those cognitions occurring in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhin), there would be no absence [of the object]. || 27 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is this state of being joined and separated also caused by a cause, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If that [state] arises, it is certainly composed of vibration (spanda) and resides within the vital breath."
It would indeed exist [only] because of that; in the absence of the vibration of the vital breath, it would not exist. || 7-28 ||

"Consisting of vibration" (*spandamayī*) means that its nature (*prakṛti*) or root cause is vibration; thus, the meaning is that it is entirely dependent upon vibration. For the intention is that an object moving from one place to another is either conjoined with or disjoined from another object. And since vibration rests upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the body] is so [dependent] through this traditional succession.

The state of being subject to conjunction and disjunction must also certainly reside in the vital breath (prāṇa) alone; thus, in the absence of the vibration of the vital breath, that [state] would not exist.
According to the principle that "in the absence of the cause, the effect is also absent," the meaning is: from where could its existence possibly arise? || 28 ||
Now, let it be granted that there is either conjunction or disjunction—or let it not be; what need have we for such a concern?

For it was proposed here that when the consumption of time occurs through the process of swallowing the vital breath (prāṇa), there would be only one complete consciousness; so tell us, how can that very [proposition] be accomplished?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Due to the absence of that [object], there is no absence of consciousness; rather, that very [consciousness] is that [object].
Because of the absence of its [the object's] division into conjunction and disjunction, there would be no absence even of consciousness; for...

The sense is that whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something must be its effect. This being so, that primordial cognition which is consciousness is indeed this very same [consciousness], and not another consciousness; the meaning is that there would be only one single, complete consciousness.
Now, one might object: "In that case, would there not be an appearance of non-duality for a single consciousness alone, due to the unification of preceding and succeeding moments?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And in reality, this [consciousness] is not long, because temporal distinctions are excluded. (7.29)

The cognition "this" is not subtle either, because it is long in its object; for length and so forth depend on time, and this cognition has no contact with time at all, since it is not delimited by time. || 29 ||
Thus he says:
"For this very reason, in reality, consciousness does not touch time;
likewise, in reality, even its eternity would not be possible, for that [eternity]..."

What is being stated is the state of following through the three times, and not a state of constant manifestation; for if it were so, it would mean that manifestation occurs in all three times. As they say:
"Wherein there is no cognition of time—neither 'always,' nor 'then,' nor even 'at one time'..."
"Therefore, this doctrine of yours is neither eternal, nor is it described otherwise.
(Upaniṣadstotra 12.5) Now,
if indeed there exists in reality only one consciousness (*saṃvit*) unconditioned by time, then how is this...?
Anticipating the objection—"How can worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which is based on external distinctions, be established?"—he says:
"Therefore, consciousness alone, though one, appears in various forms in such and such ways. (7.30)
Even though it is non-conceptual, consciousness experiences conceptualization within the sphere of objective entities;

therefore, due to the absence of contact with time, consciousness— though singular and non-conceptual— is [perceived] as manifold with respect to the object of entities, which consists of a confluence of various appearances.

Likewise, that which perceives and reflects upon forms such as blue or non-blue is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus, there is no disruption even of external worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). || 30 ||
An objection might be raised: "Even if she is reflected upon in such and such a manner, how can she be only one? Anticipating this, he says:
"As long as another vibration has not arisen, so long does that [state] persist. (7.31)
A single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would consist of as many [moments] as it takes to imagine a manifold object;

therefore, from the aforementioned cause— characterized by the production of the conjunctions and disjunctions of those respective objects and so forth— a further movement (*spandāntara*) directed toward another object of conceptualization has not yet arisen.
The meaning is that even while imagining an object in various ways, there would be only one single, very long conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not many;
this applies even when [an object] such as blue is being conceptualized as having the nature of a confluence of multiple appearances.

The sense is that there is indeed a unity of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), because there exists a single continuous synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*); otherwise, this [conceptual thought] would not even attain its own essential nature. || 31 ||
Regarding this, it is said:
"But for those who know it in this way, conceptual construction is not possible. (7.32)

For indeed, no one whatsoever could ever exist as a single [individual] even within the three worlds—these being the Buddhists. "In this way" means that the arising of other conceptual constructions occurs only upon the emergence of another vibration (*spanda*), and not within a single vibration itself. "Single" refers to that by which...

External worldly transaction, which is based on numerous supports such as the concealment of memory (*smṛti-apalāpa*) and so forth, would thus be established. He demonstrates this very point: "Indeed, conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is said to be cognition colored by words (*śabdārūṣaṇā*). (33)

And if that [consciousness] were only successive in this way, who could conceptualize what, how, or as what? Even a conceptualization as small as "a jar" would not exist; what then to say of [the perception of] stability? (7.34)

And there is no conceptual construction whatsoever that is established solely upon the phonemes (*mātrā*), as you claim. For it has been said: "Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression. This [cognition] is "colored by words" (*śabdārūṣaṇā*); it is "successive" (*kramikā*), because of speech.

Because they arise sequentially, and because conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is thus successive, the moments that have arisen have perished, and new ones have not yet emerged; therefore, what subject (*pramātā*)— even one constructed by thought— is there who could be a conceptual self, since there is nothing to be conceived as having arisen and then perished?

Furthermore, due to the absence of a connection between preceding and succeeding [phonemes] and so forth, how could one conceptualize? The meaning is that the very acquisition of the nature of conceptualization would not occur. For this very reason, since the phoneme *ṭ* is absent at the time of pronouncing *gh*, and since the former has already perished by the time of pronouncing the latter, in the word "ghaṭa"—

The meaning is this: if even such a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were not established, then let alone any consideration of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) and so forth, what talk can there be even of its mere existence? For in that [Mādhyamika] system, there is no such conceptual construction whatsoever of which even a single part could be considered definitively established.
For if that were the case, the vow of their momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) would be violated; such is the intended meaning. || 33-34 ||
Is it not our view that there is no single, persisting cognition that accompanies everything like the thread of a garland? It is not that multiple, momentary cognitions do not exist;
rather, it is those very [cognitions], when aggregated, that will possess the capacity for external practical activity—so what [is the problem]?
Anticipating the objection, "What is the fault?", he says:
"And there is no collection of cognitions, because they do not exist simultaneously. (7.35)
"Because they do not exist simultaneously," because it is stated that their cessation occurs immediately after their arising. || 35 ||
Therefore, in that view, this entire conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), being purely conceptual, would not be established; thus he says:
"By that, this conventional practice born of conceptualization has simply vanished.
He then says: "Therefore, our own position alone is superior."
Therefore, as long as another vibration does not arise, that [state] shall remain one.
Consciousness may touch even millions of dharmas whose nature consists of those conceptualizations;

as long as another movement of thought— concluding with a different conceptualization— does not arise, it continues to conceptualize the flood of dharmas consisting of such qualities as "cowness," "whiteness," and "mobility."
This must indeed be a single, alternative cognition, by which this entire worldly transaction, animated by a single unifying synthesis, would be established. || 36 ||
And he says that this was not stated as his own original invention because it is unprecedented:
"Therefore, [the Lord] consists of the reflective awareness of the noble powers of the eighty-one words. (7.37)
It has already been established that conceptual thought (vikalpa) bestows the state of Śiva;
therefore,
despite its nature of reflecting upon multiple attributes, it takes the form of the "Pervasive Sky" (vyomavyāpin) because of its characteristic of unity.

We have already stated previously that pure consciousness (*śuddhavidyā*), though it consists of various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) through its awareness of the manifold powers such as the Heart and others, bestows nothing other than the state of Śiva, which is the ultimate fruit, because it is essentially one.
Now, [one might ask]: "In this way, within a single movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*), beginning from the wheel consisting of a single aggregate..."
Since the natural arising of all the cakras— from the beginning of the cycle consisting of thirteen hundred and eighty-two thousand [beats] until its end—
continues spontaneously, how can yogins attain a specific understanding regarding particular cakras? Such is the doubt.
He pacifies [the doubt] by showing an illustration: "Just as it would happen through effort in this way: 'I shall make my ears dance. (7.38)
Just as the intellect follows the movement of the rotating wheel through effort,
so too, by means of an effort belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) preceded by the desire "I shall make my two ears dance," it happens for the yogi that,
according to the maxim of the quivering of a cow's ear and so forth, the two ears themselves appear to be dancing.

In the same way, even from an effort directed toward the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that is primarily focused on a single *piṇḍa* or other such wheels (*cakra*), the intellect becomes fixed upon that very wheel; the meaning is that the awakening becomes established specifically within the wheel intended for the commencement [of the practice]. This is the underlying point here: indeed, in this world, wherever a yogin may be engaged in any activity, [the result follows accordingly].
The recitation of any mantra whatsoever must necessarily be performed with the equality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); otherwise, the accomplishment of the task will not occur. As it has been said:
"One should mutter [the mantra] with the equality of the vital breath; from that, success will certainly arise."
"Otherwise, O beautiful one, one does not attain success, but incurs ridicule.

Therefore, whether it is the arising of another wheel whose nature is a single *piṇḍa* or otherwise, the procedure is exactly the same, because the equilibrium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is without distinction everywhere. || 38 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, the rule is that recitation, fire-oblations, worship, and so forth, possess equality with the vital breath. (7.39)

It is called *homa* because even there, the utterance of mantras occurs. Therefore, from the reason stated as "from the arising of the wheel" (*cakrodayāt*), there is no contradiction whatsoever; for while the numerical count is based on the greater or lesser number of phonemes with respect to the natural flow of the breath, [the designation *homa*] is based on the presence of mantra-utterance. || 39 ||
"What is the authority for this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the Siddhāmata, the Kuṇḍalinī power is equal to the vital breath (prāṇa) and is beyond mind (unmanā).
And this very point was stated by the Supreme Lord in the Yoginīkula. (7.40)

The connection [of this passage] is as follows: "This very [reality] has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata* and in the *Śrīyoginīkaula*. The supreme power of the Lord, known as the *varṇakuṇḍalinī*, which manifests externally in the form of mantras consisting of various single-syllable clusters (*ekapiṇḍa*) and so forth—if indeed that [power] is identical with the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The meaning is that one should ascend through the equilibrium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and then, as the *unmanā*, one should shine forth in identity with Śiva.
As it is said there:
"One should perform the recitation (*japya*) equal to the vital breath; perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) equal to the vital breath."
"In this way, the power known as Kuṇḍalinī, who is equal to the vital breath and is Manonmanī.
Thus [ends verse 40].
The Śrīyoginīkaula scripture states:

"Having established the division pertaining to the principle of Śakti within the wheel of words, mantras, and syllables, the knower of mantras shall partake in the fruit at the beginning of recitation and other rites. (7.41)
In such a wheel where the syllables of the mantra are primarily based on the words,

the yogi— having made a division within the words according to the principle of Śakti, and having caused each individual word to arise through its specific division in accordance with every movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra)— knows the arising of the mantra during recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites.
"He shall become a partaker of the fruit" means that he shall obtain the fruit as is appropriate. || 41 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is this division, or what is its fruit?", he says:
"One should eliminate the rise of the hundred as numbered by two, three, seven, and eight.
Here, [the number] is calculated according to the aggregates of words such as one, two, three, seven, eight, and so forth, for the wheels, as previously stated.

That is to say, by resorting to the division extending up to the wheel consisting of many words and clusters [of phonemes] arising within the hundred-fold [breath-cycle], one should "cause the movement of the breath to cease," which means one should perform the swallowing of the breath (prāṇagrāsa). For this alone is the primary fruit for yogins: the entry into supreme consciousness, which is not limited by time.
Thus it is said. And so, one must pay attention to this very point; thus he says:
"In this way, the mantras, the vidyās, or the lords of the wheels (cakranāyakas) abide within Śakti. (7.42)

O Dear One, having understood them in the form of word-clusters (padapiṇḍa), they should always be applied to the Great Reality (mahātattva) which is eternally risen, established in the state of Sadāśiva.
But those who are unyoked on the path of power, and whose mantras have not been recited with the *udaya*, do not achieve success even if recited with effort hundreds of millions of times. (7.44)

Having thus understood everything previously stated, the mantras or vidyās— of which the *cakras* are primary— abide as power (*śakti*) in the form of words and syllable-clusters (*padapiṇḍa*) according to the process of words, clusters, and so forth just described; they are "situated in power," meaning they have arisen through the equilibrium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and should be employed at all times during recitation and other practices by the yogins as is appropriate for them.
Success would be attained. Otherwise, indeed, because it is eternally emergent, for this very reason it is the supreme goal; because it is the Great Reality (*mahātattva*);

because it is situated in emergence due to the predominance of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), for this very reason it bestows that success; and because it is always of the nature of the auspicious and of the nature of power (*śakti*)—if [the senses] are not joined to the central abode (*madhyadhāman*), then likewise by means of the emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The meaning is that those mantras and so forth which have not been recited even through the entry—that is, by implication, the exit—do not achieve success even if recited with effort for hundreds of millions of times; they are incapable of bestowing that full [result]. As it has been said:
When the practitioner does not find [the truth] regarding the two paths of emanation and withdrawal,
which consist of the nature of rising and setting, the mantras yield only meager results.

"When recited, meditated upon, and worshipped, they do not grant worldly enjoyment or liberation; rather, impelled by the command of Śiva, they bestow the fruit of injury. By the phrase "mantras or vidyās," that which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration is [referred to].
The distinction between mantra and vidyā has also been indicated in the aphorisms. || 44 ||
Now, one might object: "Since all mantras and so forth are without distinction, why is this specific rule established, or rather, why not otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the case of all *mālā-mantras*, mental recitation (*japa*) is prescribed."
Or rather, one should perform it silently; one should not calculate the arising of their power.
"In all" means even among the [other] sciences; "mental" (mānasa) refers to this. As it has been said:
"That which the self does not hear is called mental recitation (japa);
that which the self hears by itself, one knows as whispered (upāṃśu)."

"O Goddess, that which others hear is designated as 'with sound' (*saśabda*). (Svacchanda Tantra 2.147). The word *vā* indicates an alternative; the negation of "with sound" is established by the context of the meaning.
Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not just been stated that mantras do not achieve success when they are not applied to the path of Śakti?
So how can this be said—that 'one should not imagine the arising of their power'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In all foot-mantras, practitioners who are constantly disciplined should perform recitation as much as is possible according to the power inherent in those words. (7.46)
The number designated as "padas" in those [mantras] is indeed that great;
having produced that many risings (udaya) starting from the utterance of the three *pada*s in sequence.
In the wheel known as the twelvefold, when divided by twelve, there would be one hundred and fifty;
for its arising is indeed one hundred and forty-four.
When sixteen hundred and ninety-two have elapsed,
it is declared that one hundred and twelve [breaths] are equal to half a cycle (cārārdha).
In the [cycle] called the sixteenfold, when divided by sixteen, there are eighty-four;
its rise is indeed two hundred and fifty-six. (7.50)
The wise declare that three-eighths more than this [twenty] are added here;
when eight times eight is increased by twelve, it becomes twenty-eight and a half.
Since that [text] consists of seven hundred and sixty-eight [verses], it is called the *Udayasaptaśatikā*.

For, in all mantras whose primary element is the word (*pada*), such as those consisting of the Vidyās and so forth, the practitioners of yoga have established the practice of recitation (*japa*) and so on once the equilibrium between the words and the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) has been attained.
Practitioners should recite at all times exactly as much as they are capable of performing; by doing so,

relying on the sequence such as the mention of three words (*tripadokti*) regarding those [mantric] words, and according to the principle that "multiplicity is fully realized in the three," one should gradually divide each single word into many words, [thereby attaining] the entirety of the Supreme.

Because it is impossible to utter [the mantra] all at once due to the equality of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should bring forth an amount of the measure of the word-parts (*padāṃśa*) within the power of the breath; then, that very same amount, measured by the word-parts, shall constitute the count of the recitation (*japa*) designated as a "word" (*pada*). This is the point here.

The state of being [is as follows]: not only is it impossible to utter a mantra consisting of multiple words all at once within the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti), but because it consists of many syllables,
even a single word must be divided part by part, so that one may [utter] each individual [syllable] gradually.
Thus, for yogins who utter [the mantra] with the equality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in its respective parts, the recitation of one hundred thousand times and so forth will be accomplished.
As it is said there:
"The division within the wheel of the words, mantras, and syllables resides in the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*)."
Having placed [the mantra] upon the feet, the knower of mantras should perform the recitation daily.
One should eliminate the hundredfold arising counted as two, three, seven, or eight;
thus, the mantras, vidyās, or lords of the wheels abide within the Śakti.
O Dear One, having understood them in the form of word-clusters,
they should always be applied to the Great Principle (mahātattva) which is eternally risen, situated in the state of Sadāśiva.
"But those who are unyoked on the path of power, and whose [mantras] have not been recited with the impulsion, do not achieve success despite effort...
Thus it is said. And likewise:
"In all garland-mantras, mental recitation is prescribed;
one should never perform the arousal of power (śaktyudaya) in them."
O lady of excellent hips, for them, mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is prescribed;
however, in some cases, whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa) is proclaimed in the scriptures.
In all the great mantras, up to the extent that their power reaches,
they can be constantly recited by the best of practitioners who are ever-yoked in meditation.
"The number designated for those words is indeed as many as there are;

having brought about that much of an arising, starting from the utterance of the three words in sequence. Therefore, one should effect the arising of the *mālāmantra*s and so forth in their entirety within the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*).

It cannot be done—it has been stated that one should not conceive of the arising of power in these [mantras] in its entirety; for if it were so, then because the recitation (*japa*) would yield only a small fruit, it would be considered inferior.
As it has been said:
"The lowest form of recitation (japa) is said to be that which is devoid of the counting of breaths.

Thus [it is said]. He demonstrates the very division of the words with the verse beginning with "twelve," etc.: "In the one called 'twelve,'" meaning in the wheel consisting of twelve parts, such as the *mālā-mantra* and so forth, "in the twelfth."
When each group of twelve words is divided twelvefold— thus making a total of twelve times twelve, which is one hundred and forty-four—
the emergence of one hundred and fifty breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) occurs for each of those as well. Thus it is said.

There would be twenty-one thousand six hundred movements of the vital breath (prāṇa). Likewise, when the wheel consisting of sixteen parts is divided twelvefold, there are one hundred and ninety-two divisions;
since ninety-six remain [unaccounted for], this is the [remaining] emergence (codaya). Thus, it is in that which is called the sixteenfold [wheel].
The sense is that when the wheel is divided sixteenfold,
there would be two hundred and fifty-six sixteen-parts; since eighty-four breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) remain for each of those [sixteen], this rising occurs by means of eight parts of a movement.

Thus, when the wheel consisting of sixty-four squares—divided into eight groups of eight—is divided twelvefold, there arises for each square a group of twelve breath-movements: twenty, eighteen, and twenty-eight;
and likewise, because nine hundred and sixty remains as a half, there is an eighth part (pādārdha) as the remainder.

Since the wheel consisting of sixty-four [petals] multiplied by twelve results in that number characterized as seven hundred and sixty-eight, thus in all these cases, the movements of the vital breath (prāṇa) amount precisely to twenty-one thousand six hundred.
He concludes this very point:
"This arising of the wheels has been proclaimed, bringing benefit to practitioners. (7.52)

Now, one might object: "The arising of the wheels occurs in accordance with the arising of the movement of the vital breath; what then is that [movement] such that even this [arising of the wheels] could occur?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having restrained the mental fluctuations, one has attained rest within the wheel."
Indeed, this is the arising of the movement [of breath], which lasts from the moment one emerges until one finds rest.

In this context, indeed, the yogi— having restrained the mental fluctuations consisting of conceptual construction and having turned them inward— attains rest within the mantra whose nature is the single mass (*ekapiṇḍa*) and so forth of the *cakra*;
having attained identity with the central abode (*madhyadhāma*), he rises up from the heart.

The meaning is that after exiting as far as the *dvādaśānta* (the limit twelve finger-breadths beyond the head) and re-entering within, one should rest right in the heart; until then, this constitutes the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 53 ||
Explaining the three-fold nature (trairūpya) in this very context, he also states the division of [the breath] into *siddhi* and so forth:

"But here, in the full emergence (*samudaya*), there are three [phases]: entry, the single essence, and exit; for this very reason, in the case of accomplishment (*siddhi*), the central emergence is said to be the best. (7.54)
Furthermore, here, from the moment of the arising of the breath until its entry [into the center] through complete identity with the central abode,
when it has reached fullness— meaning completion according to the aforementioned movement—
there are three modes characterized by entry, identity, and exit; therefore:

The meaning is that, among the three modes, the "middle emergence," characterized by identity (*aikātmya*), which is the cause of accomplishment, is said to be "better"—that is, superior—even compared to entry. || 54 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for such a statement?", he says:
"Indeed, the groups of mantra-cakras and vidyā-cakras, when freed from arising at the beginning or the end and joined with arising in the middle, become possessed of accomplishment. (7.55)

"One who knows the arising of the mantra-cakra and understands the meaning of the arising of the vidyā-cakra will attain success quickly; so it is proclaimed in the venerable Trika system of twenty [verses]. (7.56)

The "arising of the beginning and the end" refers to the exit and entry [of breath], while the "arising of the middle" refers to identity with the central abode (*madhyadhāma*). The particle *hi* indicates the reason. Thus, the meaning is that a yogi who knows the arising of the wheels of Mantras and Vidyās in this manner shall attain perfection without delay. || 56 ||
One might object: "For a yogi who has conquered the vital breath (prāṇa) and has ascended, what indeed is impossible that he could not accomplish?
But how can this be achieved by one who is merely desiring to ascend and is still in the process of conquering the vital breath?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

One should always recite the vidyā or the cakra—endowed with the arising of the principles (tattvas)—either two, three, or four times by measure (mātrā), whether as a distinct entity or eternally [united]. (7.57)
Each mantra, consisting of clusters, syllables, and words, resides within the principle of Śakti;
however, that mantra which consists of many syllables, or which is a Vidyā, or even a Cakra— 7.58.

That [mantra] situated in power (śaktistha) is not [to be recited] there; however, the division consists of ending with "oṃ" and "namaḥ. Furthermore, a yogi who desires to ascend should practice daily two, three, or four times, according to the gradation of his proficiency, in the sequence of one, two, and so forth.

"By three circumferences of the knees [is one] mātrā, and by three triple snaps of the fingers [is another]," as defined in *Mālinīvijaya* 17.12; by means of such *mātrās*, one should [perform the recitation] of a vidyā consisting of many syllables, or a cakra consisting of many clusters (*piṇḍa*), or a mantra consisting of many words, word by word, cluster by cluster, and syllable by syllable.

Having rendered a single aggregate—whether a syllable (*akṣara*) or a word (*pada*)—which is distinct [from its parts], as residing within the principle of the power of breath (*prāṇaśaktitattva*) according to the reasoning previously stated, one should always recite it as being endowed with the emergence of the principles (*tattvodaya*), through identity with the central abode (*madhyadhāma*).
This means that one should perform a hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) and so forth. For this very reason, it is devoid of any division into words and the like.

Furthermore, a yogi who desires to ascend by means of a mantra or the like that consists of many syllables should not perform the arousal of the *śakti* (power), because such a complete restraint of the breath (*prāṇanirodha*) is impossible; the meaning is that he should not conceive of the rising of their power. Now, if [it is argued] that because these [mantras] consist of many syllables, [they cannot be performed] in their entirety...

Fearing that it might be objected, "It is impossible to bring about the arising within the power of *prāṇa* according to the sequence just described; let this be otherwise," he says, "In that regard," and so forth. [The mantra] "ends with *āṃ namaḥ*";
however, unlike other mantras, there is no division of these [syllables] according to the sequence of words (*pada*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so on.

Since even by a mere fraction of a fraction [of these mantras] the arising of power would be accomplished, it follows that those who desire to ascend [the path] should not perform the recitation (japa) of such mantras at all— this is what has been stated. || 59 ||

Furthermore, for the yogin who has ascended, there is not only this threefold division—entry and so forth—within the full manifestation (*samudaya*) alone, but it also applies to its constituent parts; thus he says:
"Therefore, within this emergence of the principles (*tattva*), each day and night [is divided] into thirty [parts]. (7.59)
It is analyzed and further divided into groups of thirty each;
therefore, for the reason stated previously, in this commenced *Tattvodaya*,
by means of the metaphorical identification of cause and effect, [it refers to] the emergence of the wheels (*cakrodaya*).

The day-and-night cycle, which consists of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, is divided into three parts each; the meaning is that the prāṇa alone or the apāna alone undergoes division through three modes, characterized by entry, oneness, and exit.
By means of that, both flows of prāṇa and apāna consist of thirty-six [units].

Each [of these] has a threefold nature beginning with entry; thus, for each finger-breadth, there is an emergence of twelve [units]. In this way, the division of the Self is again thirty by thirty, starting from entry and so forth.

The meaning is that it partakes of three modes characterized by entry, exit, and their unity. By this, it is established that the emergence of entry and the other phases occurs for every four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
thus, for the yogi who has ascended to that state, such an emergence of the wheels (*cakrodaya*) occurs even within the limited portion of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*).
The intended meaning is that it would be accomplished.
Having thus explained this as a digression, he returns to the subject at hand: "But when, having rested upon the first emergence, one should rise up by means of the second," (7.60).
And by means of the yoga of successive halving, there would then be the aforementioned half-rising;
however, when time manifests equally as a full rising within the triad, it shines forth.
Then, during the expansion of entry and repose, there occurs the arising of its own three-fold aspect.

Therefore, having "reposed" in the "prior" primary arising— which is the nature of the central abode— and having remained in identity with that, "when one expands" by means of the "second" mode, which consists of emergence.

One should ascend by way of the *prāṇa*; that is to say, one should "enter" by means of the third mode, which consists of the *apāna*, making an entry as far as the heart. Then, due to the connection of each of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* with half [of the cycle] respectively, it consists of twenty-one hundred and sixty thousand [breaths].

Half of the aforementioned time constitutes the arising of ten thousand one hundred and eight breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*). Furthermore, when that time— consisting of twenty-one thousand six hundred movements which forms the "full" (*pūrṇa*) cycle— is in a state of equilibrium within the triad known as entry, rest, and emergence, [it is the state of Śiva].
Then, for each of the [stages] beginning with entry (*praveśa*), the meaning is that there would be the arising of its own "third part," which consists of seven thousand two hundred.
But was it not previously asserted—
"All this path rests within internal consciousness" (Tantrāloka 6.28)—
so how is it that here the path of time is said to reside specifically in the vital breath?
Anticipating the question, "In what is this state of being established said to reside? he says:
"Thus, this expansion of time is established in the vital breath (prāṇa) alone. (7.62)
"He [is] in the vibration, he [is] in that consciousness; therefore, the entire universe is established within it.

Regarding the word "prāṇa," it is used because of its predominance, though it applies to apāna and the others as well. "He" refers to prāṇa. "In the vibration" refers to the activity of breathing (prāṇana) which is of a general nature and consists of the primary outpouring. "In the void" (khe) refers to...

In the case of the empty subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*): the meaning is that "he" (the subject) becomes designated by such terms as "vibration of breath" (*prāṇaspanda*) and so forth, surging outward due to the longing for objects of cognition (*meyautsukya*). "That" refers to the void (*kha*), because consciousness itself manifests in the form of the void through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*). "By that" refers to what has been stated.
By means of the indirect cause, [it is said] "the universe," referring to the sixfold path. As he will state:
"This entire path is established in pure consciousness alone;
for that which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky."
"Through the gateway of consciousness, its creation resides in the void, the intellect, the vital breaths,
the primary channels and their subsidiary wheels, and in the external body"— thus [it is said in Tantrāloka 8.4].

Thus, he states that the creation and dissolution of the universe depend entirely upon consciousness: "Therefore, since the emergence and dissolution of the universe are established in consciousness... (7.63).
Therefore, on the path ending with *śakti*, their vibrations are truly innumerable.

Since time is ultimately grounded in consciousness through a continuous succession, and since the creation and dissolution of the universe have consciousness as their sole agent, [these vibrations] belong to that path ending with *śakti*.
Regarding the previously mentioned vibrations (*spanda*) consisting of emanation, withdrawal, and so forth:
"Since within that [supreme] emanation there are innumerable emanations and withdrawals of worlds,
it is therefore called the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) belonging to Śakti."
The meaning is that, by the reasoning stated in such passages, because all intermediate vibrations (*spanda*) are included [within this], although they are innumerable,

they are real and ultimately true (*pāramārthikī*) because their sole nature is pure Being (*sanmātra*). For whatever movement exists externally is, in its very essence, nothing but consciousness— this is the intended sense.

And this is not our own invention alone; for it is stated even in the scripture (*āgama*) as follows: "It is said in the *Śrīmālinītantra*: 'In whichever part of the body [the breath] resides... (7.64).

That modification which arises— whether in the eye or any other limb— preceded by the thought, "This entire manifestation is mine," on the part of a yogin who possesses immersion in supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvidāveśa*), that very [modification] is the ultimate reality (*tattvam uttamam*).

That which is its vibration—namely, the manifestation of all entities as non-different from itself—is the supreme reality; the meaning is that it is the ultimate reality because it does not transcend consciousness.
As it has been said there:
"O Goddess, wherever in any limb a modification arises, that is preceded by volition; that is the reality, the supreme reality. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.42).
Now, let this be so; even there, of this vital breath (*prāṇa*)...
Anticipating the question, "Why is form said to reside in the body? he says:
"Time is established in the vital breath (prāṇa), and the body is pervaded by that [time]. (7.65)
Therefore, the form of this [Self] established in the body is now described.

In the phrase "pervaded by that" (*tadāviṣṭā*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is used because the vital breath has entered into the body.
Now, one might ask: "How indeed can there be an entry of that [consciousness] into the body? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The final gross state of the pulsations of consciousness and the movements of the vital breath is the *suṣi* (the cavity). (7.66)
Having attained the form of a channel (*nāḍī*), it extends this body;
because it is the final stage of consciousness (*cit*) and the other [principles] whose natures were previously defined, due to their readiness to produce effects,
it is therefore the grossness designated by the term "cavity" (*suṣi*) arising from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of consciousness and the rest.
That solidification as an external form is she [the power of will]:
"Manifest from the tip of the big toe, she has gone from the navel to the heart;
she is to be known as Suṣumnā, having emerged from the lotus of the Brahmarandhra."
"Created by the Supreme Lord for the movement of the vital breaths of living beings"—

according to such statements, first, by means of the analogy of the central pillar, one should extend this body, which will have the dimensions to be described, by assuming the form of the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*), through all its various divisions and subdivisions.
The meaning is that, by the production of other channels, one should make it continuous like a net.
Therefore, he states that scripture also teaches this:
"For this very reason, it is said in the Śrī Svacchanda Tantra: 'Just as a leaf [is held] by its own fibers... (7.67).
In that same way, the body is pervaded by the channels through the relationship of door and gateway;
just as a palāśa leaf is pervaded on all sides by its own subsidiary fibers hanging from the central fiber,
so too is the body pervaded by the primary and secondary divisions in the form of doors and gateways.

The meaning of the sentence is: by means of the channels (nāḍīs) which are connected to the central channel (madhya-nāḍī) and situated in a relationship of subordinate and primary. As it is said there:
"They are indeed situated below the navel at the root of the penis, in the center of the navel."
From that, O beloved, the channels have issued forth horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
There, ten principal channels are situated like the spokes of a wheel;
from them, seventy-two thousand channels have branched out.
Furthermore, others have emerged from these, and yet others from those, again and again;
as many as there are millions of pores of the skin, so many channels are said to exist.
Just as the leaf of a Palāśa tree is pervaded everywhere by its fibers. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.11)

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: since it has been stated that "all [the channels] are filled with wind," and so forth, there is no disagreement that all the *nāḍīs* indeed carry the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and that the entire body is pervaded by them; so how is it that [the path] from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* is the location of *mattagandha*?
Or rather, why has the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) been said to extend only as far as thirty-six finger-breadths? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Extending from the big toe of the foot up to the Brahmakuṇḍalikā situated above. (7.68)
The entire duration of time is contained within eighty-four finger-breadths;
they know that the state of extremely subtle time extends slightly beyond the limit of the *dvādaśānta*.
In ninety-six [finger-breadths], by moving down six times two [steps], there are one hundred and eight;

the Brahma-cavity (*brahmakuṇḍalikā*) situated above is the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*). The total time previously mentioned [amounts to] eighty-four finger-breadths because the body consists of three and a half cubits. "From here," thus [it is said].
"Gone" means "stationed. This should be connected with the phrase "in ninety-six finger-breadths" from the preceding context.
And since twelve finger-breadths are taken as an addition in that case, the two measurements—of the preceding and following [parts]—are coarse and distant due to the proximity of the subtle sound.

And this is established by the sense of the context. "Below" means from the big toe. Regarding the phrase "by a double stride of six," the meaning is that since there is a stride of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) consisting of two times six, just as there is a limit of twelve [finger-breadths] above, so too it should exist below.
Now, one might object: "If there is such a variety of measurements for the body, is there not also some degree of excellence (or variation) regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this regard, within the interval between the arising and the dissolution of the vital breath moving through the middle [channel]... (7.70).
All those diverse creations and dissolutions occur through the sequence within the wind (vāyu). Here,

within this body delimited by the threefold means of knowledge, all the aforementioned processes of manifestation occur in the interval between the rise and dissolution— the exit and entry— of the vital breath (prāṇa), which flows predominantly through the center.

The processes of emanation and withdrawal occur; however, the meaning is that their diversity arises, as before, solely from the internal sequence of the apāna breath, and not from the diversity of the body.

Now, he concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half of the verse: "Thus, this emergence of the cycles (cakrodaya), which is to be cultivated through subtle reflection, has been described by me according to the perspective of both experience and scripture."
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Arising of the Cakras," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
By the phrase "subtle investigation," it is stated that this [reality] is accessible only through the utmost attentiveness; may there be auspiciousness.
This seventh chapter, concerning the practice of the specific assemblage of mantras and the contemplation of their experiential manifestation, has been explained by the one named Jayaratha.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Emergence of the Wheels" (*cakrodayaprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
May this Jayakīrti be victorious—he who has divided the petals of the world from the lotus of the universe.
Like the sun, he causes it to blossom by virtue of its abiding in the single stalk of consciousness.

Now, with the second half [of the verse], he begins to describe the nature of the path of space (deśādhvan): "Next, this procedure for the path of space, as seen in the Śiva-scriptures, is proclaimed through both concise and expanded formulations. (1)
Anticipating the objection, "Even though there are infinite intermediate objects of knowledge (*prameya*) to be expounded, why is only this one mentioned here?",
he says: "This path of time, consisting of the Lord's power of action (*kriyāśakti*), has been investigated."
Now, the path of space (deśādhvan), which arises from that [path of time] and is produced by the diversity of forms, is described.

The word "atha" (now) signifies immediate succession. The threefold path of time (*kālādhvan*)—consisting of the levels (*pada*), mantras, and phonemes (*varṇa*)—has been examined; therefore, following that succession, the examination of the path of space (*deśādhvan*) is also appropriate here.
For this very reason, [the text] proceeds in order to present the worlds (*bhuvana*), principles (*tattva*), and limited powers (*kalā*).
The four chapters to be explained [hereafter] concern this. Regarding the phrase "born from that" (*tajjaḥ*): it means that he is born from the Lord himself;
he alone has thus manifested externally in various ways. As they say:
"The flow of the essence of consciousness, having become solidified, has attained a state of possessing form."
"I worship the manifest form of Bhairava, which is the very nature of the universe.
Thus [ends verse 2].
Now, one might object: "If this is so, is this sixfold path distinct from that which is of the singular nature of Consciousness, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This entire path is firmly established in pure Consciousness alone."
That which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky.

The phrase "well-established" means that [the object] is not distinct from that [consciousness]. Here, the second half of the verse serves as the reason by way of contrast (*vyatireka*); the sense is that if it were otherwise, it would be like "a flower in the sky"—that is, it would be nothing at all.
Now, one might object: "If this path is indeed not distinct from consciousness itself, then how is it that it appears everywhere as an external differentiation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of consciousness, [it appears] in the void, in the intellect, and in the vital breaths, which are created by it."
The establishment of the paths (adhvan) occurs within the primary and secondary wheels of the channels (nāḍīcakrānucakra), as well as outside the body.

For consciousness itself, by its own sovereignty, conceals its true nature and manifests the sixfold path— though it is not distinct from it— in such a way that it appears as if distinct, both within the subject (the knower) consisting of the void, vital breath, intellect, and body which it has brought forth, and in the external object of knowledge.
Thus it has been said:
"The establishment of the paths (adhvan) within the void and so forth occurs through the emission of that [consciousness] by means of the door of Śambhavi.
The phrase "in the primary and secondary wheels of the channels (nāḍī)" should be construed with the term "winds" (marut) as being in grammatical apposition. || 4 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, let it be; what is the fault [in that], and what further purpose is served by defining it?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard, this path (adhvan) must be defined in this way, because its systematic process..."
Continuing this very [practice], the yogi shall swiftly attain the state of Bhairava.

"Prakriyākramam" means the sequential arrangement [of the principles] from Kālāgni up to Anāśrita in their respective order. "Anusandadhat" means that by means of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) "I am Śarva," the yogi brings about a state of resting within his own Self and very quickly [attains liberation].
One should attain identity with the consciousness of another. || 5 ||
And this is not our own invention alone; thus he says:
"When one stands pervading all objects by the mere desire to see them, then what is the use of saying more? so it is stated in the Spandaśāsana (8.6).
Just as an object manifests through one's own direct perception at the moment of the desire to see it, so too, when the yogi—
preceded by the contemplation "I am Śarva"— remains having embraced within his own self all objects included within the principles from Earth up to Śiva, then...

The fruit—which consists of the wonder of immersion into the state of Supreme Bhairava through the complete dissolution of all that is to be known—is experienced by one’s own consciousness alone. What is the use of saying more on this point? It means there is no other purpose. "One will realize this for oneself"—this is the fourth quarter [of the verse]. || 6 ||
One might ask: "Would this indeed occur merely through the knowledge of the process of the paths? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having known the entire path, one should dissolve it into its respective lords;
those [lords] one should gradually cause to merge, as before, into the wheel of the body, the vital breath, and the intellect. (8.7)
All that is contained within one's own self-awareness; that consciousness, whose nature is fullness, when worshipped, is the fire of universal dissolution for the ocean of saṃsāra.

"In those lords" means in Brahmā and the others. "Those"—the lords as well—one should "dissolve" into the imagined forms within the Self consisting of body, intellect, vital breath, and the void, "as before," according to the method established by the path of time; that is, starting from the body, one should cause them to rest in each subsequent stage.
Until, in due course, one brings that entire aggregate— the body and so forth— under the sway of one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) as the opportunity arises;

by means of which, that awareness, having become full through the swallowing up of all objects of knowledge (*vedya*), being "worshipped"— that is, being cultivated repeatedly in that manner— by setting aside the appearance of duality and the like...
The meaning is that it should manifest as consisting of supreme non-duality. || 8 ||
Now, [it may be objected]:
"Furthermore, below Kālāgnirudra is situated the cauldron (kaṭāha), ten million yojanas in thickness; above it are the worlds."
There are nine billion nine hundred million,
seventy million, one hundred thousand, and ten thousand eggs.
According to the statement beginning with, "Arbudas, vṛndas, and likewise kharvas,
as well as innumerable padmas— thus [the worlds] are manifold" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.4), since the worlds are infinite, their presiding deities are also infinite.
Fearing that if one were to pursue each of these individually, no one would reach the end even in thousands of births— and thus this would be impossible to accomplish— he said:
"In the venerable *Dīkṣottara*, the Guru spoke of these Lords of the Paths."
"The Guru" refers to Śrīkaṇṭhanātha; he "spoke" with absolute certainty.
He recites the very text found therein:
"Brahmā [presides] from Ananta up to Pradhāna; Viṣṇu [presides] over the individual soul (pums) up to Kalā. (8–9)
Rudra resides in the knot (granthi) and Māyā; Īśa resides in the sphere of Sādākhya;
Anāśrita Śiva resides beyond that; and the Supreme (Para) pervades all these as their pervader.

The connection is as follows: Brahmā pervades everything from Ananta, who resides beneath the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍakarparikā), up to Pradhāna. This same construction should be applied to what follows as well. Regarding the phrase "and at the knot," the word "and" (ca) implies that Rudra also pervades Māyā, which is situated within that knot. "Riśaḥ."

Thus [is] Īśvara; "the sphere of Sādākhya" refers to the three principles beginning with Śuddhavidyā. "From that"—meaning from the sphere of Sādākhya—above, in the place of the Śakti-tattva, [is] "its pervader," which [refers to] all five of those [principles], beginning with Brahmā and ending with Anāśrita.

The meaning is that the supreme Śiva is the pervasive cause of all causes. And because of this necessity, for those who rule over these [causes], this is, on the contrary, an easy means; therefore, it has essentially been stated that there is no other knowledge higher than this. || 10 ||
It is with this very intention that the venerable *Svacchandaśāstra* also says as follows:
"Thinking that [the state] has thus attained the nature of Śiva, it was described in the *Svacchandaśāsana* that there is no knowledge superior to the *prakriyā*. (8.11)
As it is said there:
"There is no liberation equal to initiation; there is no knowledge higher than Mātṛkā; there is no wisdom superior to Prakriyā; and there is no yoga that does not perceive the Unmanifest. (11.198)
Thus [ends the section]. 11.
Now, one might object: "If time is thus being contemplated, how can there be a direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of consciousness?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the Triśiraḥśāsana, consciousness is conceived as having a root, a middle, and a tip."
The agitation of the thirty-six principles is memory, which is the conceptualization of duality. (8.12)
This state of being, whose divisions are unimpeded, is the root for attaining awakening;
this state of all principles is undivided within its own self alone. (8.13)
The center of awakening may possess the characteristic of being both support and supported;
it is characterized by abiding in its own nature through the differentiation of the various principles (tattva). || 8-14 ||
That supreme awakening, however, is the consciousness-awareness (*cidbodha*), waveless and vast bliss.

Indeed, in the *Śrītriśirobhairava*, it is stated by implication that awareness itself—when conceived as the root, the middle, and the tip—is manifested as the unfolding of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). By means of this...
From the pursuit of that [object], there shall be the direct realization of consciousness. He recites that very point by way of its object, beginning with:

"Memory," and so forth. Here, indeed, that which is called "the sense of 'I'" (asmibhāva)—which is deeply rooted in the intellect's egoism and, having first distinguished the *guṇas*— [The text continues: ...and having distinguished the *guṇas* previously... [rest of the verse].

The meaning is this: by the statement found there, "One should investigate the elemental constituents (bhūtadharma) in the sequence beginning with earth," the limited subject (*pramātā*)—who consists of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) residing in non-self entities such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is characterized by memory and conceptualization of duality; for he is indeed [that].
"One should conceptualize the universe through differentiation alone, thinking 'I know this.

One should not conceptualize the object merely as having the nature of existence; rather, one should do so even for that which is non-existent, such as in the case of memories and conceptualizations concerning a deceased father and so forth—as it has been said in the *Smṛti*: 'Therefore, from this very [fact], of the 'this-ness'..."

The meaning is that, due to its predominance, it possesses an unimpeded division consisting of clearly manifest distinctions. And that root situated in consciousness, having reached the supreme limit of consciousness, is called "grossness"—this is the meaning.
Likewise, this state of those respective principles shines forth as differentiated.

The manifestation of past entities and so forth, by the principle of "this am I," comes to rest within one's own self, which is of the nature of consciousness; for this very reason, it is "undivided," meaning that with distinctions dissolved, it becomes the center of consciousness rather than its periphery, because at the outset there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Because of the appearance of difference, the phrase "characterized by some kind of relationship between support and supported" (*kiṃcidādhārādheyalakṣaṇam*)—by the word *kiṃcit* (some)—is revealed to be neither primarily characterized by difference like the root of consciousness (*bodhamūla*), nor primarily characterized by non-difference like the summit of consciousness (*bodhāgra*).
For this very reason, because it exists in the interval between them, it is called "intermediate" (*madhyama*). Thus:

The state of abiding in one's own self, which consists of the reflective awareness of "I," through the "differentiation"—that is, the radical cutting away—of the distinctions between the categories (tattvas), is the "peak of consciousness.
This is consciousness whose nature is the non-differentiation of all entities; it is consciousness that has reached its supreme limit.

This is the meaning. For this very reason, that [reality] is of the nature of universal consciousness (*cidbodha*), and not of the nature of atomic consciousness (*aṇubodha*); it is waveless, and not agitated;
it is "the great bliss" (*bṛhat sukham*), having the form of the bliss of the universe, and not having the form of non-bliss and so forth. As it has been said there:
The conceptualization that arises through differentiation regarding the domain of the thirty-six principles,
which consists of a clearly manifest sense of duality, is called the limited knower (mitamātṛ).
O Bhairavī, the consciousness that abides in the limit is the grossness of awareness;
this state of all the principles (tattvas) is not to be perceived through divisions.
One should know that which is established within one's own self as being in the midst of awakening;
this is the relationship of support and supported for that which abides in both.

One established in that state does not perceive the characteristics of abiding in one's own nature through the differentiation of the divisions of reality, for [all things] abide within the interior of the space of consciousness.

One should know that which has passed as "past," that which remains at the stage of attainment as "middle," and that which is to be known as remaining at the final stage as the "summit of awakening" (bodhāgra) in this context.
One should understand the knowledge of Śakti as characterized by supreme bliss;
know that it is eternally arisen happiness, which is described as being free from waves.
"That which is called 'great bliss' is declared to be the awakening of consciousness. || 14 ||
Thus, for the yogi who cultivates the identity with consciousness (*saṃvid*) even throughout the sixfold path, the state of Bhairava itself shall arise; so he says:
"One for whom the past, future, cities, and so forth, have been brought to the state of oneness with consciousness... (8.15).
Bhairava, the Supreme Lord, is uninterrupted consciousness.
Not only is this stated here, but it is also stated elsewhere; thus he says:
"And it is stated in the venerable Devyāyāmala as being beautiful with the thirty-six principles. (8.16)
"Meditating upon the sixfold path, one becomes identical with Śiva immediately.
The word "meditating" (dhyāyan) means perceiving [the path] as non-different from one's own consciousness. As it is said there:
"O Goddess, the entire path, radiant with the thirty-six principles..."
"Meditating [upon this], one immediately attains the supreme, eternal state.
Thus [it is said]. || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "If indeed this sixfold path is of the very nature of consciousness, then since consciousness is not delimited by space and so forth, how could there be a spatial arrangement such as 'above' and so on?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even though this Lord does not transcend pure consciousness... || 8.17 ||
In the case of the Full [Moon], there is no real establishment of top, middle, or end;
nevertheless, such a distinction exists for those who perceive it and for the one who explains it. (8.18)
The conceptualizations of being "middle," "beginning," and so forth, follow one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For those such as the perceiver (*pratipattr*) and others, because their form is contracted (*saṃkucita*), they possess the conceit (*abhimāna*) of having grasped a body and so on;
thus, they might imagine a spatial arrangement such as "above" and so forth in accordance with that [conceit], but in reality, such an arrangement could not possibly exist.

For this very reason, even that which is above would be below in relation to something else. Therefore, this arrangement depends entirely upon the perceiver and so forth—that the earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*) exists within all other principles, while the other principles exist outside of it. || 18 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Therefore, they know that which pertains to earth [arises] from the restriction of the perceiver's volition" (8.19).
The reality (tattva) that resides within the interval of all things and is enveloped by all coverings—

the earth-reality (pṛthivītattva) itself— is the ultimate limit of grossness; because it is easily understood as the starting point [of manifestation], the arrangement of the worlds (bhuvana-sthiti) is first described therein— thus he says:
In this regard, the arrangement of the worlds within the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) is now described.
He describes that very [state]: "Ananta, the leader of the Kaṭāha-Rudras who indulge in desire, mounted upon a boat in the midst of the water, reeling from the drinking of wine. (8-21)
Meditating upon the god Bhairava, he was surrounded by nāgas.
By implication, it means "within the water," [referring to] that which is situated above it. As it has been said:
"That Hūhuka, the support of Śakti, is situated upon the surface of the waters.
