For this very reason, due to its proximity to the water-element (aptattva), it is located beneath the cauldron (kaṭāha).
It is established that [the soul] resides outside, not within; as it is said in the venerable *Nandiśākhā*:
"The thickness of the shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍakaṭāhaka*) extends for ten million *yojanas*."
In the same way, O beloved, the interval situated above should be known; it is now being described.

"O Goddess, the Brahmāṇḍa is said to consist of ninety-eight crores [of yojanas]," beginning thus, [it continues]: "O fair-complexioned one, one should know that Hūhuka, the Lord of the World, who stands beneath the shell (kaṭāha), is Ananta, the support of Śakti."
Thus it is said; and in the *Śrītriśirobhairava* as well:
"Ananta, who is outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), is called the support of the universe. And regarding his abiding within:
"That [world] measures ten crores, and by means of ships it is equal everywhere;
above that, O Queen of the Gods, is a further darkness measuring one crore"—
thus has the measurement of the worlds and so forth been stated.

It would exceed the measurement and number of the worlds existing within the Brahmāṇḍa that is about to be described; thus, there would be an inconsistency in that calculation. Now, if this is so, then regarding that Infinite One: "One should purify the worlds within the pavilion of the Brahmāṇḍa."
First, there is Anantabhuvana, Kauṣmāṇḍa, and Hāṭakeśvara.
Following the world of Ananta is the great world of Kālāgni;
then the worlds of Śarva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, and the supreme world of Rudra.

What would be the meaning of such statements as, "These eight are proclaimed to be situated within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)," which prescribe their internal location? Furthermore, [there is the statement]:
"A single fragment of Brahmā’s egg is ten million [yojanas] in measurement."
Above that is Kālarudra, accompanied by the ten Īśānas.
"His city is ten million [yojanas] in extent, while its flames extend for a hundred million;
Ananta is below, Padma is above, and the others are situated in their respective order.
Thus it is said. And likewise:
"Below, Rudra, who reaches the end of time, resides in the midst of the station of the Lord of the Ten;
above is Padma, below is Ananta, and others follow in succession.
According to such statements, his world is indeed within the world of Kālāgni and not separate from it.

There is no inconsistency whatsoever even in the enumeration of the worlds that is about to be described. Furthermore, in this context, the measurement of the worlds as stated in the *Śrīsiddhātantra* regarding Ananta is certainly not to be accepted,
because it is traditionally held that "the division of Tantras arises from the distinctions of [the paths of] action (*kriyā*) and so forth."

"Therefore, whatever has been stated in a particular [system] must be performed according to that, and not according to another tantra," because their procedures (*prakriyā*) are distinct. And so, here the measurement of the hells is thirty-two crores, whereas there it is twenty-one. As it has been said:
"Above that are twenty-one crores of terrible hells. And here too [it says]:
"Within the Egg, Ananta... (8.393).
Thus, [if this were not so], the statement to be made later—"The eight [powers] together with Śarva... (8.397)—would be contradicted; what, then, should be understood in this regard? This is it:
It should be understood that the infinite one exists externally; for it is said in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka*:
"Within the pavilion of the cosmic egg..."

Such passages do not establish that there is no end to the infinite; rather, this is because the sequence of purification and its stability have already been explained previously, and it is only this much that is intended here.
As it has been stated therein:
Therefore, O Pārvatī, listen to the initiation of the worlds (bhuvanadīkṣā) according to its true nature;
this was previously taught by me in its entirety at the beginning.
"Nevertheless, O beautiful lady, I shall speak to you here in brief," having thus begun, [he continues]:
"Now hear their classification, O one honored by the lords of heroes."
Thus it is said. And therein, for this group of six beginning with Asya, their stationing is prescribed strictly outside [the Egg]. As it has been stated:
"That golden Egg of the earth which shines forth from the Lotus-born [Brahmā], beneath its lower portion shine those who act as the authors of the examples previously seen."
Beginning with: "By the grace of Viśvakarman, [the crest-jewel] upon the head of the serpent Śeṣa," and continuing:
"With the surging waves of nectar from the moonbeams of infinite power..."
Therefore, embraced [by that], it surges upward from below due to its attainment of the higher state.
"The world of that infinite hero shines with its own splendor,
always like a lake for the clusters of lotus-faces of his infinite consorts"—
thus [the author] specifies.
"Then, by the radiance of the crest-jewel of Hūhuka-Rudra, which was like the sun in the sky,
the city— filled with hosts of heroes— was cleared of darkness," and so forth; [this describes] the worlds of the Hūhuka-Rudras.
O Maheśvarī, these cities, bound by the great rope of Bhairava,
were formerly hidden here within the waters by the one whose self is Śiva.

Having described their location and measurement with the words, "All [the mountains] are one hundred thousand [yojanas] high and situated in the whirlpools of the waters," and so forth, [it continues]:
"The egg of Brahmā, however, extends for a hundred crore [yojanas] all around."
"And Kaṭāha is remembered as being ten million [yojanas] in extent, together with the hundred Rudras.
Furthermore:
"[... one should purify the worlds within."

What has been stated thus should be explained primarily by way of the analogy of the village of wrestlers (*mallagrāma*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. For in this case, since the purification of the worlds from Ananta down to Śatarudra cannot occur simultaneously, [the process must be understood sequentially].

Only the sequence itself is intended to be expressed, and not even the internal or external nature [of the levels], because if that were the case, there would be no distinction regarding their purification. Thus:
"Below these, indeed, is the world of Kālāgni, and from that..."

"And likewise, O Goddess, the Hūhukas who dwell within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)"—this and other such passages are also to be explained in this way. The authors of the *Saṃgraha* proceeded by taking this very point in its literal sense; thus they stated it accordingly in various places, so that [the soul] remains within.
The seed of delusion has taken root. And thus Somaśambhu says:
"Now Huhuka, Kālāgnirudra, and Hāṭaka;
then Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Śarva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu as the seventh."
"And Rudra—these eight Rudras reside within the shell.
Thus it has been variously conceptualized by the teachers; with the intention of demonstrating their view, [the text says]:
"Within the egg, Ananta... (8.393).
Thus, [the text] will state later on: "The eight [energies] together with Śarva... (8.397); therefore, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. As for what he will say...

That is incorrect; for this [Ananta] is distinct from the Ananta who resides outside the realm of Hūhuka-Rudrādhipati and is to be purified separately, as he is another who belongs to the retinue within that world of Kālāgni.
Indeed, it should not be stated that he is to be purified separately within that very same principle.

Because its purification occurs precisely through the purification of Kālāgnirudra; otherwise, the same would apply even to the lotuses and other [elements], whereby numerous Rudras within [the body] would have to be purified, and thus more than one hundred and eight [Rudras] would result in the Vṛtti. Likewise, by others as well, even though it remains in the external region...
Furthermore, the claim that [the Śatarudra] is identical with either one of the ten groups of Śatarudras situated below is also incorrect;
for if that were so, its meaning would already be established by its inclusion within those very groups, and thus there would be no reason to mention it separately.
Moreover, the assertion that the measurement of the worlds (*bhuvana*) stated in the *Śrīsiddhāntatantra* should not be accepted here is likewise untenable.
For if indeed some measure of the infinite universe were stated here— as it is for the hells and so forth— then,

because of the difference in its systematic arrangement, that which is taught in other systems would simply not be acceptable; yet the measure of the universe must necessarily exist, and since it is not mentioned here, it is precisely because of this [omission] that there arises a desire for it.

It must necessarily depend on something from somewhere else—so what indeed is this hostility toward the *Śrīsiddhātantra*? Or rather, since its extent of one hundred thousand [verses] is also stated in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka*, let that be consulted; what insistence can we possibly have against it?

For whatever inconsistency might be alleged regarding our reckoning of the number of inner worlds (*antarbhuvana*) would be established in either case—so enough of this prolixity. Regarding the phrase "of the Kaṭāha-Rudras," this refers to the Hūhuka-Rudras residing beneath the Kaṭāha; and therefore, by their purification alone...
The sense is that this constitutes purification. As it has been said:
"By that which is purified, the pure cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) are [purified] here along with the *ūhakas*" (Svacchandatantra 10.6).
Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, the purification of each respective world occurs precisely through the mediation of its corresponding Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*).
It must be understood as it has been said:
"No one there is afflicted by suffering, except for the pain born of the bodiless god [of love];
indeed, the heroes sport there with women in playful delight. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.8)
Thus: "mounted upon a boat," as it has been said:
"Ananta is situated below, mounted upon a boat in the midst of the waters.
"Reeling from drinking wine," as it has been said:
"The glorious Mahāmatta, ever devoted to the great drink in the water"—
by the phrase "meditating upon Bhairava," it is indicated that because of his exclusive devotion to Him,
[the Lord says]: "O Lord of the World, by the command of Śiva, no harm shall come to this practitioner through you."

"One must create an obstruction for the traveler so that his path remains free from harm" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.64), and so forth; thus, his state of compliance with that command has been revealed from the very beginning by way of a general implication. Regarding the phrase "by the Nāgas," as it has been said:
Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Vajrin, Kārkoṭa, Niṣāda, and both Kambala and Aśvatara.
"And surrounded on all sides by these very great nāgas.
Thus, it is established that he himself also possesses the form of a nāga. As it has been said:
"With arms raised, of massive body, in the form of a nāga, and of great strength."
"Standing upon the world, he supports it with a thousand hoods.
For this very reason, he is described in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka* as having Śeṣa as his couch (*āhita*). || 21 ||
Now he begins to describe the worlds within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa):
"And above the world of Kālāgni, it rises for ten million yojanas. (8.22)
Out of fear that the worlds might be reduced to ashes, he does not look upward.
By implication, "upward" refers to the lid (*kaṭāha*) of the cosmic egg; and that [lid] has a thickness of ten million *yojanas*. As he will state:
"Below and above, the lid in the egg is ten million *yojanas* thick" (Svacchandatantra 10.162).

Thus: "He does not look upwards," as it has been said: "The Lord does not look upwards so that this world may be reduced to ashes. For this very reason, His upward-facing mouth remains unopened; thus, it is everywhere stated that He possesses exactly four faces.
As it has been said:
"He is three-eyed and four-faced, bearing a garland of blazing fire-flames. (22)

One might object: "Since it has been stated in such passages as, 'For whoever is superior in qualities to another is held to be above him' (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.60), it would be logical for this [world] to be situated above the hells; so how is it said to be below them?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And although he pervades the entire universe, since he is burning this earth, || 8-23 ||
Because he was manifested prior to the hells, he is considered to be below them.
And it was stated previously:
"Since his manifestation occurred before the fires of time from the hells, therefore..."
"Even though he is all-pervasive, he [remains] beneath that... (Tattvārthacintāmaṇi 6.142).
The flame of the pervasive Lord extends for ten crores [of yojanas], and half of that is empty space above.
Above that are the lords of the hells, who experience exclusively suffering;
they are situated below, in the middle, and above, surrounded by various subdivisions. (8.25)
In those [hells], namely Avīci, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava, there are eleven, eleven, and ten respectively; thus, their total is fifty-three.
The distance between each of these [peaks] is ninety-nine million yojanas;
the interval between those numbering four hundred thousand is one hundred thousand [yojanas]. (8.27)
Kūṣmāṇḍa is above, his domain being one hundred million minus one lakh; he is its lord.
"Half of that" refers to five crores. "Empty" means devoid of people due to the fear of smoke, heat, and so forth.
As it has been said:
"Above this, O Goddess of gods, O fair-faced one, are five crores;
no one dwells here, scorched by smoke and heat" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.30).
"Above that" means above the void (*śūnya*). "In due order" refers to the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); therefore, [this occurs] in Raurava.

Eleven [hells] are included within Kumbhīpāka, and ten within Avīci; thus, including himself, those three hells amount to thirty-five, delimited by the number "five and three" (śarāgni). As it has been said:
O Dear One, one should purify Avīci, the eleventh among the hells;
O Goddess, one should personally purify Kumbhīpāka as the twelfth.
One should likewise purify that which is known as Mahāraurava;
O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall now explain these thirty-five [hells] in brief.
Avīci, the mass of worms, the Vaitaraṇī river,
as well as the iron [forest], the Śālmali tree, and the mountain of swords.
Socchvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, Pūtimāṃsa, Para,
Taptatrapu, Kṣārakūpa, and likewise Jatulepa.
They are included within Avīci; now hear concerning Kumbhīpāka, Asthibhaṅga, Krakacacchedakūpa, and Kaṭaṅkaṭa.
Indeed, Vasāmiśra, Ayastuṇḍa, and Trapulepa are proclaimed;
Kumbhīpāka is to be known, and likewise Tīkṣṇāsika.
Heated iron, as well as the path of the razor’s edge,
and the blazing thunderbolt— these twelve are proclaimed.
Eleven other terrible hells, beginning with Kumbhīpāka, are to be known; now learn from me those that follow in the great king Mahāraurava.
Kālasūtra, Mahāpadma, Kumbha, Sañjīvana, Ikṣuka, Pāśa, Ambarīśaka, and likewise Ayaḥpaṭṭa.
"The Daṇḍayantra, the Amedhya, and another of terrible form;
Mahāraurava is situated above these. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.81–90).
Regarding the word "of these," it refers to the twenty-nine [hells] included within the thirty-two hells.
"Koṭi" means ninety-nine lakhs. "Antara" means each is of the nature of zero;
by that, there are thirty-two koṭis. Among those, one hundred and forty-four is the primary [number], and within that, thirty-two, and within that, three—thus it would be stated. As it has been said:
"Beyond this, O lady of excellent hips, the hells are proclaimed;
fifty crores [of them], O Goddess... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.31). Likewise:
Among them, O beloved, one hundred and forty are preeminent;
and among those, there are another thirty-two who are the most excellent lords of the hells.
"The lords of the kings of kings [attain] three...

Thus, the intention behind such instruction is this: when the abundance of the initiate's sins has been determined according to their relative degree, purification from the hells is performed extensively; otherwise, however, it is done concisely. Above...
Thus [ends the section] on the hells. ||27||
Now, one might ask: "Who indeed dwells in such hells, and who does not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Those who perform black karma through conduct contrary to the scriptures. (8.28)
There, those who have sought refuge even once in the Supreme Lord Śiva with one-pointed mind are tormented by the terrifying world-guardians until the end of their experience. (8.29)
Those who are joined with hell do not go [to the dark realm], for that [darkness] bestows only a small measure of pleasure upon them.
"Because of acting contrary to the scriptures" means because of the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited.
"Bringing about a paucity of happiness" is due to its being incomplete because of negligence. As it has been said:
"These most terrible hells are proclaimed to be triangular."
Indeed, it is for the downfall of those living beings who are devoted to unwholesome actions.
Of those who perform cruel deeds, the deceitful, and the evildoers;
of those of the lowest and merciless castes, whose very souls delight in harming others.
For those who take pleasure in the wives of others, those who revile the scriptures of Śiva,
those who misappropriate the property of the gods, and those who are slayers of Brahmins or parents;
For those who kill cows, those who are ungrateful, those who betray the trust of friends, those who steal gold or land, and those who abandon purity and right conduct;
For those devoid of compassion and courtesy, whose minds are intent on malice and falsehood,
and who persist in the paths of unwholesome action, hells have been fully described.
Indeed, people who delight in unwholesome actions fall into hell;
I shall explain that to you briefly, in due order and according to the truth.
He who possesses truthfulness, patience, non-violence, purity, ritual bathing, freedom from deceit, compassion, and lack of greed does not fall into hell.
Peaceful, self-controlled, joyful in soul, free from egoism, equanimous, non-malevolent, without envy, and devoid of longing for the prosperity of others.
Freedom from envy, absence of pride, devotion to Śiva, lack of fickleness, delight in recitation and meditation, steadfastness, and the avoidance of miserliness.
Vows and observances, as well as the study of sacred texts and the performance of the three daily rites;
faith in all things, straightforwardness, modesty, and self-respect.
Vital energy, tranquility, contentment, avoidance of unpleasant speech,
always acting after due deliberation, and the constant restraint of the mind and ego.
Freedom from hypocrisy, absence of pride, lack of deceit, and a disposition toward knowledge;
devotion to the worship of ancestors and gods, and seeking refuge in cows and Brahmins.
Offering oblations into the fire, giving gifts to the guru, attending upon those possessed of knowledge,
delighting in solitude, meditating, and finding contentment in the Self alone.
Non-interference in the affairs of others, indifference toward those who are innocent, freedom from anger, and absence of laziness— these are proclaimed as the virtues.
He who devotes himself to these dharmas is fit for immortality;
even those human bonds that are proclaimed to be infinite perish.
For embodied beings who are righteous and devoted to the conduct of Śiva,
one should therefore understand this and apply the mind to dharma.
He whose mind is undisturbed, free from conceptual construction, and stainless,
goes to the supreme worlds and does not behold the hells.
"He whose intellect is undeluded, who is free from sin toward all beings, who is without guile and truthful—he does not behold the hells. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.53–71).
Thus [ends the section]. 29.
Then, in sequence, [the heights] are nine thousand [yojanas], with intervals of one [thousand]. || 8-30 ||
Each of the eight netherworlds (pātāla) is one [in extent], and in the eighth, Lord Hāṭaka resides.

Because of the proximity of the word "thousand" [to each], there is one thousand; thus, their measurement is established as eighty thousand [yojanas]. Regarding "the eight netherworlds," it is as has been stated:
Ābhāsa, Varatāla, Śarkara, and Gabhastimat;
then Mahātala, Sutala, and beyond that, Rasātala.
"The eighth is to be known as Sauvarṇa, endowed with all objects of desire" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.96). Regarding the term "eighth," it refers to that which is called Sauvarṇa. As it has been said:
"And above that, the netherworld (pātāla) celebrated as Sauvarṇa [is situated]."
"There the god Hāṭaka, the Supreme Lord, dwells" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.116).
And although it is said here regarding the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*): "Therein dwell, without distinction, three types of beings: asuras, nāgas, and rākṣasas."
And they were described, O fair-faced one, in each individual netherworld.
In the seven netherworlds (pātāla), there are likewise to be known other lords of the worlds:
Bala, Atibala, Balavān, and Balavikrama.

By such statements as, "Subala, Balabhadra, and Balādhyakṣa are proclaimed [as lords]," each of them exists as a separate sovereign of a world-sphere (*bhuvana*); nevertheless, regarding these, it is said:
"The purification of all is desired through the pure Hāṭaka."

By such statements as these, purification occurs through the purification of Hāṭakarudra alone; thus, because [the process] would be redundant, no instruction regarding that has been given here. || 30 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the reason for designating him in this way?", he says: "Śrīkaṇṭha, whose self is appointed to each world, forcibly [produces] many [beings]. (8.31)
"In this way, he bestows the *siddhis* according to the teaching of the venerable *Raurava*.
'Siddhis' refers to those consisting of *sālokya* and the rest. As it is said there:
'This Lord Śrīkaṇṭha has his self appointed to each world.'"
Having become gold, he performs the guardianship of the gates of Pātāla.

"Having forcibly broken the mechanical devices in the netherworlds (pātāla), that Mahodaya causes the practitioners who have mastered the true mantras to attain the supernatural powers (siddhis). Thus [ends verse 31].
Now, one might ask: "To whom does he grant these accomplishments (siddhis)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Those who observe vows but are engaged in improper actions, those who perform forbidden conduct... (8.32).
Even those who have been initiated, if they have violated their commitments and do not perform the required expiations,
remain in that state as defilers of the Vāmācāra.

Those who subsist on the portions of wealth belonging to the gods, fire, or [their] livelihoods are established in the highest state; those devoted to the service of other mantras, such as the lower-level Gāruḍa and others, remain below.
These various types of servants stood before the Lord of Gold.

The cause for being established in improper action (*vikarmasthatva*) is the performance of forbidden conduct. They are said to have "lost their observances" (*luptasamayāḥ*) due to contact with *caṇḍadravya* and other such things. For this very reason, because they do not perform penance (*prāyaścitta*), they have fallen away from the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it has been said:

"One who, being a practitioner of mantras, does not perform expiation when there is a transgression of the rules, incurs a fall from accomplishment... Thus, "those established therein" refers to those devoted to the Left-hand practice (vāmācāra); by that, it includes both those who perform such [left-hand] rites and those who are hostile toward them.

— thus it would have been said. And the qualification "O God," and so forth, applies to them alone; for others, there would indeed be only the state of being a denizen of hell. As it has been stated: "If one, together with sons, cattle, and kinsmen, should desire to go to hell..."
"One should exercise authority over the gods, and over cows and Brahmins.
Thus [it is said]: "Those established in the highest state," and "The Śaiva [tradition] is superior to the Vedas and the rest..."

Because of such statements as these, they abide in the progressively higher teachings. The phrase "of diverse natures" means that they are differentiated as superior, middling, and so forth, according to their respective karmas.
And this [result] for them is like a *niḥṣyanda* (outflow) fruit, but not direct. For if it were so [direct],...
O Goddess praised by heroes, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras,
all those who are appointed to the office of a teacher are remembered as Śivas.
"Otherwise, those lowest of men who perceive [it] by means of their prior nature are cooked in hell for three years known as *sāda*. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.411). Likewise, [it is said]:

"O Goddess, by uttering the caste of one born before [him], a man becomes liable for expiation; he is cooked in hell for three days for Rudra, five days for Keśava, and for one fortnight for Pitāmaha. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.542)
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as these. || 34 ||
Anticipating the question, "What would happen to them when their enjoyment has ceased?", he says:
"But if they, even there, worship the Lord of Gods with devotion... (8.35).
They dissolve sequentially into the principle of Īśa and then into the supreme Śiva;
however, those who behave otherwise, whose natures are intent upon enjoyment therein, [do not]. (8.36)
Distressed by the torment of the fire of time and intent on piteous lamentation, they dissolve into the principle of Guṇatattva; from there, at the beginning of creation, they emerge once again.
They are cast down by their mothers into bodies of the lowest of the low, preceded by a flood of terrible torments, in accordance with their own past actions.
Among those at the end of their human lives, some who are knowers of mantras are liberated in due course, while others are bound according to their previous actions.
Thus, this account of the Gaṇas, by names such as Hulahula and others, was proclaimed by the Blessed One in the venerable Ānandādhikaśāsana. (8.40)
Above Pātāla, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas], is the crust of the earth (bhūkaṭāhaka).
However, according to the Siddhātantra, the surface of Pātāla is surrounded by Yakṣīs.
The city of Bhadrakālī is where practitioners sport with those [energies]. "Deveśam" refers to Hāṭaka. "Otherwise" means by way of being averse to its worship.
"By the Mothers" refers to the Aparā-śaktis. As it has been said:

"Those [powers] which, embracing the Rudra-entities, cause even the most minute souls to fall lower and lower, being merged in sense objects alone, are known as the 'more terrible' (ghoratara) others. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.31). Regarding the phrase "even there," it refers to the human state; those [others] are inferior to that.
The meaning is that those who do not know the mantra experience various [births] according to the fitness of their respective actions, such as their specific caste and so forth.
Nor is this something we have stated merely on our own authority; thus he says, "It has been taught," and so on. That which was stated therein:
Beginning with: "The Mātaṅgas, the Hulahulas, and others who are causal agents possessing divine forms;
the Kāpālikas, the Kaṅkālas, and the beautiful Mahocchuṣmas," and continuing: "Thus, they are beyond numbering, [arising] from the great Caṇḍeśvara."
But those initiated into the teaching of Śiva who have been plundered by violent substances [are lost].
"Those who live by means of fierce substances are known as *brahmarākṣasas*. Likewise: "They too, dwelling in the netherworld (*pātāla*), take delight in various enjoyments."
"In Pātāla, the kings of spirits (bhūtarāja) exist, arrogant with power.

Thus, the "earth-dome" (bhūkaṭāhaka) is the support for human beings. In this way, up to this point is half of the Brahmāṇḍa; its dome (kaṭāha) is one crore [yojanas], the city of Kālāgni is one crore, and its flames [are likewise].

Ten crores [of Yojanas] for the Dhūma hell, five for the hells, thirty-two for Kūṣmāṇḍapura, ninety-nine lakhs for the Pātālas, eighty thousand for the eight Pātālas, and twenty for the Earth-Cauldron (bhūkaṭāha); thus, there are fifty crores. In this very context:
He demonstrates the specific [instruction] taught in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata* with the words, "In the *Siddhātantra*, etc. As it is said there:
"Above Pātāla is Bhadra, the auspicious abode of Bhadrakālī."
She is proclaimed as the leader of all yakṣiṇīs.
There are sixty-four thousand cities of yakṣiṇīs,
and in each city there are as many as one hundred million maidens.
"There the practitioners, possessing great strength through the removal of impurities, sport together with them;
having understood the ritual manual of the Yakṣiṇīs according to the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*.
Thus it is said.
"And further above that, there is another hundred thousand [yojanas] of darkness that is exceedingly difficult to endure;
the ground resembles glowing coals and is illuminated by heated stones.
Thus it is said.
And above that, there is nothing at all for fourteen hundred thousand leagues;
then again comes the abode of the Nāgas, which causes infinite fear.
"Surrounded by a hundred thousand black serpents a hundred-thousandfold," thus it is said:
"The betrayer of mother, the betrayer of father, the betrayer of teacher,
the killer of a fetus, the slayer of children, and the great beast who is a eunuch— these go here."
"He shall remain in the netherworld (pātāla) for as long as he remains a defiler of the path of mantra.
Thus [ends verse 41].
Having thus described one half of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) ending with the "earth-crust" (bhūkaṭāha), he now shows what lies above that, beginning with the worlds:
"Beyond that is darkness, then the heated earth, then the void, and then the serpent-worlds. (8.42)
These are the places of torment for those who revile their gurus, mantras, and so forth.
Above (or within) that earth is Mount Meru, sixteen thousand [yojanas] high.
Its base is as vast as the [preceding] magnitude; its upward extent is twice that;
its height is like that of a thousand oceans; it is golden and the abode of all the immortals.
"Sahasrāṇi" refers to thousands of *yojanas*. "Submerged" means, by implication, within the shell of the earth (*bhūkaṭāha*).
"Its root-expansion" (*tanmūlavistāra*): the word "its" (*tat*) refers back to the sixteen thousand.
"By twice that" means by thirty-two thousand. "The height is [measured] by the oceans and the Vasus [eight] thousand" (*sahasrābdhivasūcchraya*).
The meaning is that its height is eighty-four thousand [yojanas].
As it has been said:
"In the center of that [world] is the great Meru, made of gold... (Svacchandatantra 10.121).
Having begun with these words:
"It rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
it is planted sixteen thousand yojanas deep below."
"The width at the top is double the width at the base. (Sva 10.123).
Now, even if this [mandala] possesses such a measure, what is its form? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"With a circle in the middle, above, and below, and a square [at the base].
The term "samudvṛtta" means that, having first attained the state of being perfectly octagonal, it is then circularly raised upwards.

Therefore, it is square at the lower Brahma-portion, eight-sided in the middle Viṣṇu-portion, circular in the upper Rudra-portion, and shaped like a shallow bowl (śarāva) at the top on the head; such is the meaning.
But surely, in this way, its having such a form is indicated by [the statement]: "The unmanifest is characterized by four, eight, and sixteen parts," as well as:
"That ear is like a hen's egg... and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "How could the supreme Lord's *liṅga* possibly exist according to such statements?", he says:
"And that *liṅga* belongs to Bhairava, and the earth is its pedestal. (8.45)
Indeed, all the gods are absorbed therein, for it is always worshipped there;
in the center is the assembly hall of Meru made of precious elements, and its banner is in the direction of the Lord.
That Lord, the peak of Jyotiṣka belonging to Śambhu and a portion of Śrīkaṇṭha,
descended fourteen thousand [yojanas] from Manovatī.
The Cakravāḍa mountains encircle the four directions, and here reside the World-Protectors;
Amarāvatī is to the east of the Lord [Indra], and to the south of it [is the city] of the southern protector.
To the north of that city dwell the Apsarases, Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Vināyakas; while to the west of it lies the city of Agni, named Tejovatī, in its own direction.
The Viśvedevas, Viśvakarman, and those who follow them in succession [reside there];
and to the south is Saṃyamanī, situated in order to the west.
The Mātṛnandas, the Svasaṃkhyātas, the Rudras, their practitioners (sādhakas), Kṛṣṇāṅgāra, Nirṛti, and the Piśācakas are located to the east of that [city]. (8.51)
The *Rakṣasas*, *Siddhas*, and *Gandharvas* are situated further and further to the north of it;
the host of *bhūtas* is to the south of it, [the river] known as Vāruṇī Śuddhavatī.
Successively to the north of these dwell the Vasus and the Vidyādharas; to the south of Vāyu is Gandhavatī, and further to its south are the Kinnaras.
The goddess Sarasvatī with her lute, as well as Nārada and Tumburu, and Mahodaya and Indu—these are the secret [deities] of this [direction], again and again in the west. (8.54)
Kubera, the Karmadevas, and likewise their practitioners;
to the west of that illustrious Maheśa is Hari.
On the right, on the right, [are] Brahmā, the Aśvins, and Dhanvantari in sequence.
The two words *ca* (and) indicate a cause; [they mean] that he is worshipped, by implication, in the three worlds. As it has been said:
"Meru shall exist in the form of a liṅga..."
Having begun thus:
"Brahmā [is] square at the bottom...
and so forth.
"In the middle is Viṣṇu, who is eight-cornered..."; and, "Above, however, is Rudra, who is circular in shape on all sides."
Mount Meru arises as the linga, and the earth is its pedestal.

"He is the abode (ālaya) of all the gods; by that he has attained the state of being a sign (liṅga). All this world, beginning with Brahmā, including the moving and the unmoving, is dissolved (līna) within him.
Thus [it is said].
"Thus has this sign been described by you, which is honored throughout the three worlds.
Mount Sumeru is composed of gold and has a summit shaped like a shallow bowl."
Thus [it is said].
The term "dhātuḥ" refers to Brahman. As it has been stated, beginning with:
"Above that is his divine assembly hall, named Manovatī... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.123).

"Endowed with all enjoyments and qualities, [it belongs] to the Great-Souled Brahmā. (Svacchandatantra 10.124). Regarding the phrase "in the direction of Īśa," the word "that" refers back to the assembly hall (*sabhā*). And although there are three peaks here, they are mentioned here because of their predominance. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
It is joined with three peaks made of gold, refined gold, and jewels;
that made of jewels is prescribed for Tryambaka, while the silver one is for Trivikrama.

"...the golden [city] of Kanakāṇḍa... Thus it is said. Regarding the term "world-protectors" (lokapā), this is used in the sense of abundance. "To the south of that" means to the right of it. By this, the sequence is established: the city of the Apsarases is to the south of that, and the city of the Siddhas is to the south of that, and so forth.
And here, by the Apsarases and others, their own cities called Kāmavatī and so forth are indicated;

this should be understood likewise in subsequent cases as well. And here, according to the principle that "the sense of 'and others' (ādi) is obtained from the plural number," the Ādityas are also included—thus, within this interval, there are four [cities].

Otherwise, there would not be twenty-six cities. The word "that" (tām) refers to Amarāvatī. By this, it should be understood that the Vināyakas are to the left of that very city. "In the direction of Śva" means in the southeast corner (the fire-corner).
That [rule] is to be applied later as well. "To the west of that" means to the west of it. Following that...

Thus, this should also be applied to what follows. And it is established by the sense that these two cities are situated before the city called Saṃyamana, which is to be described hereafter; for all these cities indeed face the east, whereby there is a division of east, west, and so forth within them.

"Mātṛnandā" is the name of the city. "Numbered by the breaths" means eleven. "Their practitioners" refers to the attendants of Yama. Regarding the term "Rudras," it is like the eye of a crow [applying to both preceding and following terms]. "In sequence" means that after Mātṛnandā comes the city of the Rudras, who are the attendants of Yama.

Immediately after that, [it says] "of eleven. "Rākṣasas" refers to those designated as *nistriṃśas*. "To its south"—that is, by implication, to the north of the Śuddhavatī. "In front" means to the east.
"Vīṇāsarasvatī" means she who possesses the Gāndharvaveda. "Her practitioners" means...

The Yakṣas are the attendants of Kubera. [They dwell] to the south, which implies [the south] of Amarāvatī. From the use of the dual number in the phrase "in the north and the south," it should be understood that there is but one city for both the Aśvins and Dhanvantari. || 55 ||
He concludes that very point: "In this Bhairava Cakravāṭa, thus the principal cities are eightfold. (56)
Furthermore, twenty-six others are recorded as being situated in the intermediate space.
The term "principal" (*mukhyā*) is used because they are connected to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*); the term "others" (*anyā*) refers to those that are secondary (*gauṇya*). As it has been said:
"Fourteen *yojanas* below the abode of Brahmā..."
The Cakravāṭa mountain range extends for thousands [of yojanas] all around.
That is designated as the Eight Heavens; there dwell the guardians of the world.
To the east of Indra’s city, renowned by the name Amarāvatī, lies his capital.
Tejovatī is proclaimed as the city of Citrabhānu in the southeast;
to the south belongs the city named Saṃyamanī, belonging to Yamarāja.
Kṛṣṇāṅgārā is proclaimed as the city of the Lord of the Rākṣasas in the southwest;
to the west, the city of the Lord of Waters is remembered as Śuddhavatī.
To the northwest, O beloved, is the city of Vāyu named Gandhavahā;
and to the north is the city of Soma named Mahodayā.
In the northeast is the city of the Lord of Īśa, named Yaśovatī;
O Goddess, hear now of the twenty-six cities situated between these.
To the south of Amarāvatī is the city of the Apsarases called Kāmavatī;
it is made of gold, and to the south of that indeed is the city of the hosts of Siddhas.
To the south of that city is another auspicious city of the Ādityas, renowned by the name Aṃśumatī, adorned with rubies.
The divine city of Kusumāvatī, renowned among the Sādhyas, shines resplendent;
to the west of Agni lies Revatī, the city of the Viśvedevas.
To the west of that city, O Goddess, is the divine city of Viśvakarman;
to the west of Dharmarāja is known the city of Mātṛnandā.
There the Mothers play, reeling from their drinking of honey-wine;
to the west of that city of the Rudras is the golden city named Rohitā.
There, the Rudras bearing tridents are the attendants of Yama;
to his west, the city known by the name Guṇavatī is to be known.
To the east of Nirṛti is the city named Piṅgalā, belonging to the eleven Rudras, and possessing a gateway with a vajra-rampart.
O Goddess of the gods, the Piśācas known as Sukarmas reside there;
near the northwestern direction is the auspicious city of Kṛṣṇavatī.
In that very place dwell the Rākṣasas known as Nistriṃśas;
and on the northern side of that is the golden city Sukhāvatī.
Mitra dwells right there, surrounded by many servants.
North of this [city] is another famous golden city named Gāndharvī.
"Gandharvas, surrounded by divine maidens, dwell there" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.130–145). Likewise:
"The army of the Siddhas belongs to the Bhūtas on the south of Varuṇa."
The region known as Hema belongs to the Vasus, and further north belongs to Varuṇa.
To the north of that, O Goddess, is the city named Siddhavatī;
it is proclaimed as the city of all the Vidyādharas.
O Goddess, to the south of Vāyu stands the city named Siddhā;
there dwell the Kinnaras in palaces resembling gold and the sun.
To the east of Vāyu’s [abode] is that of Gāndharvī, made of gold, belonging to Citraratha,
the chief of the Gandharva kings, which resounds with divine Gandharva music.
The Blessed Lady herself resides there, adorned with the seven musical notes,
clothed in the three scales (grāmas), and embellished by the girdle of the musical modes (jātis).
Her limbs are variegated with modulations and melodic expansions; she arises from the emergence of various tānas;
she is endowed with primary and secondary characteristics; and she is veiled by the middle [register].
There, the goddess Sarasvatī was being sung of by the Gandharvas;
to her east were indeed the beautiful abodes of Tumburu and Nārada.
Behind Soma, the women of the Guhyakas are proclaimed.
To the east, indeed, is the city of Soma named Citravatī;
and to the north is the variegated city of the high-souled Kubera, composed of all kinds of precious minerals.
Surrounded by twenty-six thousand koṭis of yakṣas, the illustrious and supreme one dwells in unsurpassed enjoyments.
To its east is a city named Śubhā, made of Jāmbūnada gold;
there indeed dwell the Karma-devas, who have attained divinity through their own actions.
To the west of the Lord of the Mountains lies the glorious city of Viṣṇu;
there dwells the illustrious Śrīpati, Janārdana, who resembles the flax flower,
holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and is clad in yellow garments.
On the southern side of the mountain is the city named Padmāvatī.

To the south of that city, O Goddess, is the city named Kāmasukhā, belonging to Brahmā— the lotus-born one who sits upon a great lotus, who wears a garland of lotuses, and whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals.
O Goddess of the gods, the Aśvins and likewise Dhanvantari are remembered to be there;
and to the north of Amarāvatī is the city renowned as Mahāmeghā.
"And that divine abode of the Vināyakas is established there" (Svacchandatantra 10.146–161).
Thus [it is said]. || 56 ||
And this is the place of enjoyment for those who have performed meritorious deeds; thus he says:
"Those men who, devoted to sacrifices and works of public utility, dwell in the meritorious land of Bhārata. (8.57)
Those who, residing on Meru, worship Śambhu even once in the prescribed manner—
the word "on a holy day" (puṇye) indicates their distinction from other regions— and "in the prescribed manner" means according to the procedure described in the Purāṇas; this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"O Goddess, those men in the meritorious land of Bhārata who are devoted to sacrifices and works of public utility, and who worship Tryambaka even once—they go to Meru. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.169)
Thus [ends the verse]. 57.
Now he begins to divide the regions and so forth beneath Meru: "To the east, south, west, and north of Meru are the supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas). (8.58)
Mandara, Gandhamādana, Vipula, and Supārśvaka are the mountain-foot hills; they are white, yellow, blue, and red respectively. (8.59)
It is called "Viṣkambha" because it acts as a support for the earth. || 59 ||
Thus it is said: "Having supported the earth with these [mountains], Mount Meru stands motionless.
And since a separate measurement for these has not been stated, [they are understood to be equal].

It should be understood that these constitute a portion of the region known as Ilāvṛta, which will be described later; moreover, they are situated near Mount Meru, for otherwise they would not possess the nature of trees and mountains. And in each of these four mountains, there exist gardens, lakes, and wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas); thus he says:
They say that the forests known as Caitraratha and Nandana, as well as Vaibhrāja and Pitṛvana, are the groves [of the gods]. || 8.60 ||
The four lakes are, in order, Rakta, Udamanasa, Sita, and Bhadra;
and their respective trees are the Kadamba, Jambu, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha.

And among these four immovable mountains (*acala*), three [of them] are each mentioned in sequence. Here, the remainder is that the river Jambūnadī arises from the juice of the *jambū* tree. As it has been said:
"The *kadamba* is to be known on Mandara, and the *jambū* indeed on Gandhamādana."
The Aśvattha is to be known in Vipula, and the Nyagrodha in Supārśvaka.
There are lakes and groves here; Aruṇoda is to the east, Mānasa should be known to be to the south, and Sitoda to the west.
"To the north is Mahābhadrā, and beyond that the Caitraratha forest;
then Nandana, and finally the grove known as Pitṛvana, situated in sequence.
Thus it is said.
The Jambu tree on the summit of Gandhamādana is said to be of that same size;
the juice arising from its mass of fruits should be known as being like nectar.
O beloved, by that [river], the Jambūnadī became exceedingly swift;
having circled Meru clockwise, it enters its own source at the foot of the Jambū tree.
"From contact with that, gold is produced as an ornament for the gods;
by means of that, Jāmbūnada—the most excellent of ornaments—is born in the world. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.191) || 61 ||
Jambudvīpa extends all around, from Mount Meru down to the salt ocean.
It is one hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent and is divided ninefold by the boundary mountains on all sides; that is to say, it is circular in shape. As it has been said:
"Jambudvīpa is situated beneath Meru in the form of a circle."
"It has an extent of one hundred thousand yojanas... || 63 ||
He demonstrates its ninefold nature as follows:
"Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat—these three are on the south. (8.63)
One hundred thousand, ninety thousand, and eighty thousand respectively;
Nīla, Śveta, and Triśṛṅga are likewise situated on the right side.
These six boundary mountains of Meru extend from east to west;
Mālyavat is to the east, and that known as Gandhamādana is to the west.
Those two, extending from east to west, are thirty-four thousand [yojanas] long;
these eight, and then two others each, follow in sequence starting from the east.
Jāṭhara, Kūṭa, Himavat, Yātra, Jārudhi, and Śṛṅgin;
thus is the division established here, described for the sake of determining the regions (varṣas). 8.67.

"To the south" refers to Meru when it faces east. "A hundred thousand [yojanas]" is because Jambudvīpa is of that same dimension. Likewise, although these extend across all the continents, externally they follow their respective circular proportions accordingly.
There is a decrease in the length of Hemakūṭa and Himavat, whereas their width remains unchanged.
As it has been said:
"Extending as far as the salt ocean, they are two thousand [yojanas] in width. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.201)

Thus: "That many" refers to the measure of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) and so forth. Regarding "thirty-four thousand," this is because it will be stated later that Ilāvṛta is divided by Nīla and Niṣadha and has such a measurement;
however, in terms of its width, it is one thousand. As it has been said:
To the east of Meru, O Goddess of the Gods, the mountain Mālyavat shines forth for thirty-four thousand yojanas.
"It shines, extending from south to north, with a width of one thousand [yojanas];
likewise, on the western side, there is Gandhamādana, equal to that. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.204).
And here, regarding the four mountains named Nīla, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana—
It should be understood that the height of these mountains is forty thousand *yojanas*, while that of the others is ten thousand. As it has been said:
"Nīla, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana..."
"It is forty thousand *yojanas* in height" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.205).
Likewise, in the Śrī Mṛgendrottara:
"...ten in height, nine in the intervals."

Thus, Jambūdvīpa is divided into nine parts by eight mountains—namely, three each situated to the south and north, and one each situated to the east and west. The word "thence" (tataḥ) refers to from these eight. "Kūṭa" means Hemakūṭa; "Himavat" implies [the range] together with Kailāsa.
"Pāriyātra" refers to the Pāriyātra mountain, and by implication, it includes Niṣadha as well. As it has been said: "Jaṭhara and Hemakūṭa are situated in the eastern part;
Kailāsa and Himavat are situated in the southern part."

"The Niṣadha and Pāriyātra mountains are situated to the west, while the Jārudhi and Śṛṅgavat mountains are established to the north" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.208). And these supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvata) are located in fixed places; thus, there is no [uncertainty] here.
The disjunction caused by another disjunction consists of nine parts. || 67 ||
He says that very thing:
"Beneath the circular mountain range (cakravāṭa), there is a square region called Ilā, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, where the sun and moon do not shine, and the lifespan is three faces. (8.68)
To the west of Meru is Gandhamādana; to the west of that is Ketumāla, adorned with seven principal mountain ranges.
To the east of Meru is Mālyavat; to the east of that is Bhadrāśva, where the lifespan is ten thousand years, and there are five kulaparvatas.
From east to west and from south to north respectively,
these are determined to be thirty-two thousand and thirty-four thousand [yojanas].
To the north of Meru is Śṛṅgavān; beyond that lies the region of Kuruvarṣa, which is shaped like a bow and measures nine thousand [yojanas].
There, the lifespan is thirteen thousand years.
Then, to the north of Kuruvarṣa and in the northwestern ocean,
there are two islands, Candra and Bhadraka, measuring five thousand and ten thousand [yojanas] respectively.
Between the two white-peaked mountains of Meru, in the middle, is a golden region;
it is nine thousand [yojanas] in width, and the lifespan there is twelve and a half [thousand years].
There, indeed, to the left of Śveta and Nīla, in between them, lies Ramyaka;
it is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, and the lifespan there is twelve thousand years.
To the south of Meru are the Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha mountains; between them lies the region called Harya, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, where the lifespan is one thousand years more than that.
Right there, between the two, the Hema and Himavat mountains,
is Kinnara, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, where the lifespan is one thousand years greater than that.
Right there, to the south of Meru, lies Himavat;
to the south of which is Bhārata, nine thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a bow, a land for the experience of the fruits of karma.

The term *ilākhyam* means that this region is called *Ilāvṛta* because it is presided over by the sovereign named Ilāvṛta—this is the sense. This will become clear further on, so no effort has been made to explain it here. In the same way, one should understand the cause for the application of those names in other regions as well.

And that [region] extends nine thousand [yojanas] in width on all four sides of Mount Meru. Calculating the sixteen thousand [yojanas] at the base of Meru in the center, it totals thirty-four thousand; for this very reason, the measurement stated for the lengths and so forth of Mālyavat and Gandhamādana is exactly as given, and thus it is in every direction.

It is square due to its symmetry, but not oblong like other continents. Its lack of sun and moon is caused by its position below the Cakravāṭa mountain range. Regarding the phrase "with a lifespan of three mouths," because of its proximity to the word "thousand," it means a lifespan of thirteen thousand [years]. As it has been said:
Surrounding Mount Meru on all sides, the delightful region of Ilāvṛta is described as being nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, situated below the Cakravāṭa range.
Extending for four yojanas in all four directions, it was square on every side;
there, neither the heat of the sun's son nor the rays of the moon reached.
"For the worlds indeed prevail when illuminated by the light of Meru" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.211).
"Their lifespan is proclaimed to be thirteen thousand years" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.213).
And thus: "to the west," meaning not the Viṣkambha mountain situated to the south. Regarding "with seven," as it has been said:
"Jayanta, Vardhamāna, Aśoka, and Hariparvata..."
"Viśāla, Kambala, and Kṛṣṇa—there are seven principal mountain ranges there" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.218).
Regarding the phrase "the lifespan is ten thousand years," it should also be explained as referring to Ketumāla. For it is said:
"And they live for ten thousand [years]."
Thus [it is said]: "together with the five mountain ranges of the *kulās*. As it has been stated:
"Kaurañja, Śvetaparṇa, Nīla, Mālāgraka, and Padma—these are declared to be the five mountain ranges of the *kulās* there" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.220).

Thus: "these" refers to the two regions known as Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva. "In order" means according to their respective enumeration. Therefore, from east to west, there are thirty-two thousand [yojanas] each for Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla, while Mālyavān and Gandhamādana are each one [thousand].

One thousand [yojanas], eighteen on both sides [of Ilāvṛta], and sixteen for Meru—thus, Jambudvīpa, extending from east to west, measures one hundred thousand yojanas; and thirty-four [yojanas] to the north and south. This is understood simply by defining the dimensions of Ilāvṛta.
Śṛṅgavān is the third mountain; "outside of that" means to the north of it as well.
"Like a bow" means it is ring-shaped (*valayākāra*), due to its proximity to the salt ocean. As it has been said:
"It is proclaimed to be nine thousand *yojanas* in length and shaped like a bow" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.225).

Thus, regarding the statement concerning the measurement of the length, the intention here is that this matter is already understood from the very definition of the measurement of the horns. The same should be understood for what follows as well. "Thirteen" means, by implication, thousands. As it has been said:

"The lifespan in Kuru is thirty thousand years; the people subsist on the fruits of the Kuru trees, are born as twins, and possess the luster of blue flowers. Regarding the phrase "in the ocean," it means within the ocean. As it has been said:
And having entered the salt ocean in its northern direction for exactly four thousand yojanas, O fair-faced one.
"Candradvīpa is proclaimed to be one [thousand] more [than that], extensive;
the island of Bhadra is proclaimed to be ten thousand yojanas. (Svacchandatantra 20.229).
Regarding the phrase "of those two," it refers to Śveta and Śṛṅgin, who are situated on the left half of Meru. By that...
"To the south of Śṛṅgavat and to the north of Śveta"—this is established by the sense of the text. Regarding the phrase "twelve and a half":
this means twelve thousand plus a half, that is, twelve thousand five hundred. As it has been said:
"In the Hiraṇmaya [world], the lifespan is twelve thousand five hundred. [This occurs] "in between."
By implication, this means [the mountains] are to the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla. "Those" refers to thousands.
By implication, "in between them" means to the south of Niṣadha and to the north of Hemakūṭa. As it has been said:
"To the north of Hemakūṭa and to the south of Niṣadha..."
"Harivarṣa is thus described... (Sva. 10.236). "Twelve" refers to twelve thousand [yojanas]. "Kainnara" is the name for Kiṃpuruṣa. As it has been said:
"To the south of Hemakūṭa and likewise to the north of Himavat..."
"The [region] named Kiṃpuruṣa is a varṣa... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.238).

Regarding the phrase "its lifespan is more than a thousand [years]," the meaning is that where the lifespan exceeds those nine thousand by one thousand—that is, a lifespan of ten thousand years—this [is the case]. Of this...
"To the south" means, by implication, to the north of the salt ocean. As it has been said:
"To the south of the lord of the Himalayas and to the north of the salt ocean is the land known as Bhārata; therein, happiness is recorded to be meager. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.240)

Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, because the salt ocean is circular in shape, it is described as being "like a bow. And although this [land] is a land of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*) like other continents, it also possesses the status of a land of action (*karmabhūmi*);
thus he says, "a land of action. As it has been stated:
"But there resides one quality, which is the acquisition of auspicious and inauspicious fruits," [as stated in Svacchanda Tantra 10.246]. || 78 ||
For the regions between the oceans are indeed only lands of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), and not lands of action (*karmabhūmi*) as well;
thus he says:
"Ilāvṛta, Ketumāla, Bhadrāśva, Kuru, Hiraṇmaya, and Ramyaka."
And in the region of Hari-kinnara-varṣa, it is a land of enjoyment, but not a land of karma.
Now, might it not be possible for even a land of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi) in some cases to possess the nature of a land of action (karmabhūmi), as was stated previously:
"But if they worship the Lord of Gods there with devotion,
they dissolve into the principle of Īśvara and gradually [into] the supreme Śiva"?
Otherwise, those who exist devoted to the enjoyment of that [world], being intent on their own pleasure,
will be solely occupied with piteous cries of distress from the torment of the fire of time.
"Then, at the beginning of creation, they are dissolved into the principle of *guṇa*,
and subsequently cast down by the Mothers, preceded by a flood of terrible torments.
Having raised the doubt, "How can this be said, that anything other than Bhārata is merely a land of experience (*bhogabhūmi*)?", he says:
In this regard, although there is generally an absence of ritual action even here,
there may still be a ritual purification of the fettered souls (paśu) through such firm consecration.

The phrase "the state of being a land of action" (karmabhūbhāvaḥ) means "the status of being a land of action"—this is the sense. Now, one might object: even here [in the intermediate state], there is no status as a land of action in abundance, since animals and others merely experience the fruits of their prior karma here, rather than also acquiring new karma. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "even here."
The particle *api* is displaced [in the compound]; therefore, it should be construed as "even for those that are without objects" (*akarmaṇām api*).

And their lack of being objects [is due to] their unsuitability according to the mode of conventional perception (*anyavat-pratīti-vṛttena*), whereas according to the mode of reality (*vastu-vṛttena*), there certainly exists for them the latent impression of an object (*karma-saṃskāra*) due to the firmness of their respective respective predispositions (*vāsanā-dārḍhyāt*); thus, even for these...
The meaning is that its effect must indeed be either auspicious or inauspicious. || 80 ||

One might object: "Even so, it would not be established that this [land] is a land of action (*karmabhūmi*), while elsewhere it is a land of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), since for some there would be no karma here, yet it would exist elsewhere. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For even those who are without the purificatory rites (*asaṃskāra*) may exist in Bhārata and elsewhere as well."
From the firm impressions of the past and from the will of the Lord, [arise] the auspicious and the inauspicious.
In other places as well, karma is observed to exist, and that has been seen since ancient times;
there, the Tretā age is eternal, whereas in Bhārata, however, there are four yugas.

"Without formative impulses (*asaṃskārāḥ*)" means because of having renounced action (*karma*). "'In another place'" means among places such as heaven and so forth. The single word *api* (even/also) is displaced in its order; therefore, it should be construed as "even [both] auspicious and inauspicious. Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", it is said:

"And that was seen in the ancient [texts]. By "in the ancient," he means in the *Purāṇas* and so forth, which consist of the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and other such works. For in those, it is stated that Janaka possessed freedom from ritual action (*akarmitva*) even while in Bhāratavarṣa, whereas Nahuṣa was joined with inauspicious karma even while in heaven; therefore, what was said regarding the abundance [of such examples] in the *Bhārata* is appropriate.

[The distinction is that] elsewhere it is a land of action (*karmabhūmi*), whereas [in other places] it is a land of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*). "There" refers to [regions such as] Ilāvṛta and so forth. As it has been said:

"In none of the eight [sub-continents] does there exist a state characterized by the three ages (*yuga*); O fair-faced one, it should be known that the state characterized by the four ages exists only in the region called Bhārata. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.247)
Thus [ends the verse]. 82.
The land of Bhārata, like Jambudvīpa, consists of nine divisions; thus he says:
"And here in Bhārata, there are nine divisions, divided by the waters of the ocean into five hundred [yojanas] of land and an equal amount of water. (8.83)

"By the ocean water," meaning by that which extends in eight directions, because in that very manner the state of being ninefold is accomplished. For just as Jambudvīpa is divided into nine parts by eight mountains, so too is this [world-system] by the oceans; however, these [oceans] extend from east to west.
"Thus all [are included]. As it has been said:
"O Dear One, nine divisions are recorded there, separated by oceans;
for each individual continent, one thousand [yojanas] are proclaimed."
"Five hundred [yojanas] are to be known as land, and likewise five hundred as water" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.251).
As for that which is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "In the stream of the nine oceans, there are nine islands here at the half-land."
This and what follows has been stated with reference to the ocean of the perishable (kṣara); otherwise, there would be ten oceans here.
And thus, while there is ocean water on both sides of all the continents, for the one called Kanyā, it is only on the south, because of its [proximity] to the five-hundred-yojana ocean of Varuṇa.

Because it is partitioned. Therefore, for this [land], the Himavat alone is to the left and not another ocean; for if it were otherwise, then because it would be separated by another ocean, the Himavat would be inaccessible to its inhabitants just as it is to those of other continents.
Thus, it is established that this [land] is measured precisely by its proximity to the Himavat. As it has been said there:

"The island known as Kumārikā is considered to be near the Himavat. Thus, even its extent of a thousand *yojanas* is understood by implication to be of a single solid landmass; for this very reason, in the venerable *Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka* and other texts, [it is described as such].

In order to demonstrate the division of the boundaries from the vicinity of Himavat, the measurement is specified as extending for a thousand *yojanas*, beginning from the particular lake named Bindusaras situated at its foot. Thus it is stated therein:
"Beginning with: 'To the south of the snowy banks and to the north of the ocean-wreathed [mountains],
there is the region of Kuru, which has the configuration of a bow.'"
The lake named Bindusaras is closely situated upon the Snowy Mountain;
from that time forth, one region has been filled everywhere with virtuous people.
King Bharata, fierce as a planet against the moon of his rival, gave to his daughter, a maiden of the earth, that measure of land which had not been taken away by water.
"Therefore, this island is celebrated as being known by the name Kumārikā;
it extends for a thousand yojanas and is endowed with various castes and stages of life.
Thus it is stated in the Śrī-svacchanda-tantra as well.
"From Bindusaras onwards, it is proclaimed as the region called Kumārī;
it extends for a thousand yojanas and is endowed with various castes and stages of life. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.254). || 83 ||

And he states the division of the names of these nine regions: "Indra, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, Nāgīya, Gabhastimān in the east, Saumya, Gāndharva, Vārāha, and the one called Kanyā—these are the regions up to the ocean. (8.84)
"Up to the ocean" means beginning from the ocean; by this, it extends from Indradvīpa near the salt sea to Kanyādvīpa near the Himavat mountains. "Tāmra" means copper-colored.
Regarding "prāk," Gabhastimān comes first, followed by Nāgīya. "Vārāha" refers to Vāruṇa.
As it has been said:
"Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimat,
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Vāruṇa."
"And the ninth is proclaimed as the island known as Kumārikā. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.253). || 84 ||
And in the ninth [continent], Kanyādvīpa, situated in the middle of the southern ocean,
there are six subcontinents adorned by the seven principal mountain ranges.
Aṅga, Yava, Malaya, Śaṅku, Kumuda, Varāha, and Agastya situated on Malaya;
and right there on Trikūṭa is Laṅkā—these six are indeed the sub-islands (upadvīpas).
"Situated in the middle of the ocean to the south" means she resides in the center of the Ocean of Varuṇa.
As it has been said:
"She stands in the middle of the Ocean of Varuṇa, near the one called Kumārī."
Beyond a hundred yojanas, six islands are recorded.
Aṅgadīpa, Yavadīpa, and Malayadīpa;
another island named Śaṅku, and Kumuda beyond that.
"And Varāha shall be the sixth... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by the seven Kulādris," it is as stated: "Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and the Ṛkṣa mountain..."
"The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these mountain ranges shine forth. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.257).
Regarding the statement "Agastya resides on Malaya," it has been said:
"On the island of Malaya, the mountain named Malaya is described."
"At his foot is indeed Trikūṭa, and Laṅkā is situated upon it" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.259).
"There, on that best of mountains, Malaya, is the peak of Agastya."
"And there is the highly meritorious hermitage of Agastya, radiant as crystal" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.262). Thus [it is said]. 86.
And here, raising the doubt as to what kind of world this is, he says:
"The inhabitants of the continents and subcontinents are for the most part various kinds of Mlecchas;
they are liberated and enriched with gold and jewels—so it is stated in the venerable Ruru-śāsana. (8.87)

"Mlecchas" means those excluded from the conduct of the [four] castes and [four] stages of life—this is the meaning. By the word "mostly," it is indicated that in some cases even those of good conduct may exist. Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", it is said: "Thus in the venerable Ruru-śāsana. This has been stated:
In that regard:
"In the region called Kumārī, the subjects are devoted to the conduct of their castes and stages of life;
the others are mostly Mlecchas, yet abound in gems and gold. (87)
One might object: "In that case, what is the purpose of accumulating merit or demerit here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Whatever action has been performed or even exhausted [through experience] in Bhārata, from the Avīci hell up to Śiva, by means of that [action], there is liberation; but [this occurs] especially in the place called Kanyā. (8.88)
"Karma" refers to the auspicious and inauspicious. "Exhausted" means by means of ritual action, knowledge, and so forth.

The meaning is that through this karma—whether performed or exhausted—one may experience enjoyment within those various principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, or from that state, liberation may occur. As it has been said:

"In that very place, whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of that [action], worlds exist, ranging from those of Śiva down to the midst of the Avīci hell" (Svacchandatantra 10.248). Likewise:

"Whatever action— whether white or black— is performed by living beings when the [soul] is in the state called *kanyā* (maiden), that is the seed which bestows the experience of its fruit in heaven, hell, or liberation. (88)
Now, one might ask: "What is the reason that this [attainment] occurs especially on the Island of Maidens (Kanyādvīpa)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Right here in Bhārata, there are ten million Rudras beginning with Mahākāla."
Because of that, birth here [in this world] is difficult to obtain for those who have performed five hundred [meritorious acts], such as bathing in the Gaṅgā and other [sacred sites].
"In this very place" means on the island known as Kanyā. As it has been said: "In its center is a great island called Kumārīdvīpa;
there, ten thousand auspicious Rudras have descended in their full number."
"And it is the cause for attaining cattle, and through its recollection, it destroys sin. Likewise:
"O fair-faced one, [the places] such as Mahākāla and Ekāmra, and so forth..."
Ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) are said to exist, which yield the fruit of great desires.
"And there are five hundred rivers there, such as the Gaṅgā and others" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.249). Thus, it is because of the abundance of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth. || 89 ||
Is it not said regarding other world-ages: "The people possess the luster of fresh lotus petals, they are exceedingly delicate,
they subsist on the juice of jambū fruits, and they are devoid of old age and death" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.213)?

By such statements as these, people are [generally] abounding in happiness; yet here, by such statements as “People are seized by the fear of disease, suffering, and possess meager prosperity” (Svacchanda Tantra 10.240), they are abounding in suffering— so, in this context, by what is it meant that “birth is difficult to obtain”?
Anticipating the question, "Was this said by way of a mere sign? he says:
"In other lands, one merely carries out one's karma through experience like an animal;
however, for those born in Bhārata, there is that which is to be attained even beyond the reach of their desires. (8.90)
"Beyond all desires," because [the attainment of] enjoyment and liberation is of the greatest magnitude. || 90 ||

If this is so, and [the attainment] were to be achieved without distinction by all those born in Bhārata, then why was it said, "But especially in the land called Kanyā"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The diversity of various castes, stages of life, conducts, pleasures, and pains."
Because of that [event] in Kanyādvīpa, this is the supreme land of action (karmabhūmi).
As it has been said:
"O fair-complexioned one, those qualities previously mentioned that exist in the world of Bhārata, O beloved, they reside right there in the world known as Kumārī. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.255)
Thus, it follows that only those residing here would attain heaven or hell as a result of performing auspicious or inauspicious deeds. ||91||
Regarding this, it is said in the *Rauravavārtika*: "For men who perform white and black deeds here, the higher and lower [states], namely heaven and hell, are indeed accomplished. (8.92)
"What is the authority for this?"—to this it was said: "In the *Rauravavārtika*. It is stated there:
"For men performing white and black deeds, heaven and hell—the higher and the lower—quickly come to fruition here."
Thus [ends the verse]. 92.
He summarizes this very point:
"Thus, that Jambū [continent] which lies around the base of Meru is seventeenfold in detail, but in brief, it consists of nine divisions. (8.93)
"Of seventeen kinds" means eight beginning with Ilāvṛta and nine beginning with Indradvīpa. "By nine" means by those beginning with Ilāvṛta together with Bhārata. (93)
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for this division? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Of Svāyambhuva Manu there were ten sons; from among them, three became renunciants.
Then, in the land called Jambūdvīpa, there was a king named Agnīdhra. (8–94)
He had nine sons, and from them this land became divided into nine regions; Nābhi was the ninth of them, and his grandson was Bharata, the son of Ṛṣabha.
He had eight sons, with his daughter as the ninth portion;
by those nine, that region measuring one hundred thousand yojanas was divided into nine parts.
"Śrutāḥ" refers to the grandsons. "A king named Jambu" means from among these [regions].
The son of Ṛṣabha is Ārṣabhi; for this very reason, he is called the grandson (naptṛ). "The eight sons" refers to those previously mentioned, beginning with Indra. As it has been said:
The son of Svāyambhuva was named Manu; his son was Priyavrata.
Then ten sons were born to him, preeminent in heroism and strength.
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vapu, Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Sāvana, and Satra.
Medhāsatru and Agnibāhu—these three were renunciants;
those remaining among the seven islands were consecrated as kings of great power.
Likewise, in Jambūdvīpa there was Agnīdhra; his nine sons are recorded as Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, Hari, and Ilāvṛta.
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya,
and the ninth named Kuru— these are remembered as the lords of the nine regions (varṣas).
Born indeed from Agnīdhra were heroes of exceeding strength and prowess;
O Pārvatī, the nine regions here are marked with their names.
The son of Nābhi was the highly heroic Ṛṣabha, who was devoted to dharma;
his son, moreover, should be known as the powerful Bharata.
That excellent region, Bhārata-varṣa, is to be known by that very name.
Furthermore, O beloved, eight sons and one daughter were born to him as well.
In this land of Bhārata consisting of eight islands, eight sons were established;
however, the ninth, named Kumāra, was assigned to the daughter.
"Indeed, those islands were proclaimed by Bharata after their names" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.283).
"From that" means from Jambudvīpa, which measures one hundred thousand yojanas.
Its extent of one hundred thousand yojanas from east to west has already been demonstrated; however, as for its [extent] from south to north—

Now it is said: there, the six regions beginning with Bhārata each consist of nine thousand [yojanas]—thus making fifty-four; the mountain ranges beginning with Himavat each consist of two thousand—thus making twelve; and together with the sixteen thousand at the base of Meru, there is Ilāvṛta.
Thirty-four thousand [yojanas]—thus, Jambūdvīpa is one hundred thousand yojanas.
Now, he shows the specific configuration even outside of that:
"The Salt Ocean is exactly one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure; outside of it are the mountains in front of it."
Ṛṣabha, Dundubhi, Dhūmra, Kaṅka, Droṇa, and Indu are indeed the [names of] water. (8.97)
To the west are Varāha, Nandana, and Aśoka, along with Balāhaka;
to the south are Cakra and Maināka, and between them stands the Vāḍava fire.
To the south of the ocean, after traversing eight thousand yojanas, there is a mountain named Vidyutvat, three thousand yojanas high and as wide; here dwell those who subsist on fruits.
Besmeared with filth, with long hair and beards, behaving like cattle, naked, living for eighty years, and subsisting on grass. (8.100)
"The doors there must always be unbarred for the sake of attaining the cave (bilasiddhi);
this has been sung by the Gurus in the venerable Rauravaśāsana. (8.101)
Thus has this Salt Ocean been described;
beyond it are these six continents, each surrounded by its own ocean.

The six continents—Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomedha, and Abja—are each twice the size of the preceding one and are presided over by six sons of Manu. There are six oceans consisting of milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, wine, and sweet water. (8–103)
Medhātithi, Vapuṣmat, Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havis, and King Saṃvara—these were designated as the Agnīdhras among the Śākas and other regions of Jambudvīpa. (8.104)
"Lavaṇa" means the salt-water ocean—the "ocean of alkaline water"—this is the meaning. "Indu" is the moon.
As it has been said:
"Terrified by the fear of Vṛtrāri, the mountains entered there."
"I shall now describe those twelve great heroes in brief:
Ṛṣabha, Dundubhi, and Dhūmra entered from the eastern side; Candra, Kaṅka, and Droṇa entered from the north."
Then Aśoka, Varāha, and Nandana as the third—
these other mountains there entered the salt ocean.
Cakra, the one named Maināka, and the third, Balāhaka—
these mountains, O lady of excellent hips, have entered from the south.
"The submarine fire (vaḍavānala) indeed stands between Cakra and Maināka" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.273).

Regarding the word "to the south," it means in proximity to Cakra, Maināka, and so forth; "khākṣi" refers to twenty. Regarding "by the gurus," it refers to the feet of Bṛhaspati. As it has been stated therein:
Having traversed twenty thousand yojanas,
there stands on the southern ocean one renowned as Vidyutvān.
That mountain was three thousand yojanas in length and likewise in height;
it was a thousand yojanas broad, and there the inhabitants subsisted on grass, leaves, and fruits.
With limbs smeared and covered in filth, with long beards and hair,
those naked people lived for eighty years, subsisting on cow dung.
"In that regard, the excellences of the cities consist of entrances through unmechanized (natural) openings.
Thus, "doubled in sequence" means that there are two hundred thousand [yojanas] in Śākadvīpa and four hundred thousand in Kuśadvīpa;
such is the order of the meaning. "Abja" refers to Puṣkara. "Ikṣu" itself is "aikṣava."
"Madhurāmbukaḥ" means one whose waters are sweet. It is accompanied by "dyutimatā" (the radiant one), as implied by the context; "haviḥ" means the sacrificial offering.
As it has been said:
"Jambudvīpa, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, along with Śālmali..."
"Gomeda and the one called Puṣkara— these are the seven continents, O Pārvatī" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.284).
"Salt water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and likewise sugarcane juice..."
And the Madyoda; these are proclaimed as the seven seas of sweet water.
Jambudvīpa is recorded as being one hundred thousand yojanas in measurement;
it should be known as circular, and outside it, the salt-water ocean is equal to that.
"In this way, the oceans are situated around the continents with a doubling of size" (Sva. 21.287).
O fair-faced one, Agnīdhra is thus designated in Jambudvīpa.
In the Śāka [continent], there is one named Medhātithi, who is embodied, in the region called Kuśa.
"Then King Jyotiṣmat is remembered on Krauñca, Dyutimat on Śālmalī;
Havya on Gomedha, and likewise Saṃvara on Puṣkara" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.290). Thus [it is said]. 104.
And he further divides the six continents:
"The five [continents] beginning with Śāka consist of as many segments as are fashioned by the seven mountain ranges.
The one named Puṣkara is divided into two; here, Hari, Yama, Varuṇa, and Indu are located in the east and the other directions. (8–105)
