"They are that many," meaning exactly seven, because they are situated along the sides of the seven mountain ranges. "Two-petaled" means they are divided in the middle by one mountain in the form of a circular ring. "In the east and so forth" refers to the four directions—as it has been said:
Medhātithi had seven sons who were consecrated as rulers in Śākadvīpa:
Śānta, Ubhaya, Śiśira, Sukhada, Nandaka, and Śiva.
Kṣemaka and Dhruva—these are marked by the names of the regions; they are known as the seven regions. Now learn from me concerning the mountains.
"Gomeda, Candrasaṃjña, Nārada, Dundubhi, as well as Ṛṣabha, Somaka, and Vaibhraja are the Kulaparvatas. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.294).
In former times, seven sons were established by Vapuṣmān upon Kuśa:
Śveta, Lohita, Jīmūta, Harita, and likewise Vaidyuta.
Mānasa and Suvrata are marked by the very names of the years;
likewise are Kumuda, Urva, Varāha, Droṇa, and Kaṅkata.
"Mahiṣa and Kumuda are indeed the seven boundary mountains. (Sva. 10.300).
"Seven sons of Jyotiṣmān were established in Krauñcadvīpa."
The bamboo and the maṇḍalaka are also declared to be sprout-born (udbhijja).
And Rathakāra, Lavaṇa, Dhṛtimat, and Supratāraka.
And Kapila—these kings were marked by the names of the [respective] rain-clouds.
"Vaidruma, Hemanābha, Dyutimān, Puṣpadantaka, Kuśala, and Harimarda— these seven are the Kulaparvatas. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.305).
Cursed by Dyutimān, his sons were consecrated as kings over Śalmala:
Mano’nuga, Uṣṇa, Pāvana, and Andhakāraka.
"Munirdundubhi and Kuśala—these are remembered as them. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.309).
"Then Krauñca, Vāmana, Andhakāra, and Divākṛti..."
"Dvibindu, Puṇḍarīka, Dundubhi, and the Kulādris. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.311).
"Havyarāja consecrated his seven sons in the Gomedha sacrifice."
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, and Marīcaka.
"Kumuda, Unnata, and Mahābhadra are thus remembered. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.315).
"Udaya, Kesara, Jaṭhara, and then Suraivata..."
"Śyāma, Ambikeya, and Meru—these are the mountains situated at the boundaries. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.317).
And thus: "In the place called Puṣkara, Saṃvara is the leader there."
Two sons, renowned by him, were established in the place called Puṣkara.
"The mountain named Mānasottara is ring-shaped. (Sva. 10.323).
"Dhātakī is the king in the middle; Mahāvīta is the king on the outside. (Sva. 10.324).
Thus:
"Learn from me also of the cities of the four world-protectors here:
that of Indra is named Ekasārā, and the city of Yama is Saṃyamanī."
"And *sukhāhvā* and *vāruṇī* are indeed the two forms of Soma, *vibhāvarī*. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.327).
Thus [it is said]. || 105 ||
He summarizes up to this point:
"Five hundred and three lakṣas, two koṭis, and five ayutas—this is the measurement in yojanas from the end of the Svādharṇava up to the peak of Meru. (8.106)
In that regard, Jambūdvīpa consists of fifty thousand [yojanas]; the salt ocean is one hundred thousand;

Śākadvīpa and the milk ocean are two hundred thousand; Kuśadvīpa and the curd ocean are four hundred thousand; Krauñcadvīpa and the ghee ocean are eight hundred thousand; and Śālmalidvīpa and the sugarcane-juice ocean are sixteen hundred thousand.
Gomeda is thirty-two [lakṣas], the ocean of wine is thirty-two, Puṣkara is sixty-four, and the sweet-water ocean is sixty-four; thus, starting from half of Meru and ending with the sweet-water ocean,
the measurement is two crores, fifty-three lakṣas, and fifty-three thousand yojanas.
This would be the measurement. As it has been said:
"Two crores and fifty-three lakhs beyond that, plus fifty thousand;
these are the seven continents together with the oceans."
Thus [ends the verse]. 106.
Outside the seventh ocean is the golden land, ten crores and one lakh [yojanas] in extent; the Lokāloka mountain is said to be ten thousand [yojanas] in height and breadth.
Some maintain that the eight Rudras, together with the world-protectors (lokeśas), are situated within the eight directions of the Lokāloka mountain;
others hold that they exist solely within the interior of the Lokāloka, for the sun is there, not outside.
"The golden earth" means, by implication, for the sake of the gods' play. "The mountain beyond the world" refers to the Lokāloka mountain. As it has been said:
"Beyond that, O fair-faced one, is the golden earth extending for a hundred million [yojanas]."
Beyond this is the Lokāloka mountain, intended for the sport of the gods.

"O fair-faced one, Mount Parvata is circular in shape, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent, and one hundred thousand *yojanas* in height" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.331). Regarding the phrase "together with Lokeśa," it has been said:

"The world-protectors (lokapālas) and the Rudras of unfailing power are stationed there" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.333). Regarding the word "some": this refers to Līlākāra and others. For they have explained it differently, stating that because they embody all the world-protectors, the Rudras themselves are the world-protectors stationed there.
"Therefore, O Goddess, it is called Lokāloka; there the Rudras are stationed, all possessing unfailing power, stainless, and making the earth their abode."
Kardama, Śaṅkhapāla, Parjanya, Svarṇaloma,
Ketumān, and Rajana are situated from the east to the northeast.
Because there exist scriptural passages contradicting this, such as: "The world-protectors (lokapālas) stand outside [the sun], pervading all this.
It is not "outside," because the Sun is equal in height to the Lokāloka mountain and because he resides within Meru and the space between them. Therefore...

It is called *lokāloka* because it is where there is light for those worlds situated within it; thus, it is that which has both light (*āloka*)—meaning illumination—and non-light (*aloka*)—meaning darkness—both internally and externally. As it has been said:
"O beautiful goddess, the sun shines within it, but not outside."
Thus [ends the verse]. 108.
Thus, he demonstrates the diversity of the sun’s movement while it exists within the space between Meru and the Lokāloka mountain:

"The two paths of the ancestors and the gods, which lie to its north and south respectively, are the two tracks belonging to its own class; they call this very thing the sun’s two solstices, northern and southern. (8–109)
In this regard, as the sun moves in proximity to Meru, its path is the northern one;

however, due to its proximity to Lokāloka, it is the southern one. And these two paths are designated by the terms *suvīthī* and *ajavīthī*, meaning they are referred to by the names "the Good Path" and "the Goat Path. As it has been said:
"The path of Śuvi is to its north, while the path of Aja is to its south" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.339).
These two are indeed the paths of the ancestors and the gods—thus it is said that they are "the paths of the ancestors and the gods. Among them, the path of Aja is the path of the ancestors.
The *suvīthī*, however, belongs to the gods. As it has been said:
"The *ajavīthī* is the southern path, while the *suvīthī* is the northern course;
likewise, the divine path of the ancestors is described in due order."
Thus, these two paths alone are the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana); so it has been said:
"These two alone constitute the northern and southern courses. As it has been stated:
"Above Lokāloka is the southern course of the sun; likewise, the northern course is proclaimed to be there to the north. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.337). || 109 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the proof for this claim that the sun's northern course is due to its proximity to Meru, while its southern course is due to its proximity to the Lokāloka mountain? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For all [beings], Meru is to the north and the Lokāloka is to the south."

"Of all" refers to those residing in [the regions] beginning with Varṣāṣṭaka. For in Ilāvṛta, the sun itself does not shine; thus, what opportunity is there for any variation in its movement? Indeed, the Lord Sun, with respect to Mount Meru, [shines] from the east over the three regions beginning with Bhārata situated in the southern direction.
From the west, it rises over Ketumāla; from the south, over the three regions beginning with Kuru situated in the northern direction;

and from the east, over Bhadrāśva situated to the west—thus rising from the north and establishing itself in the eastern direction according to its own emergence, it illuminates all [the continents] and casts the Lokāloka mountain into shadow toward the south, by which means...
From its proximity to or distance from that [point], the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), and so forth would result.
Not only is there such variety in its movement alone, but even in its rising and setting—as he says: "One should contemplate the rising and setting of the sun in this manner. (8.110)
The word "ittham" (thus) means by way of a clockwise rotation—that is, by revolving around Meru.
Regarding this, it is said:
"It is midnight in Amarāvatī and likewise sunset in Yāmyā;
it is midday in Vāruṇī and sunrise is recorded in Saumya. (8.111)
That which is sunrise in Amarāvatī is midnight in the abode of Yama;
at that same time, it is sunset in the north and midday in the east—such is the movement of the sun.
Indeed, O gentle one, here on the northern side of Meru, in the city named Mahodayā, when the rising of the sun is observed for those coming from Vāruṇī, then, because two watches have elapsed,
it is midday in the city named Gandhavatī in Vāruṇī.

In the southern city called Saṃyamanī, situated in the southern direction, the sun sets; after the lapse of four watches, light is no longer seen because it has been obscured by the shadow of the mountain—this is the meaning. [Likewise] in the eastern city called Amarāvatī...

And it is midnight when the sun rises in the western quarter (Vāruṇī), because at that time it is setting [in Amarāvatī] and sunrise will occur there two watches later. Furthermore, that which is sunrise in Amarāvatī and the sight of the sun for one approaching from the northern quarter (Saumyā) is midnight in the abode of Yama, because the sun is about to rise there two watches later.
At the time of sunset in Kevāruṇa and at the time of sunrise in Saumya, it is midday there because of the circularity [of the sun's path];
for now, four watches have passed [in the former case], while in Saumya, two watches have elapsed— thus, by this very sequence, [midday occurs] in the eastern and western intermediate directions.
The rising and setting of the sun are also to be considered—thus it has been said: "In this manner, the coming and going of the sun.
As it was stated:
"Midnight in Amarāvatī is sunset for Yama. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.338)
Thus it is said:
"When his rising is seen in Amarāvatī, at that very moment he sets in Vāruṇī; such is the coming and going of the Sun."
Thus it is said; and this should also be applied to the other continents, because the rising of the sun is the same everywhere.
Having thus explained this as a digression, he returns to the subject at hand:
"The darkness outside the Lokaloka mountain consists of thirty-five crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand [yojanas]. (8.113)
The king of oceans named Garbhoda, measuring seven sāgaras, lies beyond the Lokāloka mountain; within its womb is the entire earth.
As it has been said:
"Outside of that is a terrible darkness, difficult to behold and devoid of living beings;
it is recorded as being thirty-five crores and nineteen lakhs [of yojanas]."
"Forty thousand *yojanas*, O fair-faced one" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 10.341).

Thus, the measurement of the seven [oceans], beginning with the salt ocean and so forth— which consists of twenty-seven million *yojanas* through an increase that doubles from one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) onwards— is equal to that [measurement].
This is the meaning. Regarding the term *samudrarāj* ("king of oceans"), it is because it encompasses the seven oceans, beginning with the salt ocean (*kṣāra*). As it has been said:
"Since those seven oceans that have been described are remembered as being within its womb, it is therefore called Garbhoda, the bearer of the essence of all oceans" (*Mṛgendrāgama*).
Thus [ends the verse]. 114.
And here, in the place of *tamas*, he clarifies what was taught in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvaramata*:
"In this *Siddhātantra*, on the shore of the ocean of the womb, there is a mandala known as Kauśeya; there Garuḍa resides, surrounded by the wings of the Siddhas. (8-115)
They sport upon the mountain peaks; here there are nine principal mountain ranges (kulādri).
From there flow thirty rivers of hot water that descend into the netherworld (pātāla).
In the four directions is the Naimira garden, which is constantly frequented by yoginīs;
beyond that is Meru, then the nāgas, then the clouds, and then the golden egg.
"On the shore" means on the side beyond this [ocean]. For there, at the junction of the Lokāloka mountain, is the Garbhoda ocean.

"The Naimira garden" means that which is known by the names Naimira and Puṣpa. "The serpents" refers, by implication, to the ground made of jewels. "The clouds" refers, by implication, to the region above Mount Haricandra.
"Hemāṇḍaka" means a golden vessel—a small bowl made of gold—this is the meaning. As it is said there:
"On the further shore of the Garbhoda ocean is a region named Kauśeya;
there dwells the Lord of Gods, surrounded by Garuḍa."
"With thousands of perfected beings (siddhas) who pride themselves on strength equal to his own,
they remain upon the mountain peak, sporting again and again.
Thus it is said.
"Hulahāla, Varakrodha, Koṭaka, Mūlaparvata,
Rodhaka, Vāmana, and Kāṇḍa are to be known as the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
Thus it is said.
"Furthermore, at the edge of the mountain, there are thirty rivers, each a yojana in width;
they are known to have hot water and flow toward the depths of Pātāla.
Thus it is said.
"Furthermore, on the bank of that river is the flowerless forest of Nimi;
there, O Goddess of the Gods, the Yoginīs sport, arrogant in their power.
Thus it is said.
The ground outside the forest is situated on all sides;
it is dry and devoid of water, whereas the inner ground is born of jewels.
"It is crowded with elephants from every quarter and purified on all sides;
therein are many tuskers resembling Mount Meru and Mandara.
Thus [it was said].
"Then, having even surpassed those, the great mountain known as Hariścandra rose up, situated in the form of a ring. Thus [it is said].
"Therein are present the clouds, Saṃvarta and others, making a great roar.
And again: "Furthermore, that golden egg is seen, exceedingly radiant."
Thus [ends the section]. || 117 ||
He summarizes that very point:
"Fifty million [yojanas] by the shell of Brahmā’s egg and half of Meru; thus, in the ten directions, the region known as Bhūrloka extends for fifty million. (8.118)

Therein, beginning from Meru and extending to the edge of the sweet waters (Svādūdaka), the golden ground previously calculated measures two hundred fifty-three million five hundred thousand [yojanas];
the width of the Lokāloka mountain is ten million; and the region of darkness is ten thousand.

Forty-one thousand nine million, three hundred and fifty million, plus Garbhoda; together with the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa, which measures one hundred and twenty-seven million, there are thus fifty crores in total— so it is said.
"In the ten directions"—thus, there would be hundreds of millions of earth-worlds in every respect. || 118 ||

And this world of earth (bhūrloka) is the abode for all fourteen types of created beings; thus he says: "This world of earth is pervaded by six classes—beasts, birds, wild animals, trees, humans, and reptiles—as well as by piśācas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and yakṣas. (8.119)

And for the holders of knowledge (vidyābhṛts), what need is there to say more? For the entire creation of beings, through their own conceit, there is enjoyment and residence according to their desire. (8.120)

"Tree" (*taru*) refers to the stationary (*sthāvara*). "Of the knowledge-bearers" (*vidyābhṛtām*) refers to those who constitute a particular class [of beings]. "Or rather, what need is there for much?"—the intention is that their description by way of the relationship between the class and its members would result in endlessness. "Of all" means of the fourteen kinds. By the word "through conceit" (*abhimānataḥ*), [it is implied...]

It has been shown that this state of being a locus for enjoyment and so forth consists essentially of mere conceit (*abhimāna-mātra*) and is not at all real. Regarding the term "dwelling" (*nivāsa*), it refers to certain [beings] even in the absence of enjoyment; therefore, the intention is that this very point must be purified right here. Thus it has been said:
"The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra, as well as the Saumya, Prājāpatya, and they know the Brāhma to be the eighth. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.351).
"Beasts, birds, and wild animals, as well as other reptiles;
the fifth is the immobile, and the sixth is the human womb."

"The maṇḍala of saṃsāra, which is said to be composed of the divine origins and consists of fourteen types, should be purified within the world of earth (bhūrloka). (Svacchanda Tantra 10.353). || 120 ||
Now he describes the Bhuvarloka and the regions beyond:
"The Bhuvarloka extends one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the Sun;
within that interval, there are ten paths of the wind, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas]. (8.121)
First, the path of the wind (*vāyupatha*) spread therein is discussed.
The phrase "up to the sun" (*ā arkāt*) means as far as the sun. As it has been said:
"From the surface of the earth up to the sun, the measurement is one hundred thousand [yojanas]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.422)
Thus: "at intervals of ten thousand" means that they proceed by way of ten thousand [steps]—this is the meaning. "Therein" means from the midst of the ten paths of the wind. || 121 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Fifty yojanas above that is the wind named Ṛtarddhi. (8.122)
He becomes the nourisher of living beings; from there he becomes Prācetasa.
Fifty yojanas above that, and then another hundred yojanas upward— || 8.123 ||
Here, these winds are like generals, and these clouds are mute, yet they release lightning;
they stand at a distance of only one *krośa* from the earth, raining down water.
Above those, at a distance of one hundred [yojanas], are clouds that rain down living beings such as frogs;
fifty above that is the Ogha [cloud], which rains down poisonous water.
Other clouds arising from the Skanda wind are the Piśācas in the Ogha wind;
fifty yojanas above that are the clouds known as Mārakas.
In that place dwell those Vināyakas born from Mahādeva,
who seize the performed merit of men whose selves are unrefined.
Fifty yojanas above is the Vajrāṅka [region], where there are winds, stones, and clouds;
here, the lowest of the Vidyādharas are firmly established in the Vajrāṅka.
"Fifty *yojanas* above" means from the surface of the earth. Regarding the term "the nourisher," it is as stated:
"He who increases the growth and the strength of the plants, and who causes the entire earth to swell—that imperishable one nourishes [it]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.424)
Thus: "fifty *yojanas* above" means that just as the power of immortality (*ṛtarddhi*) is situated fifty *yojanas* above the surface of the earth, so too,
having established another interval of fifty *yojanas* above that, this—

This is the meaning. He is called "Prācetasa" because he was created by the Pracetasas and because he dwells together with the fire named after them; for this very reason, he possesses both the quality of nourishing and the quality of burning. As it has been said: "The wind named Prācetasa was fashioned by the Pracetasas."
He indeed destroys the trees, and at times he may set them in motion.
"Agni, named Prācetasa, dwells together with him [there]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.427).

Regarding the phrase "above that by a hundred," the meaning is: having traversed a hundred *yojanas* even beyond Prācetasa. This same method of interpretation should be applied to what follows as well.
Because they do not possess such designations and because they rain down living beings such as frogs and so forth, they are called *sattvavahā* (carriers of sentient beings).
As it has been said:
"Beyond a hundred *yojanas*, the clouds are known as *sattvavahā*."

"And they rain down fish, frogs, and tortoises during foul weather" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.430). And it is precisely because they rain down poisonous water that they cause calamities and the like. As it has been said:
"The obstruction of the wind is proclaimed to be fifty *yojanas* above."
"But in that [period], disease-bearing clouds rain down poisonous water; by means of that, afflictions caused by Māra arise for all embodied beings. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.432) Thus it is said.
Indeed, the divine Piśācas born from the body of Skanda dwell in the Ogha;
thirty thousand crores are recorded as the followers of Skanda.
"They indeed worship the Son of Hara with divine flowers" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.442).
Regarding the phrase "in that place," it refers to the wind named Amogha. "Of those with unrefined souls" means of those who possess doubt. As it has been said:
"But above that, from those [levels], the god Amogha stands as Marut;
in him, those clouds of Māra are firmly established in the Amogha. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.433)
The formidable Vināyakas, born of Mahādeva, are unfailing;
thirty thousand koṭis of them are established in that wind.
And as it is said: "Those who take away the performed karma of men who have not disciplined themselves" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.444).
And regarding the phrase "clouds raining stones," they are so named because they rain down stones. They are the lowest of the Vidyādharas.

Because their accomplishment is minor in comparison to the vidyādharas who will be described later, for this very reason these [beings] attain those respective states of movement solely by mounting the mātaṅgas found there. || 128 ||
And he states the cause for their attainment of this state:

"Those who died while engaged in knowledge or manly exertion, and those who died while accomplishing [rites] such as in the cremation grounds—they are perfected siddhas, established in the wind marked by the vajra. (8.129)
"In the contest of knowledge and manliness," that is, in rivalry regarding the science of Garuḍa and so forth; the word "dead" implies that they died at the end of this [distance].
As it has been said:
"The wind named Vajrāṅka is situated at a distance of fifty yojanas."
"And in that [region] there are clouds named Upalās, which rain down stones. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.434).
"Likewise, in Vajrāṅka and in the wind [region], there are the Mātaṅgas, who perform cruel deeds."
Resembling crushed collyrium, they are terrible and renowned by the name Tāpanas.

The lowest among the Vidyādharas are those who travel by means of the mind or the wind; and those who [attain their power] through the prowess of spells, or by means of Vetālas and other spirits from the cremation grounds.
"Having accomplished [their goal], those perfected ones are then established in this wind" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.446). Thus [it is said]. 129.
Fifty yojanas above the Vajrāṅka mountain are the clouds that rain down lightning and thunderbolts;
here dwell the Apsarases and those men who have performed meritorious deeds.
Those who die by a precipice, by fire, by water, or who do not retreat in battle,
or those who die while recovering stolen cattle or releasing those condemned to death, abide in the world of lightning.

He explains the state of being a merit-maker (*puṇyakṛttva*) with the words beginning "in Bhṛgu," and so forth. This is because it is traditionally taught that those who die in Bhṛgu and other such places [attain this state], as is the case for those whose *smṛti* has been lost. As it is said:
"And in Bhṛgu, for one whose *smṛti* has been lost..."
Thus it is said:
"Having reached the ultimate limit, abandoned by physicians,
deprived of the taste of flavors, and tormented by diseases."
A man who, turned away from his kin and abandoned by his own people, prepares to cast off his body and ascends Mount Bhairava, shall indeed obtain the fruit thereof.
"Otherwise, he would cause his own body to fall [into ruin] and incur the fruit of killing a Brahmin.

By the word "in battle," it is meant by implication for the sake of those who have sought refuge and so forth; for otherwise, these individuals would be self-killers—how then could there be the attainment of this state? As it has been said:
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, enveloped in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. (Rig Veda Upanishad 3.12). They are situated—by implication, in celestial chariots. As it has been said:
At exactly that many yojanas from there is the Vaidyuta wind;
the Vaidyuta clouds dwell within it, and they are indeed called Vaidyutas.
"Due to the agitation of the wind, that great thunderbolt arises among them" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.435).
"In that [thunderbolt], the Apsarases of lightning are dispatched by Vāsava."
They always remain there for the protection of the earth and the city.

"Those supreme men who do not retreat in battles—whether by falling from a cliff, into fire, or into water; or those who die while recovering cows or liberating prisoners—they go upward from there in celestial chariots marked with jewels. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.449)
Thus [ends verse] 131.

From the Vaidyuta cloud to the Raivata cloud, there are clouds that carry nourishment; above them are the clouds that release the waters of disease, and immediately after those are the Saṃvarta clouds.
Those who have attained perfection through *rocanā*, collyrium, ashes, and so forth, reside right there on Raivata;
that wind is Viṣāvarta, the abode of those who vomit wrathful waters.
Fifty years beyond that, in that very place, there are stormy years born of fire;
and likewise, there are specific classes of Vidyādharas who [worship] the Supreme Lord.
They always worship with the Gāndharva [tune] while stationed at Viṣāvarta;
beyond a hundred Viṣāvartas, there arises the Durjaya [region] born of breath.
The clouds that cause the winds at the time of dissolution are situated here in the realm of Brahmā; the Puṣkara clouds, which move with the wind, and the Gandharvas reside in the Parāvaha wind.
The Jīmūtas and Meghas— those known by those names— as well as the best of the Vidyādharas,
and those worlds called Rūpavratas, are established in Āvaha.
In Mahāvahe, however, there are clouds created by Īśa that bring benefit to living beings;
in Mahāparivahe, the clouds arise from the skull of Maheśvara.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "ashes etc.," sandals and so forth are also intended. As it has been said:
"Fifty *yojanas* above that, Raivata is remembered;
there dwells the one named Puṣṭivaha, who rains down nourishment (*puṣṭi*) upon embodied beings. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.436)
Thus it is said:
"On Mount Raivata, however, the great-souled Siddhas are indeed well-established;
there they obtain yellow orpiment, collyrium, ashes, sandals, antelope skins, and so forth."
"Having accomplished [their goal], those great-souled ones become perfected beings (*siddha*) capable of assuming any form at will" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.451).

And as for the word "above," it means from Raivata. "In the interval between them" means that very space of fifty *yojanas* which is an interval of the nature of emptiness—this is the meaning. Thus it has been said:
"In the Śaṃvarta [wind], those clouds that bestow disease rain down sickening water; indeed, those clouds remain for fifty yojanas in that [region]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.437).
Thus, they are called "clouds of foul weather," because they cause foul weather. Regarding the phrase "by means of the Gāndharva [wind]":
By means of the flute, lute, and so forth. As it has been said:
"The wind named Viṣāvarta is situated fifty [yojanas] above;
in that place, the clouds named Krodhodaka are firmly established."
They will be full of anger and passion, as well as full of strife;
they will bring about the destruction of kings and likewise the ruin of the subjects.
"And they indeed bring about rain when those clouds pour down. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.440).
"In the great wind Viṣāvarta, the hosts of Vidyādharas are said to reside."
"And those ten and thirty crores [of beings] are adorned with divine ornaments. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.453).
"The clouds born of smoke belong to the Fire element; they are known to bring cold and overcast weather."
Like those who have boarded a ship caught in a whirlpool of poison, they go along depending upon that wind.

And regarding this, it is said: "There, the birds are skilled in the Gandharva arts, sharing the nature of Gandharvas; they know the methods of the flute and the lute, and they can assume any form at will" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.455).
Furthermore, in this context, because of the reading in the commentary of Uddyotakara, the phrase "even in Saṃvarta and in the great wind" [is understood].

Regarding the point of confusion—namely, why the *vidyādharas* are not mentioned in the *Saṃvarta* [chapter] but are mentioned in the *Viṣāvarta*—the reading conjectured by us alone is correct, because it has been accepted by the great authorities (*mahājana*). Likewise:
"The obstruction of the wind is proclaimed to be above one hundred *yojanas*" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.431).

In passages such as these, the reading conjectured by us alone should be accepted; otherwise, even in that [opponent's] own system, the meaning of the word *tāvat* in such passages as "tasmādūrdhvaṃ tu tāvadbhyaḥ... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.432) would not be coherent. Furthermore, "Durjaya" is the name of that [deity].
Wind. As it has been said:
"The clouds named Brahmajā indeed arise from the breath of Brahmā; they are situated above Durjaya, at a distance of a hundred yojanas. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.456)
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "and the Gandharvas," the word "and" (ca) includes the clouds known as Durjaya and others as well.
As it has been stated:
"In that very place, those named Durjaya are the protectors of Indra."
They remain established by relying upon the wind named Parāvaha.
Ten crores of clouds named Puṣkarāvartaka, born from the lotus-born [Brahmā], are proclaimed to be endowed with great heroism and power.
The wings of the great-souled mountains that were severed by Śakra,
Parāvaha carries them away like an elephant carrying men.
"In that [region] dwell the Gandharvas named Vāyugamas, whose abode is the sky" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.461). From that time onwards,
their continuous residence is to be understood, as there is no scriptural statement establishing any interval between them.

"Tatsaṃjñāḥ" means those having the name *jīmūta*. As it has been said: "Those clouds named *jīmūtas*, which arise from the life-force (*jīva*) for the sake of the gods, are supported by that second wind, Āvaha."
"In that [place] there are ten groups of Vidyādharas named Jīmūtakas" (Svacchandatantra 10.462).

Regarding the term "Rūpavratās," the meaning is: those whose vow consists in the assumption of forms—like those who mock forms—but not in [the pursuit of] an objective reality; they live by means of that vow. This has been stated in the venerable Svacchanda[tantra]:
"And those worlds which consist of form, their support is therein. This half-verse was not seen by the author of the *Uddyota*; therefore, one should not be misled.
"Created by Īśa" means fashioned by Umāpati. As it has been said:
From that [place] comes the great-carrying wind where the Droṇas reside;
therein the Droṇas are proclaimed as the protectors of the clouds.
"For they were indeed created by me in the past for the welfare of all beings. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.463).
"Clouds" refers to Saṃvarta and the others. As it has been said:
"The clouds named Saṃvarta arise from the skull above."
"The wind named Mahāparivaha is their common support. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.464) || 138 ||
He summarizes this very point:
"This path of the wind, ending with the Mahāparivaha, extends from the Ṛtarddhi [cloud] upwards.
Thus, here, starting from the Ṛtarddhi, it reaches ten thousand yojanas up to the end of the Mahāparivaha.

Having calculated seven hundred and fifty [yojanas] for the intervals between the sixteen winds according to the stated sequence, the remainder must be divided equally, as there is no specific scriptural statement to the contrary; by doing so, the measure for each would be five hundred [yojanas] and seventy-eight and a half krośas.
The daughters of Agni and the Mothers are presided over by the power of Rudra.
In the second [circle] are the Siddhas and Cāraṇas born of their own karma;
in the fourth are the eight divine weapons; and in the fifth, moreover, are the elephants of the quarters.
In the sixth [region] is Garuḍa, in another the Gaṅgā, and elsewhere the all-pervading Vṛṣa;
but Dakṣa is firmly established in the ninth by the power of Brahmā.
In the tenth [region], on the path of the Maruts, are the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Maruts;
the body of the sun's orb is nine thousand yojanas in extent.
That power of knowledge, consisting of the three qualities, blazes as the sun by the Lord's will;
the Svarloka is defined as extending from the Bhuvarloka up to the pole star (Dhruva).
The moon is one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the sun; that is the power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva.
One hundred thousand from the moon is the stellar sphere, and from that, two hundred thousand [yojanas].
They know that from each starting point, beginning with Bhauma (Mars) and ending with Sūryasuta (Saturn), there is a group of five;
from Saturn, the group of the Seven Sages (is at a distance) of one hundred thousand [yojanas], and from that, Dhruva is likewise situated.
Brahmā himself, in another form, is the immovable Dhruva in the station of Brahmā;
having become a cloud, he stands as the fixed pole above all the celestial chariots.
"The Mothers" refers to Brahmyā and the others. "In the second" means on the path of Vāyu. "Beyond that" means in the third. "Eight" refers to the Nārāca and other weapons. As it has been said:
"And here, on the fourth path, dwell the deities of the weapons."

"Barbed arrows, bows, discuses, double-edged swords, spears, tridents, javelins, shafts, and mallets" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.468). Regarding the phrase "the elephants of the directions," these are Airāvata and the others. As it has been said:
"O Goddess of the gods, Airāvata and the others dwell on the fifth path."
Erāvata, Añjana, and Vāmana the great elephant.
Supratīka, Karīndra, and likewise Puṣpadanta;
Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and Sārvabhauma as the eighth.
"The world-elephants (diggajas), renowned by that name, are stationed in their respective directions" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.471).
"In another" refers to the seventh [chapter]; "elsewhere" refers to the eighth. There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas. As it has been said:
And here are Aṅgāraka, Sarpi, Nairṛta, Sadasatpati,
Budha, Dhūmaketu, and the one renowned as Jvara.
Aja, Bhuvaneśa, Mṛtyu, and likewise Kāpālika—
these are remembered as the eleven Rudras, who bring about the fulfillment of all desires.
[The other eight are] Dhātṛ, Dhruva, Soma, Varuṇa, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyūṣa and Pradoṣa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
These have indeed been declared as the Vasus; now learn from me the Ādityas:
Aryaman, Indra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, and Gabhastimat.
"Mitra is indeed proclaimed as the lowest of the non-lowest;
Vivasvat, Parjanya, and Dhātṛ—these are remembered as the twelve" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.499).
"Threefold" means twenty-seven thousand [verses]. "He heats" means he illuminates the universe.
— this is the meaning. For the very nature of knowledge is its luminosity—this is the intended sense.
As it has been said:
"This power of knowledge belonging to the Supreme shines forth, assuming the form of the sun."
Thus [it is said in Svacchandatantra 10.498]. Starting from the Bhuvarloka, the phrase "from the sun" means from that which is situated at the end of the Bhuvarloka.
Regarding "the power of action" (*kriyāśakti*), it is because she causes the nourishment of the universe. As it has been said:
"The power of action of Śiva indeed shines forth in the form of the moon. (Svacchandatantra 10.501)
Thus: "not the asterisms" refers to the *maṇḍala*. As it has been said:
"The constellation-maṇḍala is situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] above the moon" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.501).
"By two hundred thousand" means above; therefore, it is above the constellation-maṇḍala.

Bhauma is two hundred thousand [yojanas] from there; beyond that is Budha, and finally Saura at the end. "By a hundred thousand" refers to the upward direction. As it has been said: "Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu..."

"Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci are proclaimed as the seven sages" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.505). The word "tathā" means "above by a hundred thousand [yojanas]. The phrase "become a sacrificial post" (medhībhūtaḥ) means having attained the state of being a place of binding. Regarding the word "of the celestial chariots" (vimānānām):

[This refers to] those connected with the planets and so forth. As it has been said: "O Goddess, Brahman itself, having been appointed to the station of Dhruva in another form, its host of luminaries remains bound and revolves eternally."
"But he should be known as motionless when presided over by the power of Śiva. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.510). || 146 ||
Having raised the doubt, "Even though these are bound here, what is their support?", he says:
"All those that are bound here are understood to be within the circle of wind (anilamaṇḍala).
Having raised the doubt, "And how many circles of wind are there?", he says:
There are seven layers of Maruts, beginning with Āmegha, according to their primary nature. (8.147)

"Svariti" means in the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). Regarding the phrase "beginning with the clouds" (*āmeghādyā*): "āmeghāt" means from the clouds; those things of which that is the first are "beginning with the clouds.
As it has been said:
"From the clouds, from the sun, from the moon, from the stars, and from the circle of planets..."
"From the instruction on the Seven Sages, the seventh extends as far as the Pole Star" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.512).
Likewise:
"The first layer of the earth, extending up to the clouds, is Āvaha."
And the second is that which proceeds from the clouds up to the sun, known as Pravaha.
That which is known as Udvaha is situated above the Sun and likewise above the Moon;
and that which is the fourth, Saṃvaha, is situated above the Moon and likewise above the stars.
Likewise, from the stars upward to the planets (Graha), that wind is Vivaha;
and from the planets upward to the sages (Ṛṣi), that which is the sixth is Parāvaha.
Likewise, above the Seven Sages and up to Dhruva, the seventh is the Vātaskandha wind-layer known as Parivaha. (Purāṇa) || 147 ||
And who reside here? To this he says:

"Furthermore, those devoid of knowledge who perform sacrifices, oblations, and so forth, go to heaven; upon the exhaustion of that [merit], they return to the human world by virtue of the remainder of their merit. (8.148)
Summing this up, he introduces another point:
"Thus, from the earth to the Pole Star (Dhruva), there would be fifteen lakṣas;
from heaven to the Mahān [world], there are twenty-five crores and eighty lakṣas. (8.149)
The ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas, beginning with Mārkaṇḍa, were established there; and the gods, having relinquished their offices, remained stationed in that great place.
In that great intermediate space, there are other people who enjoy their respective offices;
from Mahalloka, eight crores [of yojanas] away is Janaloka, where Kapila and others reside.
Many Siddhas who partake in bliss reside right there;
here dwell tens of millions of Janas, Tapolkas, and the high-minded Sanaka and others.
There, the Prajāpatis, who are born from the self of Brahmā, hold authority;
the abode of Brahmā, which is the truth of austerity, extends for sixteen crores [of yojanas].
Abiding there, that Self-existent One manifests this universe;
likewise, the Vedas and other [scriptures] are manifested through meditation on ritual action.
Above that is the seat of Vairiñca, which is the limit of bliss;
two crores [of yojanas] above the seat of Brahmā, the city of Viṣṇu is described.
Through meditation, worship, and recitation, the devotees of Viṣṇu go to His abode;
from the Vaiṣṇava realm, along with seventy million [beings], they reach the world of the Supreme Lord.

On the path of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is the locus of Rudra’s activity of creation and destruction, the Bhuvarloka extends for one hundred thousand [yojanas]. Beyond that is Soma, and beyond that as well is the circle of the constellations—thus, three hundred thousand [yojanas]. Then, from Bhauma (Mars) up to Saura (Saturn), each planet occupies two hundred thousand [yojanas], totaling ten [hundred thousand].

From there, [the distance to] the Seven Sages is one hundred thousand [yojanas], and from there to Dhruva; thus, from the earth up to Dhruva, the distance is fifteen [hundred thousand yojanas]. The phrase "starting from heaven" (svargataḥ) means beginning from the world of Svarga.
"The gods" refers to those residing in their respective worlds, such as Saṅkrandana and others.
"But those inhabitants of the three worlds whose offices have ceased, such as Saṅkrandana and others— for them, Mahāloka is recorded as the place of dissolution.
It was precisely with this intention that [it was stated] previously:
"It is said: 'The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakas, and others sport in that which is called Mahat. As for the word 'others,' these are the performers of various sacrifices, such as Kapila and so forth.
Thus it has been stated.
"Ekapāda, Jahnu, Kapila, Āsuri, Bhautika, and Vāḍvali are the inhabitants of Janaloka. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.508). Likewise:
"The gods named Śādhyas dwell there, always happy.
This refers to twelve koṭis of Arka. "Of those born from the Self of Brahmā" means, by implication, those born from his mind (mānasa).
As it has been said:
"Śanaka, Sananda, Sanatkumāra, Sanandana, Śaṅku, and Triśaṅku are the inhabitants of the world of Tapas. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.520).
Thus it is said.
"The mind-born lords of creatures [arose] there from Brahmā...
Thus, "he manifests" means "he creates. "Others" refers to the Śikṣā, Kalpa, and so forth.
"The seat" (āsana) means the world (bhuvana), for it is that upon which one sits. As it has been said:
Perfected through the knowledge of action, firmly established in non-duality, they have attained the state of bliss;
they have reached the state of bliss.
"The Ṛgveda is embodied therein, possessing a luster like that of sapphire" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.525);
"To the north is the Yajurveda, resembling pure crystal" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.526).
Thus: "The eternal Sāmaveda stands in the western quarter. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.527).
"Then [the one] dark like collyrium stands to the south, likewise.
(Svacchanda Tantra 10.529). "The six limbs, the Itihāsas, and all the Purāṇas indeed..."
As well as the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, the Mīmāṃsā, and the Āraṇyakas.
"The utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, as well as the secret doctrines, and the *gāyatrī*— wherever these abide, there the four-faced God [Brahmā] is present. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.530)
"And: 'O Dear One, at a distance of ten million yojanas above Satyaloka, it is known as the Brahmāsana... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.533).
The phrase "that state" (tatpadam) refers to the station of Viṣṇu. "From the Vaiṣṇava [station]" means above that—this is the meaning.
To the question, "Who reside here? he says:
"Those who are devoid of initiation and knowledge, yet intent on the worship of the Liṅga. (8.157)
"Devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, they never go below to the fierce city within the Egg," according to the system found in the *Śivadharmottara* and other such texts. (157)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, do these remain right there, or do they proceed even further beyond that?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"All those Rudras who reside there and have been initiated by Śrīkaṇṭha go to Śiva. (8.158)
Upon the exhaustion of their office, together with the host of Rudra’s daughters,
they go to Śiva— the Supreme— meaning that they are liberated by attaining identity with Him.
"Now, does this world alone possess such majesty, or are there other worlds as well?
To this he says: "And above each Rudra-city, [there is another], increasing further and further. (8.159)
Regarding this, it is said:
"Below the Egg of Brahmā and above Rudra is the city of Daṇḍapāṇi;
by the will of Śiva, he pierces the Egg and creates the path to liberation. (8.160)
Sarva, Rudra, Bhīma, Bhava, Ugra, Deva, Mahānātha, and Īśāna—these are the seven auspicious lords of the worlds from the realm of Bhūrloka. (8.161)

"Brahmāṇḍa" means beneath its shell—this is the meaning. "'Dṛṇāti' (he pierces)" means he shatters it, making it free from obstructions—this is the meaning. "'The Great God'" refers to Mahādeva. Starting from the Bhūrloka, by him... [the rest of the sentence continues].
"From Śarva, the lord of the Bhūrloka, up to Īśāna, the lord of the Satyaloka"—this is the sequence.
It follows by implication that Paśupati is the lord of the Rudraloka. || 161 ||

And here, he states that there is also a hierarchy of higher and lower among the worlds: "The seven worlds are composed of gross particularities, while the others are composed of subtle ones"—thus the Guru has correctly described [this] in the Ruru[-tantra]. (8.162)

By "specifics" (*viśeṣa*) is meant the gross elements (*bhūta*); by "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is meant the non-specific *tanmātras*. Thus they say: "The *tanmātras* are the non-specific; from these five [arise] the five gross elements.
These are known as the specifics... (Sāṃkhyakārikā 38).
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", it is said: "Thus the Guru has correctly explained [this] in the Ruru[-tantra]. (162)

Regarding this, he says: "Those five gross specific elements (viśeṣa), known as the 'abundances' (prabhūta), which were fashioned from his own body by Brahmā at the beginning of creation—these seven worlds consist of them. (8.163)

By means of subtle gross elements born from the tanmātras, which serve as the substrata for their respective marks, and by means of the coverings of the worlds consisting of smell and the other qualities, they are supported by one another. (8.164)

"By those which possess the *liṅga* and have the body as their substratum"—this is the meaning. Therefore, [it means] by those which are the causes for the covering of the worlds. "'Supporting one another'—the meaning is: existing through mutual support by way of being both general and particular. (164)
He summarizes this very point: "From Kālāgni up to Daṇḍapāṇi, there are ninety-eight crores [of yojanas].
Above that, within the Egg, is the solid Kaṭāha, measuring one crore yojanas. (8.165)
Fifty koṭis above the surface of the earth and likewise below;
there, fifty koṭis are calculated from below up to the edge of the terrestrial shell (bhūkaṭāha),
while fifteen lakṣas from the surface of the earth up to the pole star (dhruva) constitute the "great" [height].

Two crores and eighty-five lakhs [make up the Egg]; the world of humans is eight [yojanas], Tapoloka is twelve, Satyaloka is sixteen, the world of Brahmā is one, that of Viṣṇu is two, that of Rudra is seven, and the shell is one—thus, there are fifty crores [of yojanas]. (165)
He summarizes this very point:
"In this way, a hundred million earths would constitute a single grain of gold. (8.166)
Up to the limit of the hundred Rudras, one should pierce that which is difficult to subdue with *huṃ phaṭ*.

It is called "rice-grain" (*taṇḍula*) because of its circular shape—this is the meaning. "Thence" means expanded; for this very reason, it is said to extend up to the limit of the hundred Rudras. Regarding "difficult to subdue":
The meaning is that because its essence is superior even to the essence of a diamond (*vajrasāra*), it cannot be pierced even by the gods. As it has been said:
"In this way, one hundred million [units] are to be known as the earthly element (*pārthiva-tattva*);
up to the limit of the hundred Rudras, the golden [element] is to be known as circular."

"O fair-faced one, one should pierce that which is harder than the essence of the Vajra and is impenetrable even by the thirty gods, by means of the application of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.621) || 166 ||
Anticipating the objection—"Where indeed do the hundred Rudras reside, such that even a limit for them is mentioned?"—he says:
"Ten in each direction; thus, there are one hundred Rudras outside. (8.167)
And that [egg] supports the entire universe on all sides by its own power;
as it has been said:
"In each of the ten directions, ten [units] in succession, all around."
I shall explain them in successive order, according to the sequence beginning with the east.
"Kapālīśa, Aja, Budhna, Vajradeha, Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa" (Svacchandatantra 10.623).
"Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana,
Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.625).
"He is Yāmya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and he who is designated as the Kartṛ; he is the uniter and the disuniter, as well as Dharma and Dharmapati. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.627).
"Nairṛta is the fierce destroyer, with a cruel gaze and terrifying;
he has hair standing erect, deformed eyes, smoky [complexion], and red fangs. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.629).
Bala, Atibala, the mighty Pāśahasta,
Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Janāntaka.
"Meghanādī and Sunādī... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.632).
[The powers] Śīghrā, Laghvī, Vāyuvegā, Sūkṣmā, Tīkṣṇā, and Bhayānakā;
"Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikhī, Karpadī, Meghavāhana" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.634).
"The Lord of Treasures, handsome, fortunate, with a gentle body, wearing matted locks."
"Lakṣmī, Ratnadhara, Kāmī, Prasāda, and Prabhāsaka" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.636).
"Then Vidyādhipa, Sarvajña, Jñānadṛk, and Vedapāraga."
"Śarva, Sureśa, Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla, Bali, and Priya. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.638).
"Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Akrodhana, and Mārutāśana."
"Grasana, Ḍambareśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭraka" (Svacchandatantra 10.640).
Also: "Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Tridaśeśvara."
"Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabhas, Lipsu, and Trilocana" (Svacchandatantra 10.642).
"Known as the Śatarudras, they remain pervading the cosmic egg" (Svacchandatantra 10.644).
Thus, "by his own power" means by the greatness of his own heroic energy—this is the meaning.
Raising the objection, "What indeed is meant by the term 'egg' (aṇḍa), even if it were related to Brahman?", he says:
"The nature of the egg has been described by the teachers in the venerable Raurava and other scriptures. (8.168)

He recites that very text: "That mass of reality which has become oriented toward manifestation, having fallen away from its state of pure potentiality (śakti), being subject to addition and subtraction, and undivided, is called the Egg (aṇḍa). (8.169)
When the upper *sattva* is permeated by a trace of *tamas*, it is a skull;
when the lower *tamas* is rubbed away and permeated by *rajas*, it is *sattva*. (8.170)
There, because the first verse is difficult [to understand], he explains it himself:
"The term 'mass of entities' (vastupiṇḍa) refers to that which possesses the collection of Śiva and Śakti;
it is said that the 'egg' (aṇḍa) exists, and its manifestation is called 'becoming manifest' (saṃmukhībhāva). (8.171)
Nevertheless, there may be a state of being "egg-like" (aṇḍatā) for those powers submerged in Śiva;
for that purpose, there is another statement, for they do not fall away from their power. (8.172)
To prevent the over-extension [of the definition] to the body, senses, and so forth, another term [“appropriation”] is employed;
for there is no appropriation whatsoever of anything in the case of the body, senses, and so on. (8.173)
To the question, "How can there be oneness in what is a collection of body and sense-faculties?
it is stated that [the cognition] is "undivided" (*anirbhakta*), which demonstrates its belonging to the same genus (*sājātya*). (8.174)
Indeed, the term *aṇḍa* refers to a "mass" (*piṇḍa*), that is, a collection of "entities" (*vastūnām*) such as bodies, senses, and so forth;
this is its defining characteristic—this is the meaning. For when it is stated thus: "His powers [are] this entire universe... regarding Śiva as well.
By such statements as these, since [the Egg] partakes of the collection of powers beginning with *tanu*, the consequence follows that it is a *tattva* (ontological principle).
Thus, its manifestation (*vyakti*)— its becoming present and its first appearance externally—
is what is expressed by the phrase "become oriented toward manifestation," and not something that occurred previously.

By this [definition], there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), for according to the principle that "this Self is manifested once and for all," it is manifest at all times. Even so, it would follow that the collection of powers (*śaktisamūha*) which possesses identity with the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) would constitute the Egg (*aṇḍa*). For of those powers...
The manifestation externally in the form of this or that object is merely occasional;
in order to exclude that [occasional nature], another statement is provided: "fallen from the state of power" (*śaktirūpataḥ*).
For he, precisely because he has turned toward manifestation, [is distinct] from the subtle form consisting of power.
"Fallen away" (*pracyutaḥ*) means manifested externally as an individual (*vyakti*) by way of its grossness—this is the sense.

However, even when the powers (*śakti*) are oriented toward manifestation, there is no falling away from their nature as power, for that would entail the consequence of the destruction of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Even so, let it not follow that the state of being an egg (*aṇḍatā*) applies to the body, senses, and so forth.

The word *bhū* is employed as a separate term [in the verse] in the form of "*āvāpavān*. That which possesses *āvāpa*—the insertion of other entities—is so described, because the fourteenfold class of beings is inserted (*āvāpanāt*) into their respective wombs (*yonisu*). However, this does not exist in the case of the *tanu*s and so forth, because they are dependent on others; such being the case, [the *tanu*s are not *āvāpavat*].

And because another substratum is untenable. Now, even so, since the body and other factors are not one, how could there be a designation of this [consciousness] as a unity by way of being a composite? To this it was said:
"undivided. Because its division is not perceived, it is simply the commonality (*sājātya*) that provides the life-force for its unity.
He demonstrates this so that, as in the case of the cognition of a city and so forth, its unity alone would be logical. || 174 ||

Now, one might object: "If this were so, then there would be a state of being a 'mandala' for each individual principle (tattva). To preclude this, the term "mass of reality" (vastupiṇḍa) is also employed; thus he says: "Even without the term 'mass of reality,' it would occur for each [principle] individually."
Even so, why is that [nature] not present in the principles (tattvas) which have the nature of the cosmic egg? (8.175)
That which consists of the flow of the qualities (guṇas), the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the gross elements (bhūtas) is emitted within the reality-level (tattva);
it is designated by the word "entity" (vastu), comprising the body, the senses, and the worlds.
Since "form" (rūpa) has been mentioned, the aggregate of those is called an "egg" (aṇḍa).

For by the word "entity" (vastu), the principles (tattva) are also denoted, just as the body and so forth are; thus, their collective mass is an egg—how could that be? If that were so, then for the earth-principle (pṛthvī-tattva) as well...

The state of being a single egg (aṇḍa) cannot be predicated [of the whole] alone; or, if it were so predicated, the same would apply to each individual part as well—thus, the employment of the term "mass of matter" (vastupiṇḍa) would be entirely redundant. This is true; however, the earth-principle (pṛthvītattva) is the ultimate limit of grossness, and therefore other principles are also situated within it.

They are perceived directly—thus it has been said that even though this [universe] is one, it possesses, as it were, a nature consisting of multiple principles (*tattva*). As they say: "The cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) consists of the five elements.
If this is so, then everything exists everywhere; thus, the earth-principle (*pṛthvī-tattva*) also exists within the other principles.
"Existence"—thus, that same fault remains as before. True; nevertheless, the point is this:

while earth and the other elements exist in a subtle form within the higher principles (*tattvas*), here they exist in a gross form. [One might object: "Even so, would it not still follow that there are multiple entities?"
Thus, by the word *vastu*, both the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, or the objects such as sound and so forth, are expressed.

[The author] shows the doubt: "In that case, would even the principle (*tattva*) such as *prakṛti*, which consists of those aggregates, possess the nature of an *aṇḍa*?"—this is indicated by the words beginning with "But if this were so... Here, the word *guṇa* refers to *prakṛti*. This is the point here.

The resolution is as follows: it is intended here that the word *vastu* denotes specifically the particularized form of *dharma*, such as the body (*tanu*) and so forth, and not in a general sense; thus, it is only that collection [of specific dharmas] which is called an *aṇḍa*, and not even the collection of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*. || 176 ||
And here, any possible objection has already been refuted—as he says:
"And that state of being an aggregate would belong to the Lord who bears the universe as his body. (8.177)

It has been shown that other differentiators have been employed for that purpose. Furthermore, the fact that the Lord possesses a universal form (*viśvavapuḥ*) is the reason for the existence of His being the aggregate of those [differentiators]. Regarding the term "differentiators" (*bhedakāni*), it means "distinguishers" (*vyāvartakāni*). || 177 ||
Others, however, have explained this differently; thus he says:
"In those very states, within the circle of the paths (adhvamaṇḍala) dependent upon Māyā... (8.178).
Others say that the application of the term *bhedaka* (differentiator) is intended so that it should not be understood as a mere egg (*aṇḍa*).

The phrase "in those consisting of just that much" refers to the body (*tanu*) and so forth. The second [interpretation], however, has not been explained by [the author] himself because it is easy to understand; thus it is now being explained: of that egg, which is permeated by a trace of darkness (*tamas*).
The upper skull, which is the subsequent one, is *sattva* permeated by *rajas*;

the meaning is that even when there is a permeation by other qualities (*guṇas*), it is devoid of the quality called *tattva*, and even when there is a commingling with *tamas*, it is primarily that [quality] alone. But the middle...
The meaning that *rajas* is predominant is established by implication. As they say:
"The creation is expansive in *sattva* at the top, expansive in *tamas* at the root, and expansive in *rajas* in the middle, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 55)
Thus [ends the section]. 178.
Having thus explained the nature of the egg through this context, he returns to the subject at hand:
"For those hundred Rudras who bear the egg of Viriñca have been described in this manner. (8.179)
Their husbands are the eleven Rudras of great radiance.
Regarding the phrase "eleven," it means one for each direction and one for all of them collectively. As it has been said:
"The White One indeed stands to the east of the Egg... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.646).
Thus:
"In the southeast [direction], the Vaidyuta [fire] is like fire... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.648).
"In the south of the Egg is Mahākāla... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.649).
"In the southwest is the one named Bikaṭa... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.650).
Thus:
"In the western egg, he who is Rudra is remembered as Mahāvīrya" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.651).
"In the northwestern direction, Vāyuvega [resides] within the Egg... (Sva.
To the north of the one named Śubhadra... (Sva. 10.653)."
Thus:
"The one named Vidyādhara is a Rudra in the northeast... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.654).
"Below is another Kālāgnirudra... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.656).
"Enveloped by these is Rudra... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.657).
Thus:
"Vīrabhadra, surrounded by the Rudras, is situated above the Egg;
he is the eleventh [leader] with great bodies... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.658).
And so it is said. Furthermore, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, there is this specific distinction: that therein, for each group of ten, one among them alone is the Lord (*pati*).
However, Vīrabhadra remains indistinguishable in both cases. (179)
Thus it says: "Then Ananta, Kapālī, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala. (8.180)
In Śīghra are Nidhīśa, Vidyeśa, and Śambhu along with Vīrabhadra.
The essence of Śrī Vīrabhadra consists in his sovereignty over all; as it is stated therein:
"Ananta is the first among them, and Kapālīśa is the next."
Agni, Rudra, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala as well.
"Śīghra, Nidhīśvara, and another, Sarvavidyādhipa; Śambhu and Vīrabhadra, possessing the brilliance of smokeless fire. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.14). || 180 ||
And how do these abide therein? To this he says:
"Just as bees cover the *kadamba* flower with honey and masses of filaments. (8.181)
In that same manner, Śiva, Rudra, and Brahmā possess innumerable retinues;
their arrangement consists of eighty million, ten million, and one hundred million [respective attendants]. (8.182)
"And presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, they create and destroy;
such is the lordship of the gods," according to the Rauravavārtika (8.183).
As it has been said:
"For these stand surrounding the cosmic egg, just as bees surround honey,
or just as a kadamba flower is encircled by its filaments."

Thus: "Śaras" means five; "niyuta" means ten lakṣas. Therefore, one koṭi, ten lakṣas, eighty-five thousand—that is the measure of each of those worlds. And what is the authority for this? It is said: "Thus in the Rauravavārtika."
As it is stated there:
"The extent of that settlement is proclaimed to be one hundred and eighty-five million yojanas."
Thus:
"Presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, those [gods] of great power bestow sovereignty upon the gods' hearts' desire and take it away."
And thus it is said. || 183 ||
And here, this much is the distinction from other [traditions]—as he says:
"But in the Siddhātantra, outside of the golden egg (hemāṇḍa) consisting of ten billion, there are one hundred eggs, each successively double in size, composed of silver and so forth. (8.184)
In those [periods], the Brahmās shall exist in succession with lifespans doubling [at each stage];
they perish in due order, and at their conclusion, the principle consisting of water [remains].
The word "hundred" is intended merely as an illustration of their number, for they are actually infinite.
As it has been said:
"Two separate [groups] are innumerable, and each of those two separate [groups] is likewise innumerable. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.50)

Thus: "twice-twofold" means two hundred crores, four hundred crores, and so forth. By the word "silver and so forth," the inclusion of copper and other metals is intended. The phrase "twice the lifespan" and so on is said in comparison with those who have not practiced celibacy (*abrahma*).
As it is stated there:
Above that, the cosmic egg named Kālānala stands at double the size,
extending as far as a full hundred such cosmic eggs of Brahmās.
O Goddess, honored by heroes, their increase is remembered as twofold;
and their lifespan shall be twice that of the first-born Lotus-Born One.
"Now I shall fully declare the names and domains of the eggs:
Kāñcana, that which is named Kāla, Vetāla, and Mahodara," and so forth.
"Know that the hundredth Gahvara stands above them all. Thus ends [the passage].
Likewise: "The first is declared to be Kāñcana, and the second is Raukma."
Copper and iron likewise; thus they are established in this sequence.
At the end of a great eon (mahākalpa), all beings including the gods and Pitāmaha perish;
indeed, within each hundred of hundreds of great eons, one intermediate eon (antarakalpa) is exhausted.
This continues until the remaining cavity of the great cosmic egg is exhausted;
at the time of the great dissolution, its destruction occurs through a universal dissolution.
Thus [ends verse 185].

Thus, there exists a measure for the other principles as well, through a progressive increase; so he says: "In this system, from earth onwards, water and the rest [increase] tenfold in successive order up to the ego (ahaṅkāra). From that [ego], the intellect (dhī) would be a hundredfold. (8.186)
From this, the manifest male principle is ten thousandfold;
destiny is a hundred-thousandfold from that, and its [result] is ten-millionfold.
From that, Kalānta is ten millionfold; from that, Māyā is one hundred millionfold;
Īśvara would be one billionfold; and from that, [Sadāśiva] is ten billionfold.
And she pervades that which is called Sādākhya by means of the multitude and number of her powers;
the Goddess, as Vyāpinī, remains having pervaded the entire path.
"Therefore, they know the supreme Śiva-tattva to be immeasurable and pure.

Regarding the phrase "successively higher": just as water is tenfold [in extent] compared to earth, and fire is greater than that, and so on until finally the ego (ahaṅkāra). "Of that" refers to the activity of ego (ahaṅkriyā). "Vid" means knowledge (vidyā).
The word *vyaśnute* means "he pervades. "Everything" refers to [the levels] from Śakti down to the Earth. As it has been said:
"Now, above [these], the principles (tattvas) beginning with Water and ending with Śiva are established in ten ways through successive conjunctions."
Above that is the ego (ahaṅkāra), and above that the intellect (buddhi) is situated in a hundredfold manner;
O lady of excellent complexion, the primordial matter (pradhāna) should be known as being a thousandfold above that.
Human effort is said to consist of ten thousand units, while destiny is recorded as one hundred thousand;
beyond that, O lady of excellent vows, it extends up to ten lakhs, which constitutes a single *kalā*.
Māyā, however, exists pervading all that is moving and unmoving in ten million ways; Vidyā, possessing ten times the qualities of Māyā, stands pervading Māyā.
This [level] is pervaded by Īśvara with a hundred-fold increase;
Sādākhya extends for a thousand crores, and above that are Bindu and Nāda.
Indeed, the Śakti remains pervading a multitude of yojanas;
the Goddess remains pervading the entire path as the all-pervasive one.
"Therefore, O fair-faced one, the Śiva-tattva is to be known as immeasurable. (Svacchandatantra 1.673) || 189 ||
And this has not been observed anywhere else; therefore, nothing beyond this is a cause of liberation.
Thus he says:
"From water up to the Śiva-principle, nothing has been seen by anyone as being other than Śiva. (8.190)

Apart from that, what is the authority for the statement that the supreme knowledge of Śiva is the cause of liberation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And so Mahādeva has said in the venerable Svacchandaśāsana. (8.191)
He recites that very point by way of its meaning:
"The bound soul does not attain liberation otherwise, even through hundreds of [other forms of] knowledge;
the knowledge of Śiva does not arise without having received the initiation of Śaṅkara. (8.192)
That [power] is both primordial and belonging to the Supreme Lord, and furthermore, it is human;
as it has been said: "And there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.6).

Thus [it is said]. "Prāktanī" means that, by the force of practice in various previous births, it has attained the state of being a non-means (anupāya). "Pārameśī" means that it is directly authored by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), like [the teachings of] the Vidyeśvaras and others. "Pauruṣeyī" means...
According to the sequence of the scripture, this was composed by the Teacher.
As it is stated there, beginning with: "That which has been seen by those with the knowledge of bound souls (*paśu*), whose vision is deluded by false paths... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.674).
"Without the grace of the Lord, this knowledge is not obtained;
nor does spiritual transformation occur for embodied beings without having received initiation."
But when, due to a specific cause, the power that brings about liberation arises,
one should, by the will of Śiva, attain the auspicious initiation consisting of knowledge.
Then, through the divine nature consisting of mantra-yoga, the bound soul (paśu) shall attain liberation;
otherwise, the bound soul does not attain liberation even by means of hundreds of [other] knowledges.
He to whom everything has been revealed by Śiva, who possesses infinite forms,
he alone attains liberation— he is Śiva himself, the Great Lord manifest.
"Therefore, this primary knowledge was previously taught by me to you. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.706). || 192 ||
Now he begins to describe the worlds within the sevenfold reality (aptattva): "Above the Śatarudra [world] is the blue-glowing Jayā belonging to Bhadrakālī. (8.193)
The victorious city of Kālī cannot be reached through sacrifice, charity, or austerity;
those who are devoted to her and are well-initiated into her maṇḍala go there.

"Nīla" refers to sapphire (*indranīla*). "Those who are well-initiated into its maṇḍala" means that, according to the statement beginning with "Therefore, [one should seek refuge] in the Lord of the World," they have attained that particular world—this is the meaning. || 194 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the use of attaining that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Supreme Goddess grants liberation through seedless initiation (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*).
Again, one might ask: "How can this be so by merely attaining this world-realm while remaining within the principle of water (*aptattva*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He performs initiation for men as far as the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa).
Established here in this world, they attain such a state;
for this divine Goddess, the Blessed One, exists through the names and forms of all goddesses.
Concealed by the power of yoga, she is a maiden who nurtures the world.
By the statement, "It is inconceivable and immeasurable... (Sva. 10.727), it is the most excellent, by which its greatness is thus described here. || 195 ||
Then Vīrabhadra, with a retinue of ten million, possessed a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
And his city, named Vijaya, belongs to those who, remembering Maheśvara, die in the waters, in the deserts, in fire, or by the severing of their heads.
They go to the awakening of Aiśāna, to Vīrabhadra of great luster;
above Vairabhadra, it extends threefold in width to ten million [yojanas].
The egg of Rudra is an egg consisting of water, situated in the form of a rainbow.

The phrase "in the Marus" refers to those who die while remembering Maheśvara on the Great Path (*mahāpatha*); this is the connection in all instances. Otherwise, they go to the realm of lightning, as was stated previously. [Regarding] "the Lord..."
"Bodha" is fierce energy (*raudraṃ tejaḥ*), for it has arisen from the wrath of Rudra—this is the intended meaning.
"'Above Vīrabhadra'" means above the city named Vijaya belonging to Vīrabhadra. "Śālilamaṇḍa" is the watery enclosure; the world is primarily composed of that.

Up to this point: for this very reason, that cosmic egg (aṇḍa) which stands above all the worlds belonging to the principle of attainment (āptattva) and below the principle of fire (tejastattva) is designated by the term "Rudra’s Egg" (rudrāṇḍa).
And here too, it is the Lord Mahātman himself who is known by the name Vīrabhadra.

The intention is that Rudra abides in a subtle form. And "that [measurement] is ten million [yojanas] from the support" means that this is the measurement above. "Extended threefold" means that its lateral measurement is three times ten million [yojanas]. And this is not with respect to all the *tattvas*.
This must be explained, because it has already been stated that the measure of that [water] is ten times greater than the earth.
As it is said:
"O Goddess of the Gods, above this world there is indeed a great enclosure."
And the mother-cloud, thick and standing in the form of Indra’s bow, appeared.
That auspicious [palace] stands like a canopy in the midst [of space],
and there resides that Great-Souled One, measuring only the size of a thumb's tip. Its width, extending upwards, is said to be indeed ten million *yojanas*.
"The watery enclosure, O Dear One, has an extent three times that [of the previous one] across. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.758).
"It is renowned as the Egg of Rudra, O Dear One, and as the World of Rudra. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.759).
And thus it is established: that at the very commencement of the [level of] Adhvatattva is the world of Bhadrakālī;
for this very reason, it is said there that [it is] "above the Śatarudras," whereas at the end, there are two cities of Vīrabhadra in their gross and subtle forms. || 198 ||
Raising the doubt, "Are other worlds situated within that [space] or not?", he says:
"Up to the world of Vīrabhadra, and likewise up to the abode of Bhadrakālī. (8.199)
It is adorned by thirteen other worlds.

The word *āṅ* is used here in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*); thus, starting from the abode of Bhadrakālī up to the world of Vīrabhadra—meaning, including the abode of Bhadrakālī—thirteen worlds are situated.

This is the meaning. Regarding the word "upashobhitam" (adorned), one should not be misled by the explanation of the author of the Uddyota that it implies the attainment of the state of being water (*aptattva*), nor that such a reading alone constitutes the scripture (*āgama*). || 199 ||
He states those very [results]: "Then, from the earth together with its mountains, by means of concentration on the subtle element of smell... (8.200).

The wise, having mastered the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra), go after death to that supreme region of the earth; from there, they reach the city of the waters through mastery of the subtle element of water.
Then, by dying specifically at Prayāga and other such sites, at Śrīgiri, or at the city of Śrī during the descents of Rudra’s sport, that [attainment] occurs.
From that [place] comes the city of Sarasvatī, the abode of those who know the Śabdabrahman;
those [goddesses] are suitable for Rudra due to their preeminence, while others remain situated apart from the Rudras.

In the pure [elements], Gaṅgā resides in many ways; Śrī in fire and other [elements]; Sarasvatī in water; and the eight lords of the gods, beginning with Lakula and ending with Amareśa, reside in the waters. (8.204)
“Of Śahādreḥ” means [of the mountain] joined with Meru and the other mountains previously mentioned—this is the meaning.

“From the concentration on the subtle element of taste” (rasatanmātradhāraṇāt) means by means of the concentration on the subtle element of taste. “The deceased go”—this is the connection with what precedes. [This occurs] during the descents of Rudra’s play, and not otherwise.
The intention is that through the desire to show favor, there would not be the attainment of merely this much [in that state].
This will become clear further ahead, so no effort has been made here. The word "that" refers to the city of Śrī;
its connection is with the preceding verb "they go. The phrase "of those who know the Śabdabrahman" refers to those who know song.
And for those established in the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the principle of speech (*vāktattva*),
it is said: "Hāhā, Hūhū, Citraratha, Tumburu, as well as Nārada,
Viśvāvasu, and Viśvaratha— these are experts in divine song."
Having united the self with the mind and abandoned desire for the fruits of action,
they indeed attained the station of Sarasvatī, O goddess worshipped by the gods.
"And those embodied beings who, having meditated on the retention of speech, release their vital breaths, they indeed—those best of men—attain the world of Sarasvatī. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.843).
By the word "in the waters," the object of knowledge known as the "junction of the principles" (*tattvayojanā*) is also indicated.

The same should be understood for what follows as well. By the word "eight," it is recalled that the previously introduced number is also to be added, so that with Bhadrakālī, Bhū, Abdhī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī, along with the pentad of worlds, there are thirteen. As it has been said:
Lakulī, Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi, Āṣāḍhi, Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, Prabhāsa, and Amareśa as the eighth.
"This is declared to be the group of eight *pīṭhas*... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.17).
Furthermore, in the venerable *Svacchandaśāstra*, [it says] regarding these: "Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara..."
Āṣāḍhi, Diṇḍimuṇḍa, Bhārabhūti, and Lākula.
"The one known as the Guhyāṣṭaka resides within the enclosure of water, O Dear One" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.854)—

such is another reading [found] in the beginning. Here, although the sequence follows the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra*, the intention behind their placement everywhere according to the methodology of the previous scriptures is as follows:
Since this very group of eight worlds (bhuvaneśāṣṭaka) is declared to be the most important among all the tattvas in all the scriptures, for this very reason,
in the context of the *Pratiṣṭhā* [tattva], the inclusion of all worlds everywhere occurs precisely through the acceptance of these seven groups of eight beginning with that [first one]. || 204 ||
Thereafter, the fiery principle (taijasa-tattva) is established here as the fire of Śiva;
and those who have resorted to the meditative concentration on fire (vāhnī-dhāraṇā) enter into this fire.
In the Taijasa [world], there is a group of eight leaders beginning with Bhairava and ending with Harīndu;
this is the world of Prāṇa, belonging to Vāyu, which is tenfold and again tenfold.
Having meditated, or having abandoned their life-breaths while maintaining concentration right there,
those great-souled ones enter [the supreme state], becoming like the wind and taking on the form of space.
The group of eight beginning with Bhīma and ending with Gaya resides in the element of air;
the world of space (vyoman) is to be attained within the element of ether through the meditative concentration on that ether.
The eight deities beginning with Sthāṇu and ending with Vastrāpada reside in the element of space (*vyomatattva*).
The word "then" (*tataḥ*) refers to the element of water (*aptattva*). As it has been said:
"Therein [reside] Bhairava, Kedāra, Mahākāla, along with Madhyama."
"...Āmratakeśvara, Jalpeśa, Śrīśaila, along with Harīndu. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 5.18).
