But in the Śrī-svacchanda [tantra] it says:
"Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpa, Āmratakeśvara..."
Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.

"It has been declared as extremely secret... (Sva. 10.873). Regarding the phrase "in Vāyu," this refers to the *tattva* of air (*vāyutattva*). It is said to be "tenfold" due to the divisions of *prāṇa* and so forth, up to *nāga*.
Since meditation and the other [limbs of yoga] are likewise [tenfold], it is again described as tenfold. Regarding "Bhīma and the others," it has been stated as follows:
"Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Aṭṭahāsa, along with Vimaleśvara; Kanakhala, Nākhala, Kurukṣetra, and likewise Gayā. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.19).
But in the Śrī Svacchanda [Tantra]—
Gaya, Kurukshetra, Nakhalam, and likewise Kanakhala;
Vimala, Atthahasa, Mahendra, and Bhima as the eighth.
"For this is indeed more secret than the secret... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.884).
Regarding the word "of the void" (*vyomnaḥ*), that refers to space. As it has been said:
"Sthāṇu and Svarṇākṣaka are the first two; Rudra and Gokarṇaka are the next two."
"...Mahālaya, Avimukteśa, Rudrakoṭi, and Ambarāpada. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.20).
However, in the Śrī Svacchanda Tantra it says:
"Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya..."
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as the eighth.
"This is the group of eight purifiers... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.887). || 208 ||
Indeed,

according to the reasoning stated in such passages as "But there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation" (Mālinīvijaya-tantra 4.6), there is no eligibility at all for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation.

What need is there to speak of liberation occurring while still alive through the practice of that [meditation], once initiation has been performed and the practice of yoga has been perfected? What doubt can there be regarding that [liberation] at the end of the body? Yogins who practice the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) and so forth [attain this].

Anticipating the objection—"How can it be said that they attain the worlds beginning with the Earth?"—he says: "Those who are uninitiated among the elements, yet possess the conceit of being the Śiva-principle... (8.209).

Even those devoid of knowledge, provided they possess mature *dhāraṇā*, may go outside the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*)—whether they have been initiated or not—into the cities of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. (8.210)
For the sake of union with those very saṃskāras, one should not seek the supreme state;
likewise for those who have died during such descents or in sacred shrines.
Having attained that state, they gradually reach the nature of Śiva.

Regarding the phrase "among the elements," the plural number is used because the earth element is predominant; or else, it refers to the practice of "mature concentration" (*prauḍhadhāraṇā*) from among those [elements], as found in the Pāśava-yoga of the Patañjali school and others.
Regarding those who have been initiated:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular [realm], he is appointed to that very place; such a person attains success..."

By the reasoning stated in such passages as "ityādi," the meaning is that they have received the *dīkṣā* (initiation) which establishes them as practitioners (*sādhaka*) for the sake of attaining the levels beginning with the Earth (*dharā*).

He states this in the verse beginning with "tāvatsaṃskāra... and so forth. "In such descents" refers to the sanctuaries of Amareśa and others situated upon the terrestrial sphere (*bhūmaṇḍala*). || 211 ||
"What is the authority for this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This has been stated again and again in the venerable *Devīyāmala*. (8.212)
"Again and again" means at every *aṣṭakā*. As it is stated there:
"Those beings who have died there go to that state in this world."
"O beloved, those who die even in these [places], having completely destroyed the worlds through their perfect practice, go blazing forth to these very stations. || 212 ||
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:
"The All-pervasive Lord spoke [this] in the *Śrīkāmikā* during the description of Kashmir.
He recites that very text:
And those who die in the great abode of Sureśvarī and in her city, [attain liberation]. || 8-213 ||
"From Brahmā down to the mixed castes, and including all beings down to the stationary, these are indeed the lineages of Rudra; thus spoke the Blessed Śiva. (8.214)

O Dear One, in the teaching of Śiva, the cities of those beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātras) and ending with the mind (manas) are situated above the covering of space (ākāśāvaraṇa) and below the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). (8.215)
"In the teaching of Śiva"—the word "stated" is to be understood as the ellipsis. As it has been said:
"O Dear One, above the covering of space and below the ego-principle, I shall proclaim the worlds... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.895).
Thus [ends the section]. || 215 ||
He states those very things: "The great mandala of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), endowed with five colors, stands covering many millions of yojanas in its interior. (8.216)
In this way, the mandalas of the subtle elements beginning with taste are [assigned] according to their respective colors;
[the lords are] Śarva, Bhava, Paśupati, Īśa, and Bhīma, in due order. (8.217)
If, by His will, the Lords of the subtle elements (tanmātreśas) produce sound and the other [objects] as well as ether and the other [gross elements],
then from that [arise] the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire— the Great All-pervading Lord.
Ugra, Cetya, and Eṣa—these are the lords; from them come Arka, Indu, and Sayājaka.
Thus, these eight forms of Śambhu are proclaimed as the supreme. (8.219)
Others, having pervaded the entire egg of Brahmā, remain established therein;
from them alone, the earth and the other elements are produced in every kalpa.
Then there is the circle of instruments (karaṇamaṇḍala) joined with the organs of action such as speech;
among these, Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Brahmā are the presiding deities.
From that [Ākāśa-tattva] arises the circle of light (prakāśamaṇḍala), from which the five sense organs of cognition are heard;
the quarters, lightning, the sun, Varuṇa, and the earth are the deities of the ear and the other senses.
Above the maṇḍala of light is situated the maṇḍala of the five objects;
this is the maṇḍala of the mind, because it is presided over by the Moon. (8.223)
The presiding deity over the external gods, whose nature consists of equanimity, sovereignty, and bliss, is therefore declared to be the divine, all-pervading Moon, the god of the mind. (8.224)
Regarding the phrase "endowed with five colors," it has been said:
"White, yellow, pale red, green, and the luster of crystal—
endowed with these five colors, its radiance is like that of Indra’s bow" (Svacchandatantra 10.897).
Thus: "having covered within" means having enclosed everything, such as space and so forth, like a canopy—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"In the beginning, however, there is the great, expansive mandala consisting of the subtle element of smell."
"It stands like a canopy, O Goddess, for many tens of millions of *yojanas*" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.896).
"For Śarva alone is the sovereign there, O fair-faced one."

"Therefore, the earth is born, impelled by Śarveśa" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.898). The phrase "by His will" implies that otherwise, how could these insentient [elements] possess causality—this is the intended meaning. The word "thus" means in the same manner as the sphere of the subtle element of smell—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
Above that maṇḍala, however, O beloved, is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra),
which is green, dark like an emerald, and resembles the wing of a blue jay.
For Bhava alone is the sovereign there, O fair-faced one;
therefore, the waters have issued forth, impelled by Bhava.
Above that mandala, however, is the mandala of the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra),
which has the radiant luster of shimmering sunbeams and a brilliance equal to a ruby.
"Rudra Paśupati alone remains there; from him, by the will of Paśupati, that splendor indeed issued forth. (Svacchandatantra 10.902)
Above that maṇḍala, however, is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra),
which has a luster equal to the dawn-red... (Svacchandatantra 10.904).
"In that very mandala, O Goddess, Īśāna is firmly established;
from him, O Beloved, Vāyu has issued forth, impelled by the will of Īśa" (Svacchandatantra 10.905).
"Therefore, above that maṇḍala is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra),
dark like the petal of a blue lotus and possessing a luster like clear water. (Svacchandatantra 10.907).
"Bhīma alone remains there as the sovereign;
therefore, the great [space] has emerged from the sky, impelled by the will of Bhīma" (Svacchandatantra 10.909).
The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) means having resorted to the respective mandala of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). And by that—

These three mandalas exist in the upper portion of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). "The Pervasive One" (vibhu) refers to Rudra; "The Great One" (mahān) refers to Mahādeva. "From them" means from the mandalas of the Sun and others, impelled by their respective presiding Rudras. As it has been said:
Above that is the realm known as Sūrya, where the all-pervading Rudra resides;
above that is the realm known as Soma, and Mahādeva is its lord.
Above that is the Vedamaṇḍala presided over by Ugreśa;
from these [elements], the Sun, the Moon, and the Sacrificer emerged.
"In every eon, indeed, they are innumerable...

and so forth. "Supreme" (*parā*) is said because the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the rest possess a subtle form. "From them" means from those supreme bodies. "Thereafter" means immediately after the subtle elements, the "circle of instruments" (*karaṇamaṇḍala*).

Thus, because its nature consists of activities such as the utterance of various sounds, the "maṇḍala"— meaning the collection— of the five principles is dominated by the instruments (karaṇa). And it has been stated that this is connected with the organs of action, such as speech, and not with the organs of perception.
"Endowed with the organs of action such as speech," etc.
As it has been said, beginning with: "And even beyond these is the mandala consisting of the instruments" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.919).
"The Karmadevas function because of that [power] in all embodied beings;
[namely] speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.921).
Regarding the phrase "in them," it refers to these five principles beginning with speech. Therefore, Fire is the presiding deity in the principle of speech.
Up to the level of *upastha-tattva* is Brahmā. As it has been said:
"The lords of the organs of action are Vahni, Indra, Hari, and Vedhas;
and Mitra... [and so forth].
Thus,
because it illuminates its respective objects such as sound and so forth above the circle of the organs of action,
the pentad of the sensory faculties of cognition (*buddhyakṣapañcaka*), which is the circle of principles (*tattvamaṇḍala*) dominated by illumination, is called "the heard" (*śruta*).
The meaning is that it is renowned as such in its true nature (*tattvena*). As it has been said:
"From those [elements] arises that which is called the Illuminator (*prakāśaka*), resembling the sun on all sides;
from that indeed proceed the five sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*)."
"The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, respectively. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.923).
Regarding "the ear and so forth," by this it is meant that the quarters are the presiding deities of the ear, up to the earth being the deity of the nose.
As it has been said:

"The nose and so forth, ending with the ear, as well as earth and the lord of waters (Varuṇa), the sun, lightning, and the directions— thus they are situated within the organs of cognition (buddhīndriya). Regarding the phrase "above the sphere of light," it refers to the principle of the mind (manastattva), wherein all five [organs] are likewise located.

It is appropriate that objects such as sound and the rest abide [within the self], since it is precisely by virtue of being their object that the mind impels those various sense organs. Thus, the intended meaning here is that this world exists for them in its supreme form. As it has been said:

"Beyond these there exists a circle of rays, resembling the lunar orb in its width and circumference on all sides; from that indeed proceed the five objects for all embodied beings. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.925)

Thus [it is said]. "The mandala of the mind" means that the mind is the primary world. "From this" means even above the mandala of light (*prakāśa*). And here, one might ask: what is the cause for Soma being the presiding deity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Since," and so forth. Since [he exists] with equality, without distinction...
Because it functions as the impeller of all the senses toward their respective objects, that which consists of the bliss of sovereignty— the wonder of absolute freedom (svātantrya)—
is the very nature of the mind; and since it takes the form of worldly activity consisting of various volitions, the mind itself is the "deity among the external deities."

The meaning is this: He is the presiding lord over the sense organs of cognition and the rest as they manifest in an external form; therefore, He is called the "Divine" (divya) Soma—the all-pervasive one who is beneficial to the heavens (dive hitaḥ) by nourishing all the gods. || 224 ||

Beyond that is the city of the ego (ahaṅkṛti), which is the source of all the senses and the birthplace of the sensory intellect (buddhyakṣa), and which is joined by the eight [beings] beginning with Sthūla and ending with Chagala.
Beyond that is the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), the sovereign of the eight cities of the divine classes of beings;
it is proclaimed to extend from the Piśācas up to the Brahmās.
These are indeed the abodes of the divine origins according to the Purāṇas;
descending [to earth], they come into being while meditating upon their own births.

It has been stated: "even after that," meaning immediately following the mind; and "of the ego-maker," meaning of the ego (ahaṅkāra). Now, one might ask: why is this [intellect] situated above the mind and below the intellect?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
"From the womb of those with spotted eyes (*śakalākṣa*), there is the birth of the sense-organ of intellect (*buddhyakṣa*).
Regarding "Sthūla," it refers to Sthūleśvara; regarding "Chagala," it refers to Chagalāṇḍa. As it has been said:
"Sthūla and Sthaleśvara, as well as Śaṅkukarṇa and Kālañjara."
"Mākoṭa, Duraṇḍa, Chagalāṇḍaka, and Maṇḍaleśvara" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.21).
And in the Śrī Svacchanda Tantra:
"Chagalāṇḍa, Duraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara."
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara;
"The eight Sthāṇus are thus proclaimed... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.889).

"Where the Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśvara), the 'Overlord of the City,' [resides] along with the eight divine origins—that is where it is. "That" refers to the eight divine origins. As it has been said:
"The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājāpatya, and the Brahma is said to be the eighth" (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 5.23).
These very cities, such as Kakubha and others, which reside within the intellect, belong to these divine origins.

The meaning is: "principal stations" (sthānāni) refers to the primary abodes of their existence. The sense is that for these [energies], which exist below in the form of the pentad, the octad, and so forth, the worlds (bhuvanāni) are secondary. The word "having descended" (avatīrya) implies [descending] below, into the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and so on; thus they "originate" (śambhavanti).
The meaning is that they undergo creation again and again. || 227 ||
Regarding this very point, he states the cause: "Impelled by the command of the Supreme Lord, driven by Māyā, and constrained by Niyati, [they belong] to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest. (8.228)
"By that [means], at the beginning of creation, they are manifested in manifold ways through names and forms.

At the beginning of Brahmā’s creation, "they are manifested"—the meaning is that they become manifest in such and such a way through gross form. "In manifold ways" means due to distinctions such as gradations and so forth. || 228 ||
And even so, there is no falling away for them from these worlds established in their consciousness; thus he says:
"The great-souled ones do not abandon their own abode by means of their very own portion. (8.229)
And this has been explained by the venerable Bṛhaspati himself in his own work; thus he says:
"And this was stated in the *Śivatanu* by our Guru, who occupies the station of authority:
'For these [eight] are the sources for the manifestation of the powers of the eight deities. (8.230)

The meaning is: the "manifestation" (*āvirbhāva*) of even the gods, such as the *piśācas* and others, refers to their becoming manifest; by that [manifestation], there are various "sources" (*yoni*) consisting of the manifestation of powers.
In that regard, within the intellect (*buddhi*)...
Their existence below [in the lower levels] is by way of their nature as powers (śakti), whereas above it is by way of their nature as individual manifestations (vyakti). || 8-230 ||
Regarding this, it is said:
"Furthermore, their bodies and enjoyments are declared below to be of a gross nature. "Of a gross nature" means having a coarse form.
He demonstrates that very point:
"There are forty worlds, each with an additional region for equal enjoyment. (8.231)
"Forty," because of the divisions beginning with Lakulya. || 231 ||

Now, one might object: "If these [categories] possess an equal nature of enjoyment and so forth, how can there be a distinction between them as the eightfold group of the Guhyas and the fivefold group? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"They are described as eightfold and fivefold solely on account of the difference in their means (*sādhana*)."
He states the very distinction between the means of accomplishment:
"These are to be reached through the yoga of devotion, the renunciation of life, and so forth. (8.232)
Among them, Umāpati alone is the Lord, possessing independent senses and a nature free from bodily organs;
beyond him, by a process of gradual progression, the eightfold class of divine beings (devayoni) becomes the object of perception.
Regarding the loss of life in this field and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including worldly duties, the initiation of a practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the like—one might ask:
does the manifestation of these things occur by itself, or through the presiding influence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of someone else?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In them," and so forth, referring to the *piśācas* and others; [this occurs] precisely because their senses are independent.

The term *vikaraṇātmā* means one whose sensory functions (*indriyavṛtti*) are dependent upon his own will. As it is stated in that very same [text]: "Furthermore, those [faculties] which are dependent on will are designated as *vikaraṇas*.
Now, do these abide everywhere without distinction, or not?

Anticipating this objection, he says: “*taratama-* etc. The word “*tataḥ*” refers to the intellect (*buddhi*). The particle *api* is displaced in the sequence; therefore, it should be construed with “*aṣṭāv api*” (even all eight). || 233 ||
Not only do these [powers] possess degrees of intensity, but even the sense organs do so—as he says:
"The sense organs of beings are the instruments for the determination of objects.
For the intention is that Piśācas and others can see even what is obstructed by means of their eyes.
Not only is there a relative gradation among these [powers] according to each respective principle (*tattva*), but there is also one among them—thus he says:
"The sovereignty produced from the [set of principles] beginning with smell and ending with the Great Principle (*mahat*) arises by an increase of one [attribute] at a time. (8.234)
In this [system], beginning with the Piśāca and ending with Viriñca, there is the nature of the powers such as *aṇimā* (atomicity).
Here, the word "scent" (*gandha*) is a designation for the earth, due to the metaphorical identification of cause and effect.
Regarding the phrase "by an increase of one," it means that whatever sovereignty exists in the Piśāca state, it is doubled from that point on.
O Rākṣasa, [the power] of Brahmā is eightfold—this is the meaning. || 234 ||
For this very reason, one must strive for this purification during initiation; thus he says:
"Having known this, one should purify the intellect together with the senses and the *puryaṣṭaka*. (8.235)
Thus, this entire universe is but the unfolding of consciousness alone; for this very reason it is said, "together with the puryaṣṭaka and the senses. || 235 ||
Not only is there the eightfold group of divine origins here, but there is also another; thus he says:

"Then they know the dark-blue group of the eight Krodheśas, beginning with Saṃvarta; and from the group of the eight Krodhanas, beginning with Balādhyakṣa, [arises] the group of the eight Tejas. (8.236)
Therefore, the eightfold yoga beginning with the "uncreated" (akṛta) is taught in the *Svacchandaśāsana*,
while that same [eightfold yoga] is taught in its root form in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana* (Mālinīvijayottara).
In the station of the Eight Yogas (Yogāṣṭaka), there is Soma and Śrīkaṇṭha; beyond that, Māyāpura is further said to belong to Śrīkaṇṭha.
Therefore, a second world for each of those two is mentioned;
therein is Māyāpura, belonging to the Goddess by whom the universe is presided over. (8.239)
In every kalpa, that Great Goddess is spoken of under different names;
thereafter, the city of the Lord of Umā was surrounded by the Mothers.
Śrīkaṇṭha himself is called the Lord of Umā (Umāpati) in his supreme form.
"Ānīla" means having the luster of a blue lotus. As it has been said:
"Śaṃvarta, Ekavīra, Kṛtānta, and Jananāśana."
The remover of death, red-eyed, greatly wrathful, and invincible.
"Their worlds indeed have the luster of the petals of the blue lotus" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.976).
Regarding the phrase "from the group of eight Krodhas," the meaning is "above that. As it has been said:
"Above the group of eight Krodheśvaras resides the great group of eight Tejas [deities]."
The commander of the forces, the leader of the hosts, the thirty-fold one, the destroyer of Tripura.
"He is all forms, he is tranquil, and he is indeed the closing and opening of the eyes" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.978).
Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*): it means immediately after the group of eight [deities of] fire. As it has been said:
"The uncreated and the created, the sovereign power (*vaibhava*) and Brahman itself..."
"The Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Auma, and the Śraikaṇṭha as well" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.981).
The word *tu* (but/however) indicates a distinction; "root" (*mūla*) refers to the primordial source (*prakṛti*). As it is stated there:
"The eightfold yoga and the Pradhāna... and so forth.
Thus [it is said]. It was stated in another form as "in the state of the eightfold yoga," and in yet another form as "furthermore.

"Of those two" refers to Umāpati and Śrīkaṇṭha; "therein" serves to distinguish between the two. "The city" means, by implication, the second one. In this way, the cause for the support of the universe is declared by the Great Goddess.
Thus it has been said:
"Thereafter, the Blessed Mother of the world herself became manifest; you are Umā, the immeasurable, the womb of the universe, and self-born. (Svacchandatantra 10.983)
And so forth:
"In the first kalpa she was Jaganmātā; in the second, Jagadyoni; in the third, she was named Śāmbhavī; and in the fourth, Viśvarūpiṇī" (Svacchandatantra 10.992).
And so forth. In the middle [of the text]:
“Known by various synonymous names such as Kātyāyanī and Durgā, she is the bestower of boons upon devoted humans and is affectionate toward her devotees.”

"You have already descended upon the summit of the Vindhya mountain," ending at (Sva 10.1003). The word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) refers to the period following the Umā-pura. Now, one might object: since [the text] begins with Śrīkaṇṭha's statement, "The city is described again," how can it be said that [this belongs to] the Lord of Umā? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Śrīkaṇṭha alone," and so forth. || 240 ||
Anticipating the question, "Who are these Mothers?", he says:

"The one belonging to Brahmā, the one belonging to Īśa, the one born of Skanda, the one belonging to Hari, the one belonging to Varāha, the one belonging to Indra, and the one together with Vicikā (Carcikā). (8.241)
Yellow, white, yellow-blue, blue, and white-red are their colors, respectively; they are situated in the southeast, northeast, north, south, west, east, and southwest. (8.242)
"In part, they were indeed brought down by the Creator into the world of men.
As it is said: "The Brahmi [deity], with the luster of a lotus petal, adorned with divine ornaments, in the southeastern direction... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1017).
Thus:
"O fair-faced one, Māheśvarī, resembling a conch shell or cow’s milk, [is located] in the northeast... (Svacchandatantra 10.1018).
Thus:
"Kaumārī, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, adorned with necklaces and armlets, [resides] in the northern direction... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1019).
Thus:
Resembling a glossy blue lotus, adorned with necklaces and earrings,
she dwells in the southern direction, worshipping the Supreme Lord.
"And she is renowned as Vaiṣṇavī... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1020).
"Resembling a dark blue cloud, adorned with all ornaments..."
"In the western direction is Vārāhī... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1021).
"White as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, adorned with necklaces and earrings,"
"In the eastern direction, however, is Aindrāṇī... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1022).
She has a formidable face, is radiant, and is adorned with all ornaments.
And [it is said]: "In the south-western direction is Cāmuṇḍā... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1023).
And [the phrase] "by a portion" means not by her entire totality. As it has been said:
"For they do not abandon the Lord who is endowed with all states of being."
They were brought down by Brahmā to the world of men with a portion [of their essence].
"For the sake of slaying the Asuras and for the benefit of human beings. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1025) || 242 ||
And their pervasion does not end with just this much; thus he says:
"They are independent, and those others are supreme, established in the highest ether. (8.243)
Since Umā dwells there in seven ways, they serve her according to their own will.
"In the supreme ether" refers to the abode of Unmanā. "Umā" is the supreme, transcendent power of the Lord, non-different from Paraśiva. As it has been said:
The Svacchandā and other supreme goddesses are established in the supreme ether;
they attend upon the Svacchanda according to the distinction between the supreme and the non-supreme.
"Umā indeed, having become sevenfold through the transformations of name and form... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1027). || 243 ||
Above the city of Umāpati stands the supreme group of eight forms.
That form of Īśāna from whom proceeds the creation beginning with Śarva and ending with the sacrificer, starting from the earth and so forth— that form is established upon Mount Meru.
Śrīkaṇṭha is on the Crystal Mountain; he pervades the world with his eight bodies for those self-controlled ones who practice the qualified yoga of Śambhu.
Or, merely by seeing that maṇḍala, they are liberated from duality and have the three [impurities] removed.

Regarding the phrase "the eight forms," it refers to the supreme [deity] who presides over them, since the lower and the intermediate [forms] have already been mentioned previously. The word "of whom" (yasya) refers to Śarva and the others who preside over the eight forms.

Regarding the phrase "from them," it means from among the eight forms (*mūrti*); "possessing the three qualities" (*saguṇam*) refers to that which has the functions of *sattva* and so forth as its primary nature, but is not of the supreme non-dual form (*parādvayarūpa*). "That maṇḍala" refers to what was taught by Śrī Śrīkaṇṭha and others. "Those for whom duality is abandoned" (*muktadvaitāḥ*) refers to those who follow the sequence beginning with Sāṃkhya.
Those who have attained absolute liberation. || 246 ||

Now, one might object: "If indeed the capacity of yoga extends only this far, how then is its attainment of even the lower and lower levels of reality (tattva) mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of the higher and lower status of the qualities (guṇas), and because of their established state as pure or impure. (8.247)
And due to the gradations of yoga, there is a diversity of fruits;
therefore, this distinction is said to arise from the difference in the attainment of the fruit of enjoyment. (8.248)

"Due to being higher and lower" means due to the relationship of subordinate and principal. "Purity" is due to being seedless (*nirbīja*); "impurity" is due to being seeded (*sabīja*). "Due to gradation" means due to having the forms of weak, medium, and intense.
"The variety of fruits" refers to the attainment of those respective principles (*tattva*), by which this distinction exists.
One [type of] yoga serves as the cause for attaining higher and higher levels among the principles (tattvas), while another serves as the cause for attaining lower and lower levels. || 248 ||
Above the eight forms (mūrti), twelve Suśivas are proclaimed;
they begin with Vāma and end with Ekaśiva, possessing the luster of saffron and great splendor.
Above that resides the lord of the maṇḍala named Vīrabhadra;
having attained union with him, one rejoices together with him. (8.250)
Beyond that, there shall be the eight Mahādevas, ending with Aṅguṣṭhamātra;
they are of pure luster, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. As it has been said:
"Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Śiva, and likewise Śarva..."
He is the sovereign of the sciences, the sole hero, and the possessor of fierce power.
Riśāna, the husband of Umā, Aja, Īśa, and Ananta,
as well as Ekaśiva and Suśiva— these are remembered as the twelve [Śivas].
"All [the deities] resemble saffron in color and possess a radiance equal to ten million suns" (Svacchandatantra 10.1038).
Regarding the phrase "above that," the word "that" refers to Suśiva. The word "then" means immediately following even the mandala of Vīrabhadra. As it has been said:
Mahādeva, Mahātejas, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Udbhava,
Ekapiṅga, Ekeṣaṇa, Īśāna, and Bhuwaneśa as their leader.
"The eight Mahādevas, beginning with Īśiva, are accompanied by [the goddess] Aṅguṣṭhamātrā. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1042).
He summarizes this very point:
"This is declared to be the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), beginning with the eightfold divine wombs. (8.251)
At the end of the eight [deities] of Mahādeva, those eight yogas are here proclaimed;
therein, that which is called Śraikaṇṭha has Umāpati as its presiding lord.
The forms are Suśiva and Vīra; the body is the group of eight Mahādevas.

And within such a principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), among the eight yogas, that which is called the eighth world, Śrīkaṇṭha, and its presiding lord who is called the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭha—[these are described].
It has been stated that "this entire manifestation begins from that very Lord Umāpati"—namely, "of him alone," and so forth. "Vīra" refers to Vīrabhadra. As it is said:
"Without presiding over Śarveśvara, Śrīkaṇṭha [acts] by the will of the Cause."
"He alone dwells in every household in many forms.
Above the intellect (buddhi) and below primordial nature (prakṛti) is that which is designated as the qualities (guṇas).
In that [state], however, the *guṇas* being agitated produce the intellect (*buddhi*).
The meaning is: the principle designated as *guṇa*, namely the *guṇatattva*. Now, one might object:
given the statement "from *prakṛti* arises the Great One" (*Sāṃkhyakārikā* 22), [the intellect] follows immediately after *prakṛti*.

Anticipating the objection—"The principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) is described by others as being the effect of that [primordial matter]; why then is the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) mentioned here in between?"—he says, "In that regard, however," and so forth. The word "however" (*tu*) indicates a reason.
"[Become agitated]" (*saṃkṣubdhāḥ*) means having fallen into a state of imbalance through their mutual relationship of subordinate and principal.
The meaning is: "ready to produce their effects. For they abide in a state of non-distinction within primordial nature (*prakṛti*). As they say:
"Primordial nature is the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*" (Sāṅkhya Sūtra 1.61).
Thus.

Furthermore, a cause that has not undergone a transformation of its state cannot produce an effect; for a seed, having reached a state of swelling through contact with water and other factors, produces a sprout and so forth, but not otherwise.
For if it were otherwise, that [sprout] would be produced even from the root. Thus he says:
A cause that has not undergone transformation into a state of imbalance is not capable of producing an effect.
For this very reason, how could primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which has not undergone any state of imbalance, be the cause for the arising of cognition?
To this he says:
"Therefore, primordial nature, consisting of the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇas*), would be the cause."

The word "by that" refers to the state of falling into disequilibrium. Therefore, one must necessarily admit the existence of the *guṇatattva*—which is the effect of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and consists of its agitation—by means of which the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*) occurs.
Now, if this is so, does the *guṇatattva* (the principle of the qualities) also produce [its effects] without agitation (*kṣobha*), or not?

Regarding that, in the first case, let the *buddhitattva* (the principle of intellect) itself produce it in that manner; what is the use of an intermediate, postulated *guṇatattva*? Or, if there is agitation, then does that [principle] also depend on another agitation?

Whether [the disturbance] exists or not? In that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), by which neither the birth of the *guṇas* nor that of the intellect (*buddhi*) could be established.

Thus he says: "But in this way, how could she [the Intellect] produce those uneven *guṇas* without a disturbance? In that regard, if there were a first disturbance, there would be an infinite regress."

Now, one might object: "Surely this fault would apply to the Sāṃkhya, but not to us; for indeed, an insentient cause is not capable of producing an effect without being stirred, as is observed in the world in cases such as the seed and the sprout. To this, he says:

"This is indeed a fault for the Sāṃkhya..."—the word "eva" (indeed) is displaced [in the compound]. Thus, it means "for the Sāṃkhya alone. Alternatively, this is not a fault even for him, because he maintains that those *guṇas* are inherently agitated (*svata eva kṣubdhāḥ*), which is accepted as the nature of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); otherwise, how [could this be]?
The production of its effect would [then] occur; for this very reason, it is said to be "of the nature of procreation" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 11).
Thus it is said:
"Or else, by that [means], those qualities [are attained]. (8.256)

If this is so, how can the statement, "The unmanifest is indeed desired; therefore, its state of equilibrium among sattva, rajas, and tamas is *prakṛti*," be consistent? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Equilibrium, however, is merely their conjunction and nothing else. Here, equilibrium refers simply to the state of the qualities being conjoined.
Even in the state of agitation, what is intended is merely their being gathered together through mutual rivalry, and not anything else;

for [in that case] there is a state of abiding without distinction due to the absence of agitation. If it were otherwise, there would be a sublation consisting of an opening for the aforementioned defects.
Thinking, "Is no fault stated there against the Sāṃkhyas, but rather only against those who maintain the reality of the *guṇas*? he says:
"But for us, however, [the world] is joined with the agitation of the will of the independent Lord. (8.257)

The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the cause of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), wherein the *guṇas* are agitated. Here, it has been stated that an insentient cause, as long as it has not attained a state of agitation, is simply incapable of producing an effect; nor, even upon reaching a state of agitation, does this cause require another agitation.

Because things exist in that way due to the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), and without that [will] there could not even be the relation of cause and effect— as will be explained later— no effort has been made here [to elaborate]. And therefore, in our system, [this is established] by the independent Lord who presides over the principle of *prakṛti*.
This desire is indeed independent; by it, the unmanifest (avyakta) is agitated, and the qualities (guṇas) are stirred.

Having attained the nature of the reality-principle of the qualities (guṇātmatattva), it becomes the "cause" of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva)—meaning it is capable of producing it. || 257 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then let the unmanifest (avyakta), being agitated by the will of the Lord, produce the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) directly; what is the use of postulating an intermediate principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), which only causes unnecessary complexity in understanding?
To this, he says:
But surely, was there not previously a disturbance of Prakṛti due to the will of the Lord of Tattvas? (8.258)
That alone would be the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*); what is the use of other imagined qualities?
He refutes this very point: "This [intellect] does not obstruct the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that constitutes the nature of causality. (8.259)

Thereafter, another agitation (kṣobha) must be produced, like the swelling and sprouting of a seed. For that indeed is called a cause which, even when undergoing agitation, maintains its own essential nature; for even a swollen seed is still called a "seed," and thus its state of agitation is likewise [the seed].

The *guṇatattva* is capable of encompassing the reflective awareness of causality (*kāraṇatvaparāmarśa*), because even in that state, there is no departure from its essential unity with *prakṛti*. Therefore, what is called the *guṇatattva* is not a separate principle distinct from the *prakṛtitattva*, but rather that very same [principle] when it is oriented toward the production of effects.
"Agitated [kṣubdha] is a different state. For if that were a separate principle (tattva), there would be thirty-seven principles.
As it is said: "O Pārvatī, the thirty-six principal principles are to be purified in this manner."
"From Earth up to Śiva... [otherwise] such statements as these would be contradicted:
'Brahmā remains pervading the twenty-four principles.'"
"...ending with Pradhāna... (Sva. 11.46).
Likewise: "...the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth."

Otherwise, even such [scriptural statements] would be contradicted, for in that case the Pradhāna would be the twenty-fifth and the Puruṣa the twenty-sixth. Therefore, just as Māyā has a twofold nature by way of being the principle of the knot (granthi-tattva), so too Prakṛti has a twofold nature by way of being both agitated and unagitated.

This must be understood so that everything may be consistent: the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), however, because of its predominance over all [other principles], is entirely distinct from them—just as a sprout is distinct from its seed; thus, it is only an effect and not a cause. Therefore, there must necessarily be a cause for the intellect situated between [the Self and the intellect].

The reality of the *guṇas* must be accepted. Thus, it has been demonstrated that there is no room for fault even for the Sāṃkhya who asserts: "Is not *prakṛti* simply the *guṇas* themselves when they are inherently agitated? For if that were the case, the unagitated form of the *guṇas* would have to be stated first; otherwise, [the system would be untenable].
In relation to what would there be agitation? For this very reason, only three stages are shown here by the phrase "like the swelling of the seed, the sprout, and so forth. || 259 ||
Having thus established the principle of qualities (guṇatattva), he now shows the collection of worlds situated within it:
"In sequence, within darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva), there stand the rows of gurus. (8.260)
By the power of their own knowledge and yoga, the supreme teachers sport, [manifesting] thirty-two, thirty-one, and even twenty-one [forms]. (8.261)
Three-eyed and liberated from the noose, they bestow grace here. "In *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*" is a collective compound (*samāhāra*). As it has been said:
"The first row of *tamas* is situated above."
Their names are now being told correctly and in due order.
Śiva, the Lord Vāmadeva, the powerful Caṇḍa,
as well as Prahlāda, Uttama, Bhīma, Karāla, and Piṅgala.
Mahendra, Dinakṛt, Pratoda, Daśa,
the famous Kaḍevara, and likewise Kaṭaṅkaṭa.
Ambuhartā, Nārīśa, Śveta, and the Ṛgveda;
the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and likewise Atharvā Suśiva.
Virūpākṣa, as well as Jyeṣṭha, the Brahmin Nārāyaṇa,
Gaṇḍodara, Yama, Mālī, Gahaneśa, and Pīḍana.
The first row is declared to be surrounded by thirty-two Rudras;
above the Rajas, however, the second row is described.
Śukla, Dāsa, Sudāsa, Lokākṣa, Sūrya,
Suhotra, Ekapāda, Gṛdhra, and Śiveśvara.
Gautama, the Lord of Yogins, and likewise Dadhibāhu;
Ṛṣabha, Gokarṇa, Deva, and Guheśvara.
Guheśāna, Śikhaṇḍin, Jaṭin, Mālin, as well as Ugraka; Bhṛgu, Śikhin, Śūlin, Sugati, and Supālana.
Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, Lāṅguli, Tridaṇḍaka, Bhāvana, as well as Bhāvya, and the supreme Lakuleśa.
The thirty Rudras are proclaimed as the second, most excellent row;
and above that of Sattva, the third row is described.
Devāruṇa, Dīrghabāhu, Ari, Bhūti, Sthāṇuka, Sadyojāta, Śaṇṭhī, Ṣaṇmukha, and Caturānana.
Cakrapāṇi, Kūrmākṣa, Ardhanārīśa, Saṃvartaka, Bhasmīśa, and Kāmanāśana;
Kapālī, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and likewise Vaṣaṭkāra;
Vauṣaṭkāra, Svāhā, and Sudhā are thus proclaimed.
"The twenty-one Rudras constitute this third row" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1058). || 261 ||
He enumerates the worlds up to this point:
from the intellect down to the qualities, both [categories] amount to one hundred and seven. (8.262)

"Of the Rudras and the worlds, others [exist] primarily within them. Regarding "of the intellect," this refers to that which takes the form of the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*). Therefore, from the earth-principle (*pṛthvītattva*) up to the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*), there are primarily [these]; otherwise, because the number of worlds would be infinite.
There would be two hundred and seven [worlds]. For instance, below the earth there is one world of Ananta; within [the earth], six for Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
outside, one hundred for the Śatarudras; and one for Vīrabhadra, their presiding lord.

Thus, there are one hundred and eight [deities]. In the water element (*aptattva*), there are nine worlds: the water element itself, its presiding deity Vīrabhadra, and the eight secret ones (*guhyāṣṭaka*). In the fire element (*tejastattva*), there are nine: the fire of Śiva (*śivāgni*) and the eight exceedingly secret ones (*atiguhyāṣṭaka*). In the space element (*ākāśatattva*), there is space itself.
And for the eight *pavitra*s, there are nine [deities]. Among the *tanmātra*s, there are eight for the *mūrti*s;

five for the lords of the organs of action (*karmendriya*); five for the lords of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*); one for Soma in the mind (*manas*); and nine for the Lord of Ego (*ahaṅkāreśa*) in the ego, including the eight *sthāṇu*s; and [one] in the intellect (*buddhi*).
There are four groups of eight known as Devayoni, Krodha, Tejas, and Yoga; thus, there are thirty-two [categories], and in the Guṇatattva, there is a triad of rows. || 262 ||
Furthermore, there is this distinction; thus he says:
"The eightfold yoga is taught in the *Guṇaskandha*, but in the *Śivatanu* [it is] again... (8.263).
"In the aggregate of qualities" means in the principle of quality (guṇatattva). || 263 ||
He recites that very text: "Having transcended the *yoni*s, there may be givers of yoga in the secondary *skandha*:
Akṛta, Kṛta, Vibhu, Viriñca, Hari, Guha, and then, by virtue of the sequence, the Goddess. (8.264)

The instruments [of action], the qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth, the effects, and the manifold expansion of cognitions—these qualities, beginning with *sattva*, have arisen from the Unmanifest for their sake. (8.265)
These givers of yoga bestow upon persons who possess the qualities [of sattva] various fruits, such as knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and lack of sovereignty. (8.266)
Beyond those is the world of the Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, the husband and sole mother of the entire universe, who sits upon the qualities of *sattva* and the others.

The term “proliferation of conditions” (*pratyayaprapañca*) refers to the fifty [letters] beginning with *a*, such as the vowels and so forth. “Of these” refers to those beginning with *akṛta* who bestow yoga. And their status as givers consists in the fact that they bestow dharma and other benefits even upon others. “From beyond” (*parataḥ*) means upward. || 267 ||
One might ask: "What would happen to this [individual] by remaining even above these? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"By which [power], through its sovereign energy (*prābhvī*) in the form of *graha*, the elements are presided over in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣan, Kṛta, Akṛta, and so forth. (8.268)
"Nīla" refers to Viṣṇu; "in the form of a planet" means by means of that which consists of support—this is the meaning.
"Adhiṣṭhāni" means presided over. || 268 ||
He explains that very locus [of power]:
"Desiring to withdraw [the world] here, he who, having entered the lotus of the four-faced one, burns the four worlds and then creates the Janaloka anew. (8.269)
By whose will Rudrāṇī emits [the world] with bodies composed of the qualities such as sattva;
the sacrificial altar is a secondary form (anukalpa) of Rudrāṇī, and there she is worshipped by means of that secondary form.

Then, because of their perception of him as Paśupati, the gods—Indra, Upendra, and Viriñca—as well as the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, and Munis, likewise performed various sacrifices. (8.271)
"Having entered into tranquility" means having presided over [the ritual]; "having burned" means, by implication, by way of taking the form of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).

"Rudrāṇī" refers to Goddess Umā. "Anukalpa" is a secondary or figurative form; "Vedī" is the pedestal consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). "Therein" means upon that altar. "Paśupati" refers, by implication, to the form of the external liṅga. || 271 ||
That supreme equilibrium of the guṇas is the unmanifest (avyakta), which stands above the guṇas;
[therein dwell] Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, and Sūraka. (8.272)
And Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikhoda—these eight are there.
"Supreme equality" refers to abiding in an undisturbed state; for this very reason, it is called "the unmanifest" (avyakta).
Here, although the summary is introduced by mentioning only the first of the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvaras) in every case, [the rest are implied].

The intention behind reading this with his own throat [i.e., orally] is that there may be no confusion among the listeners regarding the fact that many inconsistent variant readings exist here in other scriptures. As it has been said in the venerable *Ruru*:
"Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Savaṃrata, Jyotiḥpiṅgala, Sūra, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīreśa, and the one named Śikha— these are the Maheśvaras.
Thus it is stated in the venerable Nandiśikhā as well.
There are eight guardians of the world, and the Lord of Wrath known as Caṇḍa;
likewise Saṃvarta, Piṅgala, Jyotis, and the all-pervading Pañcāntaka.
"Ekapravīra and Śikhoḍa stand beyond the qualities (guṇas).
Thus [ends the verse]. || 272 ||
In this regard as well, he shows the specific distinction stated in the *Śivatanu*:
"The profound, the repository of the Puruṣa, is Prakṛti—the root, the Pradhāna, the Unmanifest. (8.273)
"Quality," "cause," and so forth—these are synonyms for that which originates from *māyā*.
Now, one might ask: what is the basis for applying these various designations here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"As many as there are individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), whose consciousness is smeared with innate and adventitious impurities... (8.274).

All those Rudras and those who enjoy the experiences arising therefrom are established here; some, however, possess instruments that are deluded, active, or dissolved, while others are devoid of instruments.

For here, all the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field), being established as Rudras, some—possessing instruments (*karaṇas*) such as those of the deluded and so forth—enjoy the experience arising therefrom, while others are indeed devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇa*). The innate (*sahaja*) is the *āṇava* [impurity]; the adventitious (*āgantuka*) are the *kārmika* and *māyīya*. || 275 ||
He explains the nature of being "deluded" (*mūḍha*) as follows:
"Those [faculties] which are incapable of action because they lack a presiding [consciousness] are 'deluded';
those which possess specific objects and are manifest are described in the scripture as 'clear' (*sphuṭa*). (8.276)

Those things which were destroyed at the great dissolution and were not produced again at creation remain dissolved; they are subject to the will [of the Lord], and their subsequent modification is designated as "re-formation" (vikaraṇa); the effect is likewise so. (8.277)

"Kṛtyam" (the function) refers to the perception of sound and other objects; for this very reason, the phrase "possessing restricted objects" is the cause for their functioning being characterized by deafness and so forth. "Non-arising during creation" is the cause for their state of dissolution.
"Dependent on will" means they are under one's own control—this is the meaning. For this very reason...
Śrīkaṇṭha and the others possess independent senses. As it is said in this very [text]:
"Among them, Umāpati alone is the Lord, possessing independent senses and being of the nature of the *vikaraṇa*. (Tantrāloka 8.229).
Thus, [the state] is fourfold according to the divisions of the deluded (*mūḍha*) and so forth. 277.
In the principle of *paṃs* (earth), there is the group of nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*) and the eight accomplishments (*siddhi*) preceding them;
likewise, there are exactly that many [eight] worlds (*bhuvana*), namely the eight beginning with *aṇimā*.
There are that many [streams], namely nine and eight. As it has been said:
"Ambā, Salilā, Oghā, Vṛṣṭi, along with Tārayā;
Sutārā, Sunetrā, and Kumārī after that."
And likewise, the nine satisfactions (tuṣṭis) are proclaimed: Uttamāmbhasikā, Tārā, Sutārā, Tārayantī, and Pramodikā.
Pramuditā, Modamānā, and thereafter Ramyakā,
as well as Sadāpramuditā— this is declared to be the group of eight Siddhis.
Aṇimā, laghimā, and mahimā, as well as prāpti;
likewise prākāmya, īśitva, and that which is declared as vaśitva.

"The power of determining [the nature of] objects according to one's will, as well as the eightfold [powers] beginning with *aṇiman*, are traditionally taught [to belong to this state]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1070).
Anticipating the question, "And what is the nature of contentment (tuṣṭi) and the others?", he says:

"In this context, contentment is that satisfaction which arises from the notion of reality regarding what is not real; success (siddhi) is the perception of something as worth accepting even when it is to be rejected. And he says that this is not our own invention alone:
And so it has been said by the followers of Kapila: || 8-279 ||

Regarding this, it is said: "The four internal [sources of suffering] are known as nature, acquisition, time, and fortune; there are five from the cessation of sense objects due to their acquisition, protection, attachment, destruction, and injury. (8.280)

Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three types of destruction of suffering, the acquisition of friends, and charity—these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis). The former three are the threefold curb upon accomplishment. (8.281)

The term "internal" (ādhyātmikyaḥ) means that they exist within the primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth, which are not the Self. In this context, it is the eightfold primordial nature itself—in its forms of the Pradhāna, Mahat, and the rest—that is the cause of the universe's manifestation, and nothing else; therefore, it is precisely therein that one finds the cause for the cessation of attachment, aversion, and the like.

For the yogin who determines [the self] to be the enjoyer and so forth, there is contentment known as "Nature" (prakṛti). And thus, since Nature is undifferentiated, everything would arise from everything at all times; therefore, it is logical that things arise from their own respective material causes—that very [cause] is the cause of the universe.

— thus, for one who determines the state of being an enjoyer and so forth in earth and the other elements solely within their material cause (*upādāna*), there is the designation "material cause" (*upādānākhyā*). Even so, since the manifestation of existence arises in dependence upon time, for one who determines the state of being an enjoyer and so forth in that very [time] as the cause of the universe, there is the designation "time" (*kālākhyā*). Even so...
"A specific fruit arises from a specific destiny"—thus, they alone possess the status of being the cause of the universe.

For one who determines that the state of being an enjoyer and so forth resides in that very [destiny], there are four [powers] called "destiny" (*bhāgya*). As for "five," it is because there are five causes for the cessation of external objects; these are acquisition (*arjana*) and the others, which apply to everything.

The engagement with sense objects is for the sake of happiness, yet that [happiness] can never arise from them; for a person striving in the threefold process—beginning with the acquisition—of sense objects, there is only supreme suffering.
Even so, their sudden and spontaneous destruction is itself a great suffering; it is not [happiness].
If this were to be accomplished without harming others, it would be more painful than pain itself.
Thus, for the yogin who maintains equanimity by perceiving these defects, the five [types of] contentment beginning with *navāmbā* have been described in sequence. And by this—

By this very recitation, Īśvarakṛṣṇa was instructed that otherwise there would have been no explicit mention by his own throat of the nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*). *Ūha* (reasoning) is a cognition regarding various objects that arises spontaneously, independent of means of valid knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
When there is such non-comprehension, the word itself is the means; when there is non-comprehension of its object, the teacher’s instruction is given once;
when there is non-comprehension even through that, repeated practice upon that very same [instruction] is required; and for these [means], there are five adversaries:
the threefold suffering, doubt, and misfortune. Among these, regarding the threefold suffering:

Having removed obstacles by means of methods seen in other scriptures, having dispelled doubt through association with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and having eliminated misfortune through generosity,
they accomplish [the goal] by means of one of the first three; thus are the eight accomplishments (siddhi), beginning with Tārā, in their proper order.

[The powers] have been described. Now, one might object: "Why should these accomplishments (siddhis) not belong to everyone without distinction? Anticipating this doubt, it was said: "The threefold 'hook' (aṅkuśa) precedes accomplishment.

The "hook" preceding [accomplishment] is characterized by error (viparyaya), incapacity (aśakti), and discontent (atuṣṭi); because it acts as a restraint, through that [hook], [the powers do not arise] without distinction.
There is no manifestation of supernatural powers among all living beings. || 281 ||
Above [the previous level], there are three rows consisting of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, pertaining to the teacher and the disciple;
even there, a triadic nature is proclaimed due to the connection with the shadow of the three qualities (*guṇas*). (8.282)
And above the rows, there should be the eightfold science of the channels (*nāḍīvidyāṣṭaka*), beginning with *iḍā* and so forth.

Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "there also": by that word it is indicated that not only was the threefold nature of the gurus mentioned due to their connection with the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) within the *guṇatattva*, but this is also the case here—as has been stated. Thus it is said:
Now hear, therefore, regarding the three rows of gurus and disciples above:
Maskarī, Pūraṇa, Kṛtsna, Kapila, and Kāśa.
Likewise, Sanatkumāra, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, and others were their portions;
as well as Kāśyapa, Nāsiketu, Gālava, and Bhautika.
Śākalya is likewise renowned, as is the supreme sage Durvāsas;
Vālmīki is the best of gurus, along with Parāśara and Gālava.
Pippalāda, the son of Sumitrā, the son of Vāyu, and Bhadantaka— these,
beginning with Maskarī and ending with Bhadanta, are proponents of both the seen and the unseen.
The first row is held to consist of twenty-two eminent gurus:
Jahnu, Tṛṇabindu, Muni, and likewise Tārkṣya.
Dhyānāśraya, Dīrgha, Hotṛ,
Ajagara, Agastya, Vasubhauma, and Upādhyāya are also celebrated.
Śukra, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Rāma the son of Jamadagni who ascended upwards,
Sthūlaśiras, Bālakhilya, and Manuja are thus proclaimed.
Vajrātreyas, Viśuddha, Śiva, and Cārurathānuga—
those beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru are intended as the second row.
Hara, Jaṇṭhī, Pratoda, and Amareśa as the fourth;
Kṛṣṇapiṅgeśa, Rudra, Indrajit, Vṛṣabha, and Śiva.
Yama, Krūra, Vikhyāta, Gaṅgādhara, Umāpati,
Bhūteśvara, Kapālīśa, and likewise Śaṅkara.
Ardhanārīśvara, Piṅgala, and another,
Mahākāla, Saṃvarta, Maṇḍalī, and Ekavīraka.
Likewise, there is another renowned one, the eternal Bhārabhūteśvara;
and there are twenty-five sages, beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru.
"Hara and the others, ending with Dhruva, are recorded as the twenty gurus" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1083).

And here, because the word "guru" is employed in both lines, it is established by implication that in the middle line, they are indeed the disciples. Furthermore, those vidyās take the form of channels (nāḍīs), and they are the presiding deities thereof.
—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Iḍā and Candriṇī, as well as Śānti and Śāntikarī; Mālā and Mālinī, as well as Svāhā and Sudhā. (Svacchandatantra 10.1085)
Thus [ends the section]. || 282 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for the persistence of the presiding deities of the channels (nāḍīs) within the principle of the individual (puṃstattva)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because the power consisting of sound (nāda), known as 'emanation' (prasara), resides within the individual (pums). (8.283)

The word *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Since [the Lord] resides within the principle of the individual soul (*puṃstattva*), and because that soul is designated by terms such as "atomic" (*aṇu*) due to its contracted nature, He alone is "Sound" (*nāda*)— that is, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by absolute freedom and supreme agency, which "sounds" (*nadati*) by perceiving the universe as non-different from His own Self.
The power consisting of that [consciousness], because of its nature of flowing outward as an external form, exists as what is called "expansion" (*prasara*);
it flashes forth in a gross form up to the limit of the power of action—this is the meaning. This is what is being said:
the power of consciousness itself, by virtue of its own sovereignty, manifests the state of having a contracted self-nature.
Desiring to grasp even the body and so forth as one's own self, one should first attain the state of being the channels (nāḍīs). As it was said previously:
"The ultimate grossness of the movements of consciousness and vital breath is the channel."
"Having attained the form of the channels (nāḍī), it should cause this body to become a continuous stream. (Tantrāloka 7.66) || 283 ||

Now, one might object: "This would indeed be so if the agency of the person were established; however, that itself is extremely difficult to maintain, for if that were the case, he would be insentient like milk and other such things. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the person is not a non-agent, and his status as the cause of the agent is firmly established."

For in this way, since the agency of the act of eating is impossible, his status as an enjoyer would also not exist. Now, you may object: "In order to establish that the worlds are effects, you accept the agency of the Person (puruṣa); however, it is our Nature (prakṛti) alone that is capable of bearing that burden—so what is the use of him?"
Anticipating the objection—"Does this not bestow unconsciousness [upon the agent]?"—it is said:
"And the causality of the agent is firmly established.

By the term "of the agent," it is meant that [causality belongs] to the agent and not to an insentient entity such as *prakṛti* (primordial matter) and so forth. And this [point] has been addressed in the immediately preceding chapter.
It will be established; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
Now, one might object: "If agency is not admitted for the person because of his insentience, then even if that were the case, [agency] would not cease"—to this he says:
"Or, even though the person is a non-agent, [agency persists] while he remains as a cooperative cause. (8.284)
The nature of the remaining effects must be accepted [as pre-existing], otherwise the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be abandoned.

In this regard, concerning the production of the universe, *prakṛti* is the cause; and it would be incapable of producing anything without depending on the *puruṣa*, since it has been stated that the production of the universe occurs precisely through their conjunction.
As they say:

"For the sake of the Puruṣa's perception, and for the sake of isolation of the Pradhāna, there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from that, creation is produced" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 21).

Thus, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [of the Puruṣa], the Puruṣa is also a cause in the production of the universe; and since it is impossible for the universe to follow the form of that [Puruṣa], he is not the material cause (*upādāna*), but rather an auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*). And in that case, his nature as an auxiliary distinct from the material effect must necessarily be admitted; otherwise—

The theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) would be abandoned; thus, even in this way, due to its transformation into the nature of the universe, it would result in nothing but insentience.

Thus, in the production of the universe, agency must be attributed to the Person (puṃs) alone, so that even when assuming various forms, there would be no loss of his own essential nature and consequently no lack of consciousness. Thus it is said: "Therefore, in such an effect, whatever power belongs to the Person... (8.285).
Having assumed as many forms, it attains fullness.

The phrase "in such a state" refers to the gross form whose essence is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). "As many" refers to the forms consisting of the channels (*nāḍīs*), the *vidyās*, and so forth. It attains "fullness" because, even in this way, it rests solely within its own self.
Now he follows the subject at hand:
"Above the eight limbs (aṅga), that which was mentioned is called the eightfold body (vigraha). (8.286)
"It has been stated"—in all the scriptures. || 286 ||
Thus it is said:

"The effect, the cause, suffering, pleasure, consciousness, that which is to be accomplished, the instruments, and the means—this group of eight constitutes the state of manifestation within the principle of the Person (puṃstattva). (8.287)

The effect is that alone which is the cause; that is, the cause consisting of the ten organs beginning with speech. By the phrase "to be accomplished by cognition," both mere knowledge and mere activity manifested by the organs of intellect and action are expressed. By "instrument," the triad of internal organs is meant. By "means,"...

The meaning is that *pradhāna* is the cause of all things. Regarding the phrase "the state of having a form" (*vigrahatāyuk*), it is because it initiates the subtle body; thus, it exists in a subtle form, since these [elements] have already been described in their gross forms, and because *māyā* will be described later in its supreme form. || 287 ||
The world of the ten bodily attributes arises from the eightfold manifestation:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from deceit, and freedom from anger toward the guru. (8.288)
Service, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness—these ten have been declared;
furthermore, the group of sixteen ending with smell resides within the principle of the individual soul (puruṣatattva) alone. (8.289)
Beginning with the city known as the "noose of the body," there are then the qualities of the intellect;
therein likewise are the eight [qualities], the threefold ego, and similarly the [three] beginning with desire. (8.290)
The nooses, divided into those of Āgantuka, Gāṇeśa, and Vaidyeśvara, exist in three kinds within the person (puruṣa), obstructing the path to liberation. (8.291)

"From the eightfold *vigraha*" means above; that is to say, within the *puruṣa-tattva* itself, and thus above even the tenfold *dharma*. Furthermore, by repeating the phrase "the fetters of the body" (*dehapāśa*) and so forth, [it refers to] immediately following this, the fetters of the body which constitute the subtle body—the objects denoted by the word "objects," such as sound and the rest.
The city of the five [senses] should also be explained. As it has been said:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are declared to be the objects of the senses, which must be purified with effort" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1096).

Thus it is said. And although this [set of sixteen] is mentioned in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra* as being distinct from the threefold *ahaṅkāra*, it is nevertheless explained here in this manner because of its common nature with the sixteen transformations (*vikāra*). Furthermore, it is the objects of sense, such as sound and the rest, that possess the supreme power of bondage in every respect.

There is no fault here, as these [fetters] are repeatedly designated in various places according to their subtle, intermediate, and gross states as things to be purified. The connection is that the fetters, beginning with desire (kāma), are declared to be threefold. And regarding their persistence here:
The causes are those that obstruct the path to liberation. As it has been said:
"Lust, anger, greed, delusion, and malice, as well as birth, death, old age, disease, hunger, thirst, and craving."
Despair and fear, intoxication and exhilaration,
passion and hatred, mental instability, and anger, falsehood, and malice.
Illusion, envy, righteousness, unrighteousness, and lack of self-mastery are to be understood as adventitious; learn from me the fetters of the groups.
The Goddess, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha,
Bhṛṅgin, Caṇḍeśvara, and Kārttikeya is remembered as the eighth.
Ananta, Tritanu, Sūkṣma, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śivottama,
Śikhaṇḍin, Ekanetra, and the supreme Ekarudra.
"At the time of initiation, one should purify the bonds consisting of the eight Vidyeśvaras. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1101) || 291 ||

Now, indeed, there are three kinds of bonds here—the *āṇava*, the *kārmika*, and the *māyīya*. In that regard, let it be granted that the sixteen transformations and so forth are designated as bonds, for they are merely the expansion (*prapañca*) of the *māyīya* bond itself; however, as for these [groups] of the *vidyeśas*:
And why is this state called "bondage" (pāśatva), when it appears to us as something unprecedented? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whatever is other than the Supreme Śiva—whose nature has been described and who is beautiful through the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness—that is called 'bondage'. (8.292)

Here, indeed, whatever is "other"—and not merely something restricted—than the "Supreme" Śiva, whose nature was previously described as consisting solely of pure light, is called a "bond" (pāśa) in its entirety; that is to say, it is intended as such precisely because of its binding nature. Now, [one might object]:...

Anticipating the objection that nothing whatsoever could exist apart from supreme light— since it is impossible for anything to manifest independently of that light— and that if such were the case, everything would be of the nature of that one alone (and thus what could possibly be designated as a "bond"?— it is said: "[from that which is beautiful through the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness]."

Thus [it is said]. For that Supreme Śiva, although his nature is the consciousness of supreme non-duality, is beautiful through his absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), whereby he conceals his own true nature and manifests through various contracted forms; for it is from this that the impurity (*mala*) pertaining to *māyā*, which consists in the manifestation of duality, attains its full power. || 292 ||

Now, one might object: "If it is accepted that the body, the senses, and so forth—which are of the nature of the object alone and are insentient—are fetters because they are distinct from Śiva, who is of the nature of the subject alone; then let that be so. But how can the subjects (pramātṛs) also be of the nature of the subject alone and yet be of a different form [from Śiva]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Thus, although the Supreme Lord has attained masculinity and is complete, it is indeed a marvel that there is a lack of recognition of His true nature; therefore, [the limited] persons arise from that. (8.293)

In this context, it is proclaimed everywhere that bondage consists in manifestation as something distinct from the supreme form of the Lord, which is called non-recognition (*akhyāti*); and since this applies equally to both the subjects (*vedaka*) and the objects (*vedya*), the path is the same for all in their state of being fetters (*pāśa*). Even so:

If their essential nature were not fully known, a mutual distinction among individuals could arise, by which their diversity would be accounted for; for instance, one person might possess only one impurity (*mala*), another two, and yet another all three. Even so, however, there would be no difference between them regarding their status as fetters (*pāśa*).

Because the Supreme Lord’s own nature remains uncomprehended, its state persists; and thus, "the status of a Vidyeśvara is an inferior liberation"—this and so forth is entirely logical. For this very reason, [it is said]:
"O Varārohā, the infinite web of bonds extends up to the end of Śamanā. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.429)
Thus it has been stated, etc. || 293 ||
Likewise, in this context as well, he states that whatever else has not been mentioned other than Śiva is to be understood solely as a bond (pāśa):
"Those bonds, whether mentioned or unmentioned, which possess the characteristics described in the Paratantra [Tantra]," [are all to be known as such].
When all those [impurities] are purified within that person, one is liberated from worldly existence.
Above the level of the Person (puruṣa) is Niyati; situated there are ten Śaṅkaras, golden-hued and very white. But in the principle of Time (kāla-tattva), those ten are Śivas.
Each attendant has a retinue of sixteen thousand crores;
in the realm of Passion is the world of Vīreśa, the city of the teachers and disciples.
And the city of Aśuddhavidyā shall be radiant with nine powers; those beginning with Vāmā and ending with Manonmanī are proclaimed [as its presiding deities]. (8.297)
In the Kalā [tattva], there is the supreme city of the three Mahādevas;
their designations are "the Śaṅkaras. They are Vāmadeva, Śarva, and Bhavodbhava.
The adamantine body, the Lord, the Giver, and the two, Krama and Vikrama.

"And the tenth is Suprabheda; these are remembered as the Śaṅkaras within Niyati. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1104). "Golden-hued" refers to the Śaṅkaras. "Very white" refers to the Śivas. As it has been said: "The Śaṅkaras are declared to be golden-hued, while the Śivas resemble crystal."
"Pure, awakened, fully enlightened, profoundly tranquil, and the supreme imperishable."
Śiva, Suśiva, Dhruva, Akṣara, and Śambhurāja.
"And these ten, O fair-faced one, are to be known as the Śivas within the principle of Time" (Svacchandatantra 10.1107).
Furthermore, "the world of Vīreśa" refers, by implication, to that which is delimited by the number eight; "the supreme" refers to another [world] delimited by the number ten. As it has been said:
"Beyond this, learn from me concerning Hari and Hara within the principle of passion (rāga-tattva):
Saṃhṛṣṭa, Suprahṛṣṭa, Surūpa, and Rūpavardhana."
"Manonmana, Mahāvīra, and Vīreśa are proclaimed [as the lords]. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1112).
"Kalyāṇa, Piṅgala, Babhru, Vīra, and likewise Prabhava..."
Meghātithi, Chedaka, and Dāhaka were the authors of the treatises.
"And likewise, five disciples and ten teachers are thus established" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1114). Here, "they" refers to the powers (*śaktayaḥ*). As it has been said:
"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Vikaraṇī..."
And likewise Balavikaraṇī and Balapramathanī.

"And likewise, she is the subduer of all beings (*sarvabhūtadamanī*) as well as the one who transcends the mind (*manonmanī*)" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1114). And here, the feminine reading alone is correct, because it has been accepted by the great authorities (*mahājana*).
It is called "supreme" (*uttama*) because of its ascent to the ultimate limit of the universe. As it has been said:
"Mahādeva, of great splendor, of great light... || 297 ||
Now he describes the threefold nature of Māyā by way of its essence as the power of the knots (granthi): "Therefore, Māyā is primarily threefold, consisting of infinite millions [of aspects]. (8.298)
It was said that she was pervaded by the apertures of the vulva; furthermore, within the body of Śaivī, there is the group of eight Mahādevas at night, extending as far as the size of a thumb.
"In the *Śrīmālinīmata*, [this is stated] by virtue of the sovereignty over the eight wheels;
[it is said] 'primarily' (*mukhyataḥ*), for otherwise, according to the perspective to be explained, there would be a lack of unity among the *puṭas*.
In the passage 'the group of eight Mahādevas at night,' the phrase 'in the body of Śivā' (*śaivyāṃ tanau*) should also be applied. Thus it has been said.
Regarding that, it is said:
"The summit of the cave, which is omnipresent throughout the manifest universe, is adorned with a thousand vaginal apertures."
There, the first lord of the cakra is Anaghaprabhāva, possessed of great splendor;
the second lord of the cakra is the powerful Rudra, known by the name Vāma.
The Lord known as Bhavodbhava presides over the third wheel by his own power;
the one with a single tawny eye is the master of the fourth wheel.
He who is celebrated as Riśāna sets in motion the fifth wheel;
Bhuvaneśa is the presiding lord of the sixth, the wheel of the worlds.
"The deity known as Prathita, who is the leader of the seventh wheel (*cakranāyaka*), is the Lord named Aṅguṣṭhamātra, the master of the eighth wheel of worlds.
And this is not stated only here, but elsewhere as well—as he says: "Likewise..."
"In the *Śrīmālinīmata*," as it is said there: "The lords of the mandala, beginning with Mahātejas and the rest, reside there in the *māyātattva*; among them are Vāmadeva and Bhavodbhava."
"Preceded by Ekapiṅga, Īkṣaṇa, Īśāna, and Bhuvaneśa, they are the size of a thumb and possess a luster equal to the fire of cosmic destruction. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.29).
And here there is yet another distinction even from the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*—thus he says:
"Those [energies] beginning with Vāmā, which were taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana* as being [associated] with Puruṣa and the rest... (8.300).
These are said to exist within the *māyātattva* itself, from Ananta onwards, in the body of Śivī;
[the phrase] "starting from Puruṣa" includes the *rāgatattva* by virtue of the word "etcetera. As it is stated there:
"In Puruṣa [reside] Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhaveśāna, and Ekavīra."
"Pracaṇḍa, Mādhava, Aja, and then Ananta and Ekaśiva. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.26).
Regarding the phrase "from Ananta," the meaning is "up to Ananta. As it is said there:
"Then the world of Vāma, from that the [world] of Bhīma, and then also that of Ugra."
"Therefore, above that [world] is the world of Bhava, belonging to every deity.
And: "Therefore, by means of various qualities, there is the excellent world of the Hero of the Wheel (Cakravīra)."
Thus:
"Above that is the best of worlds, a treasury of immeasurable qualities, belonging to Pracaṇḍa;
there, the one named Pracaṇḍa resides and governs Ekavīra and the others."
And thus it is said. || 300 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of instructing these people in this matter?", he says:
"Those who observe the skull-vow, those who offer their own limbs as oblations, and those who practice arduous austerities... (8.301).
"Fearless toward all, they observe the vow of the sword's edge and are knowers of that reality (*tattva*).
The phrase "knowers of that reality" means those who have attained union (*sāyujya*) with Vāmā and the other [energies]. As it has been said:
"The Brahmins, having known what is to be known, bear the skull-vow (*kāpāla-vrata*) and are free from attachment."
Those who are devoted to smearing themselves with ashes attain union with the Left-hand Path (Vāma).
Having attained the realization [of the goal], those who desire the exceedingly terrifying state, having sacrificed their own heads which they have cut off themselves as an offering,
go to that terrestrial abode.
Even those steadfast ones who have undertaken fierce methods of yoga and perform difficult, intense austerities,
and who meditate on the Fierce One incessantly— they too obtain qualities that are not fierce.
