Having recognized Bhava as the God, the Brahmins— whose minds were fixed in meditation and who had attained success through the granting of fearlessness to the terrified— ascended to the state of Bhava.
"Having made their own form beautiful with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
those meditators who are steadfast in the vow of the sword’s edge go to the primordial state.
Now, one might object: "Since there is also a Lord named Ananta who is the creator of these [worlds] and so forth, what is the point of attaining these various levels?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By degrees they reach that reality where the Lord is called Ananta. (8.302)
"Tattattva" means the world-level (bhuvana) of the primordial matter (pradhāna) pertaining to Māyā; "Īśa" refers, by implication, to the path (adhvan) ending with Īśvara. || 302 ||
"What is the authority for this?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And it has been stated that the station of that Lord, the sovereign of Ananta, the agent of maintenance, dissolution, and creation, and the guardian of the door of the blessed cave, is beyond [the lower levels]. || 8.303 ||
It is said [thus] in the *Śivatanu* itself: "Beyond" means upward; "the cave" refers to *māyā*. || 303 ||

He demonstrates its very function of maintaining [the world] and so forth: "It draws out and bestows upon men the qualities such as *aṇimā*, the supernatural powers, the various forms of knowledge, asceticism, happiness, and yogic attainments, from the cavity of Māyā. (8.304)

Empowered by that power, their own strength consisting of the qualities of darkness presiding over the cave [of the heart], all [the lords] from Ananta at the beginning down to Śatabhava at the end shine forth like lamps. (8.305)
Presiding over the unmanifest (avyakta), he brings forth the universe by the command of Śambhu;
for Śiva is the cause of authority over both the pure and impure streams.

Regarding the phrase "its power" (*tacchakti*), the word "its" (*tat*) refers to Ananta. By this, it is stated that he does not merely ordain the state of the *kṣetrajñas*, but also that of the Rudras.
"Qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) refers to omniscience and so forth. "Headed by Ananta" means having Ananta as their lord.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "the world," it arises from Śambhu by way of the application of the nature of cause and effect, and not merely from His own will. The reason for this is given by the words beginning with "pure" (*śuddha*). As it has been stated there:
"Since He, the Lord of Gods, presiding over the unmanifest (*avyakta*), brings forth the world."
And because it rescues those who have fallen into the great abyss of saṃsāra.
"Therefore, Śiva, who is seated by the command of the Lord and endowed with the power of Śiva-yoga,
should be known as the cause of authority over both the pure and impure currents. ||306||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the qualification for the two streams, the pure and the impure? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Those who are first established in that great state which is conjoined with the qualities of Śiva, they are the agents of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world beginning with Ananta. (8.307)

This has been described as the "cavity of Māyā," whereas beyond that is the "Cave" (guhā), which is the source of the universe. The phrase "in the great station" refers to the pure stream; its qualification is "through union with the qualities of Śiva," because of the possibility of [attaining] omniscience and other such attributes. Regarding the phrase "of Ananta and the others," "Ananta" is the presiding deity of the principle of Māyā.

Regarding the phrase "the cave of Māyā": Māyā is of the nature of a knot (*granthi*), while *guhā* (the cave) is of the nature of the principle (*tattva*). The term "beyond" (*parataḥ*) means within the impure current (*aśuddhe srotasi*). Thus, the connection is that Māyā, being twofold—both as a knot and as a principle—is the womb of the universe (*jagadyoni*). And it has been said therein:
"The venerable Cave is the supreme Māyā, the cause of the origin of the worlds;
having experienced their existence within it, the worlds dissolve once again. (307)
And here, having raised the doubt, "What is the cause for the application of the designation 'bhaga'? he says:
"Because of their arising, while they conform to the agitation of the Lord's power (pati-śakti). (8.308)
When the husband desires the goddess who complies with his wishes, he applies the designation "bhaga" to her vulva, which is filled with various objects of desire. (8.309)
"At that time, from her, offspring such as the unmanifest (avyakta) and others are born.
The word "in them" means in those [states] consisting of the attainment of creation and so forth. "Of her" refers to Māyā in the form of a knot. "Her" refers to Māyā itself in the form of a knot.

The term *pratibhagam* means "in each part. For this very reason, the number of the primordial eggs (*prakṛty-aṇḍa*) and so forth is infinite. It is precisely because of this similarity that even the worldly narrative of male and female is hinted at here. (309)
And these are uninterrupted—thus he says:
"The precise extent of those extremely subtle [energies] is not described in the ritual injunctions. (8.310)
"In the *vidhis*," that is, in the scriptures. || 310 ||
He confirms this very point by means of an illustration:
"Just as many inner rooms are fastened within a single wall, so too are there many openings for the womb within the single wall that is the head of Māyā. (8.311)
Concealed by subtle layers of illusion and secret chambers, invisible to one another, countless Rudras dwell there happily in every single cave. (8.312)
"In that place," they have attained union (*sāyujya*), proximity (*sāmīpya*), and residence in the same world (*salokastha*) with the Supreme.
The phrase "in that place" refers to *māyā* in its form as a knot.
He states the reason for their being innumerable with the words "attained union," and so forth. (8.312)
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "In this same manner, he has been described by the teachers for those dwelling in every world. (8.313)
He demonstrates the absence of any means for calculating the number of these [channels] along with their presiding deities:
"Even the words of all the Siddhas might be exhausted after being uttered for a long time; yet, due to the infinity of the wombs (yonis), the number of the currents (srotas) cannot be told. (8.314)
Now, one might ask: "Are these other streams distinct from this stream, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, that which has been described as beginning with hell and ending with the gatekeeper is but one."
By that same channel, other [experiences] of a similar nature are also to be known. || 8-315 ||
In the unmanifest state, within the cave, his own transformation is [contained] by means of the two powers of *prakṛti*;
it is woven lengthwise and crosswise, pervaded, measured, filled, and encompassed. (8.316)

For within the Cave (guhā) reside the Unmanifest (avyakta) and its constituent part (kalā), as well as its transformation; therefore, it is logical that the Unmanifest and the Part are woven through it. For a cause must indeed be that which fills out its own effect, as they say: "The cause is that which fills out [its effect]."

Thus, the very process of filling is differentiated by such expressions as "woven across and woven lengthwise. The term "belonging to the Self" refers to the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, as well as ignorance (avidyā) and the rest. 316.
Having thus demonstrated its distinction from other treatises, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"In the middle of that [wheel] are three petals; there are six Rudras in the lower and inner [petals], one above, and five—these twelve are thus described. (8.317)
"In the lower" means in the cavity; likewise elsewhere. || 317 ||
He recites those very names:
"The six are Gahana, Asādhya, Hari, Hara, Daśeśvara, Trikala, and Gopati;
in the middle is Ananta; [the others are] Kṣema, Dvijeśa, Vidyeśa, Viśva, and Śiva. (8.318)
Thus, through the transformation of those five and six [elements] situated in the petals, the state indeed revolves;
however, the infinite Lord remains eternally in the center.
As it has been said:
"Gahana, Asādhya, and likewise the Lord Hariharaprabhu; Daśeśāna, O Queen of the Gods, Trikala, and likewise Gopati."
O fair-faced one, in the lower casket within the principle of Māyā,
Kṣemeśa, Brahmaṇasvāmī, and likewise Vidyeśāna are to be known.
Viśveśa, Śiva, and Ananta is said to be the sixth;
these Rudras are proclaimed to reside above, within the enclosure of Māyā.

"Among these, however, the Blessed One Ananteśa is the Lord of the World" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1125). And here, even though they exist in a different state by means of their supreme form, there is no distinction whatsoever for Ananta—thus he says "among them," etc. Regarding the phrase "those situated within the *puṭas*":

"Upward and downward by implication. Regarding the phrase "by their reversal," the word "that" (tat) refers to the Rudras; thus, by the inversion of their upward-downward relationship within the lower and upper compartments respectively, their position is transformed—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
By the first division, the twelve Rudras are proclaimed;
however, those who are the Mahārudras established in this Māyātattva [are different].
I shall explain them to you in detail according to the division of the three types:
O Goddess, Gopati is situated there in the lower knot (adhogranthi).
Situated above the *granthi* are Viśva, Trikalā, Kṣema,
the Lord of Brahmā, and Śiva as the fifth.
"And below and above, [it is] infinite... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1130).

Thus, here there are seven worlds in the lower section by way of the nature of the supreme-non-supreme (*parāpara*), ten in the upper section, and again only one in the middle section—making eighteen in total. || 319 ||
However, there is this further distinction—as he says:

"The knot described in the *Mataṅgaśāstra* is pervaded by a pair of six-fold cavities (kapāla) situated above and below, by their reversal, and by eight [cavities] from the center located in the directions. (8.320)

Regarding the phrase "by the pair of six": this refers to the Rudras. Thus, by means of twenty Rudras—namely, the six beginning with Ananta situated in the upper skull-cap (kapāla), those beginning with Gopatī below, and the eight beginning with Vigraheśa in the middle.
The meaning is that the knot of *māyā* is presided over. As it is said there:
"O observer of good vows, above the knot there are six skull-bones in number; an equal number of beautiful [bones] are fashioned here below by the elements. (Mataṅga 8.67)
Beginning with these words, [the text continues]: "Ananta, whose nature is infinite power, is situated at the summit of all;
below him is the one named Śiva, the Rudra who is the Lord and creator of the worlds."
Then Viśveśa of great splendor, followed by Vidyeśāna;
after that another, Brahmaṇasvāmī, and immediately thereafter Kṣemeśa.
"These six are the lords of the worlds... (Mataṅga 8.82).
"Situated below these is a knot, difficult to pierce and exceedingly vast."
"Wherein that Lord of the Body (Vigraheśāna) [resides]... (Mataṅga 8.84).
Thus:
"Wherein Śarva, Bhava, Ugra, and the powerful Bhīma [dwell]..."
Bhasmāntaka, Dundubhi, Śrīvatsa, and Mahābala.
"Therefore, below that knot is the great wheel consisting of six skull-cups" (Mataṅga 8.86).
"The divine world of Gopati is also immediately after [the world] of Trikala."
Below that is the beautiful and stainless world of Daśeśa.
And likewise: "Of Hara, of the god Harihara, and of Hari... (Mataṅga 8.88). || 320 ||
Furthermore, there is another distinction; thus he says:
"In the Śrīsāraśāsana, moreover, this is specified as having six cavities (ṣaṭpuṭatā).
As it is stated therein:"
"Beneath that, Mahāmāyā is situated, consisting of six cavities. Thus [it is said].
Thus, having concluded that Māyā has the nature of a knot, he begins to state its nature as a reality:
"This reality called the 'knot' is the effect of Māyā; therefore, it is Māyā. (8.321)

Regarding the phrase "the effect of Māyā": the meaning is that the very principle of Māyā has attained a state of imbalance due to its orientation toward manifestation; however, its true nature remains unagitated. || 321 ||
Therefore, he says:
"The principle of Māyā is indeed all-pervasive, profound, formless, and the locus of the dissolution of everything.
"All-pervasive" means it is omnipresent; for this very reason, it is "profound. It is "formless" because of its subtlety.
"It is the locus of the dissolution of all," because the universe abides here through a subtle process.
For this very reason, there is no division of worlds here; thus he says:
"In that case, a division of worlds is not appropriate in this text; therefore [it is so]. (8.322)
"In the two books" means in its very gross form. || 322 ||
One might object: "Even so, since this [power] is insentient (*jāḍya*), how does it possess the capacity to manifest such effects?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That Ananta, the lord of the *māyā*-principle, having reflected upon the individual souls (*aṇu*) who have arisen..."
She simultaneously agitates the Night and gives birth through her own infinite wombs.

"It agitates" means it renders [the seed] capable of producing its effect. "By means of enclosures" (saṃpuṭaiḥ) means by means of forms shaped like the female organ (bhaga). And their infinity has been stated precisely in the *Śivatanu-grantha*. || 323 ||
For this very reason, he states that the effects are also infinite:
"Therefore, that entire network of coverings (āvaraṇa) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth, which has been described, is innumerable and diverse; yet Māyā alone is one and indivisible. (8.324)
One might ask: "What is the proof that the effect is infinite even when the cause is one?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra that the dyad consisting of Earth and the Unmanifest..."
It is innumerable, known as the power of Night (Niśāśakti), and possesses a single nature.
As it is said there:
"Two separate [groups] are innumerable, and each of the two separate [groups] is one. (Mālinīvijaya-tantra 2.50) || 325 ||
Having thus explained this as a digression, he introduces the actual subject at hand:
"The bonds previously mentioned are the five *praṇavas*, the eight measures of the Sage (*muni*), the *kula*, and the *yoni*; she is Vāgīśī, in whom one who is born is not born again. (8.326)

"Pure" is [discussed] in the section on the *puṃstattva* (the principle of the person). That "the lineage of the sage" consists of the teacher, disciple, and so forth has already been stated previously. As for "the womb," it is said:
"Speech alone gave birth to all the worlds."
Thus, by virtue of this state, he is the cause of the universe; "he is born" by the power of mantras and so forth; and "he is not born" because he has been united with the Supreme Śiva. || 326 ||
What need is there for much? Whatever has been taught regarding the lower path (adharādhvan) starting from Kalā and so forth, all that is situated right here.
Thus he says:
"At the time of initiation, for the sake of purifying what resides on the lower path, [one employs] that which belongs to the lower path."
But all that is fully established in the presence of Ananta.
For it is logical that the effect should exist within the cause in a subtle form—this is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so, what then is meant by the *praṇava* and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Sādhya, Dātā, Damana, Dhyāna, and Bhasma—these are the five *bindus*.
And [the teachings] characterized by the *Pañcārtha*, *Guhyas*, *Rudrāṅkuśa*, and *Hṛdaya*, along with their *vyūhas*. (8.328)
Including Ākarṣa and Ādarśa, these constitute the eight means of valid cognition (pramāṇas).
The term "bindus" refers to the Praṇavas. || 328 ||
And in order to state the essential nature of all these as it applies to each case, he says:
"All those who hold authority over the principle of *māyā* possess unimpaired power. (8.329)
Possessing bodies composed of illusion (māyāmaya), they enjoy their own experience; "their own" means that which is appropriate for their respective offices—this is the meaning. || 329 ||
He explains the very nature of the body as being composed of illusion:
"For at the end of the dissolution, they are withdrawn by Ananta, and [reappear] at the dawn of the day. (8.330)
Due to their lack of faith in the Infinite One, even the gods—stunned by their own conceit of independence—regard that Supreme One as merely one who has awakened from sleep. (8.331)

Those situated within the intermediate state of *māyā* know only themselves to be the cause during the "dawn," that is, at the time of renewed creation. Regarding the phrase "other than Ananta," the word "other" (*anya*) is used in relation to those who hold authority over *māyā*.
They do not know that supreme Ananta as the cause; rather, they know only themselves to be so.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: here, the understanding of the negation arises through the force of the particle *eva*; and regarding the lack of such understanding, there are two causes: [those who] consider themselves awakened while still asleep, and those who are dull-witted due to the conceit of being independent.
Furthermore, the cause for not thus understanding oneself is expressed by the phrase "situated within the interval of *māyā*. This has been stated.
It is so— although,

according to such statements as, "In the pure path Śiva is said to be the agent; Ananta is the lord in the impure," it is indeed Ananta and the others who perform creation and withdrawal, nevertheless these...

Because they are deluded by *māyā* and intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, they do not know this; on the contrary, they think, "We alone are the agents of the creation and destruction of the worlds, and there is no one superior even to us. This is because, despite their own dependence, they are intent upon imagining independence within themselves, according to the analogy of one who has awakened from sleep.

They consider both creation and dissolution to be dependent solely upon their own selves. As it has been said: "Overcome by the intoxication of power, these self-important ones think: 'There is no other supreme cause for the worlds greater than myself.'"
"I alone am the Lord of this entire world. (Mataṅga 8.73).
For all those whose vision is directed downward are deluded by the intoxication of their own creation.
Delighting in that place, they were blameless in their enjoyment of pleasures and sports.
Having properly entered into sleep at the time of dissolution through the performance of their own functions,
they are then entered by the *kṣobhikā* [power] and awaken one another.
They perceive their own creation as being of that very same kind, radiant with its arrangement;
have we perhaps arisen from sleep, subject to the power of our own slumber?
"Free from afflictions, we sport, desiring to enjoy those things acquired by ourselves; all of us are ensnared by subtle fetters and are not obstructed by gross ones. (Mataṅga 8.80) || 332 ||
Having thus described the twofold nature of Māyā as consisting of both the knot (granthi) and the principle (tattva), he speaks in order to explain its nature as power (śakti):
"Beyond this, Māyā stands as the goddess who deludes living beings. (8.332)
That power of the God of gods is capable of accomplishing the most difficult tasks;
by it, which has no enemy nor obstacle, the intellects of others have been exhausted.
"Disputants here argue, 'This is the truth, this is not'; they are the lowest of men who possess no devotion toward the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, and the Śāstras. (8.334)
Abandoning them to the true path, he certainly leads those who rely on dry logic and know how to investigate fallacious arguments onto a wrong path.
Indeed, Māyā causes them to wander in non-liberation through the desire for liberation.

She is called "the Goddess" (Devī) because she is non-different from the Lord (deva). She is said to be "the performer of the most difficult tasks" because her nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya).
"They dispute" means they harbor conflicting opinions. She is called "dry" (śuṣkā) because she is devoid of any objective reality.
Raising the doubt, "How indeed can there be the total eradication of such a thing as this?", he says:
"Severed by the sword of Śiva-initiation, and likewise by the sword of Śiva-knowledge. (8.336)

It shall not sprout again; there is no other cause for its destruction than initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the ritual action (*kriyā*). "There is no other cause" means that [no other cause] has been taught in other scriptures. (8.336)
Above Mahāmāyā is Śuddhā, then Mahāvidyā, and then Mātṛkā. || 8-337 ||
And Vāgīśvarī [resides] there, within the nine cities beginning with Vāmā; and because of her very purity, her greatness is expressed by the term "Mahāvidyā. || 337 ||
Vāmā and the others recite as follows:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, and Balavikārikā. (8.338)
Mathanī, Damanī, and Manonmanī—these three-eyed goddesses are all yellow;
these seventy million principal mantras are established here in the Vidyātattva.
In this world, there are cities shaped like lotuses, each numbering one hundred thousand billionth parts [of a unit];
within them dwell the seven Vidyārājñīs, beginning with Triguṇī, who are the sovereigns of seven hundred million [realms] each.

"Aṃśās" refers to the retinues; "lords of seven arbudas" means that by the word *arbuda* here, *koṭi* (ten million) is indicated, thus signifying the sovereignty over mantras numbering seven *koṭis*. As it has been said:
Triguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā,
Rūpiṇī, Mardinī, and Jvālā— these seven are their respective lords.
"...and likewise the Vidyārājñīs are proclaimed... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1149). || 340 ||
Above the principle of Vidyā is the principle of Īśvara; therein resides the city that ascends through the sequence, beginning with Śikhaṇḍin and ending with Ananta, consisting of eight cities.
Śikhaṇḍin, Śrīkaṇṭha, Mūrti, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Śivottama, Sūkṣmarudra, and Ananta constitute the group of eight Vidyeśvaras.

The pervasive Lord, Ananta himself, is the leader of the seven who are situated progressively higher and higher; he is to be meditated upon and worshipped, each succeeding one being superior to the last.

"The reality of these" refers to the *Īśvara-tattva*; by implication, it should be understood that the city (*pura*) there also belongs to Īśvara, wherein the Lord Īśvara resides directly. As it has been said:
"Outside of that is the *Īśvara-tattva*; hear from me now about the worlds (*bhuvana*) therein" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1149).
Beginning with these words, it continues: "The Lord, the God, the bestower of boons, whose face is turned in every direction, resides there" (Svacchandatantra 10.1152).
Furthermore, although the eight cities are covered by the enclosure, they are [nevertheless] qualified [by this description].

Regarding the statement, "beginning with Śikhaṇḍin and ending with Ananta," as well as "ascending in sequence," their respective status is due to the progressive increase in qualities (*guṇa*). For while Śikhaṇḍin performs the acts of creation and so forth, Śrīkaṇṭha is superior to him, and Trimūrti and the others are likewise superior to him.

As for what they say—"From that [Śiva], the agency of Ananta is slightly less than his due to his subtlety; from him [comes] that of Śivottama," and so forth—all of this is established here, and therefore this should not be further explained as a fault. Of these...
This is because the arrangement [of the Vidyeśvaras] is heard of in the sequence of the eight directions beginning with the East; as it has been said:

"Henceforth I shall describe the Vidyeśvaras, proceeding in order from the East to the North-East" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1159). In this same manner, their arrangement as ascending higher and higher should also be explained. || 343 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the reason for designating these as *vidyeśvara*s? he says:
"That which exists as the three and a half crores of principal Mantreśvaras—these are their leaders;
therefore, they are the *vidyeśvaras*, the universal sovereigns (*cakravartins*). (8.344)
"Three and a half crores," because at that very moment another three and a half crores had already passed away. As it has been said:
"When the world has fully arisen, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as soon as it is born..."
Three and a half crores of mantras have been ordained by Śiva.
"Having shown grace to the multitude of atoms, they have gone to the state free from affliction. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.40) || 344 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for the primacy of Ananta alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this has been stated by the Gurus in such [teachings] as the *Śivatanu* and others.
By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the *Ruruvārtika* and so forth are included.
He says that very thing:
"The Lord, seated upon the summit of the cave pierced by hundreds of apertures, is joined with eight powers. (8.345)
He creates [the universe] beginning with the Gahana and ending with Niraya, and he appoints the Rudras;
by means of Manonmanī, he uplifts men, yet he remains impartial toward them all. (8.346)
With their minds uplifted by that [initiation], they apply themselves to the contemplation of the supreme reality;
moreover, Śiva has appointed him alone among the individual souls (aṇus) who abide on the lower paths.
Having completed his specific assignment, the Infinite Lord (Anantanātha) attains liberation along with many millions of mantras of various natures; however, Sūkṣmarudra enters that abode.
Having favored the individual soul (aṇu) which was previously unestablished, the Lord establishes it in the position of Śikhaṇḍin;
thus the one Guru proceeds through the eight stations in succession until he reaches the final abode.
In the meantime, they bring about the liberation of countless living beings;
all eight of them sit upon pure lotus-thrones joined with the eight powers.
They behold the God dwelling in the heart, the supreme cause;
meditating upon that Blessed One, the infinite, the peaceful cause within their own hearts. (8.351)
Even seven crores of pure mantras meditate upon it.
[The term] "guhāmūrdha" refers to Śuddhavidyā, which abides above Māyā. The eight powers are Vāmā and the others.
He "employs" the god Ananta and the Rudras, Sūkṣma and the rest, at the beginning of creation.
Regarding "manonmanī," this refers to the ninth [power]. The intention is that the application (*niyoga*) of each of these nine powers is indeed distinct. As it has been said:
"The Supreme Lord is led to the supreme station by Unmanī."

Thus: "standing in the middle" means being neutral; for this very reason, he should perform the creation and other acts for all of these exactly as is appropriate. "Udasta" means stimulated. The particle *eva* (only) is displaced in its position; therefore, it refers specifically to those who abide on the lower path. As it has been said:
"...the Lord Ananta is said to reside in the Asita [tattva].
The term "of manifold nature" (*anekātman*) is an epithet for the millions of mantras. This has been stated in that very same place:
"When that noble splendor of Śaṅkara arises, one ascends into the light of the Lord."
"Many millions of mantras become extinguished once their functional purpose has been fulfilled.

Regarding the word "nirvānti" (they become extinguished): the meaning is that they attain *nirvāṇa* because their task is accomplished and even the desire for further office has ceased. For the Blessed Lord does not forcibly impose an office upon one who lacks the desire for it.
This is the intended meaning. "That abode" refers to the station of Ananta. Sūkṣmarudra is the second. "The subtle one" (aṇum) refers to Vijñānākala. Regarding "Śikhaṇḍin," this refers to the eighth;
for he at that time occupies the station of Śrīkaṇṭha—this is the sense. As it has been stated in that very same work:
There, when Ananta has passed away, those leaders, moving from station to station by the command of the Lord, exercise that authority in succession.
The infinite one ceases [therein], and the subtle Lord presides over that state;
this is the procedure for all mantras, wherein even the subtle state is the supreme Śiva.
"The Lord, having illuminated the nine powers beginning with Vāmā from his own splendor,
and having graced the individual soul (aṇu), establishes him in an unprecedented state in the station of Śikhaṇḍin.
Thus it is said in the venerable Mataṅga as well.
He attains nirvāṇa because his task is accomplished; he is infinite and possesses infinite vigor.
Then, once he has ascended there, Śiva assumes a body composed of the five mantras.
He grants permission to the subtle Vidyeśvara, the high-souled one;
and he, the glorious one who has obtained boons, follows the command of his master.
Established in the infinite state of his own tantra,
the one of great renown brings forth the great wheel below, which consists of the nature of illusion.
In this way, when even Sūkṣma has ceased [his activity], Śiva bestows upon the assembly of Īśas the irreproachable state of being the cause.
For as far as the ultimate limit extends for each great-souled one moving step by step,
so far is the range of the discus.
"Having fashioned the Rudra-atom endowed with the power of Śakti for the sake of non-interruption, he appoints Śikhaṇḍin to that younger station. (Mataṅgapārameśvara 5.62).
Furthermore, as for what was stated [in the Raurava]: "When those great universal monarchs have ceased,

the supreme state, which is the cause of all agency, is established," this should be understood as referring to the context of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), for in that state, everything ceases simultaneously.
"The cessation of all [these]—this was stated previously. Also in the Śrīmataṅga:
'The gods who are the lords of the pure path, the great universal monarchs, having completed their own office, proceed to the supreme state.'"

Thus: "one" means each one. "The supreme deity" refers to Paramaśiva. The word "api" (also/even) is displaced in its position; by it, [it is meant] that there are seven crores of mantras as well. || 351 ||
Now, it has been stated that Ananta alone is authorized over the lower path (*adhara-adhvan*); raising the doubt as to what this lower path—or indeed any other path—is, he says:
"The state of existence (*bhava*) begins with Māyā and ends with Avīci; however, that which begins with Ananta is also called non-existence (*abhava*). (8.352)
This [state] also, ending with the office (*adhikāra*) of the pure qualities of Śiva, is to be abandoned;
that is to say, it extends from Anāśrita and Ananta up to the end of the office. || 8-352 ||
Anticipating the question, "And what is the cause for [the soul] being subject to abandonment here?", he says:
"For even here, the state of being directed by Śiva is observed in those who are to be graced. (8.353)
And its cessation is indeed desired, because non-existence (abhava) does not occur in the lower [levels].
Anticipating the objection, "But if this is so, how then does the term 'non-existence' apply here?", it is said:
"because non-existence does not occur in the lower [levels]. || 353 ||
He explains that very cessation [of duality]:
"Because the state of being a cause and the state of being an effect recede from the Lord for those who have attained perfection. (8.354)
When Śiva is established [as the cause], those two remain perfectly neutral under the designation of "existence" (bhava).

"Causality" (*kāraṇatā*) is the state of being an ordainer; "effectness" (*kāryatā*) is the state of being ordained. "From the Siddhas" means from the liberated individual souls (*aṇu*). "Like a garment" (*kañcukavat*) means like the veil consisting of *māyā*. For that too is likewise [an obscuration].

The sense is that they indeed turn back. Since those two have attained Śiva-hood, because their nature transcends phenomenal existence (*bhava*), they are "extremely neutral" (*atimadhyasthau*), meaning they are utterly indifferent and devoid of the agitation of being the one who enjoins or the one who is enjoined. || 354 ||
Now he speaks of the subject at hand:
"But that city which consists of the fourfold [qualities] of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty... (8.355).
In this reality of Īśvara, they know the notion of the veil of form (rūpāvaraṇasaṃjñā) to be adorned by the three worlds: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. (8.356)
The subtle obscuration has been described by the supreme gurus as residing in the *īśa-tattva*.

By the phrases "in this *aiśvara* [tattva]" and likewise "in the *īśa-tattva*," it is stated that whatever collection of worlds (*bhuvana-jāta*) exists within the *īśvara-tattva* is what must be purified. Thus it has been said:
"Five and ten worlds are to be purified in the Īśvara [tattva] in sequence.
Thus, there are eight worlds of the Vidyeśvaras, four in the Rūpa-āvaraṇa, and three in the Sūkṣma-āvaraṇa; making fifteen in total. Therefore...
Precisely this point, containing the essence of the conclusion, is stated in the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra*:
"Those who, having conquered their senses, practice the divine Pāśupata vow,
attain the state of Īśvara through devotion to the ashes, recitation, and meditation."
"In that regard, the Lord Īśvara, the Blessed One, the God of gods, who is stainless, exercises his authority as impelled by the rule of Śiva’s will. (Svacchandatantra 10.1169).
Thus it has been stated. Also, in the venerable Nandiśikhā:
"In this regard, the Lord Śiva, being thus impelled, possesses the authority; those who are steadfast in the recitation and meditation upon Him go to the state of Īśvara. (356)
From this [arises] Sādāśiva, adorned with the pair of knowledge and action. (8.357)
They say that beyond the aforementioned pure veil (śuddhāvṛti) is the veil of knowledge (vidyāvṛti), which is radiant with the two powers of existence and non-existence. (8.358)
The obscuration of power (śaktyāvṛti), known as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), is therefore described in the scripture;
it is adorned by Tejasvin and Dhruveśa due to that very obscuration of power. (8.359)
Beyond that is the radiant enclosure, then the enclosure of the Vedas, and after that the enclosure of pride;
beyond the enclosure of pride is the enclosure of perfect purity, adorned by the three cities.
Above the enclosure of Suśuddha, there is the single city of Śiva;
they say that above the enclosure of Śiva is that which is known as the enclosure of liberation (mokṣāvaraṇa).
In this enclosure of liberation, eleven Rudras are described;
from the enclosure of liberation, however, the enclosure of Ekapura is fixed.
Above the Dhruva-vṛtti is the enclosure of Icchā; there those Śivas reside within the abode of Īśvara’s will, and that is called their single city. (8.363)
Beyond the enclosure of Icchā is the one called Prabuddha, adorned by the eight Rudras of the directions;
above the enclosure of Prabuddha is the great enclosure of Samaya.
Enveloped by the five worlds and containing within it infinite coverings, there exists the great world called Sādākhya, which is auspicious (sauśiva) due to its conformity with the rule (sāmaya).
In him is the god Sadāśiva; on his right and left [sides] are Knowledge and Action, while the Supreme Will is the Śakti who rests upon his lap.
By that very will, he performs the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with creation;
[he manifests as] the five Brahmās, the six limbs, the eight [forms] beginning with Sakala, and the Śivas. (8.367)
The ten and eighteen Rudras are surrounded by those very [deities];

this is the principle (tattva) called Sādāśiva, and they say that therein lies the Pure Enclosure (śuddhāvaraṇa)—this is the connection [of the words]. "Beyond the Pure Enclosure" means above the Pure Enclosure—this is the meaning.

"Vidyāvṛtiḥ" means the veil of knowledge (*vidyāvaraṇa*). As it has been said: "The designation 'existence' is actually called 'non-existence'; within that, a dual power resides. From "thence" means from the veil of knowledge; therefore, above that.

"The obscuration of power (*śaktyāvṛti*) and, beyond that, the obscuration of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇāvṛti*). Regarding the word "in the scripture" (*śāstre*), because no specific [limit] is mentioned, it applies everywhere. In that regard, there are two Rudras in the obscuration of power. As it has been said:
"Tejasvīśa and Dhruveśa are the supreme state of the means of knowledge" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1172).

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the reading observed by Uddyotakara—“*śaktyāvaraṇam ūrdhvaṃ ca*” and “*pramāṇāvaraṇaṃ cordhvam*” —is incorrect, because it has not been accepted by the great community of scholars (*mahājana*). Also, in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*:

"Tejeśvara and Dhruveśa are situated within the enclosure of Śakti"—this is our own reading. Anticipating the question, "What is the basis for applying the term 'pramāṇāvaraṇa' (the enclosure of the means of knowledge) here?", it is stated: "the enclosure of the radiant" (*tejasvyāvaraṇam*).

For Tejeśa and Dhruveśa are the supreme station of the eight means of knowledge (pramāṇas) situated within the principle of Māyā; of these two as well, this [level] is the second outer enclosure. "Vedapurā" refers to four worlds.
As it has been said:
"Brahmā, Rudra, Pratoda, and Ananta as the fourth" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1173).
Also, in the venerable Nandiśikhā:
"Brahmā, Rudra, the one called Pramāṇa, Pratoda, and the one named Ananta."

"For these four are proclaimed as the obscurations of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇāvaraṇa). The term "suśuddhāvṛt" means the "obscuration of supreme purity" (suśuddhāvaraṇa). As it has been said:
"Above that is the obscuration of supreme purity; therein they know the triad of Rudras."
"The one-eyed, tawny swan has thus been described in brief" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1174).
"The city of Śiva" means the enclosure of Śiva— this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"Above the enclosure of Śiva, there is one known as Dhruva" (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1174).
Regarding the phrase "eleven," these are Brahmā and the others. As it has been stated:
Brahmadaṇḍin, Diṇḍimuṇḍa, Saurabha, and likewise Janmamṛtyuhara; Praṇīta is the giver of both happiness and suffering.
"They are declared to be the manifestations... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1177).
"The enclosure is Dhruva" means the enclosure of Dhruva. "They" refers to all those mentioned from this point down to the earth—this is the meaning.
"She who dwells within the house of the Lord's will" means, in other words, that she is of one form with Him. It is with this very intention [it is said]:
"The manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self of the Lord exists indeed;
without that, the reflective awareness of will does not proceed" (Rijuvimarsini 1.5.10).
This and more has been stated elsewhere. Regarding the term "one": it is so called because it is to be presided over by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) alone.
"Named *prabuddha*" refers to the veil (*āvaraṇa*). As it has been said: "I shall now briefly describe the *prabuddha* veil above."
Prīta, Pramudita, Pramoda, and Pralambana.
"Viṣṇu, Madana, Gahana, and likewise Prathita;
these are declared to be the group of eight Rudras, to be known [as presiding] over the eastern direction in sequence. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1180)
Thus; the ellipsis is that [the world] is endowed with five worlds. As it has been said: "Prabhava, Samaya, Kṣudra, Vimala, and Śiva;
after that, Ghana is declared, and beyond this, Nirañjana."
"These five Rudras are indeed the syllable Oṃ... (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1182).

Regarding the phrase "encompassing the infinite enclosures," it is stated that whatever exists above as a remainder of all things exists by encompassing everything below within itself. This is the state of Śiva.

Thus ends the enclosure of Suśiva. "The world named Śāda" means that it is the direct abode of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva; for this very reason, it is called "great. Furthermore, by the author of the Uddyota:
Having postulated the half-verse, "And likewise above Īśvara, and below Sadāśiva," (*Svacchanda Tantra* 10.1186),

the claim made from this point onward that "the principle [beginning] here is Sādāśiva" is incorrect, because this half-verse has not been accepted by the great authorities. And for this very reason, even in this way...

The word "above" (*ūrdhvam*) is redundant, and the phrase "and always below Sadāśiva" is also inconsistent, since that has already been stated in that very context. Even if it were not intended [to be redundant], this must be explained somehow or other as follows: "of the Lord" refers to Rudra, who is the syllable *Oṃ*; "from Sadāśiva" refers to the presiding deity.
For that which is to be presided over must indeed be situated below the presider. As for what is stated in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*, namely:
"The reality of Īśvara has been described; above that is Sadāśiva," this too should be understood in this way: that which belongs to Īśvara is [the level of] Sādāśiva, and Sadāśiva is...

Regarding the phrase "standing there directly": otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the concluding passage on the *īśvaratattva* in both cases; therefore, one should not be misled by the commentary of Uddyotakara, who suggests that "the path well-trodden by the great masters must be followed"—enough said.
In short: "In that" refers to the world called Sadākhya; "Śuśivaḥ" is Sadāśiva;
he is surrounded by a fourfold sequence of enclosures. || 367 ||
He recites this very sequence: "Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna constitute the five Brahmans; [the mantra] 'Hṛdayam' [is the heart]. (8.368)
They say there are six limbs: the Head, the Crest, the Armor, the Eye, the Weapon, and the Limb;
together with the Sakala, Akala, Śūnya, Kalāḍhya, and Kha, the final one is Kṣapaṇa. (8.369)
The eighth is said to be labial; thus this entire group of eight is traditionally taught.
[The others are] Oṃkāra and Śiva, Dīpta, Hetvīśa and Daśeśaka, and Suśiva and Kāla.
Sūkṣma, Sutejas, Śarva, and Śiva—these ten [faces] here, starting from the east;
then Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, Vahni, Vīra, and Raurava. (8.371)
Mukuṭa, Visarendra, Induvindu, Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, Rudra, Santāna, Śiva, Parakiraṇa, and Apārameśa—these are remembered as the Rudras. (8.372)
The knowledges of all these are known by names identical to their own.

"Akala" means partless (niṣkala). "Kṣayānta" means that which exists at the end, at the conclusion. "Hetvīśa" is the Lord of Causes; "sūkṣma" means having a subtle form. The word "of all" refers to the Śivas.
And because of the Rudras, Śaivism is said to be divided into ten and eighteen branches. || 372 ||
Then [he saw] the All-pervasive Lord, surrounded by ten million sages of mantra, together with Vāma, Ādi, Rudra, and their respective Śaktis.
The seat of Suśiva is an exceedingly white lotus with countless petals, graced by the powers (śaktis) beginning with Tārā;
and the host of Śaktis and Rudras constitutes the retinue and the cushion of Suśiva.
Each one of these has, within their respective retinues, countless millions of parārdhas;
they are liberated from the impurity of māyā and are established solely in their respective offices.
In the enclosure of Suśiva, the Rudras are omniscient and fully endowed with all powers;
upon the dissolution of the bond of office, they become peaceful, identical with Śiva, and free from rebirth. (8.376)
The "Sages" (munis) are seven; the "Rudras" are those situated in the enclosures and so forth. || 376 ||
Above is the radiant enclosure of the Bindu; there, in each place, is a lotus with the luster of the moon.
There resides Śiva, beyond the state of Peace (Śāntyatīta), adorned by the lap of his Śakti.
He is surrounded by a retinue consisting of the groups of kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti;
he is encompassed by countless Rudras and their Śaktis, along with millions of Puras.

"Above" means from the enclosure of Suśiva. "Its power" refers to Śāntyatītā. As it has been said: "O lady of excellent vows, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti are remembered as the retinue of that Śāntyatīta."
"In its leftward direction, however, Śāntyatītā is situated. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1621) || 378 ||
And this has been stated by way of another formulation; thus he says:
"In the venerable Mataṅgaśāstra, the supreme reality called *laya* (dissolution) is here referred to by the technical name *bindu*. (8.379)

That supreme principle called *laya*, which is indeed this very [reality] manifested externally due to its association with qualities such as being the creator of all, is here termed *bindu* according to the technical terminology of our own scripture;
the meaning is that such a convention has been established for it in the venerable *Matanga-pārameśvara*.
As it was said there: "Therefore, that supreme reality is immovable and faces in all directions;
for one who has attained it, there is never again birth here."
Thus:
"In this manner, from that virtuous reality (tattva), there arises another irreproachable reality,
great and pervasive below, enriched with thousands of shimmering rays."
"This is called by the technical name 'Bindu';
it exists here in four states, impelling [all things] and immutable in every respect. || 379 ||
But surely, here [it is said]: "Because of the mention of the three principles called *laya*, *bhoga*, and *adhikāra* belonging to the Lord (*pati*),
this category named *pati* is proclaimed as the first" (Mataṅga).
[If one asks: "In that case, if this is so, then where again does its nature as experience (*bhoga*) and so forth reside?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which consists of the four forms, which is pure, and which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*)."
In that regard, enjoyment has been fully described; this is what has been explained here. (8.380)
Although this [reality] possesses four forms consisting of withdrawal (nivṛtti) and the rest, it is stainless because it transcends them;
for this very reason, despite being "with parts" (sakala), it is the partless (niṣkala) state because it is dissolved into the supreme reality itself.
In that regard, enjoyment (bhoga) is taught therein; thus, the principle of Sadāśiva is its locus of enjoyment. This is what is meant here.
This very point has been stated in the *Śrīmataṅgaśāstra*. As it is said there:
"The absorption (*laya*) of the Lord Śadāśiva occurs in the principle (*tattva*) that is utterly partless (*ati-niṣkala*).
That which consists of the four forms, radiant, is the 'partless-with-parts' (*sakala-niṣkala*)."
"In that [state], enjoyment is ordained for the Lord of the universe at all times" (Mataṅga 1.3.23).
It follows by implication that the locus of authority for the city is Vidyā and the rest. As it is said in that very same place:
In the state of *laya*, there is the principle known as Śiva-tattva; in manifestation (*vyakti*), the stage called Bindu;
enjoyment (*bhoga*) occurs in the station of Sadāśiva; and sovereignty (*śāsana*) resides in the station called Īśvara.
"For his authority over this womb [of creation] must always be understood as residing in the principle of Vidyā" (Mataṅga 1.7.33).
Now, one might object: "Is not 'possessing all parts' defined as the fitness for a body extending from the *kalā* principle down to the earth?
If that is possible for the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, why is his own nature as earth and so forth not perceived, just as it is for people like us? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because the state of having a body composed of earth and the other elements is extremely subtle due to the cessation [of the gross senses] and so forth,
it is not perceived by the mother, as she is absorbed in a surging, great gnosis.
"Of the Mother" refers to the venerable Lord Sadāśiva. The reason for the subtlety of Nivṛtti and the other kalās is: "because they are dissolved within the flashing Great Knowledge. || 381 ||
"Is it not a contradiction that the state of being earth and so forth, while present here, is not perceived?"— anticipating this objection, he says:
"Because of the predominance of the fiery element, the atoms of earth in gold..."
Just as they do not appear as separate, so too [the worlds] situated in the upper, lower, and vast bodies [of Rudra].

Just as, due to the predominance of the fiery atoms (*tejaḥ-paramāṇu*) in gold, the earth-atoms (*bhū-paramāṇu*), though present, do not appear separately because their hardness and other qualities cannot otherwise be accounted for, so too [the elements] do not appear because they are eclipsed by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*).
The meaning of the statement "even those residing in the bodies of the respective lords of the worlds [exist] within the creation consisting of the pure and impure self" has been explained.
Now, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"Above the Bindu is the Half-moon; its digit is Jyotsnā, and she possesses that [Half-moon]."
Kānti, Prabhā, and Vimalā—these five are then the obstructors.
Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Roddhrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā—these five kalās, the best of gurus declare, reside within Nirodhinī. (8.384)
"Tadvatī" means possessing moonlight; "tataḥ" means even above the crescent moon. || 384 ||
Since the half-moon and the other [symbols] are of the nature of the object of the mantra, it is entirely appropriate that they demonstrate a progressively subtler and more subtle form; thus it says:
"The Bindu is remembered as having half a measure (ardhamātra), while the Vyoman has four measures (catuṣkala) and is of the nature of space."
Half of that is the half-moon, and one-eighth of that is the *nirodhikā*.
"Half of that" means a fourth part of a *mātrā*; "by an eighth part of that" means by an eighth part of a *mātrā*.
He explains the very term *nirodhikā*:
"One should abandon that *nirodhikā* which obstructs the causes beginning with Brahmā;
having pierced through this *nirodhikā*, one reaches the supreme world called Sādākhya. (8.386)

"Where the Great Body of the Five Mantras abides in its supreme form"—the word "causes" (*hetūn*) refers to the causal factors. Regarding "in its supreme form": it has been stated that her supreme form indeed resides within the enclosure of Suśiva. (386)
He describes its location and form:
"Thus, above the circle of the bindu at the end of the half-moon and the nirodhinī, there is the Great One. (8.387)
The Nāda is like a lotus filament and is surrounded by great beings;
here, there are four worlds in the cardinal directions and a fifth in the center.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rodhikā, Mocikā, and Urdhvagā;
here in the center is the lotus, and there resides the one who goes upward, surrounded by those powers.
Above the nāḍī, however, is the sauṣumna; there resides the Lord who sustains that power, the Master, surrounded on the left and right by Piṅgalā and Iḍā.
The goddess Suṣumnā, who rests upon the lap of the Lord and possesses the splendor of the moon,
has strung together the entire path, both upward and downward.
The Nāda, supported by the Suṣumnā, having pierced this entire universe,
emerges from below by means of the downward power (adhaḥśakti) and from the crown of the head by means of the upward power (ūrdhvaśakti).
Dissolved in the Brahma-aperture through the channel, that unmanifest, imperishable sound resounds within all beings, indeed presided over by the power of Śiva.

Thus, it would have been said that the Half-moon (ardhendu) and the Obstructive (nirodhinī) are the very expansion of the Bindu. By the phrase "by the great persons," those who possess the form of the Lords of Mantras (mantramaheśvara) are meant. Their power is that which moves upward.
As it has been stated:
"In that [lotus] there is a very wide lotus, and the Lord, the Master of the Upper Region, resides there. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1224).
"But his power, which moves upwards, is eternally seated upon his lap. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1226).

And thus: "Sauṣumna" is the world-realm (*bhuvana*). "Its power" is Suṣumnā. "Its lord" is Suṣumneśa. "Interwoven" means pervaded by way of being woven lengthwise and crosswise. "Above" consists of Śakti and Śiva; "below" begins with Nādānta and so forth. And of this [Suṣumnā], it is precisely between the upper and lower [extremes] that...
He demonstrates its pervasiveness with the words, "Sound has the *suṣumnā* as its support," and so forth. Here, indeed, sound, presiding over the central channel called *suṣumnā*,

having risen from below by means of the downward power (*adhaḥśakti*) and attained awakening from the *mūlādhāra*, [pervades] all this through the upward power (*ūrdhvaśakti*) consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Having pierced the world by means of a sequence that transcends its respective causes, one should emerge from the top— that is, from above— of that very channel called Suṣumṇā; thereby, having come to rest at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila),
one [resides] within all beings.
"There is no one who utters it, nor is there anyone who obstructs it; the Lord, residing in the chest of living beings, utters it Himself. (Svacchanda Tantra 7.58).
According to this teaching, He resounds; and for that very reason, because no other nature such as a distinct sound arises, it is an unmanifest resonance (*avyaktadhvani*).

For this very reason, because its nature is immovable, it is "indestructible" (*akṣara*); since it is presided over by Śiva-Śakti, its essence consists solely of supreme consciousness—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Nāda, indeed, whose support is the *nāḍī*, having pierced through this entire universe..."
Having emerged from below by means of the downward power (adhaḥśakti), it reaches as far as Brahmā above.
"Dissolved in the Brahma-aperture through the channel, the unmanifest and imperishable sound resounds within all beings, presided over by the power of Śiva. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1233). || 393 ||
Above the Suṣumṇā is the enclosure known as the Brahmabila, which has three eyes.
Therein resides Brahmā, white in color, bearing a trident, five-faced, and crowned with the moon. (8.394)
On his lap is the supreme goddess Brahmāṇī, who follows the path to liberation;
she is both the obstructress and the bestower of liberation.
The word "there" refers to the enclosure of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*). The phrase "following the path to liberation" means she is situated upon that path.
This is the meaning. For this very reason, its capacity for both obstructing and bestowing that [liberation] has been stated: "She is the obstructress and the giver of liberation. || 394 ||
Having pierced that [center], the Kuṇḍalinī moves upward.
Śakti is like a sleeping serpent and is called the support of the universe;
within her reside the subtle (sūkṣmā) and the extremely subtle (susūkṣmā), as well as others, namely Amṛtā and Amitā.
Pervasive in the center, within that [space] resides Vyāpīśa, the sustainer of Vyāpinī.

"Having pierced that" means "thereupon, upwards. It is called *ūrdhvakuṇḍalī* (the upward-coiled) because she contains within her womb this entire universe in its unmanifest state; for this very reason—

It has been said that [this state] is "like a sleeping serpent"; for this very reason, because the universe unfolds from its own very wall [of consciousness], it is called the "support of the universe. By the word "power" (*śakti*), it is indicated that from this point onward is the *śakti-tattva*. This has been stated in the venerable *Nandiśikhā*:
"Thereafter, learn from me the Śakti-tattva as it is being described:
it has the form of a sleeping serpent and possesses a luster like that of a spider's thread."
"The support of all principles (tattvas) and of the worlds, O lady of excellent vows. Regarding the phrase "in her," it refers to Śakti. As it has been said:
"She is indeed Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtā and Amitā."
"The pervasive one (Vyāpinī) is to be known as being in the center; the remaining [powers] are in order from the east onwards. (Svacchanda Tantra 10.1290).
Regarding the phrase "in her," it means in Vyāpinī. As for "the Lord of the Pervasive One" (Vyāpīśa), his position is in the eastern direction relative to Anāśritabhairava. || 396 ||
Now, it is beyond dispute that the pervasive [power] is distinct from Śakti; therefore, one might ask:
does she reside within the very principle of Śakti (śaktitattva), or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This principle of Śakti is that of which this entire expansion, ending with the earth, is the manifestation. (8.397)
Beyond that is the Śiva-tattva; there, situated in the four directions, are Vyāpin, Vyomātman, Ananta, and Anātha, who partake in its power.

In the center, however, is the Anāśrita (the Unsupported); there indeed resides the God of gods, the Anāśrita, who holds his Śakti in his lap and possesses a splendor equal to hundreds of millions of suns.

The phrase "the principle of power" (śaktitattva) refers to the world-sphere of Anāśrita. The word "thence" (tataḥ) means by relying upon that very principle of power; for that [world-sphere] is indeed situated within the Vyāpinī [aspect] of the principle of power—this is the sense. The word "there" (tatra) refers to the world-sphere of Anāśrita.
"Her powers" are Vyāpinī and the others. "Anāśrita" refers to the world-level (*bhuvana*). "Her power" is Anāśritā. As it has been said:
"Vyāpinī, whose form is space, and Anantānātha are indeed Anāśritā" (Svacchandatantra 10.1250).
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, if the term *śivatattva* were explained by its own literal meaning (*svārthavṛtti*), then everything would be contradicted; for it is said:
"In this way, O lady of good vows, the *śivatattva* has indeed been described to you."
Having purified [the path], one should then proceed upwards; she is indeed remembered as the supreme Śakti.
By such statements as "She is to be known as Samanā...
(Svacchanda Tantra 10.1254), it is shown that Samanā pervades even above the Śiva-tattva. Regarding that [state], it is said:
"O Varārohā, within that [state] ending with Śamanā, there is an infinite web of bonds. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.429).
Because of such statements, an infinite web of bonds (*pāśajāla*) would follow as a consequence. Thus [it is said]:

"O fair-faced one, while casting down the path to be abandoned (*heyādhvan*), one should exhale (*recayet*) until that energy (*śakti*) is *samanā*; above that, she is known as *unmanā*" (Svacchandatantra 10.1271).

Statements such as these would be contradicted; furthermore, passages like "The Supreme Śiva is at the end of Unmanā" would also be undermined, because [Samanā] has already been stated to be below that, and if it were also a separate category (tattva), [the hierarchy would be disrupted].

[If one were to claim there are] thirty-six principles (*tattva*s), this would constitute a loss of the initial proposition. For there is no *samanā* above or within this *śiva-tattva*; rather, it is traditionally taught that below it lies only the *śakti-tattva*. As it has been said:
"Then, O fair-faced one, *śakti* is to be installed by means of the *praṇava*."
"One should purify Vyāpinī and Samanā right there above.
If Anāśrita and the others were to abide within the Śiva-tattva, then even that [Śiva-tattva] would fall under the sway of time, for they are subject to decay. As was stated previously:
Śakti dissolves again into Vyāpinī when her own time has passed;
that day-and-night within Vyāpinī dissolves into Anāśrita.
Having multiplied the time of Śakti by ten million parārdhas in the Anāśrita [Kalā], that becomes a day and a night;
and even when multiplied by a parārdha, it remains the same duration of time.
"He too goes to dissolution in the state called Sāmya, which is beyond the mind" (Tantrāloka 6.166).
And therefore:
"Above the Unmanifested Mind (unmana), there is no time."
No conceptual construction occurs for him who is partless and devoid of time.

Otherwise, scriptural passages such as "He who is beyond Śāṅkarya and Unmanā is eternal, all-pervasive, and immutable" would be contradicted. Furthermore, there is no abiding of Anāśrita and the others within the Śiva-tattva;
rather, they reside only within the Śakti-tattva, specifically in Vyāpinī. As it has been said:
"Below that, O Goddess, is the Brahmabilam; beyond that is the Śaktitattva.
Then there is Vyāpinī, joined with the five causes, and likewise the supreme [Parā]."
"O Dear One, the Samanā and Unmanā [energies] are indeed joined with the Prakriyā and the Aṇḍas.
Therefore, the explanation stated by us alone is correct; everything else should be disregarded. (8-399)
Above the Śiva-tattva is that supreme Śakti called Samanā;
she stands established as the agent of all causes. (8.400)
She bears many eggs presided over by Śiva;

the phrase "above the Śivatattva" means she is situated in the plane of Vyāpinī, even above the world of Anāśrita. Nor, in this very context, does the word *tattva* denote a world (*bhuvana*) as something previously unestablished.

Because such usage is also observed in passages such as, "The reality of the *bindu* is fully explained... (*Svacchanda Tantra* 10.1217), [the author] clarifies that [the *bindu*] is indeed its substratum, since it consists of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) and thus functions as the agent.
Mounted upon that, the Lord Śiva performs the fivefold cosmic act.
"Śiva" refers to him who is proclaimed everywhere as the nature of the thirty-six principles (tattvas). || 401 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But having ascended to this [level], why would he perform creation and so forth?", he says:
"Samanā is the instrument of that Great Lord, who is both the cause and the agent."
"Karaṇa" means [the instrument] in the activity of creation and so forth.

Now, one might object: "If in every action there were a dependence on another agent, then the agent would be a cause; and if this were the case for the Great Lord as well, his sovereignty would be undermined by his being oriented toward something higher. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But that which is not dependent upon an operation is called the efficient cause (nimittahetu). || 8-402 ||

"In activity" means in the acts of creation and so forth. For here, that very Supreme Lord, by virtue of His own sovereignty, first manifests the nature of the void and becomes renowned in the form of Anāśrita (the Unsupported) and the others; thus, since there is an absence of anything else to be depended upon, this [Lord] alone possesses ultimate reality.

Agency is pure [in the case of Śiva]; however, for Anāśrita and the others, agency—which pertains to distinct effects due to the influence of that [Śiva's] presiding power—is impure and consists primarily of a metaphorical attribution. Consequently, Anāśrita and the others perform creation and so forth solely by His will; such is His [agency].
Because direct entry into that [state] is impossible, it serves there merely as a cause (*nimitta*), just as in the case of fame resulting from knowledge, and so forth;
thus it has been said: "The cause (*hetu*) is the motive (*nimitta*). As they say:
"But when not directly dependent on the operation, the cause is accepted as the motive."
Thus [ends the section]. || 402 ||
Even with respect to that substratum, his instrument is indeed the *samana*—thus he says:
"The All-pervasive Lord presides over the pentad of causes.
"He presides" means that [the pentad] becomes fit for performing emission and so forth through being permeated by the shadow of His own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
The meaning is that one should perform [it].
And how is this so? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Always unattached, consisting of the Lordless (anātha), infinite, and having the nature of space. (8.403)
He impels the pervasive [Prakṛti] by means of his own power as an instrument;
below that is Māyā, which exists in the form of karma, where the Śakti-kuṇḍalinī resides.
"The emergence of the world begins with the effects such as *nāda* and *bindu*.

'Khavapuḥ' means having the nature of space; 'by its own power' (*svaśaktyā*) refers to this: for instance, at the beginning of Śiva’s creation, *samanā* is the instrument, and likewise for these [deities], their respective powers are the *anāśrita* and so forth. 'In the form of action' (*karmarūpā*)."

The intention is this: because it qualifies specific acts such as creation and so forth, it is indeed the supreme Lord’s power of *māyā* that flashes forth as the universal form consisting of various *nāda*s and *bindu*s.
It is called "the *Kuṇḍalinī* of Power" (*śaktikuṇḍalī*) because it encompasses the entire universe within itself through identity with its own self. (404)
And this entire universe is indeed to be abandoned; thus he says:
"That which, within the teaching, begins with the earthly element and extends up to Sadāśiva. (8.405)
All that is declared to be *prākṛta* (evolvent), characterized by both destruction and origination.
Here, Sadāśiva is the *anāśrita* (the unsupported), and *prakṛti* is *samanā*, because it alone is the root evolvent (*mūlaprakṛti*).

Having thus stated the two objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of the conjunction of the worlds (*pura*) and the principles (*tattva*), [the author now states] that which is called the summary of the worlds (*purasaṃgraha*).
He begins to set forth the object of knowledge (prameya): "Now, that which is the measure of the entire universe, as it was declared to me by my own gurus... (8.406).
That will be stated concisely so that [the meaning] may quickly enter the intellect.
By the word "by which," he means by means of a concise statement; therefore, the intention is that this is not purposeless.
He says that very thing:
"Within the egg are Ananta, Kāla, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, and Hari. (8.407)
The Rudras are one hundred, along with the heroes; the withdrawal (nivṛtti) consists of one hundred and eight worlds.
In each of the seven—water, fire, air, ether, ego, intellect, and the root—there are [eight]. (8-408)
Eighty-six worlds constitute that which is called the *kalā* of *pratiṣṭhā*.
Regarding this, some say that eight [deities] from one's own group of eight lords are to be purified here. (8.409)
Others, however, describe all the worlds as being subject to purification;
furthermore, the venerable teachers, the Bhūtirāja-miśras, state that there are one hundred Rudras in the external [world].
"Eight together with everything"—such would be this withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). [The deities of the other kalās are:
the Rudras, Kālī, Vīra, Earth, Ocean, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Guhya. (8.411)
Thus, there is the group of eight in Water; the two very secret [mantras] of Fire in Fire; those of Vāyu in Wind;
its own city [Svapura] and Gayā and so forth in Space; and the pair of worlds [Bhuvanayuga] as the eight purifiers in the Void.

Within the ego (ahaṃkāra), there is the group of eight beginning with pride (abhimāna) and the goat; then, from the ego, arise space, the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sun, the moon, the Vedas, and the eight cities belonging to the deities of the intellect and the organs of action.

There is one world for each of the ten subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and another for each of the group of organs; thus, including the world of the mind and that of ego-consciousness (*abhimāna*), there are exactly twenty-two worlds. (8.414)

In the intellect (dhi) are the eight [forms] of the divine powers; the three known as Krut-tejas and Yoga are Umā; then her husband, followed by the eight Mūrtis, the twelve Suśivas, and Vīrabhadra. (8-415)
Then, including the group of eight Mahādevas, there are seventeen in the intellect (*buddhi*);
in the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*), there are three rows, so they know there are fifty-six cities. (8.416)
The connection is that "within and outside the egg (aṇḍa), there should be the Nivṛtti [kalā] consisting of one hundred and eight worlds.
Alternatively, the word *antaḥ* has already been explained. As it has been said:
"Within Nivṛtti is the Earth, extending for a hundred koṭis [of yojanas]."
"And in that [world], there are one hundred and eight worlds at most" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.103).

Regarding "eight," the meaning is the seven groups of eight, beginning with the Guhyāṣṭaka and ending with the Yogāṣṭaka. By the word "ten" (tena), it refers to the multiplication of the group of seven by eight. As it has been said:

"In the *Pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], there is a pervasion consisting of twenty-four principles (*tattva*) and fifty-six worlds (*bhuvana*)... (Svacchanda Tantra 4.149). Here, "in the *Pratiṣṭhā*" means within that [kalā]. "Eight" refers to [the eight Rudras] together with the group of eight Krodhas.

"All" refers even to the fifty-six; they are "mixed," meaning they are primary. "By Śarva" means by the lord of the Bhūrloka; thus, there is an equality in enumeration because he [Śarva] occupies the place of Vīrabhadra.
"Rudras" are eleven. "Secret" (guhya) refers to the world-sphere of the Guhyāṣṭaka. "In between" (antarā).
"Sky and ego" means within the sky and the ego—this is the meaning. "The subtle elements" refers to five;
"of the deities of intellect and action" means of the ten [senses] consisting of the faculties of cognition and action—this is the meaning.
"A world within the collection of subtle elements" refers to that which is called the mandala of the five objects—this is the meaning.
One might ask: "Even though these [five] pentads of worlds have already been mentioned, why is this stated again? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
"fallen into the group of the senses. The meaning is that while for those [others] this occurs solely through the presiding of the mind (*manas*), here there is an abiding even in a higher form.

"Known as Krodha, Tejas, and Yoga" refers, by implication, to the three worlds governed by the triad of eight [deities] beginning with Krodha; "three rows" refers to the subjects, namely the gurus and disciples. Regarding "fifty-six cities," there are eight worlds in the water-tattva, and [the rest] in the triad of tattvas beginning with fire.
Two for each [of the five elements], making six; twenty-two in the ego (ahaṅkāra); seventeen in the intellect (buddhi); and three in the qualities (guṇas). || 416 ||

Now, one might object: "If the worlds are said to be purified within all the principles (tattvas) starting from water and so forth, why are they not mentioned as such within *prakṛti*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even though the group of eight Lords of Wrath (*krodheśvarāṣṭaka*) resides in the Root [Nature], which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmyātman*), nevertheless [they are purified] in the intellect (*dhiyi*)."
That [number] has been subtracted; it does not again reach the count in the *pratiṣṭhā* [tattva]. || 8-417 ||
Thus, from the water-tattva up to the root, there are twenty-four tattvas in the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.
[These consist of] the group of Tuṣṭis beginning with Ambā, the Siddhis beginning with Tārā, and the group of powers beginning with Aṇimā. (8.418)

The gurus, the disciples of the gurus, the host of sages, and the eightfold forms beginning with Iḍā; the city of transformations such as smell and so forth, the eight qualities of the intellect, the ego-function, and the qualities of the sense objects;
the twenty-seven adventitious factors beginning with desire, as well as those consisting of Gaṇeśa and Vidyeśa.
Thus, there are three cities within the nooses; in this manner, there are sixteen worlds here within the Puruṣa.
In Niyati there are the two cities of Śaṅkara-daśaka and Kāla-śivadaśaka;
in Rāga is the world of Suhaṣṭa; and in the pair of Vit and Kalā are the cities of Guru and Śiṣya.
Each world [consists of] three cities at night: the city of speech and the city of valid cognition.
Thus, the Vidyā [tattva] consists of twenty-seven cities, joined with the seven principles beginning with Puruṣa. (8.422)
The subtle form of Vāmeśa is pure, the object of knowledge, and measured by the splendor of Śakti;
Suviśuddhi, Śiva, Mokṣa, Dhruva, Īśa, Saṃbuddha, Samaya, and Sauśiva are the names [of these].
The seventeen cities are the Śānta [tattva], joined with the triad of the cities of Vidyeśa and Sadāśiva.
The Bindu, Ardhacandra, and Nirodhī are located in the Parasauśiva; Indhikā and the others are in the Puras of the Suṣumnā.
Then there is Paranāda, the Brahmabila, the Śakti known as Ūrdhvakundalī together with Sūkṣmā and the others, the pervasive Vyoma, Ananta, Anātha, and Anāśrita—these are the five cities. (8.425)
And the sixth is the supreme Anāśrita; then either the sixteen worlds of Samanā, or the Bindvāvaraṇa, the supreme Sauśiva, and the five worlds beginning with Indhika.
Sauṣumna, Brahmabila, Kuṇḍalinī, Vyāpinī, Pañcaka, and Samanā—these constitute the sixteen worlds; this pair of principles (tattvas) is Śāntyatītā. || 8-427 ||
The "twenty-four principles" (*tattva-caturviṃśati*) are so called because the fundamental principle (*prakṛti-tattva*) is twofold, being both agitated and unagitated.

Regarding "the gurus," therein too, three rows concerning the relationship between guru and disciple have been mentioned. Regarding "objects," the five [qualities] beginning with sound (*śabda*), which were explained immediately after the sixteen transformations (*vikāra-ṣoḍaśaka*), are the *guṇas*.

Non-violence and the other [virtues] previously mentioned are included as being properties of the body. The particle *ca* (and) serves as a conjunction; by it, within the principle of *rāga*, there are two worlds (*bhuvana*): the world of Vīreśa and the world of the Guru and Disciple. Each "world" refers to the ninefold group of powers beginning with Vāmā and the triad of Great Deities (*mahādeva*). "The three cities of the *puṭas*" refers to this.
Its threefold nature consists of the city of speech, which is the world of Vāgīśī known as the Yoni. Regarding the phrase "the twenty-seven cities," it has been said:
"The pervasion of Vidyā is held to extend from the principle of the individual soul (puruṣa-tattva) up to the limit of Māyā."
"The seven principles (tattvas) and indeed the twenty-seven worlds. (Svacchanda Tantra 4.173).

"Vāmā" refers to the nine powers beginning with Vāmā. "Īśaḥ" means Īśvara. Everything beginning with "rūpa" up to the end of the enclosure (āvaraṇa) has been previously explained. And this measure (miti), which is primarily characterized by radiance, is the enclosure of the means of knowledge (mānāvaraṇa).
—this is the meaning. "Iṣiḥ" means desire. Regarding "in the seventeen cities," it has been said:
"From the principle of Vidyā [arises] Sadāśiva;
there is pervasion across three principles, and likewise only three phonemes."
"The eleven stages are to be known as the seventeen cities" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.185).

Regarding "Parasauśiva," it is where Sadāśiva exists in his supreme form. "Anāśrita" (the Unsupported) is so called because it is the support of all. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "yadi vām" (if for you two), it refers to the sixteen worlds; as it has been said:
"One step is one mantra, proclaimed to have sixteen phonemes;
one should contemplate the extremely subtle worlds within the Śāntyatīta [kalā]. (Svacchandatantra 4.197).
Thus [ends verse 427].
Having thus explained the division according to the procedure of the *Śrī-svacchanda*, he also speaks by way of another scripture:
"And in the venerable *Mataṅga-śāstra*, this sequence consists of a multitude of cities. The word "this" refers to that which is about to be described.
Thus he says:
"The fires of time, the hells, and the principal [worlds] numbering one hundred and four. (8.428)
Kūṣmāṇḍa, Saptapātālī, Saptalokī, and Maheśvara—such is the interior of the egg; outside of that, one hundred Rudras are situated. (8.429)
Two hundred and fifty-seven locations constitute the ground;
from the midst of five groups of eight, thirty-two are within the four primary elements.
In the subtle elements (tanmātras), there are five Viśvedevas; from there, the [next] eight [are assigned].
In the ego (garva) together with the senses, the fifth [set]; in the intellect (buddhi), the eight deities; and in the [guṇas], the qualities.
The eight Yogas known as Krodhas are led by Mūla at the time [of dissolution];
and Patadru and the others, beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra, reside within the principle of Rāga.
In the Vidyā-kalana, there are twelve [deities] beginning with Ekaśiva; in the Kalanā, there are ten.
This [Vidyā] consists of three hundred [deities] beginning with Vāmā, and it possesses three joints (parvan) and is joined with the ocean (four) and the arrows (five).

"Khābdhi" means forty. Maheśvara is Rudra. "The fifth group of eight" refers to that known as Sthāṇu. There are eight beginning with Patadrūka, and also eight beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra. "In the reckoning" (kalane) means in the context of the digits (kalā). "Three-jointed" (triparvaṇī) means by means of the three known as the elements (bhūta), the states of being (bhāva), and the principles (tattva).

In that which is composed of sections (*parva*), extending from the *kalā*s down to the earth (*kṣiti*), there exists a third category of entities in relation to the categories beginning with the Lord (*pati*). As it is stated in that very same work:
"Those known as the elements (*bhūta*), states of being (*bhāva*), and principles (*tattva*), which have always flowed forth from Māyā..."
"That category consists of three sections; this is the third in the teaching of Śiva" (Mataṅga 1.1).
"Abdhi" means four, and "yuga" means four; "rasyā" means that which is to be tasted, i.e., the six *rasas*. Thus, the meaning is sixty-four. ||433||
And here, the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvaras) are diverse; thus he says:
"Some here are Śaivas, some are Anantas, and some are Śraikaṇṭhas—this is the summary.
And they are designated in this way precisely because they have been initiated by Śiva and others. As they say:
Then there are one hundred and forty fires for the hells;
furthermore, Kūṣmāṇḍa along with the seven netherworlds (pātālas) constitutes the seven worlds.
This Rudra is within the cosmic egg, and beyond it are one hundred Rudras;
thus, the earth consists of two hundred and fifty-seven locations.
From those [five] groups of eight, there are thirty-two; then, in the four elements, five [groups of eight];
then in the subtle elements (tanmātras), five [groups of eight]; then the Viśvedevas, and then another group of eight.
That which is the sixth among the five groups of eight is indeed pride (garva) residing within the sense-faculties;
it is situated in the intellect (buddhi), and from that arise the eight gods and the eight yogins.
Likewise, the eight qualities [beginning with] anger reside in the Unmanifest (avyakta);
beyond that, in Time conjoined with Necessity (niyati), reside those beginning with Patadruka.
In the principle of *rāga*, there are eight [deities] beginning with Aṅguṣṭha; in the principle of *vidyā*, there are twelve beginning with Ekaśiva;
and in the principle of *kalā*, there are ten beginning with Vāmā.
