Thus, it is declared that within the three sections there are three hundred and sixty-four worlds; within them, the lords of the worlds are diverse.
"Some are Śaivas, likewise some are Anantas, and some indeed are Śraikaṇṭhas" (*Maṭhavṛtti*).

And here, since the source scripture has been cited as corroborative, the author of that commentary has stated that it would result in excessive prolixity; thus, his statement has been corroborated. || 433 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of demonstrating the division of the worlds in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Wherever and whenever one desires to experience the enjoyments of another, there the conjunction [of the self] should be performed. (8.434)
"Then, upon its removal, purification [is performed]; however, the remainder must be dealt with internally.
This was shown by him as a conceptual construct in order to propagate the traditional scripture (āgama). || 8.435 ||
As it has been said:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is directed to that very place and becomes a possessor of accomplishment through the power of mantra..."
Thus. Now, *atha* (then) indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*). "In its abandonment" means in the relinquishing of the desire for enjoyment—this is the sense.

"Contained within" means that it is purified precisely by the purification of the *pradhāna*. "It has been shown" implies the thought: otherwise, how could such thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) arise? "By him" means by that particular teacher.
—this is the meaning. || 435 ||
Now, one might ask: "Are only this many alternatives possible here, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Other numerous alternatives as well are to be inferred by the teachers through their own intelligence.
But if indeed many such alternatives are possible, then what exactly should be accepted here?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Furthermore, in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana, one hundred and eighteen [deities] are taught. (8.436)
Therefore, here the principal [portion] to be purified is stated concisely as one hundred. This refers to the number of worlds (*bhuvana*). As it is said there:
"Thus, among all the *tattvas*, there are one hundred and eighteen."
"The worlds are to be fully known in brief, and not in detail" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.33).
[The term] "pradhāna" [is used here] because this treatise proceeds precisely under its authority. 436.
He states that very point:
"Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Narakeśa, Hāṭaka, and then Bhūtalapa. (8.437)
Brahmā is the lord of the world of sages; the Rudras are situated in the five intermediate directions.
Ananta is in the lower direction; in the east are those known as Kapālī, Vahni, Antanirṛti, and Bala.
Laghu, Nidhipati, Vidyādhipa, Śambhu, and [the one] ending with Ūrdhva, together with Vīrabhadrapati—
[these constitute the outer enclosure] with eleven [deities], and likewise the Brahmāṇḍa with five intermediate ones.
Thus, this city of sixteen is to be reckoned here as belonging to the *nivṛtti-kalā*:
Lakulīśa, Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi, Āṣāḍhi, Puṣkara, and Nimeṣa. (8.440)
Prabhāsa and Sureśa are [located] in the water, each with their own retinue; Bhairava, Kedāra, Mahākāla, Madhyāmraka, and Jalpa are [located] in the center. (8.441)
Śrīśaila and Hariścandra—these constitute the eight secret [pīṭhas] within the Mahas; [the others] are known as Bhīma, Indrāṭṭahāsa, Vimala, Kanakhala, Nākhala, Kurusthiti, and Gayā. (8.442)
This is the extremely secret group of eight: Marut, Satanmātraka, Sākṣa, Sthāṇu, Suvarṇa, Bhadra, Gokarṇaka, and Mahālayaka. (8.443)
Avimukta, Rudrakoṭi, Vastrāpada—this is the sacred [site] in the sky;
and Sthūlasthūleśa, Śaṅku, Śrutikā, and Lañjara are the bearers of the mandala.
The two eggs of Mākoṭa and the testicles of the goat constitute the eightfold group within the *ahaṅkāra*.

"Muni" refers to seven. Thus, by virtue of their specific lordship (*īśatva*), their inclusion therein is revealed. Starting from "prācyāḥ," [the term] "antaḥ" refers to Yama because he brings about the end; "laghu" refers to...
It is called "swift" because of its rapid action. As it has been stated, beginning with:
"First, the world of the Fire of Time must be purified with effort" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 5.1).
"O Dear One, by means of these five pure worlds beginning with Kālāgni,
all this that is situated within the Brahmāṇḍa becomes purified."
Outside of that are the individual worlds of the hundred Rudras;
one should subsequently purify the tenth [world], which is surrounded by its single presiding lord.
Ananta is the first among them, and Kapālīśa is another;
likewise Agnirudra, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala.
Śīghra, Nidhīśvara, and another, Sarvavidyādhipa;
Śambhu and Vīrabhadra, possessing the brilliance of smokeless fire.
"It is considered that by these ten pure [energies] numbering one, a hundred [energies] become pure. (Mālinīvijaya 5.15).
Thus, what is called "pratyātmaka" is here stated to be another name for the very same eight secret [energies].
The phrase "in that which consists of a hundred [parts] and possesses a witness" (*śatanmātrake ca sākṣe ca*) is an epithet of *kha* (space).

According to the view of some, everything up to this point is pervaded by this very group of eight; however, according to others, because it is appropriate for an effect to reside within another cause, this much is pervaded by the *ahaṅkāra*. || 444 ||
Therefore he says:
"Others say that the subtle elements and the sense organs are within the ego. (8.445)

In the intellect (dhi), the eightfold womb (yony-aṣṭaka) is said to reside; in primordial nature (prakṛti), indeed, the eightfold yoga beginning with the unmanifest (akṛta) resides. Thus, the establishment of these seven groups of eight worlds extends from the waters down to the root (mūla).
In Nari, there are Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhaveśa, Vīra, Pracaṇḍa, Gaurīśa, Aja, Sānanta, and Ekaśiva; in Vidya, there should be the pair Krodha and Caṇḍa.
Saṃvarta, Jyotiratha, Kalā, Niyati, Sūra, Pañcānta, Vīra, Śikhīśa, and the one named Śrīkaṇṭha—these three [groups] belong to Kāla. (8.448)
Samahātejā, Vāma, Bhavodbhava, Ekapiṅgala, Īśāna, Bhuvaneśa, Purassara, and Aṅguṣṭha—these eight indeed abide at night. (8.449)
This Vidyā consists of twenty-eight worlds, extending from Puruṣa down to Niśānta; these are Hālāhala, Rudra, Krud, Ambikā, Aghorikā, along with Vāmā. (8.450)
In Vidyā there are eight Vidyeśas; in Īśa and Sadāśiva there are five:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śakti, and this Śāntā, who is Sakalā. (8.451)
There are eighteen worlds...
and herein, some are designated by their own names, others by synonyms, and others by a portion of a word; this is to be inferred by oneself. And this has already been [stated] previously.
This has been confirmed. By the sense of the word *narī* (woman), the reality of *rāga* (passion) is implicitly included;

therefore, there are six [deities] beginning with Vāmā in the principle of *puruṣa*, and five beginning with Pracaṇḍā in *rāga*. As it has been said: "Then, by an extension of half a finger-breadth, the group of six cities follows in succession."
"One should contemplate four [deities] in one pair, and one in another. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 6.14).
"Sānanta" means the single Śiva accompanied by Ananta. "Niśi" refers to Māyā. "Riśe" refers to the principle of Īśvara. Thus, there are sixteen [deities] in Nivṛtti, and [twenty-four] in Pratiṣṭhā.
Fifty-six [in the Śuddhavidyā-tattva], twenty-eight in Vidyā, and eighteen in Śāntā—
thus there are one hundred and eighteen worlds.
Now, one might object: "Has not the division of worlds been described elsewhere even in relation to the Śāntyatītā [level]? Why then is it not mentioned here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"...the Śāntyatītā, however, is indeed devoid of worlds."
The intended meaning is that, in this case, there can be no such conceptualization as space and so forth.
And he concludes this with the first half of the Āryā verse:
"Thus has the division of the path of space been declared, as instructed by the venerable Śambhu. (8.452)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Path of Space," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Thus by the venerable Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, the Guru—may there be auspiciousness!
"In Jambudvīpa, he established his residence in Bhāratavarṣa;
there, a certain person named Jayaratha composed this clear commentary on the eighth chapter.
Thus [ends] the work composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda.
In the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by the venerable teacher Jayaratha, this is the eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Path of Space. || 8 ||
The Ninth Daily Lesson: The Viveka (Discrimination) on the Manifestation.

Victorious is Jayāvaha, who possesses the power to manifest the sequence of the principles (tattva) and to distinguish their divisions; who is adorned with serpents as ornaments; and who brings about the victory of his devoted followers.

Now, with the second half [of the verse], he makes a formal declaration to explain the detailed classification of the principles (tattva), which has come in its proper turn: "Now, the classification of the principles is explained in detail. (9.1)

"In detail" means because [the reality] is established according to its true nature, preceded by the removal of the superimpositions imagined by others. "In due order" means that immediately after the description of the worlds, the occasion has arrived for the description of the principles (tattvas) that follow them. || 1 ||
One might ask: "What indeed is called 'reality' (tattva), such that its divisions could even be described?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That supreme form, dense with light, which shines as the one inherent within these various categories previously mentioned, is the one God Śiva; for this is what is meant by 'reality'."

In the Pārameśvara system, that which is called "tattva" is defined as follows: it is a single form that, without deviation, persists as a common thread through many things such as the worlds; and yet, it exists in manifold ways as the nature of earth and the other elements.
Therefore, the "being" (bhāva) of those—earth and so forth—is "tattva. Thus it is.

It has been stated that this is the cause of designation; and among the various kinds of worlds described in the immediately preceding chapter, it is that supreme reality— which is a single mass of light—
that appears as the underlying persistence, since its manifestation would otherwise be inexplicable.
Shining by encompassing the entire universe—for this expansion which appears as the so-called universe is indeed His own; as they say:
"This group of thirty-five principles is said to be the very power of Lord Śiva."
Thus, for this very reason, that which extends everything is the "Supreme Form" (tat); its state is "Reality" (tattva)—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "If this entire universe is thus nothing but the single ultimate reality that is Light (prakāśa), then the separate existence of the principles (tattva) does not exist at all; so what indeed would even the conventional designation of 'earth' and so forth be?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Furthermore, when differentiation shines forth from the state of Śiva due to the savor of His sovereignty,
that supreme form which persists manifoldly is what is called "tattva" (the principle) in the teaching of the All-pervasive Lord.
Furthermore, by the power of that very Śiva’s sovereignty,
when differentiation— from the supreme state of Śiva itself, which consists of the thirty-six principles down to the earth—
has emerged in an exceedingly manifest way, that form consisting of the principle of earth and so forth appears as something persisting through many modes.
This very thing is called "the reality (tattva) of earth and so forth"—this is the meaning of the sentence. ||2||
He establishes this very point:

"For instance, because it extends from the abode of Time (Kāla) to the city of Vīrabhadra, and because of the manifestation of support, hardness, weight, and so forth, it possesses the nature of Earth (Dharā). (3)

Thus, for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) beginning with "tathā hi": since support (*dhṛti*) and the other qualities are indeed the attributes of earth, and because they are non-different in nature from it, their apprehension is established through the apprehension of earth itself; as it has been said: "The nature of earth consists in the manifestation of support and so forth. Therefore, by virtue of its connection with the dewlap and other such characteristics...

Just as the nature of "cowness" (gotva) is pervasive across various individuals such as those with broken or shorn horns, so too is the nature of "earthness" (pṛthvītva) present in the worlds from the Fire of Time (kālāgni) upwards, due to their connection with the qualities of support and so forth. || 3 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"In the same way, this should be stated for the principles beginning with water up to Sadāśiva.
Therefore, just as the nature of earth is present everywhere through its connection with stability and so forth,"
The nature of water and so forth [is established] due to the association with natural fluidity, luminosity (whiteness), and other such qualities.

One might object: "In that case, since such a nature is observed in various instances such as a physical body or a world, would not even the body, the world, and so forth, be of the nature of distinct principles (tattvāntara)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whether in its own effect, or in a flood of qualities, or even in a quality similar to itself... (9.4)
That reality exists in a manner similar to a universal, because it extends through and pervades all things;
it is, in successive order, the earth, primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), Śiva, and so forth. (9.5)
Consequently, there would be no connection between bodies and worlds.

Furthermore, the particle *vā* should be understood as indicating an alternative (*vikalpa*) and placed out of its logical order; thus, it should be construed with "even in that which possesses similar qualities.
In this way, regarding effects such as jars and bowls within their own [causal] substratum, [there is a relation] of properties...

Because the qualities (guṇas), such as *sattva* and the rest, are not identical due to their mutual suppression and manifestation, that form which exists as a pervasive concomitant— such as "earth-ness" and so forth— within the stream (*ogha*) of the limited subjects whose qualities are contracted but who are in reality nothing but Light (*prakāśa*), or throughout the entire universe, "stretches" (*tanoti*), meaning it pervades its own effects and so on.

Having established this, [it is said that] earth and the rest, as well as the individual soul (puṃs), Śiva, and so forth, are called "that principle" (tattva) respectively according to their order. Consequently, there is no such application [of the term] to the body, the world, and so on; for in its own effects, such as movement and the like, or in its respective experiences, the body and so forth do not attain the status of being the underlying "principle."

The word "ādi" (and so forth) denotes a category; by it, one should understand that other principles such as *ahaṅkāra* (egoity) also possess a pervasive presence within their own effects, such as the senses and the self.
It is precisely with this meaning implicit within it that others [have stated]:

"That which persists until the great dissolution and provides enjoyment for all living beings is called 'Tattva' (the Reality) by the knowers of that [truth], and not the body, a jar, or the like"— so it has been stated in such passages. (4–5)
If one asks, "What is the authority for such a statement?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Mataṅgaśāstra and other texts. (9-6)
And since this has been explained there in many ways in the *Vidyāpāda* and other sections, how much could possibly be written here?
Thus, for fear of excessive prolixity, I have merely set forth the proposition. And so it is said there:
"Reality (*tattva*) is that which consists of the nature of an entity, whose essence is the manifestation of its own attributes."
The reality of the state of things is manifest and clear, as seen from the traditional teachings.

"That which is unfallen from its own state, by which the world is pervaded and brought under its control, and which could not be pervaded by anything else— that is the reality within the continuum of realities.
Thus [it is said].

Likewise, following the objection: "When a collection of earth-atoms is scattered in every direction, what is its own essential nature there that is designated as the reality (tattva) of earth? [the author replies]: "The nature of clay exists therein, by which this [earth] is so designated."
"Furthermore, it is more distinguished and indestructible than even the atoms and their aggregates," and so forth; much has been said [in this regard]. || 6 ||
This being the case, the differentiation of the principles (tattvas), which consists of the nature of cause and effect, must be explained;
thus he says:
"In this regard, their established [differentiation] is shown according to the Siddhayogīśvarīmata."
The relationship of cause and effect is that which is fashioned by the will of Śiva. || 9-7 ||
The *Siddhayogīśvarītantra*, which extends to a hundred crores [of verses] and was previously described by you as being spread across three divisions—
In the Mālinīvijaya Tantra, characterized by thirty million verses,
the path of yoga has been taught by you in great detail, O Maheśvara.
Furthermore, its summary is said to consist of twelve thousand [verses];
even that extensive version cannot be grasped by those of small intellect.
Therefore, having condensed that [teaching], O Supreme Lord, please out of your grace explain in brief for the benefit of those of small intellect that which brings about all accomplishments.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe laughed and said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*, the *Mālinīvijayottara* which has not been told to anyone. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.13)
And he will say:
"The nature of the relationship between cause and effect being thus established,
we shall explain the conception of the causes as taught in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra."

Thus, by the phrase "the relation of cause and effect" (kāryakāraṇabhāva), there has been an introductory indication of that object of knowledge (prameya) called "sequence," which was listed immediately following [the previous category]. || 7 ||
But surely, in cases such as clay and a jar, there is an entry of desire; however, that [desire] belongs to the potter.

In the case of the seed and the sprout, on the other hand, there is no entry of a conscious being at all—so what talk can there be of desire, which is its attribute? Thus, how can it be said that "there is a causal relationship"?
"Is it fashioned by the will of Śiva?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In reality, the supreme Lord Śiva is the agent of all entities.
For here, indeed, the power of an insentient thing such as a seed—which is considered a cause—is only this much: that it produces either what exists or what does not exist.

It would have to produce the sprout, which is considered the effect and whose existence is currently perceived; however, the statement "the sprout is born" does nothing for the seed, because the sprout is distinct from it. If they were not distinct, then even things such as jars would necessarily arise in that same manner. Nor can it be the case that the sprout and so forth [are produced], for in that case, the sprout would simply be of the nature of non-existence.

Since it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), how could it admit existence (*sattva*), which is contrary to its own nature? Now, if it is argued that there is no such thing as "non-existence" (*asat*) for which there could be a contradiction with existence—
because [non-existence] would have to be based on both entities— and because this [notion of non-existence] is merely conventional (*vyavahāra-mātra*) regarding that which is non-existent;
Regarding the claim that [the effect] is produced by existence (*sattā*): in reality, this is merely the statement that "when the seed exists, the sprout exists.

Thus, what could be contradicted by what? But surely, if the sprout exists whenever the seed exists, then it would have to exist at all times; otherwise, it would never exist at all. Therefore, its [existence] would always...
In an existent entity (*sattva*), there can never be a connection with "otherness" (*anyathātva*); for otherness is said to be the state of being nothing at all (*akiñcidrūpatva*).

What, then, would be the purpose of such a connection? Or, if it were so, what further quality would there be in its own nature (*svarūpa*) by virtue of which even its fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra*) might arise? And yet, this is not the case.

It should be stated that "the sprout has an essence whose existence depends upon the seed," because all entities are established solely within their own intrinsic nature, and it is logically impossible for one thing to have an essence that depends on another;
and even though that which is called "non-existent" is not any kind of real entity, nevertheless, like a hare's horn—

Since there is the possibility of a nature that is non-existent [in the external world] falling upon the ground of the internal organ and manifesting there, it is indeed contradictory for that to coexist with an existent nature that has become an object of the external senses;
thus, it was rightly said: "The existence of the non-existent is a contradiction. Now, if it is [already] existent, then what of this?

What is it that one should request from seeds and so forth? If you say it is "manifestation" (abhivyakti) and its necessity, no; for even in that case, it is possible to apply the nature of being both existent and non-existent.
Nor is it logical for it to be of the nature of both, of the nature of neither, or indescribable (anirvācya).

Because such a nature [of self-causation] is contradictory, that causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) which is universally established in the world cannot be logically sustained; thus, all worldly transactional activity (vyavahāra) would utterly collapse.
Therefore, by the force of the very designation "causal relationship," one must necessarily resort to the relationship of agent and object (kartṛkarmabhāva), since...
Because the object (*kārya*) is the domain of the act of manifestation, it is indeed the *karman* (object) that is "caused" (*kāryate*), such as this or that sprout and so forth;
it is manifested by the agent (*kartā*) through the performance of the appropriate means. Thus, even the cause (*kāraṇa*) rests within the agent alone.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, by virtue of His own will, [is the sole reality].
It illuminates this entire universe, yet under the condition of *niyati* (limitation), it does so through the intervention of other manifestations;
hence arises the worldly cognition in such forms as "from the seed, the sprout," or "from clay, the jar.
[Objection: But if that is so, would it illuminate the universe as being existent or non-existent? Has not the same fault already been stated? [Reply: No.

In this context, indeed, an object manifests in three ways according to the distinction between internality, graspability, and externality; for instance, there is the internality of an object which, even prior to becoming an object of the mind for every cognizer, manifests as identical with one's own consciousness.

Immediately following this, it has been established elsewhere that for an object situated within the self of consciousness, there is both "graspability" (grāhyatva)— like pleasure and so on— by virtue of being cognizable solely by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
and also "externality" (bāhyatva)— like a jar and so on— by virtue of being cognizable by both the internal and external organs; thus,
there is the manifestation of the object externally while it remains within the self of consciousness.
This has been stated many times:
"The manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self of the Lord certainly exists;
for without that, the reflective awareness of will does not proceed."

Thus, this very relationship of cause and effect consists in the fact that the object, which is already vibrating within, is manifested as being cognizable both internally and externally. As it has been said:
"That which is non-existent is non-existent; it is not logical for that which is non-existent to possess the nature of existence."
Furthermore, even though it exists, it is said that there is no purpose served by its acquisition of existence.
"In the world, the relationship of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves within;
its being perceivable by both types of sense organs occurs through the power of some [internal reality].
And it is not at all something unprecedented that an object situated internally appears externally.
Rather, it is merely the non-apprehension of difference; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Consequently, it is rightly said:
"The supreme Śiva, possessing absolute freedom, is in reality the creator of all things.
Now, one might object: this may indeed be the case regarding seeds and sprouts, but this is not the situation regarding clay and jars.

For in that case, the potter is indeed seen as the agent; so what is the point of postulating another unseen agent?—anticipating this objection, he says: "Agency is never possible for one who is not independent. (9.8)

For a potter does not produce a jar by his mere will alone, but rather in dependence upon clay and other materials; nor would insentient things like clay comply with his will, for if they did, why would they not also attend to his desire to produce a cloth? And thus, for him—

The utility [of the potter] consists merely in imparting a refinement to the clay and so forth; even so, there is this much more [required] than the clay and other materials: that which is intended to be made, such as a jar, must flash forth in the mind at that time.
Yet, by that alone, the effect—the jar and so forth—does not manifest externally; therefore, it is indeed something else [the Supreme Lord].

Śiva, by his own will, brings about an effect through the mutual dependence of the potter and the clay and so forth during the state of necessity; as for the potter's conceit that "this was made by me," even though the lump of clay and other materials exist, that too is solely due to His majesty, and all this—
This will be explained in detail further on, so no effort has been made here; therefore, it is rightly said:

"Agency for one who is not independent is never tenable," for such a person—like a potter and the like—has merely assumed the conceit of identity with the insentient body and so forth. Thus, how [could there be true agency]?

If one were to accept autonomy that is contrary to its own nature, [it would follow that] it resides solely in consciousness; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi). || 8 ||
Therefore, he says:
"And the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, whose body is pure consciousness";
the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "for" (hi).

Now, one might object: "In both common worldly usage and in the scriptures, even an insentient entity is accepted as possessing agency characterized by autonomy; for instance, it is said that 'the wood burns' and 'Prakṛti is considered the creator of the world. So why has it been stated that 'autonomy is not possible in the insentient'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And that which is independent and that which is insentient—these two are mutually contradictory. || 9-9 ||

For autonomy (*svātantrya*) is said to be self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), while insentience (*jāḍya*) is said to be luminosity dependent on another (*paraprakāśyatva*). Nor can there be identity or even conjunction between these two— as it has been stated, "these are mutually contradictory"— and for this very reason, that insentient object [cannot be established] because it would have to reside within consciousness (*saṃvit*).

Even if that [independent] establishment [of the object] were established within its own self, it would still depend upon a cognizer whose nature is self-luminous; thus, how could autonomy be inherent in the very nature of an insentient entity? || 9 ||
Thus he says:
"Inertia is dependence upon the subject even with respect to the establishment of its own self.
As for that which is seen in the world or in the scriptures where even an insentient thing appears to possess agency, that is due to the presiding influence of an independent [subject].
It is for the most part conventional usage.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no agency; rather, let there be causality alone, which can very clearly bring about a connection even between the insentient and the sentient. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, no other form of causality is found apart from agency. (9–10)

This would indeed be so if being an effect were something other than the external manifestation of the object; for, as long as the object manifests internally, its very "being an effect" consists in its manifesting externally without abandoning that internal form. And therefore, it is in relation to that [externalization] alone that the object remains internal.

Only in relation to that [consciousness] could what exists internally manifest externally; and since this [object] resides within the subject alone, it manifests as external from that very source and not from anything else. Thus, the subject alone is the cause of effects such as a jar, and not inert matter like clay, because in relation to the latter, there is no internal or external manifestation for this [subject], whereas for the subject, there is.
Since causality is nothing other than agency, it was rightly stated: "For an insentient entity, causality—which has as its true nature nothing but agency—is not tenable. || 10 ||

Surely, this very nature of entities is such that "when this exists, that comes to be"; for otherwise, even if [the cause] were included among existing entities, how could it be said that "when that exists, this comes to be" if it did not exist?
Moreover, there is no capacity to produce an effect other than the cultivation of a non-existent form; thus, this remains established.

"In the case of entities such as the seed and the sprout, the causal relationship consists in their being of the nature of existence (bhāva)," as stated by Dharmālaṅkāra: "In this world, for another [entity], existence itself is its state of being an effect..."
Thus it is said:

"The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the generator of things, which brings about their non-existent forms. And: "Apart from intrinsic nature, there is nothing else whatsoever that things need to depend upon."

Anticipating the objection, "What is the use of the entry of consciousness (cetanā) here?", he says: "For when that [consciousness] exists, there is the existence of those [entities]; thus, their being has as its sole life-force dependence [upon it]. How could this be so for entities that are independent, since they are established in themselves? (9–11)

For Buddhists, the causal relation does not belong to a single entity alone, nor to two entities simultaneously— as in the case of a jar and a cloth— nor even when occurring sequentially, if there is a lack of necessity—
as in the case of cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth— and nor even when there is a fixed sequence, if the preceding factor is the effect.

Furthermore, it has been stated that a cause is that which necessarily precedes, whereas an effect is that which necessarily follows; therefore, when that very thing regarded as the cause— such as a seed— is present, the thing regarded as the effect— such as a sprout—
must necessarily come into existence, having not existed before.

Thus [it is said]. And here, the restriction is implied by the locative case according to the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37), which states that when something exists in one thing and does not exist when that thing is absent, it exists only when that very thing is present. This might be so for insentient things if there were no such restriction; for instance, smoke might exist even when a jar is present.
But it is not with necessity; for necessity has mutual dependence as its very life, and that is impossible for insentient things,
since they are established solely within their own selves and are ignorant of one another's news— so, when what exists, what [could arise]?

It might be so. But surely it is fire and smoke themselves—being observed in such a manner—that, even without attaining mutual identity, are said to be "restricted" (niyata) when they do not occur otherwise;
for there is no other distinct category called "restriction" (*niyama*) which would necessitate a mutual dependence between these two.

In this regard, the very rule for fire is that there is no non-smoke after it; likewise, the very rule for smoke is that there is no non-fire before it. Thus, the specific nature of these two—restricted solely to their own selves and untouched by anything else—is itself their causality and effectuality. Therefore, there is no sense of mutual dependence whatsoever.

To this it is replied: in this way, mere perception alone would be established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that a person perceives only smoke after fire and not non-smoke, and likewise perceives only fire before [the smoke] and not non-fire; yet, this cannot arise from mere perception independent of the perceptible object itself.

Since the establishment of the reality of objects is logical, one must admit some specific feature inherent in the very nature of these two [fire and smoke] which would restrict them in that way; otherwise, the fact that smoke occurs only after fire and nothing else is neither an excellence of the nature of fire, nor is it... [the excellence of the nature of smoke].
Before the smoke there was fire alone and nothing else that belongs to that smoke; how then could such a state of affairs come to be?

For one thing does not cause another to transcend its own nature, nor does it happen—even if by some stroke of fate a cloth is seen after a jar many times—that therefore those two [are related as cause and effect].
Even if two things are mutually independent, there might nevertheless arise some known regulator by which a necessary sequence would occur;
and in that case, there would even be a causal relationship between the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī— namely,
that the rising of Rohiṇī necessarily follows once Kṛttikā has risen.

If it is argued that, "In this case, there is no rising of Rohiṇī following Kṛttikā because such a thing has never occurred before, as it was observed to be so on previous days," we say: no, for this is equally applicable to smoke as well, since its rising in continuity with fire was also observed on previous days. [Objection: But surely, by virtue of the capacity of the former...

The relation between one thing and another is the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and that is not possible in the case of the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī; for the circle of constellations is fixed to the Pole Star and remains eternally revolving simultaneously,
yet it is observed to rotate sequentially like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*).

By this [reasoning], there arises the determination of priority and posteriority between these two, but not because of some specific quality inherent in their own nature. Now, is it not the case that in your system this very capacity of the prior is proclaimed: that although the subsequent does not exist when that [prior] is absent, it is seen to come into being when that [prior] exists?
Regarding the Ornament of Dharma:
"In that context, capacity is indeed its power to produce; and if that [production] does not occur when that [cause] is present, how indeed can it be called a capacity?"
"Now, how could there be a lack of capacity? Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *Traikālyaparīkṣā* also states: "Moreover, when a cause exists, the prior non-existence [of the effect] is observed."

This is so; and this point is the same here as well: that although the rising of Rohiṇī did not exist prior to the rising of Kṛttikā, it is seen to occur when that [rising of Kṛttikā] exists. Thus, even though the rule is entirely the same for both the rising of Kṛttikā and the rising of Rohiṇī, there is no relationship of cause and effect between them.

Since smoke and fire exist [in this relation], how could this distinction be accepted as credible if it were without a basis? Therefore, one must admit some knowable property inherent in the very nature of cause and effect, of which there would be positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of a signifier (*jñāpaka*).

For in every case, only that form which is actually possible within a given entity is made known, and not otherwise; if it were otherwise, there would be error, and thus the entity would not have been truly known. Furthermore, nothing else can exist apart from its dependence upon that [entity], and that [dependence] is of two kinds, consisting essentially in mutual concomitance.

Or [it might be] of the nature of intention; yet neither of these two is possible for insentient things that are accepted as being related as cause and effect. For a mutual connection between two objects would imply identity in their existence due to their reciprocal nature, like fire and heat, such that upon the disappearance of either one, [the other would likewise cease].

Furthermore, the very existence of the other would not be possible— just as there is no absence of heat in fire— and such a state does not exist between cause and effect, because fire and smoke appear as mutually distinct; for if that were the case, fire itself would not appear in the absence of smoke, or even in its presence.

To say "smoke" would constitute a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). And the second [type of connection] consists of mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*); for example, in the case of food with respect to the eater: although the eater is indeed dependent upon food, he is not perceived as being merely attached to it, but rather as having it within his consciousness (*saṃvidi*).
It attains a state of being oriented toward [the object], by which means it proceeds toward that [object] through a process of synthesis characterized by desire for it;

however, this is not possible in the case of cause and effect, because they are insentient and lack the capacity to synthesize each other's essential natures. Therefore, in every respect, [this applies] to insentient things...
It remains established that the relationship of cause and effect is not possible without some degree of cognizability (*jñāteya*).
Now, it has indeed been stated here that cognizability consists in the priority of the cause and the posteriority of the effect;
for, by making the prior existence [of the cause] the prerequisite, there occurs the manifestation of the existence of the subsequent [effect] as something previously non-existent.

For this very reason, neither the future nor the present possess the capacity to manifest that [past object], because it exists even without them; for while the former (the past) has already existed previously and thus possesses the capacity to manifest it, the latter (the future) does not, because at that time it is of a non-existent nature.

And that which is present is said to be simultaneous; simultaneity, moreover, occurs between two things that have already acquired their existence. At that time, nothing remains for either of them to do such that one could be performed by the other; thus, it should be understood that there is merely a sequence of priority and posteriority between cause and effect.
To this he says:

"If it is argued that 'he was first and then he was later,' and if the prior and posterior states are not distinct from his essential nature (svabhāva), then it remains that he is identical [before and after]. (9.12)
Now, are this priority (*pūrvatva*) and posteriority (*paratva*) distinct from their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or not?

Regarding this, the first position is not tenable—for in your own system, there exists no such entity as priority and so forth that could possess existence apart from that [intrinsic nature]; or, if they were established merely through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [they would lack objective reality].
In this way, the relation of cause and effect would also [be undermined], resulting in the collapse of one's own tenet—

since the relation of cause and effect is accepted as being the very nature (*svabhāva*) of things— as Yaddharmālaṅkāra stated: "Thus, this relation of cause and effect is indeed the very nature of things, and not..."

"It is established merely through conventional usage. Furthermore, in the view that there is no difference [between cause and effect], only two entities recognized as cause and effect would remain; thus, nothing at all would have been said regarding their relationship, nor—
In your view, apart from the nature of smoke and fire themselves, there exists some other specific relation characterized as the causal relationship; for this very reason,
it has been stated that this is to be apprehended by a synthetic cognition (*abhyuccaya-buddhi*), such that it is not merely "this is fire" or "this is smoke."

"Up to the point that the cause is also the effect. Now, by speaking thus, you have stated—without using words—that the nature of being smoke and fire is something other than causality and effectuality;
for instance, if the very nature of fire were causality, then once that fire-nature is perceived...

Why would one not perceive that [reality], given the reasoning stated in such passages as: "Since the single nature of an object is itself directly perceived, what other part could there be that has not been seen which remains to be examined by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*)?"?
By what means could this [object] also be apprehended by a cumulative cognition (*abhyuccayabuddhi*)? It is true that it would be so;

however, this is the inherent defect of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): while determining that something is fire, it determines only this much and not its causality, which would otherwise result in such a cumulative cognition through another perception. But if [you argue] that it is by means of conceptual construction...

Thus, it is established by that much alone; what further purpose is served by an additional argument? For in cases such as "cow" and "white," there is no function whatsoever for an additional cognition.
This conceptual construction displays its own artistic skill in that it differentiates even what is non-different and unites even what is differentiated. Now, [if you say...]

The greatness of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is rooted solely in its appearance; however, it is not so in this case. For neither causality nor effect-ness, unlike spatial configuration and the like, consists of a real excellence of the object (*arthātiśaya*), by virtue of which these two might be merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*); rather, they exist by virtue of having the nature of being perceived as such.

They are established as being like momentariness; thus, there is a purpose here for the intellect to provide further support, for an object cannot be devoid of form, nor can cognition be without an object of cognition.
Is it not the case that the very form of fire is the form of the causality of smoke, wherein there would be a further support from another cognition?
This is true; however, the form of being the cause of smoke is indeed distinct from the form of fire itself.

Otherwise, why would fire that has not yet reached its final state not produce smoke? For fire that has not reached that specific state would not be fire, and as for momentariness, it belongs to the yogins.

It would result in something entirely different from the perceived blue form; for while the blue and so forth possess a nature common to both the properties of cessation and non-cessation, momentariness, however, has the nature of the property of cessation alone, as it is said: "That which is validity is indeed the state of having cessation as its property."

Thus, therefore, being characterized by a luminous form and so forth is "fire-ness," and having a positive and negative concomitance that follows smoke is "causality"; while being characterized by a pale form and so forth is "smoke-ness," and following the positive and negative concomitance of fire is "effect-ness."
The nature of being an effect and the nature of being a cause, which transcend the forms of smoke and fire respectively, are established even without being explicitly stated;
for otherwise, the two entities conventionally accepted as cause and effect would ultimately result in being nothing more than a mere collection of disintegrating parts. || 12 ||
One might object: "Let it be so; for we do not intend to assert any relation consisting of a causal relationship, since all entities indeed terminate solely within their own self-nature.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
If this principle—that "the seed is the sprout"—were true regarding cause and effect, why would a pot and a cloth not also stand in a relationship of cause and effect? (9.13)
"In this being present" (*asmin sati*) means "mutually devoid of dependence. The phrase "what would not be so?

implies that since there is no distinction in their mutual independence, the relationship of cause and effect should also exist here. Indeed, in this case, because they are insentient and devoid of dependence, the relationship of cause and effect does not [arise].

This has been established. Furthermore, since there is in the world a common perception such as "the sprout arises from the seed," there must necessarily exist some cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*),
in which these two entities find their ultimate rest.
It would attain the status of being fit for the designation of cause and effect;

for, without resting within the single cognizing subject whose nature is consciousness, there could be no union—consisting of both difference and non-difference—among insentient things that are utterly perishable, like grains of sand. Therefore:
Our established doctrine is that the very nature of the relationship between agent and object (*kartṛkarmabhāva*) is itself the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*),
as it has been said:
"But for the insentient, there is no such power— that existence by which the non-existent becomes existent."
"Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect consists precisely in the reality of the agent and the object.
Consequently, this is logical: that a farmer produces a sprout from a seed, and that God [produces] an arrow from a horn or smoke from fire. || 13 ||

But surely, if the seed and the sprout are thus distinct, their status as cause and effect could not be established merely through their resting within a single cognizer; likewise, there would be an identity between the appearances of a jar and a cloth—
since all appearances rest in the cognizer alone— and therefore, those two [seed and sprout] would indeed possess a state of absolute oneness.
One must accept that for this reason, the cause itself, undergoing transformation into various forms, is called the effect.
Thus he says:
"If the seed were to transform into the state of the sprout, leaf, and so forth..."
In this regard, since the entire category of entities possesses its own fully established nature, if it is a seed, how could it ever assume the form of a sprout and so forth?
For that which lacks such an inherent nature cannot possess such a nature; indeed, a jar can never become a cloth.
For that which does not have that as its own nature, it is not logical for it to possess that as its intrinsic nature. || 9.14 ||

Now it is said: "The very nature of the seed is such that it persists in the form of the sprout and so forth in a gradual sequence"; for the proponents of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavādin*) maintain that "a single entity indeed possesses a nature that is variegated by means of a sequence. (14)
Therefore, he says:
"If it is argued that it has that as its intrinsic nature (tatsvabhāva)... [and so on].
Now, if this is so, then would not the seed or the sprout exist merely as the state of being a seed (bījatvamātra) or merely as the state of being a sprout (aṅkuratvamātra)?

Or, because [the series] comes to rest in form, would even the seed— which is by nature not a seed— possess its final form as a sprout and so forth, and likewise, would the sprout possess its initial state as a seed and so forth, which is by nature not a sprout? To this, he says:
...then the seed and sprout would rest only in themselves, because nothing else whatsoever could possibly exist beyond them. (9.15)

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single entity to possess a dual nature; therefore, there must necessarily exist some one thing by which this manifold form, appearing as the seed, the sprout, and so forth, is manifested. (15)
Regarding this, he says:
"And consequently, it follows that this [consciousness] would be something manifold in form, to that extent.
[The opponent asks: "Is this not indeed desired by us? To which he replies:
If this were so...
[then one might ask: "But even if that were the case, how could a single entity possess two mutually contradictory forms, such as being both a seed and a non-seed? To this, he says:
...for there cannot be the occurrence of mutually contradictory forms in that which is insentient. || 9-16 ||
The meaning is that a single jar cannot be both red and not-red; this might be so—if we were to admit multiplicity simultaneously—but since it occurs sequentially, what is the point of contradiction?
Therefore he says:
"Let there be a manifold form sequentially; how indeed is it contradictory that it is insentient?
For the establishment of the pre-existent effect (satkārya) consists precisely in the body of an entity as it is perceived, [being endowed] with its own inherent nature."
"It occurs in such and such a manner through a sequence; thus, that single form is indeed variegated by succession in reality.
Immersed in its own essential nature, it encompasses all that variety."

And thus: regarding the term "insentient" (*jaḍa*), the sense is that what is non-insentient, such as variegated cognition (*citravijñāna*) and the like, may indeed be variegated even simultaneously. Regarding the phrase "what contradiction could there be?"—for even a red pot might become non-red through a different cause in a successive manner.

Now, it may be argued that neither succession nor simultaneity is any excellence (*atiśaya*) in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object, but rather in consciousness (*saṃvit*). For consciousness, when cognizing a cloth immediately after a jar, or [cognizing them] together, brings forth succession or non-succession; however, there is no "non-succession" whatsoever that exists beyond the intrinsic nature of the object itself.
"Or there might be succession; even if succession is admitted in respect to a single entity, would the superimposition of contradictory attributes not still persist? To this he says:
"Succession or non-succession cannot be something additional to the essential nature of an entity. (9.17)
"In that way, those two are mere perception...

[it] would not be anything additional to its own nature"—the meaning is "nothing at all. The reason for this is stated as "those two are mere perception," for perception occurs either sequentially or otherwise.
It is by means of succession and non-succession that the nature of an entity is conventionally expressed. || 17 ||
"But surely, if perception is also of such a nature, what is its cause?"—to this he says:
"And why is perception likewise [dependent on sequence]?
For here, indeed, the perceiver perceives each respective collection of objects only through either succession or simultaneity.

Thus, even for perception, there is an incompatibility with succession and non-succession; and although the perceiver is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), such a state [of succession or non-succession] occurs precisely because its very essence consists in the perception of succession and non-succession.
He raises this very doubt: "For that which is his perceiver, even though it has the nature of consciousness... (9.18).
If it is argued that [the object] would be perceived sequentially because its nature is to be perceived sequentially, then the same objection applies here as well; thus he says:
"In that case, what is this sequence of it, given that nothing other than it is perceived? (9.19)

For the connection between succession and non-succession was stated with respect to the object of perception (*upalabhya*) by way of its perception (*upalambha*), and that [connection] was also stated by way of the perceiver (*upalabdhr*). However, there is no further perceiver for the perceiver, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); thus, how could there be succession for this [perceiver]? This is what was meant by the statement: "Because nothing other than that is perceived."
Thus [ends the section]. 19.
Even if one relies on the position that [the perceiver] is its own nature (svabhāva), it would ultimately result in nothing more than the very form of the perceiver itself;
thus he says:
"If it is said to be the nature, then it cannot be something additional to the essential form."

Now, if it is argued that although sequence is not distinct from the essential nature [of the object] because it constitutes its very being, it nevertheless appears as if distinct due to the autonomy of consciousness, then you have arrived at our own philosophical position; thus he says:
Even though the sequence does not exceed its own essential nature, it exists by virtue of its own inherent character.
If manifestation occurs through His absolute freedom, what else need we say?
Thus, the venerable Śiva alone is designated as the sole agent. (9.21)
What indeed is its agency? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And this agency of his is the manifestation of things just as they are.
Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of things just as they are," it means [manifestation] in their various forms.
The meaning is: the manifestation of the constituent parts (mātrāḥ), namely the subjects and objects, as if they were distinct entities—meaning, their appearance as something separate. || 20–21 ||
Just as all things are manifested by the Lord through His own will, so too is the relationship between cause and effect; thus he says:
"And such manifestation exists within the relation of cause and effect. (9.22)

Now, one might object: "If, in this way, in all cases—such as the seed and the sprout, or the jar and the cloth—the Lord appears as the agent and the object, then how is it that the conventional usage of 'cause and effect' occurs only in certain instances? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For just as the coexistence with a jar appears even in the case of a cloth, so too does the state of following immediately after a jar; however, that [latter] is devoid of necessity.
Therefore, when there is an additional conformity of form, we declare that from which something invariably appears immediately after is the cause of that [effect]. (9.24)
Regarding the phrase "devoid of restriction": this is because those two [the cause and effect] are seen to be either reversed or without distinction. Now, one might object:
"In that case, would not the relationship of cause and effect also apply to you, just as it does for the Buddhist, in instances such as the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "when there is an additional continuity of form. Here, first of all, in the realm of Māyā...

There is no dispute that for an effect such as a jar, there are many causes, including clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth; among these, clay is its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), which follows [the production of the jar] through the sequence of the lump, the clod, and so on, without depending on anything else, whereas the staff and other [causes]—

Because its purpose is fulfilled merely by providing assistance through the excellence, modification, and so forth of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), that which appears as a persisting form of something through some common property is indeed its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). As even the Buddhists say:

"And because it continues even when independent, despite the difference [of the effect] which rests upon a different substance, it possesses the status of being the material cause (upādāna-hetu), just as clay is in relation to a pot and the like.
This is said; yet, even by those who speak thus, in the case of smoke and so forth, there is indeed no material causality.
That which was stated regarding its being an effect is simply their lack of knowledge concerning the distinction between its causes;

for fire is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of smoke, but rather moist fuel and the like. To illustrate: from the material cause of chaff, turuṣka, and so forth, its fragrance and other qualities also appear to persist; that alone [is the case].
Regarding its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), even worldly people possess expertise in this matter:

in cases such as the liquefaction of moonstone (*candrakānta*) by water, it is precisely the moonbeams, aided by their dependence upon the moonstone, that serve as the material cause; for otherwise, the moonstone would undergo liquefaction moment by moment.
There would be total destruction; therefore, enough with this digression. || 24 ||

Now, one might object: "If the causal relationship—which consists in a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority and is assisted by the persistence of form—is real, how could it possibly deviate? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And such a rule has as its essence nothing more than the mere appearance of things in that manner."
The manifestation "from the seed comes the sprout" does not occur at all times.
The reason why manifestation alone is the essence is stated as: "For such a manifestation does not occur at all times.
The underlying sense is that, otherwise, an sprout might even arise at some time in the absence of a seed. || 25 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Because a sprout of such a nature arises immediately after the will of the yogi, and because a restriction appears with respect to the desired form of that same kind. (9.26)
In a dream, the nature of cause and effect among jars, cloths, and so forth, appears with strict necessity, as long as there is no sublation. (9.27)

In this regard, there is indeed no dispute that yogis produce effects such as sprouts by mere will alone, without any material cause; therefore, since that sprout— which arises immediately after the yogi’s will and is produced in such a manner even in the absence of a seed— also [arises from that], [it follows that it is not dependent on a seed].
The meaning is that a rule consisting of a sequential order appears, such as "the sprout arises from the seed alone," yet this is not an absolute certainty;
for even a sprout produced by the will of a yogi belongs to the same genus as a sprout that is the effect of a seed, and is not of a different genus from a lotus root (śālūka). Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "of such a form": otherwise, because the desires of yogins would be contradicted, their very status as yogins could not be established; nor is this merely an illusion—so it has been stated. Regarding the word "desired" (iṣṭe): the meaning is "that which performs the specific purposeful action intended"—as it has been said:
"Just as for yogins, even without clay or seed, by the power of their will,
such things as jars are produced, each performing its own stable purposeful action"—
and likewise, because even in a dream, a cloth that performs the function of a jar appears according to a fixed rule.

Because the appearance of a cloth arises immediately after the appearance of a jar, this might indeed be so if there were no sublation (*bādhā*). Thus he says: "Sublation by the void. And here, is this sublation immediate or occurring at a later time? Regarding that, first, as for the latter alternative, even in the case of what occurs during the waking state...

Because sublation is possible in relation to a dream, whereas at that time there is no sublation at all, since [the dream] appears with such firmness until awakening; for this very reason, it was said: "only within that much, i.e., during the state of dreaming. (27)
Thus, an uncontradicted rule alone is the basis for the relationship of cause and effect—so he says:
"Therefore, to whatever extent and in whatever form a rule appears free from contradiction, to that extent and in that form there exists the nature of a firm cause and effect. (9.28)
One might object: "In that case, would this not result in the very position of the Sugata (Buddhist) school? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And when such a rule exists, which establishes the relationship between cause and effect, in reality, causality belongs only to that which consists of consciousness, for that [consciousness] is all-pervading. (9.29)

"That" (tad) refers to that which is indeed the "causality" of the one consisting of consciousness. "Pervasive everywhere" (sarvaga) means that it persists as the locus of rest for all appearances, such as clay, sticks, and so forth. || 29 ||
And thus, it is consistent that nothing single is a producer, but rather the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer; as it is said:
"For this very reason, in the production of a jar, the causal complex is called the cause."

"Collection" (*sāmagrī*) does not mean the individual parts taken separately, but rather those that are complete. One might object: "Apart from the staff and other such factors, what indeed is this 'collection' (*sāmagrī*) that is being spoken of? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And if a single nature is not admitted for the complete [factors] that constitute the collection... (9.30)

There would be no difference in the fruit despite the difference in causes, and that is illogical; for the word "ca" (and) indicates the reason: "one body" means that which has the complete collection of conditions as its cause and is characterized by resting in a single cognizer. Here—

If the clay, the staff, and so forth were individually the causes of the jar, then—since there is no dispute regarding the diversity of effects resulting from the diversity of causes—multiple jars would manifest; but this is not the case.
Therefore, through their resting in a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), these [factors] are designated by the term "causal complex" (*sāmagrī*).
This form must necessarily be sought after, such that it produces only a single jar;

and it is in relation to this [form] alone that there is mutual distinction among causes, from which a distinction in the effects would also arise. The word "no" (neti) is to be applied with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), for this [view] contradicts direct perception—thus he says: "And that is inconsistent. (30)
Now, it has been stated that whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something is its cause.
This condition does not exist for clay, the staff, and so forth when they are separate, but it does exist when they are complete.
What, then, is the purpose of accepting a single entity denoted by the word "sāmagrī" (the causal complex)?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "If [the cognition] conforms to that [object], it possesses that positive and negative concomitance. (9.31)
If that [unity] is the cause of this [diversity], then this "dull logic" (kuṇṭhatarka) is not pleasing to us;
for it has been rendered powerless by the very refutations of those [opposing views] immediately following [the statement that it is] "dull.
Now, if there were no identity among all these [entities] in some form or other, [how could they be related?]
It would follow, then, that even things separated by space and time could be causes; thus he says:
"And just as a complete set [of conditions], such as the staff, the string, the wheel, the hands, and so forth... (9.32).
"We consider that distant and future things likewise function as causes.
"Distant" refers to Mount Meru and so forth; "future" refers to the summer solstice and so forth. "In this way" means "likewise";
that is to say, just as a staff and other such items serve as causes for a jar, so too do distant and future things. This is what we maintain.
"—we consider by way of a logical consequence"—this is the meaning. || 32 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that here the conformity with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-anuvidhāna*) between two things existing at a great distance is unestablished? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"If Meru were there, or even if something else were to exist in the future... (9.33).
A jar would certainly not be produced if it were obstructed by those impediments;
and just as a wheel functions as a cause at a specific place and time, so too [does the causal complex]. (9.34)
Karka, Sumeru, and the others likewise remain situated up to their respective locations.

Now, is the proximity of the wheel and so forth intended in terms of space and time, or is it proximity in terms of form? In that regard, even cloth and other such things possess proximity in terms of space and so forth.

If that were possible, it would follow that even those [distant objects] perform a single causal function; furthermore, since you do not accept the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) of form, "contact" would ultimately have to consist in their being situated in a specific location and so forth,
and since this is no different for Mount Meru and other such things, they too would become causes.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that these [entities] possess a single form whose true nature is their repose within a single subject;
by means of this, while the Supreme Lord alone is the agent of their respective conjunctions and disjunctions, this entire universe may manifest. || 34 ||
Thus he says: "And so, regarding the conjunction and disjunction of those causes," (9.35).

"Śiva alone, being the one independent [agent], attains the state of agency. Now, one might object: "How can Śiva alone be accepted as the agent in all cases? For in the case of a jar and so forth, a potter is seen to be actively engaged. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Just as the potter possesses consciousness regarding the application of the wheel, the staff, and other tools; || 9-36 ||

"For she is indeed Śiva; what distinction could there be in consciousness?"— the phrase "what distinction" means "what difference," for there cannot be even the slightest other form in consciousness that exceeds its nature as consciousness.
The state of being. || 36 ||

Now, one might object: since the consciousness of a potter has a contracted nature due to being delimited by space, time, and so forth, whereas the "Supreme" (Parā) is of a non-dual supreme nature because it is undelimited, how can it be said that there is no difference between the two?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But the cognition of the potter [is so called] because it manifests through spatial limitation. (9.37)
"If [the pot] were to be cast aside as belonging to a different category from the staff,

the wheel, and so forth— [the phrase] 'cast aside from the midst of the staff, wheel, and so forth' means that this [clay] is merely a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), like the staff and other tools; and therefore, the potter does not [have a role here]."
Since [the Lord] possesses the nature of being the direct agent, it is established that "Śiva alone is the agent everywhere. || 37 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, in the creation of each single thing, Śiva is the one body of the universe. (9.38)
The conceit of agency in the person—that he is the "doer"—is also the work of the All-pervasive Lord.
Now, if this is so, then even though the potter stands on the same footing as the stick and other tools, how could he have such a conceit as, "This was made by me"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the person" (puṃsaḥ): this conceit of agency which he possesses—like a debtor's status toward a guarantor—is established in that manner by the Supreme Lord’s very power of necessity (niyati-śakti), so that the regulation of dharma, adharma, and so forth may also be established; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Thus, it is established that the relationship between cause and effect has as its very essence nothing but appearance.
Furthermore, there is a manifold variety in this [world] according to worldly treatises and so forth; thus he says:
"Precisely because it exists as the ultimate reality of such an appearance" (9.39).
The relationship between cause and effect is diverse in both the world and the scriptures.
Among these, he first demonstrates the variety found in the scriptures by way of its predominance:
"From Māyā, the unmanifest (avyakta) and kalā [arise]," according to the Rauravasaṃgraha (9.40).
In the *Śrīpūrva*, however, it is stated that the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) arises from the principle of Kalā;
this is according to the *Rauravasaṃgraha* with respect to the *Bṛhattantra*. As it is said there:
"Then, presiding over Māyā, that Supreme Lord [becomes] the Vidyeśa."
Having agitated it with his own rays, he produced the fiery portion.
"From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being;
and from that [Māyā], the Lord also emitted the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) and the *guṇas*.
And here, in the phrase "and from that the Unmanifest," the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to Māyā.
As for the words of Bṛhaspati:
"From Māyā come the Unmanifest and Kalā; from Kalā come Rāga and Vidya. This is stated in the *Śrīpūrva*, that is, the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, where it is said:
Having begun with the passage, "...having entered Māyā by means of [her] powers," it continues, "...she gave birth to the principle of Kalā."
And thus it is said: "From that very principle of *kalā*, he created the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
In this way, the Unmanifest is the effect of both *māyā* and *kalā*; such is the wonderful diversity taught in the scriptures. (40)
And for this very reason, because of such a suspicion of contradiction, whatever has been explained otherwise by others here is indeed irrelevant; thus he says:
"Therefore, from that which is called Night (niśā), having become Kali, [arises] that which is without a sign (aliṅgaka). (9.41)

Thus, when this principle explained by us has been stated, [the objection] that "it is fruitless because it is taught as being like the night" is extremely useless. "From the principle called Māyā" means from the reality known as Māyā; "without a mark" (aliṅgaka) means unmanifest (avyakta). || 41 ||
Now he shows even worldly variety: "And in the world, [variety arises] from cow dung, from insects, from volition, from dream, and from memory. (9.42)

"From a scorpion, [arising] from an insect"— that is, from a scorpion— [occurring] through the will of a yogin, or by the power of substances and mantras. Here it has been stated that even for an object manifesting externally,
its fundamental nature consists solely in being a mere appearance (ābhāsa-mātra-sāratva), as in the case of a mental construction or a dream.

Regarding the phrase "from memory": "substance" refers to gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth; for the power of jewels, mantras, and herbs is indeed inconceivable—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: a scorpion born from cow dung or similar sources is quite different [from one born from another scorpion]; it is not at all like that which is born from a scorpion.

A scorpion arising from cow dung and the like must be of that very same nature, for there is no dispute regarding the difference in effects resulting from a difference in causes; nor is it logical that two things should be considered one merely because they share a common name when their ultimate natures differ, as they have said:
"It is not logical to establish [a property] in one distinct entity on the basis of a word that is identical [in form] but not [identical in meaning],
just as it is not valid to prove that speech and other things possess horns because they possess 'cowness' (gotva). || 42 ||
Regarding this, he says: "If that [object] were something entirely different...
He replies: "That is true"—and so on.
...desire [arises] from some particularity of its own. || 9-43 ||

Surely, there exists some specific individuality consisting of place, time, form, and so forth, belonging to those scorpions born from other scorpions or from cow dung, by which their mutual difference is established; however,
that same [individuality] is equal even for those born from a scorpion, for they too possess [their own] place, time, form, and so forth.
Ordinary people perceive a difference between individuals. || 43 ||
Therefore, he says:
"But that [consciousness] is equal everywhere; there is indeed a unity in its reflective awareness.
Now, while the persistence of the cognition "this is a scorpion" may be possible there, so it is here as well.

It has been stated that they are identical: "But there exists the unity of their reflective awareness. And this is not like the cognition of a scorpion in what is not a scorpion, because there is no lack of correspondence; for here, it is precisely the reflective awareness that establishes the unity of objects, even though they appear as distinct due to factors such as distance or proximity.
This is the supreme life-force. As it has been said:

"By means of the distance or proximity of objects, by their being beyond or within the range of perception, by their being external or internal, by defects, or otherwise through the nature of the manifestor..."
"Because even those things which possess distinct appearances and shadows manifest primarily as one,
their unity is undeniable due to what is called a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in a single effect having multiple causes.

For it has been established that the relationship between cause and effect has as its ultimate reality nothing more than a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*). Precisely for this reason, the teaching regarding the transformation of the form or even the sequence of the effect is not illogical;
thus he says:
For that very reason, even regarding its own nature and its sequence, there is a different state of affairs.
In the treatises, it is logically consistent due to its diverse nature of suchness;

that is to say, "as its own form"—just as in some places the mind is said to be a sense organ of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), while in others it is called the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it has been said:
"The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and the mind are the paths of the intellect," and also: "the internal organ is threefold. (44)
Furthermore, because the sequence of cause and effect is under discussion, he shows that in the scriptures there is another primary arrangement:
"In the *Jñānottara*, [the principles] are Puruṣa, Rāga, Vidya, Kalā, Kāla, and Māyā, in order. (9.45)
In the realm of Brahmā (Vairiñca), there is no Niyati; above Kalā, Niyati is heard [to exist].
Above the triad of Puruṣa, Rāga, and Vidhi, there is the enclosure of Kalā and Niyati.
Time is said to be Māyā; this is the sequence found in the *Kiraṇatantra*.
The Person (Puruṣa), along with Necessity (Niyati), Time (Kāla), and endowed with Attachment (Rāga), Knowledge (Vidyā), and Limited Agency (Kalā). (9.47)
Thus has this sequence been taught in the *Mātaṅga-pārameśvara* and the *Jñānottara*— that is, in the *Sarvajñānottara*,
where it is said: "In reality, the Person (puruṣa) is subtle, both manifest and unmanifest, and eternal."
Thus:
"Beyond that, there shall be another [layer] known as the enclosure of Kalās.
Thus.
"Beyond this, O Guha, there would be another covering of time," and,
"Beyond this, there would be another, the Māyā-principle, which is very difficult to cross."
And thus, [the view] that there is no necessity (*niyati*) is because it is not mentioned therein in the *Sarvajñānottara*; whereas in the *Svāyambhuva*, it is called "Vairiñca. As it is said there:
"From the principle of Māyā, the principle of Time (*kālatattva*) is established in those two stages."
"In that [kala], *saṃsthā* resides; likewise, *vidyā* also [resides] therefrom again.

Here, the commentators explain that *saṃsthā* is so called because it "establishes"—that is, it "restrains" (*niyacchati*) individual souls (*aṇu*s) within [the cycle of] enjoyments; thus it is *niyati*. And here, *kāla* is encapsulated by *niyati*.
The reading "kala" (black/dark) should be accepted as it appears in the old manuscript;
otherwise, the meaning would contradict what is stated there:
"In that very place, the Person (Puruṣa) is to be known as the guardian of the house of Pradhāna."
"And from the principle of *rāga* arises that called *vidyā*, which is impure and deludes the bound soul (*paśu*).
Thus it is said:
"Then, pervading the *saṃpuṭa* [of principles] called *kāla* and *niyati* in a hundred thousand ways..."
Thus:
"Kalā is to be known from the principle of time (kālatattva), having a retinue of ten million.
Thus it is said.

"And above that would be Māyā, which also pervades downwards in ten million ways. And regarding the word "niyatya" (by necessity), it is because the sequence has been specified—namely, by way of the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). As it is said there:
"When the knot consisting of māyā is agitated by the Lord Ananta," beginning with these words, [the text continues]:
"In that same way, through the conjunction of māyā and the individual soul (aṇu), consciousness is manifested as kalā."
Thus:
"When this [universe], which was previously a mere atom, has been fashioned by a fraction [of the Supreme],
the knowledge of the atom shall arise through wisdom for one who desires to know it within that substratum of all parts."
Thus:
"From that very disposition, passion arises in a subtle form,
by which he is colored and quickly becomes an enjoyer of pleasures, intent upon enjoyment."
Thus:
"Now, having reached the sequence of time through the vision of the three coverings (kañcuka),
that subtle [self] is awakened by means of its union with the power of Śiva."
Thus:
"Now then, O tiger among sages, the power that restrains the person of immeasurable luster is presented as being coessential with the Cause."
