Now follows the exposition of the principle of the individual soul (*puṃstattva*), which is approached through self-mastery (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, the state of this sequence is established by the literal reading itself; therefore, it has not been explained by dividing it further.
Now, he follows the subject at hand.
When the reality of the causal relationship is thus established, [verse 9.48].
We shall state the conceptualization of causes as taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*": this is because this very treatise proceeds by virtue of that [scripture] alone; and the conceptualization of causes is relevant here because the detailed classification of the principles (*tattva*) has been introduced.

It would thus conclude with that very subject; therefore, there is room for the object of knowledge (prameya) called the "determination of the sequence of the principles" (tattvakrama-nirūpaṇa), which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration—this is obtained through the force of the sense (arthasāmarthya). || 48 ||
He says that very thing:
"Śiva is the nature of independent consciousness, perfectly replete with the five powers. (9.49)

"Differentiation, manifested through His sovereignty, is divided fivefold; He whose nature is sovereign vision"—the meaning is that He is of the nature of this vision which is sovereign because it requires nothing else; He is "without expectation. For this very reason, He is "fully replete with the five powers."
"It is full"—thus it has been said.
He demonstrates the fivefold division itself: "Because consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action are clearly manifest. (9.50)
The pentad of principles consists of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and that which is called Vidya.
Regarding the term *sadā*: it refers to Sadāśiva. As it has been said:
"He whose five great bodies are consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action."
"The Great Lord manifests in five ways within the groups of principles.
Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"He manifests the state of the principles consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara,
and Vidyā through the differentiated manifestation of the five powers."
Thus [ends the verse]. 50.
But surely, since everything here consists of the nature of everything else, each individual power possesses the essential nature of all powers;

so how can there be a description of the five principles (tattva-pañcaka) by way of each single power? To this he says: "Even in each one of these principles, which is perfectly replete with all powers... (9.51).
Each particular differentiation is described according to the predominance of this or that [attribute].

"This or that" refers to consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), and so forth. Indeed, in this context, the Supreme Śiva himself, whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), although devoid of desire due to his perfection, [manifests] by virtue of the majesty of his own sovereignty (*svātantrya*) with the desire to emerge outwardly.

First, by means of the gradations of the wonder of supreme bliss (*parānanda-camatkāra*), it should manifest while resting in the state of power (*śakti-daśā*) as the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I"; and immediately thereafter, it should illuminate the two branches of reflective awareness as "I am this," and therein, [it remains] solely within the locus of pure consciousness (*śuddha-cinmātra*).
When the Supreme Lord causes the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) to emerge within the "I" aspect (*ahamityaṃśa*), then,
because that [state] is indistinct due to having as its object a mass of phenomena that are like a painting merely brought into manifestation,
it is the Sadāśiva-tattva, in which Will (*icchā*) predominates— namely, "I am this. Furthermore, regarding the mass of phenomena...
When that very substratum has become manifest, and [consciousness] pours the "I" aspect into this "this" aspect,
then it is the *Īśvara-tattva*, which is dominated by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)— namely, "this-I. For this very reason,
even though there is no difference in the reflective awareness of "I," here the "this" aspect [is predominant].
This distinction arises from [the state of being] turbid or non-turbid; however, when the manifestation of the "this" aspect—
which belongs to the mass of objective entities where differentiation has fully grown— shines forth as residing solely within pure consciousness,
the "I" aspect emerges, just like that which belongs to the Lord according to the proponents of non-dualism-within-difference (*bhedādvaitavādin*).

The reflective awareness of "I am this," according to the analogy of the two pans of a balance being held equally, is the *vidyātattva*, which is characterized primarily by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); such is the division. Although this dense, singular sovereignty belongs solely to Paramaśiva, nevertheless, through his outward orientation...
The activity [of Sadāśiva] is the "principle of power" (śaktitattva), and likewise, that of Īśvara is the "principle of knowledge" (vidyātattva). With this very intention, it is stated elsewhere:
"That which, prior [to the emergence of objects], manifests as 'I' from the desireless and full [Self]..."

I salute that non-dual Absolute, whose nature consists of the entire essence of Supreme Śiva and Śakti, which, while abiding in the states of expansion, diffusion, and contraction from its own form, subsequently desires to divide itself into two branches in order to manifest its own power.
This and so forth has been stated by this [verse]. || 51 ||

Now, one might object: "If such a division were indeed possible even within this supreme form, then how could its essential nature (svarūpa), which consists of the uninterrupted light of the Supreme, remain intact?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For thus, by virtue of the perfection of his own sovereignty, he is all-pervading.
He shines through many, innumerable forms because He is devoid of limitation.
For Śiva, who is the Supreme, by virtue of the majesty of His own sovereignty,
imposes limitations upon Himself within His own nature through infinite, distinct forms consisting of past and future entities, worlds, and so forth.
Even while shining as something distinct, because its primordial nature has not fallen away, it remains essentially the uninterrupted supreme light—this is the meaning. || 52 ||
Now, one might object: "It has been stated that reality (*tattva*) is the persistence of a single form across many [individuals]; how does this apply here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Śāmbhavas, those born of Śakti, the Mantramaheśvaras, and the Mantranāyakas... (9.53)
These five groups, in their respective order, are the pure mantras;
whatever form is consistently present within each individual group shines forth [therein]. (9.54)

Thus, it is said that among these, reality (tattva) consists of [the elements] beginning with Kālāgni, just as [the categories] begin with Earth. Regarding the phrase "among these" (*eṣu*), one might ask: "What is their own group?"—anticipating this doubt, it is stated:

"These five groups, beginning with the Śāmbhava," it is said. "In order" means according to their respective sequence. Thus, the Śāmbhavas belong to the Śiva-tattva, up to the Mantras belonging to the Vidyā-tattva. The term "Śāmbhavas" refers to those belonging to Śambhu, whose nature is supreme light.

The meaning is that all these entities, such as the worlds and so forth, possess an identity with That (the Supreme), because their manifestation by another would otherwise be impossible; as was stated previously:
"Those primordial things which were mentioned earlier in their various divisions—that which is inherent within them..."
"Form shines as the supreme, dense with light; that one God is Śiva.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "born of Śakti"—this refers to Anāśrita and the others. As for the Mantramaheśvaras and the rest, they have already been mentioned previously.
And so, within these two classes belonging to one's own self, consisting of the Mantramaheśvaras and the rest, what...?
"When, by the reasoning stated in such passages as 'From the predominance of the internal state, the principle called Sādākhya appears first; but when there is a predominance of the external state,
the Pārameśvara [appears] thereafter,' the form that follows [the sequence], such as the predominance of the internal state, manifests."

It is with this intention that it is stated here, "the Śadaśiva-tattva and the Īśvara-tattva," and not with reference to presiding deities; for Śiva-hood always manifests as an internal state, while sovereignty alone radiates forth as an external state. For it is thus:
Otherwise, even Brahmā and the others would have to be reckoned as separate principles (*tattva*),

for since their status as causes is no different [from that of the earth], it would result in the fallacy of "half-old-woman logic" (*ardhajaratīya*); and if that were the case, even a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) would be a distinct principle because he presides over the earth.
It would follow [that this is the case], but it is not so; therefore, exactly what was stated is correct. || 54 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Therefore, that which those who are mocked by their similarity to mere narratives have proclaimed... (9.55).
Without even the service of a guru, they have obtained books and their desired visions;
Brahmā is the presiding deity of Nivṛtti, and he is not counted as a separate principle.

What is the logic behind counting Sadāśiva and the others separately [as distinct from Śiva], when they are contained within the Self of Anāśrita, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Īśāna, and Suśiva? (9.57)
"Why is this 'half-old-woman' logic applied to the six things designated as causes?"—thus, from its very root, that calculation is destroyed; for there is no such thing as a cause. (9.58)

Just as a king who is the lord of the earth is not a separate ontological principle [from the earth itself], so too, how could each respective lord of the kalās be a separate ontological principle? (9.59)
"By similarity of narrative" means by similarity of name, such as "Sadāśiva" and so forth. (56–59)
He concludes this very point by adding further:
"Thus, this pentad is defined as the pure path.
In that regard, it is the will of Śiva alone that is the direct agent, manifesting differentiation. (9.60)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then who is the agent in the impure path? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"In order to distribute [the fruits of action] to the hosts of conscious beings whose minds are agitated by the longing for enjoyment under the sway of the Lord's will, Aghoreśa creates here that which is other than white (i.e., the impure path). (9.61)

By the power of the will of the Lord—just described as consisting of pure sovereignty—the [power] called *lolikā* (the state of agitation) becomes clearly agitated; its capacity for remaining [inwardly] and its orientation toward [external manifestation] exist through the influence of the Lord’s will.
"His agitation, known as *lolikā*, clearly exists as a cooperative factor;
that [state] is the readiness to remain [latent], and it is directed toward [manifestation] by the power of the Lord’s will."

According to the principle to be explained hereafter, when the kārma-mala acts as a concomitant cause, there arises a longing for enjoyment— an individual (māṇava) impurity consisting of desire. For one whose conscious group (cidgaṇa)—

that is, the contracted class of subjects— is of such a nature, [the Lord] acts in order to distribute it, that is, to bring about the accomplishment of the various means for its respective enjoyments.
The Lord Aghora— the first among the Mantramaheśvaras,

elsewhere designated by the term Ananta— creates here, in our own system, the impure path (the *aśuddhamadhvāna*), beginning with the agitation of Māyā and extending from Kalā down to Earth, in order to effect the distribution [of grace].
The meaning is that [the Lord] manifests externally in manifold variety. As it has been said:
"By the power of the Lord's will, the desire for experience arises in him;
for the sake of accomplishing the means of experience for this seeker of experience, the King of Mantras [manifests]."
"He brought forth the world by entering into Māyā with his powers. Likewise: "In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent; in the impure, the Lord Ananta is the master.
Is this not so?
"Even for all beings, including the gods, there are three kinds of impurity (*mala*);

yet among them, the *kārmamala* alone is the primary cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). According to the reasoning expressed in such passages, although impurity is threefold everywhere, it is the *kārmamala* that is primary.
Regarding the fact that [the *lolikā*] is the cause of *saṃsāra*, one might ask: "What is this that is here designated as the cause of creation for the *lolikā*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The *lolikā* of the individual souls (*aṇu*s) is a desire that is devoid of action."
The impurity is the knowledge that one is incomplete; it is devoid of limitation and cessation.

That which is the desire of the atoms— being devoid of action because they lack the nature of activity, and being of the nature of mere will— is called *lolikā* (the state of longing); it is free from limitation due to the absence of any specific object, and thus it seems to long for itself.
For this very reason, there is the sense of being incomplete; for this very reason,
due to the non-manifestation of one's own nature which consists of perfect knowledge, there is ignorance— that is, contracted knowledge— and for this very reason,
because of the loss of one's own true nature, it is impurity (*mala*).
"The loss of autonomy in consciousness and the lack of awareness regarding autonomy—this is the twofold *āṇavamala* (atomic impurity), arising from the deprivation of one's own true nature.
By such statements, that which is called *āṇava* is said everywhere to be of two kinds—this is the meaning. Thus...
Karma alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra as a defilement. As it has been said:
"The efficient cause is that which is called desire...
This very capacity for atomicity belongs to the individual souls (aṇu), since when this [desire] exists...
Let there arise for these [the individual souls] the state of being the locus for those respective limitations. || 62 ||
Thus it is said:
"This is merely a state of potentiality for the inclusion of future limitations; therefore, its impurity is not a separate ontological reality, just like attachment. (9.63)
"Merely a capacity"—this is because it does not directly function as a limiting adjunct (*avaccheda*). "Of this"—that is, of impurity (*mala*).
For in this world, one thing is indeed delimited by another thing, and only through a real entity can there be a state of distinctness;
yet this [impurity] is not some kind of entity at all, but rather merely the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) of one's own full nature. Thus, what was said is correct.
—In the gathering of those respective limitations, this mere capacity alone is the impurity. || 63 ||

Now, one might object: "The Sāṃkhya has already accepted that passion (rāga) is a quality of the intellect (buddhi) characterized by dispassion, having the nature of longing for various objects; so what is the purpose of this other such principle of passion and impurity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

But that [cognition], when delimited solely by the aspect of action without further qualification, is passion (rāga) in the person; it is a property of the intellect, variegated by the diversity of actions. (9.64)

"Niravaccheda" means "without distinction. Therefore, that very *lolikā* (desire), limited solely by the general form of the thought "May something be mine," is what is intended as the attribute of the person (*puruṣadharma*). It is enumerated everywhere among the other principles (*tattva*) within the pentad of coverings (*kañcuka*), whereas [the other] is an attribute of the intellect (*buddhidharma*).

It is the very [consciousness] that flows outward as its external limit, by which this determination— characterized by various objects such as hunger, thirst, and the desire for sexual union— arises through the diversity of those respective objects;
whereas in the *āṇava* [impurity], it is merely the state of being oriented toward the general outlining of an object to be sought.
Since such an effulgence (*samullāsa*) exists, he says:
"This sense of being incomplete, and likewise the manifestation of that form.
The word *ca* (and) indicates the reason; because this sense of being incomplete is characterized by the *āṇava-mala* (the impurity of atomicity), and likewise...

The meaning is that the manifestation of the form consisting of passion and dispassion— which is considered to have the nature of the attributes of the intellect (buddhi)— manifests in various ways; for this very reason,
this [form] is like a sprout in the individual soul (āṇava), a bud in passion, and is fully blossomed in the intellect.
And it has borne fruit; enough, therefore, with this excessive detail.

Now, one might object: "Is it not our established doctrine that independent consciousness alone is the ultimate reality? From what, then, does this so-called 'impurity' (mala) arise, which appears to be distinct from that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The will of the independent Śiva is like a jar, [manifesting] in the form of a jar. (9.65)
The very desire to conceal one's own nature is the impurity (*mala*) as a real entity;

it is called a "real entity" because its nature is that of a concealed self. Indeed, in this world, the Supreme Lord, having by His own will concealed His own nature—which consists of perfect knowledge and action—
It would manifest as a contracted self-nature; therefore, it is proclaimed everywhere that contracted knowledge alone is its form. As it has been said:
"They maintain that impurity is ignorance..."
Thus [ends the verse]. 65.

But surely, since there exists only the supreme, indivisible Light, how could this thing called "impurity" (mala) attain the status of a real entity apart from that? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Just as earth and the other elements, though non-distinct [from consciousness], are conceived as having their own nature... (9.66).

"In the same way, for him (*asya*), impurity (*mala*) exists as something distinct" means "for him," that is, for impurity. "In this way" (*iti*) means that although, in reality, it is not distinct from the Supreme Light, it appears as if distinct—just like the earth and other elements. "In the scriptures" (*śāstreṣu*) refers to the *Svāyambhuva* and others; as it is said therein:
"Now, the beginningless impurity (mala) of persons is proclaimed as their state of being bound (paśutva). Likewise:
"That by which [the soul] is said to possess impurity is knowledge; impurity has a characteristic distinct from that."
Thus it is said:
"From that, the impurity (mala) of persons is traditionally taught.
Therefore, its manifestation as something distinct is not at all something new.
In this case, the objection raised by others would not be commendable; for it would only be praiseworthy if its distinctness were established independently. || 66 ||
And it is not so; he says: "But nothing [existent] is separate and independent, like a cart or the like. (9.67)

In this world, objects such as carts and the like exist externally as mutually distinct and independent entities; however, this [Self] is not so, because it is impossible for it to appear as differentiated from the perspective of the Supreme Light (paraprakāśa). For in this way, that second [entity] is present [only as a reflection]. It is by this much alone that [the differentiation of] selves [is established].

Even if there were no admixture with [other] forms, since its presence would be indistinguishable due to its all-pervasiveness, it would bring about the impurity of the form of the *aṇu*; thus, why would it not veil even the *śiva*s and the liberated *aṇu*s?
This is what was stated. || 67 ||
Is that impurity not accompanied by something else, as it resides in Śiva and the liberated souls?

[Objection: But surely, although the impurity (*mala*) is all-pervasive, it would veil the essential nature—which consists of knowledge and action—of each individual soul through its own singular power; as they say:
"The powers of impurity (mala-śaktayaḥ) are distinct for each individual soul and serve as obscurers of its qualities.

Therefore, due to the variety of transformations, that which the obscuring power undergoes as a transformation toward the cessation [of obscuration] for one particular soul would not apply to another; thus, it is not [the case that all souls are equally obscured].
It might even veil the liberated souls (muktāṇu), yet with respect to Śiva, it has no power of veiling at all, because He is by nature beginningless, pure consciousness.
Thus it is said: "There is a certain power of impurity that acts as an obstructer, and that too resides in those who are not yet liberated. (9.68)
Thus, this argument is devoid of logic and is constructed solely on the basis of blind faith.

Regarding the phrase "not gone to liberation"— meaning she has not gone to liberation, nor to the state of the liberated souls (*muktāṇu*), nor to Śiva— even if one were to admit that *mala* possesses a power,
that too would be an obscuration merely by its presence, just like [the soul's own nature], and thus the same fault remains as previously stated.

For if it were an obscuring agent, everything would either be obscured by it or nothing at all; how then could there be this certain determination? Indeed, an entity cannot be partial toward your position such that it would obscure some things and not others.

Thus, the sense is that blue can never become non-blue for anyone. Now, if it is argued that there are many such [powers] and that, due to the diversity of their transformations (*pariṇāma*), one might obstruct another—either partially or not—which accounts for the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated? This is not so; for here, indeed, in the case of all things...
Power (*śakti*) is postulated because otherwise those respective effects would be inexplicable;

just as the burning power of fire is postulated because otherwise its act of burning would be inexplicable. And that power is the very self of the entity itself, yet there is a distinction in its designation due to the difference in its functions, as they say:
"The essence of a category (padārthātman) is power (śakti), whose distinctions are superimposed due to the distinction of its effects.

For this very reason, there is a distinction in this [power] based on the distinction of its operations (vyāpāra), by which a "category" is said to possess multiple powers. Just as fire, through its connection with various operations such as burning and cooking, is called "the burner" and "the cooker."

Thus, there are many such powers; however, it is not logical for each individual power to possess further internal divisions, because there is no difference in their essential nature, because their function is one, and because there is no other means of valid cognition [to establish otherwise]. For indeed, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is postulated only for the sake of establishing what is observed.

And since that [result] is accomplished by a single power, what is the point of the laborious assumption of a distinction in the unseen (adṛṣṭa)? Likewise, if impurity (mala) also possesses a power regarding its function of obscuring, it would obscure everything;
what need is there for its non-distinction, by which its unity might be established? For this very reason, impurity too possesses some obstructing power.

Thus, the indication is made using the singular number alone; therefore it was said: "This [view] is devoid of logic," and so forth. Furthermore, since impurity (mala) is subject to transformation, if one were to postulate an obstructing power that is insentient (jaḍa), then—precisely because of its own insentience—that power would not function by itself, and thus it could not determine, "It shall veil this one, but not that one."

Because there would be an absence of such an intention, [the world] would proceed toward everything, whereby everyone would be obstructed; and if this were so, what proof would there be for a Lord whose very nature is pure consciousness? Nor is he one whose nature is beginningless, pure consciousness. Thus [it is concluded].
It is proper to say that it belongs to the beginningless [nescience] alone, because the investigation has commenced with the determination of its status as the obstructer.
He says that very thing:
"This obstructing power of the insentient does not operate by itself. (9.69)
If the universe were to proceed by itself, then the Lord would be the means of valid cognition (pramā).
In this regard, there is no dispute that what is insentient proceeds only when presided over by a sentient being;
therefore, if it is argued that the Supreme Lord himself impels that power in such a manner, that too is not so—thus he says:
If the Lord unites that power which obstructs impurity [with the soul], then— || 9.70 ||
To the question "Of what nature [is it] with respect to each atom? there is no answer in words.
Regarding "of what nature": is it stainless or stained? In the first case, one would have to apply that [impurity] even toward liberated atoms, whereby saṃsāra would exist at all times.

Furthermore, in the second case, its application is futile because that [impurity] was already present even prior to it; thus, in both ways, its application is not tenable, and it has been stated that there is no counter-argument here—"there is no further word. This is like [the case of] a jar with impurity.
Even when a group of atoms such as a cloth is obstructed by a screen, its own nature is not altered;

rather, the knower's cognition regarding that object is impeded. And if that were the case, this would be a "taint" (mala) belonging only to Śiva, insofar as his cognition regarding that object has been obscured by it.
Regarding this, he says: "Impurity is an obscuration, and it does not differentiate that which is to be obscured. (9.71)
This destroys perception, just as a cloth covers a jar;
for that which is the true nature of atoms whose forms are veiled by impurity. (9.72)
And Śiva alone would perceive that [impurity], and it would belong to Him alone as His own impurity.

Now, if this were so, then because the nature of Śiva— and likewise of the individual souls (aṇus)— is obscured by impurity which consists of the veiling of knowledge and agency, there would indeed be a destruction of their very nature.
How could this be accomplished? To this he says:
"Of the omnipresent Lord, whose essence consists solely of knowledge and action, and of the multitude of individual souls. (9.73)

The absence of that [duality] constitutes impurity (*mala*), which serves precisely for the destruction of form; "of the essence" means "of that which has that as its sole nature. "The absence of that" is so called because it causes the non-existence of knowledge and action. (73)

Now, one might object: "Surely that [attribute] is inherent; if its removal by means of impurity is accomplished, what has happened to the substrate (dharmin) such that its own essential nature (svarūpa) would be destroyed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The difference between the attribute and the substrate, and their oneness through inherence... (9.74)
This was not stated by you like the disciples of Kaṇabhuj;
for it was said previously: "In the scripture of the Supreme Lord, indeed, it is not as in the views of the followers of Kaṇāda and others."
"Some substrate is said to exist for the powers that are of the nature of attributes.
This has been explained in that very [work], and should therefore be understood from there; however, here—

For fear of excessive prolixity, I have not exerted myself further; therefore, it is your view that there is no form of knowledge or action whatsoever that exceeds Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, or the group of individual souls (aṇu). As it has been said:
"The powers (śaktis) are predominant in action, not in the nature of consciousness.
Thus, because their [powers] are cast aside by impurity (mala), their very essential nature would be destroyed;
therefore, it was rightly said: "The impurity of the omnipresent Lord and of the individual souls (aṇus) serves only to destroy their form."

One might object: "Even though form is not discarded, just as cataracts and the like act as an obscuration for the eye and other senses, will it not be exactly the same here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It cannot be obscured by that which is formless, nor by that which is formed. (9.75)
And knowledge [arises] even when the visual rays are in such a state.

Regarding the term "knowledge": it is the nature of the self, which is the form of pure, immaterial consciousness; and for such self-knowledge, an obscuration by anything—whether immaterial or material—is not logical.
Because that which is formless cannot be covered. Regarding the phrase "being such [a state]": it is possible to cover it;

for since the rays of the eyes, the sun, and so forth are material, they possess form, and thus it is indeed logical that they should be obstructed by material things such as cataracts or clouds—this is the intended meaning. || 75 ||
Now, whether this [cognition] be formless or possessed of form, what is the point of insistence?
Furthermore, since it has the nature of a knower, it would become an object of knowledge when it comes under the influence of an obscuration;
and yet, according to your own view, such a thing maintains a state of neutrality (*tāṭasthya*).

Because the relationship between the knower and the known is of such a nature, it would not be able to obscure its own essential nature, since they function separately. Consequently, because it is stainless, it would possess full knowledge and action;
thus, everyone would become omniscient? To this, he says:
And why is that very same impurity, being material in form, not perceived by knowledge? 9-76.

"Therefore, why would everyone not possess omniscience?"—this should be construed by means of the elision (*praśleṣa*) and non-elision (*apraśleṣa*) of the vowel *a* in the word "malo" (impurity), as in "malo mūrtaḥ" (impurity is material). "By the all-pervading one" (*sarvageṇa*) means by that which is pervasive because it is unobstructed by impurity, and which is omniscient—this is the meaning. "Therefore" (*tataḥ*)— [The rest of the passage follows: ...because of the absence of the veil of impurity. And "therefore" refers to the fact that [the Self] is inherently pure and all-pervasive. Thus, since the nature of the Self is eternally free from the stain of impurity, how could it not be omniscient? This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the term "all-pervading" implies that the Self is omnipresent due to its lack of spatial limitation, and "omniscient" indicates its possession of infinite knowledge. Consequently, there is no reason for any being not to partake in omniscience. This concludes the argument.

The meaning is: "by the all-pervading omniscient one" because of being unobscured by impurities; "from that" means from the non-cessation of the nature of consciousness; and "all" refers to the multitude of individual souls (*aṇu*). || 76 ||

If it is argued that since darkness consists merely of the absence of light, it is observed to act as an obscuration even though it is formless, and that the same will be the case for impurity (*mala*), that too is not so;
thus he says:
And that which is the obscuration of light by darkness is [effected] by those things that oppose it. || 9-77 ||
Resistance belongs to material atoms of light; such is not the case for that which is immaterial.
For some maintain that darkness is merely the absence of light, while others hold that its form is merely a superimposed blueness manifested by the absence of light.

Even so, by this [darkness], there is not an obscuration of light that is already established, but rather an obstruction of its very persistence; because it possesses form, the material atoms of darkness simply cause the repulsion of the material atoms of light by means of their own resistance. Thus it is between these two.
The relationship of being struck and striking is not the same as the relationship of being obstructed and obstructing; therefore, this is not an appropriate illustration here. || 77 ||
Now, one might object: "If the insentient [nature], being presided over by consciousness, were to perform some action, let that be so; what is the harm?
But how does it have the capacity to conceal consciousness itself? To this he says:
"And the dependent impurity is not capable of concealing the conscious Self. (9.78)
To conceal...
If it is argued that [the case] is like that of wine, that too is not the same here—as he says:
"Nor should the illustration of the obscuration by wine be stated;
for even wine and the like, being insentient, could certainly not obscure the self, which is itself sentient; rather..."
It is presided over by volition; for that which is insentient cannot accomplish anything at all without being impelled by volition. || 78 ||
And so it is you yourselves who [must admit this]—thus he says:
"It has been stated by you yourselves that an insentient thing cannot be an agent in its own right. (9.79)
These powers indeed impel the independent Lord.
As it has been said: "An insentient entity possesses no capacity for spontaneous engagement or withdrawal.
Therefore, since the Lord alone is the one who withdraws the fetters at that time, He is the bestower of liberation upon the souls.
"Like a sheep and so forth bound by a rope and so on," and so forth. || 79 ||
What follows from this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, [it is] impelled by the power of the Lord who knows the ripening of karma. (9.80)
Alcohol produces intoxication, which consists of the fruits of suffering, pleasure, and delusion.

By that [intoxication], even an insentient substance such as alcohol, impelled by the power of the Supreme Lord, veils the conscious Self and causes it to become intoxicated; however, this occurs in the Self that has assumed contraction consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and not in the pure nature of consciousness.
Because it is impossible to refute that [position] by the reasoning already stated. || 80 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, would not impurity (*mala*) also veil the group of conscious individual souls (*aṇu*) only when they are impelled by the power of the independent Lord? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And impurity does not veil the person when impelled by the Lord, because... (9.81).
In a person who is already pure, such a role as a prompter for the Lord is not appropriate.
Even though impurity is beginningless in this context,
the prompting of the Lord is necessarily required for its binding power, since it is insentient.

Because there is an absence of causal efficacy without the presiding of volition (*cetanādhiṣṭhāna*), [the question arises]: toward whom would that Supreme Lord impel *mala* for the sake of bondage? Toward those who are already possessed of *mala*, or toward those who are stainless? Regarding the first alternative, such impelling is useless, because they were already joined with *mala* even prior to it; as for the second...
This is impossible even with respect to liberated atoms, because that would lead to an absurd consequence; for this very reason it has been said:
"Indeed, the state of being a projector is not appropriate for a pure individual soul.
On the contrary, since there is no distinction in the purity consisting of perfect knowledge and action [in both cases], [the objection does not hold].

Either the Supreme Lord and the individual souls (aṇu) might employ impurity (mala) for their mutual obstruction, or the individual souls alone [might do so] with respect to the Supreme Lord; for when there is a great disparity in power among many compared to one,
as they say:
"When there is a conflict between two properties, that which possesses the greater number [of supporting instances] shall have its property.
Therefore it was said: "And since their stainless nature is equal, why would they not impel [one another]? (9.82)
Regarding that Lord, it is appropriate that there should be a commonality among the majority;
now, concluding this [discussion], he returns to the subject at hand:
"Therefore, the manifestation of impurity consists solely in the autonomy of one's own nature. (9.83)
This has been determined and elaborated by me elsewhere; therefore, enough of repeating it here.
"Elsewhere" refers to the first chapter (āhnika) and so forth; for this very reason, the word "again" (punaḥ) was used.
And there is no contradiction anywhere regarding this—thus he says:
"Impurity, longing, ignorance, nescience, restlessness, and manifestation. (9.84)
The defect of worldly existence, the raft [of samsara], exhaustion, emaciation, delusion, the sense of "I" and "mine," the affliction of the self, the power of illusion, and then the veil. (9.85)
"The seed of defects," "the state of being a bound soul," and "the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra"—by such etymological designations as these, he is described here and there. (9.86)
Now, one might ask: "What is this underlying object? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When this exists, existence arises; because it consists of duality, it is a flawed existence—this is the defect of existence (bhavadoṣa).
Like a couch, it carries the stream of suffering for the atoms (individual souls); therefore, it is called a raft. (9.87)

"The fault of existence" (*bhavadoṣa*) is [an example] of the seventh-case comparison according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*, because it acts like that, just as in the case of "the bed" (*mañcavat*). "The raft" (*plava*) is [an example] of the same, because it performs that function. || 87 ||

One might object: "In that case, why has the underlying meaning not been shown for everything? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The remaining words, however, are easy to understand; one should infer the appropriate meaning therein. For this very reason, we too have not explained this, out of fear of making the book too voluminous."
This must be inferred by oneself.

Now, regarding this [statement], "the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra," what is the easy-to-understand interpretation? Is saṃsāra itself the sprout, or is it the sprout of saṃsāra, of which [this] is the cause?
Dispelling such a doubt, and preceded by a demonstration of the connection with the subject matter at hand:
He introduces the impurity of action (*kārmamala*), which follows in sequence:
"Action is the cause of transmigratory existence; it is called the sprout of *saṃsāra*. (9.88)
Since the fourteen-fold variety of elemental existence is born of karma,

the second half [of the verse] serves as the reason for karma being the cause of saṃsāra; by that [reason], it is proclaimed that "the nature of saṃsāra consists of bodies and worlds, which is of the nature of Māyā."

The *kārmamala* (action-impurity) is the cause—like a sprout from a sprout—of the *māyīyamala* (illusion-impurity) described by these and other [verses]. The cause of that, in turn, is the *āṇavamala* (atomic impurity). As it has been said:
"Impurity is the cause of action; beyond that, it is the occasional [effect]."
Thus:
"The cause is that which is called longing...
and so forth. || 88 ||
Thus, since this manifold saṃsāra arises solely through the power of karma, everyone must exert effort for its very eradication; so he says:
"Therefore, in the teachings of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and so forth... (9.89).
The renunciation of "I" and "mine" is taught for the sake of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*).

In this scripture—meaning the teaching—it is indeed taught therein that whoever has fixed their mind upon the Supreme Brahman, even while performing everything, [should maintain] the sense of "I" through the conceit: "I do nothing at all."

One should abandon even the grasping at "mine-ness," thinking, "Since there is no attachment to this, there is no purpose for me in what has been done by it"; thus he would attain *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action), by which his transmigratory existence, which is caused solely by that [grasping], would no longer occur. As it is sung in the Gītā:
"Actions do not taint me, nor do I have any desire for their fruits.
He who understands me thus is not bound by actions.
"Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and dependent on nothing,
even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
Thus [it is said].
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has realized the Self, whose senses are conquered,
and whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, is not tainted.
"The knower of reality, being disciplined, should think: 'I do nothing at all.
And:
"He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment..."
"He is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. Thus it is said. || 89 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then is he not already liberated? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For even while the root impurity called ignorance remains, he is indeed free from karma. (9.90)
Due to the absence of a cause for diversity, it does not move upward nor downward;
it merely [remains] limited, not touching the non-duality with Śiva. (9.91)

"He is declared to be a *vijñānakevalī*, abiding in pure consciousness alone. The particle *api* has the sense of "also" (*cārthe*) and is displaced in its position; thus, it means "even though he is devoid of action" (*niṣkarmāpi*). "Above" (*ūrdhvam*) refers to the pure path (*śuddhamadhvānam*). He does not transmigrate because of the absence of the *āṇava* impurity known as ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the root of all taints.

Because of its state, it is neither pure nor impure below, due to the absence of the karmic impurity (*kārmamala*) which is the cause of diversity; rather, by the reasoning stated in such passages as, "Above Māyā and below Śuddhavidyā dwell the Vijñānakevalas," it occupies the intermediate region between the pure and impure paths.

Although his essential nature is pure consciousness alone, because he has lost his sovereignty, there arises a contraction of his own nature caused by a portion of the *āṇavamala*; thus, being limited, he fails to attain non-difference from the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness inseparable from sovereignty.

"Vijñānakevalī" means one whose form is consciousness (*vijñāna*)—that is, consisting of awakening (*bodha*) alone—and who is devoid of autonomy (*svātantrya*). This is what is meant by "pre-eminently stated," that is, proclaimed everywhere.
As it has been said:
"Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency."
"Even though they are identical in their characteristics such as enlightenment, those who possess mutual differentiation through the diversity of the Lord's will are the Vijñānakevalas. (91)
Now, one might ask: "Is this [individual] forever untouched by non-difference from Śiva, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But he, through the will of Śambhu, while contemplating non-difference from Śiva... (9.92).

"Gradually, having the form of the Lord of Mantras and His Leader, he attains the nature of Śiva. Regarding "gradually": this is due to the increasing intensity of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of non-difference from Śiva; for that very reason, through the excellence of its firmness, his state as a Great Lord of Mantras (*mantramaheśvara*) may even occur instantaneously (*akrameṇa*). Thus it is said.
This is the state of being. As it has been said:
"At the very beginning of the creation of the world, desiring to emit [the universe], he awakened by his own will eight individuals who were *vijñānakevalas*."
Thus: the Īśas are the Mantreśvaras; their leaders are the Mantramaheśvaras. || 92 ||

Now, it is certainly the case that the *vijñānākala* possesses the *āṇava* impurity, and since that is the cause of *karman*, how could it not produce its own effect—by which there would be nothing but its repeated state of transmigratory existence?
On the contrary, [the scripture] says that through the sequence beginning with mantras, one attains the nature of Śiva; why has this been stated? Thus [is the objection].
Incorporating one doubt within another, he raises a further objection:
"But if impurity (mala) is the cause of this karma, how [is it that the soul is not bound]? (9.93).
He does not produce a continuity of karma even for the Vijñānākala.
He refutes this very point:
"Not so; for how could that impurity [remain] when it is about to be destroyed in the Vijñānākala? (9.94)
The cause would be the state of being in the process of perishing, and it would arise solely from autonomy.
[The state of] "desiring to perish" is due to the lack of awareness even regarding that autonomy.

By such statements, there is a refutation of the internal distinctions of the nature of the ego-identification (*ahaṃbhāva-abhimāna*) with the body and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated: "How could it be a cause, since it lacks the capacity to produce its own effect? On the contrary, by its own greatness in the form of being oriented toward destruction, it is indeed in the process of perishing, which is inseparable from that [destruction].
Or rather, its very state of destruction would arise; for a seed that is about to perish cannot sprout again, nor,
while it is in the process of perishing or has already perished, could there possibly be any further requirement for it simply because it is about to perish.
With this very intention, the conceptualization of the sequence beginning with *vijñānākala* has been established everywhere;
thus he says:
"Now, in the three [states] called 'about to perish,' 'perishing,' and 'perished'... (9.95).

Within the ten stages (*daśā*), which contain internal sub-states according to their own sequential order, there is the conceptualization of the states of the Vijñānākala, Mantreśa, Tadīśa, and so forth. (9.96)

"Other states" refers to those characterized by the state of being partially about to perish, being partially perished, and so forth; and the reason for including these within [the process] is "because of their own sequential existence. For it is not the case that immediately after the stage of being about to perish (*didhvaṃsiṣutā*) and so on, there is suddenly a state of perishing as an undivided whole.

The sense is that "destruction" (dhvastatva) may manifest. Therefore, in these five states, the nature of the Vijñānākala and so forth is postulated according to their respective order. "Īśas" refers to the Mantreśvaras; "tadīśas" refers to the Mantramaheśvaras; and "ādi" refers to the Ādisiddha.

Śiva [is the ultimate reality], for otherwise there would merely be the conceptualization of him as Īśvara and so forth; and thus, due to the differentiation of these states, it follows as a matter of course that even deep sleep (suṣupti) and the fourth state (turya) possess multiple forms. || 96 ||
Therefore he says:
"And consequently, the manifold variety [of states] will be explained in relation to both deep sleep and the fourth state (turya).
Thus, it is rightly stated that the root impurity (mūlamala), desiring to destroy [the self], is not the cause of karma."
He says that very thing:
"Therefore, his own power has become stunted by its orientation toward destruction. (9.97)

"How can it be said that impurity (mala) becomes the cause of action? It is said to have become 'obstructed'—the intention being that only when its power is fragmented could it again become the cause of action. And this has been stated as a concession [to the opponent's view]."
In reality, however, this is not possible for impurity (mala); thus he says:
"Furthermore, even karma does not arise from impurity, because karma consists of action. (9.98)
And action arises from sovereignty in the form of agency, not from impurity (*mala*).
"From impurity"—the meaning is: from that which consists of non-sovereignty characterized by non-agency.
Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect exists only within the very reality of agency and objecthood.
This has been established immediately [before]. || 98 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is it that [the scriptures] state such things as: 'They maintain that impurity is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But that which constitutes its status as "karma" (action) is its capacity to yield diverse fruits.
It is well known that she [the power of action] does not exist within herself without contraction, and that [contraction] is impurity.
"She" refers to *karman* (action) by virtue of its yielding various fruits; "he" refers to contraction.
Therefore, without contraction, she lacks the capacity to bestow those respective fruits. Thus, contraction itself is impurity.

The status of being its cause is merely metaphorical; for the contracted enjoyer conceives within himself as an object of enjoyment a separate result consisting of the auspicious and inauspicious, by which he exists in various forms such as gods and humans. || 99 ||
Thus it is said: "For a diverse fruit is indeed conceived as distinct by way of being an object of experience. (9-100)
Therefore, this arrangement in the form of differentiation exists within the Self, who is the enjoyer.
Consequently, impurity (*mala*) is neither the material cause nor the auxiliary cause for the Self’s own manifestation; rather, it is like a hand to support one in performing an action—as he says:
Thus, it relies upon being a cooperative cause in the production of its own effect. (9-101)
Impurity (mala) is the cause of action (karman) by virtue of manifesting its capacity;
for without contraction, no capacity whatsoever is manifested in this [action] regarding the bestowing of diverse fruits—this is the intended meaning. || 101 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, since even the *vijñānākala*s are joined with the two impurities (*mala*) resulting from the contraction of their own sovereignty, would not such statements as 'the *vijñānakevala* is joined with only one impurity' be contradicted? On the contrary, by the statement 'the *pralayakevala* is joined with its karma,' the status of being a *pralayakevala* would result [for them]?"—thus he raises the doubt.
But if this is so, since karma exists and impurity (mala) likewise persists, how [can liberation occur]? (9-102)

"The state of being devoid of consciousness (vijñānākala) possesses such a contraction; by whom was it said that he is joined with the two impurities?"—to this he says: "Of him," and so forth. "Such" means, as before, appropriate for the state of the *pralayākala* and others, and fit for the manifestation of the efficacy of karma.
...up to verse 102.
He provides the following rebuttal:
"It is not so; for even one whose contraction has not been destroyed [can attain this] through firm contemplation. (9-103)

Thinking "I am not the doer," one abandons the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of action through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the form of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth, such as "I" and "mine. Consequently, because of this state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*), there is no connection with the impurity of action; thus, the status of the *vijñānākala* (the consciousness-deconditioned) is established. || 103 ||

One might object: "If the impressions (*saṃskāra*) were completely severed, there would be no connection between the preceding and the succeeding [moments], and thus the status of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) itself would not exist. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This firm mental state within the self that 'this action will bear fruit'... (9-104)

That *saṃskāra* exists here for the sake of the fruit, but it is not the cause of recollection. It is "firm" because it is beginningless. For within the Self, there are two kinds of *saṃskāra* consisting of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*), designated by such terms as "modification" (*vṛtti*) and so forth: either with a beginning or without a beginning. It is not the first [kind].

That [imprint] which is deposited by experience and, being awakened through the power of awakening, serves as the cause for recollection, sustains the subject's capacity for synthetic unification (*anusaṃdhātṛtva*). On the other hand, there is another [imprint], consisting of the latent impressions of action (*karmavāsanā*), by virtue of which action yields various fruits. || 104 ||

Now, one might object: "If the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of karma has been severed, what has happened to that karma such that it would not have its share of results? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though the contraction [of the ego] has not been destroyed, by the cultivation of the thought 'I am not the doer'... (9-105)
"Nor is there fruit for one who is intoxicated, deluded, and so forth, even when an expiation has been performed.
Regarding the phrase "not destroyed": this means that even when the auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*) is present, there is no fruit;
that is to say, the meaning should be understood as referring to action consisting of merit and demerit. For [the fruit does not arise] for one who is intoxicated, deluded, and so forth.

There is a continuous mental connection (*anusaṃdhāna*) such as "I am doing this"; for if an action were performed without such a connection, it would not truly be "done," so how could it bear fruit? It is precisely with this intention that [it is said]: "From the emergence of the intention, [arise] action and the rest."

Thus it has been said by others. Even when a penance (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed, one thinks, "I am not the agent here"; through this cultivation of cessation (*nivṛttibhāvanā*), because the mental engagement with those respective objects becomes slackened, they will no longer yield their respective fruits. As they say:
"Having committed a sin, one is liberated from that sin by feeling remorse; furthermore, one is purified by desisting with the thought, 'I shall not do this again. (105)
[Objection: "In that case, has it not followed that existence (*sattā*) is not the motivator for the yielding of a fruit, but rather intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*)? [Reply: This is true; thus he says:
'Whatever austerity I have practiced today, may that belong to him'—this is clear. (9-106)
"An action performed with a specific intention would not bear fruit according to that intention;
this is 'clearly'—that is, with certainty. 'Action' refers to the form of austerity. 'Would not bear fruit' means for the agent.
For since it was intended, 'May this be for another,' how could it be a giver of fruit for oneself?"
As they say:
"The desired fruit does not come to pass...
[and so forth]. || 106 ||

Now, one might object: "In this way, since the action and its fruit would reside in different substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), how can the objection regarding the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) be refuted? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But [the Lord] effects that mental impression (*saṃskriyā*) known as intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*). (9–107)

Action such as austerity (tapas) and the like, when colored by its fruit, is capable of bringing about the attainment of that fruit; for, by imparting a latent impression (saṃskāra) to the mind in the form of the intention— "May this indeed bear fruit in the hereafter"— it becomes capable of producing the attainment of the fruit.

The meaning is that in this very way, one attains skillfulness in the granting of results. For the intention is that the determination of the fruit of action depends precisely upon the intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*). As they say: "In whatever manner one intends, so shall that [action] bear fruit for him."
Thus, this objection does not arise; for it would only be so if, while the intention for the fruit were directed toward this very life, the fruit were to ripen in another. || 107 ||
But if the relationship between action and its fruit depends solely upon intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*), then that very distinction would collapse;

for everyone who performs an action without intending its fruit would not partake of that fruit, and thus heaven and hell would be rendered obsolete. This is true—provided that someone [actually intends them].
One might become intensely attached to it; therefore, he says: "But he who, even in that regard, abandons the mental impression of a result through firmness... (9-108).
He enjoys the distinguished fruit produced by the renunciation of that fruit.
Furthermore, he who, in that very pursuit, firmly abandons even the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the fruit of action—
“he who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action”— [attains the supreme goal].

By such statements as these, one should abandon attachment to that [result]; he enjoys the distinguished, supramundane fruit produced by non-attachment to that result— the meaning is that he attains the state transcending *māyā*— as is sung in the Gītā:
"For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action,
being liberated from the bondage of birth, go to the state that is free from all suffering.

But if this is so, how can the scriptural statement that even fishermen and others partake in the fruit of Śivarātri merely by staying awake, as well as the Smṛti rules on expiation for those who unintentionally drink forbidden liquor and so forth, be consistent? For it is not the case that...
Do they possess this kind of deliberation: "We do this for this purpose"? To this it is replied:

Where, indeed, is such deliberation applicable here? Is it to the essential nature of the action, or to its fruit? It cannot be to the fruit; for one does not perform [an act] with the intention, "May hell befall me because of the killing of a Brahmin."

Someone might kill a Brahmin; for in this way, there would indeed be a cessation of such an act for him. However, because in reality everyone in the world fears hell, on the contrary, even the desired fruit—such as the removal of thorns and so forth—would not accrue to him from that [act].

For at that very moment, the production of other thorns is observed hundreds of times. Nor can there be any fruit from compassionate giving, because one engages in it through compassion alone, without intending any result. If it is argued that its own nature exists right here [in the act], then that is certainly not the case for fishermen and the like.

The intention "I am awake" does not belong to this [state] in the same way it does to one who is intoxicated or deluded, because there is an absence of an unsteady state of functioning; however, due to ignorance, it lacks such firmness, which is why its possession of limited results is established. This is likewise the case in the Buddhist system for a certain [type of person].

By way of the example of a particular kind of worm, as it circumambulates the Lord Caitanya, there is indeed such an exertion in its movement; for its nature is not like that of cotton, which moves merely by being blown by the wind or other forces. Therefore, its [movement] is rightly due to the sovereign power of the Blessed One.
The attainment of a happy rebirth in another life is brought about by the power of the objective reality (*vastubala*). Even in the case of drinking what should not be drunk and so forth,

because there was no intention that it was undrinkable, one who acts unintentionally still possesses a general intention, namely, "I am drinking this," on account of which an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for him due to his lack of circumspection and other such factors.
However, it is less than that for one who acts with desire. As Manu says: "The expiation prescribed for those who act without desire is doubled for those who act with desire."
Thus, the determination of the fruits of action is indeed animated by this very [conscious] synthesis; enough with further elaboration.
He applies this very point to the subject at hand:
"By means of this sequence, he who [perceives] the entire succession of actions... (9–109).

"Even though he possesses contraction, he should abandon that state of being 'without parts' (akala) through non-egoity. Regarding "through this"—it means by way of [the practice] ending with the renunciation of fruits. Regarding "entirety"—both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Regarding "through non-egoity"—the meaning is: through non-attachment to that. Regarding "without parts"—[he becomes one who is free from the limited subjectivity].
The Vijñānākala. || 109 ||

But surely, in this way, someone might— out of the power of hatred— form an intention directed toward an enemy, thinking, "May my own misdeed accrue to him," so that even having committed a misdeed, he would not be a partaker of its fruit; would this not lead to the total collapse of the established order of the fruits of action?
Regarding this, he says:
"But in this way, would not some evil deed of one's own arise from one's intention? (9.110)
"It would be for another; you have not understood the word that is grounded in reality.

Thus—because the determination of the fruits of action depends solely upon intention (abhisandhāna), this objection belongs to one who has not understood the determination of the fruits of action; thus it is said, "it has not been understood."
And so forth. || 110 ||
He establishes this very point: "If that enjoyer were to have such an intention as he has toward himself... (9.111).
Therefore, even for one who is another, that evil deed must necessarily come to pass;
for when the intention of another is perceived, one's own intention becomes firm. (9.112)
But in the absence of such intention, this [act] possesses no connection to a fruit;
the notion "this is not my misdeed" is firmly rooted in him, and thus it leads to no result. (9.113)

Just as that doer of evil deeds has the intention within himself, "May this accrue to him," so too, if there were a corresponding reflection on the part of the "other" intended to be its enjoyer— thinking, "May this be mine"— then it would indeed be so; for [the fruit] consists of good and evil deeds.

When there is such a consciousness of intention belonging to another, one's own intention regarding the object offered to them becomes firm—that is to say, it becomes supported by the fact that one shares in the fruit thereof.
This is the meaning. Of whom...

Furthermore, since such an intention regarding one's own self does not even exist for him, how could he possibly possess the state of being a recipient of its fruit? On the contrary, it is conceivable that a contrary intention—"May no evil accrue to me"—has naturally taken root in him. For in reality, all of this...
The world is afraid of sin, and its cause is precisely the attainment of that fruit; how then could another incur the fruit of a misdeed merely through the intention of another?
Thus it would have been said: that the action should bear fruit for the one who intended it, and not for the object to whom it was dedicated.
And because there is an absence of one's own intention when aiming at another, there is no arising of the fruit. || 113 ||

Furthermore, in the absence of the agent's own retrospective awareness (*anusandhāna*), one must consider whether that performed action would bear fruit for oneself or for another, or whether it would be entirely fruitless; having thus reflected within, he briefly introduces the very position intended [by the author]:
If the intention of another is severed and no intention exists within oneself, the fruit would not accrue to either of the two, because the cause for destruction has been established. (9.114)
"Of the two" refers to the agent and the object of the act of offering; "the cause of destruction" is characterized by the absence of the internal connection between oneself and the other. || 114 ||

One might object: "Just as another person does not have the mental resolve, 'May this evil deed of theirs become mine,' so too should they not have the resolve, 'May this good deed become mine. Why, then, is it said [in the scriptures], 'Whatever austerity I have practiced today' and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Because his intention regarding the cause of happiness and happiness itself is the same—being without distinction—it is logical that he is the enjoyer of the fruits of merit and so forth. (9.115)
Furthermore, the intention "May there be suffering for me, or may it be the cause of my suffering" would not even be a common one; therefore, there is no acquisition of demerit from that. (9.116)

For the entire world desires happiness and seeks to avoid suffering; thus, it is logical that everyone intends toward happiness or its cause, even in a general sense, but not toward suffering or its cause. Therefore, it is rightly said: "One would simply become a partaker of the fruits of another's good deeds."

Nor does one share in the fruit of a misdeed; "because there is no distinction"—the meaning is: because this [act] lacks the specific form of thinking, "May the austerity performed today become my own austerity. || 116 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he returns to the subject at hand: "We speak now of that which pertains to the *jñānākala* as previously described:
because of his state of being devoid of egoism (*anahaṃyutā*), all latent impressions of karma (*karmasaṃskriyā*) have dissolved. (9.117)

By the phrase "of the one already mentioned," all the previously stated objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that establish the absence of the *kārmamala* are recalled; therefore, for this *vijñānākala*, there is no *kārmamala* at all.
Consequently, because it lacks its own functional activity—which consists in manifesting the capacity [of the *mala*]—the *mala* is about to be destroyed.

Precisely because of that reality, through a sequence beginning with the state of being currently undergoing destruction, it would reach the state of being destroyed, which is inseparable from that [process]. || 117 ||
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, karma does not exist for this [consciousness], nor can impurity (mala) act as its auxiliary; consequently, this [consciousness] attains a state of being destroyed. (9.118)
"By that" means by not acting as a cooperative cause. || 118 ||

One might object: "If impurity (*mala*) has been destroyed, then because the sense of 'I' arises everywhere in the form 'I am Śiva,' and because there is likewise [the realization of] non-existence regarding action and its fruit, would this person not again be joined with the impurity of karma (*kārmamala*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
With internal impurities cast off and brought under the sway of immersion in Śiva,
he does not fall into a state of subservience to karma, even while remaining intent on the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva).
The reason for the absence of a state dependent on karma is the fact of being brought under control by the immersion into Śiva. || 119 ||
Thus, having established that impurity (*mala*) is the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and by way of that context,
he corroborates the nature of the sprout of transmigratory existence through the teaching of the *Śrī Mālinīvijaya*, which encapsulates all the previously mentioned objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
And this very point was stated by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:
"They maintain that impurity (mala) is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence. (9.120)
Action consists of dharma and adharma, and is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Regarding that, he explains the *karmasūtra*:
"One should discern one's own effects, such as pleasure and pain, by way of their causal nature. (9.121)
"One should characterize" (lakṣayet) means that one should establish [it] in such a way by making its own existence the instrumental cause—this is the meaning.
Having raised the doubt, "In what way does this serve as its characterization?", it is said: "by way of being the cause" (hetubhāvataḥ). Indeed...
Anticipating the objection— "According to the principle that 'causes do not necessarily possess their effects,' how can a cause be established as such by necessity?"— he says:
A cause never exists anywhere without its own effect;
causality is merely a fitness, characterized by the state of being immediately followed by the fruit.

What indeed is this "capacity"? It has been stated: "the state of being produced immediately after the result. For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas and others have accepted that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) alone is the cause.
The statement beginning with "it is not necessarily [the case that] the complete causes are the cause," and so forth, was made with reference to the incomplete [causes]. || 122 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then would fire and other such factors—which have already entered into a different causal complex prior to the effect—possess causality or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the causality of the preceding factor exists through a succession..."
Therefore, this explanation contains a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound within it, namely that pleasure, pain, and so forth are its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
In that very context, he shows another explanation containing a *bahuvrīhi* compound:
"Furthermore, what is that?"
It is observed that [pleasure, pain, and so forth] occur even when the visible causes are the same. (9.123)

Due to various [circumstances], there is some other cause, and that is seen here as karma. Furthermore, by the word "that" (*tat*), it is indicated that because the previous [explanation] is untenable, this is not an alternative interpretation, but rather a conjunction through repetition; for although [the cause] is the same for every person...

When the visible causes, such as service or study, are observed, the diversity of pleasure, pain, and so forth that occurs therein cannot otherwise be accounted for; by this fact of its inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), another cause designated as "the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) is indicated—that is, it is inferred. Furthermore, because it produces specific effects, it is [inferred] by that [means].
Something specific must exist—thus he says: "And that is action.
Anticipating the objection, "Even if it is specific, how is it known to be 'action'? Let it be something else, such as a *piśāca*," he states:
"Because it is observed here. For in every case here, a diversity of effects is indeed observed due to a diversity of actions.
—this is the intended meaning. || 123 ||
He demonstrates this very point:
"Clarity, roughness, and so forth, arising in one's own limb [are produced] by one's own karma. (9.124)
An unseen cause, namely *karman*, residing in another body is postulated because it is observed that within one's own body,

various states such as serenity or harshness arise through an action of one's own, such as the application of dust or unguents; therefore, according to the maxim, "the postulation of the unseen is based on what is seen."

In this case as well, it is karma alone that is the cause, and not something such as a piśāca; rather, the meaning is that it resides in another body—that is, it has been accumulated in a different body. || 124 ||
And one should not raise an objection regarding an inconsistency on this account alone; thus he says:
"For even here, the fruit of karma is clearly seen to reside in various different bodies. (9.125)
Agricultural labor is performed in the spring, and the enjoyment of its fruit occurs in the autumn; yet that [body] is different.

Since there is no dispute here even regarding the momentariness of the body—that "the action resides in one body while the fruit resides in another body"—there is no disagreement on this point, because agricultural labor is undertaken in the spring.

The statement "that fruit [is experienced] in autumn" is only consistent with a difference in bodies due to the variety of states; thus it was rightly said: "karma residing in another body is postulated as the cause. || 125 ||

One might object: "In that case, would not the logical flaw of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) arise? Anticipating this, he says:
"Because, however, a single unifying subject (*anusandhātṛ*) is possible. (9.126)

That very same person who previously performed that diverse karma is the one who now experiences its fruit; because of this identity of continuity— since there is no lack of common locus between the action and its result in the sense that "I, by whom this was sown in the past, am that very same person who shall enjoy it today"— there is neither the destruction of what has been done, nor...
"It is rightly said that there would be the acquisition of what was not done—namely, that the fruit of action resides in various other bodies.

[Objection: "But this might be so if there were indeed a continuous connection (*anusaṃdhāna*); however, no one possesses such a connection regarding actions belonging to another birth and their fruits in this life. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even if the king is intoxicated, he might command the cook in the morning as follows: || 9-127 ||
By feeding [a guest] even without the conscious intention [to do so], one obtains that fruit;
likewise, karma acquired in another birth [yields its result] today through present consciousness. (9.128)
One enjoys the fruit even without [direct] action; the cause there is indeed the previous state of being unshakable.
For such a reflection is not possible for one who is intoxicated, such as a king or similar person:
"Indeed, yesterday I gave such an order to the cook, by which today this enjoyment—the very fruit of that command—has been obtained."

"Feed [him]"—the meaning is "enjoy [it]. Likewise here as well, there is no fault in the fact that the attainment of the fruit from karma belonging to another birth occurs even without conscious recollection (*anusandhāna*). Now, it was just stated that the determination of the fruits of karma depends solely upon recollection.

Anticipating the objection, "How can that very [state] be reversed right now?", it is said: "The cause therein is indeed prior immovability. For previously, there existed a firmly established mental connection (*anusandhi*) in that regard, such as "I act in this way," and because of the firmness of that latent impression (*saṃskāra*), its fruit appears here; thus, in this [context].

And he alone is the instigator; for it has been demonstrated immediately prior that he is never to be accepted as the agent in matters such as the fruit or its connection [to the action]. Thus, for an action that is oriented toward the granting of a fruit, the strengthening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from its previous mental engagement is necessarily required; otherwise, [the result would not follow].
Because such a state [of firmness] would be impossible; and consequently, for one who is not oriented toward that [state], such firmness could not arise.

Thus, it is possible to obstruct it by some means so that it does not grant its fruit, for in that case, even the occurrence of internal obstacles and the like is conceivable—this is the intended meaning. ||128||
Therefore it is said: "For this very reason, an action performed [is purified] by means of action or even by austerity. (9.129)
"Or it may be suppressed by knowledge when it is not yet intent upon the ripening of its fruit.
Regarding the word "therefore"—this is because, when the fruit is about to manifest, there is an indispensable requirement for the unshakable prior connection of the action.

Regarding the phrase "by means of action"—this refers to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of ritual acts and so forth. Regarding the phrase "it may be suppressed"—this means rendered unfit to yield its fruit.
One should perform [this]—this is the meaning. || 129 ||
For this very reason, karma that is oriented toward yielding its fruit cannot be obstructed; thus he says:
"Furthermore, how can that karma which has begun its effect in this body [be stopped]? (9.130)
"The final state cannot be obstructed while it is being cut off.

As for the question "How can it be cut off?"—the meaning is that it cannot be cut off by any means whatsoever. The reason for this is: "because its effect has already begun. For that which has not yet begun its very task...

First, its very state of being engaged in initiation is obstructed by some means in the interim; thus, its cessation is logical. But as for that which has already set out to initiate itself—since it is already in motion, what is there to be ceased? It has been said: "In order to cease it in its final stage."
"It cannot be done," with this very intention [it was said]: "One should not purify that which has already begun."
"...for that [karma] is indeed experienced through enjoyment.
Thus it is proclaimed everywhere. Furthermore, initiations such as the *sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā* can only occur for one whose death is imminent;
since their fruit has already been essentially bestowed even there, karma remains turned away from that [initiation].
There is no fault whatsoever in [the view that] it is to be purified. As it has been said:
"Having seen a disciple seized by old age and tormented by disease, one should then cause him to ascend and unite him with the Supreme Reality."
Thus [ends the section]. 130.

Now, it may be argued: let it be granted that the karma which produces the birth, lifespan, and body-initiating factors does not cease because its effects have already begun; however, what about that karma—whether present or past—which will initiate an effect characterized merely by experience within this very body over the course of days, months, or years? Is that not to be suppressed?
Is this possible or not?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that very body, whatever else there may be, whether of today or from the past... (9.131).
Karma can be rendered impotent by means of that [supreme] knowledge, initiation, and so forth.

"The other" refers to that which has not yet begun to produce its effects (*anārabdhakārya*), and this occurs immediately. "To render impotent" means to destroy it by stripping away its capacity to yield fruit—this is the meaning. "It is possible" means that it is not...

But it is done in that manner because it is stated in general terms: "One should not purify that which has already begun," and because no specific exception is mentioned; this is understood from the word "etcetera" (ādi).

[This refers to] mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth. As it has been said: "Those [afflictions] which are declared here to be adventitious are pacified by medicines, primarily by means of recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*)."

Thus [it is said].
