Furthermore, elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like would act as auxiliaries to that very karma which bestows longevity and has the effect of sustaining life, by means of which this [karma] remains with its capacity for activity unceased for a long time; and by virtue of which, even for those who are diligent, the death that is inevitably destined by time is postponed for some period.
Victory would consist in the nature of an obstruction. As it has been said:
"By great-souled ones who have attained perfection through elixirs, austerity, yoga, and penance—wise men who are not subject to the power of others—even time and death are conquered."

Thus, poison and the like, when administered, strike only one whose life-force (*āyus*) has been exhausted, and not anyone else. However, in that case, the agent who partakes in the evil deed merely harbors the conceit, thinking, "This was done by me. And so, this [statement] refers to karma that initiates the formation of the body.

One should not say, "Since her efficacy is not observed even in matters that can be accomplished by medicine and the like, how can there be confidence in her regarding an unseen matter? What is the use of initiation? For nothing new is produced by medicine and such means that would result in a lack of confidence.
Thus, enough with this digression. || 131 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is its destruction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For in that way, the firmness of the latent impression (saṃskāra) leads to the fruit; yet again, [it is] through firmness. (9.132)
"Whenever [the action] might perish, the action is then and there destroyed"—
this means "in such a way," namely, in accordance with the previously established continuity (*anusandhāna*).
For it has been demonstrated that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which has thus attained growth would be the cause of the fruit in this world.
As for the firmness of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) itself, which is the cause for the production of a result—that is removed because it no longer performs its function;
thus it is said: "the karma is destroyed," "ceased," "cut off," and "rendered impotent. And by these two [terms], it is stated that there is no restriction whatsoever regarding time in this case.

Thus, the summarized meaning is that even an action performed under the influence of delusion may, through the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) and other means, go to destruction for everyone without experience [of its fruit] and by way of the non-sequential path alone. || 132 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, although one who is under the sway of delusion has done nothing at all... (9.133).

Nevertheless, at the time of knowledge, all of that—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is entirely consumed. "At the time of knowledge" means at the moment of the direct realization of consciousness. || 133 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the authority for this?", he says: "And it is stated in the Śrīpara: 'The one who sees all is intensely free from taking and giving. (9.134)

In a mere moment, it would burn away everything— both the unperformed and the performed— that resides within the body. Here, someone who is all-seeing— knowing everything as being of the nature of consciousness, and for that very reason free from grasping and rejecting due to the dissolution of duality— is intensely radiant.

Having abandoned the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, one should—in a mere instant—burn away all evil deeds and good deeds residing in the body; that is to say, one should reduce them to the state of the fire of knowledge (jñānāgni). This is the meaning. || 134 ||

Anticipating the objection— "How can even action, which resides in the body, be possible for one for whom everything is grounded solely in consciousness?"— the author himself explains the phrase "residing in the body" while internalizing this very doubt:
"Residing in the body" means that she has assumed identity with the body. (9.135)
By virtue of its own freedom, consciousness itself is said to be [the agent]; therein, karma situated within it is burnt away.
This occurs through the abandonment of the latent impression of identifying with the body and by abiding in the state of being the self of the universe. (9.136)

For any refinement that occurs within that which is undivided, all-pervasive, and untouched by time is in fact a contraction; and by this [contraction], it consists of the identity of the body. (9.137)
"Consciousness alone"—the sense is that the entire multitude of phenomena is indeed the expansion of consciousness.

"Situated therein" means residing within consciousness as delimited by the body. Furthermore, the "burning" of action consists in nothing other than the subordination of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the bodily ego-sense; and that [is what follows].

It was stated that [the state] "might exist" because the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) is primary within consciousness that has resorted to the nature of the universe (*vaiśvātmya*); and that [state] arises from "abiding in the state of being the self of the universe. For indeed, in the nature of consciousness—which is non-dual, the sole ultimate reality, eternal, and all-pervading—it is not logical for any latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the body and so forth to exist as something distinct.
For that [bondage] could only exist when there is contraction, and contraction consists solely of the singular form of the body and so forth;
thus it is rightly said that for one who knows everything as being of one essence with consciousness (*saṃvid*), there occurs the burning away of karma—precisely with this intention [it was said]:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give..."
"Whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me.
Thus it is sung in the Gītā. 137.
Concluding this, he introduces another point:
"This is declared to be the impurity of karma (kārmamala), along with which the *layākalas* remain within the depths of the cave like sleeping serpents. (9.138)
Then, with their latent impressions awakened, they receive their appropriate lot and transmigrate again and again in this world, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings.

"By which" means by the *kārma* impurity (*mala*). For the *pralayākala*s are bound by two impurities. "The thicket of the cave" refers to the interior of *māyā*. By this, it is also indicated that their pervasion extends only up to this point. "From there" means immediately after remaining within *māyā*, at the commencement of creation—this is the sense. "Latent impression" (*saṃskāra*)...

—consisting of the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*), it is precisely due to their diversity that these [beings] are said to possess their respective [conditions], as they "wander" (saṃsaranti)—that is to say, by implication, conjoined with Aghoreśa. And it was stated previously:
"At the end of that day, the universe dissolves into Māyā."
"When that much of the night has passed, the Lord of the Deep (Gahaneśa) creates once again.
Thus [ends verse 139].
Now, one might wonder: "Is there only downward transmigration for these [beings] without distinction, or is there also upward movement?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But those who have begun the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of destroying the latent impressions of karma (*karmasaṃskāra*)."
Without having attained the perfection of cultivation, they have gone to their destruction.

Through the excellence of the ripening of their internal meditative cultivation, those great ones attain the state of a mantra; and from that, through various activities, they achieve results both diverse and wondrous.
"Without having attained"—the sense is that upon attaining that [state], they would indeed become *vijñānākalas*.
"Likewise, abiding within"—the meaning is that they have bestowed their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in accordance with the elimination of karmic residues.
"From the painting"—this refers, by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), to the excellence of the maturation of contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

And this should be applied as a qualification of the *karma* (action). For this very reason, it is said that even the nature of a mantra is manifold (*citram*) due to the distinctions between those with adjuncts (*sāñjana*) and those without adjuncts (*nirañjana*). The underlying idea is that because of the diversity of the cause, the effect must likewise be diverse. And regarding mantras:
It cannot be conceived otherwise than that [the Mantras] have the *pralayākala* as their material cause (*upādāna*). As they say:
"Of the Mantras who exist as *pralayākalas*, having been graced... And in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated that for the *Mantramaheśvaras*, the *vijñānākala* is [the material cause].

Since it has been stated that all [the categories] are the material causes of the Mantreśvaras, it follows by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya) that the Pralayākalas are established as the material cause of the Mantras. || 141 ||
Now he concludes the very subject at hand:
"For this *kārmamala*, which extends throughout the path ending with *māyā*, the primary cause is said to be the *āṇavamala*, whose nature is ignorance. (9.142)
"Pradhāna"—because it manifests those respective capacities. For, without this state of being a cooperative cause, it would possess no capacity whatsoever for the production of its own effects;
such is the sense. As it has been said:
"The power that brings about birth does not exist for karma without impurity;
an atom devoid of ignorance is never seen born anywhere. (142)
Now, let this be granted; however,

as for that state of agitation previously introduced in such passages as, “...whose longing for enjoyment is stirred by the power of the Lord’s will,” what is that said to be?— anticipating this doubt, he says:
The agitation of this [ego] known as *lolikā* clearly exists as its auxiliary cause;
and that [agitation], by virtue of the will of the Lord, is an orientation toward the unsuitability of remaining [in its current state]. (9.143)
"By way of cooperation"—that is to say, with the impurity of karma. || 143 ||
One might object: "Surely this would be established by the very power of the thing itself; what, then, is the purpose of the Lord's will?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For an insentient entity is never capable of anything without being presided over by consciousness."
One might object: "In that case, the Lord would by His own will assign impurity only to atoms distinct from Himself;
thus, wouldn't the doctrine of duality (bhedavāda) itself follow here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Those called 'atoms' are not anything other than the Great Lord, whose nature is Light. (9.144)
The individual soul (*pudgala*), appearing as both conscious and unconscious, is the knower of the field (*kṣetravit*) and the bound animal (*paśu*).

Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever called "atoms" other than Maheśvara, whose nature is light; for it is He alone who, through His own sovereignty, manifests within Himself the state of being both conscious and unconscious, [calling Himself] "putha..."

When the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *puṅg* in the sense of "violence" (*hiṃsā*) and "affliction" (*saṃkleśa*), one obtains *pudgala*. Thus, a *pudgala* is so called because he "perishes" (*galati*) through violence—that is, through the notion of otherness—and through affliction.

Furthermore, because he perceives the body alone—which is a field that brings about the sprouting of the seeds of karma—as the self, he is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*) due to his state of being bound.
This is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Śiva himself, having assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu)... || 144 ||
One might ask: "What would be the result of this apprehension of the state of being a limited subject (paśu), given that it appears as having both conscious and unconscious natures?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And because its nature is consciousness, it is all-pervasive, devoid of qualities, and consequently devoid of action. (9.145)
The eternal one, who desires the means for enjoyment, is described as being devoid of form;
due to his lack of consciousness, there is ignorance, and consequently, a distinction from the object of enjoyment and from other subjects. (9.146)
Regarding the term "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities): the sense is that qualities such as *sattva* and so forth belong only to insentient entities like *prakṛti*.
For this very reason, it is stated that its functional states (*vṛttayaḥ*) are also impossible for him; thus, he is called "niṣkriya" (actionless).

Consequently, the phrase "from that state of being devoid of qualities" (*tato nirguṇatvāt*) is how it should be interpreted. Regarding the term "bhogopāyepsuka" (desiring the means to enjoyment): [it refers to] the means of enjoyment...

This means that he desires to obtain causes and so forth, being solely intent upon them. "Devoid of form" (mūrtivandhya) means "formless" (amūrta). Regarding "ignorance"—the sense is that his identification with the self (ātmābhimāna) is directed toward insentient things such as the body.
And for this reason, precisely because of this insentience, he lacks the capacity to encompass and give rise to the entire universe.
And because he is permeated by the impurity (*mala*) of *māyā*, which consists of the manifestation of duality, he is said to be "differentiated from everything," as it is stated:

"His differentiation [is] from the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and from other subjects (*bhoktṛ*). Thus it has been said: "The individual souls (*aṇu*) are of the nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness..."
Thus it is said:
"The individual soul (paśu) is eternal, formless, ignorant, devoid of qualities, inactive, and powerless;
it is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and is incapable of considering the means for its own enjoyment."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 146 ||

Thus, even though they do not exceed that [consciousness], the impurity (mala) of those atoms—which appear as if they do exceed it—awakens solely by the power of the Lord's will; thereby, due to the diversity of their karma, the manifestation of various respective transmigrations occurs for them. Thus he says:
That impurity of those atoms awakens intensely by the power of the Lord’s will...
And this is not established by reasoning alone; thus he says:
"And so it has been stated in the scripture named Śrīpūrva. (9.147)
He recites that very [verse]: "By the power of the Lord's will, the desire for enjoyment arises in him;
for the sake of assisting the one who desires enjoyment, the first Mantramaheśvara [is appointed]. (9.148)
Having agitated *māyā*, he creates the manifold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
As it is said therein:
"By the power of the Lord’s will, his desire for experience (*bhoga*) arises."
"For the sake of accomplishing the means of enjoyment for this one who desires enjoyment, the King of Mantras,
having entered into Māyā with his powers (śaktis), brought forth the world.
Thus [ends verse] 148.
Nor is there any such thing as "māyā" existing apart from that; thus he says:
"And what is called māyā is the power (śakti) of the Lord, non-different [from him]. (9.149)

For indeed, that independence (*svātantrya*) of the manifestation of difference was produced by her; for that very independence of the Supreme Lord— who delights in the play of manifesting the entire universe—
in manifesting difference is itself [the power], through the expansion of non-fullness (*apūrṇatā*), which is non-distinct from Him.

It is called *māyā* because it measures (*mīnāti*) or destroys (*hinasti*); thus, it is referred to as power (*śakti*). For it is by that very [power] that this manifestation of duality is brought forth. Therefore, through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause, that [power] itself is called the "manifestation of duality. || 149 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"The first manifestation of differentiation, which has not yet reached division... (9.150).
That supreme night is the one in which the infinite future manifestations are contained within it;

for here, because it is merely the desire to overflow externally and is thus only slightly outlined, the first appearance of duality has not yet attained its division. Therefore, that [appearance] is the supreme night, meaning the Great Māyā. For this very reason...

It has been stated that within this [state], there is the internalization of the future differentiation occurring in extroversion, like a seed-pod; thus it is said: "having internalized the infinite future differentiations."
Having thus described her nature as Śakti,
she is said to be one, all-pervading, subtle, partless, the storehouse of the universe, without beginning or end, the sovereign mistress of the inauspicious (Aśiva), and free from decay.
In order to express its nature as reality by internalizing the meaning of the scriptures, he says:
"It is insentient because its form is one of difference, and since its effect is also insentient. (9.151)
She is all-pervasive because she is the cause of the universe; she is subtle because she is conceived solely through her effects;
she is eternal and one because she is inseparable from Śiva and Śakti; she is the primordial cause. (9.152)

Regarding the phrase "because it has the nature of differentiation": for this indeed is the very nature of the insentient (jaḍa), that it is manifested as delimited by [the thought], "this appears here, now," as was stated previously:
"To have a delimited manifestation is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient."
And thus, because she is measured—that is, delimited as something to be abandoned—by yogins, this is her designation.
For this very reason, she is called *aśivā* (non-auspicious). As they say:
"...*śivā* [is so called] because she bestows the manifestation of duality."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, if this [kalā] were not insentient (ajaḍa), its effect would likewise be so; as it has been stated:

"And since its effect is insentient. For if the effects of māyā, such as kalā and the rest, were not insentient, then there would follow the consequence of a plurality of conscious beings within a single body, as well as the futility of the puruṣa as the material cause. This is because [the effect] is the cause of the universe.
—Because it acts as the cause for the manifestation of the universe, which consists of effects and instruments, through the manifold gates of its various streams;
this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Since she, being all-pervasive, brings about the experience of the infinite Puruṣas..."
"All effects [are produced] everywhere through the streams that are the abodes of the universe.
Thus, she is called "the measurer" (*mātṛ*) because she measures everything. She is "subtle," meaning she is not known by all people;
for the sense is that she is postulated by those of limited vision through the logical necessity that otherwise effects would be inexplicable.

Regarding the phrase "due to the inseparability of Śiva and Śakti": Śiva is eternal, and because Śakti is inseparable from Him, it has been stated that she possesses His attributes as His substrate; thus, He is called "eternal. For this very reason, He is described as "without beginning or end" and "devoid of decay. Consequently, [He is so called] because of the negation of destruction, which is denoted by the word *mā* (non-existence).
Regarding the word *yātā*: Śiva alone is the one independent reality (*padārtha*), and Śakti is his very self-nature (*ātmabhūtā*).

According to the logical principle that "what is non-different from the non-different is itself non-different," she too is said to be one—hence the word *ekā*. For this very reason, because he is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*), he is called *niṣkalā* (without parts). And Śiva [manifests] only by virtue of Śakti.

It has been stated that [the Supreme] may manifest the universe externally even though it remains within; thus it is called the "Root Cause," and for this very reason, it is called the "Treasury of the World" and "Īśānī. Consequently, because the entire circle of phenomena (*bhāva-maṇḍala*)—though non-different from His own Self—is measured by Her, Śiva establishes it through differentiation, such that the universe is perceived within Her.
And thus [it is said]. || 152 ||
Now, one might object: "But others have stated that *prakṛti* is the root cause; how then is *māyā* designated as such here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Every effect is insentient and manifold in nature, just like a jar."
And likewise, the primary cause (pradhāna) is therefore the effect; but the self (ātman) is not conscious.

Here, inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is set forth with five members (*pañcāvayava*). It is as follows: Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) is an effect, because it is manifold while being insentient. Whatever is manifold while being insentient is all an effect, such as a jar; that which is not an effect is not manifold while being insentient.
Just as the self (*ātman*) is multiple despite being insentient, so too is the *pradhāna*; therefore, it is an effect.

This has been demonstrated many times by the proponents of the Veda, and thus it is not elaborated here for fear of excessive length. As for the claim that there is no excellence of human effort whatsoever in the act of striking down one who has already fallen—that is mere illusion (*māyā*).
Furthermore, even though it is insentient, it is established that this [Prakṛti] possesses only causality and not effecthood.
Consequently, because a cause precedes [its effects], in every instruction concerning the paths of the principles (tattvas) and so forth, she alone is mentioned first. || 153 ||
Thus it is said: "For this very reason, Māyā was previously described as existing in two ways on the path.
And its existence in two ways is stated to be by virtue of its nature as the knot of the *tattvas*—thus it is said, "existing in two ways."
For the cause must exist in a form that is either swollen or unswollen—this is the intended meaning.
But was it not just stated that Māyā is the non-deviating power (*avyabhicāriṇī śakti*) of the Lord?
How then could she arrive at a state of being (*tattvabhāva*) defined by duality? Is this not saying too little?
For just as with Māyā, the entire collection of principles (*tattvagrāma*), beginning with Kalā, is indeed nothing other than the supreme power of the Lord.
Thus, with this very intention, it is proclaimed that "His powers are the entire universe," and so forth; therefore, he says:
And just as the power of the Lord, Māyā, attains differentiation, || 9.154 ||
Likewise, the other expansion of the principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā, also possesses the nature of reality.
He establishes this very point:
"That [power] of the one whose power is restrained, which consists in the kindling of a limited capacity for agency... (9.155).

The power of the Lord is called *kalā* because it casts the individual soul downward. "Of one whose power is obstructed" means that his true nature has been concealed. "Downward" refers to the state of being a subject such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the reason for applying the word *kalā* here is precisely this downward casting. (155)
He extends this same principle elsewhere as well:
"In this same way, these [principles] beginning with Vidyā and ending with Earth are, from the perspective of ultimate reality," (9.156).
"They consist of Śiva and Śakti alone, according to the stated principle.

Regarding the phrase "according to the stated principle"—the meaning is "by following the stated principle. Therefore, just as the power (*śakti*) of the Lord (*nātha*), which consists in the kindling of his limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtā*), is called *kalā*, so too...
"Vidyā is a certain power whose nature is sensation," and so forth. || 156 ||

Now, one might object: "If the entire collection of principles (tattvagrāma), beginning with *kalā*, consists solely of Śiva and Śakti, then of what could *māyā* be the cause? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Nevertheless, the separate manifestation of *kalā* and the rest occurs through the will of the Lord. (9.157)

Therefore, since [the world] is insentient, an effect, and established as a distinct principle, Māyā is certainly remembered as its material cause (upādāna), and in some cases, it is indeed that very effect. (9.158)
"Even so" (tathāpi)—the meaning is: even while consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
From that, due to the manifestation of separation produced by the will of the Lord, there arises insentience because [the categories] such as *kalā* possess the nature of duality;
from that, there follows the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*); and from that, their persistence as separate entities. And thus, in this regard:
It has been stated that it is logical for Māyā to possess the status of a cause: "Māyā is remembered as the material cause (upādāna).
The word "in some cases" refers to the unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth; "its effect" refers to the categories beginning with Kalā. || 158 ||

Now, one might object: "The reason called 'appearing as separate' (*pṛthagbhāna*) is unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddha*), for even for a person of limited vision, such [separateness] does not exist for the parts (*kalā*) and so forth, just as it does not for the earth and other things which have been made the subject (*pakṣa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the form, variegated by such an appearance, is mutually exclusive."
Whatever indeed appears in the conceptual construction exists externally, like a jar.

Indeed, that which appears as variegated through such distinct manifestations—possessing a manifold nature due to qualities such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and being an effect (*kāryatva*), and for this very reason appearing as forms mutually excluded from one another in independent conceptual constructions (*svatantra-vikalpa*) and the like—that exists externally, just like a jar; according to the principle: "What has appeared cannot be non-appeared."

The meaning is that it exists as a real entity (*vastusat*). Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the collection of principles beginning with *tanmātra* exists externally, because they appear separately in [mental] constructs (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth; whatever appears separately in mental constructs exists externally, just like a jar or similar objects; whereas that which does not exist externally does not appear separately.

Just as the Supreme Self appears as distinct from the collection of principles beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra), [one might think] that [the world] exists outside of Him; however, although this separate manifestation of the Self persists— as seen in such passages as "this Self is manifested once for all by the Supreme Self"— it does not attain further growth, being like a flash of lightning.

Because, according to the principle beginning with "the self is not liberated from its sovereignty," there is no concealment of its being composed of the fundamental, undivided *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness); or else, [one might argue]: "The particulars are denotable, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*)."

According to the principle "that which possesses a universal," this [reason] is exclusively a *kevalānvayin* (purely positive); and here, in the case of "existence" as the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there is no unestablished positive property (*bhāvadharma*), nor is there any [reason] that is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) because it depends on both [the similar and dissimilar instances].

By the reasoning stated in such passages as, "How can that existence (sattā) be established, which is a property contradictory to an entity?"— it must be said that a reason (*hetu*) which possesses the properties of both existence and non-existence is not a valid reason, due to its being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because it establishes the existence of an external ultimate reality. || 159 ||
One might object: "But even though things like a sky-flower appear separately in mental construction and the like, they do not exist externally;
therefore, this reason is inconclusive. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"We assert the existence of the sky-flower and so forth [in that sense]; therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason]."
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thence): because even things such as a sky-flower possess external existence.

"Is this not a contradictory statement, since the non-existence of a sky-flower and the like is witnessed by all cognizers? To this he says: "The sky-flower depends upon time, space, and the cognizer because of the word 'non-existent'. (160)
"Like the earth, etc. ...

"It does not exist" is to be applied [to each case] like the eye of a crow. Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "The non-existence of sky-flowers and so forth is dependent upon time, direction, and a cognizer, because it is the object of the application of the word 'non-existent'."

That which is the object of the application of the word "non-existent" possesses a non-existence that is dependent upon time, space, and the knower, as in the case of the earth and so forth; whereas that which does not possess a non-existence dependent upon time, space, and the knower is not the object of the application of the word "non-existent," as in the case of consciousness (saṃvit); and yet, [consciousness] is indeed the object of the application of the word "non-existent."
[This is] like a sky-flower and so forth; therefore, non-existence is dependent upon time, space, and the subject.

Furthermore, as for that which is conventionally designated as "non-existent" with reference to time and so forth in such cognitions as "I do not know this here now," it has been stated many times that this is based on the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of cognition. || 160 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then what is the purpose of the conventional usage of absolute non-existence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the same way, let absolute non-existence also be analyzed in this manner.
The word "in this way" means as in the case of the non-existence of a sky-flower and the like. Therefore, the formal argument (prayoga) here is as follows: absolute non-existence...

It depends upon time, direction, and a cognizer, because it is the object of the word "non-existent. Whatever is the object of the word "non-existent" depends upon time, direction, and a cognizer, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth; whereas whatever does not depend upon time, direction, and a cognizer is not the object of the word "non-existent," such as consciousness (*saṃvit*).
And absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is the object of the word "is not"; therefore, it depends upon time, space, and the cognizer.
Having thus established the categories of reality (*tattvajāti*) beginning with those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), he now establishes the body, the worlds, and so forth as a corollary (*prasaṅgāt*).
Whatever is conceived by him, his external body exists as consciousness in that very manner.
Everything up to the end of Sauśiva is like Caitra; it possesses such a body.
Whatever kind of body one has, one's external city is of that same nature. (9.162)

Therefore, the sequence of worlds (bhuvanapaddhati) ending with Suśiva is established according to the scripture as something to be conceptualized; "in that way" means by virtue of having a body; "conscious" means presided over by consciousness; and "possessing such a body" means [as previously described].
The meaning is that it is endowed with an external body presided over by volition (*cetanā*).
"Just as" means having forms such as pure, impure, and so forth; "of that same kind" means corresponding to that.
And here there are two syllogisms: the collection of principles up to the level of Śiva...

It is endowed with an external body presided over by consciousness, just like Caitra and others. That which is not endowed with an external body presided over by consciousness is not an object of volition rooted in valid cognition, such as a jar and the like; however, everything up to the level of Śiva is an object of volition rooted in valid cognition.

The collection of principles (tattvajāta); therefore, it is conjoined with an external body presided over by consciousness. All embodied beings up to Suśiva are conjoined with specific worlds corresponding [to their nature], because they possess bodies;
for whoever possesses a body is conjoined with specific worlds corresponding [to their nature], just as the earthly body belonging to the earth.

Caitra and others: whoever does not possess a corresponding specific world is not an embodied being, just like Paraśiva; and since those from Suśiva downwards are embodied beings, they must therefore possess a corresponding specific world.
Now, one might object: "In this way, it is established that atoms have specific worlds as their objects of enjoyment;

however, since the entire path (adhvan) is a bond because it is the object of enjoyment for all atoms without distinction, does this not contradict [the former claim]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That city is to be reached by the selves, because it is a location, like any other location. (9.163)
From that, the state of being the enjoyer of the path by means of the Self is established without effort.

"That city" means everything situated within each respective level of reality (*tattva*); "to be attained" because it is fit to be enjoyed; "without effort" means without depending on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*) in this case: "The collection of those various worlds is the object of enjoyment for the atoms, because it is a location (*deśatvāt*).

Whatever is a location is an object of enjoyment for the atoms, just like a village and so forth. Whatever is not an object of enjoyment for the atoms is not a location, just like a second atom. And that collection of various worlds is indeed a location."
Therefore, atoms are the object of enjoyment. || 163 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he returns to the subject at hand:
"That Māyā, having undergone agitation, gives birth to the universe on all sides. (9.164)
Just as when an *āmalakī* tree is struck by a staff, its fruits [fall]—even though this is so, nevertheless, it appears with various sequences of priority and posteriority. (9.165)
Even within the multitude of principles that constitute the effect of Māyā, there exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect;

for although that Māyā, being agitated, produces the universe simultaneously and without succession, nevertheless, because each scripture describes it with distinctions, it appears variegated in various ways.

The meaning of the sentence is this: because priority and posteriority are manifested even within the stream of principles beginning with *kalā*, the relationship of cause and effect exists there as well—this is according to the *Āgama* (indicated by the particle *kila*). As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
"The principle of *māyā* is the seed of the universe, eternal, all-pervasive, and likewise imperishable."
Having established his own group [of powers] therein, the Lord should simultaneously cause them to vibrate.
"But when the *badarī* fruit is struck by a gentle blow, its fruits emerge from all sides—sideways, upwards, and downwards. (Svacchanda Tantra 11.60).
Thus, it is not only *māyā* that is the cause, and the universe, from *kalā* down to the earth, that is the effect.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this same nature applies even to *kalā* and the other [categories] which are its effects.

And that [nature] of theirs is mutual, as stated by the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*). Therefore, whatever is the effect is the very same as the cause, and whatever is the cause is the very same as the effect; just as *kalā* is in relation to *māyā*.
And the effect is the cause with respect to knowledge. || 165 ||
Now, one might object: "If the causal relationship between reality and its effects is described differently in each treatise, then which one is being taught here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Although that [causal relationship] is clearly seen in many ways in other treatises... (9.166).
Nevertheless, we shall explain that according to the perspective of the Mālinīśāstra;
"that" refers to the relationship of cause and effect.

But surely, even though Māyā is insentient, its status as an effect has been set aside on account of its unity, and it has been declared to be only a cause. The same should be said for Kalā and the others as well, since there is no difference in their being insentient and unitary. In this regard, their insentience is "unopposed by the opponent's view and is indeed accepted."

Having stated this by way of a rhetorical turn to refute [the doctrine of] unity, he establishes plurality: "That which they describe as being within Māyā, from Kalā down to the earth (vasudhā)... (9.167).
"This is indeed distinct for each individual, due to the differences in pleasure, pain, and so forth," they declare further on. (167)
One might object: "Even if there is no difference in the essential nature of the *kalās* and other categories, what would be lost if there were a distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this very world, within the aggregate of the means of experience... (9.168).

"How could there be a difference in experience (*bhoga*) from the simultaneous manifestation of pleasure and so forth?"—this refers to "the world," meaning that which is subject to birth and death and lacks liberation.
"In the collection of the means of experience" refers to the aggregate beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*). "Simultaneously" means—

The meaning is "simultaneously and in common. Here, it is beyond dispute that a difference in effects arises from a difference in causes. Now, if the means of experience—ranging from *kalā* down to the earth (*vasudhā*)—were non-different for every individual soul, then from where would this distinction in the experience of pleasure and so forth arise? || 168 ||

Now, one might object: "This [distinction] will arise from the difference in karma; for pleasure and the rest have karma as their cause, and that karma is distinct for each individual. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this [distinction] does not arise through a difference in karma, because that very [karma] is logically untenable. (9.169)

"Of that very [action]" means of the differentiation of karma. For it has been stated that even though there is a difference between individual selves (*ātman*), the aggregate of experiences—beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth—is one and the same. And since transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, it follows as a matter of fact that this [aggregate] is simultaneously connected to all selves. And thus it is connected.

Since *satī* (the existent) is engaged in action simultaneously by all selves—thus bestowing action upon all without distinction—how could she effect a differentiation of actions? Consequently, even though there is a difference among the selves, there is no difference in the action; thus, there would be no difference in their effects, such as pleasure and so forth.
It does not exist. || 169 ||

Thus, the aggregate of the means of experience, beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*, is indeed distinct for each individual soul (*pratyātman*), by virtue of which there arises the differentiation of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Therefore, he says: "Therefore, the group beginning with *kalā* is indeed always distinct."
Through the will of the Lord, they attain oneness in the performance of dance, song, instrumental music, and so forth.
That collection of means for enjoyment, beginning with the earth and ending with the *kalā*, which produces experience,
is determined for each enjoyer; this is to be thoroughly understood by the wise.
Otherwise, the observed distinction between pleasure and the other [feelings] would not be tenable;
it would be tenable if it were due to a distinction in their causes, provided that [the distinction] is not [merely] nominal.

"But being connected simultaneously with its agents while performing action, how will it produce distinct actions based on the difference between the agents? This is the formal argument (*prayoga*) here: the collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* is distinct for each individual self.

Because it is differentiated by pleasure, pain, and so forth; for whatever is differentiated by pleasure, pain, and so forth is distinct for each individual self, such as the body and other [physical elements]; whereas that which is not distinct for each individual self is not differentiated by pleasure, pain, and so forth, such as *māyā*.
Since the collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* is differentiated by pleasure, pain, and so forth, it follows that they are distinct for each individual self.

[Objection: But if this is so, then because of the difference between individual selves (*ātman*), there must also be a difference between the *kalās* and the other [categories]—as has been stated. And since here it is said that the difference between individual selves is not ultimately real (*atāttvika*), how could such a difference exist even for these [categories]? [Reply: Certainly, he says: "At times, through the will of the Lord, they attain unity, as in the performance of dance, song, and the like. They "attain unity" means...

To that extent, there is a dissolution of difference; for although the true nature of all subjects and objects is indeed nothing but the single principle of consciousness (*eka-cittattva*), nevertheless, this firm and deeply rooted manifestation of difference persists, brought forth by the power of *māyā*. Yet, even therein, by way of a process of re-absorption (*pratiprasava*):
In some respects, their unity appears as something created; why should it not be so everywhere?
Thus it is said: "By the will of the Lord. || 170 ||
For this very reason, because they consist of the non-dual Śiva, their purity is also possible; thus he says:
"Of all these principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā, which are yet to come into being, there exists purity for those who have been purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta). (9.171)

Regarding the phrase "of those who are to be" (*bhāvinām*): because they will be described later, this refers to *kalā* and the other [categories]. To the question "Whose purity is it?", it is said: "of them. And who are they? It is said: "those who have been purified by the descent of power" (*śaktipāta*).
Now, one might object: "Since there is no difference in their being means for experience (*bhoga*), what is the distinction between the pure and the impure [kalās]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the *kalā* is pure; such a [pure] *kalā* gives rise to that kind of agency (*karmatva*)."
By which, even though it is brief, one is swiftly liberated from this saṃsāra. || 9-172 ||
"Such"—referring to the object of the worship, meditation, and so forth, of the Supreme Lord. || 172 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"Having declared that the collection of passion, ignorance, time, necessity, primordial nature, the senses, and objects is thus pure," the omnipresent Guru spoke in the *Mānastuti*. (9.173)
"Thus"—meaning, as in the case of *kalā*. By that [means], *rāga* (passion) produces attachment precisely toward the Lord;
*vidyā* (knowledge) likewise produces discernment directed toward Him alone; *kāla* (time) effects the reckoning of His teachings and so forth;
and *niyati* (destiny) effects the restriction of one's devotion to Him and so on. In this way, the others should be inferred by oneself. Not...
"This is not our own invention," he says, with the words beginning "iti" and so forth. "Guru" refers to Śrī Vidyādhipati;
"in the Mānastuti" means in the *Pramāṇastotra*. || 173 ||
Having thus explained this as an incidental digression, he states the actual subject at hand:
"In this way, the emergence of the *kalās* and the other principles is analyzed.
He says:
From the principle of Māyā arises Kalā, which is characterized by limited agency.
As it has been said:
"She gave birth to the principle of *kalā*, through union with which a person becomes possessed of the capacity for agency... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.27).

Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated that the Self is by its very nature the knower and the agent? Then what is the purpose of this [notion] that some degree of agency is produced in it by *kalā*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For *māyā*, creating a separation of the bound soul (*paśu*) from Śiva who consists of consciousness..."
For that very reason, it is devoid of perception and action, as if in a state of deep sleep.
The meaning is that by creating a division from Śiva, who consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it conceals its own true nature.

For this very reason, because it consists of consciousness, it is said to manifest a state that is almost like being in a swoon: "it brings about a condition as if in deep sleep. "Tata eva" means "from that very [state] of bringing about deep sleep. "[He is] without vision or action."
Thus, his full knowledge and action are concealed—this is the meaning. || 175 ||

[Objection: "In that case, would the world not become entirely insentient, or perhaps even cease to exist at all, since it does not manifest as such due to the concealment of the power of vision? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For *kalā* generates a limited capacity for agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) for the individual soul (*aṇu*) through its own embrace."
And when she is anointed by him with even a minute amount, she gives birth. || 9.176 ||
One might object: "Let there be the embrace of the *kalā* by the *aṇu*; otherwise, indeed, its capacity for agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) would not arise.
But what is the purpose of this [individual soul's] embracing the *kalā*? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Mutually," and so forth.
"Anointing" (*añjana*) means "close union" (*saṃśleṣa*). (176)
He establishes this very point by means of an illustration:

"For when there is a separation from the individual soul arising from initiation that grants immediate liberation, that [power], though present and even though it clings [to him], does not in some cases produce its own fruit. (9.177)

For that *kalā*, even while remaining conjoined [to the soul], results in its own fruit— consisting of limited agency and so forth— in some individual soul (*aṇu*), by means of mere purification (*saṃskāra*) alone, like other forms of initiation; this occurs when, in the initiation of immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), the soul is separated from the *kalā* through its elevation above it.
The phrase "does not give birth" (ṅo sūte) means that she does not produce—this is the sense. || 177 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "Surely the *kalā* (limited agency) should produce its effect by its own power alone; what need is there for its union with the *puruṣa*?
He pacifies this doubt by means of an illustration:
"It is like the initial swelling [of a seed], and like the subtle stage of the sprout."
Through its conjunction with water, fire, earth, mud, and husks, the seed brings about germination. (9.178)

Just as the swelling of a seed, which constitutes its initial stage, subsequently produces its own effect through its connection with water and other factors in the form of a subtle sprout, so too it is logical that the effects of *māyā*, such as *kalā* and the rest, produce their results only upon conjunction with the *puruṣa*.
Thus it has been rightly said: "In separation from the *puruṣa*, *kalā* brings forth its own fruit."
"Agni"—here, what is intended is mere radiance. || 178 ||
Now, just as in the case of a cloth produced by the conjunction of threads, not even a single thread would fail to be its material cause (*upādāna*),

so too, according to the statement, "In that same way, consciousness (*cetanā*) is manifested through the conjunction of *māyā* and the atoms (*aṇu*), [producing] *kalā*" (Mataṅga 9.15), *māyā* would not be the material cause of *kalā*, which is born from the conjunction of *māyā* and the atoms.

Anticipating the objection, "How can we determine that [the soul] is atomic?", he says: "Even though this *kalā* is born from the conjunction of *māyā* and the atom (*aṇu*), it cannot make the atom undergo modification; rather, it causes *māyā*, which is subject to change, to do so. (9.179)
"One should not take an atom as its material cause" means that an atom cannot be its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

The reason for this is given as "unchanging" (*nirvikāraka*). For a material cause exists by undergoing a modification of its own nature and persisting as something inherent in the effect, just as clay does in the case of a jar and so forth.

It is not so for this [intellect], because that [consciousness] is eternal due to its nature as pure consciousness alone. Therefore, even though it is born from the conjunction of both [consciousness and matter], it has been stated that Māyā alone is its material cause: "But [it perceives] Māyā, which is subject to transformation"—the meaning is that [Māyā] is differentiated by the various distinctions of the transformations of its respective mental states (vṛtti). || 179 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the *kalā* cannot be the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the individual soul (*aṇu*) because it is devoid of transformation, but on what basis is this restriction made that it must be *māyā* alone? For it has been stated that the conjunction of *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman* constitutes the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Mala is the obscuring agent, while Māyā is the material cause of phenomenal existence; Karma serves as the auxiliary cause for the arising of pleasure and pain. (9.180)

For although these [impurities] are equal in being causes of saṃsāra, they each produce their own specific effects; namely, that the effect of *mala* is solely the obscuration of knowledge and action. Therefore, since its capacity is exhausted by this much alone, how could it possibly bring about the arousal of any agency?

It may also produce a constituent element (kalā) contrary to that [state]. Furthermore, since pleasure and the like are objects of the senses and are composed of the qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva*, their material cause (*upādāna*) consists of things like sandalwood paste; action (*karman*) serves merely as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*). Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), [action is not the cause] of the elements beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*).
Māyā is the material cause of all entities—this is the distinction. || 180 ||

Thus, since the individual soul (*aṇu*), whose consciousness is completely shrouded by impurity (*mala*) acting as a veil, must have some cause for the intensification of its limited knowledge and agency, and since that cannot be *karma*—
because the power of the latter is observed only in the production of experience— it follows, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), that it must be something else.
He says it is indeed *kalā* alone:
"Therefore, it is *kalā* alone—insentient and impelled by the power (*śakti*) of Anantanātha—that performs the function of strengthening the concealed consciousness. (181)

"Caitanya" means the state of being the agent of the activity of consciousness—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Is it not a contradiction that the insentient *kalā* should empower sentience (*caitanya*)? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
"Impelled by the power of Anantanātha. (181)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then let the power of the Lord (Īśa-śakti) alone empower this; what is the use of *kalā*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it is not the power of the Lord alone that will empower his consciousness."
For that [consciousness], when supported by those [faculties], does not itself become an agent. (9.182)

By one word, the power of the Lord (īśa-śakti) is indicated, and by the other, consciousness (caitanya). Here, it has been stated that if the Supreme Lord were to empower agency and so forth for bound souls— even as he does for liberated souls— by his own power alone, independent of the *kalās* and other factors, then [agency] would occur at all times and in all places.
"I shall attain the state of being a limited agent. As they say:
"For Śambhu does not manifest [the power] without the fetter (pāśa), since that [manifestation] does not have everything as its object;
nor does it manifest the power of agency in liberated souls, which is free from contact with the impurity (añjana)."
Thus [ends the verse]. 182.

Surely there is no disagreement that the person possesses agency when enjoyment is to be performed; however, we do not know at all which factor among the causal instruments (kāraka) the *kalā* is. It cannot be the object (*karman*), because, by way of strengthening consciousness, it is not an objective field with respect to the act of enjoying; nor can it be the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For that [instrument] is indeed employed by an agent; this [intellect], however, is the employer even of the agent—so how could it attain the status of an instrument like knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth? Intending here that its agency is as remote as any other factor of action (*kāraka*), he raises the objection regarding its being an instrument and then refutes it:
This *kalā* is not the primary instrument like *vidyā* and the others;
rather, it acts as the agent within the male subject (*pums*), because it functions as the instigator (*prayojaka*). (9.183)

The meaning is that "primary" (*mukhya*) refers to that which is supreme (*para*) in relation to the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest. As it is said: "That instrument by which the person (*puruṣa*), having impelled the intellect and the other [principles], effects enjoyment regarding the object of experience, and which again effects the experience within that object of experience—that is *vidyā*; she is the supreme instrument."
Thus: regarding the domain of the rule "in the sense of the male agent," the activity of the instigator (prayojaka) indeed resides in the one to be impelled (prayojya).

And so, although both possess agency, it is the person who is to be impelled—qualified by the activity of the instigator—who is the primary agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the action itself, because he possesses independence (*svātantrya*) directly toward the action. As it has been said:
"Kalā manifests its power of agency; therefore, it is the motivator. Consequently, the individual soul (aṇu), when joined with Kalā, becomes the agent (kartṛkāraka) in the act of experience. ||183||
Thus, through the relationship of the instigated and the instigator between the male and the female,
"O Brahmin, these two, existing together as if they were non-different from one another,
declare themselves to be the causal agents (kartṛ-kāraka) for the living being in the performance of the act of enjoyment."

By such statements as these, although there is no distinct characteristic [between them] because they have become a single agent and instrument, when for someone— through the grace of the Lord— a discriminative knowledge of these two arises, then that discrimination between Māyā and the Person (puruṣa) occurs, whereby, through the destruction of all karma, the state of a Vijñānākala is attained, by which this...

"A person situated below Māyā would not wander [in saṃsāra]"—thus he says: "When there arises within the two, the Person (puṃs) and Kalā, an internal knowledge of the inner [reality]—of the Lord of the Womb of Māyā (Māyāgarbheśa), his Śakti, and so forth—between which there is no perceptible difference. (9.184)

Then, through the exhaustion of all karma, there arises the discernment between Māyā and the Person (puruṣa). The state of the Vijñānakala does not go below Māyā, nor does the Person go below it. (9.185)
Ananta is the Lord of Māyāgarbha. Regarding the phrase "beginning with Śakti," the word "etc. (ādi) includes the knowledge and other [attainments] taught by Him.
As it has been said:
"But, O observer of good vows, [this is attained] through that which has arisen from the lotus-mouth of the Cause..."
Having carefully observed with the lamp of the eye of wisdom, one should act with reverence.
"This is the Puruṣa, and this is their [the guṇas'] portion, which is auspicious yet an abode of defects.
Having known the difference between these two, one who is established in himself attains liberation without doubt.
Thus, "internal" (āntara) means "inner" (antaraṅga) with respect to the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Since the destruction of all karma is established through the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* alone, what is the use of the distinction between *māyā* and *puruṣa*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When the distinction between the intellect (*dhī*) and the person (*puruṣa*) is known, [one knows] the difference between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*."
Furthermore, one's karma would not be exhausted even in a single digit [of time], for that [karma] could indeed persist.

"In the discernment of intellect and spirit" means in that form of the discernment between primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*). For it is through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*) that there occurs either non-discrimination or discrimination between primary matter and the spirit. In this context, non-discrimination is indeed the conceit of agency belonging to the reflection of consciousness that has been transferred [to the intellect].
In that very state, because it consists of the transformation wherein the fluctuations of objects have dissolved,
the non-agency of consciousness itself— which resembles the steady flame of a lamp— is discernment (*viveka*). Thus,
it has been stated that for the individual soul (*puruṣa*), discernment from *māyā* also occurs solely through the medium of *kalā*.
The particle *api* is displaced in its position; thus, the meaning is "even when [the Lord] is cognizant. Regarding the phrase "in *kalā*"—that is, when it exists.
For *kalā* alone is the direct instrumental cause for the manifestation of limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*) in action.
And it has been said:
"Because of the non-perception of karma that is to be experienced beyond the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva),
even the liberation (kaivalya) of the Sāṃkhyas is not at all tenable, due to its lack of destruction. || 186 ||

Thus, through the discernment of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the exhaustion of the person's karma extends as far as Prakṛti; however, through the discernment of Kalā and Puruṣa, it extends as far as Māyā, by which his wandering in the realms below that [Māyā] shall cease.
Thus he says:

Therefore, one who has attained realization through the Sāṃkhya perspective does not transmigrate below the Pradhāna; however, upon the discernment of Kalā and the Puruṣa, one certainly does not go below Māyā. (9-187)

"According to the Sāṃkhya view"—the meaning is: by means of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, as in the Sāṃkhya system. And it should be understood that this [discrimination] is accomplished through the sequence of meditations (*dhāraṇā*) on *prakṛti* and so forth, as taught in our own system; for otherwise, there would be a recurrence of his transmigration into those lower states.
As was stated previously:
"At the beginning of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha emits those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, the Vedas, and so forth;
therefore, such liberation is not truly complete. (Tantrāloka 6.148)
Thus [ends the verse]. 187.

Now, one might ask: "If that is so, when would he go back above Māyā? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But seeing the Self as distinct from impurity, he shall attain the state of Śiva. Now, in all three types of discernment, the subject must first be established; and that [subject]— [The text continues: ...is not perceived by the mind, nor is it perceived by the senses, nor is it perceived by the intellect. It is perceived by the supreme consciousness alone, which is free from all mental constructs. Therefore, the wise one, having realized the Self as pure consciousness, transcends the cycle of rebirth. Thus, the scripture declares: "When the seer sees the Self as stainless and free from all taints, he attains the state of Śiva. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "The Self is not an object of the senses; it is not grasped by the intellect; it is not reached by the mind. It is perceived by the light of supreme consciousness, which is devoid of all mental constructions. Therefore, the yogi who perceives the Self as pure consciousness becomes liberated while living and attains the state of Śiva. Thus, the scripture declares: "When the seer sees the Self as stainless and free from all taints, he attains the state of Śiva. This is the meaning. Moreover, it is said: "The Self is not an object of the senses; it is not grasped by the intellect; it is not reached by the mind. It is perceived by the light of supreme consciousness, which is devoid of all mental constructions. Therefore, the yogi who perceives the Self as pure consciousness becomes liberated while living and attains the state of Śiva. Thus, the scripture declares: "When the seer sees the Self as stainless and free from all taints, he attains the state of Śiva. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "The Self is not an object of the senses; it is not grasped by the intellect; it is not reached by the mind. It is perceived by the light of supreme consciousness, which is devoid of all mental constructions. Therefore, the yogi who perceives the Self as pure consciousness becomes liberated while living and attains the state of Śiva. Thus, the scripture declares: "When the seer sees the Self as stainless and free from all taints, he attains the state of Śiva. This is the meaning. Moreover, it is said: "The Self is not an object of the senses; it is not grasped by the intellect; it is not reached by the mind. It is perceived by the light of supreme consciousness, which is devoid of all mental constructions. Therefore, the yogi who perceives the Self as pure consciousness becomes liberated while living and attains the state of Śiva. Fearing that one might ask, "Since [the Self] is of the very nature of pure consciousness, how could this [realization] ever happen to anyone at any time?", he says:
"And in all cases, the descent of the Lord's power (aiśvara-śaktipāta) is the auxiliary cause here. (9.188)

Now, one might object: "If the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) here is indeed undifferentiated, then from where does this distinction arise in its effects, which consist of the three types of discernment (*viveka*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The [descent] pertaining to the office of the *māyāgarbha* belongs to the first two; but in the last case, it is stainless."
[The term] "of the one presiding over Māyā-garbha" refers to Ananta and the others. "Of the two" means [the two types of knowledge]: the discernment between Prakṛti and Māyā.

For this very reason, there is no attainment of liberation as the ultimate goal here. "Final" refers to the discernment of impurity (mala), while "stainless" refers to having liberation as the ultimate goal. "Final" refers to the discernment of impurity; "stainless" [refers to...].
Because it functions up until liberation.
One might object: "Let this [limited agency] be nothing but *māyā*; why should it be considered anything other than that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This very *kalā* is indeed inferred to be distinct from that, because of the difference in its effects. (9.189)

"Otherwise, the universe would be one, [and] there would be a denial of other [causes] for the sake of an effect"—this is because of the difference in effects. For *māyā* produces in the limited soul (*aṇu*) a state that is almost like a swoon, whereas this [power] produces a degree of agency. "It is quite another"—that is to say, distinct from *māyā*. This is what is meant by the phrase beginning with "otherwise."

This is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Regarding the word "one": if the Māyā-principle were the sole cause, then all effects, such as limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and so forth, would arise from that alone; consequently, it has been stated that this would entail the negation of the entire range of other existing principles, beginning with *vidyā*.
"Thus ends the denial of others. || 189 ||
But surely, in the venerable *Matanga* and other scriptures, it is stated that *kalā* bestows a degree of agency; for it is said therein:
"Those whose natures are slightly unfolded and whose forms are pierced by *kalā*..."
"O Sage, throbbing and trembling, they attain a state of swelling. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.9).
Such passages exist. However, in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, there is again the general principle of being the bestower of agency.
As it is said therein:

"...through union with that, he became a person, possessing the capacity for the agency of birth... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.27). And here, it is precisely by means of this [subject] that the determination of the sequence of the principles (*tattva*) has been commenced.
Anticipating the objection, "In what way has it been stated that this [kalā] possesses an agency that is contrary to its nature? he says:
"That which is called 'kalā' in the Mataṅgaśāstra and other texts is itself [the principle]. (9.190)
By means of the formulation that agency is projected through the state of possessing some degree of form—
"thus," by the aforementioned manner consisting in bestowing a limited capacity for action—
the *kalā* (power) which is taught in the *Śrīmataṅga-śāstra* and other texts resides in the male [subject].

The meaning of the sentence is this: because absolute agency is untenable, agency arises by implying a certain limited form through its own inherent capacity; thus, it is taught here in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara) by way of a general formulation. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should include the *Mṛgendra* and other texts. As it is said there:
The power of agency belonging to the individual soul is eternal and all-pervasive, like the power of the Lord;
yet, because it is veiled by darkness, it does not shine forth unimpededly with respect to its objects.
Hara, having agitated Māyā, creates that supreme reality called Kalā, which is luminous (taijasa) and serves as the instrument for activity, thereby bestowing grace upon it.
Then, by means of that atom of pure consciousness which is like a lamp,
it illuminates a single portion [of reality], having torn asunder the dense darkness.
That element which performs the functions of reckoning and impelling is *kalā*; performing impulsion by means of *tamas*, it effects expulsion.
"O Brahmin, these two, existing together as if non-different from one another,
are said by the wise to be the agent and the instrument for a living being in the performance of the act of enjoyment.
Now, one might object: "How can agency, even when qualified by some degree of form, belong to one who is ignorant?
Anticipating this doubt, he asserts the arising of another principle that bestows a certain degree of knowability:
How could that agency which is distinguished by some form of materiality come to be? || 191 ||
From that [state] of the ignorant one, [kalā] produces the limited knowledge (*vidyā*) whose nature is partial cognition.
By the word "from that," it is understood from the context to be *kalā*. As it has been said:
"Since agency is never observed in anyone without knowledge..."
"Therefore, that which has arisen from *kalā* is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) and is not primary.
The sense is that even in the case of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), full agency (*kartṛtva*) is pervaded by full knowledge (*pūrṇajñatva*). || 191 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the Sāṃkhyas do not accept the agency of the Self—so let the principle of *kalā* mentioned as its justification be set aside—but they have established its capacity for knowledge (*jñatva*) through the mediation of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. So what is the point of this [discussion]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That knowledge perceives the intellect as it moves upon the mirror of the intellect.
By means of his own self, he discerns the conditions such as pleasure, the [afflictions] beginning with delusion, cause and effect, and the web of karma situated therein. (9.193)

Here, by the word *moha*, *tamas* is also implied. Therefore, the meaning is: [he perceives] the fifty cognitive determinations (*pratyaya*) known as error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*), beginning with *tamas*, *moha*, and so forth—as it has been said:
"Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and indeed andhatāmisra—this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Self. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.5.5).
Here, the instrument itself is the cause; by that [instrument], the elements and the senses constitute the effect and the cause. [The text] says, "he discriminates."
The meaning is that one knows this pleasure through discrimination (*viveka*) as having the nature of being "neither suffering nor delusion," and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said [to be known] by its own self, in its specific form excluded from others. As it has been stated:
"Knowledge distinguishes for him his action, as well as its cause and effect. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.28). || 193 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the intellect (*buddhi*), which is characterized by various respective cognitions, may indeed be the instrument of knowledge (*vidyākaraṇa*) when it is itself the object of cognition; but what is the purpose of this [instrument] in the perception of an external object? For in that case, it is the intellect itself that exists in such a manner. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But for one whose mind is saturated with the qualities [of passion], how could there be happiness through solitude?
Even an object that is painful or characterized by delusion might appear as pleasant. (9.194)

By the phrase "intermingled with the qualities" (guṇasaṅkīrṇā), her inherent timidity is also expressed, for it has been said: "Consisting of the three qualities, she is indeed unable to show herself through discrimination;
because, being herself undiscriminated, she assumes the form of the objects."
Thus [ends the verse]. 194.

Is it not as if you have spoken this without knowing the Sāṃkhya doctrine, when you ask how the intellect (*buddhi*), being a mixture of the *guṇas*, can discern an object consisting of pleasure and so forth? For they [the Sāṃkhyas] hold that although [the intellect] is entirely covered by *tamas*, which is of the nature of veiling, [the object is revealed] through the gradual removal of that [veiling] by means of *rajas*.

They have accepted that even *sattva*, though always illuminating, when set in motion in a particular instance, would manifest pleasure and so forth in a restricted manner through a sequence; thus, the intellect (*buddhi*), consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is the one that demonstrates objects— whose nature consists of pleasure and so forth— by means of sequential discernment.
True, the intellect (buddhi) would indeed reflect an object consisting of pleasure and so forth like a mirror;

however, we maintain that it does not do so through discrimination because of its being intermingled with the qualities (guṇas). For although the intellect possesses the three qualities, due to the predominance of the portion of *sattva*, which is distinct from [the other qualities such as] blue and so forth, how could [it reflect the object] even though [the reflection] has been transferred to it?

One would determine pleasure and so forth as being distinct from suffering and the rest. For at that time, there is no perception even of suffering and the like, by means of which there could be a determination of pleasure and so forth through their distinction. Nor is mere perception itself the cognition of an object, such that a distinction might occur; for determination is the very lifeblood of that [cognition].
As it has been stated:
"Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 5).
And this [perception] would not be able to effect a discrimination of this [object] from previously perceived suffering and so forth.

Because it is impossible to investigate [the self] due to its extreme subtlety (*jāḍya*), therefore, even though pleasure and so forth are reflected in the intellect which is like a clear mirror, they must be distinguished by something else;
and that is the supreme cause called *vidyā*—this has already been stated. Thus he says:

How can an object, when being transferred into the intellect which is its own reflection, become an object of cognition? Without that [cognition], it does not exist; and that [cognition] requires another instrument within the person who is the agent.
"Let it be experienced"—the meaning is "let it be determined through discernment. "By that"—by means of *vidyā*.
"That too"—in relation to the intellect (*buddhi*). "As the agent"—in the determination of the object. || 195 ||

Now, it might be argued that since the intellect (*buddhi*) is like a stainless mirror, the reflection of the Person (*puruṣa*) would be transferred to one side of it; by virtue of which, the intellect, becoming conscious, could determine the multitude of objects transferred to the other side— so what need is there for that which is called *vidyā*?
"Must there not be another instrument [for this]? To this he says:

'But surely an entity shines forth from the light of the Person (puṃsprakāśa), which has reached the intellect (dhī) that is like a mirror polished on both sides; do not say so, for that is a reflection. (9.196)
He refutes this very point:
"For the primary meaning of 'manifestation' (bhāsana) is indeed the manifestation of the insentient object by the light of the Person (puṃsprakāśa).
Let that [manifestation] belong to the object situated externally; what is the use of this conceptualization regarding the intellect (buddhi)? (9.197)
In this regard, it has already been stated that because the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient (*jaḍatva*), it is not possible for it to illuminate objects by itself;

even when the light of the Person (*puṃsprakāśa*) is reflected into it, its insentience does not cease. It has already been established previously that a reflection possesses a single destiny (*ekayogakṣema*) with its own substratum. For externally...

Even though a conscious being such as Caitra is reflected in a mirror and the like, let it not bestow consciousness upon the mirror; on the contrary, he himself, like something insentient, would be unable to do anything at all therein. In the same way, even when reflected in the insentient intellect (*buddhi*), [the Self remains inactive].

Since the light of the person shares the same fate as that [object], it would itself incur insentience (*jāḍya*); how then could it be capable of illuminating the object? Now, it might be argued that this [light] is itself the illuminator of the object, as it was said: "Alternatively, the primary light of the person is its manifestation."

"In that case, let there be the direct manifestation of the object itself as something external; what is the use of postulating an intermediate principle called *buddhi*?"—thus it is said: "Why has the postulation of *buddhi* been made? (197).
For in this way, nothing whatsoever would manifest apart from the primary self-luminosity;
thus, "everything is indeed manifestation," and non-duality alone would flash forth everywhere.
Consequently, this entire empirical discourse of duality, consisting of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, comes to an end. That...
And since this [non-duality] is what has been undertaken for investigation here, this statement would be contrary to the subject of the proposition; thus he says:
"This is the ground of non-difference, yet difference is investigated here."

Thus, when the Supreme Light itself, through its own sovereignty, conceals its own nature and manifests as a contracted self, then this entire worldly transaction of duality unfolds, by which this person [perceives] that which has been reflected into the intellect via the channel of the senses.
One knows the object, which consists of pleasure, pain, and so forth, through knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of their mutual distinction;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the postulation of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other [faculties]. As it has been said:
"Therefore, the state residing in the intellect is within the scope of the instrument of knowledge. (9.198)

Now, one might object: "Since the object of the instrument called 'knowledge' (vidyā) is necessarily an existent thing (bhāva), and that [existent] is only external, how can it be said thus? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the reflection of existents is the object of knowledge; from that arises the conceptualization of the intellect."
If that were known directly, the very same fault already mentioned would apply.

Now, although the limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) of the individual soul (*aṇu*) has been established through the arising of its limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), one might ask: "Even though the degree of limitation is the same in both cases, why does this [soul] alone know and act only to that extent?
Anticipating this doubt, he first explains the *rāgatattva* (the principle of attachment), which accounts for this:
Since it performs some slight action, there must certainly be something else besides that.

That which is called the *rāgatattva* is precisely that which colors [the soul] therein. For it has been stated that the "limitedness" (*kiṃcitva*) of *kalā* and *vidyā* merely denotes incompleteness; however, this [passion], while being of the same nature, terminates in specific objects—thus, its presence here is necessarily required.
There must be some other cause by virtue of which the atom becomes attached to that very [object].
What is it? It is said: "That is declared to be the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*). And it has been stated:
"Passion colors this [atom] even toward its own impure enjoyments. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.28)
Thus [ends the verse]. || 199 ||
One might object: "But isn't it the property of the intellect (buddhi) characterized by non-detachment that has been stated here as the cause by the Sāṃkhyas?
So what is the use of this other principle of passion (rāga-tattva)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
