"And non-detachment alone is not the [cause] there, because even in that case there is the functioning of attachment. (9.200)
"Even in one who is dispassionate," because satisfaction remains established as a subtle attachment;

"that" refers to the *rāga-tattva* (the principle of attachment). "There too" means even in the absence of dispassion (*avairāgya*). The sense is that this very [attachment] is the cause even when there is no clinging to non-dispassion. And for someone whose longing for objects has ceased...

Even in the absence of non-detachment (*avairāgya*), attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) certainly occurs through subtle observation, because the conviction that "may something accrue to me" is never absent; this is the very power of the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*) that all qualities such as non-detachment appear in the intellect as if they were external objects.
"An especially intense manifestation. As it has been said:
"Virtue and the rest are also merely sprouts of the latent impression of attachment;
thus, this entire category of passion consists of a particularly intense manifestation."
"They are enumerated as attributes of the intellect (buddhi).

Thus, aversion (dveṣa) is also merely an expansion of this [attraction]. For even in that case, there is only the occurrence of attachment toward the removal of the undesirable and so forth; therefore, wherever there is anything to be accepted...
Or rather, the *rāgatattva* is simply a general attachment in the form of the thought "may something accrue to me," while the other [categories] are merely its elaboration;
this has been essentially established previously, so enough of further detail. || 200 ||

Indeed, agency— which has been brought by *aṇu* (limited subjectivity) to a state of partiality, by *vidyā* (limited knowledge) to a state of restricted objects, and by *rāga* (attachment) to a state of determination toward specific things— is also permeated by *kāla* (time), since the cognition "I did," "I am doing," and "I will do" would otherwise be inexplicable.
He also states the principle of time (kālatattva) which establishes that: "Time, through the units of duration such as tuṭi and so forth, therefore impels this agency. (201)
"Agency, which is delimited by its effects, will necessarily be associated with time.

Now, one might object: "Agency is indeed the sovereignty of a conscious being, and since that [sovereignty] is not distinct from [consciousness] itself, how can there be a connection between this [agency], which is eternal, and time? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
Regarding the term "delimited by its effects" (*kāryāvacchedi*): agency is indeed twofold—pure and that which pertains to *māyā*.
Of these, the former consists of the undivided self-awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) and is entirely uncolored by effects;
the other, however, is colored by effects such as "the action of a jar" or "the action of a cloth. By this, [it is shown] that even through its differentiation...

It has been stated that [the object] must necessarily be manifested—meaning "inevitably"—because the performance of an action is sustained by the sequence of the manifestation of existence and non-existence. Thus, it is established as a matter of fact that even a limited subject is indeed encompassed by this [process]. As it has been said:
"Time also, abiding through moments such as the *tuṭi* and so forth, measures this [being]. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.29) || 201 ||

Surely there is no disagreement that a person seeking a specific purposeful action (arthakriyā) takes up something and abandons something else; however, from what source does this restriction arise—that one who desires cooked food seeks fire alone and not a clod of earth, and one who desires heaven seeks the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice alone and not the Śyena? Therefore, this must necessarily be explained here.
Anticipating the question, "There must be some cause for this; what is it?", he says:
"Necessity (niyati) effects the connection within the specific sphere of effects. (9.202)

For *niyati* (destiny) would establish the restriction: "From this very cause, this very effect must arise"—as it has been said: "It effects the application within a specific sphere of effects. Thus it is stated: "Destiny joins this individual (*pudgala*) to its own action" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.29).
Thus, for one who seeks a specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), only a specific entity must be apprehended;
therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. || 202 ||

Now, since the determination of the causal relationship between the principles (*tattva*) has been introduced here, it has already been stated that *kalā* is indeed an effect of *māyā*; however, regarding the fourfold set of principles beginning with *vidyā*, [it is said]:
"From that, *kalā* was produced, as well as *vidyā* and *rāga*."
"Time, the principle of necessity (niyatitattva), the principle of the person (puṃstattva), and likewise the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti). (Svacchandatantra 11.63).
Based on such a position in the venerable Svacchandaśāstra, one might raise the doubt: regarding the level of *kalā*, is the effect [of Māyā] that of Māyā alone, or not?
Anticipating this, he says:
Knowledge (vidyā), attachment (rāga), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla)—this tetrad is the effect of kalā. And here, the sequence is as follows: necessity and time.

This has been stated in accordance with the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*; for in that [text], time (*kāla*) is mentioned immediately after necessity (*niyati*). However, the intention behind mentioning time first here is this: the function of necessity is the regulation of the relationship between cause and effect, and that [regulation] is a prior cause.
The effect is that which occurs later—how could this be without a delimitation by time?
Alternatively, because they arise simultaneously, there is no intention to express a sequence among them; thus it has been stated. Even though [this is so] in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra...

Although only this much is stated— "...he then created Vidyā and Rāga" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.27)— nevertheless, because Niyati and Kāla are accepted as effects and no other cause is explicitly mentioned, the word "eva" (only/itself) in the phrase "tata eva" (from that very [source]) [indicates this].

Since it is stated that the causality of this very *kalā* extends without distinction all the way to the unmanifest (*avyakta*), it was said that the causality of *kalā* alone results as being neither specifically distinguished nor prohibited:
"This tetrad is the effect of *kalā*."

Now, one might object: "The universe is indeed twofold, consisting of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*); in this regard, does this [set of principles] beginning with *kalā* fall on the side of the enjoyer, or otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Abiding in the state of the enjoyer, it is filled with the nature of being an enjoyer. (9.203)

The reason for the persistence of the state of being an enjoyer is expressed by the phrase "filled with the state of being an enjoyer. For the state of being an enjoyer, although initiated by the *āṇava* [impurity] and others, is "filled"—meaning augmented and brought to its final consummation in its effect—by the bestowal of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) through *kalā* and the other [impurities]. Therefore, of these...

Because that is its very nature, it abides in the enjoyer alone. Thus, the Supreme Subject Himself, whose entire store of sovereignty has first been stolen away by Māyā, becomes once again a bound soul (*paśu*) as he attains limitation by receiving back certain portions from within that entire store of sovereignty through the medium of *kalā* and the other categories.

Thus it is said. In this regard, the fact that *kalā* and *vidyā* are attributes of that [subject] is established beyond dispute. Indeed, there is no disagreement that the qualities of knowing (*jñatva*) and acting (*kartṛtva*) are attributes of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Attachment (*rāga*) is likewise an attribute of that very subject, because it is the cause for the inclination toward objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*); for if it were an attribute of the object of enjoyment, no one at all—

He would be free from passion (*vītarāga*), because the object of enjoyment is equally attractive to everyone. And it has been said: "In this context, passion (*rāga*) is that [impulse] which, toward an object of enjoyment, produces an attachment in a man through an action."
"If there were attachment toward a specific object of enjoyment, no one would ever be free from passion.
Time also functions in this way: for initially, one thinks, "I was thin, now I am stout, and by the consumption of *aśvagandhā* and ghee, I shall become even stouter," and so forth.

While manifesting succession, it should shine forth precisely as being conjoined with the subject. That very [consciousness], when again determined by time, first causes the manifestation of a succession consisting of the past and so forth from its own perspective, and then measures the object of knowledge that accompanies it, [thinking]: "That which was," "exists," or "will be."

Furthermore, the nature of *niyati* (necessity) is the regulation of cause and effect; and it has been stated previously that the relationship between cause and effect culminates in nothing other than agency (*kartṛtva*). Since agency is an attribute of the subject (*pramātṛ*), this regulation by *niyati* also belongs to the subject alone, as in: "I am this very one who acts."

This is due to [the subject's] conceit (*abhimāna*). Thus, time (*kāla*), attachment (*rāga*), necessity (*niyati*), and knowledge (*vidyā*) have *kalā* as their cause. It is rightly said—“*Kalā* and the rest abide in the state of the enjoyer”—because the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that “I now know this very thing” and “I do this” is appropriate for the subject alone, not for the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Indeed, it is precisely through union with this [limited subjectivity] that the supreme consciousness manifests a further limitation characterized by the state of being an enjoyer. || 203 ||
Thus it is said: "Māyā, kalā, rāga, vidyā, kāla, and niyati—these are declared to be the six coverings (kañcukas) of consciousness; while they persist, one is a bound soul (paśu). (9.204)

"Kañcukāni" (coverings) is so called because they cover. Regarding the phrase "in their persistence": the word "tat" (that) refers back to the *kañcukas*. As it has been said: "Māyā, Kalā, Aśuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati."
"These six are the coverings (kañcukas) of the limited self, arising from the power of obscuration.

Now, is it not the case that everywhere the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth—which constitute the nature of the object of knowledge—are called the "bound soul" (*paśu*), the "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*), and the "atomic self" (*aṇu*), for whom this inner veil of the six coverings (*kañcuka*) exists? As it has been said:
"This group of six coverings, together with *māyā*, is declared to be the inner [veil] of the atomic self" (Paramārthasāra, verse 27).
Thus [it was asked]: "How is it that six coverings (kañcukas) of consciousness are mentioned here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Indeed, within the objects of knowledge—beginning with the body and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka)—consciousness is constricted by these six; that which is beyond the object of knowledge is the individual soul (aṇu). (9.205)

The meaning is as follows: among those objects of knowledge such as the body and so forth, that cognition which—because it is of a single nature as the knower—is itself not an object of knowledge, yet has been rendered contracted and limited by this group of six beginning with Māyā, and exists as the agent of the act of knowing; this, indeed, is called the "individual soul" (aṇu) in the scriptures. And this very thing is the twenty-fifth [principle].

It is called the *puṃstattva* (the principle of the person), which is referred to as "the Person" (*pumān*), "the atom" (*aṇu*), and "the individual" (*pudgala*) in the venerable *Pūrvaśāstra* and other scriptures. By the logic already stated, the state of being a person (*puṃstva*) has arisen from the supreme consciousness itself due to the power of *māyā*; for this very reason, regarding this *puṃstattva*, [it is taught] in the venerable *Svacchandaśāstra* and elsewhere.
In various scriptures, birth is described—this should also be understood here. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The knots, the *kalās*, *kāla*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the other *mātṛkās*..."

Having introduced the subject generally with these and other words, [the author] states: "From that very [source], the principle of the person (puṃstattva) arose, which is the basis for the cognition of 'person'.
This has not been stated here by my own voice, because it was not so expressed in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*.
Now, one might ask: "Is this same sequence applicable everywhere regarding the six coverings (kañcukas), or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This very point has been stated in the *Śivatanuśāstra* once more, but by way of a different formulation."
He says that very thing:
"The obscuration, which pervades all selves, is impurity; though it is distinct, it appears as if non-distinct. (9.206)
The obscuration, which has been described as the cause of saṃsāra, is the impurity (*mala*) pertaining to the individual soul (*āṇava*).
As it is said there:
"Therefore, that [impurity] residing in all souls appears as something distinct from them, yet as if non-distinct."
"The impurity of the mind is the Mānava [ignorance], which is the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
Thus [it is said]. || 206 ||
Now, one might object: "How can this very same [power] possess both otherness and non-otherness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since she is to be consumed by the masses of rays from the fire of Śiva, she is indeed of a different nature;
yet, because she colors [everything] with her own self through a state that has no prior beginning (*anidampūrvatā*), she is therefore non-different. (9.207)
For the individual soul (*aṇu*) possessing innate impurity, there is indeed a threefold covering (*kañcuka*) from the Lord (*īśa*) and the Cave (*guhā*).

By the phrase "because it is combustible," its perishability is stated; for only that which is distinct [from the Self] undergoes coming and going—this is the intended meaning. "From whom" means from all the souls. Or else:
The reading "because it is to be flooded by the nectar-stream of consciousness" (vijñānāmṛtasaritā plāvyatvāt) should be accepted. As it is said there:
"Since [the impurity] is washed away from those [levels] by the stainless, flowing stream of the nectar of consciousness from the moon of Śiva, that [stream] is distinct."
Thus [it is said]. In the previous [context], however, it was stated that the *kañcukas* (veils/limitations) are appropriately combustible:

"by virtue of being not previously existing" (*anidampūrvatayā*), because they have been associated with [consciousness] from beginningless time; for this very reason, due to its innate nature, it is non-different [from consciousness], as its distinction is imperceptible, like the blackness of copper. As it is said there:
"Because it is conjoined with the self from beginningless time, like consciousness itself, and colors [the self] through its own activity, it therefore appears as if non-different [from it]. Thus,
even for the individual soul (aṇu) who possesses the veil of the impurity of finitude (āṇavamala), the Lord [perceives] his...
The power of cessation (*nirodha-śakti*) is the presiding deity of impurity (*mala*); the cave (*guhā*) is the locus where karma resides, which is *māyā*.

Together with these, the threefold impurity—known as the powers of Īśa, Śakti, and Māyā—is a bondage in the form of a "sheath" (*kañcuka*), because it functions primarily as a covering. As it has been said therein:
"Thus, for the person whose mind is pierced by great innate darkness (tamas), the threefold sheath proceeds from the Supreme Lord out of the cave.
This is the sense: only one who possesses these three bonds indeed becomes fit for the application of *kalā*.
For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere: "Because of the union with the *citkalā* bound by the three... and so forth. || 207 ||
Therefore he says: "For that [Self], which is as clear as a second consciousness, a subtle *kalā* is employed. (9.208)
By this [knowledge], the animal becomes capable of experience;
and its knowledge arose from the *kalā*, like the light of a lamp within a shelter. (9.209)
That which distinguishes the experience of pleasure and pain through the division of the bound soul (paśu) is *rāga*, which arises from the principle of *kalā* like a dye on a clean cloth. (9.210)
Since he does not desire the blissful experience of worldly pleasure that has been renounced, he remains thus defiled by ignorance, sustained by the power of the sheath of the three *guṇas*. (9.211)
The animal falls headlong into the womb of dense experience, rendered helpless.

Regarding the phrase "by the second": because the one consciousness, though innate, is veiled by the three coverings according to the reasoning already stated. Regarding the phrase "of the clear one": this is by its very nature. Regarding the phrase "smooth":...

The meaning is that it is "subtle" because it has just begun to manifest. And because it possesses a slight degree of luminosity, it is said to be like the light of a lamp inside a shelter. The Self (*ātman*) is comparable to a clean cloth;
it is "stained by ignorance" (*avidyā-malina*), that is, by the impurity of *āṇava* [ignorance].

And by means of *māyā* and *śakti*, which are characterized by that [bond], he is "impure"— the meaning being that his full knowledge and action are obscured. "By the power of the threefold *kañcuka*" means by the power of the threefold *kañcuka* consisting of *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga*.
The meaning is: by means of a specific capacity (*sāmarthya-viśeṣa*) that supports [attributes] such as limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*).
Thus, the mention of "six coverings" (*kañcuka*) together with the three coverings beginning with *āṇava* constitutes a different perspective (*bhaṅgy-antara*).
As for the non-mention of *kāla* (time) and *niyati* (fate), the intention is as follows:
"The purification of this principle [of Śakti] occurs through the purification of Kalā and the rest. As stated in the *Ruruvṛtti*:
"It should be understood that it is purified by Kalā and the others themselves when they are purified;
thus, there is no mention [of it] due to this underlying intention, not because of its non-existence."
Thus:
"downward-facing" means [turned away] from the orientation toward enjoyment within the sphere of Māyā. || 211 ||
Now, one might object: since impurity (mala) likewise acts as a veil in this context, it would be more appropriate to call it a "sheath" (kañcuka);
why then is it said that "there are six sheaths"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
By this, impurity is described as being like the husk of a grain, while the [principles] beginning with Kalā are like the chaff. (9.212)

"By this"—namely, by the designation of the six [principles] beginning with *māyā* as "sheaths" (*kañcuka*). They are like the layers of a coconut shell because they exist both inside and further within. Thus, for the person (*puruṣa*) who is covered by impurity (*mala*), the six sheaths constitute a kind of successive outer covering; for this very reason, it is said that they are "like husks."
As it has been said:
"And thus, the internal impurity of the person (pudgala) remains like the inner husk;
the coverings (kañcukas) would be like the outer chaff."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 212 ||
He summarizes this very point:

"Thus, regarding the specific aspect of the principle called *kalā*, which is characterized by limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*), agency has been discussed, preceded by [the discussion of] the enjoyer. (9.213)
The definition of *kalā* is agency characterized by a certain degree of form; therein,

the aspect of agency which resides implicitly within the qualifying portion (*viśeṣa-bhāga*) as the qualified portion (*viśeṣya-aṃśa*) has been discussed as being of the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), according to the stated reasoning through the sequence of the arising of *vidyā* and the other categories.
The meaning is that this was stated after investigating [the matter] in terms of its conferring the status of being an enjoyer. || 213 ||
Now, one might object: "Is there not here some 'something-ness' (kiñcitva) residing in the specific portion? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The limited power (kalā) gives birth to the primary principle (pradhāna), which is clearly distinct and consists merely of the object of knowledge, arising from that specific portion which exists here as a qualifier. (9.214)

In this context, although the agency (*kartṛtva*) is itself undivided, because it has something as its object, it acquires a certain limited form (*kiṃcidrūpatva*); thus, "this-ness" (*kiṃcittva*) would reside solely on the side of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). Consequently, having emerged by making that [limited] aspect its own motivator, with respect to the specific objects of knowledge yet to be, [it functions].

The meaning is that *pradhāna*, which consists of the commonality of all objects of cognition and has the nature of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), is brought forth by *kalā* and led to manifestation as an external form. As it has been said:
"From that very *kalā*-tattva, [the Lord] created the unmanifest (*avyakta*)... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.30).

Thus [it is said]. And that [body], being restricted to each individual person, is manifold—meaning it is many. Furthermore, although the *kalās* and other [principles] are likewise [manifold], this [body] is clearly gross in comparison to them—this is the meaning. || 214 ||

Now, since the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment are mutually dependent, how indeed can their sequential production be logically consistent? For there could be no such thing as "enjoyership" without an object of enjoyment, yet there is an object of enjoyment even without enjoyership; so how is it that *kalā* first produces enjoyership and then produces the object of enjoyment?
Having raised this doubt—“Is it so stated?”—he says:
“For Kalā brings forth both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer simultaneously;
because it intends their differentiation, they remain inseparable from one another. (9.215)

The phrase "the enjoyer" (bhoktāram) means the state of being an enjoyer residing in the enjoyer—this is the meaning. Because that [reality] consists of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, which are mutually inseparable and interdependent—this is the meaning.
For in reality, these two...
As it is stated in such passages as, "The enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment" (Svacchandatantra 1.4),

although there is non-duality due to the nature of being composed of the non-dual, the state of inseparability— characterized by mutual dependence— is demonstrated with reference to the differentiation belonging to *māyā*. Thus it has been said.
"Because of the intention toward differentiation," [it is said]. || 215 ||
One might ask: "What is the purpose of these two being thus inseparable? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed would not exist due to their mutual separation.
Regarding the phrase "due to separation": it means because there would be an absence of mutual dependence.
One might object: "In that case, let there not even be this nature of subject and object"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And when that [nature] has dissolved, for him too, Māyā would be nothing at all. (9.216)
The underlying sense is that when the agitation characterized by the nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed has dissolved, transmigratory existence itself would no longer exist.
As it has been said:
"For one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desires to act in what ought to be done..."
"When agitation is dissolved, then there shall be the supreme state. (Svacchanda Tantra 1.9). || 216 ||

Now, one might ask: "How can this be said? For elsewhere, it was previously stated that the sequence of the arising of the enjoyer and the enjoyed proceeds as follows: from *kalā* arises the principle (*tattva*) which is the nature of the enjoyer, consisting of the pair *rāga* and *vidyā*.
To this, he says:

But surely, in the venerable *Raurava* and other scriptures, it is established that Kalā produces simultaneously the dyad consisting of Rāga and Vidyā; from that [dyad], the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) arises. (9.217)

The word "tataḥ" means immediately after the expansion of the pair consisting of *rāga* (attachment) and *vidyā* (knowledge). As it has been said: "There is another branch of *kalā*, from which these—the natures of *vidyā* and *rāga*—were born in the sequence of pairs and non-pairs."
And likewise in the Śrīruru: "From the principle of Kalā, the two principles of Rāga and Vidya came into being;
and from that, the Unmanifest (avyakta)..."

Thus, the reading is by way of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). For if these were produced simultaneously, there would be only a single sentence: "From Māyā, the Unmanifest, the Kalās, and the others, together with Passion and Ignorance, came into being. However, previously, relying on the difference among commentators, it was stated: "From Māyā come the Unmanifest and the Kalās," and so forth. In that context, the author of the Vārttika [uses] the word *tat* (that).
He has explained *māyā*. But the author of the commentary [says] "immediacy" (*ānantarya*). || 217 ||
He offers this very rebuttal:

"It has been stated here that this sequence indeed appears true; for it is sufficient [to say] that one who is being affected by passion knows everything, and even while knowing, one is affected by passion here. (9.218)

It is said that although one ought to say "it is stated," with the intention that [the point] is already established as being present in the intellect, it was stated that "this has been answered without delay"; this is true, for this sequence favored by you appears here.
To explain: the meaning is that there is indeed an excessive degree of mutual sequence even between passion (*rāga*) and ignorance (*vidyā*).
For indeed, every person, whether becoming attached, knows everything; or, knowing everything, becomes attached everywhere—how could this sequence not also be possible? (218)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is it that you yourself have stated that the enjoyer and the enjoyed arise simultaneously?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Nevertheless, this reality of things has been described by us here in this manner."
And in that [state], there is no sequence whatsoever; or even if there were, it would be the reverse.
"Even so" (tathāpi) means: even though their sequential occurrence is thus [conceived]. "The existence of the entity" (vastusattā) means:

the existence of the two entities—the enjoyer and the enjoyed—which is ultimate reality. "'There is no sequence' (na kramaḥ)" is because they are mutually dependent. As has been stated by this very author elsewhere:
"And here it has been stated that, according to their actual course, this creation is indeed devoid of succession" (Tantrāloka Sāra 8, āhnika). || 219 ||

If, moreover, one were to set aside the actual existence of these entities here and speak of their sequence based on mere possibility, then conversely, that sequence could even be reversed—namely, the arising of the enjoyer immediately after the arising of the enjoyment.
Therefore, one should not be mistaken in this regard; thus he says:
Therefore, one should not engage in contrary practice regarding the procedure taught in the Śāstra.
"Regarding the procedure taught in the Śāstra" means by relying on the procedure taught in the Ruru-Śāstra;
for this alone is intended there: that from the principle of *kalā* [arise] the three principles beginning with *rāga*.

Regarding the term "arisen" (*samutpanna*): whether its arising occurs simultaneously or non-simultaneously is obtained through an investigation consisting of the determination of its essential nature, and not from the mere literal meaning alone as it is superficially heard. Thus, our own explanation is indeed superior. || 219 ||

Now, an objection might be raised: "Has it not been stated that *pradhāna* is merely the object of cognition (*vedya*), and yet there is no separate cognizability for pleasure and so forth, which exist as specific forms? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus, that which is merely the object of consciousness [consists of] pleasure, pain, and delusion. (9.220)
That which is to be experienced (*bhotsyate*) from that [source] is said to be, from the very beginning, of the nature of equilibrium (*sāmyātmaka*).

In the manner thus described, that which exists as mere consciousness (*saṃvedyamātra*)—which is to be experienced as pleasure and so forth—is to be inferred according to the principle that "it is an effect because it is perceived"; therefore, from that [inference], there is the [realization of] the specific [nature].

The meaning is: because the logical reason (hetu) is preceded by the universal (sāmānya), that which consists of identity and is of an undifferentiated nature is declared from the beginning and determined as the cause. || 220 ||
Now, an objection may be raised: "The Sāṃkhyas maintain that primordial nature (prakṛti) is the state of equilibrium among the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
how then can it be said here that this [nature] is to be understood from pleasure and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Sattva is pleasure because of its luminosity; luminosity is said to be joy. (9.221)
Suffering is passion (rajas) because its nature is activity; for activity is the sequence of that [passion] and its opposite.
Delusion is darkness (tamas), which is obscuring due to its association with the absence of illumination. (9.222)

Is it not the case that the luminous nature of pleasure (*sukha*) is unestablished? For it has been said: "Pleasure is indeed pleasure itself, not light," and "Light is called joy (*hlāda*). Joy, moreover, consists of the wonder of the "I" (*ahaṃ-camatkāra*).
Suffering (*duḥkha*), on the other hand, is of the nature of both light and non-light; for if it were of the nature of light alone, it would simply be pleasure.

Otherwise, however, there would be delusion. Regarding the phrase "because its nature is action": this is because it possesses succession due to its consisting of both existence and non-existence. Now, one might ask: "Let there be succession for suffering in this way, but from what does its being 'action' arise?
To this it is said: "For action is the succession of that and not-that. Here, "that and not-that" refers to manifestation and non-manifestation.
As it has been said:
"Consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint.
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 12)
Thus:
"Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping."
And as it is said in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (13): "In the venerable *Pratyabhijñā* as well:
'Power and bliss are the action of the Lord; their absence is that of the bound soul (*paśu*')."

"That [state] consists of the two; its passion (rajas) is suffering, and it is conjoined with goodness (sattva) and darkness (tamas). (4a.1ā.7kā. Thus, it has been stated that *pradhāna* is the unagitated form consisting of the equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. || 222 ||
Now, one might object: "If the nature of the Pradhāna is indeed unagitated, how could it be capable of producing effects?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"These very Guṇas, having undergone agitation, extend forth the effect."
Previously, for that which is unchanging, this effect could not have been of a different nature.
It has already been stated in this treatise that the wise know the *guṇas* to be a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*).

"The effect" refers to the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth. "Of a different genus" means due to the heterogeneity of the *guṇas*. Furthermore, since this was already explained previously during the description of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), no further effort has been made here. Therefore...
The sense is that this is how it must be understood. As it has been stated there:
"For that reality which is above and below, designated as the qualities of *prakṛti*, the agitated qualities therein produce the intellect" (*Tantrāloka* 8.253).

"A cause that has not undergone a state of disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*) is indeed not capable of producing an effect," and so forth; "that which does not obstruct the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the nature of causality—therefore, from that [cause], an effect arises through another agitation (*kṣobha*), like the swelling of a seed and the sprout. (Tantrāloka 8.254)

Thus far. And so, when this *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* has been introduced, the venerable lords Śrīkaṇṭhanātha and others know that the second form of *prakṛti* itself— which is established by reasoning, which is agitated and intent on producing effects, and which consists of the *guṇas*— is like a knot of *māyā*.
The meaning is that they should know [the self] as something to be instructed. As it has been said there:
"Then the qualities... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.30). || 223 ||
And here, the division of the worlds has also been shown previously, like a knot [in a thread]—thus he says:
"In this context, the world is shown as distinct according to the differentiation of the qualities. (9.224)
As it was stated previously:
"In order, the rows of gurus are established in darkness, passion, and goodness—three, thirty-two, thirty-one, and twenty-one respectively. (Tantrāloka 8.260)
Thus [ends the verse]. || 224 ||

Now, one might object: "Since this [power] is insentient (jaḍa), how can its very orientation toward producing an effect arise, by which even agitation (kṣubdhatva) could occur? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Toward the person whose longing is agitated by the power of the Lord's will..."
In order to act as the enjoyer, the independent Lord violently agitates primordial nature.

The "Lord of the Independent" (Svatantreśa) is Śrīkaṇṭhanātha. As it has been said: "Such a primary principle, together with Brahmā, having been touched by the rays of Śrīkaṇṭha in the beginning, attains manifestation at that very moment."

Thus, just as for the Sāṃkhyas, this objection does not apply to us either: namely, that because the person (puruṣa) is changeless, there would be no distinction between the states of bondage and liberation; for why should Prakṛti not proceed to produce the entire collection of transformations, beginning with Mahat, toward one who is liberated just as she does toward one who is bound?

Because its nature as an active agent has not been abandoned, and because this [nature] lacks consciousness (*acaitanya*), it does not possess the reflective awareness: "I have been seen by him," nor does it think, "I shall act for this purpose.
Therefore, there would indeed be no liberation. || 225 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Therefore, that objection raised against the Sāṃkhya—namely, 'Why does she not produce [effects] for a liberated soul, since the Spirit is subject to modification?'—is not a refutation here. (9.226)

"By that" means: by means of this agitation caused by the independent Lord acting as the agent, directed toward such a person who is necessarily [bound]—this is the meaning. "In this" means: in our philosophical system. || 226 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"From the qualities (guṇas) arises the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), which is entirely stainless;
from that, the light of the Self, though it is the knower, here attains the state of being reflected. (9.227)

The meaning is: *tat*—therefore, from that cause which is the agent, the Independent Lord (*svatantra-īśa*). "The principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*)"—it is produced from that [Lord]. As it has been said: "From them [the elements], the intellect endowed with eight qualities [is born]... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.30).
Thus. "From that" means from purity in every respect. || 227 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the light of the subject is immediate, let it cast its reflection here;
but how can the external object of knowledge do so, given that it lacks such immediacy? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the reflection of the object within that [consciousness] is produced by the senses externally."
Such [a cognition] occurs in cases such as flashes of intuition (*pratibhā*) and the like, which do not have that [external object] as their door. (9.228)
The functioning of the intellect (buddhi) is its cognition, and that [cognition] is certainly the objective support for the light of self-awareness;
although this cognition is insentient, it is nonetheless fully sufficient for that purpose.
For the reflection of an external object in the intellect is twofold: that which occurs through the gateway of the senses, and that which does not.

Of these, the first occurs in perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like; the other occurs in creative imagination (*utprekṣā*) and the like—the word "and the like" (*ādi*) including dreams and so forth. For in this case, the object would manifest to the intellect only as it has been presented by itself—this is the intended meaning. That...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the modification (*vṛtti*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), characterized by its capacity to receive the reflection of the object of knowledge—which is produced by such a contact of the senses—becomes the cognition that illuminates the object. Now, one might ask: "Since the intellect is insentient (*jaḍa*), how can its cognition manifest the object? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that... and so forth.

For what purpose? That cognition (*buddhi*) is indeed the illumination, the manifestation, the appearance of the self-awareness of the Person (*puruṣa*); its stable support, its constant substratum for the reflection—this is the meaning.
Therefore, for that reason, because it is the locus for the manifestation of self-awareness, of this [cognition]...
The meaning is this: although the cognition consisting of the mental mode (*vṛtti*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is nonetheless capable of illuminating the object. As it has been said:
"The light [of consciousness], taking the form of the object, never [appears] anywhere except through the divine gateway [of the senses]."
"Because it is the ground for the manifestation of the male principle (puṃs), cognition (bodha) is considered to be the function (vṛtti) of the intellect (mati). || 229 ||
Having thus described the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) as an instrument, he also describes its nature as a cause:

"Because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) originates from the reflection of the Person (*pums*) within such an intellect—which is a light yet turbid with objects of knowledge—it consists in the act of thinking 'I'. (9.230)
The term *ahaṃkṛt* (the ego-maker) arises by implication. As it has been said:
"From that [intellect], the *ahaṃkṛta* [arises]" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.30).
And that [ego] is such [a state]—a place of manifestation for the light of the subject (*puṃsprakāśa*), yet turbid with the object of knowledge (*vedya*).
Within the light that is the self consisting of the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), there is the ego-identification (*aham-ātmābhimāna*) expressed as "I am doing this" or "I know.
Now, one might object: "This cognition of the intellect, which has been described as a mere fragment, is experienced by the conscious principle (*cetana*)."

Anticipating the objection— "Since its state as an object of enjoyment is well-established, as it is experienced once it has arisen, and because it is thus an object of enjoyment (*vedya*), how could the conceit of 'I' (*aham-abhimāna*) take root in this thing which is the locus of the notion 'this' (*idantā*)?"— it is said:
Regarding the phrase "pratibimbitapuṃskṛteḥ"—the meaning is: with reference to the manifested person (*puruṣa*).
Even so, this ego-identification (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*) does not belong to the Self (*ātman*), but rather to the intellect (*buddhi*) which is of the nature of the non-Self;
for the reflection of the Self has the intellect as its substratum and is therefore a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that [intellect] alone.
He states its unique function: "Impelled by that [power], which consists of intense agitation, this fivefold vital air serves for life; otherwise, however, there is death. (9.231)

Regarding the phrase "in the form of agitation" (*saṃrambharūpayā*): egoity is agitation, and its activity (*vṛtti*) is also its "form" (*rūpa*), because of the identity between the activity and that which possesses the activity—so it has been said. As it is stated: "The impeller of the fivefold functional wind for the sake of life..."
"Agitation is the function of the ego... and so forth.

"Otherwise" means not impelled. Thus, the activity of the ego consists of the impelling and non-impelling of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the rest, by means of a function whose nature is agitation, through which the life of all beings [is sustained].
Or there may be death. || 231 ||

And thus, from this ego-sense—which consists of the sovereignty of pure consciousness, whose true nature is resting in one's own self alone, and which arises spontaneously—there is this specific distinction: namely, that it has become attached to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is insentient and not the true Self. As it is said:

Therefore, because it has as its essential nature the "I-consciousness" which is the sovereignty of the pure Self, this [other] is said to be "created" by means of the word *kṛti* (creation), since that [sovereignty] is uncreated. (9.232)

"This" refers to that which is characterized by egoity (*ahaṃkṛta*). "Other" refers to that which is artificial (*kṛtrima*). Now, one might ask: what is the proof for its being artificial? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "it is so stated, because of the word 'kṛti'.
For in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated that it is "characterized by egoity," and "kṛta" is indeed said to mean "artificial."
Because the root *kṛ* has this meaning. || 232 ||
Concluding this, he introduces another topic:
"Thus, this aggregate of instruments (karaṇaskandha) of the ego (ahaṅkāra) has been described.
Its aggregate of primordial nature (prakṛtiskandha) is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic. (9.233)
"Threefold"—because each one of the qualities, such as *sattva* and the others, serves as the predominant factor (*aṅgin*). || 233 ||
In that regard, he defines the extent of the *sāttvika* nature of the aggregate of primordial matter (*prakṛtiskandha*):

"From the *ahaṃkāra* dominated by *sattva*, which clearly touches upon the aspect of the enjoyer, the group of six consisting of the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the five senses (*akṣa*) is born; however, their differentiation is now described. (9.234)

By the term "pradhāna" (the primary), the existence of *rajas* and *tamas* as subordinate qualities is indicated, because these [qualities] function through mutual union. The phrase "clearly touching the power of the enjoyer" is used because the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) consists essentially in the direct reflective awareness of that [enjoyer's] own nature.

Regarding the phrase "the hexad of mind, intellect, and senses": according to the Vedic scripture, "The senses have the mind as the sixth," this means the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya) conjoined with the mind. As it has been said:
"The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, together with the mind."
"Because it possesses the quality of light (prakāśa) and is derived from sattva, it is taijasa and sattvic.

Now, one might object: even though these [eleven organs] arise from a single ego (ahaṅkāra), how is it that the mind has everything as its object, while for the others the objects are restricted? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "But the distinction is being explained."
"Differentiation" means that which is produced by the necessity or non-necessity of the object—this is the sense.
Thus he says: "The mind, because its objects are everything, is what is intended here."
The agency over all those subtle elements is the defining characteristic of the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).

"By that" means by the reason that the mind has all things as its object. "In this context" means throughout the entire treatise. "Intended to be expressed" refers to such statements as, "From [the egoity] beginning with the elements (bhūtādi), the subtle elements (tanmātra) arise; that is of the nature of tamas. Therefore, the production of the subtle elements occurs from the egoity (ahaṅkāra) in which tamas predominates.
Thus, there is no dispute. Furthermore, even in the *ahaṅkāra* where *sattva* predominates, *tamas* may exist, because these [guṇas] function through mutual union, as it has been said:
"All are mutually paired; all go everywhere."
Thus, because the mind is born from the *sāttvika* ego characterized by that [subtlety],

its domain comprises all objects. Since the mind possesses this universal range of objects, it is known from this that the ego is the cause of all the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), by which [the mind perceives] sound and the other [objects].
And there would be the state of the grasped and the grasper. || 235 ||
And thus, by way of their respective specific functions, he declares that this triad— intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*), and mind (*manas*)— is indeed the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*):
"They call intellect, ego-sense, and mind [the instruments] for cognition, volition, and desire."
This is an act that has been performed neither by external deities nor by those who are inward-turned.
Cognition (*bodha*) is the determination of an object such as sound. Excitement (*saṃrambha*) is the conceit of "I" regarding the self.
Desire (*eṣaṇā*) is volition (*saṅkalpa*). And here, because these are actions, they must necessarily have an instrument (*karaṇa*).
That [instrument] cannot be the ear and so forth, which will be mentioned later, because those pertain to external action, whereas these [cognition, excitement, and desire] do not.
Because it has the nature of being internal (*antaḥ-rūpa*), and because it effects internal action (*antaḥ-kṛti-sādhaka*), it is distinct from that [external organ];

thus it is said to be called the "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as "intellect, ego, and mind" (*buddhi-ahaṃkṛt-manaḥ*). As it has been stated: "Desire, exertion, and cognition are not accomplished by the aforementioned external instruments."
"Thus it is established that the internal instruments are the mind (manas), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi).

Here, "intellect, ego, and mind" is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). Now, even though they are external instruments, the ears and so forth can indeed become inward-turned through a process of reflection, thereby collectively [producing] cognition and the like.

Anticipating the objection, "Since they attain the status of being means [to realization], what is the point of teaching other internal organs? he says, "external," and so forth. The meaning is that even for those who are inward-turned, it is not possible for the external senses to perform functions such as cognition. For indeed, if the external senses were [active] from the outside...

If they were to act together through a turning back toward the interior (*antarmukhatā*) to produce cognition and so forth, then at the time of the perception of sound and other objects, there would be no perception of that cognition itself. For it is held that these [faculties] perceive sound and the rest when they are externally uncombined; however, in the state of being turned inward, [they cannot do so].
How could it be that cognition and so forth belong to those [faculties] when combined? This would have to occur at one and the same time; yet this is observed to happen simultaneously.
Therefore, it is not rightly said that "the external senses themselves, turned inward and acting together, are the means for cognition and so forth. As it has been stated:

"And for those whose [minds] have turned inward and who are engaged in the purpose of the mind and so forth, the activities such as will (*icchā*) and the rest would not exist together with cognitions of external objects. (236)

Now, one might object: "Since the vital breath (prāṇa) itself, existing in inseparable union with consciousness, could provide cognition and so forth, what is the use of these internal organs (antah-karaṇas)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the vital breath is not an internal organ, because it is insentient [and] because its nature is mere impulsion."
It is certain that [the self is the cause] because it is the cause of the portions consisting of effort, desire, and cognition. (9.237)
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "And because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is insentient, it cannot be the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); this is certain.
Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that even an insentient tool, such as an axe, becomes an instrument when impelled by an agent?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because it is the cause of the factors of effort, desire, and awakening, which consist of impulsion.
For an instrument being impelled cannot exist without effort;
effort is preceded by desire; and desire is preceded by awakening.

Even if one accepts that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there must necessarily exist another instrument to account for effects such as cognition; so what fault have the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest committed? As it has been said:
"Others maintain that the vital breath is the internal organ, though it is devoid of consciousness."
"That [consciousness] exists without effort; what, then, could be the instrument for its accomplishment? || 237 ||
One might object: "Since there is no difference in their being internal in nature, let there be only one internal organ; what is the use of its threefold division?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Ascertainment, self-conceit, and conceptualization—these are not [simply] functions."
Since they are of a single form, it is clearly logical that there is a threefold nature within the internal organ (antaḥkṛti). || 238 ||
The action is not of a single form, because the roots *syati*, *man* (in *manyati*), and *kḷp* are distinct.

For even if these have a single object, their respective determinations (*avasāya*)—which function by excluding what is other than the intended object—must have distinct effects; this is the sense. As it has been said:

"Kalā, pi, mati, syati, and icchā—these are born as denoters of distinct meanings; therefore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is threefold, having the senses of desire, exertion, and cognition. || 238 ||

Now, one might object: "An instrument cannot be unconscious; and since cognition (buddhi), like the mind (manas) and ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), is not itself perceived, how can its status as an instrument be justified? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And cognition is not unperceived, because it is an instrument, just like the mind."
The doctrine that the intellect (buddhi) is imperceptible, like the primordial matter (pradhāna), is abandoned by him.
"The doctrine that the intellect (*buddhi*) is non-conscious" is what is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas. And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
the intellect is conscious, because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*); whatever is an instrument is conscious, just as the mind (*manas*);
whatever is not conscious is not an instrument, just as the primal matter (*pradhāna*); and the intellect is indeed an instrument.

Therefore, it is "cognizable. And regarding its state of being cognizable, the reason—that it is endowed with the qualities (*guṇa*)—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*). Thus:
"While the state of being endowed with the qualities is equal [in both], the mind alone is held to be cognizable."
"Indeed, your intellect is inconceivable, and your skill as a logician is praiseworthy"—such statements are to be disregarded. || 239 ||

Now, let this be so regarding the internal organs; but as for the sense organs, even though—like the mind—they are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), what is the cause for their having restricted objects?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The ego-principle (ahaṃkṛti) characterized by being the cause of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) is the instrument (karaṇa) in the ear; likewise, that which is differentiated by the nature of smell (gandhatva) [is the instrument] up to the nose. (9.240)

For when the ego (ahaṅkāra) produces the mind (manas), its specific characteristic as the agent of the subtle elements (tanmātra) is the determining factor without distinction; however, in the group of the sense organs (buddhīndriya), it is by way of restriction, whereby these [organs] come to have fixed objects. As it has been said:

"In the case of the mind (*manas*), which is produced [from the ego], that [ego] is the progenitor endowed with the capacity to produce all the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); however, in the case of the ear, it is distinguished by the capacity to produce sound; likewise, up to the nose, it is endowed with the fitness to produce smell. (Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā 8, Āhnikam)

Thus, it is precisely because they are derived from the *ahaṅkāra* that there is this restriction regarding their respective objects: that the ear grasps only sound and not touch or other qualities; the skin grasps only touch and nothing else; and so on, up to the nose, which grasps only smell. Furthermore, by those [who hold a different view]...

When it is stated, "I too am the ego-maker (ahaṃkṛta), and [the ego] is the cause of my birth," and so forth, this merely demonstrates their lack of expertise in defining the true nature of the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 240 ||
Indeed, others have stated that these [senses] are composed of material elements (bhautika), because their status as grasped object and grasper would otherwise be logically untenable. As they say:
"The sense organs—the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear—arise from the material elements."
(Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.12).
Therefore, because it is composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is the perceiver of odor alone, and not of taste and so forth;
likewise, because it has the nature of space (*ākāśarūpatva*), the sense of hearing (*śrotra*) is the perceiver of sound alone, and not [of other objects].
Regarding the phrase "of touch and so forth," he says that this is incorrect:
"Therefore, let there be materiality [of the senses] as well, because of the restriction regarding objects.
Thus, the restriction of objects occurs precisely through their being produced by the ego (ahaṅkāra) as qualified by its respective functions (vṛtti).

Because the reason is established, and because these [elements] are restricted to their respective objects, let that which has been stated by others regarding their being composed of the gross elements (*bhautikatva*) suffice;

there is no need to say anything more—this is the meaning. For if it were asserted in this way, even air would have to be perceivable by the sense of touch, since it is of the same nature as that [element]; yet this is not accepted by you.

Because air is admitted to be ungraspable [by the senses]; for a substance that is perceptible by two sense organs is both visible and tangible, and since air is a substance, how could it be grasped by only a single sense organ? Furthermore, the tactile sense organ [perceives] the triad of substances beginning with earth, as well as the qualities residing in them that possess the aforementioned characteristics.

One should not perceive tangibles because the sense of touch has air as its constituent nature (*prakṛti*), and it has already been stated that the restriction of the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver follows the sequence of their constituent natures. Likewise, the eye, being a substance of light (*tejas*),
would perceive only form (*rūpa*) residing within that [light], and not earth and the other elements, because its constituent nature is light.

In this way, there would be no sensory perception of action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), and inherence (*samavāya*), because the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*) while these [categories] do not have that nature; yet all of this is observed.
Therefore, it must be said that the sense organs are not composed of material elements—since they are the instruments of experience.
The four winds, which consist of the four substances,
sequentially grasp three of those substances, but not the wind itself.
There are three substances: the eye, and within it, indeed, the forms;
therefore, there is no fixed rule in the conceptualization of the sense organs and their objects.

"And because of the material nature of the restriction and the commonality of actions, cognitions would clearly not arise from the deities, nor [would they arise] from the inherence in the embodied soul.
Now, if there is a restriction of the senses by their material nature (prakṛti), this is what is called the restriction of objects.
Having refuted the view that [the senses] are material by establishing the reasoning otherwise, you might ask:
"What then is the reasoning for their being derived from the *ahaṃkāra*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the cognitions such as 'I hear,' 'I see,' 'I smell,' and so forth... (9.241)
Because it follows from the sense of "I," its nature as being derived from the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) is clearly established.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author means] "I touch," "I taste," and so forth. "Clearly" (*sphuṭam*)—the meaning is that this is indeed established by one's own direct experience. || 241 ||

And because these [organs] are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), their status as instruments is logical, and not otherwise; thus he says: "Therefore, their status as instruments is appropriate due to their connection with a portion of the agent. (9.242)
If the instrument were distinct from the agent, how could it be an instrument since it would be something to be impelled?

Therefore, because they are derived from the *ahaṃkāra*, because they are permeated by the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*), and because they touch upon the aspect of the agent, their status as instruments is logical; for otherwise, if an instrument distinct from the agent were desired, [it would follow that it could not function as such].
Since it is that which is impelled, how could it be an instrument (*karaṇa*)? On the contrary, because it is the object of impulsion, it is the object (*karman*)—this is the meaning. || 242 ||

And since an action cannot exist without an instrument, another instrument must be sought for that [action]; and because that too would be distinct from the agent, it too would necessarily be impelled, requiring yet another instrument—thus there would be an infinite regress.
To this, he says:
If there were a desire for yet another instrument, there would be an infinite regress in that case.

For in this way, the contracted subject who has grasped the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth, having separated his own body from the touch of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*), would bring even his own limbs— such as the ears and so forth— which are by nature parts of himself,
into the state of being instruments for the acts of perceiving objects like sound, by treating them as objective domains. Thus it is said:
Therefore, by means of its inherent sovereignty, the Agent, differentiating its own body, itself makes its own part—which touches upon the objective portion—into an instrument. (9.244)

"Therefore"—because it is logically untenable for the agent to be the instrument of differentiation. "By virtue of freedom"—the meaning is: by the power of agency. "Touching upon the objective aspect"—the meaning is: connected with objects such as sound and so forth. "Its own part"—meaning: having the form of the auditory organ and the rest.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can there be the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for an axe or the like in expressions such as 'he cuts with an axe'—where the instrument is distinct from the agent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By virtue of the identification (*tanmayībhāvanā*) with that portion of itself which has been made into an instrument."
It treats that which is absolutely distinct as an instrument, like an axe. || 245 ||

For the cognizer, being indeed contracted, identifies with that portion of himself consisting of the intellect, the organs of action, and so forth, which has been made an instrument; through the power of that identification— the conceit of non-distinction—
he regards even an axe, which is absolutely distinct, as if it were not distinct from his own hand and other limbs.

It makes [the object] an instrument; that is to say, it brings about its status as the most effective means (*sādhakatamatā*) in the act of cutting. Thus, it is established that a portion of the agent itself, when separated, attains the state of being an instrument in the primary sense. || 245 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, in the beginning, for this [individual], the impure *vidyā* alone is the common instrument (*karaṇa*) for cognition;
but for action, *kalā* is said to be the common instrument. (9.246)
"Pure" means previously. For immediately following *vidyā* and *kalā*, there is the expansion of the specific body consisting of the intellect, the organs of action, and so forth. (246)
[Objection: But surely, since *kalā* is everywhere described as the agent (*kartṛ*) who impels [the soul], how can it be designated here as an instrument (*karaṇa*)? To this he says:
"But indeed, in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, the agency of *kalā* has been proclaimed."
For when that [ignorance] exists, knowledge and the rest are capable of serving as instruments. (9.247)
For it is only when things are impelled by an agent that they can function as instruments and so forth—this is the intended meaning. || 247 ||
To this, he provides the following rebuttal:
It is said that agency itself is what necessitates the status of being an instrument; for without it, other instruments have no existence. (9.248)

The phrase “being an instrument” (*karaṇatva*) means “while [the agent] exists. The term “instigating cause” (*prayojikā*) means “primary. It follows by implication that its status as an instrument, however, is secondary. For the reason why agency alone is primary is stated through the method of negation in the passage beginning with “without that,” etc. (248).
Because she is designated as the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), she does not fall within the category of instruments; thus he says:
"Therefore, she is set apart from the general group of instruments.
She is "set apart" because her status as an instrument is not primary.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is it that *kalā* has also been described as having primary instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), since it touches upon the aspect of the agent (*kartṛ-aṃśa*) just like *vidyā*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For without *vidyā*, the other instruments have no independent existence. (9.249)
Since there can be no agency for that [Self] without *kalā*, nor any capacity for knowing, they know that *kalā* and *vidyā* are the primary instruments of the person (*pums*). (9.250)
"Of others" refers to the internal and external instruments (antarbahiṣkaraṇa) which are somehow distinct from the agent;

for even though these are somehow distinct, they possess the status of instruments through the contemplation of their non-differentiation from knowledge (vidyā) and so forth, which are of the nature of their own parts—this is the intended meaning. And the connection is that "there is no innate state of that knowledge."

For where there is agency, there must be subjectivity; the sense is that without agency, there can be no agency even in the act of knowing. "From that" [means] because the status of *vidyā* as an instrument is dependent upon *kalā*; for whatever depends on another for its status as an instrument, that [other] too—
The status of being an instrument is observed, as in the case of a hand, which bestows the state of being an instrument upon objects such as a knife. || 250 ||

One might object: "In what way is the status of these two as instruments observed through their distinction from one another, as is the case with the eye and so forth in relation to form and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he states the previously mentioned reason as follows:
"Therefore, even when [the body] is deprived of the organs of cognition and action in certain cases..."
For the blind and the lame, the manifestation of form and movement does not fail to appear. || 9-251 ||
For this very reason, because *vidyā* and *kalā* are the primary instruments, [the experience occurs] at some time or on some occasion—this is the meaning.

The terms "blind" and "lame" are indicative of the absence of the faculties of cognition and action, respectively. It is not that it does not shine, but rather that it certainly shines—this is the meaning. || 251 ||
Now, one might object: "If even the blind and others were to perceive forms and so forth, then what would be the purpose of the sense organs of cognition and action?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But rather, even when such an object is to be known, [this occurs] through the power of the common sensory organs."
"In such" means precisely in a general form—this is the meaning.
Thus it is said: "At that time, the blind person attains a cognition of the universal form alone. (9.252)

For even those such as the blind would have a manifestation of objects like form and so forth in their general aspect regarding things situated on the far side of Mount Meru, just as we do; for if there were no manifestation of form and so forth being delineated, they would not even be inclined toward external objects. || 252 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"From that very same *ahaṃkāra*, however, as it comes into contact with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the organs of action—speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet—were born. (9.253)

The meaning is: "from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) which has been described as consisting of three constituents (triskandha). Now, one might object: "Since contact with the subtle elements (tanmātra) is said to exist even in the ego-sense where *sattva* predominates, what is its distinction from that [other type]?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "But it is additional. For in the state of knowledge (*jñāna-daśā*), even though [the process] has begun...

The meaning is that here, contact (*sparśa*) culminates in action (*kārya*) by virtue of being dominated by activity (*kriyā-pradhānatayā*). By this, its *rājasa* (passionate/active) nature is revealed. As it has been said:
"Speech, hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet—these arise from *rajas*."
"Due to the sequence of karma, that which is here the *vaikārika* [sattvic] pride (*garva*) is abounding in *rajas*.
And he will say:
"This group of sense organs has been described as arising from the *rājasa* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). (9.271)
Thus [ends the section]. || 253 ||
And here, as before, because of the permeation by the ego (ahaṅkāra), he clarifies its nature as being derived from the ego:
"I speak, I take up, I quickly abandon, I emit, and I go"—that activity of the ego which is capable of action is indeed the organ of action (karmendriya). (9.254)

"I emit" (visṛjāmi) [is said] because emission has bliss as its fruit. Now, an objection might be raised: "Since there is also a permeation by 'I-ness' (ahantā) in the sensory organs (buddhīndriya), what is the distinction between them and these [organs of action]? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "[The organs of action are] capable of action. And although these [organs of action] are indeed effects of the activity of the ego-sense (ahaṃkriyā),...
The intention behind this statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is that the substratum alone is not the sense organ;
therefore, he says:
"By that [definition], one whose hand has been severed still possesses a hand consisting of the organ of action (*karmendriya*)."

"By that" means by the reason of being composed of the ego-function (ahaṃkriyā) capable of performing its specific action—this is the meaning. And since the ego-function has all bodies as its locus, it is established that those [bodies] are also likewise. As he will say:
"Therefore, they call the organs of action primarily pervasive, like the sense of touch."
"In that place, they possess their functions... (9.260). Thus, the hand, which consists of the organs of action, possesses a function distinct from its perceptible substrate;
by virtue of being a portion of the agent, it takes the form of the presiding subject.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then why is conventional usage restricted to the five-fingered hand alone as the sense organ of the hand?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The supreme primary locus of that [organ] is the hand with its five fingers. (9.255)

By the term "pradhāna" (the primary), it is indicated that even when not the primary [cause], there exists another substratum for this [action]. For this very reason, even one whose hands are severed could perform grasping by means of the mouth and so forth. || 255 ||

An objection might be raised: "Surely grasping can occur even through the mouth of animals and the like, yet that is not brought about by the organ of the hand; for the body is the locus of experience for the self, and it accomplishes the enjoyment of the fruits of various actions solely through its own respective parts. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even when taking [something] with the mouth, that which functions as the instrument therein is indeed the hand; for how could an action occur without an instrument? (9.256)

In this context, regarding the act of taking [the breath], it is said that [the breath] "abides" [therein], but the mouth and so forth are not so stated. For here, by the hearing of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) residing in the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛtyartha*) must be expressed. And the meaning of the base noun is the mouth; however, its status as an instrument is not tenable, because it is composed of material elements (*bhautika*).

Because it is devoid of contact with the agent-aspect (*kartṛ-aṃśa*). Furthermore, it has just been demonstrated that an instrument cannot be absolutely non-different from the agent; therefore, one must admit some entity characterized by that [agent] and presided over by him which does indeed touch the agent-aspect, wherein the meaning of the third case—the state of being an instrument—resides.
It would conclude that [the sense] is the hand itself—as it has been said: "That is the hand alone.

Consequently, the statement [that the hand is the organ] intends only the physical substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), because "walking, sitting, taking up [objects], and so forth are observed even in those whose feet or hands have been amputated" (Nyāyamañjarī 8, ā.).
Such is merely the prattle of others. Now, the face and so forth are perceived, whereas an unseen instrument must be postulated.
And when there is a conflict between what is already established and what is to be postulated, one should accept that which is already established.

Anticipating the objection, "By this logic, it would be more reasonable to accept only that which has already been established [as such]; so why was this said?"—it was stated: "How could an action be possible without an instrument? For the mouth and other parts are established as constituent members (*avayava*), not as instruments (*karaṇa*); indeed, it is stated that their being so [as instruments] is not tenable.
Therefore, another entity must be postulated as the instrument, such that an action without an instrument would not be possible.
"In that case, would not even the postulation of the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya) be fruitless?"—to this he says:
"But if that were so, what purpose would there be for the cognitive senses (buddhyakṣa) as well?
The word "but" (tu) indicates a reason. [Objection: But surely, since cognition depends on instruments, [the existence of] the hands and so forth [is required].

Anticipating the objection—"What is this [statement] 'dependent on instruments' that is being established as if it were fifty [verses]?"—he says: "And it is stated that perception is dependent on instruments because it is an action. (9.257)
But it is a matter of wonder that [the existence of] an instrument (karaṇa) is not accepted by others in the case of movement.
By "others" is meant the Naiyāyikas and so forth. As they say:
"The action of perceiving smell and so forth is preceded by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting."
Thus, "in walking" (gamau) means in the act of going, which consists of the functioning of the organ of feet—the sense is this.

And this is also an elliptical expression for grasping and so forth. "Astonishment" [is used] because, in this way, the logical reason of being an action (kriyātva) would be inconclusive (anaikāntikatva), since the act of going might occur even without being preceded by an instrument (karana).
Consequently, it would follow that even in the act of seeing, the state of being preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*) is not established;
this is a marvel for the Naiyāyika, that what is joined here falls apart there.
And this is his great wonder: that in his system, action (*karman*) consists of only five types, such as going (*gamana*) and so forth.

Furthermore, knowledge and the rest are the ninefold specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of the self. In that regard, even with respect to the primary action of "going," there is no requirement for a prior instrument; however, that knowledge—which is itself of the nature of a quality—requires a prior instrument. This is an unprecedented assertion. || 257 ||
Thus it is said: "Going, lifting up, and so forth, are the primary perceptions of action. (9.258)
Furthermore, in the grammatical (vaiyākaraṇa) system, this [activity] is a quality (guṇa) and an action (kriyā). Perception is knowledge whose nature is seeing. As it has been said:
"Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and going—these are the five types of action alone."
Thus:
"The specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇas) are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression."

And so it is said. Now, one might object: "The meaning of the verbal root *jñā* (to know) is indeed action (*kriyā*), namely cognition (*jñāna*), and not a quality (*guṇa*. To this he replies with the words "But this is action," and so forth. A grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) incurs no fault in speaking thus, for him there is a conventional rule that a verbal root denotes action. For the Naiyāyikas and others, however, [the status of] cognition...

Since it is recited among the list of qualities (*guṇa*), how can such a designation be consistent? Consequently, this is indeed self-contradictory on his part: that while cognition (*jñāna*) is a quality, its being preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*) is accepted because it is an action (*kriyā*), whereas for [actions] such as going (*gamana*), this is not accepted despite their being actions. || 258 ||
He states that very point:
"Action is preceded by an instrument"; thus, by the rule of universal concomitance, it is preceded by an instrument. (9.259)
To say that "knowledge is not an act of taking" is clearly a manifestation of blindness;
"a manifestation of blindness" means a delusion consisting of a failure to reflect upon what precedes and follows—this is the meaning.
"Now, do we not admit that going and other such actions are preceded by the non-employment of instruments?

Rather, we do not maintain that they must necessarily be preceded by specific instruments such as the feet; for even those whose legs have been severed go by means of their knees and so forth, and serpents move by means of their chests. Anticipating this objection, he says:
Therefore, they say that the organs of action are primarily pervasive, like the sense of touch.
"In that regard, they possess their respective functions," so say my teachers in the *Mataṅga*.

Therefore, according to the reasoning already stated, because the mere substratum of the feet and other limbs lacks the status of being the sense organs of the feet and so forth, [the senses] pervade the entire body, just like the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*).

Proponents of the theory that the organs are derived from the *ahaṅkāra* have declared these to be the organs of action (*karmendriya*). However, they possess their primary function specifically in those locations, such as the feet and so forth, which serve as their substrates; it is for this reason that everyone maintains the conviction that these very places constitute the nature of the organs. In reality, however, all of these— [The text continues: ...are indeed [the organs].
The body is that which is to be presided over. For this very reason, it is not contradictory for them to be observed performing their functions anywhere at all.
Nor is this something we have invented ourselves; thus it has been said: "In the Mataṅga [Tantra], my gurus [are the authorities].
This means that the commentators on the Mataṅgaśāstra, such as the venerable Aniruddha and others, [are the sources].

Granted that it may be so— that actions such as going cannot be accomplished without the instruments such as the feet— but from what source does this restriction arise that there are only five organs of action?
For other [organs] also present themselves, since there exist other actions such as swallowing and the like.
As they say:

"The throat [is an organ] because of the swallowing of food; the chest because of embracing the jar-like breasts; and how could the two shoulders not be called organs because of carrying burdens? (Nyāyamañjarī, Vol. 8, p. 8).

Thus, since the actions of swallowing and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable even for the throat and other such parts, one must admit that they too possess the status of organs of action (*karmendriya*); consequently, the organs of action would remain indeterminate. To this he says:
"But surely there are many other actions as well; for their sake [the organs exist]. (9.261)
The instruments [of action] must also be mentioned, and thus there would be no finality regarding the senses.
