Now, one might ask: "What is the point of saying this here, since this has already been refuted by others?
To this he says: "But this was indeed refuted by Kheṭapāla and others; it is not [the case that] actions [are unnecessary]. (9.262)
That which is a means of accomplishment would be senseless for any action whatsoever;
this is the meaning according to the venerable Sadyojyotis and others, such as Kheṭapāla.
As they have said:

"But by these [five] actions defined as 'bliss' (ānanda) and so forth, the organs of action are [designated]; therefore, there is no infinity of them due to the variety of actions. They have explained this very point; it is not by me that this is being stated as a means for performing action.
Regarding the term "karmendriya" (organ of action), it refers rather to those instruments which are the means for performing other actions such as bliss and so forth;
these are the karmendriyas. || 262 ||
"For this is not a direct resolution that satisfies us"—thus he says:
"This does not serve to quench the fever of the thirst for answers to the questions we have raised. (9.263)
For peacocks are not satisfied by waters that are turbid and mostly lifeless;
the meaning is that this [knowledge] is not sufficient to quench the torment of the thirst for questions posed by others.
For in this way, the various actions and instruments postulated by others [are likewise inadequate].
Thus, it is accepted by you that [the objects] exist. || 263 ||
"Now, if this is so, then what is the response here that might be convincing to those like you?"—to this he says:
"It is said: 'The venerable Śambhunātha has given me the answer to this. (9.264)
"Strengthened by the noble conceptualization of pure self-awareness"—
by means of this qualification beginning with "pure," he states the reason characterized by its establishment through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
He says:
In this case, the one [reality] is divided due to the differences in the continuity of karma. (9.265)

In this context, the synthesis (*anusaṃdhi*) consists of five aspects; therefore, there are five organs of action. "In this context" means when there is a differentiation of synthesis based on the differentiation of the types of actions. "Consisting of five aspects" means being of five kinds. "Therefore" refers to the fact that synthesis is of five kinds. (265)
In this regard, he first explains the differentiation of action based on the differentiation of the underlying intention:
"For the sake of relinquishing, for the sake of acquiring, and for the sake of both; without these two [respective intentions], there is no [action]. (9.266)
For the sake of resting in one's own true nature, there is a fourfold external activity;
the anus, hands, feet, and the organ of generation constitute that fourfold instrument. (9.267)
That which is the internal support of the vital breaths is action (*karman*), while speech (*vāk*) is indeed the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein.

Here, for everyone, there is a fourfold contemplation (*anusaṃdhi*): for the abandonment of what is to be abandoned, for the acquisition of what is to be acquired, for both of these together, and for resting in one's own true nature by relinquishing both those forms.

Since it is said "it is divided," the action (karman) which has that as its cause must likewise be so; because such is the nature of that action, therefore, externally, there arises a fourfold instrument (karaṇa) known by the names anus, feet, hands, and genitals—this is the connection. Even though [this applies] to all actions...
Although it possesses conjunction and disjunction, nevertheless, with respect to the specific action of going—

since that action proceeds with the aim of a single result characterized by reaching a village and so forth— its very nature consists in the taking up of another location preceded by the relinquishing of various respective locations.
The function of the foot as an organ consists in the single act characterized by both relinquishing and grasping; for this very reason, it is said to be "for the sake of the two.

Furthermore, "resting in one's own nature" (*svarūpaviśrānti*) is here described as having the form of the mere experience of bliss, which is synonymous with *nirvṛti*. For in that state, [the self] somehow...

Even though it is preceded by rejection and acceptance, the agitation consisting of the thought "this is to be rejected, this is to be accepted" would be stilled. Regarding the phrase "having the vital breath as its support": since the vital breath alone is indeed the substratum of speech, it is with reference to that very breath that this [speech] attains the status of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the act of speaking; such is the case regarding rejection and so forth.

All four types of action belong to that which has attained its existence (*labdhasattāka*). For indeed, only an established entity is abandoned, acquired, or inferred as a locus of rest. Action consisting of speech, however, functions solely in the production of sound; this is its distinction from the preceding [types of action]. It is for this very reason that the word "but" (*tu*) is used.

Regarding the counter-argument (*vyatireka*): [The opponent asks], "But surely the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself, through various conjunctions and disjunctions with the vocal organs (*sthāna*) and articulators (*karaṇa*), could produce sound consisting of diverse phonemes; what then would be the use of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*)? As they say:
"The wind, having risen from the navel, expands in the chest, turns back at the throat, and strikes the head..."
"Reversing its direction, moving within the mouth, it manifests various sounds.
This is not so; for in this way, sound consisting of diverse phonemes would be uttered at all times.
Indeed, there is no moment of time in which the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not [function].

If [the vital air] were not to participate in the conjunctions and disjunctions of various specific places and articulations (*sthāna-karaṇa*), it would not flow forth. Therefore, there must exist a vocal organ (*vāg-indriya*) distinct from that [air], by presiding over which the vital air becomes capable of producing sound, whereas otherwise it would not. || 267 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "It has been stated that the function (*vṛtti*) of the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) is simple perception (*ālocana*); what then is the function of the organs of action (*karmendriya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The various functions of these [organs] in their respective tasks have thus been described in brief. (9.268)

It is called "variegated" (*citrā*) because it consists of the forms of taking up, discarding, and so forth. It is said to be "in brief" (*samāsataḥ*) because it includes all other types of action; for there could not possibly exist any other action apart from this—this is the sense. Precisely because there is no other action, there is likewise no other instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is to be postulated, for its acceptance is established by this much alone. ||268||
Regarding this, he says: "Indeed, no action distinct from these [five] is ever observed anywhere;
for what purpose, then, should this non-cessation of the senses be postulated? (9.269)
"For whose sake" means "for what purpose"—this is the meaning. || 269 ||
Now, it has been stated that there are five organs of action and that their functions—such as grasping and so forth—are fixed as exactly five.
Given this, how can there be a mutual confusion of functions, such as moving with the hand or grasping with the foot? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The wise perform this wheel of duties without confusion;
however, the dull-witted perceive a confusion because the senses function simultaneously. (9.270)

"This very [fact]" refers to such actions as moving away and taking up. "Without confusion" means that it is not the case that the hand performs moving or the foot performs taking up; rather, both the foot and the hand perform moving and taking up respectively upon a single substratum, because they pervade the entire body.

Because these, as well as the five fingers and so forth, are the primary substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the body; "by way of co-functioning" means by virtue of being situated within a single substratum—this is the meaning. "Inert" means not knowing the distinction between the substratum and that which is supported by it—this is the meaning. For it is thus:

Since the capacities for seeing and hearing would both occur within a single eyeball in the case of snakes (cakṣuḥśravas), there would also be an absence of the sense organs of cognition due to the confusion of their functions. || 270 ||
Having thus refuted the views of Akṣapāda and others, he concludes his own position: "This group of sense organs has been described as arising from the rājasa aspect of the ego (ahaṅkāra).
By the word "this," the previously introduced group consisting of the organs of action is meant.
Having thus described the nature of the ego (ahaṅkāra) as being composed of the *sāttvika* and *rājasa* aspects, he speaks of its *tāmasa* aspect as well:
"From the ego dominated by *tamas*, which has the nature of veiling the subjective aspect of the enjoyer... (9.271).
The pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka), which is the cause of the gross elements, belongs to that [ego] named *bhūtādi* (the origin of the elements).
This is because, according to the principle "by concealing the aspect of the enjoyer," the aspect of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya-aṃśa*) predominates due to its manifestation.
And the reason for this [ego] having the name *bhūtādi* is its status as the cause of the subtle elements, which are themselves the causes of the gross elements.

Thus has been stated the cause of the elements. And it has been said: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these specific qualities are the *tanmātras*, designated by the term *tanmātra*."
"Because it differs from the group that performs the function of illumination,
and because it is itself illuminated, the *ahaṃkāra* known as *bhūtādi* is here [classified] as *tāmasa*. || 271 ||

Now, how can this be said— that "the group of motor organs (karmendriya-varga) is born from the rājasa ego (ahaṅkāra)"? For the Sāṃkhyas have established that the group of the mind, the [other] sense organs, and the organs of cognition proceeds from the sāttvika ego, while the group of subtle elements (tanmātra-varga) proceeds from the tāmasa [ego].
"But both proceed from the *rājasa*," as they say:
"The group of eleven proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego; the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) proceed from the *bhūtādi*; and both proceed from the *taijasa*. (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 25)
Thus it is said:
"The group consisting of the mind, the intellect, the sense organs, and the organs of action, as well as the group of the subtle elements (tanmātras)... (272).

In this context, the connection with the *rājasa* ego (*ahaṃkṛti*) is the unifier within these two. "Within these two" refers to the group of eleven organs and the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). It is called the "unifier" because it provides the internal cohesion that directs them toward the production of their respective effects. For the *sāttvika* ego—

Functioning as the sense organs, it—being devoid of action—desires the quality of passion (rajas) as its impeller; likewise, the quality of darkness (tamas), functioning as the subtle elements (tanmātra), does so as well.

Now, what is the point of introducing this view of the Siddhāntins or the Sāṃkhya view? For here, indeed, the investigation of the ultimate nature of the relationship between cause and effect has been commenced with reference to the venerable *Pūrvaśāstra*. And therein—

Regarding this, it is said: "From that Taijasa [ego], the mind was born as the lord of the senses; from the Vaikārika [ego] arose the senses, and from the third [Tāmasa ego] the subtle elements" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.31).
Having internalized such a doubt, let us first examine the different interpretations of that very passage.
He shows this:
"But others say that the mind is born from the rājasa ahaṃkāra, because... (9.273).

The mind is agile, swift, and capable of moving through all the senses; others, however, hold that the internal organ arises from the *sattva* quality, while the organs of cognition and action [arise from *rajas*]. (9.274)
They consider [the senses] to be touched by the portions of the perceiver and the perceivable due to the *rājasa* [quality];

that is, due to the *rājasa-ahaṃkāra*, which is designated by the term *taijasa*. Furthermore, it has been stated in the verse beginning with "light" (*laghu*) that the external sense organs are only capable of functioning toward their respective objects when presided over by the mind.

"Having made [the mind] skillful in the movement of all the senses. For this very reason, because it is the presiding deity over all the external senses, it is called here "the Lord of the Senses" (akṣeśa).
It is with this very intention that others have said:
"It is said: 'The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind' (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.16). Now, consider one who eats a long, cold, fragrant, dry *śaṣkulī* [sweetmeat]..."
Anticipating the objection— "Is not simultaneous production of knowledge also observed through such formulations as 'the five cognitions of the Brahmin Kapila arise simultaneously'?"— it is said:
"possessing velocity," meaning moving swiftly.

The meaning is that, according to the analogy of the piercing by hundreds of lotus-petal needles, the sequence, though present here, is not perceived. And thus, because it possesses activity (*kriyā*), it is connected with the quality of *rajas*; therefore, it was rightly said:
"The mind is born from the *rājasa* ego. Thus...

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that the organs of cognition and action arise from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is designated by the term "transformative" (*vaikārika*). The phrase "from the *sāttvika*" refers to that which is denoted by the term "luminous" (*taijasa*);
for because light is of the nature of illumination, it possesses such a quality—thus it has been stated. [The phrase] "from the *rājasa*" [is explained as follows].
This designation is applied because it is denoted by the word *vaikārika* and because of the predominance of its specific activity;
for this very reason, it is said that [the senses] "touch upon the portions of both the grasper and the grasped" due to their connection with that [manas].
However, the followers of the Siddhānta do not accept this—thus he says:
But the Kheṭapālas maintain that the group of organs of action is clearly [the subtle body]. (9.275)

Because the state of being an object of action arises from the *rājasa* ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*), [the organs] are born from the *rājasa* ego-sense, and not from the *sāttvika* ego-sense. For indeed, conformity to the cause is the determining factor in the nature of an effect. Furthermore, the group of the sense-faculties (*buddhīndriya*) is illuminative.

And since the group of organs of action performs action, it is logical that the emergence of these two [the mind and the intellect] occurs from a corresponding ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). As it has been said:
"Since the host of deities of the mind and the intellect is illuminating..."
"Therefore, that [group] is born from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is concordant with itself.
And:
"The group of the organs of action is born from the *rājasa* *taijasa* [ego], and it performs actions."
"For that by which, once born, there is here a conformity to the cause of the effect.

Otherwise, if their [the elements'] production were assumed in this way, the lack of fixed order regarding causes would result for all transformations. For in that case, even the group of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) would arise from that very same [source].
Why would the manifestation of both groups not arise from the *tāmasa* ego?
As they say:
"The lack of fixed order among the transformations cannot be prevented."
"When the origin from the *sāttvika* is established for the two groups, the *sāttvika* and the *rājasa*...

Now, let this be; we do not disagree on this point, for it has been established that "the relationship between cause and effect is indeed manifold. However, one must consider what is logically consistent regarding the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*. For it is precisely by means of its authority that the real (tāttvika) relationship between cause and effect [is established].
Having begun to investigate this, he says:
"But in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, however, the mind [is said to arise] from the rājasa, and furthermore from the sāttvika... (9.276).
All the sense organs [arising from the rājasa ego] appears to us as logical;
however, in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, it appears even more logical to us that the mind is born from the rājasa ego, while the organs of cognition and action are born from the sāttvika [ego].
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), with its position displaced [from its logical place]. || 276 ||
He demonstrates the very reasonableness of this point as follows: "For instance, when the functions of the external senses manifest... (9.277).
The power of the internal organ (*manas*) lies in perception,

whereas that of the external functions of the senses— meaning the ten external organs, such as the eyes and so forth— lies in the conjunction [of objects] with the mind. This is the meaning of "these."

It has been stated that the capacity [of the senses] lies solely in mere observation (*ālocana*), which consists in the manifestation of one's own non-conceptual functioning: "The power [resides] in observation, which is the manifestation of the functioning. However, if the reading is *vastu* (the object), the meaning is: "in the nature of the apprehension of that [object]. This much, however, is the distinction:
That which flashes forth as the aspect of action— consisting of speech and so on— which follows upon the perception of the sensory organs,

is entirely the operation of the mind (*manas*), whose essence consists in internal synthesis, rooted in a relationship composed of both difference and non-difference, and whose true nature is its repose within the subject (the cognizer) such as the intellect (*buddhi*). For action is indeed...
The so-called unity of many successive external moments consists in their being internalized within the subject.
Nor would such a state exist only in the non-conceptual stage, because experience occurs in each individual moment of manifestation. Therefore, in cases such as "I speak," and so forth...

The primary function of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) is a slight manifestation resulting from the predominance of contact with the objective aspect (*kāryāṃśa*), which occurs through the descent of contact with the subjective aspect of the agent (*kartṛṃśa*) regarding objects such as speech; this constitutes the first conceptualization of the cognizer, by virtue of which he is distinguished from one who is mute.
It may be so; however, actions such as speaking and the like, being optional, are merely mental operations for the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ). || 277 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for this?", he says:
"And it has been stated by the Guru: 'One should make the mind possessive of subsequent reflective awareness. (9.278)
"The activity consisting of the mother's operation has that duality as its object," so it was said by the Guru, the author of the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*. As it is stated there:
"These [cognitions] have that duality as their object, being accompanied by the mental after-cognition (*anu-vyavasāyin*)."
"It performs the functions of a mother through the conceptualizations of karma and so forth" (Ri-pra.

2.2.3). For it is the mind alone that, following conceptualization, determines even an object already determined by the eyes and other senses, and by presiding over the state of certainty, [perceives] that which possesses both unitary and manifold forms.

Depending upon this duality, one would perform these conceptualizations of action and so forth; and it has been stated that the state of being a subject for the illusory knower (*māyā-pramātṛ*) consists precisely in this much—namely, "having the activity of the subject as its essence.

For, according to the principle expressed in such passages as, "Indeed, even for a bound soul (*paśu*), this divine state exists during the state of non-conceptualization," [the subjectivity of the illusory knower is established].
If that entire collection of objects were to manifest without any distinction at all, how could the worldly course of life, consisting of both difference and non-difference, be sustained? || 278 ||
Furthermore, regarding the subtle elements (tanmātras) here, he says they arise from the *ahaṃkāra* that is primarily *tamas*, such as the *bhūtādi*:
"But the group of subtle elements [arises] from the *ahaṃkṛti* in which darkness (*dhvānta*) predominates. (9.279)

Now, one might object: "Why should the group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*) not also arise from the *ahaṃkāra* characterized by *sattva*, just as the two groups of the organs of cognition and action do? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this matter there is no dispute; for everyone agrees that the process of perception begins precisely with the objects of apprehension."
For no one disputes here that this [intellect] is the commencement of the object of apprehension, which consists of the faculty of determination (*varaṇa*).
Therefore, it is that which is manifested (*prakāśya*), not the manifestor (*prakāśaka*). How, then, could its production proceed from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*)? Thus it has been said:
"The group of the subtle elements (mātrāvarga) is also distinct from the two groups [of the organs] due to its egoity;
it is to be manifested, is characterized by tamas, and is born from that which is designated as 'the origin of the elements' (bhūtādi). || 279 ||
He demonstrates the division of the very category of the subtle elements (tanmātra) alone:
"In the earth, within the manifold sphere of fragrance consisting of pleasant scents and the like... (9.280).
That universal which is "odor-ness" (gandhatva) is what is called the subtle element of odor (gandhatanmātra);

anything else is non-fragrant. The word "etc. (ādi) indicates a variety; by it, there is the inclusion of odors that are intense or faint, those produced by that [subtle element], and those belonging to substances such as clarified butter or blood. Thus it has been said:
Regarding the examination of the ground:
"Endowed with the scents of ghee, blood, cooked food, and wine. The meaning is that "variegated" refers to the specific nature [of the ground], while "common" refers to the non-specific.

The sense is that particularities must indeed be grounded in non-particularity; for this very reason, because its particularities have not yet emerged, that smell and so forth is called a *tanmātra* (pure element) when it exists in its isolated state. || 280 ||

And because it is of a universal nature, it is all-pervasive due to its connection with every particularity; thus he says: "It is therefore called pervasive; however, because it possesses a cause, it is not eternal. (9.281)

"Destruction is the disappearance [of an entity] into its own cause; therefore, it is not eternal. Nor is this [destruction] unconditioned by time, because it is not unconditioned by space; however, it is said not to be permanent because it has a cause. For that which is produced can never be eternal—this is the intended meaning.
Even so, because there is no observation of destruction at the end, it was stated that "this is not perishable"—namely, "it is not non-firm.
For in our view, what is called destruction is simply dissolution back into its own cause;
and what is called being an effect is the external manifestation of an object that exists internally, [only] to dissolve back into that very same [cause].
"Rest is destruction. By this it is established that this [Self] is not immutable-eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*), but rather transformational-eternal (*pariṇāminitya*). || 281 ||
He extends this very principle to other cases as well:
"In the same way, this application [of the analysis] should also be joined to the tanmātras ending with the word 'rasa' (taste) and so forth. (9.282)

Now, one might object: "What is the use of these imperceptible non-particulars? Let only the particulars themselves be accepted as perceptible, by virtue of which this entire course of worldly affairs may be established?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because the state prior to the specific [effects] must necessarily belong to that which is not yet specific.

The word "necessarily" implies that a cause must exist in relation to its effect—this is the sense. He now defines the nature of these very [specifics] as being of the form of the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*):
The subtle element of sound, when agitated, assumes various forms and produces diverse sounds.
Space has sound as its essence and consists of vacuity, since it is capable of supporting the superimposition of objects;
this very space, through contact with the subtle element of touch, undergoes agitation. (9.284)
Therefore, it attains the state of air (*vāyu*) here, consisting of both sound and touch.

"Agitated" means being oriented toward the production of its effects—this is the meaning. By the phrase "bearing diverse forms, that is, specific sounds," its possession of the single quality of sound is stated. Now, [one might object: is it not sound alone?
Anticipating the doubt as to how space (*nabhas*) could exist, it is said: "Sound," and so forth.

The meaning is that since sound consists of space (*avakāśātmā*), it is the corresponding cause for space because of its nature as space. Furthermore, the reason for its being of the nature of space is stated as: "capable of sustaining the superimposition of the denotable object" (*vācyādhyāsasahaḥ*). By this...

Just as sound provides space for that which is to be expressed because it tolerates the superimposition [of objects] upon itself, so too does its effect, ether (*ākāśa*), provide space for everything. "That" refers to the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). "By that" means by way of being the cause of the subtle elements of sound and touch. Thus, there is the nature of both sound and touch.
The meaning is: the state of possessing both sound and touch as its qualities. || 284 ||
But surely it has been stated by others that sound is a quality of space alone—as they say:
"In that regard, the qualities of space are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Given this, how can it be asserted here that sound is also a quality of air? Anticipating this objection, he says:
But others say that sound is the unique quality of space; that too is logical.
For wind does not obtain its own form without space;
for each preceding element persists within each succeeding element. (9.286)
Therefore, the inseparability of wind and space from one another is traditionally taught.

By the word "that" (tad), the quality of sound belongs to space; for wind does not obtain its own form at all without space—it has a nature that is co-existent with it—this is the meaning. As it says in the subsequent [verse]:

In the element of air and the others, there is the persistence of each preceding one, such as space; thus, it is traditionally taught that space and air are inseparable from one another. As it has been said:
"For this very reason, air is indeed touch, and likewise for each subsequent [element]."

"...they say that each preceding element is the cause... Thus, this quality belongs primarily to space (ākāśa) alone as it is co-present with that [sound]; however, for air (vāyu), it is only figuratively attributed due to its association with that [space]. || 286 ||
But sound and touch, together with form, have reached a state of agitation.
They say that the fire-principle (tejas-tattva) is likewise characterized by three qualities as before;
through those three [qualities] joined with taste, water arises, and with smell added, earth—such is the sequence.

It is characterized by three properties (*dharma*). "As before" means that because each preceding element persists in each subsequent one—just as sound is attributed as a quality (*guṇa*) to air, so too are sound and touch attributed to fire—the form (*rūpa*), however, is primary [in fire]. "Together with smell" means...

That is to say, by those four. As it has been said: "From the agitated *śabda-tanmātra*, which provides the space for its superimposition (*adhyāsa*), ether (*ākāśa*) is born, characterized by that one quality alone."
But from the two qualities, sound and touch, being agitated, the wind arises;
therefore, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, only these two qualities are seen in it.
From the agitation of the qualities of sound, touch, and light, fire is produced.
Therefore, those who know the three Vedas praise its state of possessing the three qualities (triguṇatva);
for from water, which is agitated by sound, touch, form, and taste, [earth] is produced.
O lady of excellent complexion, from those four powers and the five elements—
sound and the rest— when they were agitated, the earth came into being.
"Therefore, the ground of all virtues is always clearly manifested. || 288 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only the collection of qualities such as smell is perceived through direct perception, and not earth or the like existing as something distinct from them?
Or, if they do exist so, some relationship between quality and the possessor of the quality must be admitted?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
In this regard, the collection of qualities such as earth and so forth is established through direct perception.
The phrase "collection of qualities" means that it has the nature of those [qualities], because it is non-different from the aggregate of qualities such as odor and so on.
As it has been said:
"Thus, earth and the other elements, being non-different from the aforementioned collection of odors and so forth,
are established by the direct perception of the world..."
Thus; for it is not the case that the perception of the earth and other elements would occur as something distinct from that—this is the intended meaning.
Thus it is said: "For the earth does not appear as something distinct from the stream of properties such as odor and the rest. (289)
For the cognition of earth and so forth arises only upon the perception of one or another of its qualities, such as odor, and not otherwise;

thus, earth and the rest are non-different from their qualities like odor. For that which is perceived when something else is not perceived must be distinct from it, just as earth is distinct from water and so forth. As it has been said:
A cognition never arises without the apprehension of odor and the other [sensory objects];
for indeed, a cognition of the earth arises even when water and the other elements are not apprehended.
"Therefore, earth is not other than its qualities such as odor, nor is it separate from water and the other elements. || 289 ||

Now, one might object: "If the earth is nothing but smell and the other qualities, then since the earth is of a single nature, these qualities would not be perceived in succession. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as for those who maintain the duality of quality and qualified, even though this [earth] is one..."
Just as a variegated form appears on a cloth, so do phenomena appear sequentially upon the earth.

Indeed, here among the followers of Kaṇāda and others, although there is a distinction between quality and the possessor of quality, just as this single variegated form— consisting of white, green, blue, and so forth— is perceived sequentially upon the cloth (the substratum) when that substratum is being gradually unfolded, even though it is a single quality called "form" (rūpa). Just so [is the case with the soul].

Since earth and the other elements are unitary, their properties such as odor and so forth, though uniform in nature, are perceived by people like us in succession; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. As it has been said:
"Earth and the other elements, though non-different from their qualities, are declared to possess a variegated nature."
"The sequence of numbers is like a variegated form on a cloth, yet it is enveloped [within].
Thus [ends verse 290].
"Is this not inconsistent, since even a variegated form is perceived simultaneously on a wide cloth and the like?"— anticipating this objection, he says:
"And just as variegation appears simultaneously on a wide cloth..."
In the very same way, the earth appears to yogis in its entirety as a totality of phenomena.

"By the totality of the *dharmas*" means by the coexistence— that is, the simultaneity— of the *dharmas* such as smell and so forth. While extensiveness is the cause for the simultaneous appearance of variegated colors on a cloth, here, however, it is the case for yogins who have mastered the earth and other elements regarding the appearance of the totality of the *dharmas*.
From the excellence of the dharma born of yoga, there is the state of having sharp faculties. || 291 ||

Thus, for yogins there is the proficiency of the faculties (*karaṇa*), whereas for non-yogins there is its absence; it is precisely due to this difference in means that odors and other qualities are perceived in the earth and so forth in a sequential order. This is not a valid objection, namely:
"Since the earth and other elements possess a single uniform nature, how can there be a sequential perception of odors and the rest?"

Thus it is said: "Therefore, the earth, possessing a variegated form ranging from smell to sound, appears through the diversity of means, according to the division of succession and non-succession. (9.292)

Now, one might object: "If no distinction whatsoever is possible between the earth and its odor, then how can there be a difference in cognition based on the relationship of qualifier and qualified—as in 'the earth possesses odor'—according to the principle: 'If [the object] appears despite a difference in means, from where could a difference in cognition arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, it is said that the distinction between cognitions is produced by the manifestation of a sequence;
likewise, the use of the genitive case and the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier arise from the distinction between cognitions. (9.293)

The word "tataḥ" means that from which there arises the appearance of succession and non-succession through the differentiation of means. The "use of the genitive case" refers to [expressions such as] "the smell of the earth. "The state of being the divided and the divider" means the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*)—this is the meaning.
(The reading *viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāvaḥ* is more appropriate.)
For example: "Gandhavatī, Dhara," and so forth. As it has been said:
"These [words] enter the domain of cognition because they become manifest through a sequence; this is the cause for the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified."
Thus [ends the section]. || 293 ||
He concludes the very subject at hand: "Therefore, there is here no such thing as a substratum (dharmin) distinct from its attributes (dharmas).
By the word "therefore" (tena), he means by the reason that the sequential apprehension [of attributes] is established otherwise.

Thus, it has been stated that earth and the other elements are not distinct from the streams of properties such as odor and so forth. Anticipating the question—“What are they? Where are they? How many are they? And what are they like?”—he says:
“In that regard, odors, forms, and tastes may be of many kinds on earth. (9.294)
In water, there is touch produced by maturation that is neither hot nor cold, and sound is variegated; whiteness, sweetness, and coldness are diverse, as are the sounds. (9.295)
In fire, there is whiteness, luminosity, heat, and various sounds;
in wind, there is sound that is not produced by cooking (apākaja), which is neither cold nor hot, and which is diverse.
Sound consists of phonemes; it is the reflection of words in space, and thus it is of many kinds. Among these, odor is of two types: fragrant and foul.
Form is of many kinds, such as white, yellow, and so forth. Taste is of six kinds, beginning with sweet; it is produced by digestion (*pākaja*).

Thus, [this is] because it arises from conjunction with other substances such as place, time, and so forth. As it has been said: "Its touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by heating (*pākaja*).
It is called "variegated" (*vicitraka*) because its nature consists of sounds such as *khaṭ-khaṭ*. [It possesses] the triad beginning with whiteness (*śauklya*).
It has form, taste, and touch as its objects. As it has been said:
"The [qualities] of form, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold.
They are called "variegated" (*citrā*) because they consist of flickering, shimmering, and other such forms. The same applies to what follows.

The diversity [of fire] should be understood through its forms such as *dhamadham* (roaring) and *caṭacaṭa* (crackling). Regarding its form, it is characterized by white brilliance. As it has been said:
"In that [fire], the form is white and brilliant, and the touch is exclusively hot."

Thus [it is said]. "Not produced by heat" (apākaja): as it has been stated—"Its touch, while being neither hot nor cold, is not produced by heat. "Consisting of phonemes" (varṇātmaka) means composed of expressive words—this is the meaning. "Reflections" (pratibimbāni).
As it has been said:
"The wise have declared that the collection of echoes arises in the ether alone.
Now, an objection may be raised: others have determined that sound possesses the quality of being a single attribute of space, which is intangible.
As they say:

"Sound is not a specific quality of a substance possessing touch, because it is perceptible, because it does not originate from the qualities of its causes, because it does not persist as long as the substance lasts, and because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum."
Thus [it has been said]. But how is it that sound is here said to be a quality even of earth and the other elements, which possess tangibility? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"As for the statement that sound is not a property of that which possesses tangibility," and so forth (9.297).
By whom could that which is contradicted by their own perception be accepted by the followers of Kaṇāda?
"Contradicted by one's own perception" means "sublated by experience"—this is the meaning. || 297 ||
He establishes this very point: "That which appears as 'there is a sound in the drum' is indeed uncontradicted. (9.298)
And for this reason, it is not perceived elsewhere than in its substratum—this is the intended meaning.
One might object: "Is this appearance not established otherwise, since the sound is in the drum because the drum is its cause?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And it is not by mere causality [that the drum is the agent], because of the cognition that it is the appropriator (ādāna) of that [sound]."

For in this case, the cognition is not merely "there is a sound when the drum exists," but rather "this sound has the location of the drum"; therefore, the sense is that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Objection:
But how can the auditory organ, being inactive and thus not reaching the location of the drum, [perceive it]?
Anticipating the objection that [the sound] might be the cause for perceiving the word as located in that [specific] place, he says:
"And in our view, the sense of hearing has the ego (ahaṃkṛt) as its cause; it is so in each respective case. (9.299)
"Partaking of function," it thus fully grasps the sound located in that place; for this reason— namely,

because its cause is the *ahaṃkṛt* (the ego-sense)— and because the *ahaṃkṛt* itself possesses activity due to its nature as *rajas*, its effect, the auditory organ (*śrotra*), is also said to possess activity here and there.

"Partaking of function" (vṛttibhāgī) means that in each respective location of the object, it possesses activity—that is, it is characterized by action. Consequently, the auditory organ would perceive even a sound located at the site of a drum by means of its own form alone, which is sufficient for that purpose. Indeed, in this regard, the followers of Kaṇāda [hold as follows]...
They spoke thus:
"By means of a succession of wave-like vibrations, [the sound] reaches the region of space delimited by the ear-cavity, which is accepted as the auditory organ (*śrotra*), and through conjunction..."
"The sound produced from the first sound, which arises from its own constituent parts, would generate a cognition of its own object. || 299 ||
To refute this very point, he restates it: "But as for one who says that the ear is space, differentiated by its connection with the ear-canal... (9.300).
A sound born of sound, having arrived, produces the cognition of sound;
this occurs even when there is a faint sound of a drum being heard. (9.301)
"How can there be a perception [of sound] at a distance, such that one thinks, 'This is the hearing occurring over there'?

Therefore, the intention is that this reason—"its apprehension elsewhere than its substratum"—is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For this Kaṇāda, who speaks thus, [the word] "dull-witted" is used because he is nearly at the very end [of the list of the foolish].

The particle *api* suggests that this [ear] is not fit for hearing. For if, having reached the region of space—which is indeed recognized as the auditory organ—at the location of the drum (*murajadeśe*), the final sound produced from sound were perceived, then there would be the cognition "the sound is here in the ear"; but it is not so.

"Due to distance, [the sound is perceived] in the region of the drum and so forth. Therefore, the position that the sound is perceived as inherent in the space of the ear is refuted by one's own experience—this is the intended meaning. || 301 ||
He states the reason for this very point:
"For a sound produced by another sound does not [arise] from a distant or near utterance. (9.302)
For that which has reached the space of the auditory organ, there is no distinction between being distant or near;

for there is no difference in its inherence in the location of the auditory space, whether the sound arose from a distance or from nearby, since the cause's remoteness or proximity does not affect it.
There is no excellence whatsoever within its own self.
One might object: "Granted that a sound produced by another sound cannot be the object of distant perception by virtue of being a function of the auditory organ;
however, could not the very first sound itself—having the nature of spreading as far as the ear—be perceived in such a way due to its location at a distance? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And it is not tenable that this first sound is so pervasive. (9-303)
How could that which is intense be heard by this [hearer] together with those situated there, while being itself weak, since it does not rely on other properties? (9.304)

Regarding the phrase "the first sound," this refers to a sound produced by a drum or similar instrument situated at a distance. For instance, how could this very first sound of a drum or the like, which is heard with intensity by listeners situated near its location, be heard with dullness by an ear situated at a distance?

It is heard [as such]; for that very same intense sound cannot be the substratum of another property called "weakness," because a single entity cannot possess contradictory properties. Consequently, its perception occurs only in its own substratum, such as the drum; thus, this reason is indeed unestablished (asiddha). || 304 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely the followers of Kaṇāda have put forward three reasons to refute the claim that sound possesses the property of being tangible; how then could this [objection] be refuted by the refutation of only one of those reasons, since the other two reasons remain entirely intact? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This has been refuted in many ways by others; therefore, to labor over it again is in vain.
For who is not clever at dealing a blow to one who is already fallen? (9.305)

"By others" refers to those such as Jyotsnākāra and his followers. For they argue as follows: although conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a quality belonging to tangible substances, it has been established by others that it is not preceded by the qualities of its causes; otherwise, conjunction in effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) would necessarily be produced solely from conjunction.
Because the conjunction of effects is necessarily preceded by the conjunction of their causes,
it would follow that the conjunction between a post and a hawk— arising from the action of one or both— would not exist once the hawk has departed;
nor does conjunction persist as long as the substance exists, for when the substance remains, disjunction arises.
Because that [property] is absent [in the probandum]. Therefore, both reasons are inconclusive due to their connection with conjunction;

on the contrary, taking conjunction itself as the example, [the reasons] are shown to be non-concomitant with the properties of "not being preceded by qualities of the cause" and "not persisting as long as the substance exists."
In the proof that [color] possesses the quality of being tangible, [the reason] is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the probandum.

Furthermore, in the case of the alternative of "cooking in a pot" (*piṭharapāka*), there is a very clear inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the color and other qualities produced by cooking in a jar; moreover, the property of "not being preceded by qualities of the cause" is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent.

Because sound is accepted as the very material cause [of its own manifestation], and because it is admitted that the effect, which possesses the quality of sound, arises [from that cause], it follows that [sound] does not persist as long as the substance [itself].
If it is asked: "Since sound exists in conch shells and other such objects for as long as those substances exist, why is it not heard?"—we reply: "Because it is unmanifest."

The idea that sound which is manifested is a transformation entirely distinct from that which is unmanifested is incorrect; therefore, the meaning is that sound is a property (dharma) belonging to both that which is touched and that which is untouched, and this must be understood precisely for that reason. || 305 ||
Having thus described the sequence of the collection of principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth,
he demonstrates the relationship of pervaded and pervader:
"Of these [principles] beginning with Earth, whatever group of principles was previously [enumerated]," and so forth.
Abiding as one possessed of superior qualities, he shines forth pervading that entire extent.
"Pure" (pūrveti) means that which precedes another. Indeed, although there are thirty-six principles (*tattva*) here, they are primarily threefold by nature—consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva.
Among these, the quality known as the attribute of consciousness consisting of light (*prakāśamaya-ciddharmatā*) exists in varying degrees of intensity.

It becomes distinguished as it manifests—meaning that whatever possesses a superior quality in relation to something else is its pervader (*vyāpaka*), just as Śiva is the pervader of *Śakti*, and both Śiva and *Śakti* are the pervaders of the individual soul (*nara*). It is with this very intention [that it is said]:
"That which is called Ātman, Vidya, and Śiva extends up to the region of Māyā."

"The three principles, as before, partake in the manifestation of consciousness," and so forth has been stated by others. And thus, although the deficiency— consisting of the very nature of the attribute of consciousness— is indeed indistinguishable within the category of principles beginning with *māyā* (which are of the nature of the individual soul), nevertheless...

It has been stated that while these [principles] possess a quality consisting of an increasing grossness according to their respective degrees of objectivity (*vedyatā*) in the order of descent (*avaroha-krama*),

there is a distinction based on the gradation in the order of ascent (*āroha-krama*). To the extent that a preceding principle possesses a certain abundance of qualities, such is the case for these principles, beginning with Earth (*dharā*).
It is pervasive, just as water is to the earth, and fire is to that [water] as well—so forth. || 306 ||

Now, is it not the case that, like fire and smoke, the cause is the pervader because it is never absent from the effect, and the effect is the pervaded because it is never absent from the cause? Or alternatively, like an actor concealed by a curtain, the subtle is the pervaded and the gross is the pervader— so what is the point of stating here that the qualities (guṇas) are superior?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "This pervaded-pervader relationship which has indeed been shown for the principles (tattvas) is established through the predominance of qualities (guṇas), not through causality nor through parsimony. (9.307)
The word "kila" indicates that this is according to tradition (āgama). || 307 ||
Demonstrating that this very [argument] constitutes a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the simplicity (*lāghava*) of the probans (*hetutva*), he establishes it as follows:

"For passion is clearly pervaded even by what is not its cause, such as knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even by what is not its cause," this refers to knowledge and passion based on such statements as: "The unmanifest [principles], passion, and knowledge arise from *kalā*."

Because [the effect] arises simultaneously with the constituent part (kalā). Now, one might object: "Is it not a contradiction for something to be both causeless and all-pervasive? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Since that without which [something else] cannot exist is said to be pervaded by it. (9.308)
There is no such thing as "lightness" here in our own system;
rather, because of the superiority of qualities, the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is clearly to be understood. (9.309)

"It would not exist" means that it would not undergo manifestation; for in the doctrine of manifestation (ābhāsavāda), there can be no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the existence of entities apart from manifestation—this is the sense.
Therefore, in this context, whatever does not manifest without the favor of another [is dependent upon it].
It has been stated that "this is pervaded by that," and "the other is its pervader. Here,

the phrase "in one's own system" means in the Trika scripture, whose true essence is the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*) alone— the intention being that with respect to supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*), nothing exists, whether gross or subtle.

Therefore, it is because it is untenable for being a logical reason (*hetutva*) and parsimony (*lāghava*) to serve as the basis for the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). || 309 ||

Now, one might object: "In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated that due to the superiority of qualities there is merely a relationship of higher and lower, not a relationship of pervader and pervaded; so why is this being said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For whoever is superior in quality compared to another is said to be 'above' that other."
Verticality and pervasiveness are clearly [taught] in the venerable Mālinīvijaya. (9.310)
In such cases as these, "uprightness" (ūrdhvatva) is not intended to mean either spatial or temporal elevation;

rather, it refers to the excellence of qualities arising from the gradation of the nature of consciousness. And that very [excellence] is what is called pervasiveness—thus it is said: "uprightness is pervasion. (310)
Thus, he says that the matter is concluded by this much:
"Therefore, from the state of Śiva onwards, having taken luminosity as its own essential nature, it remains fixed within itself."
The earth shines intensely like the sun, being fully pervaded by the entire collection of dharmas belonging to the series of all the principles (tattvas). || 311 ||

Therefore, by virtue of this relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) which is impelled by the excellence of qualities, it is certain that, starting from Śiva, all the principles (tattvas) possess within their own selves a collection of attributes beginning with "samgraha" and ending with "paryanta," derived from the excellence of the quality known as the nature of consciousness (ciddharmatā).
The meaning is that the earth shines as pervaded by all the principles (tattvas), existing as a pervasive presence in its full form. || 311 ||
He extends this very principle elsewhere as well:
"In the same way, even for water and the other elements, there exists a body reaching up to the abode of the *śakti-tattva*.
'In the same way' means it is pervaded by each preceding *tattva*—this is the intended meaning."
One might ask: "Even if there is a relationship of pervaded and pervader among these, what is their distinction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the distinction is that the subsequent [element] exists as power (*śakti*) itself, whereas the preceding one exists as its attribute (*dharma*).
(9) "The subsequent" refers to earth and so forth; "the preceding" refers to water and so forth. "As its attribute" means that which has that [power] as its attribute.

The meaning is: "by way of being the possessor of power (śaktimad-rūpatayā). Therefore, the earth-principle (dharātattva) is of the nature of power (śakti), while the water-principle (jalatattva) is of the nature of the possessor of power (śaktimat); and the water-principle together with the earth is power, while the fire-principle (tejastattva) is the possessor of power. This continues until the principle of power (śaktitattva) is power, whereas Śiva is the possessor of power.
By which [author] it was stated: "This group of thirty-five principles is said to be the very power of Lord Śiva," and so forth, as expressed by others. || 312 ||
And since this has been explained in detail elsewhere, it should be understood from that very source; thus he says:
"This has been demonstrated in detail in the *Anuttaraprakriyā*;
therefore, a discerning person who desires a comprehensive understanding should look there for the full exposition. (9.313)
"In the *Anuttaraprakriyā*," as stated in the *Śrīparātrīśikāvivaraṇa* and other works—this is the meaning.
(313) He concludes this very point with the first half of the verse:
"Thus, the complete elucidation of the nature of reality has been accomplished. (9-314)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Principles" (*tattvaprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
By the word "correctly" (*samyak*), the distinction from [the views of] Bhogakārika and others is indicated here; may there be auspiciousness.
Jayaratha, intending to refute the systems of Śaṅkaranandana, Sadyojyotis, Devabala, Kaṇabhuj, and others, has explained the ninth chapter.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Principles" (*tattvaprakāśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* composed by Śrī Jayaratha. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
He whose hand holds a sharp trident, blazing and raised in readiness to pierce through each and every one of those principles (*tattva*s).
Victorious is he who is the embodiment of supreme victory, the manifestation of the defeat of saṃsāra.

Now, with the second half [of the verse], he promises to describe the fifteen-fold division and other such classifications of these very principles: "The secret of the Trika scripture, which is the differentiation of the principles, is now being declared. (10.1)
He says that very thing:

"Of these aforementioned principles (tattvas) which follow along within their own respective groups, even another internal division has been proclaimed here in this scripture named the Śrītrika. (10.2)
"Even another division," characterized by fifteen [categories] and so forth—this is said in comparison to the previous one.
"In the scripture named the *Śrītrika*" refers to the *Śrīmālinīvijayottara*. As it is stated there:
"Now, of these very principles, beginning with Earth (*dharā*) and so forth, in their sequential order..."
"The proliferation [of phenomena] is described briefly... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.1),
and so forth,
up to "...Śiva is not directly divided" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.7).
Thus far. || 2 ||

He says that very thing: "From the differentiation between the possessor of power and the power itself, the series beginning with Earth and ending with Mūla is divided fifteenfold, together with its own nature, by means of the [five] vowels. (10.3)
The *pralayākala* is like Rudra, being devoid of both *kalā* and the pairs of divisions (*bheda-yuga*);
likewise, *māyā* is ninefold, and the *jñākalas* are sevenfold. (10.4)
The mantras, their lords, and the lords of the mantra-lords are threefold within the fivefold state;
yet Śiva does not undergo division, for he consists of the dense consciousness of his own singular self-luminosity.
The phrase "by means of the division of the possessor of power and the powers" (śaktimacchaktibhedena) means by way of the division of the possessors of power (śaktimat) and the powers (śakti)—

namely Śiva and the others whose natures will be described, as well as [the powers] such as Will (icchā) and so forth— each being sevenfold, thus in a manner consisting of fourteen aspects. "Mūlapaścimam" [means...]

The meaning is that there are twenty-four principles ending with *pradhāna*. "By its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*) means its own form (*svaṃ rūpam*), which is uncolored by the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth, and which appears as an external, insentient essence, just as the earth is characterized by the predominance of qualities such as smell; as he will state:

"In that regard, the essential nature of the earth-element is that which exists as a separate, insentient entity, uncolored by the limiting adjuncts of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth" (10.8). The meaning is: from the principle of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) up to the end of *kalā*, there is a group of six principles, beginning with the human level.
"Free from the pair of divisions" means devoid of the duality of division; that is to say, it is thirteenfold.

Although here, since "everything consists of everything," it would be logical for there to be a fifteenfold nature everywhere, nevertheless, by way of encompassing the lower and lower categories (*tattvas*), each category previously existed in its full form.
The consciousness of another should manifest in such a way that each preceding state remains established in each subsequent one without deviation;
for otherwise, as it is said: "That which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky" (Tantrāloka 8.3).
By the reasoning stated above, the very existence (*satta*) of the entire collection of principles (*tattva*), beginning with the earth (*dharā*), would not manifest.

However, each subsequent collection of principles, having dissolved into the form of each preceding one, comes to rest sequentially within consciousness itself due to its respective emergence; therefore, because they have come to rest in consciousness, [they do not appear as separate].
If it were capable of granting that enjoyment separately, then its two-fold division would suffer a deficiency;

for in this case, there would be only thirteen types, since the group of six beginning with the *pralayākala*—along with their powers—would constitute subjects (*pramātṛ*), and the *sakala* (the bound soul) along with his power would have become one's own essential nature (*svarūpībhūta*). As it has been said:
For when consciousness perceives the universe— which is essentially the All—
through the application of firm support, it beholds the great expansion of its own inherent potency.
For the sake of accomplishing a distinguished effect, that [power] arises there by force;
for the prior state remains established within the progressively lower principles.
Otherwise, their very existence would not be possible due to the loss of their prior state;
for within the prior nature, the entire web of principles is dissolved.
"Inadequacy for enjoyment—thus is deficiency therein a mark of difference.

Furthermore, the Sakala [the conditioned self], being endowed with power (śakti) and having become his own essential nature (svarūpa), would not differentiate his very own nature in such a way. For differentiation indeed consists in the synthesis of difference in another entity with reference to a counter-correlate (pratiyogin).

One would establish it thus: "this is the object of knowledge (*meyam*)," "this is the means of knowledge (*mānam*)," and "this is the knower (*mātā*). However, for the object of knowledge, its status as an object of knowledge involves no internal differentiation within itself. Likewise, because there is an absence of differentiation within the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, it is rightly said that there is a gradual reduction of the two types of duality. As it has been stated:

For differences do not divide the essential nature [of a thing], but rather they produce a synthesis of differences elsewhere; for they establish themselves in relation to another counter-correlate, and thus, by that very fact, they are absent in the object itself.
"The refutation of the two types of internal differentiation has been stated here in sequence;

because there is an absence of differentiation within the perfectly complete Śiva-tattva, it is therefore indivisible. The suffix -vat in the word *rudravat* signifies that [the number eleven] is possessed by the number eleven, which is indicated by the word *rudra*.

The *pralayākala* is, by implication, one whose nature has become [pure] essence (*svarūpībhūta*). This should be understood in the same way for the *vijñānākala* and others hereafter. For this very reason, only these five—the *vijñānākala* and so forth—possess the status of subject (*pramātṛtva*) here, whereby there is an elevenfold division. The term "māyā" is used because of their abiding therein (*tātsthyāt*).

The second [category] is the *apavedya*, called the *pralayākala*; therefore, that too is of eleven kinds—this is the meaning. It is "ninefold" because the four [categories] beginning with the *mantra* possess the status of subjects (*pramātṛ*) along with their powers (*śakti*).
It is "seventeenfold" because the triad beginning with the *mantreśvara* possesses the status of subjects along with their powers. Their lords (*tadīśāḥ*)...

"The Lords of Mantras (mantreśvaras)" [are so called] because the status of subject belongs only to the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvara) and Śiva, together with their Śaktis. "In three ways" is because the status of subject belongs only to Śiva, together with his Śakti. The reason for the absence of differentiation in Śiva is stated as: "He consists of the dense consciousness of the single light. For differentiation indeed...
It depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and it has just been stated that no other counter-correlate whatsoever can exist in dependence upon the supreme Light; so let this suffice.
And it has been said:
"The earth-principle (dharātattva) is divided according to the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself;
together with its own essential nature, it should be known as fifteenfold. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.2)
Thus, this great multitude of principles, beginning with water and ending with the root-nature (mūla-prakṛti),
should be understood as divided by these various distinct categories by those who desire its fruits.
By this very same method, that which extends from the principle of the individual (puruṣatattva) down to kalā is to be known as thirteenfold; like Rudra, it consists of the pralayākalas.
In the same way, Māyā is to be understood as ninefold; the Jñānakevalas are likewise [ninefold];
the Mantras are sevenfold, and the Mantranāyakas are fivefold.
"The Lords of the Lords of Mantras are threefold; Śiva himself is not divided [from them]. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.7).
Thus [ends the section]. 3–5.

Now, one might ask: "What are those powers (śaktis) and possessors of power (śaktimants) that were merely indicated by the phrase 'through the division of the possessor of power and power,' by means of which the earth would possess a fifteenfold nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Śiva, the Great Lords of Mantra, the Lords, and the Mantras; the unmanifest (akala), the manifest-yoked (yuk), and the manifest (kalā).
There are seven possessors of power, and likewise fourteen powers.
One's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the fifteenth; its ground (*bhū*) consists of fifteen aspects.

These are: the Lords (*īśāḥ*), the Lords of Mantras (*mantreśvarāḥ*), the Vijñānākala and Pralayākala who are devoid of *kalā*, the Sakala (the one with *kalā*), and the Powers (*śaktayaḥ*)—by implication, the seven powers beginning with Will (*icchā*) that belong to Śiva and the others. As it has been said:
"Those beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakalātman are proclaimed to be the possessors of power (śaktimant);
their powers (śaktis) should likewise be understood by the wise. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.3).
Here, "one's own nature" (svaṃ svarūpam) refers, by implication, to [the principles] beginning with earth (pṛthivī). || 6 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "In our own system, it is proclaimed everywhere that the universe consists precisely of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva;
so how is it that this has been stated here by relying on a distinction between subjects (pramātṛ) appropriate to systems such as Siddhānta?
Incorporating this doubt within itself, the author establishes the following:
For thus, three powers of the God have been described previously: || 10-7 ||
These very [powers] are established as the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
He describes this very threefold nature:
"In this context, the supreme aspect is the form of the knower; the intermediate aspect is the means of knowledge. (10.8)
"The object of cognition (meyo), the possessor of power (śaktimān), and power (śakti)—this is one's own nature (svarūpa).

Here, the word "this" (adaḥ) refers to the meaning of the entire sentence; thus, the supreme aspect (parāṃśa) consisting of the subject (mātṛrūpa) is the possessor of power, the intermediate aspect (parāparāṃśa) consisting of the means of knowledge (pramāṇarūpa) is power, and the inferior aspect (aparāṃśa) consisting of the object of cognition (meyarūpa) is one's own nature.

Furthermore, as for the sevenfold nature that was stated regarding the powers (śaktis) and those possessing power (śaktimats), that is merely a matter of secondary varieties; here, the fundamental state consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva alone remains, so there is no fault whatsoever. || 8 ||
Thus, from among these [categories] beginning with the possessor of power (śaktimat), he first defines their essential nature (svarūpa):
"In that regard, the essential nature of earth is that which exists as separate and insentient. (10.9)
"Unstained by the limiting conditions (upādhi) such as the measure of being a mother," etc.
Regarding the phrase "unstained": for if it were stained by those [conditions], it would indeed take on forms such as Śaktimat and so forth—this is the intended meaning. || 9 ||
Thus, although this [consciousness] is unitary, its fourteen internal divisions have the powers and the possessors of power as their cause; so he says:
"The state of being knowable by this [consciousness], through the subjects beginning with the Sakala and ending with Śiva... (10.10).
There are seven such divisions [of Śiva] consisting of those who possess power (śaktimant) whose powers are not yet manifest;
these range from the Sakala to Śiva, when their respective powers have become fully emergent.
There are seven divisions produced by the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*), making fourteen in total.
By the phrase "with their powers unmanifested," the predominance of the possessors of power (*śaktimant*) is indicated here;
however, by the phrase "in whom their selves are intensified," the predominance of the powers (*śakti*) is indicated. For, in reality, there is no distinction between the power and its possessor.

There is indeed no mutual separation between them; however, it is by taking their predominance as the basis that they are designated in such a way, namely, "this is the possessor of power" and "this is the power."

Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that the sevenfold group of subjects, beginning with the Sakala, is well-known everywhere; what is the harm? But their powers (śaktis) have not been recited anywhere—so who are they? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That which is the aspect of the means of knowledge (pramāṇāṃśa) belonging to the Sakala, consisting of Vidya and Kalā... (10–12).
That universal essence is reckoned as power, but not its divisions;
that very portion of the measure belonging to the *layākala* is supremely manifest. (10.13)

The measure of the *jñānākala* is that in which the veil of *vidyā* and *kalā* has dissolved, yet it is still associated with the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the destruction of the operation of impure *vidyā*. (10.14)
Desiring to awaken, Śuddhavidyā becomes the instrument of the mantras;
once awakened, Śuddhavidyā is conjoined with its residual impression (saṃskāra).
The means of knowledge for the Mantreśvaras is devoid of those latent impressions (saṃskāra);
the means of knowledge for the Mantramaheśvaras is said to be the instrument, which is Śakti.
That divine power of will, which exists solely as absolute freedom, is the instrument of Śiva; by means of it, he knows and acts. (10.17)

The term "universal self" (*sāmānyātman*) is used because it encompasses the expansion of the "particular self" (*viśeṣātman*), characterized by the organs of cognition and action, through *vidyā* and *kalā* alone; for this very reason it was said, "but not its divisions.
The underlying sense is that, were it otherwise, there would be infinite powers (*śaktayaḥ*) due to the differentiation of their respective functions.
And it was stated previously:
"Therefore, in the past, his impure *vidyā* alone was the general instrument for cognition; but for action, *kalā* is said to be the general instrument. (Tantrāloka 9.244)
Thus: "that very [state]" refers to that which consists of *vidyā* and *kalā*; "supremely manifest" indicates this much distinction:

for that [state] is like a serpent still asleep—this is the intended meaning. "Dissolving" means that the two [powers] are dissolving, i.e., tending toward destruction. "Desirous of awakening" means not yet awakened; thus...

There would be no connection for her with the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the destruction of the impure *vidyā*-kalā; for if she were fully awakened, there would be a connection for her even with the residual impression of the destruction of the impure *vidyā*-kalā, which exists in a state of being in the process of perishing. Therefore it is said: "connected with that residual impression."

Thus: "devoid of its residual impressions" (tatsaṃskāravivarjitā) means that she is devoid even of a residual impression in a state of perishing—that is, her residual impressions have been utterly destroyed. The sense is that not even a mere trace of impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) and the like can possibly exist at this point.

By the sense of "measurement" (māna), it is Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā); and since measurement itself is the instrument, it is designated as "Power" (śakti) in various places—as it has been said: "The instrument is called power.
[It is] "the existence of mere sovereignty," as was stated previously.
"This single dharma of his operates by encompassing everything; therefore, he is joined with the power of absolute sovereignty—this is the direct rule. (Tantrāloka 1.67).
For this very reason, it is called "the Lordly" (aiśvarī); "by that [power] he knows and acts"—this applies to all [the powers].

That everything, even though it perceives and acts solely through the power consisting of impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) and limited agency (kalā), and other such matters should be understood in this way. ||12-17||
Having thus, by way of digression, explained the nature of all the powers beginning with Sakala, he speaks of the subject at hand:

"The seven subjects (mātṛs) from Śiva down to Sakala are twofold, because their powers are either suppressed or predominant; the differentiation between them consists in the differentiation of the objects of cognition. (10.18)

Now, if the object of cognition were to differ according to the difference among cognizers, then among many cognizers, a single blue object would not be known as one, but rather as something distinct for each; yet this is not the case,
for even when there is a difference in place, time, state, and cognizer, there is no distinction whatsoever within the very nature of the blue object itself.
Anticipating the doubt, "Is this not perceived?", he establishes this very point by internalizing that objection:
"For indeed, so-called 'knowability' (vedyatā) is the very own-nature (nijaṃ vapuḥ) of the entity.
By this, the sūtra has provided an indication of the object of knowledge (prameya) called "the property of the thing" (vastudharma), which was mentioned in the subsequent enumeration.
Is it not the case that this proposition is unestablished? For in the cognition of blue, there is no distinction whatsoever belonging to the blue itself;
rather, it belongs to the cognizer, since he who was previously ignorant subsequently acquires knowledge. As for the statement:
"Even that which is indirect may become direct, and even that which is direct may become indirect..."

Anticipating the objection—"By such statements as 'the object is apprehended according to the distinctions of place, time, and so forth,' is it not being said that perceptibility or non-perceptibility is a property (dharma) of the object itself?"—he states the reason for this very point: [The text continues: "Even that [distinction] is intended solely with reference to the excellence of the cognizer. Thus he explains the cause right here.
For what could possibly appear here in the cognition, "I know that which is to be known by Caitra"?

In the cognition "I know blue," let it not be understood that the state of being known (*vedyatā*)—insofar as there is the manifestation of mere blue—is a property of the object; however, in the cognition "I know the blue that is known by Caitra," does it manifest as mere blue, or rather as blue qualified by being known by Caitra? Regarding the first [alternative]:

There would be no distinction between these two cognitions—"I know blue" and "I know the blue that is cognizable by Caitra"—yet such is not the case, as it contradicts experience. In the second alternative, however, is the state of being cognizable by Caitra an attribute inherent in the blue itself, or does it reside in the cognizer? It cannot, first of all, reside in the cognizer.

Since two things residing in different substrata cannot stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified due to their differing levels of status, if [knowability] were inherent to itself, then the meaning of the proposition—"knowability is the very nature of the entity"—is established. || 19 ||

But surely, even if they reside in different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), let there be the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) because of the cognition "the object is known"; for in this awareness— "I know the blue as cognizable by Caitra"—
it would mean saying "I know the object known by Caitra," and [this involves] knowledge.
It has already been largely established that the excellence belongs to the knower alone, and not to the object of knowledge; thus he says:
"But surely, here it is only Caitra’s consciousness that shines forth.
However, the property called 'knowability' does not appear as belonging to the entity, in the same way that blueness [appears] in the object. (10.20)
"Here" refers to the object, such as blue and so forth. || 20 ||

Now, one might raise the objection that knowledge is indeed an action, and that action is to be inferred from its fruit; and that fruit is the property of the object called "manifestation" (prakaṭatā), which is itself "knowability" (vedyatā)?— anticipating this view of the followers of Kumārila, the author refutes it:

And if the property of being cognizable were part of the nature of an entity by its very essence, then it would be cognizable to everyone, just like the properties of a jar, blue color, and so forth. (10.21)

The expression "the jar, blue, and so forth" (*ghaṭanīlādi*) is a designation in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant. For in this way, the state of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) is its configuration, the state of being blue (*nīlatva*) is its color;
and by the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are such properties as being an effect (*kāryatva*), being a cause (*kāraṇatva*), and so on.

In that case, the property known as "knowability" would be non-distinct for all [objects], which would entail the consequence that there are no blind people and so forth, and everyone would be omniscient. || 21 ||

If it is argued that, because it is produced by the cognition of a specific cognizer, it would be knowable only for that person and not for everyone— this is not so; for even in that case, just as a cloth produced by a weaver does not belong to him alone (since it is common to all),
so too knowability would exist through the very same lack of distinction for everyone, and not otherwise.
In that case, the restriction—that [the property] belongs only to that which produces it—is logical; thus he says:

"Even so, if an entity possesses the property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) by virtue of the power of the cognizer’s consciousness, this fault remains, just as in the case of a cloth made by a weaver. (10.22)

"The fault applies to all in that same way" means that if [the status of being] a cognizer were produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), then just as [the status of being] the cognized is so [produced], the status of being the cognizer would likewise be so;
for the cognized and the cognizer are mutually dependent. But this is not the case, just as it is with the cognizer.
