Because the object of cognition lacks consciousness, it cannot be associated with the intellect (*buddhi*); therefore, one should not suspect that, like duality and so forth, it is produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) due to its grossness, and thus it has been resolved in another manner. And even if this so-called "cognizability" (*vedyatā*) were indeed an attribute of the entity, like its blueness and so forth...

Dharma must exist; so, is it cognizable or not? If it were uncognizable, it would be nothing at all, for an object does not attain the status of being a real entity unless it has ascended into consciousness—this has been stated extensively elsewhere.
Now, if it is indeed cognizable, then it must be manifested as such, like blueness and other qualities; otherwise, it would remain entirely unknown.

It might be so; however, in that case too, there would be another state of being known, and for that too yet another, such that an evident infinite regress (anavasthā) would arise, destroying the very root [of cognition], whereby the knowability of any object whatsoever would not be possible, and the entire universe would end up as if in a swoon. Thus he says:
As for that property called "knowability," if it were itself unknowable, it would be like a flower in the sky;
if it were knowable, then there too would have to be another "knowability," resulting in an infinite regress. (10.23)
Consequently, nothing would be cognizable, and the entire world would be as if in a swoon.

[Objection: But surely, by virtue of various specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), cognition possesses a form that manifests this or that particular object, whereby there is a restriction for each respective action, such that one says, "This is the cognition of blue," or "This is the cognition of yellow."

In the same way, let it be stated that even for an entity, its form is conditioned by the specific adjuncts of a particular cognizer, so that the restriction of relation may be established— such that "this is perceptible to Caitra alone" and "this is perceptible to Maitra.
Thus he says:
But surely, let it be said that its form is embellished by the adjunct consisting of the cognizer. (10.24)
The nature of an entity consists in its manifestation as an object, just like this cognition;

however, this [position] is untenable because cognizers perceive it as non-unitary due to the factors of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For if this were so, there would be a differentiation [of the object] just as in the case of cognition, since the external object possesses a form conditioned by various specific limiting adjuncts.

It would follow that one object cognized by Caitra is one thing, while another object cognized by Maitra is something else. For that very same cognition of blue cannot subsequently become a cognition of yellow; nor is this acceptable to you, since you admit that every object exists as a single entity external [to consciousness]. And thus:
Is this [object] colored by its being cognizable by a single cognizer, or is it colored by its being cognizable by all cognizers?
In that regard, if it were colored by its being cognizable by a single cognizer, it would be uncognizable for any other cognizer;
even if it were colored by its being cognizable by multiple cognizers, it would not be [cognizable] for anyone individually. Thus, it would be [uncognizable] in every respect.
The entire world would surely fall into a swoon. || 24 ||
Thus it is said: "If [an object] is cognizable by one cognizer, it cannot be cognized by another cognizer. (10.25)
If [an object] were knowable by all knowers, it would not be knowable by a single knower.
Therefore, there is no such thing as "knowability" belonging to an entity; thus he says:
"Therefore, there is no property whatsoever called 'knowability' that belongs to an entity. (10.26)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how can an existent entity (bhāva) become the object of the act of cognition?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The very emergence of consciousness is itself the state of being an object of cognition for that entity."

Now, consciousness is one thing and the object another; how then, upon the arising of one, can there be a specific excellence called "knowability" belonging to the other? For when a jar arises, nothing happens to a cloth.
Furthermore, consciousness is undifferentiated among all selves; thus, its arising [would affect all equally].
Fearing that [if this were so], there would be no distinction among all [cognitions] and thus even the restriction of their respective objects would not be established, he says:
"For where cognition, whose nature is the grasping of an object, [resides] within itself... (10.27).
The object to be manifested is contained within it; toward that [object], this alone constitutes its state of being known (*vedyatā*).
Indeed, in this world, because cognition is produced by an object, it possesses the object as its domain (*viṣayatva*);

even though there is no distinction in its status as a producer (*janakatva*) from the eyes and other sense organs, the restriction of the domain is due to the inherent nature of things (*vastusvābhāvya*), by which [it is determined that] "this..."
There might be such [cognitions] as "this is the perception of blue" or "this is the perception of yellow";

and such [cognitions], by the power of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by both seen and unseen factors, would manifest that very object only with respect to that internal self (*pratyagātman*) in which they exist as inseparable (*ayutasiddha*). This indeed is...
And since it is stated that the object is what is cognized, there is no fault whatsoever. || 27 ||
He provides the following rebuttal:
"To this we say: if knowability were not a property of things," (10.28)

They would remain indeed unknowable, even when knowledge—characterized by the apprehension of an object and inherent in the self—is described as existing; this is the meaning. For even so, nothing at all happens to the object, since there is neither identity of form nor identity of locus between knowledge and the object.

Because these two differ in their essential nature by virtue of being the grasped and the grasper, and because cognition—though consisting in the apprehension of an object—is nonetheless inherent in the knower; and it is precisely with this intention that it is said:
"For the supreme state is manifestation."

Thus and so forth has been stated by others. Furthermore, when there is an excellence (*atiśaya*) in one thing, nothing whatsoever would occur in another; if it is argued that "knowledge is the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of the object because it is produced from the object"—this is not so, for that which is produced from something does not become its manifestation, just as smoke [is produced] from fire, yet it is merely located within it.

The logical mark (liṅga) would [be valid] if an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) were ascertained; however, such ascertainment does not exist here, because even in the absence of an object, cognition—whose nature is the manifestation of that [object]—arises through error and the like.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "Objects would indeed be unperceivable. || 28 ||
He confirms this very point by means of an illustration:
"For just as, even though the jar's form—such as its broad base and so forth—exists... (10.29).
A cloth that does not have that as its nature does not attain the form of having a broad base and so forth;
likewise, even when cognition exists, it does not possess the nature of being inherent in the cognizer. (10.30)
How could entities that possess the nature of being unperceivable attain the state of being perceivable?
Just as a cloth— which lacks the broad-base-and-bellied shape of a jar— cannot assume the form of a jar because it consists of warp and woof threads, so too [the unmanifest cannot become manifest].

The meaning of the sentence is this: even though cognition—inhering in the knower—consists in the manifestation of an object, entities that are themselves of a non-luminous nature would not be manifest at all. || 30 ||

Thus, not only would the object itself fail to manifest according to your view, but even the great further fault that nothing at all manifests would ensue—so he says: "Behold this very great disadvantage, that the object itself [is not perceived]. (10.31)
The nature of that consciousness is luminosity, yet its substrate is not luminous;
likewise, the mind, the lamp, the eyes, and so forth, are also non-luminous. (10.32)
What indeed is this so-called "luminosity" when the entire world is asleep?

Here, there is no dispute that the external object, which is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), is by nature non-luminous; likewise, the cognition (*jñāna*) which is the effect with respect to that object is also by nature non-luminous.

Because at the time when the object is manifested, its cognition is not manifested; for at the time of grasping the object, there is no grasping of that cognition, since the cognition and the object do not appear simultaneously. As they say: "Indeed, two forms do not appear simultaneously."

"And this object consists of knowledge," because there is no apprehension of any distinction [between them]. And its substratum is the self (*ātman*), which is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); furthermore, the circle of internal organs such as the mind and the eyes, which—like the objects—are intended as instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) acting as auxiliaries.

It is indeed of a non-luminous nature because it is eternally beyond perception; and although, according to your own view, the lamp—being a causal instrument—is the illuminator of itself just as it is of another, it would not function in that way if it were itself unknown.
Furthermore, since it was precisely the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) that was undertaken for examination, this [lamp] too is meaningful [as an example].

This is what is meant by the term "vārtā" (the common usage). Therefore, if this entire causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were itself of an unmanifest nature when it brings about the manifestation of an object, nothing at all would be manifested; consequently, all this [world] would be blind.
Furthermore, because the self and the mind are imperceptible (*pārokṣya*), their conjunction as well— [...is likewise imperceptible.]
Since it has already been explained that the non-inherent cause is nothing other than non-light, it is not mentioned separately here.

Now, it might be objected: since the very nature of cognition, like that of a lamp, is the illumination of an object, why this objection—"even though cognition consists of the illumination of an object, the object is not illuminated"? For the intrinsic nature of entities is not subject to questioning. To this he says:
Indeed, the nature of cognition, like that of a lamp, is the illumination of objects. (10.33)
Just as in the statement "Caitra lives here," there is a specific excellence (atiśaya) called "living" belonging to Caitra alone and not to another,
so too, with the intention that in the phrase "the object is manifested," there is some excellence belonging to the object itself and not to the cognition, this very point is presented with derision:
He provides the resolution by means of a sequence of formulating various positions regarding existence and non-existence:
"In this matter, something unprecedented has been understood; therefore, let us dance! Let that which constitutes the nature of knowledge—the manifestation of objects—be defined. (10.34)
If the object is the manifestation, then the object, or rather the cognition itself, is that manifestation; or else, that which is the manifestation of the object is called its "form" (rūpa). (10.35)

Regarding this which is called "the illumination of an object as the nature of cognition," let it be examined what the meaning of "object" is here: is there a grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇya) such that "what is the object and what is this illumination?",
or is it a conjunction (samuccaya) such that "the object and the illumination", or rather, "the illumination of the object"?
It is merely a relationship. || 35 ||
In this regard, although the first two positions were merely suspected as possibilities,
since they are not intended by the opponent, he does not refute them; rather, he analyzes [the argument] specifically to refute the third position:

If the genitive is used in the sense of the agent, the aforementioned fault is indeed difficult to remove; if, however, this genitive is in the sense of the object, then the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇic) remains implicit in the mind. (10.36)

If indeed the object possesses agency in the act of manifesting itself, then how can there be such a pre-eminence belonging to cognition? For it has been stated many times that when one thing possesses pre-eminence, it does not affect another.
Thus: "Just as, although the jar exists in the form of its broad base and so forth... (10.29).
By these and other such arguments, the insurmountable fault would follow that the [cognition] assumes the form of another.

Now, if the object is the patient (*karman*) in the act of illumination, then, since a verb that is intransitive in its simple form (*aṇi*) becomes transitive when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added,
the expression "knowledge illuminates the object" is established.

The relationship between the instigator and the instigated is characterized by the performance of actions capable of [accomplishing] that [result], and is distinct from such acts as commanding or entreating. || 36 ||

And thus, because the operation of the instigator (prayojaka) is grounded in the operation of the one being instigated (prayojya), it follows that an object shines forth only by means of knowledge while it is itself shining forth; however, this is not tenable, since an object that is shining forth by itself does not depend upon the operation of an instigator.

Because the application of knowledge would otherwise be rendered useless. Now, if it is argued that even while an object is not yet manifesting, it is said to be "active" and "the object of operation" by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*) to manifest— distinguished from things like a sky-flower— that too is entirely untenable.

For that which does not manifest by itself—such as a non-white palace—is incapable of manifesting even when assisted by another, just like an insentient object. Furthermore, when its capacity (*yogyatā*) is examined in terms of whether it consists of manifestation or non-manifestation, it does not transcend incapacity and futility; thus, the manifestation of the object [is established].
The notion that "this is the form of knowledge" is incorrect.
Thus he says: "And so we demonstrate this: does the light shine?
It is not even non-light; yet, even so, it is nothing at all. (10.37)

In this regard, what does light illuminate? It does not illuminate, because it would be purposeless—this is the meaning. Nor does even that non-light illuminate, because it lacks the capacity; such is the connection.
This being the case, neither is there an external object to be illuminated, nor is there a cognition that illuminates.
It was said that "something might exist," yet it was also stated: "even so, there is nothing at all. || 37 ||

"Now, if this is so, how is the well-known relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*)—as in worldly expressions such as 'Devadatta leads Caitra to the village'—possible? To this he says: "In that case, how is it that in the world the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) does not apply when the instigated, whether moving or not moving, [is affected] by the activity of the instigator?"
The sense is that something might exist.
On this very point, he replies:
"It is said that when consciousness is present, it is the primary object of the sense of causality (ṇyartha); however, in the case of insentient things, it is merely figurative. (10.38)

In this context, the ultimate meaning of the *ṇi*-suffix consists of the intention of both the impelled (*prerya*) and the impeller (*preraka*). Therein, although the activity of the impelled has already commenced by its own autonomy, [the *ṇi*-suffix] characterizes it as being marked by a reflection on dependence;
and in the case of the impeller, even though the impelled is autonomous, [the *ṇi*-suffix] refers to the impeller’s own self once it has fully apprehended that dependence of the impelled.
The intention (*abhiprāya*) is characterized by the reflection upon the state of being dependent;

through this, the primary relationship—consisting of the status of the instigator and the instigated and taking the form of a confluence of both intentions—manifests. However, in cases where [the intention belongs] to the instigated, the instigator, or both...
Because it is insentient, an intention animated by reflection is not possible; therefore, such [intention] does not exist there at all.

Nevertheless, one should employ figurative usage (lakṣaṇā) in various instances accordingly, as in: "the arrow causes [him] to go," "the cow-dung fire causes [him] to study," or "the wind causes the mountain to fall. || 38 ||
Regarding this, it is said:
"For instance, although Caitra is capable of going, because his movement depends on another, he speaks thus while thinking: 'O Master, I have been sent. (10.39)

The master also, perceiving his [the disciple's] capacity for travel and clearly seeing his state of dependence, speaks the words "I shall send you," apprehensive that he might otherwise turn back. (10.40)
Thus, the fundamental connection with the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇyartha) exists only between the instigator and the one being instigated;
on account of that intention, others in the world may also employ it in such a manner. (10.41)
In the expression "he causes the arrow to go," however, one who considers himself the impeller comes to be so designated figuratively by performing the activity known as momentum (vega). || 10.42 ||
In the case of the statement "the wind causes the mountain to fall," both of them are insentient;
they are merely conceptualized by observers as having the forms of an impeller and an impelled object. (10.43)
Regarding "of the impelled and the impeller," this refers to such cases as "he causes the arrow to go" and "the wind causes the mountain to fall.

Regarding the phrase "anticipating [the possibility of] non-occurrence," the meaning is that even though the agent has the capacity to go, he might at some time not go due to indifference or other factors.
Therefore, even when the one being prompted is actually going...

The meaning is that [the action] must necessarily exist through the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*). "In this way" means by the convergence of the intentions of both the one being prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*). "By his intention" means having reflected upon the nature of the primary object. "Others too in the world" refers to...

"Another," meaning one who is neutral, distinct from both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*). "In that manner" means by way of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated;

"performing the impression (*saṃskriyā*) called velocity" refers to the archer who possesses desire, effort, and so forth, during the drawing and releasing [of the bow]. Of the one whose bow has been drawn...

For indeed, his action in the finger, produced by the conjunction of the finger [with the bowstring] and depending on the immediately preceding effort characterized by the desire to release the arrow, results in the disjunction between the string and the finger; from that, upon the destruction of the [original] conjunction,
[the arrow's motion arises] from the conjunction of the bow and the string, depending on the impression (saṃskāra) characterized as elasticity residing in the bow.

An action arises in the bow; depending on its own cause, it acquires a momentum (saṃskāra) called velocity (vega). Depending upon that [momentum], the contact between the arrow and the bow becomes a push (nodana);
from that, an action consisting of motion first arises in the arrow, and depending upon that push, there is precisely what is called velocity in the arrow.

He initiates a formation (*saṃskāra*) because, until the arrow falls, there is the initiation of successive actions. He considers himself the impeller; this very thing is the basis for the metaphorical designation here, for it is precisely because he considers himself the impeller that he is called "the impeller" by people through figurative usage. For in reality, between the impelled and the impeller—
That form is mutually dependent. Where,
due to the insentience (*jaḍatva*) of the impelled, there is no state of being impelled consisting in the recognition of dependence,
how can there be a primary state of being an impeller for the impeller who possesses such recognition, in relation to that [insentient object]?
It might be argued that, because he considers himself an instigator, one would figuratively employ the term "instigator" for him in worldly usage;

thus it was said: "it arises by way of metaphor. This is as in expressions such as "the cow-dung fire teaches," where, although the instigator is insentient and thus primary instigation is impossible, [the term is used figuratively].
Due to the figurative usage based on the notion of being impelled, the learner is conventionally treated as "impelled.
"Parikalpitau" means they are metaphorically designated. And in that context, the seed is the action originating from air which produces the disjunction of parts. 43.
He concludes this very point:
"In this way, when there is a connection with an insentient object, the primary sense of the causative suffix (ṇyartha) is not applicable.
Let this matter rest; I have already explained it at length elsewhere. (10.44)

Regarding the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*), it must be between either a non-inert entity and another inert entity, or [between two non-inert entities]. Even so, concerning the meaning of the causative suffix *ṇiC*—which is characterized by the performance of what is capable [of that action]—is it a case of having an object for an action already set in motion, or rather an object for an action not yet set in motion? Much more [remains to be considered].
He says, "it need not be elaborated here," with the words beginning "let it be" (*āstām*). "Elsewhere" refers to the *Rakīrṇaka-vivaraṇa* and other such works. (44)
He applies this very point to the subject at hand: "This manifestation [occurs] with respect to the object; therefore, it must be a metaphorical designation.
Regarding the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*): it refers to the connection between the insentient and the sentient, or between one insentient thing and another, as just mentioned.

Because the primary sense [of the causal relation] is absent in this case, it is a "metaphorical usage" (*upacāra*). Just as in the case of "the mountain throws down the wind" due to its sluggishness, the relationship between the instigator and the instigated is not primary,
so too is it here with respect to knowledge and the object in the statement "knowledge illuminates the object."

"Even in the case of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator. For according to the Naiyāyikas, even cognition is itself insentient because it is an object of knowledge, just like an external object; it is only through its connection with that [cognition] that the self becomes sentient.
As they say:
"...because of its union with consciousness, it is conscious...

This will become manifest very soon; therefore, no effort has been made here [to elaborate]. And if this is accepted, then just as the falling of the mountain—the object to be employed—is established as real in its own operation, so too is it here.
It must be admitted that the object to be employed is manifested. Thus it is said: "If it exists, then it must shine forth; for that [object] is just like a falling mountain. (10.45)

This was stated figuratively by way of concession; however, in reality, even that [figurative usage] is not possible here due to the absence of a cause, for a figurative application without a cause is not logical—thus he says:
"In a figurative application, there must indeed be some cause."
"By someone" means by whatever [agent] is intended in a particular case. He demonstrates this very point:
"In the expression 'the wind causes it to fall,' the cause is the action performed by that [wind]. (10.46)
In the case of a mountain, it undergoes a fall due to the destruction of its conjunction;
however, in this case, the cognition of the object does not effect anything at all.
How indeed could that [action] be a figurative designation (*upacāra*) if it were itself non-existent?

For its meaning is: "produced by the conjunction of the wind with the self, which is a substance possessing velocity. "Action" (*kriyā*) means, in other words, motion (*karman*) that produces the disjunction of parts. For action arises from conjunction.

Therefore, there is a division of parts, from which follows the destruction of conjunction, and from that, falling; thus, because falling here has a cause, it possesses reality. But in this case, regarding the position that [the universal] is a distinct entity, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

By the reasoning stated above, nothing at all is produced by cognition with respect to the object; thus, due to the absence of a causal basis (*nimitta*), how could figurative designation (*upacāra*) not cease? Furthermore, even when that cognition arises, how could the object be manifested? Or else, let there be figurative designation even without a causal basis.

"What will be achieved by this?"—to this he says: "For even that [object] would be non-existent. Indeed, in a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), an actual identity between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) is not logically possible;
for if it were, then even an unmanifested object might attain such a state through the metaphorical attribution of manifestation.
For a boy does not become fire simply through the application of the term "fire," such that he would also perform its purposeful activity characterized by burning and so forth.
Thus it is said: "The object, though not yet manifested, is [said to be] manifested through metaphorical attribution. (10.48)
For does such a child indeed burn by means of contact with fire?
"Unmanifested" (aprakāśita) means that its property known as luminosity has not yet arisen;
the sense is that "such" refers to one whose primordial form is undiminished and who remains unmanifested. Now, [one might ask], what is this "contact"?

If that [the boy] were non-existent in every respect, how could such conventional usage as "the boy is fire" and so forth be established everywhere without contradiction? Or is it rather the case that there is a connection with qualities similar to those associated with the [actual] fire, such as sharpness and the like, which are metaphorically attributed to him?

If it is argued that there exists a real basis (*nimitta*) by virtue of which such metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) might manifest, this is not so; for even in this case, what could the real basis be by which we might metaphorically attribute luminosity to the object? Therefore, the metaphorical usage here is merely non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*). Thus he says:
Furthermore, the seed of fire—such as sharpness and so forth—that exists in a spark is real. (10.49)
But what is the basis for the metaphorical attribution of luminosity (*prakāśatva*) where there is truth?
[The answer is: because the sharpness and so forth present in the child are real, being similar to the sharpness and so forth residing in fire.
What is the basis?—the meaning is: none at all. Now, what is the use of this?

Indeed, through the investigation of signs such as existence and non-existence, it is precisely because he knows the distinct nature of the object and the subject that a conscious person, intent upon his purpose,
employs such conventional expressions as "the boy is fire," and so forth. In the same way...

Anticipating the objection—“Could one employ the linguistic convention ‘this object is manifest’ with respect to an object that is actually unmanifest, for the sake of a purpose known as its fitness for various worldly transactions?”—he says: “For when consciousness is established, such metaphorical usage is indeed appropriate; for that [consciousness] is clearly [self-evident]. (10.50)
That [recognition] too consists of superimposition and has its life-force in synthesis;
moreover, as yet there exists no consciousness whatsoever, nor even this cognition.
That which is unmanifest [is not perceived] by another; even if it were to be manifested by that other, this same rule would apply.
To say "that too" is a superimposition (*adhyāropa*). Furthermore, according to your view, there is no synthesizing subject (*pratisandhātā*);
for he must be either a conscious being (*cetana*), namely the self (*ātman*), or consciousness itself, namely cognition (*jñāna*). Yet, at present, the self has not yet become conscious.
This is established, because it is accepted that even that which is inherently insentient (*acetana*) possesses sentience when in conjunction with cognition (*jñāna-yoga*).

And since this conjunction with cognition is possible—just as it occurs for the self (*ātman*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), so too for objects, sense-faculties, and the like through being produced [in them], and for pleasure and the like through inherence in a single substrate (*ekārtha-samavāya*)—it would follow that objects and the rest are sentient. Nor is there [an objection] here...

We perceive a restrictive cause (*niyamanimitta*) by which consciousness arises from inherence (*samavāya*) [in a specific substrate] and not from mere inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), and so forth.

As for the claim that "even though the relationship is without distinction, this particularity is produced solely by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity," that is merely sketching a way of fleeing from the problem. Thus he says: "And even now, there exists nothing whatsoever..."

Nor is there the conventional usage that "the conscious one" refers to knowledge itself in its nature as consciousness, because since that [consciousness] is of the nature of an attribute (*dharma*), it is inappropriate to designate it as the substratum (*dharmī*). Furthermore, this would be tenable only if that knowledge were self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*) by nature; but it is not so—thus he says:

"Even this cognition is non-manifest. Regarding "non-manifest," it is because at the time of the manifestation of the object, the non-manifestation of that [cognition] is admitted. Now, even though it is not manifesting, for us—unlike the followers of Śabara—it is not imperceptible (*parokṣa*) or eternally inferable; rather, [it is directly perceived].

Since it is indeed known by another cognition produced from the contact between the self and the mind immediately after the apprehension of the object, how could it be of a non-luminous nature, such that it would not deserve the designation "conscious"? To this he says:
"If its manifestation were by something other than itself, this same rule [would apply]. This...

The term *vidhi* means the manner (*prakāra*) by which an object is manifested—this is the meaning. For, if an object were to be manifested by another cognition, a relationship of the prompted and the prompter (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*) would necessarily follow; yet that [relationship] cannot be established in any way, whether primary or secondary. Thus, the very manifestation of the object remains unproven.

Thus, even if one cognition were cognizable by another cognition, since there would be no primary connection with the object, illumination itself could not be established. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*)— having a nature that is not self-illuminating—
to be the synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*), in the absence of such synthesis.
Since the superimposition of life upon that [body] is untenable, how could figurative usage (upacāra) be established here? Enough of this prolixity.
But surely, even if it is illuminated by another, just as a lamp is the illuminator of an object, so too should cognition be;
why then has it been said that because it is knowable by another cognition, cognition—being of a non-luminous nature—cannot illuminate the object? To this, he says:
But surely, a lamp is the illuminator of form; how can it be so? (10.52)
"But will not the entire collection of refutations previously stated apply here as well?
To this he says: "In this case too, do these conceptualizations of reasoning not apply?
These 'conceptualizations of reasoning'" refers to those just mentioned, which are based on both primary and secondary meanings.
The meaning is: the various modes of rebirth.
In this regard, not only is [the opponent's position] refuted by logic, but there is also an inconsistency—as he says:
"Just as a lamp would illuminate a form by its own nature... (10.53).
Such [an object] shines by itself, but knowledge does not shine in that way.
"Does not shine in that way" means because it is not self-luminous by nature. For this very reason, the word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction;
thus, at the time of illuminating an object, the lamp shines by itself as well, but knowledge does not.

And for this reason, according to the principle that "that which is unestablished cannot establish what is to be established," how could cognition, which does not manifest itself, manifest another?— this is the intended meaning.
He further confirms this very disparity by means of another illustration:
"And this lamp sufficiently bestows the state of being manifest upon all things. (10.54)
Otherwise, they would not manifest if there were no distinction; such is the rule:
"it bestows luminosity"—the meaning is that it imparts brilliance by means of the diffusion of its own light—whereby even a blue cloth [is so perceived].

"The confusion regarding the red cloth"—this is the common saying of the disputants. Likewise, it has been stated that without the imparting of luminosity, there would be no manifestation of objects at all—"otherwise, they would not shine forth. For this very reason, when a lamp is nearly extinguished, nothing whatsoever [is perceived].
It was stated, "it should illuminate"—the word *alam* meaning "sufficient" or "capable" by means of illumination.
Furthermore, it has been stated many times that knowledge does not bestow any excellence whatsoever upon the object.
And even if knowledge were to do something for the object—like a lamp providing illumination—[it would still be insufficient].
If one were to maintain that [knowledge] bestows [the state of being known], then its non-difference from that [object] must be asserted;

for a lamp, through its intermediate operation consisting in the pervasion of its own light, bestows the state of being illuminated upon an object, whereas no such intermediate operation is possible here for knowledge. And yet—

It has been stated that the claim "it illuminates an object" cannot in any way be established without non-difference—namely, "if there is non-difference, such a rule [applies]. "Such a rule" means the manner of the capacity to bestow the state of being illumination upon an object, according to the analogy of a lamp; this is the meaning. And therefore, illumination...
Thus it is established that [consciousness] manifests itself in the form of various objects, which consist essentially in the expansion of its own power.
Thus it is said: "Therefore, this aforementioned Light alone is the Supreme Śiva. (10.55)
"In whatever way it manifests, in that very way its nature as an entity becomes clear.
The phrase "as previously stated" refers to the beginning of the first chapter (*āhnika*). As it has been said:
"And the supreme reality of the object of knowledge is Śiva, whose essence is light" (*Tantrāloka* 1.52).
[The manifestation occurs] in infinite ways such as these. "In whatever way" means by whichever nature, such as blue and so forth—this is the meaning.

And since, according to the reasoning previously stated, there is indeed non-difference between light and the object, then just like the blueness of the blue, its state of being manifest is also a property inherent in its own essential nature; thus, what was said is logical.
The state of being an object of knowledge is the innate nature of an entity.
Therefore, he says:
"And thus, that which is called 'blueness' manifests in some way. (10.56)

In the same way, the state of being an object of cognition (vedyatva) shines forth, and that follows upon the objective aspect (bhāvāṃśa). Now, this unique particular (svalakṣaṇa), which consists of the manifestation of the object, is indeed indivisible; in that case, does the property called "being an object of cognition" fall upon the objective aspect or rather upon the aspect of manifestation?

Anticipating this objection, it was said: "And that follows upon the aspect of existence. For this very reason, the inclusion of both types of authoritative force (pramāṇabala) taught in the Śābara-bhāṣya by this [text] does not foster the charge of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta); thus he says:
Therefore, there are two [views]: that the fruit is the manifestation of the object, or that it is consciousness. || 10.57 ||

The followers of Kumārila maintain that [the connection] is protected from the contrary side (*vipakṣa*) and is also a mutual conjunction (*sandhāna*), characterized by the manifestation of the object. The Prābhākaras maintain that it resides in consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). "From that" refers to the reason just mentioned, namely, the non-difference (*abheda*) between the object and its manifestation. From the contrary side...

Thus, if manifestness were a property of the object (*arthadharma*), the object would be manifest to everyone, and consequently, all would be omniscient. Furthermore, if it were a property of the cognizer (*pramātṛdharma*), the object would be nothing at all [to that cognizer] and would thus remain entirely imperceptible;
for these and other such reasons, [manifestness] is protected [from being a property of either]. For indeed...

Now, it is appropriate to state that the manifestation of an object occurs without any distinction whatsoever, because the subject is one and all objects are non-existent [independently]; and even though in the realm of Māyā there are distinct subjects, nevertheless,
an object being manifested exists as residing within the subject, according to the specific difference of each respective subject.

Just like pleasure and so forth, each [cognition] is indeed determined individually; and consciousness, although it is a property of the subject (*pramātṛ*), does not abandon its connection with the object, because the object has the subject as its essence.
Thus, there is no room at all for the mediation of objects in the case of one who is omniscient regarding everything. And for that very reason, of those two...

The meaning is that there is no difference whatsoever between mutual conjunction and the position of manifest awareness; thus, by this much, it has been established that knowability, like blueness and so forth, is indeed an attribute of the object.
He demonstrates this very point by means of an illustration: "For instance, a hidden thief is clearly [perceived] as 'knowable by Caitra'. (10.58)
Having perceived this, he did not quickly take [the fruit], even though he was overcome by the desire to seize it;
for she was looking at him with respect, using the side-glance of her three-fold eye. (10.59)
A lover perceives his own body as if sprinkled with nectar;
likewise, one who is intent on seizing various objects does so quickly, without investigating their relative degrees of excellence,
once he has clearly ascertained that "this is known by Caitra," just as a thief [ascertains it].

The meaning is this: although there is a multitude of objects that ought to be most highly acquired, he does not take hold of them at all; thus, being incapable of either acquiring or abandoning them, he remains as if painted in a picture, motionless, because he is for the most part afflicted by a state of bewilderment regarding what ought to be done. And [this applies to] the lover as well.

"This beloved, unattainable even by hundreds of desires, looks at me with a side-long glance full of respect— not merely for the sake of gratification like a courtesan, nor with a gaze cast from a distance— but she does not cease looking at me for even a moment. Thus [he thought] of himself.

He perceives his body as if sprinkled with nectar and experiences within himself a supreme excellence of bliss— this is the meaning. For if that cognition of the object were an attribute of the cognizer, then how could a thief not take an object simply because it has been perceived by Caitra, or how could a lover [not take another's wife]?

It is rightly said that "one should perceive one's own body as if sprinkled with nectar upon seeing a beloved," for knowability (*vedyatā*) is a property of the object (*bhāvadharma*). Furthermore, two examples are provided to demonstrate the difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belonging to knowability as it resides in various objects.
That which causes suffering in the former case and causes happiness in the latter case.

Now, one might object: "If an object consists of consciousness (*saṃvit*), then its state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) would mean that it is nothing other than consciousness itself; and since consciousness is not a property (*dharma*) of the object, what then is this 'state of being an object of knowledge' that you call a property of the entity?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And this is not merely the awareness of cognition following upon the aspect of the object.
If that [object] performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*), what indeed could it be other than a *dharma*?

For this state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is not of the nature of knowledge; rather, it is nothing but pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), since it follows upon the aspect of the entity. Precisely for this reason:

Since it is distinct from mere consciousness of that [object], it follows by implication that it possesses the property of being an objective aspect (*bhāvāṃśadharma*); and if this were so, what would be its basis?

To this it was said: "it performs causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākara*). And that causal efficiency has just been demonstrated. It was further stated that if such a property is not admitted, then even something like blue would have to be a property.

"If it were anyone else, who could he be? By the use of the term "object" (*mātra*), the superiority of the state of being an object (*vedyatva*) over the consciousness of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃvitti*) is implied. This additional factor must be either a distinct entity (*bhāva*) or a property (*dharma*) thereof;

however, the state of being an object is not a distinct entity, for while that [consciousness] possesses the state of being an object, it is not the case that the state of being an object is itself that [consciousness].
And for this reason, it is rightly stated that "the state of being cognizable (vedyatva) is a property of the object (bhāvadharma)."
"Is it not the case that the very same fault has already been stated here—that an entity possessing the property of being an object of knowledge would become so for everyone?
This is not so," he says: "And as for what was said: 'An entity possessing the property of being an object of knowledge [would apply] even to all'... (10.61).

"Let it be so"— this [argument] of yours is like a poorly aimed weapon that destroys its own side. This delusion belongs to you alone, in that, due to a misdirected effort consisting of an incitement toward Vāsudeva who was not fighting, the Vāruṇī mace [killed] the user himself.
Just as Śrutāyudha was slain, so too would Dūṣaṇa, if employed against my side,
slay only your own side; likewise, in your view, even an object that is not surpassed by knowledge,
if it were to attain the state of being known, would then— due to the lack of distinction in its being surpassed— be knowable to everyone.
It may be so.

In our position, however, there exists only Śiva, who is independent and whose very nature is self-luminous; since there is nothing else in relation to Him, and thus no object at all exists, for whom could He shine? Thus he says:
"But for us, who maintain that there is only the state of Śiva as self-luminous... (10.62).
The very statement that "it shines for another" does not even exist [in ultimate reality].

However, in the realm of *māyā*, although there is a differentiation of subjects (*pramātṛbhed*), it has been stated previously that the object— because it consists of each respective subject— is determined individually, just like pleasure and so forth.
"This is not only logical according to the doctrine that the reality of things consists solely in a single cognizer;
it remains so even if there were an actual difference between the cognizer and the cognized. Thus he says:
"And that statement, 'This blue is for everyone,' and 'That is the jar' [remains valid]. (10.63)
That too has been grasped by those of deluded intellect as being "for the most part unknown" (*aviditaprāyam*).

Regarding the phrase "for the most part unknown," they have accepted it without even discerning whether we are here citing the color blue as an example to demonstrate that knowability (*vedyatā*) applies without distinction to everything, or whether we are indeed citing knowability itself.
This is the meaning.
He demonstrates this very point along with its reasoning:
"For the blackness perceived in the body of Kālāgnirudra... (10.64).
"Is your blue [color] perhaps yellow? Let it not be so; yet it is not non-blue.
This blue is not blue with respect to anything, nor is it blue only with respect to that which stands before it. (10.65)
That [quality] must be cognizable only for that very person, ultimately by way of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
The quality known as "blackness" which is perceived within the body of Kālāgnirudra cannot belong to Caitra;
for one substrate of attributes (*dharmī*) cannot be possessed of the attributes of another substrate.
This is well said. To demonstrate the absolute impossibility of one attribute belonging to another, it is stated:

"to the body of Kālāgnirudra. Now, one might object: "If the blueness residing in one thing does not belong to another, would that [blueness] then become yellow for that other?"—thus he raises the doubt with the words, "Is it perhaps yellow?"

He refutes [the objection] with: "Let it not be so, but let it not be blue. For that which is yellow cannot become blue simply by saying "it is not yellow"; nor is it logical to say that the redness of a jar is itself the dirtiness of a cloth. Therefore, just as blue is [perceived] by everyone—this is the illustration.

We do not know what the intended meaning is. If, however, this is stated for the purpose of illustration—that blue is indistinguishable from everything because it is an object of cognition—then this very subject of the argument has been made the illustration itself, and something contrary to your own doctrine has been asserted, as it was said: [text omitted].

[This was said] "by those of deluded intellect. Here, however, in our own view, since there is no manifestation of subject and object as separate from the perspective of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), what could manifest for whom? Thus he says:
"This blue does not exist for anyone. But even though [it appears] clearly from the perspective of another subject...

Since the object consists of the subject according to the reasoning previously stated, for whomsoever there is blue, for that very person it must be an object of cognition (*vedya*)—thus he says, "or blue," and so forth.
The particle *eva* (only/just) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). Now, one might ask: what is the cause for the restriction that "blue is indeed an object of cognition"?

"Do we not perceive something [as external] due to differences in place, time, and so forth, since even indirectness (*pārokṣya*) is possible?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "Ultimately, [it is] through the medium of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*). For that which is not known through mental construction and the like would not be "blue" for that person; indeed, there is no such thing as a cognition [of blue] apart from its being known as blue.
For it has been stated that "existence" is nothing other than manifestation itself, apart from [the individual object] named Nīla.

"In your view, although there is no difference in the 'otherness' of a property that depends on another, why is such a restriction not accepted here as it is observed elsewhere? To this he says: "And just as knowledge is asserted by you to have the nature of illuminating an object... (10.66).
Likewise, let that state of being knowable by its knower be called the future form [of cognition].
For you have stated that the nature of cognition is, in general, the essence of the manifestation of an object;
yet, although there is no difference in its manifesting all objects, it is impossible for it to do so simultaneously and in its entirety. This—

Cognition is accepted as being essentially the manifestation of a determinate object, such that one says, "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow"; likewise, in our position as well, let it be stated that the future property called "knowability" (vedyatā) is related to a specific cognizer— what is this misplaced insistence?

If that which is an object of knowledge for one knower should likewise be so for another, then if you resort to some other basis such as "causality" (*janakatva*) in that case, it is the same here as well; for in the realm of *māyā*, there is the conceit that "knowability" (*vedyatva*) is produced by the knower. Therefore, this is precisely the procedure of the Naiyāyikas.
"The basis of conventional discourse resides within the sphere of Māyā"—this is the traditional teaching of the ancient masters.
And we do not see even a trace of an opportunity for this objection; thus he says:
"Nor is there here any fixed knower of cognition, as you maintain. (10.67)
When each individual is a knower with respect to an object, let that which is known be called its "form" (*vapus*).
For just as, according to you, an object does not exist independently as something distinct from cognition,
so too here there is no such thing as a "knower" distinct from the manifestation of the object, by virtue of which [a distinction could belong] to a single cognizer.
If it were objected: "Why should an object that is manifest not be so for another subject as well?", [we reply]:

in our system, by way of the process of creating a pair of subject and object that are mutually corresponding, whoever possesses a consciousness inseparable from the manifestation of a particular object is the subject of that object; whereas one who does not possess such [consciousness] is not.
Since he would not be its cognizer at all, how could it manifest for him? Thus, it is established that [an object] is perceivable only by a specific cognizer.

"Even after hearing this which we are stating again and again, he will only become an object of ridicule if he does not grasp it"—with this in mind, [the author] says: "Let that very state of being knowable by various knowers appear to everyone indeed. (10.68)
I think that one who objects in this manner would attain the status of the foremost among the deaf;
for that state of being an object of knowledge does not appear in that way to anyone other than another. (10.69)

Regarding the phrase "the state of being the foremost among the deaf": for while a deaf person simply does not hear, this [subject] does not hear even though he is hearing; thus, he surpasses even him—this is what is meant.
For, because his nature is consciousness inseparable from the manifestation of that object, he exists in such identity with respect to some other [subject].
That state of being an object of knowledge does not manifest at all for him; the meaning is that for him, an entity would never even reach the state of being an object of knowledge.
And since it has been stated that "thus, what is called 'knowability' is the very innate body of the entity," why is such groundless anger directed toward this? To this he says:
"When it is said that [it] is the form of the entity, what is this misplaced distress?"

Now, an objection has been raised: "If the position is taken that knowability (*vedyatā*) is an attribute of an entity (*bhāvadharma*), then—just as in the case of blueness and so forth—it would follow that knowability itself must have a knowability whose nature is distinct from itself; thus, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. How, then, is this to be avoided? To this, he says:
By this path of policy, she has been eradicated from the root.
"Infinite regress... by this logical path"— that is, just as it is not logical for the state of being cognized by one subject to have a connection with another subject, so too [is it here].
The meaning is that, because the same principle applies, there is also a connection with another state of being knowable. || 70 ||
He establishes this very point:
"For in that way, it is not similar to other things such as blue and so forth;
rather, this cognizability (vedyatā) is a property (dharma), by connection with which [the object] possesses all properties. (10.71)

The substratum (dharmin) attains the state of being cognizable (vedyatva), just as it possesses existence (sattā) through inherence (samavāya). Now, in your view, what is this so-called "cognizability"? Is it merely a property (dharmamātra), or is it a distinct category of quality (guṇapadārtha) consisting of the nature of cognition? In that regard, if it were merely a property, it would certainly not exist [as a separate entity].
If it were of the nature of the attribute of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa-rūpa*), then according to the principle that "attributes are devoid of attributes" (*nirguṇā guṇāḥ*),

how could this [knowledge] possess another attribute of the same class called "knowability"? Just as knowability may be an attribute of blueness by virtue of being of a different genus (*vaijātya*), such is not the case for that [knowledge].

This "otherness of cognisability" (*vedyatāntara*) is distinct from other properties such as blueness and so forth; rather, this property of cognisability, by way of inherence (*samavāyavṛtti*), is the cause for the designation of "cognisable" in its own substratum, without which that substratum— though its body is variegated by all [other] properties— would not itself [be so designated].
Furthermore, for that which is devoid of both being an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and not being an object of knowledge, even the designation "the knowable" would be difficult to establish.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the property called 'knowability' (*vedyatā*) is itself unknowable, then it is unestablished; how, then, could it cause the subject (*dharmin*) with which it is connected to be treated [linguistically]? Anticipating this doubt, [the author proceeds to resolve it].
He provides an illustration: "like existence (sattā) and inherence (samavāya). By this, qualities (guṇas), actions (karmans), and particularities (viśeṣas) are also implied. || 72 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"For you say that existence (sattā) acts upon both the real and the unreal, as well as upon the real. (10.72)
Inherence also [distinguishes] things that are conjoined from those that are not conjoined;
and ultimate particularity, which consists in exclusion, [distinguishes] things devoid of exclusion. (10.73)

Just as whiteness is distinct from what is not white, and movement likewise [from its absence], so too the substratum (dharmin) itself exists, endowed with various attributes such as blue and the like. (10.74)
That which was previously unperceivable attains perceptibility through the property (*dharma*) consisting of the state of being perceivable.

The phrase "he performs" is to be supplied as a complement to each sentence-meaning. The word "being" (*satī*) refers to [the power] by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). The phrase "closely joined" (*saṃśliṣṭaḥ*) means that it is itself of the nature of a function (*vṛtti*). The word "final" (*antyaḥ*)...
It exists (*bhava*) in eternal substances (*nityadravya*), which are denoted by the word "end" because they do not abide at the end of origination and destruction;

that is to say, it is "situated. "Particularity" (*viśeṣa*) means a differentiator, because it distinguishes its own substratum from everything else. "Whiteness" (*śvetimā*) [is so called] because it is itself...

The meaning is that "that which is white in form makes [something] non-white. Likewise, the intended sense is that "it would make a non-goer a goer. This should be construed as: "having attained the state of being an object of knowledge (vedyatva), it remains. Indeed, this is your doctrine: namely, that there are two kinds of existence (sattā) in the form of the supreme universal—existence as essential nature (svarūpasattā) and...

And [the other type] is inherent (*samavāyinī*). Among these, the inherent [existence] occurs only in substances, qualities, and actions, whereas essential existence (*svarūpasattā*) occurs in universals, particulars, and inherence. As it has been said: "Existence is that which effects the three categories..."

Thus it is said. In this regard, just as the three categories beginning with substance (dravya) are neither existent nor non-existent by their own nature, but are existent due to their inherence in existence (sattā), so too existence itself, being existent by its very nature, is not subject to the inquiry of whether it is existent or non-existent. By this, another universal (sāmānya) is also indicated; for [the term] "cow" [is applied].

By its own nature, it is neither a cow nor a non-cow; rather, it becomes a cow through its connection with "cowness" (gotva). However, since cowness itself is inherently such by its very nature, it does not require a further connection with another universal (jāti). Just as an effect resides in its cause, or a universal resides in its particular, being itself devoid of the mode of existence [of the substratum], it exists through the relation of inherence (samavāya-vṛtti).

Furthermore, inherence (samavāya), while existing in its own substratum, does not require any other mode of existence such as inherence itself, because it is inherently of the nature of an occurrence. And just as [the category of] generality (sāmānya) serves as the cause for the cognition of continuity among entities and acts as an antidote to doubt, so too [does inherence].
In this context, "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) refer to properties such as qualities and actions, which are the causes of the cognition of exclusion; for these too,

when they serve as seeds of doubt through their connection with universals (*sāmānya*), or at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), they are the causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion that establishes the distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous substances among eternal substances.

The ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) are accepted as being established for those like me through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), whereas for yogins they are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, entities (*bhāvas*) are neither inherently excluded (*vyāvṛtta*) nor non-excluded; rather, they are excluded by way of their connection with exclusion. Thus, it is by means of the particulars themselves that they are excluded, according to this method of explanation.

Particulars (*viśeṣas*), however, because their very nature is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpatva*), cannot be conceptualized as being either excluded or non-excluded. Just as a cloth is neither white nor non-white by its own nature,
but becomes white through its connection with the quality of whiteness, whereas the quality of whiteness itself is not [white] simply because it is of the nature of whiteness.
It seeks another whiteness inherent within itself. Just as a goer is neither a goer in himself nor a non-goer, but becomes a goer through connection with the action of going;
and just as the action of going, being of the very nature of going, does not require another going within itself—so too is an entity, even though endowed with all its attributes.
It is not known by itself, nor is it unknown; however, because of its connection with knowability (*vedyatā*), it is known.
Furthermore, since knowability itself is known by its own very nature, it is not appropriate to question whether it is known or unknown; thus, we desist from further inquiry.
[Objection: But surely, just as existence (*sattā*) exists by its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), so too does knowability exist by its own essential nature alone.
If it is said that [the Self] is "to be known" (vedya), then its own nature would result in a duality of being both the object of knowledge and the knower;
and that is not tenable due to contradiction. Anticipating this objection, he establishes self-knowability as resting precisely within self-luminosity:
And knowability, while appearing, is itself like the properties of blue and so forth.
Non-luminosity attains luminosity from its own nature, which is self-luminous;

and when objectivity itself shines forth, then, although it does not shine by means of a form appropriate to insentient things like blue and so forth, it attains luminosity precisely from its own essential nature called self-luminosity.
It shines by itself; however, it does not assume the status of an object (*karmabhāva*) in relation to itself—this is the meaning.
And for this reason, the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) cannot itself become an object; thus he says: "If the universe indeed finds its rest in the Light, then... (10.76).

For this one who has accomplished all tasks and is independent in every respect, there is no other dependence whatsoever. Indeed, for an object of knowledge (*vedya*), being an insentient thing, its state of being an object consists in its dependence [on consciousness]; but once it rests within consciousness, what else could it require that would result in it becoming an "object of knowledge" even while it is already an object?
Thus it has been said: "There is no other dependence whatsoever," and "of one who has accomplished what was to be done. || 76 ||

Now, one might object: "If the nature of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) consists essentially in resting within the Light, then how can it be a property of an entity (*bhāvadharmatva*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And just as differentiation is manifested by Lord Śiva through His absolute freedom... (10.77)

In the same way as blue and other [qualities], this property of being cognizable (vedyatā) is likewise called a "property" (dharma); by the sense of the word "property," it refers to the state of being (bhāva). // 77 //
Now, let it be granted that "knowability" (*vedyatā*) is indeed an attribute of an object; what doubt could we have about that?

But how is this so—that there is likewise a lack of unity among multiple subjects? For even when there is a difference between subjects, there is no distinction whatsoever within the blue object itself by which such a thing [as a difference] could occur? Anticipating this objection, he says:
Thus, since knowability is established, let it be a property of the entity; what cause for pity is there? (10.78)

But this must be considered by all the subjects mentioned up to the end [of the scale]: since the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) would be of a single nature, how then could there be a fourteenfold division? (10.79)
To this, he provides the following response:
It is said that if this future form is described as being complete, then that very one is called the all-pervasive Lord Bhairava, the Blessed One. (10.80)

Now, if that sequence of parts and sub-parts is merely imagined through its own inherent majesty, then why endure it? What, in fact, has been accomplished by this aforementioned conceptualization? (10.81)

For such is the nature of entities, both complete and incomplete. In that state of completeness, the Supreme Light itself, being self-luminous, unfolds in such a way that what could possibly be called an "objective entity" (bhāvārtha) exist? And as for the incomplete form, it exists through the power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī) in the form of attributes, subjects, and so forth.

Since it is conceived as such by the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti) alone, this entire worldly transaction (vyavahāra), animated by duality, must simply be tolerated; what offense has been committed by this conceptualization of the sequence of fifteen [tithis] and so forth, that there should be such hatred toward it? || 81 ||
Thus, a single blue object, appearing through a sequence of various parts and sub-parts, is indeed differentiated in each respective way; so he says:
"Therefore, whenever and in whatever form an object shines forth in such-and-such a manner..."
Then, "in such a way, that very form"—this is the supreme Upaniṣad.

"By which body" means by that which is the object of knowledge for all subjects, from the *sakala* (the embodied) up to *Śiva*, whether their states are intensified (*udrikta*) or not intensified (*anudrikta*).
"That form" refers to the object of knowledge of the *sakala*, the object of knowledge of the *pralayākala*, and so forth. || 82 ||

Now, one might object: "If the state of being cognizable by various subjects such as Sakala and others has somehow been rendered differentiated solely due to the difference between those subjects, nevertheless, that [cognized object] remains of a single nature because it does not perform its causal function differently;

thus, even that which is cognized by them is of a single nature. Consequently, is the postulation of a sequence such as the 'fifteen-fold' (pāñcadaśya) and so forth not merely a conceptual construction?"

Having raised this doubt, he asserts a difference in causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) in order to establish the difference in the nature of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*): "I know what is to be known by Caitra; then [I know] by two, or even by many;
[and I know] by means of the mantra, by that Great Lord Śiva, whose power is overflowing. (10.83)
In whatever manner an entity appears through such-and-such [causes], it undergoes an incalculable variety of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth. || 10-84 ||

Just as an entity appears, so too is its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); it is not by means of something else that possesses different powers—that is, one whose powers are not augmented. Thus, by Caitra... [and so forth]. (84)
Demonstrating that very point by way of illustration, he clarifies it:
"For thus, indeed, when all the members of the audience are one-pointedly focused, they perceive the dance and song as an ocean of the essence of nectar. (10.85)
In this context, indeed, from among the discerning spectators, a single cognizer,

through the very firmness [of his conviction] regarding the words... [is led to think] "by me," [thereby perceiving] the excellence known as the state of being an object of manifold cognition (bahuvedyatā) of the dance, song, and so forth.

The meaning is that one should contemplate this as having the essence of a most wonderful marvel, which is accessible solely through one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*). For indeed, compared to a dance or similar performance perceived by a single subject, this [state]— perceived by many subjects— possesses a preeminence over all objects of cognition (*sañcetya*), by virtue of which...
To that same extent, there would be identity of the subject. || 85 ||
Regarding this, it is said:
"Therefore, it is stated that in the instruction on the observation of wrestlers and actors, there is an identity with all subjects, which brings about the experience of the full form. (10.86)
The word "tataḥ" (therefore) refers to the reason characterized by being perceivable by many subjects (*bahumātṛvedyatva*). It is said—"by all"—as it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Cognizing subjects situated in different locations [perceive] that very same object, such as a jar, simultaneously..."
"Being experienced, they attain oneness with that [consciousness] in that respect.
By "in its full form," it is meant that this alone is the full form, namely, that in which all other objects of knowledge have dissolved away.
In that very state, reflective awareness (parāmarśana) consists in having no desire for anything else. || 86 ||

"But surely, since the consciousness of each individual [subject] regarding dance and so forth remains thus established separately, what is the use of its being cognizable by multiple subjects? To this he says:
"If they were satisfied with the consciousness of only that much of an object for each individually..."
What common quality could there be among them by virtue of which there might be a unity of the cognizer? (10.87)
For in this way, there would be the perceptibility by multiple subjects for the members of the assembly; because of their merging [into one], what benefit could there be?
None at all—indeed, even the extraordinary wonder that is witnessed by one's own experience would be utterly suppressed.
This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that respect, such an experience of wonder occurs precisely because of the identity of the subjects."
Anticipating the objection, "How could this be so?", he says: "And how could there be identity with the subject?

For when multiple objects appear as knowable within a single reality, the very process of ascending toward the reflective awareness consisting of repose in one's own self serves as the seed for the subjects to attain identity by means of the dissolution of duality.
In this way, one may also become a vessel for a multitude of such joys. || 87 ||
For this very reason, he says:
"But when that object is permeated by the complex of properties consisting of its respective states of being cognizable, then it is rightly said to be other than its previous dry form. (10.88)
"From the dry [state] prior to arousal" means from that which is perceivable by each individual subject and is for the most part devoid of flavor;
"other" means entered into another form that produces unsurpassed aesthetic wonder—this is the meaning.
The reason for this is: "interwoven with the complex of properties consisting of those respective states of being objects of knowledge," which constitutes the unity of the subjects. || 88 ||

Not only in the world, with respect to all cognizers, does being an object of cognition (vedyatva) thus perform various purposeful actions (arthakriyā), but even in the scripture, with respect to other cognizers— it says: "In the scripture as well, that specific state of being an object of cognition performs a particular purposeful action."
And likewise, even more so, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara [Tantra]. (10.89)
In this way, one should remember the sixfold path as presided over by him;
for the presiding of the Lord consists in the thorough knowledge of the universe. (10.90)
"Known in this way as being perceivable by its Lord, it performs the task at hand even more effectively"—
this is the meaning, as there is no disagreement anywhere. He illustrates this very point with the words beginning "And thus," and having explained it himself, he applies it to the present context.

By the words "the substratum" (*adhiṣṭhānam*) and so forth, [the author] states that for us, unlike for those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*), there is no separate universe such that there could be a relationship of controller and controlled as described by them. Thus the Lord has said:
"The substratum of the universe is its manifestation. For He consists of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*), and of consciousness...
The object is said to be precisely that which is to be experienced, the substratum, and that which is to be presided over;

therefore, when the universe— characterized by the six paths— is known in this way through various modes of being experienced and as being experienced by Śiva, it becomes the subject matter of the ritual of initiation and other such activities.
It performs such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—this is the meaning.

In this way, by being the object of knowledge for the Mantramaheshvaras and others, there occurs the attainment of their respective specific levels of reality (*tattva*); thus, the variety of purposeful action here is incalculable. || 91 ||
Concluding this and introducing another point, he says:
"In this way, it is established that the property called 'knowability' (vedyatā) appears as belonging to the entity. (10.91)
"But when there is no association with that manifestation, it is called 'own-nature' (*svarūpa*).

Regarding the phrase "when there is no association with that manifestation," the meaning is: when there is no reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) of that attribute known as "objectivity" (*vedyatā*). Therefore, [the object] is simply "blue," devoid of any commingling with other manifestations.
When reflected upon, the manifestation, being of a universal nature, is a single one; thus it is said that this is the fifteenth essential form. || 92 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even when 'blue' is reflected upon in its own nature, it is reflected upon as consisting of all attributes internalized within it; thus, the coloring by being knowable to another subject is indeed unavoidable?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
Of one who dispels the suspicion that there might be a connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), though [the matter] remains unclear. (10.92)
The meaning is as follows: that form by which an object shines forth from one's own self is its own true form;
however, the suspicion of being joined with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is what is meant by "another appearance" (*ābhāsāntara*).
It is said to be "unclear" because, in the case of a real entity, [its nature is obscured] by the confluence of the appearances of space and time.
The sense is that clarity would arise upon the attainment of its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*). "Of one's own self" refers to the subject (*pramātṛ*);

"by which body" refers to the body in its general form; and "one's own body" refers to one's essential nature (*svarūpa*). For here, in the realm of *māyā*, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) rests within the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Functioning to exclude other superimposed properties,

it excludes other appearances even though they are not distinct from its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, it reflects upon nothing but the blue as a universal (*sāmānya*), and not even existence (*sattā*), which is inseparable from its own nature.

The intended meaning is this: how could there even be the possibility of being colored by another property called "knowability" at the stage when there is only the reflective awareness of "blue"? || 93 ||

One might object: "Surely, by means of a conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) that excludes other attributes (*dharmāntara*), the state of being cognizable by another subject (*pramātrantaravedyatā*) should be excluded; for without that [other attribute], its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) would not even exist. But how could its being cognizable by that [specific] subject (*tatpramātṛvedyatā*) be concealed?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the cognition "I know the jar," [the self] is not colored by the state of being an object of knowledge.
It is designated that "the jar alone appears in its own nature.
Now, in this case, there is indeed self-cognizability (*svayaṃvedyatā*) by virtue of being the object of the act of knowing expressed as "I know";
furthermore, cognizability by another subject (*pramātrantaravedyatā*) is necessarily present, even if [the jar] is not within the range of perception for people like us, at least ultimately.

Since it has been stated that even for worms, omniscient beings, and others, [the object] would be an object of knowledge (*vedya*), how then can it be said that "the jar appears in its own nature as not colored by the state of being an object of knowledge"? To this he says:
"But in that case, the state of being self-known is in relation to the mantras and so forth. (10.94)
Moreover, it certainly exists...

This objection arises from one who has not grasped our intended meaning; for we have not stated that a jar possesses the quality of being uncolored by cognizability (*vedyatā*) by its own nature, but rather that it appears as possessing the coloring of cognizability.
Furthermore, in the cognition "I know the jar," there is no such reflective synthesis as "I know [both] its self-cognizability and its cognizability by an omniscient being";
rather, this reflection on knowledge expressed as "I know" simply rests upon the sense of the "I" (the self). Thus he says:

"...let it be that [the object] does not exist; however, it does not appear as something existent. Nor would there be self-awareness in every case by virtue of its being inseparable from the reflective awareness of its own nature.
Thus he says:
The supreme directions beyond Mount Meru are indeed unperceivable, having the form of the fire of time.
In the cognition "this is mine," the supreme pure reality shines forth.
"Pure" means devoid of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that distinguishes between the states of being cognized by oneself or by another—this is the meaning. || 95 ||

"Is it not a contradiction that a pure object is manifest, yet its status as an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is established, while it is also said to be non-objective (*avedya*)? True; however, it is an object of cognition because it is manifest, but it is not manifest *as* an object of cognition. Thus he says:
Although it is an object of knowledge because it manifests, it is not so by way of appearing as an object of knowledge. || 10.96 ||
For manifestation is indeed unobjectifiable; thus, to what [category] do we apply it?

"That" (tad) refers to the pure reality, whose nature consists solely of its own essence. "Unobjectifiable" means not conjoined with any other appearance of objectifiability—this is the meaning. The reason for this is that it does not exist as an object of cognition (*vedyatvena*).
Regarding the phrase "because of manifestation": [one might object], "Indeed, it has been stated that 'for one whose perception is not itself perceived, the seeing of an object is not established.
