Thus, if the state of being an object of knowledge does not manifest, how can that which is to be known exist by way of its own nature?"

Anticipating the objection, "Could it be that [the light] is manifested? he says, "For manifestation... and so forth. Manifestation is indeed light (*prakāśa*), and it has been stated that this light has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its very life. Furthermore, in the cognition "I know the jar," that [light] cannot exist as an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*)—as the jar does—because there is no determination that "it is an object of knowledge"; on the contrary, [it is the subject].

The non-perception of the Kālāgni fire and other such things has already been demonstrated; therefore, why this objection: "If the object is manifest, how can there be a non-manifestation of its state of being an object"? || 96 ||
And thus, the conceptualization of the sequence beginning with the fifteenth [tattva] is indeed real—so he says:
"In this way, this earth consists of fifteen [aspects], and likewise water and the others. (10.97)
Since all these [categories] have their knowability directed toward the Sakala [subject], they terminate in the Unmanifest (avyakta).

By this, there has been an introductory indication of the rule of the principles (tattva-vidhi), which was mentioned in the subsequent enumeration immediately following the object of knowledge known as the property of things (vastu-dharma). || 97 ||
But is it not said: "Men endowed with this [series] beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth are to be known as Sakala... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.35)?

Having stated thus that the *sakala* [subject] exists up to the level of *kalā*, one might ask: "How then has his status as a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) been said to extend up to the *avyakta*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But as for what is said—that [the subjects] are endowed with [the principles] beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dharā*... (10.18)

The term "all" (*sakalā*) is an indication of the predominance of his six sheaths (*kośa*). For by this statement, it is not said that the person (*puruṣa*) exists up to the level of *kalā*; for if that were the case, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "the person is the twenty-fifth. Rather, what is meant is that these [sheaths] are predominant in him.
Regarding the phrase "the six coverings beginning with Māyā": for these are not augmented in the case of the *pralayākala*, whereas they have been destroyed in the case of the *vijñānākala*. || 98 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"Those whose coverings consist of the essence of the manifest impurity, consciousness, passion, limited agency, and so forth... (10.99).
Those known as Sakalālayas have all their coverings (kañcukas) rendered subordinate;
however, the Jñānakalas are those whose coverings have been destroyed—this is the established conclusion. (10.100)
"Rasa" [is used] six times. || 100 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the aspect of the object of cognition, such as the body and so forth, is predominant, the subject is not primarily 'sakala' (the limited one) at all;
so how can there be this state of fifteen-foldness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, even when the object of cognition is predominant, the person has [still] manifested the *kañcukas*."
The limited cognizer (sakala) indeed exists; therefore, the state of fifteen-foldness is established.

Although in the Sakala state the body and so forth—the objects of knowledge—are indeed predominant, nevertheless, due to the emergence of the sheaths (kañcukas) such as vidyā, which are the impellers of the kalās of knowledge and action, the status of being a knower (pramātṛtva) certainly exists; thus, the fifteenfold division is beyond reproach. || 101 ||

One might object: "Since the objective aspect (vedyāṃśa) is predominant, as in the case of earth and the other elements, it would be logical for the individual soul (puruṣa) also to possess fifteen aspects; so how can it be said that 'from the non-human [state] onwards, it is devoid of the pair of divisions'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the state of fifteen aspects exists even within the sakala [soul], which is situated inside earth and the other elements."
Indeed, even here in this object of knowledge, there exists an internal interval, for there is the subject.

By the phrase "situated within the earth and so forth," the predominance of the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) of this [consciousness] is further reinforced. For this very reason, it is called the "object of knowledge" (*prameya*). The underlying intention is: if [consciousness] were of a single nature consisting solely of the subject (*pramātṛ*), how could such [distinctions] be logically consistent? Regarding the phrase "within the *sakala*": when, however, the *pralayākala* is the subject here, then...
"Only on the thirteenth day"—thus all is well. 102.
One might object: "What is the use of teaching this fifteenfold division? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Because they possess contraction [of the elements] such as being enveloped by gross matter and so forth, and expansion beyond them, the fourteen [principles] beginning with Earth—due to their being both stable and mobile—are [thus established]. (10.103)

"Therefore, in the *Vijayottara*, those [states] in which insentience has become one's own nature on the path of the vital breath and the body, yet which partake of subjectivity, are called 'concentrations' (*dhāraṇā*). (10.104)

Indeed, with reference to this very point, it is stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara* that within the twenty-four principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), there are fourteen meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇās*) prescribed for each principle, together with the maintenance of an insentient nature; such is the connection. Among these, [the first] pertains to the *sakala* [state].

The three impurities (*mala*) are the gross *āṇava* and the others; the two impurities are called "covered" (*āvṛta*) based on the etymology that they are the covering of the *pralayākala*. For the *vijñānākala*, there is the primordial *āṇava* impurity.
Since the mantras have the *pralayākala* as their material cause (*upādāna*), they possess contraction due to being covered by that [impurity].

Because they are the material cause (*upādāna*) of all things, the Mantreśvaras possess a gross nature; thus, that which is designated by the term "contraction" (*saṅkoca*) refers to them. For the Mantramaheśvaras, there is expansion, due to the gradual dissolution of contraction according to their respective capacities. Śiva’s state of pervasion (*vyāptṛtā*) arises from his being devoid of limitations such as space and time.
"Pervasiveness" means that they resort to or serve it, having that as their objective support—this is the meaning. Now, one might object:

"In that case, there would be seven concentrations (dhāraṇās), not fourteen? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Because of being steady and unsteady. "Steady" means inactive through resting in one's own self.

The form of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is trembling, consisting of vibration, and active; it is the very nature of power (*śakti*). For this very reason, in this context concerning the totality of those powers, [it is said]: "In that same way, one should contemplate the body, but devoid of activity" (*Mālinīvijayottara* 12.29).
Thus it has been said:
"One should meditate on the body as being devoid of activity... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 12.26).
And those [states] arise from the gradual dissolution of duality, each according to its own nature.

It has been stated that they "reside upon the state of the subject consisting of the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth," as expressed in the phrase "on the path of the vital breath and the body. Furthermore, regarding those who possess the status of a subject, they have been described there in the context of the section on the retention of power (śaktidhāraṇā), which possesses all powers in its essential nature. As it was said there:
"In one's own body, [one should meditate on] that which resembles gold, four-cornered, and marked with a thunderbolt" (Mālinīvijaya 12.22), and so forth.
Regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other elements, however, there are meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) such as those of the *pralayākala* and *vijñānākala*. As it is said:
"In the fourth [stage], one should meditate on that which is located in the heart, extending twelve finger-breadths in length" (Mālinīvijaya 12.30).

And so forth. In the phrase "yellow and so on," the word "and so on" (ādi) includes white and other colors within the water-principle (*jalatattva*) and others. All of this is [taught] in the passage:
"Furthermore, for one who has first performed the sequence of the rite of immersion (*āveśa*) by the Guru alone..."
"He should begin the conquest of the stages through the power of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*)," as stated in *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra* 12.21, and so forth.
"These twenty-four [principles] have been declared; each is fivefold in ten ways."
"The *dhāraṇās* of the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Earth are beneficial for yogis when practiced in brief.
Since this has been explained in detail in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* itself, ending with these words, it should be understood from that very source; [it is not repeated] here.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, it has not been corroborated word-for-word. || 104 ||
Having thus defined the state of the fifteenth [day], he now defines the thirteenth and others as well:

"But when the state of being an object (*meyatā*) is attributed to the person (*pums*), who extends up to the limit of *kalā*, then the portion of the *kañcuka* (envelopes) arising from that becomes the object; he possesses no subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*). (10.105)
Therefore, the status of being a cognizer does not exist for that which is designated as "the All" (sakala),
because its thirteenth nature is devoid of the duality of power and the possessor of power.
The *layākala* is the subject whose coverings have become attenuated; situated there, he is joined [to Māyā].
Those beginning with the *vijñānākala* are likewise as previously described, having entered into *māyā*. (10.107)
Even that submergence of the coverings (kañcukas) which occurs within the principle of Māyā, whose nature is the object of knowledge, is itself an object of cognition;
for Māyā is extremely subtle, being one with those coverings. (10.108)
In this context, the Vijñānākala alone is thus the subject (mātṛ) when enveloped by the kañcukas;
likewise, even when the Akala is situated within Māyā, it possesses elevenfold nature. (10.109)

When consciousness alone remains as the object of knowledge, well-established through the destruction of the coverings, it is the mantras themselves—whose awakening is about to emerge—who possess the status of the subject. (10–110)
When even those mantras are objects of knowledge, then the knower is their Lord;
for he possesses full awakening through his emergence, yet when he himself attains the state of being an object of knowledge, [he becomes the Lord].
This Mātṛmantramaheśvara has manifested in a fully perfected form;
when he has attained the state of being known, the supreme Śiva is self-luminous.

The subject (pramātā) is that which manifests all objects of knowledge through identity with itself; this refers to the group of six principles beginning from the principle of the individual soul (puruṣa-tattva) up to the principle of limited agency (kalā). The meaning is: because these six coverings (kañcukas), having emerged, constitute the objects of knowledge (meyatva) for "this" [subject]. Thus, there is a state of thirteen.

Because both the Sakala and his power have become his very nature by virtue of being objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, an objection may be raised: "In this context, it has been stated that the Sakala is the object of knowledge and the Pralayākala is the subject (*pramātṛ*); what then is the status of the Vijñānākala and the others? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "The Vijñānākalas and so forth..."

"As before" means that even in the case of the limited subject (*sakala-pramātṛ*), their status as subjects is exactly as it was previously. Now, one might ask: "If the *māyā-tattva* is to be known, why must the submergence of the coverings (*kañcuka*) also be known? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because *māyā* is the unification with the coverings. Here too, there is a reason.

The term *susūkṣmikā* means that the causal state (*kāraṇadaśā*) is indeed one in which divisions have not yet emerged; this is the intended meaning. The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) is used because [the state] has become the very nature even of the *pralayākala*, whose coverings (*kañcuka*) have been suppressed.
The phrase "of the mantras alone" is used so as not to include the *vijñānākala* as well, by which [otherwise] there would be a ninefold division here. That is the Lord (*Īśvara*).

Thus says Mantreśvara. The phrase "identity with his own self" means that [the relationship] is not one of identity-in-difference (bhedābheda) and so forth, as is the case with the mantra and the Mantreśvara; this is the intended meaning.
Since this has been largely determined at the very beginning of the Āhnika, no further effort is made here. || 112 ||

Now, one might object: "If even He has become an object of knowledge, who then is the knower? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Śiva is the knower; for that which is not-measurable (meyo) does not have its manifestation dependent on another. (10.113)
Objectivity does not exist there, for this Lord is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

Objectivity consists in being illuminated by another (*paraprakāśatva*), and since that [objectivity] does not exist in Him because He is self-luminous, how could Śiva be an object (*meya*) like any other subject (*pramātrantara*)?—this is the meaning. || 113 ||
One might object: "Surely the manifestation of all things would be established simply by their being manifested by another;
what is the point of also accepting that they are self-manifesting? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If no self-manifesting entity whatsoever were accepted here... (10.114)
For if manifestation were to arise from non-manifestation, there would be an insurmountable infinite regress;
consequently, the entire universe would remain in a state of deep sleep, yet it does not appear so. (10.115)
If manifestation were admitted to arise from that which is itself unmanifest, the postulation of further subjects would never cease;

thus, a clearly evident infinite regress (anavasthā) would fall, destroying the very root [of cognition] such that nothing at all would manifest, and the entire universe would be as if in a swoon. Furthermore, this leads to the ultimate conclusion of the opposite of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga-viparyaya).
He demonstrates the consequence with the words "And it is not thus," and so forth. || 115 ||

Now, one might object: "If the universe indeed shines forth, then why harbor such animosity toward the first [principle] appearing in that same way? By this line of reasoning, let its self-luminosity be established; what is the use of an intermediate [process]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For that [universe] appears with a manifestation dependent on another, whereas Śiva is that other;

indeed, the universe shines forth only in dependence upon another subject (*pramātṛ*) and not by itself, so its manifestation is dependent on him. And it has been demonstrated many times previously that this other subject is none other than Śiva himself.
And that very [consciousness] is admitted to be self-luminous; for otherwise, nothing at all would be manifest.
Since this [Self] is established from the very beginning, nothing is accomplished for it by any means of proof (*pramāṇa*)—thus he says:
"If this [Self] is self-luminous, what is the use of other displays of reasoning? (10.116)

For it was stated from the beginning that the supreme life-force (*jīva*) is indeed the very essence of the means of knowledge (*māna*); on the contrary, it was established in the very first chapter (*prathamāhnika*) that the establishment of those means depends upon that [life-force]—this is the meaning. As it was said there:
This which is called manifestation shines everywhere;
since it cannot be denied, what is the use of postulating means of knowledge for it?
"Even those means of valid cognition which extend the life of objects— their supreme life-force is that very same Supreme Lord. (1.55) || 116 ||

One might object: "Since Śiva is self-luminous, does he not possess the quality of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), given that otherwise such teachings as 'this Self shines forth once and for all' would be untenable? How then can it be said that 'Śiva is not an object of knowledge'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Is it not the case that even in Śiva, who is self-luminous, there exists such an objectivity? (10.117)

The meaning is as follows: otherwise, how could there be the conventional usage of "instruction" and "instructor" as it exists—such as it is, witnessed by all the world and long established? || 117 ||
Accepting this very point, he specifies further:
"True, but he was created in that way by the Supreme Lord for the sake of being an object of knowledge. (10.118)
Having been led to the stage of the Mantramaheśvaras and others, he is made to rest therein.
This is so; however, [it is said]:
"...the self binds itself by itself."

Thus, by this figurative turn of phrase, that Śiva—having been brought to the state of being an object of knowledge because he was created as such for instruction by the Supreme Lord through His own sovereignty—is established as presiding over the ten stages beginning with the Mantramaheshvaras; this is the meaning. || 118 ||

One might object: "In that case, the very nature of Śiva would not be fully realized, and thus even the cultivation of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth performed therein would be entirely useless? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And such an object of knowledge does not belong to one whose consciousness is unconditioned. (10.119)
The state of being an object of knowledge is logically impossible for the Full (Pūrṇa) due to mutual contradiction.

Thus, because He presides over the ten levels beginning with the Mantramaheśvaras, this Śiva, though an object of knowledge, is likewise of the nature of unconditioned, full consciousness—He is indeed Śiva; such is the meaning. Not... [end of fragment].
In such a case as this, it is logical that there is knowability [only] in Śiva, because of the contradiction between insentience and sentience existing in one and the same thing.

(119) Now, if Śiva alone is indeed the nature of the object of knowledge, then why would the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Śiva not bear fruit even in the case of grass, leaves, and so forth, since there is no difference in their state of being [Śiva]?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"In the same way, even though [the object] has the nature of being an object of knowledge, in reality it does not [lose] its nature as Śiva. (10.120)
"It is true that whatever state one abandons, the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of that will bear fruit.
The meaning of "whatever" (*ko'pi*) is even grass, leaves, stones, and so forth; it is with this very intention [that it was said]:
"From grass, from a leaf, from a stone, from wood, from a wall, from dry land, or from water..."
"Arise! Go! O Lord, be my refuge; where indeed is Your abiding?"—thus and more was said by the Teachers. || 120 ||
And this has not been stated even in the scriptures merely because it is unestablished; rather, it is for this very reason of logic. Thus he says:
"In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, it is stated by him that Śiva is not directly divided. (10.121)

Now, one might object: "In this context, by saying 'Śiva is not divided,' only the negation of division is stated, but not a division [of Śiva] itself resulting from his attainment of different stages (bhūmikāntara). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the word *sākṣāt* (directly), this entire meaning has been made clear."

Thus, by refuting a lesser number, the state of fifteen-foldness and so forth has been taught. Now, in order to further consolidate that very point by refuting a greater number while addressing possible doubts as they arise, he says: "But surely Śiva must possess a single form; therefore, [the deities] would exist according to his power. (10.122)
Regarding the Great Lord of Mantras (Mantramahānātha), who possesses the three Vedas, what dispute could there be here?
Anticipating the question, "Where else has there been dispute? he says:
"Of the mantras of Maheśvara and Īśa, as well as of the two Kevalins. (10.123)
Each [individual] indeed exists with infinite divisions, just like a "sakala" (one who possesses all).
The phrase "just like a sakala" means that everything beginning from his body and so forth is distinct, whereby there is a differentiation of the continuum (*saṃtānabheda*).
Therefore, he says:
"From that, when the object is the *layākala*, there exists the *layākala* subject. (10.124)
In this way, there would be thirteen [categories], and not eleven;
even if the Vijñānākala were an object of cognition, there would be another, the Jñānākala. (10.125)
Thus, the Mother would be elevenfold, and certainly not ninefold;
likewise, when other lords of mantras (mantreśas) arise within the mantras and their respective lords.
If they are objects of cognition (*vedyatva*), there would be nine or seven; how then could they be seven or five?
This is because the *layākala*s and the others are infinite. By the term "Lord of Mantras" (*mantreśa*), one refers to the *mantreśvara*s;
by that, the possibility of other *mantra*s and other *īśvara*s is established. In that regard, as for the *sakala*:

There is no dispute that when all [subjects] are internalized, there is a state of fifteenfoldness (*pañcadaśya*) because only the seven subjects— including the *sakala* together with their powers— exist; and when the *sakala* itself dissolves into its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a state of thirteenfoldness (*trāyodaśya*) because the six subjects beginning with the *layākala*, together with their powers, exist.
However, if a *layākala* were perceivable by another *layākala*, then because the subjects (*pramātṛ*) would remain in that same state,
there would be only thirteen [categories]; likewise,
even if a *vijñānākala* were perceivable by another *vijñānākala* and so forth, according to this very same logic, for each individual subject...
How was it stated that "two divisions would predominate"?
[It is said: "...the *pralayākala* is like Rudra;
likewise, *māyā* is to be known as such; and the *jñānakevalas* are ninefold."
"Likewise, the mantras are of seven kinds, and the leaders of the mantras are of five kinds" (Māyāvajrī, 2.6). || 126 ||
Having conceded this, he provides a rebuttal:
"It is said: True, this conceptualization exists; however, it is quite clear... (10.127).
Just as there is differentiation (*bheda*) here in the *sakala* [state], it is not so in the *pralayākala* and other states.
Now, one might ask: "What is this clearly manifest differentiation in the *sakala* state that does not exist in the *pralayākala* and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
It is clear that there exist infinite intermediate varieties of such distinct classes of birth. || 10-128 ||

This entire fourteen-fold [universe] possesses a differentiation such that it is perceived directly as being "of this kind. The term "differentiated" (bheditā) means the state of possessing distinctions such as gods, humans, and so forth—this is the meaning. || 128 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated everywhere that it is precisely the *pralayākalas*, whose latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) have awakened, who become *sakalas* in various ways? Therefore, how could that very absence of differentiation which exists among them [the *pralayākalas*] also belong to the *sakalas*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But in the state of dissolution (laya), even though that distinction exists, it arises from mere latent impressions (saṃskāra) alone.

The state of being *akala* (devoid of kalās) serves as the reason for the absence of differentiation (*viśeṣa*) in the case of the *sakala* [subject], because even though differentiation exists merely through latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it cannot result in actual differentiation. For indeed, in the case of the *pralayākala*, [the text says] "na... [and so forth].

Whether in the state of non-experientiality (*apavedyatva*) as in "I have had some thought," or even in the state of experientiality (*savedyatva*) as in "I slept happily," where there is no perception of external objects at all, what need is there to mention the perception by another subject, by which a thirteenth [subject] might exist? || 129 ||
Furthermore, even for those such as the Vijñānākala, there is no difference consisting of even mere latent impressions (saṃskāra); thus he says:
"For the Vijñānakevalas and others, there is indeed no distinction even in that much. (10.130)
However, it is Śiva’s mere freedom that unfolds as their differentiation.

For, although they possess a single nature consisting of pure consciousness and so forth, it has been stated that their mutual difference consists solely in the unfolding of the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty.
As it has been said: "It is solely Śiva’s freedom that unfolds for the sake of their differentiation," and:
"Even though there is identity in their defining characteristics such as consciousness, those [entities] possess mutual difference."

"Likewise, through the non-differentiation of the Lord's will, they are the Vijñānakevalas" (Rigvidhānaprakāśa 3.2.7). Therefore, since the Vijñānākalas and others possess a single nature consisting of pure consciousness and so forth,
where there is no such differentiation, what need is there to speak of those who, in ascending order, are endowed with complete power of vision and action?

The [categories of] Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantramaheśvaras have not been mentioned here by their own name. Consequently, the distinction of the Pralayākalas and others from the Sakala is as follows: since there is no state in which a Pralayākala and so forth is an object of cognition for another Pralayākala and so forth, there is no such increase in their number.
The Blessed One taught. ||130||
With this intention, he says: "Perceiving the distinction here, such as that of the Sakala [and others]... (10.131).
The All-pervasive Lord did not speak of the thirteenth state and so forth in relation to the *layākala* and others;
by this much, the basis for the knowability of the nature of existence (*bhāvadharma*) has been established through the fifteenfold division and so on. (10.131)

Now, however, in order to establish that very point, he raises this doubt: "Is it not the case that, in comparison with the *pralayākala* and *vijñānākala*, the state of being an object (*vedyatā*)—which is their very root—does not even exist? He asks:
"But let it be granted that objectivity is a property of entities; however, [this does not apply to] the *layākala* and *vijñānākala*. (10.132)
They do not perceive anything here at all; how, then, can there be dependence upon that?
For the *pralayākala* and the *vijñānākala*, being like yogis who have entered a void-like samādhi or are like a sleeping serpent, know nothing whatsoever. Thus it is said.
It is a marvel that those two lack the very status of being knowers; how, then, in comparison to them, could the state of being known (vedyatā) be an attribute of an existing entity? || 132 ||
He provides the following rebuttal:
"Listen: while this reality of the essential unity of consciousness is thus established... (10.133)
Consciousness indeed exists even in the insentient; what then need be said of that which is about to perceive?
At the moment of its own awakening, the one who is liberated through dissolution (laya-kevalin) shall indeed perceive.
And its awakening is twofold: for the state of mantra and for worldly existence.

For in this philosophical system, where the ultimate reality is the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvid-advaita-paramārtha*), if even insentient objects such as blue or pleasure are sentient there, then what need is there to speak of subjects such as the *pralayākala* who are desirous of awakening?

The state of being a knower indeed exists for both the *pralayākala* and the *vijñānākala*, by virtue of which the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) also becomes an inherent property of their being. (134)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then when and for whom does awakening occur? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and other such means arising from the systems of the Vaiṣṇavas and others... (10.135).
Just as it is, so too the conditioned [soul], through its own various lower and higher refinements,
may become either dissolved or awakened, thereby attaining the state of mantra or the lordship over it.

But those who are devoid of autonomy and are forcibly brought under the sway of delusion awaken from the state of the *layākala* due to their own residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of worldly existence. (10.137)

The phrase "in that manner" (tathā) means according to their respective hierarchy of lower and higher levels. Furthermore, the respective hierarchy of the Vaiṣṇava and other systems has already been determined at length previously, so no effort is made here.
As it was stated before:
Furthermore, those who have begun the practice of meditation for the sake of destroying the formative forces of karma,
yet have met their end before reaching the perfection of that meditation;

"By virtue of the excellence of the ripening of their internal contemplation, those great ones attain the status of mantras; from the wondrous arises the even more wondrous through their activity. (9.141).
Thus, they are "devoid of autonomy."
The meaning is that they lack the capacity for the practice of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and so forth as taught in other systems, such as Vaiṣṇava and others.
For this very reason it was said: "Overpowered by force by delusion. || 137 ||
It is not only the *pralayākala* that is understood to be twofold, but the *vijñānākala* as well—
thus he says:
"The *jñānākala* also awakens to the state of Mantreśvara and Maheśvara."
Neither for the sake of becoming a mantra-master and the like, nor even for the sake of wandering through cyclic existence at any time. || 10-138 ||
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "for the sake of [attaining] the state of a Mantra, etc.," he specifies that it is not for the sake of Śiva-hood alone;
namely, "for the sake of the state of a Mantreśvara or a Maheśvara. The *īśas* are the Mantreśvaras. (138)
Now, it may be argued that for the Vijñānākala,
even while the root impurity known as ignorance remains,
there is no movement upward nor downward, because of the absence of any cause for such diversity.
Merely by virtue of his limitation, not yet touching the non-duality with Śiva,
he is called a Vijñānakevalin, established in pure consciousness.
Furthermore, "reflecting upon his non-difference from Śiva by virtue of the will of Śambhu,
he gradually attains the nature of Śiva,
taking the form of a Mantra, a Mantreśvara, and a Mantramaheśvara"— according to this and other previously stated principles, let him be designated as such.
Regarding the question, "How then is he awakened even for the sake of transmigratory existence?"—
anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For his descent differs according to whether he is a man of realized knowledge (vijñānin) or a yogi."

For, according to our system, because the Vijñānākala has entered [the world] as a possessor of consciousness (vijñānin) and a yogi, he does not undergo transmigration like others; thus it is said: "His descent is distinct."
Thus, he confirms the awakening that has been brought about for him:
"And it is said that the Lord of the world, desiring to emit the universe, awakened [him]. (10.139)
"In the Śrīpūrvaśāsana it is said that there are eight [beings] consisting solely of consciousness (vijñānakevala).
It is stated therein:
'Desiring to emit the world, at the very beginning of creation, by his own will...'"
"He awakened eight individuals who were solitary in their consciousness. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 1.19) || 139 ||

Now, it is undisputed that as long as the two—the *layākala* and the *pralayākala*—are unawakened, they lack the status of being knowers (*veditṛtva*). And when they are awakened, they attain the nature of all the *mantras* and so forth; therefore, from that perspective alone, at that time, the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) would be a property of the entity (*bhāvadharma*), and not from the perspective of the *layākala*. Thus it is also [the case].

Anticipating the objection, "Would not the sequence beginning with the fifteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] be disrupted?", he says: "Therefore, that capacity for awakening which these two possess when they are about to awaken... (10.140).
By the force of that [consciousness], knowability exists here precisely through the state of being fit for knowability.

Therefore, according to the principle just mentioned, when these two— the *pralayākala* and the *vijñānākala*— are about to awaken, that is, in the state of desiring to awaken, immediately thereafter...

Since the state of being a knower necessarily manifests, there is a capacity or fitness for cognition; and with respect to that, even the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*)—insofar as it consists in such fitness—is possible in the case of the earth and other elements. Thus, what room is there here for any contradiction? (140)
He illustrates this very point:
"For instance, even when her beloved is in a deep sleep, [she perceives] her arrival as something unexpected. (10.141)

Thinking, "He will see me," the woman going to meet her lover does not feel [her presence] within her own limbs; for, due to her beloved being stupefied by deep sleep, she anticipates that he will perceive her within himself, and thus the woman going to meet him experiences such an excess of joy— even while he remains asleep.
The state of being a knower exists by virtue of a fitness (*yogyatā*) whose nature consists in the connection with the awakening to existence; it is for this reason that it was stated thus. || 141 ||
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand:
"In this way, Śiva also thinks: 'Let this be made known to him. (10.142)
"I shall go" or "I shall create"—at that moment, that is merely its capacity;
such is the knowability of that entity, and its state as an enjoyer is likewise of that same extent.
For who could conceive of the manifold experience of the *layākala*? [The author says:

"This entire collection of objects will, at the occasion of his own awakening, become an object of knowledge for this *layākala* and the others in its full intensity—and not merely by way of potentiality as it is now. Therefore...
The meaning is this: the Lord Śiva also reflects, "I create this pair, which is mutually conforming, in the form of the grasped and the grasper";
at that time, even in states such as those of the *pralayākala*, knowability (*vedyatā*) is a property of the object (*bhāvadharma*) by virtue of its inherent capacity alone.

Now, it may be granted that the state of being an object (*vedyatā*) of an entity—whether figurative or primary—exists by virtue of mere suitability; however, how could the state of being a knower (*veditṛtā*) be so? For that [state] is the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*), and enjoyment is the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth; thus, in the absence of those [pleasures and pains], there would be no state of being a knower in the *layākala* and other such states, as it depends upon them.
And how could even the state of being an object of cognition (vedyatā) persist?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "the state of being an enjoyer," and so forth.
"To that extent" means consisting merely of a capacity distinct from the stage of actualization in the form of the experience of pleasure, pain, and so on.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "What is this unprecedented technical definition being formulated? Is it not improper to speak without metaphorical license that even a child is an 'experiencer' (bhoktṛ) based on a connection with future experience, just as one cannot properly say that even a child is an 'old man' simply because he possesses the latent state (bhāvanā) of old age? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The manifold... (citro).

"‘Hī’ and so forth. For enjoyment (*bhoga*) is established for various enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) through a manifold variety characterized by differences in place, time, state, and nature; just as the experience of pleasure, pain, and so on is clearly evident as enjoyment, it is not appropriate to restrict [the definition] to that alone, because such a state exists even in the case of the non-evident. Thus..."

Even when [the object] has been cultivated but is not yet clearly manifest, the transaction of enjoyment would indeed occur by virtue of mere fitness, because enjoyment is established in such and such a manner according to the suitability of each respective enjoyer. || 143 ||
He demonstrates that very point:
"For in whatever way consciousness [occurs], that indeed is experience, whether it be clear or unclear. (10.144)

Even though it is capable of being recollected, it does not abandon its state as an object of experience, whether in a clear or unclear manner, or otherwise. The word "api" (even/also) is displaced in its order; "otherwise" means [in a manner different from the aforementioned].
The meaning is: because of its vividness, it is unfit to be remembered—like grass, pebbles, and so forth, which were not noticed while traveling on a path. || 144 ||
He provides an illustration for this very point: "Even one who is stupefied by deep sleep [remains] with his body embraced by his beloved. (10.145)
"He too is called the enjoyer; he also previously conceived of himself as an enjoyer.
[The word] "is called" means by people. "He too" refers, by implication, to one who is awakened. "Previously" means even during the state of being profoundly deluded—this is the meaning. || 145 ||
The state of being the enjoyer and the enjoyed does not occur only in a state of delusion through mere capacity, but even in a state free from delusion—as he says:
"Even one devoid of mere imagination [sees] a certain noble lady before him. (10.146)
Upon seeing her about to be enjoyed, he immediately experiences great joy;
this is the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) concerning a woman of good family, characterized as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
"About to be enjoyed" means that, by the power of destiny, she is one whose enjoyment is to be performed—this is the sense.

Therefore, immediately upon seeing her with impetuosity, as if having attained his desired gain through a longing filled with agitation, he should attain a state of exhilaration— an essence of bliss appropriate for sexual union— by which his status as an enjoyer may be realized. || 146 ||

Now, one might object: "If even a woman of good family, while being enjoyed by one man, were to be an object of enjoyment for another merely by virtue of her inherent fitness, then, since there is no distinction [in that fitness], she should be so for everyone as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And then, having seen her, even one who shares a similar disposition... (10.147).

"No one else perceives it in that way; whom then can we find here?"—this is the meaning [of the phrase] "on the occasion of the joy of either one. "Even one who shares a similar disposition" means even one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth are identical to those of that very enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). || 147 ||

One might object: "Is it not the case that those who maintain a theory of causal necessity without a cause are themselves to be censured, since they claim that even when the cause is identical, the effect occurs only in some instances and not in others?
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the point by means of an illustration:
This is well-established in the world: that perception occurs in this regard even without an external cause.
The connection is as follows: when people say "it becomes clear," "as if submerged," "as if extinguished," or "the vision [is restored]," this is established in the world;
that is, even though the cause is the same, the effect occurs only in certain instances, and thus it occurs without [an apparent] cause.

The meaning is: "due to the absence of a well-known cause. By this, even when there is no difference in the collection of visible causes, experience characterized by the clarity of vision and so forth may occur only in certain instances due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa); thus, [this is established] by way of logical possibility even in a state of non-delusion.

Since the state of being an enjoyer and the state of being an object of enjoyment are observed [in these cases], it is established that the distinction of fifteen-foldness and so forth is valid, as this condition applies equally to the *layākala*s and others. || 148 ||
He concludes:
"In this way, this detailed classification of the principles has been fully set forth. (10.149)

Now, one might object: "Since the single earth is perceived by Sakala and the others either individually, or in pairs, triads, and so forth, through their combination, why should there not be an even greater number than fifteen? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of the mutual difference between powers and the possessors of power, [there is a distinction] even in those [perceptions] produced by them."
Because there is mutual difference among the various particulars, as well as with other principles. (10.150)
There is no limit anywhere for one who performs the counting of divisions and subdivisions;
and in this way, the manifold variety of the worlds and so forth is established—thus he says:
"For that very reason, this diverse arrangement of the worlds and so forth exists. (10.159)
As it has been said:
"This infinite variety has been briefly described in its full extent; likewise, the garland of worlds is clearly divided by these same distinctions. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.8)
Thus [ends the verse]. 159.
He demonstrates this very diversity here:
"Even though both possess an earthly nature, there is no equality between the worlds of Rudra and Viṣṇu;
what then can be said of other cases, whether regarding enjoyment or essential nature? (10.152)

Since there is a diversity in the nature of enjoyment between the worlds of Rudra and Viṣṇu, despite their being equally composed of earth, what then can be said of other realms—such as the worlds consisting of earth, water, and so forth? Thus it is said: "What talk could there be of anything else? (152).
Now, one might object: "Let the detailed explanation be given, by which such diversity in the worlds and so forth is established? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Although that detailed account cannot be directly expressed by us, nevertheless, let it be discerned as it is being told merely by way of its general path. (10.153)

Thus, the detailed exposition consisting of divisions and subdivisions—which was briefly indicated here by the statement of apprehension beginning with "due to the difference between power and the possessor of power" (śakti-śaktimatoḥ)—is now set forth merely as a mere indication of its direction. || 153 ||

In this regard, the fourteenfold fundamental division of powers (śakti) and possessors of power (śaktimat) has just been stated; however, due to their mutual differentiation, further intermediate varieties may also arise—thus he says: "When there is a mutual differentiation of the seven mother-powers (mātṛśakti)..."
Form consists of forty-nine essential natures, and beyond that there is an additional one.
"Fifty-one" refers to the seven powers of the subjects, beginning with Sakala, multiplied by those same seven. || 154 ||
Now, one might object: "How can a power belonging to one thing pierce another?
For surely a jar does not possess the state of being a warp and woof that belongs to a cloth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Since everything has everything as its essence, therefore [the power] resides within the Universal Mother."
The emergence of the powers of the letters, kalās, and so forth, truly exists in reality. || 10-155 ||
One might object: "Granted, this may be possible in reality, but it is not perceived as such.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Let that [consciousness] be indistinct; nevertheless, it is capable of providing at least a portion of differentiation."
For the intention here is that the demonstration of differentiation was undertaken with reference to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*).
Thus, when there is mutual differentiation among those possessing powers (śaktimant), even for the forty-nine selves,
there would be a manifoldness as previously indicated— due to the mutual differentiation even within the divisions created by them— as he says:
And among those various divisions as well, there is a great many further subdivisions.

The phrase "mutually" implies differentiation; thus, "the state of manifold division" means that by multiplying forty-nine by forty-nine, there are twenty-four hundred and one varieties—this is the meaning.
He now analyzes what was stated regarding [their differentiation] "along with other principles."
When the primary divisions and subdivisions [of the ritual] are differentiated by means of water and other substances,
the infinity of the ritual procedure is said to be expressed through the various modes of the primary division.

The meaning is: "of the primary divisions and sub-divisions" refers to the forty-nine forms and their sub-varieties. Furthermore, when these [secondary] ones are multiplied in this manner, what can be said regarding the infinity of the method of division? This is what is meant by the phrase "when there is division," namely, in the sequence of one, two, three, and so forth.

"By way of the primary divisions"—the meaning is: by way of the fourteen-fold primary division, just like that. By this, it is stated as a restatement (anuvāda) that even for the primary divisions, such as earth and the others, when they are divided according to the sequence of one, two, three, and so on, there would also be an infinity of methods of division; thus, it is a rule (vidhi). || 157 ||
Not only is there this variety among them, but there is also another way—thus he says:
"The innate powers of the eyes and other senses, whether manifest or latent, clearly extend even further distinctions. (10.158)

"Even though that portion of Śakala which consists of the aspect of valid cognition (*pramāṇāṃśa*) and is of the nature of knowledge and art (*vidyākalātmaka*), being universal in nature, is reckoned as *Śakti*, yet its divisions are not. (10.12)

This has been stated previously; nevertheless, because a universal is invariably concomitant with its particulars, the presence of the powers of the eyes and so forth must necessarily exist here as well.
Thus it was said that for the Sakala [perceiver], the powers of the eyes and so forth are both manifest and latent.
They bring about the imposition of another distinction. || 158 ||
This very principle is extended to the *layākala*s and others as well:

"In this same way, for the *layākala*s and others, another distinction is proclaimed based on the intensity or the exhaustion of that latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is designated as a 'state' (*pada*). (10.159)

"Regarding the phrase *tatsaṃskāra* (their residual impression): the meaning is that it is the residual impression (*saṃskāra*), that is, the latent trace (*vāsanā*), of those powers such as sight and so forth. Even for the *layākala*, the power consists essentially of *vidyā* and *kalā*, just as it does for the *sakala*; however, because it exists in the form of a residual impression, it is not manifest in that way for him. As it has been said:"
"For the *layākalas*, that very same portion of the means of knowledge (*māna*) is most clearly manifest.

Now, one might object: "If there is the manifestation and disappearance of the powers of the eyes and so forth, what does that have to do with their perceptibility, such that there would be the emergence of this other kind of distinction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even while relying on a power that has been suppressed, [the Self] remains in a state of indifference."
That which one knows as if without entering into it is indeed a different kind of objectivity.

As if entering, as if immersing, as if expanding, and as if whirling, the state of being known appears as something other; herein, the distinction is that which is appropriate for causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

The meaning is: "as if not entering," in the manner of [placing] grass, pebbles, and so forth, that is, by remaining on the surface. In the sequence beginning with "as if entering" (*āviśyeva*), there is a progressive decrease in intensity. For "entering" (*āveśa*) is becoming one with that;
"immersion" (*nimajjana*) is a penetration into its interior consisting of attachment; and "expansion" (*vikāsa*) is a spreading out due to eagerness for that.

"Vighūrṇana" (whirling) is a vibration consisting of an upward surging due to that orientation; "vidataḥ" means of one whose own power is overflowing—this is the meaning. Now, since there is no difference in the result, what is the purpose of this distinction which consists merely of words?

Anticipating this objection, it is said: "In this context, difference is that which is conducive to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). For one whose power has not manifested, even what is seen is as if unseen and does not nourish satisfaction in that way; however, for one whose power has manifested, there arises a supreme excellence of wonder as he perceives the object through direct contact.
This distinction, which is produced solely by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), would exist; why then is it said to be a mere matter of words?
He confirms that very point, which contains positive and negative concomitance, by means of an illustration:
"When one power is concealed and another arises quite clearly, a further distinction should be understood, like the sight of a lute-player. (10.162)
For in the case of a lute-player, when the powers of sight and the other senses are suppressed, there arises the power of hearing alone.
[162] He distinguishes between the concealment and manifestation of power as follows: "The concealment and manifestation of power [occur] through another of its own powers or from something else."
Whether being perceived or not being perceived, they manifest a state of manifold diversity. || 10-163 ||

For in some cases, the emergence and disappearance of the power of the eyes and other senses occur through their own attention or lack of attention; in other cases, as with a lute-player, they arise from another sense-power such as hearing; and in yet other cases, they arise from external factors such as mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
And all this, whether being perceived or not being perceived, constitutes the infinity of distinctions. || 163 ||
And this entire range of divisions should first be applied even according to the manner of each individual entity, such as earth and the rest; thus he says:
"In this way, whatever state belongs to these principles, beginning with earth..."
Even the so-called "jar" exists therein, demonstrating differentiation.

"In that regard"—that is, in the state known as a single jar; for when a reality possesses such manifold states, who indeed could say how many divisions there are?—this is the intended meaning. || 164 ||

Now, one might object: "If this emergence and disappearance of power is said to belong only to the subject (*pramātṛ*) and not to anything else, how can objects of cognition such as a jar be differentiated by such diversity?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In this case as well, what is called "knowability" is identity with the knowers;
therefore, this jar, being knowable by all, is indeed the Sakala [level of reality] itself. (10.165)
As long as this [reality] is knowable solely by Śiva, it appears as Śiva alone; indeed, for as long as consciousness shines, it shines as a single body.

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (from that): because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*), it is established that whatever object is known by a particular subject is of the very nature of that subject. For it has been demonstrated extensively above that an object is indeed composed of its respective subjects. Indeed, consciousness manifests itself in as many forms as consist of the nature of the object and the subject.
To that extent, it consists of the identity with each of those [objects], meaning it is essentially the indivisible supreme light.
As it has been said:
"O Dear One, as long as these are not knowers, how can they be objects of knowledge?"
"The knower and the known are indeed one; therefore, there is no such thing as impurity.

Having thus established the fifteenfold nature [of the elements] through their distribution and combination within the categories of existence and worlds starting from Earth, he now describes them collectively, including the core of the scriptures, by way of their substratum in the principles (tattvas).
Herein, the entire category of the Earth-principle (dharātattva) is shown.
The fifteenfold nature previously mentioned has been stated here in its entirety. (10.167)
That light which shines forth through the non-differentiation of the earth-principle (dharātattva) is indeed Lord Śiva; herein, the earth is Brahman—such is that doctrine. (10.168)

Those who, by the will of Śiva, impel those striving to bestow the supernatural powers (siddhis) residing in the principle of earth (dharātattva), they are the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvaras).
Now, the fifteenfold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) of the entire principle of Earth (*dharātattva*), which was previously described as divided into both individual and collective distinctions,
is demonstrated in its totality by setting aside its fragmentation through the presentation of intermediate sub-varieties; for it is exactly so.

In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, which has already been introduced, it is stated that he first points out the seven subjects (*pramātṛ*) who constitute its foundation, beginning with the word "Earth" (*dhara*). Now, one might object: since Śiva is called *brahman* because he nourishes (*bṛṃhaṇa*) all the ontological categories (*tattva*), how can he be established as having a fixed, limited nature?

Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Earth is Brahman. As the Śruti states: "This Brahman is indeed the Earth. The intention is that by the will of Śiva, Śiva himself is the impeller even of those [elements] here. || 169 ||
Who, then, are those to be impelled? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Lords of Mantras (mantreśas) and the Mantras that clearly express them are indeed impelled;
having practiced the yoga pertaining to the Earth-principle through the knowledge of Śiva. (10.170)
But they are not like the dualists, such as the Pāśupatas, Sāṃkhyas, or Vaiṣṇavas;
for they have not attained the state of being subject to the burden [of karma], and they enjoy the condition of being Vijñānākala.
Those who have reached dissolution at the end of a kalpa through the enjoyment of reality (tattva),
being endowed with the state of deep sleep, are here called the "isolated ones of dissolution" (pralayakevalas).
The term *mantreśāḥ* refers to the lords of the mantras, such as the hundred Rudras and others, who are denoted by their respective mantras.
As it has been said:
"Being impelled, they are established by power upon the ground that constitutes the denotable aspect."
The lords of mantras abide as everything from the hundred Rudras up to Viriñca.
"The mantras arise from the agitation of the earth within the power of Śiva’s resonance (nādaśakti);
they are the designators of that [reality] and are intent upon bestowing their respective fruits.
Thus, "as if distinct" means through the perception of duality; "those who have not attained the eternal abode" refers to those who have not reached the state of ultimate stability.

Because they dissolve prematurely without reaching the perfection of cultivation—meaning that while [the stages] beginning with earth have dissolved, they have [actually] dissolved into water and so forth;

for it was stated previously that at the time of cosmic dissolution, the *pralayakevalins* abide in progressively higher levels of the *tattvas*. Thus, they are "endowed with the state of deep sleep."
The meaning is: "remaining in the state of deep sleep. || 172 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the nature of the *pralayākalas* consists in their being dissolved into their respective *tattvas*, and since that [dissolution] cannot exist in deep sleep—which consists merely in the persistence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the body and other such subjects—how can these [subjects] possess that state? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Indeed, in the state of deep sleep, the dissolution of the principles (tattvas) is clearly perceived;
otherwise, from what source would the fixed perception of dreams arise? (10.173)

"Otherwise" means in the absence of that dissolution into reality (*tattva*). Here, indeed, just as in the waking state, the sequence of dream following deep sleep is observed as a fixed rule; for one who does not rest upon this [state] consisting of the repose of the internal and external organs [cannot experience it].
Because it "ascends to the state of dream," the causal state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) necessarily precedes the state of dreaming; and since an effect must arise in conformity with its cause,
that deep sleep— which consists essentially in the dissolution of the [lower] principles— must consist of the entities, worlds, and so forth appropriate to those very principles.
The creation of a dream is perceived, such as the climbing of mountains and so forth for one merged with the earth, or the crossing of the ocean and so forth for one merged with water. || 173 ||

Now, one might object: "If even in deep sleep there is a dissolution of reality consisting in the dissolution of all objects of knowledge, then what occasion is there for the memory that arises from the impressions of the experience of those very objects which were necessarily present? To this doubt, he says:"
Even the state of deep sleep appears variegated and as both clear and unclear, because we observe a variety of recollections such as "I slept happily" and so forth. (10.174)

It is called "variegated" (*citram*) because it consists of the three *guṇas*; for this very reason, it has been said: "clear, unclear, and so forth. Among these, in the clear state where *sattva* predominates, one thinks, "I slept happily"; in the unclear state where *tamas* predominates, one thinks, "I was not conscious of anything at all"; and by the inclusion of the term "and so forth," [it refers to] the clear-and-unclear state where *rajas* predominates.

The diversity of memory is seen in such recollections as, "I slept in discomfort. Since this [memory] would otherwise be inexplicable, there is no such rule that all objects of cognition must dissolve during deep sleep, which would contradict the memory of one who has awakened—this is the intended meaning. || 174 ||
And this should not be said— that this memory arises from the experience of the touch of the pleasure of a cotton bed and so forth—
for he says: "At the very moment that subtle instant, he awakens as if from sleep."
At that very moment, this is a memory; it is not a memory born from a cognition produced by an object. || 10.175 ||

For this would indeed be so if first there were awakening, then the experience of pleasure and so forth, and then, upon the occurrence of awakening, a memory born from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [experience]. But it is not so here, because awakening and memory occur in a single moment. Thus he says: "At the very moment..."
"He awakens" means that at that very moment, memory occurs. || 175 ||

For this very reason, those who claim that even in the absence of stable awakening, memory arises from such an experience— occurring at intervals through the logic of a flash of lightning for one who is awakened here and there— should be regarded as mere exaggerators;
thus he says:

Therefore, as for what is said by the deluded—that this is merely the memory of the pleasant touch of a mattress and so forth occurring intermittently for one who is awake—how could that be so? (10.176)
"Why is that?"—the meaning is that it is indeed without cause. || 176 ||
Those individuals here who have ascended to the earth, whose impurities are turbid due to being mixed with the manifestation of illusory karma, are to be known as *sakala*. (10.177)
By the words beginning with "māyā," their bondage by the three impurities (trimala) has been stated. || 177 ||

Having thus pointed out the seven types of subjects (*pramātṛ*), he speaks in order to point out their seven powers (*śakti*) in general: "In the performance of their respective functions, of this very [sevenfold] group..."
That which is agitation is clearly said to be the group of seven powers.

For Śiva is indeed of the nature of infallible consciousness; as for those three powers of his, by virtue of assuming the form of the subject through the power of his absolute freedom, [they appear as such]. (10.179)
The three types of cognitions ending with the mental [cognition] remain as if indifferent;
however, due to the coloring by the form of the object and by virtue of the nature of the subject-form, [they appear as such]. (10.180)
These three—will, knowledge, and action—are considered to end with their respective [objects].

"Respective activity" means the activity or operation of each one, such as a pillar or the like, or creation and so forth; this is the meaning. And this has been stated specifically elsewhere by this very [author]. For example:
In that very place called the Earth, which appears as if divided,
that which is perceived separately as pillars and so forth is the power of Śiva on this earth.
In this very [reality], which possesses manifold states, it performs creation, dissolution, maintenance, grace, and withdrawal, extending from the level of the Sakala up to Śiva.
In this world, the power of the Great Lord of Mantras (Mantramaheśāna) is the sovereign over the principles (tattva);
for indeed, by sheer force alone, she [projects] individual souls (pudgala) into the various groups of principles and mantras.
That power of Maheśa which impels resides on the plane of consciousness;
by means of it, one perceives the true nature of the elements, such as yellow and so forth.
This power of mantra is considered to protect one from its opposite;
it bestows perfect eagerness regarding the enjoyment or non-enjoyment of those respective realities.
The state of impurity consisting of just that much is indeed the power of the "isolated-in-knowledge" (jñānakevalin);
because of the orientation toward the karma residing in those various awakened and expanded principles.
The power directed toward the enjoyment of those [objects] belongs to the *pralayākala*;
however, that state which exists during the immersion into the manifestation of the impurities of *māyā* and *karman* [belongs to the *sakala*].

"The power that effects enjoyment, which follows various states produced by external, internal, and sensory [factors], resides in all individual souls (*aṇu*s). Now, in our system, the universe consists of nothing other than the nature of *nara*, *śakti*, and *śiva*; therein—
Having raised the objection, "In that case, since this has already been proclaimed there, why is it stated here as something new?", he says: "Śiva," and so forth.
In this regard, there is no dispute that Śiva is the supreme subject (*parapramātā*), whose nature is eternal consciousness.
And his power, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, manifests itself in both pure and impure forms.

It brings forth the six types of subjects (*pramātṛ*). Among them, the triad beginning with the Mantra-Maheśvaras possesses pure subjectivity because they do not depend upon objects of perception (*grāhya*) and so forth; however, the triad beginning with the Vijñānākalas possesses impure subjectivity because they do depend upon objects of perception and so forth. For this very reason, it has been said:

"Acquired by the power of autonomy," and "due to the coloring by the form of the object of perception. "Ending in three types of mantras" means they consist of the forms of Mantramaheśvaras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantras—this is the meaning.
"As if indifferent" means undisturbed; for if they were disturbed, they would become Śaktis.
The state of being. || 180 ||
He summarizes this very point:
"In this way, subjectivity is sevenfold; likewise, its agitation is the state of the means of knowledge. (10.181)
"Mānatā" means by way of being the nature of power (śakti)—this is the meaning. || 181 ||
One might object: "In this case, would not only the fourteenth [day] or the pair consisting of Śiva and Śakti be indicated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But that which is devoid of contact with consciousness in the form of the subject..."
Pure and insentient is its essential nature; thus the universe consists of these three aspects.

It is pure precisely because of the avoidance of contact with consciousness; for this very reason, it is insentient (*jaḍa*) and non-spiritual (*anātman*) due to the predominance of its state as an object of cognition—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"But when, through the forgetting of immersion in the subject, insentience becomes manifest..."
"Because it arises from dependence, that nature consists of the human [subject].
Thus, even in the sequence beginning with the fifteen-fold [division], it has been stated that the ultimate reality is indeed the Trika: "In this way, the universe is essentially the Trika. (182)
He extends this same principle elsewhere as well: "In the same way, the wise one should speak of water and the other elements as well, divided by their various distinctions.

Now, it is certainly not the case that anyone disagrees that Śiva and Śakti are essentially of the nature of unswerving consciousness; for it is Śakti herself, manifesting through the forms of will, knowledge, and action, who appears as the sixfold group of subjects.
This has been stated; however, since that power is without distinction everywhere, the state of fifteen-foldness (pāñcadaśya) would also be possible even up to the level of the Mantramaheshvaras.
Anticipating the objection—"Why then was that very state not described, setting aside the thirteen-foldness and so forth?"—he says:
By this method, however, [the distinction] is generally found in all the various divisions. || 10-183 ||
This fifteenfold division exists up to the level of the Mantramaheśvaras;
nevertheless, because it lacks clarity, it has not been discussed here, even though it does exist. (10.184)

The meaning is that [this applies] to all the divisions ending with the Mantramaheśvaras—by implication, to the Pralayākalas and so forth—and for this reason, what was stated [previously] regarding the thirteen-fold [division] and so on is contrary to logic; such is the intention. It is indeed true, but because this is not as clear as the case of the thirteen-fold division and so on, it has not been mentioned here. (184)

"Surely, if each successive lower form were to dissolve into each preceding higher form, it would lose its very own nature; therefore, does not the suspicion regarding the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) and so forth become entirely groundless in that case?"—
anticipating this objection, he says:
And this has been aphorized by the Creator in the *Śrīpūrva*,
for it speaks of the states of waking and so forth through the passage beginning with "by virtue of being the sovereign of active operations" (10.185).
Even though Śiva is undivided, according to the internal subtle awakening,

the Lord has indicated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that although Śiva is undivided, He possesses the nature of waking and so forth; for just as there are the states of waking and the rest, there is likewise a fifteenfold division and so on, higher and higher.
"It may arise. And thus:

"By virtue of being the presiding lord over the activity of Śaṃ, and because it impels that [activity] while depending on it; due to the cessation of desire and the state of self-abidance, though undivided, it is fivefold. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.35)

In this context, the waking state (*jāgarā*) is characterized by the predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), as Śiva is possessed of activity. The dream state (*svapna*) is characterized by the predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), consisting of various unique creations through His sovereignty as the presiding lord (*adhipati*). [The deep sleep state] consists of the withdrawal from indifference through [the powers of] knowledge and action.

The state of deep sleep (sauṣupta) is dominated by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), as it is characterized by impulsion. The fourth state (*turya*) is dominated by the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), because through the cessation [of duality] via the fullness of that which is to be desired, [bliss prevails]. The [state beyond the fourth] is dominated by the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), because, being devoid of [limited] bliss, there is repose in one's own perfectly full nature, which is the self of all and everything.
The phrase "transcending the fourth" (turyātīta) means having the nature of five states.

The expression "in accordance with the subtle consciousness residing within" means by relying on the subtle consciousness whose sole form is the subject (pramātṛ). For [this is the nature] of consciousness...
The sense is that everything may exist within by virtue of having the nature of consciousness. || 185 ||
In this regard: "This entire path, though sixfold and exceedingly extensive, which will be described, is established within the single vital breath (prāṇa). (Tantrāloka 6.5)

By such statements as these, [the author] shows that the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) exists within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) just as it does externally; thus, he begins to describe the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) and so forth by virtue of its presence therein: "Now, the network of principles situated in the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*) is being analyzed. (10.186)
This division into fifteen and so forth is exactly as the venerable Śambhu has taught;

by the phrase "the venerable Śambhu has taught," it is implied that because this [teaching] has come down through the lineage of gurus, its foundation is an uncontradicted and well-established tradition. (186)
He says that very thing: "In this case, when the entire object is to be grasped, there are sixteen moments (tuṭis). (10.187)
In the movement of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), [the divisions] are conceived as two and a quarter finger-breadths each;

this applies to every object to be grasped—that is, to the object of knowledge consisting of the principles (*tattva*), states of being (*bhāva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, the word "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) here...

"A *kṣaṇa* is traditionally held to be one-eighth of a human blink" (Svacchanda Tantra 11.199). Thus, it exists within a specific duration of time consisting of two such *kṣaṇas*. As it has been said:
"Two *kṣaṇas* should be known as a *tuṭi*... (Svacchanda Tantra 11.199).
Thus, "with parts" means "accompanied by a fourth part"—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"A *tuṭi* is a breath joined with one and a quarter finger-breadths... (Tantrāloka 6.64).
He analyzes this very point:
"Therein, the first is supreme non-duality, consisting of an undivided essence. (10.188)
The second is perceived as having the nature of the manifestation of the subject; the last, however, has attained the state of its own essential nature through identity with the object. (10.189)

Indeed, the final moment of perception cannot be distinguished as separate from the first; for the first moment consists of a *tuṭi*, which is a unit of time. Regarding the phrase "without division," it is as stated:
"Śiva is not directly divided [from it]" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.7).

Thus [it is said]: "in the form of the manifestation of the subject. For it has already been stated that the manifestation of the six subjects is indeed [the manifestation] of Śakti alone. "The final" refers to the sixteenth moment of time, consisting of a *tuṭi*.
"Due to identity with the object" means because of the predominance of the state of being an object (*grāhyatva*) itself, according to the respective case. Now, [an objection:]...

Since three *tuṭis* are here employed as both Śiva and Śakti by virtue of their being one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then— relative to the twelve subjects and their powers that are to be described subsequently—
there would be one *tuṭi* remaining in excess. Therefore, does this [excess *tuṭi*] subsume within the essential nature, or does it belong to the side of the subject?

Anticipating the objection, "How can it be deposited?", he first determines—even though it is to be explained last—that which remains, namely the penultimate moment (*upāntyakṣaṇa*), which has arrived by way of the discussion on the final moment (*antyakṣaṇa*) according to the principle of looking ahead at what is yet to come (*anāgatāvekṣaṇanyāya*). He does so with the words "it is not to be distinguished" (*na hi pravibhāvyaḥ*). The word "separately" (*pṛthak*) implies [separation] from the final moment.

The term "upāntya" (penultimate) refers to that moment situated near the end, consisting of the fifteenth *tuṭi*; for it is there, having attained an internal swelling, that the state of being an object (*grāhyatā*) itself manifests directly at the conclusion—this is the intended meaning.

In this way, he divides the remaining twelve *tuṭis* into the forms of the Great Lords of Mantra (*mantramaheśvara*) and their powers (*śakti*), and so forth: "The six moments that remain, beginning from the third moment... (10.190).
That [state] is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), consisting in the covering of the emerging conceptualizations;
it is called "the third" in relation to the first and second [moments]. It lasts for six moments, comprising both the form of the power-holder (śaktimat) and the power (śakti). ||190||
One might object: "But how can there be a covering of these arising conceptual constructions? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For they know that very form of Śiva to consist of the supreme power. (10.191)

For that hexad of moments, being composed of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), is traditionally taught to be, in sequence, the very form of Śiva and the essence of the Supreme Power (paraśakti), in relation to the possessor of power (śaktimat) and his power (śakti). || 191 ||
Having thus explained one group of six moments, he explains the next as well:
"The second middle group of six consists of the state that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara);
even this establishment of conceptual thought has gradually attained full clarity. (10.192)

It is called "middle" because it exists within the interval between the last [element] of the first hexad and the penultimate [element]; for this very reason, since the first hexad is the higher (*para*) and its own nature—consisting of the final and penultimate—is the lower (*apara*), it possesses the character of being both the higher and the lower (*parāparapadātmaka*). Thus it has been stated. "The establishment of conceptual construction" (*vikalparūḍhi*)...
Because it belongs to the realm of illusion (māyīya). "Successively" means according to the respective predominance of the sense of "this-ness" (idantā). || 192 ||

Now, one might object: "Since Śiva is of an undivided nature, it is Śakti alone who is the seed in each respective division; and since her manifestation occurs only in three ways—as will, knowledge, and action—what occasion is there for a description of a group of six? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

In this first group of six, the three goddesses quickly touch upon both the state of unfolding (pronmeṣavṛtti) and the state of closing (nimeṣavṛtti), thereby attaining the state of being a group of six.

By the phrase "the state of unfolding" (pronmeṣavṛttitām), its nature as power (śakti) is indicated; and by the phrase "the state of closing" (nimeṣavṛttitām), its nature as the possessor of power (śaktimat) is indicated. || 193 ||
Or he avoids [the first group] and applies them elsewhere—
thus it is also in the second hexad; however, here, by way of the path of the object of perception (grāhya),
having reached the state of coloring (uparāga), they abide as both supreme and non-supreme.
In this first group of six, those goddesses, by virtue of the mere effulgence of their own freedom, remain undeviating from their supreme nature even when an adjunct is desired to be grasped.

Now, one might object: "If, even in both hexads, the three goddesses exist in this manner through the process of unfolding (unmeṣa) and closing (nimeṣa), then let there be only one hexad; what is the purpose of a second? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But rather... and so forth (verse 195).
Now, if these terms—will, knowledge, and action—are indeed distinct, then there would be no excellence produced by will in knowledge, nor by both of them in action; for it is said:
"Since the prior state remains established within each successive lower reality..."
"Otherwise, their very existence would not be possible due to the loss of what preceded"; fearing that such statements would be contradicted, he says:
"And there is indeed some excellence in them, too, as they proceed from one to the next."
That which is revealed by the steadfast ones who possess the wealth of solitude, even after having made it manifest. || 10-196 ||

Right here, he shows another opinion in two ways: "Some, however, by casting one *tuṭi* into the object and even one [tuṭi] into the subject through identification (*tādātmya*), know [the cycle] as seven and seven. (10.197)

In this regard, some [teachers], having cast the single fifteenth *tuṭi*— the penultimate one— into identity with the nature of the object of perception (*grāhya*) which is the final *tuṭi*, and having thus described the essential nature through the unification of the final and penultimate *tuṭis* as we have stated, [proceed to] [discuss] the first seven *tuṭis* out of the remaining fourteen *tuṭis*.
