The view of certain authorities is that [the seven moments] are designated as the seven subjects (*pramātṛ*) and the other [seven] as their seven powers (*śakti*).

By the word "also" (*api*), the phrase "some" is included; thus, some [authorities], having assigned one *tuṭi* to the side of the grasper, implicitly define the final [moment] as being the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
In the same way, there is another group of fourteen; such is the opinion of others. || 197 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then which [view] is correct? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this subtle consciousness, whatever form those who are intent on conceptualization experience, what is the use of verbal boastings regarding that? (10.198)

Thus, for yogins who possess direct experience, only that which is established through their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is valid cognition, and nothing else. In this regard, what is the use of our or others' verbal activities, which are mostly mere prattle and devoid of experience? And by this [it is refuted] the previously mentioned...

It has been demonstrated that one's own position is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Since for a single cognizer there exists the nature of both the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and its powers (*śakti*), according to their states of being undisturbed or disturbed,
it is logical to designate them through their close proximity alone, rather than as separate entities from the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Since it is logical that the sprouting [of the seed] occurs through fullness in the final *tuṭi*, preceded by the attainment of swelling in the penultimate *tuṭi*, enough with further elaboration. || 198 ||
He concludes this very point:

"Thus, the process pertaining to the vital breath (prāṇa), from the earth up to the root [of the subtle body], has been explained according to the succession of gurus within the fifteenfold division. (10.199)
By the phrase "through the succession of gurus and lineage," it is established that this [tradition] is based solely upon its renown. || 199 ||
Having thus taught the fifteen-fold division (*pāñcadaśya*), he also teaches the thirteen-fold division and others:
"But when there is a decrease in the divisions (*bheda*) in sequence, there would also be a decrease in the *tuṭis*.
'When there is a decrease in the divisions' means in the nature of the thirteen-fold, eleven-fold, and so on; 'decrease' refers to this."

Because it is subsumed within the category of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). For, in whatever measure the two types of differentiation—consisting of the totality of that [nature] and its powers (*śakti*)—diminish, in that same measure the two *tuṭis* likewise become so.
As he will state:
"In this way, as each pair [of moments] diminishes until the distinction [between them] disappears,
so too each pair of *tuṭis* clearly undergoes diminution in succession" (10.198).
This is because each pair of *tuṭis* is deposited within the category of its own essential nature.
What is called "deficiency" is the loosening of one's stability as a knower (*pramātṛ*), and not the actual destruction of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*);
for even within the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) consisting of thirty-six finger-breadths, the number of *tuṭi*s is not lost. Therefore, in this regard:
Through the gradual dissolution of the conceptual subjects beginning with Sakala,
there arises, in successive order, the emergence of non-conceptual subjects, due to the progressive intensification of consciousness itself.
Thus it is said: "In that [state], there is the diminution of conceptual thought and the clarity of the non-conceptual. (10.200)
"In that" refers to the state where there is a deficiency in the differentiation of subjects. || 200 ||
Now, one might object: "In this case, just as in the sequence of the fifteen [tuṭis], sixteen tuṭis are established here;

how then could there be a loosening of their fixed state as the forms of the Sakala and others, by which the clarity of the non-conceptual and the diminution of the conceptual would occur?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
For just as one who has long been afflicted by suffering, having later attained a state of happiness, forgets that very suffering through the path of resting in bliss. (10.201)

Likewise, although people are established in consciousness even when conceptual construction has ceased, they do not recognize that existence [of consciousness] due to the power of resting within conceptual construction. (10.202)

"That suffering" refers to what was previously experienced for a long time. "The resting of conceptual construction" refers to its cessation. "That existence" refers to the conceptual one. Just as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that suffering—though fully developed because it was previously experienced—remains as if non-existent due to the absence of awakening through the power of resting in pleasure, so too [is the case here].

For those individuals who abide in the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpadaśā*), because their conceptualization has been exhausted, even when there is such agitation, no conceptual existence arises; for if that were the case,
they would have the direct realization of non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpakasaṃvitsākṣātkāra*), by which this defect of saṃsāra would be pacified.
Therefore, one must focus one's attention precisely here; thus he says:

"By means of the gradual diminution of conceptual construction, consciousness—which is barren of concepts—attains the manifestation of its own essential nature as the ultimate reality. Thus, let the wise person strive for focused attention upon that. (10.203)
And this is not our own invention alone—thus he says:
"In the cognition of the grasped and the grasper, there is attentiveness toward their relationship;
this is that [attentiveness] which has been described here and there, because it is the cow of plenty that milks all desires. (10.204)
In various places such as the *Śrī-Vijñānabhairava* and others, it is said:
"The perception of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings; however, this is the distinction for yogis: attentiveness toward that connection. (*Vijñānabhairava*, verse 106).

Thus, for those who are established in the state of *māyā*, rest consists precisely in the agitation of the grasped and the grasper, [thinking] "this is the grasped" and "this is the grasper. For those, however, who abide in the stage of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpaka*), even at the occasion of that agitation, [they remain aware] of that from which the arising of the grasped and the grasper occurs, or wherein it occurs.
Resting right there is the state of focused attention, by which the attainment of all desired fruits occurs. || 204 ||
Having thus spoken by way of this digression, he states the subject at hand:
"In this manner, as each pair [of moments] diminishes until the state of duality is reached, so too does each pair of *tuṭis* clearly undergo diminution in due order. (10.205)

And thus, when the twelve *tuṭis*— which consist of the relationship between the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and power (*śakti*)— are cast aside by means of their own nature characterized by the final and penultimate two *tuṭis*, only two *tuṭis* remain in Śiva? To this, he says:
For this very reason, a pair of *tuṭis* is proclaimed in the immersion (*āveśa*) into Śiva.

Now, one might object: "Since Śiva is the indivisible Self, whose sole essence is undivided and perfectly full consciousness, what possible meaning can there be for duality therein? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that the two *tuṭis* themselves exist in the form of Power (*śakti*) and the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*).
He analyzes:
"But that one *tuṭi* there is full, pure, and absolute. (10.206)
The second [state] is indeed the nature of Śiva-Śakti, consisting of all-knowingness and action;

and because of its fullness, it is pure and free from agitation—this is the meaning. For agitation is the state of Śakti, as it has been said: "It is indeed the nature of Śiva-Śakti, consisting of all-knowingness and action."
For this very reason, one who is attentive to this [state] would possess omniscience, agency, and so forth; thus he says:
"What is there that the yogi, being attentive to that [state], does not know or cannot do? (10.207)
And there is no contradiction here—so he says:
"And thus it was stated by the venerable Kallaṭa: 'The attainment of omniscience and agency occurs at the falling away of a *tuṭi*; the falling away of that *tuṭi* is another *tuṭi*. (10.208)
As for that which is stated in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*:
"At the falling away of the *tuṭi*, omniscience and so forth [arise]..."—
he explains this very point as follows:
"The fall of the first *tuṭi* is the second *tuṭi*.
That is to say, the fall, the decrease, or the diminution of the first *tuṭi* is the second *tuṭi*.
[208] Now, one might ask: why does one who is attentive during the second *tuṭi* attain omniscience and other such qualities?
One might ask: "Let that state of suchness (tathātva) belong to the very first moment (tuṭi)?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But in the first moment, everything has attained oneness, being full in every respect.
What object of knowledge (vedya) or what effect (kārya) could there be therein that is capable of being designated? (10.209)
The "object of knowledge" (vedya) and the "effect" (kārya) are stated respectively with reference to cognition (jñāna) and action (kriyā). || 209 ||
Thus, the second *tuṭi* alone is the cause for the attainment of omniscience and other powers; so he says:
"Therefore, the wise, for the sake of attaining omniscience and other powers, discern the Goddess Pratibhā, who is the first digit (*kalā*) of the manifestation of duality. (10.210)
That very power of Śiva is said [to manifest] in the third and subsequent *tuṭis*;
then, the Lords of Mantras and their powers, the Lords of Mantras and so forth, are proclaimed in succession. (10.211)

The term "initial" (*prāthamikī*) is used with reference to the manifestation of differentiation (*bhedasamullāsa*). The sense is that here, differentiation is essentially first projected. For this very reason, it is called "inspiration" (*pratibhā*), because it possesses ever-new manifestations. "That same" refers to the second form and so forth.
[The author] says "inspiration" (pratibhā). Now, if it is asked: "Surely the power of Śiva was said to reside in the second *tuṭi*;
what then is it in the third and subsequent ones?"—anticipating this doubt, he says "the third," and so forth. || 211 ||

Now, one might object: "Just as it was stated that for one who is attentive during the second *tuṭi* there is the attainment (*siddhi*) consisting of omniscience and so forth, is there likewise some attainment in these [other] *tuṭis*, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one who fixes the mind upon them, with the sole quality of attentiveness, there is an immersion into those respective attainments."
It arises by itself. || 212 ||

Regarding the phrase "those respective accomplishments" (*tattatsiddhi*): those various accomplishments, such as heaviness of the body and so forth, are described in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* and other texts within the chapters on *dhāraṇā* (concentration) and elsewhere. || 212 ||

Now, one might object: "Since Śiva-Śakti alone manifests everywhere and in every form, and since She is without distinction anywhere, why does the accomplishment (siddhi) consisting of omniscience and so forth not arise here as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

For this very reason, just as distance consists in a multiplicity of distinctions, so too in consciousness it arises from a plurality of *tuṭis*, like the lack of proximity between the senses and their objects. (10.213)

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) refers to the reason that [the principles] beginning with Mantra arise sequentially from the Lords (Nāthas) and so forth. He makes this very point clear through an illustration: "like the non-contact of the senses with their objects.
Just as, due to the abundance of intervening obstructing objects, the senses do not reach their objects...

Likewise, there is an absence of proximity even for yogins, because in their consciousness the multiplicity of *tuṭis*—which is the cause of the perception of diversity—acts as an obstruction. || 213 ||
He distinguishes this very point:
"For in whatever measure there is a decrease in the *tuṭis* through the reduction of divisions, in that same measure there is extreme proximity to consciousness, culminating in Śiva. (10.214)
Therefore, the Śiva-principle is said to be proximate from all sides and from that [state].
"Therefore" means because of the proximity of consciousness caused by the diminution of duality;
it is said to be "proximate" everywhere, as no specific distinction is made. As it has been stated:
"...there is no state that is not Śiva" (Spanda-kārikā 29).
Therefore, since everything consists of Śiva, when there is immersion (*āveśa*) into Him,
no effort whatsoever— consisting of the presentation of means (*upāya*) and so forth— is possible for the great-souled ones.
For indeed, it is only for the sake of attaining that which is remote that the application of effort should be made. || 214 ||
Thus it is said: "For this very reason, no effort is required for entry into that. (10.215)
For as there is distance, so too must there be the application of effort;
therefore, our teachers maintain that there is no room at all for means such as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like within Śiva.
Thus he says:
"The lack of scope for meditation, the instruments [of action], and so forth, within Śiva... (10.216).
For this very reason, those who possess the wealth of the tradition hold this view:

meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the like must have as their object that which is being meditated upon (*bhāvyamāna*) and so forth; however, it is not logical for this [the Self] to have such a status, because its nature is solely that of the subject (*pramātṛ*), and thus it is impossible for it to be an object of meditation and the like. As they say:
"There is no purpose whatsoever served by ritual action or even by meditative cultivation. (Śivadr̥ṣṭyāloka 7.6) || 216 ||
One might object: "Why should the application of effort be directed toward that which is remote rather than that which is proximate?
Anticipating this doubt, he dispels it by showing an analogy:
"For let the world be observed in this way, just as it is in the perception of a jar and so forth" (10.217).
In that way, does one appear as if possessing effort during the experience of pleasure?
"As if possessing effort" means because of being intent on inquiry and so forth. || 217 ||
Now, one might object: "In this way, only its internal nature—like that of pleasure and so forth—would be established, whereby it would be a means to pleasure;
however, how could its state of not being an object of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and the like be established as being caused by its identity with the supreme subject alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
They say that this "interiority" consists in possessing proximity to consciousness. (10.218)
And that [externalization] is the unfolding of consciousness as its own form, while externality is its closing;
for this very thing is called "interiority," which is said to be the manifestation of consciousness without distance or separation.
They declare that interiority consists in possessing proximity to consciousness.

One might object: "Even so, does its similarity to pleasure and the like remain exactly as it was? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And they call that the unfolding of the nature of consciousness. For what is intended here is this very state of being characterized by proximity to consciousness, which constitutes the predominance of the nature of consciousness. Therefore, it is precisely the immersion into the nature of consciousness [that is meant].
It has been stated that [the state of] externality is as follows: "Externality is its state of being closed off.

According to such statements as, "For difference from that is indeed externality... (Rigveda-prayoga 86), even though pleasure and the like are cognizable solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [they are nonetheless considered external].

It has been stated in many other places that [the object] possesses externalness precisely because it is characterized by a primary form of externality known as "expanding as something distinct. || 218 ||

Now, one might object: "If the internal nature of Śiva consists precisely in the predominance of his aspect as consciousness (cidrūpatā), and since that consciousness is self-luminous, it must be manifest everywhere; therefore, because it would be the most proximate to everyone, why does it not shine at all times? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But for those who are destined to be born, even that which is immediate does not appear as such; thus it is exceedingly remote.

"In this way" means according to the aforementioned process. For, precisely because they have come into being, they lack such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by which one would not fear them from all sides—this is the sense.
Therefore, since such a reflective awareness is impossible for them, the manifestation of consciousness remains far removed from them.
By which this vast display of saṃsāra [is produced]. As it has been said:
"If even the mere awareness of a dog constitutes an offense, how great is that offense!
Yet, by that alone, such a state is born as cannot even be described."
Thus [ends the section]. || 219 ||

Now, one might object: "In this world, distance is said to be threefold—due to separation in space, time, and intrinsic nature; yet this is not possible in the case of consciousness. How, then, can this [distinction] be stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For even that which is distant becomes near; how could its manifestation not occur here [in consciousness]?"

For even with respect to an object that is distant in space, when it comes into proximity through the power of effort, its manifestation occurs by virtue of that nearness; however, in the case of consciousness, distance is impossible to effect, because there is no such thing as moving away from it.
Having thus eliminated spatial remoteness from consciousness, he now eliminates it with respect to time as well:
"And [consciousness is not like] the seed, sprout, creeper, leaf, flower, fruit, and so forth. (10.220)
This consciousness would be gradual; therein, indeed, the sprout arises from the seed.
But here, the creeper does not arise from the sprout, nor from the seed, but rather from everything.

The reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), appearing as it does, is indeed complete in every respect; this [reality] cannot be sequential because it is not delimited by time. He describes the sequential nature of seeds and so forth with the words beginning "śūta... and so on. For even in the case of a creeper...

The point is this: if [the seed] were to arise from the seed itself, there would be no sequential order between the sprout and the creeper. Likewise, it should be understood that even for the leaf and so forth, there would be production only from the creeper and not from the sprout, whereby these [stages] would indeed possess a sequential order. Consciousness (saṃvit), however, because it is unconditioned by space and time, exists everywhere.

Since she shines forth at all times and in every respect, her state of being entirely full is expressed by the words "here," and so forth. Now, one might object: in the state of the cause, the effect is non-existent in the past, and thus it is "not yet come" (anāgata); however, here, since consciousness is occasional and therefore an effect, its being "come" (āgata) is logically established.
Anticipating the objection, "Since there is a temporal distance [between cognitions], how can it be said that this consciousness is not sequential?", he says:
"Because it is declared to be the cause of everything, and because it has arisen everywhere. (222)

If consciousness (*saṃvit*) were an effect, would consciousness itself be its cause, or some other insentient entity? In this regard, the fact that an insentient thing cannot logically function as a cause has already been established extensively above.
Furthermore, since the differentiation of one consciousness from another is untenable, consciousness is but a single, undivided whole; so what [could be its cause]?

"What is the cause, and what is the effect? The reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) alone is the cause of everything, for this entire universe is nothing but the unfolding of its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*). Therefore it has been said:
"It is arisen everywhere. And because it is arisen everywhere, it exists without any fixed location.
The remoteness of intrinsic nature has also been refuted. || 222 ||
One might object: "Granted that consciousness in its form as the subject (pramātṛ) may be the cause of everything;
but how can it attain such status when it takes the form of the cognition of specific objects of knowledge, such as a jar?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Therefore, if this movement of the vital breath should manifest even in a jar,
it would immediately find rest right there and go to dissolution in the seed of Śiva.

Therefore, because this function of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti)— which is determined by its nature as the fifteenfold [vowels] and so forth— is a cause for all things due to its universal arising, even if it were to manifest and find rest within a jar,
and even if it were to undergo arising and dissolution there with a sense of necessity, nevertheless, in that case...

The meaning is as follows: immediately upon the aforementioned reality, one should dissolve entirely into the seed of Śiva alone, and thus manifest as consisting of nothing but perfectly full light and awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*).

By the word "instantly" (*āśu*), the distinction between the sequence of powers (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*)—which arises through the succession of intermediate *tuṭi*-moments—is [overcome].
It has been stated that, because its essence consists solely of luminosity, there is no [independent] reality whatsoever. || 223 ||
For this very reason, he says:
"But there is never any succession whatsoever within the state of being Śiva.
Now, it might be argued that rest in the state of being Śiva has been described as occurring through the lineage of the mantras, their lords, the great lords (maheśas), and so forth.

Even though this sequence is not ultimately real, it is nonetheless not non-existent, because it appears as such by the will of Śiva; let it be so, with the intention that Śiva alone is the cause of everything in the sense of being the supreme cause.
But how can the intermediate causes, such as the Lords of Mantras and so forth, be set aside?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Other [factors] such as the lords of mantras and so forth are the cause; however, that [is so] due to their proximity. (10.224)
Furthermore, [the status of being a cause] arises either from non-difference from Śiva, or else, in the case of duality, from the perception of proximity.
For instance, just as clay alone, while remaining one and the same, becomes the cause of a jar through the sequence of states such as the brick,
the mound, and the lump— yet it is not logical to say that only the lump and so forth are the cause within the nature of the effect.
Because there is no such persistence [of the cause], it is appropriate to say that each particular state is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like a staff or other tools.

For this indeed is an instrument: that which, while being actively engaged in accomplishing an effect, does not intervene as a separate causal factor. Thus, in this context, Śiva alone, consisting of perfect consciousness, is the agent.
The cause of the universe is the sequence of states beginning with the Lord of Mantras (mantrādhipati), which are manifested by His own will;

it is not, however, that the state of the Lord of Mantras and so forth alone is the cause. For while they may indeed be instruments (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being employed by the agent, they do not themselves exert activity in the manifestation of the universe, nor do they [act independently].
Even in such a state, [the existence of] Śiva as the perfect conscious Self would obstruct His causality;

therefore, it has been stated that just like the powers of Will and so forth, the agency of the Lords of Mantras (Mantrādhipatis) and others is alone logical—meaning that there is no other instrument (karaṇa) besides the Lords of Mantras and so forth. As for that which...

By such statements as, "In the pure path Śiva is said to be the agent; Ananta is the lord in the impure," the causality of the Mantrādhipatis and others is expressed; that is merely figurative—so he says with the words "the cause," etc.
"That" refers to the Mantrādhipatis and so forth. "Due to proximity" means...

Just as space, time, ether, and so forth [are causes] in the production of a jar; "due to non-difference from Śiva" means that since it has been stated that Śiva is the cause, the Lords of Mantras and others are likewise called such because they are non-different from Him, just as the form and other qualities of the clay—which is the cause of the jar—are non-different from it. This is because, even within duality, there is a perception of proximity.

In the state of differentiation, these [means of knowledge] function according to their respective proximity to the subject under the influence of Māyā, like an executioner appointed by the king's command. || 224 ||
And one should cultivate a firm conviction that this alone is the supreme object to be attained; thus he says: "And by this method, constantly discriminating everything," (10.225).
Having suddenly attained the state of the Lord of the Wheel of Consciousness (*cic-cakra*) from within Bhairava himself, he concludes the present subject:
"In this way, this division residing in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is hidden within the wheel of the *khecarīs*... (10.226).
This has been revealed by me, who follows the glorious command of Śambhu.
Now, following the sequence of the principles (tattvas), he describes the states of waking and so forth as indicated in the subsequent enumeration:
"In this very path, when the state of being an object of knowledge is attained, whatever consciousness arises... (10.227).
Its own inherent variety is designated by the term "states" (avasthā).

Here, within the path of reality (tattvādhvan) and so forth— which is defined by the sequence beginning with the fifteenfold [principles] and has attained the status of an object of knowledge (prameya) as its very nature— there exists that which consists of each individual subject, beginning with Śiva.
In this way, Consciousness alone shines forth; its own manifold diversity— conditioned by various objects of knowledge manifested according to its own will,
and brought about by their respective commonality or uniqueness— is revealed.
The meaning of the sentence is that it would be designated by the terms for states such as waking and so forth. || 227 ||
He analyzes the very stages [of consciousness]:
waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), and that which transcends it. (10.228)
Thus they speak of five states when there is a single perceiver;

"that which transcends those" refers to the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). Regarding the phrase "when there is a single perceiver": for if there were multiple perceivers, one would be in the waking state while another would be in the dreaming state, and thus the very nature of these states as distinct conditions would be lost.
Furthermore, there would be no fivefold nature [of the body], for such a state of these [elements] could only exist with reference to a single substratum—this is the intended meaning. || 228 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, would not the states of waking and so forth also necessarily apply to Śiva alone, who is of the nature that transcends the fourth (turyātīta)? Anticipating this doubt, he accepts that very point:
"In that regard, this sequence of principles (tattva-paddhati), beginning from the earth-principle and ending with Śiva... (10.229).
If there is but a single cognizer within that [universe], then the states of waking and so forth must necessarily exist;
this has been revealed by Śambhunātha and is known by me through his grace. (10.230)

The word "one" refers either to Śiva in his entirety or to [the individual soul]. By the word "necessarily," it is indicated that otherwise this would not be so. And this is not being stated by us as our own invention; thus he says: "That is shown," and so forth. (230)
He states that very point:
"That which is here only the object of presiding and never the presider, the knowable residing within consciousness—that is declared to be the waking state. (10.231)
He clarifies the meaning of the particle *eva* itself: "never as a presiding controller.
The phrase "residing in consciousness" implies that otherwise it would not even possess the status of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*); this is the intended sense.
For it has been stated many times that within its own self, there is neither the cognized nor the non-cognized. || 231 ||
He elaborates on this very point:

"The elements such as Caitra and Maitra, the principles beginning with Earth, the words that serve as the instruments of denotation, and furthermore, the denotation itself, and the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). (10.232)

When this fourfold universe—consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing—is presided over [by consciousness], that state is known as waking. (10.233)

"Beings" (bhūtāni): because they are included within the fourteenfold creation of beings, by this term everything from the Piśācas up to humans—excluding stationary objects—is subsumed. "Sounds" (śabdāḥ):
although they are objects of cognition because they are included within the principles starting with Earth (dharā), they are nonetheless included here because they produce cognition in others.
It has been stated that [the means of knowledge] possesses the nature of a valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*)—namely, that they are "the instruments of expression" (*abhidhākaraṇībhūta*).
"Expression" (*abhidhā*) is so called because it consists in the cognition of an object; thus, its meaning is that it takes the form of a result (*phalarūpa*).

In this way, when this fourfold set consisting of the knower (*mātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the valid cognition (*pramā*) is itself of the nature of that which is to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*), [it is subsumed within the Lord].
Then that which is remembered as waking would indeed be this waking state—this is the meaning. || 232 ||
He demonstrates the very relationship between the presiding subject and the object presided over by analyzing it as follows:
"For that which appears internally in the cognition of the nature of volition as 'blue,' that [internal appearance] is the presiding subject and the illuminator of the external. (10.234)
That which appears as blue by way of externality, and for which there exists no state of being a presiding subject in any manner whatsoever—that is called waking. (10.235)

Whatever blue or other [object] appears within consciousness—which consists of volition and so forth—as being identical with it, that [consciousness] is the substratum; for it is the illuminator and the manifestor of the external cognition of blue and so forth—this is the meaning.
And therefore, because it is an object of cognition, the external blue [is established as such].

Since it is not able to attain the state of a presiding subject in any way whatsoever—because its nature is solely that of the object to be presided over—it is everywhere described as being essentially the waking state.
Thus, it has been rightly said: "That which is the object to be presided over is the waking state. (235)

Now, one might ask: "Even though these four are equally objects of presiding, is there any mutual distinction between them or not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard, when Caitra appears, that which is the bodily portion is described as follows:"
That which is the portion of the non-enlightened mind is the enlightened one who performs the act of cognition.
The sequence is: the awakened, the well-awakened, and the mere valid cognition (*pramā*).
The phrase "a part of the body" means that because the body is composed of the elements, it is of the nature of an object of knowledge (*prameya*);
and since its activity consists of the impelling of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, there is contact with that [object]. Thus [it is said].

The state of Buddhahood has been ascribed to the *māna* (the "I-maker") component. For, as was stated previously, it is through contact with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth that these [components] come to possess consciousness. Regarding the term "the agent of measurement" (*mitikāraka*):

one who performs measurement (*miti*) is a "measurer" (*mitikāra*); a measurer who is himself the act of measuring is a "measurer-agent" (*mitikāraka*), which means the subjective aspect (*pramātr-aṃśa*). That...

And because [the subject] consists of the nature of cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth, he is called "awakened. As for the term "well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*), because he is devoid of the turbidity of the object of knowledge and consists solely of the form of consciousness characterized by repose within his own self, he is the "pure means of knowledge" (*pramāmātra*); that is to say, he is the aspect of valid cognition (*pramiti*). || 236 ||
Nor has the state of being non-Buddha and so forth been stated by us here as our own invention; thus he says:
"For the fourfold nature is proclaimed within the waking state called Piṇḍastha. (10.237)
Now, an objection may be raised: "It has been stated that the five states, beginning with waking, are mutually distinct;
how then is there this well-known experience of their being largely intermingled, such as 'waking-dream' or 'waking-sleep'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For here, each of the four states beginning with waking is present;
"each" means in relation to one another, and thus the well-known designations such as "waking-waking," "waking-sleep," and so forth are not contradicted—this is established. || 237 ||

It is not only that such a form exists here, but even forms such as those of the unawakened and so forth—as he says: "The waking-within-waking is the unawakened; the waking-dream, however, is the state of being awakened. (10.238)
And so forth. But as for the *turyātīta* (the state beyond the fourth), how could it be distinct [from the others], given its all-pervasiveness?
Now, it has been stated that there are "five states," and the nature of the first four as being of the form of the unawakened (*abuddha*) and so on has been explained;
but what is the nature of the *turyātīta*, then?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the *turyātīta*..."

"How could there be any separation [of the fourth] since it is all-pervasive? (Śivasūtra 1.18). According to the perspective of the Śivasūtras, as in the statement, "The fourth should be poured like oil into the three" (Śivasūtra 2.30), where even the fourth is undivided everywhere, what need is there to speak further?
The intended meaning is "of that which transcends the fourth state. || 238 ||
He confirms this very point:
"And it has been said that the waking state residing in the body is both unawakened and awakened. (10.239)
"This is remembered as fourfold: *prabuddha* (awakened) and *suprabuddha* (well-awakened).
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*. It is said there:
"The fourfold [state] is indeed *piṇḍastha* (situated in the body), namely the unawakened (*abuddha*) and the awakened (*buddha*)."
"The awakened and the well-awakened... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.43). || 239 ||

Thus, although the four states are mutually intermingled, he declares that the state of the object of knowledge (*prameyapada*), described in the passage beginning with "that portion of the body which... and so forth, is the primary waking state:
"This ground of the object of knowledge is the primary one called waking; the others are intermediate. (10.240)

"Other" means that which consists of parts such as the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth, namely dreams and the like. "In between" means that which falls within those [categories] and is secondary—this is the meaning. || 240 ||
"Is it not the case that the waking state alone is the primary ground of the object of knowledge?"—
anticipating this doubt, he says:
"That portion of the designations for the elements and the principles which is said to be the substrate..."
"They call that 'situated in the body' (piṇḍastha)," according to the venerable Mālinīmata. (10.241)
Now, one might object: "In this way, on the plane of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), would not *piṇḍastha* alone be said to be primary, and not the waking state (*jāgrat*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that this is merely another name for the waking state itself:
"This worldly [state] is called 'waking' (*jāgrat*), and it is also called 'the state of being in the body' (*piṇḍastha*)."
This terminology is defined for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga. || 10-242 ||
As it has been said:
"Piṇḍastha and Sarvatobhadra are considered the two names for the waking state" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.36). || 242 ||
Now, one might ask: what is the reason for defining that which is accomplished through yoga as "piṇḍastha" (abiding in the body)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the yogin who dwells in the state of identification with that which is to be presided over..."
Identity, it is said, resides in the body; for the body is measured and is indeed a compacted whole.

The state of identity with the earth and so forth— which is a specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of the complete union (*samāpatti*) with that which is to be absorbed— belongs to the yogi who rests upon it; that identity with the earth and other elements is called "situated in the body" (*piṇḍastha*) in the scriptures, because [the reality] is measured by the earth and so forth as a unified whole (*piṇḍita*).
The meaning is: a mass of reality that has become embodied by avoiding disintegration, which contains within itself the various categories of objects, and which is all-pervasive in nature. || 243 ||

This is not merely another technical designation for the waking state; indeed, there is yet another—thus he says: "But that [state] is said to belong to the knowers who are firmly established solely in *prasaṃkhyāna*."
It is auspicious in every respect and completely full, owing to the reality of the altar existing on all sides.

The word "that" refers to the waking state. If one asks what the reason is for using this technical definition here, the following is stated in response: "It is filled on all sides by the existence of the objects of knowledge. (244)
Even so, what is the intention behind this restriction of designations only for those intent upon *prasaṃkhyāna*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because one should perceive the universe as completely filled with the existence of all things, from whatever [perspective]."
For the knower, the reality of consciousness shines forth from that very state.
Anticipating the objection— "In this case, how is the restriction that there are only three designations established?"— he says: "Indeed,
by virtue of the threefold nature of worldly usage, yoga, and enumeration..."
Three names are spoken; this same procedure applies even in cases such as dreams.

He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "This same rule applies even to dream and so forth. By this, there are the worldly designations: dream, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya); the etymological designations: the state of the word (padastha), the form (rūpa), and that which transcends form (rūpātīta); and the technical designations of knowledge: pervasion (vyāpti), great pervasion (mahāvyāpti), and accumulation (pracaya). [This applies] up to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).

Furthermore, with the perspective that will be explained later—namely, that yoga should not be "scorched"—it is stated, with the intention of enumerating the worldly states, that there are only two designations: *turyātīta* and *mahāpracaya*. || 246 ||
Having thus described the waking state, he now describes the dreaming state as well:

"That which exists by presiding over the state of the instruments [of perception], being an object of knowledge as previously described, consisting of the elements, the principles, and designations. (10.247)
That dream should be understood primarily as being on the path of conceptualization (*vaikalpika*). Furthermore,

that which was stated regarding Caitra, Maitra, and other beings— even while lying down in the waking state— refers to that which remains primarily by occupying the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the act of presiding over the reality of the elements (*bhūtatattva*).
The meaning is: this state of dream is characterized by measurement (*māna*), appearing as a shadow of what is to be measured (*meyacchāyāvabhāsinī*).

By the phrase "primarily" (*mukhyataḥ*), the intention is that although other divisions such as the waking-dream (*svapnajāgrat*) and so forth are also possible for this [state], they are secondary. Now, [one might ask] regarding that which consists of both conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*)...
One might ask: "If these two feet also possess such a nature, with reference to what has this been stated?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that object of knowledge [is found] on the path of conceptual construction. As it has been said: "Dreams are conceptual constructions" (Śivasūtra 1.9). || 247 ||

An objection may be raised: "Is it not the case that in the world, at the time of sleep, for everyone, the experience of various objects occurs through non-conceptual mental activity alone, as witnessed by one's own experience? What then [is the point of this discussion]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because there is the appearance of an equality with the objects mounted upon the path of conceptualization. (248)
This dream is also established in common worldly usage, and its similarity [to waking experience] consists in its lack of external form.

For even in the world, the state of dreaming has attained its development by referring to an appearance that is equivalent to a conceptual object, precisely because it is uncommon [to the dreamer alone] and so forth; thus, nothing unprecedented has been stated here—"and that...".

"It should be known [to occur] on the path of mental construction (*vaikalpika*). Now, one might ask: "From what source does such a similarity arise regarding the appearance of objects in both mental construction and dream? Anticipating this, it is said: "And [their] similarity consists in their non-external nature. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. The intended meaning is that precisely because they lack external form, qualities such as uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*) and so forth would apply to them here.
Thus, even though the meaning is conceptual, he divides it into two types based on clarity and lack of clarity:
"In visions such as poetic fancy (utprekṣā), dreams, imagination, memory, madness, and so forth... (10.249).
Whatever class of objects is clearly manifest, that belongs primarily to the waking state;
and this must be stated here as being the object of fear and so forth. As it has been said:
"By the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it appears clearly, just as in the case of fear and the like."
"That cognition which is non-contradictory is perception, free from conceptual construction.

For it has been stated that through intense fear, passion, and so forth, even an assailant or a beloved woman appearing before one may cause terror or longing; thus, it is said that "the range of objects of knowledge is clearly manifest. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), desire, grief, and the like are included.
As it has been said:
"Those who are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, dreams of thieves, and so forth,
perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them."

Thus [it is said]: "primarily" (mukhyatayā) is because clarity (*spaṣṭatva*) is the unique characteristic of the waking state; therefore, since the object is conceptual (*vaikalpika*), it has the nature of a dream, yet because of its clarity, it has the nature of the waking state—thus it would be called this "dream-waking. || 249 ||
Having thus described dream-waking, he now describes dream-dream as well:
"That which, even there, appears indistinct yet possesses a distinct presiding subject. (10.250)

The object of cognition that falls within another conceptual construction is called the state of dreaming. The particle *api* is displaced [in the verse]. Therefore, even when there is a presiding agent no different from that of the waking state, the collection of objects of cognition—which is indistinct because it falls within another conceptual construction—shines forth again therein, such as in the case of imagination (*utprekṣā*) and so forth.
That is called the state of dream; because it has the nature of a dream within a dream, it is the primary dream—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "Surely here the distinction between waking and dreaming has been stated on the basis of the clarity and lack of clarity of the object;
yet that clarity and lack of clarity are also observed in places such as temples due to proximity and distance.
Therefore, how can this [distinction] be established by that alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
At that very moment, he indeed knows for himself its lack of externality.

"At that very moment" means without deliberation; "of that" refers to the object that is the focus of the imaginative perception; "by itself" means not from the words of a reliable authority, as in the case of a double moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia. || 251 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Well then, what is meant by 'non-externality'?", he says: "It consists in the loss of being common to other subjects and in having an unstable nature;
for if an object were external, it would necessarily be common to all subjects and stable."
The state of being.
Now, one might ask: "In this context, is there only the distinction between dreaming, waking, and so forth, or is there something else as well?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There too, one should conceive of that fourfold division according to the same direction previously indicated. (10.252)
"Going and coming," "well-dispersed," "conjoined," and "well-composed"—

the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that this fourfold state exists not only during wakefulness but also in sleep. The phrase "as before" (*prāgdiśeva*) refers to [the states] existing as objects of cognition and so forth.

And also by way of being situated within dreams within dreams and so forth. He states this very point with the words "coming and going," etc. These [experiences] arise respectively through the connection with the coming and going produced by the movement of the breath over thirty-six finger-breadths, and through contact with objects delineated in extremely distant space and time.

There are four divisions with names corresponding to their literal meanings: [the first] because of its association with the mind alone whose sole function is conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), and [the second] because of its one-pointedness toward an object of conceptual construction (*vaikalpika*).
As it has been said:

"Having begun with: 'They maintain that dream is of two types: that which abides in the state (*padastha*) and that which is pervasion (*vyāpti*),' [the text continues: 'And that which abides in the state is fourfold. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.37)
"Going and coming, well-dispersed, gathered together, and well-composed. (Māyājāla-tantra 2.44) || 252 ||
Even in dream, there is a threefold distinction of designations just as in the waking state; thus he says:
"In this case too, as before, the worldly name for this is 'dream' (svapna). (10.253)
Indeed, sleep is considered the non-perception of external objects;
the vital breath (prāṇa) is the ground of all paths, and volition consists of the nature of comprehension. (10.254)

Yogis know that "pada" (the state/foot) is its meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and that one who abides in that state is "established in the *pada*. Anticipating the question—"What is the reason for applying the word 'dream' even in this worldly context?"—it is said: "For sleep is the non-perception of objects regarded as external. [And] "the *pada* of the entire path (*adhvan*)."
How this state [of being established] is so has already been determined in the sixth chapter (*ṣaṣṭhāhnika*).

Since everything is traversed—that is, known—by means of this, intention (*saṅkalpa*), being of the nature of comprehension, is also called "the word" (*pada*); and identity with that very [intention] is said to be "abiding in that" (*tad-sthatva*).
Thus it was stated: "Abiding in the word is absorption (*samāpatti*) in that. By that...

The meaning is: identity with the vital breath (prāṇa) and identity with volition (saṅkalpa). By the word "of the yogins," it is stated that this designation pertains to the subject of yoga. || 254 ||
Thus, he applies another designation even by virtue of being the object of the Knower: "Without depending at all upon the existence of an object situated outside [the self]... (10.255).
In the state of the knowable, knowledge, possessing autonomy, should partake of the dream-state by way of pervasion.

Indeed, in this world, having abandoned dependence on external forms, conceptual knowledge— which effects conjunction and disjunction— while remaining entirely autonomous and delineating only objects inscribed within its own self, is itself the dream.
The meaning is: one should worship and conduct oneself accordingly toward those who possess knowledge, as if they were all-pervasive. || 255 ||

And just as the object of knowledge (prameya) holds primacy in the waking state, so too does the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) here; thus he says: "This is the primary ground of the means of knowledge, for the dream state consists essentially of reflective awareness (āmarśana). (10.256)

"The reason for the predominance of *māna* (cognition) is that dream is indeed of the nature of reflective awareness (*āmarśana*). The phrase "of the nature of reflective awareness" means that it is of the nature of certainty (*niścaya*), because its form is mental determination (*avasāya*). || 256 ||
For the reflection of the object of knowledge (vedya) that appears within the object of cognition is called the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna);
it is certainly the very form of that which was previously mentioned as the presiding agent (adhiṣṭhātṛ), such as Bhūta and the rest. (10.257)
That seed of the universe, when it has become silent, is called the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*).
An objection may be raised: "But it was stated that dream consists of the activity of presiding over instruments;
how then is its nature here described as consisting of reflective awareness (*āmarśana*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For he who is the seer in both experience and conceptualization is indeed that very same one.
Therefore, there is no grasping of existence, and thus the state of "deep sleep" (sauṣupta) is spoken of.
That very one who is called the cognizer (pramātṛ) in the waking and dream states is the same in deep sleep as well;
for he is a cognizer because he cognizes, and by virtue of being a cognizer, he necessarily involves the agitation of the object of cognition (meyam), the means of cognition (māna), and so forth.

Anticipating the objection, "How can it be said that [the subject] must exist while remaining silent? he says: "For that very [consciousness] is not the grasping of an object. Indeed, the knower himself is not the object of knowledge (*prameya*), nor is he the grasping, which is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); for if that were the case, this fourfold division would not exist, and consequently, the entire worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would collapse.

It would perish; therefore, without the agitation of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meya*), the knower (*pramātṛ*) too would rest solely in his own self, whereby this state is everywhere proclaimed as "deeply asleep. || 258 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is even deep sleep—a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—referred to as 'deep sleep' (suṣupta) in common worldly parlance? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"On account of its similarity to that [state], the wise consider ordinary sleep to be deep sleep. (10.259)
The state of being a seed, then non-apprehension, equanimity, and the nature of silence.
Raising the question, "What indeed is that equanimity?", it is said: "the nature of silence.
Raising the further question, "Even in the nature of silence, what is the cause?", he says: "the state of being a seed."
Thus, because of the connection with future effects that are being anticipated, and because of the non-perception of external objects, it is called "non-apprehension. || 259 ||
And this alone is the primary state of deep sleep, like the waking-within-waking and so forth; thus he says:
"This very primary state of the subject is called by the name 'deep sleep'. (10.260)

This [reality] also possesses two designations, just as before, by virtue of being the object of the knowledge of yogins; thus he says: "And because it is form (*rūpa*), it is called *Rūpa*; furthermore, for the yogin, identity with that is *Rūpastha*. They know *Rūpin* to be the state of indifference resulting from absorption (*samāpatti*) in that. (10.261)
Since there is no further contraction of the object of knowledge for one who possesses higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), this great pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) exists accordingly. (10.262)

Because the universe has the pure subject (*pramātṛ*) as its sole essence, the "form" (*rūpa*)—namely, the subject—is so called because it "forms," that is, it makes the various objects of experience possess form by assimilating them into its own self. Identity with that [subject] is what the yogis know as "abiding in form" (*rūpastha*), and they act accordingly—this is the meaning. Now, if this is so...
Anticipating the objection—"If there is identity with the subject (*pramātṛaikātmya*) for yogins, what is the difference between the fourth state (*turya*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*)?"—he says:

"By absorption into that, there is indifference (*audāsīnya*) toward things possessing form. For here, through absorption into the nature of the subject, there is indifference—that is, a lack of interest—toward objects possessing form; but this is not as in the fourth state, where [indifference] extends to everything.

"Dissolution" (vigalanam) means that by which there would be no distinction. "By that" (tena) means by the reason of the non-existence of the contraction of the object of knowledge—this is the meaning. "'In accordance with that'" (tadanusārataḥ) means having followed the one who possesses discernment (prasaṃkhyānavat)—this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"But the Great Pervasion resides in form; even for one in deep sleep, those two [exist]. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.37) || 262 ||
Here too, as in the case of the "abiding-in-the-mass" (piṇḍastha) and so forth, there is a fourfold division; thus he says:
"Even for that [subject] who is indifferent, the object of knowledge is fourfold.
Here, this fourfold division arises from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the elements and so forth. (10.263)
Furthermore, there is another [state] which is arisen (*udita*), expansive (*vipula*), tranquil (*śānta*), and perfectly serene (*suprasanna*).

Even for a cognizer who is devoid of the agitation of the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) and so forth, the objects of knowledge—such as the elements (*bhūta*) and the principles (*tattva*)—are fourfold according to the distinctions of being "arisen" and so on, as will be explained; by that [cognizer], even [the object] is [perceived].
The meaning of the sentence is that there are precisely four distinctions—joy (*mudita*) and so forth—which arise through the power of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
It is called "arisen" (*udita*) because it persists as the nature of mere latent impression (*saṃskāra*). It is called "expanded" (*vipula*) because it grows in that very same way.
It is called "tranquil" (*śānta*) because its latent impressions have dissolved. It is called "perfectly serene" (*suprasanna*)...
This arises from the orientation toward the essence of the emerging sense of ego. As it has been said:

"Those who contemplate yoga should know that [the state] established in form is fourfold: the arisen, the expansive, the tranquil, and another which is the perfectly serene" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.44).
Thus [ends the section]. || 263 ||
Now, he defines the fourth state, which follows in sequence: "That form which consists of valid cognition and stands above the cognizer. (10.264)
The state of being oriented toward attaining fullness, which is a departure from indifference, is called the Fourth (turya); for this is considered to be the immersion into Śakti. (10.265)

The phrase "of the knower" refers to that which has been measured; for the intention is that even all four modes [of manifestation] are merely the unfolding of the sovereignty of the Full One. He demonstrates this very state of being situated above:
"the inclination toward attaining fullness is a falling away from indifference. But how is this so?

One might ask: "In the fourth state (turya), does there not arise a tendency toward the apprehension of one's own true nature simply through the subordination of indifference? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For this is considered to be immersion into Śakti.
The meaning is that immersion into Śakti—which consists of reflective awareness—is indeed its predominance.

Now, one might raise this doubt: "What is this so-called 'orientation toward attaining fullness' (pūrṇatāgamana-pratyaunmukhya)? Is its form complete or incomplete? If it is incomplete, then it is merely the states of waking and so forth; if it is complete, then it is simply the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). What, then, is this intermediate state called the Fourth (turya)? Anticipating this, he says:

However, some have asserted that consciousness is self-luminous and entirely distinct from the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower, since there exists a triad for that purpose. (10.266)

The meaning of the sentence is that some have stated that this consciousness, which is of the nature of the Fourth (*turya*), is indeed distinct from the objects of knowledge and so forth because of its self-luminosity; for otherwise, in the doctrine of illumination by another (*paraprakāśavāda*) and in the doctrine of immediate consciousness (*aparokṣasaṃvidvāda*) where it is [defined] as luminosity, it would [be known] through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the same kind.

The distinction from the knower would not be established. Now, one might ask: "From where does its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) also derive? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Because that triad exists for its sake. This means that since that triad of waking and so forth exists within that very consciousness, [consciousness] is that which possesses the object—the nature of an object—and that which possesses the *artha*, meaning the seeking or longing (*yācñā-kāṅkṣā*).

The meaning is: "tending toward rest within that consciousness. For otherwise, if even that [consciousness], which consists of resting in states such as waking and so forth, were to tend toward another rest, there would be an infinite regress—this is the intended sense. || 266 ||
Anticipating the question, "And how do these rest within her? he says:
"The object of knowledge rests in the means of knowledge, that [means] clearly rests in the knower, and he too rests in that act of measurement;
thus she alone is this Goddess, the sole life-force of the universe. (10.267)

The term *devī* means "shining," because she is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatvāt*). She is the "sole life-force of the universe" (*viśvaikajīvitam*), because everything—including the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth—rests within her. As it has been said:
"The object of knowledge attains the state of the knower; the knower attains the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvidātmatām*)."
"If it is true that the Self is consciousness itself, then this world is composed of you. || 267 ||

Now, one might object: "Since this cognition, which is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is established by the triad beginning with the object of knowledge (*meyādi*), therefore the object and the others are its life-force, but it is not theirs; why then was it said [that they are its life-force]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"It exists having transcended the three parts: the form, the vision, and 'I'."
The means that rely merely on the gateway are without means when one thinks "I see. (10.268)
This very subjectivity, whose nature is absolute freedom, shines forth;
it is the very form of the fourth state of consciousness (turya), and it is itself the essence of light.
"Form" is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), "the act of seeing" is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and "I" is the knower (*pramātṛ*).
This very pure, supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*), which is the sole life-force of the universe, transcends these three aspects;
yet, after its outward expansion in the form "I see," it returns [to itself].

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: that which consists of supreme subjectivity (*parapramātṛtā*), whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantryamayi*), is that by which one relies on the means (*upāya*)—characterized by the triad of the object of knowledge (*meyādi*) and so forth—which serves as the door for resting within one's own self; yet, in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is devoid of and incompatible with any such means. Now, [one might ask: what is distinct from the object, the instrument, and the agent?
One perceives the fourth form, which presides over the state of fruition, as luminosity;

however, no consciousness other than that manifests, of which one could say, "I see," for which a gateway might be spoken of?—anticipating this doubt, he says: "It shines. The word "and" (ca) indicates a reason; for she is the nature of the supreme subject.

Pure consciousness shines by itself; it is not, however, the ground for the emergence of conceptual constructions such as "I see"—this is the meaning. For that very [consciousness] is the self of even that light of "I see" which is considered the fourth state (*turya*);
indeed, if it were not shining even for a moment, nothing at all would manifest. (269)
Therefore, he says:
"When there is identity through immersion in that [object], the state of being a subject (*mātṛtva*) becomes manifest;
through the coloring of immersion in that, the state of being a means of knowledge (*mānatva*) arises, and furthermore, the state of being an object (*meyatā*). (10.270)
Due to the proximity of immersion (*samāveśa*) into that [state], the triad [of subject, object, and means] is [perceived] through its respective grace;
for the subject and so forth possess a certain distance when compared to the fourth consciousness (*turyasaṃvit*), as it has been said:
"in the identity with immersion into that," and "through the coloring of immersion into that."
And because of the proximity to that immersion. || 270 ||
Furthermore, the doctrine of consciousness that is distinct from the means and results of valid cognition is precisely what is followed by the established tradition of the scriptures; thus he says:
"Because the distinctions such as the object of knowledge have dissolved, this very [consciousness] is said to be 'free from affliction' (anāmaya). (10.271)
She is called "active" (savyāpārā) because she bestows grace upon [the disciple] through the Mothers and others.

She is said to be so "immediately hereafter" in this very context; for the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* will provide a corroboration not far from here, stating: "She is called both free from affliction and active. (271)
He applies this very point even through the perspective of his own philosophical system:
"Even the states of waking and so forth are established as the power (śakti) of the Lord. (10.272)

Furthermore, that [power] is twofold: the lower (apara) and the higher-lower (parāpara); however, this one is the supreme (parā). Thus, it has been stated that "that [power] is twofold"—referring to the triad beginning with waking—which is the Supreme Lord’s power; here, "she" refers to the power, while "this" refers to the consciousness consisting of the fourth state (turyā), which is supreme.
Waking and dreaming are the lower; deep sleep is the higher-lower; and the fourth state is the higher. || 272 ||
Here too, as before, there is a difference in designation; thus he says:
"Because she has fallen from the state of being a mere form (rūpaka) and from indifference, she is oriented toward fullness. (10.273)

In that state of meditative absorption, the yogi, having transcended form, perceives the universe as consisting of that [consciousness], because he is engaged in the orientation toward fullness. || 10.274 ||
Because it is reckoned through accumulation, this is considered "Accumulation" (pracaya).

When one has fallen away from being an indifferent subject due to the orientation toward fullness, and from being a limited subject, this state of the Fourth (turya) among yogis is called "Attainment" (samāpatti), even though its form is measured.
Because he has transcended the mother (the source of manifestation), he is called "beyond form" (*ūrpatīta*). The term "by accumulation" (*pracayataḥ*) means by virtue of being gathered into a mass;

for this very reason, it is said that he is "composed of that" (*tanmaya*), because the universe is perceived as if it were a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand due to its state of accumulation—this is the meaning. Thus it has been said:
"Accumulation and that which transcends form are declared to be the fourth state of perfection. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.38) || 274 ||

One might object: "In this state as well, since there is mutual intermingling, would a fourfold nature—not unlike that of waking and the other states—not be possible? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, in this [state], another fourth stage (*turya*) is not conceivable. (10.275)
It is said that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not an object of cognition, for it shines precisely as the act of cognizing itself.

Since the Fourth State (*turya*) is supreme consciousness, and its very nature is exclusively that of the cognizer, it cannot even have contact with the state of being an object; how then could this [consciousness] be so?
May it attain the nature of both the object of knowledge and the subject of knowledge, so that, presiding over both states, it may even become the Fourth-of-the-Fourth (turyaturya). || 275 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then could the states of the fourth (turya) and waking (jāgrat), and so forth, not also be possible?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the three states beginning with waking are possible for her [the Fourth] as prior conditions. (10.276)
Because it favors these three, this [state] is described in the Trika teaching as *manonmana*, *ananta*, and *sarvārtha*, according to their distinctions. (10.277)

"These states are conceivable," for the waking state and the others are indeed the unfolding of the sovereignty of the Supreme Consciousness itself; therefore he says: "Because she [the Goddess] bestows grace upon this triad. For this very reason, in accordance with the waking state and the others, she is described as being of three kinds in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara); thus he says:

"—By that," and so forth. "By that" means by virtue of being the sustainer of the three states beginning with waking. "Manonmana" (the state beyond mind) refers to the waking state, because there the mental function of thinking has transcended its own activity due to the predominance of non-conceptuality (*avikalpaka*). "Ananta" (the infinite) refers to the dream state, because it does not depend upon objects, senses, and so forth.
Because there is no restriction of place, time, and so forth; it is "for all purposes" because in deep sleep the universe exists in the form of its causal power (śakti). || 277 ||
Having thus described the Fourth state, he now describes that which transcends the Fourth:
"That which is full, of an undivided nature, and overflowing with bliss—that they call the state beyond the Fourth; that alone is the supreme station. (10.278)
One might object: "Is there not a fifth state called *turyātīta* (beyond the fourth), or does no state exist beyond this?

Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "That alone is the supreme state (*parama-pada*). It is called "supreme" because it is free from any further longing, being the abode of ultimate rest; for this very reason, it is described as having a "full and undivided form."
And [it is described as] "filled with bliss. || 278 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as three names have been assigned to each of the four states, such as waking and the rest, by virtue of worldly convention, yoga, and contemplation (prasaṃkhyāna), why are they not likewise stated here?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

In this [state], there is no existence of yoga because of the absence of cultivation (bhāvanā) and so forth; for how could there be anything to be cultivated in that which is immeasurable, undetermined, and independent? (10.279)
Because of the absence of yoga and the like, the All-pervasive Lord designated [the name] "Nāma" for this;
"because of that" means because of the non-existence of yoga and so forth. How this is so has been explained in the second chapter and elsewhere.
Therefore, since here there is only the single form of consciousness, only *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) follows; with this very intention, he says:
"But by the power of *prasaṃkhyāna*, this form [arises] through its connection with fullness. (10.280)

The state called Mahāpracaya is proclaimed here as being unsurpassed (anuttara). By the word "this form" (etadrūpam), there is a reference to that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). Now, one might ask: "In the Fourth State (turya), the designation 'accumulation' (pracaya) was mentioned;
what is the reason for its even greater magnitude here? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
Regarding the phrase "from the Anuttara," it means "due to its connection with fullness. "From the Anuttara" refers to the Fourth State (*turya*).
For while in that [Fourth State] the nature of consciousness is transcendent of the universe, here, even though it is likewise, it consists of the universe;
thus, it possesses a greatness even greater than that. As it has been said:
"The wise desire the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) to be the Great Accumulation (mahāpracaya)," so it is said in the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra (2.38). || 280 ||
For this very reason, just as there is no accumulation here, there is not even the possibility of difference; thus, no distinction has been mentioned as a differentiator—so he says:
"Indeed, because of its fullness, there is no possibility of differences within it. (10.281)
To refute that [objection], no distinction is stated as a qualifier for this [state].
But surely, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* it is said: "Manonmana, Ananta, Sarvārtha, and Satatodita..."
"In that accumulation, this one [state] is to be designated as situated within that Great Light.
By such statements, even in the *mahāpracaya* (great accumulation), the division called "constantly arisen" (*satatodita*) is mentioned.
Having raised the objection—"How then can you say that no division is mentioned in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*)?"—he says:
The term "constantly manifest" (satatodita) indicates its all-pervading nature. || 282 ||
In passages such as Sāṃkhyakārikā 13, "Sattva is light and illuminating," the very nature of *sattva* is described through its qualities of lightness and so forth; likewise here too,
by the phrase "constantly arisen," the undivided nature characterized by all-pervasiveness is revealed.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for this?", he says:
"For there is never any single difference whatsoever;
indeed, differences can only function as differentiators by depending upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin). Therefore, how could there be a single difference?"
"For that [turyātīta] is indeed said to be one's own essential nature (svarūpa). Therefore, the claim that 'there is one division here' is the prattle of a fool"—thus he says:
"In the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), there is one division, which is eternally arisen. (10.283)
Therefore, by that very [argument], its indivisibility is established;
for this very reason, the scripture also says thus—so he says: "In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, it has been stated by him..."
In that regard, because it was previously confirmed for the one established in the *piṇḍa*, he recites that very same [verse] starting from the one established in the *pada*:
"They know the other to be established in the *pada*. (10.284)
The mantras, their lords, and Śiva are proclaimed as "that which abides in form" (rūpastha);
the Supreme Power (parā śakti), though engaged in activity and yet free from affliction, is "beyond form" (rūpātīta).
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, pure, and established in its own self;
Śiva is to be known as that which transcends all, by knowing whom one is liberated. (10.286)

The subsequent [verse] concerns the act of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It has been stated that in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), the subject alone is predominant—namely, "the mantras, their lords, and the Lords with their Śaktis. Here, *Śakti* means consciousness (*saṃvit*), for it was previously stated that she is the very nature of the Fourth state (*turya*). The term "without phenomenal expansion" (*niṣprapañca*) means having an undivided nature.
For this very reason it has been said: "established in one's own self," "devoid of appearance," and "pure.
The phrase "transcending all" means that he transcends everything, including the fourth state (*turya*) and so forth, and has gone utterly beyond all things—this is the meaning. || 286 ||

Now, one might object: "Was it not previously stated here that 'having learned this from Śrī Śambhunātha, I am now showing it'? Therefore, is this [work] again merely his own invention, or is it not?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Thus [ends] the *Śrīsumatiprajñācandrikā*, which has extinguished the darkness [of ignorance]."
The illustrious Śambhunātha has described the true nature [of reality] in the waking state and so forth. || 287 ||
For Śrī Sumatinātha is indeed his supreme guru, from whose lineage this was attained by him. || 287 ||
Now, he begins to determine the essential nature of these very [categories] even according to the perspective of other teachers:
"But others, resorting to a different formulation, speak of these as follows."
The nature of the waking state and the others is now being described.
"Others" refers to the venerable authors of the *Pratyabhijñā* and others. || 288 ||
He says that very thing:
"In that regard, whatever grasping of external forms occurs by relying on the activity of the senses is the waking state; it is manifest, seated, and recurring again and again. (10.289)
Dream is a construction of one's own conceptualization, the opposite of waking;
this is the experience of the *layākala*, occurring through the power of impurity (*mala*) and karma, and not otherwise.

Due to the absence of night, sleep becomes stable in the state of non-perception of pleasure and so forth; this occurs for the *jñānākala* due to impurity (*mala*), and for the *pralayākala* due to mere experience (*bhoga*) alone. (10.291)

The meaning is this: that which is the perception of an object common to all subjects due to its externality, by way of being within the range of all the senses, is the waking-waking state. Precisely because that object is external, it remains clearly present, abiding with a vivid manifestation; for this very reason—
The meaning is that [the cognition] clearly pertains to a stable object, as it persists through repeated occurrence due to the absence of sublation.
As it has been said:
"That [cognition] which, by being within the range of all the senses, is external and stable..."

"That creation which is common to all subjects is waking" (Rigvedic-Pratyabhijñā 3.2.17). And the cause of dreaming, which is the reverse of waking, is the construction [of objects] through the volition of the Self; for in that state, because the object is a domain of the mind alone, it lacks visibility to all the senses.
Furthermore, it lacks commonality among all cognizers and lacks repeated persistence.
As it has been said:
"Even on the path of the mind alone, because of the delusion that it is an object of the senses..."
"The creation of entities with clear manifestation is considered the state of dream" (Rigvedaprakāśa 3.2.16).
Furthermore, as for that which has been described here as "clarity of manifestation," that too—
Since there is an absence of the state of being an object for all the senses and so forth, this is indeed the opposite of the waking state; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

The phrase "this is the experience of the *layākala*" means that here the *layākala* is precisely the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*); for this very reason, it is indicated by the statement that even in the waking state, the *sakala* is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). As it has been said:

"In that regard, with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), the *sakala* is considered the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), while the power (*śakti*) that has attained the form of the act of apprehension (*grahaṇākāra*) is accepted as the *sakala* [subject]. Now, one might ask: why does the *layākala* not undergo experience (*bhoga*) in the same manner as the *sakala*, such that it would attain stability?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But not," and so forth.

For although experience (*bhoga*) arises for this [individual] due to the conjunction with the two impurities of *āṇava* and *kārmika*, it does not attain growth because of the absence of the *māyīya* impurity, owing to the non-attainment of a substratum such as a body and so on. As it has been said:
