"That which is known as the *pralayākala*, because it abides in the *kārmamala*, experiences that enjoyment (*bhoga*); due to the presence of *māyā*, it does not attain stability.
By the word "pleasure and so forth" (*saukhyādi*), things such as blue and the like are meant. As it has been said:
"...the state of deep sleep, comparable to cosmic dissolution. (Ri. Pra. 3.2.15).
"...the emptiness of the object of knowledge. (Ri. Pra. 3.2.13).

And thus [it is said]. And that is the state of the *jñānākala*; this is the ellipsis. Here the reason is: "because of its fitness for experience arising solely from the *āṇavamala*, which consists essentially of desire. || 291 ||

Now, one might ask: "Do even the Vijñānākala beings possess the connection with the impurity of individuality (āṇavamala), and does the capacity for experience caused by that [impurity] exist for them? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Those who are inherently non-different, yet possessed of duality—both the insentient and the sentient—are intended to be brought forth [into manifestation]."
There, in the fourth state, reside the three: the Mantra, the Lord of Mantras, and the Supreme Lord.
Until they are capable of entering within the terrifying awakening,
phenomena— whose own essence has dissolved— are themselves non-dual.
They are said to reside in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta-pada*) within that which consists of fifteen aspects.

For those *vijñānākala* beings, although they are inherently non-different because their nature is a single form of pure consciousness, they are nevertheless intended by the Supreme Lord’s will to possess differentiation. Precisely because they thus participate in duality, they are insentient (*jaḍa*).
And because they participate in non-differentiation, they are non-inert—thus it was said, "both inert and non-inert. As they have stated:

"Even though there is identity in their characteristic of consciousness and so forth, those who possess mutual differentiation through the non-differentiation of the Lord's will are the Vijñānakevalas. (Rauravāgama-pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 3.2.7)

Thus it is said: "Abiding therein"—meaning those abiding in the waking state and so forth, namely the *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānākala* who, according to their respective fitness, have attained the nature of *mantras* and so on, and are thus the subjects (*pramātṛ*) in the fourth state (*turya*), because *mantras* and the rest have them as their material cause (*upādāna*). As it has been said:
When there is no perception of the specific means of pleasure, pain, and so forth,
that experience consisting of their general nature arises as memory during the waking state.

In that state, those who are "isolated by pure consciousness" (vijñānakevalas)—arising from the mere impurity of deep sleep—are differentiated from one another though inherently non-different; they are both insentient and sentient, and are intended to be made objects of the Lord's desire to act.

"And having entered therein, they thus [attain] this fourth state (*turya*) through their sovereignty, by means of the sequence of abiding as Mantras, Lords of Mantras, Lords of Mantras, and Great Lords.
This is the sense: for all [beings] are indeed oriented toward resting in supreme consciousness. Therefore...

In the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), all entities whatsoever—consisting of both subject and object—possess a single identity with supreme consciousness; because they are unable to maintain their own individual essence, they consequently become non-dual in themselves and manifest in the form of pure Śiva and Śakti. This is the meaning.

The word *yāvat* indicates the sequence of the progressive dissolution of differentiation; and regarding the fifteen-fold sequence, it has been stated that these are the states of waking and so forth: "Thus, in that which consists of fifteen. (293)
Thus, despite the difference in opinions, he brings the states of waking and so forth to rest in a single essential form:
"Whatever form appears most clearly to anyone, let that be considered 'waking. (10.294)
That which appears unstable was previously such a dream;
that which appears indistinct is deep sleep, even when it occurs right here before one. (10.295)
That fourth state, which arises by virtue of the connection between these three and which is like the thread of a garland, should be understood as present within all divisions. (10.296)

"That which has all dualities melted away by the surging radiance of the weight of non-duality—that they call the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). One should apply this [explanation] everywhere in this manner. (10.297)

"With its predecessor" (*sapūrva*) means "previously experienced"—this is the meaning. "Indistinct" (*asphuṭa*) means that in deep sleep, because the universe exists in the form of power (*śakti*), its form is unmanifest—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "If this is so, then nothing at all would appear here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which even before that... (*tatpuro 'pi yat*).

The meaning is that from deep sleep, that [state] arises even in the state prior to waking. For this very reason, there occurs the memory, "I slept happily," and so forth; for this very reason, it was stated immediately after:
"it has come to memory in the waking state. "Of the triad" refers to waking and the others. "In all distinctions" means...
The meaning is: "in the various sub-states such as waking-within-waking. It is said to be "like the thread of a garland" because it pervades all [states]. For this very reason it has been stated:
"The fourth [state] should be infused into the three like oil" (Śivasūtra 3.20).

Thus, because in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) there is an absence of both the pursuer and the pursued, there is not even a trace of duality; therefore, the essential nature of the states beginning with waking has been described according to the intended meaning of both systems. Having thus explained the fivefold sequence of states beginning with waking within the fifteen-fold order (pāñcadaśyaka), [the author proceeds].
He extends this principle to the thirteenth lunar day and others as well, stating: "In this manner, one should apply [this method] everywhere. || 297 ||
He says that very thing:

"But in the case of the *layākala*, the wise person should everywhere follow the entire sequence, wherein his own nature is waking, while the states prior to that—such as dreaming and so forth—are [the subsequent stages]. (10.298)
"Preceding that" means preceding its own nature from the *layākala*—this is the meaning.
"Everywhere" refers to [the levels] up to Śiva. || 298 ||
Thus it is said:
"Even within the one perfect Lord, the fourth state (turya) is said to be beyond [the three];
bliss is the fourth, while will itself is the seed-stage, which is deep sleep. (10.299)
The power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is said to be the dream state, while the power of action (kriyāśakti) is the waking state.

Nor is this a mere metaphorical designation—as in the expression "the boy is fire"—as he says: "And there can be no such metaphorical usage, for everything exists there [in that state] in reality. (10.300)
If that were not so, there would be no primary status anywhere, nor even a metaphorical one;

for in that reality which is of the singular nature of consciousness and is full, the entire collection of entities exists as if by its own power (*prabhā*), otherwise nothing at all could manifest. As it has been said:
"The manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Lord exists indeed;
without that, the reflective awareness of will (*icchāmarśa*) does not proceed" (Ri.

Pra. 1.5.10). Consequently, for those such as the *sakala* [limited subject], that [will] would not be primary precisely because of the absence of manifestation; and if that were the case, [the following would occur]:
Since even metaphorical usage would be precluded in the absence of a primary sense, the fivefold states beginning with waking must indeed exist in reality even for Śiva. (300)
Regarding this very point, he states its establishment through authoritative means:
"And this has been clearly stated by the Great Lord in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra. (10.301)
He states this very point in sequence through both the literal and the implied meaning:
"In that regard, the triad consisting of the essential nature (svarūpa), power (śakti), and the manifest (sakala)—this is the waking state within the fifteenfold division. (10.302)
In the Ageless [state], there are dream and deep sleep; the fourth (turya) partakes of the classes beginning with mantra;
and the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) consists of Śakti and Śambhu. Furthermore, in the thirteenfold [classification]... (10.303)
The nature of the waking state is different [from the others], as previously described in the cases of dissolution and isolation;
the waking and dreaming states are one's own, while the two beginning with deep sleep and the fourth state are there as before.
Even within the division of the Vijñānākala, there are the Mantras, the Lords of Mantras (Mantranāyakas), their Īśvaras, Śaktis, and Śambhus; thus, there are five states beginning with waking.
In the sevenfold division known as Mantra, there are the Mantreśas and Maheśvaras;
Śakti and Śambhu are said to be the five states beginning with waking.
The essential nature, the mantra, the Great Goddess Śakti, the Mantra-Maheśvara, and Śambhu—these are the five [aspects] within the Mantreśa who possesses five divisions. (10.307)
One's own action, knowledge, and will, and Śambhu as the fifth—these are described here as the threefold states of waking and so forth within the division of Maheśa. (10.308)

The *svarūpa* (essential nature) extends from the earth (*dharā*) up to the unmanifest (*avyakta*); because of the proximity of the word "sakala" (the manifest), its power (*śakti*) is likewise included.
The two *akalas* are the *pralayākala* and the *vijñānākala*. Regarding the *svarūpa*, it includes the *sakala* along with its power up to *kalā*;
the rest is as previously described. Thus, those two *akalas* correspond to the states of dreaming and deep sleep; the fourth state (*turya*) partakes of the class of *mantras* and so forth.

One should follow [the sequence] up to *turyātīta* and *śaktiśambhu*. By the term "in the *pralayākala*," it is implied that this refers to the object of knowledge (*vedya*); thus, the meaning is that it occurs within the elevenfold division. "Its own" refers to the essential nature consisting of the *pralayākala* and so forth, which previously became the state of dream. "The two" refers to...

The powers of the *vijñānākala* are [distinguished] by that; thus, the power of the *vijñānākala* is in the dream state, while the *vijñānākala* itself is in the deep sleep state. "As before" means that, accordingly, the *mantras* and so forth are in the fourth state (*turya*), while Śakti and Śiva are in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). The phrase "in the division of the *vijñānākala*" means in the ninefold division.
"One's own" (*svam*) refers to that which previously lay within the states of dreaming and deep sleep in the form of the *vijñānākala* and so forth.

By the phrase "the waking state and the others," the sequence is indicated; thus, the *vijñānākala* together with its power (*śakti*) is the waking state, up to the *Śiva* and *Śakti* who are beyond the fourth state (*turyātīta*). "One's own" also refers to the form of the *mantra* and so forth.
That which was previously the waking state while lying down in the dream state—by that [waking state], the Mantreśvaras exist in the dream;

the Mantramaheśvaras in deep sleep; Śakti in the fourth (turya) state; and Śambhu in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). "Svarūpa" (one's own nature) refers to the form of the Mantreśvaras and so forth, which was the dream stage prior to the waking state.

Starting again from the power of the Mantramaheśvaras, the states beginning with dream (svapna) arise in succession. "Sva" refers to the form of the Mantramaheśvaras and so forth, up to the waking state; Śambhu is the fifth, which is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). And in our system, it has been stated that, in reality, the threefold nature of Śiva’s power alone is proclaimed.
Action, knowledge, and desire. || 307 ||
Not only may the states beginning with waking be examined up to this point, but they may also be so even in Śiva, in whom the existence of duality has dissolved; thus he says:
"Because of activity, because of sovereignty, because of the loss thereof, and because of being the impeller."
Due to the cessation of desire and due to being established in his own nature, Śiva, though one, is fivefold.
This has been stated immediately prior [to this point] by the author of the text and has been explained by us through analysis; therefore, no further effort is made here. As it was said there:
"In that regard, the threefold reality consists of one's own nature (*svarūpa*), power (*śakti*), and the manifest (*sakala*)."
Thus, this is the waking state within the fifteenfold division.
In the Ageless (akala), two [states] are to be fully known as the states of dream and deep sleep;
the group consisting of Mantra, Mantreśvara, and Mantramaheśvara is traditionally taught to be the Fourth (turya).
O fair-faced one, Śakti and Śambhu are to be fully known within the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta),
in the thirteenfold division, as both the essential nature and the manifest whole.
The Mantras, Mantreśvaras, Mantreśānas, Śaktis, and Īśas are also as before;
even in the division of the Pralayākala, both [the Vijñānākala and the Pralayākala] are themselves [included within] the Vijñānakala.
The Mantras, the Lords of Mantras (Mantreśvaras), the Supreme Lords of Mantras (Mantramaheśvaras), as well as the Śaktis and the Lord of Śaktis (Śaktīśa), are likewise [to be worshipped] as before.
Within the ninefold division thus proclaimed, one's own [mantras] are the Mantras and the leaders of Mantras.
Their lords, Śakti, and Śambhu are proclaimed as the five states;
likewise, even in the sevenfold division, there are one's own [states] consisting of the Mantreśas, Īśas, and Śaktis.
O lady of excellent complexion, these five alone are to be fully known:
Sva, Śakti, Svā, Nijeśāna, and Śaktiśambhu—thus is the pentad.
In the triad, one should discern the distinction between Śakti, Śaktimān, and Śiva;
[the former] by virtue of being the sovereign of activity, and [the latter] by virtue of being the impeller independent of that [activity].
"And [it is] non-different because of the cessation of desire and because of being established in one's own nature"—thus [it is] fivefold (Mālinīvijayottara 2.27–35).

Furthermore, the differentiation of the subject (*pramātṛ*) has been stated at every step within all three objects of knowledge (*prameya*), namely the properties of things (*vastudharma*) and so forth; therefore, it is not mentioned separately here. || 308 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half-verse: "Thus has this path of reality been shown by us in detail.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Divisions of Reality."

Regarding the phrase "in detail" (*vistarāt*): for in the previous section this was stated briefly in thirty-six ways, whereas here it is presented differently, according to a sequence of fifteenfold divisions and so forth for each *tattva*; such is the sense. The word "now" (*atha*) at the end is for the sake of auspiciousness; may there be peace (*śivam*).
Jayaratha, having achieved victory over the true nature of the disagreements between the Kaumārilas and the Naiyāyikas,
has proclaimed this most lucid method of commentary in the tenth chapter.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Divisions of the Tattvas," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. 10.
The Eleventh Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
One whose continuity of the paths has been shattered by the power of the awareness of the great and terrifying roar of one's own Self.
May Jayotsāha, whose enthusiasm for victory shatters the fortress of worldly existence, be victorious!
Now, with the latter half [of the verse], he begins the path of the *kalās*:
"The path of the *kalās* will be described in accordance with the venerable command of Śambhu. (11.1)
One might ask: "What indeed is called 'time' (kāla), for which there could even be a technical designation as a path (adhvan)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as, in the midst of the previously mentioned worlds, each belongs to its own respective group..."
That reality which is differentiated by following after another is called "name. (11.2)
Likewise, within those very principles (tattvas), that which consists of following its own class and is excluded from other classes is called a "kalā" in the teaching of Śiva. (11.3)
"Among the principles" means in their midst; "its own class" refers to forms such as a single principle, according to the method to be explained;
"excluded" means like the nature of a cow being excluded from horses and the like. || 3 ||

Right here, he presents another alternative view: "Others, however, say that this extremely subtle power which exists within the principles (tattvas) is called their 'kala' (aspect/fragment), just as the earth is the supporter [of all things]. (11.4)
It is called "extremely subtle" because it is postulated through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its effects, yet it is itself unperceivable.

Just as the sustaining power (*dhārikā śakti*) is inherent in the earth, so too is the power called "withdrawal" (*nivṛtti*), which, by turning back from outward-directedness that has reached its ultimate limit, acts as a restrainer (*kalayitrī*).

Thus it would have been said. In this way, the power called *Pratiṣṭhā* (Establishment) is that which effects the establishment of the twenty-four principles—from water (*āpaḥ*) up to the root-nature (*mūla*)—by means of the very linguistic convention of their differentiation. Likewise, for the other powers as well, [the power called *Vidyā*] functions through the cognition of their nature as contracted selfhood, the pacification of the plane of Māyā, and the transcendence of that [plane].
And it should be understood that they receive their respective names from their specific functions. || 4 ||
And in reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between these two positions; thus he says:
"In these two positions, the entity does not appear as divided, because a persisting universal is not accepted [by us] as it is by the Naiyāyikas and others. (11.5)

Since, even in the former position, it was not intended that the universal (*sāmānya*) be characterized merely by concomitance—as the Naiyāyikas and others maintain—but rather as having the nature of power (*śakti*), there is no distinction between the two cases, because the concomitance of the nature of power remains the same in both. Thus, there is no superiority [in one over the other]. || 5 ||
And here there is also the opinion of others; thus he says:
"Others say that at the beginning of initiation and other rites, for the sake of easily grasping [the system], the group known as 'kalā' was devised by Śiva as a basis for the rules (samaya). (11.6)
One might object: "Is not what is called 'convention' (samaya) merely a designation based on arbitrary will?
And since that is not ultimately real, it is unreal; for this very reason, one could even venture another convention, so that there would be no fixed rule?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
And the convention established by the God of gods does not lapse into unreality; thus it is not false, nor does there arise any other convention. (11.7)

The reason for its not being non-ultimate, its not being untrue, and its not giving rise to another convention is that it was created by the God of gods; otherwise, all three of these [objections] might well be possible here—this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
Now, one might ask: "What among these [levels] is to be followed, or what is to be easily grasped?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Cessation (nivṛtti) resides in the earth-principle; establishment (pratiṣṭhā) pertains to the sphere of the manifest."
Vidyā is at the end of Niśā, and Śāntā is at the end of Śakti; this constitutes the fourfold Egg.
"This egg is fourfold" means that this very [reality] consists of the four eggs through the equal pervasion of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*. As it has been said:
"The earthly, the primal-nature (*prakṛti*), the illusory (*māyīya*), and the empowered (*śākta*)."
Thus, these four eggs have been described in brief.
By the phrase "ending with Śakti," it is revealed that there is room for other *kalās* beginning from the level of Vyāpinī. 8.
Thus he says:
"In the principle (tattva) of Śiva, [the state] is tranquil and transcendent; the supreme Śiva is beyond even *kalā*.
By the phrase "in the principle of Śiva," the *Śakti-tattva* is implied by context, as it consists of the non-differentiation of all things.
In the thirty-sixth [chapter], immediately following which,

another form is perceived— though it is conceptually constructed as beginning with the thirty-seventh and so on— for the purpose of illuminating the swallowing up of the stain of all conceptualization from the perspective of those to be instructed. Therefore, it has been said:

"Śiva is supreme, transcending the kalās. The term "transcending the kalās" means that he is *niṣkala* (without parts), because he is devoid of all *kalās*. For this very reason, he is called "supreme."
He establishes this very point:
"For here there is no classification, no convention, nor even any mental construction. (11.9)
In the abode of the radiance of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), which shines in every direction, classification is appropriate.

This consists of two aspects: the first is the *samaya* (the conventional agreement), and the other is *kalana*, which is the conceptualization of things in such and such ways. Here, the reason is that this abode is the locus of the radiance of absolute freedom in every respect.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since Śiva is to be known as the agent of all actions according to the initial instruction, how could he be subject to such a state of being an object of cognition? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But by virtue of his sovereignty, his own nature does not deviate from the attribute of the cognizer. (11.10)
In order to establish that the ultimate reality consists of the instruction and its penetration, the Lord is clearly perceived as bringing about the state of being understood. || 11.11 ||
Therefore, even within the Śiva-tattva, the association with *kalā* is taught.
By the word "therefore," it is meant that although [Śiva] possesses the nature of a knower (*boddhṛtva*), due to his own sovereignty he manifests himself as the object of knowledge (*boddhyatvena*).
"Association with *kalā*" means a connection with such-and-such conceptualization—this is the sense. As it has been said:

"By his own sovereignty, the Lord, having fashioned through volitions such as 'I am the Lord' and so forth, causes the self—which is liberated by virtue of its non-dual nature through that very sovereignty—to engage in worldly transaction. (Ri.Pra. 1.5.16).
This has been established in many ways previously, so no further effort is made here. And by this much...
The essential nature of the *kalās* has been explained. || 11 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so, and we have no disagreement with you on this point; however, why is 'egg-ness' (*aṇḍatva*) said to extend only as far as *Śakti*, and not to the pervasive [principles] such as *Ākāśa*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And what is called an 'egg' (*aṇḍa*) is the cause for the maintenance of the division of the worlds. (11–12)
They say that this is the obscuration (āvaraṇa), for it exists as far as the end of power (śakti);
"that" refers to the obscuration. || 12 ||

"Now, [one might object]: 'In this case, while there is the existence of the worlds in their distinct divisions, there is no cause for them, nor is there a cosmic egg (aṇḍa) or a covering (āvaraṇa). This statement is unprecedented.
To this, he says:
Although previously [described], the sequence of worlds (bhuvanapaddhati) exists even within the principle (tattva) called Śiva.
Even so, since it is said to be non-obstructive (*apratigha*), there is no possibility of concealment (*āvṛti*) within this;
[this applies] even to the reality-level (*tattva*) called Śiva—meaning also to the Pervasive (*vyāpinī*) and others—by virtue of being located therein.
It is "non-obstructive" because its nature is that of the void (*śūnya*) due to its transcendence of the universe; and in the absence of concealment, this very [state] is [the case].
The reason is stated by means of a qualification. || 13 ||
[Objection: "But surely 'resistance' (pratighāta) is a property of material things (mūrta), and materiality can only exist in earth;

therefore, it is not logical for the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) to arise elsewhere, setting that [earth] aside. To this he says: "Indeed, in this way, having set aside the earth, [it would have to arise] in Power (śakti), Primordial Matter (prakṛti), or Māyā... (11–14).
Moreover, even if it is non-obstructive, how is the formation of an egg possible?
On this point, our teachers have said that the pentad beginning with earth [is the cause]. (11.15)
This alone appears as direct perception; there is nothing else whatsoever.
In its state as an object of cognition (*meyatva*), it exists as the gross and the subtle; in its state as a means of cognition (*mānatva*), it exists by virtue of being the instrument. (11–16)

Through the manifestation of agency, the thirty principles (tattvas), which consist of differentiation, arise clearly within the state of the agent; their non-differentiation is considered to be Night (niśā).

When the distinctions of being the effect, the instrument, and so forth have dissolved, they declare that the pentad ending with Śiva consists in the sovereign freedom that is intent upon expansion. (11.18)

The meaning is that since there is nothing whatsoever other than the fivefold [elements] beginning with earth which is established by direct perception, the emergence of the entire universe occurs solely by depending upon them as its foundation. For,
while this [universe] is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), the emergence of the thirty *tattvas* occurs through their differentiation by the force of the aforementioned five causes.

And thus, there is no disagreement that this twofold pentad of earth and the other elements consists of these very forms, both gross and subtle; likewise, the five sense organs, which take the form of valid cognition through contact with a portion of consciousness, have this very [pentad] as their root.
The sense is that there can be no such thing as "measuring" (mānatva) apart from the object to be measured (meyam).
Due to contact with the aspect of the agent, even this pentad of organs of action, which takes the form of instruments, has only that [object] as its objective support;
for it is impossible for something to be an instrument without an effect to produce, and in the state of being an agent, it must necessarily have an object as its domain. Thus.
The pentad of principles beginning with the mind (*manas*) is also thus; otherwise, indeed, agency itself would not manifest.

Although the triad of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is certainly included within the category of instruments (*karaṇa*), nevertheless, because they are the most intimate to the agent and because [agency] proceeds through the door of the external organs, [they are treated separately].

This has been stated with reference to contact with external objects. And since primordial nature (prakṛti) is the cause of the instruments of agency, such as the intellect (buddhi), it is designated in this way because it indirectly brings about the manifestation of agency. The same applies to the pentad of coverings (kañcuka), beginning with necessity (niyati).

"Right now, he knows this very thing to some small extent with his entire being" (Paraśurāmakalpasūtra 17, verse)—by such reasoning as this, since agency itself is what is being reinforced, one must rely upon that [agency]. Now, one might object:
"In that case, would Māyā and the rest be something other than that? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Non-difference from that," and so forth.

By the word "that" (tat) here, there is a reference to earth and the other elements. The sense is that, in this non-difference, the effect would exist in a subtle form. Regarding the phrase "with the impulse toward expansion":
it is because of the contraction of "this-ness" (idantā) and the consequent emergence of "I-ness" (ahantā), and [the subsequent re-emergence] of "this-ness."
Even for that which is contracted, its being grounded in the object of knowledge (*meyaniṣṭhatva*) is indeed beyond dispute; thus it was rightly stated by our teachers:
"There is nothing whatsoever other than the pentad beginning with earth. (18)
Nor was this merely stated as his own invention; thus he says:
"And in the venerable Kālottara and other scriptures, it is likewise stated extensively:
'These five principles indeed pervade the entire universe. (11.19)
He states that very point with the words beginning "five," etc. "These" refers to earth and the other elements. As it has been said therein:
"Earth, water, fire, air, and space. (19)
For this very reason, this same pervasion is said to apply everywhere even to Sadyojāta and the others; thus he says:
"Therefore, in the body of the five mantras, [the sequence] beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna is spoken of in various places as extending from the earth element up to the ether. (11.20)

"By that" means by the aforementioned reason of the pervasiveness of the earth and the other elements throughout the world; "there and there" refers to the *Śrīkālottara* and other such texts. As it is said therein:
"The right side is to be known as earth, while the left is proclaimed to be water."
Aghora is said to be fire, and Vāyu is remembered as Tatpuruṣa.
"Ākāśa, however, is Īśa; he himself is the god Maheśvara.
Also, in the Śrīpara: "Śadya is earth, Vāma is water, Aghora is fire, Nara is air," and so on.
"The Lord is the ether...
Thus, it has been established that obscuration occurs only up to the limit of Śakti;

consequently, there is no obscuration in the Vyāpinī and the levels above it—thus he says: "Therefore, the Śiva-principle would be the Void beyond the void (śūnyātiśūnya), being unobscured (anāśrita). The word "therefore" (ataḥ) refers precisely to the limit of Śakti.

This continues as long as there is the possibility of obscuration. Regarding the term *śūnyātiśūnya*: from the "void" (*śūnyāt*), that is, from the pervasive state (*vyāpin*) and so forth, because even the latent impressions of existence (*bhāvasaṃskāra*) have been exhausted, it is the "supreme void" (*atiśūnya*), the thirty-sixth reality (*tattva*)—this is the meaning. Precisely for this reason, due to the disappearance of obscuration, it is called "unobscured" (*anāvṛta*).
Consequently, the designation "egg" (aṇḍa) does not apply here; thus it is rightly said that the state of being an egg extends up to the level of Śakti.
One might object: "In this way, it would follow that the thirty-sixth principle is transcendent to the universe;
consequently, the statement that the supreme principle consists solely of autonomous consciousness and comprises the entire universe would be a hollow verbal assertion.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But that which is the essence of all non-differentiation, autonomous, and beautiful with consciousness; || 21 ||
They declare that the thirty-seventh reality is named Paraśiva.

Indeed, in this system, although it transcends the universe, its single form consists of the universe; it is the supreme reality whose nature is autonomous consciousness, which is everywhere proclaimed as the thirty-sixth reality. Regarding that:

And those practitioners who have fallen into the state of ignorance misinterpret this, asking: "How can there be a conjunction of contradictory attributes within a single form? It is with this very intention that this form has been set apart from the others and called the thirty-seventh. For in reality, no such principle exists at all.

It is possible; for if that were the case, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural statements as "the thirty-six principles are the faces [of Śiva]. However, no such contradiction exists here, because that [contradiction] would require two distinct entities as its basis.
Yet not even a single entity is possible here, for the entire universe does not exist in relation to the Supreme Reality (paraṃ tattvam).

There is no such thing as a real entity here that, by virtue of being transcended or being identical with it, would give rise to a contradiction. Therefore, because the thirty-sixth reality itself possesses the nature of being the undifferentiated self of all, its single form is conceptually designated as the thirty-seventh.
Because of the distinction [between them], such instruction is given specifically for those perceivers. || 21 ||

One might object: "Let it be so; what is the fault? Even for this form [of the subject], since its state of being an object is postulated again during the instruction on meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, then whose status as the cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) would there be?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
When, according to the principle already stated, the state of being an object of cognition is likewise postulated for that [subject], || 11-22 ||
"When it abides as uninterrupted, that is called the thirty-eighth," according to the stated method; for "its own form [arises] from sovereignty" (*Tantrāloka* 11.10), and so forth.
The word "that" (*yat*) refers to the third form in relation to the transcendent universe (*viśvottīrṇa*) and the others; for in reality, indeed—

Even though its nature consists of transcending the universe and so forth, according to the principle that "independent consciousness is the ultimate reality," undivided pure consciousness alone is its supreme form,
which is designated as the thirty-eighth. || 22 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, if that [consciousness] too is postulated as an object of cognition, another cognizer must be postulated for it, and yet another for him, resulting in an infinite regress? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And there would indeed be no such infinite regress; let this be seen by the great-souled ones. (11.23)
He demonstrates this very point:
"Whatever object of knowledge appears, when that ceases, that which shines forth is determined to be Reality (tattva); it manifests in the heart as the thirty-sixth [principle]. (24)
"In its destruction" means in the cessation of that object of knowledge (*vedya*) which culminates in *samanā*. "That which" refers to the single form of the knower (*vedaka*);
"it shines" means that it would be directly realized by everyone without any effort—this is the meaning.
As they say:
"O Lord, when the objects of knowledge have ceased, by whom would You not be seen as the One? (Uttara-stotra 1.8).
"The thirty-sixth" means the form that transcends the universe—this is the meaning. || 24 ||
Now, is its nature simply the state of being distinct from the universe, or is there something else beyond that?
To this he says:
"Is that nothing, or is it something?"—its form remains thus subject to such inquiry.

Among these, the first position is far from tenable, for the absence of a jar cannot itself be the nature of a cloth; therefore, without even considering this, he shows another position in the teaching:
"Its nature is one, consisting of consciousness, bliss, and sovereignty. (11.25)
The thirty-seventh [verse] shines forth clearly, and therein there is no further expectation.
Therein, by means of consciousness (*cit*), the beauty of awakening is expressed, and by means of bliss (*ānanda*), the nature of total non-differentiation is stated.
For it is precisely in the state of power (*śakti*) that the universe exists without differentiation—this is the intended meaning. Thus, in this instruction...

And it has been stated that a form exceeding the thirty-six would have been taught: "Thus, in this teaching, the thirty-seventh shines forth. For it has already been explained that that which is transcendent of the universe cannot itself be composed of the universe. And thus, by [the passage] beginning with "consciousness-bliss... [it is established].
The direct, ultimate form has been described; it has been stated that there is nothing else further to be desired here—and in that regard, there is no other desire. || 25 ||

Since it is precisely because [the object] is thus to be taught that its state of being an object of knowledge (vedyatva) is once again established, there must necessarily be some knower (vedaka) for it; but who, then, is that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that [object], whose state of being an object of knowledge has been established, shines forth where—that [locus] is composed of consciousness (cinmaya). (11.26)
That [thirty-seventh] is also taught as the thirty-eighth for the sake of meditation;
if indeed it were so, then the thirty-seventh would become [the thirty-eighth] once again. (11.27)
"Cinmayaḥ" means having the nature of unconditioned consciousness alone—this is the sense. Now, one might object:

"Is this not precisely that infinite regress, wherein if a state of being an object of knowledge is imagined for him, another subject must exist for him, and yet another for that one as well? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "So too," and so forth (verse 27).
One might object: "How can the thirty-seventh [category] be the same as the thirty-eighth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The nature of its attributes—such as being undivided, autonomous, and consisting of consciousness—is exactly the same; the only difference is that [in the latter case] there is the act of making [the object] an object of knowledge. (11.28)
There is no dispute that the imposition of contradictory attributes is a cause of difference;

however, since [the two] are indistinguishable in their nature as the undivided self and so forth, that very [imposition] is not present here—so from where could this difference between these two arise? For, insofar as there is merely the quality of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) added here, [it does not constitute a difference].
By which one [principle] is conceived as the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the other as the cognizer (*vedaka*).

When such a supreme reality (*para-tattva*) manifests as the imagined state of being an object of cognition, it is then called the thirty-seventh; otherwise, it is the thirty-eighth. And it is not only of the thirty-eighth...
If the state of being an object (*vedyatva*) were imagined as something other than the thirty-seven [principles], it would follow that some entirely unprecedented form has been asserted;
nor could such a state be imagined for another cognizer distinct from it.
Thus, the relationship between the object and the cognizer (*vedya-vedaka-bhāva*) is merely reciprocal, like the conventional usage of action—therefore, there is no infinite regress.

There is some room for consideration. For, in fact, it is stated in all the scriptures that the supreme reality (*paratattva*) is nothing other than uninterrupted pure consciousness (*bodhamātra*), which is celebrated as being thirty-sixfold;

yet, through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), there occurs such an emergence of differentiation (*bhedollāsa*) by which, in relation to the subject under the influence of *māyā* (*māyā-pramātṛ*), [the state of] the great teachers (*mahāguru*)...

The instruction is according to the scripture—enough of this grinding of what is already ground! Ah, why say "according to the scripture"? What indeed is this scripture? It is certainly not the primary treatise under discussion here, for nothing of this [kind] was stated therein; on the contrary, in that [treatise], regarding initiation and so forth—

"This assignment (nyāsa) is proclaimed for the piercing of the thirty-six principles" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 6.6)—this and similar statements are indeed contradictory [to the present system]. Furthermore, in various places, such as in the *Tattvādhvaprakāśana*, the author has followed that very doctrine. Nor does there exist any scripture of this kind [that supports the contrary view].

It has been confirmed. Since all other scriptures that set forth the ritual procedures (*prakriyā*) are likewise [in agreement], what indeed could be that other scripture which, by not being transgressed, constitutes such a teaching as something entirely unprecedented?
For there certainly exists such another scripture. And so it is said in the *Śrīkularatnamālā*:
"I shall proclaim the path of reality (tattvādhvan) so that you may understand it, O lady of excellent vows:
first there are the two powers of movement (cara-śakti), and above those, the pentad is traditionally taught."
And then, O Goddess, there is the group of four, the two apertures, birth itself, pervasion, the union with Vaikuṇṭha, and the pervasion of the uvula.
O Goddess, the eighth cavity is the half-moon, O Beloved, and Kuṇḍalī;
likewise, Śānta, Praśānta, and the eternally risen Bindu.
One should know that above is the Nāda; beyond those are the six cakras.
The Śakti-tattva consists of the six cakras, and the Śiva-tattva is likewise.
"These thirty-eight principles (tattvas), O fair-faced one, as well as this path (adhvan)—how could one who does not know the worldly [path] perform initiation?
Thus it has been said. Now, here the Supreme Lord has indeed promised to expound the path of the principles (tattvādhva).

The direct designation has been made only for the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth principles, and not even for the other well-known principles; what then can be said of the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth? On the contrary, it is mostly obscure, fragmented, and disjointed.

We do not know what it is that has been stated as "unprecedented. Is it not the case that the teaching of all the principles (*tattva*) is already established here? However, even though there is a well-known and undisputed consensus regarding thirty-six principles, [this text] speaks of thirty-seven and thirty-eight as something new.

Lest there be confusion among those of tender heart who follow the scriptures, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is compassion, has expressed this according to the stated method as being essentially nothing more than a mental construction— conceived from the perspective of the subject under the influence of *māyā*— due to its hidden meaning; and that [realization] is attained through such things as service to the Guru, which involve hardships not previously seen.
And how could this be understood in such a way by those who are devoid of self-reflection?

Thus, at the outset, a state of being somewhat indistinct (*mliṣṭaprāyatva*) is observed; yet in reality, the designation of all the *tattvas* remains firmly established. And so, by the word "moving" (*cara*) here—

Since the root *car* has the sense of "going," it denotes the action of moving; and since an action cannot exist without an instrument (*karaṇa*), this power—which consists of the organ of the feet—is postulated as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). Of this power, which, although pervading the entire body, possesses a duality...

Due to the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the presiding subject and the object presided over, the primary locus of presiding is the pair of feet; since the teaching on the sequence of the principles (*tattvakrama*) has been commenced, the Earth-principle (*dhara-tattva*) is indicated— thus, it is first [mentioned] as having reached the ultimate limit of grossness.

The meaning is that the *dharātattva* (earth-principle) is thus remembered. Above that, the group of four ending with space (*ākāśa*), beginning with water (*ap*), is repeated; thus, "above that is the pentad and the tetrad"—the twenty principles from the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) up to the *puruṣa* are remembered. In this way, the twenty-five principles have been stated.

Thus it is established. Although the term "tetrad" (catuṣka) ought to be mentioned immediately after the subsequent section, it is mentioned here with the intention of demonstrating that it is compatible with both [contexts].
Furthermore, by mentioning these merely by way of enumeration, their well-known status even within other philosophical systems is indicated.

It is called a "sign" (*nimitta*) for this very reason; thus it is said that it is "remembered" (*smṛta*), and not that it is "spoken" (*ukta*). Immediately after that, [it says] "having two apertures" (*dvirandhra*): there are two apertures, the two paths characterized by knowledge and action.

The "birth" (*janma*) residing therein refers to the state of being something limited (*kiñcitva*), occurring through the process of re-emergence (*pratiprasava*) of that which had been concealed by the power of the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpagopanā*).

It is a re-manifestation; by this, it would be said that these two principles, consisting of *kalā* and *vidyā*, serve as its support. Furthermore, because the sequence of the *kañcukas* is not real, these two are mentioned immediately after the *puruṣa-tattva* due to their predominance.

The meaning is as follows: *vyāptiḥ* (pervasion) is a specific attainment (*viśiṣṭāptiḥ*), consisting of an attachment (*āsaṅga*) characterized by the thought "may something [good] happen to me," which is delimited solely by the object in its general form; this is the *rāgatattva*. By the phrase "with Vaikuṇṭha," it is meant that there is a "clashing" or "meeting" (*śaṅghaṭṭa*) with Viṣṇu, who resides in the region of the throat.

The reality of *niyati* (restriction) has been explained. For this [reality] also, according to the sequence to be described in the initiation by finger-measure (*aṅguladīkṣā*), the location is precisely the throat, since there is no great distance [between them]; such is the intention.
Alternatively, for Vaikuṇṭha, who effects maintenance, the primary function is indeed the preservation of *niyati*.

The state of being such [as the effect] has been stated for this [category] called *kārya*. "Pervasion" (*vyāpti*) refers to the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), because it is all-pervasive; for there is no collection of objects existing within the belly of the universe that is not permeated by Time. "The tongue" (*lambikā*) refers to *māyā* by virtue of its location therein. As it is said: "The sequence according to the purpose (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence according to the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)."

The meaning is as follows: "By means of stability, there is the piercing of the *bindu*"; or, that by which something is known (*vedyate*) is *vidyā*, which is the thirty-second *tattva*. Likewise, he [Abhinavagupta] says: "The Lord is the external unfolding (*unmeṣa*)... (Ri.Pra. 3.1.3).

By such statements, [it is shown that] for this very reason, because he is engaged as the agent of the act of knowing (*vidikriyā*), the Lord (*īśvara*)—whose form shines forth externally—is the reality (*tattva*) designated by that name. Furthermore, the qualification "half-moon" (*ardhendu*) is applied to him because it aims at summarizing only a portion of his objects of knowledge (*prameya*). For this very reason:

Even for one who has not yet reached the end of *nāda*, the formation of the end of *nāda* must be explained. "Nāda" refers to the principle (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva—this is the meaning. By repeating the word "above" (*ūrdhve*), [it is indicated that] even above Sadāśiva is "Kuṇḍalī," as in:
"...above that is Śaktikuṇḍalī."

From this statement, [it follows that] there is *śakti*. Furthermore, due to the removal of obscurations as appropriate, the form of *vyāpinī* is "tranquil" (*śānta*), and that of *samanā* is "perfectly tranquil" (*praśānta*). And these three—beginning with *kuṇḍalī*—are situated above the *brahmarandhra*; this is the meaning. And that...
The eighth *randhra* (opening) is counted by reversing the sequence starting from *nāda*, because it possesses that same number [of elements].

By this, the thirty-fifth *tattva*, which is of such a nature, namely the *śakti-tattva*, is described. Now, if this is so, then in the statement "the six *cakras* are above that," what is referred to by the word "that"—is it *nāda*, or rather...?

One might ask: even though the triad beginning with Kuṇḍalī is separated [from the others], why is it said that "there are six wheels" (*ṣaṭ cakrāṇi*) when such is the case? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "The principle of power (*śaktitattva*), however, is the six wheels.
The meaning is that the six wheels are nothing other than the principle of power. For [they belong to] the Supreme Lord.

The power itself, called autonomy (*svātantrya*), which inheres [in the Lord], manifesting through the threefold form of internal and external aspects— such as *samanā* and so forth, and will (*icchā*) and so forth— is said to be the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*),
the principle of power (*śaktitattva*). For here, the word *cakra* is derived from the verbal root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting."
Form (rūpa) is intended [here]; by that, it is divided into sixfold according to the manner previously described—this is the meaning. Now, one might object:
"Since it has been stated that 'this group of thirty-five principles is said to be the power of Lord Śiva alone,' there is no dispute that the Śiva-principle is indeed the thirty-sixth."

Since there is an undisputed consensus throughout all the scriptures (*āgama*) that it is exactly so, how is it that the summary states, "these thirty-eight principles"? Anticipating this objection, it is said: "exactly so" means that the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) themselves are sixfold unfolding (*vikasvara*). For this [word] is derived from the root *kas*, meaning "to unfold."

The objection: Even so, since the Śiva-tattva is expanded sixfold, there would be forty-one tattvas; thus, the flaw remains as before—that there should be only thirty-six—and how can it be said that "there are thirty-eight tattvas"? This is not so.

For, according to the principle stated, even though Śiva—the thirty-sixth—is self-luminous, when the status of being an object (*prameyatā*) is conceptually attributed to him during instruction, contemplation, and so forth, it is by means of a subject (*pramātṛ*) of that very same nature; as the saying goes: "As is the Yakṣa, so is his offering."
The thirty-seventh form is postulated as "that which is to be cultivated" (bhāvya);
for that [thirty-seventh] also having such a nature, there is a thirty-eighth;
and for that also having such a nature, in order to avoid infinite regress, there is again the very same thirty-seventh form.
"It is conceptualized as the subject"— thus, since each of these three also possesses the nature of both subjectivity and objectivity, the Śiva-tattva has six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*),
by which it is concluded that "there are thirty-eight principles. But even so...

The claim that "there are thirty-eight principles" is not tenable; for if even the thirty-seventh is conceived as an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), then by the aforementioned logic, let the thirty-sixth alone be the knower (*pramātṛ*).
What is the use of postulating a thirty-eighth principle which only leads to an infinite regress? Thus, let there be only the four wheels.

Regarding the Śiva-tattva: Now, has not the resolution already been stated here? For how indeed can it be consistent that for this very thirty-sixth principle, although it transcends the universe from the perspective of the subject limited by Māyā, it is nonetheless composed of the universe; and although it is the subject, it is also the object?

This [objection] remains to be set aside. And both of these are pacified by the very arrangement of thirty-seven and thirty-eight [factors], since it has been stated that the purpose is fulfilled precisely because the two have distinct objects; furthermore, an infinite regress would otherwise result.
Let it be that the assumption of thirty-eight [categories] might serve as a powerful support for the sake of making the meaning easily understood by listeners, even if it is not strictly possible;
however, in reality, it has already been stated that the thirty-six alone are all-encompassing. Therefore:

Having taken to heart such statements as "If the first [consciousness] exists in that way, what is the basis for its aversion?", the authors of the *Śrīpratyabhijñā* and others accept the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the thirty-sixth principle, Śiva, as established by logic; thus, nothing new has been said here— what then?

Only this much has been stated: "By his own freedom, the Lord, having fashioned himself—who is by nature non-dual—as liberated through the volitions of Īśvara and so forth, carries out worldly activity. (Rijuvimarsini 1.5.16)

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the author of the treatise, relying precisely upon that as his foundation and with the intent of wishing to explain the meaning of that scripture, has stated this; thus, everything is well-established. || 28 ||

Having thus explained this as an incidental digression, in order to introduce the subject at hand, he says: "Not only is the entire universe pervaded by these [principles] in this manner, but also by way of another method— namely,
that they are situated respectively at the end of the Earth, at the end of the Guṇas, and at the end of Māyā."
Smell, taste, and form [dissolve] inwardly through the process of becoming subtle. || 11-29 ||
This being the established principle, even at the end of the Śakti-tattva there exists a certain ever-present subtle touch, for which yogins have a longing. (11.30)
But at the conclusion of that contact, there arises a consciousness whose nature is the pure space of consciousness;
established in which, one attains the supreme state consisting of self-luminosity. (11.31)
"Tactile sensation (*sparśa*)" refers primarily to the touch of a crawling ant. As it has been said:
"O Goddess, having pierced through *Śakti*, [the power] then becomes pervasive (*vyāpinī*) within what remains of the skin;
there, experience occurs just like the touch of an ant" (Svacchandatantra 4.382).

Thus, because he possesses subtlety and is distinct from both the gross and the subtle, he is described as "some indescribable one. For this reason, he alone is the supreme goal, as it has been said: "for whom yogis yearn. Nor is he present here merely by way of the maxim of the "unexpected gourd."

Thus it was said: "When this principle is established. By this, the meaning is that one relies on the logical principle that smell resides in the earth, taste at the end of *prakṛti*, and form at the end of *māyā*, existing there in a subtle form.
For this very reason, because all states of being are withdrawn at its end, [it is] "of the nature of space."

It has been stated: "Consciousness is of the nature of pure knowledge. And here, by the mention of its being of the nature of space (*vyoma*), one should understand that it possesses the nature of air and so forth, due to the metaphorical identification of the quality and the possessor of the quality within the beginning of the sequence starting with *Śakti*.
By implication, the word "supreme" (*parām*) refers to consciousness. || 31 ||

Now, one might ask: "Even though there is no difference in these qualities being attributes of the elements (*bhūta*), what is the proof that for the yogi it is touch alone that is desirable, and not form and the others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore [arises] the point (*bindu*), from that the sound (*nāda*), from this the form, and from that the taste."
Thus it has been stated in the *Spanda* that [the breath] acts as an agitator, but touch is not so. (11.32)

Even for yogins who are intent upon contemplating the supreme reality—which is designated by terms such as *ihonmeṣa*—as long as their identification with the body (*dehāhaṃbhāva*) has not been uprooted, forms and other sensory objects will manifest from that very [reality] and function as agitators; for the manifestation of forms and so forth, like that of the *bindu* and *nāda*, constitutes an obstacle to the attainment of the supreme reality. Thus, they do not [lead to liberation].

Likewise, regarding touch—it has been stated in the *Śrī Spandaśāstra* and other texts: "In that regard, [the senses] set forth for embodied beings as agitators in no time at all" (*Spanda-kārikā* 4.12)—this is the second half-verse. As for form, it is the perception of the various shapes of visible objects even in the dark.
Even in the absence of a flavorful object, there is the tasting of nectar and the like from the tips of flickering [flames].
Now, one might object: "Granted that touch may be thus desirable, what is the fault?
But as for the five principles beginning with earth remaining in such a state, what is the proof?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And this is the doctrine of Maheśa, which he declared in the Śrīpūrva [Tantra]:
"The [five powers] are the sustainer, the nourisher, the awakener, the purifier, and the space-provider. (11.33)

Employing these terms, [one describes] the innate nature of cessation and so forth as "the cognizer," because of the predominance of perception due to the luminosity of light; and as "the purifier," because of [the purification] of the lower and lower levels of beings, states, and so forth.

The meaning is that she loosens the state of insentience and the like—which consists for the most part of what is worthless—in order to gather up the essence whose nature is consciousness. As has been stated by this very [author]:
"Due to the bond of dense insentience, [the world] has attained a state of being charming..."
Because she loosens [the knot] by bursting the knot that is situated at the lower station,
she is called by that very name: "the path for the flow of tranquilized power."
Thus: this is indeed the usage of the root *pūñ* in the sense of "purifying. The reading *utpūyinī*, however, is an archaic (*aiśa*) one.
The meaning is: by means of these words, which convey the nature of being the earth and so forth.
Concluding this, he introduces another topic: "The procedure for the five principles has been declared; now the three principles are being explained. (11.34)

The Self extends up to the Vijñānākala; up to the Vidyeśvara is the remainder; in the threefold principle (tritattva) it is Śiva, and in the single principle (ekatattva) it is the Supreme Śiva. (11.35)
As it has been said:

"The reality of the Self is declared to extend up to the Vijñānākala; that which ends with the Īśvara is called Vidyā, and they know the remainder to be the state of Śiva. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.47)
Thus, here by this [verse],

the scope for the objects of knowledge— such as the conceptualization of the principles (*tattva*)— which were introduced in the subsequent enumeration as "the conceptualization of the principles by means of one, three, five, etc. (Tantrāloka 1.296), has been shown.

Now, since the pentad of principles beginning with Earth is described as pervading all principles, there is no disagreement that it constitutes the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) itself; however, one might raise the doubt:
"Are the paths beginning with *tritva* (the triad) a separate path, like the *kalā*s and so forth, or do they likewise constitute the path of principles? Anticipating this, he says:
These two divisions are both produced solely by the differentiation of the principles (tattva);
thus, this is indeed the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), and there is no contradiction with the established doctrine of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).

"This" refers to that which was explained in the two immediately preceding chapters. Since this manifold variety of divisions belongs precisely to the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) by virtue of its encompassing those respective pervasions (*vyāpti*), therefore...
"The path is proclaimed to be sixfold."
Thus, there is no refutation whatsoever of such recognition (pratyabhijñā), as has been stated; and in this way, there is no impairment of the established state of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan). || 36 ||

He extends this very principle elsewhere as well: "Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Yati, Kāla, Māyā, Vidyeśa, Sauśiva, and Śiva—even in the ritual involving the nine principles, there is the nature of the sacrifice of the principles. (11.37)
In this manner, the wise one should state the same principle even regarding the procedure known as the eighteen-fold [rite].
And it has been said:
".................. we shall explain the ninefold reality (navatattvī)."
Having begun thus:
"Nature and the Person, as well as Necessity and Time;
Māyā, Vidyā, likewise Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva."
"Thus. Regarding the word *nyāya* (logic/reasoning), the meaning is that it is precisely the means of proof for the state of being the sacrifice of reality (*tattvādhvarūpatā*). As it has been said:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, intellect, ego, the [three] qualities, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) itself."
The Puruṣa, Niyati, Kāla, and likewise Māyā;
Vidyā, Īśvara-tattva, Sādākhya, and the sphere of Śakti—
thus there are eighteen tattvas.
Thus [ends the verse]. 37.

One might object: "Since initiation could be accomplished through any one of the paths, such as that of the principles (tattva) and so forth, for what purpose was its sixfold nature stated from the outset? Furthermore, why is there this internal diversity even therein?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For wherever there is a desire for enjoyment, it arises from the predominance of that [desire] in its application. || 11-38 ||
Furthermore, initiation possesses infinite varieties due to the inclusion of other [paths].

For there are many candidates for initiation; thus, according to their respective dispositions, a certain path may be primary while the others are secondary, whereby initiation itself is likewise infinite.
In this way, even within the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), some principle may hold primacy while another remains subordinate,
which is why there are thus many divisions. Even when this is the case,
there is no loss of their status as the path of principles, because such a form is produced solely by the differentiation of the principles themselves.
Thus it is said: "By that [means], there may be a procedure for the thirty-six principles up to the single principle. (11.39)
That very path of reality (tattvādhvan) has been taught by the Lord both in detail and in summary.
By the word "by him" (tena), it refers to the aforementioned method. It has been taught throughout all the Āgamas, as it is said:
"By thirty-six principles, by half [of them], by half of that again, or by five..."
"Or stability should be achieved by one means for the sake of higher and lower manifestations.
Now, by the maxim: "If one can find honey at the threshold, why go to the mountain?"—
if initiation (dīkṣā) were accomplished by this very concise method consisting of a single principle alone, [what would be the point?].
Anticipating the objection, "What is the use of these other extensive methods?", he says:
"And this is the rule for a single principle (ekatattva) with respect to a perfectly awakened teacher. (11.40)
And because Śambhu was pleased with the disciple who had abandoned all desire for enjoyment—the meaning is that he was a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) alone—[he bestowed this upon him]. || 40 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "Is it not stated everywhere that the Śiva-principle is to be attained through initiation (*dīkṣā*), and since that is already established from the very beginning, what is the use of this [initiation], whether performed separately or collectively? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having repeatedly expanded differentiation by means of His power, which is of the nature of absolute freedom... (11.41)
The Blessed Lord remains eternally resting within His own undivided self.

This alone is the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord: that He manifests differentiation in this manner, and yet, through the sequence of initiation and so forth, causes [all things] to rest within His own self, which is the non-dual, singular ultimate reality.
It was precisely with this intention that it was stated previously:
"Constantly dissolving this entire universe into his own consciousness and emitting it forth once again from that state, he perpetually attains the nature of Bhairava" (Tantrāloka 5.36).
Thus it has been stated, and so forth. || 41 ||
Now, concluding the very subject at hand, he introduces another point: "In this way, the division of the threefold path is according to its gross, subtle, and supreme natures. (11.42)
That which consists of the principles (tattva), the kalās, and so forth, has been described as belonging to the objective portion (meyabhāga);
now, the form residing in the subjective portion (mātṛbhāga) is described in three ways. (11.43)

It has been stated [in this way] from the eighth chapter onwards. The term "threefold" (tredhā) means existing within words, mantras, and phonemes by way of being gross, subtle, and supreme—this is the meaning. For this indeed is the supremacy of the phonemes:
that both words and mantras, whether gross or subtle, are pervaded by them alone. Therefore...
And thus, space has been granted for the object of knowledge (prameya) called the "classification of the divisions of time" (varṇabheda-krama), which was indicated in the subsequent summary;
he says this:
"That form which consists of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and pertains to the maternal portion of time..."
For it is called "the state" (pada) because of its immersion in the nature of realization. || 11-44 ||
And that very state is the mantra when it has fallen away from agitation;
for the Mother speaks in secret, being established in silence. (11.45)

The meaning is as follows: that which, by relying on the aspect of the subject (*pramātṛ*), consists of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is agitated due to its outward orientation and is called *pada* (the step); thus it is designated in the Āgama.
For a *pada* is that which consists of comprehension, in the sense that "by this, an object is stepped upon—that is, known."
Because even the temporal paths (adhvan) are permeated by the nature of consciousness, this very fact constitutes the reason for their being of the nature of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
for without the penetration of light, nothing that is to be illumined could ever manifest—this is the intended meaning. And when that very state...

Having fallen away from the form that consists of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and having attained an undisturbed form due to its inward-turned nature, it then becomes the *mantra* whose essence is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Because, due to the absence of agitation and because it abides in a state of neutrality, it is "one who speaks in secret"—meaning its essence consists of internal reflective awareness (*antaḥparāmarśa*). For this very reason, it is called "mantra."
The sense is: is this a designation based on its etymological meaning? || 45 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since this [consciousness] is silent, what proof is there that its nature consists of internal reflection?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Nevertheless, it does not abandon its nature as reflective awareness."
The Self, whose nature is the means of valid cognition and self-reflection, does not undergo agitation like an ordinary human being.
And regarding mantras and words, it has been stated by him in the Trika teaching that their own nature is indeed indivisible within the supreme state, which is both motionless and stirred.

For, according to the reasoning stated in such passages as "Even when [the light] has become silent, it does not abandon its nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)," it does not lose its essence of *vimarśa*; thus, like the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this [result] also possesses *vimarśa*.

Such is their intrinsic nature that there is no difference whatsoever between the two in their essential form. For this very reason, according to the method to be explained, the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* states that words and mantras possess one and the same form; however, this alone is the distinction between the two: that the *māna* (the means of knowledge) is the agitated state, while the *mātṛ* (the knower) is the tranquil state.
Furthermore, he is "unperturbed"—as it has been said: "But he does not undergo perturbation like a human being," and "In the supreme state, there is no vibration nor agitation. (47)

Having thus described the nature of the paths of the *pada* and *mantra* according to their gross and subtle divisions, he now describes the path of the *varṇa* as the supreme state: "In the abandonment of indifference and in the non-descent of agitation..."
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) should be in the portion belonging to the Mothers; this is the measurement previously described.
Since she consists of non-differentiation due to her nature as the Fullness,
she here abandons the state of indifference that presides over the condition of the limited subject,
yet does not descend into the agitated form appropriate to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, by implication, that very cognition (*pramiti*) previously described as being of the nature of fullness (*pūrṇatā*),

when it takes recourse to the aspect of the subject (*pramātṛ-aṃśa*), constitutes the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). This state, through resting solely in its own self, results from the subsiding of agitation (*kṣobha*) and involves the internalization of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth.
The meaning is: having a nature that is non-different from that. || 48 ||
For this very reason, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is taught here precisely because it is capable of encompassing both the words and the mantras;
thus he says:
"Therefore, from [the level of] Kṣamā onwards, there is the state of being a single phoneme in each respective principle (tattva). (11.49)
Having performed [the ritual] in the supreme Śiva, the sixteen syllables are said to be [contained] from the visarga onwards.

Precisely because of the fullness of this state, having added only a single letter starting from *kṣa* within the thirty-four principles beginning with Earth (*kṣityādi-tattva*), [one reaches] the "supreme."

Because it is complete and is considered all-pervasive, within the thirty-sixth *tattva* called Śiva— known as "Śaiva"— which possesses power (*saśaktika*), the sixteen vowels beginning from *visarga* and ending with *a* are taught in direct order (*anuloma*) during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) for the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*), as this is appropriate there. (49)
Now, one might object: "If that state indeed consists of undivided and perfectly full consciousness, from where does this division arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, the vibration of power (śakti-parispanda) has already been described previously. (11.50)

Furthermore, it has been stated many times previously that this sixfold division of the paths (*adhvan*) is nothing other than the vibration of that [Supreme] Power. When the mere relationship of "belonging to it" (*tasya*) was to be expressed, the locative case in *tatra* indicates that [the division] is actually grounded upon that very foundation. || 50 ||
He promises to summarize this very point:
"Now, everything is stated for the sake of the experience of bliss.
By "everything," he means the collection of the six paths.
He states that very point:
"The *nivṛtti* [kalā] consists of one word, one mantra, one syllable, sixteen cities, and the earth;

the other [kalā, *pratiṣṭhā*] consists of the number of elements (twenty-five), the number of syllables (thirty-three), the number of tastes (six), the number of arrows (five), the city (nine), and the word of the weapon-mantra. (11.51)

The fifth [kalā] consists of the syllable *muni*, the principle (*tattva*) *arṇa*, the mantra of two words, the principle *vasu*, the world *akṣibhuvana*, the subsequent kalā, the syllable *agni*, the principle *tattva*, the mantra of one word, and the world *sainyabhuvana*. (11.52)
Sixteen phonemes, one word, and one mantra—this is the state beyond peace (śāntyatītā).
This triad of Āryā verses was spoken by Abhinavagupta for the benefit of his disciples as a summary. (11.53)
The term "padamantravarṇa" is a collective compound (samāhāra). "One" refers to the form of the syllable *kṣa*.
"The sixteen puruṣas" refers to the sequence beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Vīrabhadra.
Furthermore, this division of the worlds (*bhuvanavibhāga*) is [discussed] at the end of the eighth chapter.
"In the Śrīpūrvaśāsana, moreover, one hundred and eighteen [deities] are mentioned.

Here, the principal ones among them, which are to be purified, are stated concisely. Since this has been declared as the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) by such passages as [verse 8.4.36], it should be investigated from that very source; why [is it not done so here]?
By virtue of the weight of the text that corroborates this, it is said that "cessation" (nivṛtti) is what is called "the sustainer" (dhārikā) here.

"Fires" (agnayaḥ) are three; "eyes" (nayane) are two; by these [are indicated] the twenty-three principles beginning with earth and ending with the Unmanifest (avyakta), as well as the letters beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṅa*. "Flavors" (rasāḥ) are six; "arrows" (śarāḥ) are five.

Thus, there are fifty-six cities. Regarding the "weapons," there are five arrows; therefore, there are two words of four syllables and three words of five syllables, making five words and [five] mantras.
"The other" refers to *Pratiṣṭhā*, which is synonymous with *Āpyāyinī*. "Sages" (*munayaḥ*) refers to seven; therefore—
The principles (*tattva*) begin with *puruṣa* and end with *māyā*, and the phonemes (*varṇa*) begin with *ja* and end with *gha*. Regarding the phrase "two [and] eight":

by that, there is one five-syllable word and a second two-syllable word; these are the two mantras. "Vasus" are eight, and "eyes" are two; thus, there are twenty-eight worlds (*bhuvana*). Regarding the phrase "the other part":

*Vidyā* is another synonym for *bodhi*. "The fires" (*agnayaḥ*) are three; by that, the letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*, as well as the principles (*tattva*) of Vidyēśvara and Sadāśiva [are indicated]. "Single" (*ekaka*)—by that, a word or mantra consisting of three syllables [is meant]. "Armies" (*śainyāni*) refers to the eighteen *akṣauhiṇīs*. "The fourth" (*turyā*)...

The "purified" (*utpūyinī*) is another synonym for the "tranquil" (*śāntā*). "Sixteen" refers to those beginning with the letter *visarga* and ending with the letter *a*. Thus, a single word and a mantra consist precisely of these sixteen vowels. Regarding "the reality" (*tattva*), it is the thirty-sixth, known as Śiva; and although it possesses power (*śakti*), it is considered one because of its primacy, for power is not...
The sense is that it must be distinct from that which possesses power (*śaktimat*).

In reality, however, there are only two principles intended to be all-pervasive; it is with this very intention that the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* states: "This deposition is proclaimed according to the division of thirty-six principles" (*Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* 6.6).
Thus it has been said. Furthermore, since worlds do not exist within the Śāntyatītā [Kalā], there is no mention of them here. As it was stated:
"The Śāntyatītā, however, is indeed devoid of worlds. (8.452)

Thus, even with reference to this, the division into words and phonemes is to be understood. In this way, there are one hundred and eighteen worlds (*bhuvana*), thirty-six principles (*tattva*), five digits (*kalā*), ten words (*pada*), an equal number of mantras, and fifty phonemes (*varṇa*); such is the sixfold path (*ṣoḍhādhvan*).
This is the summary of the meaning. As it has been said:
"The first [vowel] is pervaded by the *dhārikā* [power]; therein one single principle (*tattva*) is intended.
One should contemplate each individual syllable, whether a word-syllable (*pada-arṇa*) or a phoneme-syllable (*anu-arṇa*), separately."
From the world of Kālāgni up to the supreme city of Vīrabhadra, the sixteen cities are to be known; thus the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidha-adhvā) is proclaimed.
And with the second [syllable], Āpyāyinī, one should perceive the principles (tattvas) therein,
beginning with the twenty-third [earth] and so forth, as well as the syllables beginning with Ṭa and Va.
There are five steps, six and fifty mantras, and seventy-five cities;
there are seven principles (tattvas) with Bodhinī, and her fourfold cities.
In the third [section], there are seven syllables, consisting of two pairs of *padamantra*s;
in the fourth, however, they know there are three principles (*tattva*) associated with the *utpūyinī*.
One should perceive three phonemes, one mantra, and one word;
in brief, one should know these as the eighteen worlds.
The Śiva-tattva is supreme and tranquil; there, Kalā provides space.
One should discern the sixteen vowels as the mantra and the single word.
"Thus, the sixfold path has been briefly proclaimed. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.57).

The intention behind Abhinavagupta’s mention of his own name here is this: that this entire collection of objects of knowledge, both in its detailed expansion and its concise summary, belongs uniquely to me alone.
Proficiency. || 53 ||
Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not already been established that the sixfold path (ṣoḍhādhvan) is nothing other than the vibration of the power of the Supreme Lord?
So how is it that its nature is now described as having an external form in the guise of the categories (tattvas), worlds (bhuvanas), and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This entire path, possessing the state of non-difference from Bhairava, appears as if it were independent, attaining independence through His sovereignty. (11.54)
Although in reality this entire path is non-different from the Full Light, nevertheless,
by His very will, it manifests with autonomy as if it were something distinct from Him, whereby it appears as an external form. 54.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the path of the *kalās* and so forth may manifest externally through its own autonomy because it belongs to the objective portion (*meyabhāga*); however, since the path of the *mantras* and so forth belongs to the subjective portion (*pramātṛbhāga*), how could it have such a manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For thus, the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) situated within the form of the Mother has been defined;
