indeed, although the path of mantra and the others reside within the portion of the subject (pramātṛ), they are likewise entirely autonomous.
Thus, this entire path has been described without distinction—this is the meaning, as stated immediately before.

Now, one might object: "Is this not a contradiction, that this path of mantra and so forth, which resides within the domain of the subject, should manifest with autonomy? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes this very point:
"For when the state of the signified is swallowed by the reflective awareness of consciousness... (11.55).
Devoted to the protection of the mind through the knowledge and action of Śiva, she possesses the skill and eagerness for the playful manifestation of the entire multitude of powers.
Falling away from the form consisting of the conceit [of duality], consciousness attains the state of the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*).

For when the entire collection of external objects has been assimilated into one's own self through the act of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*)— which takes the form of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the activity of consciousness— then [the state of] the entire nature of the functioning of the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, [is realized].

Due to an eagerness— that is, a longing— for the "play," which is the external expansion of the multitude of powers (*śakti-nikurambaka*), there arises a proficiency consisting of an orientation toward that [expansion]; having descended from such a form composed of the *māna* (egoic pride) which is thus agitated, she is therefore [the power] of Śiva.
"Insofar as knowledge and action are, for the Lord, nothing but reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)," according to the principle stated in *Rauravāgama-pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya* 1.8.11 and elsewhere,

that which is dependent upon knowledge and action— whose sole essential nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)— and whose ultimate reality is that alone, is this very contemplation (*manana*), namely, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that "this is [it]. Likewise...

This protection is the ground of rest for the supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); therein, the reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*)—being intent upon that, withdrawn from outward orientation, and resting solely within it—becomes the contracted subject-form of consciousness.
Having attained the state of the path of mantras (*mantrādhvatā*), it manifests as identical with that—this is the meaning. || 56 ||
For the manifestation of consciousness is twofold: agitated and unagitated.

Among these, when it is unagitated in its state as the subject (*pramātṛ*), it is the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*); otherwise, when it is in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is the path of word (*padādhvan*). Thus he says:
Having attained the nature of the means of valid cognition, the path proceeds to the state of being the ground.
He demonstrates this very point:
for instance, the subject brings about the repose of the Mother [the Goddess of Speech] by assembling those many phonemes;
indeed, having agitated the various phonemes such as *va*, *da*, *ka*, and so forth, through the production of this or that word (*pada*).
One should attain each respective object by which there is a cessation of agitation within one's own self.
One might object: "In the case of the collision [of phonemes], there would be agitation only of the phonemes themselves and not of the knower;
what, then, is the purpose of its cessation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that collision is sequential and consists essentially of internal discourse. (11.58)
The specific form of conceptual thought is clearly characterized by immersion in experience;
therefore, our Guru declared that the state [of consciousness] consists of the nature of valid cognition. (11.59)
It is sequential because speech consists of preceding and succeeding forms; for this very reason, it is said to consist of mental discourse (*sañjalpa*),
since one speaks by synthesizing [the sounds] through the manner of saying, "The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those preceding it, is the signifier."

The sense is this: without mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), since there would be no attainment of a complete word, how could the comprehension of meaning occur through sequential phonemes? And this very point [is established] by the principle that "conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cognition of an object capable of being associated with a word," and so forth.

He states that this is its "real form," namely, "the own-form of conceptualization. Now, one might ask: even so, what kind of agitation (kṣobha) does the subject experience? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "clearly consisting of immersion in enjoyment," meaning it consists of the sensation of pleasure, pain, and so forth, arising from the experience of various objects. "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Because it consists of immersion in enjoyment, it takes the form of agitation within the subject.
Although the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is relevant here by virtue of its being a denoter and its belonging to the same genus,

according to the principle that "no knowledge arises devoid of a supporting basis," the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would not even exist without an object of cognition (prameya).

Thus, by means of this immediate sequence, he designates the triad of paths beginning with *kalā*, which resides within the objective portion (*prameya-bhāga*). Even therein, when the object of knowledge assumes the form of the means of knowledge (*māna*), there is the path of *kalā* (*kalādhvatva*); otherwise, however, in its subtle or gross states, there is the path of *tattvas* (*tattvādhvatva*) and the path of *bhuvanas* (*bhuvanādhvatva*). Thus he says:
Without abandoning its immersion in the nature of the means of knowledge, it assumes the state of being an object of cognition.

Through its connection with the process of movement, the path is said to consist of *kalās*, even when it pertains to the pure state of being an object of knowledge, which possesses both subtle and gross aspects. (11.61)
The Guru should follow, in due order, the path of reality (tattvādhvan) and the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) by means of *kalanā*.

For *kalanā* is indeed conceptualization (*vikalpana*), and that alone is the true nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—as has been stated many times before. The word “pure” (*śuddhe*) means devoid of the penetration of the status of being a means of knowledge (*pramāṇatāveśa*). || 61 ||

Thus, immediately after the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), he begins to describe the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), which consists of the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) and is based upon their mutual relationship: "That form of the objects of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower which stands above... (62).
Let this path, consisting of phonemes, be seen as abiding solely within the nature of valid cognition (*pramātṛ*);
that is to say, it is the resting place for all three, beginning with the object of cognition (*prameya*), which stands above [them]. He says the same thing:
For the yogi, there is the savoring [of reality] through resting solely in the surging consciousness. || 11-63 ||

By virtue of the capacity for all denotation, their powers are unrestricted; they are created with respect to an object that arises simultaneously with their own self and extends as far as the limits of the earth. (11.64)
Touching so many objects without distinction within their own ground of consciousness,
those multitudes of phonemes bear a true consciousness whose nature is valid cognition.
In this regard, according to the principle stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle, imperishable Speech," the multitude of phonemes has not attained mutual division because succession has not yet unfolded.

When the object— consisting of the various principles (tattvas) beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Earth— is present as non-different from one's own self within the Lord’s own cognitive plane, in the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), while perceiving those very objects from Śuddhavidyā down to Earth as non-distinct from Himself, [the subject] perceives them through the "thisness" (idantā) veiled by the "I-ness" (ahantā).
The meaning is that the virtuous ones have been created—that is, they have been brought forth—with discernment as their essence.

Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that these [words] possess denotative power only with respect to specific objects, and not with respect to all objects? Why, then, has this been said? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "sarvābhidhāna... and so forth.
It is with this intention that even the grammarians have stated: "Every word is endowed with the capacity to convey every meaning," and so forth.
To the question, "Even if there is the capacity for all denotations, what is the cause [for a specific usage]? it is said: "The surging," and so on.
For in the supreme consciousness, because it is filled with all things, everything exists—this is the intended meaning.

And those very phonemes "sustain" (*bibhrati*)—that is, they nourish—the ultimate consciousness, which consists of the repose within the triad of the knower and so forth, and whose nature is valid cognition; they manifest as being essentially identical with that consciousness.
—this is the meaning. || 65 ||

Now, one might object: "Since even children and others who are ignorant of the linguistic derivation of word-meanings can indeed possess valid cognition (*pramā*), why was it said that 'only the phonemes bear [it]'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Children, animals, and other subjects of cognition who do not participate in linguistic convention..."
They too [realize] this self-awareness, whose essence consists of unartificial refinement.

"Resorting to various distinct [forms], they attain a manifold state of subjectivity, whose essence is unartificial *saṃskāra*—that is to say, whose ultimate reality is spontaneous self-reflection (*svārasika-parāmarśa*). Now, one might object: if one relies upon a means of knowledge (*pramā*) whose essence is the innate, undivided self-reflection whose sole nature is consciousness...

Raising the objection, "Even though there is no difference in the lack of linguistic proficiency among children, animals, and so forth, how could there be such diversity in their status as subjects (*pramātṛ*) toward one another?"—it is said [in response]: "distinctly distinct," meaning that [their subjectivity] is characterized by a contraction brought about by the penetration of the *māyā* of their own respective freedom. (As it has been said:)
"Legal transactions proceed even among animals by virtue of that [name].
This [power] is not only the basis for the manifold subjectivity of those who do not employ conventions, such as children and others, but also for those who do employ conventions, namely the learned;
thus he says:
And [he attains] a firm rooting in this consciousness of infinite, uncreated colors. (11.67)
If these [phonemes] proceed according to convention, they also proceed as being beyond conventional operation;
for in this consciousness of phonemes— which has the nature just described and is uncreated because it is not itself subject to contraction— it is infinite.

When even linguistic conventions— which consist of the conjunction of word and meaning, are based on the causes of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as grasped through the processes of inclusion and exclusion (āvāpa-udvāpa), and have the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) as their essence— attain a state of established rest,
then those very conventions attain the status of non-conventional functioning.

According to the principle expressed in such passages as, "The expressive power in the word is indeed eternal, just like heat in fire," [the relationship] consists of a connection whose essence is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is distinct from the occasion of conventional designation (*saṅketa*).
The meaning is that they become "touching the object. The particle *api* is displaced in its order [in the verse]. || 67 ||

He establishes this very point by means of the method of negative concomitance (vyatireka) as well: "But without this [intuition], all conventions, even those performed many times," [would be impossible]. (11.68)
Because they would never find rest, they would lead to an insurmountable infinite regress;
for a child is taught by searching for the conventional designation within that very [process]. (11.69)

For, without this aforementioned firmness of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūḍhatā*), all linguistic conventions— even those established many times, such as "a tree is a *taru*, [it is] a *śākhī*"— fail to attain rest; thus,
by the maxim "one explains words only through words," they lead to an irresolvable infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
They would continue to search for another convention and never cease—this is the meaning.
For, by whatever convention a child is being educated, another convention such as "What is a tree? A taru, a śākhī," and so forth, is indeed sought therein. || 69 ||

Now, one might object: "What is the use of searching for another means of convention for this [child]? Understanding will arise through the pointing out [of objects] with a finger and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when a finger and so forth are pointed out, his cognition is not free from conceptual construction (avikalpa) in that way."
Conceptual construction is rooted in language, and language has its life in convention. || 11-70 ||

For this child or other person being instructed, when an object standing before them is pointed out with a finger as "this is a jar," the cognition characterized by the relationship between signifier and signified— namely, "this is what is signified by the word 'jar'"— cannot, due to the interpenetration of the word, initially be free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).

According to the principle beginning with, "If, however, conceptualization is [dependent], then those conceptualizations have words as their source," conceptualization is rooted in words, and words have convention (*saṅketa*) as their sole ultimate reality;
thus, if another convention were required, an infinite regress would necessarily ensue. (70)

Therefore, one must accept that the collection of phonemes itself— whose essence is pure awareness (*saṃvit*), whose nature is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and which does not depend on conventional signs— is the locus of rest, so that the infinite regress may be stilled; thus he says:
Therefore, that infinite and indeed non-deceptive collection of phonemes, which is accompanied by the reflective awareness of consciousness, is always unfolding. || 11.71 ||

"Of such a kind" means independent of conventions and the like. "Always" means even at the occasion of employing artificial, illusory phonemes—this is the meaning. For in this world, whatever valid cognition (*pramā*) arises, it must necessarily involve a differentiation of phonemes in the form "this is thus."
The state of being. || 71 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has already been established that the phonemes belonging to *māyā* do not appear as distinct entities within valid cognitions (*pramā*), what purpose indeed is served by these extraordinary, *māyīya* phonemes? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And precisely because the phonemes belonging to Māyā have extended their procreation, those which are described as the virility within the phonemes of Māyā [attain their fruit]. (11.72)

Let it be accepted that those [cognitions] which are independent of convention constitute valid knowledge (*pramā*), as has been established in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* and other texts. As it is said therein:
"That power of the Creator of the world which is described as inherent (*samavāyinī*)."
Having thus established the introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*),
he begins with the passage: "In that regard, having first entered [the state], she differentiates herself into the nature of the Mother," and so forth.
Having awakened by that [power], the Lord, having agitated the womb with his powers,
created the phonemes (varṇas) which have an equal number of syllables as it.

"Embraced by those various [syllables], they become bestowers of the fruits of all desires for the foremost of practitioners; it is not otherwise, O Goddess worshipped by heroes" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.28).
The word "those" refers to the phonemes belonging to the level beyond Māyā (*amāyīya*). Let them be grasped; for otherwise—

As previously stated, because of the occurrence of infinite regress, the very production of valid cognition would not take place; the implication is that, by this, the entire universe would become as if mute. || 72 ||
He illustrates this very point: "For in this way, when the words of others are heard, one's own [nature] is obscured. (11.73)
He for whom there is no valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding an object is not a knower (*mātṛ*) with respect to that object.

For even in the case of the words of another which have been heard, if one’s own valid cognition regarding their subject matter is obscured—that is, if it remains covered due to inattention or other causes—one is unable to comprehend those words of another; therefore, he [is not a knower].
In that regard, the insentient does not attain the status of a cognizer; thus, it cannot be the knower of that object—this is the meaning. || 73 ||

One might object: "Is there not indeed an understanding [of the meaning] through the necessity of explaining the otherwise inexplicable recitation of that [text] at the beginning of another's discourse? What, then, is the need for a formal means of valid cognition? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Like a parrot, he merely recites, following solely the sequence of those [words]. (11.74)
However, when one attains the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that is self-established through the attainment of autonomy, one possesses true understanding.

Indeed, one whose cognition is obstructed is insentient; following only the sequential nature of those other statements, he merely recites the words of others and so forth like a parrot, [though] regarding their subject matter...

Furthermore, its status as a knower (*boddhṛtā*) is indeed its own, belonging to itself; when that valid cognition (*pramā*) is attained, the agency (*kartṛtā*) of the self—that is, its sovereignty (*svātantrya*)—is attained therein. This is the completion of the sentence. It is not only in this way that, upon the attainment of valid cognition, its status as a knower pertains solely to another's speech and so forth.

[The author] says that agency may even exist in one's own [nature]: "For he whose awakening of self-validating cognition [occurs] through the suppression of the emergence of opposing views... (11.75).

That cognizer should become master over the collection of phonemes within his own [utterance], such as a sentence and so forth; for that cognizer whose "opposing factors"—consisting of inattention and the like—have been "uprooted" through the "subjugation," that is, the eradication, of even their first emergence, his own cognition becomes awakened. He, in his own...

The meaning is: one becomes master over a collection of phonemes in the form of great sayings (*mahāvākya*) and so forth, and one would become independent in composing sentences and the like, initiated by those very phonemes oneself. || 75 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then even though there is no difference in the awakening of valid cognition (*pramā*), why is it that some cognizers produce only sentences and the like, while others produce treatises and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In whatever way that uncreated nature is further transcended... (11.76).
In such and such a manner, the gradation of wonder (*camatkāra*) is perceived.

Regarding the phrase "of that nature" (*tadrūpam*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the reflective awareness of the awakening of valid cognition (*pramābodha*). Regarding "wonder," the meaning is the excellence of the capacity for the successive composition of sentences and so forth. || 76 ||

But surely, since valid cognition (*pramā*) consists of an unconditioned, innate, and supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), its awakening must be all-encompassing and not partial; so how can it be said that "its nature is exceeded according to [the degree of] each [individual]"? Anticipating this objection, he says:
When each subsequent [element] is submerged within the preceding letters of Māyā; || 11.77 ||

Regarding the dissolution of each preceding constituent within the convention, there is indeed a distinction in intuitive flash (*pratibhā*) for those beginning with children in this world; for, starting from the first convention,
as each subsequent convention is established according to the previous one, it is intended as an outward expansion of the reflective awareness (*saṃvid-vimarśa*) of consciousness.

With the intention of resting within that [ultimate reality], when there is an identity— by virtue of the "immersion" of each subsequent element into each preceding element consisting of the nature of the convention— the former elements, which constitute the rest of all contractions, [attain that state].

The meaning is as follows: when the phonemes, whose nature is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), are entirely "immersed" within one's own self—that is, have attained a state of identity with that [Self]—then the "divisions," which are the specific distinctions or varieties consisting of gradations, of "intuition" (*pratibhā*), which is the awakening of valid cognition, [cease]. ||77||
For this very reason, even an unimpeded flow of poetic talent (*kavitva*) and eloquence (*vaktṛtva*) extending in every direction may sometimes occur; thus he says:
"Even when the greatness of the initial surge is present, they remain established within the self of *pratibhā*. (11.78)
"They certainly attain a state of being endowed with poetic power and eloquence in every respect.

Regarding the phrase "in the greatness of the primordial surge": the meaning is that [it occurs] in that which possesses greatness through the "primordial" (*ādya*), i.e., the first, "surge" (*udreka*), i.e., the upward-throbbing state, and which exists in the immediate vicinity of the abode of supreme consciousness. || 78 ||

Furthermore, upon ascending to the supreme state (paradhārā), there would be only the yoga of all-encompassing knowledge and action; thus he says: "As long as [one remains] in that abode which is free from the conceptualization of conventional signs... (11.79).
What is there that one who has found rest in the consciousness-nature (cinmaya) does not know, or what is there that he cannot do?
Therefore, the scripture also says thus:
"For this very reason, when the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) is attained, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are to be worshipped. (11.80)
Or, when omniscience and other such states are accomplished, what accomplishment could there be that is not composed of that [consciousness]?

Therefore, because their essence consists solely in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the letters are said in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* and other texts to be worthy of worship as the cause for the attainment of mastery over speech (*vāksiddhi*) and the attainment of the status of a Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
— this is the meaning. As it is stated therein:
"Furthermore, the distinction between the letters is proclaimed by means of the collective [form]:
having meditated upon her in the heart in the form of a woman, adorned with white garments and the like..."
Seated upon the navel-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
that which is the seed-syllable of all scriptures shall then manifest incessantly.
One should contemplate it as emerging from one's own mouth,
taking the form of a string of pearls, filled with shimmering rays of light.
Commenced with syllables resembling stars, it possesses immeasurable luster;
within half a month, it unceasingly disgorges a collection of scriptures.
Established in samādhi, one may [recover] within a month in a dream, or within six months at will;
even those scriptures that have been lost, both in their textual form and in their meaning.
If the yogi has attained the state of pure consciousness, he knows the year and so forth;
this is described in brief as an incidental result.

"The attainment of equality with the Vidyeśvaras and other supernatural powers (*siddhis*)" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 19.55). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of powers such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth is intended. As it is said there:
"Alternatively, someone may employ this [mantra] in rites of subjugation and the like."
Then it quickly fulfills the desired aim of the practitioner.
"The entire sequence of phonemes, possessing the color of the risen sun... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 19.61).

Now, while it may be granted that it is appropriate for these phonemes, when properly worshipped, to be the cause of the accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) and so forth, how is it that they further serve as the means for accomplishing feats such as subjugation (*vaśya*)?
Anticipating the objection, "How can they be united?", it is said: "What accomplishment is there that is not composed of that? (80)
And for this very reason,

according to the principle stated in [Tantrāloka] 11.73, "And those which are determined as the vitality (*vīrya*) within the phonemes of *māyā*," these phonemes have as their sole essence the mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the phonemes of *māyā*.

They must necessarily be approached as being of the nature of *vīrya* (vital potency); otherwise, like mere arrangements of written characters, they would not bring about any accomplishment (*siddhi*). He confirms this through corroboration from scripture (*āgama*), stating:
"As it was said by the Giver of Boons in the venerable *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*: (11.81).
By that which is concealed, the remaining castes are clearly concealed as well.

He states this very point with the words beginning "by that" (*tena*). "By that" means by the *vīrya* (vital potency) whose nature is the mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of consciousness. "Concealed" (*guptāḥ*) means having their own selves hidden. As it is said there:
Having observed the total absence of refinement among men everywhere,
as well as the violation of their agreements, those lowest of men acted accordingly.
Therefore, the power of all mantras has been kept secret;
by that secrecy they are protected, while the remaining letters are merely phonemes.
"O Great Goddess, when these mantras of hidden power are employed even according to the prescribed ritual, they do not achieve success for him, even if recited hundreds of millions of times. (81)
He concludes that very point:
"Thus, he who shines forth through the states of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge... (11.82).
In six ways, that path attains purity through the purification of its own body (*svavapuḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "through the purification of its own body," the meaning is: in the purification of its own unique nature consisting of *kalā* and the rest—that is, in the removal of the impurity of attachment to enjoyment (*bhogāsaṅga*). || 82 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then should the path, which is directly sixfold, also be purified in its entirety, or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When purification occurs through a single form, [the other forms] therein possess another mode of being. (11.83)

The Guru, possessing continuous contemplation, should perform the purification by internalizing [the mantra] through any one [of the methods], such as the *kalā* and so forth, from among those listed. "In purification" means when the act of purification is to be performed. || 83 ||
If one is likewise unable [to do so], there is another sequence; thus he says:
"But if there is no power to include [them within the breath], one should purify the subtle [element] by means of the subtle. (11.84)
That [seed], being purified, does not produce a subsequent continuity because of its state as a seed;

"subtle" means a delicate cause—this is the meaning. Just as the phonemes (varṇa) belong to the path of the signifier (vācaka-adhvā), and the ritual portions (kalā) belong to the path of the signified (vācya-adhvā). || 84 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the purification of the sixfold path that is to be purified?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Purification is the single-minded concentration on attaining this or that respective experience in its many forms. (11.85)
Mastery over that, the renunciation of that, the realization of its nature as Śiva, absorption in that, and the dissolution of that—all this occurs both sequentially and non-sequentially. (11.86)

"Single-mindedness directed toward the attainment of this or that enjoyment" means: the "attainment" of the experience—consisting of pleasure and pain acquired through prior karma—of that specific individual soul (*aṇu*) who is considered fit for initiation, according to the principle stated in [Svacchandatantra] 4.120: "When [the fruit] has been earned, the experience consisting of suffering and happiness must be enjoyed."

In that context, "state of being an object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatā*) refers to one-pointedness, as it is said: "For the sake of experiencing the remaining fruits of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior karma" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 4.114).
Likewise:

The meaning is that, according to the principle stated in [Svacchandatantra] 4.115, "Those with divided bodies are emitted into the wombs of the Vāgīśīs," there is a firm resolve to assume birth by means of the creation of various bodies for the sake of attaining those respective objects of experience—this is what is meant by "lordship over that. Regarding "over that": of that...
The "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) of the soul (*aṇu*) undergoing initiation is its entitlement (*adhikāra*) to experience.

"Its renunciation" means the "renunciation" regarding the object of that soul's experience, which is its completion; it is an expiation (*niṣkṛti*) consisting of the total exhaustion [of karma] by way of enjoyment. As it has been said:

"Whatever objects exist in the form of the world, which consist of things to be experienced, once the fruits of karma have been fully enjoyed and nothing remains, that is traditionally known as 'expiation' (niṣkṛti). (Svacchandatantra 4.125).
This refers to the realization of that [world] as being of the nature of Śiva; for that individual soul (aṇu)...

By the statement beginning with, "That consciousness, abiding at the summit of the pure reality, has the luster of gold" (Svacchandatantra 4.133), [it is shown that] through the removal of various veils, it takes the form of the supreme good (*śreyaḥ*). Its "knowing" (*vedana*) as the stainless self is the meaning of its "extraction" (*uddhāra*) from the lower path once it has been purified. Regarding the phrase "absorption into that" (*tallīnatā*), it refers to that [consciousness].
Absorption (*laya*) is the state of being dissolved in objects of enjoyment through attachment to another, whose true nature is the repose within the self. As it has been said:
"Absorption is [the state] where, through supreme delight, one is completely [immersed] even in that which consists of pleasure and pain" (*Svacchanda Tantra* 4.120).
"Its rejection" means the rejection of that [absorption] from enjoyment, which is the non-connection with enjoyments once again.
Separation (*viśleṣa*) consists in the absence of the state of being an enjoyer. As it has been said:
"Separation is liberation from enjoyment; for it is traditionally held that [liberation] occurs when there is an absence of enjoyment" (Svacchandatantra 4.126).
And here, with the sole intention of describing the nature of purification (*śuddhi*), the sequential order is not intended.

Such is their designation. Thus, this entire collection of purificatory rites (saṃskāra), characterized by birth, eligibility, enjoyment, dissolution, atonement, separation, extraction, and so forth, is designated as "purification" (śodhana).

It arises sequentially from the form described in the venerable *Svacchandaśāstra* and other scriptures for those who possess the most intense descent of power (*tīvratīvra-śaktipāta*). And [it is said]:
"By whichever path the Guru [leads the disciple], [that path] is devoid of birth and so forth."

Or, it may be performed through the non-sequential [process] (*akrama*), whose nature will be described in the passage beginning with: "He should perform [the rite] ending with a single *tattva*... (18.2). || 86 ||

Now, one might ask: should all of this be performed without mantras or with mantras? For if it were without mantras, nothing would be accomplished because it would be like the mere daydreams of students; thus, that [position] would be trivial. But if it is with mantras, then [the result] is inconceivable.

Since the power of mantra possesses inconceivable majesty, may all prosperity come about effortlessly and without sequence; what need is there for a sequence by which "for the completion of the embryos within the wombs, three oblations are offered with the Bhairava-mantra"?
"But having performed the oblation, the rite of generation should again be performed by him with three oblations" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.118). Likewise:
"The separation is to be offered with the heart-mantra, and the expiation again with the head-mantra" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.164).
Having raised this doubt—namely, "Why was it stated thus?"—he says:
"And for this very reason, those mantras, being purifiers of manifold forms, extend a diverse purification in the Siddhānta, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other systems. (11.87)

Therefore, because birth and the rest— which constitute the collection of *saṃskāras*— occur both sequentially and non-sequentially, those [mantras] such as *Hṛdaya* and so forth, which were taught in the Siddhānta and other systems, are purifiers that possess a variegated form (*citrarūpin*) due to their function of performing specific purifications. [The mantra] "citrām" [refers to] that which is indeed sequential and manifold, by way of the forms of birth and so forth.
"Who, then, would bestow purity upon those that are non-sequential?"—anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But as for those mantras known as Anuttara, Trika, and Akrama, they indeed grant everything at all times; however, the preeminence [of each] belongs to someone, somewhere. (11.88)

Furthermore, those mantras which are taught in the threefold sequence known as the Siddhānavāmakamālinī, whose nature consists of the unsurpassed three-fold purpose— it is said that all of these [mantras] effect every kind of purification at all times, and not merely the root-mantra and so forth, as is the case with what is taught in other scriptures.
The meaning is that they bestow [the fruit] either successively or simultaneously. Now, if this is so, then how is it that [the scripture] also says:

"Then, having placed the mantras within himself, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the impregnation in the womb, endowed with all the rites for the embryo, by means of the three syllables and the half-syllable" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.60)?
Having raised the doubt: "By such statements as these, has it been said that [the rule] pertains only to specific, restricted rites? he says:
"But in some cases, for someone, there is primacy. It is with this very intention that it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"In the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*), which effects complete purification on the path up to the level of Māyā..."
In rites where no mantra has been specified, the wise man should employ an *apara* (lower) mantra.
And likewise, from Vidyā up to Sakalā, one should join the Parāparā [Kalā];
above Īśvara, one should perform the eightfold [rite] beginning with Pibanī.
"And furthermore, the wise one should not perform any rite enjoined by the ritual rules in the Niṣkala [state] using the six limbs above the Sakala [state]" (Mālinīvijaya 9.71);
thus it has been stated. || 88 ||
For this very reason, it is stated here that all mantras are established as purifiers within the path;
thus he says:
"Therefore, in the scripture known as the Śrīpūrva, by virtue of their nature as purifiers..."
The arrangement of the mantras, beginning with Parā and Aparā, is established within the path. || 11-89 ||

The word "hence" (*ataḥ*) is used because [this system] bestows everything upon all the triads of mantras. The phrase "by way of being the purifier" (*śodhakabhāvena*) means that they function as purifiers, and not as things to be purified (*śodhyatvena*), as is stated in other scriptures. As it is said there:
"In the Niṣkala [state], the single-syllable *pada* consists of three syllables and one syllable, and then two. (Mālinīvijaya Tantra 4.19)
"Thus, the three eggs are pervaded by the letter ŚA; the fourth is pervaded by the trident (the letter RA).
That which transcends all is pervaded by the emission (the letter HA); this is held to be the pervasion of Parā. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.25)
Thus far. || 89 ||

Now, one might object: "In other cases, it has been stated that the root mantra alone possesses the power of purification (*śodhakatva*), while the other mantras, such as the *hṛdaya* and so forth, possess both the state of being purified (*śodhyatva*) and the state of purifying (*śodhakatva*).
Likewise here, why is it said that only the mantras of the three powers (*śaktitraya*) possess the power of purification, and not [the others]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And there is the state of being a purifier for the [nine] goddesses of impurity, for the triad of goddesses, for the three deities, for the faces, and for the group of eight limbs. (11.90)

Or rather, what need is there for excessive detail? In the sequence of the heavy foundation consisting of the site of the gateway, everything is purifying, with the exception of the mantras used in the ritual of the world-guardians' weapons.

The intended meaning is that, furthermore, in this context, the mantras of the doors and so forth possess neither the quality of being purifiers nor the quality of being objects to be purified. || 91 ||

Now, one might object: "How can it be possible for the six paths to be that which is purified and the mantras, such as Parā and Aparā, to be the purifiers, if—as you have stated—there is no relationship between them, making them like two iron rods [standing independently]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And as for this state of being purified and that which is the purifier attributed to the time-cycle (adhvan),
it is stated in the teaching that these are logically consistent with non-difference from Śiva due to His absolute sovereignty.

But surely, since non-difference from Śiva is uniform, what is the cause for this diversity—namely, that in one case there is the state of being purified (*śodhyatva*) and in another the state of being the purifier (*śodhakatva*)? To this he says: "That [is it]. Nor is this merely our own invention;
thus it is said: "And this has been stated in the teaching. By "in the teaching," he means in that which consists of the non-dual method (*advayanaya*).
As it has been said:
"In every case, whether in a general state or within the range of sensory objects, the nature of everything is Bhairava;
and since there is no other reality apart from that, such is the teaching of non-duality."
Thus:
"the scripture of non-duality" means "the state of non-duality"—this is the meaning. || 92 ||
He establishes this very point: "All this indeed shines within the eternal Supreme Lord in the form of a reflection, and not as something external. (93)
"By way of the nature of a reflection" means by way of being non-different from its own nature; for this very reason it has been said:
"but not as something external. || 93 ||

One might object: "In the case of a mirror and the like, there is a variety of reflections because they are produced by external objects being presented to them; however, in this case, since there is no external source due to the nature of repetition, that [variety] must be projected solely by consciousness (cit). Therefore, because consciousness is one, there could be no such variety of subjects, objects of knowledge, and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Within the auspicious sky of consciousness alone, such notions as this body and so forth arise among transmigrating beings as something distinct, like the perceptions of a snake, a garland, or a wave in a rope. (11.94)

Indeed, here in Śiva alone— who, being of the nature of pure consciousness, is like the sky due to the emptiness of objective existence— there arises for the subjects under the influence of *māyā* this reflection-like cognition of the various manifold collection of entities consisting of bodies and so forth,
as well as subjects and objects of knowledge, just as the perception of a snake arises in relation to a rope.
The meaning is: they are distinct by their own nature, but not distinct in terms of being the objective support for different cognitions. || 94 ||

Now, one might ask: "Is even the cognition of a snake in a rope merely an illusion? To leave no room for such a doubt, he establishes its very nature as an illusion: "For the dream-object is established by the prior death of the body."
What is the nature of the transition to another body and so forth at death, or how does the birth of a body occur? (11.95)

For [this occurs] even within the body of some person such as a child—a first-time infant—situated in the state of childhood; or within the death of one whose father and others have been consumed by fire; or within the deep sleep of one who has attained [such a state]; or even within the interior of one currently existing [in such a condition].

Another body—whether situated in a later stage such as youth, or another body existing in a prior state of life or in a state of activity—and by the word "etcetera," blue objects and so forth appearing in the sphere of dreams and the like, are merely illusion; this is the meaning. For such things do not [exist] in that manner.

The intention is that the body and so forth exist in dreams and the like. Now, one might object: "Granted that the body exists in such a state, let it be; however, by this much, has it not been said that there is an appearance of something absolutely non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "What kind of bodily manifestation could there be at death? Indeed, in this context:

The existence or non-existence of the appearing form must be investigated; yet here it is not merely the body that appears, but rather [the body] as situated in its specific state, and thus it does not exist—therefore it was rightly said that "the non-existent body and so forth appear. Or, let it be so there.

In some way, existence is mediated by the mere substratum; however, in the case of death, since the reduction of that body to ashes is directly perceived, how can the appearance of what is absolutely non-existent be refuted? || 95 ||
Not only does this alone appear in dreams and so forth, but even that which is otherwise absolutely impossible appears as well—
thus he says:
"Even in a dream, by the power of the manifestation of the generality of mere appearance..."
Just as particular features appear [in dreams], yet they are not cultivated [as real]. || 11-96 ||

In this context, indeed, because there is a manifestation in that manner through a mere generalization— arising from a mere reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) culminating in things such as the mere decapitation [of one's head] while setting aside the specific substratum (*niyatadharmin*) in dreams and so forth— and precisely for this reason,
because the appearance of a generality is impossible without a particular (*viśeṣa*).

Even particularities such as the cutting off of one's own head, which cannot even be contemplated through force, "appear"—that is, they flash forth in a manner that cannot be denied. Thus it is rightly said: all this manifests solely as the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatā*), and not as something external. || 96 ||

Now, one might object: "If it is indeed consciousness alone that thus manifests, then how could all things—which have as their essence the single reality of consciousness—attain mutual diversity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Just as certain *śālagrāma* stones bear various forms..."
Likewise, the consciousness of the heart is like a painting on the canvas of the stages beginning with Māyā and ending with Bhūmi. || 11-97 ||

For just as certain *śālagrāma* stones, despite the lack of distinction in their being mere stones, are by their very nature the referents of terms such as "seal" (*mudrā*) and so forth, because they possess various specific configurations of conch shells, discs, and the like, and thus bear diverse forms; even so [is it here].

Although the cognizer, the object of cognition, and so forth are themselves undifferentiated aspects of consciousness, they appear as a variegated lake through the path of the entire extent of the universe— from Māyā down to the earth— which, though projected by the sovereignty of consciousness itself, takes the form of diverse limiting adjuncts (upādhi) because the categories beginning with *kalā* are restricted to each individual soul.
The meaning is: [these are] reflective awarenesses of distinct and diverse forms. || 97 ||
Is it not the case that "this alone is the difference between entities, or the cause of their difference:
namely, the attribution of contradictory properties or the difference in their causes"?

Anticipating the objection— "According to such principles, how could there be such a state [of diversity] if consciousness were indeed one?"— he says: "Cities, oceans, mountains, and so forth, conform to His will."
They are not themselves existent or non-existent, nor are they of the nature of being both cause and non-cause. || 98 ||

He establishes this very point with the words "not by itself" and so forth. For the collection of objects such as cities and the like is not real as something external in its own right; for if it were so, it would have either a gross or a subtle form, yet neither of these is possible here. To explain: [this is because] that which appears as having a single form...

Because of the association with contradictory properties such as shaking and not shaking, a gross object could not possess oneness; thus, there is a sublation regarding grossness. Furthermore, since atoms must necessarily enter into mutual conjunction, they would entail having six parts; thus, there is also a sublation regarding subtlety. Nor is it non-existent, for that which is non-existent...

Because of the application of manifestation (*bhāsana*), and for this very reason because existence (*sattā*) is not absent, it has been stated that "this is not a cause because non-existence (*asattā*) is not absent, nor is it an effect. Indeed, neither causality nor effectuality is possible without existence prior to arising and without non-existence [prior to it]. Thus it was said.
Before [that]. 98.

One might object: "In the world, this conventional practice regarding cause and effect and so forth is long-established—namely, that fire is the cause and smoke is the effect—and existence and non-existence are invariably concomitant with that; so why has this been said? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Through the total eradication of long-established necessity and the setting in motion of that which was not yet established, this independent Bhairava of the consciousness-sky remains. (11.99)

For here, it is indeed the unfolding of the Supreme Lord’s very power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) that fire is the cause and smoke is the effect; it is not, however, an inherent nature (*svabhāvatva*) belonging to fire and the like. For if that were the case, the relationship of cause and effect would be strictly fixed, yet such is not the case—since [smoke can exist] even without fire.
The manifestation of even non-existent smoke is seen through the will of a yogi;

this has been stated because of the uprooting of long-established necessity (*niyati*) and the setting in motion of that which was not yet established. Therefore, the agency over all things belongs here to consciousness alone in its full form—this has been demonstrated many times previously.
Now, one might object: "If consciousness alone, being of a full nature, manifests in such and such ways, then what is this so-called 'difference'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that which partakes in non-difference from Bhairava, who is entirely full as pure consciousness alone..."
The absence of the conceit "I am" is that which differentiates [the practitioner] within the mandala of existence.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that this differentiation has as its essence nothing more than the manifestation of non-apprehension (akhyāti). || 100 ||

Now, one might object: "In the case of seeds, sprouts, and the like, there is no penetration of consciousness at all, whereas in the case of clay, pots, and so forth, there is such penetration; however, that [penetration] belongs to the potter and is not complete. Therefore, how can it be said that agency everywhere belongs to consciousness alone, which is of a complete nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Just as no other agent is established by any means of valid cognition in a dream, so too should it be understood in all cases that self-awareness is established by itself. (11.101)

Just as here in dreams and the like, no agent conceived as a cause— distinct from one's own self-evident consciousness (*svasaṃvit*)— is established for the jars, sprouts, and so forth appearing therein; likewise, it is the same everywhere, even in the waking state and elsewhere.
The meaning is: one should understand that the agency of consciousness alone is fully realized in manifesting all states of being across all conditions. || 101 ||
One might ask: "What is the purpose of such an awakening? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He who knows thus may indeed sport in the variegated garden-city of the mind, [realizing]: 'I alone abide as the cities of the elements, states of being, and the principles. (11.102)

Indeed, he who reflects thus—"I alone manifest as the self of the universe"—perceives the mind itself as a variegated city (*citra-pura*) due to its connection with an excellence of diverse wonders; however, this does not occur in a forest or similar place, because there is no such gradation of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra-tāratamya*) there.
Rather, it is the garden (*udyāna*), which is filled with a multitude of infinite states. In that [garden]:
"He should play"—the meaning is: resting in fullness within his own self alone, he becomes liberated even while living. || 102 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely, even those who do not desire it, all involuntarily encounter the entire range of modifications beginning with birth and ending with destruction; therefore, some other cause such as karma must be sought for this.
How then can it be said that consciousness alone is the agent in all cases? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Thus, the various phenomena of birth and death—the thought "I am born" and "I have died"—appear upon the wall of the mind, fashioned by itself, within that which is unborn and immortal. (11.103)
As it is sung:
"It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it shall not cease to be again."
"Unborn, eternal, ever-lasting, and ancient, this [Self] is not slain when the body is slain. (Gītā 2.20). || 103 ||
Now, one might object: "If birth and death do not exist, how can there be the established order of this world and the next?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The states of 'this world' and 'the next world' are merely the consciousness of 'here' and 'there'."
Now, one might object: "In this case, since 'here' and 'elsewhere' as well as 'time' consist of space and time, how can consciousness be of the nature of pure consciousness alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In reality, for consciousness, there is neither space nor time at all.

One might object: "Granted that space and time do not belong to consciousness itself; however, for the object of cognition—the thing to be known which is the object of the act of cognizing—space and time must exist as its support by virtue of being its substratum. Without them, how could there be a fixed regularity (naiyatya) regarding past, future, and so forth, even if this is personally witnessed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
If this creation had been material and not composed of consciousness, then why would not even a single mountain be perceived from within it? (11.105)
In this regard, what indeed is this so-called universe: is it a form external to consciousness, or is it composed of consciousness?

If it were a form, then because everything would be merely that which is supported, what could support what? Furthermore, if it were composed of consciousness, what would even the meaning of the relationship between the supported and the supporter be? Or, in that case as well, consciousness alone would be the supporter.
That upon which all this [universe] shines forth as its support. || 105 ||

Now, one might object: "Has not the sequence of the relationship between support and supported been stated everywhere—namely, that earth is the support of water, water of fire, fire of air, and so forth? So why is this being asked:
'What is supported by what? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In the sequence of the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum, beginning with the group of the gross elements and the subtle elements,
at the end is the power consisting of consciousness, which, being of the very nature of Śiva, is the ultimate sustainer.

For even in this way, one must necessarily admit at the end that consciousness alone is the sustainer; otherwise, the infinite regress—such as "What sustains the earth, and what sustains that?"—would never cease.
Furthermore, this is because the existence of the earth and other elements cannot otherwise be accounted for than as objects of consciousness.

Only within the state of being composed of consciousness does this relationship of support and supported cohere; thus, the one Blessed Lady, Consciousness alone, is the cause for the manifestation and the maintenance of the universe, by which no fault whatsoever arises. || 106 ||
Thus it is said: "Therefore, consciousness alone is thus the agent and the sustainer; she is Śiva.
From her, all entities exist therein; she is their power, and she is the support. (11.107)

"Recognition" (pratīti) means consciousness (saṃvit). Now, an objection is raised: since it has been stated that power alone is the sustainer, what further purpose does the relationship of container and contained serve within the Śiva-realm, which is the nature of the perfectly full consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Power is the sustainer."
Regarding the word "tataḥ": the meaning is that "therein" refers to Śiva himself. It has been stated that she consists of consciousness and is indeed of the nature of Śiva. || 107 ||
And this is not something unprecedented; thus he says:
"Even that which is purely volitional does not fall downward despite being without a support.
Let the universe be contemplated in this way as resting within its own foundational power. (11.108)
Just as in cases such as "the four-tusked elephant runs in the sky," that which arises in a conceptual cognition—

such as an elephant— even without an external support, comes to rest within its own sustaining power (*dhārikā-śakti*) which consists of pure consciousness alone; and thus, it does not fall downward at all.
It remains established by its own self-sustaining power; in the same way, let this entire universe also be contemplated and grasped with certainty—this is the meaning. || 108 ||

One might object: "How can a conceptual illustration—being non-substantial—be consistent with the universe, which is a real entity whose nature as earth and so forth manifests in the form of jars and other objects?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The state of being earth and so forth is merely the habitual identification of this [body] as "I am dense" and so on; until finally, at the end, the nature of Bhairava is realized as "I am consciousness. (11.109)

The intention is this: even the entire universe, consisting of dense, liquid, and other forms, if it does not attain the sprouting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within consciousness in its various modes, can never rest upon the reality of an object existing external to consciousness. || 109 ||

Now, one might object: "If the collection of objects such as the earth, whose essence is nothing but undecaying and non-setting pure consciousness, is admitted to consist of solid, liquid, and other forms, then how is its connection with arising and passing away to be resolved?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Just as colors such as blue appear in a gem or in a rainbow, so they appear in Śiva;
yet in ultimate reality, there is never any arising or passing away of these.

Now, one might object: "Since the arising and destruction of various objects are undeniable when based upon their respective fixed locations and times, how can it be said that these have neither emergence nor disappearance? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
To say that creation occurs "in this place" or "at this time" is inconsistent;
for even space and time are created by the Lord, whose nature is consciousness.
And even in the state of illusion, there is no fixed rule regarding space and time; thus he says:
"In what is considered the waking state, within the range of three and a half cubits, and during a single watch, various dreams occur that perceive diverse directions and times. (11.112)

For even in the waking state, there appear manifestations that assume the waking condition— possessing various notions of space and time such as the earth, mountains, and sky, as well as days, months, years, and kalpas— within the limited spatial extent of the body and within time consisting of watches and so forth.
They are perceived—what indeed is the rule governing these two? || 112 ||

And thus, those who also assert the momentariness of entities based on the restriction of time consisting of extremely contracted moments are likewise refuted by this same line of reasoning; so he says:
"For this very reason, we do not consider that which is called a 'moment' to be anything at all."
Or even in a single moment of action, many rapid actions would occur simultaneously. (11.113)
Therefore, those who attained the contraction of existence for a moment must surely have relied upon this channel while adhering to the view of emptiness. (11.114)

Therefore, precisely because there is no restriction regarding place and time, no fixed moment called a "kṣaṇa" is established, by virtue of which even in a single moment of arising and so forth, there could occur "many" uninterrupted "swift" actions, such as subsistence, causal efficiency, destruction, and the like.
Because even a single moment would consist of many internal sub-moments, it could not be established as a "moment" at all;
for since one does not admit that entities persist beyond a moment,
and since the moment itself would be unstable, there would be no stability even for a moment— thus, only emptiness remains as the final resort.
If that were so, what would be the use of imagining a succession of rungs such as the system of consciousness (vijñānanaya) and the rest? ||114||
Now, one might object: "If space and time do not exist as real entities, what then is this thing called 'empirical transaction' (vyavahāra)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, that which [is capable] of making existing things void, and likewise [of making] non-existent things..."
Because he is independent, that Lord Śiva, our Master, is capable of making [all things] manifest.

"Of the existent" (sataḥ) means by way of external form. "To render void" (śūnyīkartum) means to establish [them] as consisting of pure consciousness (saṃvinmaya) by means of setting aside their externality—this is the meaning. "Of the non-existent" (asataḥ) means those whose own nature is void because their essence is nothing but pure consciousness—this is the meaning. "To make manifest" (sphuṭīkartum) means...
To manifest externally. || 115 ||
He concludes the very subject at hand:
"Thus, the Supreme Lord is celebrated as having the universe as His form;
however, the existence of anything separate from Him, such as the earth and so forth, is not tenable. (11.116)
And since this has already been stated previously, it will not be analyzed further;
moreover, we shall now desist from the numerous refutations of external objects.
"Pravyaramyata" means having ceased; that is to say, having come to rest or reached completion. || 117 ||
Now, he concludes the subject matter of this daily lesson with the first half of the verse:
"Thus, in this manner, the detailed exposition of the path beginning with *kalā* has been determined. (11.118)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Kalā and the Other Principles," in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 11.
It is clear; may there be auspiciousness. || 118 ||
One named Jayaratha, who knew the true nature of the complete classification of the sixfold paths,
indeed composed this commentary on the eleventh chapter.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Kalā and the Other Categories," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
Adorned with the straight necklace of the crescent moon whose essence is nectar, [he perceives] the entire upper sphere.
May he, who brings victory and causes the wise to rest within their own consciousness, be forever victorious.
Then, in order to reveal the application of the path by means of the second half [of the verse], he says: "Now, the application of this path in the present context is being revealed. (12.1)
"In the context" means in the sacrifice and so forth. || 1 ||
He says that very thing:

"In this way, this entire path, as it resides within consciousness, likewise resides through that [consciousness] in the void, the intellect, the vital breath, the network of channels (nāḍī), and the body. (12.2)
And externally, he is present everywhere—in the form of the *liṅga*, the physical image, fire, the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), and so forth;
thus he exists both collectively and individually, through sequential and non-sequential order.
"By that door" means by way of consciousness (*saṃvit*); for the void (*śūnya*) and the rest are created by it alone. As was stated previously:

"By way of consciousness, the establishment of the paths (*adhvan*) occurs in the void, the intellect, and the vital breaths—which are created by it—as well as in the channels (*nāḍī*), wheels (*cakra*), and secondary wheels, and externally in the body. (Tantrāloka 8.4)

Thus: "Externally" refers to the subject [who perceives] emptiness and so forth; "form" refers to the self of the disciple; and by the word "etcetera," [it includes] the ritual jar (*kumbha*) and so on. As it has been said:
"The path that resides in the jar, the mandala, and the fire, as well as that which resides within the body of the disciple..."
"And even in the Sūtra, the junction of the paths (adhvasandhi) is proclaimed to be in one place.

Here, "collective" (samasta) refers to all six kinds [of paths], while "individual" (vyasta) refers to any one of them, such as *kalā*, which is intended to be purified. Regarding "successively and non-successively" (*kramākramāt*): "successive" (*krama*) consists of the gross, subtle, and supreme levels, while "non-successive" (*akrama*)...
Its nature consists of a single stroke. || 3 ||
One might ask: "What is the purpose of its abiding in this manner? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"This path that is established externally, extending as far as the principle of consciousness (saṃvit), [Śiva] should manifest his own appropriate form there, in each respective place, through his absolute freedom. (12.4)

Beginning from the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) and extending to the external world, this sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidha-adhvā*) which is established here and there— in each path consisting of worlds, levels, and so forth— one’s own contracted self [is expanded] by means of its own sovereignty through such [realizations] as, "I alone am the supreme *Haṃsa*" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.395).

The meaning is that through one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), one should manifest the appropriate, uncontracted form whose essence is the Supreme Śiva (*paraśivātman*), and thereby bring about identity with that—this is the sense. As it has been said:
"At the boundaries of this entire universe, on all sides..."
"Having meditated upon the Śaiva reality through the process of the paths, [one attains] great prosperity. (Vi.bhai.
57) By this, the object of knowledge called "contemplation of non-duality," which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration, is also briefly set forth.
Now, one might object: "How could this appear even to a limited subject such as the body and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Everything and every form indeed shines forth even for him."
For we cannot endure being restricted in any way, even in a dream.
"Avaccheditām" means the state of having a contracted nature. As they have said:
"Even a single locus of Brahman does not transcend its possession of all forms, and it is beyond conceptualization."
Thus [ends the fifth].
One might ask: "What is the purpose of such a manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, one should behold the body as filled with all the paths of the universe, variegated by the activity of time, and the abode of the vibration consisting of space and time. (12.6)
And what follows from that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Being perceived in such a manner, he who consists of the deities within the universe is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and gratified; one who is thus possessed by him is liberated. (12.7)
"This state is not attained only through such contemplation regarding the body and so forth, but even externally"—thus he says:
"In this manner, whatever one may see anywhere—a jar, a cloth, a linga, a sacrificial mound, a book, water, or anything else—one should attain identity with that. (12.8)
One might object: "Surely it has already been stated everywhere that the attainment of the state of pure consciousness is the cause for worship and so forth;
why then is this being said again? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, the offering of objects is considered 'worship' when performed non-dualistically."
Likewise, the contemplation of the complete form is called dhyāna. || 12-9 ||
Bringing about unwavering firmness through the contemplation of its perfection,
he should contemplate the vessel of recitation by means of internal mental discourse.
There, intent on the rite of oblation, one should dissolve the individual distinctions of the entities offered and bestow their true nature as rays of light.

"Firmness" (*dārḍhya*) means up to the point of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means by means of the firmness of continuous recollection (*anusandhāna*). "He should give" (*dadyāt*) means he should manifest as the nature of its rays—this is the meaning. It has been stated that this very thing is called "offering" (*homa*): "intent upon the act of offering" (*homakriyāparaḥ*). || 11 ||
Anticipating the question, "What would happen for one who practices in this way?", he says:
"For one who acts in this manner and perceives everything with equanimity, unwaveringness is the pure vow; this is the equality proclaimed by Nandiśikha. (12.12)
Everything consists of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted, and so forth. As it is said therein:
"O Goddess, equanimity toward all things is indeed prescribed here in this vow.
A practitioner of the vow is neither a mendicant on account of his bodily impurities, nor does he become restrained merely by observing silence."
As long as the Supreme Lord, the all-pervading Śiva, has not been realized,
the practitioner, observing his vows, should remain constantly inward-turned and devoted to spiritual practice.
O Dear One, because the one Śiva dwells within all beings,
equanimity is therefore the root of all vows and the supreme vow.
"O auspicious lady, whatever other vows there may be, they all attain the state of being limbs [of this one] from hereon;
therefore, O Goddess, this is declared to be the supreme vow among all vows.
Thus [ends verse 12].
And this indeed is the supreme samādhi—thus he says:
"In accordance with the sequence of the rules for worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and vows, the ancient teachers declared that the attainment of complete stability is samādhi. (13)
The ancient masters, the former teachers such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others, have said:

"When one possesses an equal mind toward all beings in this world, whether they are oneself or others, thinking 'I am Śiva, I am without a second'—that is remembered as the supreme samādhi. (Netratantra 8.18)
Thus [ends the section]. 13.
Now, one might ask: "In such practices as worship and so forth, is anything external required, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In these matters of worship, recitation, and the like, regarding the dual state of being both external and internal,"
In the flood of material reality, there is no injunction whatsoever, nor is there any prohibition whatsoever.
In the mass of substances situated externally, such as wine and the like; and in those situated internally, such as the stalks and clarified butter and the like. || 14 ||
Now, one might ask: "Why is there a state of indifference (*upekṣaṇīyatva*) in this case? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"There is no utility here whatsoever for the purification of conceptual constructs (*kalpanāśuddhi*), the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), and so forth.
Anticipating the further doubt, "What is the proof for this?", he says:
And it is stated in the Śrītrikasūtra regarding the performance of sacrifice: || 12-15 ||

"Both ignorant of the rule and knowing the rule," and so forth, in great detail—in the *Śrītrikasūtra*, that is to say, in the *Śrīparātrīśikā*, which indicates the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) of the Trika;
such is the meaning. And likewise, it says there:

"One who was ignorant of the ritual becomes a knower of the ritual with respect to sacrifice," as stated in [Parātrīśikā, verse 20], and much more has been said; since this has already been explained previously, no further effort is made here. || 15 ||
"Now, even if this supreme power (parāśakti) is thus eternally manifest here, nevertheless,
for one devoid of external conduct, the state of Kaula is difficult to attain."
Having raised the doubt—"By such statements as these, the external application has been taught in some way; so what is this that has been said?"—he says:
"When, in whatever manner, by whatever means, and wherever one's own consciousness becomes clear... (12-16).

Then, in that manner, by him, there, each respective object of enjoyment and that very procedure—all this indeed is ordained here; thus he says: "One should employ everything here, both worldly and transworldly. (12-17)
But one who is trembling when [the state of] immovability has been reached should forcibly diminish that trembling.

"In immovability" means in a state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka)—this is the meaning. "Trembling" refers to the form of doubt and so forth. "Should forcibly diminish" means one should apply oneself with effort toward that very [state]. || 17 ||
Thus it is said: "In whatever manner and by whatever means—whether sequentially or even simultaneously. (12.18)
In this way, as doubt dissolves within, one should become diligent;
"doubt" (*vicikitsā*) here means apprehension, and by this, the object of knowledge known as trembling and shrinking is also expressed.
And what follows from this? He says:
"One should satisfy the goddesses residing in the intellect, the objects of action, and the senses by means of those very things that have been prohibited. (12.19)
"By prohibited [substances]" refers to those prescribed in such passages as, "Whatever substance is loathed by the world," and so forth. || 19 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the authority for performing such prohibited acts? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And one should rejoice in the hero's vow"—this is the statement from the *Bhargaśikhā*.
It is said there:
"One should rejoice in the hero's vow and practice it accordingly.
Thus [it is said].
One might object:
"What has doubt and the like done that such an effort should be made to diminish them? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For instance, doubt, impurity, languor, and contraction—these [are what they do]. (12-20)
Within the prison of saṃsāra, the gross pillar appears as a jar.
Mālinya is ignorance consisting of the *āṇava* impurity. *Glāni* is the lack of enthusiasm arising from that. As it has been said:
"Lassitude is the plunderer of the body, and its origin is from ignorance" (*Spanda-kārikā* 3.8).
Thus: contraction (*saṅkoca*) is the limitation of the subjectivity consisting of the body and so forth; and here, by the word "pillar" (*sthūṇā*), firmness is indicated. || 20 ||
Now, one might object: "Surely there exists a seed for doubt that is difficult to uproot—namely, 'this is to be done' and 'this is not to be done.
Therefore, how can one be diligent in diminishing that [doubt]? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The mantras are of the nature of phonemes; whatever substance is composed of the five elements... (12.21)
As for the entire collection of living beings whose nature is consciousness, what confusion could there be therein, and how?

For confusion occurs only among things of distinct natures, yet mantras and the like possess no inherent nature whatsoever— as has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "the nature of the phonemes" and "composed of the five elements."

And regarding the term "the conscious self" (cidātman): this has already been established previously at the time of stating the equality between negation and injunction; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. || 21 ||
Thus, because of the absence of any cause for this, its very occurrence is impossible; so he says:
"Due to the absence of any confusion, what is this doubt even regarding that [occurrence], clearly? (12.22)
One should not entertain doubt; thus, through non-concern, doubt dissolves.
Here, the word *saṅkara* (confusion) is an indicator for both the possible and the impossible that are being conflated.
"What is this?"—it means there is nothing [substantial] at all. Even though she is thus without cause, in her...

"One should not entertain doubt when [the state] manifests through negligence"—thus he says: "one should not have suspicion even toward that. And so, the removal of that [doubt] would be accomplished with ease—thus it is said: "in that way, doubt dissolves effortlessly. (22)
And here there is not only reasoning, but also scripture; thus he says:
"In the *Śrīsarvācāra*, the *Vīrālī*, the *Niśācarakrama*, and so forth... (12.23).
For this is extensively detailed in the scriptures, as it is stated here and there:
"The sequence" refers to the *Kramadarśana*, and by the word "etcetera," the *Śrīgamaśāstra* is included. (23)
He cites a portion of that very text:
"From doubt arises exhaustion; through doubt one becomes a vessel for obstacles. (12.24)

"The fool suspects out of ignorance; from that [doubt] come creation and dissolution. This is the second half of the verse beginning with "Through doubt one goes to an evil state; therefore, one should abandon doubt," found in the *Śrīsarvavīra*. Therein it says: "The fool suspects out of ignorance; from that [doubt] come creation and dissolution."
All mantras consist of phonemes, and all phonemes consist of Śiva.
Water is traditionally defined as that which is drinkable and undrinkable; the earth is that which is edible and inedible.
That which is beautiful and ugly is all called fire.
Wind is traditionally defined as the touchable and the untouchable, while space is said to be the void.
The offering, the one who offers, and those who accept the offering—all this, O Goddess, consists of the five elements; nothing exists anywhere that is devoid of them.
"One should generate the desire: 'How is doubt to be removed?
Thus it has been said. And much has been stated in the seventh chapter of the *Śrīvīrāvalī*, some of which was already corroborated previously;
however, for fear of making the book too voluminous, it is not written again here. One should look for that [in the original source].
This is how it should be understood. Also in the *Śrīniśācara*:
"From conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises doubt (*śaṅkā*); that doubt is of the nature of bondage. No other bondage exists apart from the doubt born of conceptual construction."
Having begun with these words, much has been said, such as: "The doubt regarding mantras, the doubt regarding the self, and the doubt regarding the principles (tattvas) are considered supreme;
I shall describe the sixfold [doubts] so that you may attain liberation. This is also stated in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*.
"...one should always be free from doubt.
Thus [ends verse 24].
This is established not only by reason and scripture, but even by the authority of the Guru; thus he says: "And the illustrious Utpaladeva, the Guru of our Guru, has said [the same].
He states that very point as follows:
We praise that path of Maheśvara, which is a thunderbolt to all doubts. || 25 ||
As it has been said:
"We praise the path of Maheśvara, which is a thunderbolt to all doubts, a fire of time to all misfortune, and the end of all that is inauspicious. (Uttara-stotra 2.28)
Thus [ends the section]. || 25 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half of the verse:
"O wise ones, do indeed understand from this great detail this individual (āṇava) means for attaining the unsurpassed state, which has been shown."
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Application of the Paths," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 12.
"Whose means have been shown" means that the means consisting of the various locations and so forth has been demonstrated by him;
may there be auspiciousness. 26.
Jayaratha, whose playful impurity of doubt has been cast away by the power of contemplating his non-difference from Consciousness,
