has here immediately composed this commentary on the twelfth chapter of the work.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Application of the Paths" (*adhvopayogaprakāśanam*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. 12.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination).
May Jayavardhana, whose movement is as bright as the full moon, increase the prosperity of happiness.
He who nourishes the world with the showers of the nectar of his own descent of power.

Regarding the doubt: "Since, according to such statements as *'In this consciousness, no differentiation of fruits should be imagined by the wise'* (Mālinīvijayottara 2.25), the attainment of the state of Anuttara is the sole fruit for those [practitioners] of the individual means (*āṇavopāya*) and so forth, then let only one means be taught;
what is the purpose of these three?"—[the following is said:]...

Wishing to set aside the distinction of qualification already taught, he makes a formal promise in the second half [of the verse] to declare the discernment of the sequence of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*):
"Now, as for who here is a vessel for qualification, or how— enough of that."
In order to analyze this, the sequence of the various descents of power (śaktipāta) is now described.
"Here" refers to the three means, beginning with that of the individual (āṇava).
"Now, since a 'discrimination of the descent of power' (śaktipātaviveka) has been stated by others, what would be the point of one here as well? Certainly;
however, having restated that very [position] and refuted it, our own established doctrine will be set forth. Thus he says:
"In this regard, some here declare this method of the descent of power..."
Having demonstrated and refuted that [position], his own view will be presented. || 13-2 ||
"This ritual" (imaṃ vidhim) means the manner of discerning the descent of power (śaktipāta) that has been introduced—this is the sense. || 2 ||
Now, one might raise the objection: "In this system, liberation arises from the knowledge of the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and that [knowledge] has dispassion and so forth as its cause;
so what is the purpose of postulating an unseen descent of power (śaktipāta)?"—incorporating this doubt, he first demonstrates the superiority [of this system] over Sāṃkhya:
In this regard, that which is perceived as existing and partaking in pleasure, pain, and delusion—being thus uneven—is postulated as having an equal cause. (13.3)
That unmanifest [nature], which consists of various forms such as *sattva* and the rest, is insentient;
like a jar or other objects, it is an effect, and its single cause is that Night. (13.4)

The meaning is as follows: regarding the points to be addressed—namely, the restatement and refutation of the views of others concerning the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and the presentation of our own doctrine—it is said here with the intent of establishing the sequence of that descent of power.
"This" refers to everything from Mahat down to the earth; it is "uneven" precisely because it partakes in pleasure, pain, and delusion.
The meaning is that its form consists of the qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the rest, existing in a state of mutual relationship as subordinate and principal.

"Of such a nature" means having the inherent nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion. "Equal" means having qualities that do not exist in a state of subordinate and principal relationship—this is the meaning. For this very reason, [it is distinct] from sattva, rajas, and tamas...

It has been stated: "Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium. The word "sa" (it) refers to the cause. Now, let this Sāṃkhya doctrine be granted—that this state of disequilibrium rests upon a state of equilibrium; and that equilibrium is eternal, unitary, and not preceded by any cause, whereas beyond that [equilibrium], there exists another principle (*tattvāntara*) which serves as its cause.
"What indeed would be the superiority over that [Pradhāna] such that it could not possibly exist?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that," and so forth.

Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is an effect, because while being insentient (*ācaitanya*), it is manifold; for whatever is insentient and manifold is entirely an effect, like a jar; whereas that which is not an effect is not thus.
In that case, since it is insentient, it cannot be manifold like the Self; and since it is insentient and manifold, the Unmanifest is therefore an effect. And it was stated previously:
"Everything that is insentient and manifold in nature is an effect, just as a jar."
"And likewise, the Pradhāna is therefore the effect, but the Self is not conscious. (9.156).
Furthermore, since the Unmanifest is an effect, what is its cause? To this it was said: "Its sole cause is that Night. (4)

Now, one might object: "In that case, let Māyā alone be the cause of the universe for you, just as Prakṛti is for us; what need is there for a Lord (Īśvara) who presides over it? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"She [Māyā] is insentient because she possesses the same nature as her effects, and indeed, the effect already exists within her."
From the creative impulse (kalā) up to the earth (dharaṇī), she was incapable of procreation due to her insentience.
Therefore, the Lord (Īśa) must agitate this [Māyā], for its agitation constitutes its fitness for procreation.

Now, one might object: "If Māyā is insentient because she is a product, then by that same logic, it would follow that the potter is also insentient, just like the jar. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From Kalā down to the Earth..."

"And its effect indeed always exists within it. For in the state of necessity (*niyatidaśā*), that which appears as the persisting essence of something in some form is its primary cause—just as clay is for a jar—and within that [cause] alone does its existence reside; this is the intended meaning. "By that" means by way of being capable of production (*sūtyakṣamatvena*).

For this reason, it has been explained that liberation would not arise from the mere knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* and so forth; for without the descent of the Lord’s power (*īśvara-śaktipāta*), such knowledge of the distinction itself could not even arise—so what opportunity would there be for liberation, which is caused by that? This has already been established previously and need not be discussed here.
Again, an effort is made. Anticipating the objection—"Surely, if this [Prakṛti] is agitated by Īśvara, what indeed could she produce?"—he says:
"And for each individual soul (pums), she produces various beginningless objects of experience. (13.6)

"Objects of enjoyment" refers to the entire range from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*). Furthermore, her procreation in this manner is neither for her own sake, because she is insentient (*jāḍya*), nor for the sake of the Lord, since He consists solely of pure consciousness.
To the question "Then for whose sake is it?"—anticipating this doubt—it is said: "For the sake of the beginningless and diverse individual souls (*puṃs*)."
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since there is no distinction in their nature as subjects (*pums*), why does that [power] not operate toward liberated souls (*muktāṇu*) as well?
To this he says:
"And if the subject is without distinction, why does that [power] not [operate] toward liberated souls?"
Now, it might be argued: "It is precisely because this [impurity] coexists with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of karma that it possesses such capacity for production;

however, since the latent impressions of karma do not exist at all in liberated souls (*muktāṇu*), how could this [capacity] apply to them? To this he says: "From what source does their absence of the latent impressions of karma derive?"—and so forth.
The sign is the formative force of karma, and that does not exist within them.
If this is argued, [we reply: from what indeed could there be an absence of karmic impressions for them?
"From what" means "from nothing at all"—this is the meaning.

Since the exhaustion of karma does not occur through experience alone— for experience is conceived in two ways, either sequentially or non-sequentially— then, in the case of sequential experience, the consequence of further karma is unavoidable, and thus its exhaustion would never occur; whereas, in the case of non-sequential experience, there could be no experience of these [karmas] at all.

For in this way, the very nature of action—which consists in the sequential granting of its fruits—would be abandoned; yet this is not the case. Thus, in either scenario, the exhaustion of karma cannot be established. As it is said: "For the consequence of other portions of karma remaining after [the experience of one] is difficult to overcome. (13.8)
The simultaneous experience of [the fruits of] actions is not logical, for they indeed ripen in succession; since an action bears its fruit, why should it ever abandon its own nature? (13.9)

If the destruction of karma results from knowledge, then from what does that [knowledge] arise? If it arises from being impelled by the Lord, then from what does He [arise]? If it arises from dharma, then from where does that dharma come? If it comes from karma, then let that be explained. (13.10)

Now, if the destruction of karma through knowledge is accepted on the basis of such statements as, "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37), then what is the cause for that knowledge itself?
It has been stated thus; but why?
For regarding that [knowledge], many other causes have been described by others, such as the thorough investigation of the six or sixteen categories (*padārtha*);
we do not know which among those is the one fixed cause for that [knowledge]. In this regard:

With reference to the section concerning the doctrine of the *Seśvara-mīmāṃsā*, he says "Īśvara," and so forth. "From dharma" means from that object characterized by injunctions such as "one should sacrifice," which is designated by terms like *apūrva*—this is the meaning.
To the question "What is the cause of that [dharma] as well? it is said: "Whence is that too? [The answer is: "From action (*karman*)," for that which is enjoined...

Since an action, due to its momentariness, is incapable of yielding a fruit that arises after a long interval, a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) must be postulated for persons as an intermediate factor to establish this; this is designated as "dharma" or "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*), by virtue of which the entire systematic arrangement of the fruits of actions is rendered possible.
As they say:

"Action prescribed for the sake of a fruit that occurs after a long interval cannot, according to the wise, be otherwise [than through an intermediate cause]; thus is the *apūrva* (unseen potency) understood."

Thus [it is said]. "That" refers to the action by which the attainment of knowledge might occur through the medium of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). By the question "Let it be told," which is posed with reproach, the utter impossibility [of such a thing] is indicated. || 10 ||
He says that very thing:
"Indeed, there is no such karma by which knowledge is brought forth;
and if that knowledge were born of karma, it would certainly fall into the category of [worldly] fruits. (13.11)
The meaning is: "If it were to fall into the mass of causes, it would take on the form of the fruit. || 11 ||

Furthermore, it is not logical that the exhaustion of one action should occur through the fruition of another action; thus he says: "How could [the fruit] of one action burn away the prior mass of karma?
For, since there is no distinction in their being fruits, even a fruit consisting of heaven, cattle, and so forth, would produce knowledge."
The intention is that [the fire] would also burn away karma.

One might object: "Even though there is no difference in their being the fruits of karma, why is it that by the power of the Lord's will, knowledge alone burns away other karmas, while [the attainment of] heaven, cattle, and so forth do not? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "How could it be so for the Lord, who is devoid of hatred, passion, and the like, yet [acts] in some cases? (13.12)
Such an intention exists nowhere else because there is no cause for differentiation.

"Somewhere" refers to cognition; "elsewhere" refers to [the attainment of] heaven, cattle, and so forth. Because there is no cause for differentiation—since for the Lord, who is free from passion, hatred, and the like, there is no such distinction whatsoever by which [a difference could arise] even without...
One should conceive of one sign as that which burns, and the other as that which is burned.

And even though knowledge is a fruit of action, its power to burn away other actions is not merely brought about by the will of the Lord, but is rather established through the force of reasoning; thus he says:
"But in this way, knowledge would indeed burn away the webs of karma, for karma [is the fuel]. (13.13)
This [ignorance], acting as a concomitant cause, produces fruits such as heaven;
ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, and even by the fruit of other actions.

In this context, ritual action characterized by the performance of the *agnihotra* oblation and so forth, being accompanied by ignorance— as stated in such passages as "But the *kārma* [bond] belongs to the ignorant agent" (*Rigveda-prayoga-ṛjuvimalā* 3.6)— would produce its respective fruits, such as heaven and the like, only through the cooperation of that ignorance.

And ignorance, being destroyed by knowledge that has arisen as the cause for the cessation of other actions, results in karma whose capacity to produce its fruit is obstructed due to the actual absence of its auxiliary causes; this much is what is meant by the statement, "Knowledge burns away the webs of karma."

Now, if indeed karma is rendered such that its capacity to produce fruit is obstructed by means of removing ignorance— which serves as a cooperative factor for the yielding of results— then what is to be understood in a case where ignorance is not removed and karma is rendered fruitless?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Fasting and other such acts would otherwise be the fruit of evil karma;
for it is indeed accepted that [the ritual] renders evil karma fruitless. (15)

In this context, indeed, other [practices] such as fasting and so forth— indicated by the word "and so on" (ādi)— which are prescribed in other scriptures like the *Smṛtis*, and likewise [qualities] such as sinlessness (*anaghatva*),
would constitute a defective fruit of action; in that case, the established order of the fruits of action would perish.

This is the meaning. Indeed, because even without the cessation of ignorance, [the practice] renders fruitless sinful acts such as fasting and other rites of atonement (*prāyaścitta*), as well as actions contrary to one's own welfare such as being bitten by a dog; that is, it indeed makes their capacity to produce results obstructed.
This has indeed been accepted by you yourselves, who maintain the doctrine of karma; for Śātātapa says: "One bitten by a dog, even if of pure conduct, shall fast for three nights. (15)
Thinking that the question of whether action is rendered fruitless by means of the removal of ignorance— or not— might lead to a very remote and difficult deliberation, he says:
"If that which is called 'ignorance' is the absence of knowledge, then what is it?"
Or is it prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) or destruction (dhvaṃsa)? In the first case, does this apply to all cognitions? (13–16)

Alternatively, the first position regarding any cognition is impossible, because it relies upon a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) in the form of "the absence of cognition. [The term] *dhvaṃsa* refers to absolute non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Regarding that, he first analyzes prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). First:
By the phrase "of someone" (ityādinā), it is meant that it belongs to a specific individual. "The former position" refers to the view characterized by the non-existence of all consciousness.

For no such sequence is possible; he says this regarding one for whom, in this beginningless saṃsāra, there has never been anything that was not the self: "There is no such person whose consciousness has ever arisen [in that way]. (13.17)

Indeed, there is no atom in this beginningless existence; what, then, could be the sequence of continuity? For if it were so, [the world] would become like a jar or similar objects due to its total insentience and muteness—this is the intended meaning. Having thus rejected the position that all consciousness is non-existent, [he now rejects] the position that a particular cognition is non-existent.
He objects: "And since it is established that there is prior non-existence of future cognition... (13-18).
Even for the liberated soul, that [nature] certainly exists; yet it does not exist prior to its birth.
If it is argued that "knowledge will arise in this liberated one," then let this be examined. (13.19)

"Of those that are to be" (*bhāvinām*) means "of those that will come into being. The underlying intention is that if that which has already occurred were non-existent, there would be only a *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (non-existence through destruction). The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this applies not only to bound souls such as ourselves, but even to liberated individual souls (*muktāṇu*). "That" refers to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of future cognition.

How so? He says: "janamata" and so forth. For it has been stated that this prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) must exist prior to the arising [of the effect]. Now, let this be considered regarding the knowledge about to arise in this liberated soul (muktāṇu): why is it that knowledge does not exist as something yet to come (bhāvī) in the liberated soul? || 19 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Why is knowledge not cultivated here? Surely because the body and so forth have not yet arisen.
Why is that? Because of the exhaustion of karma. Why is that? Because of the destruction of ignorance. (13.20)
How can there be the destruction of ignorance when consciousness is a prior non-existence?
This ignorance is indeed a prior non-existence, because its production as a positive entity is impossible. (13-21)

In this world, even among bound souls (*baddhāṇu*), although objects are presented through the connection with the intellect and external senses, it is the knower alone who is conventionally designated as "knowledge"; yet in reality, there is no arising or passing away of knowledge.
Among liberated souls (*muktāṇu*), however, because of their freedom from the bondage of connection with the body, senses, and so forth, [knowledge remains constant].

It has been stated that even the conventional discourse regarding arising and so forth is rejected from afar by the phrase, "because there is no birth of the body and so on. Furthermore, conceptual cognition (vikalpajñāna) need not even be suspected here, precisely because of liberation.
As for the phrase, "due to the destruction of ignorance," it is said that actions accompanied by ignorance indeed bear fruit.

This has already been stated. Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, in the case of a liberated soul (muktāṇu), there would be no ignorance characterized by the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of future knowledge; how then can there be the removal of ignorance? For even in the case of a liberated soul, there must necessarily be the prior non-existence of future knowledge—to this he replies: "For in the case of prior non-existence..."

Regarding the phrase "the non-existence of consciousness": the meaning is "of some future consciousness," that is, of consciousness (*saṃvit*). Now, one might object: "In the case of a liberated soul (*muktāṇu*), there is no consciousness at all that is yet to arise; so of what could there be prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)? To this he says: "Prior non-existence," and so forth.
Now, if future knowledge is impossible in the case of a liberated soul, what is the reason? To this he says:
"Why is that future knowledge not present? Surely because of the non-birth of the body and so forth.
This is the sharp, circular whirlwind that destroys all positions. (13.22)

For in this way, the non-arising of future bodies and so forth is caused by the absence of future cognition; therein also lies the exhaustion of karma, therein also the destruction of ignorance, therein also the non-production of future cognition, therein also the non-arising of future bodies and so forth,
and therein also the exhaustion of karma— thus revolving, it brings about the destruction of the very root.
Since this would result in the fallacy of circular reasoning, it is not correct to say that ignorance is the prior non-existence of knowledge. || 22 ||

Nor is it logical here that even non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) [should apply]—thus he says: "Now, if this ignorance were indeed destruction, then it would be eternally present in liberated souls; therefore, let the manifestation of the effects of Māyā exist within them. (13.23)

Regarding the phrase "always abiding": because experience—which consists of pleasure, pain, cognition, and so forth, produced by various objects—has absolutely ceased, and because ignorance always persists even with respect to those [objects], the karmas associated with it also bear fruit; thus, there is the manifestation of the impurity of *māyīya-mala*, which has that [ignorance] as its cause.
The meaning is: let there be the manifestation even of its effects, from the *kalā* down to the earth; otherwise, liberated souls would not differ from bound souls. || 23 ||

Having thus rejected the position of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), he introduces the alternative of relative negation (*paryudāsa*): "Now, ignorance is not a non-entity; rather, it is considered to be false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
That very [false knowledge] is the auxiliary cause for actions in regard to their own performance. (13.24)

Now, if false knowledge (mithyājñāna) is indeed the auxiliary cause (sahakārikāraṇa) for the performance of actions by their agents, does it then occur as an auxiliary cause only at the time of the production of their results, or rather from the very moment of their own production?
It must be stated that [the karma] continues until the fruit is reached; thus he says:
"Then what action should be said to produce its own fruit?
At that very moment, while false knowledge exists, it attains the status of a cause. (13.25)
Now, at the very moment when an action is performed, it exists in its own nature;
if there is false cognition [of that action], then from such an action comes the fruit. (13.26)

"At that very moment" (*tadaiva*) means at the very time when the effect is produced by means such as a staff, just as in the case of clay; "by such [a cause]" (*tādṛśāt*) means accompanied by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Therefore, just as a sprout and so forth might arise from a final seed accompanied by earth and other factors, so too [does it happen here].
From action accompanied by false knowledge arises a fruit characterized by various experiences such as enjoyment and so forth. || 26 ||
He refutes this very point in sequence:

"In the first position, once dissolution has occurred and the prior creation is being set in motion, there is no possibility whatsoever of false cognition due to the absence of bodies and so forth. (13.27)
Furthermore, in the latter case, whenever, by whomsoever, or wherever an action is performed, all of that is accompanied by ignorance. (13.28)
"Inevitably," [it is said] because for no one whatsoever would there be an exhaustion of karma.

"Pralaya" (dissolution) means in the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*), which is the supreme absorption (*prakṛṣṭe laye*) due to the complete cessation even of those who are devoid of body, vital breath, and intellect. "Prācyā" means primordial, that is to say, belonging to the beginning; here, in the initial creation.

There is no disagreement that the Lord, in accordance with their respective past actions (*karma*), effects the conjunction of atoms with this or that body and so forth; however, action bears fruit only when accompanied by ignorance (*ajñāna*),
and since there would be no substratum for that ignorance in the absence of a body and the like, it could not exist at that time.

Because of the absence of that concomitance, since the capacity of those karmas to produce their fruits has been obstructed, the creation would not be accomplished; thus, even the mere activity of the Lord toward that end would not be established, and consequently, nothing at all would exist. Now, [if it is argued] from the very time of the origination of the karmas...
Since ignorance persists until the attainment of the fruit, it would necessarily accompany these [actions] at all times; thus, the karma of no one would ever be exhausted,
for it has been stated that karma is destroyed only through the destruction of ignorance, and that ignorance is what is meant here.
Since it persists as something that is always following along, how could such a state of being come to be? || 27-28 ||
For even an action performed by a knower would, by its very nature as an action, be accompanied by ignorance;
since that capacity to become a vessel for obstructed results exists there as well, what need is there to speak of those who are ignorant?
Or, let it be granted that an action performed by a knower is free from association with false knowledge.
"But how could that which was performed prior to the attainment of knowledge be fruitless? To this he says:
"Even though one has become possessed of knowledge, if one performs some action... (13.29)
But if that [present effort] were fruitless, what would become of the mass of previous karma?
The meaning is: even for a knower, if the infinite previous karma were rendered fruitless, no cause whatsoever could be possible—this is the sense of the question, "What would be the outcome?"

Now, one might object: "What is the use of this position of ours? Let the former position alone suffice: since the dissolution has already occurred, even in the absence of bodies and so forth, knowledge is indeed possible for the atoms because their nature is consciousness.
To this, he says:
Now, even at the time of dissolution, due to its connection with the nature of consciousness... || 13-30 ||
How can it be that the cognition of atoms is indeed false?
If you say it is due to their inherent nature (svabhāva), then why is it not so in the case of the liberated Śiva? It is certainly not so. (13.31)
"Let it be granted that they possess knowledge; but from where does their falsity arise?"—thus it was asked:

"How is it that this is false? Now, if the falsity of knowledge arises simply from its being knowledge, then since there is no difference in their nature as consciousness (*cit-svabhāvatva*), why does it not apply equally to liberated souls (*muktāṇu*) or even to Śiva?
"What is the connection with false knowledge?"—to this he says: "In the case of one who is liberated or Śiva, is it not so? Indeed, it is not."

Surely, ignorance is not intended here in its general sense, but rather in the form of the non-perception of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, as described by the Sāṃkhyas; he states that very point: "And that which is called non-perception is the cause in the transformative [principle]."
For that [determination] occurs with respect to the primary [object], due to its connection with both confusion and distinctness. || 13-32 ||
For the sake of perception, that which is produced by the intellect—aided by its unique capacity for human goals—extends from the beginning up to the earth; therein lies the focus of the mind.

The non-distinction of the mental modification from the Self, due to the grace of the light of the Puruṣa, whereby the intellect illuminates the object along with itself—that is called experience (bhoga). (13.34)

The meaning is that [the Lord] is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for the transformation of *pradhāna*—that is, for the sake of the transformation of *pradhāna* into the various forms of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. And it has been stated that this very [cause] exists for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctness and non-confusion of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). For it is said: "That indeed..."
"For the sake of perception through the conjunction of both mixture and distinction. As they say:
"Without creation, bondage is indeed not possible for the *puruṣa*;
creation exists for the sake of its liberation..."
Thus it is said. Regarding that, he first states its "transformability" (pariṇāmitva) with the words "pumartha... and so forth.

This is the unique capacity, not shared by anything else, characterized by the tendency toward the production of effects, directed toward the purpose of the Spirit (puṃs), which is defined as the realization of the Self that is delimited by the attainment of the Spirit's isolation (kaivalya) from Pradhāna.
The meaning is that it is associated with that [Pradhāna] and acted upon by it. As it has been said:

"For the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception, and likewise for the sake of Pradhāna’s isolation (kaivalya), there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from that, creation proceeds."

"From primordial nature (prakṛti) arises the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among that group of sixteen, the five elements arise. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22).
Now, let the Pradhāna transform in this manner, whether through confusion or through distinctness.
Anticipating the question, "What, then, is meant here by 'vision' (darśana)? he says: "In that regard, etc.

In this context, when there is thus a transformation of *pradhāna*, although the intellect (*buddhi*)—which assumes the forms of various objects through the power of the transferral of the light of the *puruṣa*—is itself insentient, [it appears as sentient].

Due to its abiding in a state of volitional activity, even though the person (puruṣa) remains indifferent, through the medium of the reflection of his own image upon the intellect (buddhi)— which, like a stainless mirror, appears as both [the self and the object]— there arises a mental modification (vṛtti) consisting of the thought, "I know this."

The meaning of the statement is as follows: because of the conceit of being the agent, there is a semblance of identity; that very [semblance] is called "experience" (bhoga), which consists in the perception of a confusion arising from the transfer of the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) into the intellect (*buddhi*), which is joined with the reflection of the object. As it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse: *kartṛtayevābhimānāt sārūpyaṃ sa eva viṣayacchāyāyoginyāṃ buddhau cicchāyāsaṃkrānteḥ sāṅkaryadarśanātmā bhogo bhaṇyate.* [The English translation: Because of the conceit of being the agent, there is a semblance of identity; that very [semblance] is called "experience," which consists in the perception of a confusion arising from the transfer of the reflection of consciousness into the intellect, which is joined with the reflection of the object. As it has been said:

"Therefore, through its conjunction with that [Purusha], the insentient linga appears as if it were sentient; likewise, although the gunas are the agents, the indifferent [Purusha] appears as if he were the agent. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20).
Having thus described the state of confusion (*sāṅkarya*), he clarifies the state of discernment (*vaiviktya*):

"I am indeed the intellect, characterized by the nature of transformation; as for that other [Self], let him be someone else entirely, distinct from me, the single Self. Such is the consciousness of discernment. (13.35)
Since its purpose for that person has already been accomplished and it is deprived of auxiliary causes, it does not produce [an effect] for that person at all, but indeed for another. (13.36)

By the phrase "having the nature of transformation" (*vikṛtidharma*), its mutability and lack of consciousness are established; for this very reason, in order to indicate its distinction from the Spirit (*puruṣa*), which possesses consciousness and other such qualities, it was stated that [the Self] is "some unknown being" (*kaścit*) and "different from me" (*mad-vilakṣaṇa*). As they have said:
"The manifest and the Pradhāna are composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; the Puruṣa is the opposite of these. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 11).
In reality, when the shadow of the object has ceased in the intellect (*buddhi*) of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa...

The transfer of the reflection of pure consciousness (*cicchāyā*), which resembles the flame of an unflinching lamp, is called the knowledge of discernment (*vaiviktyajñāna*), wherein it is figuratively expressed that "nature is one thing and the person (*puruṣa*) is another.
As it has been said:
"Thus, from the practice of reality, the knowledge that 'I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I' arises— pure, absolute, and free from error, without remainder" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 64).
And thus, because the purpose of the person, which consists in the vision of both [the self and the non-self], has been accomplished, for this very reason...

The meaning is that, due to the absence of the auxiliary cause—the soul’s sole fitness for the purposes of the Puruṣa—Nature no longer produces [effects] with respect to that Puruṣa who has attained discriminative knowledge; she becomes one whose productivity has ceased.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, the Puruṣa, established in himself like a spectator, beholds Prakṛti— whose productivity has ceased due to the fulfillment of its purpose, and who has desisted from the seven forms."

"Thinking 'I have seen [Him],' the one [Puruṣa] becomes indifferent; thinking 'I have been seen,' the other [Prakṛti] ceases [her activity]. Even though there is a conjunction between the two, there is no further purpose for creation" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 66).
Nor, because Prakṛti has thus ceased her procreative function, does it follow that [liberation] would occur indiscriminately for everyone...

It was stated that this would lead to the consequence of non-liberation; however, [the author says] "for indeed, [it is] other," meaning "other" refers to the knowledge of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*) which has not yet been attained. || 35-36 ||
He introduces this very point briefly for the sake of refutation:
"In this regard, the property of both the person and the root is 'non-perception';
or rather—let this alternative stand aside—for now let this be discussed. (13.37)

For if this ignorance, consisting of non-perception, were an attribute of the person (puruṣa), then because it would be subject to modification through either constant bondage or the arising of knowledge, the person would be devoid of consciousness. And if that [ignorance] were an attribute of primordial nature (prakṛti), what would happen to the person such that he would be bound? Consequently, there would be no liberation for him at all.

The intention is as follows: since both faults would descend upon the position that [the self] possesses both natures, and so forth, when analyzed in detail, it would result in a state of extreme profundity—or rather, in fact, in a contradiction.
This is what is meant by saying, "Let this objection, which I am raising according to the perspective to be explained hereafter, be resolved."
But let this be explained. || 37 ||
He says that very thing:
"Experience [continues] until discrimination. What then is the limit there?
If, upon the attainment of discrimination, the vision of the entire source [of manifestation] arises, is even that [vision] still [experience]? (13.38)
In the former case, it may occur either generally or through specific [causes] due to a single birth;
in the latter case, it would never occur because of the connection with future time.
It is with this very intention that it was stated, "And because of the activity for the sake of isolation" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 17),
and so forth; for even if the complete perfection of all [eight] powers were indeed the attainment of discrimination, [it would still not be sufficient].
Since it is impossible for it to be the fulfillment of another birth, it must be a limit;
so, does that [limit] exist merely as the nature of birth, or rather as the nature of birth qualified by the self of earthly objects such as jars? To this he says:
"Does it exist through universals or through particulars? And neither of these two is tenable—thus he says:

"Eastern," and so forth. "In a single birth" means that even in a single individual instance, the universal exists in its entirety. "Never" is said because future specific births are infinite. (38–39)

"Surely, let the latter position alone be accepted; for the objection regarding infinity would not arise, since [the cognition] does not depend on all particularities (*viśeṣa*) but rather relies upon only a few?"—thus he raises this doubt:
"If [it were so], then through only certain particularities, [cognition] would occur simultaneously for all [of them]."
Due to beginningless conjunction, what mutual diversity could there be between them? || 13-40 ||

In this world, since the beginninglessness of the connection with *prakṛti* is equal for all persons (*puruṣa*), the discernment (*viveka*) of that [connection] might arise either simultaneously or without great delay, immediately following the attainment of a specific birth determined by *prakṛti*, just as the ripening of rice stalks occurs in autumn; such is their mutual relationship.

Since diversity and succession would be impossible [under such a view], enjoyment and liberation could not occur sequentially; thus, even the ignorance described by the Sāṃkhya does not adopt the status of a Naiyāyika [category]. 40.
Therefore, he says:
"For this reason, even from the Sāṃkhya perspective, this ignorance is not at all tenable.
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even from the Sāṃkhya perspective," it is indicated that this is not only untenable according to the sequence previously stated.
This has been stated [in the sense that] "even by this view..."

Now, one might object: "Since here only worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) are to be accepted, let those alone be analyzed; what is the use of discussing whether [the world] is joined with or separated from ignorance (*ajñāna*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Without ignorance, neither bondage nor liberation can be established. (13.41)
These two [states] are logically consistent, yet they are not tenable according to the arguments already stated;
for there would be no fixed distinction such as,
"this one is bound, this one is liberated."
Thus [ends the section]. 41.

One might object: "Let there be no question of whether [this] is logical or illogical; what is the use of this concern of ours, since the distinction between bondage and liberation can be established simply through the existence of the atoms of *māyā*? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even though the existence of *māyā*, karma, the atoms, and the will of the deity remains... (13.42)

There is no connection between bondage and liberation because the cause of their distinction is impossible. Regarding the phrase "by the will of the Lord" (devecchā): the intention is that without the presiding power of Īśvara, Māyā and the rest, being insentient, would be unable to perform even the slightest action. Therefore, [it is said] "from that," meaning because ignorance is illogical. Connection...

The reasoning is as follows: "Because no cause for such differentiation is possible. For, since [conditions] such as *māyā* are restricted to each individual soul (*puṃs*), and since the Lord (*Īśvara*) is free from passion and hatred, there could be no basis whatsoever for the distinction that "this one is bound" and "this one is liberated"—this is the intended meaning. || 42 ||

Thus, one must postulate some kind of obscuration, denoted by the term "ignorance" (ajñāna), which acts as an impediment to the knowledge and agency inherent in individual souls (aṇu); for it is by means of this that the distinction arises between one who is bound and one who is liberated—
so he says:
Therefore, by the word "ignorance" (ajñāna), [there is the negation] of the attributes of knowingness and agency. || 13-43 ||
A wise person must state that there is some obscuration of the atoms of consciousness by means of the word "ignorance" (ajñāna), as it has been said:
"Impurity, ignorance, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the essence of concealment, and darkness."
"For ignorance (avidyā), obscuration (āvṛti), and stupor (mūrcchā) are stated there to be synonyms.
Thus [ends verse 43].
And what is that like? He says:
"Established as having the nature of a veil, it is non-different from its own essential nature. (13.44)
And because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its division, that [Self] is one among all individual selves;

it is non-different from its own nature, like a partless entity—this is the meaning. Even so, there is no proof for a plurality of composite wholes (*avayavin*), namely, the so-called "difference of causes"; such does not exist here.

"It is so," it is said; because there is a lack of evidence for its being manifold, it is one. By the use of the plural number in the phrase "in all selves" (*nikhilātmasu*), it is shown that although this [impurity] is one, it possesses many powers; otherwise, its capacity to veil all selves would not be possible, or else, upon the liberation of one, all would be liberated.
As they say:
"The powers of impurity are distinct for each individual soul, and they are the obscurers of its qualities. (44)
And is such a thing eternal or an effect? If it is an effect, from what does its production arise?
To this he says: "From what could that have been produced? If [you say] from Māyā, then how indeed is she [produced]? (13.45)
"This [bondage] occurs only in some cases and not in the liberated self"—this would be the objection from the opponent if no cause for such a distinction can be found. (13.46)
Because there is no origination, it is eternal and does not perish.
If its production were from *māyā*, then it would produce this [world] for everyone, or perhaps for no one at all;
thus he says: "If from *māyā*," and so forth. And therefore, [it would follow that] liberated souls, like bound souls...

If one were to argue that this [falsehood] applies without distinction, then the very same objection raised previously would follow. For it has already been stated that if knowledge is false simply because it is knowledge, then—since there is no difference in its essential nature—that same [falsehood] must also apply to liberated souls (*muktāṇu*); for a thing [cannot be both true and false].
The sense is: "it would fall on your side. Now, if it has no cause whatsoever, then let it be eternal—thus he says "the cause," and so forth. "By that" means by the non-attainment of a cause;
and this is the reason for the absence of origination: because of the absence of its cause, there is an absence of origination.
Therefore, because this is eternal, it is said that precisely due to its eternity it is not subject to destruction, and thus it does not perish. || 46 ||
It does not perish only because of its eternity, but also due to other causes—as he says:
"Precisely for that reason, even when there is oneness, because of its being common to other selves. (13.47)

Therefore, because of that previously stated reason—namely, the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its differentiation—and because unity exists, this [consciousness] does not perish, since it is common to both self and other; this is the connection with what precedes.
For, due to its unity and commonality to all, if it were to perish in one place, it would perish everywhere simultaneously.
"May all be liberated"—this is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object: "Since this is merely of the nature of the absence of knowledge, it is nothing at all; what purpose is served by this triviality?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Nor is it non-existent, because it performs a function; nor is it unreal, because it is conventional."

"Because of its capacity for purposeful action" means that it possesses agency with respect to purposeful action characterized by the veiling of consciousness—this is the meaning. Furthermore, even so, it has not been stated that its nature is solely cognition, "because it is a concealment of that [consciousness]. For consciousness itself cannot be the concealer of consciousness—this is the intended sense.
Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so, but what is the cause of the connection between this [power] and the selves?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Nor is the conjunction of this with the selves based on a cause, because such a cause is impossible. (13.48)

"Because that is impossible"—for what kind of person would the postulated cause apply impurity: to those who are already stainless, or to those who are already stained? In the first case, because there is no distinction in their stainlessness, it would either apply even to Śiva and the liberated souls, or else it would not apply to anyone at all, just as it does not to Śiva.

[The opponent’s] understanding [is as follows]: "Furthermore, its application to the second [self] is useless because it was already stained even prior to that; therefore, it is established that the relationship between the selves and that [impurity] is indeed beginningless. As they say: "The beginningless impurity has a beginningless relationship..."
Thus [it is said]. Scripture (*āgama*) also, beginning with the passage: "Due to the connection with beginningless impurity... and so forth.
"Why is pure crystal [soiled], and why is copper stained with impurities? Just as there is a cause for that [staining] in those cases, there is none for the pure Self, which is Śiva. (48)

Having thus stated the nature of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of limited agency) by way of its individual components, he speaks as follows to summarize it in its totality and to establish that very [impurity] as the cause of the other impurities:
"Therefore, a single entity, being existent and eternal, is eternally connected with the selves."
That ignorance is inert matter, a stain, and the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra. || 13-49 ||

Thus, this kind of impurity belonging to the individual soul (*āṇavamala*) is the cause—like a sprout—to the *māyīya* impurity, which has been described by the passage beginning with, "The *māyīya* [impurity] takes the form of the body and the worlds... and so forth; it is the *kārma* [impurity].
Impurity (*mala*) is its cause; that is to say, it is the direct and indirect instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for both types of impurity. As it has been said:
"Impurity is the cause of karma, while the latter is the effect (*naimittika*)."
Thus [ends the section]. || 49 ||

One might object: "If such a stain is eternal, or if it is eternally bound to the individual souls (aṇu), then saṃsāra would never cease, and thus the consequence of non-liberation (anirmokṣa) would follow. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When the obstructing power of that [stain] remains dormant due to the rays of Śiva..."
Then that atom is touched; when it is touched, its own powers of knowledge and action become manifest. (13.50)
"This [individual soul] enters [the state of liberation], impelled like a sun-gem by the sun.
"He remains indifferent" means he withdraws from his own activity called "obstruction"—this is the meaning.
"He is touched" means he becomes a recipient of the descent of Śiva's power (śaktipāta)—this is the meaning. By that...

Just as a sun-crystal (sūryakānta), when touched by the rays of the sun, enters into its own activity characterized by blazing forth, so too this [individual], purified by the descent of Śiva’s power (śaktipāta), becomes one whose own sovereignty of consciousness is fully manifested within his own perfect knowledge and action— this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how could there be mutual diversity in the manifestation of their own nature even among pure souls, given that there is no difference in their immersion into perfect innate knowledge and action? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And by virtue of the gradual progression of the intensity of indifference toward the obstructive power. || 13-51 ||
Therefore, they speak of the manifold nature [of the self] in the manifestation of one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*).
Thus, regarding that manifestation of the individual souls' own consciousness which occurs due to the cause of contact with the rays of Śiva,
its diversity is due solely to the power of the impurity (*mala*)— the obstructive power (*roddhrī śaktiḥ*)— which is connected to it.

The gradation of neutrality— which consists in indifference toward one's own activity— is that which, through its various degrees reaching up to the supreme limit, serves as the cause for the mutual distinction among selves, even though they are all equally pure. || 51 ||

Now, one might object: "Has it not been taught everywhere that the descent of power (śaktipāta) belonging to the Supreme Lord, manifested within one's own consciousness, is the cause [of liberation]? So how is it that here the ripening of impurity (malaparipāka), which consists of the indifference of the obstructing power (rodhaśakti), is mentioned instead? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This very thing is designated in the scriptures as "the descent of power" (śaktipāta). || 13-52 ||

"Sa" refers to the touch of the rays of Śiva, which has been introduced as having the ripening of impurities as its cause. "Eṣa" (this) refers to that which has just been directly perceived. "Is defined" means it is established by its own technical terminology by the venerable teacher Kheṭapāla and others—this is the meaning.
Having thus presented the procedure for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) according to others, he refutes it:
"To this it is replied: first of all, this [notion of] impurity (*mala*) is not tenable in such a way;
this was already stated in the preceding section (*pūrvāhnika*), so what is the point of repeating it? (13.53).

"In this manner" means in the form already stated. "In the first part of the day" refers to the beginning of the ninth chapter. [The question is: what is the fruit of repetition? That which exceeds that must be discerned—this is the intended meaning. || 53 ||
He states that very point:

"What could this 'ripening' (pāka) of impurity be? If it were the destruction [of the impurity] of other selves, then because it is said that there is only one impurity, it would follow that [all others] possess purity. (13.54)

Now, even if impurity (*mala*) were restricted to each individual soul and beginningless like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it would still be destroyed; yet, if this destruction were to have a cause, [the following applies]. (13.55)

The cause is either karma or the will of the Lord; for karma is not of such a nature [to account for this], as one might ask, "What is this ripening? Nor is it simply impurity (*mala*), for that has already been essentially refuted previously—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "impurity is one," for if impurity were one, then even in a single instance...

If that [obstructive power] were destroyed, it would follow that all [souls] would attain liberation simultaneously; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the universal liberation of the world at once. Furthermore, it is not logical for the obstructive power to be manifold—as was established previously—by which a state avoiding simultaneous liberation might occur; rather, let this very [power] be accepted as restricted to each individual soul.

It was stated that by this [explanation], no fault whatsoever arises: "Now, [the impurity] is restricted to each individual soul. But one might object: "Granted that the impurity (mala) is either unrestricted or restricted in this way, since it is beginningless (anādi), how could its destruction be possible? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though beginningless, the impurity may perish, just like antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva)."

For even though prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is beginningless, it would perish upon the production of its effect—this is the intention. And if the destruction of that which is beginningless is admitted despite being illogical, is this [destruction] caused or causeless? If it has a cause, what is that cause? To this he says: "Even so," and so forth. In that regard, first, as for karma...

"It is not logical for [the soul] to be the cause"—thus he says, "karma," and so forth. "Of such a kind" means that which is the cause for the destruction of impurity (*mala*), because [karma] is solely the cause of its experience (*bhoga*). Nor is it the will of God (*īśvarecchā*);
for is that [will] independent as the cause of that [experience], or dependent? (It is certainly not dependent.)

Because there is no other factor to be depended upon besides the varying degrees of the ripening of impurity and karma; and because that [divine action] is impossible when impurity is to be destroyed;
nor is it independent, for since the Lord is free from passion and hatred, it would follow that he acts in that manner toward all beings without distinction. || 55 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"And why is it that the independent will of God acts in such a manner only in certain instances? (13.56)
And if this [existence] were causeless, its destruction would be reckoned as occurring in the second moment;
thus, *saṃsāra* would be neither begun nor completed. To this he says:
"If its destruction were causeless, let it perish even before [the second moment]."
The meaning is: "Let it perish even sooner; let this other state of persistence not be shown to me."

Now, it might be argued that because a continuous succession of subsequent moments that are closely similar occurs, [the entity], though destroyed, remains as if undestroyed, so that it does not go out of sight—to this he says: "If it is said that it produces a similar subsequent moment, then that is simply permanence. (13.57)

For in this way, by proceeding as a continuum and initiating another moment independently, it would not undergo interruption—this has been stated: "That is indeed stability. For, unlike the final moment of a jar, the occurrence of another causal complex (sāmagrī) is not possible for this [moment], by which [interruption] might occur.
If a dissimilar effect were produced, there would be a destruction without continuity. || 57 ||
And this has been stated while accepting the destruction of impurity; however, in reality, such destruction would not belong to it—thus he says:

"Furthermore, the destruction of an eternal entity, whose birth is not dependent upon a cause, is never observed. As for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), since it is a non-entity (*avastu*), let it be so. (13.58)

Anticipating the objection—"How can it be said that there is the destruction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), since its birth does not depend on a cause?"—he says: "But prior non-existence is a non-entity. Let it be so;
for since that prior non-existence is a non-entity, there could be no fixed rule regarding it. However, in the case of an entity (*bhāva*), this rule applies.
"That which is the infinity of the beginningless. || 58 ||
Now, [the author] states that there is no destruction of the impurity (*mala*), but rather its power is obstructed—namely:
"Furthermore, this so-called 'maturation' (*pāka*) of this [impurity] is simply the obstruction of its own power;
thus it would remain with its power blocked for all [souls], like poison or fire. (13.59)
Furthermore, if its power were to arise again, it would produce its own effect like poison or fire;
thus, even those who are liberated would not be liberated, nor do we admit the existence of such a power in Him. (13.60)
If indeed the ripening [of karma] were merely the obstruction of its own power, then just as poison or fire— whose powers to kill or burn are obstructed— would affect everyone without distinction,
so too this [karma], with its obstructing power blocked, would cause everyone to be liberated simultaneously. And thus:

If, due to some cause, upon the removal of an obstacle, its own power were to re-emerge— just like poison or fire— it would remain indistinguishable toward all; thus, even those liberated through great effort would suddenly become bound again for them, according to the principle of reversion (*pratiprasava*).

Since the possibility of cessation is thus rendered doubtful, there would be no certainty whatsoever regarding either bondage or liberation; consequently, what person acting with discernment would strive to abandon bondage and attain liberation? Furthermore, we do not comprehend what the name of this power might be, by which—
One might ask: "Could there be a ripening (pāka) of this [karma] that acts as an obstacle? To this he says: "And we do not admit such a power (śakti) for it. (60)
Now, if it is said that its power is "obstructive" (rodhikā), then what would it obstruct? To this he says:
"If [it is called] 'obstructive,' of whom [among men]?"—namely, of their states of knowledge and agency.
If this is so, then does its status as an obstructor consist merely in its presence, or...
Anticipating the objection that [the Lord] would be of no effect, he says:
"If [the Lord] were an obstructer by virtue of his mere existence, there would be no possibility for liberated souls or bound souls. (13.61)

In that case, if its power of obstruction were due to mere proximity, then since that proximity would be no different [for all], it would likewise apply even to liberated atoms; consequently, this entire world would be as if blind and mute, remaining nothing but bound. || 61 ||

To refute the second position as well, he says: "And the impurity (mala) effects nothing other than mere proximity, because [if it did], it would follow that the selves are subject to transformation and thus impermanent. (13.62)
For if, by virtue of its proximity, impurity or its power were to impart some excellence whatsoever to the selves, then it would follow that they are subject to modification and impermanence;
thus, there would be a collapse of your own established tenet. || 62 ||

Now, one might object: "Could it not be that the impurity does nothing at all to the selves, but rather veils their inherent qualities such as knowledge and agency, by which they are said to be bound?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The person (pudgala) is merely the state of being a knower and an agent, and it is not the substratum of those [qualities].
If that [substratum] were obstructed, alas, the destruction of form (rūpa) would follow as a consequence. (13.63)
Thus, what would be the consequence of those [obscuring] veils for the selves? Rather, knowledge and action alone constitute the nature of the selves;
it has already been stated previously that by the mere presence of such-and-such a veil, the destruction of their very nature would follow:
"For the multitude of individual souls (aṇu), which are all-pervasive and whose essence consists solely of knowledge and action..."

"The absence of that [distinction] is the impurity which serves precisely for the destruction of form. The distinction between a property and its substratum, as well as their unity through inherence—that has not been asserted by you, like the disciples of Kaṇabhuj. (Tantrāloka 9.74–75)
Thus [ends the section]. || 63 ||

In this context, what is called the "veiling" (āvaraṇa) of knowledge and action by impurity (mala) is defined as their non-manifestation to the observer, just as a cloth [conceals] a jar. Furthermore, that [impurity] cannot render a real entity (vastu) into a non-entity (avastutā), such that knowledge would become ignorance. Consequently, either everyone would be liberated, or everyone would remain bound.
Thus, even if impurity (*mala*) were present, no systematic distinction between bondage and liberation could be established. To this he says:
"And obscuration, which consists in invisibility, does not produce any otherness in the object; knowledge cannot be obscured, just as [the nature of] a jar [cannot be changed by darkness]. (13.64)

In this regard, not only is it so, but even obscuration itself is impossible—thus he says, "like a jar," and so forth. For an obscuration of formless consciousness by a stain that is either material or immaterial is not tenable; rather, such an obscuration could only occur between two material things—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, since action is merely a sprout of knowledge, it is not mentioned here separately; on the contrary,
one should understand that the impurity which has come to obscure this [knowledge] is what must be removed, so that the state of being a knower itself may be intensified— thus he says:
How can that very knowledge which is to be obscured by an obscuration fail to know it? If it were so, then obscuration would exist in name only. (13.65)

"By that which is obscuring" means by that which is intended as an obstruction—this is the meaning. "Obscuration" refers to impurity (*mala*) because it functions as such. Consequently, since this [consciousness] would not be suppressed, one would know everything just like the impurity itself; thus, everyone would become omniscient—[a conclusion] devoid of reality.
It has been stated that there would be a concealment that relies solely on words; as it was said: "And thus, there would be a concealment by name alone. (65)
And if indeed its ripening consists solely in the obstruction of its own power, then what is its obstructer?
If it is God—does He act independently, or does He depend on the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*)?
If He were independent, He would act in that same way toward everyone; thus he says:
And who is the obstructer of that power which is to be obstructed? It is God. If it is argued that He lacks dependence [on anything else] in that regard, the answer has already been given previously.
Regarding the word "given": as it has been said— "The will of the Lord is independent; why should it be so only in some cases? (Tantrāloka 13.56). || 66 ||
Furthermore, regarding the latter position, he asks: "What is said concerning the very equilibrium of karmas, in relation to which this [desire] might proceed?"—and so he says:
"Then, having regard for the equilibrium of karmas, his desire proceeds."
Its nature must also be explained; for what indeed is the equality of actions? (13.67)

He says that very thing: "Due to the greatness of the sequence of experience, at some time regarding the fruit, when two karmas are obstructed by mutual opposition, they remain in such a state of equilibrium. (13.68)

In this context, due to the power of the sequence of experience (*bhogakrama*), when many karmas have been exhausted, there may be at some indefinite time two karmas that, although ripe, possess fruits that are mutually contradictory; because of their opposition regarding the fruit, they remain obstructed and stay indifferent toward bestowing their own respective, specific experiences.

Furthermore, because they have not yet reached maturation, the karmas that follow immediately after do not turn toward the experience of their results; this state, characterized by the opposition between two conflicting karmas, is called the "equilibrium" (*sāmya*) of karmas—this is the meaning of the sentence. || 68 ||
Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be such an equilibrium of karma, what need has the Lord for this [equilibrium]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And the omniscient Lord, having perceived that impurity as a portion of time..."
That goal and that time are obstructed by the avoidance of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

The word "that" (tam) refers to [time] characterized by obstructed and contrary actions; and in observing that, omniscience is the reason by way of a qualification. Raising the doubt, "What is the proof for the existence of such a time?", he says: "It is to be defined," and so forth. And such a time as this...

The meaning is: it is characterized by the exclusion of pleasure and so forth; it is established through self-awareness because all [beings] are devoid of the experience of pleasure, pain, and the like. || 69 ||
For this very point he refutes:
"Since the fruit is to be given in that same way by actions of sequential, pure, or mixed forms, what is this mutual obstruction? (13.70)

For in this world, there are three kinds of actions: wholesome, unwholesome, and variegated. Among these, wholesome and unwholesome actions possess a pure form because their nature is determinate; the variegated, however, possesses a mixed form because its nature is indeterminate. Therefore, it is logical that these occur in a sequential order.

Because they cannot exist simultaneously, as their essential natures are mutually exclusive, they must therefore yield their own respective fruits only in succession. What kind of mutual obstruction could there be among these regarding the fruit, since it is impossible for them to function simultaneously even at any single moment? For these...
It has been stated many times that in performance, persistence, and the granting of fruit, there is indeed a sequential unity of life. || 70 ||

Granted that these two opposing actions might remain obstructed with respect to their fruit at some point in time; however, in that interval, would some other action produce its fruit or not? If it were to produce a fruit, then what is the use of that obstruction, since actions would proceed according to their sequence as before?

Because [the fruit] remains in the state of being about to be given; otherwise, if it were not to bear fruit, then even the karma that bestows birth and lifespan would not bear fruit, and consequently the body would fall at that very moment due to the obstruction caused by the power of impurity (mala). Thus he says:
"And when those two are obstructed, birth and lifespan would also not exist; therefore, [the body] would fall."
If it is argued that the body is merely the cessation of experience and so forth, then [we reply]: surely not. || 13-71 ||
If Śaṅkara obstructs the impurity when the portion of karma that bestows birth and lifespan is present, does he fear the karma that grants experience? (13.72)
"Now, has it not been stated that even karma which bestows birth and lifespan would not bear fruit at that time?
Surely this was intended with reference to karma that grants experience (*bhoga*). Thus he raises the objection:
"If it is argued that there is a cessation only of those two [types of karma] that grant experience. But if this is so...

Even if the Lord were to obstruct impurity (*mala*) despite the non-cessation of the karmas that produce birth and lifespan, He would obstruct impurity without even depending on the cessation of those karmas that grant experience; why then would He fear them such that He must necessarily depend upon their cessation? To this, he says: "But," and so forth. (72)

Nor is this a certainty— that the Lord, in the form of the moment of time (*kālakṣaṇa*), whose nature is the equilibrium of karma and who is devoid of the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, restrains the power of impurity (*malaśakti*)— for even if such an experience were to occur a hundred times,
no one at all would perceive any sign of the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*śaktipāta*), which is the cause for the cessation of the power of impurity.
"It is perceived"—thus he says:
"Even if they experience a state hundreds of times devoid of joy and pain, it has been observed frequently that they do not attain immersion in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion. (13.73)

Joy and distress are pleasure and pain; this is the immersion into the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion (*bhakti*). For devotion is indeed the first sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). As it has been said: "In this regard, the first sign is unwavering devotion to Rudra" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 2.14).
Thus [ends the verse]. || 73 ||
Now, fearing that the opponent, having been driven from every position, might resort to a different view by clinging to a mere straw, he raises this objection:
"Nevertheless, the Supreme Lord, depending upon the greatness of time..."
One should say, "He does so; what kind of time is this? || 13.74 ||

"The majesty of time" means the manifold variety of time, ranging from the sequence of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and instants (*lava*) up to the *kalpa* and *mahākalpa*. "He acts in such a way" means that he might obstruct the power of impurity (*mala*).
Now, if this is so, [what then of] space, time, and the rest?

Since the majesty of time is indeed indistinguishable due to its being common to all, we do not know what specific aspect of that [majesty] the Lord requires for the obstruction of the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*).
Thus it was said: "It must be stated what kind of time this is. (74)
For in that case, if there were a dependence on that [liberation] in a general sense, everyone would be liberated simultaneously;
yet, when sought here, no such distinction is found. Thus he says:
"Furthermore, this experience is beginningless, and karma is beginningless along with the person (pudgala)."
And therefore, the time for the succession of enjoyments is equal for everyone. (13.75)

Consequently, since there is no distinction in the beginninglessness of karma, its experience, the person (*pudgala*), and so forth, it would follow that for the sequence of experience, all persons— having avoided even the remotest distance from exhaustion— would have an equal duration of time,
such that the impurities and their potencies would cease simultaneously or in immediate succession, just like the fruits of trees at the end of the season.
If it were thought that maturation would arise [for everyone], it would follow as a consequence that there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the liberation of all beings. || 75 ||

However, there might be this distinction if any one among the triad beginning with karma were to possess a beginning— that is, if there were a point of reference such that by one [karma] a single kalpa is experienced, while by another two kalpas are experienced; and for this very reason, from a specific sequence of experience characterized by being long or short, there would also be a leveling of the karmas— thus he says:
For if there were a beginning for anything, this diversity would arise from this group [of causes]: "this one has experienced [pleasure] in this kalpa, but that one has experienced both. (13.76)
"From such a sequence of enjoyments, there might be an equality of karmas;
but this is not the case for you. Therefore, this [position] is in every respect entirely flawed. (76)
And thus, there is not only this much fault, but yet another as well; so he says:
"By means of this seed of the method, I consider [it] to be the cause of manifold variety. (13.77)

The activity of the world as it has been established does not hold true in that manner—meaning, by this [reasoning] just mentioned, characterized by the lack of distinction regarding the beginninglessness of karma and so forth. The word "I think" (*manye*) is used in the sense of probability. || 77 ||
He demonstrates that very impossibility [of their being identical]: "The individual souls (aṇu), covered by beginningless impurity, [are distinct] from the nature of vision and action. (13.78)
How is it that all [souls] are equal, yet have resorted to various successions of karma?

Since, in this world, atoms are entirely without distinction due to being shrouded by beginningless impurity, it is logical that they remain undifferentiated even while resorting to a succession of karma; for their karma is likewise without distinction.
Since such diversity does not exist [in Him], how could He serve as the cause for the diversity of that world?
Now, if the cause here is a craving for enjoyment (*bhogalolikā*), from where does the variety of that [craving] itself arise?
To this he says:
"If it is varied by way of a craving for enjoyment, then surely from where [does that craving come]? (13.79).
"Seti" means "desirous of enjoyments. "Nanu" is used here as an objection. || 79 ||

Now, if it is argued that even for the variety of the craving for enjoyments (*bhogalolikā*), the cause is the variety of karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*), then that same fault recurs: what is the cause of the variety in those [impressions] themselves? To this he says:
"If it is said to be due to the variety of beginningless karmic impressions (*anādikarmasaṃskāra*)."
That very diversity must be explained; from what [source] do necessity and passion arise?
If this greatness belongs to those two, why are they not partakers of inconsistency?

"Anādi" (beginningless) is an adverbial modifier. By that, the meaning is: having been beginningless, she [the *vāsanā*] is diverse due to the variety of karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*). Thus, since the latent impression of karma is deposited by karma, its diversity [follows].
The diversity of karma is the cause; therein lies the craving for enjoyment; therein lies the diversity of karmic impressions;
and therein lies the diversity of karma itself—thus revolving, this descent into a cycle is difficult to escape and brings about the destruction of the very root. Now, it is said:
"This is not the cause for the variety [of experience] arising from a craving for enjoyment (*bhoga-lolikā*), but rather this is the manifestation of destiny (*niyati*) and attachment (*rāga*).

Thus he says, beginning with "destiny" (*niyati*). For the nature of attachment is precisely the craving for enjoyment, thinking "may something happen to me"; however, the nature of destiny is "this very thing [shall happen]. Therefore, it is those two alone [that are responsible].
"Those two which produce the variety of longing for enjoyments"—this too is not [the case], as he says with the words "those two," etc.
For it is *niyati* (destiny/limitation) that restricts one here and there by means of the very variety of objects, or *rāga* (attachment) that colors one;
thus, even regarding that variety, another cause must be sought, and for that too, yet another.
It is evident that an infinite regress would result, which would cause the destruction of the very root.
Now, if it is argued that the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is the cause for the diversity of karma, that too is not so; thus he says:
"But the will of God, if independent [of other factors], cannot be conceived as the cause of differentiation. (13.81)

That [divine power] cannot be dependent, because there is nothing else besides impurity (*mala*) and karma to be depended upon; nor can it be independent, because since God is free from passion and hatred, He is impartial toward all beings, and thus the diversity [of the world] would be untenable.

One might object: "Since the world has never been otherwise than it is now, as is known from such [scriptural] cognitions, the variety of karma is simply established as it stands; what is the use of this search for a cause? To this he says:
"Now, if [the existence of karma] is established merely by its beginninglessness, which is devoid of reason..."
In that case, let this established order suffice; let this further impurity be in vain.
"In that case, beginningless and diverse karma alone will suffice to sustain all established orders;
so what is the use of postulating this useless impurity?"—thus it was said: "Enough then with this impurity; let it be in vain. (82)

He establishes this very point: "For indeed, as long as Māyā does not operate upon the person (pudgala), there is no karma; nor is its activity without a cause, for the impurity (mala) is measured by that [activity]. (13.83)
And if beginningless karma were to serve as the cause for such imagined activity that is the effect of māyā, what would be the purpose of postulating a separate impurity (mala)? || 13.84 ||

In this regard, first of all, the established order is as follows: during the state of dissolution of the selves (*ātman*), as long as the impurity consisting of *māyā* has not become active, the impurity of *karman* cannot possibly exist; otherwise, their subsequent connection with *kalā* and the other categories would not be possible. Furthermore, it is not logical for this [impurity] to be without a cause.

Because it would follow that either existence or non-existence would be eternal; therefore, since the impurity of karma cannot otherwise be accounted for, the impurity called *āṇava* is inferred as its cause. As the scripture also states:
"The efficient cause is called desire (*abhilāṣa*), and the effect resulting from it follows thereafter."

Thus, even so, if in the case of karma existing within the sphere of *māyā*, karma itself—consisting of its beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is accepted as the cause, then the postulation of *mala* (impurity) is redundant. || 84 ||

Even if this were accepted—that there be no such thing as "impurity" (mala)—then, according to your view, no systematic arrangement of karma consisting of experience and liberation could be established; thus he says:
"But then, let there be no impurity with respect to karmas of manifold forms."
When things are revolving in a continuous stream, no fixed determination is possible. || 13-85 ||

For when impurity (*mala*) is absent, even though karma continues to manifest in diverse forms, it is entirely ineffective toward everyone—like one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus, its persistence as a cause of experience (*bhoga*) is not tenable, nor is its persistence as a cause of liberation (*apavarga*). For that [liberation] occurs only when there is equilibrium (*sāmya*), and that...

Because this [world] possesses diverse forms, it could never be so; for that which, being diverse at the beginning and in the middle, cannot tolerate uniformity, how could it be otherwise at the end?—this is the intended meaning. || 85 ||

Regarding this, it is said: "Just as, because actions are diverse, there is no uniformity at the beginning or in the middle, so too this particular form of the self may become something else at the time of its manifestation. (13.86)

The word "even" (*api*) is displaced; by it, [the meaning is] "even at the time of manifestation. "This"—meaning some form of the Self—would not be equal [to the state of liberation]. This is the underlying intention here: for you, when impurity (*mala*) exists, even if there is equality regarding one's karma, its ripening is held to be the cause of liberation. And where...
Since impurity itself does not exist there, what purpose would action serve, in relation to which such a state might even occur? || 86 ||
