In this way, the distinction between bondage and liberation as conceived by you is utterly destroyed, and your elaborate display of scripture is rendered useless; thus he says:
"In this manner, this entire sequence beginning with bondage and liberation is indeed cut off."
It has been examined that bondage arises from ignorance and liberation from knowledge. (13.87)
Now, let this be; even if one were to concede the existence of impurity (*mala*), the equality of karma (*karmasāmya*) is not logically consistent—thus he says:
"When these two karmas are in opposition regarding their own fruits, at some point in time..."
If they remain indifferent, then let this action be understood [as such]. || 13-88 ||
What room, then, is there for the descent of Śiva’s power (śivaśaktinipāta) by that much?
If indeed, at some contrary time, two actions remain obstructed regarding the bestowal of experience, then, by virtue of propriety, let some other action itself be awakened in the interim.
Let that [karma] exert itself to yield its own fruit by being rejected;
yet, by the mere obstruction of karma, what occasion is there for the descent of Śiva’s power, according to the maxim of the sudden appearance of a pumpkin? || 88 ||
For in this way, at the time of dissolution, the falling [of the seed] upon the atoms would necessarily occur simultaneously,

because at that time the power of all karmas to grant experience is obstructed; moreover, if an equilibrium of karma were admitted, there would be no purpose served by the descent of Śiva’s power— thus he says:
At some time, when there was this indifference on the part of those two, then—
Because their mutual opposition remains unremoved over time, those two [opposing karmas] will not bear fruit in the end, nor will other intervening karmas. (13.90)

Because the time has arrived, these [senses] have been obstructed and have become objects of enjoyment for the two who have departed; thus it is always so in the case of livelihood, and likewise at the fall of the body.
Once liberation has arisen, let us set aside such conceptualizations as the descent of power (*śaktipāta*);
for even if two contradictory actions remain blocked at some point in time,
they would persist in that very same state because their contradiction has not been removed even at a subsequent time.

Furthermore, other karmas that have reached their time [for fruition] are obstructed because they have attained a state of being merely "to be experienced" (upabhogyatā), since their time has already passed; thus, at some point, no karma whatsoever would ever bear fruit. And in this way, within the continuous flow of worldly activity, even the karma that bestows life-span would gradually be exhausted in the interim.

The fall of the body would necessarily occur, and thus liberation would be accomplished without any effort at all. Therefore, by the maxim: "If one should find honey on the branch right here, why should one go to the mountain?
the conceptualization of a descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is rendered useless. || 91 ||
Now, it might be argued: "When two actions are obstructed, they always obstruct any subsequent action as well;

however, that [subsequent action] may bear fruit at some point in the future. To this he says: "Why should it not bear fruit in that very first moment, since no specific cause for its [later] occurrence has been stated—what is the need to wait for another action?"
Then, in the moment immediately following the conjunction of those two neutral actions, || 13-92 ||
Why is it that another action does not likewise produce its fruit at that very moment?

Now, if it is held that no other action whatsoever bears fruit there, but rather those two very actions themselves bear fruit when they are released from their obstruction, then by what is that removal of their obstruction effected?
Thus he says:
"Then, in another moment, those very same [causes], now devoid of obstruction... (13.93).
Consequently, by what is the avoidance of the connection between those two [cause and effect] effected?
Furthermore, does that [avoidance] arise from themselves or from something else? If it arises from themselves, let it be so from the very beginning;
if it arises from something else, since there is no certainty as to what that might be, let this matter rest. (93)

Now, it was argued that the Supreme Lord might effect the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) in dependence upon the equilibrium of karma; however, neither of those two can serve as the cause for the diversity of the descent of power—which is divided into distinctions such as intense, moderate, and mild—because they themselves lack internal variety. To this, he says:
Karma is equal by its very nature, and it does not possess degrees of intensity.

It would not be the case that "it is not Śiva’s will" regarding that effect, namely the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), nor would it possess degrees of intensity, because it consists of equality and is eternal. "That" refers to the degree of intensity.
For an effect must conform to the sequence of the qualities of its cause—this is the intended meaning. || 94 ||
In this way, even concealment (*tirobhāva*), like grace, is not tenable according to your view—thus he says:
"And this which is called concealment, from what would it arise again? (13.95)
Whatever was to be accomplished by the equalization of karma has indeed already been performed.

For this is precisely the function of the equalization of karma: that, having regard for it, the Lord effects the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) upon the individual souls (*aṇu*). And since that has already been done by him previously, there is nothing further to be done thereafter.
The meaning is this: from what could that which is called concealment (*tirobhāva*) arise? Upon its arising, we perceive no cause whatsoever.

It cannot be *mala* (impurity), because that has already reached maturity. For once it has matured—having accomplished its purpose—it would not transform again into a binder of the person (*puruṣa*). For if it were so...

Even if established with great effort, the systematic arrangement of the scriptures would fall into disorder. Furthermore, it is not the case that this [impurity] possesses the capacity to grant experience only when conjoined with the stain of karma; nor is there any equality between them, because [the impurity] has fulfilled its purpose by being the sole cause for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). || 95 ||
"Now, what is the use of these [other causes]? Let it be said that the will of God alone is its cause"—to this he replies:
"But if the will of God is the cause, then [the same objection] must be stated as before. (13.96)
For in that regard, it has already been stated many times previously that this [power] is not independent, as it is the cause of that [manifestation].

Nor is it dependent [on anything else], because there is no other thing to be depended upon besides impurity (*mala*) and karma; furthermore, such dependence would be impossible in the case of the effect, which is concealment (*tirobhāva*). Thus, the claim of the proponents of duality—that God is the performer of the five-fold act—is refuted.

By this very same method, other conceptualizations—such as whether the Lord’s will acts as an eternal cause or a non-eternal cause—have also been refuted; thus he says: "By this, those other dependencies which were postulated regarding the Lord’s will [are also discarded]."
For they too are refuted by the criticisms directed against [theories of] eternal causes, non-causes, and so forth. (13.97)

In that regard, if there were no cause, the fault would be that there must be either eternal existence or eternal non-existence. If the cause were eternal, there would be eternal existence alone. And if the cause were non-eternal, what indeed is this other non-eternal cause?
Since such a thing cannot be determined, nothing at all would be established. || 97 ||
Now, if it is argued that the Supreme Lord might effect the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) in dependence upon dispassion and so forth, that too is not the case; thus he says:
"Dispassion is a distaste for enjoyment; merit is a certain kind of discernment."
Association with the virtuous, and constancy in the practice of worshiping the Supreme Lord and other such rites. || 13-98 ||
The occurrence of a crisis, the examination thereof, certain signs in the body, service to the scriptures, the fulfillment of the multitude of enjoyments, and divine knowledge. (13.99)
If this [dependence] belongs to the Lord, then it is to be refuted as before.

"And this is to be refuted as before" means that if the required factors—such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth—are not causes, then there is the fault that they must either exist eternally or not exist at all. If, however, they are caused, is the cause eternal or occasional?

In that case, there would be constant existence in the first instance, and in the other, what else could be the occasional cause? It cannot be the will of God (*īśvarecchā*), for if that were so, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor can it be the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*) or the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*); for if these were the effects of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then those very factors [would have to be its causes].

Let it be that [the world] depends on what is spoken by a Lord; what is the use of these intermediate postulated [causes]? Nor can any other cause be asserted, because for that too, a fixed rule would be impossible. || 99 ||

Now, one might object: since detachment (*vairāgya*) and the other qualities are observed everywhere to have an invariably concomitant coexistence with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), on this basis it may be conjectured that the Supreme Lord surely effects the descent of power in dependence upon detachment and the rest; for otherwise—

How could there be this coexistence of these [qualities]? Regarding the dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth present before one, he says: "What is the use of investigating the cause if the effect is already perceived?"—according to this maxim, what is the point of such a search for a cause? He explains:
And there is deviation (vyabhicāra) both collectively and individually, as well as by way of their essential nature. (13.100)

Furthermore, there is mutual interpenetration and a great deal of logical inconsistency here regarding the effect of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). In this matter, must all factors such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the rest be required by the Lord collectively, or individually? In either case, there is deviation from the rule. To begin with, they cannot be taken collectively.

Because such a nature is not observed in those who possess the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); nor are they [the means] individually, since even among Buddhists and others there is an absence of the descent of power despite their possession of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Furthermore, qualities such as dispassion and the rest cannot possibly exist even when considered in terms of mutual inclusion—thus he says:
"And by its very nature, there is the entry of mutual dependence.
For it is said: "Detachment (vairāgya) is defined as the turning away from enjoyments."

Therefore, it need not be stated separately that there is a distaste for enjoyments, because that is already included therein. Furthermore, this is a greater logical inconsistency: that the Supreme Lord should require anything at all.
For even if He required only a mere trifle, His sovereignty would be compromised. What [more need be said]?
Furthermore, regarding that collection of objects wherein nothing at all can be accomplished even in the absence of a single one—
alas for this sovereignty, since by its own will it is unable to accomplish anything whatsoever!
As they say:
"Of what use is such sovereignty, which is like a kingdom dependent upon ministers? Nothing whatsoever is fashioned by mere whim, independent of the requirements of practical conduct. (100)

"We do not know what the sequence is for those who maintain the distinction [between the levels of grace] regarding the procedure for the descent of power (śaktipāta)—thus he says: 'Therefore, we do not conceive of what this sequence of the procedure for the descent of power is. (13.101)
Having thus refuted the opinion of others regarding the procedure for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by means of a restatement [of their view], he speaks in order to demonstrate his own position:
"In this way, [this teaching] bestows liberation from the fainting fit caused by the entry of the poison of delusion."
I shall speak this great medicinal herb of the scriptures, which was uttered from the mouth of the illustrious Śambhu.
He elucidates that very point:
"The Lord is autonomous, whose nature is consciousness, and whose essence is light by his very being;
through his engagement in the play of concealing his own form, he becomes the manifold atom. (13.103)

In this context, there is only one Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness and who consists of light; however, unlike the light of the sun and other sources, He is not insentient. For this very reason, He is autonomous, and for this very reason, because He performs the play of the dissolution and emergence of the entire universe, He is the Divine (deva) by His very nature, and not [dependent] on anything whatsoever.

In relation to this: by concealing its own nature as the one Self whose vision and action are complete, the individual soul (ātman) becomes manifold—a limited atom of vision and action that assumes various artificial forms—whereby this vast proliferation of transmigratory existence unfolds. 103.
Now, one might ask: "What, then, is the meaning of saṃsāra in this context? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By means of karmas consisting of conceptualizations of forms imagined by himself, he binds his very self here through his own freedom; thus it has been described. (13.104)

For here, that very [Self], by its own will, through various conceptual constructions such as "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"—which have as their ultimate reality nothing more than these manifold mental constructs—[acts] by means of karmas;
for it is said: "Even there, karma alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra" (Rig-pa'i rim-pa, Chapter 3, Verse 10).

The meaning is as follows: by this primary mode of expression, [the Self] binds itself through its own sovereignty by means of the *kārma* impurity (*mala*), and transmigrates through the manifold variety of various births, lifespans, and experiences; this has already been stated for the most part at the beginning of the ninth chapter—so what further need is there for an elaboration of that?
He is not only bound by his own freedom, but he even liberates himself—thus he says:
"This is indeed the majesty of the Lord's sovereignty, that He, though consisting of limited individuality (aṇutā), again touches His own perfectly pure nature. (13.105)

For this too is indeed the unfolding of His sovereignty: that even while existing in the form of an atom, He touches His own perfectly pure nature by means of a reversal; He reveals Himself, whose essential nature is full vision and action, though it had been concealed—this is the meaning. || 105 ||
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then why does he manifest himself in this way toward only a certain person?
Is there perhaps some aversion toward others? To leave no room for such a doubt, [the author] says:
"It should not be asked how it is that he manifests thus toward only a certain person."
For there is indeed no person whatsoever who can be subjected to such an inquiry.
For in our view, unlike the proponents of dualism (*bhedavādin*), there exists no such thing as a person (*puruṣa*) distinct from Him to whom this objection could apply—
namely, whether He should liberate all or none at all.
Rather, it is the Lord Himself who, through His absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*), manifests as both pure and impure, which constitutes His very nature.
"His own form is indeed just like that. || 106 ||
Now, let it be granted that this is so; nevertheless, even if this [consciousness] rests upon the state of differentiation, why should this objection not apply?
If you think thus, what is the purpose of the objection? To this he says:
"If He is indeed the Lord in that way, and His own nature is such."
What question can there be regarding the nature of that which has such manifestation as its very essence? (13.107)
"What is there to be questioned?"—the meaning is that there is nothing at all; for the intrinsic nature of an entity is indeed beyond questioning—this is the intended sense. || 107 ||
And this has not been stated by us alone; thus he says: "Our supreme preceptor, the most excellent teacher, has said this in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*.
He states this very point:
Because he possesses the nature of Śiva through the expression of the fivefold activity, for his own ritual action... || 13-108 ||
Where is there any search for other causes in that which is already active?

The statement "this is the one whose fivefold activity consists of the five types of tasks beginning with emission" refers to that very nature of Śiva; [it acts] for its own purpose, which consists of grace and so forth.
Since this deity has already become active, where is there any search for other causes such as passion, hatred, and so forth?
For there is simply no occasion for seeking such causes;
thus, how could it fail to bestow grace characterized by the manifestation of its own essential nature? It cannot be otherwise.
It is subject to censure.

Now, one might object: "If there were no cause for the performance of an action or for the enjoyment of its fruit, the person would simply not engage in activity at all; so why was it asked, 'Where is the search for other causes'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Whatever kind of fruit [arises] for the person when there is the appearance of his own nature as concealed. || 13-109 ||
In that regard, the atom (individual soul), being existent, possesses autonomy; for that [autonomy] arises from action.
Indeed, when the person has assumed limitation, there is a fruit consisting of pleasure and so forth, characterized by intensity, mildness, and the like.
With respect to that fruit which is to be experienced, his autonomy regarding the act of experiencing—that is, his agency—is what constitutes [his freedom].

That [pleasure] belongs only to one who already exists as an *aṇu* (individual soul), because it is born of action and not innate; therefore, another cause such as a woman must necessarily be sought, for otherwise, how could there be the experience of that [pleasure]?

Now, one might object: "If atomicity consists in the concealment of one's own nature (*svarūpagopana*), and if karma arises from that, and consequently saṃsāra is caused by that [karma], then would not the beginninglessness of these two—[atomicity and karma]—as accepted by all disputants be contradicted?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And that desire of the Lord to conceal His own nature serves as the efficient cause. (13.110)
Therefore, there is an beginningless establishment of both karma and impurity (*mala*).
Here, the very desire of the Lord to conceal His own nature is the cause of the *āṇava* impurity;

that [concealment] is precisely the non-manifestation of one's true nature (*svarūpākhyāti*). And karma is necessarily concomitant with this non-manifestation, occurring when the [true] form is not fully realized.

Since there is no connection [of the soul] with that [impurity], it is that very [impurity] which is the cause of even that [karman]; thus, regarding the beginninglessness of impurity (*mala*) and karman, the path is the same. However, once it has arisen, karman also depends upon impurity. As it has been said:
"The cause is called desire (*abhilāṣa*); beyond that is the effect (*naimittika*)."
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: let non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) be the individual impurity (*āṇavamala*); but from where does its nature as desire (*abhilāṣa*) arise?

For in the act of desiring, there is no agent, since [the self] has its true nature concealed; nor is there an object of action, because that which is to be desired has not yet manifested up until the present moment.
How, then, can the scripture beginning with "The cause is called desire" attain the status of a valid authority?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Concealment is the incompleteness of that which is of a complete nature, and that [incompleteness] is to be fulfilled. (13.111)
The impurity of *lolikā* (restlessness) arises from a longing for the differentiated state out of desire.

Indeed, in this context, the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the perfect nature is called "incompleteness" (*apūrṇatvam*). And that [incompleteness] is merely an orientation toward fulfillment through a differentiated state, by virtue of being fit for a longing directed toward that fulfillment. Thus...
It is rightly said that the impurity known as *lolikā* and also as *abhilāṣa* is proclaimed in all the scriptures: "..................
here, however, the impurity is desire" (*Svacchandatantra* 4.105).

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: like those who maintain the doctrine of duality, regarding the impurities (*mala*) and so forth as well as the Lord (*īśvara*), [it is stated]: "Just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has proceeded without beginning, so too Śiva is traditionally held to be beginningless, the liberator from saṃsāra."
One might object: "According to this principle, let beginninglessness be asserted simply as a matter of equal status;
why then posit a causal relationship (hetu-hetumadbhāva) that only creates such complexity in the system? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Without [the state of] being Śiva, whose nature is pure self-luminosity... (13.112).
Nothing else is tenable; therefore, Maheśvara is the cause here.

In this context, since the existence of impurity (*mala*) and the rest cannot otherwise be accounted for, the reality is simply the repose within the consciousness of Maheśvara—the pure, self-luminous Self.
Maheśvara alone is the cause, as was previously stated:
"That which does not rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky" (8.3). Now, if this is so, then what is the use of these [impurities] such as *mala*, which are like internal goiters?
Might the will of the Lord alone be the independent cause at the beginning of the creation of the universe? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, [the Lord] depends upon Māyā for the triad of creation, maintenance, and destruction. (13.113)
It is well-established that impurity (*mala*), as well as action (*karman*), are indeed the will of Śiva alone.

For here, by the reasoning already stated, it is the will of the Lord alone that is capable of performing His own threefold function—characterized by creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—throughout the universe; however, this applies to impurity, action, and *māyā*.

And having regard for this, the Supreme Lord—by the statement, "In the pure path Śiva is said to be the agent; Ananta is the lord in the impure," and so forth—performs creation and the other cosmic acts through the mouth of Ananta within the path governed by Māyā. Nor does he [require]...

Since the Lord possesses absolute sovereignty that is independent of anything else, he must necessarily depend upon impurity (*mala*) and other factors; otherwise, how could there be a diverse creation and so forth for each individual soul? Thus, everything is well-established.
Now, it has been stated that at the beginning of creation, the Supreme Lord requires the impurities (mala) and so forth for the threefold set of tasks;
but regarding the remaining two tasks, namely grace (anugraha) and the rest, does He require those [impurities] or not?—
anticipating this doubt, he says:
But in some cases, Śiva manifests in his own essential form. || 13-114 ||
Now, one might object: "Is this not like the 'half-old woman' fallacy, wherein God would perform some actions dependently and others independently? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, for Him [the Lord], impurity and karma are not at all to be depended upon by the individual soul."
If the nature of being an atom were abandoned, how could that [atom] serve as a cause? (13.115)
Therefore, one should establish the state of being independent of *māyā*.
For how could that which is the cause of impurity, limited agency (*aṇutā*), and so forth, become the cause for their removal?
Indeed, clay, the wheel, the string, and other such factors are the causes for the existence of a jar's jar-ness, not for its destruction.

Or, in the production of a skull-cup and the like, nothing is required [from the agent]; thus it is rightly said that in the act of bestowing grace, the two—impurity (*mala*) and karma—which are opposed to that, are not to be depended upon. In this same way, the independence from *māyā* here must also be established; for when even impurity and the rest are not to be depended upon, what need be said of *māyā*?
It has been stated that "in view of that" [refers to] independence from *māyā*; therefore, one should establish this very point.
Therefore, when grace is to be bestowed, it is logical that the Supreme Lord alone possesses agency independent of anything else;
thus he says: "by that."
The pure, self-luminous Śiva alone is the cause here. || 13-116 ||

Now, one might object: "If the Supreme Lord were to bestow grace in this way without depending on anything else, from what source would there be any gradation (taratamabhāva) in that grace? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And He, by His mere freedom (svācchandyamātra), manifests [this] gradation."
Is it not the case that [the claim] "merely by one's own will" is unproven, since— just as for someone following worldly laws—
the power of the Supreme Lord’s grace might descend even in dependence upon [one's] karma and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The perfections of lineage, birth, body, action, age, and religious observance.
Devotion to Śiva that is independent [of other means] is the descent of power (śaktipāta) for those who do not seek fruits;
whereas that devotion which is motivated by the desire for fruits depends upon ritual action and the like.
Therefore, while there may be a distinction here regarding the fruit [of worldly action], such is not the case regarding liberation (*apavarga*).

For devotion to Śiva alone is the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), by means of the metaphorical identification of the sign and that which is signified. Indeed, devotion is its primary characteristic, as it has been said:

"In this regard, the first sign is unwavering devotion to Rudra" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 14.8). The phrase "for those seeking no fruit" refers to those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*). The word "first" means prior.
And it has been stated that since the action required is diverse, there is also diversity in its respective fruits.

Therefore, there may be a distinction in this case regarding the fruit; however, since liberation (*apavarga*) does not depend upon action, this distinction does not exist there—thus he says: "But in liberation, it is not so."

One might object: "How can it be consistent for one whose devotion directed toward both enjoyment and liberation is indeed single and undivided, that in one case he depends upon ritual action and in the other he does not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even for one who clearly intends both the pair of enjoyment and liberation... (13.119).
In the former case, one requires action because of its diversity, but not in the latter;
"because of its diversity" refers to what was stated:
"One who wishes to produce a specific quality in the effect must resort to a specific cause."
"There are also various and diverse distinctions regarding enjoyments, which are connected to karma.
The word *uttara* here means *apavarga* (liberation). As it has been said:
"For one desiring liberation, there are no distinctions with respect to the path leading to the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*)."
"For they do not praise [anything] in Brahman...
and so forth. Thus it is established that the first is the supreme descent of power (*śaktipāta*), while the second is the non-supreme. As he will say:
"This is the essence to be known here: [the state] of the perfectly full conscious Self."
Supreme light is the descent of power, free from all limitation.
"Even such [a descent of power], when characterized by a limitation to a portion of worldly enjoyment, is that other descent of power which ultimately bestows the state of Śiva. (13.252).
Now, one might ask: even in the case of concealment (*tirobhāva*), does the Lord depend upon impurity (*mala*) and so forth, as he does in the case of creation and the rest?
Anticipating the objection, "How much more so [is this true] when it appears as a favor?", he first states its very nature, which implicitly includes independence from impurity (*mala*) and the like:
"Even though its form is not manifested, it is as if manifested by that... (13.120)
Having remained [in that state] and having grasped the mantras and so forth, he should abandon them; this is his disappearance (tirobhava).

For some, indeed, due to the actual absence of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), even though their form is not manifested, act out of hypocrisy for the sake of deceiving others solely by the will of the Supreme Lord.

Having remained as if in a manifested form through the observation of devotion, faith, and so forth, one receives the mantras and other teachings prescribed in the Śaiva scriptures following a formal initiation; yet, if one subsequently abandons them due to a lack of respect, that constitutes his *tirobhava* (concealment). Even for one whose own true nature (*svarūpa*) has been thus concealed...
The statement is made according to the analogy of a boil or a carbuncle bursting, by which there would never be for him an emergence from saṃsāra. As it was said by this very [author] elsewhere:
"But someone, through the will of the Lord, with a mind that is not properly confident..."
One who practices the conduct while indeed censuring others is said to be "concealed."
"The sin arising from the disparagement of great mantras, vidyās, conduct, and so forth, shall in every way cast that person into a place of terrible torment. (Tantravārttika 3.73) Thus [it is said].
Now, in order to bring to completion what was commenced with the words "I shall speak the great medicinal herb of scripture," he says:
"In the Śrīsāraśāstra, the Blessed One spoke of this reality. (13.121)
"This matter" refers to the definition of the procedure for the descent of power (śaktipāta) as accepted by us. || 121 ||
He says that very thing:
"One should oneself envelop one's own self—without doubt—from the Avīci hell up to the end of Śiva—with numerous states consisting of merit and demerit. (13.122)
In the same way, that very Lord of Gods, by means of the collection of powers, envelops [all things]; he himself binds, and he himself indeed releases.
One is oneself the enjoyer, oneself the knower, and oneself indeed the observer;
oneself is both enjoyment and liberation, oneself is the Goddess, and oneself is the Lord.
Just as the heat of fire is itself single-syllabled (ekākṣara), so too [the Self],

by means of manifold states consisting of dharma and adharma— meaning, primarily by the variegated karmic impurity which is the cause of transmigratory existence— is [manifested]. "In that same way" means that [it manifests] its own self by itself.
"By the aggregate of powers" means by means of [the powers] such as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and so forth; "one should envelop" means one should preside over [them].

For this very reason it is said: "He binds himself alone and he releases himself alone. For this very reason it is said: "The enjoyer" and "the knower," because enjoyment itself is bondage and the state of being a knower is liberation.
Thus it is said: "And there are no [entities] exceeding this," as he himself has stated: "both enjoyment and liberation.

For this very reason, he says that one should perceive this entire universe as consisting solely of one's own Self—namely, that one should perceive [it] "by oneself" (svayam) in its proximity (upa). "The Goddess" refers to Śakti; "Ekākṣarī" refers to Parābhaṭṭārikā.
He clarifies this very point with the words: "just as heat [is inherent] in fire. As it is said:
"The heat of fire is to be known as [inherent]... (Netratantra 1.26).
He explains this very point according to its essential meaning:
"In this context, 'reality' refers to the manifestation of the nature of one's own self through sovereignty. (13.125)

In this context, it is stated that by the very sovereignty of one's own self, there is a manifestation as liberated just as there is a manifestation as bound; this is the true meaning that has been established—this is the sense. || 125 ||
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well; thus he says:
"It is also stated in the venerable Niśākula: 'Those of small intellect, whose minds are conditioned by falsehood, suffer through their investigation of impurity (mala) and māyā. (13.126)
O beloved, what can a speck of dust do to a crystal stone?
For just as a blue stain in the sky is merely a false perception of impurity, one should therefore abandon the suspicion of being stained.
"They are afflicted" means they experience affliction in vain;

the sense is that just as dust on a crystal stone or the blueness in the sky cannot actually produce any impurity or the like in those two, so too [it is with] the Self whose nature is pure and enlightened.
"Stain and karma are imagined solely by one's own desire"; thus, one should abandon that doubt, for in reality none of this exists—this is the meaning. As it is said there:
"O Dear One, in reality no stain exists, nor anything stained."
Due to the impurity of one's own mind, impurity is said to reside within the self.
Those of small intellect are afflicted by deliberating upon impurity and illusion;
O Beloved, what can dust on a crystal stone do to it?
Impurity is merely ignorance, while knowledge is pure by its very nature;
for one whose awakening is of a pure nature, there can never be bondage.
"Just as there is blueness in the sky, so too is there impurity in the conscious self. || 127 ||
The venerable Vidyāguru has also stated this very same thing in his *Pramāṇastutidarśana*;
he says as follows: [he states that very point].
That which is accepted by the profound thinkers is the descent of power during the interval between the pervasion and destruction of dharma and adharma. (13.128)
Proclaiming that [liberation] according to their own whims, those such as the Stavaka and others would assert an independence in You that is indifferent to reality.
Here, however, the Gāhanikas [assert] that Māyā alone is the cause of the universe.

By those proponents of difference who assert that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*)— that is, the extension (*prasaraṇa*)— of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) toward the production of an effect, [they maintain] its destruction or obstruction; and within that very self,
at a time characterized by equilibrium (*sāmya*), they accept that very descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which is dependent upon that [equilibrium].
The meaning is that authors of hymns and the like, by merely expressing their own will, proclaim Your sovereignty regarding the object of Your praise as being independent of anything else. || 128 ||
Thus, by this much, the reality of the [six] philosophical systems and so forth has been analyzed;
now, in order to describe the variety of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he says:
"The manifestation of gradation consists of the intense, the moderate, and the mild. (13.129)
These very [levels] of the descent of power (śaktipāta) each abide in a threefold manner.

That which was described as the manifestation of the gradations of the descent of power—namely, its intensity, mediocrity, and mildness—each of these abides in a threefold manner; thus, by way of forms such as "intense-intense" and so forth, there are nine varieties of it.
—this is the meaning.
He demonstrates this very point by way of its result: "The most intense descent of power [occurs] spontaneously through the falling away of the body. (13.130)
It bestows liberation either at that very moment or at another time according to its relative intensity;
furthermore, from the middling-intense [intensity], all ignorance is completely dispelled.
Since one knows the nature of the self as both bondage and liberation by oneself alone, that great knowledge which is intuitive (*prātibha*) is independent of scriptures and teachers. (13.132)

The word "spontaneously" (svayam) means without the cause that is the falling away of the well-known body. "At another time" (anyakāle) means either when [death] is imminent or when it is distant. Furthermore, since this indicates a threefold division according to the degrees of intensity (taratamabhāva), there are twenty-seven varieties when each of these is considered in that same way.

It is implied. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction; therefore, in this case, unlike the previous instance, there is no cessation of the body, but rather of ignorance. "By himself alone" means not from a teacher or from scripture, because such knowledge arises for him solely through his own intuitive insight (*svapratibhā*); it is for this very reason that his greatness [is established].
The reason is the lack of dependence on teachers and scriptures. || 132 ||

Now, one might ask: does this [teacher] perceive his own nature as bondage and liberation only with respect to himself, or also with respect to others? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The moon of the Teacher, by whose light of intuition the darkness is stilled..."
It destroys darkness and heat, expanding the vision filled with bliss.
"Darkness and heat"—these two were the disciples. 133.
Now, it must be investigated: who indeed is this person who has become a vessel for such intuitive insight?
It cannot be the teacher (*śāsitṛ*), because at the time of acquiring proficiency (*vyutpatti*), that [status of being a teacher] does not exist.
For one might be called a "teacher" only when, having acquired proficiency oneself, one proceeds to instruct others; nor can it be...
The disciple, because his proficiency must be imparted by another; not knowing which of these two he is, the author raises this doubt and says:
"He is the disciplined one (śiṣṭa) because of being both object and agent, while the other is the disciple (śiṣya) by virtue of being the object."

Because he is being taught (*śiṣyate*), he is the object (*karman*) with respect to his own intuition (*svapratibhā*) since he possesses the proficiency to be produced by that intuition; however, because he is not to be taught (*śāsyatva*) by another, he is intended as the agent (*kartṛ*) through the desire to express his autonomy.

Consequently, due to the status of being like an object (*karmavadbhāva*)—as in the case of "the field is reaped" (*lūyate kedāraḥ*)—the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object, resulting in the form *śiṣṭa*. Others [say...]
Thus, they possess such intuitive insight.
And this very [Lord] is "Self-born" (svayambhū), because he exists in all scriptures by himself, without dependence on the instruction of a guru or others; thus he says:
"He is the Residue (śiṣṭa) everywhere—in the Smṛtis, words, time, lineages, and so forth. (134)
The self-arisen one (Svayambhū), who is fully established in the intuition of the meaning of the scriptures, has been described.
As it was stated previously:
"In some cases, reasoning proceeds spontaneously by itself."
"And that [power] is declared in the scripture to be innate (sāṃsiddhika), consisting of one's own self-realization. (4.40)
[Objection: But if the manifestation of intuition (*pratibhā*) arises spontaneously by itself, then from where does this restriction—that it belongs only to some—arise?
[Reply: Quite true, there is no such restriction; thus he says:
"No living being whatsoever is devoid of that teaching which is its very root. (13.135)

For the very root of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is the reality that consists of creative intuition (*pratibhā*). And yet, not even the most base animal is devoid of that intuitive reality, for it would otherwise be impossible for them to possess skill in their own appropriate activities. Therefore:
"It is said: 'By virtue of which even the linguistic conventions of animals are extended. (135)
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then why does such an undifferentiated intuition not arise for everyone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even in that case, there is an infinity arising from degrees of intensity, based on firmness or instability."

Thus, although intuition (pratibhā) arises without distinction, it possesses an infinite variety due to its manifestation in varying degrees of intensity; for it depends upon being either firm or trembling— the meaning is that, initially, it may be either stable or shaking.
And since she, while trembling, requires logic and so forth for her steadiness to arise, he says:
"She requires logic, scripture, the guru, debate, practice, and so on. (13.136)
Vāda is discourse concerning one who is free from passion. || 136 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that even knowledge which is initially wavering attains firmness on its own in certain cases; so why is there a need for reasoning and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For wavering cognition indeed returns to stability by itself."
For some, [this] firmness arises through reasoning and other means, whether used alone or in combination with others.

"By means of reasoning and so forth" refers to those things required for thorough corroboration. "Whether alone or otherwise" means either individually or collectively. Furthermore, he whose consciousness becomes firm by itself is said to be "without support," as previously stated; however, he for whom it [becomes firm] through reasoning and so forth is "with support."
Now, one might ask: "Is there, then, some distinction here regarding the fruit [of this practice], or not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"To the extent that the lack of dependence on anything else occurs in the intuitive [knowledge] (prātibha), to that same extent is this Guru supreme, having reached the further shore of consciousness. (13.138)
It is not only for an intuitive (*prātibha*) teacher that superiority exists due to independence from others;

this applies even to a constructed (*kalpita*) one, provided he possesses some scriptural portion by virtue of which he, though constructed, is called "unconstructed" (*akalpita*). Therefore, the state of being intuitive is superior in every respect—thus he says:

Even though his infinite knowledge has been learned from another, whatever he knows through the power of inspired intuition (*pratibhā*), in each and every case his state of Śiva-nature is most excellent. (13.139)
As was stated previously:
"By whatever means one may propitiate the Guru with devotion,
he then comes to know the meaning of the scriptures through the application of the sequence of that [Guru's] initiation."
He who, having attained consecration, becomes "constructed" (kalpita),
is indeed skilled in turning back the entire flood of bonds, even while still existing [in that state].
Whoever attains sudden awakening regarding some subject matter of a treatise through the application of sequential order— that person is indeed both conceptual and non-conceptual.
"That part of it which is unconstructed is considered the most excellent. (4.73) || 139 ||
Thus, because the intuitive teacher is indeed non-conceptualized, there is nothing external whatsoever that must be depended upon;
so he says:
"And for him, there is no sequence beginning with the status of a *samayin*, nor is there any consecration."
For us who follow the path of intuitive insight, there is no such thing as a continuous stream [of consciousness], nor is there the vow of sacred knowledge.

Since this [body] is presided over by that primordial knower, Mahādeva, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) serve to accomplish that very presiding; however, for him [Mahādeva], it exists by its own nature.

Indeed, no refinement such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), or the like, is of any use for this Guru who follows the path of direct intuition (*prātibha*), because he has been presided over by Mahādeva himself as the primordial Guru.
For it is precisely for the sake of achieving that divine presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that such refinements have been prescribed. That very [point is as follows]:
Furthermore, since this [self] is established by itself, what would be the use of these futile conceptualizations? || 141 ||

One might object: "Even so, does it not follow that this person has already received initiation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He is initiated by the goddesses; therefore, with devotion in the teaching of Śiva, by that very reason—namely, through their spontaneous presiding over him [in the teaching of Śiva]..."
Being endowed with devotion, which is the first sign of the descent of power (śaktipāta), he is initiated by the goddesses;
the meaning is that he has obtained his authority from them alone.
Having raised the doubt, "Even if this [reality] is thus non-imagined, might there still be some aspect of it that is imagined?", he says:
"Furthermore, by means of its firmness, resistance, and differentiation, that too [becomes imagined] of its own accord through the power of [habitual] resolve. (13-142)

One should acquire one's own spiritual refinement from a guru through asceticism, recitation, and other such means; that guru, moreover, is one of intuitive realization (*prātibha*), characterized by degrees of intensity— intense, moderate, or mild— and rooted in firmness and unwavering stability.

Gradually, either through his own self-cultivation or from a guru via vows and so forth, he should effect for himself the purification (*saṃskāra*) characterized by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, by means of which he becomes what was previously described as "the fashioner of the unfashioned. And thus:
But he who, through the cultivation of his own being as sharing in that very nature,
knows the scriptures even without another [teacher], is declared in the scripture to be a Guru, the fashioner of the unfashioned.
Its subdivisions also arise from superior, middling, or inferior means;
or else from meditative cultivation, meditation, recitation, dreams, vows, or fortitude.
"The one of great intelligence attains the unimagined and sublime consecration. (4.53) || 142 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But what is the authority for this?", he says: "For it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka [Upaniṣad]: 'One should oneself sprinkle the body... (13-143).
Beginning with these words and concluding with that final perfection, one becomes truly consecrated in this way, and not by the waters of external jars. (13–144)
As it is stated therein: "At the beginning of a vow and at the beginning of recitation (*japa*), and likewise at their conclusion,
having performed the sacrifice according to rule, one should then consecrate oneself with one's own [mantra]."
"If there should be a lack of prosperity, one should imagine it with the mind alone,
because this entire world is established within the mind," and so forth.
Then, having meditated upon a jar of nectar adorned with a digit of the moon,
the wise one should contemplate that [deity] being bathed by it upon the head.
"One should be thus consecrated, not with the waters of external jars;
he who has been consecrated in this manner is authorized for recitation and other rites.
Thus ends [the passage]. 144.
And this has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well—as he says:
"In the *Śrīsarvavīra*, the *Śrībrahmayāmala*, and so forth, that very thing was likewise described by Maheśa; how much more of this could possibly be written? (13–145).
"In this way, what could intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-vijñāna*) not accomplish for whom?
For everything is known through intuition," so said the great sage Śeṣa. (13.146)
Right here follows the citation of the authoritative source beginning with "yat" and so forth; the word "ūce" (it was said) refers to the *Pātañjala-sūtras*.
Regarding this, some dispute that this [intuition] is not the cause of all success; thus he says:
"But others say that for one who is free from desire, such a teacher is intuitive (*prātibha*). (145–146)
Since that which is desired is produced by a causal complex, the teacher is consecrated in this [rite]. || 13-147 ||
The power of destiny does not cease even when the fruit is to be accomplished;
therefore, one who has been consecrated and has observed the vows of knowledge bestows the fruit.

"Of one who is without desire" means of one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). For in the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), since they are accepted as being practiced according to one's capacity with the inclusion of all constituent parts, their result is produced by a collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*); in that regard, it is not the case that the Guru alone—who has received initiation, consecration, and so forth from another, and who himself has observed the vows of knowledge—is the bestower of the fruit.
Furthermore, this intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) is of such a nature. For this is the majesty of necessity (*niyati*):

that from a specific cause alone, a specific result must arise. Thus, how could there be any deviation for the practitioner who abides in that state of necessity? This is the intended meaning. || 148 ||
But our teachers do not accept this; thus he says:
"Our teachers, the seers of reality, led by the venerable Somānanda, Kalyāṇa, and Bhavabhūti, have declared that this is false. (13–149)
For thus those wise ones stated in their commentary on the *Triṃśikāśāstra*; he recites exactly what was said there:
"That innate knowledge is called the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). (13-150)
In its absence, that knowledge which was acquired for its sake is held in high regard;

for that higher cognition known as *prātibha* is described in all the scriptures as being like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), since through it there may arise the attainment of all fruits, such as those desired by one's wishes.

In the absence of that innate (sāṃsiddhika) knowledge, however, that [knowledge] which you favor as being acquired— such as the individual (āṇava) and other forms of knowledge— is artificial because it must be imparted by a teacher and others; for the sake of that [innate knowledge], one must attain rest within the Śāmbhava [state] alone, through the relationship of means and end.
It is precisely for the sake of manifesting innate knowledge that [the Guru] is honored;
by virtue of this, he alone is proclaimed everywhere as the primary locus of repose. || 150 ||
Regarding this, he states the scriptural authority: "For one who knows thus according to reality, there is that which leads to Nirvana. (13.151)
Initiation becomes certain even when devoid of offerings of sesame and clarified butter;
likewise, anyone who knows this according to reality, even if they have not seen the maṇḍala, [attains it]. (13.152)
He shall always possess success; he is a yogi and he is initiated.
One who was ignorant of the rules becomes a knower of the rules regarding the performance of sacrifice.

By means of these and other such statements spoken in the *Triśikā* that belong to the Great Lord (Māheśvara), it is clearly described that knowledge is the true essence of the purificatory rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 13-154 ||

In this world, whoever knows innate knowledge (*sāṃsiddhika-jñāna*) according to its true nature— for him, initiation leading to liberation occurs spontaneously and without doubt, even without external ritual action. Therefore, being initiated, he is both eternally destined for perfection and a yogin, whether he is ignorant of or cognizant of external ritual action.
Or one may become an agent in the act of sacrificing directed toward objects such as those for the fulfillment of desires;

by such and other statements of the Māheśvaras, it is taught that innate knowledge (*sāṃsiddhika-jñāna*) is indeed the true essence of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 154 ||
Furthermore, regarding that knowledge which is caused by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth for those devoid of [innate] knowledge, he says:
"But for those separated from knowledge, the means to knowledge is ritual action such as initiation.
Let this matter rest for now; it will be addressed in its own proper context later. (13-155)

"Let it be set aside for now," because there is no occasion for that [discussion] at this point when the variety of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is being examined. For this very reason it was said: "It will be addressed in its own proper context.
"Its own proper context" refers to the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). (155)

Now, one might object: "In that case, since even the means of knowledge characterized by the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth, serve as the cause for the manifestation of authentic knowledge—just like intuition (*pratibhā*)—why is such emphasis placed on intuition alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Even the authority of the Guru, the scriptures, and other means are truly instrumental only because this supreme intuition is itself the cow of plenty that grants all desires.

The meaning is that even for the guru and other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the supreme state alone is the logical means; that itself is their place of rest. For this very [supreme state] is the cause for the fulfillment of all desired objects by bringing about identity with the supreme reality (*paratattva*); thus it is said to be "the cow of plenty that grants all desires."

For it has been stated more than once that, through the relationship of means and end between the means beginning with the individual (āṇava) and the ultimate, there is repose in non-conceptual knowledge alone within the Śāmbhava state, which is the nature of intuitive flash (pratibhā). || 156 ||
Therefore he says:

"That form which, through the sequence of the application of means, is then without means and beyond sequence—that is the supreme reality, ascertained with certainty in each respective context. (13.157)

In the conjunction—that is, the mutual relationship—of the means (upāya) such as the individual (āṇava) and others, there exists a sequence consisting of the individual, the empowered (śākta), the Śambhava, and so forth; by relying upon that very sequence, the form which consists of intuitive flash (pratibhā) arises as the "beyond-means" (nirupāya) and thus as "without sequence" (akrama). That alone is the supreme reality (paraṃ tattvaṃ) in each respective context.
This is well-established in all the scriptures; there is no disagreement on this point—this is the meaning. || 157 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, what is the purpose of imagining a refinement (*saṃskāra*) within one's own self through another teacher who is himself intuitive (*prātibha*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But he who is graced by the duality of both intuitive and external refinement..."
Because he cannot be assisted by any other, that Guru is said to be the direct bestower of boons.
As it has been said:
"But he who, although his form is unconstructed, has acquired refinement from another source for the sake of firmness in correspondence, becomes Bhairava in person. (4.77)
Thus [ends the verse]. 158.

And thus, even for one who possesses such intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), [the degree of intensity] may arise through the various gradations of the external means (*bāhyopāya*)— ranging from weak to intense— by which even a medium-intense descent of power (*madhyatīvra-śaktipāta*) may be distinguished by further divisions such as "intense" and so forth; thus he says:
Whether it be for one's own liberation alone or for the liberation of the entire universe, a flash of realization arises like that of a firefly, a jewel, a star, the moon, and the sun. (13–159)
And here, by the force of the illustration, it is understood that even while liberating some people at intervals, [this occurs] progressively further on. || 159 ||

Now, there is certainly no disagreement that here, for the full perfection of intuition (*pratibhā*), the direct descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of medium-intensity is the cause; however, one might raise the doubt: "How could something else, external [to that], attain the state of being intuitive even through some degree of cultivation? Anticipating this, he says:
Therefore, this scripture composed by us is for the sake of intuitive realization;
he who practices it is truly a guru, for those who merely mimic the meaning of reality are impostors.

Therefore, he who would practice this treatise of mine entitled *Śrī Tantrāloka*— composed for the purpose of making manifest the state of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through the gradual emergence of intuition according to its varying degrees— becomes, immediately thereafter, one of intuitive insight (*prātibha*) due to the attainment of complete awakening.
The Guru would be such that by the mere casting of his glance, this entire world would attain that same nature. As was stated previously:
"Thus, the wise man who [recites] these thirty-seven [verses] always..."
"One who practices the daily rites thoroughly shall become Bhairava himself;

for when one possesses the fully perfected thirty-seven-fold awakening, one becomes Bhairava—what wonder then that even limited individuals (aṇu) attain the state of Bhairava through his very glance? (1.286)

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Is this not a great mockery, that there should be such praise for one's own work? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "For those who mock are indeed not the true reality. But was it not just now stated that "not a single living being is devoid of intuitive insight" (*pratibhā*); so what [is the point]?

Anticipating the objection—"Does [the realization] arise through dependence on the scriptures and so forth belonging to others?"—he says: "Due to the lack of understanding that depends on others, everything does not appear in this way; one does not know [it] without the instruction of another, because of the dullness of the descent of power (śaktipāta). (13.161)
Indeed, because he has set out to subsist solely upon another,

he does not manifest with such eloquence as would otherwise be required for his livelihood; this is because, due to the dullness of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he cannot do so without the words of another.
He knows only a little; in every respect, he remains dependent upon his teacher and the scriptures—this is the meaning. || 161 ||
And this has not been stated by us merely as our own invention; thus he says:
"And this is clearly established in those various scriptures.
By the phrase "in those various [scriptures]," he indicates that this point is not contradicted by any scripture.
He demonstrates this very point:
"And it has been stated thus in the *Kiraṇa*: [it arises] from the Guru, from the scripture, and from oneself. (13.162)
"Likewise, some are fit for knowledge (jñāna), and others are fit for conduct (caryā).

By the word 'likewise' (tathā), it is implied that some are fit for yoga and others are fit for ritual action (kriyā). By this, it is hinted that even for these [latter types], there is a dependence on scripture and so forth, because their objects are restricted. || 162 ||

Now, one might object: "Is this not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), namely, that knowledge arises in dependence upon a teacher and scripture? For this is established by common worldly experience; what is the point of presenting a formal proof here? Furthermore, what is the proof for the claim that for some, this [knowledge] arises spontaneously (*svataḥ*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This has been explained in detail in the venerable Nandiśikhātantra. (13–163)
It is described as "unbroken" (abhagna) by means of questions and answers;
"unbroken" means undivided (akhaṇḍa). || 163 ||
He says that very thing: "Śiva is indefinable there; what means can be described? (13.164).
When this question was posed by the Goddess, the illustrious Śambhu explained:
"What is the means?"—meaning, for the practitioner (sādhaka), by which knowledge might arise regarding Śiva, even though He is indefinable.
As it is said there:
"Thus the Supreme Lord Śiva has been described as indeed indefinable. O God, please explain the means [to realize Him] out of a desire to bestow grace upon Your devotees. (164)
What did he determine? He says:
"In this matter, discernment alone is the means, for it causes one to abandon that which is to be abandoned. (13.165)
And to him, O lady of beautiful hips, he grants supreme intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*).

"Discernment alone" means that discernment itself is the sole primary factor, whose nature consists of self-reflection—this is the meaning. "The abandonable" refers to states belonging to *māyā* and so forth. "To him" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). (165)
What follows from that? He says:
"When he is endowed with intuitive insight (pratibhā), then, being liberated, he may liberate others. (13.166)
By the descent of the Supreme Power (para-śakti), the person (puruṣa) has the impurity of Māyā destroyed.
As it is said there:
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, discrimination (viveka) is indeed the supreme means therein."
Having understood the worthlessness of cyclic existence, a living being should seek liberation.
In this impermanent world, Śiva alone is indeed auspicious—the auspicious (eternal), all-pervading Lord.
When one abandons illusory states and contemplates with true being, [then one attains Him].
And to him, O lady of beautiful hips, he grants supreme intuitive knowledge;
when endowed with such intuition, he is liberated and can then liberate others.
When the impurity of Māyā has been destroyed by the descent of the Supreme Power (paraśakti),
the person attains the supreme state, having gone to which he is not born again.
Thus [ends the section]. 166.
But has it not been stated immediately prior:
"O Goddess of Gods, having liberated [the disciple] from the extremely terrible bondage of the paths by means of initiation,
the Guru should then bestow upon the child the qualities such as omniscience"?
By such statements as these, it was said that liberation comes through initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now, however, intuitive realization (*prātibha*) is being discussed;
what, then, has been stated here? To this he says: "But surely, previously liberation was said to come through initiation; how then can it now come from intuitive realization? (13.167)
"How so?"—the meaning is: which of the two is the valid authority?
As it is said there:
"By means of initiation, the individual soul has already been declared [to have crossed] from the ocean of existence..."
"You speak now of liberation as if it were merely a matter of intuition; how can that be so?"
O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, O Enemy of Kāma, tell me clearly the authoritative means here: is it intuitive insight (*prātibha*) or initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*)? Tell me this with its explicit meaning.
Thus [ends verse] 167.
The Supreme Lord also answers this, saying:
"When this question was posed by the Goddess, the speech of the All-pervasive One proceeded:
'O Dear One, a living being is liberated through initiation (dīkṣā) as well as through intuitive insight (prātibha). (13.168)
However, there is this much distinction between these two; thus he says:
"But that initiation depends upon the Guru for the liberation from the bondage of what is to be bound;
whereas his innate, intuitive nature (prātibha-svabhāva) bestows the perfection of absolute isolation (kevalībhāva). (13.169)
The meaning is: dependence on another for the purpose of being bound, binding, or liberation. || 169 ||
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is achieved by the realization of this state of isolation (kevalībhāva)? To this he says:
"Isolation surely results in liberation through the Supreme Reality;
for you have indeed declared these three principles to be Man, Śakti, and Śiva. (13.170)
The soul is not bound; the power of bondage is the instrument that touches upon agency.
It is declared from the scripture of the Guru that Śiva is the agent of all this for the individual soul (aṇu). 13-171.
Since that was spoken regarding discernment (*viveka*), let what follows it be explained. O God of gods, how is discernment [attained], or what is it that is discerned by means of this?
"By means of the supreme reality alone"—the meaning is that one whose self consists solely of the supreme reality would indeed be liberated.
Even so, the Goddess asks again, beginning with "But surely," and so forth.
Here, it is stated in all the scriptures that the universe consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva. In that regard:

In the act of binding, the person is not what is bound; rather, the power consisting of the penetration of the agent and the object is the instrument that touches upon agency, and Śiva is the agent— all of this has been taught as something to be instructed to the individual soul (aṇu) by the Guru and according to the scriptures, so that for him—
Great knowledge (mahājñāna) arises preceded by the manifestation of the distinctions between the bound, the binder, and the act of binding.

Furthermore, that very same [knowledge] is declared to be the "higher than the higher" (anuttara) through discernment (viveka), based on the subsequent scripture. How, then, does this practitioner attain discernment; what is the method for its production, or what is it?
"Let that which is to be discerned be stated; let it be determined by the elimination of doubt, error, and so forth"—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
"Reality is declared to be threefold, consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva."
It is of the nature of Śiva, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation, and untainted.
O Maheśvara, you have explained that power as having those [qualities] as its attributes;
the reality of the human being has been illustrated by way of the relationship between the bound and the binder.
The principle of power (śaktitattva) has been declared by you in relation to both agency and instrumentality;
and that is clearly established by individual souls (aṇus) through the Guru’s tradition.

How can that [knowledge] be obtained through discrimination? This is stated by you once again, as well as regarding intuitive knowledge and that which has been received through the oral tradition of the guru.
Why has this duality been taught now for my confusion?
O Śaṅkara, explain clearly what follows from this.
O God of gods, how is discernment attained, and what is it that is discerned, by which the individual soul achieves certainty and ultimately liberation?
Thus, "nṛ-śakti-śiva" is a copulative compound (dvandva) in the sense of a collective aggregate, according to the tradition of the Guru. || 172 ||
And in order to resolve this, the Supreme Lord replied; thus he says:
"When this had been said by the Mistress of the Supreme Lord, Śiva, the primordial Guru, spoke.
He states that very thing:
The triad of principles beginning with Śiva [is known] through the authority of the Guru's tradition. (13.173)
Through statements consisting of reversals of the superior and the inferior, that which is established attains the state of intuitive insight (*prātibha*).

For indeed, the triad of principles (*tattvatraya*)— consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva— is established through the scripture of the Guru by means of dialogues in the form of questions and answers, each according to its true nature.
Having reached its growth, it attains the state of *prātibhatā*; the meaning is that intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*) arises for him.
Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated more than once that the state of intuitive insight (*prātibhatva*) is an ultimately real entity (*vastusat*)?
How then can it be said here that the three principles beginning with Śiva alone attain the state of intuitive insight through the greatness of the Guru and others?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
For one who has been purified by contemplation, the bonds have indeed been severed by the sword of initiation.

The blossoming of that reality is called *prātibha* (intuitive). For when the bonds have been severed by the sword of initiation from a guru, and the practitioner has been permeated by contemplation through the scriptures (*āgama*), the reality of intuition—which is indeed truly existent—reaches a state of full expansion; it is this very thing that is so described.

Regarding "intuitive knowledge" (*prātibha-jñāna*), it has been said: "In that case, [the goal] is to be accomplished through the authority of the tradition from the mouth of the Guru when the Great Lord is present;
through the penetration of the power of Śiva, the Guru awakens the disciple."
Through words that invert the superior and the inferior, he is empowered by the Lord's power;
and by that power, the impurity of *māyā* is destroyed for one who is perfectly awakened.
O Dear One, that expansion which arises in one whose bonds have been severed by initiation and who is cultivated through contemplation— that is this very knowledge.
"That is declared to be intuitive (prātibha), arising from the cultivation of the knowledge of reality.
Thus [ends verse 174].
He makes this very point clear to the heart by means of an illustration:
"Like a fire covered by ashes, [the power] becomes manifest in the intuitive intellect (prātibha) through the arrival of weightiness. (13.175)

Just as a seed sown in the proper season and well-watered grows accordingly, so too does intuitive insight (*prātibha*) manifest clearly through the yoga, sacrifice, and recitation taught by the Guru. (13.176)

For just as fire covered by ashes may burst forth through the breath from the mouth and so on, or just as a seed sown and watered at its proper time reaches manifestation in the form of sprouts, shoots, and the like, so too does intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*).
"By means of the yoga of sacrifice and other practices taught by the Guru. As it has been said:
"Just as fire covered by ashes, when that [ashes] is removed and kindled by fuel, becomes possessed of great luster through the power of the wind, O fair-faced one."
"The powerful one, whose radiance is light—thus this would clearly come to pass.
And:
"Just as a seed, having been well-watered, in due course over time..."
Abounding with sprouts and shoots, it was endowed with those flowers and fruits.
"Likewise, O Dear One, the pervasive branch is the intuitive knowledge (prātibha) received from the Guru.
Thus [it is said]. || 176 ||

Having thus described intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*) as it has come down through the lineage of the Guru, [the author] now describes that same [knowledge] as it is innate (*svābhāvika*) when assisted by the right recipient; first, he defines the very nature of discernment (*viveka*): "This discernment, which transcends the senses, is that which brings about discrimination."
Then, the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati) manifests by itself.

But when intuitive knowledge (prātibha) has arisen, other knowledge involving the senses—whether accessible through speech, sight, or hearing—is dependent on something else, O fair-faced one. (13.178)
A wise person should abandon that [empirical object] by resorting to the intellect, just as one sets aside a lamp during the day.

Furthermore, that object characterized by pure consciousness—which transcends the senses and lies beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition—should enter the path of inquiry; that is what is called "discrimination" (*viveka*), which consists of self-reflection. When that [discrimination] exists...
Spontaneously and independently of anything else, intuitive knowledge (prātibha-jñāna) regarding the bound, the bond, and the binder would flash forth; once that [knowledge] has arisen,
one should rely upon right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), which stands in the place of the sun, and like a lamp in the daylight, cast aside all other contracted forms of cognition.
It is to be reached by the organs of action, indicated by speech, and by the organs of perception, indicated by the eyes and ears;
it is also to be reached by the internal organ together with the senses. Therefore, one should abandon dependence on anything else.
By disregarding these, one should come to rest in the Great Light alone—this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"When discernment reaches the stage of investigation regarding that which transcends the senses,
the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati) spontaneously enters the realm of inquiry."
But when intuitive knowledge (prātibha) has arrived, other knowledge involving the senses—
comprehended through speech, sight, and hearing— is dependent on something else, O fair-faced one.
"A wise person, relying on awakening, should abandon that just as one discards a lamp by day.
Thus it is said.
For this very reason, its distinction from those of limited vision also arises; thus he says:
"For one in whom discernment has become manifest, [this occurs] within the range of the cognitive senses. (13.179)
For the practitioner in whom discernment has arisen, the consciousness becomes variegated by such things as hearing from afar and piercing through [objects],
regarding sense-objects such as sound;
that is, it takes as its objects things remote in space, time, or form.
The meaning is that his realization arises. As it has been said:
"I shall describe to you the characteristics that manifest for one in whom discrimination has appeared, and by which particular sense organ [it occurs]."
"In this manner, for whatever is to be accomplished, a great proficiency arises in that very person:
the discernment of hearing from afar, as well as reflection and vision.
Thus it is said.
Now, the playful activities proclaimed in all the tantras are to be experienced in an instant by one who is strengthened by the knowledge of Śakti.
O lady of excellent vows, one who knows the Kula consisting of the six wheels and sixteen supports performs mantra-piercing and other rites, as well as self-stabilization, possession, and so forth.
"In an instant, O Daughter of the Mountain, he enters other cities," and so forth.
For one in whom discernment has fully matured, however, because of this very aversion toward supernatural powers (siddhis), there occurs rest solely in supreme consciousness; thus he says:
"But through the discernment of all states of being, one turns away from all states of being. (13.180)
With a soul completely detached from worldly pleasures and solely imbued with the state of Śiva,
O lady of beautiful hips, this greatness of intuitive insight (prātibha) is thus established.
One should perceive Śiva, who is both internal and external, like one's own reflection in a mirror.

Indeed, in this world, consciousness alone is the true essence of all entities, and not any external form such as blue or the like; through such discernment, one becomes free from subjection to those [objects], and for that very reason—

Because his nature is detached from games such as entering the bodies of others, he rests primarily in the reality of Śiva, which consists of supreme light; thus, like a mirror through the emergence of reflections from an original object, he perceives himself everywhere— both internally and externally— as nothing but Śiva.
"One should see"—that is, one should directly realize—the universe as having the form of a single, solid mass; this is the meaning. Now, one might ask:
"How can this person be able to perceive Śiva simultaneously both externally and internally?
Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "This is established as the majesty of the intuitive consciousness (prātibha)."

And thus, since for him there is nothing whatsoever to be abandoned or to be adopted, he should abandon the specific meditations and other practices that serve as the basis for limited accomplishments (siddhis) which achieve nothing, and instead grasp the supreme consciousness itself— thus he says:
Then, knowing the truth regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, one should meditate upon one's own consciousness.
The word "tadā" (then) means: when the greatness of intuitive cognition (*prātibha*) is thus established.
As it has been said:
"By the discernment of all states of being, one becomes turned away from all states of being."
Discriminating, with a self thoroughly detached, and solely intent upon the state of Śiva.
"O lady of beautiful hips, this is prescribed as the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*) belonging to the intuitive genius (*pratibhā*).
Thus it is said:
"Just as one sees one's own reflection appearing in a mirror, O beloved,"
"One should contemplate the omnipresent and all-pervading Lord Śiva, who abides both within and without,
as being like a dream or a magical illusion— this is the yoga of accomplishment."
Having thus observed this characteristic of intuitive insight, O auspicious lady, the practitioner [should proceed].
"One who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted should then meditate upon the all-pervading Śiva.
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "If the supernatural powers (siddhis) are of no use, for what purpose were they mentioned?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

For the "net of accomplishments" has been taught as a cause for inspiring confidence in others; through the contemplation that those who have attained accomplishment in this very life shall be liberated at the end of the body. (13.183)
For so-called "attainment" (siddhi) is merely a conviction for others; otherwise, who could have confidence that liberation occurs at the end of the body? || 183 ||
Furthermore, he who, by not depending on the cognition of others, attains firmness in the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the supreme reality itself, is liberated even while living; thus it is said:
"But due to the firmness of the contemplation of the Supreme, one is declared to be liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)."
He summarizes this very point:
"This definition has been declared for you regarding the division of intuitive knowledge (prātibha). (13.184)
And here, this is not the only characteristic; there is yet another as well—thus he says:
"Capability in matters of cursing and favoring through such practice.
By the word "capability," it is meant that of one for whom discernment has become manifest. For one whose discernment is fully matured [is capable] even in activities that are like mere play.
By maintaining equanimity through non-attachment toward supernatural powers (siddhis), he rests in the supreme reality itself;
thus, being himself liberated, he may liberate others as well. || 184 ||
Regarding this, he says: "But by being indifferent toward them, one is liberated and may liberate others. (185)
