Now, one might object: "Since the Self is by its very nature pure consciousness, what indeed remains for it that manifestation could effect? What use would it have for such [manifestation]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Bound by association with the elements, the senses, and so forth, the individual soul (aṇu) will certainly wander in transmigratory existence."
That very [consciousness], when endowed with creative intuition (pratibhā), is called the principle of power (śaktitattva). || 13-186 ||
Through the descent of that [power], one is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and becomes Śiva himself;
yet, when joined with the elements, senses, and so forth, that same individual soul (aṇu) remains bound.
When it is endowed with discernment (viveka), it is called the principle of power (śaktitattva).

One should abide in the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) so that one may attain the capacity to perform various tasks, such as bestowing grace or exercising restraint; having taken firm root in that very state, one is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and becomes Śiva himself.
Thus, by disregarding the state of atomicity (*aṇurūpatā*), through the process of ascending the ladder of powers (*śaktiniḥśreṇikā*), and by having ascended to the supreme level,
one should come to rest in the highest consciousness alone— this is the meaning. By this,
that which was introduced through the objection and its resolution— the nature consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva— is [established].
It has been established that these three principles themselves must attain the nature of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-vijñāna*). As it has been said:

"O Goddess, when the Great One (*mahān*), which is gross and endowed with the three qualities (*guṇa*), is bound through its connection with the elements, the senses, and so forth, it then becomes the subtle atom (*aṇu*)."
Bound by that [karma], O woman of excellent complexion, the atom (aṇu) wanders through saṃsāra;
when that very same [atom] is endowed with creative intuition (pratibhā), it is called the principle of power (śaktitattva).
By the descent of that [power], a living being is indeed liberated from the ocean of existence;
having abandoned the six causes, he attains dissolution in the Śiva-principle.
"Thus, O beloved, everything has been told to you regarding how the two divisions [arise].
Thus [it is said].

Even though intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) has been established in this way, the Goddess asks again regarding the duality [of its nature]: "But surely, that knowledge was said by the Teacher to be both sensory (*sendriya*) and supersensory (*atīndriya*). (13.187)
And since that [knowledge] is born of discrimination (*vivekaja*) by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), how could it be devoid of the senses?

Here, first of all, knowledge consisting of heaviness (*gaurava*) is said to be "with the senses" because it is accomplished by the internal organ, the intellect; however, that knowledge born of discrimination is "without the senses. In that regard, one should "resort to the intellect" for that knowledge born of discrimination.
The meaning is this: by such statements, even if [the Self] is characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*), how could it be devoid of senses?
It would be absolutely non-existent, like the horn of a hare. As it has been said: "Knowledge from a teacher is indeed said to be with the senses; [knowledge] beyond the senses is [otherwise]."
O Lord, the birth of discernment does not proceed without the intellect.
"But how, O Śaṅkara, can its lack of sense faculties be asserted?
To me, this appears as equal to the horn of a hare.
Thus [he spoke].
Thus addressed, the Blessed One replied, saying:
"Being thus questioned, he declared that [the world] arises from the singular latent impression of dullness within the mind and the intellect. (13.188)
The state of being a sense-organ (*akṣatva*) arises through withdrawal; when that [state] is severed, Śiva is the illuminator.

Here, because of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized solely by the dullness of the mind and the intellect, there is a state of being a sense-organ (*indriyatva*) through a preeminent distinction from the object—both that which is to be conceptualized by one another and that which is to be determined.
Since these two constitute bondage, when that duality— which is the cause of the impressions of insentience—

is severed and ceased through the aforementioned nature of the self and by means of supreme discrimination (*viveka*), then Śiva alone, the illuminator, who is consciousness itself devoid of the senses, unfolds everywhere.
Established is the supersensuous nature of knowledge born of discrimination.

"Has it not been said that the latent impression (saṃskāra) itself, being of the nature of insentience, is the basis for differentiation?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "The latent impression of all entities is proclaimed to be their 'otherness' (paratā). (13.189)
"Otherness" (*paratā*) means differentiation—this is the meaning. It is "proclaimed by all," with reference to which it was previously stated:
"The characteristic of the insentient (*jaḍa*), indeed, is the state of being a limited manifestation" (3.101).
Thus it has been said. As it was stated:
"O Mistress of the Gods, the status of being sense-organs (*indriyatva*) belongs to the mind and the intellect by virtue of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Because they are insentient, their state among those [organs] constitutes the bondage of being sense-organs."
"The severance of that [bond] through the method of discernment reveals the Śiva-principle; this purification of all states of being is proclaimed as the state of transcendence. (189)
And that [distinction] does not exist here—thus he says:
"Mind and intellect are not distinct from one another due to any other cause;
for these two are the causes of discernment, augmented by the power of the Lord. (13.190)
For in this world, when the discernment (*viveka*)— the root cause— is manifesting, the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) do not become distinct from one another,

because they both arise as that very form [of discernment] through the concealment of their own individual natures within some other cause whose essence is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). This is why these two are not separate.
The meaning is: [the yogi] who has attained identity with that [state] which is augmented by the power of the Lord. || 190 ||

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then knowledge could not arise at all without the mind and the intellect; therefore, what is the point of investigating whether [the self] is devoid of senses and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But, O Dear One, the attainment of knowledge does not occur for one who is devoid of mind and intellect."
But by virtue of its other-nature, that subtle principle is called Śakti-tattva.
For indeed, the attainment or manifestation of knowledge cannot occur by abandoning either the mind (*manas*) or the intellect (*buddhi*);

rather, it is these very two—the mind and the intellect—which, through the dissolution of their own respective natures according to the stated reasoning, produce this knowledge by presiding over the subtle power-nature (*śākta-rūpa*). Thus it has been said.
"But because of its other-nature, that subtle principle is called Śaktitattva.
Thus [ends verse 191].
Now, one might object: "If this is so, why has discrimination (*viveka*) also been stated here as a cause? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Discrimination of all states of being arises from the pure state; it is 'of great scope' (*mahāśaya*).
The meaning is that "of great scope" refers to that which is capable of embracing all states of being.
Now, an objection may be raised: "Has it not been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) also, like a mirror, is capable of reflecting all entities—both the enjoyer and the enjoyed?
So how can you set that aside and say that such a nature belongs to discernment (*viveka*) alone? To this, he says:
The principle of intellect (buddhitattva), however, consists of the three qualities (guṇas) and is superior, inferior, or middling. || 13-192 ||
Furthermore, the dull sense organ, though it has attained powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, is a cause of bondage;

and because it consists of the three *guṇas*, it is said to be superior, inferior, or middling. Precisely because it has attained powers such as *aṇimā*, it causes attachment to the web of enjoyments and is thus a cause of bondage. As it has been said:
O Great Goddess, the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) is the sphere of the substrate of primordial matter (pradhāna);
it consists of darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva), which are respectively the lowest, intermediate, and highest.
"Enveloped by a web of enjoyments through the various distinctions such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, by the maxim, "If one should find honey on the threshold, why should one go to the mountain?"— if liberation were to arise from intuitive insight (*prātibha*) alone, then what would be the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is accomplished through manifold exertions?
Again the Goddess asks:
"But surely, if liberation comes through intuitive insight (prātibha), what is the use of initiation in the ritual of Śiva? (193)
As it has been said:
"O Great Lord, if an individual is liberated through intuitive insight (*prātibha*),
then for what purpose is initiation performed for a child in the sacrificial rite of Śiva?"
Thus [ends the section]. || 193 ||
The Supreme Lord has also answered this, saying:
"Indeed, children, fools, and women are ignorant regarding initiation;
yet they are liberated through the severing of bonds and awakened in the sacrificial path of Śiva. (13.194)
Therefore, O beautiful one, initiation exists among these [beings] as the instrumental cause;
for through initiation, upon the liberation from bonds, [knowledge] born of discrimination arises from the state of purity.
"In these" refers to ignorance in the form of the ignorant and so forth; therefore, the distinction is that initiation has the ignorant as its object.

"As the cause" means [the cause] of liberation and awakening. For this very reason, when their bondage has been released through initiation, knowledge born of discrimination—intuitive (prātibha) in nature—shall arise from their state of purity.

Now, one might object: "Why has this not been established through logic alone, rather than by reciting the text word for word? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This text, as it has been recited, [is intended for those] who themselves are incapable of understanding it."
Through the correspondence with the words of Śiva, their awakening shall attain firmness. || 13-196 ||
And this has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well—as he says:
"In the venerable *Niśāṭana*, knowledge is said to be threefold according to the self, the guru, and the scripture;
the primary [knowledge] is one's own realization, which carries one across the ocean of conceptual constructs. (13.197)

For doubt, which is rooted in conceptual construction and concerns objects such as the divine reality that constitutes the essence of the mantra-substance, is indeed pacified by one's own direct realization. || 13-198 ||

Although it has been stated here that knowledge is threefold— derived from the guru, from scripture, and from oneself— nevertheless, because it delivers one from the ocean of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*), the knowledge arising spontaneously from one's own realization is primary;
for in those possessed of intense or middling descent of power (*śaktipāta*), the root of conceptualization is primarily [overcome] through one's own conviction alone.
The sixfold doubt concerning mantras and so forth shall be pacified; one should come to rest in the non-conceptual self-awareness—this is the meaning. Regarding the term "parts" (*aṃśa*):
since the Siddhas and others are parts of the mantra, they are included within the very doubt concerning mantras, because they are of that same nature.

The word *ādi* (and so forth) denotes a category (*prakāra*). By this, the doubt concerning the universal (*jāti-śaṅkā*), which is a sub-category of the doubt concerning the substance (*dravya-śaṅkā*), is also included. As it has been said there:
"This knowledge is threefold: the self, the scripture, and the mouth of the guru."
Through its predominance, self-perception becomes the means for crossing the ocean of conceptual constructions.
From conceptual construction arises doubt; that doubt is of the nature of bondage.
Indeed, no other bondage exists apart from doubt born of conceptual construction.
For one who is joined with the mental exertion of conceptual construction, there will certainly be no superior state;
for there is doubt regarding the mantra, doubt regarding oneself, and likewise doubt regarding the ritual substance.
Suspicion regarding living beings is thus considered one thing, while suspicion regarding divine acts is held to be another;
suspicion is recorded as being fivefold, and suspicion regarding the principles (tattvas) is recorded as the final one.
"I shall describe the sixfold method by which you will attain liberation. Beginning thus, [the text continues]:
"Therefore, with every effort, [one should practice] that which is the cause for gaining conviction in one's own self."
It brings about self-awareness for human beings and consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva.
One should realize [the truth] within oneself according to the conditions, by means of the various types of dissolution;
for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction is permeated by supreme non-duality.
"He is liberated; there is no doubt about this—I tell you the truth. (198)

An objection may be raised: "Surely this was introduced as being said with reference to the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*; so why is the meaning of subordinate texts such as the *Śrīmannandiśikhā* being explained here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having taken up this very same internal meaning, [it is stated] in the *Mālinīmata*..."
The connection with what precedes is that "it has been described in the Mālinīmata. He recites that very [verse]:
"Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of his own fitness... (13-199).
The power of Śiva is connected [to the soul]; it is peaceful and bestows the fruit of liberation.
Through that connection, someone is liberated at that very moment.
Having said this, he speaks again concerning the object known as "intense-intense": "The identity with ignorance ceases for someone. (13.201)
Pervaded by the power of Rudra and desiring to go forth by the will of Śiva, he is led toward a true guru for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (13.202)
Having propitiated him and received the Śaṅkara initiation from him when he is pleased,
one shall go to Śiva either at that very moment, through [the exhaustion of] experience, or upon the fall of the body.

And he explains this himself: "The meaning of this is that whatever manifestation of the Self, consisting of reflective awareness, occurs with respect to its own nature—that alone is declared here to be a certain kind of time. (13.204)
"Yogyatā" (fitness) here is said to be the state of being worthy of union with identity (*tādātmya*) with Śiva.

The meaning of these four verses is as follows: whatever manifestation (*kalanā*) there may be of the Self—which is distinct from outward-directedness and consists of the reflective awareness of one's own nature—that very [manifestation] here is a certain...

Time is of the nature of internal contact that is distinct from the equilibrium of karma and other such factors, as it has been said: "at a certain time. It is "fit" because it is worthy of the yoga characterized by identity with Śiva; its state of being fit is "fitness," which is the capacity to grasp that very form—thus it is said, "by virtue of fitness."
Now, one might object: "In the self-reflection of one's own nature, no external cause whatsoever need be required;

therefore, let that [reflection] have existed even before, or else let it not exist even now? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Why was it not so before? Why is it only now?"—this is not a coherent argument. (13.205)
Indeed, there is no time whatsoever that exists apart from such manifestation;
for if it were otherwise, [the world] would be independent of that Supreme Light, which consists essentially in the reflective awareness of its own nature as such a manifestation.

There might be some independent time that could be questioned on its own authority as to why this was not so previously as it is now; yet that very time, when it rests within the state of being manifested,
because it is itself manifested, attains identity with the Light, and thus cannot exist apart from it.
To say "it does not exist" is simply incoherent.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, then how is it that the multitude of entities appears as intermingled with the manifestations of past, present, and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But through its sovereignty, let the power of time unfold in such a manifestation. (13.206)
But that [power] described as Śiva’s majesty is not for the sake of being questioned.

However, within the sphere of *māyā*, let the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) indeed manifest through His sovereignty as the cause for the appearance of past, present, and so forth; yet, in the supreme Light (*prakāśa*), it serves only to establish non-difference from Him.
Since it is not capable [of acting independently], it has been stated many times before that it is merely the expansion of that [consciousness].

Thus, when there is an awareness of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), the power of Śiva becomes connected [to the self] because of its fitness for identity with Śiva; this is the meaning of the first verse.

Now, one might object: since it has been stated in such passages as, "In all three states, they perform their activities while being pervaded by the power of Śiva, whose nature is to remain concealed," these [souls] are always connected with the power of Śiva; so at what time [could they be otherwise]?
Having raised the doubt, "Why is it said that 'she is connected'? he refutes it:
"But surely..."
The great power of Śiva remains eternally bound with the individual selves;
she is truth, yet her nature is concealment, while in her state of peace she perceives her own true form.

"Consisting of concealment" means because of the veiling of the nature of the luminous self; "the vision of one's own nature" means that which illuminates one's own perfectly full nature through the removal of those various veils—this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"Vāmā is that which vomits forth the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra), consisting of the obscuration of one's true nature. Likewise:
"In due order, [she emits] the succession of objects and latent impressions (saṃskāra) obtained through all enjoyments..."
"Desiring to withdraw [the universe], she is the Great Fullness (Mahāpūrṇā), Jyeṣṭhā, the sole path to liberation.
Thus [it is said]. || 207 ||
But surely, since this [power] is intent upon performing various functions such as veiling its own nature and so forth,
it is precisely the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayi*), that unfolds everywhere;
so how can it be said that "Vāmā" consists of concealment and "Jyeṣṭhā" is peaceful?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"For agitation is indeed duality, while oneness is its subsidence; therefore, [the state] consists of that. (13.208)

For differentiation (*bheda*) is indeed agitation (*kṣobha*), not tranquility (*śāntatva*); and unity (*aikya*) and non-differentiation (*abheda*) are indeed peace (*praśama*), not agitation. Therefore, this power (*śakti*) consists of that [duality], being both composed of agitation and composed of peace; hence it has been said that "this is of the nature of concealment and is tranquil."
Now, one might ask: "Granted that this is so, does she, once pacified, reveal her own nature immediately, or by some gradual process? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But being bound and established by that peace, she partakes of the nature of power."
By the firmness of that power, Śiva becomes one who has abandoned his atomic nature.
Bound again by that peaceful power of peace, the Self, remaining established,
partakes of the very nature of power and becomes directly situated in the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā); therefore,
having abandoned the state of the limited individual (aṇu), it attains firm stability within that very power.
The meaning is this: by resorting to the state of being overwhelmed by that immersion (*āveśa*), one becomes Śiva;

through the removal of the various veils (*āvaraṇa-tiraskariṇī*), one becomes of the nature of pure consciousness whose true essence is full agency (*pūrṇa-kartṛtva*). As was stated immediately prior:
"That very [Self], when endowed with creative intuition (pratibhā), is called the principle of power (śaktitattva).
Through the descent and immersion into that, even a bound soul (paśu) is liberated from the ocean of existence. || 209 ||
Now, one might ask: "Does the attainment of its own nature (svarūpalābha) occur only while the body exists, or even when it no longer exists?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that case as well, by virtue of degrees of intensity and so forth, [it occurs] quickly or after a long time."
His body may fall [from its place], or it may become like wood and other such [inanimate] things.
Now, one might object: "In our own system, which consists of the non-dual supreme consciousness whose essence is wonder (*camatkāra*),

if liberation were indeed a state like that of wood or other inanimate objects even while alive— merely through the severance of all qualities— then what occasion is there for derision toward the followers of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), who describe liberation in such a manner?"
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"One whose consciousness is turned outward toward all worldly transactions succeeds when permeated by the most intense and supreme power. (13.211)

Possessing the most intense power, he—by whom consciousness has been turned away (*parācīnita*) from all external activities, having made it directed outward (*parāci*)—becomes one whose continuous mental application (*anusaṃdhāna*) is averted;
he succeeds, meaning he becomes a recipient of the attainment of the experience of the wonder of supreme consciousness (*para-saṃvit*). This is the meaning.
Concluding this matter in this way, he introduces another point:

"Thus far the subject matter of the text; however, elsewhere it is clear that there is another section of the text which indicates the portion concerning those who have received a medium-intense descent of power. (13.212)

"Previously mentioned subject" refers to the subject of the most intense (*tīvratīvra*) descent of power (*śaktipāta*). "This much" refers to the form of one and a half verses. "Elsewhere" refers to the two other descents of power known as the moderately intense (*madhyatīvra*) and the mildly intense (*mandatīvra*).
By the first part or portion of the second descent of power, known as the moderately intense—
It indicates [the state] through its second part by implication, and that in turn indicates this third [state], which is called "mild-intense. As he will say:
"The portion of the text ending with 'ŚA' is clearly the subject matter of the second [chapter]."
But another [teacher], with respect to the procedure for the descent of power (śaktipāta) known as "mild" or "intense," [says]: |||
Thus [ends verse] 212.
He explains that very point:
"The state of ignorance in the person consists in consciousness being contracted within the heart;
but when that contraction has ceased, one's own true nature shines forth. (13.213)

In this context, within the heart—which is the essential nature consisting of reflective awareness (vimarśa)—when that [nature] is contracted and reduced to a subordinate state, the cognition in the limited individual (puṃs) which consists of incomplete manifestation is itself the state of ignorance; the meaning is that there is identity with that [ignorance]. If that very [state], caused by contraction, ceases for someone, [then liberation occurs].

Then his own unique and non-common nature shines forth, and he becomes possessed of full knowledge and action—this is the meaning. And for the cessation of that [limited state], the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*śaktipāta*) alone is the cause. Upon its arising, various signs are produced by which [he recognizes this]. His...
Everyone should perceive that the descent of power has occurred. || 213 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"By the phrase 'possessed by the power of Rudra,' that group of signs mentioned here is described; [namely] unwavering devotion to Rudra. (13.214)

The accomplishment of mantras, mastery over all principles, the perfection of activities, poetic skill, and the capacity to understand the meaning of all treatises—these arise from that sequence. (13.215)
Due to the application of their respective degrees of intensity, there may be a state of these [powers] being either separate or combined;
therein, the wise man should deliberate upon their predominance in both enjoyment and liberation.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*. As it is said there: "The immersion into the power of Rudra (*rudraśaktisamāveśa*) is eternally established therein;
and when that exists, one should observe these signs of his."
In this regard, the first sign is unwavering devotion to Rudra;
the second is the accomplishment of mantra, which produces immediate conviction.
Mastery over all principles is remembered as the third characteristic;
the accomplishment of the task already undertaken they call the fourth sign.
"Fifth, one should know poetic skill (*kavitva*), which is charming and adorned with ornaments;

and the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises for him spontaneously. (8.13). Regarding "perfection of actions" (*kṛtyasaṃpada*): it is for the completion of actions (*kṛtya*) that have been undertaken.

— this is the meaning. "By its sequence" (tatkramāt) means by the sequence of that Rudra-śakti, according to its respective excellence—this is the meaning. For this very reason he says "sva" and so forth; "by its own gradation" (svatāratamya) means, by implication, by the gradation of the Rudra-śakti.
"Even there" (tatrāpi) means even in such a state of being both distinct and unified—this is the meaning. To illustrate:

By the statement, "Devotion alone, when it has reached its highest limit, is called liberation," it is shown that devotion and the like are primary for liberation, while mantra-perfection and the like are primary for worldly enjoyment; elsewhere, they are merely incidental. And this entire collection of signs is found in this very [text].

It is well known that [the title] *Granthakāra* appeared [as his name]. As the Gurus say: "That fivefold mark (*lakṣmapañcaka*) which arises suddenly due to his knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures—in which the [teachings] declared in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* were clearly perceived by people."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 216 ||

Concluding this, he distinguishes between the sections of weak and intense [grace]: "This entire section ending with the word 'sa' (he) clearly concerns the second subject; the other, however, concerns the procedure for the descent of power known as weak and intense. (13.217)
He explains this very point:
"By the power of his own [innate] capacity, whether weak or intense, the desire to go forth arises in him toward a true guru, through the influence of Śiva’s will. (13.218)
This very point is indicated in the scripture as stated by the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*):

"By means of the yoga that is under the sway of Śiva’s will. The meaning is that, by virtue of the power of Śiva’s will—that is, through His sovereignty—Śiva’s power (*śaivī śakti*) is connected to Him independently, without requiring anything else.

"And its application is of many kinds," thus it is analyzed according to the strength of the power [of the disciple] as being weak or intense. "He too" refers to the true guru. "In this very scripture" refers to the one currently under discussion, known as the *Śrīpūrva*.
He recites that very [verse]: "Furthermore, he who knows all these principles (tattvas) according to their true nature... (13.219).
That guru is declared to be equal to me, for he reveals the potency of the mantra;
those who are seen, honored, or touched by him with a joyful heart [attain liberation]. (13.220)
Men are liberated from sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes—those living beings who, impelled by Śiva, have been initiated by him. (13.221)
Having obtained the fruit according to their desire, they go to the state that is free from ailment.
"In accordance with reality" means by way of the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) and so forth, as the all-inclusive nature of everything—this is the meaning.
"Equal to Me" is the statement of the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭha. This very [statement] reveals the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra.

This has been elucidated by such passages as these. "Those who are deemed worthy" means those who have been meditated upon. "They are liberated" because they have been consumed by the fire of knowledge. "Impelled by Śiva" means those upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred. "The fruit according to their desire" refers to the characteristics of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
An objection is raised: "What is the sign that, by the will of Śiva, a desire to go toward a true guru arises in him?
Anticipating this, he says:
"Through the application of the reflective awareness: 'What is reality? Who is the knower of reality? (13.222).
Through inspired eloquence and association with friends, one should desire to go to a guru;
through such a longing to go, that very teacher is attained.
Whether already perfected through the application of degrees of excellence and so forth, or even one who is still being refined, there arises for him—

by virtue of the descent of Śiva’s power (śiva-śaktipāta)— either an intuitive flash of insight (pratibhā) characterized by such reflective awareness, or an encounter with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). For one in whom such an intuitive flash does not arise spontaneously, [the following applies]:

"Due to attachment to that"—thus, when such an intuition has arisen in either case, one should desire to go toward a true guru (*sadguru*). Therefore, through the application of the desire to go, once the journey is undertaken, the teacher is reached by him.
And that teacher, due to the intensity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), is a *sāṃsiddhika* (one who has attained realization spontaneously), possessing the characteristics previously described.
Otherwise, however, he is consecrated.
And thus, by way of this indicative characterization, he also distinguishes the internal degrees of intensity:
"First, it partakes of differentiation—suddenly, gradually, in its entirety, or partially. (13.224)
For the attainment of the Guru is said here to be divided by such distinctions as these;
therefore, he immediately receives initiation that bestows Śiva.
When he knows everything in its true nature as being of the essence of knowledge,
he is then called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), having become Śiva.
In that regard, the attainment or acquisition which pertains to the previously mentioned division and concerns the perfected object is—

due to the varying degrees of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)— either in its entirety or in part, by means of the teacher, according to the method previously described, whether it belongs to the omnipresent [Self] or to a portion thereof, either simultaneously or sequentially.

It may be divided according to such distinctions as these; likewise, one should follow the same logic regarding the object of refinement (*saṃskṛta-viṣaya*), whether it be imagined (*kalpita*) or unimagined (*akalpita*). And from such a teacher, he receives initiation in such a way that, becoming Śiva at that very moment, he understands everything exactly as it is.
And he is declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta). As it has been said: "At that very moment, one shall go to Śiva. || 226 ||
One might object: "Even when there is a connection with a body, how could he possess such a nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For even his connection with a body is clearly for the sake of his Śiva-nature.
The sense is that at that time, he can no longer have the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth.
And this initiation is of many kinds; thus he says:
"For in this [initiation], there is indeed a distinction based on the teaching, the union, and the gaze. (13.227)

From the scripture, from transmission, from the demonstration of the conduct of equanimity by the teacher, and from the majesty of the mantra, mudrā, and so forth—through their various combinations and individual distinctions. || 13.228 ||
"By means of ritual action" refers to the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the internal form.

"By means of discourse" refers to the [teaching of] reality (*tattva*). "By means of union" refers to mere conjunction. "By means of scripture" refers to exposition. "By means of the demonstration of equal conduct" refers to through equality.

By disregarding distinctions such as caste and so forth; that is to say, by the demonstration, contemplation, and performance of external conduct. "Of the sacrificial porridge" (caroḥ) refers to the *kuṇḍagolaka* and others. "By action" (*kriyayā*) means by means of rites such as fire-offerings (*homa*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction. [This occurs] through the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the form of the internal aspect.
Thus, the meaning is that [this occurs] through the sequence of yoga, by means of the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the internal form in relation to the external body.
And this may occur either individually or collectively, depending on the gradation of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*);
thus it is said: "by way of the distinction between collective and individual."

And by means of this [practice] of such a kind, according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "the equilibrium of both through discourse," even while the body exists, repose in supreme consciousness arises, whereby one becomes a fit recipient for the designation "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). Thus he says:
And at that time, even while remaining within the body, he is said to be liberated.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", he says:
"And it has been stated in the two scriptures known as the Śrī Ratnamālā and the Āgama.
He recites that very passage:
But at the time when the non-conceptual state is revealed by the Guru, || 13-230 ||
At that very moment, it is said, he was liberated; only the machine remains, for the machine is incapable of acting.
Now, one might object: "If at that time the body and so forth are like a machine, then how can pleasure and pain exist?
And if they do exist, would there not be a lack of liberation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Due to the connection with *prārabdha* karma, the body experiences pleasure and pain. (13.231)
"One should not have doubt regarding that," as it is stated in the *Śrīgamaśāstra*.

[This refers to] the body, the notion of a body, and so forth, which are non-self (*anātman*). "One should not have doubt" means that because one experiences pleasure and pain, one thinks, "I am not liberated. Now, one might object: "But this doubt is not without foundation."
Anticipating the objection, "How then was it stated thus?", he says: "And that has been defined in the Śrīgamaśāstra.
The particle *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of *hi* (for/indeed).
He recites that very [verse]:
"For the body, produced in another birth, is indeed nourished by ignorance. (13.232)

By that karma, even the wise are afflicted within the body. Now, since it is possible for three types of karma—those which have begun the present body (*prārabdha*) and those which grant birth, lifespan, and experience—to exist, how can there be a reference using the singular "by karma" (*karmaṇā*), and what is the purpose of the pronoun *tat*? [Response: It is because [the affliction] occurs simultaneously with the exhaustion of all three. Or rather, the singular is used because the three are considered as a single collective whole. Furthermore, the pronoun *tat* refers to the karma that has begun the present body, because that is the most proximate. Alternatively, the singular is used because the affliction by the other two types of karma is merely secondary, while the affliction by the *prārabdha* karma is primary. Or else, the singular is used because the affliction by the other two is included within the affliction by the *prārabdha* karma. Or again, the singular is used because the affliction by the *prārabdha* karma is the most significant; for even though one possesses knowledge, as long as the *prārabdha* karma remains, one must necessarily endure its fruition. Thus, the singular is used to indicate the predominance of the *prārabdha* karma. As for the pronoun *tat*, it refers to the *prārabdha* karma because of its proximity. However, some maintain that the pronoun *tat* refers to all three types of karma collectively, on the grounds that they are equally causes of affliction. But this view is incorrect, because the affliction caused by the other two types of karma is not simultaneous with the exhaustion of the *prārabdha*. Therefore, the singular is used because the affliction by the *prārabdha* karma is the most significant, and the pronoun *tat* refers to the *prārabdha* karma due to its proximity. This is the established conclusion.

Anticipating the two-fold doubt—namely, "How can there be logical consistency since no object can be characterized that is both denotable by a word and referable by a mental pointer?"—he says, internalizing these concerns:
"The persistence [of karma] exists as a single integrated unit that bestows birth, lifespan, and experience. (13.233)
Because there is a connection [indicated] by the word "hi" following the singular number, it is said:

"from the singular number," meaning "as an object"; and "the connection characterized by the relation of cause and effect in the form 'since... therefore...'"—that which possesses such a connection is of this kind; "hi" refers to the meaning of the particle *hi*.

Thus, it is referred to by that word—this is the meaning. Because it bestows birth, lifespan, and experience, that threefold karma—described as a single unit acquired in previous lives—is the cause by which the body presided over by Māyā comes into being; therefore, while the physical frame exists, even the wise are afflicted.
The meaning of the *Śrīgamagrantha* is that [souls] appear as if bound due to the experience of pleasure and pain;
by this, it is explained that "one may go to Śiva through [the exhaustion of] experience."
Now, however, he explains that one shall go to Śiva upon the fall of the body:
"Through practice, application, transition, piercing, striking, and restraint. (13.234)
Either through the power of the mantra of the oblation or by means of the application for severing the bonds,
one should effect that which bestows immediate liberation or that which instantly separates the vital breaths.
Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated contemplation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Method (*yukti*) consists of the application of the "net" (*jāla*) and so forth, as will be described hereafter. Transference (*saṃkrānti*) is the entry into another's body and the like.
Piercing (*vedha*) is that which will be described in the form of mantras and so forth. Impact (*ghaṭṭana*) is the dispersal of the vital breath.
The "obstruction" (rodha) of the vital breath consists in its stabilization within the central channel by means of abandoning its coming and going.
"Of the mantra" refers to [mantras] such as Kālarātri. "Immediately" (sadyas) means at the very same time as the initiation (dīkṣā).

And this [rite] is not to be performed at all times; thus he says: "In that regard, however, there is this rule: one should perform it when the moment of death is near, and not otherwise, because the karma already set in motion is not thereby purified. (13.236)
And this was already stated previously: because of the power of the mantra, even though he has been deprived of his life-breaths, he still enjoys the remaining fruit. (13.237)
Having clearly spent the remainder of that birth in various ways, one is then swiftly liberated through the cessation of other karmas. (13.238)
"Otherwise" means when death is not imminent. As it has been said:
"Having seen the disciple seized by old age and tormented by diseases, one should then cause him to ascend and unite him with the Supreme Reality."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Let this [initiation] belong even to one whose death is not imminent; what is the restriction? For if this were performed, liberation would occur at that very moment—so why the delay involving dependence on the moments of proximity to death? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "Because the *ārabdhṛ* karma is not purified. Now, this...

If [it is argued that] just as there is a purifier of karma for that which is yet to be, let there be one for this too; and if not for this, let there be none for that either—having raised this doubt, it is said: "And this has already been stated. "Previously" refers to the ninth chapter. As was stated therein:

"How can that karma which has already begun its operation in this body be cut off when it has reached its final stage? Indeed, it cannot be obstructed. (131) And so forth. Now, [one might object]: "By the power of this mantra, surely there is only the separation of the vital breaths (*prāṇaviyoga*)."

If [it is argued that] since the agent who performed [the action] no longer exists, for whom indeed would this fruit of the action ripen—so what is the use of investigating its purity or impurity? Anticipating this doubt, he says "mantra," etc. The meaning is: of the *śeṣa* (remainder), i.e., of the residual karma that initiates the body, which remains after [the primary karma] has been purified.

Therefore, having exhausted— that is, brought to completion through experience— the remainder of the *prārabdha* karma consisting of various lifespans, enjoyments, and so forth from that previous birth, one attains liberation (*apavṛjyate*) because of the absence of any other karma, whether future or otherwise, that might cause delay.
"He is liberated"—this is the meaning. Therefore, it is rightly said that one should perform that [rite] at the very moment of death. || 238 ||
Therefore, he says:
"For this reason, one should not perform the life-taking initiation without knowing the moment of death;
for its sole fruit is the transgression of the command of the Supreme Lord. (13.239)
Thus, it has been made known that nothing whatsoever can be accomplished except by transgressing the command of the Supreme Lord. || 239 ||
Thus, concluding the present topic, he introduces another:
"This triad of one has been determined; now there is another regarding the descent of power (śaktipāta).
The phrase "this triad of one" refers to that which is called "intense" (tīvra).
He says that very thing: "But when initiation has been performed with an intensity that is middling, [the result] is not so firm. (13.240)
One knows one's own self to be Śiva-hood, and at the end of the body one becomes Śiva;
yet it is not so firm because of the absence of the direct realization of the knowledge of one's own self, whose nature is free from conceptual construction (avikalpa).
Anticipating the question, "What is the authority for this?", he says:
"And it has been stated in the *Niśisañcāra* and the *Yogasañcāra* scriptures. (13.241)
He recites that very point by way of its meaning:
"But by remaining in the body through conceptual thought (vikalpa), one attains the state of Śiva at the end of the body.
As it is said there:
"But one whose mind is joined with conceptualization may attain auspiciousness through the alms-gathering.
Thus [it is said].
Even when there is a middling-middling descent of power (śaktipāta), one remains eager for the attainment of Śiva.
Wherever one intent on enjoyment is joined [to a state], having experienced that, upon the dissolution of the body, he becomes Śiva;
however, if he is joined to some principle within the "slow" (manda) [state], he remains right there.

At the end of the body, having experienced the enjoyment pertaining to that [specific] principle (*tattva*), one subsequently proceeds to Śiva. "Wherein" refers to whichever principle or other level one has intended. "That" refers to the very web of enjoyments obtained through the practice of yoga and so forth, belonging to that [level]. "Having experienced" implies by means of this very body. Therefore it is said: "upon the dissolution of the body."

"Śiva" means: in that very [state] where the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has commenced; "somewhere," meaning in whatever [place] is desired; "appointed," which implies even while being eager for the attainment of Śiva; "having enjoyed," which implies by means of another body. For this very reason it is said: "having enjoyed the experience pertaining to the principles (*tattva*) at the end of the body. As it was stated by this same author elsewhere:

Even one who is intent on Śiva [attainment] from the *madhyamadhyā* [level] becomes desirous of enjoyment; thus, through initiation (*dīkṣā*), he becomes a vessel for knowledge. And he, having experienced enjoyment with this very body obtained through the practice of yoga, becomes Śiva himself at the end of the body. But from the *nikṛṣṭamadhyā* [level], having experienced enjoyment with another body—
"He attains the state of Śiva. (Tantrasadbhāva 11, Āhnika).
Even so, a certain degree of gradation (tāratamya) is possible here, by which another distinction might arise;
thus he says:
"In that case as well, because of the possibility of gradation, there is slowness or speed. (13.244)
There is also the yoga of abundant or meager enjoyment, and the sequence of the diminution of the body and the [lower] planes.
Among these, the first type pertains to the *putraka* (spiritual son); it has been established that the remaining two types pertain to the *śivadharmiṇ* and the *sādhaka*. Now, however—
He defines the remaining descent of power (*śaktipāta*) as having worldly phenomena as its object:
"In the cases of intense-mild, moderate-mild, and mild-mild [descent], there is a desire for enjoyment. (13.245)
"Ultimately, by means of the supreme [intense] method, one attains Śiva. Here, in this manner,

regarding the descent of power (śaktipāta) known as "mild," for the seeker who follows worldly dharma, there arises— by virtue of the context— a desire for enjoyment that is progressively more intense, preeminent, and principal according to its respective degree.

This is the meaning. Even so, this worldly being, at the end, through the prescribed method of initiation appropriate for himself, attains Śiva; that is, he is indeed liberated—this is the meaning. As has been stated by this very [author]:
"When the longing for enjoyment is predominant, then [there is] dullness..."
"Because there is eagerness for that [initiation] as a means consisting of the yoga of the supreme Lord's mantras;
and because the yoga of the supreme Lord's mantras and so forth culminates in liberation, it is of the nature of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
Even therein, due to gradations, there is a threefold division. This is the intended meaning here: he who...

A certain person, possessing either intense or mild *śaktipāta* and remaining within the worldly order (*lokadharmī*), may, by the power of initiation (*dīkṣā*), at the end of the body, experience enjoyments in some desired world-realm (*bhuvana*) and thereafter attain the state of Śiva. As it is said: "Having established the one who follows the worldly order in the [respective] world-protecting deity of the system..."
"One should effect the attainment of those qualities for Śiva, or for one who desires liberation. (Mṛta.
And he will further state:
"Upon the dissolution of the body that was commenced, he enjoys the powers such as *aṇimā*."
"Having enjoyed [the fruits], he goes upwards to where he is joined with the Sakala or Akala state" (15.31).

And someone else, possessing a moderate descent of power (*madhyama-śaktipāta*), having enjoyed enjoyments for some time in a certain world-realm (*bhuvana*) or the like, being initiated by that Lord, shall eventually attain the state of Śiva.
One who possesses a very mild descent of power (śaktipāta), having enjoyed worldly enjoyments for a very long time in that very state through the sequence of attaining sālokya, sāmīpya, and sāyujya,
shall thereafter receive initiation from that very source and attain the state of Śiva.
He explains this very text from the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* according to another interpretation:
"Others [interpret] the passage beginning with 'one who desires to go' as being connected to the preceding text" (13.246).
They bring [the soul] within the range of the descent of power known as "moderately intense.

It is "connected with the preceding section," meaning it is linked with the preceding text beginning with the words "together with ignorance" (*ajñānena saha*). This is stated right here by way of a qualification.
The cause is the sphere of the impact of the power known as "intermediate-intense."
He says that very thing:
"When even this [person], though possessed by a supernatural vision (*pratibhā*), [seeks] a connection with a corroborative instance... (13.247).
When he desires to go [to the supreme state], then he should be led to a true guru;

for when, through the penetration of Rudra’s power, his ignorance has ceased and his intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*) has arisen, this person possesses a medium-intense descent of power (*madhyatīvraśaktipāta*).

The meaning is as follows: when one desires the application of corroboration and, wishing to generate firmness in that corroboration through the reasoning previously stated, becomes desirous of going to the teacher’s family (gurukula) with the intent to depart, then he is led toward the true guru by the supreme power of the Lord; at that time, his inclination toward him is produced.
And this would not occur without distinction; thus he says:
"Not everyone who is entered by intuitive insight (pratibhā) is led by that power to a true guru. (13.248)

Thus he says: "The state of being desirous of departing (*yiyāsutva*) must be stated, and certainly not otherwise. The connection is that "the state of being desirous of departing" was already mentioned [previously] with the word "state" (*brūta*). "Otherwise" refers to the case where everyone is the agent of the action of reaching a true guru through their own power. "Must not be stated" refers to the state of being desirous of departing. For if indeed...

Every teacher who possesses intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*) should, by his power, be led toward a true guru without distinction; for even without the use of the term "one desiring to go" (*tad-yiyāsu*), [it is said]: "The practitioner (*sādhaka*), possessed by the power of Rudra, by the will of Śiva..."
"For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, one is led toward a true guru"—
this much alone should be stated.
Regarding this, it is said: "One who is permeated by the power of Rudra is led toward a true Guru. (13.249)
For in this way, the intuitive teacher would not possess the distinction between having a foundation and being without a foundation;
such is the intended meaning. || 249 ||

Therefore, even though one possesses intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*), it is only one who disregards the firmness of corroboration (*saṃvādadārḍhya*) who becomes desirous of going [to the supreme state], and no other; thus he says:
"By that, one whose mind is filled with the knowledge arising from attained discrimination..."
Through the firm establishment of mutual discussion and so forth, one clearly becomes desirous of striving [for liberation]. || 13-250 ||
Nor is this interpretation without foundation; thus he says:
"It was stated by the Great Lord in the *Nandiśikhātantra*, within the first six chapters:
'Then, a longing for the divine Śiva arises in bound souls (paśus). (13.251)
When the supreme atoms are indeed endowed with the conceit of being Śaivas,
at that very moment they are liberated, because they have been initiated by the Guru.
It is understood that they have accomplished what was to be accomplished merely by attaining [this state].

Even though the atoms, which were previously most extremely bound, become liberated at the very moment they are endowed with the Śaiva sense of self-identity (*abhimāna*) consisting of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*), nevertheless, at that time, their...

With regard to their prior state, for the sake of strengthening the conviction of bound souls (paśus), there arises in them a longing for the Guru and a desire to go [to him]— in accordance with such statements as, “Śiva, acting for the benefit of the world, appears in the form of the Guru”— because it is through the Guru that they are initiated.
The meaning is that they become refined (*kṛtasaṃskārāḥ*).
And therefore: "But he who, though his form is not contrived, has received refinement from another for the sake of establishing firm consistency, he is Guru Bhairava in person" (Tantrāloka 4.77).

By such statements as these, it is understood— that is, the intended meaning is realized— that through the mere attainment [of this state], for the sake of strengthening the purification received from the Guru or others, they become those who have accomplished what was to be accomplished and whose bonds of worldly existence are severed. As it is said there, immediately following that half-verse:
When the omnipresent Lord, the embodiment of the Guru, assumes tranquility through His power,
He, the powerful Master, enters into the individual souls by means of initiation through His own power.
"It cuts through the web of bonds, and the accumulations of bondage are cut away; therefore, it is called 'the cutter of bonds' (bandhanikṛntī) in the sacrifice to Śiva. Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "If this passage beginning with *yiyāsuḥ* refers to the subject of the medium-intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then what would be the case for the weak-intense descent? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But the passage beginning with *tam ārādhya* has as its sole scope the weak-intense [descent of power]. (13.253)
However, it is established by implication that a text concerning an extremely intense object is exactly as previously described.
He summarizes that very point: "This ninefold descent of power (śaktipāta) has been described by Śambhunātha.
He establishes this same meaning through the method of essential intent (tātparyagati):
This should be known as the essence here: the perfectly full conscious self.
Supreme light is the descent of power (śaktipāta) free from all limitation;
yet, even while being such, it is characterized by the limitation of the portion of experience (bhoga). || 13-255 ||
This is another descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which bestows the state of Śiva in the end.

Here, within this ninefold descent of power, the essential point to be known is this: that supreme light which exists even in the limited self as its nature of perfect consciousness—that is the supreme descent of power.
It is said:
because he is free from limitation—due to the dissolution of those various adjuncts (*upādhi*)—his essential nature is undivided consciousness;
this is the meaning. Furthermore, this is another descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which [occurs] by virtue of his being the self of perfect consciousness.
Even though it is manifest, it is delimited by the portion consisting of experience; for this very reason it has been said: "In the end, it bestows the state of Śiva."
Now, one might ask: what is the cause of such a descent of power (*śaktipāta*); is it karma, or something else?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because in both cases, [the cause] is karma and so forth, which reside within Māyā. (13.256)

"There is no activity"—thus he is entirely independent. "There is no activity" means that this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is not produced by [any external cause]. Here, by way of a qualification, the reason is "one who dwells within *māyā*. For whatever [is the case], such as karma and so forth...
The intention is this: since the atom exists within *māyā*, how could it become the cause for transcending that [state]?
As was stated previously:

In that regard, for this [individual soul], the impurity and karma are not to be depended upon as long as its atomic nature has not been abandoned; for if that [atomic nature] is lost, how could they serve as its cause?
"One should proceed to establish the state of independence from *māyā* for this very reason. (13.115).
And by this [verse], following the diversity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), the establishment of independence from *māyā*—which was indicated in the subsequent enumeration—is accomplished.
A garment was given.
And for this reason, the state of Bhairava would arise for those of pure soul even without dependence on ritual action and the like;
thus he says:
"Therefore, those Rudras who are within the sphere of Māyā, and those who are above it," (13.257).
Upon the exhaustion of their respective offices, they forcibly become Bhairavas;
for those who are not overcome by Māyā are independent of karma and other such factors.
"By the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta) alone, they have attained various supernatural powers (siddhi).
The meaning is: "by force" (*haṭhāt*) refers to the power of the descent of the Supreme Lord's grace, which is independent of karma and other such factors. Now, one might object:
since karma and the like are impossible above Māyā, let their independence [from those] be granted; however, what about within Māyā?

How can this be consistent given that [the world] arises from that [Māyā]? Or, if that were the case, why would there be the emergence of those various accomplishments (*siddhi*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those which, by means of Māyā," and so forth. [He refers to] each respective accomplishment characterized by enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

"But surely these [adepts] have attained their respective accomplishments through rituals such as worship and recitation; how then can they be independent of ritual action and the like? To this he says:
"Indeed, [they attain it] through worship, recitation, meditation, the service of Śaṅkara, and so forth. (13.259)
"How can those [mantras], having attained the status of being mantras and so forth, be independent of ritual action?
He refutes this very point:
"Not so; for in such cases as meditation on and the recitation of Śiva who has transcended [all categories]," (13.260).
First of all, let their very manifestation be investigated:

here, first of all, this must be considered— how it is that for these pure souls, at the very outset, there is this [manifestation] which is transcendent of such things as karma moving within māyā, and which is untouched by them.
The meaning is: why is Śiva engaged in those objects such as meditation, recitation, and so forth; what is the cause for that?
An objection is raised: "Has it not already been stated here that karma, its equilibrium, and so forth are the causes? Anticipating this, he says:
"Karma, its equilibrium, dispassion, the ripening of impurities, and so on, are [all] refuted. (13.261)
If the will of the Lord is the cause, then the descent of power (śaktipāta) alone is the sole cause.
It has been refuted immediately [above]. If the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is the cause,

then you have come over to our own position, namely, that for pure souls, the sole cause in various instances is the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) belonging to the Supreme Lord, which is independent of karma and other such factors.
And thus, it is not logical for recitation (*japa*) and the like to have the status of an object (*karman*); so he says:
"In this way, recitation and the like are indeed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), but they are not the object. (13.262)

For that action which, by yielding inferior enjoyment, conceals the true nature of the enjoyer, is indeed well-known in the world; however, we have no concern with its conventional designation. (13.263)

Thus, since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is the sole cause, ritual action characterized by recitation and so forth is nothing other than the Supreme Lord’s own power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which unfolds His essential nature; it is not, however, "action" (*karman*) as that term is commonly understood in the world. For such worldly action is inferior and limited, bestowing only partial enjoyment upon the enjoyer and failing to reveal His full nature.

The meaning is that it conceals itself by contracting in such and such a manner, and thus veils [itself]. Now, if it is argued that even recitation (*japa*) and so forth are well-known in the world as being "action" (*karman*), then what learned person would engage in a dispute over a mere name? Thus he says: "But we place no weight on the designation. (263)

Now, one might raise the objection: "If these [beings] are not overcome by either māyā or karma, then because they are already perfect, how could there even be a desire for various specific accomplishments (siddhi)? Having presented this doubt, he refutes it:
If it is asked why they have such an intense longing for enjoyments, the answer has already been given:
this independent Supreme Lord is the manifestation of manifold forms. (13.264)
However, through its sovereignty, the bond of concealment nourishes its state as an enjoyer within experience;
yet it remains its own very nature, devoid of impurity, karma, and the like. (13.265)

In the phrase "it has been given," at the beginning of the exposition of his own doctrine, he clarifies that very point in brief with the words beginning "in variegated [forms]," and so forth. This Supreme Lord, who is of the nature of consciousness, is indeed one alone;
yet, through His own sovereignty, He appears in manifold forms consisting of various subjects, objects of knowledge, and so on, in a variegated manner.

It has been established that [the Self] shines forth. Therefore, because of the manifestation of multiplicity even within unity, there occurs through the majesty of its own sovereignty a concealment (*tirobhāva*), which is the hiding of its true nature (*svarūpagopanā*). This constitutes bondage, which, nourishing the state of being an enjoyer during experience, proceeds by first manifesting contraction (*saṅkoca*) and functions as the bestower of birth, lifespan, and experience.

Binding oneself through actions imagined by one's own conceptualized selves, one nevertheless— by means of the process of unwinding and by setting aside the nature of adventitious impurities such as karma— returns to one's own perfectly pure form; thus, only the Supreme Lord remains, who is autonomous and whose essence consists of perfect vision and action.
—this is the meaning.
As was stated previously:
"The Lord is, by his very nature, autonomous, of the form of consciousness, and light."
Due to its connection with the play of concealing form, the atom is manifold.
It has been described that, by means of actions consisting of conceptual constructions of forms imagined by itself,
it binds itself here through its own autonomy.
"This is indeed the majesty of the Lord's sovereignty,
that He, though consisting of atomicity, again touches His own perfectly pure nature. (13.105) || 265 ||
Surely,
by such statements as "His powers are this entire universe," all this world has as its very essence the expansion of the Supreme Lord’s power.

Incorporating the objection that "just as the existence of those [powers] is worldly, so too are auspicious and inauspicious actions; therefore, how can it be said that only an action such as recitation (japa) is their power, and not the action itself?"— [the author] states, preceded by a supporting citation, that although there is no difference in these [actions] being of the nature of power (*śakti*), there is nevertheless a distinction between them.
He analyzes:

"It has been said that this very power of action belonging to Śiva, when residing in bound souls (paśu), is the binder; therefore it is called karma, which effects the concealment of one's true nature. (13.266)
And that power of action (kriyā-śakti), when known, brings about immediate accomplishment.

This very power of action belonging to the Supreme Lord, while residing in the bound soul (paśu)—who is characterized by the apprehension of duality such as "I am doing this"—produces bondage alone because it consists of the agitation of rejection and acquisition. Therefore...

Action is said to bestow pleasure, pain, and so forth, because it causes the loss of one's true nature (svarūpa). As it has been stated: "That which is commonly known in the world as action, by bestowing inferior enjoyment, veils the nature of the enjoyer..."

Thus, she who abides in her own path—which consists of Śiva and Śakti—realizing that "this entire universe is indeed nothing but this very consciousness," as a knower, would immediately bring about each respective supernatural power (*siddhi*).
Therefore, it has been said: "The ritual action of recitation and so forth is the power of the Supreme Lord, not mere karma. As it has been stated:

In the Śrīspanda: "This power, whose nature is action, belongs to Śiva; residing in the bound soul (paśu), it is the binder; established upon its own path, when known, it brings about accomplishment. (4.18)
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the 'accomplishment' (siddhi) intended here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this context, accomplishment is said to be the manifestation of uninterrupted self-awareness. (13.267)
She is the imperishable Great Lakṣmī of sovereignty over enjoyment and liberation;
and it has been stated that she exists here even while the body remains, as the "imperishable Great Lakṣmī of enjoyment and liberation."
One might object: "But surely we see in the world that various supernatural powers (siddhis) are indeed attained even through the grace of Viṣṇu and others;
why then is it said that such things must occur only from the descent of Śiva’s power (śivaśaktipāta)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whatever form of Viṣṇu and the other gods exists in the Lord, that [form] is by its own nature... (13.268).
By virtue of the application of differentiation, she is situated within the state of māyā;
therefore, because of the union with that nature, the descent of power (śaktipāta), although already present, [becomes manifest]. (13.269)
It bestows only that much enjoyment, but not ultimate Śiva-nature.
Whatever form of Viṣṇu or others exists here within the Supreme Lord, that, by virtue of its own spontaneously manifested connection with difference, occupies the intermediate state of Māyā.

Even while remaining established by assuming the form of Viṣṇu and others, the descent of power (śaktipāta) would only bestow such enjoyment as is appropriate for his specific office, but not ultimate Śiva-hood; whereby it remains inferior to the descent of power from the Supreme Lord.

One might object: "How can Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and others, who dwell within the path of Māyā, possess the capacity for grace—even though it is inferior and consists of worldly enjoyment and the like? He dispels this doubt by means of an illustration:
Just as even a king, by his own independent will, bestows favor upon someone. || 13-270 ||
Likewise, through the penetration of the power of Īśa, Viṣṇu and the others are also fully capable here; as it is said:
"This living being is ignorant and not the master of its own pleasure and pain."
"Impelled by God, one may go either to hell or to heaven.

According to this view, even a king or similar person, though still within the sphere of *māyā* due to being impelled by God, favors someone according to his own will through a portion of his own [merit]; likewise, Viṣṇu and others do so as well by bestowing worldly enjoyments (*bhoga*).
They are capable—meaning, they are able—to bestow grace upon gold.
And what follows from that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Then, by virtue of the descent of power (śaktipāta) pertaining to the office within the womb of Māyā... (13.271).
Someone who discriminates between primary matter and the Spirit, having proceeded from that very source which is superior, quickly attains discrimination through awakening. (13.272)

In an instant, he becomes the knower of the internal nature of both the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and *kalā*, as well as of *puṃmāyā*. Then, because of that very capacity of theirs, with reference to the dwelling within *māyā* (*māyāgarbha*),
a certain follower of Kapila or others [is reached] through a mild descent of power (*śaktipāta*) proceeding from them.

One who knows the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) has transcended nature and is liberated from the bondage of materiality; and another, through that very same intense descent of power (śaktipāta) belonging to the office of the Māyāgarbha, quickly realizes the distinction between the individual soul (pums) and the limited agency (kalā).
The meaning is: in an instant, he becomes a knower of the interior of Māyā and has thus completely transcended Māyā.
One might ask: "Even so, what is the purpose of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because even action that rests upon the *kalās* is completely brought to an end. (13.273)
But the previous *jñānākala* is a possessor of karma (*karmī*), because he remains established upon that [substratum].
As it was stated previously:
"Then, through the destruction of all karma, there arises the discernment between Māyā and the person (*puruṣa*)."

"Because of the state of being devoid of *vijñānakala*, the person (*puruṣa*) does not descend below *māyā*. (9.185) Now, one might ask: "In that case, even for one who has discerned the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, does karma cease absolutely or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the former," and so forth. "The substratum" refers to *kalā* and the rest. Now, in this way...
In that case, like us, he would be merely bound; so what is the use of the knowledge of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But he never again enters into creation at the very root of *prakṛti*. (13.274)
But in the *māyādhara* [state], it is emitted through the impulsion of Ananteśa;
that it is "emitted" is because of being bound by the three impurities (*mala*). As was stated previously:
"When the distinction between intellect (*dhī*) and the person (*pums*) is known, and when the difference between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* is realized..."
Moreover, one's karma would not be exhausted even in a single kalā, for that [exhaustion] could only occur there.
"Therefore, one who has attained realization through the Sāṃkhya view would not transmigrate below the level of Pradhāna" (9.187).

Now, let this be granted; however, for one who possesses the knowledge of the discrimination between Māyā and the individual soul (puruṣa), would there be only the state of a Jñānākala, or is there something even more distinguished than that? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Having attained the state of being devoid of consciousness (vijñānākala), he [proceeds] solely by virtue of his office (adhikāra). || 13-275 ||
"From Śiva, he always attains the state of being the Mantra, its Lord (Mantranātha), and so forth;

'by virtue of his office' means that only his office remains—this is the meaning. 'Always' implies that it should never be otherwise—this is the intended sense. 'From Śiva' means not by the impulsion of Ananteśa."
As was stated previously:
"Furthermore, by means of Śiva’s will, perceiving his non-difference from Śiva, he gradually assumes the form of the Mantreśas and their leaders, and attains the nature of Śiva. (9.93)
Thus [it is said].
One might object: "Let it be so; but what happens next from this descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Supreme Lord?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This descent of power which comes from the Supreme Lord indeed [arises] from impurity (mala). (13.276)

It is said that liberation comes from being separated from what is called ignorance; furthermore, this descent of power (śakti) from the Supreme Lord Śiva— and not from another lord such as Viṣṇu— is alone the bestower of liberation by manifesting the state of Śiva, because it is [separation] from that which is called ignorance.

The meaning is that he is the "separer," one who has been separated from impurity (*mala*) in its substantial form. As was stated previously: "But seeing the Self as distinct from impurity, one attains the state of Śiva" (9.188).
Now, one might ask: "Why is it that he alone is thus? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the state of Śiva is not revealed by anyone else. (13.277)
"By another" means by one related to Viṣṇu and so forth; for they are indeed deluded in this regard—this is the intended meaning.
Therefore, he says in the *Svacchandaśāstra*: "In the midst of the night, it was stated by him that there are three hundred and sixty-three deluded disputants, beginning with the Vaiṣṇavas. (13.278)

"Śiva-knowledge alone bestows the attainment of Śiva-hood. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis; thus, the meaning is that Śiva-knowledge alone—nothing else—bestows the attainment of Śiva-hood. This has been corroborated many times previously. And so, that which is...
The presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Supreme Lord’s power bestows the attainment of Śiva-nature;
that alone is designated by the term "descent of power" (*śaktipāta*), and not otherwise. For there is nothing whatsoever in this world that is not presided over by the Supreme Lord’s power.
Thus it is said: "The descent of power (śaktipāta) is discussed as culminating in the attainment of the state of Śiva. (13.279)
Otherwise, what indeed could exist that is not presided over by the power of Śiva?

Therefore, by the reasoning already stated, the powers of Viṣṇu and others, even though they preside over their respective domains, do not bestow liberation; for this reason, they are not enumerated here as instances of the descent of power (śaktipāta).
This has been stated by this very [author] elsewhere:
"Since the [attainments] of Vaiṣṇavas and others do not culminate in liberation—just like the favor of a king—there is no detailed analysis of them here;
however, it has been stated that the presiding presence of Śiva’s Power (śakti) exists everywhere. That [Power], moreover, is not merely the Jyeṣṭhā."
"But rather, they are terrible or even more terrible. (Tantrāloka 11.11a).
And therefore:
"They cause the individual souls (aṇu) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower."
"Other [powers], even more terrible, are known as those who embrace the Rudra-germs.

Thus, for the Vaiṣṇavas and others— who are presided over by such powers as described above and who maintain a reliance on duality— there is no qualification for this knowledge of Śiva, which is non-dual in nature as pure consciousness.
Thus he says:
"Therefore, in this [system], Vaiṣṇavas and others have no qualification whatsoever. (13.280)
"For since they function solely within the realm of difference, they are far removed from non-duality.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If at some point even these [limited subjects] are connected with the Śiva-power which is favorably disposed toward them, then what should be done? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But by the sovereignty of the Great Lord, even they may become oriented toward Śiva. (13.281)
For these, there is a twofold refinement: first by the extraction of the *liṅga*, and then by initiation.
"By the extraction of the *liṅga*" refers to the procedure to be described, consisting of fasting and so forth. (13.281)

Now, one might raise the objection: "If he is presided over by the supreme power of the Lord, then let his purificatory rite, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), be the same as for others; what is the purpose of this twofold [process]? He pacifies this doubt by showing an illustrative example:
When the impure residual odor has been removed, the water-pot is consecrated with flowers.
That consecration for him is twofold; such is not the procedure for a pure jar.
He concludes this very point: "In this way, this venerable descent of power (śaktipāta) has been described here as independent."
But surely, in that case, there would be a contradiction with other scriptures, wherein it is stated [in the Mataṅga] that this depends upon the equilibrium of karma and so forth:
"This activity of the nature of tranquility (śama) would be painful and very difficult to perform."
Thus it is said; and also in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"When [the disciple's] karma has been pacified, at that very moment, by virtue of his fitness, he is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power (*tīvra-śakti-nipāta*)."

"Just as Śiva is omniscient, being devoid of even the slightest lack of knowledge"— having raised the doubt, "Is this what was meant by that?", he says: "In this very manner, the *Mataṅga*, *Kiraṇa*, and other scriptures are to be understood."
However, for fear of increasing the bulk of the book, that has not been written out and included here. || 13-284 ||
The meaning is that this [verse] should be explained by following the sequence beginning with the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
This has not been stated only in our own tradition, but even in the Purāṇas and other texts that depend upon the meaning of the Śruti;
thus he says:
"And even in the Purāṇa, devotion is held to arise solely through His grace."
By this [path], those whose minds are absorbed in that state attain supreme perfection.
"But it is by his grace alone that devotion arises in men"—this is the first half-verse [of the following]. (285)
He explains this very point:
by the word "only" (eva), dependence on ritual action and the like is negated.
Grace (prasāda) is the state of becoming stainless; through it, there is the attainment of the nature of fullness. (13.286)
For by that very self, Śiva shines forth as inherently full.

In this regard, it has been stated that the Lord, through his own sovereignty, assumes the state of a limited individual (aṇutā) by manifesting contraction; yet, turning back, he reveals his own stainless and perfect form.

That [state] is His grace, which is clarity or the removal of impurity; and by virtue of that state of being stainless, there is a state of fullness, because He Himself is Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
