Thus, although He assumes various limitations of the contracted self through that very nature, He shines forth as complete.
One becomes one whose nature is the restored fullness of vision and action (dṛkkriyā), as it has been said: "They attain the supreme perfection. || 286 ||
He demonstrates this very point by way of contrast: "But in some cases, [the mind] may be devoid of contact with the great siddhi that is the state of Śiva. (13.287)

For the devotion that exists toward Vaiṣṇavas and others does not arise from Śiva alone; moreover, that devotion which is directed toward Vaiṣṇavas and others— who, according to the reasoning stated above, lack the attainment of the state of Śiva— does not proceed from Śiva alone, independent of karma and other factors.
It would not arise from the Supreme Lord—this is the meaning. || 287 ||
Now, one might object: "Has it not just been stated that nothing whatsoever can exist without being presided over by the power of Śiva?
Therefore, how can it now be asserted that devotion toward Viṣṇu and others does not originate from Śiva? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He becomes auspicious therein; this is the cause, and not he alone.
"Moreover, it is stainless and yet dependent on the attainment of limits such as ritual action (*karma*) and so forth.

Here, in the context of devotion toward Viṣṇu and others, the words "moreover" (*api tu*) and so forth are stated in order to distinguish between its state of being absolute (*kevalatva*) and its state of being stainless (*nirmalatva*). "Attainment of limits" (*prāptāvacchid*) means...
The meaning is: [the Self] has accepted the stain of limitation (saṅkoca) by being delimited through the assumption of forms such as Viṣṇu and others. || 288 ||
Now, one might ask: "Of what is this the meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But this is the very lifeblood of that [teaching] by which they attain supreme perfection. (13.289)
For indeed, in the absence of that uniformity, the aforementioned supreme perfection of devotion would not be established—this is the intended meaning. ||289||
And this has been approved even by our gurus, who are experts in logic and scripture; thus he says: "Even our supreme guru, the venerable Utpaladeva, said:
'O Lord, at the time of the descent of power (śaktipāta), You never engage in deliberation. (13.290)
What has happened to me today, that you delay in the act of manifesting yourself?
For you have declared, by means of the two words "karhicit" (at some time) and "prāpta" (attained), that you are independent [of external causes]. (13.291)

The connection [of the text] is as follows: the venerable Utpaladeva has also stated that, regarding the procedure for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of the All-pervasive Lord, there is both its rarity and its lack of attachment [to external conditions], because it is independent [of such factors]. As for the deliberation concerning fitness and unfitness that arises in that regard:

Since you do not perform [this] even at some time or occasion when it has been brought about by logic—even through forgetfulness—because here your sole basis is your own will, independent of karma and other factors; for this very reason, it is difficult to obtain here. For that which occurs in the world depending upon some means is said to be easily obtained.
By means of that accumulation, the attainment of that [state] will surely occur; for this very reason, there is also the quality of being free from partiality (*arāgitva*) here.

For Viṣṇu and the others appear as if overcome by passion and aversion, since they favor only those people who have performed [meritorious deeds] and not those who have not; you, however, perform this entirely without regard for anything else. For this very reason—
The address "O Lord" (Īśa) is according to the sequence of the independent and sovereign descent of power (śaktipāta), which is free from all dependence.
He did not express this solely by means of the two words "karhicit" and "prāpta," but also by means of the latter half [of the verse];
thus he says:
"[He describes] the variety of that very descent of power (śaktipāta) by means of the latter half. (13.292)

"By the distinctions described as 'obstruction,' 'delay,' 'speediness,' and so forth"—that is to say, immediately following [the previous statement]. For here [the sense is]: "Why do you delay toward me?
Why do you waste time through obstruction and the like? Reveal your own light immediately!"
The intended meaning.

This has been stated not only by teachers established in the non-duality of consciousness, but even by the commentators on the Śaiva scriptures; thus he says: "Also by the venerable Aniruddha, [who spoke of] the power of the All-pervasive Lord as the 'Unfolding' (unmīlinī)... (13.293).

While explaining [the scriptures], O Mātanga, the Lord’s state of non-reliance (nirapekṣatā), which consists in the manifestation of His own essential nature, has been described even with respect to stationary beings. (13.294)

The connection is as follows: the venerable Aniruddha has also described in great detail that power (*śakti*) falling [upon an object] is never dependent; thus, he has described its independence in full detail. Regarding the phrase "the unfolding power" (*unmīlinīṃ śaktim*), it is stated therein:
"When his power, colored by passion for Śiva, unfolds, it falls down, exceedingly radiant and characterized by eternal grace. (1.4.45).
By the phrase "down to the level of immobile beings," [the author] reveals the true nature even of those who are utterly unworthy.
It has been indicated.
Now, he begins to describe the variety of spiritual authority (*adhikāra*), which is rooted in the variety of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*):
"Thus, while this variety of the descent of power remains established... (13.295).
The diversity of the *samayin* and other initiates arises from distinctions such as degrees of excellence and so forth.
He states this very point:
"Someone, by the grace of Him [the Guru], through the mere attainment of the status of being a portion of Rudra... (13.296).
The initiate (*samayin*) who is described here shall gradually attain the state of Śiva;
whereas one who is bound to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), being a spiritual son (*putraka*), attains it swiftly and without succession.
Due to the intervention of worldly enjoyments, one practitioner may achieve [the goal] slowly while another does so quickly;
some have their duties fully completed within the fivefold set of tasks.
That Guru, established in form (rūpa), also partakes in the distinctions of enjoyment, liberation, and so forth,
through the application of both the concise and the detailed methods for the fourfold group beginning with the Samayin.
The diversity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) consists of distinctions such as gradual (*krama*) and non-gradual (*akrama*).
"Gradually" means after the initiation of a spiritual son (*putraka-dīkṣā*) and so forth; for this very reason, the descent of power here is mild.
"Swiftly" means immediately upon the fall of the body. "Non-gradually" means even while the body still exists—this is the meaning.
It has been stated that the interval between [the attainment of] enjoyment (*bhoga*) may be long or short—this is expressed by the phrase "long or short.

This means that, with respect to the disciple, there is a distinction regarding enjoyment, liberation (*mokṣa*), and so forth; for it has been stated that he himself possesses the full capacity for the task at hand. And precisely because of this gradation, there is also a gradation between those two [enjoyment and liberation].
This is expressed by the word "distinction" (*bheda*). Regarding the phrase "through the combination of concise and expanded [teachings]" and "by means of sequence, non-sequence, and so forth":
therein, in terms of sequence, one is first a *samayin*, then a *putraka*, and then an *ācārya*; this constitutes the totality (*sāmastya*).
In terms of non-sequence, someone may be only a *putraka* and not even a *samayin* at the outset; or someone may be only an *ācārya* and not [even a *putraka*] at the outset.
Whether one is a *samayin* or a *putraka*, there is a distinction between them.
Not only is there such variety in the descent of power (śaktipāta) through both gradual and instantaneous means, but also by another method—as he says:
"In the Siddhānta, the descent of power is gradual; in the Vāmaka, it is [instantaneous] after that. (13.300)
In the Dakṣa, Mata, Kula, Kaula, Ṣaḍardha, and Hṛdaya [traditions],
it occurs either by way of transgression or suddenly, indeed without sequence.
Because the meaning of the Trika alone is supremely excellent, it should be construed in grammatical apposition with "in the heart of the Six-and-a-Half [Tantras]. As it has been said:
"From the Veda comes the Śaiva; from that, the Vāma; from that, the Dakṣa; and from that, the Mata."

"Then the Kula, then the Kaula, and the Trika is the supreme, most excellent of all. Thus, from the Siddhānta up to the Ṣaḍardha, according to their respective degrees of gradation, there occurs a corresponding state of the descent of power (śaktipāta); this is the intended meaning.

"By virtue of transcendence" means: immediately after the Siddhānta, then the Dakṣa [Tantra], then the Kula, and then the Trika; thus, it is indeed the sudden, non-sequential [path], which is the very meaning of the Trika. || 301 ||
Nor has this been stated without foundation; thus he says:
"It is stated in the *Śrībhairavakula* that a Guru who has been well-consecrated by the five initiations, having transcended the lower currents, indeed enters the *Trika* scripture. (13.302)
In this regard,
it is traditionally held that in the Siddhānta initiation is that of the *hotṛ*, in the Tantra it is known as *yojanikā*,
in the Trika it is *samāveśavatī*, and in the Kula it is considered to consist of *stobha*.

By the statement beginning with "In the Kaula tradition, initiation consisting of essential identity (sāmarasya) is declared to be fivefold," even a teacher who has been thoroughly purified by this fivefold initiation is one who belongs exclusively to the Trika scripture— a stream of Śaiva and other scriptures that transcends lower stages.
The meaning is "consecrated as the head of all. As it has been said:
"Even a teacher consecrated in the Vāma path, though he knows the supreme reality, must undergo further refinement in the Bhairava [tradition], and likewise in Kula, Kaula, and Trika."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 302 ||

Now, one might object: here, since it has been stated in such passages as, "For all [scriptures] originate from Śiva and bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva," there is no distinction whatsoever between them, whether in terms of their cause or their result.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how is it said that this is the higher [teaching] and this is the lower scripture? he says:

"For the All-pervasive Lord has established the status of 'higher' and 'lower' among the scriptures—such as the venerable *Sarvācāra*, *Hṛdaya*, and others—by means of distinctions such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and conduct (*ācāra*). (13.303)

Knowledge consists of both duality and non-duality, while action is either external or internal. It has been demonstrated many times that it is precisely on account of these two that there exists this hierarchy of lower and higher levels. || 303 ||
He recites that very point:

"Even a teacher who has been consecrated in the Vāma path and knows the supreme reality (paratattva) still deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once more in the Bhairava Tantra. (13.304)

Now, one might object: "If he has indeed been consecrated in the Śaiva tradition and so forth, and by that alone knows the supreme reality, then what is the purpose of his undergoing further purification in the Bhairava Tantras and other systems? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:
"The Śaivas, Vaimalas, Siddhāntins, Ārhats, and those who follow the Kāruka [traditions],"...
All those animals are to be known as belonging to the Bhairava mandala of the Mothers.

Even those who have been consecrated by the Mātṛmaṇḍala, Kula, Kaula, and so forth, as well as the Bhairava Tantras and other such systems, are still merely bound souls (paśu)—this is established by implication. || 305 ||
This has also been stated regarding the Kula, Kaula, and other systems implied by the word "etcetera"—thus he says:

"And it is stated in the *Kulakālīvidhi* that for Vaiṣṇavas, and especially for those who have taken refuge in the practice of smearing themselves with ashes (*bhasmaniṣṭhā*), there is no fitness at all [for this practice]," and so forth. (13.306)
"Of those who have reached the culmination in ashes" refers to the followers of Śiva and others. || 306 ||
This has not been stated only here, but elsewhere as well— as he says—
the venerable Maheśvara has stated it in brief in the Svacchandaśāstra;
he recites that very passage:
But he who is devoted to other scriptures does not bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
He establishes this very point:
"For a guru is considered one who has received initiation through the sequence beginning with that of a *samayin*;
and since he acts thus by the power of his own capacity (*śakti*), what connection can there be [between him] and the Vaiṣṇavas and others? (13.308).

The word *ittham* (thus) functions like the "crow's eye" [applying to both parts of the sentence]; therefore, the meaning is: one who has received initiation through this sequence of the *samayin* and so forth, starting from the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of the Supreme Lord.
In the manner thus described, what lineage indeed could there not be for those such as the Vaiṣṇavas, who delight in other scriptures, regarding their status as gurus here?

There is no connection whatsoever, for according to the reasoning already stated, they do not even possess the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvara-śaktipāta*); what then can be said regarding the sequence beginning with the initiate (*samayin*), such as hearing the scriptures or receiving initiation?
This is the intended meaning.
Now, one might ask: "Could this teacher not be someone who has acquired such a form merely by displaying feigned devotion and the like out of hypocrisy?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

If one were to acquire that knowledge through deceit, eavesdropping, or similar means, there would be an expiation; therefore, what kind of qualified person could there be for this [teaching]? (13.309)

One might object: "Let this teacher, though devoted to other scriptures, accept the Śaiva scripture through some pretext or the like, or let him undergo penance; what concern is this of ours, since he certainly continues to grace his disciple? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
A disciple who is possessed by the desire for fruits and whose success depends solely on that [desire] will certainly be cooked in hell, even if he practices penance.

A disciple desires some fruit, and since that depends upon the guru, may he not achieve its accomplishment through encountering a false guru; on the contrary, [it is said]: "...but association with him is the fifth."
By saying this, the meaning is that through the performance of penance and service to the Guru, he will certainly be cooked in hell; thus there would be a great calamity. As it has been said:
"When they do not know the reality, they grasp at the Kaulika [teaching] out of hypocrisy."
Having begun with: "By which those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin) desire to go to hell," [it continues]:
"The vessel of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna-bhāṇḍa), indeed spoken by Bhairava, is of great significance."
Having personally adopted the proper conduct, he bestows the grace of initiation.
Those who sell animals for their own enjoyment— such being their nature—
fall thereafter into a most terrible hell together with those very animals.
"Together with their sons, friends, and servants, and even along with seven generations of their lineage,
they are truly unable to achieve purification through expiatory rites. (310)
One might object: "Since devotion—the sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—is observed toward his guru and the deity, he must have been appointed to such a task by Śiva himself;
what fault is there in him that this should happen? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This is a mode of concealment (*tirobhāva*), in that he has been appointed to such a [duty]."
When [the disciple] is with a guru, his devotion to Śiva is not called a descent of power (śaktipāta). || 13-311 ||

And by this, immediately following the establishment of independence, the manifold nature of concealment (*tirobhāva*), which was indicated in the subsequent summary, has also been introduced. || 311 ||

Now, one might object: "Let it be so; but what should be done by that Guru with respect to the knowledge which has been acquired by this disciple through deceit, eavesdropping, and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But when, by virtue of [the disciple's] manifold variety, he should recognize such [a state of his]..."
Therefore, one should extract from that knowledge the state of being engaged with what is contrary [to reality]. || 13-312 ||
And one should abandon that sinful conduct and become intent upon knowledge.
For if [the opportunity] passes at a later time, then at the very outset there would be no bestowing of knowledge—this is the intended meaning.
"Vaicitryam" means manifoldness, such as various types of activities, speech, and so forth. "Upāharet" means [one should bring about].

By means of the method to be described, characterized by the withdrawal of knowledge; "one should abandon" means one should not engage in dwelling with them or similar activities—this is the meaning. The reason for this is stated as "a sinful conduct. Having done so, one should perform expiation; thus it is said: "He should be solely intent on knowledge. That very [point is as follows].
He makes this clear to the heart by means of an illustration:
"Just as a king, having seized wealth from a thief, punishes him. (13.313)
Likewise, having acquired Śaiva knowledge from Vaiṣṇavas and others, one of right understanding should exercise restraint;
this is the implied meaning. And in this context, that [restraint] consists essentially of renunciation and so forth, as has already been stated.

Now, was not knowledge first taught to him by the Guru with a serene mind as being indeed changeless? And by that alone [he attained it], for it is said: "At the time when the changeless was revealed by the Guru..."

Anticipating the objection—"By such statements as 'At that very moment he is indeed liberated,' one has already achieved all that was to be done; so how can this [liberation] come about again?"—he says: "For he [the limited soul], even when the knowledge of Śiva has been fully heard, remains entirely fixed in the state of duality. (13.314)
"He does not abandon" means that this most excellent of bound souls (paśu) is firmly presided over by the Left;
he has been rendered hidden by Śiva himself and established there by the force of necessity (niyati). (13.315)
How can one who is dependent upon another proceed along the path?
For he does not abandon it because of a lack of confidence therein; this is due to being firmly presided over by the contrary [force].
"Dependent upon another" means by the power of necessity (*niyati*). As it has been said:
"Vaiṣṇavas, Saugatas, those who follow the Śrutis, as well as those who propound the Upaniṣads (Śrutyanta)—
these and others are never authorized in the teaching of the Lord.
Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, the scripture also says the same; thus he says:
"And it is declared in the Svacchanda Śāstra that those who are devoted to the Vaiṣṇava and other [sects]... (13.316).
"Indeed, Māyā causes them to wander because of their desire for liberation when there is no liberation.
Anticipating the objection— "Granted that Māyā may cause Vaiṣṇavas and others to wander, but what happens to one who, though being a Vaiṣṇava or similar, is actually a Śaiva?"— he says:
A Vaiṣṇava and others, while incorporating the Śaiva scriptures into their own doctrine, [act in this manner].
"Certainly, one who has fallen into doubt will come to fall away from both; for by attempting to combine them, there is no confidence in either case."
Now, one might ask: "Even so, what is the cause for falling away from both? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because of the transgression of the rule (samaya) regarding his own vision and the vision of others. (13.318)
Since one incurs transgression from such an act, one should not follow this procedure.
As it has been said:
"Now, if one who relies on the Vedas again seeks after the Śaiva [path]..."
Having lost his Vedic knowledge and lost his Śaiva knowledge, he will come to exist once again.
If the salutation at the junctions of the day (sandhyā) and other rites must be performed according to the Vedic system,
and if there is an omission of Śiva-mantras, an expiation is prescribed.
If the Śivadharmas are indeed placed at the beginning, then the Vedic dharma is corrupted;
or even when they are practiced together, there is a defect in the beginning, middle, and end.
Furthermore, a contradiction in practice leads to a state of mental distraction;
what undertaking, what beginning, or what end can there be for one beset by doubt?
"Furthermore, at the outset, I shall perform something out of respect for both;
even if there is a contradiction in the sequence of ritual actions, there is a mutual expiation.
Thus it is said.
This has not been stated only in the Svacchanda Śāstra; it has been said elsewhere as well—as he says:
"And such [a thing] was stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Gahvara. (13.319)
He recites that very point: "The knowledge of Śiva does not manifest among those devoted to other scriptures.
The meaning is: "It does not manifest" because they are not qualified for it.
He shows that very point by analyzing it:
"Therefore, that [practice] does not belong to the Siddhāntin in the Left [tradition], nor does it belong to him in the Right; it is not accepted in our [Trika] system. (13.320)

The connection is as follows: "In the Kula, Kaula, and Trika [systems], each preceding one is not qualified for the subsequent one. However, there is this specific distinction here: it has been stated that each preceding one is qualified for everything in the subsequent [system]. Thus, "each preceding one is qualified for the subsequent."
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "If, despite an equal degree of proficiency in other sciences, each preceding one is qualified for the subsequent, then why is each succeeding one not qualified for the preceding? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"One who is limited does not know the unlimited, nor does one established in infinity [know the limited]. (13.321)
The "All-enduring" (Sarvasaha) is situated below that; the Guru is situated above and is the presiding authority.

Here, due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he exists as infinite, yet remains delimited, contracted, and a limited subject (pramātṛ). [He leads one] toward the undelimited—the full subject in whom no delimitation exists, who is free from all boundaries.

Because he does not know [the other] as being of that same nature, he does not fear him. Therefore, due to his being unconditioned, the Guru who abides above is the one authorized over the limited [disciple] who stands below—such as a Vaiṣṇava and so forth—and not the one standing below over the one above. For how could he, whose knowledge is contracted, [be so]?
One shall become a fit vessel for plunging into perfect knowledge.

Now, one might object: "In that case, how could a Guru who possesses full knowledge and resides on a higher level bestow authority upon those below him, such as Vaiṣṇavas and others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By touching his own lower [level], he brings forth the activities of the lower levels. (13.322)
That which the supreme Guru, situated above, brings to fruition— that is,

because the Guru situated above has attained the direct realization of his own Self through the descent of the supreme nectar of complete non-dual knowledge, all lower ritual actions [are rendered superfluous].
By breathing life into them, he brings them to fulfillment; by bestowing complete enjoyment and liberation, he makes them fruitful—this is the meaning: that he is the supreme one who transcends all.
One might object: "Even if such a Guru resides on a higher level, what can he do for a Vaiṣṇava or others situated below him?
For is he not a fit recipient for their grace? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even one who stands within the vision of those below may become a servant of such a Guru as this. (13.323)
One who, ignited by such a descent of power (*śaktipāta*), would immediately lead this [soul] upward— namely,
even one belonging to a lower system of vision (*darśana*) such as Vaiṣṇava and so forth,
being ignited from among such [practitioners] by an intense descent of power, reaches such a state situated above.

One should serve the Guru, who indeed would swiftly lead even a Vaiṣṇava or others—who stand below and possess a downward gaze—to the upward state, making them manifest as one with supreme consciousness; this is the meaning.

One might object: "Just as each preceding [level] has authority over each subsequent one, why is it that each subsequent level does not likewise have authority over each preceding one? He pacifies this doubt by showing an illustrative example:
"In the case of a field or sacred seat (pīṭha) that is demarcated like various mountains and rivers... (13.324).
In each successive consciousness, the lower [element] does not possess the capacity for the higher;
just as in this world,
when one reaches the various elevations and depressions of the earth’s regions— such as mountains and rivers— one encounters distinct boundaries at each ascending level.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: in a field or location that is predominantly a fortress (*koṭṭa*), one situated in a progressively lower or deeper place is not qualified; likewise, even regarding higher knowledge, a Vaiṣṇava or similar follower situated at a lower level is not qualified for the successively higher [levels] such as Śaiva and so forth.
This has not been stated solely with reference to another, but even with reference to oneself—as he says:
"Even one who knows each successive teacher as higher and higher remains lower and lower [than the ultimate reality]. (13.325)
One who performs an office while transgressing the scripture becomes a vessel for punishment.
Regarding "transgressing the scripture," it has been said:
"One should not exercise authority when a great Ācārya is present."
"But whoever acts under the influence of delusion, the Śākinīs indeed curse him.

Now, let it be so that there is a hierarchy among the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others; however, when the descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Supreme Lord is equal for the Śaivas and others alike, what is the cause for their mutual distinction?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The diversity of fitness for knowledge arises solely from the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta). (13.326)
He demonstrates that very variety:

"Knowledge consists of three types—the scriptural, that consisting of reflection, and that consisting of contemplation—and among these, the latter is superior because it is the sole cause of liberation. (13.327)
And knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-jñāna*) is of two kinds, distinguished by being either weak or well-practiced; thus he says, "of two natures" (*dvātmeti*). As it has been said:
"Knowledge is declared to be threefold; among these, the first is held to be that which is heard (*śruta*)."
Furthermore, there is that consisting of reflection and that consisting of cultivation.
The thorough comprehension of the meaning of the treatise is considered the learning of one who is focused;
it consists of knowing "this is here," "that is there," and "this is applicable in this context."
Having thoroughly examined the meaning of all the treatises, there is a systematic arrangement;
and that knowledge consisting of reflection is taught as being of two kinds.
There is a distinction between that which is practiced with ease and that which is not; among these, the well-practiced is supreme.
When that is perfectly accomplished, there arises that which consists of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
"Since the yogi, having attained yoga, would obtain the fruit of yoga;

thus, by the distinction of their realization, the man of knowledge (jñānin) is said to be fourfold. This refers to the answer concerning those four types of knowledge, beginning with that derived from the Vedas.
That which follows from the middle is that consisting of meditative cultivation—this is the meaning. || 327 ||

He demonstrates by analyzing how [this knowledge] is the sole cause of liberation: "How could one effect extraction from the principles (*tattvas*) or union with either the *sakala* or *akala* [states] without that supreme knowledge consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? (3.328)
"From the principles" means from the impure ones; "somewhere" means according to one's own preference.
For even a teacher who possesses knowledge, if he has not performed the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of those respective principles, how could he act in this way?—this is the intended meaning.
(328) Now, [an objection]: "But..."
"Only two are declared to be givers of liberation in the Śaiva tradition: the man of knowledge (jñānin) and the yogi.

Since such statements declare that even the yogi is a cause of liberation, how can it be said here that knowledge consisting solely of contemplation (bhāvanā) is its sole cause? Anticipating this objection, he says:
But the yogi, even though he has attained various specific siddhis, becomes a unifier in the highest state, beginning with Sadāśiva, solely by virtue of his well-practiced knowledge. (13.329)

One might object: "Since the realization of each respective reality arises for the yogin through the power of yoga alone, he could simply effect the union of the disciple with those various realities by that means itself; what need is there for such knowledge on his part? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Whatever perfection born of yoga he may attain regarding the lower principles is not a means for liberation, even if it remains with him like wealth and a wife.

Now, one might object: "Who has said that there could not be the attainment born of yoga (*yogajā siddhi*) in the higher principles (*tattva*), such as Sadāśiva and the rest, by virtue of which one might liberate this entire world? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He in whom the attainment of all the paths has arisen is indeed Sadāśiva."
How can he, having attained the status of a guru, directly liberate mortals?

This is the summary of the meaning here: in this system, the knower (*jñānin*) is of four kinds; it has already been stated that each succeeding one possesses greater excellence than the preceding. Consequently, even a knower who lacks the practice of yoga—provided he has attained the state of Bhairava through the grace of the higher knowledge consisting of well-practiced contemplation—is [liberated] in every respect.
It has been stated that within the sequence beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*), the knowledge consisting of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) alone is more excellent and superior.

The yogi is of four kinds: the one who has attained (*saṃprāpta*), the one who is striving (*ghaṭamāna*), the one whose yoga is perfected (*siddhayoga*), and the one who is fully accomplished (*susiddha*). Among these, the "one who has attained" is simply one who has received the instruction on yoga.

And these two—the one who is striving (*ghaṭamāna*) and the one who is solely intent upon that practice—are not themselves established in either yoga or knowledge; therefore, what can they do for another? However, for one who has attained perfection in yoga (*siddhayoga*), there also exists knowledge well-practiced; it is only by means of employing that [knowledge] that he is a liberator, and not otherwise.
Thus it has been said:
"The yogi, however, because he possesses well-practiced knowledge, is the one who joins [the self] to the supreme state."
"And even though the perfection born of yoga is established for him, it is not the means for liberation.
And it has been said:
"The progressive superiority of these [means] has been declared."
Among the knowers of reality and the practitioners of yoga, he was the supreme master of perfected yoga.
"For since he possesses knowledge, even though he was previously devoid of the fruits of yoga" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).
As for the *susiddha* [adept], it is said:
"Furthermore, however one may remain, right there and then..."
While enjoying its fruit, one is by no means diminished by it.
"He who is well-perfected, O Dear One, should be known as equal to Sadāśiva" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).

According to such statements, he is indeed Śiva himself, whose nature is eternally unswerving. Thus, when he attains the status of a Guru, how could he not liberate mortals directly, setting aside the [lower] Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras)? But [if one considers] the lineage...
"What occasion is there here for stating that 'he should indeed liberate'?—this is the meaning.
As has been stated by this very author elsewhere: "But since he who is perfected is Śiva himself, what more need be said there?
Therefore, having thus deliberated upon the distinction between knowledge and yoga, one who possesses well-practiced knowledge alone...
It is stated everywhere that "the Guru is the bestower of liberation," and for this reason we too have declared it so here.
Regarding this, he says:

"In the Mālinītantra, having deliberated upon the nature of knowledge and yoga, it was stated that one who possesses well-practiced knowledge is declared by the wise to be the giver of liberation. (13.332)

The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) and is displaced in its position [in the verse]. Therefore, it is stated that only one who possesses well-practiced knowledge is the Guru who bestows liberation. From this, the following is established; thus he says: "Therefore, the possession of well-practiced higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) alone is the single defining characteristic of a Guru."
The meaning is: "one" implies that there is no second state of being a yogin.

But surely, the Guru has also been described as being "qualified" (*yogya*); how then is it appropriate to speak in this way? True; however, there is this distinction: it has been stated that the man of knowledge (*jñānī*) is superior to the practitioner of yoga (*yogin*). Even so, one must determine where a man of knowledge or a practitioner of yoga should be appointed as a Guru, and where they should be avoided. That—
And here, that which has been received from the mouth of our Guru is being revealed; thus he says:
"This division, however, as taught by me, is shown by Śambhunātha. (13.333)
"This" refers to that which is about to be described. || 333 ||
He says that very thing:
"One intent on the knowledge of liberation should make a teacher who possesses well-practiced realization;
one should abandon another even if already obtained. And so it was said by Śiva.

"Another" refers to knowledge that has not been well-practiced. Now, one might object: "Since the fault of abandoning a guru—who is [otherwise] attained through such statements as 'From abandoning the guru, death occurs'—has been declared, how can this be said?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And so it was stated by Śiva. This is not without authoritative proof.
This is the meaning. || 334 ||
He recites that very point:
"Just as a bee seeking fragrance goes from flower to another flower, so a disciple seeking higher knowledge should go from one guru to another guru. (13.335)

An objection may be raised: "The disciple seeks consciousness, and since he has somehow already obtained that from this [first] teacher, what is the point of his going to another teacher? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having encountered a teacher devoid of power, how could one rely on him for the knowledge of liberation?"
O Goddess, when the root of a tree has perished, from where could flowers, fruits, and the like come?
"Lacking power" means being incapable of bestowing knowledge and so forth; for how could he, being himself ignorant, act for another?—this is the intended meaning. || 336 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely here meditation (*bhāvanā*) is primary, and since it will certainly bear fruit even if performed toward an unqualified teacher, why abandon him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even while observing the splendor of ever-increasing excellence..."
Who else, therefore, would be more cursed by fate than one who occupies such a lowly position? (13.337)
Thus, one who desires enjoyment, liberation, and so forth must necessarily take refuge in an especially exalted Guru, by means of whom their attainment may occur without effort; thus he says:
"But he who should desire both enjoyment and liberation, as well as supreme knowledge..."
One should take refuge in that guru who possesses well-practiced knowledge and has attained perfection in yoga.

The phrase "one perfected in yoga" (yogasiddha) means the third type of yogi, namely the Siddhayogin; and for him, knowledge that has been well-practiced is necessarily present—thus he is called a "knower of well-practiced knowledge," as was immediately confirmed [by the previous statement] that he possesses knowledge as well. || 338 ||
If such a guru is not found, what then should be done? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In his absence, however, one should resort to a man of knowledge for the sake of realization and liberation.
The phrase "for the sake of realization and liberation" means that [the teacher] is the cause of those two.
Anticipating the question, "Even so, what should one who desires enjoyment do? he says:
"In the case of enjoyment, [one should approach] that yogi who is capable of bestowing its fruit. (13.339)

The word "should resort" (śrayet) is understood as a carry-over [from the previous verse]. And that [state], by implication, is measured as existing between the states of the manifest (ghaṭamāna) and the perfected (siddha) yoga. "That" refers to the characteristic of enjoyment (bhukti). || 339 ||

Furthermore, even if a yogi who has attained [the goal] or is striving toward it is unable to grant even a mere enjoyment (bhukti), yet is skilled in teaching the means thereto— one should disregard him and instead appoint a wise teacher (jñānī-guru) who,
by teaching that very means, may gradually bring about liberation; thus he says:
When a Yoginī is incapable of bestowing the fruit and teaches only the means, it is better that a Knower (jñānin) should instruct in the means and also grant liberation. || 13-340 ||

Now, one might object: "If even a limited knower (jñānin) must be made one's guru, then from where would a disciple seeking that higher realization obtain its fulfillment? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If indeed even a single knower is not himself complete, then [how could there be fulfillment] through the sequence of parts and sub-parts?"
Having taken up the various forms of knowledge, one should cultivate consciousness as an unbroken circle.
Therefore, one should make use of innumerable gurus in order to fulfill one's own consciousness.

For even if not a single guru endowed with perfect knowledge can be found, then by taking up various forms of knowledge from each individual guru who possesses limited knowledge, following the sequence of part and sub-part, [one attains fulfillment].

One should bring about the complete, undivided circle of knowledge within one's own self; therefore, since such [knowledge] comes from only a single guru, for the sake of fulfilling one's own consciousness,
one should, even with great effort, attend upon innumerable gurus in the absence of that [one], and not otherwise.
The meaning is that there would be some transgression.

Furthermore, by virtue of having received an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*), one should approach a Guru who possesses full knowledge; through his grace, the complete perfection of the self's own realization (*vijñāna*) shall arise for him without effort—
thus he says:
But the fortunate seeker of knowledge obtains a guru who possesses complete realization.

And in this regard, I myself am the example: by me, seeking knowledge, [the venerable Śaiva scriptures] such as the *Śaiva-śāstra*— which provide refuge in the supreme good, though its name alone is proclaimed therein, and which consist of the supramundane reality that is both dual and non-dual— [were studied].

Only one auspicious teacher was obtained, who possessed complete knowledge; he was the illustrious Śaṅkhadhara, whose name is well-remembered, [an authority] in worldly fields such as grammar, logic, and epistemology. || 342 ||

Now, one might object: "If indeed complete knowledge can be obtained effortlessly from a single guru who possesses full realization, let that be so; why then is the effort of gathering various gurus and other requirements undertaken for that purpose?"
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having made the ocean of knowledge mixed with the mere flashes of intuition from the various streams of teachers and scriptures, would one not flood it with one's own droplets? (13.343)
The term *srotas* refers to a continuous stream or the flow of a river; *pratibhā* is the manifestation [of reality] appearing directly before one's eyes. The meaning is:
"What would it not flood—that is, what would it not make into a vessel for sharing knowledge?"—meaning that it would indeed do so for everything.
And this has also been stated by the Gurus; thus he says:
"From the *Ātapa* up to the *Moṭaka*, for me who possesses the lineage of gurus, there is no poverty of instruction for me, who am a disciple of all. (13.344)
The illustrious teacher Kallaṭa has described it thus;
with this very intention, I too have served various teachers—so he says:
"I too, for this very reason, out of curiosity regarding the perspectives of the lower scriptures... (13.345).
I did not serve the logicians, the followers of the Vedas, the Buddhists, the Jains, the Vaiṣṇavas, and so forth;
this was out of curiosity, and not out of respect. Here, "logicians" refers to the Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others.
Now, one might object: "Just as there is such superiority of Śaiva and other gurus over Vaiṣṇavas and others, is there likewise a mutual superiority among those who abide by lower teachings, or not?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Through the application of rituals pertaining to the mundane, the inner-self, the supramundane, the paths, and so forth. || 13-346 ||
One should contemplate [the deities] as progressively superior due to the abundance of excellence in their awakening:

the worldly (loka), such as the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; the inner self (adhyātma), such as the Vedānta; and that which transcends the worldly path (atimārga), such as Sāṃkhya and Pātañjala—likewise, [one should contemplate the superiority] of the Agniṣṭoma and other rites.
The meaning is: by means of the prescription of *karma* (ritual action) and of *yoga*, which consists in the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind,

one should discern— that is, come to know— the gurus who possess progressively higher excellence, beginning with those of the Vedic tradition, due to the increasing degree of refinement of their perfect realization (*samyagbodha*).
Thus, even among sages who possess an excellence of awakening according to their respective stages—such as the Vaiṣṇava and others—a desire to know our teaching has arisen; so he says:
"In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, the inquirers are sages such as Nārada and others. (13.347)
First were the Vaiṣṇavas and the Buddhists, who were learned in the Siddhāntas and other systems; thereafter, their eyes became eager for the moonlight of the knowledge of the meaning of the Trika.

Thus, through familiarity with the teacher and the scriptures in their proper order, progressing higher and higher, there shall arise an excellence of awakening; therefore, one should not entertain doubt regarding the multiplicity of teachers. Thus he says:
"Therefore, one should never have any hesitation concerning the multiplicity of teachers."
Is it not said: "One should never associate with one who is devoted to another guru, who is a fool, who serves other scriptures, who commits violence against the Śakti, or who is hostile?"

Having raised the objection—"By such statements as these, the untouchability of one who is devoted to another guru has been declared; why, then, was it said that a discerning person will necessarily experience doubt upon approaching another guru?"—he says in response: "The fool who is devoted to another guru, who serves other scriptures... (13.349).
The transgression that has been traditionally taught should be understood as being "in this manner";
"in this manner" means by the method that is about to be described.
He says that very thing: "Whoever is authorized in a particular scripture is called the guru therein. (13.350)
In that regard, one who is not authorized is called "another guru";
"not authorized in that" means, for example, as a follower of the Siddhānta in the Left-hand path.
He makes this very point clear by means of an illustration:
"Just as one seated within a [royal] circle [subjugates] a king belonging to another circle... (13.351).

One who desires to conquer his own circle perishes while practicing [therein]; likewise, one who seeks to attain progressively higher knowledge and accomplishments perishes by relying [on lower ones]. (13.352)
One meets with destruction by [attacking] a teacher lower than one's own;
just as in this world, someone situated within that very same mandala might wish to conquer that very mandala which is their own abode, even though they are unqualified for it.

The meaning is: by serving a king within another mandala, one perishes; let there be no victory for him over that [other king], but rather some other misfortune may arise. In this way, remaining only in ever-higher knowledge, and [attaining] its very accomplishment—

The meaning is: one who desires to attain that [state] by resorting to a teacher who is progressively lower and lacks the requisite qualification meets with ruin; for him, neither enjoyment nor liberation will arise from such a union, but rather there will be the state of transgression (*pratyavāyitva*).
This has not been stated solely with reference to one's own system, but also with regard to other systems as well;
thus he says:
"In this very way, one who desires supernatural powers [seeks them] from a scripture that stands above [their own]. (13.353)

One who is devoted to the illusory scriptures meets with destruction; and it is said in the venerable Ānanda [Tantra]: "Having resorted to ritual action (karma) out of worldly inclination... (13.354).
He feels disgust with that, and when it proves fruitless, he resorts to another;
thus wasting away day by day, he is cooked in the Raurava and other hells.
And this is not established by mere logic alone; thus he says, "And it has been stated," and so forth.

If anyone, even while undertaking a progressively higher scriptural action, should feel aversion toward it in their heart and fail to reach firm resolve therein, then that [action] is fruitless, and another scriptural action belonging to the realm of *māyā* [is required].

One should properly take hold [of this teaching] from the heart; otherwise, in this world, wasting away day by day and being diminished by wealth, wife, and so forth, one will be cooked in the Raurava and other hells in the next world, becoming a partaker of the fruits of evil—this is the meaning. And such a reading is found hundreds of times in ancient manuscripts.
It has been seen.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, that even one established in a higher teaching would incur sin by feeling attachment toward a lower or lower teacher and so forth, then what would become of one who desires to attain the progressively higher paths while abandoning the lower teachers and so on?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

But he who, desiring to reach the ever-higher paths, would abandon a lower scripture by means of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—he is fortunate, for he has been turned toward the upward path. (13.356)
In this very way, the specific refinement of our own philosophical vision has also been stated on account of those who are to be favored;
thus he says:
"For this very reason, it is described here specifically within the Śaiva scriptures."
This is a purificatory injunction for those who lack confidence in the meanings of other treatises. (13.357)
And this alone is not the sole reason for the superiority of this system; rather, there is another as well—thus he says:
"Therefore, even one who has fallen elsewhere is to be graced here by the supreme Śaiva [system], provided he has not fallen anywhere below. (13.358)
"Higher and higher" means, for example, as in the case of a Vaiṣṇava entering a Śaiva [temple], or "he on the left and he on the right.
"In some cases" refers to instances such as among the Vaiṣṇavas and others.

For in this way, just as in our own system, even there [in the other systems] some specific refinement (*saṃskāra*)—consisting primarily of the removal of marks (*liṅgoddhāra*)—must have been taught for him. Thus he says:
"Therefore, by all the omniscient ones, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, in their own..."
Nothing such as the extraction of gender-marks and so forth is recorded in the teaching.
"By the omniscient ones"—for they know thus: that those who abide at ever-higher levels, such as the Śaivas and others, are not objects to be favored by our [lower] systems of vision.
Now, one might object: "If these [deities] are omniscient, why do they teach such an inferior knowledge while setting aside that most excellent Śaiva knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In this way, Viṣṇu and the others are those who know only the supreme reality of Śiva."
Having resorted to delusion, they gave such instructions to certain people who were possessed of wrong views.

"Kāṃścit" (some) refers, for now, to those who are fit for instruction. "Tathā" means in a manner characterized by inferior knowledge—this is the sense. And because of that alone, under the influence of delusion, they hold a contradictory conviction that "this alone is the truth"; thus it is said, "they have resorted to doubt due to delusion."
And because they were attached to that very [view], even Brahmā and the others taught that same thing with firm conviction;
thus he says:
"Such a mind as that, which is incapable of touching the truth..."
Having seen this, it was likewise declared by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, as well as by the Buddhas.
"Of such a kind" means contradictory; for this very reason it is said to be "incapable of touching the truth.

"Even by the Buddhas"—that is, even by those awakened to the supreme reality of Śiva—this is the meaning. "In that way" means by a manner consisting of inferior knowledge, appropriate to their respective dispositions; this is the meaning. || 361 ||
He concludes the subject matter of this chapter with the first half-verse of the summary:
"Thus, this descent of power (śaktipāta) has been analyzed according to both reasoning and scripture.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Descent of Power."
Thus it has been analyzed; may there be auspiciousness.
Jayaratha has clearly expounded the meaning of the thirteenth daily lesson, empowered by the majesty of his own innate vitality manifested through the descent of the Supreme Lord’s grace.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Descent of Power" (*śaktipātapradarśana*), in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter:
"Viveka" (Discrimination),
which [reveals] for the sake of the beloved of the Yoginīs the sequence for the removal of the concealment of the worlds.
We offer tribute to him, who strengthens us by his power for the sake of strength.

In this context, it has been stated everywhere that the Supreme Lord performs fivefold acts (*pañcavidhakṛtya*). Among these, the triad beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) was previously shown during the occasion of defining the variety of dissolution (*saṃhāra*), and grace (*anugraha*) was shown in the immediately preceding chapter; now, the remaining act known as concealment (*tirobhāva*) remains to be discussed.
He speaks in order to establish the fifth function by means of the second half [of the verse]:
"Let the nature of concealment (tirobhāva) be explained in detail.
The intention behind this mention, even at the commencement of initiation (dīkṣā), is that it must first be abandoned.
Once that which is supremely to be attained has been demonstrated, there will be rest.
He introduces that very point:
"By his own nature, the Supreme Lord [establishes] the sequence of necessity and non-necessity. (14.1)
Because he manifests by touching [all things], he is therefore called "Svacchanda" (the Independent One).
The meaning is that his own nature (*sva-bhāva*) is his will (*icchā*); thus, he is "Sva" (his own) and "Bhāva" (nature), from which [the name Svacchanda arises].
In that regard, he demonstrates its manifestation through the touch of the transcendence of necessity (niyati): "Relying upon necessity regarding both action and its fruit, this Great Lord... (14.2).
He ordains the intermediate states of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. The phrase "intermediate states" is used in relation to the great Śākta creation and so forth.
These, moreover, concern the three cosmic eggs beginning with Earth. As was stated previously:
Kālāgni is the destroyer on earth; at the end of Māyā, he is the sovereign of the principle of Time (kālatattva).
Śrīkaṇṭha alone is the cause of both creation and destruction at the Root (mūla).
"Therefore, the intermediate state is the *tallaya*... (6.172). || 2 ||

Furthermore, he states that for him there is no fixed contact with destiny elsewhere: "But in the great creation, which is characterized by the infinity of successive emanations and reabsorptions... (14.3).

That one God, the soul of all, the Lord who has arrived through the power of necessity (niyati), demonstrates His very greatness by means of this creation and dissolution characterized by infinity. As was stated previously:
The glorious Aghora, at the end of Śakti, is both the destroyer and the creator;
for from him proceed the countless creations and dissolutions of worlds within his own creation.
"Therefore, being included therein, the great emanation is said to be Śākta. (6.173).
It is said "having emerged from Niyati," for this [Śākta level] is not the field of karma, such that there would be an inclusion of Niyati here in consideration of it.
Not only is there a relinquishing of necessity (niyati) here [in the primary creation], but this also applies to the intermediate creations and so forth—as he says:
"And whatever creation and maintenance occurs in the intermediate [creation], even there it is unrestrained. (14.4)

"He does not abandon [it], for he remains here having cast off the necessity of the body; thus he does not abandon it. For if that were not the case, there would be a fragmentation of his sovereignty—this is the intended meaning.
Anticipating the question, "What is the difference between abandoning necessity and not abandoning it?", he says:
And when, by necessity alone, through the process of veiling its own nature... (14.5)
Then the sequence of the fruits of karma experiences suffering, delusion, and so forth;
but having abandoned the karmic constraint, one is freed from being enveloped by suffering and delusion.

"He remains desiring to manifest [himself], independent regarding concealment"—this means by relying on that sequence of veiling his own nature. "Independent" is the reason for abandoning the restriction of karma; with this very intention, he will say:
"And it was not the greatness of his own karma that caused him to remain in such a state.
Anticipating the objection— "What indeed is called 'concealment' (tirodhāna), wherein even the All-pervasive Lord is independent of karma and other factors?"—
the author, while internalizing this doubt, first presents an illustration by way of its effects and then declares its essential nature:
Just as, due to the sovereignty of light, even one who has awakened appears as if unawakened. (14.7)
He remains as if not yet crossed over, yet he behaves as if he has already crossed;
just as in this world one who is enlightened remains like the unenlightened due to the arising of the ego-reflection (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), according to the maxim:
"Even those free from passion conduct themselves as if possessed by passion."

One remains established while concealing the support of one's own innate power (*svātmavīrya*); likewise, someone who has not yet crossed over— due to the absence of the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvara-śaktipāta*)— though his form is not yet manifested, acts as if he has crossed over and as if his form were manifested, out of hypocrisy for the sake of deceiving others.

One might perform acts such as devotion and faith; however, in reality, the fact that he possesses no conviction or regard for the mantras and tantras of the Supreme Lord is what is meant by "concealment" (tirodhāna)—this is the meaning.
As was stated previously:

"Even though its form is not manifest, because it remains as if manifested by that [consciousness], when one takes up the mantra and so forth and then abandons them, that is its concealment (tirobhava). (13.121) || 7 ||
Now, here indeed,
by such statements as "I am Śiva, I am without a second," even one who has not yet attained the state of Śiva proceeds in that manner for the sake of realizing identity.
Anticipating the objection—"If it is traditionally taught that one should cultivate [the state], and if his activity is exactly like this, then what is the fault?"—he says:
"And just as the Buddha, even while performing those foolish activities, was not hostile... (14.8).

"O fool, such conduct is indeed pleasing to you; however, even while acting so, he remains an enemy within the heart. Because of this lack of a [true] heart, there is no rest for him"—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
Nor was this stated by us alone; thus he says:
"The venerable Lord of Vidyā has also spoken in such a manner in the *Mānastotra*. (14.9)
That very point— he recites it:
"Those who have received initiation into your path of instruction,
yet fall into error through the power of delusion while practicing together..."
Surely there is no application of the light of the sun for them; for what contraction could lotuses feel from the rays of the sun? (14.10)
Even those who have known what is to be known and stand in the position of a protector,
if they follow a wrong path instead of your way, are not truly correct;
for their understanding generally arises from mere inferential cognition and the like.
False awakening is like a lamp made from snake-fat. || 14-11 ||
For just as copper pierced by the foremost of elixirs does not return again to its own original nature,
so too was that nectar not drunk by those dwelling upon the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, in this [state], there are the afflictions of the sufferings of thirst and hunger. || 14-12 ||

Even though they have entered into Your teaching, those who have fallen into error therein have not experienced the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); therefore, although they understand the reality of Your teaching through its superficiality,
they have nonetheless gone onto the wrong paths such as Sāṃkhya and the like— thus, they are indeed truly permeated by the power of dissolution (*vilaya-śakti*).

This is the meaning. For they possess a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) produced by that [vision], just as in the case of a snake, a corpse, or a lamp; by means of which they perceive this otherwise. Indeed, when a snake, a corpse, or a lamp is present, everything is seen as consisting of snakes. And therefore, because other modes of perception would otherwise be impossible, [this is established].
This is determined: that these [seeds] have not undergone germination because they were rendered latent according to your doctrine.
For copper pierced by mercury would never again become copper, nor would those who have drunk nectar ever again suffer from thirst and the like. || 12 ||
And thus, it is precisely the activity of the awakened one that, by being rejected, causes this [state] to disappear; so he says:
"Then that activity of the awakened one—consisting of mantra-practice, ritual worship, and so forth—if kindled by aversion, burns him within, because that burning is indeed doubt. (14.13)
The cause of internal burning is "kindled by hatred" (*dveṣeddha*); that is, it is ignited by hatred, meaning it is stimulated by being the object of hatred.

For it is by that very hatred that he comes to have such a state—this is the sense. As it has been said: "Arising from anger toward the great mantras, vidyās, conduct, and so forth, which are being censured."
"The sinner shall be cast in every way into that terrible abode of torments.

Now, what is the meaning of "burning" (*dāha*) here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Burning is indeed that very doubt, because of which [it occurs]. For doubt is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that alone is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). As it has been said:
"Every conceptual construction is saṃsāra...
Thus it is said; and in that very context, its state of being "intensely burning" is explained as concealment (tirobhāva). || 13 ||
Now, one might ask: "In this case, is the cause his own previous karma manifesting, or is it something else?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Nor is it the power of his karma such that he remains in this state."
For what indeed is that action, or why is the rule here the same as the previous one?
Such is the cause of concealment; "in this way" means by acting with aversion toward the activities of the awakened one.

Indeed, there is no such karma whatsoever that could serve as a cause for concealment, for that [karma] bestows birth, lifespan, and experience, and it has been stated that nothing within this [category] constitutes concealment—what indeed...?

Regarding the phrase "that karma": there exists no such latent impression of karma (*karmāśaya*) whatsoever that could serve as its cause—thus he asks, "From what cause? And so, just as it was previously stated that grace (*anugraha*) occurs solely through the will of the Supreme Lord, independent of karma and other factors, so too does concealment (*tirodhāna*).
Thus it has been said: "The procedure here is the same as the preceding one. "Procedure" (vidhi) refers to the manner of resolving an objection. || 14 ||
Therefore he says:
"Consequently, that is the will of the Supreme Lord by which this [soul], thus deluded, seeks to become a vessel for suffering to be experienced throughout infinite time. (15)
Now, one might object: "If the mere will of the Supreme Lord is indeed the cause here, then from where does this diversity of suffering among these beings arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even there, due to the diversity of will, [the result] consists of three types: pertaining to this world, the next world, or both."
There is likewise a distinction even within suffering, produced by its duration or its brevity. || 14-16 ||
He demonstrates this very point:
"The concealment [of the self] for Kāla, Kāma, Andhaka, and others who dwell in the city of Paulastya, as well as for others, is indeed painful both here and in the hereafter. (14–17)

The inhabitants of the city are the residents of Tripura; "of others" refers to Citrasena and the rest. Because of the word "and" (ca), this also applies here [to the other two cities], since for Kāla and the others, grace was exercised immediately after the burning right here [in this world]; whereas for Paulastya and the others, grace was not accomplished in either case [neither before nor after the burning]. || 17 ||
Not only is His mere will the cause of this [concealment], but there is also another;
thus he says:
"And there is also another concealment, consisting in the transgression of the rules (samaya)."
It consists of the transgression of the *samaya*, because of the metaphorical identification of cause and effect.
Anticipating the objection, "What is the authority for this?", he says:
"As was stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Ānandagahvara. (14–18)
"O Goddess, due to the transgression of the *samaya*, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years.
Here, the restriction that it must be exactly "a hundred years" is not intended; thus he says:
"Even there, the sequence is manifold, due to the distinctions of weak, intense, and so forth. (14–19)

Having thus described the nature of concealment (*tirobhāva*), he also indicates its removal: "And by the sovereignty of the Great Lord, even one who is concealed may, of his own accord, or through another, again fully attain grace. (14.20)

In this regard, he first describes his own arrival with a disposition toward bestowing grace: "When, through further grace, there is the performance of penance and so forth, and initiation and the like have been carried out according to the [individual's] capacity, one shall become composed of the nature of Śiva. (14.21)

The sense is that the performance of the expiation should indeed occur spontaneously; "accordingly" means in accordance with one's own fitness, which consists of the intense, mild, or other degrees of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). || 21 ||

He speaks also by way of another door: "Even one who has passed away and whose life-force has departed is favored through the descent of power (śaktipāta) by taking hold of his kinsmen, friends, and teachers, and is initiated and so forth. (14.22)
Here too, as before, there is a variety of forms; thus he says:
"In that case as well, there is a distinction based on the speed or slowness of time and so forth;
such is this descent of power (śaktipāta) by which one attains the nature of Śiva. (14.23)
"So be it," [he said], for a long time or quickly. || 23 ||
He summarizes the very object of knowledge previously mentioned:
"In this way, the agency consisting of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace—this fivefold agency is the state of Śiva belonging to the self that is consciousness. (24)
Now, one might object: "Granted that consciousness possesses this so-called agency—the state of Śiva—regarding the fivefold set of acts at the beginning of creation;
but what is the purpose of this instruction for someone like me? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one who considers his own self to be complete and independent in the performance of the fivefold acts..."
For the yogi, worship, recitation, meditation, and yoga shall be perpetually manifest. || 25 ||

For the very essence of images and the like is that they are enlivened by the Supreme Reality; and since this is always present for the yogi who possesses such a realization, it is said that "they too are ever-arisen. || 25 ||

And thus, this alone is the supreme goal by which liberation may occur even while one is living; therefore, one should never be attached to enjoyments and the like, which appear for but a moment and are largely artificial—thus he says:
"One should never take delight in the affairs of a magician."
Even that enjoyment which belongs to Sādāśiva is bondage for those whose nature is [otherwise] appropriate.
Now, one might object: "Is it not your own doctrine that Śiva consists of both knowledge and action? Then how can it be said that sovereignty alone is Śiva-hood? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Śiva-hood is precisely the state of being the knower; that is what is called sovereignty here."
The sense is that there is no difference whatsoever between knowledge and action; as it has been said:
"There is no knowledge devoid of action, nor is there action devoid of knowledge."

Furthermore, the agency (kartṛtva) here in the form of being a creator—according to the analogy of a potter and so forth—is not intended [as the primary meaning], because that is not the primary [agency]. For that [primary agency] is the substrate of the agency whose nature is pure sovereignty, since without it, this [secondary agency] does not arise. Thus he says:
Its agency is not primary, like that of a potter, because it presides over [the material cause]. (14.27)

Now, one might object: "In that case, even for those like us, there is no primary agency (kartṛtva) just as in the case of a potter and the like; therefore, enough with this conceit of being Śiva within oneself. For if that were so, the world would follow our mere will, and yet it does not? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Knowing this, one should never at any time entertain a sense of fragmentation, thinking:
"If I am Śiva, why does the universe not follow my will? (14.28)
"Fragmentation" means limitation. || 28 ||

He establishes that very non-apprehension [of the object] as follows: "In the cognition of 'I', it is either Śiva or the Supreme Lord who flashes forth with the thought, 'Let them follow my will,' or else a body and so forth are created. (14.29)
Śiva certainly possesses this [nature], yet this body has been fashioned by you in that manner; what other "bodiness" could there be for him? So why should this be a ground for censure? (14.30)

The phrase "ahaṃvidi" means in the consciousness of "I. In that case, if Śiva alone, who is autonomous, were to manifest here, then the world's conformity to His will would be established as a matter of course. But if the body and so forth are merely created [entities], how could this be so for them? For they are indeed insentient.

He was created with his full knowledge and power cast aside; otherwise, indeed, he would not even possess the nature of a body. Thus, it has been said that this is not to be censured, for what else could it be called?
Therefore, one should maintain the conceit "I am Śiva" alone, and not in the body or other such things, by which [one realizes] the true reality itself.

Through an excellence of firmness, it would attain growth. By this much, the object of knowledge known as the fullness of gnosis (*jñānaparipūrṇatā*) has been stated; and that alone is the supreme thing to be attained, as it has been said:
"One should never take pleasure in the account of a magician."
Thus [ends the section]. || 30 ||
Anticipating the objection, "But what is the authority for this?", he says:
"And it has been stated in the *Siddhasantāna-śrīmad-ūrmimahākula*.
By "in the *Ūrmimahākula*," he means in the *Ūrmikaula*.
He recites that very [verse]: "Those who have performed exertion through the rotation of the breath, the movement of the air, the projection of the vital force, and so forth... (31).
"Those who are deluded regarding [lower practices such as] sorcery and the like are indeed deluded regarding the supreme state.

Anticipating the objection— "If this is so, then how is it that in all [scriptures] the departure (*utkrānti*) consisting of the dispersal of the vital breaths and so forth is said to be a means to the supreme state?"— he says:
In every case, even that departure which occurs with great reverence leads to liberation.
She is proclaimed in the essential scriptures as the means for enjoyment,
as it is sung:
"Having restrained all the gates of the body and having confined the mind within the heart..."
Having fixed his vital breath at the crown of his head, he remained established in yogic concentration.
"Uttering the single-syllabled Brahman 'Om' and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal. (8.12-13).
This means that among the essential scriptures, such as the *Viṣvā*, *Pradhāna*, *Ūrmi*, *Kaula*, and others—this is the sense.
"By way of being a means to enjoyment," and not by way of being a means to liberation;
and by this, the uselessness of the upward departure (utkrānti) has been indicated.
To establish that very point, he recites the relevant passage from that same work:
"If the Lord is omnipresent, tell me, where will He go after departing? (14.33).
If, on the other hand, it were not all-pervading, then it would be like a jar;
this application of the procedure for the departure [of the soul] is described as occurring by means of a single part. (14.34)
But how can there be any consistency with the concept of "departure" (utkrānti) regarding the partless reality of Śiva?
[The soul] is said to be like a jar because it is essentially contracted by having a restricted location, time, and form.
Furthermore, this method of departure is described as a yoga characterized by a single location and spatial restriction.
That which is called "transcendence" (*utkrānti*) consists in abandoning each successive lower state and ascending to each successive higher state.

However, this does not apply to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), because it is partless (*niraṃśa*) due to being free from conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence. As it is said therein:
Transmigration exists wherever there is the conceptualization of a measure;
where there is no measure, in the manifestation of emptiness, transmigration does not exist.
If the Blessed One is all-pervading, tell me what is the use of the upward departure?
If the Blessed One is not all-pervading, tell me what is the use of the upward departure?
This application of the procedure for the departure of the soul (utkrānti) is described only in part;
because of the omnipresence of the Self and of Śiva, even that [departure] does not exist.
"That which is not touched by the extremes of 'it exists,' 'it does not exist,' 'it both exists and does not exist,' or 'it neither exists nor does not exist'—
because it is beyond the range of speech, that is what is called reality (tattva) here," beginning with these words.
"If the deity is omnipresent, tell me, where will it go after departing?
But if it is not omnipresent, then it would be like a jar."
"Therefore, this yoga of departure is an illusion consisting of darkness.
Thus [it is said].
Anticipating the question, "And how can this [power] be a means for enjoyment (bhoga)? he says: "Just as, from the earth up to the air, by means of jumping, water, fire, and fasting... (14.35).

The movement of the self through the sky [during] the process of departure (*utkrānti*) is likewise. Just as Bhṛgu and others experienced enjoyment sequentially through the four principles beginning with earth, so too does one experience it here in the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*) by this [process], for the effect follows the sequence of the qualities of its cause.
"It must be so"—this is the sense.
And for this reason, those who desire to attain the supreme reality should not perform this [rite]; thus he says:
"Therefore, one should not cause the individual soul (jīva) to depart by means of the longing for the supreme reality. (14.36)

"But if departure [from the body] is not a means to liberation, then how does one reach the eternal state after abandoning this physical body?"— anticipating this objection from the *Śrīmālinīvijayottara* (17.25) and other passages, he says:

However, that which is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* regarding the characteristics of the departure [of the soul] (*utkrānti*) is not for the sake of a means to liberation, but rather for the purpose of abandoning worldly experience, since there is a desire for it to be so. (14.37)
"In that manner" means by way of the process of departure. || 37 ||

For indeed, for those yogins who possess identity with the supreme consciousness awakened by the power of the descent of the Supreme Lord’s grace, the very abandonment of the body is the sole means, due to their aversion to the enjoyment of external objects.
Thus it is said:

One who has attained perfection through recitation, meditation, and so forth, by virtue of autonomy and the descent of power (śaktipāta), if he becomes dispassionate toward worldly enjoyment, may thus abandon the body. (14.38)
And this has not been taught here as something entirely unprecedented; thus he says:

"It is indeed heard that even for Bhīṣma and others, who possessed the power of death at will, there occurred an approach to the end of life upon the attainment of a distaste for worldly enjoyment. (14.39)
One might object: "Is not the natural inclination toward renouncing enjoyments at the end of life an inherent cause?
For a living being who has abandoned the tasting of flavors cannot survive by any means; so what is the use of teaching the means for that?
Indeed, in cases such as 'one who is hungry should eat,' there is no need to rely upon scripture. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The body that has attained the state of perfection through yoga, mantras, the nectar-substance, excellent offerings, and so forth,
cannot indeed be abandoned otherwise than by means of the yoga according to the stated sequence.
The meaning is that one who possesses accomplishment has attained stability. || 40 ||
And this was not stated merely on the basis of one's own imagination; thus he says:
"And such [a teaching] has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the Mālinītantra:
'Or else, considering even all enjoyment to be deformed... (14.41).

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: by saying "thus, etc.," and by the Supreme Lord saying "possessing an internal reality that is unperceivable by all," and so forth, such a thing was stated. It is called "deformed" (*virūpaka*) due to the varying degrees of the wonder of immersion into supreme consciousness, and not because of having abandoned the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*).
"By all" means by those who understand the meaning as it is generally presented. The inner reality here is this:
liberation occurs for him through the very conceit of the identity "I am Śiva" within his own self, whereas the casting off of the body occurs by means of this [practice].
It is with this very intention that it is said here:
"...he attains the eternal state. (17.25). Likewise:
"...he enjoys the fruit declared for initiation."
Thus it has been said: therefore, the very conceit of performing the fivefold acts such as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is the supreme means for liberation within one's own self. Thus he says:
"In this way, the teaching on the sovereignty of one's own self regarding the duties of emanation and so forth. (14.42)
That alone shall be the primary initiation which bestows Śiva-hood upon the disciple;
nor is this without authority—as he says:
"And it is stated in the venerable *Niścāra* [Tantra] by means of the Bhairavian splendor. (14.43)
Those whose minds are free from conceptual construction perceive the entire universe as pervaded [by Śiva];
