however, one whose mind is possessed of conceptual construction shall go to Śiva upon the falling of the body.

Through the application of external initiation and so forth, and by means of the conceptualizations of conduct and observances, one becomes free from conceptual construction right now; thus, one is liberated while living—of this there is no doubt.

"By means of splendor" (*tejasā*) means by means of that whose essence is perfect knowledge and action; for this very reason it is said: "of one whose mind is free from conceptual construction" (*vikalpojjhitacetas*), which means those who are established solely in the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaita*). "Of one whose mind is joined with conceptual construction" (*vikalpayuktacitta*) is because the non-duality of consciousness has not yet been realized even now. "Even today" (*adyaiva*) means even while the body still exists.
As it is said there:
"The entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by the splendor of this very Śiva;
thus do the sages, the Siddhas, and the deities known as Vīras perceive."
But those men on earth whose minds are free from conceptual construction perceive [the truth];
however, one whose mind is joined with conceptual construction may attain Śiva through the practice of alms-gathering.

"But he whose mind is exhausted of conceptual construction perceives himself as the auspicious and imperishable through the purity of his being; he is liberated while living, without a doubt. Thus, liberation belongs to those who possess non-conceptual states even while alive, but for others...
Thus it is established that [this occurs] immediately after the fall of the body.
Now, one might object: "What proof is there for the claim that what was not accomplished while one is alive will be accomplished once dead?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"[The state of being] like the mass of roots of the withered tree of saṃsāra..."
If, due to the internal presence of conceptual construction, even tiny sparks of the fire of ultimate reality should arise, then at their conclusion,
the mass of the fire of stainless awakening blazes forth intensely.

Because it is consumed by the woodworm of pure conceptualization— such as "this entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is my own power"— it is like a withered tree; and those [concepts] which, acting as its support,
are essentially like a mass of roots and are impure because they sustain differentiation (bheda).
Since they are obscured by mental constructions (*saṅkalpa*) and thus not directly manifest,

even if these fragments of immersion in You— though resembling mere sparks from the ultimate mass of the fire of consciousness— should occur during states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then, by necessity, at the end of the body, once again...

Furthermore, the fire of ultimate reality (paramārthavahni), ignited by the blowing of repeated practice, blazes forth intensely; having first extinguished the state of being a limited embodied subject (dehapramātṛtā) and so forth, it attains a state of supreme radiance as the supreme subject (parapramātṛtva)—this is the meaning. || 46 ||
He concludes this very point with the first half-verse:
"In this way, this commencement of initiation has been shown as approved by the scriptures.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrītantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Commencement of Initiation. || 14 ||
It is in accordance with the scriptures, and not merely one's own invention; may there be auspiciousness!

Jayaratha has thus explained this fourteenth chapter on daily practice, which was suddenly brought forth by him whose own full consciousness had been stolen away by the concealment and destruction wrought by the Unfavorable One (Ahi).

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Commencement of Initiation," in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named *Viveka* written by the venerable teacher Jayaratha. 14.
